sents: lead
Battletoads is a video game media franchise by Rare that began with the original beat 'em up game Battletoads in 1991.
lead
Starring three anthropomorphic toads named after skin conditions, Rash, Zitz, and Pimple, the series was created to rival the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles games series.
lead

The original Battletoads game for the NES was renowned for its extreme difficulty, but still received a cult following, spawning sequels for various platforms including a crossover with the Double Dragon series and a modern reboot after a 25 year gap in releases.
lead
In each of the games, the objective is to defeat the toads' nemesis the Dark Queen and her army of space mutants.
Series
Originally released for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) in 1991 by Rare, the game was distributed by Tradewest in Europe and North America, and by Masaya Games in Japan.
Series
It was subsequently ported by Arc System Works to the Sega Genesis and Game Gear in 1993, and by Mindscape to the Amiga and Amiga CD32 in 1994.
Series
Battletoads: An LCD game was released by Tiger Electronics in 1991.
Series
Battletoads (Game Boy): A spin-off of the original also released in 1991.
Series
Battletoads in Battlemaniacs: Released in 1993 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) and developed in 1994 for the Sega Master System (but not released until 1996).
Series
Battletoads in Ragnarok's World: A stripped down port of the original game for the Game Boy, released in 1993.
Series
For the first time in the series, the game offers players a character selection screen.
Series
Battletoads Arcade: An arcade game released in 1994, also known as Super Battletoads.
Series
Battletoads (2020): An Xbox One and Microsoft Windows game developed by Dlala Studios in collaboration with Rare, it was released on August 20, 2020.
Series
It features three-player couch co-op multiplayer and high resolution hand-drawn 4K 2.5D graphics.
Series
Battletoads and Battletoads Arcade are included in Rare Replay, a compilation of 30 Rare games released for the Xbox One in 2015.
History of production
In 2013, Phil Spencer from Microsoft 's Xbox team mentioned his fondness for Battletoads while asking the fans what Rare games should be brought back for the Xbox One.
History of production
In 2014, "Battletoads" was re-trademarked in the United States.
History of production

Spencer appeared publicly in a Battletoads T-shirt in 2015, just days after Microsoft Studios ' Ken Lobb (creator of 2013's Killer Instinct reboot) said they have plans to bring Battletoads and other classic Rare series back "someday".
Other
Battletoads: The Official Battlebook, the Tradewest-authorized guide to the Battletoads console games, was written by Steve Schwartz and published in 1994 by Prima Publishing.
Animated pilot
Intended as the pilot for a full-fledged series, the special was syndicated by Bohbot Entertainment in the United States on the weekend of Thanksgiving 1992 as part of their "Kids' Day Off" package.
Animated pilot
Buena Vista Home Video released the pilot on VHS in January 1994.
Animated pilot

It received an official YouTube release on August 5, 2014, on a YouTube channel run by the Canadian company DHX Media (now WildBrain), which currently owns the rights to most of DIC's cartoon library.
Animated pilot
A comic with the backstory of Battletoads, written by Rare employee Guy Millar, was also published in Nintendo Power.
Reception
In 2010, Game Informer included Battletoads among ten gaming franchises that deserve a revival, and precisely, "a true HD sequel".
Reception

In 2012, Forbes listed it as one of five video game franchises "that need to come back from the dead", adding that a modern Battletoads "should retain its side-scroller qualities while adopting the 2.5D style" similar to Mark of the Ninja.
Prank call
Beginning in early 2011, 4chan users organized a mass prank calling to the Gold and Silver pawn shop, home to the popular television show Pawn Stars.
Prank call
Battletoads developer Rare has acknowledged the prank via an achievement named "Do You Have Battletoads?" in their 2015 game compilation Rare Replay.

The Ultimate Team is a crossover of Technos Japan 's Double Dragon and Rare's Battletoads game franchises, although Technos had little or no credited involvement in production beyond the Double Dragon license.
lead
The game features the characters from the Double Dragon series, Billy and Jimmy Lee, two young martial arts experts; also included are the three humanoid toad protagonists from the Battletoads game.
lead
It is also the first Battletoads game to feature all three toads as playable characters.
lead
The game's engine and design are directly based upon the Battletoads series.
Plot

The first level of the seven-level game takes place on the tail of Colossus, the second on the interior corridors of the ship in level two, the third in the ship's base, and the fourth where the player attempts to destroy the ship from the outside while on a small space craft.
Plot
Although the ship is successfully destroyed, the Dark Queen and the Shadow Boss survive by escaping in a missile hull, thus making the fifth level's goal to board it.
Gameplay
It has three play modes: a single-player, a "2 Players A" mode where the players can hit each other, and a "2 Players B" that doesn't have that.
Gameplay
Like the prior Battletoads installment, there are only three continues and no password system, and in the two-player modes, if one player loses all lives, both players have to start a level over.
Gameplay
The 16-bit versions have identical gameplay to their NES counterparts, attacks and jumping are triggered by only two buttons.
Development
The NES version features 3D scrolling and other advanced special effects uncommonly sophisticated for the console.
Development
The Game Boy version is similar to the NES version, but it is only for one player.
Development
The sprites are the same size although the screen is smaller (leaving less room for movement) and the 3D effects are absent.
Development
The logo on the game cover art is one of Rare's first uses of 3D graphics.
Contemporaneous

Nintendo Power asserted that the game has confusing depth perception, but "great action, graphics and theme make this one of the strongest titles this year", and is better than Battletoads in Battlemaniacs (1993).
Contemporaneous
The NES version was nominated for Nintendo Power Awards 1993 in the categories "Graphics & Sound", "Theme & Fun", "Play Control", "Villain" (The Dark Queen), and "The Best Overall Game".
Contemporaneous
Other reviews, such as Electronic Gaming Monthly critic Martin Alessi and Mike Weigand of Electronic Games, found the visuals amazing for an 8-bit game, citing its parallax scrolling effects.
Retrospective

Matt Hull of Hardcore Gaming 101, reviewing the NES version, praised the humor of the moves and sound effects, "superb" music, "very smooth" controls, and for having the same 16-bit-looking graphics as the prior Battletoads game, particularly the animation, backgrounds, parallax scrolling, and the Colossus.
Retrospective

Hull appreciated its more forgiving difficulty in comparison to the original Battletoads, Thornburg stated it was still unfair at times, noting "unbalanced fights", "moving down a rope too fast for the screen and being killed by seemingly nothing or being overcrowded by enemies at the most frustrated moments".
Retrospective

An AllGame critic, Brett Alan Weiss, was harsh on the SNES version, calling it "an unnecessary creation, except to line the pockets of the companies involved", and too similar in looks and gameplay to its 8-bit counterpart, thus not taking enough advantage of the 16-bit console's capabilities.
Retrospective
The game was featured on the lists of "top 11 video game crossovers" by UGO Networks and the 15 most bizarre crossovers in gaming by GamesRadar.
Retrospective
In 2018, Complex listed the game 28th on its "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".

fes_bucky_o_bunny.title: Bucky O'Hare
sents: lead
Bucky O'Hare is a fictional character and the hero of an eponymous comic book series and spin-off media, including an animated TV series and various toys and video games.
lead
He was created by comic book writer Larry Hama and comic book artist Michael Golden between 1977 and 1978 and made its publishing debut in Echo of Futurepast #1 in May 1984 Continuity Comics.
lead
The storyline of Bucky O'Hare follows a parallel universe where a galactic war is ongoing between the United Animals Federation (U.A.F.) and the sinister Toad Empire.
lead

The U.A.F. is an interplanetary republic run by sapient mammals, while the Toad Empire is controlled by a vast computer system known as KOMPLEX, which has led the highly consumerist toad population to fight an expansionist campaign against the rest of the galaxy.
Overview
The original Bucky O'Hare was published by Continuity Comics between 1984 and 1985.
Overview
The series ran in issues #1-6 of the comics anthology series Echo of Futurepast, with Hama writing and Michael Golden on pencils.
Overview
All six parts were collected into an oversized graphic novel in 1986.
Overview
The series was intended to run for six issues, but only five were published between January 1991 and March 1992, leaving the expanded version of the story incomplete.
Overview
Hama wrote a second Bucky O'Hare arc, which was never published.
Overview
When the animated series was broadcast in the United Kingdom in 1992, DC Thomson published their own Bucky O'Hare comic, which ran bi-weekly for twenty issues from March to December of that year.
Overview

The first six issues of the series re-printed the original US series (#1-5 using the expanded version, and #6 using the original Echo version), after which the series moved on to original material (incorporating elements of the animated series) written by Peter Stone, penciled by Andre Coates, and inked by Joel Adams.
Overview
The cartoon, meanwhile, ran from September 1991 to January 1992, along with a series of action figures.
Overview
During that period, Konami produced two tie-in video games based on the property: an NES version and an arcade version, both released in 1992.
Characters
Jenny – first mate and pilot, a female cat from the planet Aldebaran with mysterious magical and psionic powers common to the females of her species.
Characters
Because of the Prime Directive of the Aldebaran Sisterhood, she keeps these powers secret from the other members of the crew.
Characters
Bucky and his crew decide to keep Willy a secret from the Toads.
Characters
AFC Blinky – an advanced AFC ("Android" First Class).
Characters
Storm Toad Death Kommandos – a berserker platoon of the most savage and fearless storm toads, who are kept confined until circumstances require them.
Characters
The U.S. comic only ran this one plotline.
Characters
To coincide with the TV series in the early '90s, a UK comic reprinted the issues, then produced a further fifteen issues written by Peter Stone, and illustrated by Andre Coates and Joel Adams.
Characters
In 2007, Vanguard reprinted the original Bucky O'Hare comic and two of the UK issues in a digest size collection, similar to a manga.
In other media
Bucky O'Hare and the Toad Wars! is a syndicated animated television network show which aired in 1991.
Video games

A Bucky O'Hare game was released for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1992, which required Bucky to rescue each of his crew members (except Bruiser, who is not featured in the game) on a series of planets.
Toy line
In 1991, the toy company Hasbro released a line of action figures based closely on the Bucky O'Hare series.
Toy line

Most of the major characters were represented: Bucky O'Hare, Deadeye Duck, Willy DuWitt, Blinky, Bruiser and Commander Dogstar were the heroes released, and Toadborg, Air Marshall, Storm Toad Trooper and Al Negator were the villains that made it to the shelves.
Toy line
There are several photographs available online of the unreleased figures, some completely painted with accessories, and others as unpainted prototypes.
Toy line
At least one photo shows the fully packaged Jenny, likely because this figure was completed in time for the first release, but was delayed to be part of the second.
Toy line

The mobile configuration of the chief villain Komplex (Komplex-2-Go in the arcade game), Digger, and Tri-Bot (a minor villain from the final episode) are the other unpainted prototypes known to exist from these photos.
Toy line
More recently, both an unpainted prototype and a fully finalized figure of Jenny was revealed online in a review video.
Toy line
In 2017, Boss Fight Studios began to release new Bucky O'Hare action figures.
Toy line
The first two to be released were Bucky O'Hare and the much anticipated First Mate Jenny.
Legacy
During the 1990s, VHS tapes were released by Family Home Entertainment.
Legacy
Due to Sunbow Productions ' lack of a US home distributor currently (it was formerly Rhino, then Sony Wonder, which has shut down), the cartoon had been stalled in releasing a Region 1 DVD.
Legacy

A company called Exposure Entertainment was supposed to have released the 13 episodes on DVD in North America, in Region 1 NTSC format for the first time, but the overall release was either very rare and limited, or no set had appeared at all.
Legacy

The same company had a similar issue with their first season release of Biker Mice from Mars, but it did have a Region 2 PAL DVD release in the UK by Metrodome Distribution, which as of 2013 is now out of print.
Legacy

Hasbro has recently acquired the rights to most of their cartoon library, and since the toys were produced by Hasbro, it may be possible for the series to see a DVD release in Region 1 eventually, if Hasbro did acquire the rights to the cartoon and if they can find a distributor for the show.
Legacy
Comic book artist Neal Adams and Continuity created a short online 3-D cartoon of Bucky O'Hare.
Legacy
In 2006, Neal Adams was reportedly working on a Bucky O'Hare film project.
Legacy
The graphic novel Neal Adams Presents Bucky O'Hare and the Toad Menace was re-released in 2008 in manga format by Vanguard Press.

fes_vice_project_gloom.title: Vice: Project Doom
sents: lead
Vice: Project Doom, known in Japan as Gun-Dec (ガンデック), is an action video game developed by Aicom and published by Sammy Corporation for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
The game was released in Japan on April 26, 1991, and in North America on November 1991.
lead
Vice: Project Doom is a side-scrolling platformer with noticeable similarities to the Ninja Gaiden series for the NES, with the addition of gun shooting and driving segments as well.
lead
The player assumes the role of a secret agent who must uncover a conspiracy involving a new kind of alien substance.
lead
A Sega Mega Drive conversion titled Deep Scanner was in development, but never released.
lead
It was released on Nintendo Switch Online in August 2019.
Gameplay
The very first level, as well as Stage 10, are driving stages, while Stage 4-2 and 11-1 are shooting stages; the rest are standard side-scrolling/ parallax -scrolling stages.
Gameplay
As usual of the genre, the player has a health gauge and a limited number of lives.
Gameplay
In the main stages, Hart can switch between one of three weapons: a Laser whip, a.44 Magnum revolver, and a supply of M-24 Stick grenades.
Gameplay
The laser whip is a short-range weapon that can be used infinitely, while bullets and grenades are limited and must be replenished by picking additional supplies dropped by defeated enemies.
Gameplay
Other power-ups include Meat and other health-restoring aids, and as well as coins that will give the player one extra life for every 100 collected.
Gameplay
In the main segments, Hart can jump, attack, crouch, and climb ladders like in most other action games.
Gameplay
Hart drives a Ferrari F-40 red; the player maneuvers the car through the road while shifting between three gears and shooting at enemy vehicles with the car's equipped gun.
Gameplay

The game's stages are Route 246, Waterfront (Construction Site), Chinatown, Port, Ricardo Range, Warehouse 0001, Train and Sewers, Power Plant, Bio-Tech Laboratory, Harbor, and finally the BEDA Corporate Headquarters.
Plot
The information received leads Hart to a secret research base in the jungle, where he fights a certain flying cyborg.
Plot
A fight ensues between them, and Hart defeats the director of the corporation, first as a human, then as a monster.
Reception
Allgame gave Vice: Project Doom an overall rating of 2.5 stars out of a possible 5 stars.
Reception
The May 1991 issue of the North American gaming magazine Nintendo Power gave this game an overall rating of 3.8 out of 5.

fes_sunguy.title: Sunman (video game)
sents: lead
Sunman is an unreleased action video game developed by EIM and planned to be published by Sunsoft for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1992.
lead
Despite being mostly complete, it was never commercially released.
History
In an interview with planner/director Kenji Eno, it was confirmed that this was originally intended to be a Superman game.
History
The game was obtained by The Lost Levels, a website that specializes in unreleased and prototype video games, from a European collector without any information on what it was.
History

The early, rough prototype of the ROM was also made for release on The Lost Levels, and it indeed had sprites of Superman as the original sprites for the main character, and the background music played in-game replaced with John Williams's Superman Theme.
History

Another unreleased Sunsoft cart in the US can be made to confirm that this was indeed Superman originally, as the levels are identical to Sunman, but they are in a less finished form, and the player is able to skip levels by pausing and pressing the select button.
History
In February 2014, a ROM hack was released by a user with the pseudonym Pacnsacdave of a full Sunman to Superman NES conversion.
History
The hack changes the title screen, cutscenes, and sprites to those of the actual Superman prototype ROM.

fes_clash_at_demonhed.title: Clash at Demonhead

Programmer(s): Norihiro Hisamatsu Tomiko Narusawa Mayumi Sano

sents: lead
Clash at Demonhead, known in Japan as Dengeki Big Bang!
lead

(Japanese: 電撃ビッグバン!, Hepburn: Dengeki Biggu Ban!, Blitz Big Bang!), is an action-adventure platform game released by Vic Tokai for the Nintendo Entertainment System on January 27, 1989 in Japan and December 1989 in North America.
Gameplay
There are over 40 routes the player can take in the game, and the player must explore the world to progress.
Plot
Bang learns from the hermit that the demon can only be destroyed with the Sword of Apollo.
Plot
The only way to defuse the bomb is with the medallions, but with no instructions, Bang can only guess where each medallion is placed, and is working against a countdown timer that triggers the bomb.
Plot
When Bang succeeds, the alien voices its disdain that humanity will live on and announces that the alien race intends to leave Earth to its own devices and never return.
Reception
Allgame gave the game a score of 2.5 out of 5.
In popular culture
The band also appears in the 2010 film adaptation of the novels, Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, as well as in the subsequent video game adaptation.
In popular culture
The band is named after the 1989 video game, as well as their drummer - Lynette Guycott - being named after Tom Guycott.
In popular culture
The creator of the comic book, Bryan Lee O'Malley, reportedly said that it was the first NES title he ever played.

fes_wyrm_journey_to_the_center_o.real: Wurm: Journey to the Center of the Earth
fes_wyrm_journey_to_the_center_o.title: Wurm: Journey to the Center of the Earth

Designer(s): Shoichi Yoshikawa Hiroshi Kazama Masasuke Aruga

sents: lead

Wurm: Journey to the Center of the Earth, released in Japan as Vazolder: The Underground Battle Space (地底戦空バゾルダー, Chitei Sen Kū Bazorudā), is a multi-genre video game developed by Cyclone System and published by Asmik and SOFEL for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1991.
Gameplay

Wurm has a variety of different styles of play, with side-scrolling travel stages in the VZR vehicles, overhead shooting levels, levels where the protagonist Moby leaves the vehicle to explore underground ruins, and first-person shooting levels with boss monsters.
Gameplay
Boss monsters have a probability meter that has to be raised up to 100% before that enemy can be eliminated.
Plot

The plot of this video game deals with mysterious earthquakes that emerge in the year 1999, and the government dispatches explorers in powerful digging machines called Vazorudas or VZRs (renamed WURM in the US manual, but the name is never used in the game).
Reception
Nintendo Power gave the game a rating of 14.8 out of 20 in their September 1991 issue, while GamePro assigned the game a 16 out of 25 two months later.

sfes_metrood.title: Super Metroid
sents: lead
Super Metroid is a 1994 action-adventure game developed by Nintendo and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is the third installment in the Metroid series, following the events of the Game Boy game Metroid II: Return of Samus (1991).
lead
Players control bounty hunter Samus Aran, who travels to planet Zebes to retrieve an infant Metroid creature stolen by the Space Pirate leader Ridley.
lead
Following the established gameplay model of its predecessors, Super Metroid focuses on exploration, with the player searching for power-ups used to reach previously inaccessible areas.
lead
It introduced new concepts to the series, such as the inventory screen, an automap, and the ability to fire in all directions.
lead
The development staff from previous Metroid games—including Yoshio Sakamoto, Makoto Kano and Gunpei Yokoi —returned to develop Super Metroid over the course of two years.
lead
The developers wanted to make a true action game, and set the stage for Samus' reappearance.
lead
Super Metroid received acclaim, with praise for its atmosphere, gameplay, music and graphics.
Gameplay

Super Metroid is a 2D side-scrolling action-adventure game, which primarily takes place on the fictional planet Zebes from the original game—a large, open-ended world with areas connected by doors and elevators.
Gameplay
The player controls Samus Aran as she searches the planet for a Metroid that has been stolen by Ridley, the leader of the Space Pirates.
Gameplay
The "Moon Walk" ability, named after the popular dance move of the same name, allows Samus to walk backwards while firing or charging her weapon.
Gameplay
The X-ray Scope is used to see items and passages through hidden walls and other surfaces.
Plot
Samus Aran brings the last Metroid to the Ceres space colony for scientific study.
Plot
A single Metroid that has grown to enormous size attacks and nearly destroys Samus, but relents at the last moment.
Plot
It is the larva that was stolen from Ceres; because Samus was present at its hatching on SR388, the Metroid has imprinted on Samus, recognizing her as its "mother".
Development
Super Metroid was developed by Nintendo R&D1 with a staff of 15 managed by Gunpei Yokoi.
Development
Intelligent Systems, who co-developed the original Metroid with R&D1, handled the programming.
Development

Shortly before the game's release, the North American Entertainment Software Rating Board, a self-regulating organization, was formed in response to the increasing violence in games such as Mortal Kombat (1992).
Development
The game was demonstrated at the Winter 1994 Consumer Electronics Show, and was named the best Super NES game at the show by GamePro.
Audio
The music for Super Metroid was composed by Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano, and uses 16-bit versions of music from previous games.
Audio
A soundtrack album, Super Metroid: Sound in Action, was published by Sony Records on June 22, 1994.
Audio
It contains 38 tracks and has a running time of 58:49.
Release
The game was released by Nintendo in Japan on March 19, 1994, in North America on April 18, and in Europe on July 28.
Release
It was re-released through the Nintendo Power service in Japan on September 30, 1997.
Release
Super Metroid became available as a Wii Virtual Console game in North America on August 20, 2007, in Japan on September 20, and in Europe on October 12.
Release
The game was later released on the Wii U Virtual Console in May 2013, initially available during the trial campaign for a cheaper price before reverting to its regular price the next month.
Release
The New Nintendo 3DS -specific Virtual Console also received the release in April 2016.
Release
In September 2017, Nintendo released the Super NES Classic Edition, which included Super Metroid among its games.
Release
Super Metroid and other Super NES games were added to the Nintendo Switch Online subscription service in September 2019.
Reception
Super Metroid was one of the highest rated games on review aggregator GameRankings.
Reception
Slate found the newly added auto-mapping feature something that players really needed, saying that it was the only feature in Super Metroid that the original Metroid should have had.
Reception

James Leach agreed with Nicholson and Mott that Super Metroid was what Mega Man X should have been, containing "everything I look for: playability, hidden tricks, powerful weapons and steamingly evil baddies".
Reception
IGN called Super Metroid ' s Virtual Console version a "must-own", commenting that although the game was released nine months after the Wii launched, they felt that it was worth the wait.
Reception
For players who have never played Super Metroid, IGN claims that they owe themselves as gamers to "finally find out about what you've been missing all these years".
Reception

Despite admitting that the Virtual Console version was essentially "nothing more than a no-frills, emulated version of a 13-year-old SNES game" that was no longer cutting-edge, he was still pleased with it and reiterated his belief that Super Metroid is "one of the best 2D action adventure games ever produced".
Sales
In Japan, Super Metroid was the ninth-best-selling video game of 1994, with 531,000 copies sold that year.
Sales
With the help of strong marketing from Nintendo, Super Metroid sold well in North America, topping the Super NES sales chart in May 1994.
Sales
By late 2003, the game had shipped 1.42 million copies worldwide.
Accolades

Electronic Gaming Monthly named Super Metroid a Game of the Month for May 1994, gave it an Editors' Choice award, awarded it as the Best Action Game of 1994, and named it the best game of all time in 2003.
Accolades
IGN ranked Super Metroid 3rd (2003), 10th (2005) and 7th (2007) in its top 100 games of all time lists.
Accolades
Likewise, IGN readers ranked the game 11th in its top 99 games of all-time list in 2005, and 4th in its top 100 games in 2006.
Accolades

Richard George of IGN also ranked Super Metroid 3rd in its top 100 SNES games, crediting its "flawless action, impeccable level design, out-of-this-world atmosphere, a totally badass heroine and an enormous overworld to explore".
Accolades
Game Informer placed the game 29th on their top 100 games of all time in 2001.
Accolades
In 2018, Complex listed the game 3rd on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Accolades
In 1995, Total! rated the game 17th on its "Top 100 SNES Games".
Accolades
In 1995, Flux magazine listed Super Metroid 62nd in their "Top 100 Video Games".
Legacy
Andrew Webster of Ars Technica found the game's atmosphere impressive, and noted that the developers had perfected the aspect on solitude, a concept introduced in the first Metroid game.
Legacy
Game Informer writer Joe Juba cited the game's ending as "one of the most memorable and empowering moments in gaming history".
Legacy
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine called the game "challenging, deep and undeniably epic", placing it 24th on a list of the greatest Nintendo games.
Legacy
Super Metroid, alongside Konami 's 1997 game Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, is also credited for establishing the " Metroidvania " genre.
Legacy
Super Metroid: Redesign, created by "drewseph" in 2006, features new items, expanded areas and modified physics.
Legacy
In 2011, a Japanese hacker named "SB" released a ROM hack titled Metroid: Super Zero Mission, which intends to combine elements from Super Metroid and Metroid: Zero Mission.
Sequels
Nintendo did not release another Metroid game for eight years, as the series had not matched the success of the Mario and Legend of Zelda franchises.
Sequels
Yokoi left Nintendo in August 1996, amid the failure of the Virtual Boy, and died in a car accident in October 1997.
Sequels
Fans eagerly awaited a Metroid game for the Nintendo 64 (N64).
Sequels
According to Nintendo producer Shigeru Miyamoto, Nintendo did not develop a Metroid game for the N64 as they "couldn't come out with any concrete ideas".
Sequels
Sakamoto said he could not imagine how the N64 controller could be used to control Samus.
Sequels
Nintendo approached another company to make an N64 Metroid, but the offer was declined because the developers thought they could not make a game to equal Super Metroid.
Sequels

In late 2002, Nintendo released Metroid Fusion, a 2D sequel developed for the Game Boy Advance by Nintendo R&D1, and Metroid Prime, a first-person game developed for the GameCube by American developer Retro Studios, and the first Metroid game to use 3D graphics.
Sequels

Metroid Prime received three spin-offs, 2009 compilation Metroid Prime: Trilogy, containing Prime, its 2004 sequel Metroid Prime 2: Echoes, and 2007 Wii sequel Metroid Prime 3: Corruption, and an upcoming fourth sequel.
Sequels
In 2010, Metroid: Other M was released, taking place between Super Metroid and Fusion.
Sequels

After a long development period, a fifth 2D game and sequel to Fusion, Metroid Dread, was released in 2021 for the Nintendo Switch to critical acclaim and developed by Metroid: Samus Returns developer MercurySteam.

sfes_legend_of_zeldo_a_link_to_th.real: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past
sfes_legend_of_zeldo_a_link_to_th.title: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past
sents: lead
The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is an action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is the third game in The Legend of Zelda series and was released in 1991 in Japan and 1992 in North America and Europe.
lead
The story is set many years before the events of the first two Zelda games.
lead
The player assumes the role of Link as he journeys to save Hyrule, defeat the demon king Ganon, and rescue the descendants of the Seven Sages.
lead
It returns to a top-down perspective similar to the original The Legend of Zelda, dropping the side-scrolling gameplay of Zelda II: The Adventure of Link.
lead
It introduced series staples such as parallel worlds and items including the Master Sword.
lead
A Link to the Past is widely considered among the greatest video games ever made, with particular praise for its presentation and innovative gameplay.
lead
It was ported to the Game Boy Advance as A Link to the Past and Four Swords in 2002, and sold 6.5 million copies across both platforms by 2004.
Gameplay
A Link to the Past puts the player in control of its protagonist, Link, and is viewed and controlled from an overhead perspective, much like the original The Legend of Zelda.
Gameplay
Where Link could only move in four directions in the original The Legend of Zelda, Link can now move diagonally as well.
Gameplay
While Link can enter the Dark World via portals, he can only exit the Dark World using an item called the Magic Mirror.
Setting

A Link to the Past is a distant prequel to the original The Legend of Zelda and Zelda II: The Adventure of Link, and, within the official chronology, is the first game in the "Defeated Hero" timeline that connects to an alternate reality scenario where the Hero of Time does not succeed in Ocarina of Time.
Story
Originally the Golden Land where the omnipotent Triforce resided, it was turned into the Dark World when Ganon seized the Triforce and his evil corrupted the land.
Development

In 1988, development of a new NES The Legend of Zelda video game began, but one year later, the project was brought to Nintendo 's next console; the Super Famicom (known as the Super NES in other regions).
Development
At the time, most Super NES game cartridges had 4 Mbit (512 KB) of storage space.
Development
This game broke the trend by using 8 Mbit (1 MB), allowing the Nintendo development team to create a remarkably expansive world for Link to inhabit.
Development
Like Super Mario World, this game used a simple graphic compression method on the Super NES by limiting the color depth of many tiles to eight colors instead of the Super NES's native 16-color tiles.
Development

Storage space was also saved by eliminating duplication: The Light World and the Dark World are almost identical in layout (though using differing texture tiles), and the Dark World exists in the ROM only as an "overlay" of the Light World.
Development
Producer Shigeru Miyamoto originally intended the game to feature a party, "one that consists of the protagonist,... a magic user, and a girl".
Music
The overworld theme of The Legend of Zelda ("Hyrule Overture") returns in A Link to the Past, redone in S-SMP style.
Music

While the first game originated the "Hyrule Overture", many recurring motifs of the Zelda scores come from A Link to the Past, including "Zelda's Lullaby" (Princess Zelda's Theme), "Ganondorf's Theme", "Hyrule Castle" (Royal Family Theme), "Kakariko Village" and "Select Screen/Fairy Cave".
Music
A soundtrack to Kamigami no Triforce, entitled The Legend of Zelda: Sound and Drama, was released by Sony Records in Japan on June 22, 1994.
Music
The first disc is 44 minutes long and features rearranged versions of a selection of the game's themes, along with a bonus drama track.
Music
The second disc features 54 minutes of the original arrangements for the game and those of the original NES game.
Localization
The most common change was the removal of religious references to conform with Nintendo of America's content guidelines.
Localization
The most obvious change was made to the subtitle, which was renamed from Kamigami no Triforce ("Triforce of the Gods") to A Link to the Past.
Easter egg
In 1990, Nintendo Power held a contest, requiring players to take a photo of the "WarMECH", a powerful and rare enemy in Final Fantasy.
Easter egg
As a result, a hidden room exists in A Link to the Past containing 45 blue rupees and a greeting from Chris Houlihan, the winner of the contest, reading "My name is Chris Houlihan.
Easter egg
There was no wide awareness of the room until the 2000s, more than a decade after the release of A Link to the Past with the increased popularity of the Internet and Super NES emulators.
Easter egg
The Game Boy Advance re-release, The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past and Four Swords, removed the ability to access the room, though it could still be found in the game's code.
Easter egg
The Virtual Console re-releases on the Wii, Wii U, and New Nintendo 3DS, as well as the version present on Nintendo Switch Online, contain the room, being emulations of the original game.
Reception
It was the first game to receive a near-perfect score of 39 out of 40 from Famitsu magazine.
Reception
A Link to the Past was reviewed in Dragon magazine by Sandy Petersen in 1993, giving it 5 out of 5 stars.
Reception
In 1995, Total! listed the game 2nd on its "Top 100 SNES Games".
Reception
In 1996, GamesMaster rated the game 80th on their "Top 100 Games of All Time".
Reception
In 2005, IGN editors placed it 11th in its "Top 100 Games", while readers voted it to 5th place, before IGN later ranked it the second best game of all time in 2015 and 2019.
Reception
In 2006, Entertainment Weekly chose it as the best game of all-time and it was inducted into GameSpot ' s list of the greatest games of all time.
Reception
Members of GameFAQs ranked it the 4th best, and readers of Japanese magazine Famitsu ranked it 31st in a 2006 poll.
Reception
It also placed 3rd in Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s list, 23rd in Game Informer ' s, and 3rd in a best 200 Nintendo games list by Nintendo Power.
Reception
In July 2007, readers of the magazine Edge voted it sixth in a poll of the 100 best games of all time.
Reception

The Escapist, G4TV, GameSpy, Good Game, IGN, Nintendo Life, and PALGN referenced the Chris Houlihan room in articles which discuss video game easter eggs and secrets.

If only two players are active, the game ensures that all puzzles generated do not require a third or fourth player to solve.

On November 22, Nintendo released A Link Between Worlds, which takes place in the same world, but features a new storyline, new puzzles and original dungeons.
A Link Between Worlds
Height and depth play a large role by taking advantage of the 3D feature of the 3DS, while maintaining the traditional top-down perspective.
