sfes_secret_of_manna.title: Secret of Mana

Platform(s): Super Nintendo Entertainment System, Mobile phone, iOS, Android

sents: lead
Secret of Mana, originally released in Japan as Seiken Densetsu 2, is a 1993 action role-playing game developed and published by Square for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead

It is the sequel to the 1991 game Seiken Densetsu, released in North America as Final Fantasy Adventure and in Europe as Mystic Quest, and it was the first Seiken Densetsu title to be marketed as part of the Mana series rather than the Final Fantasy series.
lead
Set in a high fantasy universe, the game follows three heroes as they attempt to prevent an empire from conquering the world with the power of an ancient flying fortress.
lead
Rather than using a turn-based battle system like contemporaneous role-playing games, Secret of Mana features real-time battles with a power bar mechanic.
lead
The game has a unique Ring Command menu system, which pauses the action and allows the player to make decisions in the middle of battle.
lead
An innovative cooperative multiplayer system allows a second or third player to drop in and out of the game at any time.
lead
Secret of Mana was directed and designed by Koichi Ishii, programmed primarily by Nasir Gebelli, and produced by veteran Square designer Hiromichi Tanaka.
lead
The game received acclaim for its brightly colored graphics, expansive plot, Ring Command menu system, and innovative real-time battle system.
Gameplay
Like many other role-playing games of the 16-bit era, Secret of Mana displays a top-down perspective, in which the player characters navigate the terrain and fight off hostile creatures.
Gameplay
The player takes each Orb to a blacksmith, located in most towns, who uses it to reforge one weapon.
Story
With the last of his strength, Dyluck warns that Thanatos has sold his soul to the underworld and must not be allowed to have the Fortress.
Development
Secret of Mana was directed and designed by Koichi Ishii, the creator of the game's Game Boy predecessor, Final Fantasy Adventure.
Development
The team hoped to build on the foundation of Final Fantasy Adventure, and they included several modified elements from that game and from other popular Square titles in Secret of Mana.
Development

The party system also received an upgrade from the first Mana game: instead of temporary companions who could not be upgraded, party members became permanent protagonists and could be controlled by other players.
Development
The real-time battle system used in Secret of Mana has been described by its creators as an extension of the battle system used in the first three flagship Final Fantasy titles.
Development
According to Tanaka, the game's battle system features mechanics that had first been considered for Final Fantasy IV.
Development
Similarly, unused features in Secret of Mana were appropriated by the Chrono Trigger team, which (like Final Fantasy IV) was in production at the time.
Development
According to Tanaka, the project was originally intended to be Final Fantasy IV, with a "more action-based, dynamic overworld".
Development
Secret of Mana was originally planned to be a launch title for the SNES-CD add-on.
Development

One of the most significant changes was the removal of the option to take multiple routes through the game that led to several possible endings, in contrast to the linear journey in the final product.
Development
Secret of Mana was announced as being released in July 1993 as recently as that April, marketed as a "Party Action RPG", before eventually being released in August instead for the Japanese market.
Development
In South Korea, it was released the same month in August 1993.
Development

The English translation for Secret of Mana was completed in only 30 days, mere weeks after the Japanese release, and the North American localization was initially advertised as Final Fantasy Adventure 2.
Development
Critics have suggested that the translation was done hastily so that the game could be released in North America for the 1993 holiday season.
Development
The Japanese release only named the three protagonists in the manual, while Western versions omitted the characters' names until the enhanced port on the iOS.
Music
The original score for Secret of Mana was composed and produced by Hiroki Kikuta.
Music

Kenji Ito, who had composed the soundtrack for Final Fantasy Adventure, was originally slated for the project, but was replaced with Kikuta after he had started on other projects, such as Romancing SaGa.
Music
Secret of Mana was Kikuta's first video game score, and he encountered difficulties in dealing with the hardware limitations of the Super NES.
Music

Kikuta worked on the music mostly by himself, spending nearly 24 hours a day in his office, alternating between composing and editing to create a soundtrack that would be, according to him, "immersive" and "three-dimensional".
Music
Rather than having sound engineers create the samples of instruments like most game music composers of the time, Kikuta made his own samples that matched the hardware capabilities of the Super NES.
Music
Kikuta stated in 2001 that he considered the score for Secret of Mana his favorite creation.
Music
Kikuta's compositions for the game were partly inspired by natural landscapes, as well as music from Bali.
Music
An official soundtrack album, Seiken Densetsu 2 Original Sound Version, was released in Japan in August 1993, containing 44 musical tracks from the game.
Music

An English version, identical to the Japanese original aside from its localized packaging and track titles, was later released in North America in December 1994 as Secret of Mana Original Soundtrack, making Secret of Mana one of the first Japanese games to inspire a localized soundtrack release outside of Japan.
Music
An album of arranged music from Secret of Mana and its sequel Seiken Densetsu 3 was produced in 1993 as Secret of Mana+.
Music
Secret of Mana+ contains a single track, titled "Secret of Mana", that incorporates themes from the music of both Secret of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3, which was still under development at the time.
Music
The latest album of music from the game is a 2012 arranged album titled Secret of Mana Genesis / Seiken Densetsu 2 Arrange Album.
Music
Music for the 2018 remake, which features remastered versions of the original soundtrack, was overseen by Kikuta and arranged by numerous game composers, such as Yuzo Koshiro and Tsuyoshi Sekito.
Music
The soundtrack was released as an album, also titled Secret of Mana Original Soundtrack, shortly after the remake's release in February 2018.
Music
A rendition of the soundtrack was commissioned for the first ever BBC Proms gaming music concert in 2022.
Re-releases
In 1999, Square announced they would be porting Secret of Mana to Bandai 's handheld system WonderSwan Color as one of nine planned games for the system.
Re-releases
A mobile phone port of Secret of Mana was released on October 26, 2009.
Re-releases
A port of the game for iOS was revealed at E3 2010, and released on Apple's App Store on December 21, 2010.
Re-releases
The enhanced port from the iOS version was released on Android devices in 2014.
Re-releases
A port for the Nintendo Switch was released with ports of Final Fantasy Adventure and Trials of Mana as part of the Collection of Mana on June 1, 2017, in Japan, and June 11, 2019 in North America.
Re-releases
The game was released as one of the games included on the Super NES Classic Edition on September 29, 2017.
Re-releases
In August 2017, a 3D remake of the game was announced for PlayStation 4, PlayStation Vita and Windows and was released on February 15, 2018.
Sales
Dengeki Oh magazine ranked it the second best-selling video game of 1993 in Japan, where 1.003 million units were sold that year, just below Street Fighter II Turbo.
Sales
In South Korea, it was the top-selling game from November to December 1993.
Sales

Edge reported in November 1993 that the game was "the most widely covered game of the year in Japan" with a high number of sales, but was initially released in North America "completely un-hyped and mostly unheard of".
Sales

Despite this, Secret of Mana went on to become the second top-selling Super NES game on the monthly US Babbage 's chart in October 1993, below only Mortal Kombat, with Secret of Mana remaining in the US top ten SNES game charts for a year up until October 1994.
Sales
In the United Kingdom, it was the fourth top-selling game in November 1994, and the second top-selling SNES game that month (below Donkey Kong Country).
Sales
Next Generation reported in 1996 that the game had sold more than 500,000 copies in the United States alone.
Sales
According to Square Enix, Secret of Mana had shipped 1.83 million copies worldwide as of 2003, with 1.5 million shipped in Japan and 330,000 abroad.
Contemporary reviews

GamePro ' s review praised the graphics, plot, "first-rate gameplay" and "positively massive" world "dwarfing even Zelda ", while stating the gameplay and multiplayer were "rough around the edges", concluding it to be "one of the finest action/RPGs" on the SNES.
Contemporary reviews
Secret of Mana was awarded Game of the Month in December 1993 and Best Role-Playing Game of 1993 by Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Contemporary reviews
Edge ' s review said that Secret of Mana was better than contemporary role-playing games Ys I & II, The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, and Landstalker: The Treasures of King Nole.
Contemporary reviews

The review stated that Secret of Mana "includes some of the best game design and features ever seen: simultaneous threeplayer action, the best combat system ever designed, the best player interface ever designed, a superb control system, and yes, some of the most engrossing and rewarding gameplay yet".
Contemporary reviews

Peterson concluded that Secret of Mana was one of the best SNES role-playing games and that it was "a much larger game than Zelda, with many more types of monsters, character options, and fortresses to explore".
Contemporary reviews

Computer and Video Games said in 1994 that Mana was "doing for adventure games now what Zelda did several years ago" and that Mana is "one of the best games for the SNES this year and more playable than" Donkey Kong Country.
Contemporary reviews
Next Generation said in 1996 that many players considered it "the RPG equivalent of Lord of the Rings."
Retrospective reception
In 2008, Lucas Thomas of IGN reviewed the Virtual Console release of Secret of Mana and stated that it was considered one of the best video games ever made.
Retrospective reception
In 2014, Edge magazine described Secret of Mana as "one of the high points of the 16bit era".
Retrospective reception
A writer for the magazine noted that, 20 years after Secret of Mana ' s release, its reputation as a SNES action RPG had been surpassed only by that of The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past.
Retrospective reception
Secret of Mana has placed on numerous top game lists since its release, and is the 13th highest-rate SNES game on aggregator website GameRankings.
Retrospective reception
In 1995, Total! rated Secret of Mana 12th on their "Top 100 SNES Games of All Time," with Super Play ranked it eighth on its list of the best 100 SNES games of all time the following year.
Impact

In 2006, Level magazine claimed that Secret of Mana ' s rocky development was Square's main inspiration to move their games, such as the Final Fantasy series, from Nintendo consoles to Sony consoles in 1996.
Impact
Secret of Mana was an influential game in its time, and its influence continued into the 2010s.

sfes_secret_of_nevermore.title: Secret of Evermore
sents: lead
Secret of Evermore is an action role-playing game developed and published by Square for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It was released in North America on October 17, 1995, in Australia in February 1996, and in Europe in March 1996.
lead
A Japanese release was planned to follow the North American release by a few months but was ultimately cancelled.
lead
The story of Secret of Evermore follows a boy and his shapeshifting pet dog as they are inadvertently transported to the fantasy world of Evermore.
lead

The player guides both characters through Evermore, a world composed of separate realms, each resembling a different period of real-world history: "Prehistoria" (prehistory), "Antiqua" (classical antiquity), "Gothica" (the Middle Ages), and "Omnitopia" (an imaginative future world).
lead
The gameplay shares many similarities with Secret of Mana, such as real-time battles, a ring-shaped menu system, and the ability to switch control between the two characters.
lead
Despite similar game mechanics and a similar title, it is not an entry in the Mana series.
lead
Secret of Evermore is unique in that it is the only game developed by Square designers in North America.
Gameplay
Secret of Evermore takes many of its interface and gameplay aspects from Secret of Mana.
Gameplay
Swinging a weapon or running causes the gauge to fall to 0%.
Gameplay
Most swords, axes, and spears can cut through vegetation, while some weapons are required to break rocks and other barriers.
Gameplay
In the four worlds of Secret of Evermore, the in-game currency changes.
Gameplay
Most vendors only specialize in one type of good, and some rare items require an extensive amount of trading to obtain.
Alchemy
A unique element of Secret of Evermore is its magic system.
Alchemy
Some Alchemists make their home in out-of-the-way areas and will dispense rare formulas if the player manages to seek them out.
Alchemy
Alchemy Formulas require pairs of ingredients to be used; some are available throughout the game, and others are only native to certain environments.
Alchemy
Although there are dozens of Formulas available to be found within the game, only nine can be equipped at a time.
Setting
Most of the game takes place in the fictional world of Evermore.
Plot
The story of Secret of Evermore begins with a black and white flashback to 1965, in a small town called Podunk, USA.
Plot
A butler dressed in a white tailcoat greets the boy when he appears, only to lock him in a room with several attack robots.
Plot
In each realm, the boy encounters a citizen of Podunk involved in an original experiment gone awry 30 years before.
Plot
At the last moment, Ruffleberg appears and deactivates Carltron, who promptly freezes in place.
Development
In early 1994, the development of Secret of Evermore began at SquareSoft, the Redmond, Washington, office of the Japanese parent company Square.
Development
The concept of an "American-flavored Secret-of-Mana-like" game was dictated from overseas.
Development
The studio had a naming competition which resulted in Secret of Evermore; composer Jeremy Soule claims to have been the team member who submitted the name "Evermore".
Development
Many elements of Secret of Evermore were copied from Secret of Mana because they had proven to be effective.
Development
It was decided that it would be single-player to preserve memory—it was originally planned to be only 12-megabits.
Development

Using computer software, including Alias 3D modeling software running on SGI workstations, the game's artwork and design were mapped out by three animators, four background artists, and a 3D rendering artist.
Development
The final product of Secret of Evermore was produced using another company program, SIGIL (Square Interpreted Game Intelligence Language).
Development
There is a persistent misconception that the game is, or was released in lieu of, a follow-up to Secret of Mana.
Development
Other Square titles such as Final Fantasy VI and Chrono Trigger were being localized simultaneously with the production of Secret of Evermore.
Development

Fehdrau explained in an interview that Secret of Evermore was not created in place of Trials of Mana and that the team that developed Secret of Evermore was assembled from newly hired staff and would otherwise never have been assembled.
Development
Secret of Evermore was released on October 17, 1995, in North America.
Development
In 1996, it was translated into German, French and Spanish for the non-English-speaking market in some PAL territories, including Australia and New Zealand.
Music
Jeremy Soule composed and produced the score for Secret of Evermore, his first video game project.
Music
In high school Soule was a big fan of video games, but he felt most of their scores "lacked drama and intensity".
Music
Soule was hired by Square Soft after they had reviewed the demo to score Secret of Evermore.
Music
The soundtrack was released on a CD containing 29 tracks, the first eight of which are arranged versions of the original sound.
Music
The disc was published by Square and was only available initially to those who pre-ordered Secret of Evermore.
Reception
Secret of Evermore received positive reviews from most media outlets.
Reception
A highlight for some critics was gameplay, particularly the unique alchemy system and aspects also found in Secret of Mana such as the ring menu.
Reception
Others argued that Secret of Evermore was a decent first attempt by the American team.
Reception

Video Games praised Squaresoft USA's very first title, noting that while the menu and control schemes were taken from previous Square games, its mood, story, and setting were enough to set it apart from the earlier titles.
Reception

In a retrospective review, Allgame editor Scott Alan Marriott described the game as "a good, solid RPG, but those expecting memorable characters or a dramatic, involving story will most likely be disappointed".
Reception
One reviewer, however, noted that he missed the Japanese-style art found in other Square games and although the art in Secret of Evermore was good, it was aimed at an American audience.
Reception
In 2018, Complex rated Secret of Evermore 41st in their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Times" list.

sfes_final_fantasia_ii.title: Final Fantasy II
sents: lead
Final Fantasy II is a 1988 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer as the second installment of the Final Fantasy series.
lead
The game has received numerous enhanced remakes for the WonderSwan Color, the PlayStation, the Game Boy Advance, the PlayStation Portable, iOS, Android and Windows.
lead
As neither this game nor Final Fantasy III were initially released outside Japan, Final Fantasy IV was originally released in North America as Final Fantasy II, so as not to confuse players.
lead
Following enhanced versions for iOS and Android in 2010 and 2012 respectively, the game was re-released again as part of the 2021 Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster series.
lead
The game's story centers on four youths whose parents were killed during an army invasion by the empire of Palamecia, who are using hellspawn to conquer the world.
lead
Three of the four main characters join a rebellion against the empire, embarking on missions to gain new magic and weapons, destroy enemy superweapons, and rescue leading members of the resistance.
lead
The Game Boy Advance remake adds a bonus story after the game is completed.
lead
Final Fantasy II introduced many elements that would later become staples of the Final Fantasy franchise, including chocobos and the recurring character Cid.
Gameplay

Characters and monsters are no longer separated into separate windows in the battle screen as they were in the first Final Fantasy, and players can see their current and total hit points below the battle.
Gameplay
Players can also fight with less than four characters in their party, which was not possible in the first game.
Gameplay
The game introduces a "back row" in battle, within which characters or enemies are immune to most physical attacks, but can be harmed with bows and magical attacks.
Characters
Final Fantasy II features four playable characters as well as several secondary characters who are only briefly controlled by the player.
Story
There the party finds only a mother with her son, learning that all but one of the dragoons are dead, partly as a result of imperial poison.
Story
After placing an egg of the last wyvern in a cavern, the party returns to Altair and finds the Hilda they rescued is a lamia in disguise.
Story
The party returns to Fynn and sees that many towns have been destroyed by a cyclone summoned by the Emperor.
Story
The party calls upon the newly born last wyvern to take them to a castle inside the cyclone, where they confront and kill the Emperor.
Soul of Rebirth

Climbing to the highest floor, the party meets the Light Emperor, who explains that when Firion and his allies killed him, his soul was split, with the Emperor's "dark half" falling to Hell and acquiring more power, while his light half—the Emperor they now see—ascended to Heaven.
Development

During the development of the first installment in the series, Square 's management decided to manufacture 400,000 copies of the game to make a sequel possible, then the original Famicom (NES) version successfully shipped 520,000 copies in Japan.
Development

Using the experience gained from the first installment, which focused more on fitting story ideas into their new gameplay system and game world, the developers fully crafted the story of Final Fantasy II first.
Development
The experience system was designed to be a more realistic advancement system than that of the first game.
Development
Several members of the original staff from the first game reprised their jobs for Final Fantasy II.
Development
Nobuo Uematsu composed the music, as he had for the first game, while Yoshitaka Amano was again the concept artist.
Development
The game was released one day before the one-year anniversary of the first game's release.
Development
In April 1989, the game was novelized by its original scenario writer Kenji Terada under the title Final Fantasy II: Muma no Meikyū (lit.
Music
Although the two soundtracks were composed separately, the soundtrack to II has only been released as a combined album with the soundtrack to Final Fantasy I.
Music
They were first released as All Sounds of Final Fantasy III in 1989, which was then republished in 1994.
Music

An arranged album of music from the two soundtracks titled Symphonic Suite Final Fantasy was also released in 1989, while Final Fantasy & Final Fantasy II Original Soundtrack, a combined soundtrack album for the PlayStation versions of the games, was released in 2002 and re-released in 2004.
Versions and re-releases
Final Fantasy II has been remade several times for different platforms, and has frequently been packaged with the first Final Fantasy in various collections.
Unreleased English version
Assigned to the project was Kaoru Moriyama, whose later work included script translations for Final Fantasy IV and Secret of Mana (known as Seiken Densetsu 2 in Japan).
Unreleased English version

In 2003, when the game was finally released to English-speaking audiences as part of Final Fantasy Origins, it was released with new graphics, music, and a brand new translation under the supervision of Akira Kashiwagi.
Unreleased English version

A fan translation of the original game was also created prior to the release of Origins, and makes use of an original translation as the existence of the prototype cartridge was not common knowledge at the time.
Re-releases

In addition to its original Famicom release, Final Fantasy II was re-released on the WonderSwan Color in 2001, and both singularly and as part of a collection with Final Fantasy I for the PlayStation in 2002.
Re-releases
It was released on the Game Boy Advance in 2004 as part of Final Fantasy I & II: Dawn of Souls, on the PlayStation Portable in 2007, and for the Japanese Wii Virtual Console on June 16, 2009.
Re-releases
The Final Fantasy III collection included the original game with only minor changes.
Re-releases
The WonderSwan Color remake of the game was first released on May 3, 2001, and later included as a bundle with a special Final Fantasy II edition of the console.
Re-releases

It was published both individually (in Japan only) and alongside Final Fantasy I in a collection entitled Final Fantasy Origins (or Final Fantasy I+II Premium Collection in Japan); this was the first release of the game outside Japan.
Re-releases
The port was re-released as part of the Final Fantasy 25th Anniversary Ultimate Box package in December 2012.
Re-releases
Final Fantasy II was again released in a new format in 2004 for the Game Boy Advance as part of Final Fantasy I & II: Dawn of Souls.
Re-releases
In 2005 and 2006, Square Enix released a version of Final Fantasy II for three Japanese mobile phone networks.
Re-releases
To celebrate the Final Fantasy series' 20th anniversary, the game was released in Japan for the PlayStation Portable in 2007.
Re-releases

The release for the Japanese Virtual Console for the Wii on June 16, 2009, for the Wii U on December 11, 2013, and for the Nintendo 3DS on February 12, 2014, is identical to the original Famicom release, incorporating none of the updates of the later versions.
Re-releases
On February 25, 2010, Square Enix released a port of the PSP version modified with touchscreen controls for the iOS platform.
Re-releases
Following this, a touchscreen port was brought to Android in 2012 through the Google Play store.
Reception
According to Square's publicity department, the original Famicom release sold 800,000 copies.
Reception
As of March 2003, the game, including all re-releases at the time, had shipped 1.28 million copies worldwide, with 1.08 million of those copies being shipped in Japan and 200,000 abroad.
Reception
Despite having only been released in June of that year, as of September 2007 the PlayStation Portable version had shipped 90,000 copies in Japan and 70,000 in North America.
Reception
Despite these high sales, the game had sold the fewest copies of any of the first ten main games in the Final Fantasy series.
Reception
Upon release, Famicom Tsūshin (now Famitsu) gave the original Famicom version a score of 35 out of 40, based on a panel of four reviewers giving it ratings of 9, 9, 9 and 8 out of 10.
Reception
This made it one of their three highest-rated games of 1988, along with Dragon Quest III (which scored 38/40) and Super Mario Bros.
Reception
It was also one of the magazine's five highest-rated games up until 1988, along with Dragon Quest II (which scored 38/40) and Zelda II: The Adventure of Link (which scored 36/40).
Reception
The 1989 "All Soft Catalog" issue of Famicom Tsūshin included Final Fantasy II in its list of the best games of all time, giving it the Best Scenario award.
Reception

Retrospectively, G4 described the stat-building system as an "Innovation", noting that "computer RPGs took the "level" system wholesale from tabletop role-playing games and made it a genre staple, but FF2 eliminated levels altogether", but that what "sounds novel at first wound up being a huge mess".
Reception
Famitsu magazine scored the WonderSwan version of the game a 30 out of 40, and GameSpot noted the Dawn of Souls ' mostly outdated graphics but praised its length and bonus content.
Reception
The Dawn of Souls release was named the IGN Game Boy "Game of the Month" for March 2004, and the package was rated 76th in Nintendo Power ' s Top 200 Games list.
Reception
The story was considered to be much more involved and deep than the first Final Fantasy, as it involved romance and the death of characters.

sfes_fantasia.title: Final Fantasy III
sents: lead
Final Fantasy III is a role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer.
lead
The third installment in the Final Fantasy series, it is the first numbered Final Fantasy game to feature the job-change system.
lead
The story revolves around four orphaned youths drawn to a crystal of light.
lead
The crystal grants them some of its power, and instructs them to go forth and restore balance to the world.
lead

Not knowing what to make of the crystal's pronouncements, but nonetheless recognizing the importance of its words, the four inform their adoptive families of their mission and set out to explore and bring back balance to the world.
lead
The game was originally released in Japan on April 27, 1990.
lead
The original Famicom version sold 1.4 million copies in Japan.
lead
It had not been released outside Japan until a remake, also called Final Fantasy III, was developed by Matrix Software for the Nintendo DS on August 24, 2006.
Gameplay
The gameplay of Final Fantasy III combines elements of the first two Final Fantasy games with new features.
Gameplay

The turn-based combat system remains in place from the first two games, but hit points are now shown above the target following attacks or healing actions, rather than captioned as in the previous two games.
Gameplay
Auto-targeting for physical attacks after a friendly or enemy unit is killed is also featured for the first time.
Gameplay
The character class system featured in the first game also reappears, with some modifications.
Gameplay

Whereas in the original game the player chooses each character's class alignment at the start of the game and is then locked into that class for the duration of the game, Final Fantasy III introduces the "job system" for which the series would later become famous.
Gameplay

Final Fantasy III is the first game in the series to feature special battle commands such as "Steal" or "Jump", each of which is associated with a particular job ("Steal" is the Thief's specialty, while "Jump" is the Dragoon's forte).
Characters

Final Fantasy III focuses around four orphans from the remote village of Ur (while in the remakes players only begin as Luneth, slowly picking up the other three characters as they progress; a change from the original and from other early Final Fantasy titles), each starting off as an Onion Knight in the original game.
Characters
Appearing in a female-like form, the Cloud of Darkness refers to herself in first-person plural because her two tentacles have minds of their own.
Story
Following an earthquake, a hidden cavern in Altar Cave opens.
Development
The completed game was one of the largest ever released for the Famicom, published on a 512 KB cartridge, the second-highest capacity available for the console.
Development
Square developed and released Final Fantasy III during the same period that Nintendo released its 16-bit Super Famicom console, intended as the successor to the original 8-bit Famicom.
Development

Nowadays we know that when you've got a platform like PlayStation, you'll have PlayStation 2 and then PlayStation 3, and where you've got Xbox, you move on to Xbox 360 - you can sort of assume what's going to happen in the future.
Development
But back then, that was the first time that we'd seen a new generation of consoles, and it was really difficult to predict what was going to happen.
Development
Square planned to localize and release the game outside Japan; however, plans to localize the game were scrapped.
Music

Final Fantasy III Original Sound Version, a compilation album of almost all of the music in the game, was released by Square/ NTT Publishing in 1991, and subsequently re-released by NTT Publishing in 1994 and 2004.
Music

A vocal arrangement album entitled Final Fantasy III Yūkyū no Kaze Densetsu, or literally Final Fantasy III Legend of the Eternal Wind, contains a selection of musical tracks from the game, performed by Nobuo Uematsu and Dido, a duo composed of Michiaki Kato and Sizzle Ohtaka.
Music
The album was released by Data M in 1990 and by Polystar in 1994.
Cancelled WonderSwan Color remake

Bandai unveiled their WonderSwan Color handheld system in 2000 and had immediately headed up a deal with Square to release enhanced remakes of their first three Final Fantasy titles on the new console.
Cancelled WonderSwan Color remake

Although Final Fantasy and Final Fantasy II were both released within a year of the announcement, Final Fantasy III was ultimately delayed from its late 2001 release date, even after Bandai picked up the game's publishing rights.
Cancelled WonderSwan Color remake
Although the game was never formally cancelled, the official website was taken offline once production of the WonderSwan Color consoles ceased in 2002.
Cancelled WonderSwan Color remake

When we developed FF3, the volume of content in the game was so huge that the cartridge was completely full, and when new platforms emerged, there simply wasn't enough storage space available for an update of FF3, because that would have required new graphics, music and other content.
Versions and re-releases
There are two distinct Final Fantasy III versions: the original 2D Famicom version, and a completely remade 3D version.
Reception
Upon release, Famicom Tsūshin (now Famitsu) gave the Famicom version a score of 36 out of 40, based on a panel of four reviewers giving it ratings of 9, 9, 10 and 8 out of 10.
Reception
This made it one of their three highest-rated games of 1990, along with Dragon Quest IV and F-Zero, both of which scored 37 out of 40.
Reception
It was also one of the magazine's six highest-rated games up until 1990, along with Dragon Quest II, Dragon Quest III and Zelda II: The Adventure of Link.
Reception
In Famicom Tsūshin ' s 1990 Game of the Year awards, Final Fantasy III was voted the runner-up for the Grand Prize, with 37,101 points, behind Dragon Quest IV.
Reception
In 2006, readers of the Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu voted the original Final Fantasy III the eighth best video game of all-time, above Dragon Quest IV.
Reception
As of March 2003, the original Famicom game had shipped 1.4 million copies in Japan.
Legacy

From 1991 to 1992, Kadokawa Shoten 's Famicom gaming magazine, Maru Katsu Famicom (マル勝ファミコン) published Legend of the Eternal Wind, from Final Fantasy III (悠久の風伝説 ファイナルファンタジーIIIより, Yūkyū no Kaze Densetsu Fainaru Fantajī Surī-yori), a manga serialization of Final Fantasy III illustrated by Yu Kinutani.
Legacy
It was subsequently collected into three tankōbon under Kadokawa Shoten's Dragon Comics imprint: Legend of the Eternal Wind 1, 2, and 3.
Legacy
The characters reprise their roles in the sequels, Dissidia 012 and Dissidia NT.

sfes_final_fantasia_mystic_quest.title: Final Fantasy Mystic Quest

Writer(s): Chihiro Fujioka Yoshihiko Maekawa Ted Woolsey

sents: lead
Final Fantasy Mystic Quest, released as Mystic Quest Legend in PAL regions and as Final Fantasy USA: Mystic Quest in Japan, is a role-playing video game for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It was released as a spin-off to Square 's Final Fantasy series of video games.
lead

Final Fantasy Mystic Quest was first released in North America in 1992 and marketed as a "simplified role-playing game... designed for the entry-level player" in an attempt to broaden the genre's appeal.
lead
The game's presentation and battle system is broadly similar to that of the main series, but differs in its inclusion of action-adventure game elements.
lead
It was also the first Final Fantasy game to be released in Europe.
lead
The player controls a youth named Benjamin in his quest to save the world.
lead
His goal is to reclaim a set of stolen crystals that determine the state of the world's four elemental powers.
lead
The gameplay takes a departure from the main series in a variety of ways, eliminating many series staples such as random battles, save points, manual equipment, and the party system.
Exploration
The game features a unique way of traveling the world map.
Battle system

The game's battle system relies on conditional turn-based combat, where the characters and enemies cycle through rounds in battling each other, with the first action of the turn awarded to the fastest character.
Battle system
Character health is represented by an incremental life bar, although the player may choose to have it displayed in numerical fractions as in most role-playing games.
Customization
The weapon arsenal in Final Fantasy Mystic Quest is considerably smaller than most role-playing games.
Customization
The spell catalog in Mystic Quest is limited compared to most other Final Fantasy games.
Customization
Notably, the Heal spell and potion act as a cure-all for status ailments, eliminating the need for unique status recovery items.
Customization
Similarly, the Cure spell and potion each restore 25% of player's maximum hit points regardless of level, so there is no need for a range of potion or spell strengths.
Story
While exploring, his village is destroyed in an earthquake.
Story
After proceeding through the first stage of the Focus Tower, and arriving in the province of Aquaria, Benjamin locates Phoebe, and learns that Spencer is trapped underground by thick ice floes.
Story
Finding the Old Man in the back of the Life Temple, they find that he holds the only bag of wakewater, and to use it on the plant in the center of town.
Story
Back in Aquaria, they find that the wakewater does not work, and reviving the crystal is the only thing that will save the town and Spencer.
Story
The only way the road works is when there is no wind, so Benjamin and Kaeli proceed to Mount Gale and stop the wind by defeating a powerful monster at the top.
Development

Square had already released several Final Fantasy spin-offs in North America, including the first three titles in the SaGa series as Final Fantasy Legend, and the first Mana series game as Final Fantasy Adventure, and wished to further break into the popular American consciousness.
Development
Mystic Quest was developed in a graphic and gameplay style similar to Final Fantasy Legend III (part of the aforementioned SaGa series).
Development

Even the jump feature from Final Fantasy Legend III has been reproduced, and almost all of the icons - from caves to the enemy sprites - are a color-upgraded version of Final Fantasy Legend III ' s character set.
Development
With the more traditional RPGs, it takes a good 15 or 20 hours of playing before you're finally hooked".
Development
Because the game was marketed towards a younger demographic, the game sold for US$ 39.99.
Release
The European release had its title changed to Mystic Quest Legend to avoid confusion with Final Fantasy Adventure, which had been released in Europe as Mystic Quest.
Release

Final Fantasy Mystic Quest was first unveiled in June at the 1992 Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago, where it was a popular venue, and the game was later presented in more detail in the Fall 1992 issue of the Ogopogo Examiner.
Audio

It was one of the first games bearing the Final Fantasy name not to be composed by series regular Nobuo Uematsu, after Final Fantasy Adventure (known in Japan as Seiken Densetsu: Final Fantasy Gaiden) and the Final Fantasy Legend trilogy (known in Japan as the Sa·Ga trilogy).
Audio
The album was first released on one compact disc by NTT Publishing on September 10, 1993.
Audio
The track "Last Castle" was written in a short time, and was used to create imagery of a field, but its length left very little space for the "Battle 3" song.
Reception
According to Square's publicity department, Final Fantasy Mystic Quest sold a total of 800,000 units, with roughly half of these sold in Japan.
Reception
On its original North American release, it scored 16/20 in GamePro, 14.9/20 in the November 1992 issue of Nintendo Power, 29/40 in Electronic Gaming Monthly, and 86% in Electronic Games.
Reception
IGN rated the Wii Virtual Console release a 6.0, or "Okay", citing an extremely repetitive and simple battle system, and very little character development.
Reception
1UP.com rated the game a "Not Worth It!", calling it "handholding" and "insubstantial".
Reception
On April 1, 2006, GameSpot included Mystic Quest in an April's Fools list entitled "Top 10 Final Fantasy Games", which mostly consisted of spin-offs from the main series and unrelated games.
Reception
In October 2010, the game was released on Nintendo's Virtual Console.
Reception
Famitsu has also reported that Square was preparing the game for release on the Android mobile platform in 2012.
Reception
In 2018, Complex ranked the game 66th on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".

sfes_lufio_ii_rise_of_the_sinistr.real: Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals
sfes_lufio_ii_rise_of_the_sinistr.title: Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals

Designer(s): Ryu Kurugami Tomonari Matsumoto Samichi Sugiura

sents: lead
It is the second game in the Lufia series.
lead
The game is a prequel to Lufia & the Fortress of Doom.
lead
It follows the story of the first main character's ancestor, Maxim, and explains the origins of the war between mankind and a group of gods called the Sinistrals.
lead
Lufia II made a number of changes from the first game.
lead
Dungeons no longer have random encounters and there are hundreds of puzzles throughout the game, ranging from simple to extremely challenging.
lead
It also introduced new skills, such as a variety of weapons that could be used to stun monsters or solve puzzles, and IP attacks.
lead
In 2010, Square Enix released a re-imagining of the original game titled Lufia: Curse of the Sinistrals.
Gameplay
The main player character, Maxim, gains a number of tools and weapons which can only be used in dungeons (similar to The Legend of Zelda titles), such as a bow and arrow, bombs and a hookshot.
Gameplay
Capsule monsters are special creatures which the player may only find on specific locations of the world.
Gameplay
The Ancient Cave, a randomly generated dungeon composed of 99 floors, is presented to the player as a side-quest in the town of Gruberik.
Gameplay
Red chests contain items which can only be used inside the cave for the duration of the playing session.
Gameplay
As soon as the player leaves the cave, all items from red chests disappear, except for "Iris Treasures", which cannot be equipped and serve only as collectibles.
Gameplay
The rare blue chests contains items which can be used outside the cave and brought back to the cave on subsequent journeys.
Plot
The game is a prequel, set 99 years before Lufia & the Fortress of Doom, which tells the story of how the Sinistrals first appeared in the world and the battles fought against them.
Release
The Australian version was released in 1997, one year after the North American version.
Reception
The game held an aggregate review score of 80% on GameRankings based on five reviews.
Reception
Upon release in Japan, Famitsu gave the game a score of 30 out of 40, while it received a perfect score of 10 out of 10 in their Reader Cross Review.
Reception
In Japanese polls of all-time favorite Super Famicom games, Lufia II was consistently voted one of the top five between 1995 and 1996.
Reception
Upon release in North America, three GameFan reviewers each scored it 90 out of 100; all three praised the storyline, puzzles, dungeons, graphics, and soundtrack.
Reception

Retrospectively, Corbie Dillard of Nintendo Life praised the "unique visual stylings, the efficient turn-based combat system and the beautifully orchestrated soundtrack", and called it one of the best RPG games for Super Nintendo console.
Reception
IGN ranked Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals 34th on their "Top 100 SNES Games of All Time".
Nintendo DS remake
An action-RPG remake of Lufia II for the Nintendo DS was developed by Neverland, with much of the staff of Lufia II involved in the project, and released in 2010.

sfes_lufio_the_fortress_of_doom.title: Lufia & the Fortress of Doom

Composer(s): Yasunori Shiono Aki Zaitsu Naomi Kuroda

sents: lead

Lufia & the Fortress of Doom, known as Estpolis Denki (エストポリス伝記, Esutoporisu Denki, officially translated Biography of Estpolis) in Japan, is a role-playing video game developed by Neverland and published by Taito in 1993, for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is the first title in the Lufia series of video games and the only game from the series released under the Taito label in North America.
lead

The game's plot follows The Hero, Lufia, Aguro, and Jerin on a quest to prevent the resurrection of four superpowered beings called Sinistrals, and frequently delves into the political and personal lives of the subjects of kingdoms all around the world.
lead
Top-down exploration is mixed with traditional turn-based combat using 2D sprites.
lead
The game was generally well-received, and has spawned multiple sequels on the Super Nintendo as well as the Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance and the Nintendo DS.
Gameplay
Lufia & the Fortress of Doom plays much like a traditional role-playing video game and features 2D character sprites and environments.
Gameplay
The battles themselves take place from a first-person perspective, and require the player to use each character's strengths, such as physical attacks or magic use, as in many other mainstream RPGs.
Gameplay

An interesting quirk in the battle system, reminiscent of older RPGs like the early Dragon Quest games, makes it such that when ordering two characters to attack a particular enemy, and the first character defeats the enemy, the second character's attack will still target the defeated enemy and thus miss.
Gameplay
The player's progress is saved in one of three available slots on the cartridge's built-in battery back-up system by speaking to a priest at a church found in most towns.
Starting characters
Guy: Guy is a longtime friend of Maxim who has no knowledge of magic himself but is physically the most powerful character.
Non-playable characters
From their floating Fortress of Doom, they gathered their strength, only to be defeated by Maxim and his friends years ago.
Non-playable characters
Daos is the Master of Chaos (Infernos in the Dutch version), while Amon is the Master of Terror; this is the only game in the series where this localization error occurs.
Development

Taito began to develop a port of Lufia & the Fortress of Doom for the Sega Mega Drive/Genesis, but the game, primarily intended for a North American release, was not released because of Taito America's closure in 1995.
Development
At least two full-page advertisements were made in U.S. magazines, the second one announcing a delay to spring 1995, with the tagline "It's worth the wait".
Development
A ROM image of the Mega Drive version was leaked online in 2014 by a former programmer of the port.
Reception
In the United States, it was the top-selling Super NES game in February 1994.
Reception
Upon release, Electronic Games scored it 93%, calling it "the best RPG so far this year".
Reception
In Dragon, Sandy Petersen gave the game 3 out of 5 stars.
Reception
GamePro gave it ratings of 4.5/5 for graphics, 4/5 for sound, 4/5 for control and 4.5/5 for overall fun factor.
Reception
Lufia was runner-up for GamePro ' s 1993 Role-Playing Game of the Year award, which was won by Secret of Mana.
Reception

Some reflect on it fondly for its story and characters, while others criticize it as being inferior to other console RPGs of that era, such as Secret of Mana, the Final Fantasy titles, or its prequel Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals.

sfes_illusion_of_gaya.title: Illusion of Gaia
sents: lead
Illusion of Gaia, known in PAL territories as Illusion of Time, is an action role-playing video game developed by Quintet for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
The game was released in Japan by Enix in 1993, and in North America and PAL territories by Nintendo in 1994 and 1995.
lead
Set in a fantasy reimagining of Earth, the game's plot centers on a boy named Will who is chosen to save the world from an impending disaster.
lead

During the course of the game, the player guides Will through levels based on ancient ruins of real-world civilizations and Wonders of the World, such as the Great Pyramid and the Great Wall of China.
Gameplay
While Illusion of Gaia has a large cast of characters, Will, Freedan and Shadow are the only playable characters in the game.
Gameplay
Each has unique abilities, and certain areas are impassable without a specific character.
Gameplay
Enemies reappear only when Will loses all his lives or leaves an area and returns.
Gameplay
When an enemy is killed, it may leave behind a gold sphere worth some number of life points.
Gameplay
If Will dies with 100 or more points, the player resumes play at the start of the current stage instead of losing outright.
Gameplay
There is only one healing item (herbs), and they are rare.
Gameplay
Unlike most games of its type, areas visited previously cannot be revisited, except in the last third of the game.
Gameplay
The only side quest, finding all the Red Jewels, cannot be completed if the player fails to find some before advancing the story.
Setting
The story is set in the age of exploration, a period roughly corresponding to the 16th century.
Setting
Many return with nothing, and some are never seen again.
Story
Later the comet is revealed to be an ancient weapon from the last Blazer War, and has the power to change the shape of the world.
Story
Saddened by that fact, Will and Kara join one last time to form Shadow to return to Earth.
Story
Will's friends are depicted in what appears to be a modern-day school, implying that even if they forgot about their time together, they remained friends in the "real" world.
Development and release
The game is often considered an unofficial trilogy along with two other Quintet games, Soul Blazer (1992) and Terranigma (1995).
Development and release
It was released for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, in Japan on November 27, 1993, and in North America on September 26, 1994.
Development and release
For example, the prototype version contained a different title screen, based on the original Japanese-version title screen.
Development and release
In the leaked prototype, the title was presented as SoulBlazer: Illusion of GAIA.
Development and release
Some of the script of the English-language prototype was different from the final version.
Development and release
When Nintendo decided to be the United States publisher, the title was changed and a logo was specifically redesigned to resemble the logo of Nintendo's popular The Legend of Zelda game franchise.
Version differences

Most notably, the native tribe encountered near Angkor Wat were originally cannibals, with the skeletal remains lying around the village being the remnants of their own tribesmen, whom they had eaten to survive.
Version differences
A translation error in a sequence near the middle of the game suggests that Seth's consciousness has been absorbed into that of a sea monster named "Riverson".
Version differences
Of these, only the French version made significant changes, adding references to existing people or myths, such as Edgar Degas, Franz Kafka, Chrysaor and Nosferatu.
Reception
Quintet reported that Illusion of Gaia sold 650,000 cartridges sold worldwide, including 200,000 copies in Japan, 300,000 copies in North America, and 150,000 copies in Europe.
Reception
In comparison, Soul Blazer had sold 295,000 cartridges worldwide.
Reception
On the other hand, Illusion of Gaia enjoys a sense of worldliness that Soulblazer didn't have.... you never know quite what's coming next, and that's the best thing that could be said about an RPG".
Accolades
Illusion of Gaia was rated the 186th best game made on a Nintendo system in Nintendo Power ' s Top 200 Games list in 2006.
Accolades
In 2018, Complex ranked Illusion of Gaia 86th on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Accolades
In 1995, Total! rated the game 41st in their Top 100 SNES Games, complimenting the graphics and gameplay.
Accolades
IGN ranked Illusion of Gaia 74th on their "Top 100 SNES Games of All Time".

sfes_terranigmo.title: Terranigma

Producer(s): Masaya Hashimoto Shinji Futami Jun Toda

sents: lead
Terranigma is a 1995 action role-playing game developed by Quintet for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), with manga artist Kamui Fujiwara acting as the character designer.
lead
The game tells the story of the Earth 's resurrection by the hands of a boy named Ark, and its progress from the evolution of life to the present day.
lead
The game is considered the third and final entry in an unofficial trilogy of action RPGs created by Quintet, also including Soul Blazer (1992) and Illusion of Gaia (1993).
lead
The game has been met with critical acclaim for its presentation, gameplay, and story, although it has been criticized for its difficulty.
Gameplay
Each attack is meant for dealing more damage to certain kinds of enemies, though in most cases there is little to no difference regardless of the technique used.
Plot
The first chapter of the game, "The Outset", introduces Ark, a mischievous boy who lives in Crysta, the only village in the underworld.
Plot
The only person not affected by the curse, the Elder, guides him to resurrect the continents of the surface world in order to unfreeze the people.
Plot
For the first time ever, a human being leaves Crysta to explore the underworld, which is portrayed as a frozen wasteland of imposing crystal mountains and rivers of magma.
Plot

Beruga provides Ark with an insight into his personal image of paradise: a perfect world where all insignificant life is killed with a virus named Asmodeus and everyone else is made immortal by turning them into zombies.
Plot
Ark's last dream pictures him as a bird flying above the world that he helped to exist, watching it grow older.
Release
Terranigma was first previewed in mid-1995 and slated for an October launch window.
Release
It was first released in Japan on October 20, 1995, by Enix for the Super Famicom under the name Tenchi Sōzō.
Release
The title was then released in Europe on December 19, 1996, by Nintendo.
Release
It was also released in Spain in April 1997 and in France on the summer of 1997.
Release
The game wound up never being published in North America because Enix had already closed its US subsidiary by the time the localization was finished.
Release

Except for the guide book, none of these materials have been released outside Japan, though Club Nintendo published a 32-page comic illustrating scenes from the game up to the events of the third chapter in Germany.
Release
A Japanese soundtrack album titled Tenchi Sōzō Creative Soundtracks, with 33 compositions and six arranged tracks of the game's music, was released by Kitty Enterprises on October 25, 1995.
Release
A petition by the game's Japanese fanbase, backed by artist Kamui Fujiwara and co-composer Miyoko Takaoka, began in July 2021 to either re-release or remaster Terranigma.
Reception
GameFan ' s Kei Kuboki described it as Quintet 's "best (...) effort" and being "among the most memorable titles".
Reception
The game holds a 74.14% rating based on seven reviews at review aggregator GameRankings, and was given the "Silver Hall of Fame" award from Famitsu.
Reception
It received a 23.3 out of 30 score in a public poll taken by Family Computer Magazine.
Reception
Famitsu ' s four reviewers gave Terranigma a score of 30 out of 40.
Reception
Likewise, The Super Famicom ' s three reviewers gave it a 78 out of 100 scores.
Reception
Superjuegos ' s Marcos García also regarded Terranigma as one of the best and most ambitious action role-playing games for SNES, stating that it surpasses Illusion of Time and Secret of Evermore.
Reception
Lorente also gave high remarks to the Mode 7 maps, audio, controls and absorbing plot.
Reception
In November 1997, in its 60th monthly issue, Nintendo Acción listed it as the 11th best game they had ever reviewed.
Reception
Player One ' s Christophe Pottier also stated that the game was excellent and "technically perfect" presentation-wise.
Retrospective coverage
1Up.com ' s Jeremy Parish described it as Quintet's best-known Super Nintendo action-RPG, noting the quality of the gameplay, music and deep story themes.
Retrospective coverage
Jeuxvideo.com ' s Zashy regarded its graphical effects as among the most beautiful on SNES while giving positive remarks to the playability, longevity, soundtrack and storyline.
Retrospective coverage

Zashy noted that its difficulty can put some players off but nevertheless claimed that " Terranigma will undoubtedly remain the title that marked the end of the reign of SNES in the most poetic way possible".

sfes_breath_of_fyre.title: Breath of Fire (video game)

Designer(s): Yoshinori Takenaka Yoshinori Kawano Makoto Ikehara
Composer(s): Yasuaki Fujita Mari Yamaguchi Minae Fuji Yoko Shimomura Tatsuya Nishimura

sents: lead
Breath of Fire is a role-playing video game developed by Capcom originally for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
Initially released in Japan in April 1993, the game was later made available in North America in August 1994 by Square Soft, who handled the title's English localization and promotion.
lead
It is the first entry in the Breath of Fire series.
lead

Recognized by Capcom as their first traditional role-playing video game, Breath of Fire would set the precedent for future entries in the series, and features character designs artist Keiji Inafune, as well as music by members of Capcom's in-house sound team Alph Lyla.
lead

In 2001, the game was re-released for the Game Boy Advance handheld system with new save features and minor graphical enhancements, with the English version being released in Europe for the first time.
lead
In 2016, it was released for the New Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console.
lead
In 2019, it was released for the Nintendo Switch SNES games library.
lead

Set in a fantasy world, Breath of Fire follows the journey of a boy named Ryu, one of the last surviving members of an ancient race with the ability to transform into mighty dragons, as he searches the world for his sister.
Characters

Each character hails from a different clan made up of anthropomorphic animal-like beings or humans with fantastic powers, with their assortment of magic spells and personal field abilities that can be used out of battle to help the player progress through the game and find hidden items.
Characters
The main character is a young man named Ryu, one of the last surviving members of the Light Dragon Clan, who have been driven to near-extinction by their enemy, the Dark Dragon Clan.
Story
The Dragon Clan—a race of humans who are able to transform into dragons—differ from the others in that their members appear (for the most part) to be human.
Story
Each key has a unique magical property which affects the surrounding landscape; the Light Key is hidden in the port town of Auria, providing boundless prosperity for its residents.
Story
Ryu's first destination is the town of Nanai, under which the Earth Key is sealed.
Development

The game's English release in August 1994 was a joint effort between Capcom USA and Square Soft, who handled most of the title's localization and promotion in North America due to Capcom USA's lack of experience with text-heavy role-playing games.
Development
Breath of Fire' s English localization was handled primarily by Ted Woolsey, whose previous works included Final Fantasy Legend III, Final Fantasy Mystic Quest, and Secret of Mana.
Development
In March 2001, Capcom Japan announced that Breath of Fire would be ported to Nintendo's Game Boy Advance handheld system with new features and a more "intuitive" gameplay system.
Development

Two months before the 2001 Electronic Entertainment Expo in Los Angeles, Capcom USA announced that they would be publishing an English version of the game initially for release the following September.
Audio

The music for Breath of Fire was composed by four members of Capcom's sound team Alph Lyla: Yasuaki Fujita, Mari Yamaguchi, Minae Fuji, and Yoko Shimomura, originally credited under the pseudonyms "Bun Bun", "Mari", "Ojarin", and "Pii♪", respectively.
Audio

Although no official soundtrack for the game was made available during its original release, the background themes from the title would later be included on the Breath of Fire Original Soundtrack Special Box released in March 2006, which featured music from the first five games of the series.
Contemporary

While the title was initially only "modestly successful" in North America, Nintendo Power noted a spike in sales following the release of the game's sequel in December 1995, calling it "a rare second wind".
Contemporary
The game was mostly well received by critics during its release in North America in 1994.
Contemporary
Game Informer awarded it a score of 9 out of 10.
Contemporary

Electronic Gaming Monthly praised the title's "excellent graphics and sound", ultimately stating that "Even if you're not a fan of these kinds of more deliberately- paced games, you'll still get hooked on this one!" Its five reviewers gave it ratings of 8, 8, 7, 8 and 9 out of 10.
Contemporary
GameFan ' s three reviewers gave it scores of 94, 90 and 90 out of 100, concluding that it has "beautiful art work, a great story, very good fight scenes, and some of the most amazing music".
Retrospective
Retrospectively, the Super NES version maintains a 78% average score on aggregate review website GameRankings.
Retrospective
The game's re-release on the Game Boy Advance maintains a 76% review average on Game Rankings and a 79% on Metacritic.
Retrospective

It debuted on the Japanese software charts as the third highest-selling game of its first week, selling 22,236 copies, and would go on to sell a total of 63,407 copies in the region by the end of 2001.
Accolades
In 1997, Breath of Fire was ranked 82nd in Nintendo Power' s list of the top 100 games released on Nintendo consoles, and in 2006, it placed 161st in the magazine's top 200.
Accolades
In 2002, Breath of Fire became runner-up for "Best Game Boy Advance Role-Playing Game" in IGN's Best of 2001 awards.
Accolades
In 2018, Complex rated Breath of Fire 27th on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Accolades
IGN ranked the game 43rd in its Top 100 SNES Games.
Legacy
Breath of Fire influenced two officially licensed manga which were first serialized in Japanese magazines.
Legacy

The first, Breath of Fire: Ryū no Senshi by Hiroshi Yakumo, is a re-telling of the events of the video game which was first published in Family Computer Magazine before being released as a two-volume collection by Tokuma Shoten.
Legacy

Breath of Fire: Princess of the Wings) by Kouji Hayato, takes place after the events of the game and focuses on the relationship between Ryu and Nina, and first appeared in Monthly Shōnen Jump before also being released in a two-volume compilation by Shueisha Jump Comics.
Legacy
Hayato followed up the manga with a side-story called Breath of Fire Part II: Chiisana Boukensha (ブレスオブファイア PART2 ~小さな冒険者~, lit.
Legacy
Breath of Fire Part 2: Little Adventurers), which featured the adventures of Ryu and Bo's sons, which was later released as its own single volume.

sfes_breath_of_fyre_ii.title: Breath of Fire II
sents: lead
Breath of Fire II is a role-playing video game developed and published by Capcom.
lead
First released in 1994, the game was licensed to Laguna for European release in 1996.
lead
It is the second entry in the Breath of Fire series.
lead
It was later ported to Game Boy Advance and re-released worldwide.
lead
The game was released on Wii 's Virtual Console in North America on August 27, 2007.
lead
Nintendo of Europe's website mistakenly announced it for release on July 27, 2007, but it was in fact released two weeks later, on August 10, 2007.
lead
In 2013, it was released for the Wii U Virtual Console.
lead
In 2016, it was released for the New Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console.
Gameplay
Like the previous game, only four characters may be in a party at a given time, but now may not be freely switched outside of certain areas.
Gameplay
Each character has a unique Personal Action that may be performed outside of combat that allows the player to access certain areas, destroy objects, avoid traps, or move about the game more easily.
Story
Breath of Fire II is set in a fantasy world 500 years after the events of the original game.
Story
The story opens on Ryu, age 6, living in the village of Gate with his sister Yua and father Ganer, a priest for the Church of St.
Story
To gather information, Ryu travels to Coursair, a town with a large coliseum, and becomes a challenger in the arena against Katt, the coliseum's most popular fighter.
Story

To communicate with the people of Tunlan, the party first retrieves the Famous Flute from Sten's hometown of HighFort, where Sten is forced to confront his past as a former soldier and help rescue the kingdom from Shupkay, another demon in disguise.
Story
After saving Tunlan's princess from demonic possession, the party uses the Therapy Pillow to visit Gandaroof's mind, which is being destroyed by the demon Aruhameru.
Story
Aruhameru claims that Gandaroof possesses knowledge that threatens his "God", and reveals that he destroyed the people of Gate's memory of Ryu.
Story
Tiga attempts to rescue her, only for both him and Claris to be killed.
Story
The party travels deep underground to the demon stronghold, where they meet the last remaining members of the Dragon Clan.
Development

While the character designs for the original Breath of Fire were conceived by company head of development Keiji Inafune, the cast of Breath of Fire II was created entirely by artist Tatsuya Yoshikawa, who had previously only provided promotional art for the game's predecessor.
Development
The game was released in North America one year after the Japanese version in December 1995, and would later become the first Breath of Fire title to become available in Europe in April 1996.
Development

Three days before the release of the original Breath of Fire on Nintendo's Game Boy Advance in July 2001, Capcom announced that they would similarly port Breath of Fire II to the handheld, with an initial release date some time in 2002.
Development

To celebrate the game's release in December 2001, Capcom of Japan held an art contest for fans to submit artwork featuring characters from the first two Breath of Fire games, with the winner chosen by the Game Boy Advance version's staff.
Development
In January 2002, Capcom USA announced that an English version of Breath of Fire II would be heading to North America the following April.
Development
A European version would also be released in July 2002, published by Ubisoft.
Audio
In January 1995, the Breath of Fire II: Shimei no Ko Original Soundtrack was released in Japan by Sony Records, and featured 28 selected themes from the game on a single disc.
Audio

A complete musical selection from the title would not be made commercially available until 2006, with the release of the Breath of Fire Original Soundtrack Special Box, which contained all music from the first five games of the series.
Audio
In order to promote the game, Capcom hired J-pop singer Mio Watanabe to record a theme song that played during the game's television commercial in Japan called "Owaranai Ai" (終わらない愛, lit.
Audio
Unending Love), which was released as a single in December 1994 by Alfa Records.
Reception
Breath of Fire II was released the same week as Sony's PlayStation console in Japan, and debuted on Japanese software charts as the seventh highest-selling game of its first week with 89,700 copies.
Reception
It was given an 8 out of 10 in two separate Reader Cross Reviews printed by Famicom Tsūshin, and it would go on to sell a total of 350,000 copies in the region by the end of 1995.
Reception
The game became popular enough to be re-released in the region for the Nintendo Power flash RAM peripheral in September 1997 at a reduced price.
Reception
The four reviewers of Electronic Gaming Monthly generally found the game worth getting for its high quality sound and lengthy quest.
Reception
While remarking that there are very few cinematic scenes compared to the first Breath of Fire, he was pleased with the complexity of both the main story and most of the side quests.
Reception

Similar to the original Super Nintendo Entertainment System release, the Game Boy Advance version met with mostly positive reception from critics, with the Japanese version receiving a 29 out of 40 score from Weekly Famitsu magazine.
Reception

GameSpot compared the game to the previous version, calling it a "faithful translation of the SNES game" and praised the title's new save feature allowing players to record their progress at any time, but found that its music "leans toward the bland side of things" and "lack personality".
Reception

GamePro awarded the Game Boy version a perfect score as well as an Editor's Choice Award, stating that the only flaw was the game's low difficulty, declaring that "In the realm of today’s high-powered next-gen role-players, BOFII is an excellent time-killer".
Reception
The game would later be nominated for "Best Port of a 16-bit Classic" and "Best Role-Playing Game on Game Boy Advance" in GameSpot's Best and Worst of 2002 Awards.
Reception
The Game Boy Advance version holds a 75% review average on GameRankings, as well as an 81% average on Metacritic.
Reception
Breath of Fire II ' s Virtual Console release in 2007 met with mixed response.
Reception
In 2006, Nintendo Power ranked the game 171st in its list of the top 200 games released across all Nintendo consoles, ten places behind the original Breath of Fire.
Reception

In 2018, Complex listed the game 75th on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time" writing: "Breath of Fire II isn’t too different from the original, but different enough to not be a direct clone.
Reception
But it’s not as good as the first one." IGN rated the game 53rd in its Top 100 SNES Games.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.

sfes_world.title: Super Mario World

Platform(s): Super Famicom / Super NES, Game Boy Advance

sents: lead
Super Mario World, known in Japan as Super Mario World: Super Mario Bros.
lead
4, is a 1990 platform game developed by Nintendo EAD and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
The player controls Mario on his quest to save Princess Peach and Dinosaur Land from the series' antagonist Bowser and the Koopalings.
lead
The gameplay is similar to that of earlier Super Mario games; players control Mario through a series of levels in which the goal is to reach the goalpost at the end.
lead
Super Mario World introduces Yoshi, a ridable dinosaur who can eat enemies.
lead
Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development developed the game, led by director Takashi Tezuka and producer and series creator Shigeru Miyamoto.
lead
It is the first Mario game for the SNES and was designed to make the most of the console's technical features.
lead
The development team had more freedom compared to the series installments for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES).
Gameplay
Super Mario World is a 2D side-scrolling platform game in which the player controls Mario or Luigi, the protagonists of the game.
Gameplay
The majority of the game takes place in 2D linear levels, populated with obstacles and enemies, which involves the player traversing the stage by dashing, jumping, and dodging or defeating enemies.
Gameplay

The game ends when the player runs out of lives, although the player can continue from the most recent save point (a successfully completed castle, fortress or haunted house) by selecting " Continue ".
Gameplay

Super Mario World includes a multiplayer option which allows two players to play the game by alternating turns at navigating the overworld map and accessing stage levels; the first player controls Mario, while the second player controls his brother, Luigi.
Gameplay
The game introduces Yoshi, a dinosaur companion Mario can ride who is able to eat most enemies.
Gameplay

The default Yoshi is green, but the game also has hidden blue, yellow, and red Yoshis; the player can obtain each colored Yoshi by finding its egg in the Star World areas and feeding it either five enemies, a Super Mushroom, a Fire Flower, a Cape Feather, or a Starman causing the baby Yoshi to mature.
Gameplay
Although the main objective is to navigate through seven worlds to reach the end of the game, the player can beat the game much faster by using secret Star Road routes.
Gameplay
To access a hidden world, the player needs to find keys scattered throughout the game's levels.
Gameplay
Exploring these secret stages can lead to other stages, such as the Special World.
Plot
3, the brothers Mario and Luigi decide to go on vacation with Princess Toadstool to a place called Dinosaur Land, a prehistoric-themed world swarming with dinosaurs and other enemies.
Development
The game was directed by Takashi Tezuka, while Shigeru Miyamoto, the creator of both Super Mario and The Legend of Zelda, served as producer.
Development

Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development handled development with a team of ten people, including three main programmers and a character designer, most of whom had worked on past Super Mario titles.
Development
In a retrospective interview, the core team said Miyamoto wielded the most authority during development.
Development
Super Mario World was the first Mario series game developed for the then-upcoming Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
Development
The inspiration for Yoshi can be traced back even further; Miyamoto designed a green dragon for the 1984 game Devil World which shared many similarities with Yoshi.
Development
3, Miyamoto had a number of sketches around his desk, including an image of Mario riding a horse.
Development
Hino originally produced a design that Tezuka deemed too reptilian, and "didn't really fit into the Mario world", so he encouraged the designer to create a "cuter" character.
Development
3, composer Koji Kondo decided to reuse the same themes for Super Mario World, albeit in a rearranged form.
Development
As Super Mario World was the first game developed for the SNES, Kondo felt "overjoyed" at being able to compose music by using eight sounds at once.
Release
Super Mario World was first released in Japan on 21 November 1990 under the name of Super Mario World: Super Mario Bros.
Release
The game was released in North America on 23 August, 1991.
Re-releases
The game was re-released in a special version of Super Mario All-Stars, Super Mario All-Stars + Super Mario World, as a pack-in game for the SNES in December 1994.
Re-releases
All-Stars contains enhanced remakes of the first four Super Mario games released for the NES: Super Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros.
Re-releases
Super Mario World was ported to the Game Boy Advance as Super Mario World: Super Mario Advance 2 between 2001 and 2002.
Re-releases
2, Game Link Cable support for four players in the Mario Bros.
Re-releases
The SNES version was released on the Wii 's Virtual Console in Japan on 2 December 2006, in the United States on 5 February 2007, and in Europe on 9 February 2007.
Re-releases
It was released for the Wii U in North America and Japan on 26 April 2013, and in Europe on 27 April 2013, along with the full launch of the Wii U Virtual Console.
Re-releases
On March 3, 2016, the game was released for the Virtual Console service of the New Nintendo 3DS.
Re-releases
Super Mario World was also one of the 21 SNES games included in the Super NES Classic Edition released in September 2017.
Re-releases
On 5 September 2019, Nintendo released Super Mario World on their Nintendo Switch Online service as a launch title.
Reception
Nintendo has sold 20.61 million copies of the game worldwide, making it the best-selling game for the SNES.
Reception
In the United States, Super Mario Advance 2 for the Game Boy Advance sold 2.5 million copies and earned $74 million in revenue by August 2006.
Reception
During the period between January 2000 and August 2006, it became the second highest-selling portable game in the United States.
Reception
In December 2019, review aggregator GameRankings ranked Super Mario World as the 78th highest-rated game of all time, with an aggregate score of 94% based on nine reviews.
Reception
The visuals and presentation were two of the most praised aspects of the game.
Reception
Karn Bianco from Cubed3 enjoyed the game's relaxed visual style, and praised Nintendo for keeping everything "nice and simple" designing a game perfect for children.
Reception
Critics commended the game's replay value and unique gameplay in comparison to older Super Mario games.
Reception
Navarro similarly felt the game featured some of the best and most challenging levels the series has offered thus far, saying "nothing about the game feels out of place or superfluous".
Reception
In retrospect, Sleeper believed the game's biggest achievement was its level design, calling it an "unrivalled master class" with a constant sense of momentum.
Awards
The game received 1991 Game of the Year awards from Nintendo Power and Power Play.
Awards
In 2009, a poll conducted by Empire voted it "the greatest game of all time".
Awards
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine placed the game 7th in a list of the greatest Nintendo games of all time.
Awards

In its final issue in October 2014, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked Super Mario World the third-greatest Nintendo game of all time, behind The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Super Mario Galaxy.
Awards
In 2012, Nintendo Power similarly named Super Mario World the fifth greatest game of all time, a step up from its eighth best ranking in their 2006 poll.
Awards
In 2007, Retro Gamer ranked it as the best platform game of all time, while USgamer listed it as the best Super Mario platform game ever in 2015.
Awards
In 1996, GamesMaster ranked Super Mario World 3rd on their "The GamesMaster SNES Top 10" list.
Awards
In 1995, Total! listed the game 11th on its Top 100 SNES Games, at the time they opined Super Mario World is "a contender for the best game ever."
Legacy
As a pack-in game for the SNES, Super Mario World helped popularise the console, and became the best-selling game of its generation.
Legacy
Yoshi became one of the most important characters in the Mario franchise, re-appearing in later Super Mario games and in nearly all Mario sports and spin-off games.
Legacy
Yoshi appears as the main playable character in Super Mario World ' s 1995 prequel Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island, which helped lead to multiple video games focused on the character.
Legacy
A Super Mario World clone, Super Mario's Wacky Worlds, was in development for the Philips CD-i device by NovaLogic from 1992 to 1993, but was cancelled because of the console's commercial failure.
Legacy
In a poll conducted in 2008, Yoshi was voted as the third-favourite video game character in Japan, with Cloud Strife and Mario placing second and first.
Legacy
DIC Entertainment produced an animated series of the same name, consisting of thirteen episodes, which ran on NBC from September to December 1991.
Legacy

In a similar way, Super Mario World is one of the four games whose assets are available in Super Mario Maker, a custom level creator released for the Wii U in 2015, in its port to Nintendo 3DS in 2016, and its 2019 sequel.
