sfes_kirbo_s_dream_lund_3.title: Kirby's Dream Land 3
sents: lead
Kirby's Dream Land 3 is a 1997 action - platform game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
Starring Kirby, it is the fifth installment in the Kirby series and the third game under the Kirby's Dream Land name.
lead
Although the first game was largely unrelated, Dream Land 3 features many similar characters to Dream Land 2.
lead
Dream Land 3 was followed by Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards in 2000.
lead
Kirby's Dream Land 3 was the last SNES game published by Nintendo in North America.
lead

Problems with the game's PAL conversion prevented it from being released in Europe and Australia for many years; it was eventually released for the Virtual Console in those regions in the form of an import from North America on July 24, 2009, for the Wii and on July 25, 2013, for the Wii U.
lead

The game was re-released on the Virtual Console in North America on January 5, 2009, for the Wii and on May 8, 2013, for the Wii U and in Japan on April 28, 2009, for the Wii and on May 8, 2013, for the Wii U.
lead
It was also included as part of the 2012 Wii compilation Kirby's Dream Collection and the Nintendo Switch Online SNES game service.
Plot
After Dark Matter is defeated, Kirby and Gooey set off on the journey home, only to pause hesitantly at several points along the way.
Gameplay
Kirby's Dream Land 3 is a traditional platformer Kirby game; the player controls Kirby, whose objective is to get to the end of each stage.
Gameplay
Additionally, some parts of the game world require a certain ability to be accessed, such as blocks that can only be destroyed by the ability displayed on them.
Gameplay
Zero is the game's secret and true final boss; defeating him is key in achieving the best ending.
Gameplay

Zero is famous for being a rare example of graphic violence in a first-party Nintendo game – Zero fights Kirby by opening cuts on his sclera and shooting blood out of the cuts at him, as well as summoning small Dark Matters to use as projectiles.
Gameplay
Although he is eventually defeated, Zero reappears in Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards as '0 ' (pronounced zero two), still retaining his ability to spit blood and his motif as a giant eye.
Gameplay
As a reference to his previous fight with Kirby, 0 wears two large plasters on the top of his 'head', covering the wound left from his iris bursting out of his body.
Kirby's allies
At any time during play, Kirby can summon Gooey—a blue, long-tongued blob first seen in Dream Land 2.
Kirby's allies

When controlled by the computer or also a second human player, Gooey's abilities are similar to Kirby's: He can swallow enemies using his long tongue, then either spit them out or copy their abilities to a limited extent.
Kirby's allies
Rick the Hamster, who can only jump once but can stomp on enemies, run faster, doesn't slide on ice and can scale walls.
Kirby's allies
Kine the Ocean sunfish, who can only jump once but can stomp on enemies, swim more efficiently in water (even against strong currents), and can let Kirby inhale underwater.
Kirby's allies

Pitch the Bird, who has more versatile copy ability variants than the other Animal Friends, but cannot fly against strong winds like Coo can and is much more limited in flying due to his small size, only being able to fly like how Kirby can float.
Kirby's allies

ChuChu the Octopus, who can only float for a limited time before gradually descending, but is able to cling to and walk across ceilings and can grab items with her tentacles (identically to Gooey's tongue; in both cases, this function is only usable without ability as it replaces Kirby's inhale ability).
Development
Kirby's Dream Land 3 uses a mode of the SNES termed "pseudo high-resolution" (which allows for color blending between two adjacent pixels) to blend dithered sprites.
Reception
Kirby's Dream Land 3 received mixed to positive reception from both critics and fans.
Reception
GameRankings gave the SNES version an aggregated score of 66.25% based on four reviews.
Reception
IGN gave Dream Land 3 a fairly positive review of the Virtual Console re-release, "It's not Super Star.
Reception

But once you get past that, you can appreciate Dream Land 3 for what it is -- a direct, numbered follow-up to the series that started on the Game Boy." Nintendo Life initially gave the game a 6 out of 10, criticizing the lack of difficulty but praising the stylized graphics.

Kirby Super Star, released as Kirby's Fun Pak in PAL regions, is a 1996 anthology action - platform game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is part of the Kirby series of video games by HAL Laboratory.
lead
The game was advertised as a compilation featuring eight games: seven short subsections with the same basic gameplay, and two minigames.
lead
The game was later released for the Wii and Wii U Virtual Consoles.
lead
Nintendo re-released Kirby Super Star in Japan, the United States and Europe in September 2017 as part of the company's Super NES Classic Edition.
lead
The game was released on the Nintendo Switch Online service on December 12, 2019.
lead
An enhanced remake titled Kirby Super Star Ultra was released for the Nintendo DS in 2008 and 2009 to commercial and critical success, selling just under 3 million copies.
Gameplay
Like Kirby, Helpers can float continuously, but can only use the copy ability they were based on.
Game modes
While most retain the same game mechanics, they have different stories and objectives.
Game modes
Spring Breeze: an abridged remake of the first Kirby game, Kirby's Dream Land (1992), with the gameplay enhancements of Kirby Super Star.
Game modes
Kirby must make his way to a castle to challenge King Dedede, who has stolen food from the citizens of Dream Land.
Game modes
There are also two secret areas and a mini-boss that moves across the world map.
Game modes
It takes place across three levels of varying length; whoever earns the most points by the end of all levels wins, with bonus points awarded to the first to finish each race.
Game modes
Players can choose to race either King Dedede or a "ghost" (the player's best attempt at the race), or simply race alone for the fastest time.
Game modes
60 treasure chests are hidden across four areas.
Game modes
Some treasures reference other Nintendo franchises, such as the Triforce (The Legend of Zelda), Captain Falcon 's helmet (F-Zero), and Mr.
Game modes
Milky Way Wishes: the largest mode in the game.
Game modes
The Arena: a boss attack mode that challenges the player to fight every boss in the game with only one life and a free selection of power-up at the start of the game.
Development
Although a Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) title, the Kirby Super Star prototype was developed for the original Nintendo Entertainment System.
Development
According to Sakurai, although the prototype was for internal use only, it was almost complete and some of Kirby's animations were nearly identical in the final game.
Development
The prototype was used to test out ideas before implementing them in the final product; Sakurai said having the game operating on an internal build made it easier to develop ideas.
Development

By creating an "omnibus" collection of quick-to-beat individual scenarios, each complete with their own unique gameplay, I thought I could provide a lot of content without causing players to grow tired of any one style.
Development
The game was also the first in the series in which Kirby's appearance changed depending on his copy ability.
Development
The omnibus format was chosen because Sakurai noted most SNES and some NES games were of considerable length, and prices were high.
Development
Spring Breeze, a remake of Kirby's Dream Land, was designed for beginners and is thus Super Star ' s first mode.
Development
Originally, Sakurai was going to remove copy abilities to remain faithful to the original game while teaching beginners how to play, but ultimately did not.
Development
This was partially due to the influence of Rare 's Donkey Kong Country (1994), a game that incorporated computer-generated (CG) graphics.
Release
Kirby Super Star was one of the last SNES games, released just three months before the launch of the system's successor, the Nintendo 64.
Release
Publisher Nintendo released the game in Japan on March 21, 1996, in North America on September 20, 1996, and in Europe on January 23, 1997.
Release
The Wii version was released in Japan in October 2009 and in the West in May 2010, and the Wii U version was released worldwide in May 2013.
Release
The game was also included in Kirby's Dream Collection (2012), a 20th anniversary compilation of Kirby titles for the Wii.
Release
Nintendo released the game on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System app via its Nintendo Switch Online subscription service on December 12, 2019.
Release
A special version with the secret modes unlocked was later released on June 9, 2022.
Reception
Kirby Super Star was both a critical and commercial success, selling over one million copies in Japan.
Reception
Captain Cameron of GamePro gave it a perfect 5 out of 5 in sound, control, and FunFactor, and a 4.5 out of 5 in graphics.
Legacy
Kirby Super Star was given an enhanced remake in the form of Kirby Super Star Ultra to celebrate the series' 15th anniversary.
Legacy
The remake was released in North America on September 22, 2008, to critical and commercial success, selling just under three million copies worldwide.
Legacy

Many of the music tracks in Kirby Super Star have been remixed in various games, such as the Super Smash Bros. series; the Nintendo 64 game, for instance, had a new version of the Gourmet Race theme as Kirby's theme song.
Legacy
In reference to the scope of the mode of the same name, the arena is amongst the largest stages in the game's catalog, and thus supports up to eight players.
Legacy
It features a unique mechanic dubbed the "Danger Zones", stage hazards that instantly KO any fighter whose damage percentages exceed 100%.
Legacy
In 2021, Charlie Rosen and Jake Silverman arranged the composition "Meta Knight's Revenge" for The 8-Bit Big Band.

sfes_kirbo_s_dream_coarse.title: Kirby's Dream Course

Designer(s): Shinichi Shimomura Kensuke Tanabe Hideki Fujii

sents: lead
Kirby's Dream Course is a 1994 miniature golf video game developed by HAL Laboratory and Nintendo EAD and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
A spin-off of the Kirby series and the first released for the SNES, players control the pink spherical character Kirby through a series of courses by launching him towards the goal hole at the end.
lead
Kirby can hit enemies to collect power-ups that grant him unique abilities, such as those that allow him to destroy certain obstacles or fly around the level.
lead
HAL Laboratory originally designed Dream Course as a standalone game called Special Tee Shot.
lead

Though it was previewed in several magazines and displayed on the packaging for the console, HAL replaced the game's original characters with those from the Kirby series following its popularity on the Game Boy.
lead
Special Tee Shot was later released for the Satellaview peripheral in Japan.
lead
Dream Course received favorable reviews, both at release and retrospectively, for its unique design and absurdity.
lead
Some were critical of its high difficulty level and controls.
Gameplay
Kirby's Dream Course is a mini golf video game set at an isometric perspective, similar to games such as Marble Madness (1984).
Gameplay
When only one enemy remains, that enemy transforms into the goal hole (providing two stars).
Gameplay
In multiplayer, players compete for the most stars, and a player may connect with a star claimed by the other player for themself (turning pink to yellow and vice versa).
Development
HAL originally designed the game as a standalone title called Special Tee Shot in 1992, which featured its own original characters and art assets.
Development

Following the appearance of an unnamed yellow Kirby in Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards (2000), a yellow color palette became a recurring colorization for additional players playing as a Kirby in the Kirby and Super Smash Bros. series (often as the second player).
Development
Kirby's Dream Course was released in Japan on September 21, 1994, as Kirby Ball.
Development
It was released in North America on February 1, 1995, and in Europe later in the year.
Development
Special Tee Shot was later re-released in 1996 for the Satellaview, a peripheral for the Super Famicom that played games via satellite broadcasts.
Development
Dream Course was digitally re-released for the Wii Virtual Console in 2007, and the Wii U Virtual Console in Japan in 2013.
Development
In 1995, Nintendo and HAL began work on a sequel named Kirby Ball 64 / Kirby Bowl 64 for the then-upcoming Nintendo 64.
Development
Kirby Ball 64 / Kirby Bowl 64 was designed to take advantage of the system's analog stick to allow for more precise movement, in addition to utilizing gouraud shading for its graphics.
Development
The sequel was never released, though some of its concepts were later implemented into Kirby Air Ride (2003).
Reception
A writer for Next Generation found its mini golf-inspired gameplay unique compared to other games, as did a reviewer from Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Reception
Staff from Nintendo Life compared its silliness to Electronic Arts ' Zany Golf (1988), and that it possessed fun gameplay and a balanced level of difficulty.
Reception
Thomas believed Dream Course ' s unique concept made it incomparable to other games.

sfes_kongo.title: Donkey Kong Country
sents: lead
Donkey Kong Country is a 1994 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
It is a reboot of Nintendo's Donkey Kong franchise and follows the gorilla Donkey Kong and his nephew Diddy Kong as they set out to recover their stolen banana hoard from the crocodile King K.
lead
The single-player traverses 40 side-scrolling levels as they jump between platforms and avoid obstacles.
lead
They collect items, ride minecarts and animals, defeat enemies and bosses, and find secret bonus stages.
lead
In multiplayer modes, two players work cooperatively or race each other.
lead
After developing Nintendo Entertainment System games in the 1980s, Rare, a British studio founded by Tim and Chris Stamper, purchased Silicon Graphics workstations to render 3D models.
lead
Nintendo sought a game to compete with Sega 's Aladdin (1993) and commissioned Rare to revive the dormant Donkey Kong franchise.
lead
Rare assembled 12 developers to work on Donkey Kong Country over 18 months.
Gameplay
Some feature unique game mechanics, such as rideable minecarts, blasting out of cannons resembling barrels, and swinging ropes.
Background
In 1985, the British game developers Tim and Chris Stamper established Rare Ltd.
Background
The brothers previously founded the British computer game studio Ultimate Play the Game and founded Rare to focus on the burgeoning Japanese console market.
Background
Rare demonstrated it was possible to reverse-engineer the NES and showed several tech demos to Nintendo executive Minoru Arakawa; impressed, Arakawa granted Rare a Nintendo developer licence.
Background
Rare developed more than 60 NES games, including the Battletoads series and ports of games such as Marble Madness.
Background
When Nintendo released their next console, the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), in 1991, Rare decided to limit their output.
Background
Around 1992, Rare invested their NES profit in Silicon Graphics, Inc.
Background
The move made Rare the most technologically advanced UK developer and situated them high in the international market.
Conception
Though they had purchased the workstations to produce games for the Nintendo 64, which was in development at the time, Rare discovered it was possible to use them with the 16-bit SNES.
Conception
Rare tested the SGI technology with Battletoads Arcade (1994) and began developing a boxing game, Brute Force, using PowerAnimator.
Conception

Nintendo wanted a game to compete with Sega's Aladdin (1993), which featured graphics by Disney animators, when Nintendo of America chairman Howard Lincoln learned of Rare's SGI experiments during a trip to Europe.
Conception

After impressing Nintendo with a demonstration of Brute Force, Tim Stamper—inspired by Mortal Kombat ' s use of digitised footage in place of hand-drawn art—suggested developing a platform game that used pre-rendered graphics.
Conception
The franchise had been largely dormant since the unsuccessful Donkey Kong 3 (1983), so Nintendo figured that licensing it posed minimal risk.
Conception
Conversely, the lead designer Gregg Mayles recalled that it was Nintendo that requested a Donkey Kong game.
Conception
According to Mayles, Nintendo codenamed the project "Country" (based on Rare's location in Twycross), leading to the title Donkey Kong Country.
Conception
Rare assembled a team of 12, the largest in their history at that point, and development began.
Conception
Nintendo was sceptical of Rare's approach to graphics, concerned it would make the game unplayable.
Conception
One in attendance, the Game Boy creator Gunpei Yokoi, felt the game "looked too 3D", but Mayles said Donkey Kong ' s creator, Shigeru Miyamoto, was supportive and gave Rare his approval.
Conception
Donkey Kong Country was the first Donkey Kong game that was neither directed nor produced by Miyamoto, who was working on Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island (1995).
Conception
Miyamoto was still involved with the project and Rare said he provided crucial input.
Conception
Nintendo is usually highly protective of their intellectual properties, but was relatively uninvolved with Donkey Kong Country, leaving most of the work to Rare.
Conception
Rare spent 18 months developing Donkey Kong Country from an initial concept to a finished game, and according to product manager Dan Owsen, 20 people worked on it in total.
Conception
It cost an estimated US$ 1 million to produce, and Rare said that it had the most man hours ever invested in a video game at the time, 22 years.
Design

The stages were painstakingly arranged so that the player could "go first time" past obstacles (if there was a swinging rope then when it came on screen it was swinging towards you so you could jump onto it straight away)...
Design
Rare drew inspiration from the Super Mario series, Mayles citing Super Mario Bros.
Design
Rare featured barrels as a primary game mechanic to pay homage to the original arcade game, and included hidden collectibles like coins and balloons to add depth.
Design
Diddy Kong originated from Rare's search for a game mechanic akin to Super Mario ' s power-up system in that he would serve as the player's health.
Design

Donkey Kong Country did not have much scrapped content; Gunn said he only regretted that Donkey Kong walks across dotted lines instead of paths on the world map, which could not be implemented due to time constraints.
Design
One scrapped idea, a collectible that would evade the player by running or hiding, served as the basis for the Jinjos in Rare's subsequent game Banjo-Kazooie (1998).
Design

Reviewing Donkey Kong Country for release, Nintendo directed Rare to reduce the difficulty to appeal to a broad audience, reasoning that the secrets would provide sufficient challenge for hardcore gamers.
Design
At this point, Miyamoto made some last-minute suggestions, such as Donkey Kong's terrain slap, that were incorporated.
Design
Nintendo's Kensuke Tanabe flew to Twycross to localise the game with Rare.
Characters
Because Donkey Kong did not have much of an established universe, Rare was free to expand it with new characters.
Characters
Unlike the original Donkey Kong Jr., Rare did not want Diddy to share his build with Donkey Kong, so they based him on a spider monkey and made him agile to give him distinct moves.
Characters
Naming the character was a challenge, and Rare dropped their preferred "Dinky Kong" due to legal problems.
Characters
Rare staff spent hours at the nearby Twycross Zoo recording gorillas for reference, which they described as "a complete waste of time".
Characters
The antagonists, the Kremlings, were recycled from a cancelled Rare game.
Characters
Rare's initial story was extensive and spanned 15 pages, but Nintendo had it condensed to fit into an instruction manual.
Graphics
Donkey Kong Country was one of the first games for a mainstream home video game console to use pre-rendered 3D graphics, a technique used in the earlier 1993 Finnish game Stardust for the Amiga.
Graphics
Rare developed a compression technique that allowed the team to incorporate more detail and animation for each sprite for a given memory footprint, which better preserved the pre-rendered graphics.
Graphics
Nintendo and Rare called the technique Advanced Computer Modelling (ACM).
Graphics

Rare briefly feared competition from DMA Design 's Uniracers (1994), which also featured pre-rendered graphics, but the staff was relieved upon learning that the player character was Uniracer ' s only element that was pre-rendered.
Graphics
The game was Rare's first to require multiple programmers, and they worked with little guidance.
Graphics
To help, Nintendo provided Rare with research material regarding apes, barrels, and caves.
Graphics
The ACM process pushed the SNES hardware to its limits; Betteridge said Rare wanted to do everything they could with the hardware similar to what they had done with the NES game Battletoads (1991).
Music
Rare asked Wise to record three jungle demo tunes that were merged to become the "DK Island Swing", the first level's track.
Music
Wise cited Koji Kondo 's music for the Super Mario and Legend of Zelda games, Tim and Geoff Follin's music for Plok!
Music
(1993), synthesiser film soundtracks released in the early 1980s, and rock and dance music from the same decade as influences, and wanted to imitate the sound of the Korg Wavestation synthesiser.
Music
Wise wanted to compose in the style of 1940s jazz but was restricted by the SPC700's limitations; he "used a lot of small samples and made very synthesised" to work around them.
Music

Since Donkey Kong Country featured advanced pre-rendered graphics, Wise wanted to push the limits in terms of audio to create "equally impressive" music and make the most of the small space he was working with.
Music
Wise considers the track his favourite and the game's biggest technological accomplishment in regards to the audio.
Music
Wise said his primary focus was to make the most of the SPC700, and he input the music by hand to save memory.
Music
Eveline Novakovic contributed seven tracks, including the world map theme, as her first SNES project.
Music

According to Beanland, the track was intended for an internal progress video about another Rare game, Killer Instinct (1994), before Nintendo decided to use it in a Donkey Kong Country promotional trailer.
Marketing
Lincoln unveiled Donkey Kong Country at the Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago, which took place from 23 to 25 June 1994.
Marketing

According to the Los Angeles Times, Nintendo spent US$ 16 million on marketing Donkey Kong Country in America alone; at the time, major games typically had an average marketing budget of US$ 5 million.
Marketing

Marketing materials emphasised the revolutionary graphics—often noting that Rare's SGI workstations had been used to create the Jurassic Park (1993) film's dinosaurs —and positioned Donkey Kong Country as a direct competitor to Sega's Mega-CD and 32X platforms to remind players it was not for next-generation hardware.
Marketing

Nintendo World Report wrote that Exposed was "probably the first time most people outside of Nintendo learned about the " and the promotion allowed players to see the game for themself at home, rather than having to learn about it secondhand from a magazine.
Marketing
A soundtrack CD, DK Jamz, was released via news media and retailers in November 1994, with a standalone release in 1995.
Marketing
The competition version of Donkey Kong Country is the rarest licensed SNES game; only 2,500 cartridges are known to exist.
Context
Donkey Kong Country was expected to gross at least US$ 140 million in the US if it matched sales projections.
Context

The Nintendo 64 was not due for release until 1996, so Donkey Kong Country, wrote USGamer, served as Nintendo's "bluff" to make it seem that the SNES could hold its ground against next-generation hardware.
Sales
Donkey Kong Country set the record for the fastest-selling video game at the time: it sold over 500,000 copies within a week, and sales reached one million copies in the US alone in two weeks.
Sales

In its second week on sale in the US, the game grossed US$ 15 million, outpacing the week's highest-grossing film (The Santa Clause, US$ 11.5 million) and album (Miracles: The Holiday Album, US$ 5.2 million).
Sales
Donkey Kong Country sold six million copies worldwide in its first holiday season, grossing $400 million in worldwide sales revenue.
Sales
Based on available sales figures, it is the third-bestselling SNES game and the bestselling Donkey Kong game.
Reception
Diehard GameFan and Total! said it changed expectations for 16-bit and platform games, and Entertainment Weekly wrote it "is to most 16-bit games what most 16-bit games are to their Atari forebears.
Reception
EGM said that the graphical quality prompted questions about the purpose of 32- and 64-bit hardware.
Accolades

Donkey Kong Country was the only video game included in Time ' s Best Products of 1994 list, coming in second behind the Chrysler Neon, and it became the first game to win the Favourite Video Game Kids' Choice Award at the 1995 Kids' Choice Awards.
Post-release
In April 1995, following Donkey Kong Country ' s success, Nintendo purchased a 25 per cent minority stake in Rare, which increased to 49 per cent over time.
Post-release

Rare was the first non-Japanese studio to enter such a relationship with Nintendo, making them a second-party developer; Nintendo published Rare's subsequent games and allowed them to expand its staff from 84 to over 250 and move out of the farmhouse to an advanced development site elsewhere in Twycross.
Post-release
Rare was one of the first developers to receive Nintendo 64 software development kits and decided to start spending more time developing fewer games.
Post-release
Nintendo and Rare's partnership produced acclaimed Nintendo 64 games such as GoldenEye 007 (1997), Banjo-Kazooie (1998), Perfect Dark (2000), and Conker's Bad Fur Day (2001).
Post-release
Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest, released in 1995, features Diddy rescuing a kidnapped Donkey Kong from K.
Post-release

Other teams at Rare used Donkey Kong Country ' s technology in the fighting game Killer Instinct and Donkey Kong Land, Donkey Kong Land 2 (1996) and Donkey Kong Land III (1997), which attempted to replicate Donkey Kong Country ' s visuals and gameplay on the handheld Game Boy.
Post-release
Rare followed Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! with Donkey Kong 64 (1999), the first Donkey Kong game to feature 3D gameplay.
Post-release
In 2002, Rare was acquired by Nintendo's competitor Microsoft and the Donkey Kong rights reverted to Nintendo.
Rereleases
In 2000, Rare developed a port of Donkey Kong Country for Nintendo's Game Boy Color (GBC) handheld console.
Rereleases
The GBA version was released in Australia on 4 June 2003, Europe on 6 June, in North America on 9 June, and in Japan on 12 December.
Rereleases
The GBA version sold 1.82 million copies, including 960,000 in the US by August 2006.
Rereleases
Between January 2000 and August 2006, it was the 19th highest-selling game for a Nintendo handheld console in the US.
Rereleases
In September 2012, the game was delisted from the Virtual Console for unknown reasons, though Kotaku ' s Jason Schreier suggested it may have been related to licensing problems with Rare.
Rereleases
Donkey Kong Country returned to the Wii U 's Virtual Console in February 2015 and was added to the New Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console in March 2016.
Legacy
The game inspired an animated series that ran for 40 episodes from 1997 to 2000, and Diddy Kong starred in a Nintendo 64 racing game spin-off, Diddy Kong Racing (1997).
Legacy

Following Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!, the Country series went on a hiatus until Donkey Kong Country Returns, developed by Retro Studios, was released for the Wii on Donkey Kong Country ' s 16th anniversary in 2010.
Legacy
Wise, who left Rare in 2009, returned to compose Tropical Freeze ' s score.
Retrospective assessments
Eurogamer wrote that it became popular to dislike it in the early 2000s, and it was often described as one of the most overrated video games.
Retrospective assessments
Hardcore Gaming 101 said it was the one element that had unquestionably aged well and contained some of the 16-bit era 's most memorable music.
Retrospective assessments

In 2014, USGamer described Kent's claims as "seemingly apocryphal ", and in 2019, the video game historian Frank Cifaldi said the Electronic Games issue with the Miyamoto interview did not contain the alleged quote.
Influence
Nintendo and Rare's partnership continued until Star Fox Adventures (2002) for the GameCube, after which Rare was acquired by Microsoft.

lead
It is a reboot of Nintendo's Donkey Kong franchise and follows the gorilla Donkey Kong and his nephew Diddy Kong as they set out to recover their stolen banana hoard from the crocodile King K.
lead
The single-player traverses 40 side-scrolling levels as they jump between platforms and avoid obstacles.
lead
They collect items, ride minecarts and animals, defeat enemies and bosses, and find secret bonus stages.
lead
In multiplayer modes, two players work cooperatively or race each other.
lead
After developing Nintendo Entertainment System games in the 1980s, Rare, a British studio founded by Tim and Chris Stamper, purchased Silicon Graphics workstations to render 3D models.
lead
Nintendo sought a game to compete with Sega 's Aladdin (1993) and commissioned Rare to revive the dormant Donkey Kong franchise.
lead
Rare assembled 12 developers to work on Donkey Kong Country over 18 months.
Gameplay
Some feature unique game mechanics, such as rideable minecarts, blasting out of cannons resembling barrels, and swinging ropes.
Background
In 1985, the British game developers Tim and Chris Stamper established Rare Ltd.
Background
The brothers previously founded the British computer game studio Ultimate Play the Game and founded Rare to focus on the burgeoning Japanese console market.
Background
Rare demonstrated it was possible to reverse-engineer the NES and showed several tech demos to Nintendo executive Minoru Arakawa; impressed, Arakawa granted Rare a Nintendo developer licence.
Background
Rare developed more than 60 NES games, including the Battletoads series and ports of games such as Marble Madness.
Background
When Nintendo released their next console, the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), in 1991, Rare decided to limit their output.
Background
Around 1992, Rare invested their NES profit in Silicon Graphics, Inc.
Background
The move made Rare the most technologically advanced UK developer and situated them high in the international market.
Conception
Though they had purchased the workstations to produce games for the Nintendo 64, which was in development at the time, Rare discovered it was possible to use them with the 16-bit SNES.
Conception
Rare tested the SGI technology with Battletoads Arcade (1994) and began developing a boxing game, Brute Force, using PowerAnimator.
Conception

Nintendo wanted a game to compete with Sega's Aladdin (1993), which featured graphics by Disney animators, when Nintendo of America chairman Howard Lincoln learned of Rare's SGI experiments during a trip to Europe.
Conception

After impressing Nintendo with a demonstration of Brute Force, Tim Stamper—inspired by Mortal Kombat ' s use of digitised footage in place of hand-drawn art—suggested developing a platform game that used pre-rendered graphics.
Conception
The franchise had been largely dormant since the unsuccessful Donkey Kong 3 (1983), so Nintendo figured that licensing it posed minimal risk.
Conception
Conversely, the lead designer Gregg Mayles recalled that it was Nintendo that requested a Donkey Kong game.
Conception
According to Mayles, Nintendo codenamed the project "Country" (based on Rare's location in Twycross), leading to the title Donkey Kong Country.
Conception
Rare assembled a team of 12, the largest in their history at that point, and development began.
Conception
Nintendo was sceptical of Rare's approach to graphics, concerned it would make the game unplayable.
Conception
One in attendance, the Game Boy creator Gunpei Yokoi, felt the game "looked too 3D", but Mayles said Donkey Kong ' s creator, Shigeru Miyamoto, was supportive and gave Rare his approval.
Conception
Donkey Kong Country was the first Donkey Kong game that was neither directed nor produced by Miyamoto, who was working on Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island (1995).
Conception
Miyamoto was still involved with the project and Rare said he provided crucial input.
Conception
Nintendo is usually highly protective of their intellectual properties, but was relatively uninvolved with Donkey Kong Country, leaving most of the work to Rare.
Conception
Rare spent 18 months developing Donkey Kong Country from an initial concept to a finished game, and according to product manager Dan Owsen, 20 people worked on it in total.
Conception
It cost an estimated US$ 1 million to produce, and Rare said that it had the most man hours ever invested in a video game at the time, 22 years.
Design

The stages were painstakingly arranged so that the player could "go first time" past obstacles (if there was a swinging rope then when it came on screen it was swinging towards you so you could jump onto it straight away)...
Design
Rare drew inspiration from the Super Mario series, Mayles citing Super Mario Bros.
Design
Rare featured barrels as a primary game mechanic to pay homage to the original arcade game, and included hidden collectibles like coins and balloons to add depth.
Design
Diddy Kong originated from Rare's search for a game mechanic akin to Super Mario ' s power-up system in that he would serve as the player's health.
Design

Donkey Kong Country did not have much scrapped content; Gunn said he only regretted that Donkey Kong walks across dotted lines instead of paths on the world map, which could not be implemented due to time constraints.
Design
One scrapped idea, a collectible that would evade the player by running or hiding, served as the basis for the Jinjos in Rare's subsequent game Banjo-Kazooie (1998).
Design

Reviewing Donkey Kong Country for release, Nintendo directed Rare to reduce the difficulty to appeal to a broad audience, reasoning that the secrets would provide sufficient challenge for hardcore gamers.
Design
At this point, Miyamoto made some last-minute suggestions, such as Donkey Kong's terrain slap, that were incorporated.
Design
Nintendo's Kensuke Tanabe flew to Twycross to localise the game with Rare.

Because Donkey Kong did not have much of an established universe, Rare was free to expand it with new characters.
Characters
Unlike the original Donkey Kong Jr., Rare did not want Diddy to share his build with Donkey Kong, so they based him on a spider monkey and made him agile to give him distinct moves.
Characters
Naming the character was a challenge, and Rare dropped their preferred "Dinky Kong" due to legal problems.
Characters
Rare staff spent hours at the nearby Twycross Zoo recording gorillas for reference, which they described as "a complete waste of time".
Characters
The antagonists, the Kremlings, were recycled from a cancelled Rare game.
Characters
Rare's initial story was extensive and spanned 15 pages, but Nintendo had it condensed to fit into an instruction manual.

Graphics
Rare developed a compression technique that allowed the team to incorporate more detail and animation for each sprite for a given memory footprint, which better preserved the pre-rendered graphics.
Graphics
Nintendo and Rare called the technique Advanced Computer Modelling (ACM).
Graphics

Rare briefly feared competition from DMA Design 's Uniracers (1994), which also featured pre-rendered graphics, but the staff was relieved upon learning that the player character was Uniracer ' s only element that was pre-rendered.

The game was Rare's first to require multiple programmers, and they worked with little guidance.
Graphics
To help, Nintendo provided Rare with research material regarding apes, barrels, and caves.
Graphics
The ACM process pushed the SNES hardware to its limits; Betteridge said Rare wanted to do everything they could with the hardware similar to what they had done with the NES game Battletoads (1991).

Rare asked Wise to record three jungle demo tunes that were merged to become the "DK Island Swing", the first level's track.
Music
Wise cited Koji Kondo 's music for the Super Mario and Legend of Zelda games, Tim and Geoff Follin's music for Plok!

(1993), synthesiser film soundtracks released in the early 1980s, and rock and dance music from the same decade as influences, and wanted to imitate the sound of the Korg Wavestation synthesiser.

Music

Wise considers the track his favourite and the game's biggest technological accomplishment in regards to the audio.
Music
Wise said his primary focus was to make the most of the SPC700, and he input the music by hand to save memory.

Eveline Novakovic contributed seven tracks, including the world map theme, as her first SNES project.

sents: lead
Harvest Moon, known in Japan as Farm Story (牧場物語, Bokujō Monogatari), is a farm simulation role-playing video game developed by Amccus for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
The game first was released in Japan by Pack-In-Video in 1996, in North America by Natsume Inc. in 1997, and in Europe by Nintendo in 1998.
lead
The European version shipped with language localizations for Germany and France.
lead
It is the first game in the long-running Story of Seasons video game series, previously known as the Harvest Moon series in western territories.
lead
The game has been re-released on the Satellaview, Nintendo 3DS, Wii, Wii U and Nintendo Switch.
Gameplay
While the only care that chickens require is feeding, cows must be continually talked to, brushed, and milked to retain their health.
Gameplay
After dark, the only business in town that the player can access is the bar, where a number of non-player characters gather to drink and talk.
Development
Yasuhiro Wada was producer for the game, and the last game he worked on was Magical Pop'n.
Development
The following merge with Victor Entertainment led to the downsizing of Wada's development team, shrinking from ten members to only three.
Release
The game was released on August 9, 1996, in Japan for the Super Famicom.
Release
It was released in North America in 1997, and Europe in 1998.
Release
Despite the recent release of the Nintendo 64 the game would sell over 100,000 units.
Satellaview version
BS Bokujō Monogatari (BS 牧場物語) was an episodically released ura - or gaiden -version of the original Harvest Moon consisting of 4 unique episodes on the Satellaview.
Satellaview version
Due to the nature of SoundLink broadcasts these games were only broadcast to players between 6:00 and 6:50PM on broadcast dates.

The game was never released outside Japan and as with all other Satellaview titles it has never been re-released as a stand-alone title.
Satellaview version
A single rerun of the broadcasts was conducted in the same weekly format from November 4, 1996, to November 30, 1996, at 5:00 to 5:50PM.

The game received mainly positive reviews and has a GameRankings standing of 73%.

For the release of Harvest Moon on the Wii 's Virtual Console, IGN rated the game at 8.5, praising the game's still gorgeous 16-bit graphics and addictive gameplay.

sents: lead
Earthworm Jim is a 1994 run and gun platform game developed by Shiny Entertainment, featuring an earthworm named Jim, who wears a robotic suit and battles the forces of evil.
lead
The game was released for the Sega Genesis and Super Nintendo Entertainment System, before being subsequently ported to several other video game consoles.
lead
It was well received by critics, and received a sequel, Earthworm Jim 2, in 1995.
lead
In 2009, Gameloft developed and released a remake for mobile phones and Nintendo DSi which was later ported to PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 as Earthworm Jim HD.
lead
In February 2018, Gameloft's contract with Interplay ended and all of the ports developed by Gameloft were removed from digital stores.
Gameplay
The game plays as a 2D sidescrolling platformer with elements of a run and gun game as well.
Gameplay
Two villains made their only appearance in this game: Chuck, a junkyard man with a tendency to vomit bizarre objects; and Doc Duodenum, a crazed organ of a giant alien.
Gameplay
In between most levels, a racing level called "Andy Asteroids" is played.
Development
Inspired by the success of the Sonic the Hedgehog series with its first and second installments, they decided that they wanted to start the franchise as a video game, a rare approach at the time.
Development
Almost all levels were first programmed by Dave Perry on the Genesis and then converted to the Super NES by Nick Jones.
Development

"For Pete's Sake" was coded simultaneously on both platforms by Andy Astor, and "Andy Asteroids" and "Snot a Problem" were originally programmed on the Super NES by Nick Jones and then converted to the Genesis.
Development

The game's unique atmosphere, world, and characters were because the company had previously always been restricted to doing licensed games, like 7up 's Cool Spot, where they had to conform to the other company's preset limitations.
Release
The original version was released for the Genesis in October 1994.
Release

The game was released in Japan physically only on Super Famicom on June 23, 1995, published by Takara, while the Japanese Mega Drive version was available exclusively via the Sega Channel service on December 1, 1995.
Release
The Special Edition was later ported to Windows 95 by Activision.
Release
This version included a secret room which, when reached by the first 200 players, would display a password and a toll-free telephone number.
Release
A direct port of the Game Gear version was also brought to the Master System, but only in Brazil.
Release
However, it only has 4 levels, and the boss in "What the Heck?" is missing.
Release

A conversion of the game was also being developed by German studio Softgold and planned to be published by Atari Corporation for both the Atari Jaguar and the Atari Jaguar CD, but it was never finished due to the departure of Normen B.
Release
Kowalewski from Atari, who was the lead developer of the port, sometime between or at the end of 1995.
Release
The alpha prototype, which consisted of basic character animations, and the source code of the conversion are currently lost.
Release

The game also had an MS-DOS port released in a package titled Earthworm Jim 1 & 2: The Whole Can 'O Worms (along with the MS-DOS port of Earthworm Jim 2) with redrawn graphics and missing the level "Intestinal Distress".
Release
In 2001 Game Titan ported the Super NES version to the Game Boy Advance.
Release
The game was re-released digitally on some platforms in the late 2000s as well.
Release

Release
The Genesis version was also re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on September 15, 2022.
Release
The MS-DOS version was re-released through DOSbox emulation on GOG.com on October 7, 2008, and on Steam on November 4, 2009.
High-definition remake
In 2009, Gameloft released digitally an updated remake of the game on a number of mobile/handheld platforms.
High-definition remake

While the extended version of the "New Junk City" level from the "Special Edition" is included, "Big Bruty" ("Special Edition" new level) and "Who Turned Out the Lights?" (secret level from the original release) aren't present.
High-definition remake
The only new addition for the DSiWare version was an extra minigame that involved the player using the system's camera on their own face, in order to mimic the same faces Jim would make on-screen.
Reception

Earthworm Jim was awarded Best Genesis Game of 1994 by Electronic Gaming Monthly, GamePro gave the Genesis version a perfect score, and Famicom Tsūshin scored the Super Famicom version of the game a 30 out of 40.
Reception
The game has been noted for its fluid animation, featuring a hand-drawn style that was unusual for 16-bit releases.
Reception
Next Generation reviewed the Genesis version of the game, and stated that "Sure, it's only a slick 16bit platform game.
Reception

GamePro and Electronic Gaming Monthly remarked that whereas most Sega CD ports simply add enhanced music, Earthworm Jim included many worthwhile additions such as new animations, new levels, and the new homing missile weapon.
Reception

Electronic Gaming Monthly reviewed that the Game Gear version has impressive graphics by portable standards but is crippled by the Game Gear's limited two-button control, frequent screen blurring, and frustrating difficulty.
Reception

Reviewing the Windows 95 version, Maximum claimed "it's not only a damn fine platform game, it's probably the best the PC has seen to date." They particularly praised the non-frustrating challenge and the strong personality of the graphics.
Reception

Computer Game Review remarked, "If you found Pitfall, The Mayan Adventure entertaining, you'll want to check this one out." Computer Games Strategy Plus named the computer release of Earthworm Jim the best arcade title of 1995.
Reception
Reception for the 2010 remake, Earthworm Jim HD, was less positive.
Reception
Similarly, the iPhone version of the game was criticized for its sloppy controls, mostly due to being touchscreen only.
Reception
The game sold more than 1 million copies by 1995.

Accolades

Accolades
In 2018, Complex rated the game 54th on their The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time writing: "Earthworm Jim was unlike any other game out there at the time, and it’s still quite original today.
Accolades

Ga-roo-vy!" In 2017, Gamesradar ranked the game 19th on their "Best Sega Genesis/Mega Drive games of all time." They felt the game's free-form shooting and platforming kept the game fresh and relevant and called the game "a jolly side-scrolling adventure".

A sequel, Earthworm Jim 2, was released in 1995.

It was released in late 1995 and early 1996 depending on region and video game console, initially being released for the Sega Genesis and Super Nintendo Entertainment System, before being ported to other platforms.
Gameplay
New power-ups include the chip butty, which increases Jim's suit power to 200%.
Gameplay
The last level of the game, "See Jim Run Run Jim Run", is not a typical boss fight, but rather, a race against Psy-Crow through an obstacle course to get to Princess What's-Her-Name.
Versions and releases
The game, much like the first, was developed for the Sega Genesis and then ported over to the Super NES.
Versions and releases
Rainbow Arts ported the game to MS-DOS along with the first game, in a package titled " Earthworm Jim 1 & 2: The Whole Can 'O Worms ".
Versions and releases

On a 1994 conference held on CompuServe with Shiny Entertainment prior to its release, David Perry stated that they were considering making a version of the game for the Atari Jaguar, which never came to fruition.

A Game Boy Advance port, developed by Russian studio SuperEmpire Inc, based on the Super NES release, was released in 2002.
Versions and releases
The Genesis version was later released for download on the Wii via the Virtual Console in 2009, as well.
Versions and releases
The Super NES version was re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online Service in March 2022.

Reviewing the Genesis version, one reviewer for Electronic Gaming Monthly disapproved of the game, remarking "where the first had technique, this one just gets cheap", but the remaining three declared it a worthy sequel.
Reception

The PlayStation port, which contained the same content as the original releases, received a poor review 3/10 score from Computer and Video Games, due to there being no significant improvements, despite the obviously more powerful hardware of the PlayStation.
Reception
The 2002 Game Boy Advance release was panned by critics as well, but this time due to the game having an "unfinished" game engine, glitched graphics, and an unpredictable save system.
Reception
IGN stated that "the action tends to slow down in the most unlikely locations...and the gameplay's inconsistent...load a game where you instantly die for no apparent reason".
Reception
GameSpot nominated Earthworm Jim 2 for its 2002 "Most Disappointing Game on Game Boy Advance" and "Worst Game on Game Boy Advance" awards.

In 1996, GamesMaster ranked the Mega Drive version second in their "The GamesMaster Mega Drive Top 10." In 1998, Saturn Power listed the Saturn version 90th in their Top 100 Sega Saturn Games.

lead

It is the third arcade version of Street Fighter II, part of the Street Fighter franchise, following Street Fighter II: Champion Edition, and was initially released as an enhancement kit for that game.
lead
Released less than a year after the previous installment, Turbo introduced a faster playing speed and new special moves for certain characters, as well as further refinement to the character balance.
lead

lead

lead

The only character exempt to this change is M.

The pitch change in the characters' voices when they perform a variation of their special moves based on the strength level of the attack was removed, but the voice clips of the announcer saying the names of each country were restored, along with the barrel-breaking bonus stage that was removed in the first SNES port.

1 for PlayStation 2 and Xbox, as well as Capcom Classics Collection: Reloaded for the PlayStation Portable.

lead
It refines and balances the existing character roster from the previous versions, and introduces four new characters.
lead
It is the first game on Capcom ' s CP System II hardware, with more sophisticated graphics and audio over the original CP System hardware used in previous versions of Street Fighter II.
lead
Super Street Fighter II was followed in 1994 by Super Street Fighter II Turbo, a fifth version of Street Fighter II, which further balances the characters and adds features.

After the first set, the players are re-arranged by outcome.
Tournament Battle
The winning players are sent to either of the first two cabinets, and losing players are sent to the others.
Tournament Battle
In the finals, the players competing for first place are sent to the first cabinet, the third-place players to the second cabinet, and so on.

In Japan, Game Machine listed Super Street Fighter II in its November 1, 1993 issue as being the most-popular table arcade game at the time.

Eventually, 2 million copies were sold worldwide.

sfes_mega_robo_man_x.title: Mega Man X (video game)

sents: lead
Mega Man X is a 1993 action - platform game developed and published by Capcom for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead

It was the first Mega Man game for the 16-bit console and the first game in the Mega Man X series, a spin-off to the original Mega Man series that began on the Super NES's predecessor, the Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
Mega Man X was released in Japan on December 17, 1993 and was released in both North America and Europe the following year.
lead

Taking place a century after the original Mega Man series, Mega Man X is set in a futuristic world populated by both humans and "Reploids", robots capable of thinking, feeling, and growing like their human creators.
lead
Because of these complex attributes, many Reploids are prone to destructive, renegade activity and are thereafter referred to as "Mavericks".
lead
The plot of the game follows the protagonist X, an android member of a military task force called the "Maverick Hunters".
lead
With the help of his partner Zero, X must thwart the plans of Sigma, a powerful Maverick leader wishing to bring about human extinction.
lead

With the transition to more advanced gaming hardware, series artist Keiji Inafune explained that the development of Mega Man X involved reinventing Mega Man through gameplay expansion and a more mature storyline while still maintaining the basic concepts on which the franchise was built.
Plot
Mega Man X takes place in an unspecified time during the 22nd century (21XX) and approximately 100 years after the original Mega Man series.
Plot
Among the ruins, Cain finds a large capsule which contains a highly advanced robot with human-level intelligence and emotions, and even free will, the likes of which the world has never seen before.
Plot
The robot was buried while running a 30-year diagnostic program to ensure these features.
Plot
Cain decides to duplicate X and, within several months, completes the first "replicate android " or "Reploid", a robot who can think, feel, learn, and grow exactly like a human.
Plot
X, guilt-ridden at having helped design such a dangerous race, joins forces with the only other remaining Hunter, Zero, in order to stop Sigma at any cost.
Plot
X proceeds to track down and exterminate eight of Sigma's most powerful Mavericks, then rendezvous with Zero outside Sigma's stronghold.
Plot
Another battle ensues, ending similar to their first meeting with X at Vile's mercy.
Plot
After the credits, a message from Sigma reveals that X merely destroyed a temporary body, and that Sigma's spirit lives on.
Gameplay
The original Mega Man series on the NES consisted of 2D platform games that focus on run-and-gun gameplay.
Gameplay
The player can return to the game at a later point using a password system; the password will retain any number of the eight stages cleared and most power-ups.
Gameplay
The player can also collect hidden "Heart Tanks" that extend X's maximum life energy and "Sub-Tanks" that can store extra energy for later use.
Gameplay

When certain conditions are met, a secret capsule can be unlocked which gives X the ability to perform the " Hadouken ", an attack used by characters (Ryu, Ken, Akuma, Sakura, Gouken) from Capcom's Street Fighter series.
Development
Inafune created the character Zero, whom he originally intended to be the game's main, playable protagonist.
Development
The development team additionally wanted the world of Mega Man X to be much more sophisticated than in the first Mega Man series.
Development
Sigma, however, was written as a once-good character suffering an "unforeseen error" that leads him to be completely evil.
Development
The first three were responsible for one track each.
Development
Iwai and Horiyama would later compose the soundtracks for Mega Man X2 and X4 respectively.
Development
The Japanese division of Sony Records published an arranged album featuring ten songs on March 9, 1994.
Development
Music using the SNES instrumentals was included as part of the Capcom Music Generation: Rockman X1 ~ X6 soundtrack released by Suleputer in 2003.
Development
The success of the Mega Man series allowed Capcom to continue releasing NES titles well into the 16-bit era.
Development
A teaser for an SNES incarnation of the Mega Man series first made its way into a preview of Mega Man 6 in the spring 1993 issue of the Japanese Club Capcom fan magazine.
Development
Mega Man X was announced in North America in a March 1993 Game Players magazine interview with Capcom's Senior Vice President Joseph Morici.
Development
The tentatively titled "Super Mega Man" was originally to have a "fairly large memory configuration and a battery backup ".
Development
The autumn 1993 issue of Club Capcom announced Rockman X for a December 1993 release in Japan, divulged several plot and gameplay details, and showed Zero as a silhouetted " Blues -like character".
Development
Leading up to its release, the game was covered by the North American press surrounding the summer 1993 and winter 1994 Consumer Electronics Shows.
Reception and legacy
Game Players summarized Mega Man X as "a near-perfect cart with classic gameplay, excellent graphics and sound and tons of hidden items and power-ups".
Reception and legacy

Websites such as IGN, GameSpot, GamesRadar, and 1UP.com retrospectively held Mega Man X as a successful milestone in transitioning the Mega Man series from its increasingly stale existence on the NES to the SNES.
Reception and legacy

Brett Elston of GamesRadar stated, " X was a total reinvention of the series, a perfectly executed update that had fans anticipating its release with a fervor the franchise hadn't seen since the Mega Man 2 and 3 days."
Reception and legacy
The game's title initially proved a source of some confusion; the gaming media reported that many gamers mistook the "X" for the roman numeral 10.
Reception and legacy

Mega Man X was ranked number 58 in Nintendo Power' s "100 Best Nintendo Games of All Time" in its 100th issue in September 1997, number 103 in the publication's "Top 200 Games" list for its 200th issue in February 2006, and the 11th best SNES game of all time in its August 2008 issue.
Reception and legacy
GamePro similarly listed it as the eighth greatest 16-bit video game.
Reception and legacy
Game Informer considered it the 120th best game of all time in its own 200th issue in December 2009.
Reception and legacy
IGN named it the twelfth-best on its own top 100 SNES games list in 2011.
Reception and legacy
In 2018, Complex listed the game 15th on their "The best Super Nintendo Games of All Time." They felt the game was one of the best Mega Man X games in the series.
Reception and legacy
In 1995, Total! rated the game 28th on its Top 100 SNES Games.
Reception and legacy
The SNES version sold 1.165 million copies worldwide as of 2001, making it the 41st best-selling Capcom game of all time.
Reception and legacy
IGN's Jeremy Dunham speculated that the game's more mature storyline and its inclusion of numerous gameplay extensions over the original Mega Man series helped create a "unique cadre of fans".
Reception and legacy
The game was followed by seven direct sequels and three related titles: Mega Man Xtreme, Mega Man Xtreme 2, and Mega Man X Command Mission.
Reception and legacy
Another video game spin-off series, Mega Man Zero, began in 2002 on the Game Boy Advance handheld as a result of the immense popularity of the character Zero.
Re-releases and remakes
After the SNES version debuted, Mega Man X was ported by Rozner Labs to the IBM PC for MS-DOS in 1995 and was packaged with a six-button game controller.
Re-releases and remakes
Mega Man X received a separate PC release for Windows in Japan in 1996, based on the North American MS-DOS version.
Re-releases and remakes
Majesco Entertainment republished the SNES version of the game in 1997.
Re-releases and remakes
Nintendo also republished the game in Japan on its Nintendo Power cartridge service in 1998.
Re-releases and remakes
Mega Man X, alongside its next five direct sequels and Mega Man: Battle & Chase, was compiled and made available on the Mega Man X Collection in North America for the GameCube and PS2 in 2006.
Re-releases and remakes
An enhanced remake titled Mega Man Maverick Hunter X, or Irregular Hunter X (イレギュラーハンターX) in Japan, was released worldwide for the PSP between 2005 and 2008.
Re-releases and remakes
With the launch of the PSP, Keiji Inafune and his team debated on whether or not to create a Mega Man X9.
Re-releases and remakes
"So, we decided that instead of going the X9 route, let's go back to the series' roots and rediscover what makes the X series so classic," Inafune concluded.
Re-releases and remakes
According to Yoshikawa, the character illustrations were updated to resemble both toys and the designs of Mega Man X8.
Re-releases and remakes
Like the original game, Maverick Hunter X has received very positive reviews from critics, accumulating aggregate scores of 82% on GameRankings and 79 out of 100 on Metacritic.
Re-releases and remakes
Capcom released a port of Mega Man X onto FOMA and i-mode compatible mobile phones in Japan in 2007.
Re-releases and remakes

Mega Man X has also been made available for purchase on the Virtual Console service in Japan and North America in 2011 for the Wii, and later in Europe in 2012, as well as for the Wii U in 2013 and the New Nintendo 3DS in 2016.
Re-releases and remakes
The game was ported to the Android operating system in Japan as a free download on November 18, 2011.
Re-releases and remakes
Another remake of Mega Man X was released on the Apple iOS (iPhone and iPod Touch) on December 21, 2011.
Re-releases and remakes
Nintendo re-released Mega Man X in September 2017 as part of the company's Super NES Classic Edition.
Re-releases and remakes
A limited physical cartridge re-release was announced in May 2018 published by iam8bit in celebration of Mega Man' s 30th Anniversary.
Re-releases and remakes
The release will be limited to 8,500 copies, with 7,500 produced in opaque light blue cartridges 1,000 in glow-in-the-dark translucent blue, with each color in a random box.

sents: lead
Mega Man X2 (stylized as MEGA MAN X²), known as Rockman X2 (ロックマンX2) in Japan, is a 1994 action - platform game developed by Capcom for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
The game was released in Japan on December 16, 1994, and in North America and PAL regions in 1995.
lead
It is the direct sequel to Mega Man X, released one year prior.
lead
Mega Man X2 takes place in the near future in which humans try to peacefully coexist with intelligent robots called "Reploids", with some of the Reploids going "Maverick" and threatening daily life.
lead
The plot follows the android protagonist X, a "Maverick Hunter" who has saved humanity from the evil Sigma six months earlier.
lead

A trio of Mavericks calling themselves the "X-Hunters" has arisen, intent on destroying X by luring him with bodyparts of his comrade Zero, who died in the conflict with Sigma's right hand robot named Vile.
lead
Mega Man X2 features much of the same action - platforming elements as the first installment of the series, following the traditional gameplay of the original Mega Man series.
lead
The player is tasked with completing a series of stages by destroying enemies, gaining various power-ups, and winning the special weapon of each stage's boss.
Plot
Mega Man X2 is set in an ambiguous year during the 22nd century ("21XX") in which the world is populated both by humans and mechanical beings known as "Reploids" (replicant androids).
Plot
The events of the first Mega Man X game entail the hunter X's fight to stop Sigma, a Maverick overlord bent on the destruction of humanity.
Plot
Cain that the X-Hunters have attacked Maverick Hunter headquarters and stolen any collected parts and the control chip.
Plot
Just as X annihilates the last of the X-Hunters, Sigma reveals himself to have been behind the plot.
Gameplay
Mega Man X2 is an action - platform game in the same fashion as the first Mega Man X and the original Mega Man series.
Gameplay
Like the first Mega Man X, players can locate and acquire numerous hidden power-ups.
Development
Mega Man X2 was developed by a team at Capcom, which included artists Hayato Kaji and Keiji Inafune, as well as designers Sho Tsuge, and Yoshihisa Tsuda.
Development
A majority of the people who worked on Mega Man X2 had either been heavily involved with the development of the first Mega Man X or were completely new to the franchise.
Development
According to Tsuda, it was Inafune's decision to bring Zero back to life in Mega Man X2 simply because he thought it would be "a shame" to keep him dead.
Development
Inafune felt particularly attached to Zero, a character whom he had designed and originally intended to be the main protagonist of the X series.
Development
Even though Inafune had mostly relinquished his character design duties in Mega Man X2, he refused to allow any drastic changes to the illustration of Zero.
Development
The game's antagonists, the X-Hunters, were present as several illustrations within Inafune's sketchbook prior to the completion of the first Mega Man X.
Development

Mega Man X2 has an in-cartridge enhancement by Capcom called the Cx4 chip, a digital signal processor which allows for limited 3D graphical effects like rotation, enlarging, and shrinking of wireframe objects.
Development
The company held weekly meetings devoted to utilizing the chip to its maximum potential in Mega Man X2.
Development
Tsuge commented that the Cx4 was their "greatest adversary to date" as they were instructed to use it in as many ways as possible.
Development
The musical score for Mega Man X2 was chiefly composed by Yuki Iwai.
Development
The Mega Man X2 soundtrack, featuring the original SNES instrumentals, was included as part of the Capcom Music Generation: Rockman X1 ~ X6 compilation released by Suleputer in 2003.
Release
The game was released in Japan on December 16, 1994, and in North America and PAL regions in 1995.
Release
Mega Man X2 was included in the Mega Man X Collection for the GameCube and PlayStation 2 in North America in 2006.
Release
The game was also released on Japanese mobile phones in 2008 and 2009 and worldwide on the Virtual Console in 2011 and 2012 for the Wii and in 2013–2014 for the Wii U.
Release
In 2006, Mega Man X2 was included as part of the North American Mega Man X Collection for GameCube and PlayStation 2.
Release
A version for i-mode and EZweb -compatible mobile phones was made available in Japan between 2008 and 2009.
Release
Mega Man X2 was released on the Wii Virtual Console service in Japan on December 27, 2011, in PAL regions on May 31, 2012, and in North America on June 14, 2012.
Reception
Reception for Mega Man X2 has been primarily positive by virtue of its graphics, sound, and a persistently enjoyable gameplay model which critics and fans of the Mega Man series had come to expect.
Reception
Comparing the game to the first Mega Man X, GamePro ' s Chris Nicolella called Mega Man X2 "improved in almost every way".
Reception

GameSpot editors Christian Nutt and Justin Speer were appreciative of Capcom's attempt at expanding Mega Man X2 over its predecessor in all aspects, especially the story, which they called "involving... with engaging characters".
Reception
IGN named Mega Man X2 as the 31st-best game in its list of the top 100 SNES games of all time.

Light's new lab assistant, Auto, and where these bolts can be spent on items and power-ups, a feature that originally debuted in the Game Boy Mega Man titles.

Just one week before the game went into its beta stage, the team decided to include this mode on the conditions that Mega Man and Bass be the only playable characters and that it would have no bugs.

Gregory Ballard, the president of Capcom's North American division, admitted the company was too conservative in shipping copies of Mega Man 7 when it launched in the region in September.
Development
The music and sound composition of Mega Man 7 was a collaboration of ten people, including Ippo Yamada, who was pulled in to work on the game while he was working on another project.
Development
A CD soundtrack for Mega Man 7 containing 37 pieces of music was published for the first time in Japan by Team Entertainment on November 21, 2007 amidst the franchise's 20th anniversary.
Reception and legacy
Critically, Mega Man 7 has received a moderately positive reception in both past reviews and more contemporary retrospectives.
Reception and legacy
Tony Mott of Super Play found the game to lack improvement over its 8-bit counterparts in gameplay, stating that the level layouts are "muted and appear regular when compared to the X series".
Reception and legacy
Brett Elston of GamesRadar similarly noted Mega Man 7 as feeling far too similar to the earlier games and that it pales in comparison to the SNES's more relevant and inventive Mega Man X.
Reception and legacy
"It's still worth a play to see the 16-bit jump," Buchanan summarized.
Reception and legacy
Thomas of IGN described the introduction of Mega Man's rival Bass as the seventh installment's most important contribution to the franchise.
Reception and legacy

In spite of Mega Man 7 technologically moving the series from its NES roots to the next generation of consoles, it would eventually transition back to an NES visual and audio style similar to the first six titles many years later.

sfes_mega_robo_man_bass.title: Mega Man & Bass
sents: lead
Mega Man & Bass is a 1998 action - platform game developed and published by Capcom.
lead
It is a spin-off game in the original Mega Man series and was originally released in Japan for the Super Famicom on April 24, 1998.
lead
It was later ported to the Game Boy Advance (GBA) handheld in 2002, and localized in English and released the following year.
lead
Wily many times, the robotic hero Mega Man is called into action once again when a powerful being known as King steals the blueprints to the creations of Dr.
lead
Light in order to create an army for robotic dominance over humans.
lead
Having learned of the threat, Mega Man's rival Bass decides to take matters into his own hands.
lead
The game is an action - platformer where the player advances by defeating bosses and acquiring their signature weapons.
lead
Mega Man & Bass lets the player choose between either of its title characters, each of which plays differently from the other.
Plot
Proto Man is the first to arrive at the scene.
Plot
The pair explains that humans are the ones who created robots in the first place, which confuses King, who teleported Proto Man out of his castle after the battle.
Plot
Proto Man tells Bass that although he is a strong robot of free will, he can never defeat his rival because he has nothing for which to fight.
Gameplay
Bass is able to rapidly fire his arm cannon in eight directions, though shots cannot be fired while moving or pass through walls unless a certain upgrade is obtained.
Gameplay
After the introduction level, the player can only choose between three Robot Masters.
Gameplay
In a similar fashion to previous installments in the series, enemies often drop bolts after they are destroyed, and these can be exchanged for various restorative items and upgrades.
Gameplay
Some upgrades are unique to either character, such as Mega Man's ability to call on his dog Rush to search for items, or an adaptor for Bass to combine with his wolf Treble to temporarily fly.
Gameplay

Most of the CDs are hidden either behind obstacles that need to be destroyed with a special weapon or accessed with a character-specific ability, making it impossible to collect them all on a single playthrough.
Development
Mega Man & Bass was developed for the Super Famicom after the release of Mega Man 8, which preceded Mega Man & Bass on the two 32-bit consoles, the PlayStation and Sega Saturn.
Development

According to series producer Keiji Inafune, Mega Man & Bass was intended for younger players who still owned a Super Famicom and did not have the means to experience Mega Man 8 on one of the newer systems.
Development
Designer Hideki Ishikawa recalled the development of Mega Man & Bass as "one big party".
Development
Graphically, Mega Man & Bass uses many of the same two-dimensional sprites and animations as Mega Man 8.
Development
Two of the eight Robot Master bosses in Mega Man & Bass (Tengu Man and Astro Man) are borrowed from Mega Man 8.
Development
Iwamoto originally denoted Ground Man as "Drill Man" despite there already being a Robot Master by that name in Mega Man 4.
Development
The company commemorated the 15th anniversary of the Mega Man franchise with the GBA version of the game.
Reception and legacy
The GBA port has received generally positive critical reviews, currently holding an aggregate score of 79% on both GameRankings and Metacritic.
Reception and legacy
Most critics found the game to be a solid yet conventional action-platformer that successfully adheres to the classic Mega Man formula.
Reception and legacy

GameSpy contrarily criticized its lack of innovation, declaring, "Anyone that hasn't tried a Mega Man game yet would be better advised to spend $15 on a new copy of Mega Man 8 on the PSOne rather than paying $30 for an inferior retread of the same game".
Reception and legacy
Harris additionally observed a heavy amount of trial-and-error for the levels themselves where the player must die several times before completing each one.
Reception and legacy
According to Famitsu, Mega Man & Bass for the GBA sold 91,097 copies in Japan between its release date and the week of December 23, 2002.
Reception and legacy
Rockman & Forte: Challenger from the Future) was released for the WonderSwan handheld in 1999.
Reception and legacy

As Mega Man & Bass was released directly after Mega Man 8 and it shares plot and gameplay characteristics with the rest of the numbered titles in the series, many believed it to be the ninth main game in the series; however, the actual Mega Man 9 would not be released until 2008.
Reception and legacy

Inafune explained in an interview with the Brazilian magazine Nintendo World that the ninth installment follows the storyline of Mega Man 8 and that the worlds for Mega Man & Bass and Mega Man 9 are meant to coincide with one another, as evidenced by a schematic of Bass in the ending of the game.
Reception and legacy
In 2010, Bass was made playable via downloadable content in Mega Man 10.
Reception and legacy
Nintendo Power listed Mega Man & Bass as the 14th best GBA game of all time in its 20th anniversary issue in 2008.

sfes_mega_robo_man_soccer.title: Mega Man Soccer

Composer(s): Toshio Okamoto Norihiko Togashi Kenichi Tomizawa

sents: lead
Mega Man Soccer is a soccer video game for the Super NES.
lead
The game is based on the original Mega Man series of action - platform games.
lead
Mega Man Soccer was released in Japan on February 17, 1994, and in North America in March of that same year.
lead
Mega Man Soccer is a traditional soccer game with exhibition matches, tournaments, and leagues that can be played both single-player and multiplayer depending on the mode.
lead
The game features characters and Robot Masters from previous entries in the original Mega Man series.
lead
Each character has a unique special shot that will temporarily disable anyone that comes in contact with the ball.
lead
This aspect of Mega Man Soccer was met with critical praise, but overall reception has been average, particularly due to its perceived poor play control.
Gameplay
The "Exhibition" mode lets the player play a single match with a team created using any of the game's 20 characters on one of a dozen themed soccer fields.
Gameplay
For the first section of this mode, the player is given a team composed entirely of Mega Man robots, and is tasked with defeating eight teams of Robot Masters in an order of the player's choosing.
Development
Mega Man Soccer was first announced in an interview with Capcom's Senior Vice President Joseph Morici in the March 1993 Game Players magazine.
Development
Series artist Ryuji Higurashi recalled seeing the characters Guts Man and Heat Man in preview screenshots for Mega Man Soccer.
Development
Guts Man was originally featured as part of a sketch for the game's Japanese cover art; when he was cut from the final draft of the game, he was replaced by Proto Man.
Reception
GamePro ranked the game at number four on its "10 Weirdest Sports Games Ever".
Reception

The list compared it to sports games in the Mario series, stating that the latter makes more sense in having only one of each character, unlike Mega Man Soccer, which can have multiple copies of characters on the field at one time.
Reception
In 2018, Complex rated Mega Man Soccer 61st in their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".

sfes_act_razer.title: ActRaiser
