Genre(s): Platform, city-building, Action RPG, god game

sents: lead

ActRaiser is a 1990 video game developed by Quintet and published by Enix for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, It combines traditional side-scrolling platforming and sections with city building and god game elements.
lead
A sequel, ActRaiser 2, was released for the Super NES in 1993.
lead
In 2007, ActRaiser became available on the Wii 's Virtual Console download service in Europe, North America, and Japan.
lead
A version of the game was also released for European mobile phones in 2004.
lead
A remake, Actraiser Renaissance, was released for several platforms in 2021.
Gameplay
Although the Master is never directly controlled, the player interacts with the world by controlling an angel and an animated statue.
Gameplay
Once all four lairs have been sealed the population will begin to build the most advanced homes available to the people in that region.
Plot
The plot follows a godlike being known only as "The Master" (God in the Japanese version) in his fight against Tanzra (Satan in the Japanese version), also referred to as "The Evil One".
Version differences
Finally, there is a "Professional!" mode, unlocked after completing the game, containing only the action segments with a level design similar to the original Japanese release.
Ports
Square Enix released a limited version of the game for mobile phones, published by Macrospace on September 1, 2004.
Ports
It was released in Japan on March 20, 2007, in Europe on April 13, and in North America on May 28.
Actraiser Renaissance
A remake under the title of Actraiser Renaissance was released in September 2021, for Android, iOS, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Windows.
Music
A single disc soundtrack for the game was released on January 25, 1991, in Japan.
Music
A shorter arranged soundtrack titled Symphonic Suite from Actraiser was released on September 21.
Music
In 2004, a medley of music from the game arranged by the original composer was performed live at the second annual Symphonic Game Music Concert in Leipzig, Germany.
Music
The soundtrack was re-released by Wayô Records on vinyl and CD in 2021 as ActRaiser Original Soundtrack & Symphonic Suite.
Music

Koshiro would later return to not only fully recreate the original soundtrack for Actraiser Renaissance, but also composed fifteen new tracks, in both the original SNES sample quality and Renaissance's own higher quality audio.
Reception
The game sold about 620,000 copies worldwide, with 400,000 copies sold in Japan, 180,000 in the US and 40,000 in Europe.
Reception
Geoffrey Douglas Smith of AllGame wrote while the game was not the height of its genre, the unique combination and the orchestrated soundtrack result in enjoyable adventure.
Reception
Super Gamer magazine gave a review score of 84%, calling it a brilliant mix of a strategic gods game and platforming elements.
Reception
ActRaiser was awarded Best Music of 1993 by Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Reception
In 1997 Electronic Gaming Monthly editors ranked it the 75th best console video game of all time.
Reception
ActRaiser was inducted into GameSpot 's Greatest Games of All Time in December 2003.
Reception
It was rated the 150th best game made on a Nintendo System in Nintendo Power 's Top 200 Games list.
Reception

In 2007, ScrewAttack ranked ActRaiser #1 on their "Top 10 Big Names That Fell Off", which listed games that were popular in days past, whether good or bad, but have since faded into relative obscurity (ActRaiser was discussed positively).
Reception
In 2018, Complex ranked ActRaiser 33rd on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Reception
In 2017, Gamesradar listed ActRaiser 23rd on its "The best SNES games of all time".
Reception
In 1995, Total! placed the game 91st on its "Top 100 SNES Games".

sfes_act_razer_2.title: ActRaiser 2

Designer(s): Hitoshi Ariga Hiroshi Hayashi Naoko Suzuki

sents: lead
ActRaiser 2 is a side-scrolling platform game for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System developed by Quintet and published by Enix in 1993.
lead
The game is a sequel to the original ActRaiser, but the storyline is not directly connected to its predecessor.
lead
Otherwise, the given story draws concepts from the famous religious epics Paradise Lost and the Divine Comedy.
lead
Unlike the original game, which alternately combined platform game sequences and god game sequences, ActRaiser 2 is only a platform game.
Gameplay

Gameplay for ActRaiser 2 consists primarily of side-scrolling platform action, similar to the "Professional!"/"Action" mode from the original game, while completely removing the city building simulation.
Gameplay

Like the original, each area contains two "acts"; the first act of an area consists of monsters spawned from a lesser demon named after an unfavorable condition, while the second act consists of monsters spawned from the primary evil, named after one of the seven deadly sins, with heightened challenge and peril.
Gameplay
The side-scrolling action for ActRaiser 2 is more advanced than its predecessor.
Gameplay
Armed only with a sword, and a shield which can deflect some attacks, the Master becomes heavily dependent upon magic.
Gameplay
Magic is executed by holding down the designated button to "charge up" and is then released, consuming a magic scroll which is limited when the Master enters an area.
Gameplay

This is different from the first ActRaiser in which the player had to select a particular magic before descending down to the world to fight monsters and was limited to only that magic for the duration of battle.
Gameplay
In ActRaiser 2, each magic is designed for particular situations and some magic is more powerful than others.
Gameplay
The game's difficulty is also increased in that monsters require much more damage to be destroyed.
Synopsis

After the player slays the first six deadly sins, the Tower of Babel (renamed "Tower of Souls" in the western versions), the final staged level of the game, appears, in which the Master fights the final sin, Destruction, a mechanically engineered god representing Pride.
Development and release
According to developer Quintet, ActRaiser 2 was made at the request of Enix of America, and designed according to their specifications.
Reception
ActRaiser 2 was seen by some game writers as not as good as the original.
Reception
The game sold about 180,000 copies worldwide, with 40,000 copies sold in Japan and Europe respectively and 100,000 sold in the US.
Reception
Levi Buchanan of IGN wrote that while not as good as the original game, ActRaiser 2 ' s allusions to Medieval religious texts and apocryphal storytelling is "more than welcome".
Reception
In 2018, Complex rated Actraiser 2 81st on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Reception
In 1995, Total! ranked the game 38th on its "Top 100 SNES Games".
Legacy
In 1996, Sega announced that they would be publishing a Quintet-developed remake of ActRaiser 1 and 2, tentatively titled Act Remix, for the Sega Saturn.
Legacy
Quintet started coding a third game in the ActRaiser series, for the Nintendo 64, but never finished it.
Legacy
In May 2008, Fumiaki Shiraishi, the lead programmer for Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles: My Life as a King, noted in an interview that he would like to make an ActRaiser sequel.

sfes_super_castlevein_iv.title: Super Castlevania IV
sents: lead
Super Castlevania IV is a 1991 action - platform game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It has been re-released multiple times, including for the Super NES Classic Edition.
lead
Super Castlevania IV features expanded play control, 16-bit graphics featuring Super NES's Mode 7, and a soundtrack featuring new pieces and arrangements based on previous Castlevania music.
lead
A reimagining of the events of Castlevania on the NES, the game takes place in 1691 Transylvania, where the vampire hunter Simon Belmont must defeat the vampire Dracula.
lead
The game received critical acclaim and is considered one of the greatest video games of all time.
Development and release
His first 16-bit game, Ueno's team possibly started development on it during 1989.
Development and release
Ueno liked the original Castlevania for the Nintendo Entertainment System the most and wanted to make a pure action game that was similar to it.
Development and release
Ueno only considers Super Castlevania IV a remake of the original Castlevania to some extent.
Development and release
The game was released in Japan on October 31, 1991 for the Super Famicom.
Development and release
Factor 5 created a short demo of the game running on the Mega Drive and presented it to Konami.
Development and release
It was re-released on the Virtual Console in 2006 for the Wii, in 2013 for the Wii U, and in 2016 for the New Nintendo 3DS.
Development and release
In September 2017, it was included on Nintendo's Super NES Classic Edition, a miniature replica of the Super NES featuring many built-in games.
Development and release
The game is included in Castlevania Anniversary Collection, a compilation of past Castlevania installments released on May 17, 2019 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One.
Audio
On June 21, 2017, the game's music was released on vinyl by Mondo.
Reception
Nintendo Power gave the game four overall scores of 4.0, 4.0, 4.5 and 4.5 out of 5.
Reception
In 1994 the game was reviewed by Sandy Petersen in Dragon #209's "Eye of the Monitor" column.
Reception
In a 1997 Castlevania retrospective, GamePro said it "is still one of the all-time best games".
Reception
It was named by Nintendo Power in a 2006 issue as the 66th best game made on a Nintendo system.
Reception
Official Nintendo Magazine placed the game at 70 on their list of the 100 best Nintendo games ever.
Reception
Game Informer ' s review opined that it "perfect the classic formula" due to its whip and less stiff gameplay.
Reception
In 2018, Complex listed the game 13th on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time", writing: "Next to Symphony of the Night, this is the best Castlevania game of all time.
Reception
The control is perfect, the progression is perfect, and even the ramping up of the difficulty is flawless, as it gets difficult in all the right spots.
Reception
Also, it has the best soundtrack ever." In 1996, GamesMaster ranked the game 55th in its "Top 100 Games of All Time".

sfes_castlevein_draculo_x.title: Castlevania: Dracula X

Composer(s): Tomoya Tomita Masanari Iwata Harumi Ueko Masahiko Kimura

sents: lead

Castlevania: Dracula X, titled Castlevania: Vampire's Kiss in Europe and Akumajou Dracula XX in Japan, is a 1995 action - platform game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is the second Castlevania installment to be released for the Super NES.
lead
It is a remake of Castlevania: Rondo of Blood, which was previously released in Japan on the PC Engine Super CD-ROM in 1993.
lead

While the plot is similar to Rondo of Blood and it uses many of that game's graphics, it features new levels and altered gameplay elements, rather than being a direct port because of the limits of the Super NES cartridge format and exclusivity agreements with PC Engine maker NEC.
lead
It was released on July 21, 1995 in Japan, in September 1995 in North America, February 22, 1996 in Europe, and on June 22, 1996, in Australia.
lead
The game received mixed reviews, with journalists considering it inferior to Rondo of Blood and criticizing its high difficulty.
lead
The game was re-released as a Wii U Virtual Console download in Japan on April 23, 2014, in North America on October 2, 2014, and the PAL regions on November 13, 2014.
lead
It was released again for New Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console download in North America on December 29, 2016, and in Europe and Australia on January 26, 2017.
Reception
Castlevania: Dracula X for the Super NES received mixed reviews, with most critics stating that it is an inferior conversion of the PC Engine game.
Reception

On the release of the game, Famicom Tsūshin scored Dracula X a 24 out of 40, and Electronic Gaming Monthly scored it a 6.75 out of 10, saying it is a good game in its own terms but does not hold up to previous Castlevania games.
Reception
In 2018, Complex rated the game 82nd on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".

sfes_contro_iii_the_alien_wars.title: Contra III: The Alien Wars

Composer(s): Miki Higashino Masanori Adachi Tappi Iwase
Platform(s): Super NES, Game Boy, Game Boy Advance

sents: lead
Contra III: The Alien Wars is a 1992 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
It is the third home console entry in the Contra series after Contra (1988) and Super C (1990) for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES).
lead
In PAL regions, it was retitled Super Probotector: Alien Rebels and the player characters were replaced with robots.
lead
The player is tasked with fighting off an alien invasion of Earth across six stages.
lead
Four stages feature side-scrolling action traditional to the series while two are presented from an overhead perspective.
lead
It is the first Contra title to have been directed by Nobuya Nakazato who later directed other games in the series.
lead
He designed Contra III to feature more comical elements, a more cinematic soundtrack, and tighter stage design than its predecessors.
lead
Contra III received positive reviews, with critics praising its arcade quality derived from its sound and visual design.
Gameplay
There are six stages in total; four are side-scrolling while two are presented in an overhead perspective using the Super NES's Mode 7 rendering mode.
Gameplay
The stages each feature unique controls, giving the player the ability to rotate the screen to navigate.
Gameplay
The player has limited bombs, and using them will damage all enemies on the screen.
Development
Although this was Nakazato's third year at Konami, Contra III is the first Contra game he worked on, having only previously done informal playtesting for Super C (1990).
Development
Nintendo Power reported the name change to Contra III in its coverage of Winter CES in 1992.
Development
The restriction is that graphics can only move horizontally along the scanline to achieve the illusion that they are actually sprites in the foreground.
Development
Contra III was released in Japan on February 28, 1992, and North America on March 26.
Development
In Europe, the game was retitled Super Probotector: Alien Rebels and released on September 12, 1992.
Reception
Along with Computer and Video Games (CVG), they admired the use of Mode 7 on the top-down stages, with EGM extending their praise to the boss design on those stages.
Reception
Mean Machines wrote that the score rivaled that of ActRaiser (1990).
Reception
CVG called it a cross between Strider (1989) and Midnight Resistance (1989), and enjoyed the athletic climbing ability of the characters.
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 51st in a list of the greatest Nintendo games, calling it "Hectic, relentless and very challenging".
Accolades
In 2018, Complex listed Contra III as the 21st best Super Nintendo game.
Accolades
They praised its intensity and wrote: "If not for, this would be the best Contra in the entire series, by far." IGN ranked the game 24th in their "Top 100 SNES Games of All Time."
Ports and rereleases
Contra III was released again for the Wii U Virtual Console in Japan and North America in November 2013, and Europe received the unmodified Contra III on the Wii U in January 2014.
Ports and rereleases
In May 2016, Contra III was added to the Nintendo 3DS eShop for North America and Europe for exclusive use with the New Nintendo 3DS.
Ports and rereleases
Contra III was included in the 2017 Super NES Classic dedicated console.
Ports and rereleases
It was released in June 2019 for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Windows.
Contra: The Alien Wars (Game Boy)
Factor 5 developed a port for the Game Boy; it was released on September 23, 1994 in Japan, and in November in North America.
Contra: The Alien Wars (Game Boy)
The game was released in Europe in October as Probotector 2 with the player characters redrawn as robots.
Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (Game Boy Advance)
At E3 2002, Konami announced the development of a remake of Contra III for the Game Boy Advance.
Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (Game Boy Advance)
The port was titled Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX and released in November 2002 in Japan and North America, and February 2003 in Europe.
Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (Game Boy Advance)
The secondary weapon slot and bombs were omitted from the port, and the Mode 7 stages were replaced with side-scrolling stages from Contra: Hard Corps.
Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (Game Boy Advance)

Contra Advance received "mixed or average" reviews per ratings aggregator Metacritic; IGN criticized the removal of the Mode 7 stages for eliminating variety and GameSpot was troubled by the weaponry changes.
Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (Game Boy Advance)
In November 2015, the game was added to the Wii U Virtual console in North America and Europe.
Legacy
Contra III is director Nobuya Nakazato's first project in the Contra series, later acting as producer and director.
Legacy

Programmers Hideyuki Suganami and Mitsuru Yaida left Konami shortly after Contra III to work at the then-newly-founded Treasure, where they helped develop Gunstar Heroes (1993) and Alien Soldier (1995), which both expanded on the run and gun game formula defined in Contra III.

sfes_super_turrikan.title: Super Turrican (1993 video game)

lead

The game only features 4 worlds and ends with the H.

Giger -inspired alien boss, despite a representation of 'The Machine', similar to that featured in Mega Turrican, appearing in the prologue.

sfes_super_turrikan_2.title: Super Turrican 2

Artist(s): Frank Matzke, Tobias J. Richter, Andreas Escher

sents: lead
Super Turrican 2 is a 16-bit shooter game for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, developed by Factor 5 and marketed by Ocean Software in 1995.
lead
Part of the Turrican series, it is the sequel to Super Turrican for the same platform.
lead
The game was released on the Virtual Console in North America on September 29, 2008.
lead
However, it was retired without any explanation in October 2013 in the same region.
lead
It was also re-released as an aftermarket cartridge for the original SNES console in 2022, also including a score attack level for Super Turrican.
Story
Long since his last defeat, The Machine has returned and the defenses of the star system are no match for The Machine's phasers launched from deep space.
Story
Civilizations were destroyed in an instant and the whole system fell under the spell of evil, with just a few tiny cries for help escaping the boundaries of the system.
Story
But seconds later, only one of the ships manage to escape the dangerous influence of the black hole.
Story
Shipwrecked somewhere in this devastated realm is the last remaining survivor of the assault squad team sent by the United Freedom Forces.

sfes_axelei.title: Axelay
sents: lead
Axelay is a 1992 scrolling shooter video game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead

Set in the fictional solar system Illis where an alien empire known as "Armada of Annihilation" invades its planets including the Earth -like Corliss (Mother), players take control of the titular D117B space fighter craft as a last resort to stop the alien invasion by recovering its lost weaponry.
lead

The gameplay mainly consist of both vertical-scrolling and horizonal-scrolling stages in the same vein as Konami's own Life Force, with players choosing three different weapon-types that increase in number as they progress through the game.
lead
Headed by Super Castlevania IV producer Kazumi Kitaue, Axelay was developed by most of the same team that would later go on to form Treasure, the creators of Gunstar Heroes.
lead
Though first launched for the Super NES, the game has since been re-released through download services for Nintendo consoles.
lead
The title became popular and regarded by publications as a classic of the shoot 'em up genre, garnering praise for its visuals, music and an advanced selection of weapons available at the time.
lead
A sequel, Axelay 2, was planned but never materialized due to low sales of the first game.
Gameplay

Axelay is a scrolling shooter similar to Konami's own Life Force where players take control of the D117B space fighter craft as a last resort to stop the Armada of Annihilation by recovering its lost weaponry through six stages, each with a boss at the end that must be fought before progressing any further.
Gameplay
The gameplay varies quite a bit from that of traditional 2D scrolling shooters.
Gameplay
Similar to Life Force, levels transition between vertical and horizontal scrolling layouts, forcing the player to select weapons that will be most effective for each level.
Gameplay
In the top-down stages, enemies and objects are warped as they come into view to produce a pseudo-3D effect, in addition of parallax scrolling effects.
Gameplay

Getting hit by enemy fire or colliding against solid stage obstacles will result in losing a life and once all lives are lost, the game is over though players have the option to continue playing via a limited number of credits.
Gameplay
Although there is an ending, the game loops back to the first stage after completing the last stage, with each one increasing the difficulty and enemies fire denser bullet patterns.
Plot
As a last resort against the alien forces, the D117B fighter is sent out to recover its lost weaponry and put a stop to the invasion.
Plot

Having traversed the cloud covered Cumuluses, the space colony Tralieb, the largely populated Urbanite, the watery Cavern, and Sector 3 Lava Planet, the Axelay D117B fighter makes its way to the fortress of Armada of Annihilation and completes its mission.
Development and release

Ueda stated that one of the enemies in the last stage previously appeared in other shoot 'em up games by Konami such as Life Force and Flak Attack, as his then-president at Konami liked the enemy's attack.
Development and release
Axelay was first released in Japan by Konami on 11 September 1992.
Development and release
The game was originally intended to be a Japanese exclusive but was given an international release in response to numerous letters from consumers and critics.
Development and release

The soundtrack was released on a single 22-song disc published by King Records on 21 October 1992, while the tracks "Unkai" and "Colony" were included on the Konami All Stars 1993 and the Perfect Selection Konami Shooting Battle II compilation discs respectively.
Development and release
The title was re-released on the Wii 's Virtual Console service in Australia and North America in 2007 and later in Japan in 2008.
Reception
They gave it a 4.5 out of 5 for control and fun factor and a perfect 5.0 for graphics and sound.
Reception
Nintendo Power scored Axelay 3.75 out of 5, praising its graphics but noting that its head-on perspective takes some getting used to.
Reception
Super Play listed it number 36 on its list of the top 100 SNES games of all time in 1996.
Reception

The following year, it was listed as number 91 on Electronic Gaming Monthly 's 100 best games of all time in their 100th issue, which cited its Mode 7 effects, the boss visuals, and the strategy involved in choosing the weapons loadout before each level.
Reception
The website ScrewAttack called it the #6 best 2D shooter.
Reception
Nintendo Power magazine later called it the #18 best game on the SNES.
Reception
Axelay was included as one of the titles in the 2010 book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
Reception
In 1995, Total! ranked Axelay 88th on their "Top 100 SNES Games." IGN rated Axelay 55th in its Top 100 SNES Games.
Reception
They praised the game calling it "A visual stunner on the SNES" and felt that the unique application of the Mode 7 made Axelay feel like two games in one.
Retrospective reviews
Both IGN and GameSpot gave the Virtual Console re-release of Axelay a 7.5 out of 10.
Retrospective reviews
Nintendo Life gave the game a score of 80 out of 100.
Legacy
After finishing Axelay two times consecutively on the highest difficulty level, a message promising Axelay 2 appeared but the planned sequel never materialized due to low sales of the first game.
Legacy
The Axelay D117B fighter makes an appearance in Konami's Airforce Delta Strike as an unlockable aircraft.

sfes_gunfarce.title: GunForce
sents: lead
GunForce (also known as GunForce: Battle Fire Engulfed Terror Island) is a side-scrolling run and gun video game produced by Irem for arcades in 1991.
lead
The game was ported by Bits Studios and published by Irem for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in 1992.
lead
The sequel, GunForce II, was originally known in Japan as Geo Storm.
Reception
In Japan, Game Machine listed GunForce on their July 1, 1991 issue as being the tenth most-successful table arcade unit of the month.
Reception
In the September 1991 issue of Japanese publication Micom BASIC Magazine, the game was ranked on the number fifteen spot in popularity.

sfes_wild_gunz.title: Wild Guns
sents: lead
Wild Guns is a 1994 space Western shooting gallery video game developed by Natsume for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
Set in the Wild West with steampunk and sci-fi influences, the story follows Annie and her bounty hunter Clint, seeking revenge for the death of her family.
lead
The player controls either Annie or Clint sidestepping and jumping in the foreground while shooting down enemy robots in the background and dodging enemy bullets.
lead
These gameplay mechanics combine elements from third-person shooters and light gun games.
lead
Development lasted five months on a small budget with a team of only three core members and two support staff.
lead
The team leads had previously worked together on The Ninja Warriors (1994) for the Super NES, and so chose to develop for that system.
lead
Wild Guns was heavily influenced in its gameplay and artistic design by arcade games such as Blood Bros. and Dynamite Duke.
lead
The game's scenery, characters, and sound design drew ideas from the Western film genre and the science fiction manga Cobra, creating a space Western setting.
Gameplay
Single player and cooperative modes are available, as well as target practice allowing two players to compete to achieve the highest score.
Gameplay
Only five bombs can be held at a time, which can be used to clear the screen of enemies.
Gameplay
When a player's bullets hit bullets fired by enemies, a gauge at the bottom of the screen will fill.
Gameplay
Once filled, the player will be awarded with a Vulcan gun, the most powerful weapon in the game which grants invincibility.
Development
The team chose to develop for the Super NES because the three had worked together previously on The Ninja Warriors (1994) for that system.
Development
The screen shaking and mirage -like effects that occur after explosions were influenced by the film RoboCop 3.
Development
The game's music was created using PC-98s, a Roland W-30 keyboard, and a MIDI sequencer.
Development
Originally, the reticle could only move up and down, and lateral movement was done by moving the player side-to-side; this, however, proved to be cumbersome and was changed.
Development
The "Look Out!" text bubble was added because of difficulty judging bullet distances due to the screen's artificial 3D depth.
Release
The game was released in Japan on August 12, 1994.
Release
The North American version of Wild Guns was set to be released in the third quarter of 1994 and was reviewed at the time, but the release was unexpectedly delayed until the third quarter of 1995.
Release
A 32X version was reportedly planned for 1996, but never materialized.
Release
The game has since become a rare collector's item.
Release
The game was rereleased on the Virtual Console for the Wii in 2010 and Wii U in 2014.
Release
The game was added to the Nintendo Switch Online subscription service in 2020.
Release
An enhanced remaster titled Wild Guns Reloaded was released for the PlayStation 4 in December 2016.
Release
Natsume released Reloaded on Windows in July 2017, marking the company's first ever release on the personal computer.
Release
On April 17, 2018, Reloaded was released on the Nintendo Switch.
Reception
Famitsu gave it a score of 26 out of 40.
Reception
Critics and Natsume themselves have acknowledged Wild Guns as a cult classic.
Reception
Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu gave the PS4 version of the game a score of 29 out of 40.

sfes_run_sabre.title: Run Saber

Run Saber is a side-scrolling action game developed by Horisoft and published by Atlus for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
The game was released in North America on June 8, 1993, and in Europe in 1993.
lead
Run Saber features side-scrolling fighting as the two main heroes, Allen and Sheena, the Run Sabers, fight to save the planet.
lead
The gameplay is similar to Strider, Valis and some elements of Psycho Dream.
lead
Run Saber was not released in Japan, despite being developed by a mostly-Japanese team.
Gameplay

Originally, the boss at the end of the Tong City level was supposed to be a woman lying on her side, but Nintendo felt that this violated their content guidelines as they did not want to depict or reference violence against women on their hardware, so the woman was changed into a dead woman and was approved.
Plot
Humanity's only hope is a new weapon known as Project Saber, three cyborgs that are genetically enhanced to supernatural levels.
Plot
Kurtz, the first Saber, malfunctions and escapes to Earth before the project is complete.

sfes_metal_worriers.title: Metal Warriors

Artist(s): Chris Hockabout Harrison Fong Jesse Clark

sents: lead

Metal Warriors is a side-scrolling action - platform run and gun video game developed by LucasArts and published by Konami exclusively for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in North America in April 1995.
lead
It is often confused by many to be a direct sequel to Cybernator, which was created by NCS Corporation and released earlier in 1992 on the console.
lead

Set in the year 2102 where dictator Venkar Amon has waged a war against the United Earth Government for three years, players assume the role of lieutenant Stone from the titular freedom-fighting group taking control of several mecha suits in a last-ditch effort to overthrow the Dark Axis military force on Earth.
lead
Its gameplay mainly consists of action and shooting mixed with mission-based exploration using a main seven-button configuration.
lead

Metal Warriors was created by most of the same team who previously worked on Zombies Ate My Neighbors at LucasArts, including designer Mike Ebert and programmer Dean Sharpe, and uses an improved version of the same game engine that was previously implemented in the latter.
lead

Development on the project was immediately approved by Kelly Flock after release of Zombies Ate My Neighbors in 1993 to positive reviews and took influence from various mecha anime series and video games, most notably Cybernator.
lead

It was originally intended to be published by Nintendo as a first-party title during Christmas amid the 3D era before publishing duties were ultimately handled by Konami instead, who produced a limited run of copies in total as a result.
lead
Nevertheless, it has since gained a cult following, in addition of being referred by publications like IGN as one of the best titles for the Super Nintendo.
Gameplay

At any given time or when it is almost completely destroyed, players can abandon their suit and scramble around the stage to find a new one, allowing to remain in the game even if their assault suit was destroyed.
Gameplay
Stone can also fit into smaller spaces and scout ahead without attracting the attention of most enemies, as some of them ignore unsuited marines.
Gameplay
The players have a limited number of continues to keep playing before the game is over.
Development and release
Metal Warriors was developed by most of the same team headed by Mike Ebert and Dean Sharpe who previously worked on Zombies Ate My Neighbors at the American studio LucasArts.
Development and release

Ebert has explained in recent years that the team had originally desired to implement a split-screen two-player co-op mode in Zombies Ate My Neighbors but it was not possible due to the engine not being fast enough at the time, however they were able to do so on the project.
Development and release

The game originally was previewed by Nintendo Power in their July 1994 issue under the title Battledroids, which proved to be difficult to obtain due to being an official terminology from George Lucas ' Star Wars.
Development and release
Metal Warriors was first showcased to the public during Winter CES in 1995, before being released exclusively in North America on April of the same year.
Development and release

Sharpe has since stated that a version for the Sega Genesis would not have been possible without his involvement due to several programming tricks used in order to run the game on the Super NES, before the idea was ultimately scrapped after Nintendo picked up the project for release.
Development and release
A Game Boy Advance conversion was in development by animator Leonard Robel at LucasArts without the original team but it was never released due to internal conflicts.
Reception

Game Informer said that this last feature "adds a whole new level of playing to the game, making you think through the missions on two levels; where can I take my mech and where can I take my pilot." Since its initial release, it has gained a cult following.
Reception
In 2011, IGN placed the title on their Top 100 SNES Games list at #33, praising its originality and two-player versus mode.
Reception
Most critics described the game's difficulty as extremely challenging without being frustrating, though a few complained at the lack of a password system.
Reception

VideoGames, which was most vehement about this complaint, nonetheless added that " Metal Warriors is still a white-hot game", and applauded it for giving "a lot of leeway" in how the players can explore the stages and engage enemies.

sfes_ogre_battel_the_march_of_the.real: Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen
sfes_ogre_battel_the_march_of_the.title: Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen
sents: lead
Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen is a 1993 real-time tactical role-playing game developed by Quest Corporation.
lead
Originally published for Super NES by Quest in Japan and by Enix America in North America.
lead
It is the first installment of the Ogre Battle series.
lead
It was directed by Yasumi Matsuno, and designed by Matsuno with Akihiko Yoshida.
lead
The story of Ogre Battle focuses on a band of rebels as they lead a revolution against a corrupt reigning Empire, ruled by an evil Empress.
lead
Ogre Battle was ported to the Sega Saturn and PlayStation, with enhancements made to the original gameplay.
lead
It was later released for Virtual Console, and mobile phones.
lead
A successor, Tactics Ogre, was released in 1995 for the Super NES.
Gameplay
In accordance with this element, vampires and werewolves will only be seen in the evening, with the former appearing in coffins during the day, and the latter appearing as normal men.
Gameplay
There are also four hidden stages accessible through the main game with an additional stage as an easter egg.
Battle
The unit that caused the most damage is the victor and forces the other unit to retreat.
Alignment
In Ogre Battle, the alignment statistic indicates how lawful (good) or chaotic (evil) a character is, on a scale from 0 to 100.
Alignment

A player whose alignment is relatively high will not necessarily be penalized for employing units of low-alignment soldiers; rather, a mix of high- and low-alignment fighters results in the most potent fighting force.
Alignment
Provided the player keeps low- and high-alignment characters in their own separate units, and only liberates towns with high-alignment units, he or she can still see the best ending.
Alignment
For example, one can employ a few decidedly low-alignment units to slaughter enemy units, reserving high-alignment units for liberation purposes only.
Classes
There are several different classes available in Ogre Battle, but any given character is limited to a subset of class changes depending on their race.
Classes
Finally, the two human class trees are unique in that they have the most branches in their tree and characters can be demoted to move along a different path.
Classes
Each character has a terrain type where they move fastest and fight the best (some classes also get additional attacks), with flying characters able to move quickly over all terrain.
Plot
Before Rashidi dies, he uses his blood to release Diablo, the king of the Underworld who was sealed away after the first great Ogre Battle.
Development
Matsuno had never played a tactical game before this, but on staff recommendations played Nobunaga's Ambition to get a feel for the genre.
Development
A challenge faced by the team was creating a 3D-like display on the limited SNES hardware.
Development
The angled perspective on battles was to contrast against the common first-person or overhead top-down views of other RPGs at the time.
Development
Ogre Battle was Yoshida's second title while working at Quest, having first done artwork for Musashi no Bōken.
Music
It was Sakimoto's first attempt at orchestral music, as he had previously only done with in techno and electronic music.
Music
A soundtrack album for the game was released in April 1993 by Datam Polystar.
Music
A further compilation arrange album, featuring tracks from both Ogre Battle and its sequel, was released in October 1996.
Releases
Ogre Battle was released in Japan by Quest on March 12, 1993.
Releases
The SNES version was published by the American branch of Enix in May 1995.
Releases
In 1998, an updated edition of the Super NES version was released by Quest as a download for the Nintendo Power Cartridge in Japan.
Releases
The Super NES version was re-released in North America on the Wii 's Virtual Console on March 2, 2009, for 800 Nintendo points ($8).
Releases
The SNES version was ported to mobile devices with additional downloading maps and released in Japan by Square Enix for FOMA on September 1, 2010, and for EZweb on May 12, 2011.
Releases
A PlayStation port was developed by Quest and published by Artdink on September 27, 1996.
Releases
This version was localized into English under the title Ogre Battle: Limited Edition by Atlus USA in July 1997.
Releases
The Japan-only Sega Saturn port was developed and published by Riverhillsoft on November 1, 1996.
Reception
Originally planned to have a relatively small 200,000 copy print run, encouragement by Nintendo after a positive press showing had Matsuno persuading Quest to double that number.
Reception
The game sold through all 400,000 copies shortly after release, turning it into a commercial success.
Reception
The North American printing by Enix was limited, apparently just 25,000 units, selling out quickly and prompting several reorders.
Reception
It consequently became a collector's item, with unboxed cartridges selling for over $150 each in 1997.
Reception

GamePro ' s Scary Larry gave it a mixed review, commenting that the game is "unique", but that the gameplay consists largely of tedious war simulation management, offering no direct control over the combat.
Reception
He concluded that, with "13 endings, engrossing gameplay, and a wizard's bag full of secrets, Ogre Battle is a must-buy for RPG fans, whether or not you played the 16-bit version".
Reception
Ogre Battle was listed as the #180 best game made on a Nintendo System in a "Top 200 Games" list published by Nintendo Power.
Reception
In 2018, Complex named Ogre Battle number 34 on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Reception
IGN ranked the game 41st in its Top 100 SNES Games.

sfes_tactics_ogrr.title: Tactics Ogre
sents: lead
Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together is a 1995 tactical role-playing game developed and published by Quest Corporation for the Super Famicom.
lead
It was later ported to the Sega Saturn (1996) and the PlayStation (1997), the latter released in North America in 1998 by Atlus USA.
lead

The second entry in the Ogre Battle series, the story takes place in the war-torn kingdom of Valeria, where protagonist Denim Powell works in a local resistance force against occupying powers, ending up caught in the ethnic conflicts driving the war.
lead
Battles are turn-based, taking place on grid-based maps from an overhead perspective with a focus on positioning and using character class abilities.
lead
Production lasted two and a half years, with Ogre Battle creator Yasumi Matsuno acting as director, writer and lead designer.
lead
The storyline was inspired by conflicts in Europe and Asia, based heavily in personal and political drama over the fantasy-themed narrative of Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen.
lead
The gameplay, inspired by the video game Solstice, uses a chess-inspired combat system in contrast with the real-time battles of its predecessor.
lead
Hiroshi Minagawa was art director, while the characters were designed by Akihiko Yoshida.
Gameplay
An ability unique to the lead character is "Persuade", which has a chance of recruiting enemy units in battle.
Gameplay
The narrative's branches occur in its first three chapters, with events coming back together for the final chapter's events before playing out an ending based on earlier decisions.
Synopsis

Survivors of Tartare's Dark Knights use the stolen Zenobian sword Brunhild to break the seal on a portal leading to the realm of Asmodeus, attempting to use its power to repel Denim's forces but are instead killed.
Development

The production of Tactics Ogre began at series developer and publisher Quest Corporation following the unexpected commercial success of Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen upon its 1993 release.
Development
The concept for Tactics Ogre was in place by 1992, though Matsuno's team had begun work on an untitled 3D action title which was abandoned when Quest Corporation requested a sequel to Ogre Battle.
Development
Memory limitations were a constant issue, with walking and running animations being the only ones that could be on-screen at all times.
Development
The switch from real-time to turn-based tactics was born from Matsuno's boredom with the first game's systems, a situation he compared to the differing paces and audiences for Alien and Aliens.
Development
The quarter-view perspective was directly inspired by Solstice, a game Minagawa enjoyed.
Development
Minagawa created a prototype design which he showed Matsuno, which formed the technical foundation for Tactics Ogre.
Development
The 3D-style levels were created using the custom-built Hermit technology, which could create large-scale levels based on positional data using a small amount of system memory.
Development
The battle system was inspired by chess.
Scenario
Inspired by the acceptance of involved storylines with the Final Fantasy series, Matsuno decided to create a "thoroughly written scenario".
Scenario
The initial pitch included the first chapter's narrative split, a conversation scene between Hamilton and Tartare, and Hamilton's fate.
Scenario
Story, system and tutorial text totalled 300,000 characters, the memory for which had been set aside at the start of production with a large scenario in mind.
Scenario
While March of the Black Queen was the fifth chapter, Matsuno felt the gameplay of Tactics Ogre was a poor fit for the sixth chapter which would have directly continued the first game's narrative.
Scenario
The portrayal of ethnic conflict was fairly rare in Japanese games of the time.
Scenario
Rather than focusing only on ethnicity, Matsuno wrote the scenario to show how a conflict based on any differences between groups could be resolved.
Scenario
The implementation of multiple story routes was inspired by sound novels and gamebooks of the time.
Scenario
The originally-planned protagonist was Hamilton, but after Matsuno created the character of Denim he focused the story around him.
Scenario
Denim's and Vice's names were respectively inspired by the material denim and the clothing brand Levi's, connecting to their origin in the world's lower social ranks.
Scenario
While originally considering the Chaos route to be the canon series of events, he later summarized the endings as alternate coexisting timelines with no "correct" choice.
Scenario
Matsuno originally planned for more divergence in the story paths, but memory limitations meant these and other systems relating to unit loyalty were trimmed down.
Scenario
The variations in Denim's endings as Valeria's king were dictated by a hidden algorithm of how the different factions viewed Denim, a version of Ogre Battle ' s Chaos Frame.
Scenario
A cheat was included in the final game to show it through the Warren Report screen, but Matsuno lost the memo describing it and was only found by fans in 2014 through data mining.
Music
The music was composed by Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata, who had previously worked on the first Ogre Battle.
Music
A soundtrack album, featuring the original sound tracks on the first disc and in-game midi versions on the other two discs, was published by Datam Polystar on October 25, 1995.
Music
Tracks from Tactics Ogre were featured in the compilation album Ogre: Grand Repeat, published by Datam Polystar on October 25, 1996.
Release
Tactics Ogre was released in Japan on October 6, 1995, eighteen months after its initial announcement due to Matsuno wanting further polish in the character animations.
Release
The game's subtitle was inspired by the song of the same name by British rock band Queen.
Release
This version was re-released in Japan for Virtual Console on the Wii U on January 30, 2009.
Release
A Virtual Console version for New Nintendo 3DS was released on November 21, 2016.
Release
It was ported to and published on the Sega Saturn by Riverhillsoft on December 13, 1996.
Release
Further unique music was also created for the different endings.
Release
A PlayStation port was developed by Kuusou Kagaku and published by Artdink on September 25, 1997.
Release
Artdink reissued this version in Japan on December 2, 2000.
Release
It was released in North America on May 6, 1998, dropping the original subtitle.
Release

The Super Famicom original was never released outside Japan, a fact attributed to the console's waning lifespan, its complexity in narrative and mechanics, and a lack of interest from Western players.
Release
A fan translation of the Super Famicom version, which transcribed the PlayStation script using a patch, was released by translation group Aeon Genesis on April 25, 2010.
Release
A fan translation of the Saturn version, which transcribed the PlayStation Portable script, was released on February 27, 2023.
Reception
The Super Famicom release has sold over 500,000 copies in Japan.
Reception
The Saturn version had sold over 70,000 units by February 1997, making it one of the console's best sellers at the time.
Reception
Review aggregate website GameRankings gave the PlayStation release a score of just over 81%, based on six reviews.
Reception
The Super Famicom version was awarded Best Import Strategy Game of 1995 by gaming magazine GameFan.
Reception
In March 2006, the Japanese Famitsu magazine readers voted on their 100 all-time favorite games, and Tactics Ogre was named number seven.
Reception
In 2017, IGN placed Tactics Ogre as the 20th best RPG of all time, citing the mature themes, and multiple story paths and endings.
Reception
In 2019, Famitsu conducted a poll of over 7000 readers to determine the best games of the Heisei era (1989-2019), with Tactics Ogre placing 15th.
Reception
In a retrospective of tactical RPGs for the PlayStation, 1Up.com ranked Tactics Ogre as one of the best available at the time.
Legacy
Matsuno left Quest in 1995 once Tactics Ogre was completed, eventually joining Square (later Square Enix).
Legacy
Together with a number of Tactics Ogre staff members who followed him, he developed Final Fantasy Tactics (1997) for the PlayStation.
Legacy
Final Fantasy Tactics proved a success, and Matsuno went on to create multiple titles set within its fictional universe of Ivalice including Vagrant Story (2000) and Final Fantasy XII (2007).
Legacy

The latter would be his final project for Square Enix, as he departed the company in 2005 citing ill health, though he would return in later years to collaborate with Square Enix on a freelance basis.
Legacy

While he left Quest after completing Tactics Ogre, Matsuno had been planning a third Ogre Battle title which would blend gameplay elements from the first Ogre Battle and Tactics Ogre into a mainstream experience.
Legacy
Minagawa would reassemble most of the original staff, including Matsuno, for a PlayStation Portable remake of Tactics Ogre, released in 2010 in Japan and 2011 in the West.
Legacy
A new update of the game was released on November 11, 2022, Tactics Ogre Reborn.
Legacy
It was made available for PC, Playstation 4 & 5, and Nintendo Switch.

sfes_fire_emblum_japan.title: Fire Emblem

First release: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light April 20, 1990

sents: lead
Fire Emblem is a Japanese fantasy tactical role-playing game franchise developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo.
lead
First produced and published for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1990, the series currently consists of seventeen core entries and five spinoffs.
lead
The core gameplay revolves around discrete battles between the player's team of characters and enemy non-player characters across grid-based maps.
lead
The player and enemy each take turns moving their characters across the map and having them perform combat-based actions.
lead
The games also feature a story and characters similar to traditional role-playing video games, and occasionally social simulation aspects as well.
lead

A notable aspect of gameplay is the permanent death of characters in battle, rendering them unusable upon being defeated, although this aspect of the game can be turned off starting from Fire Emblem: New Mystery of the Emblem onwards.
lead
The series' title refers to the "Fire Emblem", a recurring element usually portrayed as a royal weapon or shield representing the power of war and dragons.
lead
The development of the first game began as a dōjin project by Shouzou Kaga and three other developers, and its success prompted the development of further games in the series.
Gameplay
Each character has a specific character class which gives them set abilities and affects how far they can move across the field; some classes have innate skills unique to them.
Gameplay
During a battle, a character gains experience points by performing actions, such as attacking an enemy, healing an ally, or slaying a foe, which typically offers the most experience points.
Gameplay
Most games use a Weapon Durability system: after being used a certain number of times, a character's weapon will break.
Story and themes
The continents of Archanea and Valentia are the settings of Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, Gaiden, Mystery of the Emblem, and Awakening, and were the planned setting for Fire Emblem 64.
Story and themes
Genealogy of the Holy War and Thracia 776 are set in Jugdral, which is distantly connected with Archanea and Valentia, while The Blazing Blade and The Binding Blade take place in Elibe.
Story and themes

In Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light and other games set in Archanea, it is a shield inset with five magical gems named after its connection to dragons and weapons of war, being the "emblem of flame".
Development and history

The first Fire Emblem game, Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, was originally never intended as a commercial game, defined by creator Shouzou Kaga as a dōjin project with three other job-holding students.
Development and history
Kaga worked on the Fire Emblem series until Thracia 776, when he left Nintendo and began development on Tear Ring Saga for the PlayStation.
Development and history
After Thracia 776, the Fire Emblem series had several releases on portable devices.
Development and history
In 2001, Marth and Roy, from Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light and The Binding Blade respectively, appeared as playable characters in Super Smash Bros.
Development and history
By 2010, the series was suffering from declining sales and Nintendo told Intelligent Systems that if their next Fire Emblem failed to sell above 250,000 units, the series would be canceled.
Development and history

As the only music composer at Intelligent Systems when Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light was in production, she acted as both composer and sound director, up until Thracia 776, when she left the company to become a freelancer after completing the score for Paper Mario.
Development and history
Katsuyoshi, who was unsatisfied with his work on the series, stepped down for Thracia 776.
Development and history
The designer for Thracia 776 was Mayumi Hirota, whose brief tenure with the series ended when she left Intelligent Systems with Kaga after the game's completion.
Main series
The first entry in the series, Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, was released in 1990 for the Japanese Famicom.
Main series
A second game for the Famicom, Fire Emblem Gaiden, was released in 1992.
Main series
In 1994, Mystery of the Emblem was released for the Super Famicom, containing both a remake of Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light and a sequel of the first game.
Main series
Two more games were released for the Super Famicom in 1996 and 1999 respectively: Genealogy of the Holy War and Thracia 776.
Main series
The next entry released was The Binding Blade in 2002 for the Game Boy Advance.
Main series
It was released overseas under the title Fire Emblem in 2003 in North America and 2004 in Europe, becoming the first official release of the Fire Emblem series in these regions.
Main series
Melee for the Gamecube in 2001, and the earlier release (and success) of Advance Wars in the West, prompting Intelligent Systems and Nintendo to finally release Fire Emblem in the West.
Main series
The final entry for the Game Boy Advance, The Sacred Stones, was released in 2004 in Japan, and in 2005 in North America and Europe.
Main series
The ninth installment in the series, Path of Radiance, was released worldwide on the GameCube in 2005.
Main series
It was the first Fire Emblem game to feature 3D graphics, voice acting, and full-motion animated cutscenes.
Main series
A direct sequel to Path of Radiance, Radiant Dawn was released for the Wii in 2007 in Japan and North America, and 2008 in Europe.
Main series
In 2008, the series returned to handheld systems with two releases for the Nintendo DS.
Main series
Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon, an expanded remake of the first game, was released in 2008 in Japan and Europe, and 2009 in North America.
Main series
Shadow Dragon makes use of unique DS features unavailable to the Famicom and introduced new characters, added additional story elements, revamped mechanics, and modernized graphics.
Main series
A Japanese-only entry, New Mystery of the Emblem, was released in 2010 for the DS as an expanded remake of Mystery of the Emblem.
Main series
The series moved to the Nintendo 3DS with Fire Emblem Awakening, the thirteenth game in the series, released in 2012 in Japan and 2013 in North America and Europe.
Main series
The second entry for the Nintendo 3DS, Fates, was released in June 2015 in Japan, February 2016 in North America, and in May 2016 for Europe and Australia.
Main series
A third entry, Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia, was released on the Nintendo 3DS in April 2017 in Japan and in North America and Europe the following month.
Main series
Echoes is an enhanced remake of Gaiden, maintaining many of the unique features of Gaiden while revamping the graphics and script, and adding several ease-of-play improvements.
Main series
A Fire Emblem game was announced for the Nintendo Switch during a Fire Emblem focused Nintendo Direct in January 2017.
Main series
The game was officially revealed as Fire Emblem: Three Houses during the Nintendo Direct presentation at E3 2018, and was released in July 2019.
Main series
Fire Emblem Engage, a second entry for Nintendo Switch, was announced during a September 2022 Nintendo Direct and released in January 2023.
Spin-offs and cameos
In 1997, an episodic prequel to Mystery of the Emblem titled BS Fire Emblem: Archanea Senki-hen was released through Satellaview.
Spin-offs and cameos
A crossover with the Shin Megami Tensei series, Tokyo Mirage Sessions ♯FE, was released in December 2015 in Japan and worldwide in June 2016 for the Wii U.
Spin-offs and cameos
On January 17, 2020, an enhanced version titled Tokyo Mirage Sessions ♯FE Encore was released on Nintendo Switch.
Spin-offs and cameos
Fire Emblem Heroes is a spin-off gacha game for Android and iOS, and was released in February 2017 for mobile devices.
Spin-offs and cameos
A crossover with the Dynasty Warriors series, Fire Emblem Warriors, was released for the New Nintendo 3DS and Nintendo Switch in 2017.
Spin-offs and cameos
A second Warriors game, based on Three Houses, and titled Fire Emblem Warriors: Three Hopes was announced in a Nintendo Direct on February 9, 2022 and released on June 24, 2022.
Cancelled games
A Fire Emblem game was initially in development for the Nintendo 64 and its peripheral 64DD.
Cancelled games
Originally codenamed Fire Emblem 64, it was first revealed by Shigeru Miyamoto in 1997.
Cancelled games

Ultimately, due to poor sales for the 64DD and internal structural changes at Intelligent Systems, Fire Emblem 64 was cancelled in 2000 and development shifted to what would become Fire Emblem: The Binding Blade.
Cancelled games
Work done for Fire Emblem 64 was incorporated into The Binding Blade.
Cancelled games

An additional RTS-based game for the Wii was planned and would have been released after Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn, but after trial and error and an unfocused development schedule, the project was cancelled.
Cancelled games
Intelligent Systems never planned a Fire Emblem game for the Wii U.
Cancelled games
Nintendo producer Hitoshi Yamagami said such a game would need to sell 700,000 copies to be profitable.
Cancelled games
A rumored Fire Emblem remake for the Nintendo 3DS was being developed by AlphaDream, but was cancelled following the company's bankruptcy surfaced in late 2019.
Cancelled games

According to the reports, it was one of the many video games that had been in development, but were ultimately scrapped for the platform, with many speculating those projects could be moved to the Nintendo Switch.
Reception
Sales in Japan were the highest with Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light but progressively declined with future games, which sold 329,087; 324,699; 776,338; 498,216 and 106,108 copies respectively.
Reception
As of 2002, total sales had reached over two million copies.
Reception
Awakening topped the total sales of both Radiant Dawn and the Mystery of the Emblem remake in its first week.
Reception
It went on to sell 2.35 million copies worldwide and become the best-selling Fire Emblem game in Western territories at the time.
Reception
In 2007, a Japanese public poll named Mystery of the Emblem as one of the country's All Time Top 100 video games.
Reception

In 2014, Destructoid writer Chris Carter praised the series' mechanics, and at the same time chose Mystery of the Emblem, Path of Radiance, and Awakening in his list of the five best games in the series.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
The game bore multiple similarities to the Fire Emblem series, and Nintendo filed a lawsuit against Tirnanog for copyright infringement.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
The first suit failed, and the court ruled in Tirnanog's favor.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
Nintendo filed a second lawsuit, and this time was awarded a cash settlement of ¥76 million.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
Nintendo attempted taking a third lawsuit to the Japanese Supreme Court in 2005, but the second ruling was upheld.
In other media
A short, two episode original video animation series based on Mystery of the Emblem released in 1996.
In other media
These anime episodes were released in North America in 1998, five years before The Blazing Blade was localized, making them the first official Fire Emblem media to be released in the region.
In other media

Two trading card games have been made with the Fire Emblem franchise: Fire Emblem: Trading Card Game, which was released from 2001 – 2006, and Fire Emblem 0 (Cipher), which was released in 2015 and was discontinued in late 2020 with the twenty second expansion pack being the last one.

sfes_super_boomerman.title: Super Bomberman

Mode(s): Single-player, co-op, multiplayer (up to four players via Super Multitap)

sents: lead
Super Bomberman is an action, maze game, part of the Bomberman series, released for the Super NES in 1993.
lead
It is the first in the series to be released in Europe keeping the Bomberman title instead of being called Dynablaster or Eric and the Floaters.
lead

Super Bomberman spawned its own series of sequels; including Super Bomberman 2, Super Bomberman 3, Super Bomberman 4, Super Bomberman 5, Super Bomberman R, Super Bomberman R Online, and Super Bomberman R 2.
Gameplay
The screen shows the top down view of a grid of 143 (13 x 11) squares.
Gameplay
The grid restricts the movement of characters so they can only move horizontally or vertically around the screen.
Gameplay
Most levels start with the grid being partially filled with destructible soft walls.
Normal Game
Each world has eight stages with the last stage being a boss fight.
Normal Game
The player makes progress through the game by clearing all the enemies from the stage and then exiting via a door that is hidden under one of the destructible walls.
Normal Game
World 5 differs from the rest in that the player fights robot Bombermen in an arena.
Battle Mode
Because the standard SNES control deck only has two controller ports, in order to play with more than two human players, a multitap device is required.
Battle Mode
All bomb blasts are instantly fatal in Battle Mode.If one of the players are the last player remaining they win the round and receive a gold trophy.
Battle Mode
The overall winner is the first person to win a set number of gold trophies (i.e. the first person to win a certain number of rounds).
Battle Mode
The number of trophies needed is configurable when starting the game and ranges from 1 to 5.
Battle Mode
The Speed Round, which is Stage 12, is considered to be the most competitive as it requires a large amount of skill to control the fast-paced players and bomb detonation.
Battle Mode
During a Battle Game, the effects of all the items last for one battle only.
Battle Mode
Only items such as Ice Cream, Pancakes, Apples (Etc.) give points and other items such as a clock that adds additional time to the game time.
Super Multitap
Super Bomberman was originally bundled with a multitap device to allow more than two players to play simultaneously.
Super Multitap
Hudson Soft later released a second multitap (the Super Multitap 2) on its own for people that had purchased Super Bomberman unbundled, or one of the other multitap enabled games.
Super Multitap
Eventually there were 54 Super NES games that utilised the multitap.
Reception
Super Bomberman was met with very positive reception from critics on both the Super Nintendo Entertainment System and J2ME.
Reception

The four reviewers of Electronic Gaming Monthly gave Super Bomberman a unanimous score of 9 out of 10 and their " Game of the Month " award, and asserted that the game's addictiveness is on the same order as that of Tetris.
Reception
Game Informer ranked it the 90th best game ever made in 2001.
Reception
In 2011, IGN rated the game 49th on their "Top 100 SNES Games of All Time".
Reception

In 2018, Complex rated Super Bomberman 37th on their The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time and they opined the game is "probably best four-player game for the SNES." The game went on to sell over 918,484 copies in Japan alone and it also received a Platinum Editor's Choice.

sfes_super_boomerman_2.title: Super Bomberman 2

Programmer(s): B. Hanawa Teturou Kiyomoto Toshiyuki Suzuki
Mode(s): Single-player, multiplayer (up to four players via Super Multitap)

sents: lead
Super Bomberman 2 is a video game developed by Produce! and Hudson Soft and released on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It was released in Japan on April 28, 1994, in North America later the same year, and in Europe on February 23, 1995.
lead
It is the second installment of the Super Bomberman series, part of the larger Bomberman franchise, and the only installment without a 2-player story mode (although one was originally planned).
Story Mode
There are 5 worlds total, and at the end of each world is a boss.
Story Mode
Each boss is first battled on foot before retreating into a giant machine.
Multiplayer
In Battle Mode, 2 players (4 with a multitap) can face off against one another in one of 10 arenas designed specifically for multiplayer.
Story
5 evil cyborgs called the Five Dastardly Bombers are bent on taking over the universe.
Reception
Next Generation reviewed the game, rating it five stars out of five, and stated that "This is truly God's perfect party game."
Reception

Next Generation ' s 1996 lexicon of video game terms included the joke entries "Bomb-o'clock" and "Bombaholic", in which they referred to Super Bomberman 2 as "the videogame of choice for game developers everywhere".
Reception
Later that year they named it the 3rd best game of all time, saying it "epitomizes the Japanese art of taking a ludicrously simple concept, and then executing that concept faultlessly.

sfes_super_boomerman_5.title: Super Bomberman 5

Programmer(s): Hiroki Toyama Masato Tobisawa Mittu Takahashi
Artist(s): Kozue Sato Naoto Yoshimi Shoji Mizuno
Mode(s): Single-player, co-op, multiplayer (up to five players via Super Multitap)

sents: lead
Super Bomberman 5 is a video game released by Hudson Soft in early 1997.
lead
It is the fifth installment of the Super Bomberman series and the final Bomberman game to be released on the Super Famicom.
lead
The game was released in two variations: a standard cartridge and a gold cartridge, which was sold through CoroCoro Comic.
lead
The gold cartridge included extra maps in battle mode.
Gameplay
The single-player portion of Super Bomberman 5 is nonlinear, giving players a choice of which level they'd like to complete next.
Gameplay
Depending on your path, you can accumulate 100% of completion.
Gameplay
After finishing 100%, the game map is reset, which allows player to finish the maps 200%.
Gameplay
In multiplayer, there are nine characters to choose from, and over 10 maps to play on (though the extra three maps in the gold version can be unlocked in the normal cart as well).
Gameplay
A create-a-character mode, which is unique to Super Bomberman 5, lets players choose their character and color and allows them a number of points.
Gameplay
If you enter in password menu (Options → Password) 0413, the maps in battle mode will change.
Gameplay
There are also 10 playable characters in Battle Mode, nine of which are bosses in Normal Mode.
Development and release
3 variants of this game have been released, a standard cartridge and a gold cartridge, which was sold through CoroCoro Comic.

sfes_zombies_ate_my_landlord.title: Zombies Ate My Neighbors
sents: lead
Zombies Ate My Neighbors is a run and gun video game developed by LucasArts and published by Konami for the Super NES and Sega Genesis consoles in 1993.
lead
One or two players take control of the protagonists, Zeke and Julie, in order to rescue the titular neighbors from monsters often seen in horror movies.
lead
Aiding them in this task are a variety of weapons and power-ups that can be used to battle the numerous enemies in each level.
lead

Various elements and aspects of horror movies are referenced in the game with some of its more violent content being censored in various territories such as Europe and Australia, where it is known only as Zombies.
lead
While not a great commercial success, the game was well-received for its graphical style, humor and deep gameplay.
lead
It spawned a sequel, Ghoul Patrol, released in 1994.
lead

Both games were re-released as part of Lucasfilm Classic Games: Zombies Ate My Neighbors and Ghoul Patrol for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Xbox One and Microsoft Windows by Disney Interactive in June 2021.
Gameplay

In each of the 48 stages, which includes seven optional bonus levels, the players must rescue numerous types of neighbors, including barbecue chefs, teachers, babies, tourists, archeologists, soldiers, dogs, and cheerleaders.
Gameplay
Each level has at most ten neighbors, and each neighbor type is worth a different number of points.
Development
Zombies Ate My Neighbors was originally developed by LucasArts.
Development
The monsters in the game are based on classic horror films released in the 1950s and more modern films like Friday the 13th and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre.
Development
The North American SNES game was later released with a variant cover art in limited quantities.
Release
In October 2009, the Super NES version of Zombies Ate My Neighbors was re-released for the Wii Virtual Console.
Release

In May 2021, the game and its sequel were announced for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Xbox One and Windows, with a port developed by Dotemu and co-published by Disney Interactive and Lucasfilm Games.
Release
Lucasfilm Classic Games: Zombies Ate My Neighbors and Ghoul Patrol was released on June 29, 2021.
Reception
Although not an immediate success, Zombies Ate My Neighbors became a cult classic years after its release.
Reception
Upon its release, it got above average praise, earning an 84.5% on Gamerankings.com.
Reception

Mike Seiblier of Sega-16 said the variety of weapons shows off the game's "tongue in cheek nature by giving you weapons and items like silverware, dishes, soda can grenades, a weed whacker, keys, bazookas as well as health packs".
Reception
The game has been regarded as one of "the most requested additions to the VC system even before the Wii launch".
Accolades
Mega ranked the game 42nd in their "Top 50 Mega Drive Games" in 1994.
Accolades
They called the game "Incredibly fun and funny." In 2018, Complex listed the game 48th on its "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time" list.
Accolades
In 2017, GamesRadar rated the game 21st on their "Best Sega Genesis/Mega Drive Games of All Time" In 1995, Total! ranked the game 43rd in their Top 100 SNES Games.
Accolades
In 1996, GamesMaster listed the Mega Drive version ninth in their "The GamesMaster Mega Drive Top 10."
Legacy
In 1997, LucasArts released a game for the PlayStation and the Sega Saturn titled Herc's Adventures, which uses the same basic gameplay format and mechanics as Zombies Ate My Neighbors.
Legacy
Programmer Chris Long cited Zombies Ate My Neighbors as a major influence on his 1997 game Swagman.
Legacy
Day of the Tentacle, another game developed by LucasArts, is referenced in Zombies Ate My Neighbors through a secret level.
Legacy

Comparisons to the game Dead Rising, released for the Xbox 360 in 2006, have been drawn, Lucas Thomas of IGN saying: " Zombies Ate My Neighbors is basically a comical 16-bit template for the new Xbox 360 release, Dead Rising.
Sequels and spin-offs
A sequel entitled Ghoul Patrol was released in 1994, which was also well-received.
Sequels and spin-offs
Originally, Ghoul Patrol was not intended to be released as a sequel to Zombies Ate My Neighbors, but was re-worked as such to increase sales.
Sequels and spin-offs
An unofficial, spiritual sequel, Demons Ate My Neighbors, has been in development by Tuned-Out Games since 2020.

sfes_pilotwangs.title: Pilotwings (video game)

Programmer(s): Shuhei Kato Hajime Yajima Takumi Kawagoe

sents: lead
Pilotwings is a flight simulation video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
The game was originally released in Japan in December 1990, shortly after the launch of the Super Famicom in the country.
lead
It was also released as a launch title for the SNES in August 1991 in North America, with a European release following in 1992.
lead
In Pilotwings, the player attempts to earn pilot licenses through lessons in light plane flight, hang gliding, skydiving, and the use of a rocket belt.
lead
Bonus stages and levels involving an attack helicopter are also available.
lead
Each event offers unique controls and gameplay mechanics.
lead
To increase the realism of the game's flight simulation, the developers extensively utilized the SNES's Mode 7 capability, which mimics 3D graphics by rotating and scaling flat objects.
lead
The game was well-received upon its release, largely thanks to its graphical presentation.
Gameplay
Each area features 2—4 events, which may be played in any order.
Gameplay

In the skydiving, rocket belt, and hang glider modes, landing on moving platforms rewards players with a perfect score, and a bonus stage for extra points may be earned by falling into the water of a target area.
Development
Nintendo EAD completed Pilotwings and two other games (Super Mario World and F-Zero) within 15 months of the debut of the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
Development
Pilotwings was released in Japan on December 21, 1990, one month after the system's launch, and was later released in North America in August 1991 as a launch title.
Development
Six tracks from the game, including a rearranged version of the skydiving theme, appeared on the Nintendo Super Famicom Game Music album, released in Japan on March 4, 1992.
Development
Six piano -arranged versions of songs from the game were included on the Nintendo Super Famicom Game Music: Fun Together with Beyer CD, which was released in Japan on November 30, 1993.
Development
A flight simulator game resembling Pilotwings called Dragonfly was shown during the official unveiling of the SNES to the Japanese press on November 21, 1988.
Development
The game was used to demonstrate the system's Mode 7 graphics system, which allows rotation, scaling, and other effects to be used on flat images to create a 3D effect.
Reception and legacy
The game drew praise for its presentation, with publications describing the game's use of Mode 7 graphics as "stunning" and "jaw-dropping".
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings was generally seen as a showpiece title for the Super NES, demonstrating its Mode 7 features, built-in sprite scaling, and high-end sound chip in a conspicuous manner.
Reception and legacy
Official Nintendo Magazine remarked in 2009, "This early SNES title is still enjoyable enough to be considered a true classic."
Reception and legacy
In February 2006, Pilotwings was listed as the 153rd best game on a Nintendo console by Nintendo Power.
Reception and legacy
IGN listed it in their "Top 100 Games of All Time" at number 74 in 2003, and at number 91 in 2007.
Reception and legacy
It was named the 16th best game on the Super NES by GameDaily in 2008, while Game Informer listed it at number 131 in its "Top 200 Games of All Time" in 2009.
Reception and legacy
Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game number 61 on its February 2009 "100 Best Nintendo Games" list.
Reception and legacy
In April 1996, Super Play listed it as the tenth greatest game for the Super NES.
Reception and legacy
In 2018, Complex rated the game 77th on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Reception and legacy
In 1995, Total! placed the game 20th on their Top 100 SNES Games.
Reception and legacy
In 1996, GamesMaster listed Pilotwings 30th in its "Top 100 Games of All Time."
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings sold over two million copies worldwide by 1996.
Reception and legacy
A sequel, Pilotwings 64, was released for the Nintendo 64 in 1996 as a launch title for its respective system.
Reception and legacy
A second sequel for the Nintendo 64, which showed off the console's capabilities, was cancelled due to lack of development resources within Nintendo.
Reception and legacy
In 2003, it was announced that Factor 5 was working on a GameCube incarnation of the Pilotwings series.
Reception and legacy
However, an anonymous blogger claimed in late 2009 that Factor 5 had indeed finished working on it, but that Nintendo was not confident in publishing it.
Reception and legacy
Nintendo finally announced a new title in the series, the Nintendo 3DS title Pilotwings Resort, at E3 2010.
Reception and legacy
The new title was released as a launch title for the 3DS in North America on March 27, 2011.
Reception and legacy
The game has been featured in the Game On historical exhibition organized by the Barbican Centre, including a display at the Science Museum in London in 2007.
Reception and legacy
Nintendo re-released Pilotwings on the Wii Virtual Console service in PAL regions and North America in 2009 and in Japan in 2010, and then on the Wii U Virtual Console in 2013.
Reception and legacy
On September 5, 2019, the game became available on the Nintendo Switch Online service for the Nintendo Switch.

sfes_f_zilch.title: F-Zero (video game)
sents: lead
F-Zero is a 1990 racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
It was released in Japan on November 21, 1990, in North America in August 1991, and in Europe in 1992.
lead
F-Zero is the first game in the F-Zero series and was a launch game for the SNES.
lead
F-Zero was rereleased for the Virtual Console service on various Nintendo platforms and as part of the Super NES Classic Edition in 2017.
lead
The game takes place in the year 2560, where multi-billionaires with lethargic lifestyles created a new form of entertainment based on Formula One races called "F-Zero".
lead
The player can choose between one of four characters in the game, each with their respective hovercar.
lead
The player can race against computer-controlled characters in 15 tracks divided into three leagues.
lead
F-Zero has been acknowledged by critics for setting the standard for the racing genre and the creation of its futuristic subgenre.
Gameplay
Each has their own selectable hovercar, and each hovercar has its own unique performance abilities.
Gameplay
An on-screen display will be shaded green to indicate that a boost can be used; however, the player is limited to saving up to three at a time.
Gameplay
Unlike most F-Zero games, there are three iterations of Mute City that show it in either a day, evening, or night setting with slightly different configurations.
Gameplay
In BS F-Zero 2, Mute City IV continued the theme with an early morning setting.
Setting
F-Zero is set in the year 2560, when humanity's multiple encounters with alien life forms had resulted in the expansion of Earth's social framework.
Setting
The multi-billionaires who earned their wealth through intergalactic trade were mainly satisfied with their lifestyles, although most coveted more entertainment in their lives.
Setting
The game introduced the first set of F-Zero racers: Captain Falcon, Dr.
Development and releases
