F-Zero was released alongside the SNES in Japan on November 21, 1990, in North America in August 1991, and in Europe in 1992.
Development and releases
Only it and Super Mario World were initially available for the Japanese launch.
Development and releases
Takaya Imamura, one of the art designers for the game, was surprised to be able to so freely design F-Zero ' s characters and courses as he wanted since it was his first game.
Development and releases

Mode 7 is a form of texture mapping available on the SNES which allows a raster graphical plane to be rotated and scaled freely, simulating the appearance of 3D environments without processing any polygons.
Development and releases
The Mode 7 rendering applied in F-Zero consists of a single-layer which is scaled and rotated around the vehicle.
Development and releases
1UP.com 's Jeremy Parish stated that F-Zero and Pilotwings "existed almost entirely for the sake of showing off" as they outclassed the competition.
Development and releases
The game was downloadable over the Nintendo Power peripheral in Japan and was also released as a demo onto the Nintendo Super System in 1991.
Development and releases
An F-Zero jazz album was released on March 25, 1992, in Japan by Tokuma Japan Communications.
Development and releases
The game was re-released for the Virtual Console service on the Wii in late 2006, then on the Wii U in February 2013, followed by its New Nintendo 3DS release in March 2016.
Development and releases
Nintendo re-released F-Zero in September 2017 as part of the company's Super NES Classic Edition.
Development and releases
It was also later included as one of the 20 SNES games for Nintendo Switch Online subscribers in September 2019.
Reception
F-Zero was widely lauded by game critics for its graphical realism, and has been called the fastest and most fluid pseudo-3D racing game of its time for home systems.
Reception
Eurogamer 's Tom Bramwell commented "this abundance of Mode 7 was unheard of" for the SNES.
Reception
IGN 's Peer Schneider assured readers F-Zero was one of the few 16-bit era video games to "perfectly combine presentation and functionality to create a completely new gaming experience".
Reception
Kasavin felt it offered exceptional gameplay, with "a perfect balance of pick-up-and-play accessibility and sheer depth".
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine called the game "Blisteringly fast, seriously challenging and insanely fun", ranking the game 66th on a list of greatest Nintendo games.
Legacy
IGN credits the game for having inspired the future creation of numerous racing games inside and out of the futuristic subgenre, including the Wipeout series and Daytona USA.
Legacy

Toshihiro Nagoshi, President of Sega 's Amusement Vision, stated in 2002 that F-Zero "actually taught me what a game should be" and that it served as an influence for him to create Daytona USA and other racing games.
Legacy
In 1995, Total! rated the game 50th on their Top 100 SNES Games summarizing: "It’s old and basic but this garish futuristic offering still pushes your driving skills to the limit.
Legacy

In 1997 Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it the 18th best console video game of all time, citing its tight controls, the different handling characteristics of the four craft, and the competitive opponent AI.
Legacy

IGN ranked F-Zero as the 91st best game ever in 2003, discussing its originality at time of release and as the 97th best game ever in 2005, describing it as still "respected as one of the all-time top racers".
Legacy
In 2018, Complex listed F-Zero 31st on its "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time."
Legacy

Nintendo initially developed the sequel of the first F-Zero game for the SNES, although it was broadcast in several versions on the St.GIGA subscription service for the Satellaview attachment of the Super Famicom instead.
Legacy
The sequel was released under the Japanese names of BS F-Zero Grand Prix and BS F-Zero Grand Prix 2 during the mid-1990s.
Legacy
BS F-Zero Grand Prix contained a new track along with the original 15 tracks from the SNES game and four different playable vehicles.
Legacy
IGN states BS F-Zero Grand Prix 2 features one new league containing five tracks, a Grand Prix and a Practice mode.
Legacy

Although the F-Zero franchise made the transition to 3D graphics on the Nintendo 64 with the release of F-Zero X in 1998, Mode 7 graphical effects continued to be used for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) installments Maximum Velocity (2001), GP Legend (2003), and Climax (2004).
Legacy
The free online racing video game, F-Zero 99 (2023), was released through the Nintendo Switch Online (NSO) subscription service.
Legacy

In a similar vein to the NSO exclusives like Tetris 99 and Pac-Man 99, the game reuses graphical aesthetics and gameplay, and recontextualizes it as an battle royale — players choose the same vehicles and tracks from the 1990 game.

sfes_super_plumber_kart.title: Super Mario Kart
sents: lead
Super Mario Kart is a kart racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
The first game in the Mario Kart series, it was released in Japan and North America in 1992, and in Europe the following year in 1993.
lead
Selling 8.76 million copies worldwide, the game went on to become the fourth best-selling SNES game of all time.
lead
Super Mario Kart was re-released on the Wii 's Virtual Console in 2009, on the Wii U 's Virtual Console in 2013, and on the New Nintendo 3DS 's Virtual Console in 2016.
lead
Nintendo re-released Super Mario Kart in 2017 as part of the company's Super NES Classic Edition.
lead
In Super Mario Kart, the player takes control of one of eight Mario series characters, each with differing capabilities.
lead
In single player mode players can race against computer-controlled characters in 4 multi-race cups consisting of 20 tracks (5 in each cup) over three difficulty levels (50cc, 100cc and 150cc).
lead
During the races, offensive and speed boosting power-ups can be used to gain an advantage.
Gameplay
The goal of the game is to either finish a race ahead of other racers, who are controlled by the computer and other players, or complete a circuit in the fastest time.
Modes
Initially, there are three cups available – the Mushroom Cup, Flower Cup, and Star Cup – at two difficulty levels, 50 cc and 100cc.
Modes
By winning all three of the cups at the 100cc level, a fourth cup – the Special Cup – is unlocked.
Modes
Winning all four cups at 100cc unlocks a new difficulty level, 150cc.
Modes

If a player finishes in the fifth to eighth position, they are "ranked out" and the race must be replayed – at the cost of one of a limited number of lives – until a placing of fourth or above is achieved.
Modes
Points are accrued by finishing in the top four positions in a race; first to fourth place receive nine, six, three and one points.
Modes

The finishing order for that race will then become the starting grid for the next race; for example, if a player finished in first place, then that player will start the next race in the same position.
Modes
The racer with the highest number of points after all five races have been completed wins the cup.
Modes
In time trial mode, players race against the clock through the same tracks that are present in Mario Kart GP mode, attempting to set the fastest time possible.
Modes
Mario Kart GP is the same as in single-player, the only difference being that there are two human-controlled and six computer-controlled drivers.
Modes
Each player starts with three balloons around their kart which can be popped by power-ups fired by the other player.
Modes
The first player to have all three of their balloons popped loses.
Characters
In 2005, Nintendojo called the sprites "not-so-pretty" when they are rendered at a distance, and IGN has commented on the dated look of the game.
Characters

Super Mario Kart was the first game to feature playable characters from the Mario series other than Mario or Luigi in a non-platforming game and the selection and different attributes of the characters is regarded as one of the game's strengths, IGN describing a well-balanced "all-star cast".
Characters

All of the characters present in Super Mario Kart have gone on to appear in later games in the series, except for Donkey Kong Jr. and Koopa Troopa, who have only appeared intermittently after being replaced by Donkey Kong and Wario respectively in Mario Kart 64.
Tracks
Each of the four cups contains five different tracks for a total of twenty unique tracks, additionally there are four unique Battle Mode courses.
Tracks
The tracks have received positive commentary with GameSpy describing them as wonderfully designed and IGN calling them perfect.
Tracks
When naming its top five Mario Kart tracks of all time in 2008, 1UP.com named Battle Mode Course 4 at number three and Rainbow Road – along with its subsequent versions in the series – at number one.
Tracks
The track themes in Super Mario Kart influenced later games in the series; recurring themes that first appeared in Super Mario Kart include haunted tracks, Bowser's Castle and Rainbow Road.
Development

The game did not start out as a Mario series game and the first prototype featured a generic kart racer character; the team decided that characters three heads tall would best suit the design of the karts.
Development
Notable in the development of Super Mario Kart was its use of Mode 7 graphics.
Development
First seen in F-Zero, Mode 7 is a form of texture mapping available on the SNES which allows a plane to be rotated and scaled freely, achieving a pseudo-three-dimensional appearance.
Development
1UP.com have credited the use of Mode 7 with giving the game graphics which at the time of release were considered to be "breathtaking".
Development
Retrospective reflection on the Mode 7 visuals was mixed, with IGN stating that the once revolutionary technology now looks "crude and flickery".
Development
The DSP-1 chip that was used in Super Mario Kart went on to be the most popular DSP chip to be used in SNES games.
Reception

Super Mario Kart received critical acclaim and proved to be a commercial success; it received a Player's Choice release after selling one million copies and went on to sell 8.76 million copies worldwide, becoming the fourth best-selling game ever for the SNES.
Reception
In Japan, it was the top-selling game in September 1992 and became a multi-million seller in 1992, eventually selling a total of 3.82 million in Japan.
Reception
In Europe, it was the top-selling game during the first quarter of 1993, above the Sega Mega Drive titles Sonic the Hedgehog 2 and Streets of Rage 2 during the same period.
Reception
In the United Kingdom, Super Mario Kart was the top-selling Super NES game in February 1993, and it went on to be the seventh best-selling game of 1993 with more than 250,000 sales in the country.
Reception
Aggregate scoring sites GameRankings and MobyGames both give an average of more than 90 percent.
Reception
Another aspect of the game to have been praised is its gameplay, which Thunderbolt has described as the "deepest most addictive... to be found on the SNES console".
Reception
Retrospective reviews of the game have been positive with perfect scores given by review sites including Thunderbolt and HonestGamers.
Reception

In 1995, Total! rated the game 16th on its "Top 100 SNES Games." In 1996, Next Generation listed it as number 37 on their "Top 100 Games of All Time", commenting that the controls are elegantly designed to offer "supreme fun".
Reception
In 1996, GamesMaster ranked the game 16th on their "Top 100 Games of All Time".
Reception

In 1999, Next Generation listed Super Mario Kart as number 7 on their "Top 50 Games of All Time", commenting that, "Imitated a thousand times, but never, ever, equalled, Mario Kart changed the rules for the driving game and gave the world one of the most engrossing and addictive two-player experiences ever".
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it as the 15th best console video game of all time, attributing its higher ranking than Mario Kart 64 (which came in 49th) to its superior track design and powerups.
Reception
IGN ranked it as the 15th best game ever in 2005, describing it as "the original karting masterpiece" and as the 23rd best game ever in 2007, discussing its originality at time of release.
Reception

The Age placed it at number 19 on their list of the 50 best games in 2005 and in 2007 Edge ranked Super Mario Kart at number 14 on a list of their 100 best games, noting its continued influence on video game design.
Reception
Games UK's list of the hundred greatest games of all time which praises the appealing characters and power ups and 1UP.com ' s "Essential 50", a list of the fifty most important games ever made.
Reception
The game placed 13th in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s 100 greatest Nintendo games of all time.
Reception
Guinness World Records ranked it at number 1 on a list of the top 50 console games of all time based on initial impact and lasting legacy.
Reception
Game Informer ranked the game at 35 on their top 100 games of all time in 2001 praising how the game's Mode 7 revolutionized racing games.
Reception
In 2018, Complex listed Super Mario Kart seventh on its "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Reception
In 2019, The Strong National Museum of Play inducted Super Mario Kart to its World Video Game Hall of Fame.
Legacy
In 1994, less than two years after the release of Super Mario Kart, Sega released Sonic Drift; a kart racing game featuring characters from the Sonic the Hedgehog series.
Legacy
Apogee Software released Wacky Wheels for PC and Atari Corporation released Atari Karts for the Atari Jaguar in 1995.
Legacy
Super Mario Kart is credited as being the first non-platforming game to feature multiple playable characters from the Mario franchise.
Legacy
Mario series characters have made cameos in games from other series such as SSX on Tour and NBA Street V3, both published by EA Sports.
Legacy

Following this model the Mario series has gone on to become the best selling video game franchise of all time with 193 million units sold as of January 2007, almost 40 million units ahead of second-ranked franchise Pokémon, also by Nintendo.
Legacy
Super Mario Kart was re-released on the Japanese Virtual Console on June 9, 2009, and later in North America on November 23, 2009.
Legacy
Previously, when naming it as one of the most wanted games for the platform in November 2008, Eurogamer stated that problems emulating the Mode 7 graphics were responsible for its absence.
Legacy
The game was released for the Wii U Virtual Console in Japan during June 2013, and in Europe on March 27, 2014.
Legacy

In addition, North American users were able to get the game starting from August 6, 2014 to celebrate the 22nd anniversary of the game, which included the new game update of Mario Kart 8 on August 27, 2014.
Legacy
In 2016, the game was re-released for the New Nintendo 3DS.
Legacy
Nintendo re-released Super Mario Kart in 2017 as part of the company's Super NES Classic Edition.
Legacy
Super Mario 3D World has a stage with a look based on the Mario Circuit racetracks from Super Mario Kart.
Legacy
Mario Kart DS contains remakes of the Mario Circuit 1, Donut Plains 1, Koopa Beach 2, and Choco Island 2 courses.
Legacy
Mario Kart Wii has remakes of the Ghost Valley 2 and Mario Circuit 3 courses.
Legacy
Mario Kart 7 has remakes of the Mario Circuit 2 and Rainbow Road courses.
Legacy
The most recent entry, Mario Kart 8, has remakes of the Donut Plains 3 and Rainbow Road courses, though the latter is only available as downloadable content in the original release.
Legacy
The enhanced Nintendo Switch port of Mario Kart 8, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, later added remakes of the Mario Circuit 3 and Bowser Castle 3 courses as downloadable content.
Sequels
The first sequel, Mario Kart 64, was released in 1996 for the Nintendo 64 and was the first Mario Kart game to feature fully 3D graphics.
Sequels

Although reviewers including IGN and GameSpot felt that the single-player gameplay was lacking compared to its predecessor, the simultaneous four-person multiplayer modes – a first for the Nintendo 64 – were praised.
Sequels
The second sequel, Mario Kart: Super Circuit, was released for the Game Boy Advance in 2001.
Sequels
Mario Kart: Double Dash was released for the GameCube in 2003.
Sequels
Mario Kart DS, released for the Nintendo DS in 2005, was the first Mario Kart game to include online play via the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection.
Sequels
It went on to become the best selling handheld racing game of all time, selling 7.83 million units.
Sequels
Mario Kart Wii was released for the Wii in 2008 and incorporates motion controls and 12-player racing.
Sequels
Mario Kart Wii went on to be the worldwide best-selling game of 2008.
Sequels
Mario Kart 7 for the Nintendo 3DS was released in 2011, which features racing on land, sea, and air.
Sequels
Mario Kart 7 added the ability to customize the kart and to race in first-person mode.
Sequels
Three Mario Kart arcade games have been released, Mario Kart Arcade GP in 2005, Mario Kart Arcade GP 2 in 2007, and Mario Kart Arcade GP DX in 2013.
Sequels

The most recent entry in the series is Mario Kart 8 for the Wii U, which was released at the end of May 2014, which brings back gliders and propellers from Mario Kart 7 as well as 12-player racing in Mario Kart Wii.
Sequels
Mario Kart 8 includes a new feature called Mario Kart TV, where players can watch highlights of previous races and uploading them to YouTube.
Sequels
An enhanced port, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, was released on the Nintendo Switch on April 28, 2017.
Sequels
The game keeps most elements from the Wii U version, while adding more characters, kart parts, battle modes, and battle stages.
Sequels
The port received universal critical acclaim, and has sold over 20 million copies as of August 2020, becoming the best selling game for the console.
Sequels
The only other Mario Kart games to feature the coin collecting of the original are Mario Kart: Super Circuit, Mario Kart 7, and Mario Kart 8.

sfes_star_vixen.title: Star Fox
sents: lead
Star Fox is an arcade style rail shooter and third person action-adventure video game series created by Shigeru Miyamoto, produced and published by Nintendo.
lead
The games follow the Star Fox combat team of anthropomorphic animals, led by chief protagonist Fox McCloud.
lead
Gameplay involves many adventures around the Lylat planetary system in the futuristic Arwing fighter aircraft, in other vehicles, and on foot.
lead
The original Star Fox (1993) is a forward-scrolling 3D rail shooter, but later games add more directional freedom.
lead
The first game in the series, developed by Nintendo EAD and programmed by Argonaut Software, uses the Super FX Chip to create the first hardware-accelerated 3D gaming experience on a home console.
lead
The Super FX Chip is a math co-processor built into the cartridge to help the Super NES render graphics.
lead
Super FX has been used in other Super NES games, some with increased processing speed.
lead
Its reboot, Star Fox 64, is the first Nintendo 64 game with Rumble Pak support.
Star Fox
The first game, Star Fox, or Starwing in Europe and Australia, was released for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in 1993.
Star Fox
Developed by Nintendo EAD and programmed by Argonaut Software, it uses the Super FX chip to provide 3D graphics during a period of predominately 2D games.
Star Fox
The concept was inspired by a shrine to the Japanese fox deity Inari Ōkami, which Shigeru Miyamoto visited regularly.
Star Fox 64

Star Fox 64, or Lylat Wars in Europe and Australia, introduced fully spoken dialogue, off-the-rails movement, new vehicles and characters, multiplayer, and rudimentary on-foot gameplay through an unlockable multiplayer mode.
Star Fox 64
It was released in 1997 for the Nintendo 64 and came bundled with the Rumble Pak, a force feedback controller attachment.
Star Fox 64
Star Fox 64 retells the main story of the original Star Fox canon, with new characters and gameplay elements.
Star Fox 64 3D
Star Fox 64 3D is a remake of Star Fox 64 for the Nintendo 3DS, released in 2011, as the second Star Fox game on a handheld console.
Star Fox 64 3D
The game was announced in a conceptual trailer for the Nintendo 3DS at E3 2010.
Star Fox 64 3D
With a few exceptions, the gameplay in Star Fox 64 3D is very similar to that of the original version.
Star Fox 64 3D
The player can enable "Gyro Controls", using the 3DS's internal gyroscope sensor to control the Arwing.
Star Fox 64 3D
A new multiplayer "Battle Mode" allows up to 4-player LAN multiplayer (via Download Play), or to battle against CPU opponents.
Star Fox Adventures
Developed by Rare, it is predominately an action-adventure game in which Fox is armed with a mystical staff.
Star Fox Adventures
Traditional space shooting is limited to small segments between chapters.
Star Fox Adventures
Its roots can be traced to Dinosaur Planet, a game Rare was developing late in the life cycle of the Nintendo 64, but cancelled by Nintendo and converted into a Star Fox game.
Star Fox Adventures
Taking place eight years after the events of Star Fox 64, the main antagonist is an army of dinosaurs called the Sharp Claws, led by General Scales.
Star Fox Adventures
The gameplay of Adventures resembles that seen in most 3D The Legend of Zelda games.
Star Fox: Assault
Developed by Namco, Star Fox: Assault was released in 2005 for the GameCube.
Star Fox Command
Star Fox Command was developed by Q-Games for the Nintendo DS, and was released in 2006.
Star Fox Command
It is the first Star Fox game for a handheld console and the first to offer online multiplayer.
Star Fox Command
Each character has a unique ship with different abilities.
Star Fox Zero
Star Fox Zero was developed by Nintendo and PlatinumGames for the Wii U and released in April 2016.
Star Fox Zero
The first Star Fox game on a home game console in over 10 years, the game is controlled using the Wii U GamePad's gyroscope feature.
Star Fox 2
Star Fox 2 was originally cancelled even though it was completely finished.
Star Fox 2

Many of its new ideas were implemented for the then-forthcoming Star Fox 64, such as the rival team Star Wolf, all-range mode, charge shot, and a multiplayer mode (though Star Fox 2s multiplayer mode was no longer featured in the final beta).
Virtual Boy game
Cinematic camera angles were a key element, as they are in Star Fox 2.
Virtual Boy game
At both E3 1995 and at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show 1995, the demo showed an Arwing doing various spins and motions.
Virtual Boy game
One observer called it "an intriguing technical demo featuring a Star Fox-like spacecraft doing a lot of spinning and zooming in 3D.
Virtual Boy game
Attendees to these two events were given 3D glasses to watch the demos and tech videos that were played on screens at the show floors, and from these videos.
Arcade game
Originally planned as a companion game for Star Fox: Assault, an arcade game was abandoned and never released.
Arcade game
It was scheduled for release in 2004–2005, but was cancelled for unknown reasons.
Star Fox Armada
The game was pitched to Nintendo by Retro Studios, but never made it to the development stage.
Star Fox (Nelsonic Game Watch)

Shortly after the release of the first Star Fox game, in June 1993, Nintendo teamed up with Kellogg's and Nelsonic to develop and release a promotional LCD-based Star Fox Game Watch coupon in boxes of Corn Flakes.
Star Fox Guard
Star Fox Guard was first shown at E3 2014 under the name of Project Guard, and was announced under a final name in a March 2016 Nintendo Direct.
Star Fox Guard
Guard was released for the Wii U in April 2016, coinciding with the release of Star Fox Zero.
WarioWare series
(not ROB 64 from the Star Fox series, but rather the R.O.B. attachment for the NES), who is armed with a large NES Zapper.
WarioWare series
In WarioWare Gold for Nintendo 3DS, another SNES-styled Star Fox microgame appears, this time challenging players to not crash into anything when their ship is on the verge of being destroyed.
Nintendo Power comics
A monthly Star Fox comic strip, illustrated by Benimaru Itoh, was printed in issues 45 to 55 of Nintendo Power in 1993.
Nintendo Power comics
Fox, Falco, and Andross were the only 3 characters whose backgrounds were fully explained in the story.
Lylat Wars Comic
The official Club Nintendo magazine in Germany released a Star Fox 64 comic drawn manga-style to retell the game's storyline.
Manga
A one-issue Star Fox comic by Kazumi Sakamoto (坂本かずみ) was printed in the Comic Bonbon 1993 Spring Vacation Jumbo Edition (春休みジャンボ増刊号), published in April of that month.
Manga
A one-issue Star Fox comic by was printed in the 1993 Spring Break Edition (増刊号 ９３年春休み増刊) of Corocoro Comic.
Manga
A Star Fox 64 comic by Takahiro Yamashita is within the April and June 1997 issues of Bessatsu Corocoro Comic.
Star Fox: Farewell, Beloved Falco
The manga was released on the official Star Fox Adventures Japanese website, and it chronicles the events between Star Fox 64 and Star Fox Adventures.
Star Fox: Farewell, Beloved Falco
In the beginning, Katt Monroe returns from Star Fox 64 along with a rag-tag team of roughnecks with apparently an inside lead on the fact that Shears is evil.
Star Fox: Farewell, Beloved Falco
The manga ends with the Star Fox team seeing Dinosaur Planet broken apart and deciding it is worth checking out.
Star Fox Zero – The Battle Begins
A 14-minute web video of Star Fox Zero produced by Shigeru Miyamoto, Production IG, and Wit Studio, features the Star Fox team in an anime-styled battle of the first level in Star Fox Zero: Corneria.
Arwing
From Star Fox 64 onwards, the two side pods are a distinctive blue color.
Arwing
The Arwing is also an easter egg in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time but can only be accessed by a gameshark code.
Arwing
In Bayonetta 2, miniature Arwings replace Bayonetta's guns when she is wearing the game's unlockable Star Fox costume.
Landmaster
The Landmaster M1 tank first appeared in Star Fox 64 (1997, Nintendo 64) as a tracked light tank in two of the game's missions and one of the game's multiplayer maps.
Wolfen

This ship would have first appeared in Star Fox 2, but was instead first seen in Star Fox 64 on the planet Fichina (mistranslated as Fortuna in Star Fox 64, fixed in 64 3D) – or alternatively – Bolse.
Reception
The Star Fox series has had mostly positive reviews, the most acclaimed being Star Fox 64, and Star Fox Zero received the most mixed reviews.
Reception
115 spot on EGM's "The Greatest 200 Videogames of Their Time", and 82nd best game made on a Nintendo System in Nintendo Powers Top 200 Games list.
Reception
It also received a 34 out of 40 from Famitsu magazine, and a 4.125 out of 5 from Nintendo Power Magazine.
Reception
Next Gen Magazine pointed out Star Fox as helping pioneer the use of 3-D video game graphics.
Reception
As Star Fox Adventures took a different approach to the franchise, many fans complained it was too much like a role-playing adventure game, such as The Legend of Zelda.
Reception
In October 2009, Shigeru Miyamoto said that he was disappointed that sales of the Star Fox series in Japan had decreased during the preceding period.
Reception
Typing "do a barrel roll" or "Z or R twice" into the search bar, the screen rotates 360°.

sfes_star_vixen_2.title: Star Fox 2

Programmer(s): Dylan Cuthbert Takumi Kawagoe Yasuhiro Kawaguchi

sents: lead
Star Fox 2 is a rail shooter game developed by Nintendo and Argonaut Software and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
It was completed in 1995 but did not see an official release until 2017 on the Super NES Classic Edition.
lead
Like the original Star Fox (1993), Star Fox 2 pushed the graphical capabilities of the SNES with Argonaut's Super FX chip.
lead
Dylan Cuthbert was the lead programmer, with Shigeru Miyamoto returning as the producer and Katsuya Eguchi as the director.
lead
Star Fox 2 introduces semi-real-time gameplay, new ship types, new playable characters, and a more advanced 3D game engine.
lead
The story continues the battle against Emperor Andross, who seeks to destroy the Lylat system.
lead
By 1995, 3D technology was advancing quickly and the 3D game market was expanding, with competition from the Sony PlayStation and Sega Saturn consoles.
lead
Concerned that the 16-bit graphics of Star Fox 2 would compare poorly against newer games, Nintendo canceled the Star Fox 2 release to prioritize its upcoming Nintendo 64 console.
Gameplay
When the player's ships make contact with enemy forces, the game switches to an action perspective, piloting the Arwing ship directly with controls and gameplay similar to the first Star Fox.
Gameplay
The objective is to beat all enemy forces present in the map while defending planet Corneria, preventing its damage level from reaching 100%.
Gameplay
If Corneria's damage level reaches 100% or the player runs out of extra ships, the game ends.
Gameplay

General Pepper employs a satellite that can shoot down enemies on a limited basis; the player must also defend this installation from special enemies that can take over the satellite and use its cannon to fire at Corneria.
Plot

After his defeat in the original Star Fox, the antagonist, Andross, returns to the Lylat system and launches an all-out attack against Corneria, using his new fleet of battleships and giant missiles launched from hidden bases to destroy the planet.
Plot
Star Fox 2 features six playable characters, more than any game in the series until Star Fox Command (2006).
Development
Like its predecessor Star Fox (1993), Star Fox 2 was co-developed by Nintendo EAD in Japan and the British company Argonaut Software.
Development
Argonaut had a contract with Nintendo to create three games; after Star Fox, Argonaut programmers Giles Goddard and Dylan Cuthbert worked on Stunt Race FX (1994) and Cuthbert on Star Fox 2.
Development
Edge reported in December 1993 that development on a sequel to Star Fox had begun.
Development
The team decided early on to use the Super FX 2 chip in the game cartridge.
Development
The original chip was designed to calculate 3D math quickly and was first used in Star Fox.
Development
The Super FX 2 had more memory and ran at 21 MHz, twice as fast as the original chip.
Development
Cuthbert also rewrote parts of the engine to run in parallel in RAM to free more Super FX 2 processing for more advanced features, such as planar clipping and advanced collision detection.
Development
Such free-roaming gameplay was planned for the original Star Fox, but it was made on-rails because of the original Super FX chip's limited computing powers.
Development
Cuthbert also retooled the engine to increase the frame rate from 20 to 30 frames per second, but it was not steady so they locked the frame rate at 20 FPS.
Development
Freely explorable environments were the only gameplay element planned for the original Star Fox carried into Star Fox 2; all other ideas were new.
Development
Miyamoto took great interest in Cuthbert's platforming gameplay (before Super Mario 64 's release in 1996).
Development
Because of the Super FX 2's greater computing power, the team decided to have the fighters visibly transform into bipedal Walkers.
Development
Eguchi wanted to explore a more roguelike game system and use similar game mechanics to Star Luster (1985).
Promotion at Winter CES
Star Fox 2 was playable on the show floor at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show (Winter CES) in Las Vegas in January 1995.
Promotion at Winter CES
All three magazines thought Star Fox 2 was better than the original.
Promotion at Winter CES
Edge was more critical, writing that Star Fox 2 was Nintendo's attempt to keep the SNES relevant.
Cancellation
By mid-1995, Star Fox 2 was nearing completion, and was planned for release in August.
Cancellation
However, 3D technology was advancing quickly and the 3D game market was expanding, with competition from the Sony PlayStation and Sega Saturn.
Cancellation
The consoles ran impressive 3D graphics that captured the public's attention.
Cancellation
Nintendo was concerned that the 16-bit Star Fox 2 3D visuals would be compared to the superior 3D capabilities of competing consoles.
Cancellation
Cuthbert said that Star Fox 2 would be "compared directly against games such as Ridge Racer, which felt like you finally had an arcade machine's power in your home".
Cancellation
Nintendo decided to prioritize its upcoming Nintendo 64 console, including a new Star Fox game, Star Fox 64.
Cancellation
According to Cuthbert, Miyamoto wanted a clear break between 3D games on the SNES and Nintendo 64.
Cancellation
The Super FX 2 chip also raised the cost of production, which would have made Star Fox 2 an expensive release.
Cancellation
Star Fox 2 was canceled in mid-1995, when it was about 95% complete.
Cancellation
The August issue of GamePro printed that it had been delayed to 1996, while Electronic Gaming Monthly wrote that it had been canceled in their September issue.
Cancellation
Nintendo Power wrote in their September issue that "rumors of the demise of Star Fox 2 have been greatly exaggerated", with a release most likely coming in the first half of 1996.
Release
For many years, the completed version of Star Fox 2 remained in Nintendo's archives.
Release
In 2015, Miyamoto told journalists: "In my memory, I enjoyed but I'm not sure I would release it, I'd rather have people play a new game".
Beta leaks
In the years following cancellation, ROM images of incomplete builds of Star Fox 2 were leaked anonymously onto the internet.
Beta leaks
The first ROMs leaked in the late 1990s were early test builds with numerous software bugs.
Beta leaks
The emulation community was inspired by the release to improve Super FX chip handling in their Super NES emulators.
Beta leaks
A fan translation patch was also released which took four people and over 100 hours of work.
Beta leaks

Speaking about the final beta ROM, he said: "The basic parts are there, but there is an adage in game development, 'The last 10 percent is 90 percent of the game' and the ROM is missing that last 10 percent of iteration and refinement".
Official release
When compiling a list of games to include on the Super NES Classic dedicated console, the system's producer proposed the inclusion of Star Fox 2.
Official release
The device was announced along with Star Fox 2 's inclusion in June 2017.
Official release
The Super NES Classic was released on September 29, 2017, in North America and Europe and on October 5 in Japan.
Official release

The version is the localized English ROM that was completed in the 1990s, though Cuthbert suspected Nintendo had to make minor changes, such as altering screen flashing, to get it past modern regulations.
Official release
Promotional artwork for Star Fox 2 was created by Takaya Imamura, the original Star Fox character designer.
Official release
In December 2019, Nintendo released a video of upcoming games for its Nintendo Switch Online NES and Super NES services.
Official release
The update includes Star Fox 2 as a part of its portfolio of games, playable by those with an active Nintendo Switch Online membership as of December 12, 2019.
Reception
Star Fox 2 received generally favorable reception from critics during its inclusion on the Super NES Classic Edition in 2017.
Reception
Eurogamer ' s Christian Donlan described it as an unusual but "wonderfully surprising and inventive" sequel that builds upon the first Star Fox, due to its more roguelite nature.
Reception
Rairdin wrote that it was the most important game in the Star Fox series, and one of the greatest Super Nintendo games.
Reception

HobbyConsolas ' David Martínez commended the Arwing's transformation mechanic, open levels and introduction of new Star Fox members and Star Wolf but criticized the game's short length, technical shortcomings and controls, feeling that it was not well-rounded as the first entry.
Reception
Digital Trends ' Mike Epstein felt that Star Fox 2 took some of the biggest risks the Star Fox franchise had attempted.
Reception

GameSpot ' s Michael Higham gave positive remarks to the land vehicle sequences, freedom of approach to manage an incoming threat and off-rails 3D dogfights in space, but criticized its poor technical performance, short length, and lacking sense of adventure when compared to the first Star Fox, among other aspects.
Legacy
After Star Fox 2 was canceled, Argonaut's contract with Nintendo ended.
Legacy
The company collaborated with Nintendo in 2006 to develop Star Fox Command, and again in 2011 for Star Fox 64 3D.
Legacy
Cuthbert found the experimentation with Star Fox 2 personally helpful in his career.
Legacy
Star Fox 2 inspired the design of later Star Fox games.
Legacy
Free-range flying and grounded vehicle gameplay were implemented into Star Fox 64, as was the Star Wolf team.
Legacy
Nintendo and Q-Games played Star Fox 2 to gather inspiration on its strategic gameplay elements for Star Fox Command.
Legacy
Miyamoto asked Cuthbert to make Command more similar to Star Fox 2 than the original Star Fox.
Legacy
The Arwing's ability to transform into the Walker was re-introduced in Star Fox Zero (2016).
Legacy
Cuthbert believes a lot of the platforming experimentation they ran in Star Fox 2 gave Miyamoto confidence for Super Mario 64.

sfes_stunt_race_fz.title: Stunt Race FX
sents: lead

Stunt Race FX, known in Japan as Wild Trax (ワイルドトラックス, Wairudo Torakkusu), is a racing video game developed by Nintendo and Argonaut Software and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is the second game to use the 3D-centric Super FX powered GSU-1.
lead
Stunt Race FX was added to the Nintendo Switch Online service on September 5, 2019, its first re-release in more than two decades.
Gameplay

The player can choose between three vehicles (F-Type is like a Formula One, COUPE is a coupé, and 4WD is a monster truck), a fourth unlockable (2WD), or a fifth in bonus games (TRAILER which is a semi-trailer truck).
Gameplay
Each course is constructed of 3D polygons, complete with road bumps, overhead passes, and detailed billboard advertisements.
Development
In 1991, Nintendo and Argonaut Software began developing a custom 3D cartridge chip called the Super FX chip to enable create polygonal 3D graphics on the Super NES.
Development
The primary goal was what became the hit game Star Fox, but during the Super FX's development, Nintendo and Argonaut experimented with general 3D game development.
Development
3D polygonal graphics are the game's main highlight, and producer Shigeru Miyamoto had his designers emphasize realistic vehicle dynamics.
Development
The direction, weight, and force applied by each tire to the road surface is unique, making it quicker and easier for the car's tail to drift when cornering compared to other vehicles.
Development
In early development, the 2WD vehicle was not a part of the car roster.
Development
In its place was a three-wheeled vehicle called the 3WD, bearing a color scheme very close to the 4WD's blue paint job.
Reception
Stunt Race FX ' s sales had surpassed 1 million copies by 1998.
Reception
In the United Kingdom, it was the top-selling SNES game in October 1994.
Reception

Electronic Gaming Monthly commented that Stunt Race FX is a disappointment after the first Super FX game, Star Fox, because "the game feels awkward with the touchy steering and the feeling of speed just isn't there.
Reception
Game Zero scored it 94 out of 100, saying the controls are "out of this world!" and the "attention to detail is truly superior".
Reception
Edge gave it a 9 out of 10 rating, as "one of the best racing games currently available for any home system".
Reception
In the British television show Bad Influence!, a few reviewers combined their ratings into an overall score of 4 out of 5.
Reception
IGN ranked the game 86th in its Top 100 SNES games of All Time.
Reception
In 2018, Complex rated it 90th on its "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time".
Reception
In 1995, Total! ranked it 21st on its list of Top 100 SNES Games.
Reception

Zoey Handley of Destructoid said the game's contemporary reviews are mostly positive but biased by the simple standards of the time, and that as a child she considered it good only as a rental because its replay value is so short and the primitive graphics induce nausea.

sfes_yoshu_s_cookie.title: Yoshi's Cookie
sents: lead
Yoshi's Cookie is a 1992 tile-matching puzzle video game developed by Tose and published by Nintendo for the NES and Game Boy platforms in 1992.
lead
A Super NES version was released the following year, developed and published by Bullet-Proof Software.
Gameplay
The player mixes and matches the cookies such that entire rows or columns consist only of cookies of the same type.
Development
Yoshi's Cookie originally began development as an arcade game called Hermetica (ヘルメティカ, Herumetika), which was being produced by game developer Home Data.
Development
Nintendo obtained the licenses for the 8-bit (NES and Game Boy) versions of Hermetica, and developed the game into Yoshi's Cookie, which now featured Mario characters.
Release
Yoshi's Cookie was first released in Japan on November 21, 1992, for the Nintendo Entertainment System and Game Boy.
Release
Five months later, it was released in North America in April 1993, and in Europe on April 28, 1994.
Release
The Super NES version was released in June 1993 in North America, on July 9, 1993, in Japan, and in Europe during the same year.
Yoshi no Cookie: Kuruppon Oven de Cookie

National, a brand of Panasonic, released 500 copies of a special limited edition of Yoshi's Cookie for the Super Famicom, titled Yoshi no Cookie: Kuruppon Oven de Cookie (ヨッシーのクッキー クルッポンオーブンでクッキー), which worked with a peripheral called the Kuruppon Oven to show players how to make the cookies in the game.
Yoshi no Cookie: Kuruppon Oven de Cookie
In October 2010, a copy of this edition was valued at ¥ 157,500 (equivalent to US$1,924 in 2010).
Remake and emulation
Yoshi's Cookie was remade and included in the Nintendo Puzzle Collection for the GameCube, released in Japan on February 7, 2003.
Remake and emulation

The NES emulated version was also re-released for the Wii 's Virtual Console service on April 4, 2008, in Europe and Australia, April 7, 2008, in North America, June 10, 2008, in Japan, and November 11, 2008, in South Korea.
Remake and emulation
It was discontinued from the service on October 11, 2013, in Japan and Europe, and October 18, 2013, in North America.
Reception
GamesRadar ranked it the 48th best game available on the Game Boy and Game Boy Color.
Reception
The Washington Post in 1993 called the game "simple, but addictive, just like all puzzlers from the Big N.
Reception
You might have nightmares about that NES coming back to life." Nintendo Power rated Yoshi's Cookie the fifth best NES game of 1993.
Reception
IGN ranked the game 50th on their Top 100 SNES Games."

sfes_pocky_rocko.title: Pocky & Rocky (video game)

Artist(s): Shunichi Taniguchi Tomoyuki Nishiyama Yoshihino Hattori

sents: lead
Pocky & Rocky is a 1992 scrolling shooter video game developed and published by Natsume for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (Super NES).
lead
It is the sequel to Taito 's 1986 arcade game KiKi KaiKai.
lead
Pocky & Rocky follows the adventures of a young Shinto shrine maiden, Pocky, and her new tanuki companion, Rocky, as they attempt to save a group of goblins from evil forces.
lead
Gameplay takes place from a top-down perspective and features both single-player and cooperative modes.
lead
The game was generally well-received by critics.
lead
It was followed by Pocky & Rocky 2 (1994) and Pocky & Rocky with Becky (2001).
lead
A new entry, Pocky & Rocky Reshrined, released in 2022.
Gameplay
A limited-use special bomb attack can be used to hit several or all the enemies present on the screen.
Gameplay
A floating being called "Help man" is hidden in each level that will drop power-ups when found.
Release
Pocky & Rocky was licensed by Taito to Natsume, who developed and published the game for release in Japan in 1992 and the rest of the world in 1993.
Release
In Japan, Pocky & Rocky was broadcast on the Satellaview service on June 6, 1997.
Reception
The graphics of the game, especially the backgrounds and enemies, received praise for being colorful and well-animated, many comparing it to The Legend of the Mystical Ninja in graphical style.
Reception
In 1996, Super Play ranked the game 91st on their Top 100 SNES Games of All Time.
Sequels
In Pocky & Rocky 2 (1994) for SNES, Pocky and Rocky must work together once again to stop a forced marriage between a princess and a tyrant.
Sequels
In the second sequel, Pocky & Rocky with Becky (2001) for Game Boy Advance, the duo are joined by their friend Becky to stop a hydra dragon.
Sequels
The latest entry, Pocky & Rocky Reshrined, was released for the PlayStation 4 and Nintendo Switch in 2022, and on Windows in 2023.
Sequels
UFO Interactive Games released a spiritual successor to the series, Heavenly Guardian (2007), developed by Starfish for the PlayStation 2 and Wii.

sfes_plonk.title: Plok!
sents: lead
Plok! is a platform game developed by British studio Software Creations for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
lead
It was released in late 1993 by Tradewest in North America, Nintendo in Europe, and Activision in Japan.
lead

Players portray the hood-headed titular protagonist, the king of the island Akrillic who is protecting it from fleas spawned by the Flea Queen, who is under the island's ground, as well as other bosses trying to overthrow Plok's power.
lead
His versatility lies in his four separable limbs, which can be used to shoot at targets and enemies, and several power-ups scattered throughout its colorful stages as " presents."
lead

' s history began in the late 1980s as a self-funded coin-op project by Ste and John Pickford named Fleapit; they worked on it while at Zippo Games and programmed it for Rare 's 'Razz Board' hardware.
lead

It was cancelled in 1990 following the closure of Zippo Games, but was revived as a SNES game developed at Software Creations after the Pickfords were promoted to higher positions, with Ste becoming an art director and John a producer.
lead
Software Creations self-funded the game with the Pickfords owning intellectual property rights.
lead
The game was to be ported for the Sega Genesis, but the reissue was cancelled for unknown reasons.
Gameplay

Saving is limited to two "Permanent Continue Positions" after the completion of the Bobbins Brothers and Rockyfella boss fights which the player can return to even after the game is reset, and there is no password feature.
Gameplay
The only limitation is that he cannot shoot limbs while somersaulting.
Gameplay
Plok's secondary attack takes the form of "Speed Blade," a buzzsaw -like jump that not only gives him increased speed as items but also dispatches enemies at the highest damage possible.
Gameplay

For fleas, for the player to complete the level, Plok must destroy every single one of them in every level (with the exceptions of Cotton Island, Legacy Island, and Fleapit), where the last one drops a flag which levitates to its flag pole and allows the player to progress.
Plot
Plok wakes up one morning and notices his big square flag on the pole on his house's rooftop has been stolen, and goes out searching for it.
Plot
Plok encounters the two giant creatures who are responsible for placing the fake flags, the Bobbins Brothers, whom Plok's grandpappy had warned him about, and fights them.
1988: Rare hires Zippo Games

In the summer of 1988, Ste and John Pickford, workers at Zippo Games which was owned by John and their friend Steve Hughes, were struggling to complete games for 16-bit Atari ST and Amiga computers, many getting canceled.
1988: Rare hires Zippo Games
Zippo Games was the only company to have been consulted by Rare for NES work.
1988–1989: Fleapit

After more motivation from John, Ste moved to clear sheets of paper to do more sketches, where the character's colors, poses, size (32x40) and "extreme expressions" involving an opening mouth were conceived.
1988–1989: Fleapit

As a result, the Pickfords made a deal with Rare to use the hardware to produce their dream game as well as to own the game property and receive a big chunk of revenue from board sales; however, the deal also made all of the funding up to the brothers.
1988–1989: Fleapit
As development went on, Rare was profiting mostly from selling NES titles, making them less focused on Razz Board games such as Fleapit.
1988–1989: Fleapit
In 1989, Rare, the first company outside of Japan to have a Game Boy, instructed Zippo Games to develop a game for the handheld console; however, this meant stopping the development of Fleapit.
1988–1989: Fleapit
Rare and Zippo Games' relationship worsened; Zippo never completed a Game Boy product as instructed and was bought out by Rare in 1990 to be renamed Rare Manchester, which was shut down.
1988–1989: Fleapit

Fleapit was cancelled half-completed in 1990 as a result of Zippo Games closing and funds running out; Ste admitted in 2014 a desire to produce a coin-op caused improper business decisions, such as rejecting more financially-rewarding console work.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations
After leaving Zippo, John phoned Richard Hay, the head of Software Creations, the first company outside of Japan to have a development kit for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations
Hay hired the Pickfords right away to use it to design and program Equinox (1993), a sequel to the NES title Solstice (1990).
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations
While the brothers and Hay considered many consoles, such as the NES, Super NES, and Game Boy, only a Super NES title came into fruition.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations
Plok! was the Pickford brothers' first experience as project managers, as well as the first time they collaborated with other developers to turn their ideas into a finished product.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations

Buckley later admitted to Plok! being his most "proud" work. and Kong admittined that his experience as the game's tester prepared him for being lead designer on Team Soho 's PlayStation 2 title The Getaway (2002): "QA is great grounding for designers.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations

Although Pickfords allowed Buckley and Brooke to offer many contributions, development was not without conflict, the biggest argument occurring late in development regarding difficulty; while Buckley and Brooks felt it was proper, the Pickfords found it overbearing.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations
To settle the dispute, the first eight stages which were originally for Cotton Island were moved later as the Grandpappy Plok dream stages, with eight new easier Cotton Island stages created.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations

Kong also reported one of the publishers wanted the first level's difficulty decreased, so the staff decreased the bouncing sprouts' hit points from two to one; however, in the tutorial segment of the final game, the sprouts take two hits as Plok fires an extra arm.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations

While Software Creations did have collectible continues (named "Plokontinues") for Plok!, it did not produce a save battery due to being too costly, and passwords were scrapped out of fear gaming magazines would spread them around.
1990–1993: From Zippo to Software Creations
Kong recalled most of the game was completed close to the end of Equinox ' s testing.
Graphics and art

Unlike other hardwares that used bitmap grids that encode colors and transparency through binary numbers, the Razz Board hardware stored pixels as bytes, with the first six bits determining color, the seventh bit setting its vertical position relative to its predecessor, and the eighth its horizontal.
Graphics and art
For instance, using a bitmap system to create a 32-pixel line requires a grid of 1,024 pixels (32x32) with 992 of them transparent, while making the same line took only 32 bytes in Razz Board.
Graphics and art
This meant sprites weren't restrained to perfectly square sizes, which Ste took advantage of when creating the text font although setting an arbitrary limit of 22x29.
Graphics and art

For the SNES game, Brooke designed two new fonts for 16x16 and 8x8 bitmap grids: one based on Ste's font for Fleapit, in turn based on his lettering in concept drawings, and another for the silent movie-esque screens in the Legacy Island levels.
Graphics and art
Software Creations' leader and Plok! executive producer Mike Webb reported compressing 50% on the game's 16-megabit graphics data (equivalent to Street Fighter II) to eight megabits.
Graphics and art
Ste drew the illustrations in black and white, due to being focused more on shape than on color and photocopying technology only allowing monochrome prints.
Graphics and art
The color scheme was formulated originally for an 8-bit arcade title; to achieve a "natural" look, colors were scrunched into extreme areas of the RGB color wheel.
Graphics and art
John's first plan for taking the most advantage of the Razz Board was with how Plok was animated; since he had separable limbs, all of his six parts were independently-moving static sprites.
Graphics and art
The fleas, although animated traditionally with frames, were only two legs to make animating extreme poses simpler and for the sprite to not be too busy.
Graphics and art
Ste reported "5 or 6" frames for all of the fleas' movements.
Graphics and art

For the SNES console, Brooke altered the design of Plok and the fleas only slightly, but Plok's animation method was transformed; the SNES has the traditional bitmap method of executing pixels, thus he was animated frame-by-frame by Brooke.
Concepts and design
The Bobbins Brothers and Womack were transferred from Fleapit (although Womack went through a massive redesign by Brooke that Ste appreciated) while the Penkinos were originally-conceived for Plok!.
Concepts and design
The "floating" limb movements were coded in John's first prototype of Fleapit, with the idea of removing limbs incorporated later on as the Pickfords experimented.
Audio
Ste reported Geoff doing around 75% of the work and being far more open for discussion with the team, and Tim being more "elusive".
Audio

Plok! continues the Follin brothers' incorporation of old rock music influences; "A Line in the Sand", for instance, was inspired by the works of Stevie Wonder, and its guitar solo being influenced by Queen guitarist Brian May.
Audio
A breathing sample in the boss theme was also used in Equinox and Spider-Man and the X-Men in Arcade's Revenge (1992).
Audio
Rare composer David Wise has expressed admiration for Plok!, claiming his work on Donkey Kong Country to be inspired by the Follin brothers' soundtrack.
Publishing

Shigeru Miyamoto expressed a strong interest in working on the game; when Plok! was only half-finished, he wrote a letter to Hay claiming it was the third-best platform game below Sonic and Mario and that he would make it the second-greatest in the genre above Sonic but below Mario.
Publishing

While Nintendo's reasons for this remain undisclosed, Ste believes that Miyamoto found it, particularly its mini-race levels, too similar to the then in-development first-party title Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island.
Promotion
The Pickfords, despite owning the IP and developing Plok!, were never consulted on promotion.
Promotion

In the United Kingdom, Nintendo released a VHS tape, Super Mario All-Stars Video (1993); hosted by Craig Charles, the video features a segment of testers at Nintendo UK promoting upcoming games, including Plok!
Promotion

Tradewest's US print advertisement depicted the top half taken up by Double Dragon and Battletoads, the bottom half a picture of the Plok character; the only info revealed was that Plok! was published by the two other franchises.
Promotion

Nintendo's UK print ad depicted a faux desktop screenshot with an image of an angry old lady in the house as the wallpaper; the only Plok! visual depicted was its box art, placed in the bottom right and very small-sized.
Promotion
Plok! was first announced in June 1993; upon its announcement, an N-Force journalist called it one of the most "surreal" games in the September 1993 line-up.
Promotion

Tradewest presented Plok! at the summer 1993 Consumer Electronics Show; a GameFan writer called Tradewest "one of the most impressive third party line-up," highlighting Plok! as a "a colorful new action title with a lead character that hurls his arms and legs at attackers."
Contemporaneous reviews
Upon release, some critics declared Plok! the best Nintendo release of 1993 as well as another classic by the company, the best platform game of the year, and one of the all-time best in the genre.
Contemporaneous reviews

Reviews also enjoyed its humor, such as with Plok's limbless movements, his power-ups, and nonsensical story; Humphreys felt it would help the game be enjoyed by even the biggest detractors of kid-friendly platformers.
Contemporaneous reviews
' s gameplay and eulogized its playability, perfect control, and variety.
Commercial performance and plans for a franchise

The Pickford brothers garnered IP ownership for the Plok character, common in other media economies but rare in the video games industry; and planned a franchise out of it, such as sequels, ports, and merchandise.
Commercial performance and plans for a franchise

A Mega Drive version was planned using a Software Creations worker's software for automatically converting SNES titles into Mega Drive games; 80% of the code was automatically converted, according to Ste, with the other 20% requiring hands-on work.
Commercial performance and plans for a franchise
Ultimately, however, despite Webb announcing the port's completion in an April 1994 interview, it was never released for unknown reasons.
Commercial performance and plans for a franchise
During marketing, a Plok model was created in 3D Studio 4 for a promotional photo of Software Creations.
Commercial performance and plans for a franchise

Ste, in 2004, publicly stated developers and producers with more finances knew about previews of the Fleapit coin-op, which may have influenced them to produce games like it; there are no other reports verifying this.
Legacy
In 2009, North American company Super Fighter Team released Zaku, a horizontal shooter for the Atari Lynx which features a special guest appearance by Plok.
Legacy
From there, the webcomic takes place 20 years after the game as it features new characters and some returning ones like Rockyfella.
Legacy

In later years, Plok was ranked the 26th all-time best SNES title (which also named it the best platformer produced in the United Kingdom) in 1996, the 19th best platform game by Gamereactor in 2014, and was listed in Edge editor Tony Mott's 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die in its 2013 edition.
Legacy
Games starring characters with floating body parts used as weapons, such as Dynamite Headdy (1994) and Rayman (1995), were released shortly afterwards and garnered much wider exposure.
Legacy

When listing Plok! on a list of "The Most Unappreciated Platformers of the '90s" for Kotaku, Ben Bertoli wrote it was "influential for portraying a world, named Akrill, based on craft supplies and cloth, a concept that Nintendo itself has come to rely on for many games.
Legacy

The game also provided players with power-ups and vehicles, such as flamethrowers and jetpacks, the likes of which had not been seen in a single game." Sepia-toned flashback stages also made up a chunk of Mickey Mania (1994).

sfes_aero_the_acro_rat.title: Aero the Acro-Bat

Producer(s): David Siller Jeff Spangenberg Jay Moon
Designer(s): David Siller Nigel Cook Team Aero
Programmer(s): Richard Cowie Carl Wade Jeff Spangenberg Darrin Stubbington David Brevik David Crummack

sents: lead
Aero the Acro-Bat is a 1993 video game developed by Iguana Entertainment and published by Sunsoft.
lead
It was released for both the Super Nintendo Entertainment System and Sega Genesis.
lead
Aero the Acro-Bat, a red anthropomorphic bat, was created by David Siller.
lead
In 2002, Metro 3D released a version of the game for the Game Boy Advance, with a battery back-up (which the original versions lacked).
lead
The GBA version was titled Aero The Acro-Bat - Rascal Rival Revenge in Europe and Acrobat Kid in Japan.
lead
The Super NES version of the game was released on the Wii 's Virtual Console in the PAL region on July 23 and in North America on July 26, 2010.
lead

The Super NES version was announced to be re-released on August 2, 2024 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S, alongside a new localization in Japanese made by Shinyuden as Aero: Acrobat Kid for the Nintendo Switch users in Japan.
lead
A sequel, Aero the Acro-Bat 2, was released in 1994, followed by the spin-off Zero the Kamikaze Squirrel.
Plot
A spoiled, rich kid named Edgar Ektor was a regular attendant at The World of Amusement Circus and Funpark, but was banned after a failed prank almost killed a lion.
Plot
20 years later, Edgar became a powerful and evil industrialist.
Plot
Aero the Acro-Bat is the circus' greatest star and the only hope for rescuing the performers (including his girlfriend Aeriel) and putting a stop to Edgar's evil schemes.
Gameplay
Aero can attack enemies by shooting limited stars or by doing an aerial diagonal drill attack at his target when he is in the air.
Gameplay
When Sunsoft converted the game for the Super NES they changed the bonus level to utilise Mode 7 as a straightforward level to maneuver above an overworld map.
Development
The final concept was designed by David's son Justin Siller, who was inspired by mixed themes from the 70s and 80s.
Development
Some of the enemies, items and in-levels that Siller proposed never made it in the finished game.
Development
Originally Aero was going to be released for the original Nintendo Entertainment System, but by this time 16-bit consoles were on the market, so the NES version was cancelled.
Development
Plans were made by Sunsoft to port the game to Atari Jaguar sometime in 1994, but this version was never released.
Development
Metro 3D found the game very promising for marketing and Siller directed the port during its development.
Release

Promotional artwork of the game was shown at 1993 Winter Consumer Electronics Show in Nevada as well as the prototype version at the 1993 Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago, where it stood out well above other exhibits.
Release
By late 1993, Sunsoft was giving away free copies of the Super NES or Genesis version of the game to the first 100 people that sent them a 3x5 postcard to their address.
Release
Ratalaika Games are re-releasing Aero the Acro-Bat for Switch, Xbox Series, PS4, and PS5 with a worldwide release planned for August 2, 2024.
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the Super NES version an 8.3 out of 10 and the Genesis version a 7.6 out of 10.
Reception
NintendoLife gave the Virtual Console release of the Super NES version a 6 out of 10.
Reception
Four reviewers in GameFan gave the Genesis version 93, 97, 87, and 90 Video Games: The Ultimate Gaming Magazine gave both the Genesis and SNES versions 8 out of 10.
Reception
Conversely, Digital Press gave the game only 3 out of 10.

sfes_zero_the_kamikaze_chipmunk.title: Zero the Kamikaze Squirrel
sents: lead
Zero the Kamikaze Squirrel, released years later in Japan as Zero: High Flying Squirrel, is a video game developed by Iguana Entertainment, and published by Sunsoft in 1994.
lead
It is a spin-off/sequel of the Aero the Acro-Bat series.
lead
The game was released for the Sega Genesis in October 1994 and for the Super NES in November 1994, along with the release of Aero the Acro-Bat 2.
lead
The main star is Zero, Aero's rival from the previous games.
lead
A remake for the Game Boy Advance was planned in 2003, but it was cancelled.
Plot

During the events of Aero the Acro-Bat 2, Zero receives a telegram from his girlfriend Amy telling him that an evil lumberjack named Jacques Le Sheets is deforesting their homeland Stony Forest to produce counterfeit money and has also captured her father.
Development
Some of the enemy boss sprites were rendered with 3-D Studio.
Development
The game was showcased at 1994 Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago.
Reception

The four reviewers of Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the Genesis version an 8.25 out of 10, praising Zero's innovative techniques, especially his dive and swoop moves, and the colorful graphics, which one of the reviewers said surpass the Genesis's theoretical color limits.
Reception
Captain Squideo of GamePro, in contrast, commented that while most of Zero's moves are fun, the dive and swoop moves are too difficult to control.

f64_spy.title: GoldenEye 007 (2010 video game)
sents: lead
GoldenEye 007 is a 2010 first-person shooter video game developed by Eurocom and published by Activision for the Wii, with a handheld version for Nintendo DS developed by n-Space.
lead
It is a modern reimagining of the 1995 James Bond film GoldenEye as well as a remake of the 1997 video game of the same name, developed for the earlier Nintendo 64 console.
lead
The game was officially announced by Nintendo at their E3 2010 conference presentation.
lead
The game was released on 2 November 2010 in tandem with another James Bond game, Blood Stone, which was also released for the DS, but not the Wii.
lead
Nintendo, the publisher of the Nintendo 64 game, published the Wii version in Japan the following summer, where it remains Wii-exclusive.
lead
It was the fifth James Bond game developed by Eurocom and their second under Activision, after the PlayStation 2 version of 007: Quantum of Solace two years prior.
lead

Although not as critically acclaimed as its original Nintendo 64 version, the game received positive reviews from critics, with many calling it a return to form for the series, with particular praise for its gameplay, campaign, voice acting, multiplayer and controls.
lead
An enhanced port of the game, titled GoldenEye 007: Reloaded, was released in November 2011 for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3.
Setting
Although Pierce Brosnan starred as Bond in GoldenEye and was featured in the 1997 game, subsequent Bond actor Daniel Craig 's likeness and voice are featured in the 2010 game.
Setting
The plot has been modified to match the style of the first two Craig reboot era films, which also meant the exclusion of Q and Miss Moneypenny (who later returned to the franchise in Skyfall).
Setting
Judi Dench (who portrayed M since the original GoldenEye) reprises her role in voice only, as does Rory Kinnear as Bill Tanner.
Plot
Onatopp and Ourumov hijack the helicopter but Bond is able to plant his smartphone on board, and MI6 is able to track the helicopter to a remote base in Siberia.
Gameplay
While GoldenEye 007 is a re-imagining of the film, the game does have noticeable differences.
Gameplay
The original GoldenEye 007 featured a cheat menu which is available from the start in the re-make.
Gameplay
GoldenEye 007 also provides players using the Remote with Nunchuk or Wii Zapper with the ability to peer around cover by tilting the Nunchuk.
Gameplay
The game does not open with any gun barrel sequence like the Craig films prior to the release of Spectre which was the first 007 film to open with it since Die Another Day.
Multiplayer
GoldenEye 007 features both offline split screen for up to four local players and online play for up to eight players.
Multiplayer
Online multiplayer is provided through the free Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection, and though up to eight players can connect to a game remotely, only one local player is allowed at a time.
Multiplayer
Split screen combat provides over a dozen modifiers, including Melee Only, You Only Live Twice, and Paintball Mode from the original game.
Development

He stated, "We would love to see it, so we're exploring all the rights issues." On 7 January 2008, Xbox Evolved reported that an updated version of GoldenEye 007 would be released on Xbox Live Arcade.
Development

However, on 11 January 2008, 1UP.com reported that a GoldenEye 007 port (as opposed to a remake) had been in development at Rare for several months, but stated that the title would not be released on the Xbox Live Arcade since "Microsoft and Nintendo couldn't agree on the financial side of things".
Development
However, Perfect Dark, a Nintendo 64 title which used the same engine as GoldenEye, would later make it to Xbox Live Arcade, and the near-complete port of "Goldeneye 007" was leaked online in 2021.
Development
It was revealed at E3 2010 that a new Goldeneye video game would be released for the Wii in November 2010.
Development
GoldenEye 007 is built on a modified version of the IW game engine from another Wii game by Eurocom, Dead Space: Extraction.
Development

Originally, Free Radical Design (now Crytek UK) were approached by Activision to develop the game because former Rare staff were working there, with the PS3 and Xbox 360 initially being considered as target platforms early into development.
Development
Free Radical Design even rebuilt the first level, "Dam" for those consoles.
Development
Wilson spoke in June 2010 about Daniel Craig 's participation in revisiting the story from the original film.
Development
"When we first pitched the game to him, he was really excited about it.
Development
David Arnold, composer of the 007 film scores from Tomorrow Never Dies until Quantum of Solace, composed the game's score.
Development
Nicole Scherzinger performs the title song " GoldenEye ", a cover version of the film's theme which was originally performed by Tina Turner.
Reception
Although not as critically acclaimed as its original Nintendo 64 version, GoldenEye 007 received positive reviews.
Reception
Aggregating review websites GameRankings and Metacritic gave the Wii version 83.67% and 81/100 and the Nintendo DS version 68.82% and 64/100.
Reception
Japanese game magazine Famitsu gave the Wii version a 34 out of 40 score, and the NDS version a 22 out of 40.
Reception
IGN awarded the game a 9.0 out of 10 and an Editor's Choice Award, praising its multiplayer component and its well-crafted story while criticising the lack of voice chat.
Reception
The reviewer, Craig Harris, concluded by acknowledging that the game—as of its release—is the Wii's best first person shooter.
Reception

Gaming Nexus gave GoldenEye 007 an A−, stating, "instead of standing in the original GoldenEye ' s shadow, Eurocom has created a brand new game that is just as compelling and addictive as the original." GameSpot reviewer Tom McShea also praised the game, awarding it an 8.5 out of 10.
Reception
Joystiq scored the game 4 out of 5.
Reception
Nintendo World Report awarded the game an 8.5/10, with the reviewer stating, "Frankly, I haven't seen a more impressive Wii shooter." The Official Nintendo Magazine gave GoldenEye 007 a score of 90%.
Reception
GameTrailers scored the game at 8.6 of 10, indicating that while most aspects are well-done, the game's performance suffers from inconsistent framerates, particularly during splitscreen play.
Reception
Digital Trends' gave the game 8 of 10, complaining of the enemy AI's simplistic strategies and lack of adaptability.
GoldenEye 007: Reloaded
At the 2011 San Diego Comic-Con, Activision unveiled GoldenEye 007: Reloaded, a remastering of the Wii game for the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 consoles.
GoldenEye 007: Reloaded
The game features high-definition graphics due to running on a new game engine, an achievement system, new "MI6 Ops Missions", and PlayStation Move compatibility for the PlayStation 3 version.
GoldenEye 007: Reloaded
The game was released on 1 November 2011 in North America, and on 4 November 2011 in Europe.
GoldenEye 007: Reloaded

Activision also released a PlayStation 3 bundle called "GoldenEye 007: Reloaded – Double 'O' Edition"; the bundle features the game itself, the PlayStation Move motion and navigation controllers, PlayStation Eye Camera, the Sharp Shooter peripheral, and access to the downloadable character Hugo Drax.
Reception
GoldenEye 007: Reloaded received generally mixed to positive reviews.
Reception
Aggregating review websites GameRankings and Metacritic gave the PlayStation 3 version 75.60% and 72/100 and the Xbox 360 version 73.20% and 72/100.

f64_perfect_dusk.title: Perfect Dark
sents: lead
Perfect Dark is a 2000 first-person shooter developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64.
lead

The first game of the Perfect Dark series, it follows Joanna Dark, an agent of the Carrington Institute research centre, as she attempts to stop an extraterrestrial conspiracy by rival corporation dataDyne.
lead

The game features a campaign mode where the player must complete a series of levels to progress through the story, as well as a range of multiplayer options, including a co-operative mode and traditional deathmatch settings with computer-controlled bots.
lead
As a spiritual successor to Rare's 1997 first-person shooter GoldenEye 007, Perfect Dark shares many features with its predecessor and runs on an upgraded version of its game engine.
lead
GoldenEye 007 director Martin Hollis led the game's production for the first fourteen months of its near three-year development cycle before he left Rare to pursue other interests.
lead
The game is one of the most technically-advanced titles for the Nintendo 64, and requires an Expansion Pak to access the campaign mode and most of the multiplayer features.
lead

Shortly before the game's release, a feature that would have allowed players to place a photograph of their choice onto the face of their multiplayer character was cut due to sensitive issues surrounding the ability for players to attack images of real people.
lead
Upon release, Perfect Dark received critical acclaim and sold relatively well, eventually joining Nintendo's " Player's Choice " game selection.
Gameplay
Perfect Dark is a first-person shooter where players complete levels to unlock content and progress through the game's storyline.
Gameplay
Players manoeuvre their character from a first-person perspective and have the ability to lean left or right, look up or down, crouch, crawl, and drop from most ledges; there is no jump ability.
Gameplay
For example, the secondary function of the K7 Avenger assault rifle detects threats like explosive devices.
Gameplay
Most weapons have a finite magazine and must be reloaded after a certain number of shots.
Gameplay
The most notable of these is the shooting range, where players can test their proficiency with the game's weapons in individual challenges.
Campaign
Perfect Dark features a campaign mode where a single player controls the game's protagonist, Joanna Dark, through a series of levels collected together into missions.
Campaign
Options such as friendly fire can be disabled and only one player is required to survive a level.
Multiplayer
Perfect Dark features a multiplayer mode where up to four players and eight computer-controlled bots can compete against each other in different arenas.
Multiplayer
Pre-set behaviours range from them pursuing the highest-scoring player to exclusively chasing the player who killed them last.
Multiplayer
Other behaviours restrict bots to only attack players using fists and disarming moves.
Multiplayer
The multiplayer mode includes 30 pre-set challenges against bots that may be tackled by one or more players.
Plot

Perfect Dark is set in an alternate 2023 against the backdrop of an interstellar war between two alien races: the Maians, who resemble the archetypal Grey alien, and the Skedar, reptile -like creatures who use a cloaking device to appear human.
Plot
The player is cast as Joanna Dark, an agent of the Carrington Institute whose excellent scores in training have earned her the codename "Perfect Dark".
Plot
On her first mission, she is sent to extract a defector known as Dr.
Concept and design
Perfect Dark was developed by Rare and originally directed by Martin Hollis as a spiritual successor to the company's 1997 first-person shooter GoldenEye 007.
Concept and design

Shortly after GoldenEye 007 was released, Rare was planning to work on a game based on the GoldenEye sequel Tomorrow Never Dies, but the company was outbid by Electronic Arts, which would release their video game adaptation in 1999.
Concept and design
Working titles for the new project included "Covert Ops" and "Alien Intelligence" before the words "Perfect Dark" were decided on.
Concept and design

Hollis noted naming similarities to the 2006 first-person shooter Black by Criterion Games: "Game developers just like black, nihilism, dystopian futures, the number zero, infinity, spheres, perfection—all that kind of stuff".
Concept and design

The double slash symbol in the game's logo was inspired by the Japanese writing system, while the bad grammar of the phrase "Perfect Dark" partially alludes to Hollis' affection for the way Japanese developers use English words in their own games and products.
Concept and design
The X-Files television series inspired the incorporation of a gray alien character and the premise of aliens being investigated.
Concept and design

For example, the first level takes place in a skyscraper that lead artist Karl Hilton had always wanted to build, and features realistic environments like service stairs and an exterior area that can be explored.
Concept and design

To this end, the team created Joanna Dark, influenced by a number of fictional heroines: Kim Kimberly from the 1983 interactive fiction game Snowball, the seductive spy Agent X-27 in the 1931 film Dishonored, the eponymous femme fatale of the 1990 film La Femme Nikita, and FBI agent Dana Scully from The X-Files.
Concept and design
The name of the in-game company dataDyne was inspired by Yoyodyne from the 1965 novella The Crying of Lot 49 by Thomas Pynchon.
Concept and design
The layout of the Air Force One level was inspired by the 1997 film of the same name because it was the only reference material the team had.
Concept and design

In the game's Counter-Operative mode, the idea that the opposing player can take control of another opponent at any time was inspired by the 1999 film The Matrix, where agents can reappear as another person in the film's simulated reality.
Production
According to Rare, only 30% of the original engine remained, providing a basic framework to construct levels and animate characters.
Production
Originally, Hollis hoped that the difference between light and dark would be a significant feature of the gameplay, and the title was intended to reflect this focus.
Production

A flashlight was implemented by software engineer Steve Ellis, who had been responsible for much of the multiplayer mode of GoldenEye 007, but was ultimately not included in the game due to limitations of the Nintendo 64 hardware.
Production
Hollis was involved with Perfect Dark for the first 14 months of its near three-year development cycle, during which progress was unsatisfactory.
Production
Hollis' decision came after his four-year contract with Rare was about to expire, which he chose not to renew as he wanted to pursue other interests.
Production
