Shortly after his exit in September 1998, four additional members—Doak, Hilton, Ellis and composer Graeme Norgate —left Rare to form Free Radical Design, partially because they were unsatisfied with the working environment.
Production
In spring 1999, Rare moved its headquarters from a country farmhouse in Twycross, Leicestershire to its current multi-million office complex.
Production
Rare installed an in-house motion capture studio, which was used to capture hit animations and full walk cycles.
Production
Game designer Duncan Botwood wore a pair of heels to portray Joanna Dark in some sessions, but motion capture artist Laurie Sage performed most of her moves.
Production
Numerous secrets were added to the game to fuel the exploration efforts of players, including a piece of cheese hidden in every level.
Production
The game has two hidden passwords: one found by picking up a necklace in one level and another by reaching the highest rank in the multiplayer mode.
Production
Rare had originally intended these details to access password-protected sections of promotional websites and use them for an alternate reality game.
Production
As developers kept adding features, the game ended up using all the extra memory on their debug consoles and became too big to fit into the Nintendo 64's standard 4 MB of random-access memory (RAM).
Production
Because the developers were unable to optimise it, they made use of the Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak, which increases the Nintendo 64's RAM from 4 MB to 8 MB.
Production

Although the Expansion Pak is required to access the game's campaign and most of the multiplayer features, a limited subset of deathmatch options are available without the device—around 35% of the game is playable without an Expansion Pak, as estimated on the game's instruction booklet.
Production
The iterative nature of the game's development led Hollis to describe the ultimate number of multiplayer options as "a vast array of features I never planned".
Production

Although Rare's Nintendo -side producer Ken Lobb originally stated that the feature was removed due to technical difficulties, the actual reason was revealed to be sensitive issues surrounding the ability for players to attack images of real people.
Production
Rare's decision came after then-recent attacks such as the Columbine High School massacre, when new censorship laws were being introduced in the United States.
Production
One of Norgate's few contributions to the final Perfect Dark score was the theme of the first level.
Production
The game supports 16x9 widescreen and Dolby surround sound, and features voice acting for all in-game and cutscene dialogue.
Production
Because Perfect Dark features more than 45 minutes of voiced cutscenes, the game was shipped in a 32 MB cartridge.
Marketing and release
Although a follow-up to GoldenEye 007 was confirmed to be in development in early 1998, Perfect Dark was formally presented as Nintendo's lead game at E3 1998 in Atlanta, Georgia.
Marketing and release

Originally scheduled for a release in summer 1999 and later in December 1999, Perfect Dark was heavily trailed in video game magazines, with Nintendo Official Magazine predicting that it would be "the best shooting game this century".
Marketing and release

A working version of the game appeared at the European Computer Trade Show in September 1998; N64 Magazine described the preview as having "the kind of attention to detail that had everyone who saw drooling".
Marketing and release

A more complete version was presented at E3 in May 1999, where the game's compatibility with the Game Boy Camera was announced, and at Nintendo Space World in August 1999, alongside Rare's Donkey Kong 64 and Jet Force Gemini.
Marketing and release
Shortly before release, Rare unveiled a website for the in-game company dataDyne to promote interest in the game's storyline.
Marketing and release
The game had a marketing budget of $10 million.
Marketing and release
Perfect Dark was first released in North America on 22 May 2000.
Marketing and release
To supplement the game, Rare released a Game Boy Color counterpart, also titled Perfect Dark, shortly afterwards.
Marketing and release
In Japan, Perfect Dark was released on 21 October 2000.
Marketing and release
Perfect Dark features a different box art for each regional release.
Marketing and release
Rare's art director Kev Bayliss, who created the North American and European artworks, designed the North American version in one day because Rare needed it very quickly.
Marketing and release
For the Japanese release, a completely different image was requested by Nintendo, who originally considered releasing the game in Japan under the title "Aka to Kuro" (赤と黒, lit.
Marketing and release
"Perfect Dark" does not translate well into Japanese, and the title "Aka to Kuro" was considered sufficiently edgy.
Marketing and release
According to NPD 's Toy Retail Survey Tracking system, Perfect Dark was the second best-selling game of May 2000 in North America, behind Pokémon Trading Card Game.
Marketing and release
The Japanese launch saw sales totalling 35,000 units in its first week.
Marketing and release
As a bestseller, Perfect Dark joined Nintendo's " Player's Choice " game selection on 21 December 2000.
Marketing and release
23 on the all formats chart for the week of 24 December 2000.
Marketing and release
As of March 2003, Perfect Dark had sold almost 1.3 million copies in the United States and 77,000 copies in Japan.
Marketing and release
Total sales in the United States reached 1.5 million by December 2007.
Marketing and release

In a 2011 interview with Eurogamer, game designer Chris Tilston revealed that lifetime sales for the game reached 3.2 million, but did not clarify if the figure accounted for units shipped to retailers.
Reception
Perfect Dark received critical acclaim from video game publications.
Reception
The most praised aspects of the game were its graphics, artificial intelligence, and number of multiplayer options.
Reception
GameSpot claimed that, as a console first-person shooter, Perfect Dark is "unparalleled", while IGN journalist Matt Casamassina remarked that its extensive features set the game apart from its peers.
Reception
Similarly, N64 Magazine described Perfect Dark as "dauntingly huge", stating that it "takes everything that made its predecessor such an enduring favourite and does it bigger, better and more often".
Reception
Nintendo Power editors called the game "undeniably a work of art", suspenseful, "more compelling than most action movies and much deeper than any video game of its type".
Reception
The Electric Playground credited Rare for being able to fit such a clear-sounding experience into the limited space of a Nintendo 64 cartridge.
Reception
GamePro called the game's Counter-Operative mode one of the "coolest multiplayer modes ever", stating that the player playing as Joanna never knows which enemy the opposing player controls.
Reception
At their Best and Worst of 2000 awards, GameSpot editors awarded Perfect Dark Best Nintendo 64 Game and Best Shooting Game, and nominated it in the Best Multiplayer Game category.
Reception
Rare was recognised for its work on the game and received the BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Moving Images Award for 2000, and the Golden Satellite Award for Best Interactive Product in 2001.
Legacy

Shortly after Perfect Dark was released, Rare planned to develop a "sister" title, called Velvet Dark, for either the Nintendo 64 or its successor, the GameCube, but the project never moved beyond pre-production and was ultimately abandoned.
Legacy
Meanwhile, Free Radical Design released TimeSplitters for the PlayStation 2 in October 2000, a first-person shooter based around a completely new engine.
Legacy
TimeSplitters bears several gameplay and presentational similarities to GoldenEye 007 and Perfect Dark, including a similar aiming system and unlockable options through quick level completions.
Legacy
After Rare was purchased by Microsoft in 2002, the company released a prequel, Perfect Dark Zero, as a launch title for the Xbox 360 in 2005.
Legacy
The magazine concluded that despite Perfect Dark not standing up as a good game to play in 2009, "its currency of ideas and provocation remains sound".
Legacy

In 2015, Den of Geek considered Perfect Dark "a game that's done more for the shooter genre than often credited for", and said that the game was still ahead of its time because no game had revitalised its ideas.
Legacy
In 2001, Electronic Gaming Monthly editors ranked Perfect Dark 65th on their list of Top 100 Games of All Time, while Nintendo Power included it in their 2006 list of Top 200 Nintendo games.
Legacy
86 on their list of Top 100 Games of All Time, noting that "Everything that GoldenEye made great, Perfect Dark did too, and then some." Similarly, Edge placed the title at No.
Legacy
28 on their 2007 list of 100 Best Videogames (a list voted for by readers, Edge staff and gaming industry professionals), claiming that the game brought the Nintendo 64 era to a satisfying close.
Legacy
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked it 37th on a list of 100 Best Nintendo Games.
Legacy
A reboot, also titled Perfect Dark, is being developed by The Initiative.
Remaster

A remaster of the game, also titled Perfect Dark, was released in 2010 for the Xbox 360 through its Xbox Live Arcade download service, featuring improved frame rate, enhanced graphics and an online multiplayer.
Remaster
The remaster was developed by 4J Studios, the same studio that previously handled the Xbox 360 ports of Rare's platform games Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie.
Remaster
Some critics considered the relatively unchanged game to be outdated, but most agreed that the title was a solid revival of a classic.
Remaster
In 2015, the remaster was included in the Rare Replay video game compilation for Xbox One.

f64_thyme.real: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
f64_thyme.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
sents: lead
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a 1998 action-adventure game by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was released in Japan and North America in November 1998 and in PAL regions the following month.
lead
The game is the first in The Legend of Zelda series with 3D graphics.
lead
Ocarina of Time was developed by Nintendo's Entertainment Analysis & Development division.
lead
It was led by five directors, including Eiji Aonuma and Yoshiaki Koizumi, produced by series co-creator Shigeru Miyamoto, and written by Kensuke Tanabe.
lead
Series composer Koji Kondo wrote its soundtrack.
lead
The player controls Link in the realm of Hyrule on a quest to stop the evil king Ganondorf by traveling through time and navigating dungeons and an overworld.
lead
The game introduced features such as a target-lock system and context-sensitive buttons, which have since become common in 3D adventure games.
Gameplay
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a fantasy action-adventure game set in a three-dimensional world with an expansive environment.
Gameplay
For example, only adult Link can use the Fairy Bow, and only young Link can fit through certain small passages.
Setting
Ocarina of Time is set in the fictional kingdom of Hyrule, the setting of most Legend of Zelda games.
Story
Link collects the other two stones: the first from Darunia, leader of the Gorons, and the second from Ruto, princess of the Zoras.
Story
Ganondorf acquired only the Triforce of Power, while Zelda received the Triforce of Wisdom and Link the Triforce of Courage.
Development

Ocarina of Time was developed concurrently with Super Mario 64 and Mario Kart 64 for the Nintendo 64 by Nintendo's Entertainment Analysis & Development (EAD) division, for more than $12 million with a staff of more than 200.
Development
Development was migrated from the 64DD disk drive peripheral to cartridge due to the high data throughput of streaming 500 motion-captured character animations throughout gameplay.
Development
Initially targeting 16- megabytes, it was increased to 32 megabytes, as Nintendo's largest game ever.
Development

Four or five initial teams grew over time, each working on different basic experiments, including scenario and planning, Link's actions, transforming classic 2D items into improved 3D form, camera experiments, motion capture, sound, special effects, and the flow of time.
Development
Although the development team was new to 3D games, assistant director Makoto Miyanaga recalled a "passion for creating something new and unprecedented".
Development
The development involved more than 120 people, including stunt performers used to capture the effects of sword fighting and Link's movement.
Development

Miyamoto initially intended Ocarina of Time to be played in a first-person perspective to enable players to take in the vast terrain of Hyrule Field better and let the team focus more on developing enemies and environments.
Development
Originally Z-targeting involved a generic marker, but Koizumi changed the design to that of a fairy to make it less "robotic".
Development

To promote this instantaneous continuity of cinematic gameplay, the cutscenes in Ocarina of Time are completely generated with real-time computing on the Nintendo 64 and do not use prerendered full-motion video.
Development

Miyamoto's vision required this real-time architecture for the total of more than 90 minutes of cutscenes, regardless of whether the console had a vast medium like CD-ROM on which to store prerendered versions.
Development

Miyamoto said the real-time rendering engine allowed his small team of 3 to 7 cinematic developers to rapidly adjust the storyline and to focus on developing additional gameplay elements even up to the final few months of development, instead of waiting on a repeated prerendering process.
Development
Some of Miyamoto's ideas were instead used in Super Mario 64, since it was to be released first.
Development
Ocarina of Time originally ran on the same engine as Super Mario 64 but was so heavily modified that Miyamoto considers the final products different engines.
Development
One major difference between the two is camera control; the player has a lot of control over the camera in Super Mario 64, but the camera in Ocarina of Time is largely controlled by the game AI.
Development
Miyamoto said the camera controls for Ocarina of Time are intended to reflect a focus on the game's world, whereas those of Super Mario 64 are centered on the character of Mario.
Development
Miyamoto wanted the difficulty to be easy enough to make the game accessible to all players and said in particular that he wanted it to be easier than Super Mario 64.
Music
Ocarina of Time ' s music was written by Koji Kondo, the composer in charge of music for most of the games in The Legend of Zelda series.
Music
The button layout of the Nintendo 64 controller resembles the holes of the ocarinas in the game, and players must learn to play several songs to complete the game.
Music
Kondo said that creating distinct themes on the limited scale was a "major challenge" but feels that the result is very natural.
Music
The official soundtrack of Ocarina of Time was published by Pony Canyon and released in Japan on December 18, 1998.
Music
In 2001, three years after the initial release of Ocarina of Time, GameSpot labeled it as one of the top ten video game soundtracks.
Music

In 2011, however, a 51-track limited edition soundtrack for the 3DS version was available in a free mail out through a Club Nintendo offer to owners of the 3DS edition, as an incentive to register the product.
Music
Hero of Time, an orchestral recording of Ocarina of Time ' s score performed by the Slovak National Symphony Orchestra, was released by video game label Materia Collective in 2017.
Release
Ocarina of Time was first shown as a technical and thematic demonstration video at Nintendo's Shoshinkai trade show in December 1995.
Release
Nintendo planned to release Super Mario 64 as a launch game for the Nintendo 64 and later release Ocarina of Time for the 64DD, a disk drive peripheral for the system that was still in development.
Release

Issues regarding performance of the 64DD peripheral led to development being moved from disk to cartridge media, and thus the game would miss its scheduled 1997 holiday season release and was delayed into 1998.
Release
Throughout the late 1990s, the Nintendo 64 was said to lack hit first-party games.
Release

Next Generation wrote that "Nintendo absolutely can't afford another holiday season without a real marquee title" and that Zelda was "one of the most anticipated games of the decade", upon which the Nintendo 64's fate depended.
Release
Nintendo spent $10 million on Ocarina of Time ' s marketing.
Release
In March 1998, it was the most anticipated Nintendo 64 game in Japan.
Release
Chairman Howard Lincoln insisted at E3 1998 that Zelda ship on time and become Nintendo's reinvigorating blockbuster, akin to a hit Hollywood movie.
Release
Customers in North America who pre-ordered the Ocarina of Time received a limited-edition box with a golden plastic card reading "Collector's Edition".
Release
This edition contained a gold-colored cartridge, a tradition that began with the original Legend of Zelda (1986) for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
Release
Demand was so great that Electronics Boutique stopped pre-selling the game on November 3, 1998.
Rereleases
Nintendo ported Ocarina of Time to its next console, the GameCube, as part of The Legend of Zelda: Collector's Edition, a compilation of Zelda games.
Rereleases
The emulated port runs at a resolution of 640×480, quadruple that of the original, and supports progressive scan.
Rereleases

Another GameCube release included the original game and a second, more difficult version titled Master Quest that was included as a pre-order bonus with The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker (2002) in Japan and North America and included in GameCube bundles worldwide.
Rereleases
In November 2003, Ocarina of Time was ported to China's iQue Player as one of the five games available on its release.
Rereleases
In February 2007, Ocarina of Time was released for the Wii Virtual Console service for 1000 Wii Points.
Rereleases
Ocarina of Time was rereleased on the Wii U Virtual Console worldwide on July 2, 2015, this time including the original controller vibration.
Rereleases
It was also released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on October 25, 2021.
Nintendo 3DS remake
In June 2011, Nintendo released Ocarina of Time 3D, an enhanced port for the Nintendo 3DS handheld console.
Master Quest
After completing Ocarina of Time, Nintendo developed a new version of the game for the then-unreleased 64DD peripheral with the working title Ura Zelda, commonly translated as "Another Zelda".
Master Quest
In 1998, Ura Zelda was delayed indefinitely following problems with the development of the 64DD, and was canceled due to the 64DD's commercial failure.
Master Quest
In August 2000, Miyamoto stated that Ura Zelda had been finished and that no online functions had ever been planned.
Master Quest

Ura Zelda was released on the GameCube in 2002 in Japan as Zeruda no Densetsu: Toki no Okarina GC Ura (ゼルダの伝説 時のオカリナ GC裏) and in 2003 in North America and Europe as The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Master Quest.
Master Quest
According to Miyamoto, Ura Zelda was simple to port as it used few of the 64DD features.
Master Quest
IGN's Peer Schneider gave Master Quest a mostly positive review, likening the concept to the second quest of the original Legend of Zelda.
Reception
Upon its initial Nintendo 64 release, Ocarina of Time received critical acclaim.
Reception

The review aggregator websites Metacritic and GameRankings both rank the original Nintendo 64 version as the highest reviewed game of all time, with average scores of 99/100 from Metacritic and 98% from GameRankings.
Reception
GameRevolution noted the characters' faces, the "toughest graphical challenge on 3D characters", saying that the characters' expressions and animation featured "surprising grace".
Reception
IGN believed that Ocarina of Time improved on the graphics of Super Mario 64, giving a larger sense of scale.
Reception
EGM enjoyed that Nintendo was able to take the elements of the older, 2D Zelda games and "translate it all into 3D flawlessly".
Reception
Nintendo Power cited Ocarina of Time, along with Super Mario 64, as two games that "blazed trails" into the 3D era.
Reception
Pitchfork gave the official soundtrack album a 9 out of 10.
Sales

In the United States, over 500,000 pre-orders were placed, more than tripling the number of pre-orders for any previous game, for which it was awarded the Guinness World Record for Most Advance Orders for a Game.
Sales
Upon release, more than 1 million copies were sold there in less than a week.
Sales

In 1998, 2.5 million copies were sold, although it was released only 39 days before the end of the year; it earned $150,000,000 (equivalent to $280,000,000 in 2023) in U.S. revenues, higher than any Hollywood film in the last six weeks of 1998.
Sales
It was the best-selling video game of 1998 in the United States.
Sales

In Japan, 920,000 copies were sold in 1998, becoming the eighth best-selling game of that year; a reported 386,234 copies were sold in its first week there, surpassing the 316,000 first-week sales of Metal Gear Solid.
Sales
In Europe, Ocarina of Time was the fifth-bestselling game of 1998, grossing more than €39,000,000 or $44,000,000 (equivalent to $82,000,000 in 2023).
Sales
In the UK, it was the fastest-ever-selling game until the release of Gran Turismo 2 in 2000, selling 61,232 copies during its first weekend.
Sales
1.14 million Nintendo 64 copies were sold in Japan and 7.6 million copies worldwide.
Sales
By 2000, Ocarina of Time had sold 7 million cartridges and grossed about $400,000,000 (equivalent to $750,000,000 in 2023) worldwide.
Awards
In 1998, Ocarina of Time won the Grand Prize in the Interactive Art division at the Japan Media Arts Festival.
Awards
Edge gave it the awards for "Game of the Year" and "Gameplay Innovation" and placed it 2nd place for "Graphical Achievement" (behind Virtua Fighter 3tb).
Legacy
After publication, Ocarina of Time was featured on a number of compiled lists of best or most influential games.
Legacy
The game was placed second in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s "100 greatest Nintendo games of all time", behind only Super Mario Bros.
Legacy
Game Informer ranked it as its 11th favorite game of all time and described it as "untouchable".
Legacy

In May 2011, IGN held a tournament-style competition celebrating the 25th anniversary of the original The Legend of Zelda ' s release in which fans voted Ocarina of Time the greatest Zelda game; it beat Majora's Mask in the final round.
Legacy
Edge concluded its 2009 list with: " Ocarina of Time is here in the list not because Nintendo had the power and wisdom to make a great game, but because it had the courage to make a unique one".
Legacy
In 2022, The Strong National Museum of Play inducted Ocarina of Time to its World Video Game Hall of Fame.
Legacy
Reception for the Master Quest and Virtual Console rereleases was positive; while some considered aspects of the graphics and audio to be outdated, most thought that the game had aged well.
Legacy
The Master Quest version holds an average score of 89.50% on GameRankings and 91/100 on Metacritic.
Legacy
Game Revolution said that although the game has "noticeably aged compared to brand new RPGs... it's still a terrific game", awarding 91 out of 100.
Legacy

In 2007, former GameSpot editor Jeff Gerstmann gave the Virtual Console port 8.9 out of 10: "Even after nine years, Ocarina of Time holds up surprisingly well, offering a lengthy and often-amazing adventure".
Legacy
In November 2021, enthusiasts fully decompiled Ocarina of Time 's ROM into human-readable C code.
Legacy
In March 2022, a group called "Harbour Masters" publicly released a PC port under the name " Ship of Harkinian ", which includes widescreen support and an increased framerate, among other features.
Impact
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ' s gameplay system popularized features such as a target lock system and context-sensitive buttons that have since become common elements in 3D adventure games.
Impact
Former Rockstar Games vice president of creativity Dan Houser stated in 2012 that "anyone who makes 3-D games who says they've not borrowed something from Mario or Zelda is lying".
Impact
Dark Souls creator Hidetaka Miyazaki (FromSoftware) said that " The Legend of Zelda became a sort of textbook for 3D action games ".
Impact
CD Projekt Red (The Witcher, Cyberpunk 2077) cited Zelda as an influence on The Witcher series, including The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (2015).
Impact
Final Fantasy and The 3rd Birthday director Hajime Tabata (Square Enix) cited Ocarina of Time as inspiration for the seamless open world of Final Fantasy XV.

f64_legend_of_zeldo_majora_s_mas.real: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
f64_legend_of_zeldo_majora_s_mas.title: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
sents: lead
The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask is a 2000 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was the second The Legend of Zelda game to use 3D graphics, following Ocarina of Time (1998).
lead
Designed by a creative team led by Eiji Aonuma, Yoshiaki Koizumi, and Shigeru Miyamoto, Majora's Mask was completed in less than two years.
lead

It features enhanced graphics and several gameplay changes, but reuses elements and character models from Ocarina of Time, which the game's creators called a creative decision made necessary by time constraints.
lead
The story takes place months after Ocarina of Time.
lead
Link arrives in a parallel world, Termina, and becomes embroiled in a quest to prevent the moon from crashing in three days' time.
lead
The game introduces gameplay concepts revolving around a perpetually repeating three-day cycle and the use of various masks that transform Link into different forms.
lead
As the player progresses through the game, Link learns to play numerous melodies on his ocarina, which allow him to control the flow of time, open hidden passages, or manipulate the environment.
Gameplay
The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask is an action-adventure game set in a three-dimensional (3D) environment.
Gameplay

As a direct sequel to Ocarina of Time, the first 3D title in the series, the game retains its predecessor's gameplay systems and control scheme while introducing new elements including character transformations and a three-day cycle.
Masks and transformations
Whereas the masks in Ocarina of Time are limited to an optional sidequest, they play a central role in Majora's Mask, which has twenty-four masks in total.
Masks and transformations
Some areas can only be accessed by use of these abilities.
Masks and transformations
For example, the Great Fairy's Mask helps locate stray fairies in the four temples, the Bunny Hood increases Link's movement speed, and the Stone Mask renders Link invisible to most enemies.
Masks and transformations
Certain masks are involved only in sidequests or specialized situations.
Three-day cycle
Majora's Mask revolves around a three-day cycle (about 54 minutes in real time), in which non-player characters and events follow a predictable schedule.
Three-day cycle
Players may save their game and return to 6:00 am of the first day by playing the Song of Time.
Three-day cycle
Although returning to the first day resets most quests and character interactions, Link retains weapons, equipment, masks, learned songs, and proof of dungeon completion.
Setting and characters
Majora's Mask is set in Termina, an alternate version of Hyrule which is the main setting of most Zelda games.
Story
Link plays the Song of Time and miraculously returns to the day he first set foot in Termina.
Development
It was initially conceived as a remixed "Ura" edition of Ocarina of Time for the disc-based 64DD peripheral for Nintendo 64.
Development
By reusing game assets, the smaller team was able to finish Majora's Mask in 15 months.
Development
Another team finished Ura Zelda, but it never came out on the 64DD, which was a commercial failure in Japan and was not released outside its home country.
Development
Early in development, this system originally rewound a week, but it was shorted as seven days was deemed too burdensome for players to remember and too complex to create in one year.
Development
Aonuma cited the 1998 film Run Lola Run as inspiration for the time loop concept.
Development
Majora's Mask first appeared in the media in May 1999, when Famitsu reported that a long-planned Zelda expansion for the 64DD was in development.
Development
It had a playable demo at the Nintendo Space World exhibition on August 27, 1999.
Development
In November, Nintendo announced a "Holiday 2000" release date.
Development
The game was supported by a $8 million marketing campaign.
Technical differences from Ocarina of Time

Majora's Mask runs on an upgraded version of the engine used in Ocarina of Time and requires the use of the Nintendo 64's 4MB Expansion Pak, making it and Donkey Kong 64 the only two games that require the peripheral.
Technical differences from Ocarina of Time
IGN theorized this requirement is due to Majora's Mask ' s origins as a Nintendo 64DD game, which would necessitate an extra 4MB of RAM.
Technical differences from Ocarina of Time

IGN considered the texture design to be one of the best created for the Nintendo 64, saying that although some textures have a low resolution, they are "colorful and diverse", which gives each area "its own unique look".
Music
The two-disc soundtrack was released in Japan on June 23, 2000, and features 112 tracks from the game.
Reception
In Japan, The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask sold 601,542 copies by the end of 2000.
Reception
In the United States, it was the fourth best-selling game of 2000 at 1,206,489 copies.
Reception
In Europe, it was the eighth highest-grossing game of 2000.
Reception
Overall, 3.36 million copies were sold worldwide for Nintendo 64.
Reception
The game holds a score of 95/100 on review aggregator Metacritic, indicating "universal acclaim", based on 27 reviews.
Reception

Reviewers did not take issue with the reuse of game engine, control mechanics, and visual assets from Ocarina of Time; Jes Bickham of GamesRadar said they were already "nigh-on perfect after all" and the recycling allowed the development team to concentrate on delivering new content.
Reception

Andrew Reiner of Game Informer called it "one of the most inventive premises in all of gaming", and also stated that "without question, Majora's Mask is the finest adventure the Nintendo 64 has to offer".
Reception
Some critics found that the time restrictions made it one of the most challenging games in the series.
Reception
Multiple outlets took note of its darker tone and story compared to other games in The Legend of Zelda series.
Reception
Matt Casamassina of IGN described the game as " The Empire Strikes Back of Nintendo 64", making an analogy to the film's status as a more mature and sophisticated sequel to Star Wars.
Reception
The GamePro reviewer characterized the story as "surreal and spooky, deep, and intriguing" and the game as "living proof that the N64 still has its magic".
Reception
Majora's Mask was a runner-up for GameSpot ' s "Best Nintendo 64 Game" award, losing to Perfect Dark.
Legacy
Writing for Polygon, Danielle Riendeau observed that Ocarina of Time provided the foundations for Majora's Mask to become the "most innovative" game in the series on a structural level.
Ports and emulated releases

In 2003, Nintendo rereleased Majora's Mask on the GameCube as part of The Legend of Zelda: Collector's Edition, a special promotional disc which also contained three other The Legend of Zelda games and a twenty-minute demo of The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker.
Ports and emulated releases

The Collector's Edition was also available through the Club Nintendo reward program, with a bonus discount offered in 2004 with the purchase of The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures during the month-long "Zelda Collection" campaign.
Ports and emulated releases
The only differences are minor adjustments to button icons to resemble the buttons on the GameCube controller.
Ports and emulated releases
The GameCube version also features a slightly higher native resolution than its Nintendo 64 counterpart, as well as progressive scan.
Ports and emulated releases
Majora's Mask was released on the Wii 's Virtual Console service in Europe and Australia on April 3, 2009, and Japan on April 7.
Ports and emulated releases
It was later released in North America on May 18 and commemorated as the 300th Virtual Console game available for purchase in the region.
Ports and emulated releases
During January 2012, Club Nintendo members could download Majora's Mask onto the Wii Console at a discount.
Ports and emulated releases
A similar deal was offered at the discontinuation of Club Nintendo in 2015.
Ports and emulated releases
The game was released for the Wii U 's Virtual Console service in Europe on June 23, 2016 and in North America on November 24.
Ports and emulated releases
Majora's Mask was released through the Nintendo Switch Online Expansion Pack service on February 25, 2022.
Nintendo 3DS remake
After the release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D, a remake for the Nintendo 3DS, director Eiji Aonuma suggested that a Majora's Mask remake was dependent on interest and demand.
Nintendo 3DS remake
The remake, titled The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask 3D, was released worldwide in February 2015.
Nintendo 3DS remake

Like Ocarina of Time 3D before it, the remake features improved character models and stereoscopic 3D graphics, along with altered boss battles, an additional fishing minigame, and compatibility with the New Nintendo 3DS, particularly its second analog stick used for camera control.
Nintendo 3DS remake
The game's release coincided with the launch of the New Nintendo 3DS system in North America and Europe.
Nintendo 3DS remake
A special edition New Nintendo 3DS XL model was launched alongside the game, with the European release featuring a pin badge, double-sided poster, and steelbook case.
Cultural impact
Majora's Mask was the primary inspiration for the 2010s web serial Ben Drowned by Alexander D.
Cultural impact

Building on the horror elements of the game, Ben Drowned is framed as an urban legend about a "haunted" Majora's Mask game cartridge that causes unexplainable events in-game and in the player's real life.
Cultural impact
Victor Luckerson of The Ringer attributed part of Majora's Mask ' s enduring cult following to its ambiguous themes, malleable and receptive to reinterpretations like Ben Drowned.
Cultural impact
Skull Kid appears as a computer-controlled Assist Trophy in Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U and Ultimate, while the Moon appears as an Assist Trophy in Ultimate as well.
Cultural impact
A Skull Kid-themed mask is available as customizable headgear to be worn by Mii characters in Nintendo 3DS and Wii U and Ultimate.
Cultural impact
Ember Lab made an animated short film called Terrible Fate in 2016, based on characters from Majora's Mask.

f64_kablooie.title: Banjo-Kazooie (video game)
sents: lead
Banjo-Kazooie is a 1998 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Controlling the player characters, the bear Banjo and the bird Kazooie, the player attempts to save Banjo's kidnapped sister Tooty from the witch Gruntilda.
lead
The player explores nine nonlinear worlds to gather items and progress.
lead
Using Banjo and Kazooie's traversal and combat abilities, they complete challenges such as solving puzzles, jumping over obstacles, and defeating bosses.
lead
Rare conceived Banjo-Kazooie as a role-playing video game, Dream, for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System following the completion of Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest (1995).
lead
The 15-member team, led by Gregg Mayles, transitioned development to the Nintendo 64 and retooled the game as a platformer after the role-playing format proved too complex.
lead
Banjo-Kazooie was inspired by Super Mario 64 (1996) and designed to appeal to a broad audience, similar to Walt Disney Animation Studios films.
lead
Grant Kirkhope composed the soundtrack; Banjo-Kazooie was one of the first games to feature vertical remixing, where various sound layers fade in and out depending on the player's location.
Gameplay
There are a total of 100 jiggies to collect (ten in each world), all of which are needed to view the proper ending, and 900 notes (100 in each world).
Gameplay
The door with the highest amount of required notes has 880, although 765 are needed to enter the final section.
Gameplay
Like Super Mario 64 (1996), Banjo-Kazooie is very open and allows the player to collect Jiggies and musical notes in a nonlinear order.
Gameplay
For example, while swimming, Kazooie moves faster but also has a harder time turning directions than Banjo, who only swims when above ground.
Gameplay

By finding a spell book called Cheato in the game's overworld, the player may also unlock secret codes that increase the capacity of Banjo and Kazooie's item inventory, such as the red feathers from 50 to 100 and the blue eggs from 100 to 200.
Origins

The origins of Banjo-Kazooie can be traced back to Project Dream, a cancelled video game developed by Rare 's Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest (1995) team for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
Origins
Inspired by Japanese role-playing games and LucasArts adventure games, Dream was developed for 16 months and starred a boy who got into trouble with a group of pirates.
Origins

The game used Rare's Advanced Computer Modeling (ACM) graphics technology, first used in Donkey Kong Country (1994), to an advanced level." It involved the layering of several sprites to provide depth, achieved with "hundreds of thousands of pounds worth of rendering equipment.
Origins
Because the introduction of the Nintendo 64 made the ACM technology obsolete, Rare decided to transition the development of the game to that console.
Origins
When this occurred, the Nintendo 64 was still known as the Ultra 64.
Origins

In the 2.5D game, Banjo would have collected fruits, the equivalent to musical notes in Banjo-Kazooie, in five "fruit houses" named after the fruit in them: oranges, grapes, lemons, bananas, and cherries.
Origins

Two months into its 2.5D phase, Rare was presented by Nintendo a "really, really early" version of Super Mario 64 (1996), which exposed them to the perceived future direction it would take the video games market.
Staff and workflow
The team comprised both experienced and inexperienced people; some had been working at Rare for 10 years while others had never previously worked on a video game.
Staff and workflow
Bryan has not revealed much about the making of the cover art, other than that Rare wanted him to "tell a story" with it.
Staff and workflow
Actual work on Banjo-Kazooie started in March 1997 with a development team of 10 people.
Staff and workflow
The development of the game took 17 months to complete after Rare discarded Project Dream, the first two of these being spent experimenting with Dream ' s graphic technology.
Staff and workflow
Mayles and Bryan, in one week, attempted forty hours of normal time and 60 overtime hours for a total of 100 hours.
Staff and workflow
Mayles admitted in 2022 to having worked 102 hours in a single week.
Staff and workflow

As part of Rare's late 1990s strategy of rewarding staff with bonus royalties, the Banjo-Kazooie staff was paid 50 cents per sold game in addition to their average salaries, higher than the 17-cent-per-cartridge amount of GoldenEye 007 (1997) but lower than the full-dollar-per-cartridge total of Donkey Kong 64 (1999).
Design

However, Super Mario 64 ' s 3D aspect was referenced heavily, as it was the only game similar to Banjo-Kazooie that had been released, and Rare intended to combine it with the look of Donkey Kong Country.
Design

The developers appreciated the freedom of movement Super Mario 64 provided, but analyzed it did not take enough advantage of it; instead, it centered on quick timing and reflexes required for most 2D platformers, which Mayles considered unsuitable for 3D games due to lesser accuracy of viewing distances.
Design
Sutherland described Super Mario 64 ' s camera as it and the player character attached to each other with a string, with the only movement being tilting when he moves around the front of the camera.
Design
Rare also disliked Super Mario 64 ' s forcing of the player back into the hub world once they collect a star in the level, thinking that it hindered immersion.
Design
Difficulty balance was a major focus; for example, the musical notes were ultimately the only collectibles the player would lose if they died or exited a level.
Design
Rare decided to make an action-based game that focused totally on Banjo and his abilities, Kazooie later born out of the planning of them.
Design

Kazooie was named after a kazoo, which was considered an annoying instrument, "much like the personality of the bird" to Mayles, while the witch Gruntilda was inspired by Grotbags from the Grotbags British television series.
Writing and humour
Banjo-Kazooie continues the trend of Rare games with characters titled " the ", the name of the animal or object occasionally rhyming with the name, for example Mumbo Jumbo.
Writing and humour
Most of the dialogue was ad-libbed, and a challenge for the designers was to remember the personalities and mindsets of the characters while doing so.
Rejected concepts and features

Rare originally planned to include a multiplayer mode and more worlds, such as a mine level, but these were not implemented due to time constraints; some were included in the sequel Banjo-Tooie (2000).
Rejected concepts and features
Connell recalled encountering the team working on a four-player mode only three weeks before Nintendo's approval.
Rejected concepts and features

One scrapped feature, " Stop 'N' Swop ", would have allowed Banjo-Kazooie to interact with Donkey Kong 64 (1999), Jet Force Gemini (1999), Banjo-Tooie, Perfect Dark (2000), and Conker's Bad Fur Day (2001).
Rejected concepts and features
During development, Rare discovered the Nintendo 64 retained flash memory for several seconds after a cartridge's removal.
Rejected concepts and features
Nintendo requested Stop 'N' Swop's removal when Rare submitted Donkey Kong 64 for approval.
Rejected concepts and features
Preview coverage from July and August 1997 revealed that Tooty was originally Banjo's girlfriend Piccolo, and that there were 16 levels accessed via jiggies instead of nine.
Visuals and levels

The in-game characters were created with minimal amounts of texturing so they could have a sharp and clean look, while the backgrounds use very large textures split into 64×64 pieces, which was the largest texture size the Nintendo 64 could render.
Visuals and levels

A 2018 Nintendo Life feature discussed how the size and scope of the worlds took advantage of the limited memory and were significant in 3D video games at the time, citing the different seasons in Click Clock Wood, the organ section in Mad Monster Mansion, and Freezeezy Peak's size.
Visuals and levels
To conceive them, a theme was chosen first then all the traits and design choices, including the animal Mumbo would transform Banjo and Kazooie into, associated with it.
Visuals and levels

The incorporation of a trivia game at the end was a method of making Banjo-Kazooie unique; the section was initially planned to only have a few questions for the player to ask, but became a massive board game in the end.
Audio

Although Banjo-Kazooie was not his first project for Rare, as he previously converted David Wise 's score for Diddy's Kong Quest to a Game Boy port and helped on Goldeneye 007 (1997), it was the first time he worked on all music and sound effects for a game.
Audio
After Dream was disbanded, Rare was focused on getting Banjo-Kazooie finished as much as possible.
Release and promotion
The Nintendo 64 games presented at E3 were lauded by Nintendo Power as "pushing the boundaries of interactive entertainment, innovation, and intensity".
Release and promotion

The reaction from gamers and critics towards the game was generally positive, 64 magazine predicting it to be "the biggest hit of the year." However, it was also met with skepticism as a rip-off of Super Mario 64 and overly cute, and despised its new name.
Release and promotion
The game was then presented at the 1997 annual Nintendo Space World event, where the first five worlds were playable.
Release and promotion

N64 Magazine gave a glowing review of the panel, admitting it to be the event's most absorbing experience, even moreso than the Zelda game that got the most attention from other gamers and journalists.
Release and promotion
Banjo-Kazooie was initially scheduled for a release in November 1997, in the US 24 November, but was delayed to give developers more time for polish.
Release and promotion
When Rare met Nintendo of America 's Howard Lincoln at E3 1997, he was against a delay, complaining: "We've committed $20 million to this campaign".
Release and promotion
To fill that year's Christmas schedule, Lincoln told Rare to include Donkey Kong characters in an R.C.
Release and promotion
Eurogamer called Diddy Kong Racing "something of a testing ground for Rare's -era heroes", as it included Banjo and Conker as playable characters prior to featuring in their own games.
Release and promotion
In the following months, Rare released screenshots at such a rate that by May 1998, N64 Magazine suspected the game was completed besides testing.
Release and promotion
Banjo-Kazooie was released on 29 June 1998 in North America, 17 July 1998 in Europe, Australia in August 1998, and 6 December 1998 in Japan as Banjo and Kazooie's Big Adventure (バンジョーとカズーイの大冒険).
Release and promotion
The Japan date was shifted multiple times, set to be released before other territories in January 1998 as of November 1997, and moved to April months later.
Release and promotion
The UK date was also set to 16 March 1998 as of Christmas 1997, before being moved to July two months later.
Release and promotion

In Europe, the game was released in the summer, an active season for Nintendo 64 releases that followed a scarce period and included games of various genres, such as Quest 64 (1998), Mortal Kombat 4 (1998), Off Road Challenge (1998), Dezaemon 3D (1998) and Virtual Chess 64 (1998).
Release and promotion
It had a marketing budget of $10 million.
Release and promotion
Virgin Megastore reported that the game was topping the UK charts as of 21 September 1998.
Release and promotion
In Japan, Banjo-Kazooie entered Famitsu ' s Top 10 sales charts for the week ending 13 December 1998, selling 74,000 copies for a total of 117,399.
Release and promotion
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, the game took home a "Gold" prize for revenues above €26 million in the European Union during 1998.
Release and promotion
As of March 2003, the game had sold more than 405,000 units in Japan.
Release and promotion
As of December 2007, it had sold more than 1.8 million copies in the US.
Release and promotion
As of 2021, Banjo-Kazooie worldwide sales were 3 million, making it the tenth highest-grossing Nintendo 64 game.
Reception
At Metacritic, which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, it garnered a weighted average of 92, based on 19 entries.
Reception

The same magazine argued it was only better in terms on visuals but not gameplay, in a review published in an issue preceded by two issues that predicted it to be the best game of the summer and "the first real Mario -beater."
Reception
N64 Magazine enjoyed that the level design not only suited the combination of both characters' abilities, but also required them.
Reception
Harding opined the jumping and movement was well-above most other video games.
Reception

Critics suggested potentially high amounts of time to complete the game, estimates ranging from 35–50 hours, which was attributed to the world size, amount of objectives, challenge of the later levels, and backtracking.
Reception
GamePro stated the amount of tasks and big size surpassed most other consoles games at the time.
Reception
Shea claimed they set a benchmark for the console, absent of issues of most other games such as repetitive textures, fogging and lagging framerates.
Reception
Hyper and N64 Magazine found most of the fixed viewpoints tolerable, and appreciated the manual camera control.
Reception
N64 Magazine and Nintendo Acción found the camera control intuitive, but felt Super Mario 64 was better in terms of the camera.
Accolades
IGN awarded the game Overall Best Graphics of 1998, Best Texture Design of 1998, and Best Music of 1998.
Sequels and re-releases
A sequel, Banjo-Tooie, was released for the Nintendo 64 in 2000 and largely adopts the gameplay mechanics of its predecessor.
Sequels and re-releases
The Banjo-Kazooie series continued to be developed with the release of Banjo-Kazooie: Grunty's Revenge and Banjo-Pilot for the Game Boy Advance in 2003 and 2005, respectively.
Sequels and re-releases
A third main game, Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts, was released for the Xbox 360 in 2008.
Sequels and re-releases
An Xbox Live Arcade version of Banjo-Kazooie, developed by 4J Studios, was released for the Xbox 360 on 26 November 2008.
Sequels and re-releases
The Xbox Live Arcade version was generally well received by critics, featuring an aggregate score of 77 out of 100 at Metacritic and generally considered a solid revival of a classic.
Sequels and re-releases
TeamXbox praised its controls as very responsive in comparison to most other XBLA re-releases.
Sequels and re-releases
PALGN was also disappointed in the small amount of rewards provided by the Stop 'n Swap feature for Nuts & Bolts, only a few vehicle accessories.
Sequels and re-releases
In 2009, IGN ranked it seventh on its list of Top 10 Xbox Live Arcade Games.
Sequels and re-releases
In 2015, the Xbox Live Arcade version became one of the first backwards compatible titles for Xbox One, and was re-released as part of the Rare Replay video game compilation.
Sequels and re-releases
In 2019, this version was enhanced to run at native 4K resolution on Xbox One.
Sequels and re-releases
Ultimate on 4 September 2019, including Banjo and Kazooie as a tag team of playable fighters and a stage based on Spiral Mountain, a location in the game.
Sequels and re-releases
Banjo-Kazooie was added to the Nintendo Switch Online library of Nintendo 64 games on 20 January 2022, marking its first re-release on a Nintendo console.
Retrospective reception

Shacknews called it the fifth best Rare game in 2018, while New York magazine's Vulture website, in 2022, listed it as one of "The 25 Best Games on Nintendo Switch Online." In 2009, Game Informer ranked the game 71st in their list of the Top 100 Games Of All Time.
Retrospective reception
In 2021, it ranked number 21 on Retro Gamer ' s special edition of 100 Games To Play Before You Die: Nintendo Consoles Edition.
Retrospective reception

Banjo-Kazooie has also been cited as part of a 1990s golden age of Rare entries that showed a frequency and strong devotion to quality in the platform and shooter genres, which began with Donkey Kong Country and mostly encompassed the Nintendo 64.
Influence
Some critics noted the importance of Banjo-Kazooie ' s indication that Nintendo's EAD was not the only developer to pull off a first-rate 3D platformer.
Influence
Kirkhope recalled Rare getting tired of making Banjo games after Tooie, contributed by Rare's general philosophy being against sequels.
Influence
A frequently-cited reason for the decline, which Kotaku and The Ringer have suggested, was the overwhelming amount of collectables, of which Rare's 3D platformers were particularly notorious.
Influence

The game's developer, Jonas Kaerlev, explained that his goal was to magnify the positives of the 1998 N64 game, including exploration, charm, and puzzle-solving, while mitigating its flaws, such as endless collecting and a camera.
Influence

Many of the 3D Mario games continued to follow their linear formula until Super Mario Odyssey (2017), where the player can explore the world without a time limit and remains in it after collecting a power moon.

f64_banjo_twooie.title: Banjo-Tooie
sents: lead
Banjo-Tooie is a 2000 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 console.
lead
It is the second game in the Banjo-Kazooie series and the sequel to Banjo-Kazooie.
lead

The game follows the returning protagonists Banjo and Kazooie as they attempt to stop the plans of the witch Gruntilda and two of her sisters, who intend to vaporise the inhabitants of the game's island setting.
lead

The game features worlds significantly larger than those of its predecessor, requiring the player to complete challenges such as solving puzzles, jumping over obstacles, collecting items, and defeating opponents.
lead
It also includes a multiplayer mode in which up to four players can compete in several minigames repurposed from the main campaign.
lead
Development of the game started in June 1998, directly after the release of its predecessor.
lead
Several new features were cut from the game due to time constraints and limitations of the Nintendo 64 hardware.
lead
It is the final Banjo-Kazooie game to be released by Nintendo prior to Rare's purchase by Microsoft.
Gameplay

Carrying over most of the mechanics and concepts established in its predecessor, the game features three-dimensional worlds consisting of various platforming challenges and puzzles, with a notable increased focus on puzzle-solving over the worlds of Banjo-Kazooie.
Gameplay
Each puzzle challenge requires more Jiggies than the last.
Gameplay
Musical notes return in Banjo-Tooie, but are now used to learn new moves from Bottles' brother, a drill sergeant named Jamjars, who assumes Bottles' role from the first game.
Gameplay

All of Banjo and Kazooie's moves from the first game are immediately accessible in Tooie, and the player can acquire several new moves such as first-person aiming, new egg types, and the ability to play as Banjo and Kazooie separately, with each gaining moves they can only use while on their own.
Plot
Outside, two of Gruntilda's sisters, Mingella and Blobbelda, use their large HAG 1 digging machine to enter Spiral Mountain.
Plot
There, King Jingaling, king of the Jinjos, explains that his subjects were frightened away by the HAG 1 and scattered throughout the Isle O' Hags, the game's overworld.
Plot
He gives the two their first Jiggy (possible previously owned by the gray Jinjos that were all killed by Hag 1) as a reward for rescuing his subjects in advance.
Plot
Gruntilda plans to charge B.O.B. long enough to blast the entire island and use the stolen life force to restore her body.
Plot

The witch's most loyal henchman, Klungo, is sent out to hinder Banjo and Kazooie's progress, but after losing to them several times, resulting in beatings from Gruntilda, Klungo abandons her and sides with the protagonists.
Plot

Within Gruntilda's fortress, Cauldron Keep, Banjo and Kazooie compete with Mingella and Blobbelda in a trivia game show hosted by Gruntilda similar to that of the first game, in which losing competitors are flattened under one-ton weights.
Plot

Banjo and Kazooie fight Gruntilda and the HAG 1 atop her fortress, but she is finally defeated when she drops her most powerful magic spell inside the HAG 1 cockpit, causing the entire machine to explode, reducing Gruntilda to nothing more than her head.
Deleted Content

According to the Wiki, Cauldron Keep was originally going to be a traditional level like its predecessors called "Castle World" with collectables but was reduced to a much smaller map due to time constraints.
Development
Banjo-Tooie was developed by Rare and designed by Gregg Mayles, who previously worked on Banjo-Kazooie.
Development
Some features that were originally cut during the development of Banjo-Kazooie, such as some of its worlds and a multiplayer game mode, were instead integrated into Banjo-Tooie.
Development
An additional world set in a castle was planned, but due to time constraints, it was scrapped during development and assets from it were used in constructing Cauldron Keep.
Development
The game features roughly 150 total characters, including enemies and non-playable characters.
Development
Despite this, Rare resolved to include some of the planned bonuses within the game.
Development
The music was composed by Grant Kirkhope, who previously worked as the main composer for Perfect Dark, Donkey Kong 64, and Banjo-Kazooie.
Development
Kirkhope initially had to pause his work on Banjo-Tooie to work on other projects first, but ultimately the music score for the game was completed on time.
Development
The developers initially aimed for a fourth quarter 1999 release, but the game was ultimately delayed.
Development
Banjo-Tooie was presented at the 2000 Electronic Entertainment Expo and first released on 20 November 2000 in North America.
Development
Japanese and European releases followed on 27 November 2000 and 12 April 2001, respectively.
Reception
Upon release, Banjo-Tooie was critically acclaimed and sold 1.49m worldwide by 2008 GameRevolution considered Banjo-Tooie less repetitive than Donkey Kong 64 and a worthy successor to Banjo-Kazooie.
Reception
Nintendo Power referred to Banjo-Tooie as "the perfect cross between Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Kazooie ", noting that it features less backtracking between levels than Donkey Kong 64 does.
Reception
The publication also stated that the only disappointment was how Rare resolved the "Stop 'N' Swop" bonuses.
Reception

N64 Magazine editor Mark Green felt that, although Banjo-Tooie delivers "a decent complement of clever puzzles and enjoyable run-and-jump moments", it did not feel "as fresh or as exciting" as previous Rare platformers.
Reception
Despite the praise, Edge concluded that Rare should have innovated more instead of simply copying the formula of Super Mario 64.
Reception
At the GameSpot Best and Worst of 2000 awards, Banjo-Tooie was awarded Best Platform Game, and was a runner-up in the Best Sound and Best Nintendo 64 Game categories.
Reception
At the 4th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Banjo-Tooie received nominations for the " Game of the Year ", "Console Game of the Year", and " Console Action/Adventure " awards.
Xbox 360 version
An Xbox Live Arcade version of Banjo-Tooie, developed by 4J Studios, was released for the Xbox 360 on 29 April 2009.
Xbox 360 version
The Xbox Live Arcade version of Banjo-Tooie received mixed to favourable reviews from video game critics, featuring an aggregate score of 73 out of 100 at Metacritic.
Xbox 360 version
In 2015, the Xbox Live Arcade version became one of the first backwards compatible titles for Xbox One, and was re-released as part of the Rare Replay video game compilation.
Xbox 360 version
In 2019, this version was enhanced to run at native 4K resolution on Xbox One X.

f64_donkey_kongo_64.title: Donkey Kong 64
sents: lead
Donkey Kong 64 is a 1999 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It is the only Donkey Kong game to feature 3D gameplay.
lead
As the gorilla Donkey Kong, the player explores themed levels to collect items and rescue his kidnapped family members from King K.
lead
The player completes minigames and puzzles as five playable Kong characters—each with their own special abilities—to receive bananas and other collectibles.
lead
In multiplayer modes, up to four players can compete in deathmatch and last man standing games.
lead
Rare began working on Donkey Kong 64 in 1997, following the completion of Donkey Kong Country 3 (1996).
lead
It was conceived as a 2.5D platformer similar to Country before becoming a more open-ended game using the engine from Rare's Banjo-Kazooie (1998).
lead
A 16-person team with many recruits from the Banjo group finished it in 1999.
Gameplay
Donkey Kong 64 is a 3D platforming action-adventure game in which the player, as Donkey Kong and his friends, explores an island and collects items to progress through minigames and puzzles.
Gameplay
Most of the puzzles are simple and involve rearranging items, manipulating switches and tiles, or matching items as in the game Concentration.
Gameplay
There are five such golden banana-rewarding objectives for each of five playable characters across seven themed worlds — 200 goals in total, in addition to a connecting overworld.
Gameplay
As in other Rare games, the player often encounters an impasse such as an indestructible object or out-of-reach area, and must acquire a new ability with which to eventually backtrack and resolve it.
Gameplay
Each of the five characters begin with basic abilities and can purchase additional, unique abilities from Cranky Kong as the game progresses, which are necessary to solve certain puzzles.
Gameplay
The characters each use unique projectiles and musical instruments.
Gameplay
For example, some doors can be opened only with Donkey Kong's coconut projectiles and others can be opened only with Diddy Kong's guitar.
Gameplay
Playable versions of the original Donkey Kong (1981) and Jetpac (1983) are hidden within the game, and playing through them is required to finish the story.
Conception

The British studio Rare, which created the successful Donkey Kong Country games for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in the mid-1990s, developed Donkey Kong 64, with Gregg Mayles leading the effort.
Conception
Development began in 1997, shortly after the completion of Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!
Conception
It was originally reported as an intended release on the Nintendo 64 's 64DD add-on, but transitioned to cartridge while the 64DD was delayed and eventually canceled.
Conception
Rare artist Carl Tilley disputed the possibility of a 64DD release, recalling to Did You Know Gaming? that "Rare wouldn't have wanted to release on the DD.
Conception

Hardware sales dictated where best to sell the game." Time Extension argued that early reports of a 64DD release were "a mistake, a mistranslation, or simply talks between upper management." Grant Kirkhope stated that Project Dream was the 64DD title being developed by Rare at the time, not Donkey Kong 64.
Conception
A team of 16 people worked on the game across three years, and an additional eight members assisted in its later stages.
Conception
Rare conceived Donkey Kong 64 as a linear, 2.5D platform game similar to the Donkey Kong Country games.
Conception
The Nintendo 64 was still new, and at the time Rare did not have a common game engine.
Conception
The linear version was developed for around 18 months before it was eliminated in favor of a more open-ended approach similar to Rare's 1998 game Banjo-Kazooie (1998).
Design

Rare was unable to reuse the models from the Donkey Kong Country series, where they had been pre-rendered and modeled with NURBs using PowerAnimator; Donkey Kong 64 ' s real-time 3D graphics could only use polygons, so the team used a new tool, Gamegen.
Design
Though the real-time graphics prevented Rare from reproducing the level of detail seen in the Donkey Kong Country series, they allowed for more expressive characters.
Design
The strong emphasis on collectibles was a design choice made at the request of Rare co-founder Tim Stamper to distinguish Donkey Kong 64 from Banjo-Kazooie.
Design
Rare attempted to differentiate Donkey Kong 64 from Banjo-Kazooie through its variety of playable characters, cinematic set-pieces, and bombastic boss battles.
Design
A removed feature, " Stop 'N' Swop ", allowed data to be transferred from Banjo-Kazooie to Donkey Kong 64 to unlock in-game bonuses.
Design
During development, Rare discovered the Nintendo 64 retained flash memory for several seconds after a cartridge's removal.
Design
Nintendo requested Stop 'N' Swop's removal when Rare submitted Donkey Kong 64 for approval.
Design
Nintendo was concerned the Nintendo 64 would not retain RDRAM long enough for the feature to work and that it could potentially damage consoles.
Design
Specifically, Nintendo 64 models produced after Banjo-Kazooie ' s release reduced the amount of time the console retained flash memory, making Stop 'N' Swop nearly impossible to activate as intended.
Design
Donkey Kong 64 was the first of two games to require the Nintendo 64's Expansion Pak, a console RAM upgrade bundled with the game.
Design

The Expansion Pak was previously used to power optional higher-resolution graphics, but in the case of Donkey Kong 64, it was marketed as improving the frame rate and rendering of objects at a distance.
Design

Chris Marlow, who was working on Conker's Bad Fur Day (2001) at the time, claimed that Rare could not resolve a bug that occurred without the Expansion Pak and thus they were forced, at great expense, to bundle the game with the memory upgrade.
Music
Donkey Kong Country 3 composer Eveline Fischer was originally assigned to Donkey Kong 64; Kirkhope became involved after he was asked for assistance, and he provided Donkey Kong's voice.
Music
Nintendo of America ran a "DK Rap" contest in which fans record their own version of the rap to win prizes including a trip to its headquarters.
Promotion and release
Rare announced Donkey Kong 64 with a single screenshot on its website and coverage in the January 1999 issue of Nintendo Power.
Promotion and release
Electronic Gaming Monthly wrote that it was playable by the 1997 Electronic Entertainment Expo, though IGN said that it debuted at the 1999 event.
Promotion and release
Donkey Kong 64 was expected to be a bestseller, as the console's "crowning achievement" in graphics and sound.
Promotion and release
Donkey Kong 64 ' s sizable US$22 million marketing campaign doubled the typical budget for a major Nintendo release.
Promotion and release
The campaign included a 60-second commercial played at over 10,000 movie theaters during the holiday season, and additional advertisements via billboards, print, and radio.
Promotion and release

Nintendo projected sales of 2.5 million copies within one year, and later that year increased the number to 4 million copies (1.5 million more than for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time), including 1 million of the translucent green Nintendo 64 bundles.
Promotion and release
Polled retailers expected Donkey Kong 64 to be the top console game sold during the 1999 holiday season.
Promotion and release
It had little holiday season competition from Nintendo, as Nintendo had moved releases including Mario Party 2, Perfect Dark, and Pokémon Stadium into the next year.
Promotion and release
Rare and Nintendo released Donkey Kong 64 in North America in November 1999, and a worldwide release followed the next month.
Promotion and release

Nintendo offered a special bundle of the game and console, including a banana yellow-colored game cartridge, its required Expansion Pak, and a transparent green " Jolly Rancher -style" Nintendo 64 console.
Promotion and release
In April 2015, Donkey Kong 64 was digitally rereleased as one of the first Nintendo 64 games added to Nintendo's Wii U Virtual Console catalog.
Reception
Donkey Kong 64 received critical acclaim — "universal acclaim", according to video game review aggregator Metacritic.
Reception
It became the Nintendo 64's top seller during the 1999 holiday season and Nintendo's chief defense against competitor Sega 's introduction of its Dreamcast console.
Reception
As a bestseller, Donkey Kong 64 joined Nintendo's " Player's Choice " game selection, where high sales continued through the next holiday season.
Reception
Cumulative worldwide sales were 5.27 million, including more than 2.3 million copies in North America by 2004.
Reception
It won the 1999 E3 Game Critics award for Best Platform Game, and several annual awards from Nintendo Power, including best overall game of 1999.
Reception

Donkey Kong 64 received nominations for " Game of the Year " and "Console Game of the Year" by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences during the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards (now known as the D.I.C.E.
Reception
IGN described Donkey Kong 64 as the biggest and most ambitious Nintendo 64 game as of its release, but very similar to Banjo-Kazooie in its platforming and puzzle design.
Reception
This had become a trend in Rare's games, and Donkey Kong 64 followed the "predictable formula" of making players collect multiple sets of items and in full for a special ending.
Reception
Next Generation noted Rare's propensity for backtracking.
Reception
EGM said the puzzles and minigames are fun the first time through, but they quickly become worn when replayed with increasingly tighter time restrictions.
Reception
GameSpot, however, considered parts of Donkey Kong 64 ' s gameplay "cerebral", requiring the consideration of several simultaneous tasks to solve later puzzles.
Reception
Already familiar with concepts borrowed from Super Mario 64, Ocarina of Time, and Banjo-Kazooie, critics considered the player's tasks less innovative or interesting to decipher.
Reception
With an estimated 30 hours in basic gameplay, IGN called it Rare's War and Peace.
Reception
Even with the RAM expansion for graphics, Donkey Kong 64 ' s visuals were only found marginally — if at all — better than that of its contemporary games, such as the previous year's Banjo-Kazooie.
Reception

IGN avowed that Donkey Kong 64 was not as pretty as Banjo-Kazooie, especially in its water and backgrounds, though it still ranked among the console's prettiest games because the setting is barren and nondescript at first, and only later introduces lighting effects and richer textures.
Reception
IGN hoped for more from Rare, praising the particle effects (such as in the desert wind), but considering its dynamic lighting overused.
Reception
N64 Magazine said the enhanced effects were most often used for decoration, though they also played some role in puzzles based on illuminating paths.
Reception
The characters were praised for their personalities, animations, and portrayal of Rare's signature humor.
Reception
IGN considered the characters less baffling than those of other Rare games, and sometimes funny.
Reception
The consensus was that Donkey Kong 64 lacked the revolutionary potential of Donkey Kong Country but was of a sufficient high quality to sell well during the holiday season.
Reception

The Cincinnati Enquirer described its platform style as coupled with many others, such as Super Mario 64, Banjo-Kazooie, and Jet Force Gemini (1999): "Replace the story line, the graphics and a couple of gameplay elements and you basically have the same game".
Reception
Though hyped fans would be disappointed, IGN said that Donkey Kong 64 remains an excellent and expansive platformer with an overwhelming amount of things to do.
Reception

GameFan, on the other hand, was most disappointed by how it "truly offers nothing new" and compared its monotony and repetition with the 1999 film Eyes Wide Shut: "a big bloated project with not enough brilliant moments to justify the numbness... sitting through the whole thing", it "fails to live up to the Rare name".
Reception
Donkey Kong 64 ' s 3D platforming was commonplace by the time of its release and, according to GameSpot, would have fared better as a Nintendo 64 launch game.
Reception
With its competition considered, Daily Radar wrote that Donkey Kong 64 was simply the best 3D platform game on the console.
Reception

Edge qualified this thought: Donkey Kong 64 was the closest any third-party developer had come to outdoing Nintendo's mastery of game structure and was "a fine effort... in its own right", but its gameplay was derivative and unimaginative compared to the freedom and flexibility of Nintendo's Super Mario 64.
Reception
In a retrospective review, Nintendo Life found the Wii U controller an easy substitute for the Nintendo 64's controls.
Legacy
Rare's 3D platformers became notorious for their emphasis on collecting items, and Kotaku remembered Donkey Kong 64 as "the worst offender" with hundreds of color-coded bananas.
Legacy
Super Mario 64 breathed life into the 3D platforming genre, Donkey Kong 64 sucked it all out" and solidified Rare's reputation for making "collect-a-thon" games.
Legacy
The indie developer behind A Hat in Time, a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie, blamed Donkey Kong 64 for the "collect-a-thon platform adventurer" genre's decline in popularity.
Legacy
The game holds a Guinness World Record for most collectible items in a platform game.
Legacy

Though decently reviewed, this and Rare's subsequent Nintendo 64 releases did not meet the extolment of the company's preceding games, and lackluster sales led to a staff exodus that culminated with the company's acquisition by Microsoft in 2002.
Legacy
Donkey Kong 64 was resultingly Rare's final Donkey Kong game; the series did not receive another major installment until Donkey Kong Jungle Beat (2004) five years later.
Legacy
Electronic Gaming Monthly noted at the game's launch, that the Nintendo 64 was approaching the end of its lifecycle, as gamers turned their sights to the Sega Dreamcast and Sony PlayStation 2.
Legacy
IGN later named Donkey Kong 64 as worthy of a remake for the Nintendo 3DS handheld console.
Legacy
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine placed the game 89th in a list of the best Nintendo games, calling it "a forgotten classic".
Legacy
Sutherland believes this happened because those who played the game as children had realized the song was meant to be taken as a joke, not a serious songwriting attempt.
Legacy
Melee (2001) and Donkey Konga (2003).
Legacy
In 2017, Kirkhope composed a similar rap for Yooka-Laylee, a platform game made in homage to Rare's works.
Legacy
Movie (2023), included at the behest of Donkey Kong's voice actor Seth Rogen.
Legacy
Kirkhope was flattered by the song's inclusion but disappointed he did not receive credit; the film simply credits it as originating from Donkey Kong 64.

f64_plumber.title: Super Mario 64
sents: lead
Super Mario 64 is a 1996 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was released in Japan and North America in 1996 and PAL regions in 1997.
lead
It is the first Super Mario game to feature 3D gameplay, combining traditional Super Mario gameplay, visual style, and characters in a large open world.
lead

In the game, Bowser, the primary antagonist of the Super Mario franchise, invades Princess Peach 's castle and hides the castle's sources of protection, the Power Stars, in many different worlds inside magical paintings.
lead
As Mario, the player collects Power Stars to unlock enough of Princess Peach's castle to get to Bowser and rescue Princess Peach.
lead
Director Shigeru Miyamoto conceived a 3D Super Mario game during the production of Star Fox (1993).
lead
Development lasted nearly three years: about one year on design and twenty months on production, starting with designing the virtual camera system.
lead
The team continued with illustrating the 3D character models—at the time a relatively unattempted task—and refining sprite movements.
Controls
Super Mario 64 is a 3D platformer in which the player controls Mario through various courses.
Controls
The player can adjust the camera—operated by a Lakitu broadcasting Mario—and toggle between first-person and third-person view.
Health, lives, and power-ups
Unlike many of its predecessors, Super Mario 64 uses a health point system, represented by a pie shape consisting of eight segments.
Health, lives, and power-ups
Three switches of the same colors can be found in secret areas that turn their corresponding blocks solid and allow Mario to obtain three types of special cap power-ups.
Setting and objective
Each of the fifteen courses has seven Power Stars, and an additional fifteen are hidden as secrets and as bonuses, for a total of 120 Power Stars in the game.
Setting and objective
Some Power Stars only appear after completing certain tasks, often hinted at by the name of the course.
Setting and objective
There are many hidden mini-courses and other secrets within the castle, which may contain extra Power Stars required for the full completion of the game.
Plot
When he arrives, Mario discovers that Bowser has invaded the castle and imprisoned the princess and her servants within its walls using the power of the castle's 120 Power Stars.
Plot
The Power Stars are hidden in the castle's paintings, which serve as portals to other worlds where Bowser's minions keep watch over the Stars.
Plot
Mario unlocks two doors to different floors of the castle with keys obtained by defeating Bowser in hidden worlds.
Plot
After getting at least 70 of the 120 Stars, Mario breaks the curse of the endless stairs that block the entrance to Bowser's final hiding place.
Development
In the early 1990s, Super Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto conceived a 3D Mario design while developing the game Star Fox (1993) for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
Development
According to engineer Dylan Cuthbert, who worked on Star Fox, Super Mario FX was never the title of a game, but was the codename of the Super FX chip itself.
Development
Miyamoto reformulated the idea for the Nintendo 64, not for its greater power, but because its controller has more buttons for gameplay.
Development

At the January 1993 Consumer Electronics Show (CES), where Star Fox made its debut, Nintendo's booth demonstrated a talking 3D polygon animation of Mario's head; it returned in the start screen, programmed by Giles Goddard.
Development
Production of Super Mario 64 began on September 7, 1994, at Nintendo's Entertainment Analysis & Development division, and concluded on May 20, 1996.
Development
"There no jumping actions in 3-D we could reference at the time, so we shared in the enjoyment of going through all the trial and error with Mr.
Development
Super Mario 64 is one of the first games for which Nintendo produced its illustrations internally instead of by outsourcing.
Development
The 3D illustrations were created by Shigefumi Hino, Hisashi Nogami, Hideki Fujii, Tomoaki Kuroume, and Yusuke Nakano, and the game was animated by co-director Yoshiaki Koizumi and Satoru Takiwaza.
Development
Yōichi Kotabe, illustrator and character designer for the Mario series, made a 3D drawing of Mario from various angles and directed the creation of the character models.
Development
In an interview with The Washington Post, Yoshiaki Koizumi recalled that his challenge was animating the 3D models without any precedents.
Development
Miyamoto's guiding design philosophy was to include more details than earlier games by using the Nintendo 64's power to feature "all the emotions of the characters".
Development
Super Mario 64 was first run on an SGI Onyx emulator, which only emulated the console's application programming interface and not its hardware.
Development

The first test scenario for controls and physics involved Mario interacting with a golden rabbit, named "MIPS" after the Nintendo 64's MIPS architecture processors; the rabbit was included in the final game as a Power Star holder.
Development
Super Mario 64 features more puzzles than earlier Mario games.
Development
It was developed simultaneously with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time but, as Ocarina of Time was released more than two years later, some puzzles were taken for Super Mario 64.
Development
