According to Inagaki, the average Nintendo 64 game had about 500 sound effects, and made comparisons to Ocarina of Time, with 1,200, and The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask, with 2,000.
Development

Super Mario 64 is one of the first games to feature Charles Martinet as the voice of Mario, and Leslie Swan—then senior editor of Nintendo Power and English localizer for Super Mario 64 —as the voice of Princess Peach.
Release
Super Mario 64 was first shown as a playable prototype in November 1995 at Nintendo Space World.
Release
This version was only fifty percent complete, and only about two percent of texture mapping was finished.
Release
According to Nintendo of America chairman Howard Lincoln, Miyamoto's desire to add more was a major factor in the decision to delay the Nintendo 64 release from Christmas 1995 to Summer 1996.
Release
The game was later shown at E3 1996 with multiple Nintendo 64s set up for people to play.
Advertising and sales
Peter Main, Nintendo's vice president of marketing at the time, stated Super Mario 64 was meant as the killer app for the Nintendo 64.
Advertising and sales
The US$20 million marketing campaign included videotapes sent to more than five hundred thousand Nintendo Power subscribers and advertisements shown on MTV, Fox, and Nickelodeon.
Advertising and sales
Super Mario 64 was officially released in Japan in June 1996, North America in September, and in Europe and Australia in March 1997.
Advertising and sales
During its first three months of sale in North America, it sold more than two million copies and grossed $140 million in the United States, becoming the best-selling video game of 1996.
Advertising and sales
It was also the best-selling game overall from 1995 to 2002.
Advertising and sales
During the first three months of 1997, it was the second-best-selling console game at 523,000 units.
Advertising and sales
By early 2001, it had sold 5.5 million units, and 5.9 million by September 2002.
Advertising and sales
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, Super Mario 64 won a Gold ECCSELL prize for earning revenues above €21 million in the European Union in 1998.
Advertising and sales
It had become the second most popular game on Wii 's Virtual Console by June 2007, behind Super Mario Bros.
Advertising and sales
By March 2008, Super Mario 64 sold 11.8 million copies worldwide, being the best-selling Nintendo 64 game.
Advertising and sales
By 2015, Super Mario 64 was the 12th most sold Mario game, with 11.91 million copies sold.
Super Mario 64 DS
An enhanced remake, Super Mario 64 DS, was released for the Nintendo DS in 2004.
Super Mario 64 DS
By September 2021, 11.06 million copies had been sold worldwide.
Other re-releases
A version of Super Mario 64 was used as a tech demo for the Nintendo 64 Disk Drive (64DD) floppy drive at the 1996 Nintendo Space World trade show.
Other re-releases

Like Wave Race 64, Super Mario 64 was re-released in Japan on July 18, 1997 as Super Mario 64 Rumble Pak Version which fixed various bugs, added support for the Rumble Pak peripheral, included the voice acting from the English version, among other changes.
Other re-releases
In November 2003, it was ported to China's iQue Player as a limited-release demo.
Other re-releases
In late 2006, it was released on the Wii Virtual Console service which added enhanced resolution and compatibility with the GameCube and Super Famicom Classic controllers.
Other re-releases
In September 2020, Super Mario 64 was one of the three Super Mario games to be included in the Super Mario 3D All-Stars collection on Nintendo Switch.
Critical reviews
GamePro commented on the 1995 prototype's smoothness, and how the action "was a blast", despite the game being only fifty percent complete at the time.
Critical reviews
Ed Semrad of Electronic Gaming Monthly agreed, praising the new 3D animation of Mario characters shown in only 2D before.
Critical reviews
Brown & Sons, recalls Super Mario 64 being the most anticipated game of E3 1996, remembering a field of teenagers "jostling for a test run".
Critical reviews

Super Mario 64 received critical acclaim, with a score of 94 out of 100 from review aggregator Metacritic based on thirteen reviews, and a score of 96% from review aggregator GameRankings, which ranked it the eighteenth best video game of all time based on twenty-two reviews.
Critical reviews
Writing for GameRevolution, Nebojsa Radakovic described Super Mario 64 as one of the few "true" 3D platform games.
Critical reviews
GamePro particularly praised the combination of unprecedented technical performance and art design, calling it "the most visually impressive game of all time".
Awards
Super Mario 64 won numerous awards, including various "Game of the Year" honors by members of the gaming media, and in Nintendo's own best-selling Player's Choice selection.
Awards
At the 1997 Computer Game Developers Conference, it was given Spotlight Awards for Best Use of Innovative Technology, Best Console Game, and Best Game of 1996.
Legacy
Super Mario 64 was key to the early success of and anticipation for the Nintendo 64.
Legacy

Eventually, the Nintendo 64 lost much of its market share to Sony's PlayStation, partly due to its cartridge and controller design decisions, which were reportedly implemented by Miyamoto for Super Mario 64.
Legacy
In 2012, Super Mario 64 was among the 80 entries in the Smithsonian American Art Museum 's The Art of Video Games exhibit.
Influence
Super Mario 64 set many precedents for 3D platformers as one of the most influential video games.
Influence
1Up.com wrote about its central hub world, which provides a safe tutorial and a level selector, and is now a staple of the 3D platformer genre.
Influence
Its mission-based level design inspired game designers such as GoldenEye 007 (1997) producer and director Martin Hollis and the development team of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater.
Influence
Square Enix has stated that a coincidental meeting with Disney employees resulted in the creation of the Kingdom Hearts series, inspired by Super Mario 64 ' s use of 3D environments and exploration.
Influence

Chris Sutherland, who served as the lead designer for Banjo-Kazooie, agreed that Super Mario 64 set the benchmark for 3D platformers and claimed that any other game in the genre on the Nintendo 64 would inevitably be compared with Super Mario 64.
Influence
To increase freedom of exploration and fluid control in a 3D world, Super Mario 64 designers created a dynamic virtual video camera that turns and accelerates according to the character's actions.
Influence

Nintendo Power praised the game's camera movements along with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ' s addition of the lock-on camera and concluded that the two games were trailblazers for the 3D era.
Influence
Thor Jensen considers Super Mario 64 to be the first truly realized 3D platformer with the integration of camera control into its core gameplay, which he called the medium's true evolutionary leap.
Influence
At the time, 3D games generally only allowed the player to either control the character in relation to a fixed camera angle or in relation to the character's perspective.
Influence
Super Mario 64 ' s controls, in contrast, are fully analog and interpret a 360-degree range of motion into navigation through a 3D space relative to the camera.
Influence

In 2005, Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked Super Mario 64 the most important game since they began publication in 1989, stating that, while there were 3D games before it, "Nintendo's was the first to get the control scheme right".
Influence
In July 2021, a pristine, sealed copy of Super Mario 64 was auctioned for $1,560,000, the largest amount ever paid for a video game.
Influence
Heritage Auctions 's video games specialist said, "It seems impossible to overstate the importance of this title, not only to the history of Mario and Nintendo but to video games as a whole".
Successors
In July 1996, Nintendo insiders stated that Miyamoto was assembling a team consisting mostly of developers who had worked on Super Mario 64.
Successors
Miyamoto affirmed that work on the sequel had only commenced at the time of the E3 1997 convention.
Successors
Super Mario 64 successors include Super Mario Sunshine for the GameCube and Super Mario Galaxy for the Wii, building on its core design of power-ups and its 3D, open-ended gameplay.
Successors
Super Mario Galaxy 2 includes a remake of Super Mario 64 ' s Whomp's Fortress level called Throwback Galaxy.
Successors
Super Mario 3D Land and Super Mario 3D World are departures from the open-ended design, instead focused on platforming reminiscent of 2D games.
Successors
The ' Mario 64 Suit' and ' Mario 64 Cap', which change Mario's appearance to his in Super Mario 64, can be purchased after completing the main storyline.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches
The most popular was a pervasive rumor that Luigi existed as an unlockable character.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches
In 1996, IGN offered a prize of $100 if a player could find Luigi, to no avail.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches

In July 2020, 24 years and 1 month after the initial release of Super Mario 64, unused assets for Luigi from the scrapped multiplayer mode were discovered in the game's development files, in an event known as the Nintendo Gigaleak.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches
One popular rumor involves a "Wario Apparition", based on an E3 1996 presentation with Charles Martinet voicing a disembodied Wario head.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches
Conspiracy theorists also spread the rumor that "every copy of Super Mario 64 is personalized", claiming that certain bizarre phenomena existed in only certain copies of the game.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches
Another YouTuber, Pannenkoek2012, creates highly technical and analytical videos of Super Mario 64 glitches and mechanics, which have been covered many times by the video game press.
Rumors, conspiracy theories, and glitches

The game has also inspired challenges that attempt to beat it with certain restrictions, such as not being able to press the A button, requiring deep understanding about the game's mechanics and bugs.
Fan projects
Super Mario 64 HD, a high-definition remake of the first level of Super Mario 64, Bob-Omb Battlefield, using the Unity game engine.
Fan projects
In 2019, fans decompiled the original ROM image into C source code, allowing Super Mario 64 to be natively ported to any system.
Fan projects
Fans created ports for several more platforms, including the Nintendo 3DS, PlayStation 2, PlayStation Vita, Dreamcast, and Android.

f64_paper_plumber.title: Paper Mario (video game)

Director(s): Ryota Kawade Toshitaka Muramatsu Takahiro Ogi Hironobu Suzuki

sents: lead
Paper Mario is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 home video game console.
lead
Paper Mario is the first game in the Paper Mario series.
lead

First released in Japan in 2000 and then internationally in 2001, Paper Mario was later re-released for Nintendo's Wii Virtual Console in July 2007, the Wii U Virtual Console in April 2015, and the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on December 10, 2021.
lead

Paper Mario is set in the Mushroom Kingdom as the protagonist Mario tries to rescue Princess Peach from Bowser, who has imprisoned the seven "Star Spirits", lifted her castle into the sky and has defeated Mario after stealing the Star Rod from Star Haven and making himself invincible.
lead

To save the Mushroom Kingdom, rescue Peach, get the castle back, and defeat Bowser, Mario must locate the Star Spirits, who can negate the effects of the stolen Star Rod, by defeating Bowser's minions guarding the star spirits.
lead
The player controls Mario and a number of partners to solve puzzles in the game's overworld and defeat enemies in a turn-based battle system.
lead
The battles are unique in that the player can influence the effectiveness of attacks by performing required controller inputs known as "action commands".
lead

Although Nintendo planned to have Square, now Square Enix, develop Paper Mario, the company was occupied with developing Final Fantasy VII for the PlayStation; Intelligent Systems developed the game instead.
Gameplay
The player accumulates partners as they advance into different locations; only one partner can accompany Mario in the overworld, although the player can interchange them at any time.
Gameplay
The player can locate hidden battle upgrades in the game's overworld, which promotes one partner character to a new rank at a time.
Gameplay

Badges can also be obtained that yield bonuses ranging from added moves to gradual health restoration during combat; each consumes a set number of Badge Points (BP), meaning Mario can only equip a limited number of badges at a time.
Gameplay
The objectives and actions of each transition to Peach vary, although most are stealth -based.
Plot and setting

Mario and his friends go to the four Koopa Bros.' fortress where they save the first Star Spirit. and they find the second one in the Dry, Dry Desert inside a secret fortress ruled over by Tutankoopa.
Plot and setting

Mario becomes a suspect of murder when he finds the Shiver City's mayor unconscious; after solving the mystery (which was the mayor's own accident), Mario gets to the Crystal Palace where he saves the last Star Spirit from the Crystal King.
Development
The game was initially called Super Mario RPG 2, was slated for release on the 64DD, and was first revealed at Nintendo Space World '97, a video game trade show hosted by Nintendo.
Development

Paper Mario saw a number of re-releases for later Nintendo consoles: the Wii Virtual Console in July 2007, the Wii U Virtual Console in April 2015, and via the Nintendo Switch Online service in December 2021.
Development
In 2023, Paper Mario was fully decompiled, making an unofficial PC port and mods possible.
Development
The game had a marketing budget of $4 million.
Music
The game's soundtrack was first released in Japan on September 21, 2000, with the game's original title by Enterbrain, and distributed by the magazine Famitsu.
Reception and legacy
Paper Mario received critical acclaim, receiving a 93/100 on review aggregator Metacritic based on 15 reviews.
Reception and legacy
The game was the top-selling game in Japan on the week of its release, selling more than 276,000 copies, and the top-selling game for two weeks in other regions.
Reception and legacy
It currently ranks as the sixth-highest scoring Nintendo 64 game on Metacritic, the ninth highest rated video game of 2001, and the highest-scoring Nintendo 64 game released that year.
Reception and legacy
IGN 's Matt Casamassina praised the game's accessibility, commenting that "it serves as the perfect introductory game to any person hoping to explore the genre".
Reception and legacy
IGN claimed the game was "the best RPG for Nintendo 64", calling it "fantastically deep, intuitively designed, and wonderfully rewarding".
Reception and legacy
Although reviewers claimed that the novel graphical style was initially confusing, most welcomed the style eventually, with GameSpot claiming that it was "extremely well done".
Reception and legacy

Chester Barber reviewed the Nintendo 64 version of the game for Next Generation, rating it five stars out of five, and stated that "One of the best RPGs ever, and definitely the best RPG available for Nintendo 64.
Reception and legacy
Even if you've only been buying games for newer systems, this is a must-buy." GameSpot named Paper Mario the best Nintendo 64 game of 2001.
Reception and legacy
During the 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Paper Mario was nominated for the " Console Role-Playing " award by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.
Reception and legacy
Paper Mario also proved popular on the Virtual Console, reaching a high of "second most downloaded game" in the US in August 2007.
Reception and legacy
In 2023, enthusiasts fully decompiled the game's ROM into human-readable C code.

f64_party3.title: Mario Party 3

Programmer(s): Syunsuke Tanaka Kazuhiro Matsushita Masahide Tomita
Artist(s): Keisuke Kasahara Kayo Fujimoto Hitoshi Takiyama Hisao Okada

sents: lead
Mario Party 3 is a 2000 party video game developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead

The third installment in the Mario Party series, it was first released in Japan on December 7, 2000, in North America on May 7, 2001, in Australia on September 3, 2001, and in Europe on November 16, 2001.
lead

As with the previous installments, the player chooses between eight playable characters: Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Yoshi, Wario, and Donkey Kong from the first two games, alongside newcomers Princess Daisy and Waluigi.
lead
The game features duel maps, where two players try to lower each other's stamina to zero using non-player characters such as Chain Chomps.
lead
Mario Party 3 was the final first-party Nintendo 64 game released in North America.
lead
It was followed by Mario Party 4 for the GameCube in 2002.
lead

Content from Mario Party 3 was remastered as part of Mario Party: The Top 100 for the Nintendo 3DS and Mario Party Superstars for the Nintendo Switch, released on November 10, 2017, and October 29, 2021, respectively.
lead
The game received its first official re-release on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on October 27, 2023.
Gameplay
Mario Party 3 includes multiplayer compatibility; each game on a board map consists of four players, including at least one human player and up to four.
Gameplay

After the players and board map have been determined, the player chooses how long the board map game will last: "Lite Play" consists of 20 turns, "Standard Play" consists of 35, and "Full Play" consists of 50.
Gameplay
The player can also set a "Custom Play" that consists of any number of turns between 10 and 50, but restricted to multiples of 5.
Gameplay
Upon starting a board, players each hit a dice block to determine turn order, with the highest number going first on each turn and the lowest number going last.
Gameplay
The goal of Mario Party 3 is to collect the most Stars within the allotted amount of turns.
Gameplay
Stars must be purchased from the Millennium Star with coins, which can be earned through a selection from one of 70 mini-games that is played once at the end of each turn.
Gameplay
The first player initiates a turn by rolling a dice block that determines how many spaces they will advance on the board, ranging from one to ten spaces.
Gameplay

Boo appears in certain locations of the map, and can steal coins or a Star from another player on behalf of any player who passes him; stealing coins costs five coins, while stealing a Star costs 50 coins.
Gameplay
If all players are the same color, a 4-player mini-game is played.
Gameplay
If players are on separate colors, they will split into teams and play either a 1 vs.
Other modes
Mario Party 3 includes a Duel mode, in which two players use a selection of up to two partners to attack their opponent and deplete their health.
Other modes
The mode can either be played in 20 turns or for an indefinite amount of turns until one of the players' health is depleted.
Other modes
The game will end before the turn count expires if either player's health hits 0.
Other modes
If the turn count expires and both players have the same amount of health, whoever has the most coins wins.
Other modes
If both their health and coins numbers are the same, which is rare, the game ends in a draw.
Other modes
Duel mini-games and Game Guy mini-games are the only mini-games available to be played on a duel board.
Other modes
Unlike Battle Royale, they do not occur after every turn, but only if either player lands on a mini-game space.
Other modes
There is also a part of each map that makes the players play a duel mini game for 20, 30 or 40 coins after it is passed 5 times.
Development
Like prior games in the Mario Party franchise, Mario Party 3 was developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo.
Development
It is the first Mario Party game to have multiple save slots and the first to have Princess Daisy and Waluigi as playable characters.
Development
On August 9, 2000, it was revealed to have 70 new mini games.
Development
Later that month, Nintendo released 12 more screenshots of the game's adventure boards.
Reception
Mario Party 3 received "average" reviews according to the review aggregation website Metacritic.
Reception

While GamePro calling it "one of the last and best games you can play on the system with up to three buddies", other reviewers were critical of Mario Party 3 for largely using the same gameplay as the previous installments, with only minimal changes.
Reception
NGC Magazine wrote, "Playing against the CPU is one of the most frustrating exercises known to man."
Reception
Gavin Frankle of AllGame called Mario Party 3 the most enjoyable in the series, reasoning that it "provides enough to entice new fans and satisfy existing ones".
Reception

In 2015, IGN listed the game at number one on its list of "Best Mario Party Games," writing, "The best Mario Party games know the balance between luck and skill, and Mario Party 3 best exemplifies this rule.
Reception
Just about everything that made Mario Party 2 so great was pushed further as Mario Party 3 introduced even more strategic items, creative new boards, and some truly fun minigames."
Awards
Mario Party 3 won the "Console Family" award from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences during the 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.

f64_plumber_golf.title: Mario Golf (video game)
sents: lead
Mario Golf is a 1999 sports game developed by Camelot Software Planning and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Mario, his friends, and his enemies play golf on a variety of Mario-themed courses.
lead
Following NES Open Tournament Golf, it is the second game in the Mario Golf series.
lead
Camelot also developed a Game Boy Color version, which adds role-playing elements.
lead

The Nintendo 64 version was re-released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack, in 2008, 2015, and 2022 respectively, while the GBC version was re-released on the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console in 2012, and on the Nintendo Switch Online service on March 12, 2024.
Gameplay
The Transfer Pak connects the Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions, to exchange characters and data.
Development
Nintendo originally started development on a golf game for the Nintendo 64 tentatively titled Golf.
Development
Some time later, they recruited Camelot Software Planning to create a role-playing game, but Camelot wanted to make a simpler game to get accustomed to the Nintendo 64 hardware first.
Development
Nintendo was impressed with Camelot's prototype that they canceled their other golf game and assigned Camelot to develop Mario Golf 64.
Development
This new golf game was announced in the February 1999 issue of The 64Dream.
Reception
The Nintendo 64 version received "universal acclaim", according to review aggregator website Metacritic.
Reception
Reviews of the GBC version aggregated slightly stronger than those of the Nintendo 64 version.
Reception
IGN called the GBC version "an absolutely brilliant rendition of golf, and a perfect game for the go".
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave both versions a score of 30/40.

f64_plumber_tennis.title: Mario Tennis

Producer(s): Shinji Hatano Hiroyuki Takahashi Shigeru Miyamoto Shugo Takahashi (GBC)

sents: lead
Mario Tennis is a 2000 sports video game developed by Camelot Software Planning and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 (N64).
lead
Following Mario's Tennis, it is the second game in the Mario Tennis series.
lead
The game is known for being the introduction of Luigi 's arch-rival, Waluigi, and the re-introduction of Princess Daisy and Birdo.
lead
Camelot also developed a Game Boy Color (GBC) version, which was published under the same title in Western regions and as Mario Tennis GB in Japan.
lead

The N64 version was re-released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack, in 2010, 2015, and 2021 respectively; the GBC version was re-released on the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console in 2014, and on the Nintendo Switch Online service in 2024.
Gameplay
The game uses a control system that differs from most other video tennis games.
Gameplay
A total of seven types of shot are possible using only the two main buttons of the controller.
Gameplay
Most modes support multiplayer for up to two players in singles and up to four players in doubles.
Gameplay
The N64 version of Mario Tennis features 16 playable characters, 10 of which did not appear in the previous Mario Tennis game.
Gameplay
Notably, the character Waluigi makes his first appearance in this game, having been created to give Wario a doubles partner.
Gameplay
In addition to the player's created character, the GBC version features 25 playable characters, consisting of nine Mario series characters and 16 human characters from the game's story mode.
Gameplay
Through the use of a Nintendo 64 Transfer Pak, players are able to import their characters from the GBC version to the N64 game, retaining the characters' stats.
Gameplay
As the characters go up in levels, the player may send their improved characters to the N64 version to level up again.
Gameplay
Other features, such as the Ring Tournament mode in the N64 version and multiplayer functionality in the GBC version, are also omitted from the Virtual Console releases.
Development

At Nintendo's suggestion, Princess Daisy was brought back from obscurity after having only ever appeared in Super Mario Land and NES Open Tournament Golf in order to give Luigi a doubles partner like Mario had Peach.
Development
The game had a marketing budget of $4 million.
Reception
The Nintendo 64 version received "universal acclaim" according to the review aggregation website Metacritic.
Reception
The game was a runner-up for GameSpot 's annual "Best Nintendo 64 Game" award, losing to Perfect Dark.
Reception
Dutch magazine Power Unlimited gave the N64 version a score of 9.1 out of 10, calling it very addictive, especially with four players.
Reception
Mario Tennis sold over 200,000 copies within two weeks of its release.
Reception
During the 4th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences honored Mario Tennis with the " Console Family " award.

f64_star_vixen_64.title: Star Fox 64
sents: lead
Star Fox 64, known as Lylat Wars in the PAL regions, is a 1997 rail shooter game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It is the second installment in the Star Fox series and a reboot of the original Star Fox for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
Star Fox 64 was the first Nintendo 64 game to feature support for the system's Rumble Pak peripheral, which initially came bundled with retail copies of the game.
lead
Since its release in 1997, the game has sold over 4 million copies, making it the best-selling game in the series and the ninth best-selling game on the system.
lead
The game received critical acclaim for its precise controls, voice acting, multiplayer modes, and replay value through the use of branching gameplay paths.
lead
Like the SNES Star Fox game before it, Star Fox 64 has been deemed one of the greatest video games of all time.
lead
A stereoscopic 3D remake for the Nintendo 3DS, Star Fox 64 3D, was released in 2011, and a reimagining for the Wii U, Star Fox Zero, was released in 2016.
lead
The game was also re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack at the launch of the service on October 25, 2021.
Gameplay
Star Fox 64 is a 3D rail shooter game in which the player controls one of the vehicles piloted by Fox McCloud, usually an Arwing.
Gameplay
Most of the game takes place in "Corridor Mode", which forces Fox's vehicle down an on-rails path straight forward through the environment.
Vehicles
Each vehicle shares some tactical characteristics with the Arwing while providing its own unique gameplay elements.
Multiplayer
Star Fox 64 features split-screen multiplayer support for up to four players simultaneously.
Multiplayer

At first, users can only play using the Arwing fighter, but by earning certain medals in the main campaign, players can unlock the Landmaster tank and fight on foot as one of the four members of Star Fox equipped with a bazooka.
Multiplayer
Multiplayer is the only place where players can use a Landmaster with upgraded lasers.
Multiplayer

There are three modes of multiplayer play: a "point match" in which the player must shoot down an opponent a certain number of times, a "battle royal" in which the last player left wins, and a "time trial" to destroy enemy fighters.
Plot
In the Hard route ending from Area 6, Fox reveals Andross' true form as that of a floating brain, and finally kills him.
Plot
Shortly before his death, Andross activates his base's self-destruct system in a last-ditch attempt to kill Fox.
Plot
In a post-credits scene, Pepper receives a bill from Star Fox presenting the number of enemies killed and multiplies it by 64, resulting in the amount of money due.
Plot
If the price is between $50,000 and $69,999 (between 781 and 1,093 enemies killed) he will say, "This is one steep bill....but it's worth it".
Plot
If the price is over $70,000 (1,094 or more), he says "What?!" At this point, the bill is stamped.
Main characters
Fox is the game's protagonist and only playable character in Story Mode.
Main characters
The team's mothership, the Great Fox, is piloted by a robot named ROB 64 (NUS64 in the Japanese version).
Development
Following the release of Star Fox in 1993, series creator Shigeru Miyamoto began working on Star Fox 2 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
Development
By 1995, Miyamoto and team had largely finished development of Star Fox 2 before realizing that its release would require the upgraded Super FX 2 chip, which would increase the cost of the game.
Development
Recognizing this and that the Nintendo 64 would launch the following year with significantly increased processing power and graphical capabilities, Miyamoto made the decision to cancel Star Fox 2.
Development
Around this time, Star Fox 64 's development reportedly began with a series of experiments by character designer Takaya Imamura and programmer Kazuaki Morita.
Development

As Morita was new to 3D programming, creating something entirely new was difficult, and to make matters worse, they didn't have the final N64 hardware itself to work with, instead having to utilize a bulky development computer and a modified Super Nintendo controller.
Development
The pair decided to begin development by porting the original Star Fox, which they thought would be better for easing into 3D.
Development

As this was Morita's first attempt at learning 3D, he began with inputting his own data and placing objects like cubes on a course, and then launched basic-looking Arwings; this prototype was affectionately named "Star Box".
Development

All this would change, however, when the game that would form into Star Fox 64 was first shown off at Shoshinkai 1995, where they had displayed ten seconds of promotional footage, and from there the game's production would be properly green-lit, with director Takao Shimizu coming on board.
Development

Miyamoto had two overall goals and themes for Star Fox 64: The first was to create a more fleshed out Star Fox game, as they weren't able to achieve a high enough processing speed for the original Star Fox thanks to hardware limitations.
Development
The other goal was also to retain some of the best elements from the then-cancelled Star Fox 2, not wanting all of that development teams' efforts to go to waste.
Development
In particular, Miyamoto said: "All-Range Mode, Multi-Player Mode and the Star Wolf scenario all came from Star Fox 2 ".
Development
In regards to the All-Range mode, Morita reportedly worked on this aspect in secret initially as an experiment, inspired by what he saw from Star Fox 2.
Development
The game's branching pathways were meant to act as a middle ground between the original Star Fox 's static difficulty routes and also Star Fox 2' s more free-form gameplay.
Development
The team originally intended for the game to contain multiple underwater levels but ultimately scaled back as they found that the underwater levels slowed down the pacing of the game.
Development

With the underlying gameplay largely complete early in development, Miyamoto and the team focused the majority of their efforts on graphics, audio and dialogue, and enemy AI, seeking to harness the Nintendo 64's processing power.
Development

For example, inspired by Miyamoto being a fan of the British puppet-based show Thunderbirds, the development team animated the game's characters opening and closing their mouths in a puppet-like fashion while speaking, which reduced the overall amount of animation work required for the game.
Development
The team also realized that adding dynamic audio would enhance the 3D gameplay experience as the player's allies could audibly signal when the player was being pursued by an offscreen enemy.
Development
Edgier dialogue such as "I guess it's your turn to be thankful" was written for the character Falco Lombardi, while more supportive dialogue such as "Never give up.
Development
Star Fox 64 was also the first title to make use of the Rumble Pak peripheral, which came bundled with the game in some instances.
Release
The game was first shown publicly at E3 1996 where Nintendo released a video of an early version of the game.
Release
This early version of the game showcased only the first level (Corneria) and featured a minimalistic HUD, showing only a crude meter reflecting the player's shield gauge.
Release
Nintendo released further beta footage of the game on December 6, 1996, that showed subsequent levels, an improved HUD, and a short multiplayer segment.
Release
The game reportedly had a marketing budget of $7 million.
Release

In an interview post-release, Miyamoto said that while he was not 100% satisfied with the final version of Star Fox 64, he felt that the game made better use of the Nintendo 64's increased processing power than Super Mario 64, which was a launch title for the console and which Miyamoto had also developed.
Reception
Star Fox 64 received critical acclaim and was one of the top-selling games of 1997, second to Mario Kart 64.
Reception
Reviews hailed the level branching system, particularly its use of player performance and secret in-level triggers rather than simple path selection.
Reception
GamePro gave the game a perfect 5 out of 5 in all four categories, praising the gameplay, graphics, controls, and fun factor.
Reception

The most common criticism was that Star Fox 64 was not as much of a leap over the original Star Fox as Super Mario 64 was over previous Mario games, in particular that the gameplay was still on rails.
Reception
GameSpot reviewer Glenn Rubenstein declared Star Fox 64 "an instant classic" and "a pleasure to look at".
Reception
EGM gave it their "Game of the Month" award, with Dan Hsu calling it "a shooting fan's dream come true" and Shawn Smith "almost as good as Mario 64 ".
Reception
The GameSpot review of the Wii Virtual Console version bestows a (7.6/10), praising its simple, enjoyable shooting gameplay, and much voice acting.
Reception

The review says the game is nice to look at regardless of its graphic age, with added replay value in finding hidden paths, but found the lack of rumble support "alarming", especially since it is the first game to support the Rumble Pak.
Reception
In the first five days of the game's U.S. launch, more than 300,000 copies were sold, surpassing the record previously held by Mario Kart 64 and Super Mario 64.
Reception
It sold above 1 million units in the United States by the end of 1997, one of five Nintendo 64 games to do so.
Reception
Sales were considerably less in Japan, where it sold 75,595 copies during the first week of sale.
Reception
The game also took the #73 spot in Nintendo Power 's "Top 200 Nintendo Games Ever".
Reception
Star Fox 64 is listed as the 45th greatest game of all time by Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition in 2009.
Reception

In 1997 EGM ranked it the 39th best console video game of all time, citing its amazing visuals, huge amount of voice acting, and the deep challenge of earning medals on all stages and completing expert mode.
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 14th in a list of the greatest Nintendo games.
Remake
At E3 2010, Nintendo announced a remake of Star Fox 64 for the Nintendo 3DS, titled Star Fox 64 3D.
Remake
Nintendo exhibited a demo the same day that emphasized the technology of the Nintendo 3DS.
Remake
The remake was co-developed by Q-Games and features stereoscopic 3D graphics, quality-of-life improvements, gyroscope controls, and brand new voice recordings.
Remake
The game was released on July 14 in Japan and September 9, 2011 in Europe and North America.
Remake
This marked the first time that Star Fox 64 had been released in PAL territories under the original Star Fox name.

f64_pocket_critters_snap.title: Pokémon Snap
sents: lead
Pokémon Snap is a 1999 first-person photography game with rail shooter style gameplay mechanics developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was first released in Japan in March 1999 and was later released in July 1999 in North America and in September 2000 for PAL regions.
lead
It is a spin-off game in the Pokémon series, being one of the first console-based games for it, and featuring many Pokémon rendered for the first time in real-time 3D.
lead
The game was re-released for the Wii 's Virtual Console in December 2007, for the Wii U 's Virtual Console in 2016, and for the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in June 2022.
lead
Originally announced as a Nintendo 64DD title, the development of Pokémon Snap was moved to the Nintendo 64 due to the 64DD's delays.
lead
The gameplay is similar to other first-person games, viewing from the perspective of protagonist Todd Snap as he moves automatically on a rail.
lead
The objective of the game is to take pictures of Pokémon with an in-game camera, using items such as apples and "pester balls" to achieve better shots.
lead
After each round, players are judged based on the quality of their photos.
Synopsis and gameplay
Players start out with only a camera, but as they progress, Professor Oak will provide them with a number of special accessories used to obtain better photographs.
Synopsis and gameplay
Levels must be replayed after acquiring new accessories in order to locate hidden Pokémon, alternate routes, or photographic opportunities that yield the best scores.
Synopsis and gameplay
The first accessory, apple-shaped Pokémon food, can be thrown to either stun or attract Pokémon.
Synopsis and gameplay
The game features 63 of the original generation of 151 Pokémon.
Jack and the Beanstalk
Named after the English fairy tale of the same name, the game was intended for the 64DD, a peripheral for the Nintendo 64.
Jack and the Beanstalk
Jack and the Beanstalk was first revealed in February 1995, a year before the Japanese release of the N64, but the game was not heard from again.
Jack and the Beanstalk
However, it is speculated that some gameplay elements ended up in EarthBound 64, which started development in 1994 but was cancelled in 2000.
Jack and the Beanstalk
Benimaru Itoh, one of the art designers of EarthBound 64, said in an interview that the game was to feature seeds.
Jack and the Beanstalk
When planted, these seeds would grow in real-time, utilising the 64DD's internal clock.
Conversion to Pokémon
On 27 February 1996, Nintendo affiliate Game Freak released Pocket Monsters Red and Green (released in the west as Pokémon Red and Blue).
Conversion to Pokémon
On 1 April 1997, an anime TV series debuted, turning the franchise into a national phenomenon that was later successfully exported to the rest of the world.
Conversion to Pokémon
The game, now known as Pokémon Snap, was shown at Nintendo Space World '97.
Conversion to Pokémon

Satoru Iwata, one of the producers of the game, explained in a 2010 interview: "Originally, Pokémon Snap for the Nintendo 64 system wasn't a Pokémon game, but rather a normal game in which you took photos, but the motivation for playing the game wasn't clear.
Conversion to Pokémon

We wondered what players would enjoy taking pictures of, and later on we made a somewhat forced switch to taking pictures of Pokémon." Masanobu Yamamoto, one of the character designers, initially had a negative reaction to the switch, since it meant that a lot of work he had put into the project had to be scrapped.
Conversion to Pokémon
In 1999, Mother / EarthBound creator Shigesato Itoi posted a five-part article series about Jack and the Beanstalk on his site, 1101.com.
Support for 64DD dropped

After turning the project into a Pokémon game, the title initially continued to be developed with support for the 64DD, an accessory for the Nintendo 64 that used magnetic disk cartridges with a bigger storage capacity, and which featured an internet modem and internal clock.
Support for 64DD dropped
The device made its first public appearance at Shoshinkai 1996, but after numerous delays, it eventually received a limited, Japan-only release on 1 December 1999, with only a handful of games.
Support for 64DD dropped
Almost all of the games that would have a 64DD version, including The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Donkey Kong 64, were given an N64-only release.
Support for 64DD dropped
In January 1999, the magazine Dengeki Nintendo 64 announced that Pokémon Snap was also no longer appearing on the 64DD, being published only as an N64 cartridge.
Release and promotion
Pokémon Snap was released on March 21, 1999, in Japan, July 26, 1999, in North America, and September 15, 2000, in PAL regions.
Release and promotion
Nintendo, partnering with LodgeNet, included Nintendo 64s with Pokémon Snap for more than 86,000 hotels with the intent of capitalizing on the Pokémon franchise for the holiday travel season.
Re-releases
In December 2007, Pokémon Snap was re-released for the Wii as a Virtual Console title.
Re-releases
On April 4, 2016, Pokémon Snap was re-released in Japan for Wii U as a Virtual Console title.
Re-releases
This version was released in Europe and Australia on August 18, 2016, and North America on January 5, 2017.
Re-releases
On June 24, 2022, Pokémon Snap was rereleased for Nintendo Switch Online’s Expansion Pack.
Sales
Pokémon Snap was fourth on the chart for top-selling games in Japan for the week of its release, March 18 to March 24.
Sales
For the week ending May 21, 1999, in Japan, it ranked fifth.
Sales
In the United States, Pokémon Snap sold in excess of 151,000 copies in the first three days of its release.
Sales
Since its release, it was the most rented game, up to October 22, 1999.
Sales
For the month of November, it was featured in the United States' top 10 list of best-selling video games.
Sales
For the week ending November 27, it ranked as the 10th best-selling video game, while it remained the most-rented video game for the same week.
Sales
By the end of 1999, Pokémon Snap was the sixth best-selling video game in the United States, having sold in excess of 1.5 million copies.
Sales
In the United Kingdom, it sold 6,500 units at launch, reaching No.9 in that week's charts, and replacing Perfect Dark as the top-selling game in the N64 Top Ten chart.
Critical reception
Pokémon Snap received positive reviews from the media, scoring 77/100 on Metacritic.
Critical reception
Ars Technica editor Frank Caron commented that Pokémon Snap had become a "fan favorite", while author Marina D'Amato called it "famous".
Critical reception
Author Amit Dhir called it one of the most popular video games of 1999, alongside Gran Turismo and Final Fantasy VIII.
Critical reception

Matt Casamassina of IGN called it an "addictive, surprisingly fun" game, noting however that "Pokemaniacs are bound to be disappointed with the selection of Pocket Monsters in the game – roughly 62 out of a possible 151 in all."
Critical reception
GameSpot praised it as a "refreshingly unique game".
Critical reception

IGN editors Mark Bozon and Casamassina commented on Pokémon Snap ' s likelihood of becoming a Virtual Console title; the former called it a "cult classic" as well as a "fresh and entertaining little package".
Critical reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s four reviewers gave the game two 8/10 scores and two 8.5/10 scores.
Critical reception
The Electric Playground editor Victor Lucas called it "innovative" and "worth taking a look at".
Critical reception
The Denver Post editor David Thomas commented that the concept of Pokémon Snap should have "never worked", but it turned out to be "one of the most creative and entertaining games on the market".
Critical reception
The magazine Boys' Life called it addictive, praising the reactions of the Pokémon as "unique and always entertaining".
Critical reception
At the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Pokémon Snap was awarded Console Children's/Family Title of the Year by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.
Critical reception
Blockbuster nominated it for best Nintendo 64 game in its "Blockbuster Awards".
Critical reception
Developer Wade Tinney attributed the inspiration for the game design of Snapshot Adventures: Secret of Bird Island to both Pokémon Snap and the video game Spore.
Critical reception
The PlayStation 3 video game Afrika was said by both UGO Networks and Shacknews to be Pokémon Snap -like.
Critical reception
Thomas called the photo sharing feature a positive of its release, while criticizing its limited selection of Pokémon, similar to the review of the Nintendo 64 version from IGN.
Critical reception

IGN included Pokémon Snap in its wish list of Nintendo 3DS remakes, commenting that it could take advantage of the 3DS' ability to produce stereoscopic 3D photos would be an enjoyable feature for Pokémon Snap.
Critical reception
1UP.com used Pokémon Snap as an example of a game that would use the Wii U controller's gyroscope to look around, calling it "The coolest version of Pokémon Snap ever ".

f64_pocket_critters_stadium.title: Pokémon Stadium
sents: lead
Pokémon Stadium, known in Japan as Pokémon Stadium 2, is a strategy video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was released in Japan on April 30, 1999; in North America on March 6, 2000; in Australia on March 23, 2000; and in Europe on April 7, 2000.
lead
It was the first Stadium title released in Western regions, succeeding the Japan-only 1998 Nintendo 64 release Pocket Monsters' Stadium.
lead
The gameplay revolves around a 3D turn-based battling system using the 151 Pokémon from the Game Boy games Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow.
lead
Originally intended for the 64DD, it was later developed into a standard console game after the add-on failed.
lead
Using the Transfer Pak accessory that was bundled with the game, players are able to view, organize, store, trade, and battle using Pokémon uploaded from Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow.
lead
The game includes four stadium cups, each of which is a series of three-on-three Pokémon battles against an ordered lineup of opponents.
lead
Gym Leader Castle mode involves battles against the eight Kanto gym leaders and the Elite Four.
Gameplay
The Pika and Petit Cups only award one trophy each.
Gameplay
In each battle, the player and the opponent are only allowed to use three of their six party Pokémon.
Gameplay
Like in the Stadium, the player has to pick a team of six Pokémon and may only use three at a time for battling.
Other features
A player's Game Boy Pokémon can also be saved, researched, and traded on the Nintendo 64 in Oak's Lab.
Mini-games
To win, players must be the last one standing or have the fewest misses after five rounds.
Mini-games
": Players race to see which Sandshrew can dig for water the fastest.
Mini-games
The players with the most points win.
Mini-games
" Run, Rattata, Run ": As Rattata, players run on a treadmill to be the first to reach the goal, jumping over hurdles along the way.
Mini-games
The player with the most expensive bill wins.
Pocket Monsters ' Stadium
The first Pocket Monsters' Stadium was released only in Japan on August 1, 1998.
Pocket Monsters ' Stadium
Once intended as a 64DD launch title with a March 1998 release date, it was instead converted to a standard Nintendo 64 game on a 32 MB cartridge.
Pocket Monsters ' Stadium
Because of technical limitations, this version features only 40 Pokémon that are available for battle, instead of the full 151 Pokémon from the Game Boy versions as originally planned.
Pocket Monsters ' Stadium

Connectivity with the Pokémon Game Boy trilogy is available using the Transfer Pak in the same way as the internationally released Pokémon Stadium and later Pokémon Stadium 2 (Pocket Monsters' Stadium Gold and Silver in Japan).
Pocket Monsters ' Stadium
GameSpot reported that it had 1.4 million pre-orders by June 1998.
Pocket Monsters ' Stadium
The game sold a reported 270,000 copies in its first month of release.
International release
Pokémon Stadium 2 was announced in the December 1998 issue of The 64Dream.
International release
On February 16, 1999, Nintendo announced that it would be showing the game in a Japan-exclusive event called Pokémon Festival '99.
International release
Because the first game had met criticism for its difficulty, the AI was toned down for the sequel to make it easier for average players.
International release
Released as Pokémon Stadium throughout North America and Europe, this version supports the transfer of all first generation Pokémon to and from Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow via the N64 Transfer Pak.
Promotion
On March 6, 2000, Nintendo launched a $7 million Pokémon Stadium advertising campaign on television, print, and online media as part of a wider $30 million Pokémon promotion.
Promotion

Nintendo released a promotional Pokémon Stadium bundle featuring a Nintendo 64 console, one Gray and one Atomic Purple Nintendo 64 controller, a poster, a Pokémon Trainer's Journal, and a "Cool Porygon " promo card by Wizards of the Coast for the trading card game.
Promotion
The Smart Cards were previously available in Blockbuster's 1999 promotion for Pokémon Snap.
Reception
Pokémon Stadium received mostly positive reviews from critics, attaining a score of 78.60% on review aggregator GameRankings based on 26 reviews.
Reception
GameSpot contributor Jeff Gerstmann gave the game a 5.7 "mediocre" review, writing that the gameplay "feels scaled down and oversimplified, even when compared with the original Game Boy games".
Reception

GameFan called it "surprisingly fun, even for the uninitiated." In his review on gaming website Cubed3, Ross Morley praised the game's battle system for its "beautiful 3D models, special effects and range of options".
Reception

IGN ' s Peer Schneider wrote an 8.2 "great" review of the game, calling it "a must-buy for Pokémon fans", but also citing that "the audio is nowhere near the quality of some of the recent Nintendo releases".
Reception

Regarding the game's announcer, a frequent complaint among critics, RPGamer' s Ben Martin wrote that: "With a very limited vocabulary and continual comments throughout every single action, it certainly is a nice option to be able to turn this guy off".
Reception
Nintendo Power similarly critiqued the announcer soundbites as "tiresome", but it rated the game overall with an 8.8 out of 10.
Reception
During the 4th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Pokémon Stadium received a nomination for the " Console Family " award by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.
Reception
In its first month of sales in North America, Pokémon Stadium sold over 1 million copies, and it became the best-selling console game in the region during the year 2000.
Reception
Nintendo of America announced that it would be released as a Player's Choice title, a well-selling game with a lower suggested retail price, on December 26, 2000.
Reception
At least more than 3.97 million copies have been sold, including 3.16 million in the United States, 710,765 in Japan, and more than 100,000 in the United Kingdom.
Sequel and legacy
The game was released in 2000 and 2001 as Pokémon Stadium 2, featuring the 251 Pokémon from the first two generations.
Sequel and legacy
The game was re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on April 12, 2023.

f64_pocket_critters_stadium_2.title: Pokémon Stadium 2
sents: lead
Pokémon Stadium 2, known in Japan as Pokémon Stadium Gold & Silver, is a strategy video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It features all 251 Pokémon from the first and second generations of the franchise.
lead
It was released in Japan on December 14, 2000, in North America on March 26, 2001, and in Europe on October 10, 2001.
lead
In Western regions it was titled Pokémon Stadium 2, as it was the second Stadium game to be released outside Japan, in which it was the third game in the series.
lead

Like its predecessor, Pokémon Stadium 2 is compatible with the Transfer Pak accessory, allowing players to use Pokémon trained in the three original Game Boy Pokémon games (Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow) and the three Game Boy Color games (Pokémon Gold, Silver, and Crystal).
lead
The majority of the game takes place inside the fictional White City, where various facilities for battling, organizing, researching, and playing with Pokémon are located.
lead
The Japanese edition also features the capability to use the Pokémon Mobile System from Pokémon Crystal.
lead
The game was released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in August 8, 2023.
Gameplay
Defeating the rival will unlock Round 2, in which the player must re-challenge the Stadium, Gym Leader Castle, and the Rival at a higher difficulty level.
Gameplay
With the exception of the Challenge Cup, the player first assembles a team of six Pokémon consisting of any combination of rental Pokémon or imported Pokémon from a Game Boy cartridge.
Gameplay
In the same fashion as the first Stadium, each combatant chooses only three of their six Pokémon to use in a battle before beginning.
Additional features
The Mini-Game Park is an area in White City where up to four players can play 12 different Pokémon-themed mini-games.
Additional features
The player who has the most points after five logs wins.
Additional features
Pichu's Power Plant: As Pichu, players race to be the first to fully charge up using four electrodes.
Additional features
Rampage Rollout: As Donphan, players compete to be the first to complete nine laps around a square track.
Additional features
At the Game Boy Tower, Pokémon Red, Blue, Yellow, Gold, Silver, and Crystal can be played on the Nintendo 64.
Additional features

The Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak increases the texture resolution and overall image quality when inserted into the console, and also reduces how often data needs to be loaded when playing Pokémon Crystal in the Game Boy Tower.
Development
The success of Japan's Pokémon Stadium 2, released internationally as Pokémon Stadium, led to the development of a third entry.
Development
Scheduled for a late 2000 release, the game was to be demonstrated publicly at the 2000 Nintendo Space World festival.
Development
By July 20, 2000, the game's title was changed from Pokemon Stadium 3 to Pokemon Stadium Gold/Silver.
Development
Nintendo announced more information on October 3, including the dates of the Japanese release and official tournaments.
Development
On October 25, Nintendo set the game's North American release date for March 26, 2001.
Development
The game had a marketing budget of $7 million.
Reception
Pokémon Stadium 2 holds a 78% score on the review aggregate website Metacritic, indicating "generally favorable reviews".
Reception
GameRankings rated it 73.31% based on 18 reviews.
Reception
The game became the 18th best-selling Nintendo 64 video game with a reported shipment of 2,540,000 units.
Reception
Pokémon Stadium 2 was a nominee for "11th Annual GamePro Readers' Choice Awards" for "Best Action Game of the Year", but lost to Grand Theft Auto III for PlayStation 2.

f64_harvest_moo_64.title: Harvest Moon 64
sents: lead
Harvest Moon 64, released in Japan as Bokujō Monogatari 2 (牧場物語2), is a 1999 farm simulation video game developed by Victor Interactive Software for the Nintendo 64 console.
lead
It was published by Victor Interactive in Japan and by Natsume Inc. in North America.
lead
It is the third game in the Story of Seasons series (following Harvest Moon GB).
lead
The game was re-released on the Wii U in 2017, marking its first release in PAL territories.
lead
It was re-released again for the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in 2023.
Gameplay
The objective of Harvest Moon 64 is to restore and maintain an abandoned farm left to the player by their grandfather.
Gameplay
The local town, where most of the villagers spend their day, contains a church, a bar, a bakery, a town square, a flower shop, a library, a tool shop, among other things.
Gameplay
Unlike the original Harvest Moon for the SNES, there is a limited amount of time to work in any given day as well as a limited amount of stamina for work.
Gameplay
The dog originally belonged to the player character 's grandfather and is a throwback to the original Harvest Moon.
Gameplay
One of the other major features of Harvest Moon 64 is the ability to marry and have a child.
Gameplay

There are five eligible girls in Harvest Moon 64, represented by hearts that appear in their dialogue boxes, representative of her affection toward the player, ranging from white (indifferent) to pink (in love).
Release
Harvest Moon 64 was released in Japan on February 5, 1999, and in North America by Natsume Inc. on December 22, 1999.
Release
However, in celebration of the series' twentieth anniversary, the game saw release on the Wii U Virtual Console on February 23, 2017.
Release

This also marked the game's debut in the PAL regions (the original had been cancelled due to time constraints), as well as the game's first official re-release (as well as the first time digital) in nearly two decades.
Release
The game was re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack service on December 7, 2023.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 31 out of 40.
Reception
Many reviews claimed that although the game had a repetitive soundtrack and often glitchy visual displays, the game's captivating and unique gameplay made up for it.
Reception

Mars Publishing's Parent's Guide to Nintendo Games gave the game the only Parent's Guide Choice Award for a Nintendo 64 game because it met the requirements of a game that "displays imagination, creativity, ingenuity of the first order, while offering a playing atmosphere that is educational and enriching."
Reception
Nintendo Power ranked Harvest Moon 64 as the 278th greatest Nintendo game of all time.

f64_earthworm_tim_3d.title: Earthworm Jim 3D
sents: lead
Earthworm Jim 3D is a 1999 platform game developed by VIS Interactive and published by Interplay Entertainment for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It is the third in the Earthworm Jim series and a sequel to Earthworm Jim 2.
lead
It was the first game in the series to not be developed by Shiny Entertainment, which had recently instituted a strict "no sequels" policy.
lead
Interplay Entertainment, having recently purchased the Earthworm Jim rights, handed the franchise off to VIS Interactive.
lead

The game suffered a difficult, prolonged development cycle and was repeatedly delayed until it was released in 1999 for the Nintendo 64, with Rockstar Games publishing the N64 version in North America.
lead
It was ported to Microsoft Windows.
lead

The game was not received well, with critics claiming that the charm of the originals was lost, and that despite the long development period, the game still felt sloppy and lacked previously promoted features.
Gameplay
Earthworm Jim 3D borrows much of its gameplay from other platformers of the era, competing with Banjo-Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64.
Development
Shortly after the release of Earthworm Jim 2, its original developer, Shiny Entertainment was bought by Interplay Entertainment, and then put onto other projects.
Development
It was decided that, much like many platform game series at the time, such as Super Mario or Sonic the Hedgehog, that gameplay would transition from 2D to 3D.
Development
Development started shortly after Earthworm Jim 2 in 1996.
Development
The game was initially being developed for the PlayStation, but this version was scrapped early in 1997 in favor of the Nintendo 64 platform.
Development

Much content from previews and promotional material was no longer in the final game; most notably that the game's final packaging showed Evil the Cat as the boss of the "Fear" level, whereas Professor Monkey-for-a-Head was actually the boss of the level.
Development
The characters had to be redesigned for the shift from side-scrolling 2D to free-roaming 3D.
Development
Problems with the frame rate and animation were still arising in the game as development was over 70% complete.
Reception
Earthworm Jim 3D received mixed reviews on both platforms according to the review aggregation website GameRankings.
Reception
Many reviews called the game uninspired, mediocre, and unable to compete with many other similar, higher reviewed platform games at the time, such as Super Mario 64, Rayman 2, or Banjo-Kazooie.
Reception
A major complaint was the game's camera, with GameSpot ' s Nintendo 64 version review stating that they felt the camera was on a " kamikaze mission to destroy the game".
Reception
GameSpot ' s review of the Windows version was even more negative, concluding with " Earthworm Jim 3D has something to discourage all types of people from playing it.
Reception

Everyone else will be frustrated by the horrible camera." IGN was slightly more forgiving for the Nintendo 64 version, praising sound, graphics, and presentation, but still criticizing the camera and lasting appeal.
Reception
In one review, Boba Fatt of GamePro called the Nintendo 64 version "a disappointing experience that's more enraging than fun.
Reception
Avoid this washout at all costs." In another review, iBot said, " Earthworm Jim ' s crazy antics have made it to N64, but it appears that the system wasn't ready for him.
Reception
As 3D platformers go, Earthworm Jim 3D is middle of the road, which is frustrating because he's a character that's a lot of fun."
Reception
The PC version was nominated for the "Worst Game of the Year" award at GameSpot ' s Best and Worst of 2000 Awards, which went to Blaze and Blade: Eternal Quest.

f64_rayguy_2.title: Rayman (video game)
sents: lead
Rayman is a 1995 platform game developed by Ubi Pictures and published by Ubi Soft.
lead
The player controls Rayman, who must pursue Mr Dark to recover the Great Protoon that used to keep the balance between nature and the people of Rayman's valley.
lead
The player must navigate the valley, defeat enemies with abilities gained throughout the game, and free captured Electoons, also encountering a boss at the end of each thematic world.
lead
Michel Ancel conceived Rayman as a teenager and was able to realise the concept after being hired by Ubi Soft in 1989.
lead
He initially targeted the Atari ST and then the Super NES CD-ROM but restarted the development for the Atari Jaguar after the Super NES CD-ROM's cancellation.
lead
Ancel incorporated several childhood memories into the design and was soon joined by a larger development team.
lead
Ubi Soft made Rayman a launch title for the PlayStation in North American and Europe to compete with Japanese platform games on the platform.
lead
Rayman was first released for the Atari Jaguar on 1 September 1995, followed shortly by versions for the PlayStation, the Sega Saturn, and MS-DOS.
Gameplay
Rescuing all Electoons in the first five worlds grants Rayman access to the final world, the Candy Château, the hideout of the final boss, Mr Dark.
Gameplay
When Rayman interacts with the Magician, who is hidden in various levels, he can access hidden rooms that grant him Tings or extra lives if beaten in a given time.
Plot
Electoons return Rayman's fist at the last moment, such that he can defeat Mr Dark and retrieve the Great Protoon.
Early concepts and design
In 1988, his animation skills led him to be one of the early hires for the nascent publisher Ubi Soft, which at the time was operating with from Montreuil with six developers.
Early concepts and design
Rayman was greenlit in 1992, and Michel Guillemot gave Ancel and his team artistic freedom.
Early concepts and design
The game's style was inspired by Celtic, Chinese, and Russian fairy tales, as well as Ancel's childhood, having spent a lot of time by rivers, chasing insects, and climbing trees.
Early concepts and design
Having become interested in rendering tools such as Autodesk 3ds Max, he chose to incorporate 60 Hz animations.
Early concepts and design
Houde considered this impressive for a time where most games used sprites animated at five frames per second.
Early concepts and design
The Rayman character was named after the ray tracing rendering technique.
Production and release
When Nintendo cancelled the peripheral in 1993, that version of Rayman was also scrapped.
Production and release
It was considered lost media until rediscovered a copy dated 1992 in October 2016.
Production and release
With his permission, the programmer Omar Cornut released it online in July 2017.
Production and release
Michel Guillemot eventually assigned additional developers onto the project and allocated 15 million francs for its development.
Production and release
Rayman on the Jaguar was first displayed at the 1994 Summer Consumer Electronics Show.
Production and release
In late 1994, magazine advertisements announced Rayman as a title for the Atari Jaguar with a release in the fall or by December 1994.
Production and release
Pre-release promos of the PlayStation had advertised a release date of Rayman on 13 January 1995 in Japan.
Production and release
Later, Japanese magazines stated a release date for the PlayStation version as being June 1995.
Production and release
Similarly, American magazines reported a Jaguar release by June 1995, as well as versions for the 32X and 3DO, both of which were cancelled.
Production and release
Rayman was released on 1 September 1995 for the Atari Jaguar in Europe and on 9 September 1995 for North America.
Production and release
A version for MS-DOS was released in December 1995 in Europe and in North American in April 1996.
Reception
Captain Squideo, also of GamePro, commented that the PlayStation version was a "dazzling delight" and proclaimed it to be one of the most visually appealing games at the time.
Reception

Sam Hickman of Sega Saturn Magazine criticised the Sega Saturn version because of what he considered an overabundance of levels that played similarly with only varied attacks or an increased difficulty used as differentiation.
Sales
By the end of 1995, 400,000 copies of Rayman had been sold in Europe.
Sales
The game sold 900,000 copies globally by 1997.
Sales
It was the all-time best-selling PlayStation game in the United Kingdom, while in France it had sold 670,000 copies by 2000, becoming the second-best-selling game on the platform in the country.
Sales
According to Gamasutra, Rayman Advance ' s sales neared 600,000 units during the first half of the 2001–2002 fiscal year alone and then reached 770,000 copies by the end of March 2002.
Legacy
The commercial success of Rayman spawned a successful franchise with several sequels, including Rayman 2: The Great Escape (1999), and some of the game's elements influenced Rayman Origins.
Legacy
Ancel was honoured by the French government for his work in 2006.
Legacy
Rayman was brought to the Game Boy Color in early 2000, to Palm OS in September 2001, to the Nintendo DSi in December 2009, and to iOS in February 2016.
Legacy
Rayman Advance, a variant for the Game Boy Advance developed by Digital Eclipse, was released in June 2001.
Legacy
The game is one of twenty titles included with the PlayStation Classic, a miniature PlayStation replica released in December 2018.

f64_space_station_silicone_valle.title: Space Station Silicon Valley
sents: lead
Space Station Silicon Valley is a platform video game developed by DMA Design and published by Take-Two Interactive.
lead
It was originally released for the Nintendo 64 in October 1998.
lead
An adaptation of the game for Game Boy Color was developed by Tarantula Studios and released in 1999.
lead
A PlayStation port, developed by Runecraft, was released in 2000, under the name Evo's Space Adventures.
lead
Players control Evo, a robot reduced to a crawling microchip after a ship crash, and are tasked with taking control of animals to solve puzzles and defeat enemies.
lead
Development began in September 1995 as part of a publishing deal with BMG Interactive.
lead
When this deal fell through, the development team turned their focus to the Nintendo 64, which allowed for a more advanced environment and model processing.
lead
The hardware shaped the game's humour and style, with a soft focus look leading to a style akin to Plasticine models.
Gameplay
Players are frequently accompanied by the voice of Dan Danger, a human who is trapped in the destroyed spaceship.
Gameplay

Each level also contains a hidden objective, such as collecting a souvenir or making an animal perform a certain act; as players complete the hidden objectives, they are rewarded with a gold trophy, and collecting all trophies unlocks a bonus level.
Plot
In the year 2001, the space station Silicon Valley is launched, housing numerous robotic animals.
Plot
Believed to have disappeared forever, it reappears 1000 years later, and the many expeditions sent to retrieve the space station vanish without explanation.
Plot
Following this, the duo of Dan Danger and Evo are sent to investigate; they crash land in the station and Evo's body is destroyed, reducing him to a microchip.
Development

Space Station Silicon Valley began development in September 1995, as part of a three-game publishing deal between developer DMA Design and BMG Interactive, the other games being Grand Theft Auto (1997) and Tanktics (1999).
Development
All three games were planned to be released on Microsoft Windows, PlayStation and Sega Saturn, as they were the most popular platforms at the time.
Development

Following Take-Two Interactive 's acquisition of BMG Interactive in March 1998, Take-Two acquired the publishing rights to the game, and the team instead changed focus to develop the game for the Nintendo 64, upon discovering that Windows was incapable of processing the models and environments intended for use.
Development
Every member of the team that developed Space Station Silicon Valley began working at DMA Design at the beginning of development, in September 1995.
Development
Development began using the then-new DirectX libraries, following the release of Windows 95.
Development
The levels were designed and edited using Silicon Graphics computers, which were transferred directly to the Nintendo 64 development boards.
Development
The team found the Nintendo 64 to be more advanced than previous hardware; programmer Grant Salvona described the development kits as "the most powerful hardware available in the building".
Development

The game was presented with "distinctive 'British' humour" to distinguish it from other games; lead programmer Leslie Benzies and artist Aaron Garbut often presented the team with other Nintendo 64 games, such as Super Mario 64 (1996), to identify the differences.
Development
While similar body-swapping games already existed, such as Paradroid (1985), they had little influence on the development of Space Station Silicon Valley.
Development
The team were instead influenced by other games in development at DMA, including Grand Theft Auto and Body Harvest (1998).
Development
The game was developed with little interference from upper management; programmer Obbe Vermeij said that "only after 18 months was there a push to get everything together into a finished game".
Development
Space Station Silicon Valley entered beta in August 1998, and was first released for Nintendo 64 on 22 October 1998.
Development
A 2D remake was released for Game Boy Color in Europe in late 1999; IGN ' s Tim Jones was critical of the port, criticising the gameplay and level design.
Reception
Space Station Silicon Valley received "generally favorable" reviews for the Nintendo 64, according to review aggregator Metacritic.
Reception
IGN ' s Matt Casamassina called Space Station Silicon Valley "maybe the most original game to hit Nintendo 64", and Next Generation named it "one of the very best Nintendo 64 has to offer".
Reception
GameRevolution wrote that the game has "some of the best sound yet" for a Nintendo 64 game, praising the variety of the musical tracks.
Reception
Critics noted the graphics did not match Nintendo games like Banjo-Kazooie and Super Mario 64 but were suitable for its purpose.
Reception
Next Generation felt that the game "doesn't push Nintendo 64's hardware to the limits", and noted some occasional frame rate slowdown, but appreciated the "cute" and simplistic design.
Reception
It was named IGN ' s Game of the Month for October 1998, and in February 1999 it won Most Innovative Game from IGN, who praised it for capturing "old-school" gameplay mechanics.
Reception

In January 2007, IGN placed the game fifth on a list of "Underrated and Underappreciated Games", and in April 2009 placed it on a list of "Nintendo 64 Treasures", stating that it "remains one of the great unsung heroes" of the console.
Reception
The team attributed the poor commercial performance to the game's simultaneous launch with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which was Nintendo's marketing focus at the time.

f64_blast_corpz.title: Blast Corps
sents: lead
Blast Corps is an action game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
In the game, the player uses vehicles to destroy buildings in the path of a runaway nuclear missile carrier.
lead
In the game's 57 levels, the player solves puzzles by transferring between vehicles to move objects and bridge gaps.
lead
It was released in March 1997 in Japan and North America.
lead
A wider release followed at the end of that year.
lead
The game was Rare's first game for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Its development team ranged between four and seven members, many of whom were recent graduates.
lead
The team sought to find gameplay to fit Rare co-founder Chris Stamper 's idea for a building destruction game.
Gameplay
The game's puzzles increase in difficulty as the player progresses through its 57 levels.
Gameplay

Activating hidden communication points in each level will unlock various secret levels, where the player completes objectives against the clock, such as completing laps on a circuit or smashing specific objects.
Gameplay
Completing every stage unlocks a time attack mode, in which players are awarded medals for clearing the carrier's path in the fastest time.
Plot

To prevent this, the government hires the demolition company known as Blast Corps — founded by several former military soldiers who were stationed in the base the missiles came from, until an accident involving one of their members led the others to desert their post.
Development
Rare founder Chris Stamper famously gave Blast Corps its raison d'être.
Development
Blast Corps was among Rare 's first games for the Nintendo 64 and led a run of seven critically acclaimed Rare titles for the console.
Development
Rare founder Chris Stamper was the impetus for the project.
Development
For instance, the Mario Kart 64 "power slide" drift mechanics inspired that of Blast Corps ' s dump truck.
Development
The game's lead artist, Ricky Berwick, had developed the vehicle concepts without consideration for their in-game function, and the vehicles were only later retrofitted to the gameplay.
Development
Wakeley described these platinum challenges as "just insane" and said he could only finish four himself.
Development
He was also inspired by the Super Mario 64 demo at Nintendo's annual trade show in 1995, which introduced him to the 3D analog stick and spurred him to achieve something similar.
Development
In its 1995 trade show preview, it was originally titled Blast Dozer, a name it retained for its Japanese release.
Development

(The team had considered other titles, including "Heavy Duty Heroes", "Blast Radius", and "Power Dozer".) Blast Corps was first released in Japan on March 21, 1997, and in North America three days later.
Development
To promote the game, a three-part comic detailing the game's story was published in Nintendo Power issues #97–99, later released as a graphic novel by Dark Horse Comics.
Reception
The game received "universal acclaim", according to review aggregator Metacritic, and "unanimous critical success", according to Retro Gamer.
Reception

Trent Ward commented in GameSpot that the premise taps into childhood fantasies, while "the unique relationship between the terrain and the vehicles you pilot ensures that Blast Corps will exercise your mind as well as your reflexes".
Reception
Slo Mo instead asserted that "Over 60 levels and hidden areas within hidden areas give you your money's worth".
Reception

A Next Generation critic agreed, asserting that the vast size of the levels and numerous secrets and bonus areas make Blast Corps "one of the few Nintendo 64 games that justifies its exorbitant price tag".
Reception
Schneider described the soundtrack as between "70s pop, disaster movie score, and Country Bear Jamboree ".
Reception
Retro Gamer wrote that the game's combination of puzzles and continuous destruction made the game so unique as to defy genre classification.
Reception
Retro Gamer thought of Blast Corps as a 3D successor to "nail-biting reaction games" such as Loco-Motion.
Reception
EGM named it a runner-up for "Most Original Game of the Year" (behind PaRappa the Rapper) at their 1997 Editors' Choice Awards.
Reception
Blast Corps sold close to a million copies.
Reception
Metacritic ranked the title among the top ten games released in 1997.
Reception
It remained Metacritic's highest ranked 1997 Nintendo 64 game after GoldenEye 007.
Reception
Blast Corps was selected as Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s May 1997 Game of the Month and an IGN Editors' Choice.
Reception

Later the same year, Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it number 93 on their 100 best console video games of all time, remarking, "C'mon, not only are you driving all the vehicles you thought were mega cool as a kid – you're using 'em to plow through buildings." Four of six Nintendo Power reviewers recommended the game.
Legacy
After praising the game in a 2010 Rare retrospective feature, Retro Gamer ' s writers craved a sequel.
Legacy

Steve Ellis, who was a programmer at Rare, thought Blast Corps to be among the company's most underrated games, and though its physics were now dated, he continued to find the game fun enough to revisit regularly.
Legacy
Blast Corps is included in Rare Replay, a compilation of 30 Rare titles, released on the Xbox One on August 4, 2015.
Legacy
Blast Corps was a standout favorite among Rare Replay reviewers.
Legacy
