The game was re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in North America and Europe on February 21, 2024, and in Japan on April 24, 2024.
Legacy
Rare's Blast Corps began a run of highly praised Nintendo 64 games, including GoldenEye 007, Banjo-Kazooie, Perfect Dark, and Jet Force Gemini.
Legacy
Retro Gamer wrote that Rare had doubled the number of classic Nintendo 64 games and was an important alliance for Nintendo.
Legacy
Microsoft acquired Rare in 2002 for a record price of $377 million.
Legacy
After the industry had changed, Blast Corps designer Martin Wakeley reflected a decade after the game's 1997 release.
Legacy
In 2009, Wakeley said, a studio would rarely entrust the scope of a project like Blast Corps to a team of four recent graduates.
Legacy
The staff of Nintendo Power (1997) and IGN (2014) both listed Blast Corps in the bottom halves of their top 100 Nintendo games of all time.
Legacy
Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 84th on a list of the greatest Nintendo games.

f64_jet_force_jiminy.title: Jet Force Gemini

Composer(s): Robin Beanland Graeme Norgate Alistair Lindsay

sents: lead
Jet Force Gemini is a 1999 third-person shooter developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64 video game console.
lead
The game follows the story of three members of a galactic law enforcement team as they try to stop a horde of drones led by an insectoid called Mizar.
lead

It features a single-player mode where the player must explore a galaxy and save Tribals, a race of survivors who have been enslaved and imprisoned by Mizar, and places strong emphasis on shooting large numbers of enemies while dodging their attacks.
lead
The game also includes a multiplayer mode where two to four players can compete in traditional deathmatch games.
lead
Inspired by 80s arcade games and more recent titles of the time, such as Super Metroid and Super Mario 64, Jet Force Gemini blends elements of both shoot 'em up and action-adventure games.
lead
Works such as Aliens, Stargate and Battle of the Planets were also major influences.
lead
The game received generally positive reviews from critics.
lead
Praise was given to its detailed graphics and life-span, while criticism was targeted at its confusing controls and insistence on having to save every Tribal to fully complete the game.
Gameplay
Jet Force Gemini is a third-person shooter with shoot 'em up and action-adventure elements, in which the player controls the player character from a third-person perspective in a 3D environment.
Gameplay
By contrast, when walking around, the game plays similar to a 3D platformer.
Gameplay
In the game's single-player mode, the player must explore a galaxy that is composed of 15 nonlinear worlds.
Gameplay
Most doors open automatically, but some require a special action to be unlocked.
Gameplay
The player must collect all 12 ship parts and 282 Tribals to access the final stage.
Gameplay
Some multiplayer aspects, such as levels and characters, must be unlocked by finding the corresponding secret in the game's single-player mode.
Plot
On Earth, the Jet Force Gemini team is given the highest honors for their accomplishments.
Development
Jet Force Gemini was developed by Rare 's Blast Corps team.
Development
Work on the game began in 1997 with lead engineer Paul Mountain, who had previously worked on Diddy Kong Racing.
Development
The inspirations of the game ranged from 80s arcade classics to more recent titles of the time.
Development

The free-roaming nature of Nintendo 's Super Mario 64 influenced the scale and the openness of some of the backgrounds and settings, while the collecting and upgrading of weapons were inspired by Super Metroid.
Development
According to him, "I suppose, in short, we were inspired by all the good stuff we'd played and enjoyed playing." Jet Force Gemini also borrowed elements from non-video game sources.
Development
Most of the characters in the game were named after stars and constellations, such as Mizar and Vela.
Development

Originally, the protagonists Juno and Vela were designed as younger and more cartoon-like with large heads, but they were ultimately changed to a more mature version because Nintendo expressed concerns over a game starring two children killing a large number of creatures.
Development
The idea was to retain a character-based game, where players could see the character they were playing while keeping the tightness and accuracy of first-person shooters.
Development
Rare initially attempted to automate the change of view and targeting mode based on the context of the action, but this idea was eventually replaced with a manual system.
Development
Developers initially considered the possibility to use the 4 MB Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak, but the idea was eventually dropped.
Development
In May 1999, a playable demonstration of the game was presented at the Electronic Entertainment Expo in Los Angeles, California.
Development
A more complete version of the game was showcased at Nintendo Spaceworld in Japan in August 1999, alongside Rare's Donkey Kong 64 and Perfect Dark.
Development
The game was originally intended to be released in North America on August 31, 1999, but was pushed back to September 27, 1999, to give the developers more time to polish up the game.
Development
It was then pushed back even further to October 11, 1999, due to manufacturing delays.
Development
In Europe, the game was released on October 29, 1999, and on December 1, 1999, in Japan.
Development
Although 4Kids Entertainment obtained the rights to merchandising Jet Force Gemini and Perfect Dark toys, movies, and other recreational products, the company did not produce any merchandise.
Reception
Casamassina felt that this task was "far too tedious to truly be enjoyed." In contrast, N64 Magazine stated that revisiting previous stages with new weapons was fun and extends the game's lifespan.
Legacy
According to former Rare designer and producer Martin Wakeley, Jet Force Gemini on the Game Boy Color "was the only occasion I can remember Rare outsourcing anything.
Legacy
The game was never officially announced by either Rare or Nintendo.
Legacy
In 2000, Jet Force Gemini was ranked by IGN at number 20 in their list of The Top 25 N64 Games of All Time.
Legacy
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked it the 93rd best game available on Nintendo platforms.
Legacy
The staff called it Rare's "big hope" due to the highly anticipated but delayed Nintendo 64 game Perfect Dark.
Legacy
Subsequent games developed by Rare have featured cameo appearances of Jet Force Gemini, including Kameo: Elements of Power, Viva Piñata: Trouble in Paradise, and Banjo-Tooie.
Legacy
Players may also dress their character up as Juno, Vela, and Lupus in Minecraft: Xbox 360 Edition through the use of a downloadable content pack.
Legacy
The game is included as part of the Rare Replay video game compilation for Xbox One, with support for dual-analog controls being added post-release.
Legacy
The game was also re-released via the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on November 30, 2023 in Japan, and on December 7, 2023 in western regions.

f64_diddly_kongo_racing.title: Diddy Kong Racing
sents: lead
Diddy Kong Racing is a 1997 kart racing game developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64.
lead
The game revolves around Diddy Kong and his friends' attempt to defeat the intergalactic antagonist, a wizard pig literally named Wizpig, through winning a series of races.
lead
The player takes control of any of the featured characters throughout the game.
lead
Diddy Kong Racing features five worlds with four racetracks each, and the ability to drive a car, hovercraft, or pilot an aeroplane.
lead
Development began after the release of Killer Instinct 2 (1996), and was intended to be a real-time strategy game known as Wild Cartoon Kingdom in its early stages.
lead
As time progressed, the focus of development shifted from a Walt Disney World -influenced racing game to a unique title named Pro-Am 64, in which Nintendo had no involvement.
lead

Due to the delays of Banjo-Kazooie, Rare felt that they needed a stronger intellectual property to attract a wider audience for a game scheduled to release before Christmas 1997, thus making the decision to centre the game around Diddy Kong.
lead
Diddy Kong Racing received critical acclaim upon release.
Gameplay

The worlds are opened up by collecting balloons, except for Future Fun Land, which is unlocked after defeating Wizpig for the first time and rank 1st place in all four Trophy Races of the original worlds.
Gameplay
If the player defeats Wizpig in Future Fun Land, obtains all amulet pieces and collect all the gold medals, the player will be able to play in a mode called "Adventure 2".
Gameplay
The battle modes are not initially selectable, and must be unlocked by collecting special keys hidden in each of the worlds.
Plot
The only solution available to the island's inhabitants is to defeat Wizpig in an elaborate series of races that involve cars, hovercraft, and aeroplanes.
Plot

Timber hires a team of eight racers: Diddy Kong, the first recruit; Conker the Squirrel and Banjo the Bear, recruited by Diddy; Krunch the Kremling, Diddy's enemy who follows after him; Tiptup the Turtle, T.T. the Stopwatch, Pipsy the Mouse, and Bumper the Badger, all inhabitants of Timber's island.
Development
Development of the game began after the release of Killer Instinct 2, in which a team was split into making Killer Instinct Gold for the Nintendo 64 and a new racing game for that console.
Development
In June 1997, the game was altered to Pro-Am 64, an unrelated follow-up to the NES racing game R.C.
Development
According to Lee Schuneman, the Pro Am 64 project featured three-wheeled trikes in contrast to radio-controlled cars.
Development
With Banjo-Kazooie being delayed until the summer of 1998, the team was adamant for a release of an AAA video game in time for 1997's Christmas season.
Development
Rare felt that Pro Am 64 did not have a strong enough intellectual property to capture the attention of consumers, and thus changed the licence to feature Diddy Kong.
Development

Musgrave recalled that the ultimate goal of the game was to make it "run as fast" as Mario Kart 64, which proved difficult during development as the latter game utilised 2D character sprites whereas Diddy Kong Racing used fully 3D models.
Development
Musgrave later attributed the success of the overall project due to the "small team" of 14 people who worked on it.
Development
In an October 2012 interview, Musgrave said that Timber the Tiger would have been the main character of Pro Am 64 had the intellectual property for Diddy Kong Racing not been conceived.
Development
Rare stated that they chose not to exhibit Diddy Kong Racing at E3 because of the proprietary animation technology used in the game.
Development
The soundtrack was first released in Japan on 1 April 1998, with 42 tracks, while a version of the album was released in Europe with the same number of tracks.
Development
For its United States release only 16 tracks were featured.
Release

Due to most of the Nintendo 64's planned 1997 Christmas season line-up being delayed until 1998, Diddy Kong Racing became the main Nintendo 64 release for the holiday shopping season, and a majority of Nintendo's $200 million advertising budget for the entire year was allocated to promoting the game.
Release
The game had a $20 million marketing budget in North America.
Release

Diddy Kong Racing also held the distinction of being the only game in the North American Christmas season line-up for which development was contracted by Nintendo; the other two first-party Nintendo 64 games in the line-up, Bomberman 64 and Mischief Makers, were both licensed from Japanese third-party publishers.
Reception

The Nintendo 64 version holds an aggregate score of 89% at GameRankings based on 20 reviews and 88 at Metacritic based on 15 reviews, whereas the Nintendo DS remake received a score of 67% at GameRankings based on 42 reviews and a score of 63 at Metacritic, based on 39 reviews.
Reception
Diddy Kong Racing sold approximately 4.5 million copies worldwide; which included 3.78 million copies sold in the United States and PAL regions, and 653,928 copies in Japan.
Reception
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, it took home a "Gold" prize for revenues above €15 million in the European Union during the previous year.
Reception
It stands as the Nintendo 64's eighth best-selling game, and broke one million units sold in the United States within three weeks of its release.
Reception
The graphics and gameplay were the most praised aspects of the game.
Reception
Jeff Gerstmann of GameSpot disputed this, saying that the game has both pop-up and distance fog in amounts comparable to the average Nintendo 64 game.
Reception

Doug Perry of IGN heralded the visuals as the most "spectacular of its kind", and praised Rare's ability to master dynamic animation through enabling polygons to span larger surfaces without loss of framerate.
Reception

Although Crispin Boyer opened his review of the game for Electronic Gaming Monthly (EGM) with the warning "Don't dismiss this out-of-the-blue racer as a Mario Kart 64 clone", most reviews compared the two games.
Reception
Other critics, including Boyer's EGM co-reviewers, focused on Diddy Kong Racing ' s perceived superiority to Mario Kart 64.
Reception
Dan Hsu of EGM said it "beats Mario Kart 64 in every department", particularly mentioning the superior balance and level designs.
Reception
Edge praised the adventure and progression aspect of the game, stating that the game's single-player mode is "everything Mario Kart 64 should have been."
Reception
In a retrospective review, Andrew Donaldson of Nintendo Life stated that the game was visually "incredibly vibrant" and "captivating" for a game of the early Nintendo 64 era.
Reception
Scott McCall of AllGame acknowledged its only shortcoming was its "excessive" amount of clipping, although he admitted it was not "unbearable".
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 79th on a list of the greatest Nintendo games of all time.
Reception
EGM named Diddy Kong Racing "Racing Game of the Year" at its 1997 Editors' Choice Awards.
Reception
Diddy Kong Racing was awarded with " Console Racing Game of the Year " by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences in 1998, beating Mario Kart 64, Moto Racer and NASCAR 98.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
After the release of Diddy Kong Racing, Rare began development on a sequel named Donkey Kong Racing for the GameCube, which featured Donkey Kong as the titular character.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
A pre-rendered CG video of the game was shown at E3 2001, which displayed a parody of the speederbike scene from Return of the Jedi.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
According to Lee Musgrave, the game featured a unique mechanic which involved riding on animals rather than driving vehicles.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs

Development of Donkey Kong Racing was cancelled when Nintendo turned down the opportunity to purchase its remaining 51 percent stake in Rare, and the developer was bought out by Microsoft for £375 million in 2002.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
After the buyout, Rare took what had been done with Donkey Kong Racing and created a prototype for the Xbox which expanded into an adventure game similar to the original setup of Diddy Kong Racing.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
Musgrave stated that the concept was essentially "built from scratch" and featured a limited multiplayer version at one point.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs

The concept was in development over 18 months and evolved from being an animal-orientated racing game to an open-world game with Tamagotchi -style features, in which nurturing animals was a "key mechanic".
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
By this point, Donkey Kong Racing had evolved into Sabreman Stampede, part of Rare's Sabreman series.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
Sabreman Stampede was set for release on the Xbox 360, but was cancelled due to a lack of focus and Rare's unfamiliarity with the hardware.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
One, named Diddy Kong Pilot, with planes as the only vehicle, was planned for a release on the Game Boy Advance.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
Originally announced alongside Donkey Kong Racing at E3 2001, the game became Banjo-Pilot after Nintendo sold their share of Rare to Microsoft.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
The other, titled Diddy Kong Racing Adventure, was a rejected pitch made by Climax Studios for the Nintendo GameCube around 2004.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
The project was never announced to the public in any capacity, and only became known after a video game archivist acquired the prototype and published a video about it in November 2016.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs
As Timber was bypassed as the main character in Diddy Kong Racing, Rare's next game was planned to keep Timber as the main character, according to Kev Bayliss.
Cancelled sequel and spin-offs

This game was originally planned as Dinosaur Planet for the Nintendo 64, with Timber as a time traveller to a prehistoric period and gameplay similar to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but over time, they found it better to replace Timber with wholly new characters.
Remake
Developed by Rare and published by Nintendo, it was released in February 2007 in North America, and April in Europe and Australia.
Remake
The battle modes were restricted to multiplayer only, with the custom racetracks replacing them in Adventure Mode.
The "Diddy Laugh"
In the game's opening sequence, the sound of children laughing can be heard when the Rare logo is displayed.

f64_plumber_kart_64.title: Mario Kart 64
sents: lead
Mario Kart 64 is a 1996 kart racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 (N64).
lead
It is the second main entry in the Mario Kart series and is the successor to Super Mario Kart (1992) for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It was released in Japan on December 14, 1996, and in North America and Europe in 1997.
lead
It was released for the iQue Player in China on December 25, 2003.
lead
It was released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console in 2007 and 2016, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on October 25, 2021.
lead
Players control one of eight Mario franchise characters, who race around 16 tracks (four in each of four cups) with items that can either harm opponents or aid the user.
lead
Changes from the original include introducing 3D computer graphics for track design, and four-player support.
lead
The characters and items remain 2D sprites, but 3D track features include elevation, bridges, walls, and pits.
Gameplay
Mario Kart 64 is a kart racing game in which the player controls one of eight selectable Mario characters in several racetracks that vary in shape and theme.
Gameplay
Mario Kart 64 has 16 racing tracks divided into four cups with four tracks each.
Game modes
Mario Kart 64 has four game modes: Grand Prix, Time Trial, Versus, and Battle.
Game modes
Grand Prix mode supports both single-player and competitive multiplayer gameplay, while other modes only support one or the other.
Game modes
When the player completes a race, points are awarded based on the rank they finished ranging from first to eighth and the placement order gets carried over to the next race as the new starting grid.
Game modes
If the player ranks 5th or under, the player must restart the race.
Game modes
Unlike the original Super Mario Kart, the player can restart an unlimited number of times, instead of only being allowed three restarts.
Game modes
After finishing all four races in each cup, trophies are awarded to the players who scored the highest accumulation of points: bronze for third place, silver for second, and gold for first.
Game modes
Difficulty level is measured by engine size: 50, 100, or 150 cc.
Game modes
There is an additional unlockable difficulty called "Extra", which allows players to race at speed 100cc on tracks that are inverted left-to-right.
Game modes
Later installments call this feature "Mirror Mode" in which players race on horizontally-flipped tracks at speed 150cc.
Game modes
Time Trial is a single-player-only mode with the objective of completing a three-lap race on the selected track in the fastest total time.
Game modes
For any given course, the top five fastest total times are saved, and the fastest single lap time of any race is also saved.
Game modes
Ghost data for up to two different courses can be saved permanently only on a Controller Pak device.
Game modes
With two players, the total number of wins for each player is tracked, and in three- or four-player races, the number of 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place wins is tracked for each racer.
Game modes
Battle mode supports two to four players, and the last man standing objective has players attack each other with items inside one of four selectable arena courses.
Game modes
In three- or four-player matches, the first two players' characters to lose all their balloons will transform into mobile "Mini Bomb Karts" and forfeit the ability to win the match.
Game modes
The Mini Bomb Kart is still maneuverable by the player and can collide and inflict damage on another player only once, after which it can no longer participate.
Playable characters
Mario Kart 64 features eight playable characters: Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Toad, Yoshi, Bowser, Wario and Donkey Kong.
Playable characters
The game was originally to feature the character Kamek, a villainous character from Yoshi's Island, before being replaced by Donkey Kong.
Development
Production began in 1995 with the title Super Mario Kart R, where the "R" means "rendered".
Development
The game was developed concurrently with Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, intended to be a launch game for the Nintendo 64, but more resources were given to the other two.
Development
Some early footage of the game was showcased briefly at the Shoshinkai Software Exhibition in Japan on November 24, 1995.
Development
Miyamoto stated that the game was 95% complete, but Nintendo chose not to display a playable version due to the difficult logistics of demonstrating the multiplayer features.
Development
The prototype featured the Feather item from Super Mario Kart and a Magikoopa as one of the eight playable characters, who was replaced with Donkey Kong in the final game.
Development

Mario Kart 64 features tracks that are fully rendered in 3D, and billboarding to display the characters and items through the use of Advanced Character Modeling (ACM), the MIPS CPU, and Silicon Graphics workstations.
Development
Konno stated that, though rendering the characters as 3D models was not impossible, the display of eight simultaneous 3D characters would have exceeded the processing power of the console.
Development
Rare, developer of the Donkey Kong Country games, provided Donkey Kong's character model.
Development

The technique of rubber band AI prevents all the racers from easily separating, and the Spiny Shell item, which targets and attacks the player in first place, was added in order to keep each race competitive and balanced.
Soundtrack
The soundtrack for Mario Kart 64 was composed by Kenta Nagata, which is his first work on a Nintendo game.
Soundtrack
It was later released in a three disc collection, along with the soundtracks of Star Fox 64 and Super Mario 64.
Release
In addition to the regular release in Japan, Nintendo released a "limited edition" which was the regular cartridge bundled with a black-and-grey Nintendo 64 controller.
Release
The Japanese release in December 1996 was followed by a U.S. release in February 1997.
Release

Nintendo of America chairman Howard Lincoln stated that in addition to the time needed for the localization, Mario Kart 64 was more critical to the Japanese market, as there were fewer N64 games available in that market at the time.
Release
Mario Kart 64 was released as a downloadable Virtual Console game on the Wii in January 2007 and on the Wii U in December 2016.
Release
In October 2021, Nintendo also ported the game to Nintendo Switch Online.
Release
During the first three months of 1997, Mario Kart 64 was the best-selling console game in the United States, with sales of 849,000 units for the period.
Release
In Japan it ranked as the 10th best-selling video game in the year 1997, and the highest in Nintendo 64 software.
Release
By 2007, approximately 5.5 million copies of Mario Kart 64 had been sold in the United States and 2.24 million in Japan.
Reception
Mario Kart 64 received generally positive reviews from critics and proved to be a commercial success.
Reception
Review aggregator Metacritic ranks it as the sixth-highest ranked Nintendo 64 title based on fifteen reviews.
Reception
It has sold 9.87 million copies worldwide, making it the second- best-selling game on N64.
Reception

Detractors of the graphics felt they lacked detail (Tom Gulse from Computer and Video Games and Peer Schneider from IGN), weren't better enough than the previous 16-bit entry (AllGame 's Scott McCall and Neil West from Next Generation), and failed to fully benefit from the N64's power (Francois Caron of Jeuxvideo.com).
Reception
The use of 2D sprites was a common critique, West arguing that it made the game look 16-bit.
Reception
Mario Kart 64 ' s track design and gameplay polarised critics.
Reception
Computer and Video Games ' s Ed Lomas and N64 Magazine ' s Jonathan Nash felt that success was too dependent on getting the right power-ups.
Reception
Morley disliked Mario Kart 64 ' s wide, motorway-like track design by saying that it did not provide an "adrenaline filled" experience which players might have hoped for.
Reception
Hyper ' s David Wildgoose and Jonathan highlighted the flexible turning control with the multiple-angled joystick, calling it "perfect" and true to real-life karts.
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it a runner-up for "Multiplayer Game of the Year" (behind Saturn Bomberman) at their 1997 Editors' Choice Awards.
Reception
Mario Kart 64 placed 17th in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s 100 greatest Nintendo games of all time and 49th in Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s 1997 list of the 100 best console games of all time.
Reception
In 1998, Mario Kart 64 was nominated for Console Racing Game of the Year by the Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences during the inaugural Interactive Achievement Awards.

f64_f_zilch_x.title: F-Zero X
sents: lead
F-Zero X is a futuristic racing video game for the Nintendo 64 console.
lead
Developed and published by Nintendo, it was released in Japan, North America, and Europe in 1998.
lead
In 2000, the Expansion Kit was released in Japan, including a track and vehicle editor.
lead
The original game was ported in 2004 to the iQue Player in China.
lead
It had Virtual Console re-releases on the Wii in 2007 and the Wii U around nine years later.
lead
On March 11, 2022, the game was re-released on Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack, featuring online multiplayer.
lead
It is a sequel to the original F-Zero (1990), and is the first F-Zero installment with 3D graphics.
lead
The game has a steep learning curve and its gameplay experience is similar to that of the original.
Gameplay
F-Zero X is a fast-paced futuristic racing video game where 30 competitors race on high-altitude circuits inside plasma -powered hovercars in an intergalactic Grand Prix.
Gameplay
The game introduces 26 new vehicles, and reprises the 4 from the original F-Zero game.
Gameplay
Players get an additional spare machine for every 5 contenders eliminated.
Race modes
F-Zero X has 5 different gameplay modes: GP (Grand Prix) Race, Practice, Time Attack, Death Race, and VS Battle.
Race modes
In GP Race, the player races against 29 opponents through 3 laps of each track in a cup.
Race modes
Players get a certain number of points for finishing a track depending on where they placed, and the winner of the cup is the character who receives the most total points.
Race modes
Each cup has 4 selectable difficulty levels: Novice, Standard, Expert, and Master.
Race modes
Furthermore, the 3 cups initially available are ordered by increasing difficulty (Jack, Queen, and King respectively) and 6 tracks each.
Race modes
Eventually, the player can unlock the Joker Cup with its set of 6 tracks, followed by the X Cup.
Race modes
The X Cup is a set of 6 tracks that are randomly generated on each playthrough.
Race modes
Time Attack lets the player choose a track and complete a 3-lap race in the shortest time possible.
Race modes
Up to 3 player-contributed ghosts can be raced against simultaneously, but only 1 can be saved per track.
Race modes
Death Race has the player annihilating the 29 other racers as speedily as possible on a specialized course.
Race modes
Battle is the multiplayer mode where 2 to 4 players compete in a 3-lap race, and slots not in use by players can be operated by the artificial intelligence.
Development and release
t's not possible to measure how fast your car can go in, but it's possibly about 1,000 kilometers per hour — possibly the fastest racing game ever for a home system.
Development and release
In mid-1996, during Mario Kart 64 development, Shigeru Miyamoto said he planned a sequel to F-Zero for the Nintendo 64.
Development and release
Initially titled "F-Zero 64", Famitsu magazine revealed the project in mid-1997.
Development and release
Several key Wave Race 64 programmers including the lead programmer made up the in-house development team.
Development and release
Developed by Nintendo EAD, it is a sequel to the original F-Zero (1990), and is the first F-Zero installment with 3D graphics.
Development and release
The game debuted at the Nintendo Space World event on November 20, 1997, publicly playable for the first time.
Development and release
IGN reported this version was 60% complete and consistently ran at 60 frames per second.
Development and release

They noted that " hide most of the limited backgrounds with their girth and undulating nature which block out almost everything else." Fogging effects are used to hide background shortcomings such as where the sky and ground meet.
Development and release
The F-Zero X Original Soundtrack was released on September 18, 1998, with 29 musical tracks.
Development and release
The F-Zero X Guitar Arrange Edition was released on January 27, 1999, with ten guitar arrangements.
Development and release
The game was released in Japan on July 14, 1998, but its North American release suffered a three-month delay due to Nintendo's policy of evenly spacing the release of first-party games.
Development and release
It was released in North America on October 27, in Europe on November 6, and in China for the iQue Player on February 25, 2004.
Development and release
It was re-released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console in 2007 and around 2016, respectively.
Development and release
A March 2022 re-release to Nintendo Switch Online Expansion Pack members has a 2 to 4-person online multiplayer mode.
Expansion Kit
The 64DD is a peripheral for the Nintendo 64, released only in Japan, and designed in part to provision cartridge games with expansions on inexpensive 64 megabyte floppy disks.
Expansion Kit
The F-Zero X Expansion Kit is the 64DD's first expansion disk, released on April 21, 2000, in Japan.
Expansion Kit
The disk can save up to a 100 tracks and up to 3 ghost data per course.
Expansion Kit
The Expansion Kit disk requires the cartridge, which was programmed with "64DD hooks" to detect the 64DD and expansion disk.
Reception
The game has an aggregate average of 87.61% based on 15 reviews at GameRankings, and a metascore of 85 at Metacritic.
Reception

Peer Schneider of IGN described the gameplay as "god-like", "hair-splitting" speed; and he considered the game to rival its predecessor Wave Race 64 with its "perfectly fine-tuned controls and a fresh approach to racing".
Reception
GameSpot criticized the low polygon count on the vehicles "particularly uninspiring" and saying that the "track detail is also very limited, giving the track a spartan feel to it".
Reception
Although the optimizations are strict, critics exalted the steady rate of 60 frames per second, which some thought made up for the lack of graphical detail with little room for improvement.
Reception

According to GameSpot, F-Zero X became the first racing game to run at 60 frames per second with up to 30 vehicles on screen at the same time, but in order to keep the frame rate, polygon counts on the vehicles, textures and track detail are sacrificed.
Reception
The Electric Playground said it goes hand-in-hand to the simulation of speed in the game, but that "I wouldn't in a million years buy music like this to listen to".
Reception
GameSpot ' s retrospective review gave it 6.5/10, calling it "the black sheep of the series" when compared with the other F-Zero games in "visual style and technical flair".
Reception
IGN described it as an exceptional update to the original game that "only suffers under its generic look".
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine praised the game, ranking it 39th on a list of greatest Nintendo games.
Reception
Nintendo sold 383,642 units of F-Zero X in North America and 97,684 units in Japan.
Reception
In its first week of sale in Japan, 56,457 copies were sold, but only about one fifth of that in the following week reportedly due to the Nintendo 64 having had a small dedicated fanbase there.
Reception
F-Zero X was named as a finalist by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences for " Console Racing Game of the Year " during the 2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.

f64_wave_rays_64.title: Wave Race 64
sents: lead
Wave Race 64 is a 1996 racing video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Gameplay involves the player racing on a personal watercraft on a variety of courses while successfully manoeuvring the vehicle around various buoys.
lead
A multiplayer mode where two players can compete against each other on a chosen course is also included.
lead
The game supports the Controller Pak, which allows players to transfer saved data from one game cartridge to another.
lead

Originally referred to as " F-Zero on water", the game was intended to feature high-speed boats with transforming capabilities, but these were ultimately replaced with Jet Skis as producer Shigeru Miyamoto felt that the game would not be differentiated enough from other titles on other systems.
lead
Wave Race 64 received acclaim from critics, who praised the game's satisfying controls and dynamic watery environments.
lead
The game is credited with helping Nintendo effectively make its paradigmatic leap from the 16-bit 2D graphics of the Super Nintendo Entertainment System to the Nintendo 64's 3D capabilities.
lead
It was re-released for the Wii and Wii U 's Virtual Console in 2007 and 2016, respectively, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in 2022.
Gameplay
Wave Race 64 is a racing video game in which players race on personal watercrafts in different weather conditions and on a variety of courses.
Gameplay
In the Championship mode, the player must race opponents through a series of courses and win the first place.
Gameplay
Leaving the course area limited by pink buoys for more than five seconds will also result in disqualification.
Gameplay
Only the courses that have been unlocked in the Championship mode can be played in the Time Trials, Stunt, and multiplayer modes.
Gameplay
A Nintendo 64 Controller Pak can be used to transfer saved data from one game cartridge to another.
Development and release
Wave Race 64 was developed by Nintendo EAD and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto as one of the first Nintendo 64 games.
Development and release
Development of the game was led by Shinya Takahashi, who had been working with Nintendo since 1989.
Development and release

Takahashi, along with Yoshiaki Koizumi, who worked with Miyamoto on Super Mario 64, are credited for helping the company effectively make its paradigmatic leap from the 16-bit 2D graphics of the Super Nintendo Entertainment System to the Nintendo 64's 3D capabilities.
Development and release
Since the game's engineers only had experience with the 2D graphics of earlier Nintendo consoles, Takahashi had to guide them through the first stages of development.
Development and release
While experimenting with the Nintendo 64's Silicon Graphics technology, one of the programmers created a tech demo that served as an example of the game's wave programming.
Development and release
Originally, the game was referred to as " F-Zero on water" and would feature high-speed boats, as shown in footage from the 1995 Nintendo Shoshinkai show.
Development and release
Miyamoto explained that "boats looked pretty good at the show, but I didn't think that Wave Race 64 would be unique from similar games on other systems if we used boats.
Development and release
Jet Skis can show many maneuvers that work well in the realistic water of Wave Race 64 ".
Development and release
The game uses the Nintendo 64's alpha blending feature to make the water simultaneously transparent and reflective.
Development and release
Wave Race 64 was promoted with a marketing campaign that cost $4 million.
Development and release
It was first released in Japan in September 1996 on an 8- MB cartridge.
Development and release
In the United States, Wave Race 64 was released as the third Nintendo 64 game on November 4, 1996, featuring voice changes and renamed levels.
Development and release

It was the first racing game developed for the Nintendo 64 and the first to use the Nintendo 64's hardware capabilities to "create a believable and engaging water environment unmatched by previous games".
Development and release
In the United Kingdom, the game was released in April 1997, shortly after the launch of the Nintendo 64.
Development and release
Like Super Mario 64, Wave Race 64 was re-issued in Japan in July 1997 as Wave Race 64 Shindō Pak Taiō Version (ウエーブレース64 振動パック対応バージョン, " Wave Race 64: Rumble Pak-Compatible Version ").
Reception
Wave Race 64 was a critical and commercial success, selling more than 154,000 units in Japan by December 1996 and more than one million units in the United States by December 1997.
Reception
As of December 2007, the game had sold 1.95 million copies in the United States.
Reception
Globally, the game sold 2.95 million units, making it the best selling Wave Race game of all time, and 14th best selling Nintendo 64 game.
Reception

GamePro described Wave Race 64 as a "phenomenally fun" racing game that captivates players with its deep and challenging gameplay, while Next Generation regarded it as one of the first quality titles released for the Nintendo 64, along with Super Mario 64 and Pilotwings 64.
Reception
Graphically, Wave Race 64 was praised for its fluid animations, realistic physics, clean waters, and textured polygons.
Reception
In contrast, AllGame 's Jonti Davies felt that the game's "cheesy" and "distinctly '80s theme" soundtrack combined with the announcer's "hyperexcited cries" gives the game a light and arcade feel.
Reception
Similarly, Game Informer remarked that the waves can strike players on every turn and that one mistake can mean the difference between victory and defeat.
Reception

Although the magazine criticized the game's lack of courses, noting that most of them can be seen in a day's play, it ultimately concluded that Wave Race 64 is an example of how Nintendo's approach to game design still remains markedly different from almost every other videogames company in the world.
Reception
Glenn Rubenstein of GameSpot also praised the controls, stating that Wave Race 64 "makes the best use yet" of the Nintendo 64 analog stick.
Reception

In March 1997, EGM editors named Wave Race 64 their Sports Game of the Year and a runner-up for their Nintendo 64 Game of the Year award (behind Super Mario 64), citing the realistic physics and variety of tracks.
Legacy
After its release on the Nintendo 64, Wave Race 64 has been included in several top lists.
Legacy
In 1997, EGM ranked the game 68th on its list of 100 Best Games of All Time.
Legacy
In 1999, Next Generation ranked it 20th on a similar list, commenting that Wave Race 64, along with Mario 64, demonstrated more graphical power for the system.
Legacy
IGN editors ranked it 33rd on their 2003 list of Top 100 Games of All Time, and 37th on another list published in 2005.
Legacy
The simple concept of racing on jet skis was complicated by changing wave patterns, swells, and rising tides, and Nintendo added its trademark depth to broaden and deepen the unique racer.
Legacy
In 2006, Nintendo Power placed Wave Race 64 at 127th in its "Top 200" games list.
Legacy
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 49th on a list of greatest Nintendo games of all time.
Legacy
Wave Race 64 was released in China for the iQue Player console in 2003.
Legacy
A 1-hour demo of the game was also included with the console.
Legacy
On August 6, 2007, the game was released on the Wii 's Virtual Console.
Legacy
Unlike Nintendo 64 version, the Virtual Console release does not feature Kawasaki banners due to expired licensing deals.
Legacy
When the game was released on the Wii U 's Virtual Console in 2016, the Kawasaki banners were restored.
Legacy
The game was re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on August 19, 2022, once again with the Kawasaki banners restored.
Legacy
Codemasters producer Guy Wilday cited Wave Race 64 as a key influence in the design of their 1998 racing game Colin McRae Rally.
Legacy
According to Wilday, Wave Race 64 is "a fine example of a game with realistic physics and an incredibly well balanced control system.
Legacy
The game is easy to pick up and play but it is only after playing it for some time that you start to understand the additional nuances of the controls.

f64_1081_snowboarding.title: 1080° Snowboarding
sents: lead
1080° Snowboarding is a snowboarding video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 in 1998.
lead
In the game, the player controls one of five snowboarders from a third-person perspective, using a combination of buttons to jump and perform tricks over eight levels.
lead

1080° was announced in November 1997 and developed over the course of nine months; it garnered critical acclaim and won an Interactive Achievement Award from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.
lead
A sequel, 1080° Avalanche, was released for the GameCube in November 2003.
lead
The game was re-released in 2008 and 2016 for the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console respectively, and was re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in 2023.
Gameplay
1080° has two trick modes (trick attack and contest), three race modes (race, time attack, and 2 players), a training mode, and an options mode.
Gameplay
In 1080° ' s two trick modes, trick attack and contest, players accrue points from completed tricks.
Gameplay

The game features 24 tricks and 5 secret tricks, all of which are performed by using a combination of circular positions of the control stick, the R button, the Z button and the B button; point values are allocated based on complexity, combos, and required time.
Gameplay
The 1080° spin requires nine actions, the most of any trick in the game.
Gameplay
1080° has three race modes; in these modes, victory can be achieved by taking separate routes within a course and balancing the snowboarder after a jump to avoid speed loss.
Development and release
1080° ' s release was announced on 21 November 1997 at Nintendo's Space World trade show; the game's working title had previously been Vertical Edge Snowboarding.
Development and release
1080° was one of several snowboarding games released for the Nintendo 64 in 1998, others being Big Mountain 2000 and Snowboard Kids.
Development and release
Before the game's release, journalists were able to play 1080° at the January 1998 Nintendo Gamers' Summit.
Development and release
1080° was directed by Masamachi Abe and Misthuro Tanako, programmed by Englishmen Giles Goddard and Colin Reed, developed and published by Nintendo, and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto.
Development and release
Goddard had previously programmed the Mario face in Super Mario 64, which was released two years prior to critical acclaim and was a huge commercial success, while Reed had programmed Stunt Race FX.
Development and release
When developing 1080°, Goddard and Reed used a technique called "skinning" to eliminate joints between the polygons composing the characters.
Development and release
Tommy Hilfiger outfits and Lamar snowboards appear throughout 1080° as product placement.
Development and release
1080° ' s soundtrack of "techno and rappy beats" with "thrashy, foozed-out vocals" was composed by Kenta Nagata.
Development and release
1080° ' s development took place from April or May 1997 into early 1998.
Development and release
The game was released on 28 February 1998 in Japan and on 1 April in North America.
Development and release
Nintendo prioritized 1080° for Japanese release over other Nintendo 64 games because they wanted it out while there was still snow.
Development and release
Nintendo delayed the game's European release because they hoped to boost sales with a winter release; 1080° was eventually released on 9 October 1998 in Europe and the PAL regions.
Reception
1080° Snowboarding received "generally favorable reviews", just two points shy of "universal acclaim", according to review aggregator website Metacritic.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 31 out of 40.
Reception
1080° Snowboarding has been perceived to be a leader among snowboarding titles at the time.
Reception
Edge hailed it as the "most convincing video game emulation of the snowboarding experience so far" with an "atmosphere of sobriety" unlike any other Nintendo game at the time.
Reception
The game's graphics were of the highest quality for the Nintendo 64 at the time.
Reception

1080 Snowboarding was described by Next Generation as setting the standard for an entire genre, and by Hyper as bringing a new dimension to snowboarding as Wave Race 64 did to water-based racing, successfully capturing the excitement the sport.
Reception
GamePro said that the game was "the kind of great game that's worth snapping up as soon as it's out."
Reception
Writing for AllGame, Shawn Sackenheim considered the "highly technical" control scheme of 1080° Snowboarding one of the game's strengths despite its initial difficulty.
Reception

The music was also generally praised, with Matt Casamassina of IGN calling it "a shining example of what can be achieved on the format" and Sackenheim calling it "one of the best N64 soundtracks to date".
Reception

In a retrospective review by the Official Nintendo Magazine in 2006, Steve Jarratt commented that 1080° Snowboarding "boasted the best video game representation of snow" and was complemented by "swooshy" sound effects.
Reception
The magazine also ranked it the 87th best game available on Nintendo platforms.
Reception
The staff felt it was the most realistic snowboarding game ever made.
Reception

Kenta Nagata's soundtrack, especially its inclusion of drum and bass music, was praised in 2023 by NME 's Mat Ombler, who placed the game alongside Wipeout in helping bring underground electronic club music to a larger audience.
Reception
1080° Snowboarding won the AIAS ' Console Sports Game of the Year award at the 2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.
Reception
It was also nominated for Best Nintendo 64 Game at the 1998 CNET Gamecenter Awards, which went to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
Reception
PC Data, which tracked sales in the United States, reported that 1080° Snowboarding sold 817,529 units and earned $40.9 million in revenues by the end of 1998.
Reception
This made it the country's seventh-best-selling Nintendo 64 release of the year.
Reception
The game ultimately sold 1,230,000 units in the United States, and over 23,000 in Japan.
Reception
It did not, however, match the success of the developers' first game, Wave Race 64 which sold 1,950,000 units in the United States and 154,000 in Japan.
Reception
1080° Snowboarding was re-released on the Wii and Wii U 's Virtual Console service in 2008 and 2016 respectively, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on December 7, 2023.
Sequel
1080° Avalanche, a sequel to 1080° Snowboarding, was released for the GameCube in 2003.
Sequel
Greg Kasavin of GameSpot gave the sequel a harsher critical reception due to "frame rate issues and limited gameplay".

f64_excitebyke_64.title: Excitebike 64

Programmer(s): Sam Baker Mike Lamb Ben Stragnell
Artist(s): Jon Evans Allan Hayburn Richie Romero George Simmons

sents: lead
Excitebike 64 is a video game published by Nintendo and developed by Left Field Productions.
lead
It was released for the Nintendo 64 on May 2, 2000 in North America, June 23 in Japan, and June 8, 2001, in Europe.
lead
It is the second installment in the Excite series, acting as a sequel to Excitebike on the NES, and is the first 3D game in the series.
lead
Many real-life dirt bike gear brands are extensively featured throughout the game, such as Bell Helmets, Alpinestars and No Fear.
lead
The game received positive reviews from critics and was later re-released for Wii U via the Virtual Console in 2016.
lead
It was also re-released on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack on August 30, 2023.
lead
A third game in the series, Excite Truck, was released in 2006 for the Wii.
Gameplay

Besides the tracks main course many of the levels have hidden shortcuts, that require the player to slow down and change direction, or use a speed boost for jumping over chasms, from hill to hill, over other vehicles and buildings, choosing to follow the original game in its "extreme" jumps and physics.
Features
There is a tutorial that teaches players how to play through the 17 different tracks.
Features
Also featured is an emulated version of the original Excitebike and a 3D remake of it with the same obstacles called Excite 3D.
Features
As bonus features to the game, cheat modes were introduced, requiring the player to press buttons in a certain order to unlock a hidden "Cheats Menu".
Development
Using the N64's Rumble Pak allowed the player to feel these game experiences, as well as such things as making a hard landing.
Development
The game was revealed by Nintendo to the public at the pre- E3 conference on May 12, 1999.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 29 out of 40.
Reception

Various unlocked extras make Excitebike 64 a truckload of fun, but it's playing to get those goodies that kicks up the dirt." In another GamePro review, Dan Elektro said, "While you can't help but feel that Excitebike 64 is a few tweaks short of greatness, it's still a quality, enjoyable ride."
Reception

GameCritics said, "The game isn't perfect — I would have liked even more tracks to race on as well as a few more racers." GameSpot opined, "Some will cry about the frame rate, and some will wish the game featured real riders."
Reception
Another problem the game encountered was that it was one of the last games released for the N64 in Europe, having been released there over a year later than the Japan and U.S. releases.
Reception
The delay was due to Nintendo's struggle to keep up with the demand for the games Pokémon Stadium and Perfect Dark.
Reception
Nonetheless, the game ultimately went on to sell approximately two million units, according to information provided by former employees of Left Field Productions.
Reception
The game was nominated for the "N64 Game of the Year" award at The Electric Playground ' s Blister Awards 2000, which went to Perfect Dark.

f64_pilotwangs_64.title: Pilotwings 64
sents: lead
Pilotwings 64 is a flight simulation video game developed by Nintendo and Paradigm Simulation and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was one of three launch titles for the Nintendo 64 in Japan as well as Europe and one of two launch titles in North America, along with Super Mario 64.
lead
Pilotwings 64 is a sequel to Pilotwings for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, which was a North American launch game for its respective console in 1991.
lead
Also like that game, Pilotwings 64 received production input from Nintendo producer and EAD General Manager Shigeru Miyamoto.
lead
Pilotwings 64 puts the player in control of one of six pilots as they try to earn pilot licenses through various forms of aviation.
lead
The events are flying an autogyro, using a jet pack, and hang gliding.
lead
Several bonus tasks are offered, such as skydiving and a human cannonball test.
lead
The game also puts focus on allowing the player to freely explore its detailed 3D environments, most notably a miniature representation of the United States.
Gameplay
Pilotwings 64 is a flight simulator in which the player must complete a variety of missions involving different airborne vehicles and air sports.
Gameplay
There are three main events in Pilotwings 64 required to complete the game, each of which has its own objectives and unique flight controls using the Nintendo 64 controller 's single analog stick.
Gameplay
The first, hang gliding, usually requires the player to fly through a series of floating marker rings or snap a photograph of a particular piece of scenery before landing on a target area.
Gameplay
Pilotwings 64 also features several bonus events that are unlocked if the player performs well in the main missions.
Gameplay

Lastly, Pilotwings 64 features a "Birdman" mode that puts the character in a bird suit and gives players the opportunity to freely explore the game's detailed, object-dense environments set among its four distinct islands.
Gameplay

One of the islands is based on the United States, and has geographical replications of famous landmarks including the Statue of Liberty and Mount Rushmore (with Mario 's face replacing George Washington 's) and major cities such as Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York City.
Development
Pilotwings 64 was co-developed by the Texas -based graphics company Paradigm Simulation and Nintendo 's Entertainment Analysis & Development (EAD) and Research and Development No.
Development
Due to Paradigm's experience with Silicon Graphics workstations, Nintendo contacted the American company in 1994 concerning it becoming one of the Nintendo 64's "Dream Team" of first developers.
Development
Paradigm worked directly with a team at Silicon Graphics and spent nine months developing a technology base for Pilotwings 64 and Paradigm's other Nintendo 64 releases.
Development
Development on Pilotwings 64 began in earnest during June 1995, with Nintendo working on the game design and Paradigm working on the technical production.
Development
Shigeru Miyamoto, the producer of Pilotwings for the SNES, reprised his role for Pilotwings 64 and oversaw the project from Japan.
Development
Miyamoto's involvement was more removed than with the SNES game due to his simultaneous work on the platform game Super Mario 64.
Development
According to Miyamoto, Pilotwings 64 was designed to allow gamers to experience free flight in realistic 3D environments on the Nintendo 64.
Development
He indicated that there was never an issue as to whether Pilotwings 64 should be more of an arcade game or a simulation, as their goal was to "always have a more arcade feel".
Development
Pilotwings on the SNES makes use of the power of the 16-bit console, principally its Mode 7 capability.
Development
Similarly, Pilotwings 64 prominently demonstrates the graphical features of its own console.
Development
Gatchel suggested that just as design elements present in the game generated its production requirements, these same elements were influenced by the Nintendo 64's technology during development.
Development
The large islands within the game were created using Paradigm's own 3D development tool Vega UltraVision.
Development
Navigation of these environments is relatively smooth thanks to Pilotwings 64 taking advantage of several key Nintendo 64 hardware features.
Development
Pilotwings 64 also applies z-buffering, which keeps track of an object's depth and tells the graphics processor which portions of the object to render and which to hide.
Development
The six playable pilots in Pilotwings 64 are all named after various birds.
Development
The soundtrack for Pilotwings 64 was composed by Dan Hess with Akito Nakatsuka as arranger.
Development
The tracks were produced to complement each level, such as a "soothing" jazz -inspired musical piece played during the exploratory Birdman mode.
Development
A CD soundtrack was released by Pony Canyon in Japan on December 16, 1996.
Development
Pilotwings 64 was one of thirteen Nintendo 64 games shown at Shoshinkai show in Tokyo in November 1995 when the console was first demonstrated to the public as the "Ultra 64".
Development
The game was later displayed at the Electronic Entertainment Expo (E3) in Los Angeles during May 1996.
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings 64 was released in Japan on June 23, 1996, as one of three Nintendo 64 launch titles, the other two being Super Mario 64 and Saikyō Habu Shōgi.
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings 64 managed to sell about one unit with about every tenth Nintendo 64 console, with regional sales totaling 136,986 copies by the end of the year.
Reception and legacy
The game was one of two original releases for the system during its September 26, 1996 debut in North America, which was a few days earlier than the date set by Nintendo.
Reception and legacy
While Super Mario 64 initially sold at a one-to-one ratio with each console in the United States, Pilotwings 64 sold an average of one copy with every fourth console.
Reception and legacy
About 90,000 copies of Pilotwings 64 were sold in its first few days on sale in the country, putting the game at number four on the NPD Group sales charts for that September.
Reception and legacy
It went on to become the sixth best-selling Nintendo 64 game of 1996 in the United States.
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings 64 saw a release in European nations on March 1, 1997, when it was one of three launch games along with Super Mario 64 and Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire.
Reception and legacy
It was confirmed in early 1998 that the game had sold over one million units worldwide.
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings 64 was well received by most reviewers.
Reception and legacy
The game's combination of 3D graphics, realistic settings, and flight simulation were applauded by many news sources and major gaming publications.
Reception and legacy
In his release review of the Nintendo 64, The Seattle Times contributor Steven L.
Reception and legacy
Kent found that the flight mechanics and vast areas featured in Pilotwings 64 make it one of the most impressive games ever made.
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings 64 has been criticized for lacking innovative gameplay.
Reception and legacy

The New York Times writer Ashley Dunn characterized the game's E3 demonstration as "brain-dead" in its gameplay and suggested that even young children would rather fly a dragon on the Sony PlayStation.
Reception and legacy
Game Revolution issued Pilotwings 64 a particularly harsh review score, declaring the game to be nothing more than a graphical showcase for those with nothing better to do.
Reception and legacy

Electronic Gaming Monthly awarded Pilotwings 64 Flying Game of the Year, explaining that it shows the potential of the fun factor of flying and allows for more than one path from point A to point B, and says that "fun, variety and easy-paced action gave PW64 this award."
Reception and legacy
Pilotwings 64 was ranked number 38 in Nintendo Power ' s "100 Best Nintendo Games of All Time" in its landmark 100th issue in September 1997.
Reception and legacy
In February 2006, it was rated the 117th best game made on a Nintendo system in the magazine's "Top 200 Games" list for its 200th issue.
Reception and legacy
In July 2007, the United Kingdom video game magazine Edge included Pilotwings 64 at number 69 on its own "Top 100 Games" list.
Reception and legacy
The UK's Official Nintendo Magazine listed it at number 40 on its "100 Best Nintendo Games" in February 2009.
Reception and legacy
Paradigm announced at E3 1997 that they were producing a Nintendo 64 sequel to Pilotwings 64.
Reception and legacy
There were rumors of a sequel on the GameCube and later the Wii, development courtesy of Factor 5, but no game was ever shown.
Reception and legacy
After their briefing time at E3 2010, Nintendo announced a sequel titled Pilotwings Resort for the Nintendo 3DS, which was released as a launch title for the handheld console.

f64_kirbo_64_the_crystal_shards.title: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards
sents: lead
Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards is a 2000 action - platform game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 (N64).
lead
It is the first Kirby game to feature 3D computer graphics and follows Kirby as he attempts to reassemble a sacred crystal shattered by Dark Matter.
lead
Gameplay is viewed from a 2.5D perspective and is similar to previous Kirby titles; the player traverses levels and obtains powers by eating enemies.
lead
Kirby 64 introduces Power Combos, the ability to mix powers to create more powerful ones.
lead
In a multiplayer mode, up to four players can compete in three minigames.
lead
Development began in September 1997.
lead
The game was intended for the N64's 64DD add-on, but became a standard N64 title after the add-on failed.
lead
HAL initially planned to use the N64 controller 's analog stick for Kirby 64, but switched to the D-pad about a year before release.
Gameplay
Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards is a side-scrolling platformer similar to previous games in the Kirby series.
Gameplay
(1996) and Klonoa: Door to Phantomile (1997), Kirby 64 is a 2.5D platformer; although environments and characters are rendered in 3D computer graphics, gameplay is restricted to a 2D plane.
Gameplay
Players control Kirby using the Nintendo 64 controller 's D-pad.
Gameplay
Kirby 64 introduces Power Combos, the option to combine Kirby's copy abilities.
Gameplay
There are 28 possible combinations, which are stronger than normal copy abilities or have added effects.
Gameplay
Here, up to four players can compete in three minigames: 100-Yard Hop, a race to the finish line; Bumper Crop Bump, a competition to collect food; and Checkerboard Chase, a last man standing game.
Development
Kirby 64 was developed by HAL Laboratory as the first game in its Kirby series to feature 3D graphics.
Development
Development began in September 1997, shortly before Kirby's Dream Land 3 was released.
Development
At the time, 3D graphics were becoming common, so HAL wanted to create a 3D Kirby game.
Development
The development team had to be careful transitioning the series' art style to 3D as they did not want to disappoint Kirby devotees.
Development
The game was initially developed for the 64DD, a disk-drive add-on for the Nintendo 64 (N64), but became a standard N64 Game Pak after the add-on failed commercially.
Development
By October 1997, HAL had created a prototype to experiment with Kirby in 3D.
Development
The studio worked this prototype, which used the N64 controller's analog stick to control Kirby, until about a year before release.
Development
Saito said the prototype was nearly finished and "was pretty good," but the team felt they could do better.
Development
HAL changed the control configuration from the analog stick to the D-pad because the game was played on a 2.5D plane rather than a 3D one.
Development
At Space World in 1999, the developers observed children play with the original setup.
Development
Kirby 64 was directed by Shinichi Shimomura, who had previously directed Kirby's Dream Land 2 and Kirby's Dream Land 3.
Development
It is thematically similar to those games; Adeleine, a supporting character, and 0, the final boss, are reinterpretations of characters from Kirby's Dream Land 3.
Development

Originally, there were going to be several playable characters (including Waddle Dee, whose gameplay focused on picking up objects), but only Kirby and King Dedede remained playable in the final game.
Development
The N64's technology also made four-player minigames possible.
Development

Ishikawa spent about a year creating most of the game's music and sound effects, and believed that composing the music for the final areas as jazz music would surprise players used to the series' typical electronic influences.
Development
Publisher Nintendo announced the game at E3 1999.
Development
According to IGN, Kirby representation on the N64 was "long-awaited", as an earlier series game for the system— Kirby's Air Ride —had been canceled.
Development
Kirby 64 was released in Japan on March 24, 2000, in North America on June 26, 2000, and in Europe on June 22, 2001.
Development
GameSpot noted that unlike other Kirby games, Kirby 64 saw release before support for its system ended.
Development
It was the last traditional Kirby home console game until Return to Dream Land (2011).
Development
Nintendo re-released Kirby 64 for the Virtual Console on the Wii and Wii U in 2008 and 2015, respectively.
Development
The game was also included in Kirby's Dream Collection (2012), a 20th anniversary compilation of Kirby titles for the Wii.
Development
Kirby 64 was re-released on May 20, 2022, on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack Service.
Reception
Kirby 64 received "generally favorable reviews", according to the review aggregator Metacritic.
Reception

Critics likened it to other 2.5D platformers on the N64 including Goemon's Great Adventure (1998) and Yoshi's Story (1997), Some felt its gameplay and visuals were reminiscent of older platform games for the Nintendo Entertainment System and Super NES.
Reception
Edge viewed this as a detriment, writing that the game suffered from a lack of innovation in the midst of other Nintendo franchises establishing themselves within the growing 3D game market.
Reception
Critics believed Kirby 64 lacked in longevity and difficulty.
Reception
N64 Magazine felt the early levels were enjoyable but that later stages became stale, and opined that the game would have benefited from more complex level design.
Reception
IGN and Hyper also recommended the game as a rental to older gamers, and only as a purchase for children.
Reception
N64 Magazine called the graphics the best aspect of the game and praised the scenery and environments.
Reception
USgamer ranked it as the 13th best traditional Kirby game out of 16 in 2017, calling it "uninspired."

f64_yoshu_s_story.title: Yoshi's Story
sents: lead
Yoshi's Story is a 1997 platform game published and developed by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was released in Japan in December 1997, and worldwide the following year.
lead
The game has been subsequently re-released on the Wii, Wii U, and Nintendo Switch.
lead
Development was handled by Nintendo EAD and led by Hideki Konno and Takashi Tezuka.
lead
It was the first Yoshi platformer not to be produced nor directed by Shigeru Miyamoto, although he contributed design ideas.
lead
The score was composed by Kazumi Totaka, who provided the voice of Yoshi in the game.
lead
As a follow-up to the Super NES game Yoshi's Island, it continues within the platform genre with similar gameplay.
lead
However, Yoshi's Story is more puzzle -oriented, with most challenge being tied to the strategic achievement of a high score.
Gameplay
On each course, the goal is to fill the Fruit Frame by eating 30 pieces of fruit.
Gameplay
Melons give the most points, and each level has exactly 30 of them hidden throughout.
Gameplay
While the first page will always display four courses, the following pages will initially be limited to only one course.
Gameplay
For example, if the player collects two hearts during a course, they will be allowed to choose from course 1, 2, and 3 on the next page.
Plot
While each page consists of four courses each, the path to Baby Bowser's castle will only consist of one course per page.
Development

Originally titled Yoshi's Island 64 for the 64DD floppy drive and then moved to cartridge instead, the game was developed by the Yoshi's Island team, directed by Hideki Konno and produced by Takashi Tezuka.
Development

With the first promotional video clip from the game being revealed at Nintendo Space World in November 1996, Yoshi's Island 64 presented lush, colorful worlds of pre-rendered 3D graphics and polygonal animations, also demonstrating the Nintendo 64's ability to run 2D games.
Development
Shigeru Miyamoto said the 2D format was necessary to create the artistic style of graphics the development team wanted.
Development
The game's title was eventually changed to Yoshi's Story, being announced in August 1997, with a release of promotional screenshots from upcoming games.
Development
Shortly after, the game was noted to be getting a memory expansion, extending from 96 to 128 megabits.
Development
The completed game was unveiled at Nintendo Space World in November 1997.
Development
With the game's initial release hitting Japan on December 21, 1997, the international release was delayed from the fourth quarter of 1997 to February 9, 1998.
Audio

The recorded samples have since been constituting the official voice for Yoshi, making a second appearance in the 1999 game Super Smash Bros., to further be recycled in succeeding games that Yoshi appeared in.
Audio
Totaka has hidden his 19-note signature melody in the game, which may be heard on the Trial Mode course select screen, after the background music has looped eight times.
Audio
Published by The Original Shape CD, Inc., the 15-track CD had the characteristic trait of being shaped to outline the print on the disc, illustrating Yoshi's head.
Audio
The full soundtrack was released in Japan on February 4, 1998, published by Pony Canyon.
Audio
The third and last issue of the soundtrack, Love, Peace & Happiness: The Original Yoshi's Story Soundtrack, contained 28 tracks, and was released in Germany by Nintendo of Europe on April 9, 1998.
Game Boy Advance tech demo
When Nintendo unveiled the Game Boy Advance to U.S. game developers on April 10, 2000, one of the available demonstrations was a tech demo derived from Yoshi's Story.
Game Boy Advance tech demo

The opening displayed a pre-rendered rotating island, resembling the shape of a Yoshi, taking advantage of the system's affine rotate-and-zoom feature (akin to the Super Nintendo's Mode 7) to render a seascape in perspective.
Game Boy Advance tech demo
Screenshots from the demo show the presence of giant Shy Guys, that were primarily designed to demonstrate system's advancement from the Game Boy Color 's 10-pixel sprite limit.
Game Boy Advance tech demo
In spite of the fact that Nintendo had published a promotional image of a Game Boy Advance with the tech demo running on it, it was never released as a completed game.
Re-releases
Yoshi's Story was re-released on the Wii 's Virtual Console service in October 2007, and for the Wii U 's Virtual Console in early 2016.
Marketing and sales
According to the Japanese magazine Famitsu, Yoshi's Story sold 53,428 copies on the day of its release in Japan.
Marketing and sales
As a result, it gained the number seven rank in Famitsu ' s top ten best-selling video games chart.
Marketing and sales
The game sold an additional 118,502 copies in the region by January 4, 1998, dropping to the number eight spot.
Marketing and sales
By the end of that year, Yoshi's Story sold a total of 618,789 copies in Japan, making it the 27th best-selling video game in the country in 1998.
Marketing and sales
In the German market, it sold 150,000 units from January through September 1998.
Marketing and sales
Nintendo intended to release Yoshi's Story in North America by the 1997 holiday season, but the release was delayed until March 1998.
Marketing and sales
A Nintendo official said that the delay was "based on us demanding A-plus quality." Once the game was completed, Nintendo initially shipped 800,000 units from Japan to American retailers.
Marketing and sales
Retailers were concerned that there would be shortages (like there had been for GoldenEye 007), but a Nintendo official promised that the shipment would satisfy demand.
Marketing and sales

The trade-off is that rumble support was dropped, just like the other N64 releases." As with their review of the original release, they lambasted the lack of interesting designs and challenge.

Thomas's review for the VC release, he gave it a 6.0 out of 10, saying that "It's nonsensical.

f64_super_bash_bros.title: Super Smash Bros. (video game)
sents: lead
Super Smash Bros. is a 1999 crossover fighting game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It is first game in the Super Smash Bros. series and was released in Japan on January 21, 1999; in North America on April 26, 1999; and in Europe on November 19, 1999.
lead
The game is a crossover among different Nintendo franchises, including Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Star Fox, Yoshi, Donkey Kong, Metroid, F-Zero, Mother, Kirby, and Pokémon.
lead

It presents a cast of characters and locations from these franchises and allows players to use each character's unique skills and the stage's hazards to inflict damage, recover health, and ultimately knock opponents off the stage.
lead
Super Smash Bros. received generally positive reviews upon its release.
lead
It was a commercial success, selling over five million copies worldwide by 2001, with 2.93 million sold in the United States and 1.97 million sold in Japan.
lead
It was given an Editors' Choice award from IGN for the "Best Fighting Game", and also became a Nintendo 64 Player's Choice title.
lead
The game spawned a series of sequels for each successive Nintendo console, starting with Super Smash Bros.
Gameplay
Characters are additionally not limited to only facing opponents, instead being allowed to move freely.
Gameplay
Each stage offers unique gameplay and strategic motives, making the chosen stage an additional factor in the fight.
Gameplay

In the game's single-player mode, the player battles a series of computer-controlled opponents in a specific order, attempting to defeat them with a limited number of lives in a limited amount of time.
Gameplay
While the player can determine the difficulty level and the number of lives, the series of opponents never changes.
Gameplay
During sudden death, all fighters are given 300% damage and the last fighter standing will win the match.
Development
Super Smash Bros. was developed by HAL Laboratory, a Nintendo second-party developer, during 1998.
Development
His first idea was to include famous Nintendo characters and put them in a fight.
Development
Knowing that he would not get permission if he asked ahead of time, Sakurai made a prototype of the game without informing Nintendo, and did not show anyone until it was well-balanced.
Development
The prototype he presented featured Mario, Donkey Kong, Samus and Fox as playable characters.
Development
On October 20, 2022, Sakurai, who still had the prototype of Dragon King: The Fighting Game, demonstrated its gameplay and its differences from the final product of Super Smash Bros.
Music
A complete soundtrack was released on CD in Japan through Teichiku Records in 2000.
Release
The game was revealed as early as November 1998 and plans for a North American release were revealed in February 1999.
Release
To promote the game's launch, Nintendo of America staged an event called Slamfest '99, held at the MGM Grand Adventures theme park in Las Vegas, Nevada, on April 24, 1999.
Release
Despite this, no video footage of Slamfest '99 is known to survive, and the broadcast is currently considered lost media.
Reception
Upon its initial Nintendo 64 release, Super Smash Bros. received "generally favorable" reviews according to review aggregator site Metacritic, based on 11 reviews.
Reception
IGN criticized the game's battle stage and character offerings as "much too limited" and "routine" in the single-player experience.
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly held that its "novel concept alone makes this game worth checking out," but that, it "may not be worth the cash" for a single-player experience.
Reception
Super Smash Bros. was commercially successful, becoming a Nintendo 64 Player's Choice title, selling 1.97 million copies in Japan and 2.93 million in the United States as of 2008.
Reception

The Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences named Super Smash Bros. as a finalist for " Console Action Game of the Year " and " Console Fighting Game of the Year " at the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.

lead
It was released in North America in June 1998 by THQ, Europe in September 1998 by Konami and July 1999 by Imagineer.
lead
It is the first role-playing video game released for the system in North America.
lead
After Quest 64 ' s moderate financial success, a sequel was in consideration by the developer Imagineer.
lead
However, only the sequel's story was revealed before it was ultimately cancelled.
lead

Brian sets off to find his father, who has left the monastery of the mages - the player learns later that his father is looking for a thief who has stolen the "Eletale Book".

The player character's spells work through elemental spirits, with each of the Nintendo 64 controller 's four C buttons corresponding to one of the four classic elements (wind, earth, water, and fire).

The game differs from most RPGs in that the experience system is not based upon a traditional "level-up" model.
Gameplay
If Brian runs out of HP, the game will return him to the last inn at which he saved.

In-game time is tracked with a compass/clock in the HUD, and certain events may either only happen at night or only happen during the day.

The game was announced in early 1997, at which point it was to be titled Eltale (エルテイル) in Japan and Holy Magic Century in all other regions.

Quest 64 was developed by Japanese company Imagineer, while THQ both translated it into English and published it in North America.
Development
Expectations for the game were high upon release, as it was the first true RPG on the Nintendo 64.

Quest 64 received mixed reviews upon release with GameRankings giving it a score of 54%.
Reception
GameSpot wrote "Quest 64's individual puzzles and challenges are similarly straightforward.

Discover that there's a villain scaring everyone and making it impossible to get through Forest #1 to Town #2.

To boot, he's stolen Unique Elemental Magic Item #1 from Lord #1." The general conclusion was the game was competent enough to charm gamers who had never played an RPG before, but too simplistic and trite to interest anyone else.
