Soon after, Resident Evil 1.5 was scrapped at 60–80 percent completion.
Development restarted
During a period in which the team made no progress rewriting the scenario, Okamoto was introduced to professional screenwriter Noboru Sugimura, who was enthusiastic about the first game's story.
Development restarted

Sugimura was initially consulted on a trial basis, but Okamoto was impressed by the ease with which Sugimara solved script problems, and soon asked him to compose the entire scenario for Resident Evil 2.
Development restarted
One fundamental modification to the story was the reworking of Elza Walker into Claire Redfield, in order to introduce a connection to the plot of the first game.
Development restarted
To fulfill Capcom's sales plan of two million copies, director Kamiya tried to attract new customers with a more ostentatious and Hollywood-like story presentation.
Development restarted
The environments were created on SGI O2 computers, and each background took two or three weeks to render.
Development restarted
The maximum number of zombies displayed on the screen at one time was limited to seven, making it possible to use 450 polygons for the comparatively detailed models of Leon and Claire.
Development restarted

Other than the graphics, one of the most important new features is the "Zapping System", which was partly inspired by Back to the Future Part II, a time travel-themed film sequel that offers a different perspective on the story of the original film.
Development restarted
The voice-overs by the all-Canadian cast of Resident Evil 2 were recorded before the actual cutscenes were completed, with each of the actors selected from a roster of ten people per role.
Development restarted
Thus, she is the only main character not to appear in a pre-rendered cutscene.
Development restarted
The North American version contains more violent game over screens, which were removed from the Japanese Biohazard 2.
Development restarted
Resident Evil 2 was made more difficult (and thus longer-playing) than its Japanese equivalent to prevent short-term rentals from affecting U.S. sales.
Music
The music for Resident Evil 2 was composed by Masami Ueda, Shusaku Uchiyama, and Syun Nishigaki, except one track composed by Naoshi Mizuta.
Music
Key events of the story are supported with orchestral and cinematic compositions – a move that was inspired by blockbuster films.
Music
Two albums containing music from the game were released in January and August 1998, respectively.
Music
The first, Biohazard 2 Original Soundtrack, is the main release and includes most of the significant compositions.
Music

The second, Biohazard 2 Complete Track, largely encompasses less prevalent themes, but offers an orchestral medley and a second CD with sound effects, voice collections, and an interview with the sound staff.
Music
The European version of Biohazard 2 Original Soundtrack has an identical CD, Resident Evil 2 Original Soundtrack.
Music
Disc jockey Piston Nishizawa created electronic remixes for several of the compositions, which were later released as the album Biohazard 2 Remix: Metamorphoses.
Marketing
The game had a marketing budget of $5 million.
Releases
After its initial release for the PlayStation in January 1998, Resident Evil 2 was reissued and ported to other systems, many gaining new features in the process.
Dual Shock Ver.
The first re-release is the Dual Shock Ver., which supports the vibration and analog control functions of the PlayStation's DualShock controller.
Dual Shock Ver.
Version" mode based on the difficulty level of Resident Evil 2 ' s Western versions.
Dual Shock Ver.
The Dual Shock Ver. served as the basis for the majority of ports, such as the Windows 9x -based PC-CD version Resident Evil 2 Platinum.
Dual Shock Ver.
A "Data Gallery" was added to the main menu, allowing the player to view movies, rough sketches, illustrations, and 3D models.
Dual Shock Ver.
Developed by Sourcenext, it includes high-quality FMVs encoded at 640×480 pixels.
Nintendo 64
Released on November 16, 1999, the Nintendo 64 version of Resident Evil 2 is one of the few games released for the console to have FMVs, overcoming the limited storage space on the cartridge.
Nintendo 64
The PlayStation version with two CD-ROMs of up to 700 MB per disc was faithfully replicated (with unique enhancements) on a 64 MB Nintendo 64 Game Pak.
Nintendo 64
Across twelve months and with a budget of $1 million, Resident Evil 2 was ported to the console by a team led by nine full-time and one part-time personnel from Angel Studios.
Nintendo 64
Further help was provided by ten staff from Capcom Production Studio 3 and Factor 5.
Nintendo 64

Hidden throughout the four scenarios, they reveal new information about the series' lore and connect the story of Resident Evil 2 to those of the other installments, including some that had not been released yet.
Nintendo 64

The Nintendo 64 version adjusts its display resolution depending on the number of polygonal models currently on screen, and supports the Expansion Pak accessory for a maximum resolution of 640×480 during gameplay.
Nintendo 64
In 2018, Eurogamer called this "one of the most ambitious console ports of all time".
Other versions
A port of Resident Evil 2 for the Sega Saturn was developed at Capcom, with plans for it to use the console's 4 MB RAM cartridge, but technical difficulties led to its cancellation in October 1998.
Other versions
Tiger Electronics released a black and white sprite -based 2.5D version for its Game.com handheld in late 1998.
Other versions
In February 2013, an unfinished build of Resident Evil 1.5 was leaked onto the Internet.
Other versions
In July 2024, Resident Evil was released on GOG.com, with ports of Resident Evil 2, released on August 27, 2024 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis expected to come later.
Reception

Its original PlayStation release holds an average aggregate score of 93% at GameRankings based on 25 reviews, and 89 out of 100 points at Metacritic for both the PlayStation and Nintendo 64 versions based on 13 reviews.
Reception
Mac Donald said that the idea of actions in the first scenario affecting the second was "cool in concept", but underused.
Reception
Resident Evil 2 was also praised for its graphics, which many critics said were a substantial improvement upon those of the first installment.
Reception

Allgame 's Shawn Sackenheim awarded its graphics the highest possible score, as he found the backgrounds to be "rendered to perfection", the cutscenes "a work of art", and the animation "fluid and eerie".
Reception
Next Generation said it had "the most precise and realistic sound effects ever heard in any game".
Reception
Sackenheim described the music and sound effects as "spot on perfect" and the soundtrack "perfectly composed", and Mac Donald likened the use of audio to that of classic horror films.
Reception
Sanchez said that the puzzles were paced better than in the first game, but less interesting and too easy for experienced players.
Reception
With the exception of the critically acclaimed Nintendo 64 version, most later releases of Resident Evil 2 have received slightly lower scores than the PlayStation version.
Reception
The Nintendo 64 version was widely commended for the technical achievement of fitting a two-disc game on a single 512- Mbit (64MB) cartridge.
Reception
Eurogamer said the Nintendo 64's unique analog control "works supremely well to the point where it's borderline game-breaking".
Reception
In 2018, Eurogamer called it "one of the most ambitious console ports of all time".
Reception
Davis and 1UP.com 's Mark MacDonald were disappointed by the version's lack of features that were included in the Nintendo 64 release.
Reception
Peer Schneider of IGN found the 2.5D version for the Game.com to be frustrating and only "partially faithful" to the original release of Resident Evil 2.
Sales
Resident Evil 2 was promoted with a $ 5,000,000 (equivalent to $9,300,000 in 2023) advertising campaign.
Sales
In Italy, the game reached 100,000 pre-orders, worth over 12 billion lire or $6,600,000 (equivalent to $12,300,000 in 2023).
Sales
On the weekend following its release, more than 380,000 copies were sold, grossing $19,000,000 (equivalent to $36,000,000 in 2023).
Sales
After one and a half months, the game's global sales had topped 3 million copies, with 1.9 million sold in Japan and over a million sold in the United States.
Sales
Weekly Famitsu named it Japan's best-selling game for the first half of 1998, with sales of 2.13 million units.
Sales
According to The NPD Group, it was 1998's sixth best-selling game in the United States.
Sales
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, Resident Evil 2 took home a "Gold" prize for revenues above €29 million or $33,000,000 (equivalent to $62,000,000 in 2023) in the European Union during 1998.
Sales
With 4.96 million copies sold, the original PlayStation version of Resident Evil 2 was a commercial success, and is the franchise's best-selling game on a single platform.
Sales

By March 1999, approximately 11 million units of all versions of Resident Evil and Resident Evil 2 had been sold worldwide, including 810,000 copies of Resident Evil 2: Dual Shock Ver., totaling 5.77 million copies for both PlayStation versions of Resident Evil 2.
Sales
In Japan, 17,973 copies of the Nintendo 64 and GameCube versions were sold, and in the United States, 326,397 copies of the Nintendo 64 version were sold, totaling at least 344,370.
Accolades
It is listed as one of the 100 best games of all time by Electronic Gaming Monthly (62nd), IGN (58th), Empire (49th), Game Informer (34th), and Official UK PlayStation Magazine (6th).
Accolades
Readers of Retro Gamer voted Resident Evil 2 the 97th top retro game, and the staff wrote it was "considered by many to be the best in the long-running series".
Accolades
GameTrailers ranked it fourth on a list of the games that most needed remakes.
Controversy

In Italy, Resident Evil 2 was temporarily banned in 1999 following criticism from the political organization "Movimento Diritti Civili" (Civil Rights Movement) for its realistic depiction of violence, with the law enforcement agency Guardia di Finanza seizing over 5,500 unsold copies.
Legacy

Ted Adams and Kris Oprisko loosely adapted it into the comics "Raccoon City – R.I.P." and "A New Chapter of Evil", which were released in the first and second issues of Resident Evil: The Official Comic Book Magazine in March and June 1998.
Legacy
The 60-issue Hong Kong comics Biohazard 2 was published weekly from February 1998 to April 1999.
Legacy
In 2008, Resident Evil 5 producer Jun Takeuchi, who had previously worked on the series as weapons designer and graphics animator, alluded to the possibility of a full-fledged remake.
Legacy
Such a project had already been considered for the GameCube in 2002, but Mikami abandoned the idea as he did not want to delay the in-development Resident Evil 4.
Legacy
Spaced director Edgar Wright cited this episode inspired by Resident Evil 2 as the basis for his zombie comedy film Shaun of the Dead (2004).
Legacy
The dramas were broadcast on Radio Osaka in early 1999, and later released by publisher Suleputer as two separate CDs, Biohazard 2 Drama Album.
Remake
In August 2015, Capcom announced that a remake of Resident Evil 2 was in development.
Remake
Capcom unveiled the game at E3 2018, with trailers and gameplay footage, and a worldwide release date of January 25, 2019 for PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One.
Remake
The game uses the RE Engine, which is also in Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, and replaces the tank controls and fixed camera angles with "over-the-shoulder" gameplay similar to Resident Evil 4.

f64_turuk_dinosaur_hunter.title: Turok: Dinosaur Hunter
sents: lead
Turok: Dinosaur Hunter is a first-person shooter video game developed by Iguana Entertainment and published by Acclaim for the Nintendo 64 console and Microsoft Windows.
lead
It was released in 1997 in North America and Europe.
lead
Turok is an adaptation of the Valiant Comics comic book series of the same name.
lead
The player controls Turok, a Native American warrior, who must stop the evil Campaigner from conquering the universe with an ancient and powerful weapon.
lead

As Acclaim's first title for the Nintendo 64, Turok was part of a strategy to develop games internally and license merchandise; Acclaim acquired the rights to Turok when it purchased Valiant Comics in 1994, renaming it Acclaim Comics.
lead
Suffering from cash flow problems and falling sales, Acclaim came to rely on Turok as its best hope for a financial turnaround.
lead
Iguana pushed the Nintendo 64's graphics capabilities to its limits, and were forced to compress or cut elements to fit the game on its 8 megabyte cartridge.
lead
Bugs delayed the game's release from September 1996 to January 1997.
Gameplay
Played from a first person perspective, the 3D graphics and style of play combine elements of the run-and-gun video game Doom with exploration mechanics of Tomb Raider.
Gameplay
Turok features 13 weapons plus the Chronoscepter, ranging from a knife and bow to high tech weaponry.
Gameplay
When the player is at full health, the meter reads 100, while dropping to 0 subtracts one life, and losing the last life ends the game.
Gameplay
Gathering "life force" points scattered across the levels increases the player's life count by one for every 100 points accumulated.
Development
Turok originally appeared in comics from Western Publishing and Dell Comics in December 1954.
Development
Valiant Comics revived the series and published the first issue of their Turok series in 1993.
Development

Video game publisher Acclaim Entertainment bought Valiant for $65 million in 1994 and acquired developer Iguana Entertainment for $5 million plus stock a year later, part of a strategy to develop games in-house and make money licensing characters in different entertainment media.
Development
Turok was announced in August 1994 as an exclusive title for Nintendo's planned "Ultra 64" console, eventually called the Nintendo 64.
Development
Iguana considered a third-person perspective similar to Super Mario 64 and Tomb Raider, but decided to make the game a first-person shooter instead.
Development
According to project manager David Dienstbier, the first-person perspective was a natural way to showcase the 3D power of the Nintendo 64.
Development

While the development team benefited from Acclaim's clout as a longtime Nintendo supporter, getting earlier feedback from the publisher and more face-to-face time during production, most of the developers at Iguana were new and inexperienced; Turok was Dienstbier's first title.
Development

Due to the game's action and violent content, Dienstbier believed they were pushing the limits of what Nintendo would allow on their console, but Nintendo never asked to see or approve anything in the game.
Development
The Nintendo 64 platform had superior processing capabilities compared to most personal computers available at the time, but also came with challenges.
Development
Fitting the game on its 8 MB cartridge was difficult; ultimately, Iguana had to compress everything and reduce the quality of the music to meet size requirements.
Development

Iguana was able to use Acclaim's state-of-the-art motion capture studio, allowing humanoid characters to move smoothly and in a convincing manner; motion capture helped alleviate the problems of Iguana's limited resources and tight schedule.
Development
A stuntman recorded movements for the human characters; while the developers tried to use emus and ostriches for the dinosaurs, the results were only used as reference material.
Development

The company lost $222 million in the 1996 fiscal year due to sales falling to $162 million compared to $567 million the previous year; in the first quarter of fiscal 1997, the company lost a further $19 million.
Development
The company laid off 100 of its 950 workers since March 1996 and its stock had dropped from a high of $13.875 a share to as low as $3.
Development
Turok, Acclaim's first Nintendo 64 title, became the company's best hope of a turnaround, as there were only ten Nintendo 64 games on the market, and Turok was the only shooter.
Development
Turok was the only major Nintendo 64 software demonstrated at the September 1996 European Computer Trade Show, with Nintendo themselves absent from the show.
Development
Brown Inc analysts figured that selling one million copies of Turok could bring Acclaim as much as $45 million.
Development

Endangering Turok ' s sales was its high price—$79.99 in the US, £70 in the UK, and $129.95 in Australia —and Entertainment Software Rating Board 's "mature" rating, which suggested lower sales as parents would not buy the game for their children.
Delay and release
Originally slated for a September 30, 1996, release in North America, the game was initially delayed to January 1997.
Delay and release
Acclaim heavily marketed Turok on the covers of video-gaming magazines and in television commercials for the Nintendo 64.
Delay and release
Responding to positive pre-orders and advance sales of Turok, Acclaim announced on January 2, 1997 that a sequel, tentatively titled Turok: Dinosaur Hunter 2, would be released in late 1997.
Delay and release
Acclaim dubbed the March 4 release date of the game "Turok Tuesday", reporting that pre-sales at Toys "R" Us had exceeded expectations.
Delay and release
Acclaim stock increased in anticipation before the game's release, up $0.62 to $5.94.
Delay and release
In 1998 Turok was added to the Nintendo 64's $39.99 line.
Reception
Turok was a critical and commercial success, earning rave reviews from video game magazines and becoming the most popular title for the Nintendo 64 in the months following its release.
Reception
On the aggregate review web site Metacritic, the console version of Turok has an 85% rating, based on scores from thirteen reviews.
Reception

Douglass Perry of the multimedia website IGN compared Turok favorably to other first person shooters, saying that the title distinguished itself by allowing a level of 3D movement not possible in other members of the genre.
Reception
Video game magazine Edge said that Turok contradicted the prevailing notion at the time that only Nintendo could create superior games for the console.
Reception

In contrast, William Burrill of The Toronto Star wrote that Turok offered nothing new if players had tried a first-person shooter before, and Next Generation Online said that its similar gameplay essentially made the game "a very pretty Duke Nukem ".
Reception

Speaking to Shacknews in 2007, Propaganda Games 's Josh Holmes said that while GoldenEye 007 is commonly considered the standard-setting console shooter, Turok pioneered the console shooter first by offering open environments and deviating from the corridor-based shooters that were the standard until then.
Reception
Perry, GamePro, and Next Generation all noted that while many players would not initially like using the Nintendo 64's analog stick for weapon movement, they would become adept at the control scheme.
Reception
Polak said that the game proved the supremacy of the Nintendo 64's graphics in the console market.
Reception
Gerstmann wrote that the distance fog used to reduce the slowdown was a "neat effect" as enemies would appear out of the mist "fangs first", although it masked the console's limitations.
Reception

Next Generation said that while Turok was overall probably the best-looking Nintendo 64 game to date, the limited texture palette causes all the environments to appear similar, making the game disorienting despite the map.
Reception
Colin Williamson commented in PC Gamer that the game's popularity on the Nintendo 64 could in part be attributed to the shortage of games for the system at the time.
Reception
Like Next Generation, he said that while the graphics are impressive, the limited textures and constant fog make the game disorienting, and first-person platform jumping does not work.
Reception
Worldwide sales of Turok: Dinosaur Hunter surpassed $60 million in late June 1997, and accounted for 45% of Acclaim's revenues in the fiscal quarter in which the game was released.
Reception
Acclaim re-issued the game for the 1997 holiday season due to its sales potential for the increased console player base.
Reception
Turok was later named a Nintendo " Player's Choice " title in 1998—the only third-party Nintendo 64 game to be featured at the time —and ultimately sold about 1.5 million units.
Reception
The game generated $200 million in revenue worldwide by 1998.
Reception

In addition to Turok, the Turok franchise includes five other games: Turok 2: Seeds of Evil (1998), Turok: Rage Wars (1999), Turok 3: Shadow of Oblivion (2000), Turok: Evolution (2002), and Turok (2008).
Legacy
A Game.com version was announced, and early screenshots of it circulated in the press, but it was never released.
Legacy

In February 2017, the source code of the N64 version was sold on eBay for $2551.99 which was found on a SGI Silicon Graphics Indy development machine which originated from the Acclaim Entertainment liquidation.
Legacy
Nightdive Studios produced a remastered version of the game, along with Turok 2, for the PC.
Legacy
The remaster was released in digital stores on December 17, 2015.

f64_turuk_2_seeds_of_evil.title: Turok 2: Seeds of Evil
sents: lead
Turok 2: Seeds of Evil is a first-person shooter video game developed by Iguana Entertainment and published by Acclaim Entertainment.
lead
It was released for the Nintendo 64 console in 1998 and ported to Microsoft Windows computers in 1999.
lead
Seeds of Evil is the second game in the Turok video game series and a sequel to Turok: Dinosaur Hunter.
lead
The game follows the story of a Turok and his efforts to stop a powerful alien entity from escaping the confines of his Lightship.
lead
A different game set in the same fictional universe, also titled Turok 2: Seeds of Evil, was released for the Game Boy Color alongside the Nintendo 64 game.
lead
Seeds of Evil features a single-player campaign consisting of six levels and a multiplayer mode where various players can compete against each other in several game types.
lead
It supports the Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak, which enables an optional high-resolution graphics mode.
lead
The game was developed over a period of 21 months and was originally intended to be released on a 12 MB cartridge without a multiplayer component, but was ultimately released on a 32MB cartridge.
Gameplay
Like its predecessor Turok: Dinosaur Hunter, Seeds of Evil is a first-person shooter where the player assumes the role of Turok from a first-person perspective.
Gameplay
As Turok, the player can run, jump, climb ladders, swim and dive underwater for a limited period of time.
Gameplay
All the portals in the hub area, except for the first one, must be unlocked with keys that must be collected in the levels.
Gameplay
In the Nintendo 64 game, the player's progress can only be saved in special portals, while the Microsoft Windows version lets players save the game at any point.
Gameplay
There are five talismans in the game and every level, except for the first one, features a feather and a talisman chamber.
Gameplay

The Primagen key from one particular level usually requires the player to use the talisman from the next level, except for the Primagen key from the last level, which requires the player to use four talismans.
Multiplayer
For example, the Raptor is limited to close-range attacks, but is also extremely fast and agile.
Multiplayer
Multiplayer games in the Nintendo 64 version of the game support up to four players via split screen.
Multiplayer
In contrast, multiplayer games in the Microsoft Windows version support up to 16 players via LAN or internet.
Plot
At the end of the game, Adon states that the mysterious force which conspired against Joshua during his quest still exists, setting the stage for the sequel Turok 3: Shadow of Oblivion.
Development and release
Seeds of Evil was developed by Iguana Entertainment with a team roughly the same size as that of Dinosaur Hunter, which was composed of 18 people.
Development and release
Development started before Dinosaur Hunter was released and preliminary work on level and enemy design finished by July 1997.
Development and release
The Cerebral Bore weapon was inspired by the Tall Man's weapons from the 1979 film Phantasm.
Development and release
The game's progression, focus on exploration and mission objectives were inspired by the Mario and Zelda franchises.
Development and release
Unlike the original game, where levels shared graphic assets, Seeds of Evil features unique levels with different geometry, textures and enemies.
Development and release
Having received Nintendo 64DD development kits that included the Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak, Iguana Entertainment added an optional high-resolution mode to the game early on in the development cycle.
Development and release
In conjunction with the Expansion Pak, this mode allows the game to be played at a resolution of 640x480 pixels, a technical accomplishment for the Nintendo 64 at the time.
Development and release
Seeds of Evil was originally designed to fit in a 12 MB Nintendo 64 cartridge.
Development and release
Nevertheless, when cartridges prices fell, the storage was increased to 16MB, allowing the development team to add a multiplayer mode.
Development and release
The cartridge size was ultimately increased to 32MB, which was the largest size for a Nintendo 64 game at the time.
Development and release
The actual development of the game took overall 21 months to complete and over 10,000 hours of game testing were reportedly conducted.
Development and release
In May 1998, a demonstration of the game running in high-resolution mode was presented at the Electronic Entertainment Expo.
Development and release
With a marketing budget of $9 million, the game was fairly anticipated and worldwide retailers ordered 1.75 million copies of the game before launch.
Development and release
Seeds of Evil was originally planned to ship in October 1998 for Acclaim Entertainment 's "TurOctober" event, but the release date was pushed back to November.
Development and release
The game was released in North America on December 10, 1998.
Development and release
The game was rescheduled for a European release on December 18.
Development and release
In Japan, the game was released on June 18, 1999, as Violence Killer: Turok New Generation (バイオレンスキラー TUROK NEW GENERATION).
Development and release
A different game set in the same fictional universe, also titled Turok 2: Seeds of Evil, was released for the Game Boy Color alongside the Nintendo 64 game.
Development and release
A port of the game was released for Microsoft Windows on February 9, 1999.
Reception
Seeds of Evil received "generally favorable" reviews according to Metacritic and sold 1.4 million copies by January 1999.
Reception

Next Generation praised the game's technical aspects and improvements over its predecessor, while GameSpot described Seeds of Evil as "a landmark shooter and a must-buy", stating that the game "raised the bar for first-person shooters" like Rare 's 1997 title GoldenEye 007.
Reception
GameSpot said that the soundtrack is "well suited to the game and never intrusive", while Victor Lucas of The Electric Playground described it as "suspenseful, dynamic and always adrenaline charged".
Reception

Similarly, Tim Weaver of N64 Magazine credited the music for being "dramatically scored, with strings, tom toms, bass lines and nerve-juddering screeches as enemies spring out at you from all angles".
Reception
The multiplayer mode was praised for its use of 3D space and innovative game types.
Reception
Tal Blevins of IGN criticized the controls for its limited support of keyboard functions and the graphics for their distance fog, which was not common in computer games of the time.
Reception
At the 1998 GameSpot Game of the Year awards, the Nintendo 64 version was awarded Shooting Game of the Year.
Reception
In a retrospective review, Martin Watts of Nintendo Life said that Seeds of Evil "is quite possibly the best third-party effort ever released for Nintendo 64".
Remaster
The remaster was released for Microsoft Windows on March 16, 2017, for Xbox One on March 2, 2018, and for Linux and macOS on September 12, 2018.
Remaster
The remaster was released for the Nintendo Switch on August 9, 2019.
Remaster
Although the Nintendo Switch version was released without a multiplayer mode, it was ultimately added with the release of a patch on February 25, 2021.
Remaster
The remaster was released for PlayStation 4 on February 25, 2021.

f64_turuk_3.title: Turok (video game)
sents: lead
Turok is a first-person shooter video game developed by Propaganda Games, and published by Disney Interactive Studios under Touchstone Games.
lead
It was released for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in February 2008, and later ported on to Microsoft Windows in April.
lead
It was the only game produced under the Touchstone Games label.
lead
Turok is loosely based on the comic book series of the same title and is a reboot of previous Turok video games.
lead

Players assume the role of Native American space marine Joseph Turok, who is part of a team sent to a remote planet to apprehend General Roland Kane, Turok's former commanding officer, who is now a wanted war criminal.
lead

After crash landing, Turok discovers that the planet is home to all manner of dinosaurs, and must fight both the predatory creatures and Kane's private army on his mission to take down his former mentor.
lead
The game received mixed reviews from critics.
lead
A planned sequel to Turok was cancelled following the closure of Propaganda Games.
Gameplay
The gameplay of Turok is similar to that of most first-person shooters, with a strong focus on survival in dangerous natural environments.
Multiplayer
Multiplayer supports up to 16 people, and 4 players for three co-op missions.
Multiplayer
There can be up to 4 A.I controlled dinosaurs or insects on any map at one time.
Multiplayer

Originally, the Xbox 360 version of Turok was set to feature an achievement called "Grab Bag", which required players to kill at least one enemy, one dinosaur, one teammate, and themselves, all in the same match.
Multiplayer
A Map pack called the " Velociraptor Pack" was later released, containing two new multiplayer maps, one new Co-op map, and 2 refurbished maps, which now take place at night.
Multiplayer
The online multiplayer for the PlayStation 3 version has been permanently shutdown since February 2011.
Plot
Whiskey Company fends off the attack, but Parker and Lewis are killed and the comm unit is destroyed.
Development
The game was in development for three years with a team of 150 people.
Reception

GameTrailers, which gave the game 8.3/10, highlighted the game's use of the Unreal Engine 3, believing it to be "the best use of the tech outside of Epic's own efforts" and praising the modeling and animation of the dinosaurs in particular.
Reception
1UP.com gave the game a score of C+, specifically complaining about its stealth mechanics, the use of camera shaking, and occasional graphical glitches in the PlayStation 3 version.
Reception
Turok received 3/5 from X-Play, who commented on its aim-assist being woefully inadequate both in multiplayer and singleplayer, but praised its graphics and "outlook".
Reception
Turok was a commercial success, shifting over 1 million units in its first two months of sales.
Reception
The game was popular enough for Propaganda Games to begin working on a sequel for the Xbox 360 before the developer was shuttered.

f64_shadowguy.title: Shadow Man (video game)

Platform(s): Windows, Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Dreamcast, OS X, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch

sents: lead
Shadow Man is an action-adventure video game developed by Acclaim Studios Teesside and published by Acclaim Entertainment.
lead
It is based on the Shadow Man comic book series published by Valiant Comics.
lead
The game was announced in 1997 and was originally slated for a late 1998 release on Nintendo 64 and an early 1999 release for Microsoft Windows, but was delayed to August 31, 1999.
lead
A PlayStation version was also released on the same day.
lead
A Dreamcast version was released three months later on December 1.
lead
Shadow Man was re-released on September 17, 2013, on GOG.com, available for Windows (with a version for Mac OS X subsequently added), and later on Steam, available for Windows and OS X.
lead

Nightdive Studios, who re-released Shadow Man in 2013, developed Shadow Man Remastered, a remastered version of the game which includes 4K resolution, improved shadow mapping, per-pixel lighting, anti-aliasing and missing content that was cut from the original game.
lead
The game was released for Microsoft Windows on April 15, 2021, while the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One ports were released on January 13, 2022, and the Nintendo Switch port on January 17, 2022.
Plot

In 1888, Jack the Ripper – lamenting the fact that his ritualistic murders have not unlocked a mystical power that he believes to exist – prepares to perform the ritual upon himself at the expense of his own life.
Development
The game's development budget was more than $6 million.
Reception
The Dreamcast, PC and N64 versions of Shadow Man received favorable reviews, while the PlayStation version received mixed or average reviews, according to video game review aggregator GameRankings.
Reception

For now, I am satisfied running, searching, and shooting." PlanetDreamcast gave the Dreamcast version 6.5 out of 10, saying that it "offers a good filler game until the next batch of games hits your local store."
Reception
Jes Bickham of N64 Magazine gave the Nintendo 64 version 93%, calling it "a dark and glittering jewel in the N64's gaudy crown.

f64_command_concur.title: Command & Conquer

Developer(s): Westwood Studios (1995–2003) EA Los Angeles (2003–2010) Victory Games (2011–2013) EA Phenomic (2011–2013) EA Redwood Studios (2018–present)
Publisher(s): Virgin Interactive Entertainment Electronic Arts Sega Nintendo
Platform(s): Apple Mac, Nintendo 64, PlayStation, PC (MS-DOS, Windows), Sega Saturn, Xbox 360, Android, iOS

sents: lead
Command & Conquer (C&C) is a real-time strategy (RTS) video game franchise, first developed by Westwood Studios.
lead
The first game was one of the earliest of the RTS genre, itself based on Westwood Studios' influential strategy game Dune II and introducing trademarks followed in the rest of the series.
lead
This includes full-motion video cutscenes with an ensemble cast to progress the story, as opposed to digitally in-game rendered cutscenes.
lead
Westwood Studios was taken over by Electronic Arts in 1998 and closed down in 2003.
lead
The studio and some of its members were absorbed into EA Los Angeles, which continued development on the series.
History
Command & Conquer was released worldwide by Westwood in 1995.
History
A global war ensues between the UN -formed Global Defense Initiative to contain it and the cult quasi-state revolutionary Brotherhood of Nod, led by the enigmatic Kane, which seeks to harness it.
History
Highly successful, it was followed by Command & Conquer: Red Alert in 1996 which is set in an alternate universe where the Soviet Union wages war with the Allies.
History
The first game is sometimes referred to as Tiberian Dawn as a result.
History
The original game was followed by Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun in 1999 and its expansion pack Firestorm.
History
In 2002, Westwood Studios released Command & Conquer: Renegade, a first-person shooter.
History

A spin-off game in 2003, Command & Conquer: Generals, set in a more realistic near-future and featuring the United States, China and the Global Liberation Army was followed by an expansion pack, Zero Hour.
History
Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars was released in 2007 and followed by the expansion pack Kane's Wrath.
History
Command & Conquer 4: Tiberian Twilight, released in 2010 as the conclusion to the Tiberium saga, received mixed reviews because of its deviation from traditional gameplay and story.
History

The Red Alert series was continued by the 2000 title Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2, its expansion, Yuri's Revenge and Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 in 2008, which introduced a third faction, the Empire of the Rising Sun, which resembles Japan with futuristic robotic technology.
History
As of July 2010, the Command & Conquer franchise consists of eleven games and eight expansion packs.
History
The first three games of the series have been released as freeware to promote the successors.
History
The Command & Conquer series has been a commercial success with over 30 million Command & Conquer games sold as of 2009.
Gameplay
The Command & Conquer titles are real-time strategy games, with the exception of the first-person shooter Command & Conquer: Renegade.
Gameplay

The raw materials themselves, in games released before Red Alert 2 as well as Command & Conquer 3 require storage space in the form of refineries and, in the case of excess, "storage silo" structures.
Gameplay

Unit effectiveness against opponents follows the rock-paper-scissors (intransitivity) principle found in most real-time strategy games, and units' attack characteristics can vary according to faction.
Gameplay

Access to advanced units and abilities may be temporarily blocked if the required structures are destroyed or if they are not being provided with adequate power by the supporting "power plant" structures.
Multiplayer
All games in the series up to Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 featured two CDs that could be used for this reason.
Multiplayer
Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 was noted for being the first RTS game to enable the campaigns to be played cooperatively online; others had only supported single player campaigns.
Multiplayer
The GameSpy master servers have shut down in 2013., but some game titles can be played via Gameranger.
Tiberian series
Command & Conquer, released on September 26, 1995, is the first game in the series, which takes place somewhere between 2017 and 2020 according to the Command & Conquer: Renegade manual.
Tiberian series

Command & Conquer was well received and was widely praised by critics: " Command & Conquer is one of the finest, most brilliantly-designed computer games I have ever seen" said GameSpot reviewer Chris Hudak.
Tiberian series
Command & Conquer has attained 94% as an aggregate score from Metacritic with the less well received Covert Operations expansion pack obtaining an aggregate score of 72% after its 1996 release.
Tiberian series
Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun, released on August 27, 1999, takes place in the year 2030.
Tiberian series
In 1998, Westwood Studios, the developers of Tiberian Sun, was acquired by Electronic Arts.
Tiberian series

Compared to its predecessor, Tiberian Sun relies heavily on science fiction technologies and introduces a new isometric game engine featuring varying level terrain to give the impression of a true 3D environment.
Tiberian series

The full motion video is also scripted differently; while the cutscenes of Command & Conquer and Red Alert were filmed from a first-person perspective, Tiberian Sun used traditional cinematic shots for its FMVs featuring actors such as James Earl Jones and Michael Biehn.
Tiberian series

Command & Conquer: Renegade, released February 26, 2002, takes place in the final days of the events of Command & Conquer and was the last Command & Conquer game to be created by Westwood Studios before their liquidation in 2003.
Tiberian series
Unlike any other games in the series, Renegade is a first-person shooter.
Tiberian series
Although receiving average reviews, with an aggregate score of 75% on both GameRankings and Metacritic, Renegade was praised for its online features.
Tiberian series
GameSpy awarded Renegade its 2002 "Wish it had been better" award, condemning the single player but saying that " C&C: Renegade ' s multiplayer was innovative and fun".
Tiberian series
Online play was praised for encouraging teamwork and coordinated assaults, unlike other contemporary first-person shooters.
Tiberian series
Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars, released March 29, 2007, was a return to the real-time strategy roots of the Command & Conquer series.
Tiberian series
As a direct sequel to Tiberian Sun, Tiberium Wars is set in 2047 and features the introduction of a third faction, the Scrin.
Tiberian series
The sequel attained an aggregate score of 85% from both GameRankings and Metacritic.
Tiberian series

PC Gamer U.S. gave the game its "Editor's Choice" rating at 90%, stating that "one of the greatest RTS franchises of all time returns to glory", while PC Gamer UK gave it a more reserved rating of 82%, stating that it was "a welcome, but limited, return".
Tiberian series
Shortly after the release of Tiberium Wars, the expansion pack Command & Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath was announced.
Tiberian series

Released on March 24, 2008, Kane's Wrath limited the player to only the Brotherhood of Nod in the campaign mode, though the original factions and six new sub-factions are available for the new strategic mode and skirmish mode and it takes place in 2052.
Tiberian series
Reception was mainly positive with the expansion attaining an aggregate score of 77%.
Tiberian series

Command & Conquer 4: Tiberian Twilight, released on March 16, 2010, saw a big change in gameplay from the previous Command & Conquer by removing the resource gathering and base building elements in previous games as well as the removal of the third faction, the Scrin.
Tiberian series
The developers received approval from EA to release their game, and it entered open beta on February 26, 2014.
Tiberian series
EA announced in November 2018 its plans to remaster Command & Conquer, including expansions and Red Alert, for modern computer systems through Petroglyph Games.
Tiberian series
The Remastered Collection received a score of 82/100 on Metacritic, with 48 positive, 10 mixed, and 0 negative reviews, indicating a "generally favorable" reception.
Red Alert series

Command & Conquer: Red Alert, released on November 22, 1996, is set in an alternate universe 1950s and was originally made to be the prequel to Command & Conquer establishing Red Alert as the prologue of the entire Tiberium series of games.
Red Alert series

For PlayStation only, there was also a separate release to the original called Red Alert: Retaliation which included all the maps, missions and units of Red Alert: Counterstrike and Red Alert: The Aftermath as well as some newly filmed cut-scenes only available with Red Alert: Retaliation.
Red Alert series
Before being re-released as freeware on August 31, 2008, by Electronic Arts Command & Conquer: Red Alert had sold over three million copies.
Red Alert series
Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 was released on October 23, 2000.
Red Alert series
Since that game lacked reference to the Tiberian series, the connection established in the first Red Alert game became unclear.
Red Alert series
Red Alert 2 was received fairly positively with an aggregate score of 86% from GameRankings.
Red Alert series
An expansion pack to Red Alert 2, Command & Conquer: Yuri's Revenge was released on October 10, 2001.
Red Alert series
GameRankings reports an average score of 85% based on 31 reviews, making Yuri's Revenge the best received expansion pack in the Command & Conquer series.
Red Alert series
Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3, released on October 28, 2008, followed up on the story of Red Alert 2 and continued the series' more "light-hearted" take on Command & Conquer.
Red Alert series

Executive producer Chris Corry stated in a pre-release interview that Red Alert 3 will further differentiate the playable factions from each other and " up the silliness in their faction design whenever possible".
Red Alert series
This approach was seen as popular with Red Alert 3 obtaining an aggregate score of 82% from Metacritic.
Red Alert series
A stand-alone expansion to Red Alert 3, Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 – Uprising was released on March 12, 2009, to fairly poor reviews for the series with an average score of 64% from Metacritic.
Red Alert series

Another downloadable standalone game for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 was released known as Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 - Commander's Challenge which contained the Commander's Challenge mode of Uprising for consoles.
Red Alert series
Command & Conquer: Red Alert was released on October 16, 2009, for iOS which was a continuation of the story of Red Alert 2 and takes place before Red Alert 3.
Generals series
Command & Conquer: Generals, released on February 10, 2003, has a plotline which is unrelated to the other games of the Command & Conquer series.
Generals series
Generals uses an engine dubbed SAGE (or S trategy A ction G ame E ngine) and is the first fully three-dimensional Command & Conquer real-time strategy game.
Generals series
Based on 34 reviews, Metacritic gives it a score of 84/100 which includes a score of 9.3/10 from IGN.
Generals series
Generals has also received the E3 2002 Game Critics Awards Best Strategy Game award.
Generals series

One review noted that Generals was the first Command & Conquer real-time strategy game that did not include full-motion video cutscenes to tell the story and that it departed from the unique interface and base-building mechanics that had characterized all of the previous Command & Conquer RTS titles.
Generals series
An expansion for Generals, Command & Conquer: Generals – Zero Hour, was released on September 22, 2003, to further the Generals storyline.
Generals series
Zero Hour added 9 new armies to the game, over a dozen new campaign missions, and a gameplay mode known as Generals Challenge.
Generals series
Zero Hour obtained much the same reception as Generals with an aggregate score of 85% and 84% from GameRankings and Metacritic respectively.
Generals series
On December 10, 2011, Electronic Arts posted that the next game in the series would be Command & Conquer: Generals 2.
Generals series
In August 2012, Generals 2 was repurposed to a free-to-play game known as simply Command & Conquer.
Recent
EA revealed Command & Conquer: Rivals, which was under development by the newly formed EA Redwood Studios and released for Android and iOS mobile devices in December 2018.
Recent
In March 2024, EA released Command & Conquer: The Ultimate Collection on Steam.
Music
Klepacki returned to the series in 2008 to assist with the soundtrack for Red Alert 3.
Music
The original score for Command & Conquer: Red Alert was composed by Frank Klepacki and was voted the best video game soundtrack of 1996 by PC Gamer and Gameslice magazines.
Music

Among his most famous songs from the series is the theme of Red Alert, titled "Hell March", which accents the style of the game with adrenalized riffs of electric guitar, the sounds of marching feet, and synthesizers to a dramatic chant.
Reception
The Command & Conquer series have been a commercial success with over 30 million Command & Conquer games sold as of 2009.
Reception
In 1997, Screen Digest said it was "probably the world's biggest PC CD-ROM entertainment franchise to date."
Reception
As noted in the table below, the highest rated game is Command & Conquer with a score of 94% from Metacritic.
Reception
The highest rated game averaged over both sites is Command & Conquer: Red Alert with an average of just over 90%.
Reception
As a series, Command & Conquer games have averaged approximately 80% when including expansion packs and approximately 84% without.
Reception
Command & Conquer ' s long history resulted in Guinness World Records awarding the series six world records in the Guinness World Records: Gamer's Edition 2008.
Reception

These records include "Biggest Selling RTS Series", "Most Number of Platforms for an RTS", and "Longest Running Actor in Video Game Role" for Joe Kucan, who has played the part of Kane, the villainous mastermind of the series, for 15 years.

pboy_critred.title: Pokémon (video game series)

First release: Pocket Monsters Red and Green (Japan) February 27, 1996

sents: lead
Pokémon is a series of video games developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo and The Pokémon Company under the Pokémon media franchise.
lead

It was created by Satoshi Tajiri with assistance from Ken Sugimori, the first games, Pocket Monsters Red and Green, were released in 1996 in Japan for the Game Boy, later released outside of Japan as Pokémon Red Version and Blue Version.
lead
The main series of role-playing video games (RPGs), referred as the "core series" by their developers, has continued on each generation of Nintendo's handhelds.
lead
The most recently released core series games, Pokémon Scarlet and Violet, were released on November 18, 2022, for the Nintendo Switch.
lead
In addition to Game Freak's development, Creatures provides support through their Pokémon CG Studio, which creates 3D models for the Pokémon in the games, and also develops some spin-off titles.
lead

In 1998, Nintendo, Creatures, and Game Freak jointly established The Pokémon Company, which manages licensing, production, publishing, marketing and deals for the franchise both within Asia and worldwide through The Pokémon Company International.
lead
The core games are released in generations, each with different Pokémon, storylines, and characters.
lead
Remakes of the games are usually released around a decade after the original versions for the latest console at the time.
Gameplay
A major subplot of most games is to defeat a criminal organization, whose intents are usually trying to take over the world through the misuse of powerful Pokémon known as Legendary Pokémon.
Gameplay
The player may carry between one and six Pokémon in their active party; the first Pokémon in the lineup is automatically sent into battle when one begins.
Gameplay
In most Pokémon games, players aim to weaken wild Pokémon in battle to then throw a Poké Ball, which are used to capture the Pokémon and add it to the player's team or get sent to storage.
Gameplay
Certain Pokémon are only able to evolve by trading as well.
Development
The franchise began its ninth and current generation with Pokémon Scarlet and Violet, which were released worldwide for the Nintendo Switch on November 18, 2022.
1996–1998: First generation

Spin-off first-generation titles include Pokémon Pinball; an adaptation of the Pokémon Trading Card Game for Game Boy Color; an on-rails photography simulator for Nintendo 64 titled Pokémon Snap; a Nintendo 64 Pokémon -themed adaptation of Tetris Attack, Pokémon Puzzle League.
1996–1998: First generation
A 3D Nintendo 64 incarnation of the handhelds' battle system, Pokémon Stadium; and a co-starring role for several species in the Nintendo 64 fighting game Super Smash Bros..
1996–1998: First generation
At the Nintendo Space World in 2000, a game was revealed briefly with Meowth and Team Rocket singing a song.
1999–2001: Second generation

The second generation of Pokémon video games began in 1999 with the Japanese release of Pokémon Gold and Silver for the Game Boy Color, with Australia and North America getting the game in October 2000 and European release date of April 2001.
1999–2001: Second generation
This generation introduced 100 new species of Pokémon (starting with Chikorita and ending with Celebi), for a total of 251 Pokémon to collect, train, and battle.
1999–2001: Second generation
The Pokémon Mini is a handheld game console released in December 2001 in Japan and 2002 in Europe and North America.
2002–2005: Third generation
The third generation introduced 135 new Pokémon (starting with Treecko and ending with Deoxys) for a total of 386 species.
2002–2005: Third generation
Secret Bases can be found in bushes, trees, or small cave openings in landscapes by using the Pokémon move, Secret Power, which can be taught to virtually all Pokémon.
2002–2005: Third generation
It was around this time that the franchise was regaining its popularity, managing to ship over 100 million games worldwide.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
In 2006, Japan began the fourth generation of the franchise with the release of Pokémon Diamond and Pearl for Nintendo DS.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
The games were released in North America on April 22, 2007, and in Australia on June 21, 2007.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
The game was released in the UK and Europe on July 27, 2007.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
It was released for the Nintendo DS in Japan on September 13, 2008, in North America on March 22, 2009, and in Australia and Europe on May 14, 2009, and May 22, 2009, respectively.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
Released in Japan on September 12, 2009, the games were later released to North America, Australia, and Europe during March 2010.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
The fourth-generation introduces another 107 new species of Pokémon (starting with Turtwig and ending with Arceus), bringing the number of Pokémon species to 493.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
This generation is the first to have 3D graphics in the main series game, although it is still a mixture of both 3D graphics and sprites.
2006–2009: Fourth generation
Secret Bases also appear in Sinnoh but can only be created and housed in Sinnoh's underground.
2010–2012: Fifth generation
The fifth generation of Pokémon began on September 18, 2010, with the release of Pokémon Black and White in Japan.
2010–2012: Fifth generation
The other main series games, and the additions to Black and White, titled Pokémon Black 2 and White 2, are direct sequels.
2010–2012: Fifth generation
They take place in the Unova region two years later and were released in Japan on June 23, 2012, and in North America, Australia, and Europe in October of that year for Nintendo DS.
2010–2012: Fifth generation
This generation introduced a total of 156 new Pokémon (beginning with Victini and ending with Genesect), the most of any generation so far.
2010–2012: Fifth generation
It was also the first generation where the first new Pokémon in National Pokédex order (Victini) is not a starter.
2010–2012: Fifth generation

Spin-off fifth generation games include sequels Pokémon Rumble Blast and Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Gates to Infinity for Nintendo 3DS, PokéPark 2: Wonders Beyond for Wii, and Pokémon Rumble U for Wii U, a downloadable game.
2010–2012: Fifth generation
Various fifth generation Pokémon have appeared in Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U and Super Smash Bros.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On December 24, 2012, Japanese magazine Nintendo Dream posted a greetings card sent out by Game Freak.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
In the card, Junichi Masuda exclaimed that during 2013, they intend to further evolve the world of Pokémon.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On December 29, 2012, a new Pokémon Black 2 and White 2 commercial aired in Japan, and ending with a message, informing Pokémon fans that the latest news would be announced on January 8, 2013.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On January 4, 2013, both the Japanese and English Pokémon website confirmed that an announcement would be made on January 8.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On January 7, 2013, the Japanese website explained that the Nintendo president, Satoru Iwata would hold a 10-minute " Pokémon Direct " video conference to announce the big Pokémon news.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On January 8, 2013, Satoru Iwata announced the sixth generation of Pokémon, with the new paired games, Pokémon X and Y, which were released on the Nintendo 3DS on October 12, 2013, worldwide.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
The X and Y games are rendered in full 3D; however, only select parts of the game can be displayed in stereoscopic 3D.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
A month later, Sylveon (Japanese: Nymphia (ニンフィア, Ninfia)), a new evolved form of Eevee belonging to the games' new Fairy-type was revealed and is currently the last Eeveelution to be revealed.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On May 7, 2014, Nintendo revealed the games Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire in a teaser trailer, remakes of the third generation games Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
Greninja, the final evolved form of Froakie, would later go on to represent the sixth generation of Pokémon in the hit fighting game, Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
On August 26, 2014, Pokkén Tournament was announced and was released on July 16, 2015, in Japanese arcades and was released on March 18, 2016, worldwide for Wii U.
2013–2015: Sixth generation
In July 2016, Niantic and Nintendo released a free-to-play augmented reality game titled Pokémon Go which was released for Android and iOS devices.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
During a Nintendo Direct presentation on February 26, 2016, two new Pokémon titles were announced, titled Pokémon Sun and Moon.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
The games were released on the Nintendo 3DS on November 18, 2016, in Japan, North America, and Australia, and in Europe on November 23, 2016.
2016–2018: Seventh generation

The games were the first since the second generation to be backwards-compatible with other titles, including Pokémon X and Y; Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire; and the Virtual Console re-releases of Pokémon Red, Blue and Yellow.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
On June 6, 2017, Pokémon Ultra Sun and Ultra Moon were announced.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
The two games offer new additions to the story of Pokémon Sun and Moon, including new features, and was released worldwide on the Nintendo 3DS on November 17, 2017.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
On May 29, 2018, two new Pokémon games in the main Pokémon franchise, Pokémon: Let's Go, Pikachu! and Pokémon: Let's Go, Eevee!, were announced.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
They are remakes of Pokémon Yellow with gameplay mechanics borrowed from Pokémon Go and were released worldwide on the Nintendo Switch on November 16, 2018.
2016–2018: Seventh generation
In total, this generation introduced 88 new Pokémon, Alolan forms, trials, Z-moves, Poké Pelago, and Festival Plaza.
2019–2021: Eighth generation

During E3 2017, Nintendo and The Pokémon Company announced that Game Freak was developing a new core Pokémon role-playing game set to release for the Nintendo Switch in "2018 or later." The game is the eighth generation of Pokémon.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
Along with the announcement of Pokémon: Let's Go, Pikachu! and Pokémon: Let's Go, Eevee! it was confirmed that another core Pokémon role-playing game would be released in late 2019.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
It was clarified that the 2019 game was the one mentioned during E3 2017, not the Let's Go games.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
On February 27, 2019, on the 23rd anniversary of the franchise, Pokémon Sword and Shield were confirmed for Nintendo Switch, which were released worldwide on November 15, 2019.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
On January 9, 2020, two expansion packs titled The Isle of Armor and The Crown Tundra were announced.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
The Isle of Armor was released on June 17, 2020, and The Crown Tundra was released on October 22, 2020.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
On February 26, 2021, Brilliant Diamond and Shining Pearl were announced, remakes of the fourth generation games Pokémon Diamond and Pearl developed by ILCA and set to release later that year.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
Brilliant Diamond and Shining Pearl were released on November 19, 2021, while Pokémon Legends: Arceus was released on January 28, 2022.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
This generation introduced a total of 96 new Pokémon with 81 revealed in Sword and Shield, 8 revealed in the expansion packs, and 7 revealed in Pokémon Legends: Arceus.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
On March 6, 2020, the remake of the Mystery Dungeon, Red and Blue Rescue Team was released titled Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Rescue Team DX.
2019–2021: Eighth generation
On November 26, 2020, at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade, Pokémon teased its 2021 25th anniversary logo and details for its special celebration "soon".
2022–present: Ninth generation
On February 27, 2022, Pokémon Scarlet and Violet were announced for the Nintendo Switch, with a late 2022 release date.
2022–present: Ninth generation
The games were released on November 18, 2022.
2022–present: Ninth generation
On February 27, 2023, a two-part expansion pack was announced titled The Hidden Treasure of Area Zero.
2022–present: Ninth generation
Part One, The Teal Mask, was released on September 13, 2023.
2022–present: Ninth generation
Part Two, The Indigo Disk, was released on December 14, 2023.
2022–present: Ninth generation
An epilogue, Mochi Mayhem, was released on January 11, 2024.
2022–present: Ninth generation
On February 27, 2024, Pokémon Legends: Z-A was announced to have a 2025 release on the Nintendo Switch.
Other games
Pokémon are also in Mario Artist: Paint Studio for Nintendo 64DD as pasteable stickers, and they also appear in Picross NP Vol.
Super Smash Bros. series
Pikachu and Jigglypuff are introduced in Super Smash Bros. for the Nintendo 64, and appear in every installment of the franchise.
Super Smash Bros. series

Brawl for the Wii, Mewtwo and Pichu are not featured as playable characters, although Squirtle, Ivysaur, and Charizard make their first playable appearances as part of the Pokémon Trainer character, while Lucario appears as a separate character.
Super Smash Bros. series
Greninja made its first appearance in Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U, Charizard is a standalone character, and Mewtwo returns as a downloadable content character.
Reception
After the first five months of release, the Game Boy games sold almost 3 million copies.
Reception

The series has sold over 279 million units (inclusive of spin-off titles; 210 million for the mainline Pokémon games) as of February 29, 2016, giving it the distinction of being one of the best-selling video game series in history.
Reception

Guinness World Records awarded the Pokémon series eight records in Guinness World Records: Gamer's Edition 2008, including "Most Successful RPG Series of All Time", "Game Series With the Most Spin-Off Movies" and "Most Photosensitive Epileptic Seizures Caused by a TV Show".
Reception
As of March 2022, the series has sold over 440 million units.
Reception
The anime series has run for over 900 episodes, accompanied by 19 feature films, with a twentieth in production.
Reception
The trading card game and its expansion sets have grown to around 3,000 unique cards in total, and continue to draw a healthy player base to its official international tournaments.
Reception
The extent of global toy and merchandise sales since 1996 cover broad markets and high quantities.
Reception

IGN ranked Pokémon as the 17th greatest desired game series: "the basic gameplay premise boasts solid, addictive play mechanics, and several of the handheld RPGs deserve to be in every gamer's collection.
Reception
1 Nintendo game "not made by Nintendo", stating that having to catch each Pokémon made the games addictive.

pboy_pocket_critters_gold.title: Pokémon Gold and Silver
sents: lead
Pokémon Gold Version and Pokémon Silver Version are 1999 role-playing video games developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Color.
lead
They are the first installments in the second generation of the Pokémon video game series.
lead
They were released in Japan in 1999, Australia and North America in 2000, and Europe in 2001.
lead
The games introduce 100 new species of Pokémon and follow the progress of the player character in their quest to master Pokémon battling.
lead

Both games are independent of each other but feature largely the same plot and, while both can be played separately, it is necessary to trade between these games and their predecessors in order to fully complete each games' Pokédex.
lead
The Johto Saga of the Pokémon anime is based on the new region introduced in the games.
lead
A third game in the generation, Pokémon Crystal, was released in 2001.
lead
Pokémon Gold and Silver were critically acclaimed upon release.
New features
Trainers will call for a rematch and others will call about rare Pokémon that can be caught in a certain area.
New features

In addition, there is the possibility of encountering a shiny Pokémon, which have a different coloration than normal Pokémon of their species, and appear very rarely, around 1 in 8192 for games until Pokémon X and Y.
New features
In Gold and Silver, new moves were added, but Pokémon knowing these moves are not allowed to be traded to the first generation games.
Setting
The design of Johto was inspired by Japan's Kansai and Tōkai regions, with many of the region's temples and more traditional Japanese aesthetics finding their way into Johto.
Story
For example, Cinnabar Island has been almost completely taken over by a volcano eruption; only a Pokémon Center remains.
Story
Silver's caves is Red, the protagonist of Red and Blue, whom the player can challenge for the most difficult final battle in the game.
Development
Gold and Silver were first publicly showcased at November 1997, Nintendo Space World Expo in Japan, becoming the most popular exhibit at the program.
Development
In the same vein as the Pokémon Mew of Red and Blue, the exclusive Pokémon Celebi was included in the Gold and Silver games but is only accessible after attending a Nintendo promotional event.
Development
The first official event offering Celebi was Nintendo Space World 2000 in Japan, in which 100,000 attendees would be awarded the rare Pokémon.
Development
In order to be selected, players had to send in a postcard to enter a lottery for one of 100,000 certificates of Celebi, allowing them to enter the event and obtain it.
Development
The original intention was to release the game in 1998, even synchronizing with the supposed end of the anime 's first season.
Development

Development issues, worsened by Game Freak being sidetracked with Pokémon Stadium and the localization of the first generation, led the game to be postponed, and the original release slate was taken over by Pokémon Yellow.
Development
Programmer Shigeki Morimoto stated that part of why development took three and a half years was due to being a small team of only four programmers.
Unused and cut content

In 2018, ROM images of the early-in-development Japanese-language demo shown during the 1997 Nintendo Space World presentation resurfaced: two debug versions of the games, and two versions that were modified to work on normal Game Boy hardware and most emulators.
Unused and cut content
These ROM images were only rumored to exist until they were anonymously posted on the " Pokémon Reverse Engineering Tools" (PRET) Discord server in May 2018.
Unused and cut content
The ROMs were first released anonymously onto 4chan 's /vp/ board in May, with a formal The Cutting Room Floor release coming later that day.
Unused and cut content
Earlier in May 2018, Pokémon artist Atsuko Nishida revealed that the popular creature Pikachu was originally supposed to have a third evolution, named "Gorochu".
Release
In September 1999, the games were announced for release in Japan on November 21, 1999, and a North American release date was estimated for September 2000.
Release
Pocket Pikachu Color was slated for release in Japan on November 21, 1999, the same day as the release of Gold and Silver.
Release
In addition, an officially licensed Pikachu -themed Game Link Cable developed by Kemco was set for release in Japan on November 18, 1999.
Release

Anticipating high sales, Nintendo set its first production shipment for the games in Japan at three million, predicting that eventually more than eight million copies would be sold in the country alone.
Release
As a precursor to the North American release, Gold and Silver were displayed for audiences to interact with at the 2000 American International Toy Fair in New York City.
Release
The localized English names of the 100 new Pokémon were kept confidential by Nintendo, with the company releasing names periodically.
Release
In September 1999, Nintendo announced that Gold and Silver would be released in North America in September 2000.
Release
In May 2000, Nintendo announced the official North American release date of Gold and Silver would instead be October 16 of that year.
Release
The games had record pre-order sales — approximately 600,000 copies of the games were pre-ordered in just two months, compared to 150,000 copies for Pokémon Yellow.
Release

As the release date neared and retailers began to receive shipments of the games, some retailers—such as Electronics Boutique —opted to sell them immediately upon receiving the games; first using them to fulfill pre-orders, and then selling the remaining copies to walk-in customers.
Release
The games were reportedly obtainable as early as October 11.
Release
The games were released in Australia on October 13, 2000 and in Europe on April 6, 2001.
Pokémon Crystal
It was released in Japan on December 14, 2000, North America on July 29, 2001, and in Europe on November 2, 2001.
Pokémon Crystal
Pokémon Crystal has sold nearly 6.4 million units worldwide.
Nintendo 3DS re-release
In June 2017, The Pokémon Company announced via a Pokémon Direct broadcast that the games would be re-released worldwide via the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console on September 22, 2017.
Reception

Craig Harris of IGN gave the games a "masterful" 10 out of 10 rating, stating that: "As awesome as the original Pokémon edition was, Pokémon Gold and Silver blow it away in gameplay elements, features, and goodies.
Reception
There was particular praise given to the innovative internal clock feature, with Frank Povo of GameSpot, noting: "The first major addition to Pokémon GS is the presence of a time element...
Reception
There's a reason why Pokémon is so popular, and Pokémon Gold and Silver is going to help the series move further into the 21st century", said Harris.
Sales
Pokémon Gold and Silver continued the enormous success of Pokémon Red and Blue, beginning the formation of Pokémon into a multi-billion dollar franchise.
Sales
Upon its first day of release in Japan, the game sold 1,425,768 units.
Sales
As of April 2000, roughly 6.5 million copies of the games had been sold in Japan.
Sales
Silver proved to be the slightly more popular version, edging out Gold by approximately 100,000 copies.
Sales
In the U.S., the game generated 1 million pre-sales about three weeks before release.
Sales

Upon the first week of release in the U.S., the games had eclipsed Pokémon Yellow ' s previous record sales of a little over 600,000 copies; selling a combined total of 1.4 million copies to become the fastest-selling games ever.

lead
They are the first installments in the second generation of the Pokémon video game series.
lead
They were released in Japan in 1999, Australia and North America in 2000, and Europe in 2001.
lead
The games introduce 100 new species of Pokémon and follow the progress of the player character in their quest to master Pokémon battling.
lead

Both games are independent of each other but feature largely the same plot and, while both can be played separately, it is necessary to trade between these games and their predecessors in order to fully complete each games' Pokédex.
lead
The Johto Saga of the Pokémon anime is based on the new region introduced in the games.

Trainers will call for a rematch and others will call about rare Pokémon that can be caught in a certain area.

In addition, there is the possibility of encountering a shiny Pokémon, which have a different coloration than normal Pokémon of their species, and appear very rarely, around 1 in 8192 for games until Pokémon X and Y.

In Gold and Silver, new moves were added, but Pokémon knowing these moves are not allowed to be traded to the first generation games.
Setting
The design of Johto was inspired by Japan's Kansai and Tōkai regions, with many of the region's temples and more traditional Japanese aesthetics finding their way into Johto.

For example, Cinnabar Island has been almost completely taken over by a volcano eruption; only a Pokémon Center remains.

Silver's caves is Red, the protagonist of Red and Blue, whom the player can challenge for the most difficult final battle in the game.

In the same vein as the Pokémon Mew of Red and Blue, the exclusive Pokémon Celebi was included in the Gold and Silver games but is only accessible after attending a Nintendo promotional event.

In order to be selected, players had to send in a postcard to enter a lottery for one of 100,000 certificates of Celebi, allowing them to enter the event and obtain it.

The original intention was to release the game in 1998, even synchronizing with the supposed end of the anime 's first season.
Development

Development issues, worsened by Game Freak being sidetracked with Pokémon Stadium and the localization of the first generation, led the game to be postponed, and the original release slate was taken over by Pokémon Yellow.
Development
Programmer Shigeki Morimoto stated that part of why development took three and a half years was due to being a small team of only four programmers.
Unused and cut content

In 2018, ROM images of the early-in-development Japanese-language demo shown during the 1997 Nintendo Space World presentation resurfaced: two debug versions of the games, and two versions that were modified to work on normal Game Boy hardware and most emulators.

In addition, an officially licensed Pikachu -themed Game Link Cable developed by Kemco was set for release in Japan on November 18, 1999.

Anticipating high sales, Nintendo set its first production shipment for the games in Japan at three million, predicting that eventually more than eight million copies would be sold in the country alone.

As a precursor to the North American release, Gold and Silver were displayed for audiences to interact with at the 2000 American International Toy Fair in New York City.
