pba_fire_emblum.title: Fire Emblem

First release: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light April 20, 1990

sents: lead
Fire Emblem is a Japanese fantasy tactical role-playing game franchise developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo.
lead
First produced and published for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1990, the series currently consists of seventeen core entries and five spinoffs.
lead
The core gameplay revolves around discrete battles between the player's team of characters and enemy non-player characters across grid-based maps.
lead
The player and enemy each take turns moving their characters across the map and having them perform combat-based actions.
lead
The games also feature a story and characters similar to traditional role-playing video games, and occasionally social simulation aspects as well.
lead

A notable aspect of gameplay is the permanent death of characters in battle, rendering them unusable upon being defeated, although this aspect of the game can be turned off starting from Fire Emblem: New Mystery of the Emblem onwards.
lead
The series' title refers to the "Fire Emblem", a recurring element usually portrayed as a royal weapon or shield representing the power of war and dragons.
lead
The development of the first game began as a dōjin project by Shouzou Kaga and three other developers, and its success prompted the development of further games in the series.
Gameplay
Each character has a specific character class which gives them set abilities and affects how far they can move across the field; some classes have innate skills unique to them.
Gameplay
During a battle, a character gains experience points by performing actions, such as attacking an enemy, healing an ally, or slaying a foe, which typically offers the most experience points.
Gameplay
Most games use a Weapon Durability system: after being used a certain number of times, a character's weapon will break.
Story and themes
The continents of Archanea and Valentia are the settings of Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, Gaiden, Mystery of the Emblem, and Awakening, and were the planned setting for Fire Emblem 64.
Story and themes
Genealogy of the Holy War and Thracia 776 are set in Jugdral, which is distantly connected with Archanea and Valentia, while The Blazing Blade and The Binding Blade take place in Elibe.
Story and themes

In Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light and other games set in Archanea, it is a shield inset with five magical gems named after its connection to dragons and weapons of war, being the "emblem of flame".
Development and history

The first Fire Emblem game, Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, was originally never intended as a commercial game, defined by creator Shouzou Kaga as a dōjin project with three other job-holding students.
Development and history
Kaga worked on the Fire Emblem series until Thracia 776, when he left Nintendo and began development on Tear Ring Saga for the PlayStation.
Development and history
After Thracia 776, the Fire Emblem series had several releases on portable devices.
Development and history
In 2001, Marth and Roy, from Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light and The Binding Blade respectively, appeared as playable characters in Super Smash Bros.
Development and history
By 2010, the series was suffering from declining sales and Nintendo told Intelligent Systems that if their next Fire Emblem failed to sell above 250,000 units, the series would be canceled.
Development and history

As the only music composer at Intelligent Systems when Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light was in production, she acted as both composer and sound director, up until Thracia 776, when she left the company to become a freelancer after completing the score for Paper Mario.
Development and history
Katsuyoshi, who was unsatisfied with his work on the series, stepped down for Thracia 776.
Development and history
The designer for Thracia 776 was Mayumi Hirota, whose brief tenure with the series ended when she left Intelligent Systems with Kaga after the game's completion.
Main series
The first entry in the series, Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, was released in 1990 for the Japanese Famicom.
Main series
A second game for the Famicom, Fire Emblem Gaiden, was released in 1992.
Main series
In 1994, Mystery of the Emblem was released for the Super Famicom, containing both a remake of Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light and a sequel of the first game.
Main series
Two more games were released for the Super Famicom in 1996 and 1999 respectively: Genealogy of the Holy War and Thracia 776.
Main series
The next entry released was The Binding Blade in 2002 for the Game Boy Advance.
Main series
It was released overseas under the title Fire Emblem in 2003 in North America and 2004 in Europe, becoming the first official release of the Fire Emblem series in these regions.
Main series
Melee for the Gamecube in 2001, and the earlier release (and success) of Advance Wars in the West, prompting Intelligent Systems and Nintendo to finally release Fire Emblem in the West.
Main series
The final entry for the Game Boy Advance, The Sacred Stones, was released in 2004 in Japan, and in 2005 in North America and Europe.
Main series
The ninth installment in the series, Path of Radiance, was released worldwide on the GameCube in 2005.
Main series
It was the first Fire Emblem game to feature 3D graphics, voice acting, and full-motion animated cutscenes.
Main series
A direct sequel to Path of Radiance, Radiant Dawn was released for the Wii in 2007 in Japan and North America, and 2008 in Europe.
Main series
In 2008, the series returned to handheld systems with two releases for the Nintendo DS.
Main series
Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon, an expanded remake of the first game, was released in 2008 in Japan and Europe, and 2009 in North America.
Main series
Shadow Dragon makes use of unique DS features unavailable to the Famicom and introduced new characters, added additional story elements, revamped mechanics, and modernized graphics.
Main series
A Japanese-only entry, New Mystery of the Emblem, was released in 2010 for the DS as an expanded remake of Mystery of the Emblem.
Main series
The series moved to the Nintendo 3DS with Fire Emblem Awakening, the thirteenth game in the series, released in 2012 in Japan and 2013 in North America and Europe.
Main series
The second entry for the Nintendo 3DS, Fates, was released in June 2015 in Japan, February 2016 in North America, and in May 2016 for Europe and Australia.
Main series
A third entry, Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia, was released on the Nintendo 3DS in April 2017 in Japan and in North America and Europe the following month.
Main series
Echoes is an enhanced remake of Gaiden, maintaining many of the unique features of Gaiden while revamping the graphics and script, and adding several ease-of-play improvements.
Main series
A Fire Emblem game was announced for the Nintendo Switch during a Fire Emblem focused Nintendo Direct in January 2017.
Main series
The game was officially revealed as Fire Emblem: Three Houses during the Nintendo Direct presentation at E3 2018, and was released in July 2019.
Main series
Fire Emblem Engage, a second entry for Nintendo Switch, was announced during a September 2022 Nintendo Direct and released in January 2023.
Spin-offs and cameos
In 1997, an episodic prequel to Mystery of the Emblem titled BS Fire Emblem: Archanea Senki-hen was released through Satellaview.
Spin-offs and cameos
A crossover with the Shin Megami Tensei series, Tokyo Mirage Sessions ♯FE, was released in December 2015 in Japan and worldwide in June 2016 for the Wii U.
Spin-offs and cameos
On January 17, 2020, an enhanced version titled Tokyo Mirage Sessions ♯FE Encore was released on Nintendo Switch.
Spin-offs and cameos
Fire Emblem Heroes is a spin-off gacha game for Android and iOS, and was released in February 2017 for mobile devices.
Spin-offs and cameos
A crossover with the Dynasty Warriors series, Fire Emblem Warriors, was released for the New Nintendo 3DS and Nintendo Switch in 2017.
Spin-offs and cameos
A second Warriors game, based on Three Houses, and titled Fire Emblem Warriors: Three Hopes was announced in a Nintendo Direct on February 9, 2022 and released on June 24, 2022.
Cancelled games
A Fire Emblem game was initially in development for the Nintendo 64 and its peripheral 64DD.
Cancelled games
Originally codenamed Fire Emblem 64, it was first revealed by Shigeru Miyamoto in 1997.
Cancelled games

Ultimately, due to poor sales for the 64DD and internal structural changes at Intelligent Systems, Fire Emblem 64 was cancelled in 2000 and development shifted to what would become Fire Emblem: The Binding Blade.
Cancelled games
Work done for Fire Emblem 64 was incorporated into The Binding Blade.
Cancelled games

An additional RTS-based game for the Wii was planned and would have been released after Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn, but after trial and error and an unfocused development schedule, the project was cancelled.
Cancelled games
Intelligent Systems never planned a Fire Emblem game for the Wii U.
Cancelled games
Nintendo producer Hitoshi Yamagami said such a game would need to sell 700,000 copies to be profitable.
Cancelled games
A rumored Fire Emblem remake for the Nintendo 3DS was being developed by AlphaDream, but was cancelled following the company's bankruptcy surfaced in late 2019.
Cancelled games

According to the reports, it was one of the many video games that had been in development, but were ultimately scrapped for the platform, with many speculating those projects could be moved to the Nintendo Switch.
Reception
Sales in Japan were the highest with Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light but progressively declined with future games, which sold 329,087; 324,699; 776,338; 498,216 and 106,108 copies respectively.
Reception
As of 2002, total sales had reached over two million copies.
Reception
Awakening topped the total sales of both Radiant Dawn and the Mystery of the Emblem remake in its first week.
Reception
It went on to sell 2.35 million copies worldwide and become the best-selling Fire Emblem game in Western territories at the time.
Reception
In 2007, a Japanese public poll named Mystery of the Emblem as one of the country's All Time Top 100 video games.
Reception

In 2014, Destructoid writer Chris Carter praised the series' mechanics, and at the same time chose Mystery of the Emblem, Path of Radiance, and Awakening in his list of the five best games in the series.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
The game bore multiple similarities to the Fire Emblem series, and Nintendo filed a lawsuit against Tirnanog for copyright infringement.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
The first suit failed, and the court ruled in Tirnanog's favor.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
Nintendo filed a second lawsuit, and this time was awarded a cash settlement of ¥76 million.
Tear Ring Saga lawsuit
Nintendo attempted taking a third lawsuit to the Japanese Supreme Court in 2005, but the second ruling was upheld.
In other media
A short, two episode original video animation series based on Mystery of the Emblem released in 1996.
In other media
These anime episodes were released in North America in 1998, five years before The Blazing Blade was localized, making them the first official Fire Emblem media to be released in the region.
In other media

Two trading card games have been made with the Fire Emblem franchise: Fire Emblem: Trading Card Game, which was released from 2001 – 2006, and Fire Emblem 0 (Cipher), which was released in 2015 and was discontinued in late 2020 with the twenty second expansion pack being the last one.

pba_fire_emblum_the_sacred_stone.title: Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones

Director(s): Sachiko Wada Taiki Ubukata Kentaro Nishimura
Composer(s): Yoshihiko Kitamura Saki Haruyama Yoshito Hirano

sents: lead

Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones is a tactical role-playing game developed by Intelligent Systems, and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance handheld video game console in 2004 for Japan and 2005 in the West.
lead

It is the eighth entry in the Fire Emblem series, the second to be released outside Japan, and the third and final title to be developed for the Game Boy Advance after The Binding Blade and its prequel Fire Emblem.
lead

Set in a separate continuity to earlier Fire Emblem titles, The Sacred Stones takes place on the fictional continent of Magvel, which is divided into five nations, each built around a magical stone said to be linked to the imprisonment of an ancient demon.
lead

When one of the five nations, the Grado Empire, invades its neighbors and begins destroying the stones, protagonists Eirika and Ephraim of the royal family of Renais set out to gather allies and halt Grado's conquest, while also trying to uncover the reasons for the war.
lead
The gameplay is similar to previous Fire Emblem games, focusing on turn-based, tactical movement of units across a grid-based battlefield.
lead
Core features of the game include permanent death for characters defeated in battle and support conversations that grant advantages to certain units in battle.
lead

The Sacred Stones began development alongside Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance as a side project, sharing much of its visual design and mechanics with Fire Emblem while incorporating elements from earlier entries such as Fire Emblem Gaiden.
lead
First announced in mid-2004, it was heavily promoted in Japan.
Gameplay
Each time a unit earns 100 experience points, that unit will gain a level and some of their stats will randomly increase.
Gameplay
After a character has leveled up to 10, they have the option to be evolved using a class-specific item.
Gameplay
In each battle, the player is given command of a limited number of units and an objective to complete.
Gameplay
Different weapons also feature a minimum skill level for use, requiring units to train with that weapon type to earn the proper rank, which ranges from E to A, and then to S, the highest rank.
Gameplay
Victory goes to the last group standing or to the party with the highest score depending on the match conditions.
Synopsis
The Stones were used to seal away the soul of the Demon King Fomortiis at the end of a conflict between humans and monsters over 800 years ago.
Synopsis
The game begins when the Grado Empire, largest of the five founding nations, launches an unexpected assault on the neighboring nation of Renais, home of the royal siblings Eirika and Ephraim.
Synopsis
Eirika is forced to reach the allied nation of Rausten by passing through the new republic of Carcino, the sixth nation, and secret ally of Grado.
Synopsis
Lyon under the influence of the Demon King, declares that he will once more rule Magvel once the Stones are destroyed.
Synopsis
The twins manage to escape and retrieve the last intact Sacred Stone from Rausten.
Development and release
According to staff, development began unexpectedly in 2003 alongside Path of Radiance: the staff thought they would not be developing another entry for the Game Boy Advance.
Development and release
Some of its gameplay mechanics were borrowed from the 1992 entry Fire Emblem Gaiden, along with other unspecified mechanics from the Super Famicom entries.
Development and release

The Sacred Stones would be the last Fire Emblem game to be developed for the Game Boy Advance, along with being the last original Fire Emblem on handheld devices until Fire Emblem Awakening in 2012 for Nintendo 3DS.
Development and release
The Sacred Stones was first announced in Japan in June 2004, scheduled for release in Autumn that year.
Development and release
Two guidebooks were also published focusing on the game, the first on October 21 and the second on November 17.
Development and release
A Western release was first hinted at in a Nintendo report, revealing its prospective release of both Path of Radiance and what would turn out to be The Sacred Stones.
Development and release
It was released in 2005 in North America, Australia, and Europe on May 23, November 3, and November 4, respectively.
Development and release
The move from the first Western game to The Sacred Stones and Path of Radiance meant that any work on localizing The Binding Blade could not be managed.
Development and release
The title was later re-released as part of Nintendo's promotional "3DS Ambassador Program" as a free download on December 16, 2011.
Development and release
It was later re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console: it was released in Japan on August 6, 2014, the PAL regions on January 1, 2015, and in North America on June 18 the same year.
Reception
Upon its day of release in Japan, The Sacred Stones sold 97,842 units, achieving a sell-through rate of just over 64%.
Reception
By the end of 2004, the game had sold 233,280 units, reaching #48 in Famitsu ' s annual video game sales rankings.
Reception
In North America, The Sacred Stones was among the top 20 games in the Nintendo hardware charts, with sales of 96,000 units.
Reception
Although no exact total sales figures have been published, Nintendo cited the game as being among its successful Game Boy Advance titles for 2005.
Reception
Karen Chu of 1UP.com said the story shone through, keeping players from burning out after the battle segments.
Reception
Foster called the gameplay the game's biggest feature and greatest strength despite not having changed much since the previous game.
Reception

Parkin stated that it was quite easy to spend large amounts of time creating the perfect strategy, and that restarting a level after a character died or going to one of the EXP maps to boost character levels was extremely tempting.

pba_golden_son.title: Golden Sun (video game)
sents: lead
Golden Sun is a role-playing video game developed by Camelot Software Planning and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.
lead
It was released in August 2001 in Japan, November 2001 in North America and February 2002 in Europe.
lead
Golden Sun ' s story follows a band of magic-attuned teenagers called Adepts on a mission to protect the world of Weyard from alchemy, a potentially destructive power that was sealed away long ago.
lead
During their quest, the Adepts develop new magic abilities called Psynergy, assist others, and learn more about why alchemy was sealed away.
lead
Golden Sun is followed by a sequel, The Lost Age, which together form a complete story.
lead
Golden Sun began as a single planned game for the Nintendo 64, but production shifted to the Game Boy Advance over the course of development.
lead
After facing hardware constraints, the developers decided to split the game into two.
lead
Golden Sun was critically and commercially successful, being the top-selling game for four months in Japan and selling more than one million units worldwide.
Gameplay
During combat, the camera shifts to a pseudo- 3D view, spinning and zooming depending on the attacks and items used.
Gameplay
The player receives a "Game Over" if each character's hit points are reduced to zero; if this happens, the player loses money and the party is returned to the sanctum in the last visited town.
Gameplay
There are 28 Djinn in Golden Sun, seven for each of the four elements.
Plot
The keys to unlocking alchemy are four elemental stars hidden within the mountain shrine, Mt.
Development
Camelot originally planned to create a single game instead of a series, and in the early stages of the project created a game design document for Golden Sun on the Nintendo 64 console.
Development
When it became apparent the Nintendo 64 was being replaced by the GameCube, Camelot shifted their focus to making a game on the handheld Game Boy Advance.
Development

A major goal with Golden Sun was to make the game's magic usable outside battle for puzzles, and offer players a high level of freedom in how to approach events, rather than a linear story that could only be experienced one way.
Development
In August 2000, Camelot showed an early but playable version at the Nintendo Space World Expo in Japan.
Development
The game was intended to launch alongside the Game Boy Advance, but slipped to the summer and released in Japan in August 2001.
Development

While it was eagerly anticipated in the west, players had to make do with Japanese-language imports until the game was localized and released in North America in November, and Europe in February 2002.
Reception
Craig Harris of IGN said that Golden Sun was arguably one of the best 2D-based Japanese RPGs ever.
Reception

Rick Moulton of GamesRadar+ hailed the game as "the best handheld role-player ever", while G4 TV 's Miguel Concepcion and Game Informer ' s Andy McNamara called it the best original RPG on the GameBoy Advance.
Reception
Harris called the game the most graphically-impressive on the system, and that the sound surpassed that of the Super Nintendo's capabilities.
Reception
Ricardo Torres, writing for GameSpot, considered the only mark against the combat that if an enemy was defeated, player characters would not automatically retarget the remaining foes.
Reception
Golden Sun won "Handheld Game of the Year" at the 2002 Golden Joystick Awards.
Reception
During the 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Golden Sun in the " Hand-Held Game of the Year " and " Console Role-Playing " categories.
Reception
Golden Sun was ranked 94 on IGN ' s Readers Choice Top 100 games ever.
Reception
The publication later named the title the 24th-best Game Boy Advance game of all time.
Reception
It was rated the 31st best game made on a Nintendo system in Nintendo Power ' s Top 200 Games list.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.
Reception
Golden Sun was a commercial success, and sold 740,000 copies in the United States and another 338,000 in Japan.
Reception
It was followed by Golden Sun: The Lost Age in 2002, and Golden Sun: Dark Dawn in 2010.
Reception
Golden Sun was re-released for the Virtual Console via the Wii U eShop in April 2014, and was released for the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in January 2024.

pba_golden_son_the_lost_age.title: Golden Sun: The Lost Age
sents: lead
Golden Sun: The Lost Age is a 2002 role-playing video game for the Game Boy Advance, developed by Camelot Software Planning and published by Nintendo.
lead
It is the second installment in the Golden Sun series and was released on June 28, 2002 in Japan, and in 2003 in North America and Europe.
lead

Taking place after the events of the previous game, The Lost Age puts the player into the roles of the previous games' antagonists, primarily from the perspective of magic-attuned "adepts" Felix and his allies as they seek to restore the power of alchemy to the world of Weyard.
lead
Along the way, the player uses Psynergy to defeat enemies and discover new locations, help out local populations, and find elemental djinn which augment the characters' powers.
lead
Players can transfer their characters and items from Golden Sun to The Lost Age through a password system or Game Link Cable, and are rewarded for fully completing both games.
lead
Upon release, The Lost Age was positively received by critics and audiences.
lead
IGN ranked the game as the eighth-best Game Boy Advance title of 2003 and the 22nd-best GBA game of all time.
lead
It was eventually followed by a third installment, titled Dark Dawn, released in 2010 and set thirty years after the two original games.
Gameplay
Most gameplay outside of battle takes place either in the game's overworld or within dungeons, caves, and other locales with puzzles integrated into their layout.
Gameplay
Acquiring new Psynergy spells gives players access to new locations and secrets hidden within the game world.
Gameplay
Some types of Psynergy can only be used in either combat or in the overworld and non-battle scenarios.
Gameplay
With each "utility" Psynergy spell, the party gains access to more locations and secrets hidden within the game world.
Battle
While a battle being is conducted, the characters and background swirl around and change positions in a pseudo- 3D effect.
Battle
If all the player's characters are downed by reducing their hit points to zero, the party is returned to the last village that the player visited and loses money.
Battle
Successfully completing a battle yields experience points, coins, and occasionally rare items.
Djinn system
Not counting the ones that can only be found in the original Golden Sun, there are eleven Djinn for each of the four elements that can be allocated to each character.
Characters and setting
For most of the game, the player controls four characters.
Plot
When they reach the tower's top, the Wise One, the entity responsible for originally tasking Isaac to prevent the breaking of Alchemy's seal, confronts them.
Development and release
The Lost Age was first revealed to Japan in early 2002, with the magazine Famitsu being the first publication to review the game.
Development and release
The Lost Age was highly anticipated; it topped IGN 's list of Game Boy Advance "Most Wanted" games for 2003.
Development and release
The North American version of the game was playable at Electronic Entertainment Expo 2002.
Reception
On Metacritic, The Lost Age has an 86% aggregate rating, compared to Golden Sun's 91%.
Reception
Likewise, GameRankings gives The Lost Age an 87% overall rating, slightly lower than Golden Sun's 90%.
Reception
Conversely, The Lost Age was ranked 78 on IGN 's Readers Choice Top 100 games ever, higher than its predecessor.
Reception
It was also rated the 69th best game made on a Nintendo System in Nintendo Power 's "Top 200 Games" list.
Reception
IGN gave the sequel high praise; while most of the game mechanics remained unchanged, the addition of more complicated puzzles was welcomed.
Reception
The Lost Age subsequently became IGN's "Game of the Month" in April 2003.
Reception
The publication later named The Lost Age the best Game Boy Advance game of April 2003.
Reception
Ethan Einhorn of GameNOW felt that the only elements that set the fighting system above "typical RPG fare" were the graphics.
Reception
The Lost Age sold 96,000 units in its first week in Japan, being the best-selling game of the period.
Reception
The game sold a total of 249,000 copies in Japan and 437,000 in North America by November 21, 2004.

pba_advanced_wars.title: Advance Wars
sents: lead
Advance Wars is a turn-based strategy video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.
lead
It is the seventh title in the Wars series of video games, and the first in the Advance Wars sub-series.
lead
The game takes place on a fictional continent, where two nations, Orange Star and Blue Moon, have been fighting each other for years.
lead

The conflict enters a new stage when an Orange Star commanding officer named Andy is accused of attacking the armies of two other nations, Yellow Comet and Green Earth, without reason, resulting in a worldwide war.
lead

As with previous Wars titles, Advance Wars was not originally intended for release outside Japan, due to Nintendo feeling that Western consumers would not be interested in turn-based games because of their complex mechanics.
lead
In order to alleviate this, the developers made the mechanics easy to understand, adding in an in-depth tutorial that did not require players to read the manual.
lead

Designer Kentaro Nishimura commented that the game's success shifted Nintendo's attitude over Western tastes, and that same success is frequently credited as a driving force for Nintendo bringing another Intelligent Systems franchise, Fire Emblem, outside of Japan beginning with the seventh installment.
lead
Advance Wars was released in North America on September 10, 2001.
Gameplay
The "Campaign" and "War Room" modes both help to rank the player up (from Rank #100 to Rank #1) and to earn coins to unlock COs and maps in the "Battle Maps" shop.
Battle system
All units are limited in the types of units they can attack.
Battle system

For example, the Mech unit has a bazooka that can only be fired at land vehicles, but are more powerful for that purpose than their secondary weapons, machine guns, which Mechs can use against other Mechs, infantry, and helicopters.
Battle system
The majority of units have main weapons with a limited supply of ammunition, with the amount of ammo depending on the type of unit.
Units
There are 18 different types of military units in Advance Wars.
Units

One rule of thumb that units have to adhere to is that a portion of their fuel supply is used up each turn; ground units who run out cannot move, while air and naval units who run out are destroyed as they consume fuel even when stationary.
Multiplayer
In Versus mode, only one GBA system is used, which every participant in the game uses.
Commanding officers

Most COs provide units with innate special advantages and disadvantages, such as extra firepower, greater strength, or a shorter firing range, with some COs being better with specific units (e.g. being better with air units than naval units).
Plot

Starting with having only one choice of a CO to advise, Andy, the player will have a choice of two more Orange Star COs, Max and Sami, to advise as the story progresses, each with their own advantages and disadvantages.
Development
Advance Wars was first announced at Nintendo Space World 2000 under the name Game Boy Wars Advance.
Development
In January 2001, Nintendo France gave new screenshots from this and other Game Boy Advance games to French gaming sites with little other information.
Development
Four player mode was confirmed before E3 2001 and with it a US release date of September 10.
Development

Game Boy Wars Advance was originally scheduled for an October 12, 2001 release in Japan, but it was canceled in order to avoid competition with Game Boy Wars 3 (released for the Game Boy Color that same year).
Development
It was eventually released in a two-in-one compilation in 2004 with its sequel, Game Boy Wars Advance 2.
Development

Director Makoto Shimojo commented that the early stages of development often feature Intelligent Systems coming up with unique game mechanics for it, and upon presenting to Nintendo, typically being told that it was "too sophisticated" or "not balanced for a general audience".
Development

Shimojo commented that once he became more astute at the game, it became hard for him to judge what it would be like for a novice to play, though he comments that his goal is to ensure that the difficulty level is right enough to allow the largest number of people to play it.
Development

Advance Wars was originally intended to remain exclusive to Japan, like the previous entries in the series, which were kept in Japan due to Nintendo feeling that consumers would not be interested in turn-based games, or in such complicated games.
Virtual Console
The game was released on the Wii U Virtual Console on April 3, 2014, in North America and Europe.
Virtual Console
In Japan, the compilation which includes both Advance Wars and Advance Wars 2: Black Hole Rising games were released on the same day.
Reception
Upon release, the game received a score of 92/100 according to the review aggregation website Metacritic, indicating "universal acclaim".
Reception
It was rated the 26th best game made on a Nintendo System in Nintendo Power ' s Top 200 Games list.
Reception
Nintendo Power awarded the game a perfect 5 star rating, stating that " Advance Wars treads on new ground, taking the strategy genre to a place where gamers of all tastes will be gung-ho for it".
Reception
Gaming Age wrote: "There is a perfect blend of simplicity and complexity that makes this game so highly addictive".
Reception
GameSpot named Advance Wars the best Game Boy Advance game of 2001.
Reception
It was nominated for the publication's annual "Biggest Surprise" prize among console games, but lost to Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty.
Reception
During the 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences awarded Advance Wars with " Hand-Held Game of the Year ".
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine called the game "an almost faultless blend of fiendish strategy and Nintendo magic", placing it 72nd on a list of greatest Nintendo games.
Reception
In their October 2013 issue, Edge retroactively awarded the game ten out of ten, one of only twenty-three games to achieve that perfect score in the magazine's twenty-year history.

pba_advanced_wars_2_black_hole_r.title: Advance Wars 2: Black Hole Rising

Writer(s): Masayuki Horikawa Kouhei Maeda Makoto Shimojo

sents: lead
Advance Wars 2: Black Hole Rising is a turn-based strategy video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.
lead
It was released in North America and PAL regions in 2003.
lead
It is the second game in the Advance Wars sub-series of Nintendo Wars.
lead
It is preceded by Advance Wars and followed by Advance Wars: Dual Strike.
lead

Despite being developed in the region, the original Japanese release was canceled, but the game was later released in the region alongside the original Advance Wars as part of a compilation cartridge called Game Boy Wars Advance 1+2 in 2004.
lead
The game was released on the Wii U 's Virtual Console in North America and Europe in 2015.
lead

At E3 2021, Nintendo announced that Black Hole Rising, alongside the original Advance Wars, would be remade and released together for the Nintendo Switch by WayForward in another compilation titled Advance Wars 1+2: Re-Boot Camp.
lead
Black Hole Rising is nearly identical to the previous game in terms of core gameplay; there was only a small change in overall graphical style and some small content additions.
New features
Black Hole Rising is nearly identical to the previous game in terms of core gameplay; the only additions were to the overall content of the game.
New features

Many new maps were added for Versus mode and War Room, although most of the new maps and commanding officers are not available for use at the start of the game, and must be purchased from the in-game shop after certain conditions are met.
New features
Only one new unit, the Neotank, was added to the original set in Advance Wars.
New features
The Missile Silo can be fired by foot troops to deal area of effect damage, and pipelines act as impassable walls.
New features
Along with the two terrain features, various new special Black Hole buildings were also introduced in Black Hole Rising, although they are only found in the game's campaign.
New features
When units attack the property, the number decreases; when it reaches zero, the property is destroyed.
New features
The CO Power, introduced in Advance Wars, was a special ability unique to each commanding officer that could be triggered as the commanding officer's CO Meter filled by battle.
Plot
The Death Ray is eventually destroyed by the COs of the Allied Nations, who manage to disarm the missile and corner Sturm.
Development
It was originally announced in January 2003 under the title Advance Wars 2 to be released in North America in June of that year.
Development
As Advance Wars was not released in Japan, Black Hole Rising was also unreleased in Japan, despite the fact the games were developed there.
Development

Later, before the launch of Advance Wars: Dual Strike, the games were released in Japan on a single cartridge, Game Boy Wars Advance 1+2 for the Game Boy Advance as well as the GBA game for the Wii U Virtual Console, which contained both of the games.
Development
When a demo of the game was released at E3, it was clear that the gameplay would stay nearly identical to its predecessor Advance Wars, though new content would be added.
Development
IGN journalist Craig Harris commented after E3 2003 that " Black Hole Rising doesn't have an overwhelming sense of newness".
Reception
GameSpot said: "No GBA owner should be without it, and anyone getting their hands on a new GBA for the first time should make playing Advance Wars 2 one of their first orders of business".
Reception
The publication later named it the best Game Boy Advance game of June 2003.
Reception

1Up.com praised the core gameplay of the series, stating that "The game has changed just enough to please loyal fans, and when you've got a formula that makes for such a compelling gaming experience, why mess with it?"
Reception
GameSpot commented that one could "cynically call it a rehash", and IGN stated that "the number 2 in the title honestly doesn't deserve to be there".
Reception
Eurogamer had similar comments about the game, claiming "it's a classic, but it's so obviously a £35 mission pack, and is probably double the price it should have been".
Reception
GameSpy 's Michael Vreeland thought the game "feels a bit too similar to the first game".
Reception
During the AIAS ' 7th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Black Hole Rising was nominated for Handheld Game of the Year.

pba_metrood_fusion.title: Metroid Fusion
sents: lead
Metroid Fusion is a 2002 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.
lead
It was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 1, which had developed the previous Metroid game, Super Metroid (1994).
lead
Fusion is part of the Metroid series, and takes place between the events of Metroid: Other M and Metroid Dread.
lead
Players control the bounty hunter Samus Aran, who investigates a space station infected with shapeshifting parasites known as X.
lead
Like previous Metroid games, Fusion is a side-scrolling game with platform jumping, shooting, and puzzle elements.
lead
It introduces mission-based progression that guides the player through certain areas.
lead
It was released on the same day as the GameCube game Metroid Prime in North America; both games can be linked using the GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable to unlock additional content for Prime.
lead
Fusion was acclaimed for its gameplay, controls, graphics and music, though its shorter length and greater linearity received some criticism.
Gameplay
Samus opens most doors by shooting at them, while some only open after she reaches a certain point.
Gameplay

The player can use the GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable to connect to Fusion and unlock features in Prime: after completing Prime, they can unlock Samus's Fusion Suit, and after completing Fusion, they can unlock an emulated version of the first Metroid game.
Gameplay
In Metroid: Zero Mission (2004), players can connect to Fusion using the Game Boy Advance Game Link Cable to unlock a Fusion picture gallery, which includes its ending images.
Plot
Bounty hunter Samus Aran explores the surface of the planet SR388 with a survey crew from Biologic Space Laboratories (BSL).
Plot
Samus escapes, but the lab is destroyed.
Plot
Knowing that the X would only infect the arriving Federation troops and absorb their spacefaring knowledge to conquer the universe, Samus states her intention to destroy the station.
Plot
The computer suggests that she should alter the station's propulsion to intercept with SR388 and destroy the planet along with all X populations.
Plot
En route to initiate the propulsion sequence, an SA-X confronts Samus, who defeats it and sets the BSL station on a collision course with SR388.
Plot
The SA-X appears and attacks it, but is destroyed; Samus absorbs its nucleus and uses her newly restored Ice Beam to destroy the Omega Metroid.
Development
Nintendo confirmed a Metroid game for the Game Boy Advance in March 2001.
Development
Ken Lobb, Nintendo of America 's director of game development, said that it is a new game and not a port of the 1994 Super NES game Super Metroid.
Development
Early footage was shown at the 2001 E3 convention under the name Metroid IV.
Development
At E3 2002, Nintendo demonstrated the game again, now under the title Metroid Fusion, with updated graphics.
Development
Metroid Fusion was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 1 (R&D1), the same team that created Super Metroid.
Development
Metroid Fusion is the first 2D Metroid game with animated cutscenes; the story is revealed through text and close-ups.
Development
According to the lead programmer, Katsuya Yamano, Nintendo R&D1 did not consult previous Metroid games for programming techniques, and instead used their previous game Wario Land 4 as a reference.
Development
The developers planned to feature voice acting, but the voices were only used for warning announcements due to ROM cartridge limitations.
Release
Metroid Fusion was released in North America on November 18, 2002.
Release
In Europe, Fusion was released on November 22, followed by the Australian release on November 29.
Release
It was released in Japan on February 14, 2003, and in China on March 2, 2006.
Release
A two-disc soundtrack album, Metroid Prime & Fusion Original Soundtracks, was published by Scitron on June 18, 2003.
Release

Metroid Fusion was released on the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console in December 2011 as part of the "3DS Ambassadors" program, one of ten Game Boy Advance games for those who purchased their 3DS consoles before a price drop.
Release
Metroid Fusion was among the first three Game Boy Advance games to be released on the Wii U Virtual Console in April 2014.
Release
A sequel, Metroid Dread, was released in 2021 for the Nintendo Switch.
Reception
The Japanese magazine Famitsu gave it 34 out of 40.
Reception
GamesRadar and GamePro felt that Fusion was too short, but "love every minute of it", finding the hidden secrets and new power-ups "sublimely ingenious".
Reception
Nintendo World Report and Eurogamer called it the best 2D Metroid game and the best Game Boy Advance game so far.
Reception
Game Informer agreed, describing it as "everything you could want from a Game Boy Advance game" from beginning to end, giving it a perfect review score.
Reception
The "perfect" controls were praised by Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Reception
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine called Fusion "sleek, slick and perfectly formed", ranking it the 62nd-best Nintendo game.
Sales
Metroid Fusion has sold over 1.6 million units worldwide.
Sales
In its debut week, Fusion sold more than 100,000 units in North America.
Sales

It finished the month of November 2002 with 199,723 copies sold in the United States alone, for total revenues of US$ 5,590,768, making it the third best-selling Game Boy Advance game that month, and the tenth best-selling game across all platforms.
Sales
It sold 940,000 copies by August 2006, with revenues of US$ 27 million.
Sales
During the period between January 2000 and August 2006, in the United States it was the twenty-first highest-selling game for the Game Boy Advance, Nintendo DS or PlayStation Portable.
Sales
As of November 2004, Fusion had sold 180,000 units in Japan.

pba_metrood_zero_mission.title: Metroid: Zero Mission
sents: lead
Metroid: Zero Mission is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.
lead
It is a remake of the original Metroid (1986), and retells the story with updated visuals and gameplay.
lead
Like other Metroid games, the player controls bounty hunter Samus Aran, who travels to planet Zebes after learning that the Space Pirates are experimenting with Metroids, hostile parasitic creatures.
lead
The gameplay focuses on exploration, with the player searching for power-ups to reach previously inaccessible areas.
lead
The remake adds items, additional areas, mini-bosses, difficulty levels and a rewritten story that explores Samus's past.
lead
Zero Mission was released on February 9, 2004 to acclaim.
lead
It received praise for its new content, graphics, gameplay and improvements over the original, but criticism for its short length.
lead
Its honors included a 46th-place ranking in a list of the Top 200 Games compiled by Nintendo Power.
Gameplay
Zero Mission is the first game in the Metroid series to include a sequence in which the player controls Samus without her Power Suit.
Gameplay

In this sequence, Samus is more vulnerable to damage, must crawl through ducts on her hands and knees without the help of her Morph Ball mode, and has a weak pistol that briefly stuns enemies as her only weapon.
Plot
While searching for the stolen Metroids, the Galactic Federation locates the Space Pirates' base of operations on the planet Zebes.
Plot

As a last resort, the Federation decides to send a lone bounty hunter to penetrate the Pirates' base and destroy Mother Brain, the mechanical life-form that controls the Space Pirates' fortress and its defenses.
Plot
With both her ship and Power Suit destroyed, Samus infiltrates the Mothership, leading her to Chozodia, where a Chozo Statue offers her a trial.
Development
Sakamoto was the only member of the original Metroid development team to work on Zero Mission.
Development
One of the biggest challenges that the developers faced was adding enough elements to Zero Mission to make it feel new, while keeping the spirit of the original Metroid.
Development

Metroid Fusion had offered connectivity with Metroid Prime on the GameCube, and Zero Mission was planned to offer similar functionality with Metroid Prime 2: Echoes, but these plans ultimately fell through.
Development

The game is the first in the series to let the player choose a difficulty level at the start; each of three levels varies in the amount of damage caused by enemies with the third option only unlocked after finishing the campaign once.
Release
Nintendo revealed Metroid: Zero Mission at the E3 convention in 2003, and its North American release date of February 9, 2004 was announced later that year.
Release
It was released in Australia on March 19, in Europe on April 8, and in Japan on May 27.
Release
Zero Mission was the best-selling Game Boy Advance game in the United States in its debut month, selling 151,807 units, and was the third-bestselling game across all video game systems in that month.
Release
By May, sales dropped to seventh among Game Boy Advance games, with 31,619 copies sold and $938,681 in revenue.
Release
By February 2005, it had sold over 439,000 units in the United States and 69,000 in Japan.
Release
Zero Mission was released on the Wii U Virtual Console in Japan on June 19, 2014.
Release
This was followed by the release in Europe on March 12, 2015, and in North America on January 14, 2016.
Release
It was released for the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack service for Nintendo Switch on June 19, 2024.
Reception
The Japanese magazine Famitsu gave it a score of 34 out of 40.
Reception
X-Play and GamePro enjoyed the game; X-Play said it was "perfect for blasting space pirates on the go", and GamePro was "constantly surprised" by it.
Reception

Nintendo World Report called the game a masterpiece and the perfect example of a Metroid game, saying it mixed all the best elements from the other games and layered them on top of the original Metroid level design and concepts.
Reception
IGN felt Zero Mission was a "weak one-shot experience" that players would only after they had completed it and played it again.
Reception
Nintendo Power named Zero Mission the 46th-best game for any Nintendo system in 2006.
Reception
In their March 2010 issue, they named Zero Mission the eighth-best game released on a Nintendo console in 2010s.
Reception
Zero Mission was voted IGN ' s Game Boy Advance Game of the Month for February 2004, and IGN staff named it the best Game Boy adventure Game of 2004 and the ninth best Game Boy Advance Game.
Reception
GameSpot also named it the best Game Boy Advance game of February 2004, and nominated it for the year-end "Best Game Boy Advance Game" award.
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly also named it the best handheld game of 2004.
Reception
During the 8th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences awarded Zero Mission with " Handheld Game of the Year ".
Reception
Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 94th in a list of the best Nintendo games.
Reception
Nintendo Power also ranked it the best Game Boy Advance game of all-time in its August 2011 issue.
Reception
In 2020, IGN named Zero Mission the fifth-greatest video game remake.

pba_legend_of_zeldo_the_minish_c.real: The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap
pba_legend_of_zeldo_the_minish_c.title: The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap
sents: lead
The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap is an action-adventure game and the twelfth entry in The Legend of Zelda series.
lead

Developed by Capcom and Flagship, with Nintendo overseeing the development process, The Minish Cap was released for the Game Boy Advance in Japan and Europe in 2004 and in North America and Australia the following year.
lead
The Minish Cap serves as a prequel to Four Swords and Four Swords Adventures, telling the origins of the titular Four Sword and the villain Vaati.
lead
The game retains many elements common to previous Zelda games, especially top-down predecessors such as A Link to the Past, and includes new features and mechanics.
lead
Chiefly, the protagonist Link acquires a magical talking cap named Ezlo, who can shrink Link to the diminutive size of a Minish.
lead
The Minish Cap was well received among critics and has gained a cult following over the years.
lead
It was named the 20th best Game Boy Advance game in an IGN feature and was selected as the 2005 Game Boy Advance Game of the Year by GameSpot.
lead
The game was re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console in June 2014, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in February 2023.
Gameplay
In certain areas, the player can create multiple copies of Link; although The Minish Cap is a single-player game, this ability is inspired by the multiplayer-focused Four Swords games.
Plot
The grateful people of Hyrule would hold an annual Picori Festival, with legends stating that a door between their worlds would open every 100 years, allowing the Picori to return.
Plot
As only children can see the Picori, King Daltus orders Link to find them so that the sword can be reforged to stop Vaati and restore Zelda.
Plot
Vaati transforms into a demonic form, only to be vanquished by Link, restoring Ezlo to normal.
Development and promotion

Work on the title was suspended to allow the teams to focus on Four Swords, but in February 2003 Shigeru Miyamoto and Eiji Aonuma revealed that development of what would later be called The Minish Cap was "well underway".
Development and promotion
Nintendo launched a website for The Minish Cap in September 2004, showing concepts of Link's shrinking ability.
Development and promotion

Aonuma was reportedly impressed by what the development team was able to achieve with Hyrule Town, particularly given the restrictions of a 2D game, commenting that it even surpasses Clock Town in Majora's Mask.
Development and promotion
The game's gust jar was inspired by a gourd that can suck up anything from the novel Journey to the West.
Development and promotion
Several other aspects of the gameplay were inspired or directly lifted from Four Swords and Four Swords Adventure, both of which Minish Cap serves as a prequel to.
Development and promotion

The game contains a developmental in-joke to the Oracle of Ages and Oracle of Seasons titles in an optional side-quest which sees the player aiding three females travelers from distant lands who are looking for a place to stay.
Development and promotion
The player will only able to provide housing for two of the three women, and although their landlord makes reference to building a third house for the third woman, this never occurs in the game.
Development and promotion
A first in the Zelda series, the game was released in European territories before North America.
Development and promotion
The main cited reason for this was the Nintendo DS: with the European DS Launch scheduled for Spring 2005, Nintendo of Europe pushed to make The Minish Cap its handheld Christmas " killer app ".
Development and promotion
The game is included in the list of Game Boy Advance games that is now available for download for the Nintendo 3DS 's Virtual Console by Nintendo 3DS Ambassadors.
Development and promotion
In Europe, the game was available either as a standalone packaged game, or as part of a special pack, which included one of only 25,000 limited edition, Zelda -themed Game Boy Advance SP.
Reception and awards
The Minish Cap was the best-selling game in its debut week in Japan, selling 97,000 copies.
Reception and awards
It became the 62nd best-selling game of 2004 with 196,477 copies, and had a total of 350,000 copies overall in the country.
Reception and awards
In North America, The Minish Cap sold 217,000 copies in its debut month of January 2005, being the fourth best-selling game of the month.
Reception and awards
The Minish Cap closed the year as the seventh best-selling game of 2005.
Reception and awards
By March 2005, the game already had sold 1 million units worldwide.
Reception and awards
In the United States alone, The Minish Cap sold 680,000 copies and earned $21 million by August 2006.
Reception and awards
During the period between January 2000 and August 2006, it was the 37th highest-selling game launched for the Game Boy Advance, Nintendo DS or PlayStation Portable in that country.
Reception and awards
The game ended up selling 1.76 million copies worldwide.
Reception and awards
The graphical style especially—which continues the whimsical style of Wind Waker —was welcomed by most reviewers.
Reception and awards
The music of the game was commended by most sites; GameSpy stated that "even the music is outstanding, featuring some of the highest quality tunes to ever come out of the GBA's little speakers".
Reception and awards
Despite the criticism of the dungeon lengths, 1UP.com praised the dungeon design, proclaiming it as superior to that of other Zelda games.
Reception and awards

The Minish Cap won the 'Best Game Boy Advance of 2005' by GameSpot over such finalists as Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones and WarioWare: Twisted!; GameSpot labelled it as "the Game Boy Advance game we remember the most".
Reception and awards
In March 2007, the game was ranked as the 20th best Game Boy Advance game by IGN.
Reception and awards
The game was ranked 47th in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s "100 Greatest Nintendo Games" feature.

The Minish Cap received an average score of 90 percent from GameRankings, a site that compiles media ratings from several publishers to give an average score.
