pst_resident_weevil_director_s_c.title: Resident Evil
sents: lead
Resident Evil, known as Biohazard in Japan, is a Japanese horror game series and media franchise created by Capcom.
lead
It consists of survival horror, third-person shooter and first-person shooter games, with players typically surviving in environments inhabited by zombies and other mutated creatures.
lead
The franchise has expanded into other media, including a live-action film series, animated films, television series, comic books, novels, audiobooks, and merchandise.
lead
Resident Evil is the highest-grossing horror franchise.
lead
The first Resident Evil game was created by Shinji Mikami and Tokuro Fujiwara for PlayStation, and released in 1996.
lead
It is credited for defining the survival horror genre and returning zombies to popular culture.
lead
With Resident Evil 4 (2005), the franchise shifted to more dynamic shooting action, popularizing the "over-the-shoulder" third-person view in action-adventure games.
lead
The franchise returned to survival horror with Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (2017) and Resident Evil Village (2021), which used a first-person perspective.
History

The development of the first Resident Evil, released as Biohazard in Japan, began in 1993 when Capcom 's Tokuro Fujiwara told Shinji Mikami and other co-workers to create a game using elements from Fujiwara's 1989 game Sweet Home on the Family Computer (Famicom) in Japan.
History
Resident Evil made its debut on the PlayStation in 1996 and was later ported to the Sega Saturn.
History

The first entry in the series was the first game to be dubbed a " survival horror ", a term coined for the new genre it initiated, and its critical and commercial success led to the production of two sequels, Resident Evil 2 in 1998 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis in 1999, both for the PlayStation.
History
A port of Resident Evil 2 was released for the Nintendo 64.
History
The fourth game in the series, Resident Evil – Code: Veronica, was developed for the Dreamcast and released in 2000, followed by ports of Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
History

History
Resident Evil 4 was later released for Windows, PlayStation 2, and Wii.
History

History

History

History
In a similar vein, the Chronicles series features first-person gameplay, albeit on an on-rails path.

The first-person perspective continued in the eighth mainline game Resident Evil Village.
History
Released in May 2021, the game, set in a mysterious European village, is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard although it incorporates more action elements inspired from Resident Evil 4.
History
A new generation of remakes of older entries began in 2019 with a remake of Resident Evil 2, being released for the PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One.
History
The remake outsold the original game within a year, selling over five million copies.
History
Following in the success of the Resident Evil 2 remake, Capcom revealed a remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis in December 2019, known as Resident Evil 3.
History
In June 2022, a remake of Resident Evil 4 was announced and released on March 24, 2023 for PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC.
Story overview
The STARS team is mostly decimated by zombies and other BOWs, leaving only a handful of survivors, including Chris Redfield, Jill Valentine, and Albert Wesker.
Story overview
Chris and Jill explore the zombie-infested mansion and uncover a secret underground Umbrella research facility.
Story overview
Most of the city's residents are infected and become zombies.
Story overview
Resident Evil 6 features Leon and Chris meeting for the first time in the video game series.
Story overview
Ethan, Mia, and their newborn daughter, Rosemary, are relocated to Eastern Europe but are abducted by a cult.
Tank controls
The first game introduced a control scheme that the player community has come to refer to as " tank controls " to the series.
Tank controls
While the first three entries in the series featured this control scheme, the third, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, saw some action-oriented additions.
First-person shooter gameplay and VR
Resident Evil 7 is the first main Resident Evil game to use the first-person perspective and to use virtual reality.
First-person shooter gameplay and VR
The eighth main-series game, Resident Evil Village, also features a first-person perspective.
First-person shooter gameplay and VR
A VR version of Resident Evil 4 was released on the Oculus Quest 2 on October 21, 2021.
Live-action films
From 2002 to 2016, six live-action Resident Evil films were produced, all written and produced by Paul W.
Live-action films
Despite a negative reaction from critics, the live-action film series has made over $1 billion worldwide.
Live-action films

The series holds the record for the "Most Live-Action Film Adaptations of a Video Game" in the 2012 Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition, which also described it as "the most successful movie series to be based on a video game."
Live-action films
A reboot, Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City, was released on November 24, 2021, with Johannes Roberts as writer/director.
Animated films
The first computer animated film for the franchise was Biohazard 4D-Executer.
Television
Resident Evil: Infinite Darkness, a four-part CG anime series, premiered on July 8, 2021, on Netflix.
Television
An eight episode live-action series, two plotlines set in 2022 and 2036 follow Albert Wesker and his daughters navigating Umbrella's experiments in New Raccoon City.
Merchandise
Over the years, various toy companies have acquired the Resident Evil license, with each producing their own unique line of Resident Evil action figures or models.
Merchandise

Some models included the STARS Beretta featured in Resident Evil 3, and the Desert Eagle in a limited edition that came with other memorabilia in a wooden case, along with the Gold Lugers from Code: Veronica and the "Samurai Edge" pistol from the Resident Evil remake.
Merchandise
The guide describes and summarizes all of the key events that occur in Resident Evil Zero, Resident Evil, Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, and Code: Veronica.
Merchandise

A second Archives book was later released in December 2011 and covers Resident Evil 4, Resident Evil 5, the new scenarios detailed in Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles and Resident Evil: The Darkside Chronicles, and the 2008 CGI movie, Resident Evil: Degeneration.
Merchandise
Halloween Horror Nights 2013, held at Universal Orlando, featured a haunted house titled Resident Evil: Escape from Raccoon City, based on Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
Novels

The first Resident Evil novel was Hiroyuki Ariga's novella Biohazard: The Beginning, published in 1997 as a portion of the book The True Story of Biohazard, which was given away as a pre-order bonus with the Sega Saturn version of Biohazard.
Novels
Perry has written novelizations of the first five games, as well as two original novels taking place between games.
Novels
While no official English translation of these novels has been published yet, the last two books were translated into German and published in 2006.
Novels
There was also a Japanese novelization of the first film, unrelated to DeCandido's version, written by Osamu Makino.
Novels
The books are a two-part direct novelization of the game and are published in Japanese and German only.
Novels
The first novel, titled Biohazard: The Umbrella Chronicles Side A in Japan and Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles 1 in Germany, was released on December 22, 2007.
Novels
The second novel, titled Biohazard: The Umbrella Chronicles Side B in Japan and Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles 2 in Germany, was published in January 2008.
Comics
In 1998, WildStorm began producing a monthly comic book series based on the first two games, Resident Evil: The Official Comic Magazine, which lasted five issues.
Comics
The first four issues were published by Image, while Wildstorm themselves published the fifth and final issue.
Comics

In Hong Kong, there has been officially licensed Biohazard manhua adaptations of Biohazard 0 by publisher Yulang Group, Biohazard 2 by Kings Fountain, Biohazard 3 Supplemental Edition by Cao Zhihao and, Biohazard 3 The Last Escape, and Biohazard Code: Veronica by Lee Chung Hing published by Tinhangse Publishing.
Comics
In 2009, Wildstorm began publishing a Resident Evil comic book prequel to Resident Evil 5, which centers on two original members of the BSAA, Mina Gere and Holiday Sugarman.
Comics
Written by Ricardo Sanchez and illustrated by Kevin Sharpe and Jim Clark, the first issue was published on March 11, 2009.
Comics
On November 11, 2009, the third issue was released, and the fourth was released March 24, 2010.
Reception and legacy
Most of the games in the prominent Resident Evil series have been released to positive reviews.
Reception and legacy

Some of the games, most notably Resident Evil, Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 4, have been bestowed with multiple Game of the Year honors and often placed on lists of the best video games ever made.
Reception and legacy
That same year, G4tv called it "one of the most successful series in gaming history."
Commercial performance
By December 2022, around 135 million Resident Evil games had been sold.
Commercial performance
The first two Resident Evil games had collectively sold approximately 11 million units worldwide by March 1999.
Commercial performance
By early 2001, the series had sold 17 million units worldwide, earning more than $600 million.
Commercial performance
By 2011, it had sold about 46 million copies and was estimated to have grossed at least $1.3 billion.
Commercial performance
It is recognized by Guinness World Records as the best-selling survival horror series, with Resident Evil 2 remake being the best-selling survival horror game as of 2023.
Commercial performance
Seven of the top ten best-selling horror games in North America are Resident Evil games.
Commercial performance
The 2023 Resident Evil 4 remake sold more than three million copies in its first two days of release.
Commercial performance
It sold four million copies in its first two weeks, making it one of the fastest-selling Resident Evil games.
Commercial performance
In Japan, it was the best-selling retail game in its first week, selling 89,662 copies on PlayStation 5 and 85,371 on PlayStation 4.
Commercial performance
The Resident Evil film series was the highest-grossing film series based on video games by 2012.
Commercial performance

By 2011, the films had grossed over $600 million at the box office, bringing the franchise's estimated revenue to at least more than $1.9 billion in combined video game sales and box office gross up until then.
Commercial performance
As of 2020, the films have grossed more than $1.3 billion in box office and home video sales.
Commercial performance
The success of the video games and films have made Resident Evil the highest-grossing franchise in the horror and zombie genres.
Cultural impact
GameSpot listed the original Resident Evil as one of the fifteen most influential video games of all time.
Cultural impact
According to Kim Newman in the book Nightmare Movies (2011), "the zombie revival began in the Far East" mainly due to the 1996 Japanese zombie games Resident Evil and The House of the Dead.
Cultural impact
George Romero, in 2013, said it was the video games Resident Evil and House of the Dead "more than anything else" that popularised his zombie concept in early 21st-century popular culture.
Cultural impact

In a 2015 interview with Huffington Post, screenwriter-director Alex Garland credited the Resident Evil series as a primary influence on his script for the horror film 28 Days Later (2002), and credited the first Resident Evil game for revitalizing the zombie genre.
Cultural impact

Screenwriter Edgar Wright cited Resident Evil 2 as a primary influence on his zombie comedy film Shaun of the Dead (2004), with the film's star and co-writer Simon Pegg also crediting the first game with starting the zombie revival in popular culture.
Cultural impact

The Resident Evil films, 28 Days Later and the Dawn of the Dead remake all set box office records for the zombie genre, reaching levels of commercial success not seen since the original Dawn of the Dead (1978).
Cultural impact

Since then, zombie films have declined in popularity during the late 2010s, but zombie video games have remained popular, as seen with the commercial success of the Resident Evil 2 remake and Days Gone in 2019.

pst_resident_weevil_survivor.title: Resident Evil Survivor
sents: lead
Resident Evil Survivor is a light gun shooter video game developed by Tose and published by Capcom.
lead
It was released on the PlayStation in Japan on January 27, 2000, in Europe on March 31, 2000, and in North America on August 30, 2000.
lead
It is a spin-off of the Resident Evil video game series.
lead
It is also the first first-person perspective Resident Evil game predating Resident Evil 7: Biohazard by seventeen years.
lead
A Microsoft Windows version was released only in China and Taiwan on September 7, 2002.
lead

As the first release of the Gun Survivor series, this game was a major difference from the main Resident Evil series, substituting the third-person perspective of the previous games to a first-person view.
lead

The Japanese and European versions of the game were compatible with Namco 's GunCon/G-Con 45 light gun, making it one of the first off- rail light gun games, whereas lightgun compatibility was removed from the North American release.
lead
It was followed by Resident Evil Survivor 2 – Code: Veronica.
Gameplay
Survivor's gameplay is a combination of first-person shooter and arcade -style light gun shooter.
Gameplay
The player views the environment from the perspective of the character (first-person view) and moves the character through the environment with the controller.
Gameplay
The game borrows its enemies from Resident Evil 2, featuring the zombie models from that game, as well as creatures such as Lickers, the Ivy plants, Moth Giants and Tyrants.
Gameplay
The player's arsenal consists almost entirely of pistols, such as the Glock 17 and the CZ75 with unlimited ammo.
Plot
The pilot escapes the burning wreckage only to find himself fighting a battle against the living dead, with no memory of his identity or his reasons for being there.
Plot
Ark tells Lott to go ahead to the station first and regroup there.
Reception
Edge praised the Japanese import's well-rendered 3D environments, but criticized the long loading screens between opening and closing doors.
Sequels
The Gun Survivor series was followed by three sequels, which were released for the PlayStation 2 and utilised the G-Con 2 peripheral.
Sequels
Resident Evil Survivor 2 – Code: Veronica was released for the PlayStation 2 in 2002, based on the characters and enemies of Resident Evil – Code: Veronica.
Sequels
Dino Stalker, a spin-off of the Dino Crisis series, was also released in 2002.
Sequels
A fourth game, Resident Evil: Dead Aim, was released in 2003.

pst_silent_hull.title: Silent Hill (video game)
sents: lead
Silent Hill is a 1999 survival horror game developed by Team Silent, a group within Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo, and published by Konami.
lead
As the first installment in the Silent Hill video game series, the game was released exclusively for the PlayStation.
lead
Silent Hill uses a third-person view with real-time rendering of 3D environments.
lead
To mitigate the limitations of the console hardware, developers used fog and darkness to obscure the graphics and hide pop-ins, which, in turn, helped establish the game's atmosphere and mystery.
lead
Unlike earlier survival horror games that focused on protagonists with combat training, the player character of Silent Hill is an " everyman ".
lead
The game follows Harry Mason as he searches for his missing adopted daughter in the eponymous fictional American town of Silent Hill.
lead
Stumbling upon a cult conducting a ritual to revive a deity it worships, he discovers her true origin.
lead
Five game endings are possible, depending on the actions taken by the player, including one joke ending.
Gameplay
Accessible from the menu and readable only when sufficient light is present, each map is marked with places of interest.
Gameplay
The player finds a flashlight early in the game, which illuminates only a short distance.
Plot

Harry can later rescue Kaufmann from a monster, discover evidence of his involvement in local drug trafficking, and find his hidden bottle of aglaophotis, a supernatural liquid that can exorcise demons.
Plot
Alessa's never-healing wounds terrified her, and she fell deeper into a drug addiction fueled by Kaufmann.
Endings
The "Joke" ending features extraterrestrials abducting Harry.
Design
Despite the profit-oriented approach of the parent company, the developers of Silent Hill had considerable artistic freedom, as the game was produced in an era of lower-budget 2D titles.
Design
Toyama questioned Konami's decision to appoint him as director, as he had never directed a game before Silent Hill.
Design
The game's joke ending was inspired by a suggestion box created to find alternative explanations for the events in Silent Hill.
Design
As a young employee, Sato was initially limited to basic tasks such as font design and file sorting.
Design
He also created 3D demos and presentations and taught older staff members the fundamentals of 3D modeling.
Design
Sato eventually approached the company's higher-ups with a short demo movie he had rendered and threatened to withhold his technical knowledge unless he was assigned to 3D work.
Design
Over two and a half years, he lived in the development team's office, using approximately 150 Unix -based computers to render scenes after his coworkers left for the day.
Design
Sato estimated that the game's budget was lower than that of Japan's biggest games at the time.
Design
The game debuted at the 1998 Electronic Entertainment Expo in Atlanta, Georgia, where presentations of movies and in-game scenes received applause from the audience.
Design
Cheryl Mason's first name is based on actress Sheryl Lee, and Lisa Garland's surname is taken from actress Judy Garland.
Design
"Michael Kaufmann" combines the first name of Troma Studios producer Michael Herz and the surname of producer Lloyd Kaufmann.
Music
When he presented his compositions to the staff for the first time, they mistook the sound for a game bug.
Music
Yamaoka explained that the noise was intentional for the music, and the team only withdrew their objections after he elaborated on his reasons for this style.
Music
On March 5, 1999, the album Silent Hill Original Soundtracks was released in Japan.
Music
The 41st track, the ending theme "Esperándote," was composed by Rika Muranaka.
Music

When she arrived in Buenos Aires, Argentina, to record the translated Spanish lyrics with Argentine singer Vanesa Quiroz, Muranaka found that the syllables no longer matched the melody, and she had to recompose it in five minutes.
Music
On October 29, 2013, Perseverance Records released a "Best Of" album featuring 16 newly interpreted instrumental tracks composed by Akira Yamaoka and arranged and performed by Edgar Rothermich.
Music
The 17th track on the album is the ballad "I Want Love," performed by Romina Arena.
Release
Silent Hill was released for the PlayStation in 1999, with launch dates spanning from February to July in North America, Japan, and Europe.
Release
In 2006, it was included in the Silent Hill Complete Set in Japan.
Release
Silent Hill became available for download from the European PlayStation Network store for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable on March 19, 2009.
Release
On September 10, 2009, Silent Hill was released on the North American PlayStation Network. and it was re-released on the European PlayStation Network on October 26, 2011.
Adaptations
Titled Play Novel: Silent Hill, it was released only in Japan in 2001 as a gamebook -style visual novel.
Adaptations
A film adaptation, also titled Silent Hill, was released on April 21, 2006.
Adaptations
Directed by Christophe Gans, the film was loosely based on the game, incorporating elements from Silent Hill 2, Silent Hill 3, and Silent Hill 4: The Room.
Adaptations
The game was released on December 8, 2009, for the Wii and on January 19, 2010, for the PlayStation 2 and PlayStation Portable, to mostly positive reviews.
Reception and Legacy
The game sold over two million copies, which earned Silent Hill a spot in the American PlayStation Greatest Hits budget releases.
Reception and Legacy

In November 1999, the Verband der Unterhaltungssoftware Deutschland (VUD) awarded Silent Hill a "Gold" certification, indicating sales of at least 100,000 units across Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.
Reception and Legacy

House praised Silent Hill, describing it as "a truly magnificent work of art" and "a genuinely terrifying experience combined with a unique, gripping story and immersive atmosphere." However, the voice acting was less well-received.
Reception and Legacy
Reviewers noted that Silent Hill used real-time 3D environments, unlike the pre-rendered backgrounds found in Resident Evil.
Reception and Legacy
Despite this, most reviewers felt these factors enhanced the game's atmosphere.
Reception and Legacy
The game's lasting popularity as the first in the series was recognized long after its release.
Reception and Legacy

A 2000 list of the best PlayStation games by IGN ranked it as the 14th-best, while GameSpy 's 2005 article on the best PlayStation games placed Silent Hill as the 15th-best game produced for the console.
Reception and Legacy
In a 2006 GameTrailers video feature, Silent Hill was ranked number one on its list of the top ten scariest games of all time.
Reception and Legacy
In November 2012, Time named it one of the 100 greatest video games of all time.

pst_metal_gear_sneaky_vr_misions.title: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection
sents: lead
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection is a video game compilation published by Konami.
lead
The compilation features ports of titles in the Metal Gear franchise of stealth games, released in commemoration of the series' 35th anniversary.
lead
1 was released for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S on October 24, 2023.
lead
More volumes will be announced and detailed in the future.
Games
1 presents five individual applications, each comprising one or two games and additional versions as well as its additional content.
Games
Metal Gear Solid and its two sequels each have their own application, while the MSX versions of Metal Gear and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake are contained in one application.
Games

The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) games Metal Gear (1987) and Snake's Revenge (1990) have their own application, labeled as "Bonus Content", including extra content such as the music player and graphic novels.
Games
Metal Gear Solid and its sequels can be purchased individually, with Metal Gear Solid bundling Metal Gear and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake.
Games

Due to the original Metal Gear Solid being presented in a 4:3 aspect ratio, an assortment of wallpapers can be selected both from the main menu and during gameplay, as well as adjustments to the game's display position.
Games

The collection includes the ability to create virtual save data for other Konami PlayStation titles and virtually swap controller ports from Player 1 to Player 2, which are both relevant to the boss fight against Psycho Mantis.
Games

Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty (2001) and Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater (2004) are both direct conversions of their HD Edition remasters previously developed by Bluepoint Games and distributed as part of the Metal Gear Solid HD Collection (2011) compilation for PlayStation 3, PlayStation Vita and Xbox 360.
Games
Before release Konami announced that on PlayStation 5, Windows and Xbox Series X/S, all featured games are presented at a resolution of 1080p at a maximum performance of 60 frames-per-second (FPS).
Games
The Nintendo Switch version of the collection similarly retains a native 1080p resolution in TV Mode, but has a lower output of 720p in Handheld Mode, while both configurations run at 30 FPS.
Games
The Switch version's 30 FPS cap was noted as "bizarre" since the Shield version, which the Switch version is derived from, manages to run at 60 FPS using the same Tegra X1 chip.
Additional content

Remixes of the vocal tracks "The Best is Yet to Come" from Metal Gear Solid, "Can't Say Goodbye To Yesterday" from Sons of Liberty and the titular "Snake Eater" from Metal Gear Solid 3, was made available as pre-order bonuses.
Development

In November 2021, the digital downloads for Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty and Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater as well as the original Metal Gear Solid HD Collection were removed from digital storefronts, with Konami citing expired licenses as the reason.
Development
In July 2022, Konami announced their intentions to reinstate the games for the series' 35th anniversary.
Development

During the development of Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater, Konami began the development of the Master Collection series to make "the most complete collection that celebrates the 35th anniversary of the series, allowing fans to play the games as they were, as first released on the latest platforms."
Marketing and release
1 was announced for the PlayStation 5 during a PlayStation Showcase in May 2023, immediately after the reveal of Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater.
Marketing and release
In the original announcement, it was revealed to contain the first three Metal Gear Solid games.
Marketing and release

In June 2023, a Nintendo Direct revealed that the compilation would be released for Nintendo Switch, that it would include the Nintendo Entertainment System version of Metal Gear and its standalone sequel Snake's Revenge, and that it would include digital graphic novels for Metal Gear Solid and Metal Gear Solid 2.
Marketing and release

In August 2023, a digital release for PlayStation 4 was confirmed to be in development, and was later announced as releasing the same day as on other platforms, with PS4 players entitled to a free PS5 upgrade.
Marketing and release
1 released on October 24, 2023, alongside standalone versions of the three Metal Gear Solid games for $19.99 each.
Marketing and release
Buying the standalone version of Metal Gear Solid grants access to Metal Gear and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake.
Marketing and release

The Nintendo Switch physical release in North America and Europe only includes Metal Gear for MSX2, Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake, Metal Gear for NES and Snake's Revenge on the Game Card, while the rest of the contents have to be separately downloaded and installed to the console.
Reception

The Nintendo Switch version of the compilation was scored the highest at 78/100 on review aggregator website Metacritic, while both the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S versions garnered a comparatively lower aggregate score of 74/100.

pst_tactics_ogrr_let_us_cling_to.real: Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together
pst_tactics_ogrr_let_us_cling_to.title: Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together (2010 video game)

Platform(s): Let Us Cling Together PlayStation Portable Reborn Nintendo Switch PlayStation 4 PlayStation 5 Windows

sents: lead
Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together is a 2010 tactical role-playing game developed and published by Japanese company Square Enix.
lead
It is a remake of the 1995 Super Famicom (Super Nintendo Entertainment System) title of the same name, second entry in the Ogre Battle series.
lead
The remake retains the same strategy RPG gameplay of the original, focusing on turn-based tactical battles and the use of character classes.
lead
The game incorporates additional features such as equipment crafting and the ability to revisit branch points in the game's narrative, in addition to multiplayer functionality.
lead
The storyline, following the actions of rebel fighter Denam Pavel during a civil war within the kingdom of Valeria, was also expanded with new scenes and characters.
lead
The remake was conceived following the release of Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions (2007), taking four years to complete.
lead
It was directed by original artist Hiroshi Minagawa, who assembled most of the original staff including writer and designer Yasumi Matsuno, and composers Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata.
lead
Original artist Akihiko Yoshida returned to supervise the art direction, with many characters redesigned by Tsubasa Masao.
Content and gameplay
Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together is a PlayStation Portable (PSP) remake of the 1995 Super Famicom (Super Nintendo Entertainment System) title of the same name.
Development

Following the release of Tactics Ogre, Matsuno and a number of staff members moved to Square (predecessor of Square Enix) and developed Final Fantasy Tactics (1997), going on to develop multiple titles in its universe of Ivalice.
Development
Quest Corporation continued production on the Ogre Battle series until it was purchased and absorbed into Square following the release of Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis (2002).
Development
Matsuno remained at the company until 2005, when he left during the production of Final Fantasy XII citing ill health.
Development
Concept work for a remake of Tactics Ogre began in May 2007 at Square Enix following the release of Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions, an updated port of Final Fantasy Tactics for the PSP.
Development
Matsuno initially refused, but when Minagawa changed the plan so the remake would include changes for modern audiences, he agreed to join the project.
Design
An early plan was for players to be able to go back 100 moves in the Chariot system, but was deemed too generous and reduced to the final count of fifty.
Design
The fields and stages were rebuilt in 3D, with 2D character sprites overlaid and painted to appear like classic pixel art.
Design

The artwork was managed by Yoshida, but much of the character art and other artistic elements were reworked by Tsubasa Masao, an artist known for his work on Metal Gear Acid and Final Fantasy: The 4 Heroes of Light.
Design
While the original game featured 300,000 characters of writing, the remake's expansions pushed this number to over 700,000, more than the script for Final Fantasy XII.
Design

The team included Kazuhiro Kataoka, who had worked on Ogre Battle 64; Yuichi Murasawa and Kyoko Kitahara, who had written both Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis and titles within the Ivalice series; Motoharu Tanaka, whose work included Final Fantasy entries and Parasite Eve; and Tsuyoshi Tomooka of The Last Remnant.
Design
He originally planned to raise Denam's age to 23, but as this would have clashed with the story's themes of youthful rebellion, he settled on making him 18.
Music
A 4-CD soundtrack album was released on November 10, 2010.
Music
The first three discs included the re-recorded and new music, while the fourth disc included a selection of music from the Super Famicom original.
Release
Wallpapers and ring tones inspired by the remake were included in the mobile port of Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen, released in September.
Release
The Tactics Ogre remake was released on November 11 as a physical and digital release.
Release
Between December 2010 and January 2011, three free pieces of downloadable content (DLC) were released, featuring scenarios focusing on Denam using the World system to rewrite earlier events.
Release
An artbook featuring commentary from Yoshida and Masao was released in May 2011, and a fan book featuring artwork and developers answering fan questions was released in July.
Release
For its Western marketing, an animated trailer was created by animation studio Kamikaze Douga, depicting key scenes from the narrative and featuring a unique track created by Sakimoto.
Release
The game was released in North America on February 15, 2011, with select retailers offering a pre-order bonus of tarot carts designed by Yoshida.
Release
The European release on February 25 included a limited Premium Edition featuring the tarot set, an artbook, and a mini soundtrack CD.
Release
A PlayStation port of Tactics Ogre had been localized for North America by Atlus USA in 1998.
Reception
Upon its debut in Japan, the remake reached the top of game charts, recording sales of over 176,000 units during the first week.
Reception
By the end of 2010, it was the 48th best-selling game of the year, with sales of over 257,000 units.
Reception
In North America during February 2011, it was the top-selling PSP title in the region according to data collected by The NPD Group.
Reception

Tactics Ogre: Reborn was the highest selling physical game during its first week of release in Japan, moving 36,783 units on Switch, 12,668 units on PlayStation 4, and 7,805 units on PlayStation 5 for an opening week total of 57,256 retail copies sold.
Reception
On review aggregator website Metacritic, Tactics Ogre received a score of 87 points out of 100 based on 49 critic reviews.
Reception

Jeremy Parish, writing for 1Up.com, awarded the website's highest score, lauding the gameplay additions and technical superiority compared to the earlier PlayStation port and citing it as a masterpiece despite potential problems with lowered difficulty.
Reception

Ryan King of Play noted a lack of innovative features in its story and gameplay, but praised it as "one of the most competent, solid, well-put-together J-RPGs you will ever play", comparing it to a compressed refinement of its genre.

pst_wild_armz.title: Wild Arms (video game)
sents: lead
Wild Arms is a role-playing video game developed by Media.Vision and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
Originally released in Japan in 1996, it was later translated and released in North America in 1997 and Europe in 1998.
lead
It features a fantasy setting and motif and 2D computer graphics for normal gameplay, while battle sequences are rendered in 3D.
lead
Taking place in the fantasy world of Filgaia, Wild Arms follows the adventures of a band of miscreants and adventurers called Dream Chasers who scour the world in search of excitement and fortune.
lead
The player assumes control of a young boy named Rudy who has the ability to operate powerful weapons called Ancient Relic Machines (ARMs), forbidden remnants of a lost age that resemble firearms.
lead

Along with his companions Jack and Cecilia, the group must use their respective skills to navigate through the vast wastelands and dungeons of Filgaia and prevent an otherworldly threat from reviving their lost leader and destroying the world.
lead
Despite its release being somewhat overshadowed by hype for the upcoming Final Fantasy VII, Wild Arms was a critical and commercial success.
lead

Since the American branch of Sony Computer Entertainment had only recently lifted its policy against allowing RPGs to be released in the U.S., there were relatively few RPGs available for the system in the U.S. at that time, giving Wild Arms an added advantage in that market.
Gameplay
Special devices called "Tools" unique to each character allow the player to traverse otherwise impassable situations while not in battle.
Battle system
Unlike normal gameplay, where all character and background graphics are two-dimensional (2D), combat is rendered entirely in 3D.
Battle system
Each of the three playable characters has a unique set of abilities that can be used to defeat enemies or aid party members.
Battle system
During combat, each character has a "Force Bar" divided into 4 equal-sized sections called levels.
Battle system

Cecilia's " Mystic " ability, for example, allows an item to be used to cast a spell whether it be an attack, restorative or assist spell, and Jack's "Accelerator" gives him the option of acting first in the next combat round, regardless of his or the enemy's speed.
Battle system
Runes can be obtained either in hidden areas within dungeons, or simply whenever the story wills it.
Battle system
Most Guardian attacks, like Cecilia's magic, have a certain elemental designation that is more effective against certain enemies.
Setting

Wild Arms takes place in the world of Filgaia ("Fargaia" in the original Japanese version), a fantasy world modeled closely after medieval Europe, though the technology is comparable to that of the early Industrial Revolution, with advancements such as motors first coming into use.
Setting

Since most of the world's most advanced technology existed centuries before the start of the game, archaeologists and engineers are essentially one and the same; rediscovering old technology as they find new applications for it.
Characters

Cecilia Lynn Adlehyde (セシリア・レイン・アーデルハイド Seshiria Rein Aderuhaido "Cecilia Raynne Adlehyde" in the Japanese version) is a young princess who has spent most of her life studying at the Curan Abbey magic school.
Characters
Before she leaves, however, she is contacted by a mysterious voice who beckons her to a hidden library deep within the abbey.
Story

With their leader gone, a majority of the demons disappeared, with only a few remaining in seclusion over the next few centuries, eventually launching an attack on the castle to reclaim the incapacitated body of Mother.
Story

The Guardians tell Rudy and his companions that the demons have already begun to revive their leader, and have only to lift the seal on her cocoon -like prison by destroying the three scattered statues that lie across Filgaia.
Story

Realizing that the only way to defeat the demons is to confront them in their stronghold, the Photosphere, Rudy, Jack, and Cecilia gather the necessary materials to enter the tomb of the last remaining golem, the Earth Golem, Asgard.
Story
Even after defeating the last of the Demons, it seems too late to stop Malduke's weapon from destroying Filgaia, but the Guardians are able to pool their strength and revive the world.
Story
Rudy, Jack, and Cecilia board the teleportation device to be transported back to Filgaia, only to be stopped in mid-voyage by what is left of Zeikfried's body and his spear.
Story
The weakened Zeikfried launches a last desperate assault on the heroes, and, though defeated in the end, the energy released in the battle destabilizes the portal.
Story
In a letter she writes to Jack and Rudy, she tells them that she will send them the item they forgot to help them on their future adventures and shows up shortly after to join them on a new quest.
Development
Wild Arms was developed by Japanese software company Media.Vision and initially released in Japan in late 1996.
Development
The studio was founded in 1993 by several members of Telenet Japan who had left the Riot division after having worked on the RPG series Tenshi no Uta for the NEC PC Engine.
Development

Wild Arms' soundtrack was composed entirely by Naruke and is heavily inspired by Spaghetti Westerns, featuring instrumentation from mandolins, acoustic and electric guitars, finger cymbals, trumpets, and whistling.
Development
The game's overworld theme "Lone Bird in the Shire", contains the melody from Ennio Morricone 's " The Ecstasy of Gold " originally from The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly.
Release
First appearing as a video demo on the promotional PlayStation Jampack vol.
Release
1 in January 1997, the full English version of Wild Arms was made available in March of the same year by Sony Computer Entertainment America (SCEA).
Release
Wild Arms was later translated to both French and German for its release in the PAL region in late 1998, published by Sony Computer Entertainment's European division.
Release
The Wild Arms Original Game Soundtrack was initially released in Japan on January 22, 1997, and was re-printed two years later.
Release

After the release of the enhanced remake Wild Arms Alter Code: F and its arranged soundtrack, a complete version of the original Wild Arms soundtrack containing all of the game's music, titled Wild Arms Complete Tracks was released on April 6, 2006.
Release
On July 26, 2007, Wild Arms was released on the PlayStation Network in Japan, through which it can be played on the PlayStation Portable and, as of Operating System update 1.70, on the PlayStation 3.
Release
On December 6, 2007 this version was released on the North American PlayStation Network.
Release
On January 4, 2012, Wild Arms was released on the European PlayStation Store.
Release
The console was released on December 3, 2018.
Release
Wild Arms was released on the PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 for the upgraded PlayStation Plus service on June 13th, 2022.
Reception
It sold over 250,000 copies in Japan during the first two weeks after its release and was positively reviewed by Japanese critics.
Reception
Game Informer magazine stated it was "by far one of the best action RPGs of the year", praising the game's use of 3D battle graphics in addition to the colorful 2D graphics of normal gameplay.
Reception
Their three reviewers scored it 9, 9.25 and 8.5 out of 10.
Reception
GameFan ' s three reviewers scored it 95%, 92%, and 90%, and also gave it their "Game of the Month" award.
Reception

Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s four reviewers scored it 9, 8.5, 9 and 8.5 out of 10, earning it an "Editor's Choice Silver Award", a distinction given to games with a score averaging between 8 and 9 out of 10.
Reception
Since all of these options are available to you at all times, the role-playing element never feels constraining."
Legacy

The Wild Arms series has grown to several games since the original title's release, with a fourth sequel released in Japan in December 2006, mobile phone adaptations, a manga, and a Wild Arms anime distributed by ADV Films.
Remake
Wild Arms Alter Code: F (ワイルドアームズ アルターコード:エフ) is an enhanced remake of Wild Arms for the PlayStation 2, developed by Media.Vision and published by Sony in Japan and Agetec in North America.
Remake
The game features entirely new 3D environments, five new playable characters and many other improvements.
Remake
The game's North American release was postponed several times until it was finally released on November 15, 2005.
Remake
The North American version comes with a bonus DVD featuring the first episode of the Wild Arms anime series, Wild Arms: Twilight Venom.
Remake
The game has been graphically overhauled and now has 3D graphics both in and out of battles.
Remake
The encounter cancel system from Wild Arms 2 and 3, which allows a player to skip a random battle, is present.

pst_alundro.title: Alundra

Producer(s): Takahiro Kaneko Hideaki Kikukawa Akira Sato

sents: lead

Alundra (アランドラ, Arandora), released in Europe as The Adventures of Alundra, is an action-adventure video game developed by Matrix Software and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It was originally released in 1997 in Japan, January 1998 in North America by Working Designs and June 1998 in PAL territories by Sony-owned Psygnosis.
lead
The game's protagonist is a young man named Alundra, who learns that he has the power to enter people's dreams.
lead
He is shipwrecked on an island, near the village of Inoa, where locals have been suffering from recurring nightmares that sometimes cause death.
lead
With his dream walking ability, Alundra proceeds to try to help the locals.
lead
The narrative becomes gradually darker and more twisted as the game progresses, dealing with mature themes such as death, clinical depression, fate, religion, and the essence of human existence.
lead

The gameplay involves extensive exploration of the island and various dungeons, with an emphasis on challenging puzzle solving, real-time action combat, and platforming, as well as interaction with non-player characters in the village of Inoa.
lead

The main gameplay innovation is a dream walking mechanic, where Alundra can enter people's dreams, with each of the dream levels having its own unique twist based upon the dreamer's personality and traits.
Plot
The ship carrying Alundra is caught in a storm and is broken in half, leaving most of the crew dead and Alundra drifting unconscious.
Plot
After Melzas is destroyed, Alundra and Meia bid farewell to the villagers and depart together, before going their separate ways.
Development
The game began development before the PlayStation launched in 1994 and took three years to complete.
Release
Later, Alundra was released as a downloadable game on the PSone Classics service for the PlayStation 3.
Reception
The game had sold 143,114 copies in Japan by the end of 1997.
Reception
Following its North American release, Working Designs sold over 100,000 copies of the game in North America within a single month in early 1998.
Reception

It has a score of 86 out of 100 at Metacritic based on 9 reviews, making it the sixth highest-rated PlayStation title of 1997, and held an 84% at GameRankings based on 13 reviews at the time of the site's closure in 2019.
Reception

Next Generation stated that "Working Designs made a smart decision importing Alundra, and any gamer looking for a unique challenge is guaranteed to appreciate it." Jay Boor wrote in IGN, "Never have I been so tested and challenged since the old Genesis adventure title, LandStalker.
Reception
Both Next Generation and GamePro remarked that Alundra looks too much like a " 16-bit " game, with GamePro giving it a 4.5 out of 5 for sound, control, and fun factor but a 3.5 out of 5 for graphics.
Reception
GameSpot found that it is sometimes difficult to judge height and depth, forcing the player to proceed by trial and error.
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly and GamePro both selected Alundra as the runner-up for their 1997 Best Role-Playing Game of the Year awards, coming second only to Final Fantasy VII.
Sequel
The game was followed up by Alundra 2 in 1999.
Sequel
The sequel uses 3D graphics and has little in common with the original game.

pst_alundro_2.title: Alundra 2
sents: lead

Alundra 2: A New Legend Begins (アランドラ2 魔進化の謎, Arandora 2 Ma Shinka no Nazo, "Alundra 2: The Mystery of Magic Evolution") is an action role-playing game developed by Matrix Software and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It was released in Japan in 1999 and internationally by Activision in 2000.
lead
Unlike its predecessor, Alundra, Alundra 2 features a 3D look which opens up a new world of puzzles.
lead
Also, despite its title, Alundra 2 is a standalone sequel, and has no ties with the original.
lead
It has a whole new story with a different set of characters, including the main character, Flint.
lead
Compared to the darker storyline of Alundra, Alundra 2 has a more light-hearted storyline.
Gameplay
Alundra 2 is an action role-playing game that has the environment in 3D, the character can be moved in all directions, and the camera can be manually rotated 360 degrees.
Gameplay
The game also features unique magical ring items which grant Flint special powers such as the abilities to float in place or traverse over harmful lava.
Story
Flint eavesdrops on their conversation and it is mentioned that Mephisto can create "mechanical men" through a technology that only he understands.
Reception
Japanese magazine Famitsu gave the game a score of 28 out of 40.
Reception
But if you're a devout fan of Alundra however, you may want to tread lightly as Alundra 2 shares little in common."

pst_legend_of_manna.title: Legend of Mana
sents: lead
Legend of Mana is a 1999 action role-playing game developed and published by Square (now Square Enix) for the PlayStation.
lead
It was the fourth game released in the Mana series, following 1995's Trials of Mana.
lead

Set in a high fantasy universe, the game follows an unnamed hero as they restore the land of Fa'Diel by creating the world around them and completing a number of interrelated quests in order to restore the Tree of Mana.
lead
While incorporating action role-playing elements from the prior games in the series, such as real-time battles, Legend of Mana has its own distinct style of gameplay.
lead

Most notably, it gives the player the ability to shape the world's structure through the Land Make system, generating regions and quests in a non-linear gameplay system rather than a strong main plotline.
lead
Legend of Mana was directed by series creator Koichi Ishii, designed by Akihiko Matsui, and produced by veteran Square director and producer Akitoshi Kawazu.
lead
The game had high sales, selling 400,000 copies in its first week of release and 700,000 by the end of 1999.
lead
Reviews were less positive than for prior games in the series.
Gameplay
Like previous games in the Mana series, Legend of Mana displays an angled top-down perspective, in which the player characters navigate the terrain and fight off hostile creatures.
Gameplay
Legend of Mana, unlike previous games in the Mana series, does not feature a set journey through a fixed world.
Gameplay
Adjacent Lands are not connected; to move from one land to another the player must first return to the map screen.
Gameplay
Each Land is ranked from 0 (no presence) to 3 (strong presence) in its strength in each Spirit of Mana; this in turn causes magic of that element to be stronger in that Land.
Gameplay
Pets can also be raised with the Japan-only PocketStation peripheral, and two players can battle each other in an arena.
Setting
Legend of Mana is set in the fictional world of Fa'Diel.
Characters and story branches
Rather than a single, overarching plot, the story of Legend of Mana is composed of a multitude of quests split into three main quest arcs, numerous other quests, and a final quest arc.
Characters and story branches
The first main arc is the story of the Jumi, a dying race of people who have external jewel hearts which are considered valuable.
Characters and story branches
Regardless of which path(s) the hero decides to take, they begin the game's final story, titled "Legend of Mana".
Development and release
Legend of Mana was directed by Mana series creator Koichi Ishii, who had worked on the three previous games in the series.
Development and release
Retro Gamer, in 2011, stated that although Ishii kept the game tied to previous titles in the series by reusing gameplay elements, Kawazu had a heavy influence on the gameplay design of the game.
Development and release

Legend of Mana was designed as a 2D game, despite the PlayStation 's 3D -focus, as the console could not handle the full 3D world Ishii envisioned where one could interact with natural shaped objects.
Development and release
Content such as numerous character sprites and item game mechanics had to be scrapped for the sake of fitting the whole game on one CD-ROM.
Development and release
Legend of Mana was first announced by Square in March 1999 just before its debut at the Tokyo Game Show.
Development and release
The game was released in Japan in July 1999 with considerable hype, packaged with demos of Square's future releases Vagrant Story, Chrono Cross, Front Mission 3, and Threads of Fate.
Development and release
It was planned to be released in North America alongside the July and August 2000 releases of Chrono Cross and Threads of Fate, but was instead released early on June 6.
Music
The original score for Legend of Mana was composed, arranged, and produced by Yoko Shimomura.
Music
Shimomura was a newcomer to the series; the previous two Mana games were scored by Hiroki Kikuta, and the first by Kenji Ito.
Music
Shimomura said in 2002 that she considered the soundtrack to Legend of Mana to be the one that best expresses herself.
Music
Legend of Mana featured the first vocal track of any Mana game, "Song of Mana", which also serves as the game's opening theme.
Music
The 1999 soundtrack album Seiken Densetsu / Legend of Mana Original Soundtrack collects 55 tracks of music from Legend of Mana on two discs.
Music
The soundtrack was published by DigiCube, and was reprinted by Square Enix in 2004.
Music
The album reached #65 on the Japanese Oricon music charts and stayed on the charts for two weeks.
Music
"Song of Mana" was later made available on the Square Vocal Collection album in 2001.
Merchandise

As a promotion for Square's "Summer of Adventure" release schedule in 2000, which the North American release of the game was a part of, those who preordered the game were given a free music CD with select tracks from the game.
Merchandise
Legend of Mana was re-released in Japan late in 2000 as part of the Square Millennium Collection at a budget price along with a special music box and two character figurines.
Merchandise
A companion book titled Seiken Densetsu: Legend of Mana Ultimania including artwork and interviews was released as part of Square's Ultimania series.
Merchandise
It was published by DigiCube in 1999 and later reprinted by Square Enix in 2004 after the subsidiary's closing.
Merchandise
An artbook, Legend of Mana: Making of Mana, was published in 2000 by ASCII.
Merchandise
A five-volume manga series, created by Shiro Amano, was published between 2000 and 2002.
Reception
In Japan, Legend of Mana was a bestseller at the time of release, and sold over 400,000 units in its first week alone as the highest-selling release that week in Japan.
Reception
By the end of the year, it had sold over 700,000 copies in Japan.
Reception
Legend of Mana was also the top selling PlayStation game during the week of its release in North America.
Reception
Legend of Mana received mixed reviews from critics.
Reception
Bilyk noted that the visuals "may be the most impressive two-dimensional graphics ever to grace an RPG".
Reception
Andrew Pfister of Electronic Gaming Monthly praised them even more, calling them "the most impressive 2D artwork ever seen on a console".
Reception

Damian Thomas's RPGFan review likened the graphics to Disney animation for having "a very storybook, cutesy cartoony feel to them", while Andrew Vestal of GameSpot said that the graphics were some of the most lush and ornate 2D graphics ever made.
Reception
The game won an award for best graphics at the 4th Japan Game Awards from the Computer Entertainment Supplier's Association.
Reception
The music in Legend of Mana was also a high point in many reviews; the reviewers for Electronic Gaming Monthly called it "fantastic" and "wonderful".
Reception

Smith of IGN's review stated that the soundtrack is "as good as any you'll hear today" with a good mix of intensity, suspense, and subtle nuance, and Vestal of GameSpot termed it "excellently orchestrated" and a perfect fit for the game in each environment.
Reception
GamePro, while praising the Land Make system, found that the "focus of Legend of Mana is obscured by the over-abundance of subplots".
Reception
IGN's Smith concluded that while he enjoyed the game, he felt that it was not a complete game like Secret of Mana, but instead a collection of fun experiences.
Legacy
In November 2000, Legend of Mana was ranked number 48 on Weekly Famitsu ' s list of top 100 PlayStation games of all time.
Legacy

The game was re-released on February 21, 2002 as part of the PSone Books best-sellers series in Japan, in 2006 as part of Square Enix's Ultimate Hits collection, and re-released on the PlayStation 3 PlayStation Network store as part of the PSone Classics series on March 22, 2011.
Legacy
A remastered version was released on June 24, 2021 for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and PC.
Legacy
This version of the game was later released for Android and iOS on December 7, 2021.
Legacy
An anime adaptation by Yokohama Animation Laboratory and Graphinica titled Legend of Mana: The Teardrop Crystal aired from October to December 2022.

pst_legend_of_dragun.title: The Legend of Dragoon
sents: lead

The Legend of Dragoon is a role-playing video game developed by Japan Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation in 1999 in Japan, 2000 in North America, and 2001 in Europe.
lead
Set in a high fantasy fictional world called Endiness, the game follows a group of warriors led by the protagonist, Dart, as they attempt to stop the destruction of the world.
lead
The player controls a party of 3D character models through pre-rendered, linear environments.
lead
Combat uses a combination of turn-based mechanics and real-time commands.
lead
Notably, the game includes a quick time event called "addition" during each attack, requiring the player to press a button when two squares converge.
lead
Development began in 1996 and took three years with a production team of over one hundred, and cost $16 million, notably high for the time.
lead
The game's use of realistic CGI cutscenes drew attention from the press.
lead
On release, The Legend of Dragoon received mixed reviews, with critics comparing it unfavorably to the Final Fantasy series.
Gameplay
The Legend of Dragoon features three modes of play: the area map, the field, and the battle screen.
Gameplay
Players explore the world of The Legend of Dragoon by following predetermined routes on a linear 3D map.
Gameplay
The character can only become a Dragoon during a battle if they have obtained spirit points, which are received after successfully executing an addition attack.
Gameplay
The Dragoon form is only usable for a limited number of turns and must recharge to be used again.
Setting and characters
The Legend of Dragoon takes place on a world referred to in-game as "Endiness".
Setting and characters
Winglies are an aggressive species who are able to fly and enslaved humans 10,000 years before the start of the game.
Setting and characters
Meru is a dancer from a flower town and Kongol is the last of his species alive in the game's world.
Story
As he arrives he discovers that the town has been destroyed and his childhood friend Shana has been taken to a prison.
Story
Diaz reveals that during the Wingly reign 10,000 years ago a creature called the Virage Embryo, also known as the God of Destruction, came to the world to end all other life.
Story
Before it could be born, the Winglies used their magic to separate its body from its soul and cast the body into the sky, where it became the Moon That Never Sets.
Story
The soul of the God of Destruction was originally placed inside the Crystal Sphere, which was worn by the Wingly ruler Melbu Frahma to increase his power.
Story
The body can be summoned if the Signets are destroyed, which is done using the immense magical power contained within the artifacts that Lloyd gathered.
Story
Emperor Diaz reveals himself to be Zieg Feld, Dart's father and leader of the Dragoons 10,000 years ago.
Story
Zieg – possessed by Melbu Frahma – takes Shana and destroys the remaining Signet Spheres that seal the Moon That Never Sets, causing it to fall from the sky.
Development
The Legend of Dragoon was developed in-house by Sony Computer Entertainment, Inc.
Development
The producer was Shuhei Yoshida, and this game was both one of the last and largest projects he worked on prior to leaving Japan Studio.
Development
At the beginning of its development in 1996 the company was also creating Ape Escape and Ico, so The Legend of Dragoon began with a very small team.
Development
The production team grew to over 100 staff members and had a budget of $16 million, both considered very large for a PlayStation game.
Development
The team's strive for realism resulted in magic — a common character ability in RPGs — only being incorporated into the Dragoon state or through items with equivalent effects.
Development
There were originally no plans for CGI movies as the character models were polygon-based and there would be a disconnect between real-time and CGI graphics.
Development
The team chose the character's names by writing down 100 names between the letters A to N and then choosing the names they liked best and attaching them to the characters who fit the proposed name.
Development
Iwata originally only designed Dart and Rose, with Rose's hair being bright green.
Music
The music of The Legend of Dragoon was co-composed by Dennis Martin and Takeo Miratsu.
Music
The Legend of Dragoon was Martin's first work for a video game, and was chosen because Sony wanted a different musical style to other RPGs at the time.
Music
Martin was originally supposed to compose the game's music himself, but the game's 4 CD-length made this impractical and the Japanese staff hired Miratsu to create additional soundtracks.
Music
Martin found the limited PlayStation hardware frustrating for compositions.
Release
The Legend of Dragoon was announced in September 1999 after cutscenes from the game were shown at that year's SIGGRAPH event.
Release
The game released in Japan on December 2, 1999.
Release
A North American release was confirmed by Sony in January 2000 and released on June 13, 2000.
Release
The game was released in Europe on January 19, 2001.
Release
The game was re-released as a PlayStation Classic through PlayStation Network on December 22, 2010 in Japan and May 1, 2012 in North America.
Release

In February 2023, Sony Interactive Entertainment announced via the PlayStation Blog that The Legend of Dragoon will be digitally available on PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 on February 21, 2023 under the Classics Catalogue.
Reception
The Legend of Dragoon was given a score of 74 out of 100 by review aggregation website Metacritic based on 12 reviews, indicating a "mixed or average" reception.
Reception
During the 4th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated The Legend of Dragoon for the " Console Role-Playing " award.
Sales
Upon its debut in Japan, The Legend of Dragoon reached second place in sales behind Pokémon Gold and Silver, selling over 160,000 units and becoming the best-selling new release that week.
Sales
By 2007, the game had sold over 280,000 copies in Japan.
Sales
By 2007, The Legend of Dragoon had sold over 823,000 copies in North America.
Other media
An original soundtrack album for the game was released in Japan on January 21, 2000, by SPE Visual Works.
Other media
RPGFan's Lucy Rzeminski called the album "a passable CD if you give it a chance to sink in", praising some tracks but finding most of the album lacking in both quality and variety.
Other media
Chris Greening of Square Enix Music Online gave the album a score of 6/10, saying that while innovative at the time, it had been superseded in quality by later soundtracks.
Other media
"If You Still Believe" was included in the compilation album Game Music Collection ～Sony Computer Entertainment Japan Best～, published by King Records on January 23, 2005.

pst_legend_of_legaya.title: Legend of Legaia
sents: lead
Legend of Legaia (レガイア伝説, Regaia Densetsu) is a role-playing video game developed by Prokion and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
Contrail handled the game's production.
lead
It was released in Japan in October 1998, North America in March 1999 and Europe in May 2000.
lead
A sequel, Legaia 2: Duel Saga, was released for the PlayStation 2.
Plot
Vahn discovers a rare kind of Seru known as a Ra-Seru named Meta, which is both intelligent and capable of merging with a human.
Reception
Next Generation said, "if you can deal with the trite, hackneyed story, the new fighting engine makes this worth checking out." Famitsu scored it 27 out of 40.
Reception
During the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Legend of Legaia for "Console Adventure / Role-Playing Game of the Year".

pst_brigandeen.title: Brigandine (video game)
sents: lead
Brigandine is a turn-based strategy game for the PlayStation video game console, created by developer Hearty Robin and released in 1998.
lead
It was released in North America by Atlus the same year, under the title Brigandine: The Legend of Forsena.
lead
In 2000, Hearty Robin released an expanded version of the game called Brigandine: Grand Edition, which included multiplayer support along with other new features.
lead

In the game, the player chooses one of the nations of the fictional continent of Forsena, and has the goal of conquering the other nations by taking their castles, using troops composed of humanoid commanders and fictional creatures.
lead
Although primarily a strategy game, it also includes some characteristics of tactical role-playing games.
lead
A sequel titled Brigandine: The Legend of Runersia, developed by Matrix Software and published by Happinet, was released on the Nintendo Switch in June 2020.
Gameplay
The number of monsters which may join a troop is limited by the Rune Knight's Rune Power statistic.
Gameplay
Each nation is led by a ruler, who has a unique class but is otherwise similar to other Rune Knights.
Preparation mode
The player may navigate and view statistics of all castles on the continent (although only the castles of the player's nation may be managed).
Preparation mode
If the defending castle is occupied, a battle is marked to occur between the two groups of troops, unless the castle sending the troops is attacked first.
Battle mode
Each unit, with rare exceptions, may act once each turn, and the units belonging to the same troop must act in sequence.
Battle mode
Each side may bring at most three troops to a single battle, regardless of the number of troops that are attacking or defending the castle.
Battle mode
Once a battle starts, the attacker has 12 turns to gain victory by defeating all of the defender's troops.
Battle mode
A troop is defeated by having its leader reduced to 0 hit points, or when the leader retreats.
Battle mode
If the ruler of a nation is reduced to 0 hit points or retreats, all other Rune Knights belonging to that nation retreat.
Battle mode
If the attacker fails to gain victory within 12 turns, all their Rune Knights retreat.
Battle mode
When a Rune Knight is reduced to 0 hit points or retreats, the monsters belonging to its troop may either retreat or be captured by the opposing side.
Battle mode
Monsters which are reduced to 0 hit points are considered to be killed, and disappear forever.
Battle mode
Rune Knights reduced to 0 hit points become unavailable to be used for one in-game month, but aren't affected otherwise.
Playable nations
Lance desires to fight to avenge his father and take back the kingdom which was stolen from him.
Playable nations
Zemeckis doesn't have the ambition of power - he desires to conquer Forsena just because fighting is the only way of life he knows.
Brigandine: Grand Edition
If, after 12 turns of battle, the attacker has a unit stationed on the defender's castle, the attacker now wins.
Brigandine: Grand Edition
If, after 12 turns of battle, the attacker has a unit stationed on the defender's castle, the attacker now wins.
Brigandine: Grand Edition
Many dialog-only cut scenes were replaced by anime cut scenes.
Brigandine: Grand Edition
3D battle animations replaced by simpler and faster 2D animations.
Development
Hearty Robin, then known as Easlystaff, demonstrated the game at the September 1997 Tokyo Game Show.

pst_tales_of_destinee.title: Tales of Destiny
sents: lead
Tales of Destiny (テイルズ オブ デスティニー, Teiruzu Obu Desutinī) is an action role-playing game originally developed by Telenet Japan 's " Wolf Team " as the second main title in Namco 's "Tales of" series.
lead
Originally released in Japan for the PlayStation in December 1997, an English version was later made available in North America in September 1998.
lead

The game features many of the same development staff as its predecessor, Tales of Phantasia, including composers Motoi Sakuraba and Shinji Tamura, with character designs by series newcomer Mutsumi Inomata.
lead
Its producers gave it the characteristic genre name RPG of Destiny (運命のRPG, Unmei no RPG).
lead

A remake for the PlayStation 2 was released in November 2006, which was followed by an updated version called Tales of Destiny Director's Cut (テイルズ オブ デスティニー ディレクターズカット, Teiruzu Obu Desutinī Direkutāzukatto) in January 2008, both exclusive to Japan.
lead
The remake was also given its own unique genre name by its producers as RPG called 'Destiny' (運命という名のRPG, Unmei to iu na no RPG).
lead
Taking place in a fantasy world, the game follows the story of Stahn, a young man who comes across a sentient sword named Dymlos and his subsequent encounters with other similar sword-wielders.
lead
Eventually, he and his friends must unite against evil forces seeking a relic from an ancient war.
Gameplay
The game uses an enhanced version of the Linear Motion Battle System that debuted in the first game of the series, Tales of Phantasia.
Gameplay
Battles take place on a 2-D plane where characters and enemies act in real time.
Setting
Unfortunately, only a select few were chosen, leaving the rest of the people to remain on the bleak surface of the planet.
Setting
In the meantime, the purposeless Swordians fell into a deep stasis sleep, only to awaken when grave threats rose once again.
Main characters
Stahn Aileron (スタン・エルロン, Sutan Eruron, Stan Aileron) is a 19-year-old adventurer who grows into a powerful sword-based physical fighter, Stahn is the protagonist of Tales of Destiny.
Main characters

Leon Magnus (リオン・マグナス, Rion Magunasu, Lion Magnus) is a master swordsman of Seinegald – at age 16 the youngest in history to serve the kingdom, and a close associate of the president of the powerful Oberon Company.
Main characters
Philia Felice (フィリア・フィリス, Firia Firisu, Philia Philis) is a 19-year-old priestess.
Main characters
Garr Kelvin (ウッドロウ・ケルヴィン, Uddorō Keruvin, Woodrow Kelvin) is the 23-year-old Prince of Phandaria, and a skilled archer as well as a swordsman; Igtenos is his wind-elemental Swordian.
Main characters
Mary Argent (マリー・エージェント, Marī Ējento, Mary Agent) is a 24-year-old woman who suffers from amnesia, and is not aware of her last name due to an unknown event in her past.
Main characters
Chelsea Torn (チェルシー・トーン, Cherushī Tōn, Chelsea Tone) is the 14-year-old granddaughter of Garr's archery master, Alba.
Main characters
Bruiser Khang (マイティ・コングマン, Maiti Konguman, Mighty Kongman) is a 39-year-old powerful fighter from a battle arena.
Main characters
Karyl Sheeden (ジョニー・シデン, Jonī Shiden, Johnny Shiden) is the estranged 26-year-old son of an aristocratic family and a bard by trade.
Development
Tales of Destiny was originally developed by members of Telnet Japan and Wolf Team, who had previously worked on Tales of Phantasia.
Development
An English version was announced for North America originally for the third or fourth quarter of 1998, and would later appear at the 1998 Electronic Entertainment Expo in Atlanta.
Development

Namco America had originally intended to dub the character voices into English, and searched for "excellent voice talent to fill positions", yet the final version still retains the original Japanese audio.
PlayStation 2 versions
In a June 2006 press conference, Namco Bandai Games announced that a remake of Tales of Destiny for the PlayStation 2 was in development and due for release some time the following winter in Japan.
PlayStation 2 versions
However, the discovery of unexpected bugs led to the title being delayed past its original due date of November 22, and was instead released on November 30.
PlayStation 2 versions

Namco Bandai Games later announced in a July 2007 press conference that yet another version of Tales of Destiny would be released for the PlayStation 2 called the Tales of Destiny Director's Cut (テイルズ オブ デスティニー ディレクターズカット, Teiruzu Obu Desutinī Direkutāzukatto), and would be due for release in early 2008.
PlayStation 2 versions
The game was released in Japan in January 2008 alongside a limited special edition packaged with an artbook and soundtrack.
Audio
An official soundtrack for the original PlayStation version was released in March 2000 by Movic containing a total of 76 songs across two discs.
Audio
In May 2007, a soundtrack for the PlayStation 2 remake was made available by King Records, and featured 108 songs on four discs.
Audio
Numerous Tales of Destiny radio drama albums featuring the Japanese voice cast have been produced since 1998.
Audio
Tales of Destiny: The Heavens) was also produced by Movic and released between June and August 1999.
Audio

In December 1999, a stand-alone drama album entitled Tales of Destiny ~Proust~ Forgotten Chronicle (テイルズ・オブ・デスティニー～プルースト・Ｆｏｒｇｏｔｔｅｎ Ｃｈｒｏｎｉｃｌｅ, Teiruzu Obu Desutinī Purūsuto Forgotten Chronicle) was released.
PlayStation version
Tales of Destiny obtained a 31 out of 40 total score from Japanese magazine Weekly Famitsu based on individual scores of 8, 7, 8, and 8, earning it the publication's Silver Award.
PlayStation version
In 2006, Famitsu readers would declare it the 79th greatest game of all time in its "All Time Top 100" feature, making it the third highest-ranking Tales game on the list.
PlayStation version
The game sold over 450,000 copies in Japan by the end of 1997, and it received a "Gold Prize" from Sony in May 1998, indicating sales above 500,000 units in Japan.
PlayStation version
It went on to sell approximately 1,139,000 copies worldwide by December 2007.
PlayStation version
It was the best-selling individual single-platform Tales game, as of December 2007.
PlayStation version
The English version received generally positive reception in North America, earning a 73% average score from aggregate review website GameRankings.
PlayStation version
IGN gave the game a 7.5 of 10, stating the game was "Highly recommended, as long as you're a fan of the classic Super NES ".
PlayStation version
RPGamer was less enthusiastic, giving the game a 6 out of 10, calling it "a fairly good game" but not without its flaws.
PlayStation version
GameSpot, however, was much more negative in regards to the game, giving it a 4.9 out of 10.
PlayStation 2 version
The PlayStation 2 remake received a slightly higher score of 32 out of 40 from editors of Weekly Famitsu based on scores of 8, 8, 8, and 8, granting it a Gold Award.
PlayStation 2 version

The original version sold approximately 368,000 copies in Japan by the end of 2006, while the Director's Cut would sell 142,301 copies by the end of 2008, becoming the 92nd most-bought software title in the region that year.
Legacy
The game received a direct sequel, Tales of Destiny 2, which released in 2002 on the PlayStation 2, and was ported to the PlayStation Portable in 2006.

pst_personna.title: Revelations: Persona
sents: lead
Revelations: Persona is a 1996 role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus.
lead
It is the first entry in the Persona series, itself a subseries of the Megami Tensei franchise, and the first role-playing entry in the series to be released in the west.
lead
Originally released for the PlayStation in 1996 in Japan and North America, the title was ported to Microsoft Windows in 1999.
lead
A port to the PlayStation Portable retitled Shin Megami Tensei: Persona was released in North America and Japan in 2009, and the following year in Europe.
lead

This port featured new cutscenes and a reworked English localization that was more faithful to the original Japanese release, as the original 1996 North American localization was heavily criticized for its unfaithfulness to the original Japanese version.
lead
The PlayStation version was also released for the PlayStation Classic on December 3, 2018 worldwide, marking the PlayStation version being released in Europe for the first time.
lead
The story focuses on a group of high school students as they are confronted by a series of supernatural incidents.
lead
After playing a fortune-telling game, the group each gain the ability to summon Personas, the multiple selves within them.
Gameplay

A mixture of navigation styles are used: navigation around the students' hometown is done using an overhead view, navigation of standard environments such as outside areas and story locations use an angled third-person view, and dungeons and most buildings are navigated in first-person.
Gameplay
A Persona can only be fused using cards from certain Persona families.
Setting and characters
The game takes place in Japan in 1996, in the town of Mikage-cho.
Setting and characters
Hermelin High, the town's high school, being in Class 4 taught by Saeko Takami.
Setting and characters
All the main characters have the power to summon Personas, described in the manual as "the power of their hidden selves".
Plot
In the SEBEC route, should the protagonist decide to confront SEBEC, he is first joined by a recovered Maki, then asked by Nanjō to help save Mark, who is captured by demons.
Plot
Philemon contacts them and tells them that the only way to save Saeko is the Demon Mirror, which can remove the source of the mask's curse.
Development
The development of Revelations: Persona began in 1994, after the release of Shin Megami Tensei If....
Development
The Persona system was directly inspired by the Guardian system used in If..., originally designed by future Persona director Katsura Hashino.
Development
The first draft involved the students going on a field trip and being caught in a series of mysterious events.
Development

The first versions created were the original Maki, who had been bed-ridden for a long time, and the "ideal" version, whose inexperience with the outside world and interactions with others made her an expressionless doll.
Ports and localization
Persona was released in Japan on September 20, 1996 for the PlayStation.
Ports and localization
The game was ported to Microsoft Windows and released on March 25, 1999 by ASCII Corporation.
Ports and localization
The game was compatible with Windows 95 and 98 operating systems.
Ports and localization

It was decided to remake the original Persona as a large number of new fans had been brought to the series by Persona 3 and Persona 4, so Atlus decided to give them easier access to the beginning of the series.
Ports and localization
The game was announced in February 2009, and released on April 29 of that year.
Ports and localization
Persona was the first role-playing entry in the Megami Tensei series to be released in the west, with the first Megami Tensei release being action game Jack Bros. in 1995.
Ports and localization

The team that localized Persona was quite small, which made the process quite difficult: not only was there a large amount of text to translate, but the team needed to adjust or change the Japanese references as they feared it might alienate western players.
Ports and localization
The entire Snow Queen route was also cut from the game, leaving only the SEBEC story route open for exploration.
Ports and localization

The PSP remake's localization was similar to those done for Persona 3 and 4, with the dialogue being in tune with modern youth and keeping as close to the original dialogue as possible except for Japan-specific cultural references.
Music
Persona was Tsuchiya and Meguro's first major work, with Meguro beginning shortly before he officially joined Atlus' internal staff.
Music
The first piece composed by Meguro was "The Aria of the Soul", the theme for the Velvet Room, originally commissioned by Aoki.
Music
While he kept the original atmosphere, he also used the experience and musical techniques gained from his work on Persona 3 and 4.
Music
The official soundtrack album, Persona Be Your True Mind Original Soundtrack, was released on June 17, 1999.
Music
An arrange album, Megami Ibunroku Persona Original Soundtrack & Arrange Album, was released April 18, 1999.
Music
In Japan, the official soundtrack for the PSP port was released on April 29, 2009.
Reception
These would remain the best first-week sales in the franchise until the release of Persona 5 in 2016.
Reception
