Because the PlayStation was unable to calculate this in real time, the location of each vertex was stored in each frame at 30 frames per second.
Graphics
Gavin, Baggett, and Cerny attempted to invent a compressor in assembly language for this manner of animation; Cerny's version, although the most complicated, was the most successful of the three.
Graphics
Rubin created Crash's model with 532 polygons and animated all the game's characters.
Graphics
Since only 900 polygons could be visible on screen at a time, parts of the game's landscapes are hidden by trees, cliffs, walls, and twists and turns in the environment.
Graphics
Baggett created two-way compressors that would reduce the 128-megabyte levels down to 12 megabytes and allow them to be compatible with the PlayStation's two-megabyte random access memory.
Graphics
The levels proved to be so large that the first test level created could not be loaded into PowerAnimator and had to be cut up into sixteen pieces.
Graphics
Each piece took about ten minutes to load on a 256-megabyte machine.
Graphics
The hand-drawn cutscenes were dropped after Sony Computer Entertainment picked up Crash Bandicoot for publication, as Sony desired to push the PlayStation's 3D polygonal graphics.
Level design
The first two test levels created for the game were not integrated into the final version because they were too open and had too many polygons.
Level design
After working on those three levels, the first operational jungle-themed level, "Jungle Rollers", was created from pieces of the failed first test level arranged into a corridor between trees.
Level design

Afterward, two to three levels would be developed for each environmental theme created, with the first level featuring an introductory set of challenges and later levels adding new obstacles (such as dropping and moving platforms in the second jungle-themed level) to increase the difficulty.
Level design
The level layouts and gameplay mechanics were generally not drawn out on paper beforehand and were largely the result of trial and error by the Naughty Dog team.
Level design

On a Saturday in January 1996, Gavin and Rubin conceived the crate mechanic, reasoning that crates would be made up of a low amount of polygons and multiple types of which could be combined to interesting effect.
Level design
The first crates were integrated into the game six hours later, and many more were placed during the following days.
Level design
By February 1996 over 20 levels had been created which were in various stages of completion.
Level design
One of the last levels he created was "Stormy Ascent", which was roughly four times longer than the other levels.
Level design
Because removing the level completely was considered too risky, Stormy Ascent was left hidden within the disc and accessible to play via GameShark.
Audio
The music for Crash Bandicoot was a last-minute aspect added to the game before its showing at E3.
Audio
The sound of Ripper Roo's maniacal chortling is a sample of a hyena (voiced by Dallas McKennon) from Lady and the Tramp (1955).
Marketing and release
Sony appreciated the demonstration, but internal management issues meant that Sony would not sign an agreement with Universal Interactive to publish the game until March 1996.
Marketing and release
While preparing for the game's demonstration at the 1996 E3, the team decided to finally rename the title character "Crash Bandicoot", a name credited to Kurosaki and Dave Baggett.
Marketing and release
Universal Interactive, in an attempt to take credit for Crash Bandicoot, notified Naughty Dog that they were not allowed to attend E3.
Marketing and release

In response to this provocation, Jason Rubin drafted and printed 1,000 copies of a document entitled "Naughty Dog, creator and developer of Crash Bandicoot " to hand out in front of the Crash Bandicoot display at E3.
Marketing and release
Crash Bandicoot was first shown at E3 in May 1996 and was met with enthusiastic reactions.
Marketing and release
Crash Bandicoot was displayed at the front of Sony's booth at E3, replacing their original choice of Twisted Metal.
Marketing and release
An additional commercial featuring Sega was considered but never created due to increasing expenses.
Marketing and release
The development of Crash Bandicoot spanned a total of 18 months.
Marketing and release
It was released in North America on September 9, 1996, and in Europe on November 8, 1996.
Japanese distribution
Upon Naughty Dog's first meeting with the executives of Sony Computer Entertainment Japan, the executives handed Naughty Dog a document that compared Crash with Mario and Nights into Dreams.
Japanese distribution
Crash Bandicoot was released in Japan on December 9, 1996.
Japanese distribution
It was later re-released as part of The Best for Family range on May 28, 1998, and the PSOne Books release followed on October 12, 2001.
Reception
Storm of GameFan, who gave both the game and its competitor Super Mario 64 perfect scores, determined that " Mario 64 is a perfect action/adventure and that Crash is a perfect action/platform".
Reception

In 2009, Jim Sterling of Destructoid stated that the game has aged poorly since its initial release due to a lack of support for DualShock thumbsticks, a poor camera, and substandard jumping and spinning controls.
Reception
In 2015, the staff of Fact ranked Mancell's score as the 69th greatest video game soundtrack, describing it as "the best Funky house riffs this side of Crazy Cousins".
Reception
In 2018, the game was ranked #179 in GamesTM ' s list of "200 Greatest Games of All Time".
Sales

In the United States, the game was the second-highest renting PlayStation title at Blockbuster Video in its opening month before topping the chart the following month and staying within the top ten for two subsequent months.
Sales

The game sold over 1 million units worldwide in 1996, including 640,000 copies in the United States and Europe, becoming the fourth and fifth best-selling PlayStation game of 1996 in the United States and Europe, respectively.
Sales
In Australia, the game sold more than 100,000 copies in its first month of release.
Sales
Crash Bandicoot ' s success continued into 1997, in which it was the tenth best selling video game in the United States.
Sales

In May 1997, Crash Bandicoot became the first non-Japanese game to receive a "Gold Prize" in Japan for sales of over 500,000 units, and in September 1997, it was inducted into the Greatest Hits budget range.
Sales
By late February 1998, its sales in the United States reached 1.5 million units, while Japanese and European sales reached 610,000 and 725,000 units, respectively.
Sales

Sales continued through 1998: PC Data tracked 771,809 domestic sales of Crash Bandicoot for the year, which drew $16 million in revenue and made it the United States' 10th-best-selling PlayStation release of the year.
Sales
The game spent nearly two years on the NPD TRSTS top 20 PlayStation sales charts before finally dropping off in September 1998.
Sales
In Australia, it was the fourth best-selling home console game of 1998.
Sales
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, Crash Bandicoot took home a "Gold" prize for revenues above €17 million in the European Union during 1998.
Sales
By February 1999, 4.49 million copies of Crash Bandicoot had been shipped to retailers worldwide.
Sales

As of November 2003, Crash Bandicoot has sold over 6.8 million units worldwide, making it one of the best selling PlayStation video games of all time and the highest selling ranked on sales in the United States.
Legacy

Following the release of Crash Bandicoot, Naughty Dog developed and released two sequels, Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back (1997) and Crash Bandicoot: Warped (1998), and the kart racing game Crash Team Racing (1999), all to critical acclaim and commercial success.
Legacy

The Crash Bandicoot series established Naughty Dog's reputation in the video game industry, and they found further success with the Jak and Daxter, Uncharted and The Last of Us series; Naughty Dog later recreated a level of Crash Bandicoot within its 2016 title Uncharted 4: A Thief's End.
Legacy
After the publishing deal between Universal Interactive and Sony ended in 2000, several more games were developed for the Crash Bandicoot series by different developers, which received mixed reviews.
Legacy
Crash Bandicoot was released on the PlayStation Network in the United States on December 4, 2006, and in Europe on June 22, 2007.
Legacy
During E3 2016, Sony announced that as part of the series' 20th anniversary, the first three games of the series would be remastered by Vicarious Visions in a compilation titled Crash Bandicoot N.
Legacy
Sane Trilogy, which was released for the PlayStation 4 on June 30, 2017.
Legacy

Dark Horse Books reprinted the original developer's bible for Crash Bandicoot as a hardcover publication titled The Crash Bandicoot Files: How Willy the Wombat Sparked Marsupial Mania, which was released on March 27, 2018.
Legacy
In April 2024, a prototypical port of the game for the Sega Saturn was created by homebrew developer Frogbull, with a playable build being revealed in August.

pst_crash_bandicute_warped.title: Crash Bandicoot: Warped
sents: lead
Crash Bandicoot: Warped, known in Europe as Crash Bandicoot 3: Warped, is a 1998 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It is the third game in the Crash Bandicoot video game series following Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back.
lead
The game's story takes place immediately after the events of the second game.
lead
The game follows the main characters Crash and Coco Bandicoot as they travel through time and prevent the villains from gathering the crystals by collecting them themselves.
lead

Crash Bandicoot: Warped was lauded by critics, who noted a high quality in many areas, including gameplay, graphics and audio, and the game has been considered one of the best video games of all time.
lead
It went on to sell nearly 6 million units, making it one of the best-selling video games for the PlayStation.
lead
In Japan, the game surpassed the sales of its two predecessors and became the first non-Japanese PlayStation title to sell over 1 million copies in the country.
lead
A remastered version was included in the Crash Bandicoot N.
Gameplay
Warped is a platform game in which the player controls Crash and Coco Bandicoot, who must travel through time and gather 25 crystals scattered across time before Doctor Neo Cortex and Uka Uka do so.
Gameplay
The Time-Twisting Machine is split up into five chambers; only the first chamber is initially available.
Gameplay
The goal in each level is to find and obtain the crystal hidden in the area.
Gameplay
When all 25 Crystals are found and all five boss characters are defeated, the game is won.
Gameplay
More lives can be earned by collecting 100 "Wumpa Fruits" or breaking open a special crate to collect a life.
Gameplay
Gems are rewarded to the player if all of the crates in a level are broken open or if a secret area is completed.
Gameplay
Colored gems are found in special levels and lead to hidden areas.
Gameplay
Scattered throughout the level are yellow crates with the numbers 1, 2 or 3 on them.
Gameplay
The first five Relics the player receives unlocks access to a level in the "Secret Warp Room".
Gameplay
Every five Relics thereafter open up another level in the Secret Warp Room.
Gameplay
The levels in the Secret Warp Room must be won before the game can be completed.
Development
Production of Warped began in January 1998, with Naughty Dog given only ten and a half months and a budget of over $2 million to complete the game.
Development
It was released in North America on November 3, 1998, and in Europe on December 11, 1998.
Development
The Japanese version of Crash Bandicoot: Warped was one of the first video games to support the PocketStation, a peripheral that downloads minigames from PlayStation games.
Character and level design
The emotion sketches depicting Cortex begging for forgiveness inspired the shot design and animation for the game's cinematic introductory sequence.
Character and level design
Zembillas drew the first sketches of Tropy (and the doodle he created as Naughty Dog was describing the character to him) on January 22, 1998.
Character and level design
Zembillas drew the first sketches of Dingodile on February 4, 1998.
Character and level design
The final sketches of Dingodile were drawn on February 12, 1998.
Character and level design
A panda was originally considered but was rejected due to its similarity to the polar bear seen in Cortex Strikes Back.
Character and level design
The shark seen in the game's underwater levels was one of Jason Rubin's first PowerAnimator models.
Character and level design
The model was originally built for the first Crash Bandicoot game, but was not used until Warped.
Character and level design

The "time travel around the world" theme of Warped allowed the Naughty Dog artists to stretch beyond the limits imposed by the island-themed setting of the previous games; each time theme has distinctly unique structures and color palettes.
Character and level design
The most detailed textures of Warped are located in the Egyptian Tomb levels in the form of decorative paintings.
Character and level design
To give the desert highway some character, full-service gas stations and diners were added to the roadside to evoke a " 1950s America " flavor.
Reception

Johnny Ballgame praised the game's graphics as "incredibly clean" and "detailed", citing the water in the jet ski levels as "the most realistic-looking waves of any PlayStation game we've seen so far".
Reception

Mark Cooke praised the game's "smooth" and "cartoonish" animation as "top of the line, bested by no other game" and its "limitless" rendering distance and "beautiful" 3D models as "the pinnacle of PlayStation rendering".
Reception
Randy Nelson was thankful for the game's increased musical diversity in comparison to Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back.
Reception
By February 1999, 2.9 million copies of Warped had been shipped to retailers worldwide; the NPD Group reported sell-through of 862,506 copies in North America alone by the end of January.
Reception
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, it took home a "Gold" prize for revenues above €15 million in the European Union during the previous year.
Reception
By 2002, Warped had sold over 5.7 million units worldwide, making it the thirteenth best-selling PlayStation video game of all time.
Reception
The game's success resulted in its re-release for the Sony Greatest Hits lineup on August 23, 1999, and for the Platinum Range in 2000.
Reception
Crash Bandicoot: Warped was a bestseller in Japan, and was the first non-Japanese PlayStation title to receive a "Platinum Prize" in Japan for selling over 1 million units.
Reception

Game Informer placed the game 26th on their top 100 video games of all time in 2001 noting the game's difficulty not hard like the first game and not too easy like the second game and praising the platforming action as “fantastic”.

pst_crash_team_raising.title: Crash Team Racing
sents: lead
Crash Team Racing (stylized as CTR: Crash Team Racing) is a 1999 kart racing video game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It is the fourth installment in the Crash Bandicoot series.
lead

The game's story focuses on the efforts of Crash Bandicoot, Doctor Neo Cortex, and other ragtag team of characters in the Crash Bandicoot series, who must race against the egomaniacal Nitros Oxide to save the Earth from destruction.
lead
In the game, players can take control of one of fifteen Crash Bandicoot series characters, though only eight are available at first.
lead
During the races, offensive and speed boosting power-ups can be used to gain an advantage.
lead
Crash Team Racing was released on October 19, 1999, in North America, and on October 20, 1999 in Europe.
lead
It was praised by critics for its gameplay and graphics, though the audio was met with mixed opinions.
lead
A successor, Crash Nitro Kart, was released in 2003 for the Game Boy Advance, GameCube, PlayStation 2, Xbox and N-Gage.
Gameplay
Crash Team Racing is a kart racing game in which the player controls characters from the Crash Bandicoot universe, most of whom compete in karts.
Modes
Crash Team Racing features 5 racing modes: Adventure, Time Trial, Arcade, Versus and Battle.
Modes
In each mode, the player selects 1 from 8 characters to control.
Modes
The objective of the Adventure Mode is to save the world from the story's antagonist, Nitros Oxide, by winning races on 16 different tracks.
Modes
In the beginning of the game, the player only has access to two levels.
Modes
In each level, the player must win a trophy by coming in first place.
Modes
After beating levels, new modes become available, such as the Relic Race, in which the player races through the track alone and completes three laps in the fastest time possible.
Modes
If all of the Time Crates are destroyed, the player's final time is reduced by ten seconds.
Modes
If the player manages to collect all three letters and come in first place, a "CTR Token" is awarded.
Modes
The Purple CTR tokens are awarded for beating the Crystal Bonus Round by collecting 20 crystals under a certain time limit.
Modes
Gem Cups are racing tournaments held against computer-controlled opponents and are accessible in a secret area in the "Gemstone Valley" world.
Modes
In a "Point Limit Mode" battle, the first player to achieve 5, 10 or 15 points wins.
Modes
In the "Time Limit Mode" battle, the player with the highest points after 3, 6 or 9 minutes wins.
Modes
In the "Life Limit Mode", each player has a set number of lives (3, 6 or 9) and the battle has a time limit (3, 6 minutes or forever).
Modes
The player with the most lives at the end of the time limit wins.
Modes
If "forever" is chosen as the length, the battle lasts until only one player is standing.
Modes
Three and four players can team up for 2-vs.-1, 2-vs.-2, 3-vs.-1 or 1-vs.-1-vs.-2 battles.
Characters
Fifteen characters are playable in Crash Team Racing, although only eight of them are playable from the start.
Characters
The main antagonist of the story, Nitros Oxide, is the self-proclaimed fastest racer in the galaxy who threatens to turn Earth into a concrete parking lot and make its inhabitants his slaves.
Characters
Oxide appears only as an opponent in the game's final race and time trials, and cannot be controlled by the player.
Characters
The four boss characters, along with an imperfect and morally ambiguous clone of Crash Bandicoot named Fake Crash, become accessible as playable characters if the Adventure Mode is fully completed.
Characters
Doctor Nefarious Tropy appears as the player's opponent during the Time Trial races and an unlockable playable character, while a bonus character, Penta Penguin, can only be unlocked via cheat code.
Story
The inhabitants of Earth are visited by an extraterrestrial named Nitros Oxide, who claims to be the fastest racer in the galaxy.
Story
Challenging Earth to a game called "Survival of the Fastest", he beckons Earth's best driver to race him.
Story
After undergoing years of therapy to cope with his loss, he takes up unicycle -racing, only to get into a gruesome accident.
Development

Naughty Dog began production on Crash Team Racing after the completion of Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back; the game engine for Crash Team Racing was created at the same time Crash Bandicoot: Warped was produced.
Development
Development took place over the course of eight months on a budget of $2.4 million by a team of 16–18 staff.
Development
The characters of the game were designed by Charles Zembillas and Joe Pearson, who designed the characters of the last three installments of the series.
Development
Nitros Oxide was originally a mad scientist obsessed with speed who plotted to speed up the entire world until the end of time.
Development
The original "speed up the world" plot is referenced in a promotional comic (written by Glenn Herdling and drawn by Neal Sternecky) featured in the Winter 2000 issue of Disney Adventures.
Development

To address the complication of potentially having up to 64 kart tires on a four-player split-screen, programmer Greg Omi developed a method of rendering the tires as camera-based two-dimensional sprites.
Development
The central antagonist character Oxide was never intended to be playable in the game due to the PlayStation console's memory limitations.
Development

Said limitations further affected the game's roster of playable characters; Polar and Pura were originally to ride in the same kart and be played as a single character, but were ultimately split into separate characters, and both Komodo Brothers were to appear in the game before Komodo Moe was omitted.
Development
Crash Team Racing went into the alpha stage of development in August 1999, and the beta stage on September.
Development
98 was given a custom Crash Bandicoot -themed paint job in promotion of the game.
Development
A playable demonstration was included on a promotional compilation disc released by Pizza Hut on November 14, 1999.
Reception
Crash Team Racing was nominated for Console Racing Game of the Year at the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.
Sales
Crash Team Racing has sold 1.9 million units in the United States and over 300,000 units in Japan.
Sales
As a result of its success, the game was re-released for the Sony Greatest Hits line-up in 2000 and for the Platinum Range on January 12, 2001.
Sales

An indirect sequel titled Crash Nitro Kart was released in 2003 for the PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube, Game Boy Advance and N-Gage and was the first game in the Crash Bandicoot series to feature full motion video.

pst_spiro_the_dragon.title: Spyro the Dragon
sents: lead
Spyro the Dragon is a 1998 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead

Spyro the Dragon is an open-ended 3D platformer, featuring large, sprawling levels in which the player must locate collectable items, among which are gemstones, crystallized dragons, and stolen dragon eggs.
lead

Spyro's abilities as a dragon include fire breath, a head-on charging attack, and a mid-air glide which he can use to scale large distances, all of which must be used strategically to find items and defeat enemies.
lead

Spyro the Dragon started development following the release of Insomniac's debut game, Disruptor, which sold poorly but was generally praised by critics, impressing Universal Interactive enough to encourage them to make a second game.
lead
Artist Craig Stitt suggested a game about a dragon, and work began on a new game.
lead

Taking inspiration from the film Dragonheart, the game started out as a more mature title with a dark and realistic approach, but the direction was shifted to have a more whimsical and light-hearted tone to appeal to a wider market of consumers.
lead

The game was one of the first on the PlayStation to utilize shifting levels of detail among rendered objects, thanks to a panoramic engine developed by Alex Hastings which allowed the game's open-ended nature to be fully realized.
lead

Stewart Copeland, the former drummer for The Police, composed the game's music, and the titular character was voice acted by Carlos Alazraqui, alongside additional voices done by Clancy Brown, Michael Gough and Jamie Alcroft.
Gameplay

Spyro the Dragon is a 3D platform game; the player controls the titular character as he ventures across the realms of the Dragon World to defeat the antagonistic Gnasty Gnorc, as well as rescue his fellow dragons and recover all of their stolen treasure.
Gameplay
Another important collectible in the game is the dragons' stolen treasure, which is dispersed throughout each level in the form of multicolored gemstones.
Gameplay
There are also stolen dragon eggs that must be reclaimed by chasing and defeating thieves.
Gameplay

These attacks must be used appropriately for certain enemies and situations; for instance, some enemies carry fireproof metal armor, meaning that they can only be defeated by charging, while larger enemies can only be hit using fire breath, as they will immediately crush Spyro otherwise.
Gameplay
Sparx can be rejuvenated by consuming butterflies, which are found by killing passive creatures such as sheep that roam throughout most levels.
Plot
Spyro, a young purple dragon, is the only dragon that manages to avoid getting crystallized by the attack.
Plot
Along the way, he frees the crystallized dragons, who give him advice and urge him to recover any stolen treasure and dragon eggs along the way.
Plot

After Spyro's quest is over, he has access to Gnasty's treasure portal, which can only be opened if Spyro rescues every dragon in the kingdom and recovers all of the dragons' treasure and retrieves the stolen dragon eggs.
Plot
A secret ending can then be unlocked by retrieving everything inside of the treasure portal.
Concept
Spyro the Dragon was the second game developed by Insomniac Games, following the release of their first game, Disruptor, in December 1996.
Concept

According to programmer Peter Hastings, the dragon character was originally going to be named "Pete", but due to copyright concerns over similarities to the Disney film Pete's Dragon, the name was scrapped.
Concept
Spyro was originally going to be green, but the developers worried he would blend in with grass, so they eventually changed him to purple.
Concept
As a result, a demo of Crash Bandicoot: Warped was hidden in Spyro, and vice versa.
Design

Spyro the Dragon was unique compared to other 3D platform games of the time; Spyro's ability to glide allowed him to travel long distances in the air, meaning that the player could cross almost an entire level if starting from a high enough point.
Design
Spyro was coded with efficiency in mind, as 3D rendering technology was new at the time and the game had to fit the limited specifications of the PlayStation.
Design
Around 80% of the game's code was written using Assembly, while other parts were programmed in C due to its simplicity and speed.
Graphics

Spyro the Dragon made use of a 3D panoramic engine, developed by Alex Hastings, that could display far-away objects by utilizing varying levels of detail, a method of rendering which was new and unexplored at the time.
Graphics
This system allowed objects to be displayed from far distances while adhering to the PlayStation's limited RAM capabilities; it was one of the first video games to make use of such a system.
Audio

Alazraqui explained in an issue of Electronic Gaming Monthly that he tried to make Spyro's voice sound like "a kid at camp that everybody likes." Alazraqui did not continue in this role after the first game, being replaced by Tom Kenny for the sequels.
Release
Spyro the Dragon was first unveiled at the 1998 E3 convention in Atlanta, Georgia.
Release
It was then later released in North America on September 9, 1998, and in Europe on October 23 of the same year.
Release
On December 12, 2012, the game was digitally re-released to the PlayStation Store together with Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage! and Spyro: Year of the Dragon.
Release

A remake of the game, alongside its two sequels, was included as a part of the Spyro Reignited Trilogy compilation for the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in November 2018, followed by the Nintendo Switch and Microsoft Windows in September 2019.
Sales
In the week of November 29, 1998, it was the 3rd best-selling game in the UK, behind Tomb Raider and FIFA 99.
Sales
At the 1999 Milia festival in Cannes, it took home a "Gold" prize for revenues above €20,000,000 in the European Union during the previous year.
Sales

Spyro the Dragon received a "Gold" award from the Verband der Unterhaltungssoftware Deutschland (VUD) by the end of August 1999, for sales of at least 100,000 units across Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
Sales
By December 1999, the game had sold 1,000,000 copies in North America.
Sales
As of 2007, the title had gone on to sell a total of nearly 5,000,000 units.
Reception
Spyro the Dragon currently holds a score of 85% at GameRankings, based on an aggregate of 18 reviews.
Reception
IGN 's Craig Harris hailed it as the most fun 3D platformer he had played since Crash Bandicoot, writing "Two claws up.
Reception
Way up." Computer and Video Games called the game "easily the best 3D platform game on the PlayStation", despite noting its largely child-friendly nature.
Reception
Edge named it the best 3D platform game for the PlayStation, but criticized Spyro's limited abilities and said that the game was not as varied as Super Mario 64.
Reception

Fielder spoke positively of Copeland's compositional work, calling it "wonderfully atmospheric." Slo Mo described the music as having a "catchy, mellow jazz-rock swing to it" while also praising the voice work for its wide array of unique voices.
Reception
Fielder wrote that an overabundance of extra lives caused the game to feel "like it was aimed at a younger or broader audience," holding the final boss and the bonus level as the only exceptions.
Legacy

It was the first game in what became an expansive video game series, spawning 2 more platforming sequels for the PlayStation – Ripto's Rage and Year of the Dragon – released in 1999 and 2000, respectively.
Legacy
As of the year 2000, the series had sold more than 3.2 million copies in the U.S. and over 4 million copies worldwide.
Legacy
Insomniac stopped developing the Spyro series after Year of the Dragon, as it finished off their 4-game contract with Universal Interactive.
Legacy

Spyro being their first considerable success, Insomniac went on to develop several other successful video game franchises, including the Ratchet & Clank series of platform games and the first-person shooter series Resistance.
Legacy
The game's rendering system, new and unheard of at the time, has gone on to be used in several other 3D video games.

pst_spiro_ripto_s_rage.title: Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage!
sents: lead
Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage!, known as Spyro 2: Gateway to Glimmer in PAL regions, is a 1999 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It is the second game in the main Spyro series.
lead
A remake was released as part of the Spyro Reignited Trilogy in 2018.
Gameplay
In order to progress through the first two hub worlds, the player must acquire a talisman from each realm, which is awarded for reaching the end of the level, before facing the boss of each world.
Gameplay

Swimming lets Spyro dive underwater to reach submerged treasure and hidden tunnels, climbing lets Spyro climb up certain surfaces, and the headbash lets Spyro perform an overhead smashing attack which can break rocks and certain cages.
Characters and setting
The only characters from the original game to return as main characters in this game are Spyro, the game's protagonist, and Sparx, his dragonfly sidekick.
Development
The sequel to Spyro the Dragon was tentatively titled Spyro the Dragon 2 during its pre-production phase.
Development
The music for Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage! was composed by Stewart Copeland and was engineered and co-produced by Jeff Seitz.
Development

The character Spyro is voiced by Tom Kenny, replacing Carlos Alazraqui from the first game, while additional voices are provided by Kenny, Gregg Berger, Melissa Disney, Milton James, Mary Linda Phillips and Marcelo Tubert.
Development
The game was officially announced at the 1999 E3 convention in Los Angeles, CA.
Development
In Volume 3 Issue 1 of the Official US PlayStation Magazine, which was released in October 1999, the name "Ripto" originated from the Japanese katakana spelling of Spyro.
Development
The game was released in North America on November 2, 1999.
Development
Sony Computer Entertainment of America director of product development Ami Blaire stated, " Spyro 2 isn't just another sequel.
Re-releases
The game became available for download on the European PlayStation Network on July 26, 2007, before its predecessor was released to the same market.
Re-releases
On April 17, 2008, it was released on the Japanese PlayStation Store.
Re-releases

On May 7, 2009, the game became available for download from the North American PlayStation Store and a corrected version was re-released on the European PlayStation Store on December 12, 2012, although as the NTSC version instead of PAL.
Re-releases

Spyro 2, alongside its predecessor and sequel, received a remastered release with updated visuals on November 13, 2018 as part of the Spyro Reignited Trilogy compilation for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One.
Reception
GamePro said of the game, "If you simply loved the first Spyro, or are very intrigued by the second, you can't go wrong with Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage.
Reception
The game received a "Gold" sales award from the Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 200,000 units in the UK.
Reception

pst_spiro_year_of_the_dragon.title: Spyro: Year of the Dragon
sents: lead
Spyro: Year of the Dragon is a 2000 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation video game console.
lead
The third game in the Spyro series, Year of the Dragon follows the adventures of the titular purple dragon.
lead
After an evil sorceress steals magical dragon eggs from the land of the dragons, Spyro travels to the "Forgotten Realms" to retrieve them.
lead
Players travel across different worlds gathering gems and eggs, defeating enemies, and playing minigames.
lead
Year of the Dragon introduced new characters and minigames to the series, as well as offering improved graphics and music.
lead
Year of the Dragon received positive reviews from critics, who noted the game successfully built on the formula of its predecessors.
lead
The game sold more than 3 million copies worldwide.
lead
Year of the Dragon was the last Spyro title released for the first PlayStation, and the last developed by Insomniac Games; their next game would be Ratchet & Clank.
Gameplay
The main objective is to recover stolen dragon eggs which are scattered across 37 levels.
Gameplay
Players do not need to gather every egg to complete the main portion of the game or gain access to new levels; in fact, certain eggs can only be found by returning to the world at a later time.
Gameplay
Gems are scattered across the worlds, hidden in crates and jars.
Gameplay
If the player does not have Sparx, the next hit causes the player to lose a life and restart at the last saved checkpoint.
Gameplay
Some foes are only vulnerable to certain moves.
Gameplay
Spyro can also run through "Powerup Gates", which give him special abilities for a limited period.
Gameplay
Some of the minigames were featured in Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage! and were subsequently expanded for Year of the Dragon, while others are entirely new to the series.
Plot
Spyro meets with Sheila the Kangaroo, Sergeant Byrd the Penguin, Bentley the Yeti, and Agent 9 the Monkey, all who help him on his quest.
Development
After developing the first-person shooter Disruptor, Insomniac Games worked on a third-person platformer that became Spyro The Dragon (1998).
Development
Spyro was followed by a sequel, Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage (1999).
Development

Development of the third Spyro title spanned about ten and a half months, from November 1999 to September 2000; the development team was influenced by a host of other games, including Doom and Crash Bandicoot.
Development
The goal was that the most skilled players would be consistently challenged, while less-skilled players would not be discouraged by the difficulty and give up.
Development

The levels were made larger than those in Spyro 2, so that more areas for minigames could be added; to prevent player confusion on where to go next, these areas were designed to load separately from the main hubs.
Development

Price also noted that their personalities helped freshen the story, which he considered a much more evolved and "coherent" plot than the one originally created for Spyro the Dragon, due to the studio's greater experience.
Release
Year of the Dragon released in the United States on October 10, 2000.
Release

While the upcoming PlayStation 2 was being aggressively promoted, Sony continued to support its three marquee PlayStation 1 games, including Year of the Dragon, with a $10 million advertising campaign.
Release
The game sold more than two million units in the U.S.
Release
By June 2007, the game sold more than 3.2 million units worldwide.
Reception

GameSpot ' s Brad Shoemaker and IGN ' s David Smith noted that the game only brought minor refinements to the series, but that if players liked the previous games, they would enjoy Year of the Dragon as much or more.
Reception

While Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s Ryan Lockheart wrote that Year of the Dragon had the best camera of any 3D game he had played, other reviewers found fault with the camera, particularly when it was unable to keep up with Spyro.
Reception
Simpson and Salzman highlighted the lack of frame rate issues despite the graphics, though GamePro noticed infrequent slowdowns in the most hectic scenes.
Reception
Shoemaker considered the only flaws of the game's presentation inherent with all PlayStation games, though these weaknesses were hidden well.
Reception
Year of the Dragon was developer Insomniac Games ' last Spyro title.
Reception
They began prototyping what would become their next title, Ratchet & Clank, in the first half of 2000, while Year of the Dragon was still in production.
Reception
The next console entry in the series, Spyro: Enter the Dragonfly, was released in 2002.
Reception
Year of the Dragon was later packaged along with the first two Spyro games in the Spyro Reignited Trilogy.

pst_tony_hock_s_pro_skater.title: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater
sents: lead

Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, released as Tony Hawk's Skateboarding in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of Europe, is a 1999 skateboarding video game developed by Neversoft and published by Activision.
lead
It is the first installment in the Tony Hawk's series.
lead
It was released for the PlayStation on September 29, 1999 and was later ported to the Nintendo 64, Game Boy Color, Dreamcast, and N-Gage.
lead
Tony Hawk's Pro Skater takes place in an urban environment permeated by an ambience of punk rock and ska punk music.
lead
The player takes control of a variety of skateboarders and must complete missions by performing skateboarding tricks and collecting objects.
lead
Tony Hawk's Pro Skater was met with critical acclaim for all versions except the Game Boy Color version, which had a more mixed reception.
lead
The game resulted in a successful franchise, receiving eight annualized sequels developed by Neversoft from Pro Skater 2 (2000) to Proving Ground (2007).
lead
It is also credited with introducing skateboarding to a more mainstream global audience.
Gameplay
When this gauge is full and flashing, the player is capable of performing a special trick that is worth many more points than ordinary tricks.
Gameplay
The fifth objective involves collecting a VHS tape hidden in the level.
Gameplay
Three of the mode's levels take place in a competition setting in which the player performs for judges and accumulates the highest score within three one-minute rounds.
Gameplay
In "Graffiti", players must accumulate the highest score by changing level elements into their own color via the use of tricks.
Gameplay
"Trick Attack" is a mode in which players must accumulate the highest score by chaining tricks together.
Gameplay
The first player to accumulate the entire word loses.
Development

Following the releases of arcade game Top Skater (1997) by Sega and PlayStation game Street Sk8er (1998) by Electronic Arts, Activision identified skateboarding-simulation games as a growing market in the gaming industry and concluded that such a title would resonate with a young audience.
Development
The publisher then decided to entrust the project to Neversoft, which had recently completed the third-person shooter game Apocalypse (1998) within nine months.
Development
Although Neversoft had never developed a sports video game before, the development team was confident in its ability to accomplish the task before its given deadline of the 1999 Christmas season.
Development
The game's engine is a modified version of that of Neversoft's previous title Apocalypse, and the game's prototype used Bruce Willis 's character from that game as the placeholder player character.
Development
Once the prototype reached a functional and demonstrable state, the Neversoft team realized that they would require a professional skateboarder to aid in the remainder of production.
Development
In September 1998, Activision established contact with Hawk and arranged a meeting between him and Neversoft.
Development
By January 1999, Activision publicly announced their agreement with Hawk to include him in the game.
Development
The 900 featured in the game was itself drawn from footage of Hawk's famed performance of the feat in the X Games that summer, and was a relatively late addition as a result.
Development
The collection of VHS tapes was directly inspired by the collection of stars in Super Mario 64 (1996).
Development
Manuals were originally intended to be implemented into the game, but were omitted due to time constraints; manuals would subsequently be included in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2.
Promotion and release
Elissa Steamer 's inclusion in the game, along with the game's final release date of September 29, was presented on August 26, 1999.
Promotion and release
A playable demo with only two available skaters was integrated into the Jampack Summer '99 compilation CD released by PlayStation Underground.
Promotion and release
A second playable demo was included on a promotional compilation disc released by Pizza Hut on November 14.
Promotion and release

While Neversoft would begin development of the game's sequel, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2, shortly before the release of the first game, Activision would entrust the game's Nintendo 64 port to Edge of Reality, which had recently ported Monster Truck Madness 2 to the same system.
Promotion and release
The Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions received a multi-million dollar advertising campaign on several major youth-targeted channels in the United States beginning in April 2000.
Promotion and release
The game came bundled with the N-Gage QD that was released in 2004.
Ports
The Nintendo 64 port of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater was developed by Edge of Reality and released on March 15, 2000.
Ports
The Dreamcast version was developed by Treyarch, published by Crave Entertainment and released on May 24, 2000.
Ports
The Game Boy Color version was developed by the Japanese company Natsume and released on March 30, 2000.
Ports
The Game Boy Color version is an adaptation rather than a true port of the PlayStation version due to the limited capacity of the platform.
Ports
There are four gameplay modes in which the player can only perform a few tricks.
Ports
In "Half Pipe Mode", the player must attempt to achieve the highest score possible.
Ports
"Tournament Mode" is a five-level vertically scrolling game in which the player must race against three computer-controlled skaters and achieve the highest rank.
Ports
The N-Gage version was developed by Ideaworks3D and released on October 13, 2003, a week following the launch of the N-Gage.
Ports

The game is a faithful port of the PlayStation version and retains most of the characters, levels, control scheme and original music while adding levels from Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 and two multiplayer games.
Ports
The N-Gage version was named "Best-Mobile Game" by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts in 2004.
Ports

A remake of both the first game and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2, titled Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2, was developed by Vicarious Visions and released on September 4, 2020, for PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One, followed up a year later on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and Nintendo Switch.
Ports

The remake includes all of the original levels and skaters from the original games, but also includes improved skater creation and park creation modes, online multiplayer, and other new features, and featuring most of the original soundtracks, with a few exceptions due to licensing issues.
Reception

Doug Perry of IGN praised the game's "imaginative, deep, and amazingly addictive" gameplay, "steady and consistent" learning curve, "intuitive and natural" controls, large and complex levels, "jaw-dropping" physics and "perfect" soundtrack.
Reception
Three reviewers for Next Generation magazine - Blake Fischer, Eric Bratcher, and Greg Orlando - gave five stars out of five for PlayStation, Nintendo 64, and Dreamcast versions, respectively.
Reception
Tony Hawk's Pro Skater was ranked #36 in Game Informer ' s "Top 100 Games of All Time" in its 100th issue in August 2001.
Reception

The game was nominated for "Console Game of the Year" and " Console Sports Game of the Year " during the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, but lost to Soulcalibur and Knockout Kings 2000, respectively.
Reception
The game was included on Polygon 's 2017 list of The 500 Best Games of All Time.
Sales
Tony Hawk's Pro Skater was the third highest-selling PlayStation title of November 1999 in the United States.
Sales
From its release date to late-December 1999, the game shipped in excess of 350,000 units and was available in over 10,000 retailers nationwide.
Sales

The PlayStation version of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater received a "Platinum" sales award from the Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 300,000 copies in the United Kingdom.
Sales
The Verband der Unterhaltungssoftware Deutschland gave the PlayStation version a Gold Award for 100,000 sold copies in Germany by February 2000.
Sales
The PlayStation versions of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater and its successor were respectively the third and second highest-selling console games of 2000.
Sales
The Nintendo 64 version was the sixth highest-selling Nintendo 64 title in the United States during the week of November 19–26, 2000.
Sales
As of 2001, it has sold 3.5 million units.
Sequels

The game resulted in a successful franchise, receiving eight annualized sequels developed by Neversoft from Pro Skater 2 (2000) to Proving Ground (2007), and a 2020 remake along with the sequel, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2.
Cultural impact
In 2020, a documentary film Pretending I'm Superman: The Tony Hawk Video Game Story from Swedish director Ludvig Gür was released chronicling the development and impact of the game.
Cultural impact
Throughout the 2010s and 2020s the game's soundtrack was acknowledged as having been a major cultural influence in music, particularly in spreading punk and metal to millennials.

pst_tony_hock_s_pro_skater_3.title: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3
sents: lead
Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 is a 2001 skateboarding video game and the third installment in the Tony Hawk's series.
lead
It was published by Activision under the Activision O2 label in 2001 for the PlayStation, PlayStation 2, Game Boy Color and GameCube.
lead
In 2002, it was published for the Xbox, Game Boy Advance, Windows, Mac OS, and the Nintendo 64.
lead

It was the final official release for the Nintendo 64 (having been discontinued 3 months prior), the first game released for the PlayStation 2 supporting online play and was a launch title for the GameCube in North America and PAL regions.
lead

lead
Pro Skater 3 is also considered to be one of the greatest video games ever made.
Gameplay
The game stood out in the franchise for being the first title to have online capabilities.
Gameplay
Users could connect directly to other players online on the PlayStation 2 version—even prior to the launch of the network adapter, with a USB Ethernet adapter.
Gameplay
Due to the shut down of most Sony servers the game is no longer playable with others online, except for via programs like XLink Kai or through websites that allow users to play online through a DNS.
Gameplay
The PlayStation and Nintendo 64 versions run on the Pro Skater 2 engine, with a different revert animation that is the same as the PlayStation version of Pro Skater 4.
Gameplay
The Xbox version has an improved frame rate over the PlayStation 2 and GameCube version, as well as an additional level, the Oil Rig.
Development

Shortly prior to release, Neversoft quickly amended some of the objectives in the Airport level due to sensitivity reasons in light of the September 11, 2001 attacks, where terrorist non-player characters were instead reskinned into pickpockets.
Development
Series producer Ralph D'Amato recalled: "When 9/11 happened, we were almost finished with Pro Skater 3.
Reception
Chester Barber of Next Generation gave five stars out of five for PlayStation 2 version, highly praising the gameplay, new tricks to perform, graphics and controls.
Reception
By July 2006, the PlayStation 2 version of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 had sold 2.1 million copies and earned $77 million in the United States.
Reception
Next Generation ranked it as the 14th highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in the country.
Reception
Combined sales of Tony Hawk console games released in the 2000s reached 10.7 million units in the U.S. by July 2006.
Reception

Its PlayStation 2 version also received a "Platinum" sales award from the British Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 300,000 copies in the country.
Reception

The PS2 version earned a rare perfect 10 score from Jeff Gerstmann of GameSpot (one of only 20 titles to earn this award in GameSpot 's history), who stated that the game "makes everything before it almost unplayable by comparison".
Reception
GameSpot named Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 the best PlayStation game, best alternative sports console game and overall second-best console game of 2001.
Reception
IGN rated the game 9.7/10, stating that the game "should go down in history as one of the best twitch-fests on PlayStation 2".
Reception
The game is currently the top rated PS2 game on the review aggregate website Metacritic, with an average score of 97/100, tying with Grand Theft Auto III.
Reception
Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 was a runner-up for GameSpot ' s 2002 "Best Sports Game on PC" award, which went to Madden NFL 2003.
Reception

During the 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 was honored with the " Console Sports " award by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences; it also received nominations for outstanding achievement in " Animation " and " Visual Engineering ".
Sequel
A fourth game in the series, titled Pro Skater 4, was released the following year in October 2002.

Two Honda NSX cars from 1992 were included in the Japanese version, but were removed from the North American and European versions.

Awards), won "Best Simulation" of 1999 at the Spotlight Awards, won "Best Driving Game" and "Best Graphics" of 1999 according to the staff of PlayStation Official Magazine, and was voted the sixth best game of all time by the magazine's readers in the same issue.
