A year later, the Online version was nominated for the "Best Online Game on PlayStation 2" award at their Best and Worst of 2002 Awards, which went to SOCOM U.S.
Reception

During the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences ' 6th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the latter online version received a nomination for the " Online Gameplay of the Year " award, which went to Battlefield 1942.
Reception
By July 2006, the game had sold 950,000 units and earned $31 million in the U.S.
Reception
NextGen ranked it as the 61st highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between October 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Twisted Metal: Harbor City
A sequel project is Twisted Metal: Harbor City, though it was never officially announced and the project was later scrapped.
Twisted Metal: Harbor City
Details on the game were revealed in the PlayStation 2 port of Twisted Metal: Head-On, Extra Twisted Edition.
Webisodes

Animation S4, a producer of 3D and Flash animations, created a series of six original Flash "Webisodes" to promote the release of Twisted Metal: Black, beginning with No-Face, and including Billy Ray Stillwell, Sweet Tooth, Dollface, Bloody Mary and Mr.

pst_ape_escapade.title: Ape Escape (video game)
sents: lead
Ape Escape is a 1999 platform video game developed by Japan Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
The first game in the Ape Escape series, the game tells the story of an ape named Specter who gains enhanced intelligence and a malevolent streak through the use of an experimental helmet.
lead
Specter produces an army of apes, which he sends through time in an attempt to rewrite history.
lead
Spike, the player character, sets out to capture the apes with the aid of special gadgets.
lead
Ape Escape is played from a third-person perspective.
lead
Players use a variety of gadgets to pursue and capture the apes, traversing across several environments.
lead
The game's controls are heavily centered around the analog sticks, being the first game to require the use of the PlayStation's DualShock controller.
lead
Development of Ape Escape lasted over two years, and was generally focused on adapting to the use of the controller, which was a significant challenge for the development team.
Gameplay
For most of the game, players control Spike—a boy tasked with pursuing and capturing the apes across time, preventing them from rewriting history.
Gameplay
Throughout the game, players can gather Specter Coins, which can be found in hidden locations in each stage.
Plot
Spike must also face off against Specter, who has not only built himself an advanced Monkey Helmet further increasing his own intelligence but has also brainwashed Jake to his side.
Development
Intrigued by the potential of the controller, the team implemented its use in Ape Escape, making it the first video game to require the use of the DualShock for gameplay.
Development
Music from the game was included in Ape Escape Originape Soundtracks, published on November 18, 2011, by Terada's label Far East Recording.
Development
Ape Escape was officially announced in the April 1999 issue of Official U.S.
Development
A playable demonstration was integrated into the Jampack Summer '99 compilation CD released by PlayStation Underground.
Development
A second playable demonstration was included on a promotional compilation disc released by Pizza Hut on November 14.
Development
Promotions for the game were held on Cartoon Network during Sony's winter holiday marketing campaign of 1999.
Development
The game was released in North America on June 22, 1999.
Development
A remake, titled Ape Escape: On the Loose, was announced on May 11, 2004, during Sony's press conference at the Electronic Entertainment Expo.
Development
It was released as a launch title for the PlayStation Portable (PSP) on March 24, 2005.
Critical reception
Ape Escape received "universal acclaim", according to review aggregator Metacritic, based on 19 reviews.
Critical reception
Japanese publication Famitsu gave it 32 out of 40, based on four reviews.
Critical reception
Edge credited the distinct stages and original weapons, concluding that Ape Escape "offers enough novelty to make it worth serious consideration for anyone tired of the many me-too platformers".
Critical reception
Next Generation felt the game's "general light-hearted cuteness makes it ideal for younger players, but its originality and challenge will also appeal to the most jaded hardcore players".
PlayStation Portable version
Ape Escape: On the Loose received "mixed or average reviews" according to Metacritic, based on 35 critics.
PlayStation Portable version
1Up.com ' s Jeremy Parish criticised the porting of the game for being outdated, declaring it "a game that was better in another time, on another system, ported simply for cynical convenience".
PlayStation Portable version
Parish felt that On the Loose served "to blemish the PSP's reputation... as a dumping ground for warmed over 32-bit offerings far beyond their sell-by date".
Sales
Ape Escape sold 70,000 copies in Japan in its first three days, over 293,000 copies by the year's end, and more than 500,000 overall.
Sales
On the Loose sold over 250,000 copies, also earning the Greatest Hits label.
Legacy
Ape Escape is considered one of the most significant titles on the PlayStation console.
Legacy
Perry of IGN declared it "the best 3D platform game on the PlayStation", and GameSpot's Peter Bartholow named it "one of the best 3D platformers to date".
Legacy
Scott Alan Marriott of AllGame described the game as "one of the most enjoyable 3D platform games" on the PlayStation.
Legacy
IGN included Ape Escape in an article documenting the greatest PlayStation 3D platform games, and later named it the eighth greatest game on the console.
Legacy
In March 2004, Official UK PlayStation Magazine named it the ninth greatest game of all time.
Legacy
Game Informer ranked it 100 on its list of best games in 2001, praising its gameplay and innovation.
Legacy
A direct sequel, Ape Escape 2, was released for the PlayStation 2 (PS2) in July 2001, followed by Ape Escape 3 for PS2 in July 2005.
Legacy
Several spin-off titles were released exclusively in Japan: Pipo Saru 2001 in July 2001 and Saru!
Legacy
Million Monkeys in July 2006 for the PS2, followed by Saru Get You: Pip Saru Racer in December 2006 and Saru!
Legacy
Another spin-off, Ape Quest, was also released worldwide for PSP in January 2008.
Legacy

A series of party games has also been released: Ape Escape: Pumped & Primed in July 2004 and EyeToy: Monkey Mania in August 2004 for PS2, as well as Ape Academy 2 for PSP in December 2005, and PlayStation Move Ape Escape for the PlayStation 3 in December 2010.
Legacy

The character of Spike is available as a playable character in PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale (2012), and an ape costume is available as a downloadable outfit in some of the LittleBigPlanet games (2008–12).
Legacy
A mini-game featuring an ape from Ape Escape is included in Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater (2004).
Legacy
Ape Escape was added to the Deluxe tier of the PlayStation Plus lineup in May 2022, playable on PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 with full Trophy support.

pst_medievel.title: MediEvil
sents: lead
MediEvil is an action-adventure hack and slash video game developed by SCE Studio Cambridge and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead

The game is set in the medieval Kingdom of Gallowmere and centres around the charlatan protagonist, Sir Daniel Fortesque, as he makes an attempt to stop antagonist Zarok's invasion of the kingdom whilst simultaneously redeeming himself.
lead
Development began in 1995 at Millennium Interactive in Cambridge under the working title of Dead Man Dan.
lead
The visuals are heavily influenced by Tim Burton's The Nightmare Before Christmas.
lead
Originally conceived as an arcade-style shooter for platforms such as Windows and the Sega Saturn, Sony's purchase of SCE Cambridge Studio evolved the game into a PlayStation title.
lead
The game received mostly positive praise from critics upon release, with praise including its blend of Halloween themed visuals, but was criticised for its controls and cumbersome camera work.
lead
It was released in Europe and North America in 1998, and in Japan in 1999.
lead
It was also re-released on the PlayStation Network in 2007.
Gameplay
Dan can equip a shield alongside weapons for defence, but each type of shield has a limited amount of strength and are therefore best used sparingly.
Gameplay
In each level, there is a hidden Chalice of Souls which can be collected if the player has dispatched enough enemies (some Chalices are awarded via other means).
Plot
In the year 1286, an evil sorcerer named Zarok plotted to take over the kingdom of Gallowmere with his undead army.
Plot
In reality, however, Dan was struck down by the first arrow fired in the battle, with the king choosing to cover it up and declare Dan the "Hero of Gallowmere".
Plot
100 years later, Zarok reappears, casting a spell over Gallowmere to plunge it into eternal night, awaken his undead army and steal the souls of the living.
Plot

As Zarok uses his last breath to cause his lair to collapse in an attempt to take Dan with him (inadvertently crushing himself in the process), Dan escapes and Zarok's magical influence over the land is thwarted, thus restoring the souls back to the living and putting the dead back to rest.
Development
Development of MediEvil began in late 1995 at independent developer Millennium Interactive in Cambridge.
Development
Sorrell joined Millennium, with whom he had been working with for a while, after completing James Pond 3.
Development

According to Sorrell, the first design proposal for the game had the working title ‘ Dead Man Dan ’ and described a game that was initially a fusion of Capcom 's Ghost'n Goblins combined with the art style of Tim Burton 's The Nightmare Before Christmas.
Development

SCE Cambridge wanted the game to possess a unique lead character, thus Sorrell worked with script doctor Martin Pond whilst creating an expansive backstory for the lead protagonist, Sir Daniel Fortesque.
Development

Sony's acquisition of SCE Cambridge (which occurred within six months of Sony agreeing to publish the game) helped ease financial strain on the project, but did not assist the studio's inexperience with making 3D games.
Development
Sorrell admitted in a retrospective interview that MediEvil presented "a mountain of challenges", since they, as many other developers at the time, were new to 3D gaming.
Development

During development, the Cambridge team played beta versions of successful platformers such as Super Mario 64 and Crash Bandicoot which helped them understand how they might solve some challenges in building a 3D action game for the first time.
Development
Sorrell stated that a spline camera view was the first attempt, but he disliked it due to the lack of freedom for the player to feel as if he was exploring.
Development
Concept art and a separate level was created for this section, but it never materialised into the game.
Development
Sorrell explained that the humour was a "happy accident", and that he used it only when he thought it appropriate.
Music

The 2005 PlayStation Portable re-imagining MediEvil: Resurrection used parts of the MediEvil score, along with original elements composed by Bob & Barn that was performed by a live orchestra and choir.
Marketing and release
MediEvil was first released in North America and Europe in October 1998.
Marketing and release
The Japanese version, titled MediEvil: Yomigaetta Gallowmere no Yūsha, was released on 17 June 1999.
Marketing and release
The game was later released with C-12: Final Resistance in a two-disc pack on 9 May 2003.
Marketing and release
In 2011, MediEvil was ported to Android, although it is only compatible with PlayStation-certified devices such as the Sony Xperia Play.
Reception

IGN 's Chris Roper praised the game's sense of humour and unique presentation, but was skeptical about the game's "sloppy" controls and disjointed level designs, noting that the game's graphics did not age well over time as compared to the PSP remake which offered superior graphics and gameplay.
Reception

Many reviewers compared the visuals to be similar to Tim Burton's The Nightmare Before Christmas, Joe Fielder of GameSpot credited MediEvil for its original look and number of unique puzzles, but criticised the camera work, summarising that a "tighter camera control" would have been a necessity.
Reception

Randy Nelson of IGN considered the game to be a homage to Capcom's Ghosts & Goblins, stating that the game took too many inspirations from others and not enough innovation was put into it to make it "unique".
Reception

MediEvil was named as a finalist by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences for " Console Adventure Game of the Year " and "Console Game of the Year" during the 2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.
Reception

The Android version was described as "rather expensive" by Damien McFerran of Know Your Mobile, but he praised the humour and the amount of content, which he said made the game stand out from other 3D action games on Android.
Sales
The game has been re-released as a "PlayStation Platinum" title in 1999, meaning it sold at least 400,000 copies in Europe.
Remakes
In 2005, a "reimagining" was released on the PlayStation Portable under the title MediEvil: Resurrection.
Remakes
An eponymous PlayStation 4 remake was released in 2019.
Remakes
The original 1998 game can be unlocked in the remake by completing special objectives.

pst_medievel_2.title: MediEvil 2
sents: lead
MediEvil 2 (stylised as MediEvil II in North America) is a 2000 action-adventure game developed by SCE Cambridge Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It is the second instalment of the MediEvil series and a sequel to MediEvil.
lead

Taking place 500 years after the events of the first game, it follows series' protagonist Sir Daniel Fortesque's revival in Victorian-era London as he attempts to stop sorcerer Lord Palethorn and Jack the Ripper 's plans to terrorise the city by raising the dead.
lead
Following the positive reception of the first game, Sony Computer Entertainment commissioned SCE Cambridge Studio to make a sequel to MediEvil before the end of the PlayStation's lifespan.
lead

The original concepts for MediEvil 2 went through many transformations during development before the Cambridge team finally settled on making a sequel set during the Victorian Gothic revival, largely reminiscent of its predecessor.
lead

The game received mostly positive reviews from critics upon release, with praise including slight improvements over its predecessor, such as artificial intelligence and graphical enhancements, but was criticised for lack of innovation from the original.
Gameplay
MediEvil 2 once again sees players in control of Sir Daniel Fortesque as he travels through several levels set in Victorian-era London to thwart the evil Palethorn and his undead army.
Gameplay
MediEvil 2 adds a new feature that allows the player to select two weapons that Dan can toggle between in real-time.
Gameplay
Collecting Life Bottles hidden in certain levels expands Dan's life meter, which can be replenished via Life Vials and Life Fountains.
Plot
The game's plot takes place in 1886, 500 years after Sir Daniel Fortesque's battle against the evil sorcerer Zarok in the previous game.
Plot

Dan collects the final pages and confronts Palethorn, who steals the page from him and offers Dan the choice of joining him, but Dan refuses, saying "I'll never join you!" Palethorn then assigns his two assistants, Mander and Dogman, to stop Dan from following him, but both are killed.
Plot
With his last breath, Palethorn drops a time bomb in a last-ditch effort to kill Dan, destroying his lair in the process.
Plot

If the player has collected all the Chalices, Dan and Kiya instead go for a ride on the time machine which takes them back to the end of the first game, encountering Palethorn in a monstrous form similar to Zarok's.
Development
After the success of the first MediEvil, Sony Computer Entertainment commissioned SCE Cambridge to develop a sequel that would be released before the end of the PlayStation 's lifespan.
Development
Chris Sorrell, who previously served as director of the first game, was not involved in development, so the project was handed over to James Shepherd instead.
Development

The Cambridge studio believed it would not be difficult to make a sequel to the first MediEvil, considering that the ending of its predecessor would give the team an opportunity to set the next game in a different time period.
Development
Shepherd settled on MediEvil 2 being set in the Victorian era, the birthplace of the Neo-Gothic revival.
Development
Various features cut from the previous game were added into MediEvil 2, such as playable characters and levels that featured puzzles.
Reception
MediEvil 2 received favourable reviews, albeit less than its predecessor, according to the review aggregation website GameRankings.
Reception
The game was mostly praised for its rich detailed graphics but was criticised by many reviewers for its bad camera angles, easy difficulty, and similarity to the first game.
Reception
Perry disliked the fixed camera positioning throughout the game and outlined that the camera was "good, not great" and only a small improvement to its predecessor.
Reception

Daily Radar ' s Stephen Frost praised the game's improved artificial intelligence and harder difficulty in comparison to the first game, summarising that MediEvil 2 was "better, not perfect," although he thought that the game was still lacking in innovation.
Reception
At the 2000 BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Awards, MediEvil 2 won the best console game category.
Reception
MediEvil 2 also nominated for "10th Annual GamePro Readers' Choice Awards" for "Best Adventure Game of The Year", but lost to Shenmue for Sega Dreamcast.

pst_parappa_the_napper.title: PaRappa the Rapper
sents: lead
PaRappa the Rapper is a rhythm video game developed by NanaOn-Sha and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation in Japan in 1996 and worldwide in 1997.
lead
Created by music producer Masaya Matsuura in collaboration with artist Rodney Greenblat, the game features unique visual design and rap -based gameplay and is considered the first true rhythm game.
lead
It was ported to the PlayStation Portable in 2006 in celebration of its 10-year anniversary.
lead
A remastered version of the original PlayStation game was released for PlayStation 4 in 2017 for the game's twentieth anniversary.
lead
PaRappa the Rapper was well received by critics, who praised its music, story, animation, and gameplay, though its short length was criticized.
lead
Several publications list it as one of the best video games ever made.
lead

It spawned two follow-up titles; a guitar -based spin-off titled Um Jammer Lammy, released in 1999 for the PlayStation, and a direct sequel, PaRappa the Rapper 2, released for the PlayStation 2 in 2001.
lead
The game was also influential in setting the basic template for the rhythm game genre, including franchises such as the Bemani and Harmonix games.
Gameplay
Rank-changing aspects of a level are only apparent during the first of every two lines.
Gameplay
If the player successfully times the first line of a pair but fails on the second, the rank meter will not blink Bad or Awful.
Gameplay
Likewise, once the game has been cleared, a Good play is only necessary on the first of every two lines to be able to get Cool mode on the second line.
Development
Game development started in 1994, before the release of the PlayStation.
Development

Matsuura was particularly inspired by the musical practice of sampling and claimed "the most interesting thing about sampling was people's voices", and thus wanted to create a music game using actual voices and by extension one based around rap.
Development
One of the first designs Greenblat created specifically for the game was that of the main character, PaRappa, who initially took the form of a shrimp.
Development
The game also is one of the first PlayStation games to use in-game motion capture in order to portray more realistic character movement.
Development
The game, however, became massively successful, which prompted SCEA, despite having a strict policy against 2D games, to release the game in North America.
Reception
PaRappa the Rapper sold 761,621 copies in Japan during 1997, making it the 7th best-selling video game of 1997 in that region.
Reception
In May 1998, Sony awarded the game a "Platinum Prize" for sales above 1 million units in Japan alone.
Reception
As of 2003, the game has sold 1.47 million copies in Japan and 214,398 copies in the United States, for a combined 1,684,398 copies sold in Japan and the United States.
Reception
The game received near-universal acclaim from critics, who hailed PaRappa the Rapper as a unique game with irresistibly catchy songs.
Reception
Next Generation summarized that "The game is so well-produced and carried out that you won't even notice that the gameplay itself is based on the most primitive of concepts.
Reception
Simply put, style over substance has never been better done than in PaRappa." The one common criticism was that the game is too short.
Reception

Electronic Gaming Monthly awarded it "Most Original Game of the Year" and "Best Music", and the character PaRappa "Best Mascot" (beating out Lara Croft and Crash Bandicoot, both of whom had critically acclaimed games released that year), at their 1997 Editors' Choice Awards.
Reception
In the final issue of the Official UK PlayStation Magazine, the game was chosen as the 3rd best game of all time.
Legacy
PaRappa the Rapper is considered the first true rhythm game.
Franchise
PaRappa the Rapper was followed by a spin-off titled Um Jammer Lammy, which was released on 18 March 1999 in Japan.
Franchise
A direct sequel, PaRappa the Rapper 2, was released for the PlayStation 2 in 2001 in Japan and 2002 in North America and Europe.
Franchise

Several media adaptations outside of the video game industry were also developed, including an eponymous anime television series which aired in Japan between April 2001 and January 2002, which served as a tie-in to PaRappa the Rapper 2.
Ports
PaRappa the Rapper was released for PlayStation Portable in Japan in December 2006 and in North America and Europe in July 2007 for the game's tenth anniversary.
Ports
In conjunction with the PSP release, Sony, for a limited time, freely released the soundtrack.
Ports
In a 2008 Famitsu interview, Masaya Matsuura revealed that a brand new song created for the PSP release, "Believe in Yourself", was cut due to development time constraints.
Ports
A remaster of the game by Japan Studio for PlayStation 4 was released on 4 April 2017.
Ports
The port features graphics of up to 4K resolution, and includes all the downloadable songs from the PSP version.
Ports
A playable demo was released on 3 December 2016, celebrating the game's 20th anniversary.
Ports
Homebrew developers found that the PS4 port was actually the PlayStation Portable version running inside an emulator and with high resolution textures.
Ports
In 2016, Sony's mobile studio ForwardWorks announced they were working on a smartphone version of the game; no further details have been released since then.
In popular culture
PaRappa the Rapper was featured as a challenge on the video game-based show GamesMaster in 1998.

pst_um_jammer_clammy.title: Um Jammer Lammy

Composer(s): Masaya Matsuura Yoshihisa Suzuki Shigeyoshi Kawagoe

sents: lead
Um Jammer Lammy (ウンジャマ・ラミー, Un Jama Ramī) is a 1999 rhythm video game developed by NanaOn-Sha and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It is a spin-off follow up to 1996's PaRappa the Rapper, once again featuring the collaboration of music producer and game designer Masaya Matsuura and artist Rodney Alan Greenblat.
lead
An arcade version co-developed by Namco, titled Um Jammer Lammy Now!, was released for the Japanese arcade cabinets in December 1999.
lead
The game received generally positive reviews from critics.
Plot
On the night before MilkCan is due for their first concert, Lammy has a dream of performing alongside Chop Chop Master Onion, only to realize she had been playing a vacuum cleaner the entire time.
Plot
Lammy wakes up and realizes she only has 15 minutes to get to her concert.
Gameplay
Easy is a practice level for stages 1–6, where any button can be pressed on the line, but there is no option to save.
Gameplay

In Lammy's storyline, starting stages 2 onward unlocks various sound morphers (Flanger, Harmonizer, Wah-Wah, Distortion, and Reverb) that can be selected with the Select button whilst playing as Lammy or Rammy.
Gameplay
The player may also use the back shoulder buttons (L2 and R2) to use the guitar's wammy bar.
Gameplay
At the beginning of the game, the only mode available is Lammy's Solo mode.
Gameplay
After clearing a level with Lammy (except Stage 1), the player unlocks Co-op and Vs. modes for Lammy and Rammy.
Development and release
After the success of 1996's PaRappa the Rapper, Sony was eager to release another game in the series.
Arcade version
The arcade version of the game, entitled Um Jammer Lammy Now! is played using a unique guitar controller.
Arcade version
In 2023, after years of it being considered a lost, an arcade cabinet owned by the English broadcaster Jonathan Ross was documented online and portions of the data was archived.
North American version
Most notably, in Stage 6, Lammy no longer goes to Hell after slipping on a banana peel and dying.
North American version

Lyrics were also changed; in Stage 1, Chop Chop Master Onion says "you can play on an island" instead of "you can play in Hell" (referencing the changes to Stage 6), and in Stage 5, which features a lumberjack, anything that implied deforestation was pleasant was removed.
Digital re-release
The game was released on the PlayStation Network in Japan on February 27, 2008 and in North America on October 1, 2009.
Digital re-release
The release is playable on PlayStation 3, PlayStation Portable, and PlayStation Vita.
Music
(Millennium Girl)", was released in Japan on April 21, 1999.
Music
Three soundtracks inspired by the game have been released in Japan by SPE Visual Works.
Music
The game's original soundtrack was released on November 20, 1999.
Music
An album, MilkCan, Make It Sweet was released on June 19, 1999, which features variations on the original songs, the majority of which feature vocals by Michele Burks as Katy Kat.
Music
Finally, Parappa & PJ: I Scream!, which features remixed versions of the game's songs with original lyrics performed by Dred Foxx as Parappa, was released on September 22, 1999.
Reception
But keep in mind that the game doesn't stray far from the formula, and the game's difficulty will put off those who never mastered Parappa.
Reception

It's easily the most insane mish-mash of psychadelia yet seen on a console, and at least deserves a shot (or the whole bottle, even)", but criticized the story, calling it "the most obtuse, disjointed, drug-induced mess of a story that has ever been conceived, period".
Reception
The site even went so far as to rate the game as #40 on the list of the Top 50 Worst Game Names Ever.
Reception
The alternate U.S. version of Lammy's Stage 6, however, drew mixed praise and criticism.
Reception

Similarly, GameSpot's Gerstmann made a later update on his March 26, 1999 review by commenting on the U.S. alterations to Stage 6, exclaiming: "It doesn't really affect the game too much, since much of the game doesn't make a lot of sense to begin with".
Reception
Um Jammer Lammy won E3 1999 Game Critics Awards in the categories "Best Puzzle/Trivia/Parlor Game" and "Outstanding Achievement in Sound".
Reception
The game also received the " Outstanding Achievement in Original Music Composition " award from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences at the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.

pst_klonoah_door_to_phantomile.title: Klonoa: Door to Phantomile
sents: lead
Klonoa: Door to Phantomile is a platform game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation in 1997 and the first game in the Klonoa series.
lead
The story follows Klonoa and his friend Huepow in their efforts to save the dream world of Phantomile from an evil spirit intent on turning it into a world of nightmares.
lead
The player controls Klonoa through a 2.5D perspective; the stages are rendered in three dimensions but the player moves along a 2D path.
lead
Klonoa can grab enemies and throw them as projectiles, or use them as a jump boost to navigate through the stages.
lead
The game was directed by Hideo Yoshizawa, who conceptualized the setting as a dream world that could appeal to children and adults.
lead
The Klonoa character was designed early on and the environments and other characters were designed around him.
lead
Door to Phantomile received positive reviews, being praised for its clever platforming, impressive graphics, and cutscenes.
lead
Some critics thought it lacked in certain gameplay innovations and was excessive in its Japanese cuteness.
Gameplay
It is presented from a 2.5D perspective; the environments are rendered in 3D but the gameplay takes place on a 2D plane.
Gameplay
Enemies can be thrown into the foreground or background as well as along the 2D plane.
Gameplay
Some stages end in boss fights which take place in circular 3D arenas or head-on against a 2D plane.
Plot
After rescuing Granny from Joka, she tells them about a legend that involves the pendant, the legendary moon kingdom, Ghadius and "the dream not of this world".
Plot
Later, a noticeably guilt-ridden Huepow finally tells Klonoa the truth; that he was never from Phantomile at all and that all the memories they had shared together prior to their adventure were fake.
Development
Yoshizawa is known for having previously directed Ninja Gaiden (1988) for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
Development
The game was originally planned to be an adaptation of the manga Spriggan, but the licensing fell through.
Development
Originally the game used three buttons, but was reduced to two for quicker input and faster play.
Development
The 3D graphics and cinematics were made with LightWave 3D.
Release
The game was revealed at the 1997 E3 trade fair with a video demonstration.
Release
In previews, both IGN and GameFan compared the 2.5D gameplay to Pandemonium!.
Release
The game was also presented at the 1997 Tokyo Game Show with playable demos and an actor in a Klonoa costume.
Release
The game was published by Namco on December 11, 1997 in Japan.
Release
It was originally going to feature only a selection of songs because the entire score could not fit on a single disc.
Release
Namco published the game in North America in March 1998, and it was published in Europe on June 5 by Sony Computer Entertainment Europe.
Release
Door to Phantomile was included in a PlayStation 2 compilation of Namco games titled NamCollection in July 2005.
Release
The Japanese exclusive compilation commemorated Namco's 50th anniversary and included five original PlayStation games by the company.
Release
It was also re-released for Japanese mobile phones in July 2009, and as a downloadable PSone Classic on the PlayStation Network in December 2011.
Reception
Critics labeled Klonoa: Door to Phantomile as Namco's first notable 3D platformer and a bid for creating a gaming mascot.
Reception
IGN wrote that it was perhaps the best platformer on the market, and "the first 2.5D platformer that makes use of classic 2D game elements without sacrificing the versatility of a 3D environment".
Reception
Ulrich Steppberger of Man!ac praised the game, and only was critical of the game's short length.
Reception
Namco won "Best Character" for Klonoa at the 1997 Japan Game Awards.
Reception
The game was deemed the Platform Game of the Year for 1998 by videogames.com, which called it a " sleeper hit " and "a triumph from an unexpected source."
Legacy
Klonoa: Door to Phantomile is remembered for its blend of 2D gameplay and 3D visuals.
Legacy
Critics praised it for retaining classic side-scrolling gameplay while still keeping alongside the industry's transition to 3D.
Legacy
GameSpy, Polygon, and GamesRadar+ ranked it as the 5th, 10th, and 25th best PlayStation game of all-time respectively.
Legacy
Nintendo Power called it "arguably the best platformer released for the PlayStation" and GameSpy called it the best 2.5D game ever and of the best platformers of its generation.
Legacy
In 2015, Hardcore Gaming listed the game on their 200 Best Video Games of All Time.
Legacy
The game spawned a series of sequels, including a direct sequel titled Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil (2001) for the PlayStation 2, as well as other titles for the Game Boy Advance.
Legacy
The original game was remade as Klonoa in 2008 for the Wii, developed with key members of the original team, including director Yoshizawa.
Legacy
A compilation featuring a high-definition remaster of Door to Phantomile and the original Klonoa 2, titled Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series, was released July 8, 2022 for multiple platforms.
Legacy
An anime film set in the same universe as Door to Phantomile was announced in 2016, but was then canceled in 2019.

pst_rayguy.title: Rayman (video game)
sents: lead
Rayman is a 1995 platform game developed by Ubi Pictures and published by Ubi Soft.
lead
The player controls Rayman, who must pursue Mr Dark to recover the Great Protoon that used to keep the balance between nature and the people of Rayman's valley.
lead
The player must navigate the valley, defeat enemies with abilities gained throughout the game, and free captured Electoons, also encountering a boss at the end of each thematic world.
lead
Michel Ancel conceived Rayman as a teenager and was able to realise the concept after being hired by Ubi Soft in 1989.
lead
He initially targeted the Atari ST and then the Super NES CD-ROM but restarted the development for the Atari Jaguar after the Super NES CD-ROM's cancellation.
lead
Ancel incorporated several childhood memories into the design and was soon joined by a larger development team.
lead
Ubi Soft made Rayman a launch title for the PlayStation in North American and Europe to compete with Japanese platform games on the platform.
lead
Rayman was first released for the Atari Jaguar on 1 September 1995, followed shortly by versions for the PlayStation, the Sega Saturn, and MS-DOS.
Gameplay
Rescuing all Electoons in the first five worlds grants Rayman access to the final world, the Candy Château, the hideout of the final boss, Mr Dark.
Gameplay
When Rayman interacts with the Magician, who is hidden in various levels, he can access hidden rooms that grant him Tings or extra lives if beaten in a given time.
Plot
Electoons return Rayman's fist at the last moment, such that he can defeat Mr Dark and retrieve the Great Protoon.
Early concepts and design
In 1988, his animation skills led him to be one of the early hires for the nascent publisher Ubi Soft, which at the time was operating with from Montreuil with six developers.
Early concepts and design
Rayman was greenlit in 1992, and Michel Guillemot gave Ancel and his team artistic freedom.
Early concepts and design
The game's style was inspired by Celtic, Chinese, and Russian fairy tales, as well as Ancel's childhood, having spent a lot of time by rivers, chasing insects, and climbing trees.
Early concepts and design
Having become interested in rendering tools such as Autodesk 3ds Max, he chose to incorporate 60 Hz animations.
Early concepts and design
Houde considered this impressive for a time where most games used sprites animated at five frames per second.
Early concepts and design
The Rayman character was named after the ray tracing rendering technique.
Production and release
When Nintendo cancelled the peripheral in 1993, that version of Rayman was also scrapped.
Production and release
It was considered lost media until rediscovered a copy dated 1992 in October 2016.
Production and release
With his permission, the programmer Omar Cornut released it online in July 2017.
Production and release
Michel Guillemot eventually assigned additional developers onto the project and allocated 15 million francs for its development.
Production and release
Rayman on the Jaguar was first displayed at the 1994 Summer Consumer Electronics Show.
Production and release
In late 1994, magazine advertisements announced Rayman as a title for the Atari Jaguar with a release in the fall or by December 1994.
Production and release
Pre-release promos of the PlayStation had advertised a release date of Rayman on 13 January 1995 in Japan.
Production and release
Later, Japanese magazines stated a release date for the PlayStation version as being June 1995.
Production and release
Similarly, American magazines reported a Jaguar release by June 1995, as well as versions for the 32X and 3DO, both of which were cancelled.
Production and release
Rayman was released on 1 September 1995 for the Atari Jaguar in Europe and on 9 September 1995 for North America.
Production and release
A version for MS-DOS was released in December 1995 in Europe and in North American in April 1996.
Reception
Captain Squideo, also of GamePro, commented that the PlayStation version was a "dazzling delight" and proclaimed it to be one of the most visually appealing games at the time.
Reception

Sam Hickman of Sega Saturn Magazine criticised the Sega Saturn version because of what he considered an overabundance of levels that played similarly with only varied attacks or an increased difficulty used as differentiation.
Sales
By the end of 1995, 400,000 copies of Rayman had been sold in Europe.
Sales
The game sold 900,000 copies globally by 1997.
Sales
It was the all-time best-selling PlayStation game in the United Kingdom, while in France it had sold 670,000 copies by 2000, becoming the second-best-selling game on the platform in the country.
Sales
According to Gamasutra, Rayman Advance ' s sales neared 600,000 units during the first half of the 2001–2002 fiscal year alone and then reached 770,000 copies by the end of March 2002.
Legacy
The commercial success of Rayman spawned a successful franchise with several sequels, including Rayman 2: The Great Escape (1999), and some of the game's elements influenced Rayman Origins.
Legacy
Ancel was honoured by the French government for his work in 2006.
Legacy
Rayman was brought to the Game Boy Color in early 2000, to Palm OS in September 2001, to the Nintendo DSi in December 2009, and to iOS in February 2016.
Legacy
Rayman Advance, a variant for the Game Boy Advance developed by Digital Eclipse, was released in June 2001.
Legacy
The game is one of twenty titles included with the PlayStation Classic, a miniature PlayStation replica released in December 2018.

pst_tombo.title: Tomba!
sents: lead
Tomba! is a 1997 platform-adventure game developed by Whoopee Camp and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
lead
It was released in Japan in 1997 and in other territories the following year.
lead
The game centers on the eponymous feral child as he attempts to recover his grandfather's bracelet from an evil race of anthropomorphic pigs.
lead
Creator Tokuro Fujiwara developed Tomba! after leaving Capcom in 1995, founding Whoopee Camp as director, producer and lead designer.
lead
He chose the game's 2D side-scrolling perspective for the format's straightforward nature, and created a non-linear " event " system to differentiate the game from other platforming titles.
lead
Tomba! was received positively by critics, with praise for its controls, visuals, and varied gameplay objectives.
lead
However, the game's audio received a more mixed reception.
lead
Despite the game's lackluster commercial performance, it was followed by a sequel in 1999, Tomba!
Gameplay
Most of the game takes place in a side-scrolling perspective.
Plot
One day, Tomba's bracelet is stolen following a confrontation with a group of Koma Pigs.
Development
Tomba! was created by Tokuro Fujiwara, who left Capcom in December 1995 after 13 years as an employee.
Release
Tomba! was released in Japan on December 25, 1997.
Release
Promotional plush figures of Tomba and a Koma Pig were distributed in limited quantities around the game's original release date.
Release
The figures were also offered as prizes in a sweepstake run by Gamers' Republic in 1999.
Release
Tomba! was released in North America on July 16, 1998 and in Europe on August 28, 1998.
Release
The game is titled Tombi! in European territories; Erik Engström of Hardcore Gaming 101 speculated that the change was motivated by the fact that "tomba" is an Italian word meaning " grave ".
Release
Tomba! was re-released on the PlayStation Network in Japan on July 6, 2011.
Release
The English-language version of Tomba! was re-released on the PlayStation Network in North America on June 19, 2012 and in Europe on October 3, 2012.
Release
In the month of its North American debut, Tomba! was the third best-selling PSOne Classic.
Release
On July 12, 2023, Limited Run Games announced they would be working with Fujiwara to release an enhanced version of Tomba! on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5 and Windows.
Release
The new version will run on Limited Run Games' Carbon Engine and feature a new soundtrack by Fujita.
Release
Special Edition, was released on PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch and Steam on August 1, 2024, with a PlayStation 4 release to follow later.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 31 out of 40.
Reception
Mark Cooke of GameRevolution noted that Tomba! was the first platform game to grant such freedom, following attempts by RPGs such as The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall.
Reception

Rybicki cited the high amount of load times as a negative point, and John Broady of GameSpot criticized the limited save system as a "chore", suggesting that a system that saves the game after each event would have been more logical.
Reception
The game's visuals were lauded for their bright and colorful presentation, smooth character animation, and combination of 2D character sprites and 3D polygonal environments.
Reception
Crispin Boyer of Electronic Gaming Monthly compared the game's visuals to Klonoa: Door to Phantomile, particularly in the "almost perfect marriage" of its disparate graphical elements.
Reception

All four reviewers for Electronic Gaming Monthly appreciated the game's eccentric and lightly humorous tone, as did Rybicki, who found the game refreshing after a glut of post-apocalyptic three-dimensional third-person shooters at E3 1998.
Reception

Erik Engström of Hardcore Gaming 101 saw influences by various anime from the late 1970s and early 1980s; he compared the game's rural and fantastical setting and occasional scatological references to Akira Toriyama 's Dr.
Sequel
2: The Evil Swine Return for the PlayStation in 1999, and the game was also met with positive reviews.
Sequel
Tomba! later garnered a cult following.

pst_suiko_saga_ii_japan.title: Suikoden II
sents: lead

Suikoden II (Japanese: 幻想水滸伝II, Hepburn: Gensō Suikoden Tsū,) is a role-playing video game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation video game console and the second installment of the Suikoden video game series.
lead
It was released in late 1998 in Japan, 1999 in North America, and in 2000 in Europe.
lead
The game features a vast array of characters, with over 100 recruitable characters, of which over 40 are usable in combat.
lead
Suikoden II takes place 3 years after the events of the original Suikoden and centers on an invasion of the City-States of Jowston by the Kingdom of Highland.
lead
The player controls a silent protagonist who is the adopted son of Genkaku, a hero who saved the City-States of Jowston in a war against Highland years ago.
lead

The protagonist and his best friend, Jowy Atreides, each gain one half of the Rune of the Beginning, one of the 27 True Runes of the Suikoden setting, and become caught up in the intrigues of the invasion and the dark fate of those who bear the halves of that Rune.
lead
As with other Suikoden titles, the game also centers on the recruitment of the 108 Stars of Destiny, who together have the power to alter fate.
lead

The game was initially released to lackluster sales and somewhat tepid critical reception, with some criticism (and lack of widespread appeal) being directed at the game's simpler and more retro 16-bit sprite visuals at a time when 3D graphics were heavily emphasized across the industry.
Gameplay
The player can also recruit over 100 new characters to his cause, often involving a short sidequest to do so.
Gameplay
Like other games of the series, Suikoden II employs a unique character leveling system from most RPGs.
Gameplay

Characters have a certain number of spell usages per "spell level"; for instance, a character with four level 1 spell slots and a Fire Rune could cast "Flaming Arrows" (the level 1 Fire Rune spell) four times.
Gameplay
The player may have a party of up to 6 characters in this battle type, against up to 6 enemies.
Gameplay
Emphasis is placed on "unite attacks," unique combination attacks between specific characters in the party.
Characters

The story revolves around Riou and Jowy each acquiring one half of the Rune of the Beginning, one of the 27 True Runes that each govern an aspect of the Suikoden universe and are the source of all magical powers.
Characters
As with all Suikoden games, the principal cast of the game is the 108 Stars of Destiny, who play important or minor roles in the plot of the game.
Plot
Riou is rescued from the river by a group of mercenaries working for Jowston, led by Viktor and Flik from the first Suikoden game, but is detained as an enemy soldier of Highland.
Plot

Fleeing from the advancing Highland army, Riou and Jowy return to the now-destroyed town where Jowy was rescued, and are drawn to the mysterious shrine that is the resting place of the Rune of the Beginning.
Plot

Leknaat, the magician and True Rune bearer from the original Suikoden who oversees fate, appears and tells Riou that he has been chosen to gather the 108 Stars of Destiny to alter the fate the True Runes impose on the world.
Development and release
In the winter of 1993/1994, Konami newcomers Yoshitaka Murayama and Junko Kawano were tasked with creating an RPG for an internally developed video games console.
Development and release
Murayama, Kawano and ten other employees were instead assigned with developing Konami's first games for Sony 's upcoming console, the PlayStation.
Development and release
Committed from the start to make a franchise to rival series such as Enix 's Dragon Quest and Square 's Final Fantasy, Murayama wrote the scenario of the first Suikoden.
Development and release
With the success of the first game a sequel gained a green-light.
Development and release
After reading fan letters Murayama decided that the selling point of the first game was its story, and thus it became the main focus of the second title.
Development and release
The story for Suikoden 2 was conceived after Suikoden 1 and was mostly written by Murayama himself.
Development and release
Suikoden II was made available for download on the PlayStation Network on December 9, 2014.
Reception
In the West, the game saw a limited print run, and the lackluster initial response prevented a reprinting of the game.

pst_valkyrie_profiel_japan.title: Valkyrie Profile (video game)
sents: lead
Valkyrie Profile is a role-playing video game developed by tri-Ace and published by Enix for the PlayStation.
lead
It was released on December 22, 1999 in Japan and on August 29, 2000 in North America.
lead
As she journeys, she learns more about her original human life, removed from her memory upon becoming a Valkyrie.
lead
The game was both a critical and commercial success; it sold over 700,000 copies, and critics praised the deep and complicated gameplay system and the plot.
lead
Valkyrie Profile received an enhanced port of the game, which was released for the PlayStation Portable in 2006 under the name Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth.
lead

The PlayStation Portable version of the game received an enhanced port for Android and iOS in March 2018, and a re-release for PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 using software emulation on December 22, 2022.
Gameplay

Dungeon exploration plays more like a platform game than a traditional RPG, with Lenneth Valkyrie the only visible character and capable of jumping, sliding, swinging her sword, and shooting ice crystals.
Gameplay
Enemies are visible and attacking them gives Lenneth a first attack advantage in combat.
Gameplay
Lenneth can also engage an enemy in battle by coming into contact with them; in this case, there is a 50% chance that the enemy will have the first attack.
Gameplay
Travel on the world map occurs in a 3D third-person perspective, with Lenneth flying in the skies over Midgard.
Gameplay
When entering a city or town, the game switches to a 2D profile view and Lenneth will disguise herself as a human, allowing her to interact with inhabitants without drawing attention to herself.
Gameplay

Character development for most of einherjar consists of their "death scenes", which are often dramatic and highly emotional and often steeped in symbolism and metaphors, and dialogue between them and the Gods while in Valhalla.
Gameplay
Each chapter is further divided into periods, depending on the difficulty (16 in Easy, 24 in Normal, and 28 in Hard).
Gameplay
Not sending Einherjar and opting to keep too many special artifacts awarded at the end of dungeons will lower Lenneth's Evaluation to 0, which triggers the worst possible ending (Ending C).
Gameplay
First, it tilts the divine war in the Æsir's favor and increases Lenneth's Evaluation.
Gameplay
On Easy and Normal difficulty, the starting levels of einherjar vary, while on Hard difficulty, all characters start from Level 1.
Gameplay

The "B" and "C" endings can be achieved in any difficulty level, while the "A" ending, which completes the entire story, is only available with the completion of certain tasks in the normal and hard difficulties.
Combat
Valkyrie Profile has a unique turn-based battle system.
Combat
Charge Time replaces MP, decreases slowly on its own, and prevents casting spells when above 0.
Combat
Fighters have unique Purify Weird Souls.
Combat
Only certain scepters allow the use of Great Magic; human-forged Great Magic-capable scepters have a high chance of breaking with such use, and unbreakable ether-coated ones are extremely rare.
Combat
Damage is not capped so the party may attack an enemy until they no longer have any available moves rather than being limited to the total HP (health points) of the target.
Combat
Lenneth is also the only character who cannot be voluntarily removed from the party at any point in the game.
Combat

Most characters will only be able to equip their specified type of weapon (though some swords can be used by light and heavy warriors and samurai) and only certain weapons allow them to perform all three of their attacks (or Great Magic in the case of mages).
Characters
Some of them can only be obtained in normal or hard mode.
Characters

Lenneth is one of the three goddesses of fate (the other two being her sisters, Hrist and Silmeria) the three apparently share the same body, though only one is awake at any given time and can be distinguished by their hair color and armor.
Story
In the village of Coriander, a 14-year-old girl named Platina lives with her cruel parents.
Story
The sorceress Mystina, one of Lezard's rivals, discovers what he has been doing and takes his last remaining homunculus.
A Ending
Surt refuses Loki's offer and is destroyed.
A Ending
As one never truly accepted by the Æsir or the Vanir, Loki seeks to destroy everything.
A Ending
Freya begs her to call the other gods but she refuses to listen, saying they only cared for themselves instead humanity.
Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth
Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth is the PlayStation Portable (PSP) port of the original Valkyrie Profile developed by Tose and published by Square Enix in 2006.
Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth
In 2022, Lenneth was ported to PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5.
Reception
Valkyrie Profile sold over 310,000 copies in Japan by the end of 1999.
Reception
As of September 2005, the PlayStation version of Valkyrie Profile has sold over 709,000 copies worldwide of which 636,000 units were sold in Japan alone.
Reception
Japan-GameCharts reports that 168,515 copies of Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth have been sold in Japan as of November 2008.
Reception
Square Enix lists that the PSP re-release has sold 60,000 copies abroad as of November 2007.
Reception
As of 2016, the Valkyrie Profile series has sold 2.2 million copies in total.
Reception
Valkyrie Profile was well received by critics, with an 81/100 rating at Metacritic.
Reception
Japanese gaming publication Famitsu gave the game a 35 out of 40, including it in its top 120 scoring PlayStation games of all time in 2000.
Reception
That same year, the magazine's staff voted the game number 30 on its top 100 PlayStation games of all time.
Reception
In a 2006 reader's poll conducted by Famitsu, Valkyrie Profile was voted the 27th best video game of all time.
Reception
Due to the positive review scores and relative rarity of the game, used copies of Valkyrie Profile have sold for $300, which is more than its initial retail price.
Reception

Eric Bratcher for Next Generation gave it three stars out of five, and called it an ambitious game with a compelling combat system, great open-ended character customization, and a unique setting, but thought that it is more artistic than a modern, less management-oriented titles.
Reception
The PSP re-release, Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth, was also well received by critics, with an 80/100 rating at Metacritic.

pst_castlevein_chronicles.title: Castlevania Chronicles

Composer(s): Shin-chan Keizo Nakamura Hiroshi Kobayashi Sota Fujimori (PlayStation)

sents: lead
Castlevania Chronicles is an action - platform game video game developed by Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo for the PlayStation.
lead
Released in 2001, it includes two distinct game modes: Original Mode and Arrange Mode.
lead
Original Mode is a direct port of the 1993 game Akumajō Dracula for the X68000 home computer.
lead
This version of Akumajō Dracula is itself a remake of the original Castlevania, which was released for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1986.
lead
Players control Simon Belmont, a vampire hunter who has entered Dracula 's castle to defeat him and save Transylvania.
lead
Arrange Mode offers a modernized experience with enhanced features, including a new introductory cinematic, updated sprites, re-balanced gameplay and a remade soundtrack.
lead
These enhancements aim to make the game more accessible to contemporary players while preserving the core elements of the original.
lead

Castlevania Chronicles was later made available as a PSone Classic on the PlayStation Network in December 2008, allowing a new generation of players to experience the game on both American and Japanese platforms.
Gameplay
Akumajō Dracula was designed to take full advantage of the X68000 hardware, featuring an updated and more complex game engine than the original Castlevania.
Gameplay
The game retains all the special items and sub-weapons from the original, while introducing a new rare item called the herb, which can refill the player's health in exchange for hearts.
Gameplay
Hidden items that grant points and 1-ups are scattered throughout the game and can be found by ducking or standing in specific locations.
Development
The development of Akumajō Dracula for the X68000 was driven by a desire to enhance the original Castlevania game for the Famicom while leveraging the advanced capabilities of the X68000 hardware.
Development

The release of the X68030 during development also prompted the team to make subtle adjustments that took advantage of the newer hardware's capabilities, resulting in even smoother animations and enhanced visual effects for users of the X68030 model.
Development

The development team faced various challenges, including the need to accommodate different hardware specifications and the inclusion of intricate design elements that pushed the X68000's capabilities.
Development
The PlayStation re-release, Castlevania Chronicles, expanded on the X68000 game.
Development
Players can choose to play this "Arrange Mode" version of the game with all of the new features intact, or play the "Original Mode" version as it was originally presented on the X68000.
Audio

The game supported several sound modules including the X68000's native FM Synthesizer (Yamaha YM2151), as well as multiple MIDI modules such as the Roland LA (MT-32, CM-32L, CM-64) and Roland GS (SC-55, SC-33, SC-155, CM-300, CM-500).
Audio
Hiroshi Kobayashi, one of the composers, noted the challenges and the excitement of working on the X68000 platform.
Audio
The development team also integrated a secret option for enabling General MIDI, which was not officially advertised due to the variable sound quality across different devices.
Audio
These efforts culminated in a soundtrack that was not only memorable but also demonstrated the advanced audio design possible on the X68000 system.
Audio

In the Japanese Chronicles, unlike the US and European versions, the sound hardware selection screen automatically appears before starting a game on "Original Mode" just as it did in Castlevania (X68000).
Audio
A code must be entered to reach it in either mode in the U.S. and European versions, while the Japanese version only requires one to be entered in "Arrange Mode".
Reception
GameSpot critiqued the PlayStation version for its perceived lack of replay value and dated graphics, assigning it a modest score of 6.1.
Reception
PSX Nation's J.M Vargas assigned the game a score of 80% and concluded: "One tough mother through and through.

pst_einhandler.title: Einhänder
sents: lead
Einhänder is a scrolling shooter developed by Square for the PlayStation console.
lead
It was released in Japan on November 20, 1997 and in North America on May 5, 1998.
lead
It was also re-released for the Japanese PlayStation Network on June 25, 2008.
lead
The name Einhänder is German and denotes a type of sword that is wielded with one hand, here used to refer to the single manipulator arm possessed by the player's spacecraft.
lead
The game is based on the story of the Greek's mythology of Selene and Endymion and set in a fictional future during a war between the Earth and the Moon.
lead
The player is part of the Moon's forces and must invade enemy territories to gather reconnaissance and enemy weapons.
lead
The music of the game, mainly in a techno / trance style, was composed by Kenichiro Fukui and was published in Japan as a soundtrack album.
lead
The game received positive reviews from critics, who praised its gameplay and graphics, but felt the game's short duration and lack of two-player mode were minor flaws.
Gameplay
The game's graphics are in 2.5D, that is, in 3D with occasional shifting of camera angles, but with the player's movement restricted to a two-dimensional plane.
Gameplay
The player can choose between multiple difficulty settings and three different models of the "Einhänder" fighter, in addition to two secret ones.
Gameplay
The player's fighter can move at different speeds and is equipped with a default machine gun as well as a manipulator arm, which is used to collect gunpods left by destroyed enemies.
Gameplay
Most stages have a middle boss and an end boss, which often possess a main core and individual parts that can be destroyed.
Gameplay
Points awarded for destroyed cores are multiplied by the value of the hit counter.
Plot
The "First Moon War" resulted in the destruction of most of the Earth's surface and the creation of a totalitarian regime on the planet.
Plot
Selene's tactics consists of sending one-man fighter spacecraft called "Einhänder" on kamikaze missions to cause as much damage as possible on the planet before being destroyed.
Plot
EOS also records and relays the player's flight and battle record data back to Hyperion.
Plot
After completion of the last objective Hyperion informs the player that the battle pattern of the latest EOS unmanned fighter is complete.
Plot
The player is given the honor of being the target of the last EOS test as reward for their heroic efforts.
Plot
Yet, the pilot's name and deeds were stricken from the records and they are remembered only by veterans of the war.
Development
Einhänder was the first 3D shooter developed by Square, a company otherwise mostly known for their role-playing video games.
Development
The game was showcased at the Tokyo Game Show in September 1997 and was initially planned for a Japanese release on October 16, 1997.
Development
On June 25, 2008, Square Enix re-released the game as a digital download on the Japanese PlayStation Network.
Music
The soundtrack of the game was published in Japan by DigiCube, a subsidiary of Square, on December 21, 1997, and was reissued by Square Enix on July 18, 2007, after DigiCube's bankruptcy.
Music

pst_guilty_geer.title: Guilty Gear (video game)
sents: lead

Guilty Gear (subtitled The Missing Link in Japan) is a 2D fighting video game developed by Team Neo Blood, an Arc System Works production group led by Daisuke Ishiwatari, and published by Arc System Works.
lead
First released on May 14, 1998, for the PlayStation, it is the first installment in the series of the same name.
lead
Set in a world destroyed by a war between humans and bio-organic weapons called Gears, it follows ten fighters as they enter a tournament held to prevent resurrection of the Gears' leader.
lead
Its gameplay consists of one-on-one fights, a four-button attack configuration featuring special moves and instant kill techniques, as well as three different playable modes.
lead
Devised by Ishiwatari, it spent a year and a half in production, with influences from Street Fighter and manga.
lead
After its original release, it was brought to both North America, and Europe and the PAL region, and achieved a cult status among fans.
lead
It has received favorable critical reception, with praise towards its characters' roster, 2D graphics and fast gameplay that differentiates it from other games of the same genre.
lead
It has been labeled as one of few games of its era to cause a lasting impact on the genre, alongside the hegemonic Capcom and SNK games.
Plot
In 2010, mankind discovered an unlimited energy source of incredible power, which was labeled “magic”.

Plot
A bounty hunter named Sol Badguy defeats Testament in the second to last stage of the tournament.

Characters

Development and release
Kidooka approved the idea and gave Ishiwatari a staff of around 12 people, the so-called "Team Neo Blood", to develop it.
Development and release
Ishiwatari, however, said only four people were doing the main work and that all group had no experience in creating video games.
Development and release
With influences of the fantasy setting of the manga Bastard‼, Ishiwatari created the series hoping it would appeal not only to game fans but to anime fans too.
Development and release
Originally, the game was designed with rendered 3-D visuals, but this was later replaced by hand-drawn artwork because Ishiwatari disliked the result.
Development and release
Guilty Gear took a long time between its first announcement after Arc's then latest release— Wizard's Harmony (1995)—and its actual release.
Development and release
It was first released in Japan on May 14, 1998 for the PlayStation.
Development and release
When the contest ended, Atlus released the game on November 9, 1998.
Development and release
In the United Kingdom, the game was published by Virgin Interactive Entertainment, and was released on May 19, 2000.
Development and release
In continental Europe, it was licensed and published by Studio 3 in May 2000.
Reception
Reviews for it were generally positive, with an aggregate score of 78% from GameRankings.
Reception
IGN staff said it would be well received by fans of traditional 2D fighting video games and considered it one of the bests of the genre on PlayStation.
Reception
Writing for Electronic Gaming Monthly (EGM), a reviewer dubbed "Sushi" said it was the second best 2D fighter on PlayStation behind Street Fighter Alpha 2.
Reception

Harry Slater of Pocket Gamer and Eurogamer 's Wesley Yin-Poole affirmed it as regarded "by many to be the greatest 2D, one on one fighter of the era" and "the greatest fighting game of all time", respectively.
Reception
Slater stated "it's one of the coolest 2D fighters from a time when 2D fighters just weren't cool".
Reception

Mielke declared it is "one of the few non- Capcom or SNK 2D fighters to make any sort of impact on the genre." Though stating that Capcom was still the best developer, Nelson said Guilty Gear is "better than 90% of those on the market".
Reception
House declared "superb is the only way to describe them", asserting that they are all "pretty original".
Reception
Most of criticism, however, is directed to how the AI makes the game difficult and how there are some attacks that cause too much damage.
Reception
In spite of it, Game Informer considered the instant-kill move to be the "biggest" concept introduced by Guilty Gear.
Reception
In contrast, most of critics were positive in their conclusions.
Reception
Mielke said it "is as good as it gets", and it was described by House as "just a solid, well-executed 2D fighting game that has class, personality and a great engine".
Controversy
In a 1999 speech condemning advertisements for violent video games aimed at children, U.S.

The Guilty Gear game was the first installment of the series that is considered a cult classic among video game fans.
Legacy
It was followed by five direct sequels, Guilty Gear X (2000), Guilty Gear X2 (2002), Guilty Gear 2: Overture (2007), Guilty Gear Xrd (2014), Guilty Gear Strive (2021), and several spin-offs.

Arc System Works re-released Guilty Gear in a "reprinted edition" on September 22, 1999 for a cheaper price.

It later became available by download on PlayStation Store as a PSone Classic in Japan on May 31, 2007, in Europe on January 7, 2010, and in PAL region on January 8, 2010.

Another reviewer from the same site, GoldfishX, said the only drawback the disc has is the mastering of the CD which can make it difficult to hear the guitars on rhythm in some tracks.

Nevertheless, as it was not a problem related to composition, he still gave a perfect score to the soundtrack.

lead

Tekken 3 maintains the same core fighting system and concept as its predecessors.

Three-dimensional movement is insignificant in previous Tekken games (aside from some characters having unique sidesteps and dodging maneuvers), but Tekken 3 adds emphasis on the third axis by allowing characters to sidestep in or out of the background.

Reversals, introduced for some characters in Tekken 2, were now available to all characters.

PlayStation

The backgrounds were re-made into 2D panoramic images, the number of polygons used for each character were slightly reduced, sound effects played at a high pitch, and the game runs at lower overall resolution.
PlayStation
Namco representatives had in fact originally stated that they did not think it was possible to convert Tekken 3 to the PlayStation.

By April 1997, Tekken 3 was popular in the arcades, and the process of its home conversion was considered certain on PlayStation but merely a controversial consideration on Nintendo 64.

Arakawa had previously composed for the first two Tekken games, while Sano, Okabe and Miyake would go on to work on several future entries in the series, including Tekken Tag Tournament.

The PlayStation emulator Bleem! was released for the Sega Dreamcast that allows Dreamcast owners to play a graphically enhanced version of Tekken 3 using the PlayStation copy of the game.

The PlayStation 2 release of Tekken 5 features the arcade version of Tekken 3.
PlayStation
The PlayStation version of Tekken 3 is among 20 "generation-defining" games on the PlayStation Classic, released on 3 December 2018.

While Virtua Fighter 3 was more successful in Japan at the time, Tekken 3 was more successful worldwide.

In May 1998, Sony awarded Tekken 3 a "Platinum Prize" for sales above 1 million units in Japan.

177 on Game Informer ' s 2009 Top 200 games of all time.

pst_tekkon.title: Tekken (video game)
sents: lead
Tekken (鉄拳) is a fighting video game developed and published by Namco.
lead
It was originally released on arcades in December 1994, then ported to the PlayStation home console the following year.
lead

One of the earliest 3D polygon -based games of the genre, Tekken was Namco's answer to Virtua Fighter and was designed by Seiichi Ishii, who himself was also Virtua Fighter 's designer when he worked at Sega previously.
lead
The game was developed on the purpose-built low-cost System 11 board, based on PlayStation hardware.
lead

Tekken initially divided opinion with its presentation and unusual control system, however following its home console release in 1995 - only the third such game following the first Virtua Fighter and Battle Arena Toshinden - it quickly became popular and a best seller.
lead
It started the Tekken series, with a sequel, Tekken 2, being released in 1995.
Characters
Each has a special "sub-boss" associated with them, who will be fought in Stage 8, followed by the final boss, Heihachi Mishima.
Characters
The sub-boss characters are clones in terms of moveset, with only a handful of moves distinguishing them from the original.
Characters
All sub-bosses and Heihachi were never made playable in the original arcade version.
Characters
A total of 17 playable fighters exist in the console version.
Plot

When Kazuya Mishima was only five years old, his father, Heihachi Mishima, carried him to the summit of a mountain and threw him off to test his strength and determine whether he was fit to inherit the Mishima Zaibatsu.
Plot
21 years later, Kazuya travels across the world competing in martial arts competitions and emerging as an undefeated champion, with the only draw against Paul Phoenix, an American fighter.
Plot
Heihachi organizes and announces the King of Iron Fist Tournament to prove his power and worth.
Development and release
Tekken was not originally conceived as a fighting game.
Development and release
The project began as an internal Namco test case for animating 3D character models, and eventually incorporated texture mapping similar to that found in Namco's 1993 racing game Ridge Racer.
Development and release
In 1994, Namco acquired developers from longtime competitor Sega, which had recently created the first 3D fighting game with 1993's Virtua Fighter.
Development and release

Tekken was initially planned for the Namco System 22, the board used by Ridge Racer, but after Namco heard Sega was developing Virtua Fighter 2 for their new Sega Model 2 arcade board, before the development of Tekken was later moved to the System 11 after the meeting with Kutaragi.
Development and release
The game was originally going to be titled Rave War.
Development and release
Also known as Rave Wars, the prototype was demonstrated at the Amusement & Music Operators Association (AMOA) Expo in September 1994, before being renamed Tekken upon release.
Development and release
Directed by Virtua Fighter designer Seiichi Ishii, Tekken was intended to be a fundamentally similar title, with the addition of detailed textures and twice the frame rate (at 60 frames).
Development and release
Because it was developed for Namco's System 11 arcade board, which was based on raw PlayStation hardware, Tekken was easily ported to the latter.
Development and release
Tekken was marketed to small arcades as a cheaper alternative to Sega's Virtua Fighter 2, which was released for the more expensive Model 2 arcade board.
Development and release
Namco held a promotional tour to market the arcade game across North America in early 1995, holding video game competition tournaments in twelve cities.
Development and release
Originally released for the arcades in late 1994, Tekken was later ported to the PlayStation.
Development and release

The PlayStation 2 version of Tekken 5 features the arcade version of Tekken (being an emulated version of its arcade counterpart as well as the other two that were included in the arcade history mode).
Development and release
In 2005, Namco re-released Tekken as part of the NamCollection compilation for the PlayStation 2 to celebrate the company's 50th anniversary.
Commercial
In Japan, Game Machine listed it on their February 1, 1995 issue as being the fifth most-popular arcade game for the previous two weeks.
Commercial
It went on to be Japan's fourth highest-grossing arcade game of 1995, below Virtua Fighter 2, Street Fighter Zero and Vampire Hunter: Darkstalkers' Revenge.
Commercial
In the United States, it was one of top five highest-grossing arcade conversion kits of 1995.
Commercial
Tekken was the first PlayStation game to sell over a million units.
Commercial
In Japan, it sold 942,000 units in 1995, making it the fourth best-selling home video game of 1995, below Dragon Quest VI, Chrono Trigger and Virtua Fighter 2.
Commercial
Tekken was also a best-seller in the United Kingdom, where it was the top-selling game in October and December 1995.
Commercial
In the United States, the game sold 786,556 units, for a combined 1,728,556 units sold in Japan and the United States.
Commercial
It currently has sold 2.8 million copies as of 2024, according to Tekken developer and future director Katsuhiro Harada.
Commercial
Guinness World Records awarded Tekken with multiple records in the Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition 2008.
Commercial

These include, "First PlayStation Game to Sell Over One Million Units", "First Fighting Game To Feature Simulated 3D", as well as a record for the entire series as "The Best Selling Fighting Series for PlayStation Consoles."
Critical
On release of the PlayStation version, Famicom Tsūshin (Famitsu) scored Tekken a 38 out of 40, while giving it an 8 out of 10 in their Reader Cross Review.
Critical
In 1996, GamesMaster ranked the game 49th on their "Top 100 Games of All Time."

Sequels
