All developed elements have been integrated into Blade & Soul 2.
Sequels
Blade & Soul 2 is focusing on the all-new PVE and PVP combat experiences designed for playing on the mobile platform and on the PCs, sharing a little connection to Blade & Soul.
Sequels
The sequel was launched on August 26, 2021, for the Android, iOS, and Microsoft Windows, and is planned to be released for the console in the future.
Sequels
Cross-play function was applied for all versions of Blade & Soul 2.

pst_rival_skools.title: Rival Schools: United by Fate

Designer(s): Hideaki Itsuno Makoto Otsuki Tatsuya Nakae

sents: lead

Rival Schools: United by Fate, known in Japan as Shiritsu Justice Gakuen: Legion of Heroes, is a 1997 fighting game produced by Capcom originally released as an arcade game on Sony ZN-2 hardware, then ported to the PlayStation in 1998.
lead
A sequel, Project Justice, was released in 2000.
Gameplay

The actual fights, however, are one-on-one fights, with the partner only participating by being called in when a player has enough 'vigor' for a Team Up attack, done by pressing a punch and kick button of the same pressure.
Gameplay
The Team Ups are some kind of double team attack by the character and partner, or (for most female characters' Team Ups) heal the main character or give them more vigor.
Gameplay
The 'vigor' meter (essentially a super meter) can go up to 9 levels, with Team Ups costing two levels and super moves from a single person costing one level of vigor.
Gameplay

Attack Cancels allowed a player to cancel an incoming hit simply by timing their own hit with the attack, which would cancel out both attacks (though it does not nullify the remaining hits of a multi-hit move).
Plot
The player's team eventually faces off against Raizo Imawano, the principal of the school, and first boss of the game.
Plot

In the arcade version, character selection is initially limited to selecting two characters from the same school and free selection of any character is accessed through time; the PlayStation version, which includes all characters unlocked by default, has no such restrictions.
Development
Rival Schools: United by Fate entered development when director Hideaki Itsuno wanted to make a 60fps polygon-based fighting game.
Development

As Capcom 's earlier 3D fighting title Star Gladiator was already set to 30fps, because of things such as sword effects and backgrounds, the development team did not exceed the limitations of the arcade hardware.
Development
The game was originally called Justice Fist, and the initial story was that fighters from every country came together to decide who was the strongest.
Development
Itsuno intended for the setting to be in a school where 40 characters fought to decide who would be the class representatives.
Development
A 54% complete version of Rival Schools was the most popular Capcom game at the September 1997 JAMMA show, drawing larger crowds than Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact.
Ports
The first disc included the original arcade game and the standard modes included in most home versions of fighting games.
Ports

Capcom translated most of the games on the Evolution Disc for the English localization, and planned to include the character creation mode (rebranded as "School Life") as well, but later abandoned it, citing the amount of time it would take to translate it from Japanese to English.
Ports
On February 23, 2012, Capcom re-released the PlayStation port on the Japanese PlayStation Network.
Nekketsu Seisyun Nikki 2

In Japan, Capcom released a PlayStation-exclusive update to the original Rival Schools titled Shiritsu Justice Gakuen: Nekketsu Seisyun Nikki 2 (私立ジャスティス学園 熱血青春日記2, "Private Justice Academy: Hot-Blooded Youthful Diary 2").
Nekketsu Seisyun Nikki 2
On release, Famitsu magazine scored Nekketsu Seisyun Nikki 2 a 30 out of 40.
Reception
In Japan, Game Machine listed Rival Schools: United by Fate on their February 1, 1998 issue as being the most-successful arcade game of the month.
Project Justice
Justice Gakuen in Japan), was released in 2000 in Japan and 2001 in the United States and Europe for arcades and the Dreamcast.
Project Justice
In comparison to Rival Schools, Project Justice featured teams of 3, adding three-person team-up attacks and the ability to interrupt and stop 2-person team-ups.
Project Justice
Since at least 2013, director Hideaki Itsuno has expressed an interest in continuing the Rival Schools series by developing a third installment.
Project Justice
In August 30, 2024, Hideaki Itsuno announced hes leaving Capcom, which later means he will not be continuing Rival Schools as its likely cancelled.
Comic book
A comic book based on Rival Schools was produced by UDON Studios, with its first issue published on May 17, 2006, with art by Corey Lewis.
Comic book

Originally, the comic was to be produced by Dreamwave Productions, but when Dreamwave showed signs of financial failure, the rights of the comic were sold to UDON, which had already produced the successful Street Fighter comic.
Comic book
The comic was made available on August 31, 2007 in the U.S. and later released as a webcomic.
Street Fighter series

Following the appearance of Sakura Kasugano in the first game, Capcom has established the Rival Schools series as taking place within the same world as its Street Fighter series, with characters from Rival Schools appearing in various Street Fighter media.
Street Fighter series

On August 16, 2021, Akira was added as a playable character to Street Fighter V as part of its 5th season of downloadable content, becoming the first playable Rival Schools character in a Street Fighter game, with her brother, Daigo as her assist; Edge and Gan make cameo appearances in her accompanying stage.

pst_bushido_blayde.title: Bushido Blade (video game)

Composer(s): Shinji Hosoe Ayako Saso Takayuki Aihara

sents: lead
Bushido Blade (ブシドーブレード, Bushidō Burēdo) is a 3D fighting video game developed by Lightweight and published by Square and Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation in 1997.
lead
The game features one-on-one armed combat.
lead
Its name refers to the Japanese warrior code of honor bushidō.
lead
Upon its release, the realistic fighting engine in Bushido Blade was seen as innovative, particularly the game's unique Body Damage System.
lead
A direct sequel, Bushido Blade 2, was released on the PlayStation a year later.
lead
Another game with a related title and gameplay, Kengo: Master of Bushido, was also developed by Lightweight for the PlayStation 2.
Gameplay
Unlike most fighting games, however, no time limit or health gauge is present during combat.
Gameplay
Most hits will cause instant death, while traditional fighting games require many hits to deplete an opponent's health gauge.
Gameplay
Many of these attacks are only available in one of three stances, switched using the shoulder buttons or axis controls depending on controller layout: high, neutral, and low.
Gameplay
Similar to the weapons, each one has a different level of strength and speed, and a number of unique special attacks.
Gameplay
Characters in Bushido Blade also have the ability to run, jump, and climb within the 3D environments.
Gameplay
Because battles are not limited to small arenas, the player is encouraged to freely explore during battle.
Gameplay
The castle compound which most of the game takes place in acts as a large hub area of interconnected smaller areas including a cherry blossom grove, a moat, and a bridge labyrinth.
Gameplay
Other single player options include a practice mode and a first person mode.
Gameplay
Slash mode pits the player's katana-wielding character against a long string of 100 enemies, one after the other.
Plot
A fictional 500-year-old dojo known as Meikyokan lies within this region, and teaches the disciplines of the master Narukagami Shinto.
Plot
Several other members of the society, under penalty of death, are sent to dispatch the defector, only catching up to him (or her) within the ruins of the surrounding Yin and Yang Labyrinth Castle.
Development
Bushido Blade was the first title developed by Lightweight, a partially-owned subsidiary of the game's publisher Square at the time of its release.
Development

The director explained that the bushidō code of honor present in the game was not strictly the warrior's "way of dying" like that found in the Edo period 's famous Hagakure guide but emphasized the concept of one's own survival as found in teachings of earlier Japanese time periods.
Development
The music was released with the soundtrack for Square's Driving Emotion Type-S, also composed by the trio, on a two-disc set in 2001.
Release
Originally slated for a February 1997 release in Japan, Bushido Blade was pushed back to March to make room for the debut of Square's Aques line of sports games in February.
Release
Despite the North American-exclusive inclusion of graphic violence, the ESRB rated the game Teen, while the ELSPA gave the European release a more restrictive 18+ rating.
Reception
In Japan, Bushido Blade was the 25th best selling game of 1997 in Japan, selling nearly 387,937 copies.
Reception
The game was also added to the PSone Classics roster on the Japanese PlayStation Store in 2008.
Reception
In the United States, the game sold 324,083 units as of January 2003, adding up to 712,020 units sold in Japan and the United States as of January 2003.
Reception
The one-hit kills drew the most commentary, with GameSpot calling them "Bushido Blade's most exciting and preposterous feature, destined to earn it just as many fans as detractors".
Reception
In 1999, Bushido Blade received a nomination for " Console Fighting Game of the Year " during the AIAS ' inaugural Interactive Achievement Awards.
Reception
In November 2000, Bushido Blade was voted by the readers of Weekly Famitsu magazine as number 85 in its top 100 PlayStation games of all time.
Reception
In 2006, the game was ranked number 190 on 1UP.com 's list of The Greatest 200 Videogames of Their Time.
Reception
In 2010, GamesRadar included Bushido Blade on the list of the seven "'90s games that need HD remakes ".

pst_bushido_blayde_2.title: Bushido Blade 2
sents: lead
Bushido Blade 2 (ブシドーブレード弐, Bushidō Burēdo Tsu) is a fighting video game published by Square, released in Japan and North America in 1998.
lead
It is the sequel to Bushido Blade, which had been released the previous year.
lead
The game was re-released in 2008 for PlayStation Network.
Gameplay
Bushido Blade 2 expands on some of the aspects of Bushido Blade, while limiting or removing others.
Gameplay
The fights in Bushido Blade 2 mark the progress of the chosen character who—depending on the character—either fights to regain a legendary sword, or to destroy the opposing school.
Gameplay
Two characters in Bushido Blade 2 are exceptions to the typical opponent roster: the gun-wielding Tsubame and Katze.
Gameplay
Most of the weapons are straight from the first game, excluding the yari and the M16.
Gameplay

The yugiri (a sword which is quite similar to the nodachi but wielded like the katana), which was used by the original Bushido Blade ' s final boss Hanzaki is now a selectable weapon, but is only accessible in the final battle versus the unarmed "last member of the Kagami clan".
Gameplay

Some of the original Bushido Blade ' s selectable weapons— rapier (which does not appear as a selectable weapon, but only in Highwayman's two-sword stance when he has the long sword equipped), sledgehammer and ninjato —as well as the boss-specific "Double-Bladed Sword-Staff" and "Special Sabre", have been eliminated.
Plot
In the 13th century, on the island of Konoshima (in the Seto Naikai, Inland Sea of Japan) there existed two feudal clans, the Kagami and the Sue, both aligned to the same Daimyō.
Plot
Some 800 years later, the Shainto school, composed of the remaining descendants from the Sue clan, attacked the Narukagami Shintoryu, the Kagami clan dojo, at their headquarters, the Meikyokan.
Plot
To redeem their honor, they move to recover the Sacred Sword Yugiri and wipe out the last descendant of the Kagami family.
Characters
Most of the playable characters from the first game have returned, including Red Shadow, Mikado, Kannuki, Tatsumi, Utsusemi, and Black Lotus (now known as Highwayman).
Characters
A few NPCs from the first game have returned as playables, namely Sazanka, Tsubame, Katze, and Hongou.
Characters

As in the first Bushido Blade, all of the main characters have two outfits—one for the story mode, and one for the other play modes, while unlockable fighters use a single costume for the entire game.
Characters
Kannuki – A starting character who returns from the first Bushido Blade game.
Characters
Other than that, has no unique attacks.
Characters
The only character to have unique moves (aside from throws) with the naginata poleaxe.
Characters
The purple-eyed boy, now a little bit matured from the first game.
Characters
Has unique attacks with any sword in the game, including the sword-dances for the katana and the nodachi, with the nodachi one being unique to him.
Characters
A female ninja from the first Bushido Blade, who appears to be a student of Utsusemi.
Characters
Runs faster than most characters and has an improved running attack.
Characters
Proficient with European weapons like the long sword and broadsword, having unique leg swipes using both.
Characters
Proficiencies are mostly the same as with Utsusemi, but cannot perform a throw on the opponent, nor can he do a "million stabs" maneuver.
Characters
A male ninja, he is notable for being very fast both for running and striking, as well as having the biggest sidearms count.
Characters
Similar to a kabuki actor, he made his debut in the first Bushido Blade as a sub-boss.
Characters
Hokkyokku Tsubame – A special character in a bikini who wields an M-16 rifle.
Characters
One of the two characters to have unique strikes with it.
Characters
She is proficient in acrobatics (around which most of her unique strikes circuit) and the use of light weapons, mainly the long sword.
Characters
Uses the long sword in the sheathed stance, the fastest stance in the game.
Characters
Appeared in the original game as a hidden enemy.
Characters
Is actually Black Lotus from the first game, who has changed his identity after his betrayal of the Narukagami in the first game.
Characters
Aside, can do a backup maneuver with it and a million strikes combo.
Characters
Was also a secret character in the first game, as well as an important character in story mode.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 29 out of 40.
Reception
Next Generation said in the July 1998 issue that the Japanese import "isn't an easy game to classify.
Reception
As a sequel, it may alienate fans of Bushido Blade 1 who were anxious for more of the same.
Reception
During the week of April 3, 1998, the game was the third-best-selling game including games from other consoles.
Reception
In North America, Bushido Blade 2 was the ninth-best-selling game during the week of November 13, 1998.
Reception
The game was named as a finalist by the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences for " Console Fighting Game of the Year " during the 2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.

pst2_shin_megumi_tensai_nocturnal.title: Shin Megami Tensei (video game)
sents: lead
Shin Megami Tensei is a role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the Super Famicom.
lead
Originally released in 1992 in Japan, it has been ported to multiple systems and eventually released in the West for iOS in 2014.
lead
It was released on the Virtual Console service in Japan on Wii in 2007 and on Wii U in 2013, as well as Nintendo Switch Online in 2020.
lead
It is the third game in the Megami Tensei series and the first in the central Shin Megami Tensei series.
lead
The gameplay uses first-person navigation of dungeons and turn-based battles against demons.
lead
The player can recruit demons as allies by talking to them rather than fighting them, and two to three demons can be fused to create new demons.
lead
The story follows a player-named protagonist who lives in near-future Tokyo.
lead

When a portal to the realm of demons is opened accidentally by a scientist named Steven and is seized by Gotou, a military commander who believes that he can control the demons, the United States government orders a nuclear attack on Tokyo.
Gameplay
The gameplay is similar to that of other games in the series: players make their way through dungeons and fight against demons in a first-person perspective.
Gameplay

At some places, called "Cathedrals of Shadows", players can fuse two to three allied demons into one single, more powerful demon; as demons do not receive experience points, this is the only way for the player to increase their demons' power.
Setting and characters
Shin Megami Tensei takes place in a near future Tokyo, first in the year "199X", and then 30 years later in a post-apocalyptic version of the city.
Development
While designing the maps, Kaneko wanted to use wire-frame models, but the Super Famicom's limited capacities meant this idea was scrapped.
Character designs
The Hero's and the Heroine's clothes were designed to be futuristic; the Heroine was designed to be a protector, with clothes inspired by American football equipment.
Character designs
The Law Hero and Chaos Hero have ordinary clothes at first; the Chaos Hero was designed to look unsophisticated, with a bad posture and military clothes.
Character designs
The character Louis Cyphre was inspired by the character of the same name from the 1987 movie Angel Heart.
Character designs
According to Ito, the character Thorman's name was originally inspired by the Norse god of thunder, but after release, he realized that the name was highly similar to that of Harry S.
Character designs
The graphics for most demons were directly drawn as sprites, without concept art, to make sure that the design and the graphics would work within the hardware limitations of the Super Famicom.
Character designs
Certain important characters, and some demons who the player would be guaranteed to meet, were drawn as concept art first.
Music
Masuko considered Shin Megami Tensei to be an experimental work: it was the first time he had created music for the Super Famicom, so he was not familiar with the console's specifications.
Music
A soundtrack album, Shin Megami Tensei Law & Chaos Disc, was released on February 24, 1993, by Victor Entertainment under the catalog number VICL-40046/7.
Music
A second album, Shin Megami Tensei Sound Collection, was released on March 5, 2003, by SME Visual Works under the catalog number SVWC-7175/6.
Release
Shin Megami Tensei was first released on the Super Famicom on October 30, 1992, in Japan; it remained exclusive to that region for 22 years.
Release
Subsequent ports were released on the PC Engine (December 25, 1993), Mega-CD (February 25, 1994), the PlayStation (May 31, 2001), and Game Boy Advance (March 28, 2003).
Release

The Game Boy Advance version, which was the first time Shin Megami Tensei appeared on a portable platform, included the ability to exchange demons and items using the platform's data exchange capacities.
Release
The game was released in February 2012 for iOS and November of that year for Android.
Release
The iOS port was localized and released in North America and Europe on March 18, 2014.
Release
With the release of iOS 11 in 2017, the game is no longer compatible with up-to-date iOS devices.
Localization
In 2002, the team Aeon Genesis released an English translation patch unofficially for the original Super Famicom release of the game.
Localization
They went on to release English translations for Shin Megami Tensei II in 2004 and Shin Megami Tensei if... in 2018.
Localization
In 2021, another team released a translation patch for the GBA version that carries over the official iOS localization.
Localization
In 2022, a third team released an unofficial English translation patch for the PlayStation release.
Localization

The localization project was slow at first, as it took time to extract the files from the game, so the localization team started by playing the game in order to find out what kinds of dialogue text and system messages it contained.
Localization

A challenge for the localization team was character limitations: only four rows of text, with 28 characters each, were able to be displayed at a time, and at some points this had to be limited even further in order to avoid graphical glitches.
Localization
The Soulless Army, while Persona 4 and Shin Megami Tensei IV include several quotes and terms from the game.
Localization
The already translated Shin Megami Tensei quotes from Persona 4 ' s localization were reused verbatim in the localization of Shin Megami Tensei.
Reception
At the end of 2001, the PlayStation version was the 119th best selling video game of the year in Japan, with 85,991 sold copies.
Reception
On release, Famitsu magazine gave the original Super Famicom version a score of 36 out of 40, with all four reviewers giving it a 9 out of 10.
Reception
This made it one of their three highest-rated games of 1992, along with Dragon Quest V and World of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck.
Reception
Shin Megami Tensei was also one of only eleven games to have received a Famitsu score of 36/40 or above up until 1992.
Reception
For subsequent console ports, Famitsu gave scores of 25/40 (PCE), 28/40 (MD), 30/40 (PS), and 27/40 (GBA).
Reception
RPGFan found the story to be good and macabre, and surprisingly relevant even in 2014.
Legacy
Shin Megami Tensei II, which directly continued the story of Shin Megami Tensei, was released in 1994.
Legacy
The game developer Toby Fox cited Shin Megami Tensei as inspiration for his 2015 game Undertale, specifically its dialogue system.

pst2_shin_megumi_tensai_digital_d.real: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga
pst2_shin_megumi_tensai_digital_d.title: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga

successor: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga 2

sents: lead
Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga is a duology of role-playing video games developed by Atlus for the PlayStation 2.
lead
They are a spin-off of the Megami Tensei series.
lead
The first Digital Devil Saga was released in Japan in 2004, North America in 2005, and Europe in 2006.
lead
Its direct sequel, Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga 2, released in 2005 in Japan and North America, and 2007 in Europe and Australasia.
lead
The games were published in Europe and Australasia by Ghostlight and in other regions by Atlus and its North American subsidiary Atlus USA.
lead
Digital Devil Saga follows the Embryon, a tribe who fights against five other tribes in a digital world called the Junkyard.
lead
After being infected with a demon virus that grants them demonic powers, the Embryon must fight with and devour the other tribes to ascend to "Nirvana".
lead
During the conflict, they shelter a woman named Sera, who has the power to calm their demonic powers.
Gameplay

In the Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga role-playing games, players take control of the characters Serph, Heat, Argilla, Gale and Cielo, with the characters Sera and Roland becoming playable in Digital Devil Saga 2.
Gameplay
In Digital Devil Saga 2, characters will sometimes enter battle in a half-transformed "berserk" mode, which increases attack power while locking away magic skills and lowering a character's defense.
Gameplay
In Digital Devil Saga 2, special Karma Ring items can be assigned to characters to grant stat boosts.
Gameplay
Importing save data from the first game enables some skills and abilities learned during the first game to be transferred to the characters that learned them.
Setting and characters
The first Digital Devil Saga takes place in the Junkyard, a combat simulator program where it always rains.
Setting and characters

Each tribe holds a particular territory, and initially are devoid of emotions: the only common ground is a great tower at the Junkyard's center called the Karma Temple, which acts as a meeting place for all the tribe leaders.
Setting and characters
In Digital Devil Saga 2, two new main characters are introduced: Roland, the alcoholic leader of the Lokapala resistance group; and Madame Margot Cuvier, head of the Karma Society.
Plot
The Embryon first become conscious of their new powers when they meet the surviving Vanguards: during their time there, they are forced to kill the Vanguards' leader Harley.
Plot
Jinana, having refused to eat as she needed to, goes berserk and must be killed.
Plot
The Embryon, Sera and Angel only just escape as the Junkyard is destroyed.
Plot
In Digital Devil Saga 2, the Embryon appear in the real world, which is slowly being destroyed by the Black Sun: the only ones able to survive the sun's rays are those infected with the demon virus.
Plot
Sera was the only survivor of a group of children with the ability to communicate with God.
Plot
As Sera begins transmission, the base is destroyed, killing her and Serph.
Plot
Aided by the data avatars of the Embryon, Seraph fights God's avatar to prove humanity's worth.
Development
Production on the initial Digital Devil Saga started prior to the beginning of active development on Shin Megami Tensei III: Nocturne in 2002.
Development
During her time on the project, she collaborated with Tadashi Satomi, who had previously written scripts for the first three Persona games.
Development

Godai wrote her outline on the basis that both books and video games had stories broken into chapters, writing up the story up to the first boss battle in short story form to get a sense of the narrative and lore.
Development
Production of Digital Devil Saga 2 began immediately after the release of the first game.
Development
To tease it prior to its official announcement, a large number of unfinished plot threads and vague hints relating to the main characters' previous lives were incorporated into the first game.
Development
For Digital Devil Saga 2, the team expanded upon the systems implemented in the first game.
Development
The game's setting was inspired in Satomi's mind by the frequent reporting of natural disasters and outbreaks of diseases around the world.
Development
According to Satomi, while the first game's motif was "rain", the second game's was "sun".
Development
The team used player feedback from the first game's systems to make their adjustments.
Character design
The only one not to have a strange hair color was Sera, signifying her unique status.
Character design
Kaneko was the first to propose the game's concept, which was then worked on by other staff members.
Character design

Makoto Kitano was responsible for creating 3D representations of the game's demons, A noted element was the design of Cerberus, which combined elements of the three-headed version first designed for Devil Summoner: Soul Hackers and the shape of sharks.
Character design
One of the additional challenges was the fact that it was the first Megami Tensei title to feature extensive voice acting, inspired by the need to fully express the game's themes and story.
Music

The music for Digital Devil Saga was composed by Shoji Meguro, who had previously worked on multiple Megami Tensei games, with some additional tracks for the first game being written by Kenichi Tsuchiya.
Music
While he had previously been restricted in his music quality by the limited storage space of the CD medium, Meguro was able to play half the tracks using real-time streaming.
Music
For the first game, Meguro made heavy use of guitar-based rock music, taking his inspiration from music of the 1960s and 70s.
Music
The game's battle theme, "Hunting", was originally going to be the boss theme, but its instrumentation was considered to be wrong and so it was changed to the normal battle theme.
Music
The first game's opening theme, "Pray", was sung by Sera's voice actress Houko Kuwashima.
Music
The opening theme for Digital Devil Saga 2 was "Alive": it was written by Meguro, sung by Kayoko Momota, and had backing vocals by Yumi Kawamura.
Release
Digital Devil Saga was first announced in the Japanese director's cut version of Nocturne in February 2004.
Release
The game's formal title had only been decided upon shortly before its reveal.
Release
An eight- megabyte PlayStation 2 memory card was sold that featured artwork of Serph and his demon form.
Release
Digital Devil Saga 2 was officially announced at the 2004 Tokyo Game Show.
Release
To promote Digital Devil Saga 2, a special DVD containing selected music tracks and movie material was created as an over-the-counter giveaway for the initial print of the game.
Release
Digital Devil Saga was officially announced for the west at the 2004 Electronic Entertainment Expo for release in the winter of that year.
Release
The second game's release window was officially announced at the 2005 Electronic Entertainment Expo, to be published in North America by Atlus USA.
Release
The game arrived in stores in North America a week earlier than originally scheduled.
Release
Digital Devil Saga was the first Megami Tensei project to feature an extensive voice acting element.
Release

During localization, localization project manager Yu Namba made a spelling error during one of the early cutscenes where the name of Serph's demon form was shown: the demon's name was displayed as "Varna", when it was actually "Varuna".
Release
The error was not spotted until it was too late, and so remained in the game.
Reception
By the end of 2004, the first game sold 153,421 units in Japan, coming in at the 81st best-selling title in Japan for that year.
Reception
The second game sold 90,812 units in Japan by the end of 2005, becoming the 144th best-selling game for 2005.
Reception

Digital Devil Saga did not manage to meet its projected sales targets in Japan, and contributed to the company's console division posting a substantial loss for the 2004/2005 financial year, resulting in several staff members being laid off.
Reception
According to a representative of Atlus USA, the games' sales performances in 2005 were "absolutely fabulous".
Reception
In Europe, it was stated by its publisher that the first game had sold above expectations in the region.
Reception
Speaking in 2013, a Ghostlight representative said that the Digital Devil Saga duology had "met with great success" in Europe.
Reception
Digital Devil Saga received positive critical reception: aggregate sites GameRankings and Metacritic show ratings of 80% and 78/100 respectively.
Reception
The reviewer for 1UP.com, despite missing the demon fusion systems from earlier Megami Tensei titles, thoroughly enjoyed the game, calling it "a great Final Fantasy alternative".
Reception
Digital Devil Saga 2 received an even better reception: its aggregate scores from GameRankings and Metacritic were 83% and 83/100 respectively.
Reception
While critics generally cited a necessity for knowledge of the first game, the story and gameplay were generally cited as an improvement over the original.
Reception
Famitsu was again fairly positive, enjoying the story and characters, while also noting the accommodations for first-time players.
Reception

Dengeki PlayStation was highly positive about the game, praising its story and gameplay additions, though saying that the two games were a little too similar, and that people who had not played the first game would be confused by the story and character relations.
Reception
1UP.com's Shane Bettenhausen said that while the game shared many similarities with its predecessor, it was not as repetitive as other games such as the.hack series, and was still a good game.
Reception
Masimilla said that Digital Devil Saga 2 had managed to realize the first game's storytelling ambitions, enjoying the experience despite noting some design flaws.
Legacy
In 2011, Digital Devil Saga and its sequel Digital Devil Saga 2 ended up topping the site's "Top 20 RPGs of the Last Decade" list.
Legacy

Kurt Kalata, writing for 1UP.com in an article concerning the controversial content of the Megami Tensei series, made mention of Digital Devil Saga due to its examination of the ethics of eating others to survive.
Legacy
A manga spin-off of Digital Devil Saga titled Digital Devil Saga: Avatar Tuner - Shinen no Matou was published in Japan in 2005 by Jive.
Legacy

pst2_shin_megumi_tensai_digital_d_2.title: Shin Megami Tensei (video game)
sents: lead
Shin Megami Tensei is a role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the Super Famicom.
lead
Originally released in 1992 in Japan, it has been ported to multiple systems and eventually released in the West for iOS in 2014.
lead
It was released on the Virtual Console service in Japan on Wii in 2007 and on Wii U in 2013, as well as Nintendo Switch Online in 2020.
lead
It is the third game in the Megami Tensei series and the first in the central Shin Megami Tensei series.
lead
The gameplay uses first-person navigation of dungeons and turn-based battles against demons.
lead
The player can recruit demons as allies by talking to them rather than fighting them, and two to three demons can be fused to create new demons.
lead
The story follows a player-named protagonist who lives in near-future Tokyo.
lead

When a portal to the realm of demons is opened accidentally by a scientist named Steven and is seized by Gotou, a military commander who believes that he can control the demons, the United States government orders a nuclear attack on Tokyo.
Gameplay
The gameplay is similar to that of other games in the series: players make their way through dungeons and fight against demons in a first-person perspective.
Gameplay

At some places, called "Cathedrals of Shadows", players can fuse two to three allied demons into one single, more powerful demon; as demons do not receive experience points, this is the only way for the player to increase their demons' power.
Setting and characters
Shin Megami Tensei takes place in a near future Tokyo, first in the year "199X", and then 30 years later in a post-apocalyptic version of the city.
Development
While designing the maps, Kaneko wanted to use wire-frame models, but the Super Famicom's limited capacities meant this idea was scrapped.
Character designs
The Hero's and the Heroine's clothes were designed to be futuristic; the Heroine was designed to be a protector, with clothes inspired by American football equipment.
Character designs
The Law Hero and Chaos Hero have ordinary clothes at first; the Chaos Hero was designed to look unsophisticated, with a bad posture and military clothes.
Character designs
The character Louis Cyphre was inspired by the character of the same name from the 1987 movie Angel Heart.
Character designs
According to Ito, the character Thorman's name was originally inspired by the Norse god of thunder, but after release, he realized that the name was highly similar to that of Harry S.
Character designs
The graphics for most demons were directly drawn as sprites, without concept art, to make sure that the design and the graphics would work within the hardware limitations of the Super Famicom.
Character designs
Certain important characters, and some demons who the player would be guaranteed to meet, were drawn as concept art first.
Music
Masuko considered Shin Megami Tensei to be an experimental work: it was the first time he had created music for the Super Famicom, so he was not familiar with the console's specifications.
Music
A soundtrack album, Shin Megami Tensei Law & Chaos Disc, was released on February 24, 1993, by Victor Entertainment under the catalog number VICL-40046/7.
Music
A second album, Shin Megami Tensei Sound Collection, was released on March 5, 2003, by SME Visual Works under the catalog number SVWC-7175/6.
Release
Shin Megami Tensei was first released on the Super Famicom on October 30, 1992, in Japan; it remained exclusive to that region for 22 years.
Release
Subsequent ports were released on the PC Engine (December 25, 1993), Mega-CD (February 25, 1994), the PlayStation (May 31, 2001), and Game Boy Advance (March 28, 2003).
Release

The Game Boy Advance version, which was the first time Shin Megami Tensei appeared on a portable platform, included the ability to exchange demons and items using the platform's data exchange capacities.
Release
The game was released in February 2012 for iOS and November of that year for Android.
Release
The iOS port was localized and released in North America and Europe on March 18, 2014.
Release
With the release of iOS 11 in 2017, the game is no longer compatible with up-to-date iOS devices.
Localization
In 2002, the team Aeon Genesis released an English translation patch unofficially for the original Super Famicom release of the game.
Localization
They went on to release English translations for Shin Megami Tensei II in 2004 and Shin Megami Tensei if... in 2018.
Localization
In 2021, another team released a translation patch for the GBA version that carries over the official iOS localization.
Localization
In 2022, a third team released an unofficial English translation patch for the PlayStation release.
Localization

The localization project was slow at first, as it took time to extract the files from the game, so the localization team started by playing the game in order to find out what kinds of dialogue text and system messages it contained.
Localization

A challenge for the localization team was character limitations: only four rows of text, with 28 characters each, were able to be displayed at a time, and at some points this had to be limited even further in order to avoid graphical glitches.
Localization
The Soulless Army, while Persona 4 and Shin Megami Tensei IV include several quotes and terms from the game.
Localization
The already translated Shin Megami Tensei quotes from Persona 4 ' s localization were reused verbatim in the localization of Shin Megami Tensei.
Reception
At the end of 2001, the PlayStation version was the 119th best selling video game of the year in Japan, with 85,991 sold copies.
Reception
On release, Famitsu magazine gave the original Super Famicom version a score of 36 out of 40, with all four reviewers giving it a 9 out of 10.
Reception
This made it one of their three highest-rated games of 1992, along with Dragon Quest V and World of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck.
Reception
Shin Megami Tensei was also one of only eleven games to have received a Famitsu score of 36/40 or above up until 1992.
Reception
For subsequent console ports, Famitsu gave scores of 25/40 (PCE), 28/40 (MD), 30/40 (PS), and 27/40 (GBA).
Reception
RPGFan found the story to be good and macabre, and surprisingly relevant even in 2014.
Legacy
Shin Megami Tensei II, which directly continued the story of Shin Megami Tensei, was released in 1994.
Legacy
The game developer Toby Fox cited Shin Megami Tensei as inspiration for his 2015 game Undertale, specifically its dialogue system.

sents: lead
Persona 4, released outside Japan as Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4, is a 2008 role-playing video game by Atlus.
lead

It is chronologically the fifth installment in the Persona series, itself a part of the larger Megami Tensei franchise, and was released for the PlayStation 2 in Japan in July 2008, North America in December 2008, and in Europe and Australia in March 2009, being one of the final major exclusives for the system.
lead
It was re-released as a PlayStation 2 Classic for the PlayStation 3 in April 2014.
lead
Persona 4 takes place in a fictional Japanese countryside and is indirectly related to earlier Persona games.
lead
The player-named protagonist is a high-school student who moved into the countryside from the city for a year.
lead

During his year-long stay, he becomes involved in investigating mysterious murders with a group of friends while harnessing the power to summon physical manifestations of their psyches known as a Persona.
lead
The plot of Persona 4 was inspired by the work of mystery novelists owing to its murder mystery premise.
lead
The rural setting was based on a town on the outskirts of Mount Fuji and intended as a "'nowhere' place" and is the central setting to have players sympathize with the daily life of the characters.
Gameplay
Persona 4 blends traditional RPG gameplay with simulation elements.
Gameplay
Days are broken up into various times of day, the most frequently recurring being "After School/Daytime" and "Evening", with most activities causing time to move on.
Gameplay
Certain activities are limited depending on the time of day, days of the week, and the weather, with most evening activities unavailable if the player visits the TV World that day.
Personas
The level of Personas that can be created are limited by the protagonist's current level.
Setting and characters
Persona 4 takes place in the fictional, rural Japanese town of Inaba (稲羽市, Inaba-shi), which lies among floodplains and has its own high school and shopping districts.
Setting and characters
The game also follows the main characters into the TV World, a fog-shrouded realm filled with monsters called Shadows, which can only be accessed through TV sets.
Story
On April 11, 2011, Yu Narukami arrives in Inaba to live with the Dojimas, consisting of his uncle Ryotaro and his cousin Nanako, for one year, as his parents are working abroad.
Persona 4 Golden
Persona 4 Golden adds two new Social Links to the game; Adachi and Marie, a mysterious girl who becomes an assistant in the Velvet Room and wishes to uncover her lost memories.
Development
According to the game director Katsura Hashino, while "ideas thrown around earlier", development on Persona 4 in Japan did not begin until after the release of Persona 3.
Development
The development team consisted of the team from Persona 3 and new hires which included fans of Persona 3.
Development
Atlus intended to improve both the gameplay and story elements of Persona 3 for the new game, to ensure it was not seen as a "retread" of its predecessor.
Development
Hashino said that "to accomplish that, we tried to give the players of Persona 4 a definite goal and a sense of purpose that would keep motivating them as they played through the game.
Development

The murder mystery plot was our way of doing that." The plot of Persona 4 was "greatly inspired", according to Hashino, by mystery novelists such as Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Agatha Christie, and Seishi Yokomizo.
Development
Persona 4 was officially unveiled in the Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu in March 2008.
Development
The game's North American release date was announced at the 2008 Anime Expo in Los Angeles, California.
Development
Atlus would not make an add-on disc or epilogue for Persona 4, as had been done with the Persona 3 FES.
Development
Persona 4 allowed players full control of characters in battle.
Development
This was due to negative comments from players about most of the player team in Persona 3 being controlled by the game's AI.
Development
Unlike other role-playing games, which may have large worlds for the player to explore, Persona 4 mostly takes place in Inaba.
Development
The choice of Japanese mythical figures for the characters' Personas as opposed to the Graeco-Roman deities used in earlier games was directly inspired by the new setting.
Development
Despite living in the countryside, Persona 4 characters were designed to look and sound "normal" and like "modern high-schoolers", according to lead localization editor Nich Maragos.
Localization
As with Persona 3, the localization of Persona 4 was handled by Yu Namba and Nich Maragos of Atlus USA.
Localization
A different change was that the main characters in the English dub referred to others members of the cast on a first-name basis, while the Japanese version differed in this regard.
Localization
For the dub, the editors sometimes switched between first-name and last-name referral for dramatic effect.
Localization
Similarly, Persona 4: The Ultimate in Mayonaka Arena and Persona 4: The Golden were shortened to the previously stated titles.
Localization

Localization
A member of the English dub that also appeared in Persona 3 was Yuri Lowenthal.
Localization
Though he had dubbed characters in Persona 3, Namba wanted him to have a larger part.
Localization
Another element in the English script was that the use of swear words was increased over Persona 3: the first draft featured very strong language which was cut as it did not seem suited.
Music
Kitajoh, who had previously written music for Atlus with Growlanser VI and Trauma Center: New Blood, contributed four themes to Persona 4, while Kozuka wrote the "Theme of Junes".
Music
Persona 4 ' s two-disc soundtrack was released in Japan by Aniplex on July 23, 2008.

Reception

Reception

Reception

Development
Rogue Galaxy was first hinted in August 2003, when Level-5 revamped its website, and included a single image for a "New RPG ".
Development
No further information was provided, although, at the time, some thought the game might be the rumored Dark Cloud 3.
Development

Nothing more was heard until February 2005, when Level-5 president Akihiro Hino revealed that "New RPG" was going to be released for the PlayStation 2, quelling rumors the game was being developed for the PlayStation Portable.
Development

The name was announced on July 19, when it was also revealed that the game would feature cel-shaded graphics in the style of previous Level-5 games, such as Dark Chronicle and Dragon Quest VIII: Journey of the Cursed King.
Development
Level-5 refer to the technique as "tonal rendering " - a mixture of cel-shaded 3D graphics for the main characters, set against detailed, realistic backgrounds.
Development
He also revealed the game was the biggest project Level-5 had ever worked on, both in terms of production length and the number of staff working on the project.
Development
In an August interview with Famitsu, Hino explained the gameplay involves the player travelling the galaxy and visiting various planets, each of which has its own unique visual theme.
Development

Originally, he had planned to feature a "virtually uncountable number of planets", which would be procedurally generated as the player explored them, but this concept was later modified to a smaller number of planets, each with multiple locations.
Development
"Level-5 was created for swords and magic fantasies, but we got bored with the consistently similar worlds, so we wanted to try something new".
Development
A trailer for the game was released on August 5, as was basic plot information.
Development
One may actually get the feeling of existing in the expansive world of a massively multiplayer online RPG rather than the limited world of standard RPG".
Development
The game was released in Japan on December 8, with no date set for North American or European releases.
Development
IGN's Gantayat again praised the absence of loading times, arguing "the technical feats this game pulls off with the grey and limping PS2 hardware are impressive".
Development

GameSpot's Bethany Massimilla wrote that "the visual style of the game is strongly inspired by cel-shading techniques, but the characters here aren't the flat and cartoony sort that you might ordinarily associate with the cel-shaded style.
Music
The two-disc, sixty-one track Rogue Galaxy Original Soundtrack, was released in Japan on January 25, 2006 by King Records.
Localization improvements
In April 2006, Sony Computer Entertainment confirmed the localised version for a North American market.
Localization improvements
Also in E3 event in May, Level-5 revealed the English language version of the game is much more than a direct translation of the original Japanese version, but also to include multiple new features.
Localization improvements
Initially for October 2006, the North American release date had been pushed back to January 2007 to facilitate further refinement.
Localization improvements
At the 2006 Tokyo Game Show, the producer of the English localization, Nao Higo, called the new version of the game the "perfect version".
Localization improvements
When the second player enters the code in "Battle mode" at the Insectron tournament, they can use their team to fight the first player's team.
Localization improvements
The game is now housed on a double-layer 8.5GB DVD instead of the original 4.7GB DVD, which allows smoother graphics and additional data.
Localization improvements
Over 2000 lines of additional voiced dialogue has been added.
Reception
Game Revolution 's Tim Tackett was critical of the plot, writing that "the characters lack backstories, and the emotional pitch never leaves the realm of Saturday morning cartoons".
Reception
Grinding out levels and looking for items is rarely this rewarding, and it's obvious that Level 5 knows the depths of the role-player's mind all too well".
Reception

Since you only have direct control over one character, who'll mostly depend on the same basic attacks regardless of which weapons you've equipped, the battles don't feel particularly varied from one to the next".
Reception
On the other hand, though, this is a game that does enough differently or better than most of its PS2 predecessors that it's still well deserving of your consideration".
Reception
IGN's Jeremy Dunham praised the graphics ("It's easily one of the top 20 best looking PS2 titles ever made") and the battle system, although he was somewhat critical of teammate AI.
Reception

Though its storyline isn't on the same level as other great PS2 games in the genre, its mixture of strong combat mechanics, addictive sidequests, and absolutely stunning visual style more than makes up for what it doesn't do".
Sales and awards
Prior to the release of the game, Sony Computer Entertainment corporate executive Masatsuka Saeki had hoped it would sell a million units.
Sales and awards
Although it was the top-selling video game in Japan during the week ending December 11, 2005, selling 237,631 units, by the end of 2006, the game had sold only 356,192 units.
Sales and awards
In 2007, Rogue Galaxy: Director's Cut sold a further 29,457 units.
Sales and awards
The game won a "Future Award" at the CESA Game Awards (2005) and an "Excellence in Digital Content" award at the Digital Contents Grandprix (2006).
Sales and awards

At the Famitsu Awards in 2006, it won both "Best RPG" and a "Special Rookie Award." It was named "Game of the Month" for January 2007 and given an "Editor's Choice" award by IGN, who, in 2010, placed it at #53 in their "Top 100 PlayStation 2 Games".
Sales and awards

During the 11th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences named Rogue Galaxy as one of the nominees for 2007's " Role-Playing Game of the Year ", but eventually lost to Mass Effect.

pst2_dragon_request_viii.title: Dragon Quest VIII
sents: lead
Dragon Quest VIII: Journey of the Cursed King is a role-playing video game developed by Level-5 and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 2.
lead
It was released in Japan in 2004, in North America in 2005, and in PAL regions in 2006.
lead
It is the eighth installment of the Dragon Quest series and it is the first English version of a Dragon Quest game to drop the Dragon Warrior title.
lead
A version of the game for Android and iOS was released in Japan in December 2013, and worldwide in May 2014.
lead
Dragon Quest VIII uses cel shading for the characters and scenery and is the first game in the series to have fully 3D environments and character models.
lead
The game retains most of the series' role-playing game elements, such as turn-based combat and the experience level system.
lead
Dragon Quest VIII follows the silent protagonist and his party of allies as they journey towards the goal of defeating the wicked Dhoulmagus, who cursed the kingdom of Trodain and its people.
lead
Dragon Quest VIII was a critical and commercial success, later being released under the Sony Greatest Hits brand.
Gameplay
Players are able to pan the camera a full 360 degrees around the character, as well as look in a first-person perspective mode.
Gameplay
In the earlier games, battles were shown from a first-person perspective.
Gameplay

For this installment, the battles are shown in a first-person perspective while choosing what to do, but the view then shifts to a third-person perspective with all of the members of the Hero's party shown on the screen along with the enemies.
Plot
The only one left unaffected is the unnamed protagonist, a Trodain guard.
Plot
Marcello kills the last remaining descendant of the sages, but manages to contain Rhapthorne for a time.
Plot
In the 3DS version, the player can choose to instead begin a romance with Jessica.
Characters

The main protagonist of the game, an eighteen-year-old royal guard of Trodain and the only person present in the castle to escape Dhoulmagus' wrath unscathed, is a silent hero, and named by the player.
Characters
Jessica Albert, the only woman to join the party, is a sorceress from the town of Alexandria who seeks to avenge her murdered brother, Alistair.
Characters
In battle, he can use both magic and physical attacks effectively and has the most healing spells.
Development and release
Dragon Quest VIII was released in Japan on the morning of November 27, 2004, with a celebration at Starbucks in Shibuya, Tokyo, starting at 6:30 am.
Development and release
Horii and Square Enix President Yoichi Wada both made appearances at the event, and several of the first buyers in line received a toy Slime.
Development and release
A demo disc for Dragon Quest VIII was also released during the fall of 2005 through Shonen Jump magazine.
Development and release
The game was released in North America on November 15, 2005, and shipped with a playable Final Fantasy XII demo disc.
Development and release
In a Nintendo Direct in November 2015, it was shown that the game would be releasing for the 3DS in 2016.
Development and release
Dragon Quest VIII was the first game in the series to bear the Dragon Quest name (rather than Dragon Warrior) in North America.
Development and release
In 2003, Square Enix registered the Dragon Quest trademark in the US, making the Dragon Warrior name obsolete.
Development and release
As this installment of the series was the first after 2003 to be released outside Japan, it was the first to receive the Quest in its title.
Development and release
Richard Honeywood, of Square Enix's localization office and famous for his work with Final Fantasy VIII and Chocobo Racing, was the main force behind the game's English localization.
Development and release
The iOS and Android version removed the voice acting, akin to the original Japanese PS2 version due to hardware limitations at the time.
Development and release
Dragon Quest VIII was released in PAL regions in April 2006 under the title Dragon Quest: The Journey of the Cursed King, dropping the Roman numeral.
Music
As with most Dragon Quest games, Koichi Sugiyama wrote the game's original score.
Music
An official soundtrack for Dragon Quest VIII was released in December 2005, published by Aniplex.
Music

The 3DS versions swaps the soundtracks with the Japanese version using the symphonic suite orchestral recordings, while the North American and PAL versions use the sequenced music, which was entirely remastered, other than the original sequenced music in the Japanese PS2 version.
Music
The iOS and Android version uses the sequenced music from the Japanese PS2 version.
Reception

Released for the PlayStation 2 on November 27, 2004, in Japan, Dragon Quest VIII sold 2,167,072 units in two days, 3 million in three days, and more than 3 million within a week, becoming the fastest-selling PlayStation 2 title in Japan.
Reception
By September 2008, total worldwide shipments of Dragon Quest VIII surpassed 4.9 million copies, of which over 430,000 were from the North American release.
Reception
Dragon Quest VIII is the biggest selling game ever for the PlayStation 2 in Japan.
Reception
It was the first Dragon Quest game to receive a score of 39 out of 40 from Famitsu.
Reception
It won both 1UP.com ' s and GameSpy 's "Best RPG of E3 2005" award, ahead of runner-up Kingdom Hearts II.
Reception
During the 9th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards (now known as the D.I.C.E.
Reception
The iOS version became the 2nd top-seller of Japan AppStore in the debut half day, highlighting the influence of the series.
Reception

The Nintendo 3DS version was nominated for "Handheld/Mobile Game of the Year" at the Golden Joystick Awards, for "Best Portable Game" at Destructoid ' s Game of the Year Awards 2017, and for " Handheld Game of the Year " at the 21st Annual D.I.C.E.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.
Reception
The US release of Dragon Quest VIII received mostly positive reviews, receiving a score of 89 out of 100 on Metacritic.
Reception
Critics were quick to praise the 3D cel shaded visuals, noting that it was the first game in the series to be fully three-dimensional.
Reception
Edge magazine, however, commented that the game's substance seemed out of place for 2005.
Reception
The 1UP.com staff suggested that the player stop playing "to just look around and absorb the scenery" and said that it rivals Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas ' map of San Andreas in size and detail.
Reception

IGN writer Jeremy Dunham wrote that the "only exception in the game's mass list of progression is the plotline," explaining that it has one of the more basic Dragon Quest stories; but he also mentions that the game still manages to take a simple plot and make it entertaining.
Legacy
Dragon Quest Yangus, a roguelike Mystery Dungeon game by Cavia for the PlayStation 2, follows the storyline of a young Yangus.
Legacy
The protagonist also appears as a playable character in the 2018 crossover fighting game Super Smash Bros.
Legacy

The character would be voiced for the first time by Yuki Kaji who, according to director Masahiro Sakurai, said it was a dream of his to do voicework for both the Super Smash Bros. and Dragon Quest series.
