pst2_xenosago_episode_ii.title: Xenosaga Episode II
sents: lead
Xenosaga Episode II: Jenseits von Gut und Böse is a 2004 role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft for the PlayStation 2.
lead
It was published in Japan (2004) and North America (2005) by Namco, and in Europe by Sony Computer Entertainment Europe (2005).
lead
It is the second entry in the Xenosaga trilogy, and forms part of the wider Xeno metaseries.
lead

Continuing directly from the events of Xenosaga Episode I, Xenosaga Episode II sees protagonists Shion Uzuki and Jr. continuing to combat the plots of the U-TIC Organization and the insane Albedo Piazzolla.
lead

Gameplay is carried over from the first game, featuring exploration of environments through a linear narrative, while battles follow a turn-based system featuring a system of button combinations, multiple leveling systems, and combat featuring both the characters on foot and piloting large mecha called "E.S.".
lead
Development of Xenosaga Episode II began following the completion of Episode I.
lead
Series creator Tetsuya Takahashi gave control of the Xenosaga series to a new development team, resulting in a number of changes.
lead
The gameplay system was redesigned based on feedback from Episode I.
Gameplay
Most areas can be navigated on foot, but some require the use of mechs.
Gameplay
New items and accessories can only be gathered either through searching the environment or defeating enemies, as currency and shops are not present.
Setting
Humanity is now spread across 500,000 planets, with their governments forming the Galaxy Federation.
Setting
The planet of Miltia was lost in a space-time anomaly when an experiment involving U.R.T.Vs—an army of 669 genetically modified children designed to combat U-DO's energies—goes horribly wrong.
Setting

During the events of Episode I, main protagonist Shion Uzuki and her creation the anti-Gnosis android prototype KOS-MOS are forced to escape a Gnosis attack triggered by the discovery of a Zohar Emulator.
Plot
While on Second Miltia, MOMO, Ziggy, chaos and Jr. are attacked by U-TIC agents in powerful mechs, only being saved by Canaan's intervention.
Plot
The three were close, but Albedo became despondent when he discovered his ability to survive any injury was unique to him, meaning he could outlive his brothers.
Plot
With Miltia accessible, the Federation, U-TIC, and the Immigrant Fleet fight each other for control of the Zohar hidden on the planet.
Plot
Shion and Allen attempt to reach Miltia, but are almost destroyed by U-TIC forces and only saved due to KOS-MOS's spontaneous activation and intervention.
Development
Following the release of Episode I in 2002, the Xenosaga project was reevaluated and staff reshuffled to allow newer staff members a chance to handle the series.
Development

During this period the Xenosaga series, originally planned by Takahashi as a six-part series, was rearranged into a trilogy, with the possibility of further episodes should the series meet continued success.
Development
Development on Episode II took approximately two years, worked on by a staff of 60 to 100 people.
Development
The battle system was adjusted based on feedback that the first game's battle system was too complicated.
Development
The new E.S. mecha were designed by Kouichi Mugitani and Junya Ishigaki; each wanted to emulate the design choices of Episode I while also creating something unique to Episode II.
Development
Episode II was the last main Xenosaga game worked on by Saga prior to her leaving the project in 2005.
Development
Xenosaga Episode II was first announced in July 2003 during a special event dedicated to the productions of Monolith Soft.
Development
The game was released by Namco in Japan on June 24, 2004.
Development
The game was first shown off internationally at the 2003 Electronic Entertainment Expo, with its release window being announced by Namco in August of that year.
Development
Episode II was released in North America on February 15, 2005.
Development
Dubbing was handled by Cup of Tea Productions; Xenosaga Episode II was the company's very first project.
Development
While Episode I was not released in Europe, Namco partnered with Sony Computer Entertainment Europe to release Episode II on November 4, 2005.
Music
The original game's composer Yasunori Mitsuda refused to return to the series due to both a busy schedule and a clash of interests with Namco over the direction of the game.
Music
Hosoe, whose previous work included Street Fighter EX and the Ridge Racer series, was forced to greatly restrict his compositions' quality due to working with the limited sound hardware on the PS2.
Music
Kajura's compositions were released on a two-disc album in July 2004, while some of Hosoe's music was released on a promotional disc as part of the North American strategy guide.
Reception
During its first week on sale in Japan, Xenosaga Episode II reached second place in gaming charts, selling around 186,000 units.
Reception
The following week the game dropped to the third place with further sales of over 32,000 units, contributing to a general decline in game sales during that period.
Reception
Within two weeks of its release, the game had sold nearly 219,000 units in Japan.
Reception
According to Namco's fiscal report in February 2005, the game had sold 280,000 units in Japan by that time.
Reception
According to their later 2005 fiscal year report, Episode II was one of Namco's better-selling titles in North America, although no exact sales figures were given.
Reception
According to a later report, Episode II underperformed commercially, reaching just over 50% of Namco's projected sales target.
Reception
GamePro, while noting that the cinematics might be too long for some, enjoyed the story and its continuation of the first game's narrative.
Reception
Dunham noted that the increased visual quality and redone character designs helped in the game's presentation, though he found the soundtrack lacking when measured against the first game's score.
Reception

GamePro positively noted that the first game's mechanics had been made more approachable for series newcomers, while Massimilla felt that the simplified nature of the character growth system brought down the experience in addition to being shorter than other RPGs available at the time.
Legacy
While the team were open to further entries based on the game's commercial performance, it was designed to be the last entry in the series.
Legacy
Episode III was the last game released in the Xenosaga series.
Legacy
Released in July 2004 for mobile devices, the game was co-developed by Monolith Soft, Namco Mobile and Tom Create as part of a move to make Xenosaga a multimedia franchise accessing a wide audience.
Legacy
Co-developed by Monolith Soft and Tom Create, the scenario was supervised by Takahashi and included material which needed to be cut from the original releases of the first two Xenosaga games.

pst2_xenosago_episode_iii.title: Xenosaga Episode III
sents: lead
Xenosaga Episode III: Also sprach Zarathustra is a role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and published by Namco Bandai Games for the PlayStation 2 in 2006.
lead
It is the final entry in both the Xenosaga trilogy and the larger Xenosaga series, which forms part of the Xeno franchise.
lead

Concluding the narrative of Xenosaga Episode I and Episode II, Episode III sees Shion Uzuki and the battle android KOS-MOS search out the origins of the hostile alien Gnosis while being hunted by Shion's former employers and four powerful humans called the Testaments.
lead

Gameplay is carried over from the first two games, featuring exploration of environments through a linear narrative, while battles follow a turn-based system featuring multiple leveling systems and combat with both a human party and mecha.
lead
Concept work for Xenosaga Episode III began during the later development of Xenosaga Episode II in 2004.
lead
The development team's aim was to address issues raised by fans and staff with the previous two Xenosaga games, along with bringing the story to a satisfactory conclusion.
lead
Due to the decision to turn the intended six-part series into a trilogy, the original draft for Episode III was substantially reworked.
lead
As with previous Xenosaga titles, the subtitle was drawn from the work of German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche.
Gameplay
Some dungeons in the game are only navigable with mechs, while others enable the player to switch between navigating on foot or in mechs.
Setting
Humanity is now spread across 500,000 planets, with their governments forming the Galaxy Federation.
Setting
The planet of Miltia was lost in a space-time anomaly when an experiment involving U.R.T.Vs—an army of 669 genetically modified children designed to combat U-DO's energies—goes horribly wrong.
Characters
The main protagonists are Shion Uzuki, a former employee of Vector Industries; and KOS-MOS, a prototype anti-Gnosis battle android.
Plot
After the test, T-elos' creator Roth Mantel informs Allen that KOS-MOS will be scrapped so development can focus on T-elos.
Plot
As KOS-MOS's weaponry is the only way to break into the hyperspace pocket and save the Elsa, Shion leads the group into the facility and rescues KOS-MOS, guided at one point by Abel.
Plot

The trauma caused the young Shion to resonate with the Zohar, summoning the Gnosis and awakening U-DO; it was only Mizrahi's self-sacrifice in sealing away Miltia that prevented the chaos from spreading.
Plot
KOS-MOS is last seen drifting towards Lost Jerusalem.
Development
Development of Xenosaga Episode III began in 2004 during the final development stages of Episode II.
Development

One of the main goals when developing Episode III was not only to bring a satisfactory end to the Xenosaga storyline up to that point, but to address criticism of the short length of Episode II ' s story, while also addressing general problems noticed with both Episode I and Episode II.
Development
The scenario for Episode III includes narrative elements Takahashi originally created for Episode II, which had been cut from Episode II due to time constraints.
Development
While most of the designs were adaptions of Tanaka's earlier work, Mugitani also designed a new version of KOS-MOS and multiple new mechs.
Development
Mugitani's mech and armor designs drew from both the Gundam franchise and the 1997 film adaptation of Starship Troopers.
Development
Xenosaga Episode III was officially announced in 2005, alongside Xenosaga I & II —a Nintendo DS remake of the first two Xenosaga episodes—and Baten Kaitos Origins.
Development
With its announcement, it was widely confirmed that it would be the last installment in the Xenosaga series.
Development
The game released in Japan on July 6, 2006 by Namco; in North America, the game released on August 29 of that year by Namco Bandai Games.
Development
The game was localized for the West by Namco Bandai and 8-4; Xenosaga Episode III was one of 8-4's earliest projects.
Music
A soundtrack album titled Xenosaga Episode III: Also Sprach Zarathustra Original Sound Best Tracks, featuring selections from the game's score, was published by Victor Entertainment on July 12, 2006.
Reception
During its debut week, Xenosaga Episode III reached number 2 in the charts behind New Super Mario Bros. with sales approaching 124,000 units.
Reception
During Q3 of 2006, the game sold a total of 343,000 across Japan, mainland Asia and North America.
Legacy
Xenosaga Episode III was the last property to be released in the Xenosaga series.
Legacy

Partly to boost team morale and create a game players would enjoy, the team developed a new RPG for the Wii; originally titled Monado: Beginning of the World, its title was eventually changed to Xenoblade Chronicles.

pst2_okamo.title: Ōkami
sents: lead
Ōkami is a 2006 action-adventure game developed by Clover Studio and published by Capcom.
lead
It was released for PlayStation 2 in 2006 in Japan and North America, and in 2007 in Europe and Australia.
lead
After the closure of Clover Studio a few months after the release, a port for Wii was developed by Ready at Dawn, Tose, and Capcom, and released in 2008.
lead

Set in a fictional version of classical Japan, Ōkami combines Japanese mythology and folklore to tell the story of how the land was saved from darkness by the Shinto sun goddess Amaterasu, who took the form of a white wolf.
lead
It features a sumi-e -inspired cel-shaded visual style and the Celestial Brush, a gesture-system to perform miracles.
lead
The game was planned to use more traditional realistic rendering, but this had put a strain on the graphics processing of the PlayStation 2.
lead
Clover Studio switched to a cel-shaded style to reduce the processing, which led to the Celestial Brush concept.
lead
The gameplay is modeled on The Legend of Zelda, one of director Hideki Kamiya 's favorite series.
Gameplay
Rare Demon Fangs can be earned through combat which can be traded for unique items that are beneficial in gameplay but not required to complete the game.
Gameplay

Weapons inspired by the Imperial Regalia of Japan (the Reflector, the Rosaries, and the Glaive) can be equipped on Amaterasu as either main or sub-weapons (one each), and used in addition to other melee attacks that the player can have Amaterasu learn through the course of the game.
Celestial Brush
A game mechanic unique to Ōkami is the Celestial Brush.
Celestial Brush

The player's ink for drawing is limited by the amount available in special ink wells, preventing the player from solely using Brush techniques to defeat enemies; ink is restored in the wells over time when the Brush is not used.
Plot
Most character names below are the shortened names of the U.S. version.
Characters

Most of the human characters in the game only see her as a plain white wolf; some believe Amaterasu to be the reincarnation of Shiranui (the white wolf that fought Orochi 100 years prior to the game's present), and do not recognize her spiritual nature.
Characters

Each of its eight heads is infused with a different elemental magic power, but the entire demon is susceptible to a special brew of sake available only at Kamiki Village, allowing Amaterasu to defeat it while in its stupor.
Characters
Throughout the game, the player encounters several other characters that are inspired from Japanese folklore.
Story

In the game's present, Nagi's descendant and self-proclaimed greatest warrior, Susano, refuses to believe in Nagi's legend and frees Orochi, who escapes and curses the lands, sapping the life from Nippon.
Development
Kamiya and other members of the team introduced ideas around the nature aspect and eventually led to the game's initial prototype, which Kamiya admitted was "incredibly boring to play".
Development
While the team successfully used the photorealistic engine to produce initial prototypes, the performance on the target platform, the PlayStation 2, was not great.
Development

Sakuya, designed around a peach motif, was envisioned with what were called "level 2" and "level 3" designs where the character would wear less clothing as the story progressed, but the "level 3" appearance, effectively naked, was vetoed by Inaba.
Development

Orochi in Japanese mythology is a gigantic creature, so lead character designer Sawaki Takeyasu designed the back of the demon to include a garden and palace; this inspired the game designers to include a bell in those structures that would be Orochi's fatal weakness in the game.
Development
In 2024, Kamiya said that while Clover Studios were brought together to be a "dream team", there was strife between the various developers.
Development

Only one puzzle in the game had to be changed as it required knowledge of the steps in drawing a kanji character which would be readily known for Japanese audiences; for the Western release, these steps were demonstrated in the game.
Development
Ōkami was shown at the 2005 E3 Convention, approximately 30% complete, with a planned release in 2006.
Development
The game was released a year later, with its release in Japan on 20 April 2006, North America on 19 September 2006, in Europe on 9 February 2007, and in Australia on 14 February.
Development
The Ōkami: Official Complete Works art book was published by Udon in May 2008.
Development
The game was re-released under Sony's " Greatest Hits " in Japan in August 2008.
Naming and allusions
Issun's informal name for Amaterasu in the Western translation, "Ammy", was inspired by Kamiya, and is similar in tone with the Japanese informal name, "Ammako".
Naming and allusions
For example, a non-player character aptly named "Animal Lover" lost his rabbit named "Inaba", the last name of the head producer Atsushi Inaba.
Naming and allusions
To further convey the joke, Inaba the rabbit can be seen falling out of a tree directly underneath Atsushi Inaba's name during the closing credits.
Audio
The music in Ōkami was inspired by classical Japanese works.
Audio
In May 2006, Capcom released a 5-disc soundtrack for Ōkami in Japan.
Audio
In the North American and European release, the player can unlock a jukebox to hear the in-game music upon completion of the game. Ōkami won the best score award at the 2007 BAFTA Video Games Awards.
Audio
Mika Matsura both arranged the 10 songs, and performed it on the piano.
Audio
With the release of Ōkami HD for the Nintendo Switch, Data Disc prepared a vinyl four-disc compilation of over 60 of the game's musical tracks for release in October 2018.
Wii port

However, at the 2007 UK Gamers Day, Capcom announced that Ready at Dawn would oversee porting and development of a Wii version of Ōkami originally scheduled for release in March 2008 but subsequently pushed back to April.
Wii port
Ready at Dawn president Didier Malenfant said that, aside from the control scheme, the Wii version will be "an exact port of the PS2 version".
Wii port
...we're getting the game up and running first.
Wii port

In November 2007, Svensson said that the engine had been ported to the Wii, writing that "there are still several systems getting set up properly but there's most definitely a Wii-driven Amaterasu running around Wii-rendered environments as we speak".
Wii port

A listing posted at Capcom's website for the game in February 2008 revealed that the Wii version would support 480p and widescreen output, and IGN confirmed that the motion sensing of the Wii Remote would be used to perform the Celestial Brush features within the game.
Wii port
This site was made live on 3 April 2008, featuring wallpapers, character artwork, and fan-created art for the game.
Wii port
Svennson further noted that "if did the numbers that we did on the PS2, I'd be very happy.
Wii port
A paper parchment filter applied to all on-screen elements that is readily apparent in the PlayStation 2 version is in the Wii version, but the effect is much less significant.
Wii port
Following a delay, the Wii port of Ōkami was released in North America on 15 April 2008, Australia on 12 June, Europe on 13 June, and Japan on 15 October 2009.
Wii port
To make up for the error, Capcom offered for a limited time to replace the cover with one of three high-resolution covers free of charge to users in North America.
Wii port
The European PAL version of the cover has no such error.
High-definition remaster
Capcom later released Ōkami HD for Windows, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One on 12 December 2017 worldwide, built off the PS3 remaster.
High-definition remaster
The Windows, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One versions include both digital and retail editions, and the Xbox One version was released as a download in Japan.
High-definition remaster
This version supports 4K resolutions, though locked at a 30 frames-per-second framerate, and includes an optional widescreen presentation alongside the 4:3 aspect ratio of the original game.
High-definition remaster
The high-definition remaster was released for the Nintendo Switch on 9 August 2018.
High-definition remaster
The Nintendo Switch port has both a standard physical retail and a limited edition release exclusive to Japan, whilst the game is an eShop -exclusive in other regions.
High-definition remaster
A version of the game was released exclusively in the United States for Amazon Luna on 20 April 2022.
Sequels
The September 2009 issue of Famitsu announced that Ōkamiden was indeed a sequel to Ōkami for the Nintendo DS, to be released by Capcom in Japan in 2010, though without the input of the Clover staff.
Sequels

At the Electronic Entertainment Expo 2016 during an interview with Metro, Kamiya, now at PlatinumGames, said that he had ideas for Ōkami 2 and Bayonetta 3, though did not confirm if either game was in active development.
Sequels
In October 2019, following on financially successful releases of Resident Evil and Monster Hunter games, Capcom indicated that it was looking to revive some of its "dormant" properties.
Reviews
Ōkami received critical acclaim, with a score of 93/100 on Metacritic.
Reviews

GameSpot gave it a 9 out of 10 and selected it as an Editor's Choice, citing that its "visual design instantly stands out, but it turns out to be just one of many inspired aspects of this impressive action adventure game".
Reviews
IGN gave the game a 9.1 out of 10, as being "beautiful, charismatic, engaging and one of the most original games you'll play anytime soon".
Reviews
Electronic Gaming Monthly's three reviewers gave it a 9, 9.5, and 9 out of 10, with one saying: "I'll be surprised if you can find a better game on any system this fall".
Reviews
Newtype USA named Ōkami its Game of the Month for October 2006, heralded the pacing as "nearly flawless" and proclaimed " Ōkami is that rarest of beasts: a game without any obvious flaws.
Reviews

Eurogamer scored the game 10/10 saying: "Right from the start it conjures an atmosphere of being something special, but to keep that level of quality up consistently over 60 hours ensures that this will be a game that will be talked about for years to come".
Reviews
In 2007, Ōkami was named eighteenth best PlayStation 2 game of all time in IGN' s feature reflecting on the PlayStation 2's long lifespan.
Reviews
Famitsu gave the game a near perfect score of 39 out of 40, the 15th game to date to receive this score from the publication.
Reviews

The Wii version of Ōkami has received generally similar praise to the PlayStation 2 version, with GameSpot stating that the support for widescreen and the Wii controls "make it even more relevant today than it was in 2006".
Reviews
The Wii version was given the Game of the Month award from IGN for April 2008.
Reviews
In 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine ranked the game 33rd in a list of greatest Nintendo games.
Reviews
The high-definition release on the PlayStation 3 was praised for being the "definitive" version of the game, with the rendering in 1080p helping to make the graphics style of the game stand out.
Reviews

Cam Shae of IGN did express some disappointment that the PlayStation 3 version does not attempt to address the "pop up" of far-off objects due to draw distance, a limitation of the PlayStation 2 version.
Reviews
Oli Welsh of Eurogamer considered that the game remains as relevant as it was when it was first released in 2006, being one of the few video games of the Zelda style.
Reviews
The release of Ōkami HD for Windows, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One in 2017 was critically praised, establishing that the decade-old game still remained relevant.
Reviews
Polygon ' s Jeff Ramos considered this release the best example of a remaster, praising how well the game's art style and detail are rendered at the higher 4K resolutions.
Awards
IGN, Edge Magazine and Game Revolution rated it as the best overall game of 2006, while GameTrailers and PSM named it best PS2 game for 2006.
Awards
IGN further awarded the game the "Best Overall" and "PS2 Adventure Game", the "Best Overall" and "PS2 Artistic Design", the "Overall" and "PS2 Most Innovative Design", and the "Best Overall Story".
Awards
GameSpot awarded the game for the "Best Artistic Graphics" for 2006.
Awards
IGN named Ōkami 90th game of all time as of 2017.
Awards
In 2010, GamePro ranked it as the fifth best game for the PlayStation 2.
Awards
A 2023 poll conducted by GQ among a team of video game journalists across the industry listed Okami as the 94th best video game of all time.
Awards

The game earned the "Best Character Design" and only one of three Innovation Awards at the 2007 Game Developers Choice Awards. Ōkami won the Grand Prize in the Entertainment Division of the 2006 Japan Media Arts Festival.
Awards
The game was awarded the "Best Anthropomorphic Video Game" in the 2006 Ursa Major awards.
Awards
The HD version was nominated for "Game, Classic Revival" at the 17th Annual NAViGaTR Awards.
Sales
More than 200,000 copies of Ōkami were sold in North America in 2006, grossing approximately US$8 million and ranking as the 100th best selling game of the year in the region.
Sales
By March 2007, the total sales of the PlayStation 2 version were near 270,000.
Sales
By comparison, 66,000 copies were sold in Japan for 2006.
Sales
Kamiya said, in 2024, that these numbers made the game a "failure", which was part of the reasoning for the closure of Clover Studios.
Sales
On 30 July 2008, Capcom revealed that approximately 280,000 copies of the Wii version of Ōkami had been sold in North America and Europe since its release date.
Sales
The Wii version debuted in Japan with a modest 24,000 copies sold in its first week in the region.
Sales
It was recognized as the sixth-bestselling game in Japan on 23 October 2009.
Sales

Total sales for the game remained under 600,000 total units by March 2009, and was named the "least commercially successful winner of a game of the year award" in the 2010 version of the Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition.
Sales
Subsequently, in 2018, the game was awarded the Guinness World Record for "Most critically acclaimed video game starring an animal character".
Sales
Ōkami HD on PlayStation 4 yielded 16,536 unit sales within its first week on sale in Japan, placing it at number 18 on the all format sales chart.
Sales

As of 31 March 2024, more than 2.40 million copies have been sold for the PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch, and as of 2020, 1.065 million copies of the Windows and PlayStation 3 versions, for a combined 3.365 million copies sold by June 2023.
Sales
As of 30 June 2023, worldwide sales of the series reached 4 million copies.
Legacy
Ben Mattes, producer for the 2008 Prince of Persia video game, cited Ōkami, Ico, and Shadow of the Colossus as influences on the gameplay and artwork for the game.
Legacy

After Clover's dissolution and most of its staff's subsequent reformation as PlatinumGames, one of their next games, Bayonetta, contains several references to Ōkami; the most notable of these is when Bayonetta transforms into a panther and, like Amaterasu, a trail of flowers and plant life follows her.
Legacy

For the 2010 San Diego Comic-Con, Capcom raffled a limited run of T-shirts designed by Gerald de Jesus and iam8bit that placed Amaterasu, Shiranui, and Chibiterasu (from Ōkamiden) into a homage to the Three Wolf Moon t-shirt.
Legacy

In 2009, GamesRadar included Ōkami among the games "with untapped franchise potential", commenting: "Seriously, if Nintendo can make the same Zelda game every few years, then why can't Capcom release Ōkami 2 ?".
Legacy
In 2015, Amaterasu was featured in Archie Comics ' Worlds Unite crossover between its Sonic the Hedgehog comic lines and Mega Man series.
Legacy

Capcom submitted and got approval to publish an Amaterasu "courier" for Dota 2 just prior to the December 2017 release of Ōkami HD on Steam, with players that had pre-ordered or purchased Ōkami HD within the release period receiving the courier for free.

pst2_ika.title: Ico
sents: lead
is an action-adventure game developed by Japan Studio and Team Ico and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.
lead
It was released in North America and Japan in 2001 and Europe in 2002 in various regions.
lead
It was designed and directed by Fumito Ueda, who wanted to create a minimalist game around a "boy meets girl" concept.
lead
Originally planned for the PlayStation, Ico took approximately four years to develop.
lead
The team employed a "subtracting design" approach to reduce elements of gameplay that interfered with the game's setting and story in order to create a high level of immersion.
lead
The protagonist is a young boy named Ico who was born with horns, which his village considers a bad omen.
lead
Warriors lock him away in an abandoned fortress.
lead
During his explorations of the fortress, Ico encounters Yorda, the daughter of the castle's Queen.
Gameplay
These actions are complicated by the fact that only Ico can carry out these actions; Yorda can jump only short distances and cannot climb over tall barriers.
Gameplay
Players are unable to progress in the game until they move Yorda to certain doors that only she can open.
Development

Lead designer Fumito Ueda came up with the concept for Ico in 1997, envisioning a "boy meets girl" story where the two main characters would hold hands during their adventure, forming a bond between them without communication.
Development

Ueda was also inspired by the video game Another World (Outer World in Japan), which used cinematic cutscenes, lacked any head-up display elements as to play like a movie, and also featured an emotional connection between two characters despite the use of minimal dialog.
Development
Ueda began working with producer Kenji Kaido in 1998 to develop the idea and bring the game to the PlayStation.
Development
The game originally focused on Ico's attempt to return Yorda to her room in the castle after she was kidnapped by these warriors.
Development
The team decided to remain true to Ueda's vision, and began to use the Emotion Engine of the PlayStation 2, taking advantage of the improved abilities of the platform.
Development
The cover used for releases in Japan and PAL regions was drawn by Ueda himself, and was inspired by the Italian artist Giorgio de Chirico and his work The Nostalgia of the Infinite.
Development

On reflection, Yasuhide Kobayashi, vice-president of Sony's Japan Studio, believed the North American box art and lack of an identifiable English title led to the game's poor sales in the United States, and stated plans to correct that for the release of The Last Guardian.
Development
For its original release, a limited edition of the game was available in PAL regions that included a cardboard wrapping displaying artwork from the game and four art cards inside the box.
Development

The game was re-released as a standard edition in 2006 across all PAL regions except France after the 2005 release of Shadow of the Colossus, Icos spiritual sequel, to allow players to "fill the gap in their collection".
Soundtrack
Icos audio featured a limited amount of music and sound effects.
Soundtrack
The soundtrack, , was composed by Michiru Oshima and sound unit "pentagon" (Koichi Yamazaki & Mitsukuni Murayama) and released in Japan by Sony Music Entertainment on February 20, 2002.
Soundtrack
The last song of the CD, "ICO -You Were There-", includes vocals sung by former Libera member Steven Geraghty.
Novelization
A novelization of the game titled was released in Japan in 2004.
Novelization

A Korean translation of the novel, entitled 이코 – 안개의 성 (I-ko: An-gae-eui Seong) came out the following year, by Hwangmae Publishers, while an English translation was published by Viz Media on August 16, 2011.
Film
In 2010, Misher Films said that a film adaption of Ico may come about based on the success of their then-planned adaptation of Shadow of the Colossus.
Reception
Ico received critical acclaim, becoming a cult hit among players.
Reception
The game has an aggregated review score of 90 out of 100 at Metacritic.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu magazine scored the PlayStation2 version of the game a 30 out of 40.
Reception

The game is considered by some to be one of the greatest games of all time; Edge ranked Ico as the 13th top game in a 2007 listing, while IGN ranked the game at number 18 in 2005, and at number 57 in 2007.
Reception

Charles Herold of The New York Times summed up his review stating that "Ico is not a perfect game, but it is a game of perfect moments." Herold later commented that Ico breaks the mold of games that usually involve companions.
Reception

In most games these companions are invulnerable and players will generally not concern with the non-playable characters' fate, but Ico creates the sense of "trust and childish fragility" around Yorda, which leads to the character being "the game's entire focus".
Reception
G4TV's Matthew Keil, however, felt that "the game is so strong, many will finish 'Ico' in one or two sittings".
Reception
By 2009, only 700,000 copies were sold worldwide, with 270,000 in the United States, and the bulk in PAL regions.
Awards
The game received three Game Developers Choice Awards in 2002, including "Excellence in Level Design", "Excellence in Visual Arts", and "Game Innovation Spotlight".
Legacy

Several game designers, such as Eiji Aonuma, Hideo Kojima, and Jordan Mechner, have cited Ico as having influenced the visual appearance of their games, including The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess, Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater, and Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, respectively.
Legacy

Marc Laidlaw, scriptwriter for the Half-Life series, commented that, among several other more memorable moments in the game, the point where Yorda attempts to save Ico from falling off the damaged bridge was "a significant event not only for that game, but for the art of game design".
Legacy
The Naughty Dog team used Ico as part of the inspiration for developing Uncharted 3.
Legacy

Goichi Suda aka Suda51, said that Ico save game method, where the player has Ico and Yorda sit on a bench to save the game, inspired the save game method in No More Heroes where the player-character sits on a toilet to save the game.
Legacy
Ico was one of the first video games to use a bloom lighting effect, which later became a popular effect in video games.
Legacy
Jenova Chen, creator of art games such as Flower and Journey, cited Ico as one of his biggest influences.
Legacy
Ico was also cited as an influence by Halo 4 creative director Josh Holmes.
Legacy

Naughty Dog said The Last of Us was influenced by Ico, particularly in terms of character building and interaction, and Neil Druckmann credited the gameplay of Ico as a key inspiration when he began developing the story of The Last of Us.
Other Team Ico games
, released for the PlayStation 2 in October 2005 in Japan and North America, was developed by the same team that developed Ico.
Other Team Ico games
The game was referred by its working title "Nico" ("Ni" being Japanese for the number 2") until the final title was revealed.
Other Team Ico games
Team Ico's third game, The Last Guardian, was announced as a PlayStation 3 title at the Electronic Entertainment Expo 2009.
Other Team Ico games
Development subsequently switched to the PlayStation 4 in 2012, and the game was reannounced in 2015 and released in December 2016.
HD remaster
Ico, along with Shadow of the Colossus, received a high-definition remaster for the PlayStation3 that was released worldwide in September 2011.
HD remaster
Patch 1.01 for the digital high-definition Ico version added the Remote Play feature, allowing the game to be played on the PlayStation Vita.

pst2_shadow_of_the_colossal.title: Shadow of the Colossus
sents: lead
Shadow of the Colossus is a 2005 action-adventure game developed by Japan Studio and Team Ico, and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.
lead
It takes place in a fantasy setting and follows Wander, a young man who enters an isolated and abandoned region of the realm seeking the power to revive a girl named Mono.
lead

The player assumes the role of Wander as he embarks on a mission that might entail Mono's resurrection: to locate and destroy the colossi, sixteen massive beings spread across the forbidden land, which the protagonist traverses by horseback and on foot.
lead

The team sought to create an outstanding interactive experience by including a distinct visual design, an unorthodox gameplay template, and non-player characters with sophisticated artificial intelligence such as the colossi and Wander's horse, Agro.
lead

Cited as an influential title in the video game industry and one of the best video games ever made, Shadow of the Colossus is often regarded as an important example of video games as art due to its minimalist landscape designs, immersive gameplay, and emotional weight of the player character's journey.
lead
It received wide critical acclaim by the media and was met with strong sales compared to Ico, due in part to a larger marketing campaign.
lead
The game won several awards for its audio, design, and overall quality.
lead

A remastered version for the PlayStation 3 was released alongside Ico as The Ico & Shadow of the Colossus Collection in September 2011, developed by Bluepoint Games, who later produced a remake in high definition of the game for the PlayStation 4 in 2018.
Gameplay
Most colossi are situated in remote areas, such as atop cliffs or within ancient structures.
Gameplay

Each colossus dwells in a unique lair, and in most encounters the player must use some aspects of the current battlefield to advantage, a necessity that becomes more pronounced as the game progresses.
Gameplay
The first two battles take place on simple, vast, flat areas of land, wherein the player's only goal is to discover how to scale the colossi and attack their weak points.
Gameplay
Wander has a limited stamina gauge that decreases as he hangs onto the colossus; the player thus must act quickly when they scale the creature.
Gameplay
Aside from the colossi, who are the only enemies of the game, the environment is inhabited by natural animals.
Gameplay
Only one species, however, has an effect on gameplay: eating the tail of a certain kind of lizard increases Wander's stamina gauge.
Setting
The only point of entry to the region is a small cleft in the mountains to the north that leads to a massive stone bridge.
Characters
The only established fact regarding Mono is that she was a maiden who was sacrificed because she was believed to have a cursed destiny.
Characters

The colossi are armored, most often enormous creatures with forms ranging from various humanoids to predatory animals, and live in all manner of surroundings and environments, including underwater and flying through the air.
Characters
Some colossi are peaceful and will only attack when provoked, whereas others are aggressive and will attack on sight.
Characters
The Latin names of the colossi, though spread throughout fan related media, are not official and are never referred to within the game.
Plot
Soon after, Wander goes on to defeat the final colossus as Emon's company arrives in the Shrine of Worship to witness the last temple idol crumble.
Plot
Mono takes the child with her, following the horse to higher levels of the Shrine of Worship, and arrives at a secret garden within the shrine as the game ends.
Origin

Shadow of the Colossus is the second project of Team Ico, a group of staff members within Sony Computer Entertainment 's (SCEI) International Production Studio 1 that was led by director Fumito Ueda and producer Kenji Kaido.
Origin

The game originated from one of Ueda's concepts that he developed directly after the team submitted their debut title Ico, released in late 2001 for Sony 's PlayStation 2 video game console, for publication.
Origin
Ueda cited The Legend of Zelda series as an influence, as he grew up wanting to make a game like Zelda and designed the Colossi bosses like "inverted Zelda dungeons."
Origin
Originally, the team considered Ueda's idea alongside another concurrently-developed game.
Origin
The untitled game did not employ 3D graphics, whereas Team Ico applied them to their published game.
Origin
The team eventually scrapped their plans for a counterpart title to Ueda's intended game, which was advanced into further development.
Origin
Prior to the start of the project, Team Ico assessed the opportunity to establish it as a sequel to their first game.
Origin
Following lengthy deliberations, they decided not to pursue a sequel to Ico and to produce a standalone game provisionally dubbed NICO (a portmanteau of ni, 2 in Japanese, and "Ico").
Origin
Development commenced immediately after the December 2001 release of Ico ' s Japanese version.
Early prototypes
To develop the concept video for NICO, Team Ico formed a small internal group, which was composed of Ueda, one of Ico ' s designers and a roughly 10-person animation team.
Early prototypes
The first storyboard that outlined the video was drafted in January 2002, and the actual short film was completed that May.
Early prototypes
The video was visualized in the Ico game engine and was rendered in real-time on the PlayStation 2 hardware.
Early prototypes
The video was later exhibited at many trade shows, such as the 2006 D.I.C.E.
Early prototypes
In June 2002, a small group of staff at Team Ico started to build a prototype of NICO for testing purposes.
Early prototypes
In May 2003, Team Ico assembled a demonstrational build of NICO and presented it at a production meeting.
Early prototypes
That year, the NICO technology demo was shown across Sony's foreign offices among a lineup of prospective PlayStation 2 titles, and its exposure excited the spectators.
Early prototypes
After evaluating the limited number of personnel that was involved with NICO as well as their professional profiles, Team Ico concluded that they were not qualified to deliver an online-only game.
Production
After a lengthy preparatory phase, the game's production began in September 2003.
Production

From a pool of five hundred applicants, ten were subsequently enlisted to work on the game; however, Ueda felt that only one or two satisfied his criteria, as he expected every facet of the title to be as well-crafted as possible.
Production
Character designer Shinpei Suzuki recalled that they started to develop the game in an experimental fashion and made progress through trial and error.
Production
To plan out the design of the game's visual elements, Ueda used 3D computer graphics software instead of sketching them on paper.
Production
As Team Ico operationalized the game's physics-oriented features, they continued to refine them with reference to the Ico -inspired character designs from the NICO concept video.
Production
Some of the game's characters are procedurally animated; this technique is sparsely used due to the limited computational capacity of the PlayStation 2.
Production

Kaido admitted that Team Ico's ambitions for the game were partly unimplementable with the PlayStation 2 hardware, and that the team " sight of the cardinal rules of game design" several times during production.
Production
Ueda initially intended to incorporate 48 colossi in NICO, but their amount was afterward reduced to 24 when he concluded that his former vision was unrealizable.
Production
Eventually, Ueda settled on the released game's 16 beings due to a concern that the game would not achieve the desired quality level if the previous number of the colossi was maintained.
Production

In late 2004, following two years of development during which NICO was listed on Sony's internal schedules for forthcoming products under that respective name, Team Ico changed the game ' s designation to its final Japanese title.
Production
SCEI's European branch was determined to publish the game under the name Ico 2 in its associated regions.
Production
Shadow of the Colossus was unveiled in early September 2004–along with Genji: Dawn of the Samurai –via an announcement on the official Japanese PlayStation website.
Production
On September 10, SCEI held an official press conference where Shadow of the Colossus was presented by Ueda and Kaido to Japanese trade journalists.
Production
Later that month, a trailer of Shadow of the Colossus was revealed at the 2004 Tokyo Game Show, where Sony alluded to the game's tentative release date in the next year.
Production
At an internal meeting in February 2005, Team Ico decided to monitor player feedback to the unveiling of Shadow of the Colossus in an effort to correct the game's deficiencies.
Production
By July 2005, Team Ico entered the last phase of Shadow of the Colossus ' development.
Production
Ueda noted that the finished version of the "organic collision deformation" technology differed drastically from the iteration that the team originally developed.
Production

SCEI demonstrated Shadow of the Colossus at the 2005 Tokyo Game Show to a positive reception, and Jō Kirian of ITmedia reported that a long line of attendees queued up near the game's exposition stand at the venue.
Production
According to Ueda, Shadow of the Colossus ultimately involved a 40-person team.
Production
After three and a half years of development, Team Ico completed the Japanese and North American versions of Shadow of the Colossus in September 2005.
Design
Ueda felt that Ico ' s analogous structure to an adventure game resulted in its limited interactivity, and he wanted Shadow of the Colossus to be more player-driven by comparison.
Design

Another concern for Ueda was to materialize a unique connection between the colossi, as NPCs, and the game's audience, by ensuring that victory over an enemy evoked a conflicted sensation in the player.
Design
To have a scene like that... seemed like a mistake to them".
Design

Kaido was especially satisfied with Agro's implementation, and Ueda was inspired by the interplay between the horse and the protagonist to focus his following game, The Last Guardian, on a similar relationship.
Music

Inspired by the opening theme from Silent Hill, Ueda also intended the soundtrack to reflect a melancholic ambiance as well as the history of the game's setting, based on the narrative's elements of death and resurrection.
Music
The soundtrack was composed by Kow Otani, who had been previously responsible for the music to the 1990s-era Gamera films and a number of anime titles.
Music
Within the video game medium, his past work consisted of the soundtracks to the PlayStation 2 flight simulator Sky Odyssey and the PlayStation scrolling shooter Philosoma.
Music
Team Ico wanted to bring "a unique sound and feel" to each of the player's confrontations with the colossi.
Music
When the finalized material was delivered, the staff invited Otani to see the prototype as a means to communicate the game's direction to the composer.
Music

On December 7, 2005, an album containing music from the game was released only in Japan, titled Wanda and the Colossus Original Soundtrack: Roar of the Earth (ワンダと巨像 オリジナル サウンドトラック大地の咆哮, Wanda to Kyozō Original Soundtrack: Daichi no Hōkō).
Music
Although parts of that composition perplexed Ueda at first, he became convinced that it "was a really cool way to use the game's music" after familiarizing himself with the result.
Release

Following a July 15, 2005 news release where SCEI confirmed the publication date for the Japanese version of Shadow of the Colossus, the company divulged details about the limited first run edition of the game, which players could only acquire by pre-ordering, on August 19 of that year.
Release
On September 12, 2005, SCEI revealed that it had secured an arrangement to distribute the game through 7-Eleven 's Japanese сhain of convenience stores.
Release

The companies launched a promotional campaign: consumers who pre-ordered the game at one of the 7-Eleven's retail outlets would receive stylized bookmarks whose designs incorporated artwork from Shadow of the Colossus.
Release

On October 7, 2005, several weeks before the game was demonstrated at the 2005 Akihabara Entertainment Festival in Tokyo, Dengeki PlayStation ' s online news service reported that custom copies of the game bundled with thematic memorabilia would be available for purchase at the event.
Release
Shadow of the Colossus was released in Japan on October 27, 2005 at a list price of 7,140 yen.
Release

The limited edition of Shadow of the Colossus distributed through pre-ordering contained a different packaging from the standard edition, promotional videos that had been screened at the game's initial September 2004 unveiling, E3 2005 and the 2005 Tokyo Game Show, and production footage of NICO.
Release
Prior to its domestic launch, Shadow of the Colossus had been released in North America on October 18, 2005, accompanied by a nationwide advertising campaign that ran across multiple mediums.
Reception
Shadow of the Colossus received universal acclaim, with an average critic score of 91% at GameRankings, making it the 11th-highest rated game of 2005.
Reception

The game received strong reviews from publications such as the Japanese magazine Famitsu, who rated the game 37/40, the UK-based Edge, who awarded an 8/10, and Electronic Gaming Monthly, who granted 8.8/10.
Reception

GameSpot ' s review gave it an 8.7, commenting that "the game's aesthetic presentation is unparalleled, by any standard", while multimedia website IGN hailed the game as "an amazing experience" and "an absolute must-have title", rating it 9.7/10.
Reception
GameSpy described it as "possibly the most innovative and visually arresting game of the year for the PS2".
Reception

Concern was also expressed about the game's camera, which was described by GameSpy as being "as much of an opponent as the Colossi", "manag to re-center itself at the worst and most inopportune times".
Reception

Other critics like Game Revolution and GameSpot felt the game was too short (average playthrough time estimated 6 to 8 hours), with little replay value given the puzzle elements to each colossus battle.
Sales
Shadow of the Colossus sold 140,000 copies in its first week at retail in Japan, reaching number one in the charts.
Sales
Almost 80% of the initial Japanese shipment was sold within two days.
Sales
The game was placed on Sony's list of Greatest Hits titles on August 6, 2006.
Awards

It was nominated for "Best Original Music", "Best Artistic Graphics" and "Best PS2 Game", yet also "Most Aggravating Frame Rate" in GameSpot ' s awards for 2005, while it won "Best Adventure Game" and "Best Artistic Design" in IGN's Best of 2005 awards, who cited Agro as the best sidekick in the history of video games.
Awards
Two years after its release IGN listed Shadow as the fourth greatest PlayStation 2 game of all time.
Awards
GamesRadar awarded it Best Game of the Year 2006 (being released in the UK in early 2006, later than the US), and appears in the site's "The 100 best games ever" list at number ten.
Awards

The readers of PlayStation Official Magazine voted it the 8th greatest PlayStation title ever released in the magazine's 50th issue, and it placed 43rd in a later poll presented in the journal's 100th issue.
Awards
Destructoid named the game #1 in their list of the top 50 video games of the decade.
Awards
IGN named Shadow of the Colossus the best game of 2005, and the second best game of the decade, behind Half-Life 2.
Awards
In 2012, Complex magazine named Shadow of the Colossus the second-best PlayStation 2 game of all time, behind God of War II.
Awards
In 2015, the game placed 4th on USgamer ' s The 15 Best Games Since 2000 list.
Awards
In 2022, the game placed third on IGN ' s "Best PS2 Games Of All Time" list.
Legacy

Shadow of the Colossus has been cited as an influence on various video games, including God of War II (2007), God of War III (2010), Titan Souls (2015), The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild (2017), Death's Gambit (2018), Praey for the Gods (2019), and Elden Ring (2022).
Remastered version
A PlayStation 3 remastered version of Ico and Shadow of the Colossus was announced at Tokyo Game Show 2010 and released in September 2011 under the title The Ico & Shadow of the Colossus Collection.
Remake
Sony announced a remake of Shadow of the Colossus for the PlayStation 4 during their Electronic Entertainment Expo 2017 press conference.
Film adaptation
On May 23, 2012, it was reported that Chronicle director Josh Trank would be directing the film adaptation.

pst2_kingdom_harts.title: Kingdom Hearts (video game)
sents: lead
Kingdom Hearts is a 2002 action role-playing video game developed by Square for the PlayStation 2 video game console.
lead
It is the first game in the Kingdom Hearts series and is the result of a collaboration between Square and The Walt Disney Company.
lead
An expanded re-release of the game featuring new and additional content, Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, was released exclusively in Japan in December 2002.
lead
The Final Mix version of the game was later remastered in high definition and released globally as part of the Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 Remix collection for the PlayStation 3.
lead

The game was later ported and released as part of the bundled Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 + 2.5 Remix collection for PlayStation 4 in March 2017, Xbox One in February 2020, Windows in March 2021, and Nintendo Switch in February 2022.
lead
The game combines characters and settings from Disney animated features with those from Square's Final Fantasy series, in addition to original characters and worlds created for the game.
lead
It follows the adventures of Sora, a cheerful teenager who fights against the forces of darkness alongside his allies, including Donald Duck, Goofy and other Disney characters.
lead
The game was a departure from Square's standard role-playing games, introducing a substantial action and hack and slash element to the gameplay.
Gameplay
Donald and Goofy comprise the party in most areas, but many levels feature a character who may replace them.
Gameplay

In some worlds, the party changes its appearance, has abilities unique to that world, or both; the characters can fly in Neverland, gain aquatic forms in Atlantica which enable them to survive underwater, and wear Halloween costumes in Halloween Town to blend in with the locals.
Gameplay
Most of the gameplay occurs on interconnected field maps where battles take place.
Gameplay
As players progress through the game, they can receive certain Disney characters as summons, such as Dumbo and Tinker Bell, each with their own unique abilities.
Gummi Ship
Once the player's Gummi Ship is destroyed, it will have the option to either return to the world selection menu or retry the level.
Setting
Additional worlds are mentioned by various characters, but are inaccessible due to being destroyed by the Heartless.
Setting
Each world is disconnected from the others and exists separately, and with few exceptions, most characters in the world are unaware of other ones.
Characters
The primary protagonist of the game is Sora, a 14-year-old boy chosen to wield the Keyblade—a weapon which is a cross between a key and a sword—to battle darkness.
Characters
For most of the game, Sora is joined by Donald Duck and Goofy, who are a court wizard and captain of the royal guard respectively, and were sent from Disney Castle to find the Keyblade.
Characters
Maleficent, from the 1959 film Sleeping Beauty, leads a group of Disney villains that seeks to use the Heartless for their own gain.
Characters
Most worlds also feature a Disney villain whom the player must defeat.
Characters
On the Destiny Islands, the player meets younger versions of Tidus and Wakka from Final Fantasy X (2001), and Selphie from Final Fantasy VIII (1998).
Characters
In Traverse Town, the player encounters Squall Leonhart (also known as "Leon") from Final Fantasy VIII, as well as Aerith, Cid, and Yuffie from Final Fantasy VII (1997).
Characters
Rikku from Final Fantasy X was originally set to appear, but was replaced by Yuffie.
Story

Sora and his friends eventually arrive at Hollow Bastion, Maleficent's headquarters, where Riku takes the Keyblade from Sora and reveals himself to be its intended wielder, with Sora only receiving it in his absence; Donald and Goofy reluctantly leave Sora as per their orders.
Story
Ansem reveals Kairi as the seventh Princess of Heart, her heart having transferred into Sora's body when the Destiny Islands were destroyed.
Story
Sora and his group venture to the End of the World, the remnants of the worlds destroyed by the Heartless, to confront Ansem as he reaches the door to Kingdom Hearts.
Development
The initial idea for Kingdom Hearts began with a discussion between Shinji Hashimoto and Hironobu Sakaguchi about Super Mario 64.
Development
They were planning to make a game with freedom of movement in three dimensions like Super Mario 64 but lamented that only characters as popular as Disney's could rival a Mario game.
Development
The game began development in February 2000 and originally focused more on the gameplay with a simple story to appeal to Disney's target age range.
Development
In a June 2013 interview, Nomura stated the name of the game was inspired by Disney Theme Parks, particularly Animal Kingdom, which had recently opened when development on the game began.
Development
Final Mix included further additional content such as new items, cutscenes, and enemies, such as a new secret boss that sets up the sequel.
Music
While there are arranged melodies derived from previous Disney films, most of the soundtrack consists of original themes written specifically for the game by Shimomura.
Music
Utada was the only singer Nomura had in mind for the Kingdom Hearts theme song.
Music
The single, "Hikari," was released in Japan on March 20, 2002 and proved to be very popular; by August 2002, it had sold over 860,000 copies in Japan.
Music
The Kingdom Hearts soundtrack was released on a two CD set on March 27, 2002, in Japan and a year later in the United States.
Music
The soundtrack was later included in the Kingdom Hearts Original Soundtrack Complete, which was released in Japan on March 28, 2007.
Promotion
Kingdom Hearts was announced at the Electronic Entertainment Expo in May 2001.
Promotion
A playable demo was available at the Tokyo Game Show in 2001.
Promotion
To help market the English release of the game, Square launched the official website in April 2002, which featured trailers, a "Name-In-Game" sweepstakes, and other Internet content.
Promotion
On May 14, 2002, a press release announced a list of the English voice actors.
Re-releases
The first was the original Japanese release, followed by the North American and PAL releases, which includes additional content.
Final Mix
Originally released only in Japan on December 26, 2002, Kingdom Hearts Final Mix has several events and a number of gameplay tweaks that are not in previous releases.
Final Mix

The optional bosses first included in the English version were introduced to Japanese players for the first time, along with a new fight against " Unknown Man," in an attempt to raise interest for the sequel.
Final Mix
When first released, Final Mix included either a deck of Kingdom Hearts cards or special music CD.
Final Mix
A limited "Platinum Edition" version of Kingdom Hearts Final Mix was later released with an action figure of Sora, a sticker set, and sketches of some of the main characters.
Final Mix
It was released for the first time in North America, Europe and Australia as part of Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 Remix.
HD 1.5 Remix
During August 2011, Nomura expressed desire to release a high definition rerelease of the game though he had yet to confirm such plans.
HD 1.5 Remix

In September 2012, Square Enix announced Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 Remix, a compilation for the PlayStation 3, that includes both Kingdom Hearts Final Mix and Kingdom Hearts Re:Chain of Memories in HD and trophy support.
HD 1.5 Remix
The character models from Kingdom Hearts 3D: Dream Drop Distance were used as a base for the game's characters.
HD 1.5 Remix
Additionally, the collection includes HD cinematic scenes from Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days.
HD 1.5 Remix
It was released in Japan on March 14, 2013, in North America on September 10, 2013, on September 12, 2013, for Australia, and September 13, 2013, for Europe.
HD 1.5 Remix
In June 2013, Nomura stated that the original game assets for Kingdom Hearts had been lost some time ago.
HD 1.5 Remix
In October 2016, Square Enix announced a single-disc compilation release of Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 Remix and Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 Remix for the PlayStation 4.
HD 1.5 Remix
It was released on March 9, 2017, in Japan, and was released on March 28, 2017, in North America, and March 31, 2017, in Europe.
HD 1.5 Remix
A piece of free downloadable content for the PS4 version released in June 2017 added a Theater mode for Kingdom Hearts Final Mix; this was included by default in later ports of the compilation.
HD 1.5 Remix

On November 14, 2019, Square Enix announced that both Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 Remix and Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 Remix were coming to Xbox One, marking the Xbox debut of the first two Kingdom Hearts games and spinoffs.
HD 1.5 Remix
The two games are combined into a collection titled Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 + 2.5 Remix, and released on February 18, 2020.
Related media
The novel series consists of two volumes and was released in North America on March 25, 2008.
Related media
The manga was originally serialized in Japan by Enterbrain 's Famitsū PS2, but has since been released worldwide in four volumes.
Related media
The first volume was released on October 11, 2005, and the fourth volume was released on July 10, 2006.
Related media
The entire series was later released in a boxed set on October 10, 2006.
Related media
The first volume was ranked 95th in USA Today ' s "Top 150 best sellers" during the week of its release.
Reception
During the first two months of its North American release it was one of the top three highest-selling video games and was among the top selling titles during the 2002 Christmas and holiday season.
Reception
In November 2002, UBS Warburg listed it as the 6th highest console game in terms of sales during the week of November 5.
Reception

At the end of April 2003, Square announced that Kingdom Hearts had sold its millionth copy in the United States, which made it eligible for PlayStation's "Greatest Hits" status, and over 3.0 million worldwide.
Reception
Sales reached 1.2 million in Japan in the first quarter of 2004, and broke 4.0 million worldwide.
Reception

In December 2005, the NPD Group listed it as "one of the top ten best-selling PlayStation 2 titles of all time in North America." By July 2006, Kingdom Hearts had sold through 2.6 million copies and earned $100 million in the United States alone.
Reception
Next Generation ranked it as the seventh highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Reception
As of December 2006, Kingdom Hearts had shipped over 5.6 million copies worldwide with 1.1 million in PAL regions, 1.5 million in Japan, and 3.0 million in North America.
Reception
As of 2006, the original game and the Final Mix version had sold 6 million copies on PS2.
Reception
As of March 2022, the Kingdom Hearts series has shipped more than 36 million copies worldwide.
Critical response

In IGN 's Best of 2002 awards, it was nominated for "PS2's Best Game of 2002 Editor's Choice Award" and was a runner up for "PS2's Best Game of 2002 Reader's Choice Award." In 2007, the website listed Kingdom Hearts as the 22nd best PlayStation 2 game of all time.
Critical response
GamePro had positive comments on the overall audio and gave that aspect a perfect score.
Critical response
GamePro compared the battle system to "old N64 Zelda games " and had positive comments about Donald and Goofy's artificial intelligence.
Critical response
G4TV awarded it "Best Story" at their 2003 G-Phoria awards show.
Critical response
Fan response was also positive; Kingdom Hearts was voted as the 19th best game of all-time by readers of the Japanese magazine Famitsu, 16th by the users of website GameFAQs, and 92nd by IGN users.
Critical response
Kingdom Hearts ranked ninth on IGN's most recent "Top 25 PS2 Games of All Time" list.
Critical response
It ranked first on GamesRadar 's "Top 7 Disney Games" list in 2009.
Critical response
It was also a nominee for the Best Game Award from the CESA Game Awards for 2001–2002.
Critical response
In the making of the 2004 video game Fullmetal Alchemist and the Broken Angel the developers, Racjin, looked at other titles for inspiration, particularly Kingdom Hearts when making the game.
Sequels
Kingdom Hearts was followed by several sequels, becoming the first game in the Kingdom Hearts series.
Sequels
It was followed by a direct sequel, Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories, on the Nintendo Game Boy Advance, which was released in Japan on November 11, 2004.
Sequels
Kingdom Hearts II is the third game in the series, set one year after Chain of Memories, and was released in Japan on December 22, 2005, for Sony PlayStation 2.
Sequels
Like the first game it was re-released as Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix alongside a PS2 remake of Chain of Memories.
Sequels
A Kingdom Hearts game was developed exclusively for V CAST, Verizon Wireless 's broadband service, and was released on October 1, 2004, in Japan and on February 4, 2005, in the United States.
Sequels
In November 2008, Kingdom Hearts coded was released for mobile phones in Japan, the game takes place after the events of Kingdom Hearts II.
Sequels
A follow-up, Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days, was developed for the Nintendo DS and released in Japan on May 30, 2009, and in North America on September 29, 2009.
Sequels
A prequel was released in Japan on January 9, 2010, entitled Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep, for the PlayStation Portable, which takes place 10 years before the events of Kingdom Hearts.
Sequels
The following title in the series was Kingdom Hearts 3D: Dream Drop Distance for the Nintendo 3DS, released in 2012.
Sequels

At E3 2013, Kingdom Hearts III was announced to be in development for the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One, before being released in January 2019, followed by a downloadable content expansion titled Kingdom Hearts III Re Mind in early 2020.
Sequels
The following title, Kingdom Hearts: Melody of Memory, set after the Re Mind scenario, was then released in Japan on November 11, 2020, and worldwide two days later.
Sequels

During Square Enix's 20th anniversary event for the franchise in April 2022, a mobile title, Kingdom Hearts Missing-Link, was announced for iOS and Android devices, with a closed beta arriving in August, while the next mainline installment, Kingdom Hearts IV, was also revealed to be in development.

pst2_kingdom_harts_ii.title: Kingdom Hearts II
sents: lead
Kingdom Hearts II is a 2005 action role-playing game developed and published by Square Enix in collaboration with Buena Vista Games for the PlayStation 2 video game console.
lead
The game is a sequel to Kingdom Hearts, and like the original game, combines characters and settings from Disney films with those of Square Enix's Final Fantasy series.
lead
An expanded re-release of the game featuring new and additional content, Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix, was released exclusively in Japan in March 2007.
lead

The Final Mix version of the game was later remastered in high definition and released globally as part of the Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 Remix collection for the PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Windows, and Nintendo Switch.
lead
Kingdom Hearts II is the third game in the Kingdom Hearts series, and takes place one year after the events of Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories.
lead
Sora, the protagonist of the first two games, returns to search for his lost friends while battling the sinister Organization XIII, a group of antagonists previously introduced in Chain of Memories.
lead
Like previous games, Kingdom Hearts II features a large cast of characters from Disney and Square Enix properties.
lead
Concepts for Kingdom Hearts II began during the end of development of Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, with the game entering full development in 2003 and being announced at Tokyo Game Show 2003.
Gameplay

The gameplay of Kingdom Hearts II is similar to the action RPG and hack and slash gameplay of the first Kingdom Hearts game, though developers made an effort to address some of the complaints of no map and camera bugs with the previous game.
Gameplay
The player directly controls Sora from a third-person camera angle, though first-person perspective is available via Select button.
Gameplay
Most of the gameplay occurs on interconnected field maps where battles take place.
Gameplay
In response to criticism, the "Gummi Ship" feature of the first game was re-imagined to be "more enjoyable".
Drive Gauge

Drive Forms also give Sora new abilities that can be used in normal form, called "Growth Abilities." Sora's first two Drive Forms only combine power with one party member; later-obtained Drive Forms require him to bond with both party members.
Drive Gauge
Like in the first game, Sora can summon a Disney character to aid him in battle.
Drive Gauge

Instead of being limited to only one action, Summons now have a menu of their own and are capable of performing solo or cooperative actions with Sora, which are performed by pressing the triangle button.
Setting
As in the first game, the player can travel to various Disney-based locales, along with original worlds specifically created for the series.
Setting

While Disney-based worlds were primarily derived from the Disney animated features canon in the first game, Kingdom Hearts II introduces worlds that are based on live-action franchises with one based on Pirates of the Caribbean.
Setting
Twilight Town, an original world first seen in Chain of Memories, has a greater role as the introductory world.
Setting
The World That Never Was is a new world that serves as the headquarters of Organization XIII.
Characters
Villains unique to the worlds are prevalent, and are often presented as challenges that Sora's group must overcome.
Story
Sora revisits the worlds to solve lingering problems while seeking a path to Organization XIII's base of operations in the World That Never Was.
Story
Following a lead, Sora, Donald, and Goofy enter a passageway to the World That Never Was through Twilight Town, where Axel sacrifices himself to allow them to proceed.
Story
Atop the Castle That Never Was, Sora and company battle Xemnas, who uses what remains of Kingdom Hearts to fight them.
Story
In a post-credits scene, Sora, Kairi, and Riku receive and read a letter from Mickey, the contents of which are hidden from the player.
Development
Development plans for Kingdom Hearts II began around the completion of Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, but specific details were undecided until July 2003.
Development
The game was developed by Square Enix's Product Development Division-1, with most of the original staff from the first game.
Development
The game was originally supposed to have been released after Kingdom Hearts.
Development
Nomura had planned for the sequel to take place a year after the first and originally intended for the events of that year to be left unexplained.
Development
To explain the loss of all the abilities from the first game at the beginning of Kingdom Hearts II, Nomura had Sora's memories scrambled in Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories.
Development
The combat system was completely redone and did not use any animations from the first game.
Musical score
Like the first game, Kingdom Hearts II features music by Yoko Shimomura and Hikaru Utada.
Musical score
The Original Soundtrack for Kingdom Hearts II was composed by Shimomura and released on January 25, 2006.
Musical score
Utada's involvement was announced on July 29, 2005.
Musical score
The CD single for "Passion" was released on December 14, 2005 and "Sanctuary" was first previewed on MTV 's official website in early 2006.
Voice cast

Many of the original voice actors from the first Kingdom Hearts reprised their roles; Miyu Irino and Haley Joel Osment as Sora, Mamoru Miyano and David Gallagher as Riku, and Risa Uchida and Hayden Panettiere as Kairi.
Content editing
Port Royal, based on Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl, contains the most content edits.
Promotion

Rumors for a sequel on the PlayStation 2 were spurred in Japan when the video game website Quiter stated that "an internal (and anonymous source) at Square Japan" confirmed that development of Kingdom Hearts II had begun.
Promotion
Initial details were that it would take place some time after Chain of Memories, which takes place directly after the first game.
Promotion
At the 2004 Square Enix E3 Press conference, producer Shinji Hashimoto said that many mysteries of the first game would be answered.
Promotion
Square Enix launched the official Japanese website in May 2005, followed by the English website in December 2005.
Promotion
Although the game was announced in September 2003, a release date for the game was not set until two years later.
Release
Within a week of its Japanese release, Kingdom Hearts II shipped one million copies, selling almost 730,000 copies.
Release
The NPD Group reported that Kingdom Hearts II was the highest-selling console game in North America during March 2006 with 614,000 copies.
Release
In the month after its release in North America, Kingdom Hearts II sold an estimated one million copies.
Release
GameStop listed the game as their best-selling title for the first quarter of 2006.
Release
The game was also on IGN 's "Top 10 Sellers in 2006".
Release
By December 2006, over 3.5 million copies of Kingdom Hearts II had been shipped worldwide with 700,000 in PAL regions, 1.1 million in Japan, and 1.7 million in North America.
Release
By March 31, 2007, Square Enix had shipped over 4 million units worldwide.
Reception

Patrick Gann of RPGFan deemed the partner artificial intelligence to be superior to the first game, whereas Haynes denounced it as "absolutely terrible", attributing this to the omitted ability to issue AI commands.
Reception
The quick time events were a generally welcomed addition, with Luke Albiges of Eurogamer regarding their quality and impact to be on par with the knife fight scene in Resident Evil 4.
Reception

Bedigian declared the game to be the first instance of quick time events being successfully implemented, and admired the resulting actions as "some of the most beautiful polygon sequences seen on PlayStation 2".
Reception
Eric Bratcher of GamesRadar+ was also excited by most of the boss battles, though considered a few of them "straight-up lame".
Reception
James Mielke (writing for EGM) and Gann dismissed the first-person mode as unhelpful, with Mielke warning that the inability to see Sora's Keyblade was disorienting.
Reception

The RPG elements were described as light, with Haynes calling them a "casualty" of the increased emphasis on combat; he remarked that items were "practically useless" due to a lack of need to use them in certain places as in the first game.
Reception

While the assortment of minigames in the Hundred Acre Wood was said to be improved from the first game, the transition of Atlantica from an action set-piece to a series of rhythm minigames was derided.
Reception
Bratcher and Gann were relieved by the absence of the scavenger hunt-type quests from the first game.
Reception
The Gummi Ship segments were widely agreed to be an improvement over those of the first game.
Reception
The visuals were lauded, with Mielke and Albiges considering them among the PlayStation 2's best, and Villoria putting them on par with Square's best productions.
Reception
He added that despite the limited nostalgic value of the Disney tunes, they "never get tiring, slightly repetitive, or seem out of place".
Reception
Larsen only criticized some repetitiveness, but noted that the fast-paced action made this hardly noticeable.
Reception

However, Villoria and Gann were less than impressed; Villoria felt that the soundtrack did not meet the high standard set by the first game, while Gann complained of the synth quality and recycled tracks from the first game.
Reception
Haynes, however, assured that the Journal feature provided sufficient context, and added that it had been improved from the first game.
Reception
Gann considered the plot to be more cohesive than that of the first, as the Disney worlds held more relevance to the story.
Reception
Andrew Reiner of Game Informer promised that the story would "give you shivers and make your heart leap" despite not being as powerful as the first game.
Reception
Mielke complimented Nomura's "eye for epic drama" previously observed in Final Fantasy VII: Advent Children, which he said "touches you where games like, say, God of War never will".
Reception

Reiner and Fischer were disappointed by the amount of recycled Disney content from the first game; Reiner, describing most of the Disney-based conflicts as "tacked on" diversions, speculated that Disney "handcuffed Square Enix on being able to create new content".
Awards and accolades
The game received numerous awards, including a Satellite Award in 2006 for "Outstanding Game Based on Existing Medium".
Awards and accolades
Famitsu ' s readers ranked the game 29th on their "All Time Top 100" feature, ten places below Kingdom Hearts.
Awards and accolades
Eurogamer ranked it 34th on their "Top 50 Games of 2006" list.
Awards and accolades
Video game magazine Electronic Gaming Monthly awarded it "Best Sequel" of 2006, and Game Informer listed it among the "Top 50 games of 2006".
Awards and accolades
VideoGamer.com featured it 10th in their article "Top 10: Role playing games".
Awards and accolades
Kingdom Hearts II also received a near-perfect score, 39/40, from the Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu.
Awards and accolades
G4 awarded Kingdom Hearts II "Best Voice Over" and "Best Soundtrack" in their 2006 G-Phoria awards show.
Awards and accolades
The game was ranked the 16th greatest console video game of all time in a 2021 Japanese poll conducted by TV Asahi which surveyed over 50,000 respondents.
Versions and merchandise
The first three are the normal regional releases in Japan, North America, and PAL regions, which only differ nominally in content editing and localization.
Versions and merchandise
The European and Australian PAL releases were reformatted to run at 50 Hz to fit the definition size of PAL encoding systems.
Versions and merchandise
It provides extended information on the first two Kingdom Hearts games, as well as information on the unreleased Kingdom Hearts II.
Versions and merchandise
In North America, BradyGames published two strategy guides—a standard guide and a limited edition version.
Versions and merchandise
The latter version was available in four different covers and included a copy of Jiminy's Journal along with 400 stickers.
Final Mix
Because the first game was re-released, there was speculation whether Tetsuya Nomura would do the same with Kingdom Hearts II.
Final Mix
In September 2006, Square Enix announced Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix, featuring new scenes and gameplay elements.
Final Mix
Like the first re-release, this version would combine English audio with Japanese text and also use the "Sanctuary" theme song instead of "Passion".
Final Mix
Kingdom Hearts II was re-released in Japan on March 29, 2007 as a 2-disc set titled Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix+.
Final Mix
The first disc contains Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix with a new secret movie and additional battles and items.
Final Mix
The second disc contains Kingdom Hearts Re:Chain of Memories, a 3D PlayStation 2 remake of Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories with extra scenes and voice acting.
Final Mix
