pst2_kingdom_harts_ii_final_mix.title: Kingdom Hearts II
sents: lead
Kingdom Hearts II is a 2005 action role-playing game developed and published by Square Enix in collaboration with Buena Vista Games for the PlayStation 2 video game console.
lead
The game is a sequel to Kingdom Hearts, and like the original game, combines characters and settings from Disney films with those of Square Enix's Final Fantasy series.
lead
An expanded re-release of the game featuring new and additional content, Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix, was released exclusively in Japan in March 2007.
lead

The Final Mix version of the game was later remastered in high definition and released globally as part of the Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 Remix collection for the PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Windows, and Nintendo Switch.
lead
Kingdom Hearts II is the third game in the Kingdom Hearts series, and takes place one year after the events of Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories.
lead
Sora, the protagonist of the first two games, returns to search for his lost friends while battling the sinister Organization XIII, a group of antagonists previously introduced in Chain of Memories.
lead
Like previous games, Kingdom Hearts II features a large cast of characters from Disney and Square Enix properties.
lead
Concepts for Kingdom Hearts II began during the end of development of Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, with the game entering full development in 2003 and being announced at Tokyo Game Show 2003.
Gameplay

The gameplay of Kingdom Hearts II is similar to the action RPG and hack and slash gameplay of the first Kingdom Hearts game, though developers made an effort to address some of the complaints of no map and camera bugs with the previous game.
Gameplay
The player directly controls Sora from a third-person camera angle, though first-person perspective is available via Select button.
Gameplay
Most of the gameplay occurs on interconnected field maps where battles take place.
Gameplay
In response to criticism, the "Gummi Ship" feature of the first game was re-imagined to be "more enjoyable".
Drive Gauge

Drive Forms also give Sora new abilities that can be used in normal form, called "Growth Abilities." Sora's first two Drive Forms only combine power with one party member; later-obtained Drive Forms require him to bond with both party members.
Drive Gauge
Like in the first game, Sora can summon a Disney character to aid him in battle.
Drive Gauge

Instead of being limited to only one action, Summons now have a menu of their own and are capable of performing solo or cooperative actions with Sora, which are performed by pressing the triangle button.
Setting
As in the first game, the player can travel to various Disney-based locales, along with original worlds specifically created for the series.
Setting

While Disney-based worlds were primarily derived from the Disney animated features canon in the first game, Kingdom Hearts II introduces worlds that are based on live-action franchises with one based on Pirates of the Caribbean.
Setting
Twilight Town, an original world first seen in Chain of Memories, has a greater role as the introductory world.
Setting
The World That Never Was is a new world that serves as the headquarters of Organization XIII.
Characters
Villains unique to the worlds are prevalent, and are often presented as challenges that Sora's group must overcome.
Story
Sora revisits the worlds to solve lingering problems while seeking a path to Organization XIII's base of operations in the World That Never Was.
Story
Following a lead, Sora, Donald, and Goofy enter a passageway to the World That Never Was through Twilight Town, where Axel sacrifices himself to allow them to proceed.
Story
Atop the Castle That Never Was, Sora and company battle Xemnas, who uses what remains of Kingdom Hearts to fight them.
Story
In a post-credits scene, Sora, Kairi, and Riku receive and read a letter from Mickey, the contents of which are hidden from the player.
Development
Development plans for Kingdom Hearts II began around the completion of Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, but specific details were undecided until July 2003.
Development
The game was developed by Square Enix's Product Development Division-1, with most of the original staff from the first game.
Development
The game was originally supposed to have been released after Kingdom Hearts.
Development
Nomura had planned for the sequel to take place a year after the first and originally intended for the events of that year to be left unexplained.
Development
To explain the loss of all the abilities from the first game at the beginning of Kingdom Hearts II, Nomura had Sora's memories scrambled in Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories.
Development
The combat system was completely redone and did not use any animations from the first game.
Musical score
Like the first game, Kingdom Hearts II features music by Yoko Shimomura and Hikaru Utada.
Musical score
The Original Soundtrack for Kingdom Hearts II was composed by Shimomura and released on January 25, 2006.
Musical score
Utada's involvement was announced on July 29, 2005.
Musical score
The CD single for "Passion" was released on December 14, 2005 and "Sanctuary" was first previewed on MTV 's official website in early 2006.
Voice cast

Many of the original voice actors from the first Kingdom Hearts reprised their roles; Miyu Irino and Haley Joel Osment as Sora, Mamoru Miyano and David Gallagher as Riku, and Risa Uchida and Hayden Panettiere as Kairi.
Content editing
Port Royal, based on Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl, contains the most content edits.
Promotion

Rumors for a sequel on the PlayStation 2 were spurred in Japan when the video game website Quiter stated that "an internal (and anonymous source) at Square Japan" confirmed that development of Kingdom Hearts II had begun.
Promotion
Initial details were that it would take place some time after Chain of Memories, which takes place directly after the first game.
Promotion
At the 2004 Square Enix E3 Press conference, producer Shinji Hashimoto said that many mysteries of the first game would be answered.
Promotion
Square Enix launched the official Japanese website in May 2005, followed by the English website in December 2005.
Promotion
Although the game was announced in September 2003, a release date for the game was not set until two years later.
Release
Within a week of its Japanese release, Kingdom Hearts II shipped one million copies, selling almost 730,000 copies.
Release
The NPD Group reported that Kingdom Hearts II was the highest-selling console game in North America during March 2006 with 614,000 copies.
Release
In the month after its release in North America, Kingdom Hearts II sold an estimated one million copies.
Release
GameStop listed the game as their best-selling title for the first quarter of 2006.
Release
The game was also on IGN 's "Top 10 Sellers in 2006".
Release
By December 2006, over 3.5 million copies of Kingdom Hearts II had been shipped worldwide with 700,000 in PAL regions, 1.1 million in Japan, and 1.7 million in North America.
Release
By March 31, 2007, Square Enix had shipped over 4 million units worldwide.
Reception

Patrick Gann of RPGFan deemed the partner artificial intelligence to be superior to the first game, whereas Haynes denounced it as "absolutely terrible", attributing this to the omitted ability to issue AI commands.
Reception
The quick time events were a generally welcomed addition, with Luke Albiges of Eurogamer regarding their quality and impact to be on par with the knife fight scene in Resident Evil 4.
Reception

Bedigian declared the game to be the first instance of quick time events being successfully implemented, and admired the resulting actions as "some of the most beautiful polygon sequences seen on PlayStation 2".
Reception
Eric Bratcher of GamesRadar+ was also excited by most of the boss battles, though considered a few of them "straight-up lame".
Reception
James Mielke (writing for EGM) and Gann dismissed the first-person mode as unhelpful, with Mielke warning that the inability to see Sora's Keyblade was disorienting.
Reception

The RPG elements were described as light, with Haynes calling them a "casualty" of the increased emphasis on combat; he remarked that items were "practically useless" due to a lack of need to use them in certain places as in the first game.
Reception

While the assortment of minigames in the Hundred Acre Wood was said to be improved from the first game, the transition of Atlantica from an action set-piece to a series of rhythm minigames was derided.
Reception
Bratcher and Gann were relieved by the absence of the scavenger hunt-type quests from the first game.
Reception
The Gummi Ship segments were widely agreed to be an improvement over those of the first game.
Reception
The visuals were lauded, with Mielke and Albiges considering them among the PlayStation 2's best, and Villoria putting them on par with Square's best productions.
Reception
He added that despite the limited nostalgic value of the Disney tunes, they "never get tiring, slightly repetitive, or seem out of place".
Reception
Larsen only criticized some repetitiveness, but noted that the fast-paced action made this hardly noticeable.
Reception

However, Villoria and Gann were less than impressed; Villoria felt that the soundtrack did not meet the high standard set by the first game, while Gann complained of the synth quality and recycled tracks from the first game.
Reception
Haynes, however, assured that the Journal feature provided sufficient context, and added that it had been improved from the first game.
Reception
Gann considered the plot to be more cohesive than that of the first, as the Disney worlds held more relevance to the story.
Reception
Andrew Reiner of Game Informer promised that the story would "give you shivers and make your heart leap" despite not being as powerful as the first game.
Reception
Mielke complimented Nomura's "eye for epic drama" previously observed in Final Fantasy VII: Advent Children, which he said "touches you where games like, say, God of War never will".
Reception

Reiner and Fischer were disappointed by the amount of recycled Disney content from the first game; Reiner, describing most of the Disney-based conflicts as "tacked on" diversions, speculated that Disney "handcuffed Square Enix on being able to create new content".

The game received numerous awards, including a Satellite Award in 2006 for "Outstanding Game Based on Existing Medium".

Famitsu ' s readers ranked the game 29th on their "All Time Top 100" feature, ten places below Kingdom Hearts.

Eurogamer ranked it 34th on their "Top 50 Games of 2006" list.
Awards and accolades
Video game magazine Electronic Gaming Monthly awarded it "Best Sequel" of 2006, and Game Informer listed it among the "Top 50 games of 2006".
Awards and accolades
VideoGamer.com featured it 10th in their article "Top 10: Role playing games".
Awards and accolades
Kingdom Hearts II also received a near-perfect score, 39/40, from the Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu.
Awards and accolades
G4 awarded Kingdom Hearts II "Best Voice Over" and "Best Soundtrack" in their 2006 G-Phoria awards show.
Awards and accolades
The game was ranked the 16th greatest console video game of all time in a 2021 Japanese poll conducted by TV Asahi which surveyed over 50,000 respondents.
Versions and merchandise
The first three are the normal regional releases in Japan, North America, and PAL regions, which only differ nominally in content editing and localization.
Versions and merchandise
The European and Australian PAL releases were reformatted to run at 50 Hz to fit the definition size of PAL encoding systems.
Versions and merchandise
It provides extended information on the first two Kingdom Hearts games, as well as information on the unreleased Kingdom Hearts II.
Versions and merchandise
In North America, BradyGames published two strategy guides—a standard guide and a limited edition version.
Versions and merchandise
The latter version was available in four different covers and included a copy of Jiminy's Journal along with 400 stickers.
Final Mix
Because the first game was re-released, there was speculation whether Tetsuya Nomura would do the same with Kingdom Hearts II.
Final Mix
In September 2006, Square Enix announced Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix, featuring new scenes and gameplay elements.
Final Mix
Like the first re-release, this version would combine English audio with Japanese text and also use the "Sanctuary" theme song instead of "Passion".

pst2_final_fantasia_x.title: Final Fantasy X
sents: lead
Final Fantasy X is a 2001 role-playing video game developed and published by Square as the tenth main entry in the Final Fantasy series.
lead

Originally released in 2001 for PlayStation 2, the game was re-released as Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster for PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita in 2013, for PlayStation 4 in 2015, Windows in 2016, and for Nintendo Switch and Xbox One in 2019.
lead

The game marks the Final Fantasy series transition from entirely pre-rendered backdrops to fully three-dimensional areas (though some areas were still pre-rendered), and is also the first in the series to feature voice acting.
lead
Final Fantasy X replaces the Active Time Battle (ATB) system with the "Conditional Turn-Based Battle" (CTB) system, and uses a new leveling system called the "Sphere Grid".
lead

Set in the fantasy world of Spira, a setting influenced by the South Pacific, Thailand and Japan, the game's story revolves around a group of adventurers and their quest to defeat a rampaging monster known as Sin.
lead
The player character is Tidus, a star athlete in the fictional sport of blitzball, who finds himself in Spira after Sin attacked his home city of Zanarkand.
lead
Shortly after arriving to Spira, Tidus becomes a guardian to summoner Yuna to destroy Sin upon learning its true identity is that of his missing father, Jecht.
lead
Development of Final Fantasy X began in 1999, with a budget of more than $32.3 million ($59.1 million in 2023 dollars) and a team of more than 100 people.
Gameplay
In the game, almost all the locations are essentially continuous and never fade out to a world map.
Combat
Final Fantasy X introduces the Conditional Turn-Based Battle (CTB) system in place of the series' traditional Active Time Battle (ATB) system first used in Final Fantasy IV.
Combat
In this incarnation of the feature, most of the techniques are interactive, requiring button inputs to increase their effectiveness.
Blitzball
It is the only minigame that plays a role in the overall plot line as it is a main part of Tidus's character, and is in the first scene where the game's main antagonist, Sin is shown.
Setting and characters

Spira is very different from the mainly European-style worlds found in previous Final Fantasy games, being much more closely modeled on Southeast Asia, most notably with respect to vegetation, topography, architecture, and names.
Setting and characters
Among them are the Al Bhed, a technologically advanced but disenfranchised sub-group of humans with distinctive green eyes and unique language.
Setting and characters

Other fauna in Spira, aside from those drawn from real animals, such as cats, dogs, birds, and butterflies, include the gigantic, amphibious shoopufs (which are similar to elephants); and the emu-like chocobo, which appears in most Final Fantasy games.
Story

It begins in his home city, the high-tech metropolis of Zanarkand, where he is a renowned blitzball player and son of the famous blitzball star Jecht, an abusive father who disappeared 10 years prior.
Story
During a blitzball tournament, the city is attacked by an immense creature that Auron, a man not originally from Zanarkand, calls "Sin".
Story
Upon arriving in Spira, Tidus is rescued by Al Bhed salvagers, with the young Rikku explaining that Sin destroyed Zanarkand 1,000 years ago.
Story
Once they reach Zanarkand, Yunalesca —the first summoner to defeat Sin and unsent ever since —tells the group that the Final Aeon is created from the fayth of one close to the summoner.
Development

Final Fantasy X ' s development began in 1999, costing approximately ¥ 4 billion (approximately $ 32.3 million, or $59.1 million in 2023 dollars) with a crew of over 100 people, most of whom worked on previous games in the series.
Development

Executive producer Hironobu Sakaguchi has stated that although he had concerns about the transition from 2D to 3D backgrounds, the voice acting, and the transition to real-time story-telling, the success of the Final Fantasy series can be attributed to constantly challenging the development team to try new things.
Development
According to the Square Enix companion book Final Fantasy Ultimania Archive Volume III, 17 SEVEN TEEN was a temporary title early in Final Fantasy X ' s production.
Development

17 SEVEN TEEN ' s story differed from the final version: the protagonist, who looked similar to Tidus, traveled the world seeking a cure for a pandemic that killed people when they reached the age of seventeen.
Influences

Although Final Fantasy X was originally centered on the relationship between Tidus and Yuna, the addition of Jecht's character and his feud with his son was added later in the making of the game to provide more focus on how the father and son produce a bigger impact in Spira's history rather than the romantic couple.
Music
Final Fantasy X marks the first time regular series composer Nobuo Uematsu has had any assistance in composing the score for a game in the main series.
Music
PlayOnline.com first revealed that the game's theme song was completed in November 2000.
Music
It was first released in Japan on August 1, 2001, by DigiCube, and was re-released on May 10, 2004, by Square Enix.
Music

In 2002, Tokyopop released a version of Final Fantasy X Original Soundtrack in North America entitled Final Fantasy X Official Soundtrack, which contained 17 tracks from the original album on a single disc.
Music
Other related CDs include feel/Go dream: Yuna & Tidus which, released in Japan by DigiCube on October 11, 2001, featured tracks based on Tidus' and Yuna's characters.
Music

Piano Collections Final Fantasy X, another collection of music from the game, and Final Fantasy X Vocal Collection, a compilations of exclusive character dialogues and songs were both released in Japan in 2002.
Music
These are "Fight With Seymour" from their self-titled album, published in 2003, and "Otherworld" and "The Skies Above", both of which can be found on the album The Skies Above, published in 2004.
Music
An odd note is that the unreleased/promo CD-R (Instrumental) version of Madonna's "What It Feels Like For A Girl" done by Tracy Young was used in the blitzball sequences.
Versions and merchandise

The Japanese version of Final Fantasy X included an additional disc entitled "The Other Side of Final Fantasy", which featured interviews, storyboards, and trailers for Blue Wing Blitz, Kingdom Hearts, and Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within, as well as the first footage of Final Fantasy XI Online.
Versions and merchandise
An international version of the game was released in Japan as Final Fantasy X International in January 2002, and in PAL regions under its original title.
Versions and merchandise
Final Fantasy X was released as Greatest Hits in North America in September 2003.
Versions and merchandise
The Japanese release of Final Fantasy X International also includes "Eternal Calm", a 14-minute video clip bridging the story of Final Fantasy X with that of its sequel, Final Fantasy X-2.
Versions and merchandise
The video clip was included in a bonus DVD for Unlimited Saga Collector's Edition under the name Eternal Calm, Final Fantasy X-2: Prologue.
Versions and merchandise
It was first released in Europe on October 31, 2003, and featured English voice-overs.
Versions and merchandise
In 2005, a compilation featuring Final Fantasy X and X-2 was released in Japan as Final Fantasy X/X-2 Ultimate Box.
Versions and merchandise
The game was re-released as part of the Final Fantasy 25th Anniversary Ultimate Box release in December 2012.
HD Remaster
Final Fantasy X was re-released in high-definition for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita, in celebration of the game's 10-year anniversary.
HD Remaster
The remaster was released in December 2013 for Japan, and the following year in March for other markets.
HD Remaster
The remaster also included its sequel X-2, remastered in HD and they were released under the title Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster on a single Blu-ray disc game.
HD Remaster
The games contain all the content found in the International version, including Eternal Calm and Last Mission.
HD Remaster
Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster was released for the PlayStation 4 worldwide in May 2015.
HD Remaster
It included enhanced graphics in full HD (1080p), the option to switch to the original soundtrack and the ability to transfer save files from the PS3 and PS Vita versions.
HD Remaster
One year later, it was released for Windows via Steam on May 16.
HD Remaster
It includes an auto-save feature, 5 game boosters, 3 parameter changes, the option to skip FMVs /cinematics, 4K resolution support, audio settings and graphic options.
HD Remaster
A version for the Nintendo Switch and the Xbox One was released on April 16, 2019.
Reception
The Japanese video game magazine Famitsu and Famitsu PS2 awarded the game a near-perfect 39/40 score.
Reception
Another Japanese gaming magazine, The Play Station, gave the game a score of 29/30.
Reception
Famitsu, Famitsu PS2, and The Play Station expressed particularly favorable responses toward the game's storyline, graphics, and movies.
Reception
The game maintains a 92 out of 100 on Metacritic.
Reception
The voice casting was praised by Game Revolution who noted most of them were "above average" and called the music "rich".
Sales
Square initially expected the game to sell at least two million copies worldwide owing to the reduced PlayStation 2's fanbase, making it smaller than the last three released titles.
Sales
However, within its first day of its release in Japan, more than 2.14 million units were shipped, including 1.4 to 1.5 million pre-orders.
Sales
A million units were sold within hours, and first-day shipments were expected to generate ¥17.6 billion or $145,000,000 (equivalent to $250,000,000 in 2023) in sales revenue.
Sales
These figures exceeded the performances of Final Fantasy VII and IX in a comparable period, and Final Fantasy X became the first PlayStation 2 game to reach two and four million sold copies.
Sales
In October 2007, the game was listed as the 8th best-selling game for the PlayStation 2.
Sales
Final Fantasy X sold over 2.43 million copies in Japan alone in 2001.
Sales
By June 2002, it had sold 5.07 million units worldwide, including 2.76 million in the Asia-Pacific region, 1.47 million in North America, and 840,000 in Europe.
Sales
By March 2003, the game had sold 5.89 million units worldwide, including 2.87 million in Japan and 3.02 million abroad.
Sales
It sold 6.6 million copies worldwide by January 2004.
Sales
By July 2006, it had sold 2.3 million copies and earned $95 million in the United States ($144 million in 2023).
Sales
Next Generation ranked it as the 11th highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Sales
As of March 2013, the game had shipped over 8.5 million copies worldwide on PS2.
Sales
As of 2017, the PS2 version of the game has sold over 8 million copies worldwide.
Sales
The "Ultimate Hits" bargain reissue of the game in September 2005 sold over 131,000 copies in Japan by the end of 2006.
Sales
As of October 2013, Final Fantasy X and its sequel X-2 had together sold over 14 million copies worldwide on PlayStation 2.
Awards
Final Fantasy X received the Best Game Award from the Japan Game Awards for 2001–02.
Awards
In GameSpot 's "Best and Worst Awards" from 2001, it came seventh in the category "Top 10 Video Games of the Year", and won the "Best Story" and "Best Role-Playing Game" awards.
Awards
The game also received a PlayStation 2 Game of the Year award nomination at the 2002 Golden Joystick Awards, but lost to Grand Theft Auto III.
Awards
Readers of Famitsu magazine voted it the best game of all time in early 2006.
Awards
Final Fantasy X came in fifth on IGN 's "Top 25 PS2 Games of All Time" list in 2007 and sixth in "The Top 10 Best Looking PS2 Games of All Time".
Awards
1UP.com listed its revelation during the ending as the third-biggest video game spoiler, while IGN ranked the ending as the fifth best pre-rendered cutscene.
Awards
In a Reader's Choice made in 2006 by IGN, it ranked as the 60th-best video game.
Awards
It also placed 43rd in Game Informer ' s list of "The Top 200 Games of All Time".
Awards
In 2004, Final Fantasy X was listed as one of the best games ever made by GameFAQs, while in November 2005 it was voted as the 12th "Best Game Ever".
Awards
At the 6th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards in 2003, it was nominated for " Outstanding Achievement in Animation " and " Console Role-Playing Game of the Year ".
Awards
Readers from GameFaqs also voted it as Game of the Year during 2001.
Awards
In 2008, readers of Dengeki magazine voted it the second best game ever made.
Awards
It was voted first place in Famitsu ' s and Dengeki ' s polls of most tear-inducing games of all time.
Legacy
Due to its commercial and critical success, Square Enix released a direct sequel to Final Fantasy X in 2003, titled Final Fantasy X-2.
Legacy
Although the sequel did not sell as well as the original, 5.4 million units versus over 8 million units, it can still be considered a commercial success.
Legacy
In 2013, after the release of the HD Remaster, Nojima said that he would like to see a second sequel to X, and if there were demand for it, it could happen.
Legacy
Traversing real-time 3D environments instead of an overworld map has also become a standard of the series.
Legacy
Final Fantasy X can be considered a pioneer in 3-D RPG maps.
Legacy
The Sphere Grid system of FFX had an influence on the action role-playing game Path of Exile (2013), along with the Materia system of Final Fantasy VII.
Legacy

Kujiraoka noted that the staff received multiple requests by fans to include Tidus' and Yuna's Will look as an alternative design but Nomura said it was not possible as the company would first need to develop Final Fantasy X-3.

pst2_final_fantasia_x_2.title: Final Fantasy X-2
sents: lead
Final Fantasy X-2 is a 2003 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the PlayStation 2.
lead
Unlike most Final Fantasy games, which use self-contained stories and characters, X-2 continues the story of Final Fantasy X (2001).
lead
The story follows Yuna as she searches for Tidus, the main character of the previous game, while trying to prevent political conflicts in Spira from escalating to war.
lead
Final Fantasy X-2 was the first game in the series to feature just three player characters and an all-female main cast.
lead
The battle system incorporates Final Fantasy character classes —one of the series' signature gameplay concepts—and is one of the few entries to have multiple possible endings.
lead
The soundtrack was created by Noriko Matsueda and Takahito Eguchi in lieu of long-time Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu.
lead
The game was positively received by critics and was commercially successful, selling over 5.4 million copies on PlayStation 2 and winning a number of awards.
lead
It was the last Final Fantasy game to be released by Square before it merged with Enix in April 2003.
Gameplay
Final Fantasy X-2 is a role-playing video game in which players take on the role of Yuna as she explores the fictional world of Spira.
Gameplay
The game's sidequests include minor tasks and quests, optional bosses and dungeons, and the most minigames of any Final Fantasy at the time of its release.
Gameplay
Unlike its predecessor, in which the player's course through the world was largely linear, Final Fantasy X-2 allows players to visit almost any location at any time.
Gameplay

Players are free to engage with as many or as few optional scenarios as they choose; only a few scenarios per chapter are required to advance the game's central plot and are marked on the world navigation system as "Hotspots".
Gameplay
Achieving 100% completion unlocks a secret ending.
Gameplay
The combat in Final Fantasy X-2 uses an enhanced version of the Active Time Battle (ATB) system, in which characters and enemies take actions according to their speed.
Setting and characters

Final Fantasy X-2 takes place two years after Final Fantasy X and is set in the fictional world of Spira, which consists of one large landmass divided into three subcontinents, surrounded by small tropical islands.
Setting and characters

Spira is distinct from the mainly European-influenced worlds found in previous Final Fantasy games, being much more closely modeled on Southeast Asia, most notably with respect to vegetation, topography, architecture, and names.
Setting and characters
Among them are the Al Bhed, a technologically advanced but previously disenfranchised sub-group of humans with distinctive green eyes and unique language.
Setting and characters

Spira had been terrorized by a gargantuan monster called Sin for 1000 years, inhibiting technological advancement and trapping its people in a cycle of religious asceticism in hopes of praying Sin away.
Setting and characters

The most influential of the groups are the progressive Youth League led by Mevyn Nooj, the reformist New Yevon Party led by Praetor Baralai, and the Machine Faction led by Gippal which supplies weapons to both sides.
Setting and characters
The three main playable characters of Final Fantasy X-2 are Yuna, Rikku, and Paine, members of the sphere hunter group called the Gullwings.
Setting and characters
Yuna was inspired to join after viewing a sphere recording that appeared to depict Tidus, her lost love who vanished during the ending of Final Fantasy X.
Setting and characters
Paine is a new character designed for Final Fantasy X-2, to accommodate the game's intended action-adventure style revolving around a trio of female characters.
Setting and characters
The game's main antagonist is Shuyin, the unsent spirit of a fallen soldier during the Machina War 1000 years ago.
Story
Two years after Sin's defeat, Yuna, Rikku, and Paine recover Yuna's stolen Garment Grid from the Leblanc Syndicate in the first of several encounters in which they vie for spheres.
Story
One thousand years ago, Shuyin was a famous blitzball player in the high-tech metropolis of Zanarkand and Lenne's lover.
Story
Desiring to save Lenne who had been conscripted into the Machina War between Zanarkand and Bevelle, he infiltrated Bevelle to hijack their secret weapon, Vegnagun.
Story
The Songstress dressphere displays the scene of Shuyin and Lenne's last moments to all the concertgoers, opening their eyes to the unproductive nature of their disagreements.
Story
Players who achieve 100% completion see an additional reunion scene in Zanarkand where the pair discuss whether he is truly real or still a dream.
Development

Development of Final Fantasy X-2 began in late 2001 in response to the success of Final Fantasy X, particularly fan reaction to the "Eternal Calm" video included in the Japanese version of Final Fantasy X International, which depicts Yuna's everyday life after the game.
Development
Final Fantasy X-2 was released in Japan shortly before the merger between Square and Enix.
Development

The production team initially disliked the name "X-2", but was eventually accepted since the story was a direct continuation of the previous story and thus could not be the next numbered game in the Final Fantasy series.
Development
Maya and Softimage 3D were the two main programs used to create the graphics.
Development
Retaining the engine and locations from the original game meant that the team could spend most of their time on the gameplay systems and plot.
Development
Final Fantasy X-2 incorporated a number of elements from modern Japanese pop culture.
Development
Toriyama explained that one of the goals during development was to provide a large variety of minigames, such that "if you bought FFX-2 you wouldn't need any other game".
Development
Though work on the opening song and motion capture began early in development, the opening sequence was actually the last portion of the game to be completed.
Music
Noriko Matsueda and Takahito Eguchi composed the soundtrack to Final Fantasy X-2 instead of regular series composer Nobuo Uematsu.
Music
The soundtrack included two J-pop songs: " Real Emotion " and " 1000 Words ".
Music
Koda released her own English versions of "Real Emotion" and "1000 Words" on the CD single for " Come with Me ", with slightly different translations.
Release
As with Final Fantasy X, Square Enix released an expanded version of the game, Final Fantasy X-2 International + Last Mission, in 2004 for the PlayStation 2.
Release
In 2005, a compilation featuring Final Fantasy X and X-2 was released in Japan as Final Fantasy X/X-2 Ultimate Box.
Release
There are three books in the series: Final Fantasy X-2 Ultimania, Final Fantasy X-2 Ultimania Ω, and Final Fantasy X-2: International+Last Mission Ultimania.
Release
Gaming peripheral company Hori produced PlayStation 2 controllers modeled after the Tiny Bee guns Yuna uses in Final Fantasy X-2.
Release
They were re-released in a new silver box to coincide with the release of Final Fantasy X-2: International + Last Mission.
Release
Hori also released a vertical stand for the PlayStation 2 console, with a Final Fantasy X-2 logo that lights up in blue color when plugged in.
Release
Final Fantasy X and X-2 were re-released in high-definition for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita in celebration of the game's 10-year anniversary.
Release
Production had started by January 2012, with Kitase involved.
Release
The collection on PlayStation 3 was titled Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster.
Release
The remaster collection was also released on the PlayStation 4 in 2015, PCs in 2016, followed by Nintendo Switch and Xbox One in 2019.
Critical response
According to review aggregator Metacritic, reviews for Final Fantasy X-2 were "generally favorable".
Critical response
In 2006, readers of Japanese video game magazine Famitsu ranked Final Fantasy X-2 as number 32 in a poll on the best video games of all time.
Critical response
IGN summarized Final Fantasy X-2 as "a brilliant and addictive romp" through the world of Spira.
Critical response
Critics had mixed reactions to Final Fantasy X-2 ' s tonal shift from its predecessor.
Critical response
IGN felt the changes were part of its intrigue, praising the narrative's political elements and comedic tone compared to the first game.
Critical response
Further praise came from RPGamer, with one staff reviewer summarizing it as "a light-hearted fun game" that "may... be the most enjoyable thing to come from the series in several years".
Critical response
Whereas IGN and 1Up.com commended the music as a fitting backdrop to the action and new tone, Electronic Gaming Monthly regarded it as "too bubbly".
Critical response
RPGamer and GameSpot commented that, despite the lack of overt improvement on the first game, it was still one of the best-looking PlayStation 2 games at the time.
Sales
In 2003, Final Fantasy X-2 sold over 1.94 million copies in Japan, making it the highest-selling game of the year.
Sales
Within nine months of its Japanese release, it sold more than a million copies in North America (within two months of its release there), and nearly four million copies worldwide.
Sales
It went on to sell 2.11 million units in Japan, 1.85 million units in the United States, and more than 100,000 units in the United Kingdom.
Sales
International + Last Mission sold over 288,000 copies in Japan over the course of 2004.
Sales
As of March 2013, the game has sold over 5.4 million copies worldwide on PlayStation 2.
Sales
By October 2013, Final Fantasy X and its sequel X-2 had together sold over 14 million copies worldwide on PlayStation 2.
Legacy

After Final Fantasy X-2, Square Enix released direct sequels to other Final Fantasy games, including Dirge of Cerberus: Final Fantasy VII, Final Fantasy IV: The After Years, and two sequels to Final Fantasy XIII.
Legacy
Joseph Leray of Destructoid attributed the fan backlash against the game to its status as the first direct sequel in the series and its light-hearted and "girly" tone.
Legacy
Fritz Fraundorf of the GIA likewise praised its open-ended nature, observing that it was the first Final Fantasy game released in the wake of Grand Theft Auto III ' s popularity.

pst2_final_fantasia_xii.title: Final Fantasy XII
sents: lead
Final Fantasy XII is a 2006 role-playing video game developed and published by Square Enix.
lead
The twelfth main installment of the Final Fantasy series, it was first released for the PlayStation 2 in March 2006.
lead
Final Fantasy XII also includes elements from previous games in the series, such as Chocobos and Moogles.
lead
The game takes place in Ivalice, where the empires of Archadia and Rozarria are waging an endless war.
lead
Dalmasca, a small kingdom, is caught between the warring nations.
lead
When Dalmasca is annexed by Archadia, its princess, Ashe, creates a resistance movement.
lead
During the struggle, she meets Vaan, a young adventurer who dreams of becoming a sky pirate in command of an airship.
lead
They are quickly joined by a band of allies; together, they rally against the tyranny of the Archadian Empire.
Gameplay
Unlike previous games in the series, the player can also control the camera with the right analog stick, allowing for a 360° view of the surroundings.
Gameplay
While in towns and cities, the player may only see from the perspective of Vaan, but any character may be controlled in the field.
Gameplay
Final Fantasy XII restructures the system of earning gil, the currency of the Final Fantasy games; instead of gil, most enemies drop "loot" which can be sold at shops.
Battle system
Excluding the massively multiplayer online role-playing game Final Fantasy XI, Final Fantasy XII is the first entry in the main Final Fantasy series not to include random encounters.
Battle system
For example, the target "Ally: HP < 70%" causes the character to target any ally whose hit points have fallen below 70%.
Battle system
Unlike X, however, Espers follow hidden gambits, rather than the player's direct command.
Battle system

Some Espers have origins in Final Fantasy Tactics and Tactics Advance and others are derived from the final bosses of previous Final Fantasy games such as Chaos, the final boss of the first Final Fantasy, and Zeromus, the final boss of Final Fantasy IV.
Battle system
Final Fantasy XII introduces "Quickenings", a new Limit Break system unique compared to those in previous games in the series.
Battle system
Each character can learn three Quickenings, which are unique to that character.
Growth system
Like the Sphere Grid in Final Fantasy X, all characters may obtain all licenses on the board, but each Quickening and Esper license may only be activated by a single character.
Story
Rasler is killed in the war, the city of Nabudis is destroyed in a single explosion, and the Dalmascan King Raminas is assassinated moments after signing a treaty of surrender.
Development
Development for Final Fantasy XII began in December 2000 and was headed by Final Fantasy Tactics director Yasumi Matsuno and Final Fantasy IX director Hiroyuki Ito.
Development
It has also been noted that the similarities originate from The Hidden Fortress, the 1958 Akira Kurosawa film that inspired Star Wars.
Development
Basch was the first character designed and the developers considered him the "hero" of the story at the time.
Development
Vaan and Penelo were added last and became the heroes in the final version of the plot.
Development

In terms of general changes, the localization team introduced widescreen 16:9 ratio support and reinserted scenes that were left out of the original Japanese version for political reasons and to preserve an "All Ages" CERO rating.
Development
A playable demo of the game was shipped with the North American release of Dragon Quest VIII in November 2005.
Development

To commemorate the release of Final Fantasy XII, playable demos of the English version were available at DigitalLife's Gaming Pavilion in New York City on October 11, 2006, a day dubbed " Final Fantasy XII Gamer's Day".
Development
Final Fantasy XII once held the Guinness World Record for longest development period in a video game production, with a total of five years, spanning from 2001 until its release in 2006.
Development

At a Final Fantasy XII "postmortem" at MIT in March 2009, Hiroshi Minagawa mentioned that several years of production were devoted to the creation of custom tools used for the development of the game.
Development
It was also listed as 8th on the Guinness top 50 games of all time in 2009.
Music
Hitoshi Sakimoto composed and arranged most of the game's soundtrack, with Hayato Matsuo and Masaharu Iwata creating seven and two tracks respectively.
Music
Nobuo Uematsu, following his departure from Square Enix in 2004, only contributed the ending song, " Kiss Me Good-Bye ".
Music
Sakimoto experienced difficulty following in Uematsu's footsteps, but he decided to create a unique soundtrack in his own way.
Music
Two promotional soundtracks were released before the original soundtrack, Symphonic Poem "Hope" and The Best of the Final Fantasy XII Soundtrack, on March 1 and 15, 2006, respectively.
Music
The original soundtrack itself was released two months later in Japan on May 31.
Music
It consists of 4 CDs with 100 tracks, and includes promotional tracks not in the final version of the game.
Music
The CD single for "Kiss Me Good-Bye" was released on the March 15, 2006.
Music
A limited edition was also released, featuring a DVD containing the music video for "Kiss Me Good-Bye".
Music
Tofu Records has released an abridged version of the original soundtrack, which contains 31 songs, including "Kiss Me Good-Bye".
Merchandise

On March 16, 2006, Sony Computer Entertainment Japan released a special Final Fantasy XII package, which contained a PlayStation 2 game system, the Final Fantasy XII game, a standard DualShock controller, and a vertical console stand.
Merchandise
The drinks became commercially available in Japan on March 7.
Merchandise
The Potion was a limited edition product and is no longer available.
Merchandise
Square Enix published the series in a total of five tankōbon volumes from December 22, 2006, to August 22, 2009.
Merchandise
Studio BentStuff published three Ultimania books in 2006: Final Fantasy XII Battle Ultimania and the Final Fantasy XII Scenario Ultimania on June 16, and Final Fantasy XII Ultimania Ω on November 24.
Merchandise
Another Ultimania edition, the Final Fantasy XII International Zodiac Job System Ultimania, was released on September 6, 2007, as a guide book for the International Zodiac version of the game.
Merchandise
The game was re-released as part of the Final Fantasy 25th Anniversary Ultimate Box Japanese package in December 2012.
Merchandise
On January 26, 2007, Square Enix Product Blog revealed full-color Gabranth, Ashe, Balthier, and Vaan figures.
Merchandise
In 2007, Balthier was featured in Final Fantasy Tactics: War of the Lions as a playable character.
Reception
It is also the second Yasumi Matsuno game to garner a perfect score, the first being Vagrant Story.
Reception
Newtype USA named Final Fantasy XII its "Game of the Month" for November 2006, praised the gameplay, graphics, and story, and called it "the best RPG to have been released for any Sony platform".
Reception
Executive producer Akitoshi Kawazu was pleased by Famitsu ' s rating but admitted that he thought the game was not perfect; he felt that the storyline did not meet some fans' expectations.
Reception
Final Fantasy XII was named best PlayStation 2 game and best RPG by numerous video game journals and websites, including GameSpot, GameSpy and IGN.
Reception
The Japan Game Awards 2006 honored Final Fantasy XII with their "Grand Award" and "Award for Excellence" and the PlayStation Awards 2006 bestowed the "Double Platinum Prize".
Sales
Final Fantasy XII sold more than 1,764,000 copies in its first week in Japan, almost equaling the sales of Final Fantasy X in its first week.
Sales
A Square Enix conference report stated that Final Fantasy XII sold more than 2.38 million copies in Japan in the two weeks since its March 16, 2006, release.
Sales
In North America, Final Fantasy XII shipped approximately 1.5 million copies in its first week.
Sales
It was the fourth best-selling PlayStation 2 game of 2006 worldwide.
Sales
As of March 2007, the game had shipped over 5.2 million copies worldwide.
Sales
By November 2009, over 6 million copies of the game were sold worldwide on PlayStation 2.
Sales
As of October 2017, the PlayStation 4 remaster shipped over one million copies worldwide.
International Zodiac Job System
An expanded version of the game, Final Fantasy XII International Zodiac Job System, was released in Japan on August 10, 2007.
International Zodiac Job System
The player can control guest characters and summons, and hold L1 to double the game's running speed.
International Zodiac Job System

There is also a " New Game+ " option, a "New Game- (minus)" option (in which characters do not gain experience), and a "Trial Mode" in which the player hunts monsters in 100 different maps to gain items and money.
International Zodiac Job System
The game also includes the western version's English voices and widescreen 16:9 support, and a bonus DVD.
Revenant Wings
A sequel, Final Fantasy XII: Revenant Wings, was released for the Nintendo DS in 2007.
The Zodiac Age
In July 2017, Square Enix released Final Fantasy XII: The Zodiac Age, a high-definition remaster of the Japanese-only International Zodiac Job System for the PlayStation 4.
The Zodiac Age
The Zodiac Age was nominated for "Best Remake/Remaster" at IGN ' s Best of 2017 Awards, and won "Best Remaster" at Game Informer ' s Best of 2017 Awards and 2017 RPG of the Year Awards.
The Zodiac Age
The Zodiac Age was largely developed by Virtuos, who previously developed Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster for Square Enix.
The Zodiac Age
A version for Windows was released via Steam on February 1, 2018.
The Zodiac Age

The port included support for higher display resolutions and 60 frames-per-second rendering, options to switch between three different versions of the soundtrack, and immediate access to the post-game modes.
The Zodiac Age
Versions for the Nintendo Switch and Xbox One were released on April 30, 2019.
Legacy
The gambit system inspired similar systems used in other games such as Dragon Age: Origins and Pillars of Eternity II.

pst2_fatal_frane.title: Fatal Frame (video game)
sents: lead
Fatal Frame is a survival horror video game developed by Tecmo for the PlayStation 2.
lead
The first installment in the Fatal Frame / Project Zero series, it was released in 2001 in Japan and 2002 in North America and Europe.
lead
An enhanced port for the Xbox was released in 2002 in North America and 2003 in Japan and Europe.
lead
The game was published for both systems by Tecmo in Japan and North America.
lead
In Europe, the PlayStation 2 version was published by Wanadoo, and the Xbox version by Microsoft.
lead
It was re-released in North America on the PlayStation Network in 2013.
lead
Set in the year 1986, the story follows siblings Miku and Mafuyu Hinasaki.
lead
When Mafuyu disappears while searching for a famous novelist in the haunted Himuro Mansion, his sister Miku goes to find him.
Gameplay
Hostile ghosts can only be fought using the Camera Obscura, an antique camera that can capture ghosts.
Gameplay

When using the Camera, the view switches to a first-person view: the Camera Obscura's viewpoint is moved with the left analog stick on a controller, while the character is moved with the right stick while maintaining a view through the Camera.
Gameplay
The most damage is dealt when the ghost is very close.
Synopsis
The story, set in the year 1986, focuses on Miku and Mafuyu Hinasaki, siblings with the ability to see supernatural events.
Synopsis
The last time the ritual was performed, the sacrifice was Kirie Himuro.
Synopsis
According to staff, the first ending is canon and leads into the events of the third game.
Development
The concept came to Shibata inspired by his own dreams and encounters with what he felt were supernatural occurrences.
Development
Development began when the PlayStation 2 hardware was first introduced to Tecmo, under the codename "Project Zero".
Development

During early development, a large amount of effort went into adjusting the lighting and shading, with the most obvious in-game representation of the key colors and desired effect being Miku's torch piercing the darkness inside the mansion.
Development

The setting of the game in a classical Japanese mansion originated from Shibata's early ideas for settings within the Deception series, although these ideas were passed over as it limited the possibilities for the series' trap-setting gameplay.
Development
The story was the first part of the game to be completed.
Development

The setting was originally going to be in the then-present day, but as the team wanted to create a feeling of isolation through a lack of modern technology such as mobile phones, the setting was changed to the 1980s.
Release
The game was first announced in July 2001 for a winter release under the provisional title " Project Zero ".
Release
The game's Japanese title was inspired by the nature of the game's enemies as "beings of nothingness", along with it representing the state of someone being at their utmost during a decisive moment.
Release
The game was initially dated for December 7, but Tecmo later shifted the date forward to December 13.
Release
The game's release for North America was confirmed in January 2002 to be March 8, but the title was instead made available on February 27.
Release
Two cited examples were a haunted mansion said to be the site of numerous murders, and the legend of a tree from which a woman hanged herself when forcefully separated from her lover.
Release
An expanded port for the Xbox, titled Fatal Frame Special Edition, was released in 2002 in North America and 2003 in Japan and Europe.
Release
The game was re-released on the PlayStation Network for the PlayStation 3 in North America on April 9, 2013 as a PlayStation 2 Classic.
Reception
In its debut week in Japan, Fatal Frame sold 22,000 units, the lowest debut sales of the series.
Reception
Its lifetime sales in the country have reached 42,000 units, also making it the lowest-selling title up to that point.
Reception
Upon release on the PlayStation 2 in Europe, it sold 12,000 copies.
Reception
Chris Baker of 1UP.com similarly praised the atmosphere and enjoyed the gameplay, particularly noting its ability to make him feel like a newcomer to gaming with its late-game difficulty spike.
Reception
GameSpy 's Raina Lee, reviewing the Xbox version, called it "the only really scary game on the Xbox".
Legacy
A sequel to the game, titled Fatal Frame II: Crimson Butterfly, was released in 2003 in North America and Japan, and 2004 in Europe.
Legacy
A sequel to both games, Fatal Frame III: The Tormented, was released in 2005 in Japan and North America, and 2006 in Europe.
Legacy
Shortly after the game's release, a Hollywood film adaptation was announced in 2003.
Legacy

After a long period of hiatus, the film was re-announced in 2014, this time produced by Samuel Hadida, and was set to begin production after the completion and release of Fatal Frame: Maiden of Black Water.
