pst2_dark_clod.title: Dark Cloud
sents: lead
Dark Cloud is an action role-playing video game developed by Level-5 and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.
lead
Originally intended as a launch title for the system in March 2000, the game was eventually released in Japan in December 2000, in North America in May 2001, and in Europe in September.
lead
A spiritual sequel, Dark Chronicle (Dark Cloud 2 in North America), was released in Japan in 2002 and worldwide the following year.
lead

Uniquely combining the mechanisms of action role-playing games with elements of city-building games, Dark Cloud tells the story of a group of adventurers who band together to fight against the Dark Genie, who has attacked and destroyed many villages.
lead
The main protagonist and player character is Toan, a boy who is given a magical stone called the Atlamillia by the fairy king Simba, granting him the power to rebuild the destroyed lands.
lead
Dark Cloud was met with mainly positive reviews by critics, who praised its blend of gameplay types, although some criticized its combat as repetitive.
lead
The game sold over a million copies worldwide by 2014.
lead
It was later released via emulation for the PlayStation 4 through the PlayStation Network in December 2015.
Gameplay

When all three reach 100%, the village is complete, although it is not necessary for the player to reach 100% in all three to be able to move on to the next set of dungeons and the next village; the player must only acquire 100% in collection and rebuilding to unlock the next village.
Gameplay
Completing 100% of the villagers' wishes is not a requirement, although if the player does reach 100%, they are awarded a bonus item/ability.
Gameplay
Unlike most action role-playing games, instead of the characters leveling up, their weapons do.
Gameplay

To upgrade a weapon, the player can attach stat-increasing items (attack power, speed, ability to kill different types of monsters, elemental attributes, etc.), but a single weapon can only carry a limited number of attachments.
Gameplay
When a weapon reaches level five, it can be transformed into a "SynthSphere", which carries 60% of the weapon's power and attributes.
Gameplay
The characters themselves can only grow stronger with the consumption of particular items, which can increase their health points, water meter and defense.
Gameplay
Each character also has a unique ability that allows them to move through the dungeons; for example, Xiao can jump across chasms that other characters can not.
Plot
They defeat him, releasing him from the Genie's control, and he tells them of the legend of the "Black Demon" that nearly destroyed the world, until it was defeated and imprisoned by the Moon People.
Plot
Seda learned the only thing strong enough to defeat the Genie was Atlamillia.
Plot
No Atlamillia would exist for another 400 years, so he opened a portal to the future.
Development
Dark Cloud was the first game from developer Level-5, led by president and CEO Akihiro Hino, who also wrote, produced and designed the game.
Development
Development began immediately when the company was founded in October 1998 with a projected development time of two years.
Development
When the PlayStation 2 was announced in March 1999, Sony president and CEO Ken Kutaragi used an early demo of Dark Cloud to show the capabilities of the platform.
Development
In September 1999, Sony showed an early playable version of the game at the Tokyo Game Show.
Development
Georama mode was a major component of the demo, with both IGN and GameSpot comparing it to Legend of Mana ' s "Land Make" system.
Development
At E3 in May 2000, a 30% complete playable demo was shown.
Music
A full forty-six track soundtrack was released by Sony Music Entertainment Visual Works in Japan on January 11, 2001.
Reception
Not quite fun." In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of one eight, two sevens, and one six for a total of 28 out of 40.
Reception
Gameplay was compared by several critics to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, while the weapon system was likened to Vagrant Story.
Reception
While it's not the Zelda for the PlayStation 2 everyone was hoping for, Dark Cloud puts its own significant stamp on the adventure-RPG genre."
Reception

During the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences ' 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the game was nominated for the " Console Role-Playing " award, which went to Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance.
Sales
During its debut week in Japan, it entered the charts at number 15, selling only 19,615 units.
Sales
By the end of 2000, it had sold 35,783 units, making it to the 286th highest selling game of the year, across all systems.
Sales
In 2001, it sold a further 34,688 units, for a total of 70,471 units.
Sales
Nevertheless, it proved to have much stronger sales internationally, and ultimately sold over 800,000 units worldwide.
Sales
By July 2006, the game had sold 670,000 units and earned $22 million in the U.S.
Sales
NextGen ranked it as the 95th highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between October 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Sales
Combined sales of the Dark Cloud series reached 1 million units in the U.S. by July 2006.
Sales
The game had sold 100,000 copies in Japan and 1 million in the United States by 2014.

pst2_dark_chronical.title: Dark Chronicle
sents: lead
Dark Chronicle, released as Dark Cloud 2 in North America, is a 2002 action role-playing game developed by Level-5 and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2 (PS2).
lead
It was released in Japan before releasing in English in 2003.
lead
An emulated version of the game was released for the PlayStation 4 through the PlayStation Network in 2016.
lead
The game is a spiritual sequel to 2000's Dark Cloud, with which it shares the same basic game mechanics but features new characters and plot.
lead
Players control two main protagonists, Max and Monica, who must work together to stop the game's main antagonist, Emperor Griffon, from destroying the world.
lead
The game features themes of time traveling, with Max and Monica trying to prevent Griffon's destruction by altering the past to change the future.
lead
The game was met with positive reviews from critics, who praised the improvements over Dark Cloud, in particular the graphics and variety of gameplay styles.
lead
Dark Chronicle won several awards, and sold roughly 250,000 copies in Japan within a month.
Gameplay
Throughout most of the game, players control characters Max and Monica.
Gameplay
Each character also has a unique combat ability: Max can pilot a customizable, mech -like vehicle called the Ridepod, and Monica can shapeshift into monsters.
Gameplay
Unlike most action role-playing games in which the characters level-up, weapons in Dark Chronicle instead do the leveling.
Gameplay
Most items in this game can be broken down, or "spectrumized", which turns the item into a "SynthSphere" that can be attached to a weapon to raise specific stats, depending on its properties.
Gameplay
As in the previous game, characters can only grow stronger by consuming particular items that permanently increase their health points and defense.
Gameplay
Each Georama map must complete as many of the conditions for that map as possible; it is not necessary to achieve 100% to advance the plot in any map, but doing so earns the player bonus items.
Gameplay
Each character has a different ability and only one can be active at a time.
Plot

After leaving the town, Max is told that 15 years ago Emperor Griffon destroyed the world but spared Palm Brinks because he wanted a special stone - Max's pendant - and that Flotsam is one of Griffon's henchman.
Plot
Max and Monica use their new ability to time travel, as well as the reopening of the railroad by Mayor Need to go on a mission rebuilding areas of the world that Griffon destroyed.
Plot
During these adventures, they learn that Emperor Griffon possesses a gold atlamillia - the most powerful of the three - but desires the other two to make him all powerful.
Plot
Max and Monica use Ixion to head 10,000 years into the past to face Emperor Griffon, a young moon-person who lives in Moon Flower Palace.
Plot
The Element reveals it was born from Sirus' hatred of humans and plans to rule over the destroyed Earth.
Development

Rumors about Dark Chronicle first appeared in April 2002, when Level-5 Inc. updated its website with an image of a silhouette from its newest game, although no other details were made available at the time.
Development
The game was officially announced on May 16, when Level-5 launched a full website that revealed the new game would include Dark Cloud ' s Georama mode and had more features than its predecessor.
Development

More information was revealed at E3 later in May, when Sony Computer Entertainment announced the game would be released in Japan and Europe as Dark Chronicle and in North America as Dark Cloud 2, with a release date of late 2002 to early 2003.
Development
The invention system, which according to Sony would feature over 100 hours of gameplay, was also demonstrated for the first time.
Development

IGN and GameSpot both featured previews of the game based on the E3 demo; IGN focused on the improved Georama system and praised the cel-shaded graphics, and GameSpot looked at the dungeons, finding the combat improved from the first game.
Development
Level-5 referred to the graphic style as "tonal rendering"; the main characters have a smooth, shaded look and the backgrounds have detailed textures and lighting.
Development
The main characters have a higher polygon count than the supporting characters and are composed of 2,500 to 3,000 polygons.
Development
Supporting characters are composed of 1,500 to 2,000 polygons.
Development
An emulated version of the game for the PlayStation 4 through the PlayStation Network was released in January 2016.
Music
A two-disc album, Dark Chronicle Original Sound Tracks, was released in Japan by Scitron on February 19, 2003.
Music

GameSpot 's Brad Shoemaker wrote that " Dark Cloud 2 ' s music ranges from good to excellent", and said that "generally there are enough tunes that you won't get too bored of hearing any particular one".
Music
IGN 's Kaiser Hwang wrote that "the music in Dark Cloud 2 ranges from really good, to really really good, to exceptionally good".
Music
A remix album, Dark Chronicle Premium Arrange, was published in Japan by Team Entertainment in April 21, 2004.
Sequel

A sequel, potentially titled Dark Cloud 3, was first rumored to be in development for PlayStation 3 in an alleged leak published in 2006 by PSMania, which said Level-5 was aiming for a March 2009 release.
Sequel

In 2009, Level-5 manager Yoshiaki Kusuda said that although the company did not have a "specific plan for a sequel", it would "seriously consider making it" if fans asked for it often enough, leading Kotaku writer Stephen Totilo to encourage readers to request the game.
Sequel
Totilo reported in 2010 and again in 2012 that several people had misread the original 2009 interview, were emailing him and asking him to make it.
Sequel
Reporting on a 2017 interview that Hino gave to Nikkei Business Publications, Rolling Stone lamented that a Dark Cloud 3 was not among Level-5's plans for the Nintendo Switch.
Sequel
Hino told Polygon that Level-5 could not produce a new Dark Cloud game on its own because the license was co-owned by Sony.
Sequel
Although Level-5 has never officially released a Dark Chronicle sequel, there is some evidence that Rogue Galaxy was originally developed as Dark Cloud 3.
Sequel
Inside the NTSC-J version of Rogue Galaxy, two images named DC3-Title can be found.
Reception
Dark Chronicle received generally favorable reviews, with an aggregate score of 87 out of 100 on Metacritic, based on forty-one reviews.
Reception
GameSpot 's Brad Shoemaker scored the game 9 out of 10, calling it "one of the finest games released for the PlayStation 2 so far" and "an aesthetic masterpiece".
Reception

Every element of the game, from the georama system to the weapon upgrading to the interaction with a large cast of characters, displays a polish and attention to quality that you find only in real classics".
Reception
The publication named Dark Chronicle the best PlayStation 2 game of February 2003.
Reception
IGN 's Kaiser Hwang also scored the game 9 out of 10, calling it "arguably the best looking PS2 game out there".
Reception
He concluded that " Dark Cloud 2 takes the standard sequel road and gives us everything that made the original Dark Cloud great, only bigger and better...
Reception
From the incredible graphics, to the great sound, to the refined gameplay, Dark Cloud 2 just oozes of quality and polish".
Reception
Eurogamer 's Ronan Jennings also scored the game 9 out of 10, writing "it deserves credit for making us focus on actually doing things.
Reception
GameSpy 's Christian Nutt scored the game 4 out of 5, saying it fell just short of being a classic: "The biggest and most obvious problem with the game has to be its story.
Reception
His conclusion was: There's no question in my mind that Dark Cloud 2 is one of the most solid RPG adventures for the PS2; but... it doesn't quite live up to its potential.
Reception
If Level-5 had worked out all of the kinks, it'd be one of my favorite games for the PS2.
Reception
While it has my grudging respect, there are many games that I prefer, thanks to DC2's idiosyncrasies".
Reception
Game Revolution 's Johnny Liu awarded the game a B, praising the graphics and variety of gameplay but said it became somewhat repetitive towards the end: " Dark Cloud 2 is very serial in nature.
Sales and awards
Dark Chronicle sold 235,917 copies in Japan by the end of 2002.
Sales and awards
The game won "Best PlayStation 2 Game" (2003) from GameSpot, and nominated for " Console Role-Playing Game of the Year " (2004) from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.
Sales and awards
It was also nominated for "Best Adventure Game" at the 1st British Academy Games Awards, losing to The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker.
Sales and awards
Dark Chronicle was named "Game of the Month" for February 2003 and given an "Editor's Choice" award by IGN, which in 2010 placed it at #31 in their "Top 100 PlayStation 2 Games".

fcube_metrood_prime.title: Metroid Prime
sents: lead
Metroid Prime is a 2002 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
Metroid Prime is the fifth main Metroid game and the first to use 3D computer graphics and a first-person perspective.
lead
It was released in North America in November 2002, and in Japan and Europe the following year.
lead
Along with the Game Boy Advance game Metroid Fusion, Prime marked the return of the Metroid series after an eight-year hiatus following Super Metroid (1994).
lead
Metroid Prime takes place between the original Metroid and Metroid II: Return of Samus.
lead
Players control the bounty hunter Samus Aran as she battles the Space Pirates and their biological experiments on the planet Tallon IV.
lead
Metroid Prime was a collaboration between Retro in Austin, Texas, and Japanese Nintendo employees, including producers Shigeru Miyamoto and Kensuke Tanabe.
lead
Miyamoto suggested the project after visiting Retro's headquarters in 2000.
Gameplay

Metroid Prime is an action-adventure game in which players control protagonist Samus Aran from a first-person perspective, unlike previous games in the Metroid series, with third-person elements used for Morph Ball mode.
Items

Prime is one of the first Metroid games to address the reason Samus does not start with power-ups acquired in previous games; she begins the game with some upgrades, including the Varia Suit, Missiles and Grapple Beam, but they are lost during an explosion on the Space Pirate frigate Orpheon.
Development
According to producer Shigeru Miyamoto, Nintendo did not develop a Metroid game for the Nintendo 64 as the company "couldn't come out with any concrete ideas".
Development
Metroid co-creator Yoshio Sakamoto said he could not imagine how the Nintendo 64 controller could be used to control Samus.
Development
Nintendo approached another company to make Metroid for Nintendo 64, but the offer was declined, supposedly because the developers thought they could not equal Super Metroid.
Development
Metroid Prime was a collaboration between Nintendo EAD and R&D1 and the American company Retro Studios.
Development
Retro was created in 1998 by an alliance between Nintendo and Iguana Entertainment founder Jeff Spangenberg.
Development
After establishing its offices in Austin, Texas in 1999, Retro worked on four GameCube projects.
Development
When Miyamoto visited Retro in 2000, he suggested a new Metroid game after seeing their prototype first-person shooter engine.
Development
In 2000 and early 2001, four games in development at Retro were canceled, including an RPG, Raven Blade, leaving Prime the only game in development.
Development
During the last nine months of development, Retro's staff worked 80- to 100-hour weeks to reach Nintendo's deadline.
Development
According to senior artist James Dargie, it took them almost six months to do the first level that Nintendo approved, and then they had less than a year to do the rest of the game.
Development
Concept artist Android Jones, a lifelong fan of the series whose work included Samus's Varia Suit and most of the art in the Scan Visor, would sleep in the office and resume working when he woke up.
Development
We didn't want to make just another first person shooter....
Development
Making a first person shooter would have been a cheap and easy way to go.
Development
The game was planned to use a third-person perspective, but after Miyamoto intervened this was changed to first-person perspective and almost everything already developed was scrapped.
Development
The change was prompted by camera problems experienced by Rare, which was developing the Nintendo 64 game Jet Force Gemini.
Development
According to director Mark Pacini, Miyamoto believed that "shooting in third person was not very intuitive"; Pacini also said that exploration is easier using first-person.
Development

Pacini said that after picking that perspective, the crew decided not to make a traditional first-person shooter, instead they had to break down the stereotypes of what a first-person game is and make a fun Metroid game.
Development

Pacini said that Retro tried to design the game so that the only difficult parts would be boss battles and players would not be afraid to explore because "the challenge of the game was finding your way around".
Development

The team considered implementing the Speed Booster power-up from Super Metroid but concluded it would not work well because of the first-person perspective and the limitations imposed by the scale of game's environment.
Development
The first public appearance of the game was a ten-second video at Space World 2000.
Development

In February 2001, the game was confirmed by Nintendo, which also announced that because of its emphasis on exploration and despite the first-person perspective, Metroid Prime would be a first-person adventure rather than a first-person shooter.
Development
The game was showcased at E3 2001 in May, with its title confirmed as Metroid Prime.
Audio
Tommy Tallarico Studios initially provided sound effects, but Miyamoto deemed them not good enough for an extended presentation at Space World 2001.
Audio
A soundtrack album, Metroid Prime & Fusion Original Soundtracks, was published by Scitron on June 18, 2003.
Release
Metroid Prime was released for the GameCube in North America on November 18, 2002.
Release
In 2003, the game arrived in Japan on February 28, and Europe on March 21.
Release
In 2004, Nintendo released a Metroid Prime GameCube bundle, including a second disc featuring a trailer and a demo for Metroid Prime 2: Echoes, a timeline of Metroid games, and an art gallery.
Release
Metroid Prime was re-released in Japan in 2009 for the Wii as part of the New Play Control! series.
Release
The compilation became available for download from the Wii U 's Nintendo eShop in January 2015.
Metroid Prime Remastered

Metroid Prime Remastered, a high-definition remaster for the Nintendo Switch, was released digitally on February 8, 2023, with a physical release on February 22 in North America and March 3 in Europe and Japan.
Metroid Prime Remastered
Samuel Claiborn of IGN described it as "a perfect example of how to both honor a lauded classic and bring it up to code".
Metroid Prime Remastered
As of March 2023, Metroid Prime Remastered had sold 1.09 million copies.
Reception
Metroid Prime became one of the best-selling games on the GameCube.
Reception
It was the second-best-selling game of November 2002 in North America, behind Grand Theft Auto: Vice City; 250,000 units were sold in the first week of its release.
Reception
As of July 2006, the game had sold more than 1.49 million copies in the U.S. alone, and had earned more than US$50 million.
Reception
More than 78,000 copies were sold in Japan, and Nintendo added the game to its Player's Choice line in the PAL region.
Reception
It sold 2.84 million copies worldwide and was the best-selling Metroid game until Metroid Dread (2021).
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly awarded it a perfect score.
Reception
In 2004, the video game countdown show Filter said Metroid Prime had the best graphics of all time.
Reception

Metroid Prime appeared on several lists of best games; it was ranked 23rd in IGN ' s Top 100, 29th in a 100-game list chosen by GameFAQs users, 18th in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s 2009 list of greatest Nintendo games and 10th in Nintendo Power' s "Top 200 Nintendo Games Ever".
Reception
IGN named Metroid Prime the best GameCube game, while GameSpy ranked it third in a similar list, behind The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker and Resident Evil 4.
Reception
Nintendo Power also ranked Metroid Prime as the sixth-best game of the 2000s.
Reception

Wired ranked the game 10th in its list of "The 15 Most Influential Games of the Decade" for popularizing "exploration, puzzle-solving, platforming and story" among first-person shooters, saying that the game was "breaking the genre free from the clutches of Doom ".
Reception
Wired ' s writer continued that Metroid Prime took a massive stride forward for first-person games.
Legacy
Metroid Prime was followed by Metroid Prime 2: Echoes (2004) on the GameCube and Metroid Prime 3: Corruption (2007) on the Wii.
Legacy
The first two games were re-released on Wii as part of the New Play Control! series in Japan, and as part of the Wii compilation Metroid Prime: Trilogy (2009).
Legacy

A pinball game, Metroid Prime Pinball (2005), and the action spin-offs Metroid Prime Hunters (2006) were released for the handheld Nintendo DS console, and Metroid Prime: Federation Force (2016) for the Nintendo 3DS.
Legacy
Metroid Prime 4: Beyond is planned for release in 2025 for the Nintendo Switch.
Legacy
Metroid Prime ' s gameplay and HUD have influenced other first-person shooters such as Geist and Star Wars: Republic Commando.
Legacy
A demo of a 2D fangame version of Metroid Prime was released in April 2021.

fcube_metrood_prime_2_echos.title: Metroid Prime 2: Echoes
sents: lead
Metroid Prime 2: Echoes is a 2004 adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead

The sequel to Metroid Prime (2002) and the first Metroid game with a multiplayer feature, Echoes was released in North America, Europe and Australia in 2004 and in Japan under the name Metroid Prime 2: Dark Echoes in May 2005.
lead
The story follows bounty hunter Samus Aran after she is sent to rescue Galactic Federation Marines from a ship near Aether, a planet inhabited by a race known as the Luminoth.
lead
She discovers that the troops were slaughtered by the Ing, a hostile race that came from an alternate dimension of Aether.
lead
Samus must travel to four temples to ensure the destruction of the evil Ing, while battling them, wild creatures, Space Pirates, and her mysterious doppelgänger Dark Samus.
lead
Retro sought to differentiate Echoes with a heavier focus on story-telling and new gameplay mechanics.
lead
Nintendo launched a viral marketing campaign that included several websites written as if taking place in the Metroid universe.
lead
The single-player mode was acclaimed for its graphics, atmosphere and music, though its steep difficulty and multiplayer mode were met less positively.
Gameplay
Metroid Prime 2: Echoes is an adventure game "with heavy action elements and an emphasis on complex puzzle-solving" in which the player controls the Samus Aran from a first-person perspective.
Gameplay
Equipment players collect include the Screw Attack, which allows Samus to somersault in midair and off certain surfaces, and new beam weapons that have limited ammunition.
Plot
Samus then encounters her evil doppelgänger, Dark Samus, for the first time, and after a small skirmish Dark Samus jumps through a portal.
Plot
When she reaches the structure, she meets U-Mos, the last remaining sentinel of the Luminoth, an alien race that have fought against the Ing for decades and are now on the verge of defeat.
Plot

Samus defeats the creature and retrieves the last remaining energy, causing Dark Aether to become critically unstable and begin to collapse, but her path out of the temple's gateway is blocked by a horribly altered and unstable Dark Samus.
Development

Since the game was a first-person adventure and its deathmatch mode could not easily replicate other shooting games, Retro just tried to "make a multiplayer experience that fans of Metroid games would instantly know and recognise".
Development
The developers sought advice from the producers of the Nintendo game The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, which also used the theme of parallel worlds.
Development
Some features, such as a hidden version of Super Metroid (1994), were canceled for lack of time.
Development
Tanabe later said that Echoes was only about thirty percent complete three months before the deadline Nintendo had set for a 2004 holiday release.
Release
Metroid Prime 2: Echoes was released for the GameCube in North America on November 15, 2004, Europe on November 26, and in Australia on December 2.
Release
The PAL version lacked the standard 50 Hz mode, and offered 60 Hz mode only.
Release
In Japan, it was released on May 26, 2005 as Metroid Prime 2: Dark Echoes.
Marketing
Nintendo launched several websites to initiate a viral marketing campaign for Echoes, with inspiration drawn from Halo 2 ' s alternate reality game I Love Bees.
Marketing
Athena Astronautics gave a random selection of 25 people who replied to the offer an "interactive training manual", which was in fact a free copy of Metroid Prime 2: Echoes.
Marketing
A Metroid -related spoof of "I Love Bees" appeared online in October 2004, to which Nintendo reacted by stating that it was not involved with it.
Marketing
Never send a man to do a woman's job".
Re-releases
Echoes was re-released in Japan in 2009 for the Wii console, as part of the New Play Control! series.
Re-releases
The Wii version of Echoes was released in North America and Europe on August 24 as part of the compilation Metroid Prime: Trilogy, which also includes Metroid Prime and Metroid Prime 3: Corruption.
Re-releases
The compilation was re-released on the Wii U 's Nintendo eShop on January 29, 2015.
Critics
In December 2019, review aggregator GameRankings ranked Metroid Prime 2: Echoes as the ninth best GameCube game and the 281st best game of all time.
Critics
GameSpot and IGN praised the campaign as a lengthy and rewarding adventure and appreciated the minimum 20 hours required to complete the game.
Critics
A major criticism of Echoes focused on the game's high difficulty, with Game Informer declaring that "not only are the boss fights unforgiving, the environment is sometimes difficult to follow".
Critics

GameSpot criticized this mechanism and called it "a scavenger hunt much tougher than the rest of the game", and 1UP.com said that the only purpose it served was to artificially extend the game's length.
Critics

Serge Pennings of The Observer noted there were too few opportunities to save the game while playing, an aspect X-Play also criticized by saying that most of the game's difficulty was "because the save system is poorly implemented and downright cheap".
Awards
Echoes won an award in almost every category it was nominated for at the 2004 Nintendo Power Awards, and won awards for Best GameCube Game of 2004 from IGN, Electronic Gaming Monthly, and GameSpy.
Awards
The game was a finalist in GameSpot's 2004 "Best Action Adventure Game" category across all platforms.
Awards

During the 8th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Echoes received nominations for " Console First-Person Action Game of the Year ", and outstanding achievement in " Art Direction " and " Visual Engineering ".
Awards

It was rated the 174th best game made on a Nintendo system in Nintendo Power ' s Top 200 Games list, the 74th best game by GameFAQs users, the 15th best GameCube game by IGN, and the 13th best by GameSpy.
Sales
Echoes sold 470,000 copies in North America in December 2004.
Sales
It was the ninth-best-selling game in its debut month in Japan with 16,105 copies sold, ranking it behind Yu Yu Hakusho Forever and Hanjuku Hero 4: 7-Jin no Hanjuku Hero.
Sales
By August 2009, 800,000 copies had sold worldwide.
Sales
The game ultimately sold more than 1.10 million copies worldwide.

fcube_fire_emblum_path_of_radiants.title: Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance

Composer(s): Yoshito Hirano Saki Haruyama Naoko Mitome Atsushi Yoshida Kanako Teramae

sents: lead
Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance is a 2005 tactical role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and Nintendo SPD, and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
It is the ninth main installment in the Fire Emblem series, and the third to be released in the west.
lead
As with previous installments, gameplay revolves around positioning characters on a battlefield to defeat an opposing force.
lead
If characters are defeated in battle, they are removed from the rest of the game.
lead
The story takes place on the fictional continent of Tellius, inhabited by the human Beorc and the shapeshifting Laguz.
lead
The game begins when the Beorc nation of Daein invades its neighbor, the kingdom of Crimea.
lead
The mercenary Ike and his companions set off to restore Crimea's heir, Princess Elincia, to the throne.
lead

The group travels across Tellius, allying with other countries to free Crimea from Daein's control and confronting racial tensions and long-standing resentment between the Beorc and the Laguz along the way.
Gameplay
Before entering battle, players can choose a certain number of characters to use from a roster of up to 46 characters.
Gameplay
Once a character earns 100 experience points, they automatically level up.
Gameplay
Once the class changes, the character receives set stat bonuses, and their level is reset to level 1, while carrying over all the random stat increases aggregated up to that point.
Gameplay
After promotion, the level-cap is 20, and no character can earn experience points after achieving this level.
Gameplay
Supports are ranked from C to A, with A being the highest rank and granting the best bonuses.
Gameplay
Weapons forged at Base can also be customized with a unique name.
Setting and characters
According to legend, the goddess who made the world created Beorc in her image, and created the Laguz to fill the gap between herself and beasts.
Development
Development on Path of Radiance began at Intelligent Systems after the international success of the first localized game in the series, released overseas under the title Fire Emblem.
Development
Path of Radiance was the first Fire Emblem to have 3D in-game graphics, full-motion video cutscenes and voice acting.
Development
It was also the first home console game since Fire Emblem: Thracia 776 for the Super Famicom.
Development

Transitioning from 2D graphics to 3D graphics was one of the biggest challenges during development, especially the transition from the tilted overhead view to a character-to-character battle in third-person.
Development
By the end of development, Narihiro had some regrets about the quality of the game, saying in an interview that he considered it to be only 70% complete when released.
Development
Ike was born from the many ideas for new directions being suggested for the new 3D game, with many people wanting the protagonist everyone could empathize with.
Development
Designing all the characters to be unique under the new conditions proved a challenge.
Release
A new Fire Emblem title was first announced in April 2004, with the full reveal coming in an issue of Weekly Shōnen Jump.
Release
The game's title, story details and chosen platform were announced in Weekly Shōnen Jump, with a release date announced as some time during 2004.
Release
The game was first shown publicly by Nintendo at their Nintendo World Touch DS event in early 2005.
Release
As a pre-order bonus, Nintendo created a special CD containing selected tracks from the game, and a special calendar commemorating the series' 15th anniversary.
Release
The game released in Japan on April 20, 2005.
Release
The first western demonstration of the title was at E3 2005.
Release
It was subsequently released in Europe on November 4; and in Australia on December 1.
Localization
The biggest challenge for the team was translating from Japanese to English, which required staff from Japan to come over and check their work.
Localization
When translating the dialogue, the localization team wanted to preserve the story's depth and serious tone, despite often having a limited text and character space for interaction and expression.
Localization
While most of the time they refrained from putting out-of-context remarks in character dialogue, an exception was Anna, a recurring Fire Emblem character who featured in optional tutorial missions.
Reception
In Japan during its opening week, Path of Radiance sold 100,357 copies, selling through 64.16% of its initial shipment.
Reception
By the end of 2005, the game had sold 156,413 copies.
Reception
Although no exact sales figures have been published, Nintendo cited the game as being among its successful GameCube titles for 2005.
Reception
Reception of the game was generally positive: on aggregate site Metacritic, it received a score of 85/100 based upon 42 critic reviews.
Reception
In IGN ' s GamerMetrics List for 2005 and GameSpot ' s 2005 Readers' Choice award, Path of Radiance was at #2 in their respective lists behind Resident Evil 4.
Reception
The game was among those nominated at the 2006 Golden Joystick Awards in the "Nintendo Game of the Year" category.
Reception
The game was named by GamesRadar was one of the best GameCube games of all time in 2014, and Destructoid listed it among the five best Fire Emblem games in the series in 2013.
Reception

During the 9th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Path of Radiance for " Role-Playing Game of the Year ", which was ultimately awarded to Jade Empire.
Reception
One reviewer cited it as the series' new exemplar, while another pointed out rough edges in the graphical redesign and that the new 3D perspective made seeing some parts of the map difficult.
Reception
1UP.com ' s Shane Betternhausen was positive overall, saying " delivers a superbly paced and rewarding adventure".
Reception
RPGFan reviewer Mark Tjan said that while not the best Fire Emblem game he had played, "it's certainly a good game and worth picking up if you're searching for an SRPG worth your time and money".
Legacy
The next entry, Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn, began development in May 2005 for the Wii.
Legacy
It was released in 2007 in Japan and North America, and 2008 in Europe and Australia.

fcube_paper_plumber_the_thousand_y.title: Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door
sents: lead
Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door is a 2004 role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
The Thousand-Year Door is the second game in the Paper Mario series following Paper Mario, and is part of the larger Mario franchise.
lead

In the game, when Mario and Princess Peach get involved in the search for a mystic treasure that holds great fortune, Peach is kidnapped by an alien group called the X-Nauts; Mario sets out to find the treasure and save the princess.
lead
The Thousand-Year Door borrows many gameplay elements from its predecessor, such as a drawing-based art style, and a turn-based battle system emphasizing correctly timing moves.
lead
For most of the game, the player controls Mario, although Bowser and Princess Peach are playable at certain points.
lead
The game was announced at the 2003 Game Developers Conference, and was released late July 2004 in Japan and late 2004 worldwide.
lead
The Thousand-Year Door was acclaimed at release and is since considered one of the greatest video games of all time.
lead
It won the "Role Playing Game of the Year" award at the 2005 Interactive Achievement Awards, and is often considered the best game in the series.
Gameplay
Mario can also purchase "badges" from non-player characters (NPCs), find them hidden in the environment, or occasionally obtain them from defeated enemies.
Combat
Jumping or hammering an enemy before entering combat mode will cause a "First Strike." This allows Mario to damage the enemy before the regular combat starts.
Combat
Likewise, some enemies can strike first and damage Mario before the regular combat starts.
Combat
Some player attacks, such as Mario's hammer, can only target enemies on the ground, and spiky enemies will instead damage Mario if he jumps on them.
Combat
When a partner's HP is reduced to 0, the partner becomes inactive and cannot be used until revived.
Combat
If Mario's HP is reduced to 0, however, the game ends and the player must start again from the last saved point.
Combat
If the player wins the battle, the player is awarded Star Points; for every 100 Star Points, the player levels up and chooses to increase Mario's maximum HP, FP, or BP.
Combat
The audience starts with a maximum size of 50 and can grow up to 200 as the player levels up during the game.
Plot
The story is divided into eight chapters and a prologue, each of which primarily takes place in one of the unique areas.
Characters
In particular, the Goomba Professor Frankly, who knows the most about the mysteries relating to Rogueport, must be visited every time Mario retrieves a Crystal Star.
Characters
Most of Peach's story is spent on her interaction with the X-Nauts' computer AI TEC, who falls in love with Princess Peach despite not fully understanding the concept of love.
Story
The game opens with an introduction about a seaside town that was destroyed by a cataclysm and consequently sunk into the depths of the earth.
Development and release
Nintendo revealed The Thousand-Year Door at the Game Developers Conference of 2003.
Development and release
Before its release, the game was confirmed to be a direct sequel to the Nintendo 64 game Paper Mario and was known tentatively as Mario Story 2 in Japan and Paper Mario 2 in North America.
Development and release
A preview of the game was available at E3 2004; it included Hooktail Castle and a Bowser bonus level as playable stages.
Development and release
The game was released on July 22, 2004, in Japan, October 11 in North America, November 12 in Europe, and November 18 in Australia.
Reception
Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door was well-received, with review aggregators Metacritic and GameRankings both giving the game an 87/100.
Reception
Eurogamer rated the large amount of text as "the only major stumbling block" of the game.
Reception
RPGamer commented that the music "for the most part is done very well", but that the perceived repetitive battle music was "one of the biggest flaws" of the game.
Reception
The game won " Console Role-Playing Game of the Year " at the 8th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards (now known as the D.I.C.E.
Reception
Awards), and was nominated for GameSpot's 2004 "Best Story", "Best Graphics, Artistic" and "Funniest Game" awards.
Reception
The game was ranked 56th in Official Nintendo Magazine 's "100 Greatest Nintendo Games" feature.
Reception
Edge Magazine placed the game 93rd on their 100 best video games in 2007.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.
Reception
In 2023, GameSpot writer Brandon Hesse rated the game as the best Mario RPG of all time, describing it as the "pinnacle of the Paper Mario series" and "one of the best RPGs ever made".
Reception
In its first week of release in Japan, The Thousand-Year Door was the best-selling game, selling about 159,000 units.
Reception
It proceeded to sell 409,000 units in the country and 1.23 million copies in North America.
Reception
As of December 2007, the GameCube game had sold 1.91 million copies worldwide.
Legacy
The new approach was often critiqued by critics, and most reviewers compare the game to The Thousand-Year Door to highlight what the games were lacking.
Legacy

Paper Mario: The Origami King returned some minor elements that had been removed from the games that it followed, such as Paper Mario: Sticker Star, but most critics still derided the game for missing classic features.
Remake
A remake of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door for the Nintendo Switch was announced during a Nintendo Direct presentation on September 14, 2023.
Remake
Nintendo Life reported that the game runs at 30 frames per second as opposed to the original's 60, but noted that it did not majorly affect their gameplay experience.
Reception
The remake was equally well received upon release, with an average score of 88/100 on Metacritic.
Reception
As of June 2024, the remake has sold 1.76 million copies worldwide, nearly matching the original version's lifetime sales in a single month.
Lawsuit
In 2008, Morgan Creek Productions filed a lawsuit against Nintendo alleging that they illegally used the song "You're So Cool" from the film True Romance in an advertisement for the game.

fcube_super_bash_bros_melee.title: Super Smash Bros. Melee
sents: lead
Melee is a 2001 crossover fighting video game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
It is the second installment in the Super Smash Bros. series.
lead
It features characters from Nintendo video game franchises such as Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Star Fox, Pokémon, and Donkey Kong among others.
lead
The stages and gameplay modes reference or take designs from these franchises as well.
lead

Melee includes all playable characters from the first game and also adds characters from additional franchises such as Fire Emblem, of which no games had been released outside Japan at the time, in addition to new stages and gameplay modes.
lead

Like other games in the Smash Bros. series, Melee ' s gameplay system offers an unorthodox approach to the fighting game genre, with a counter that measures damage with increasing percentages, representing the knockback the character will experience, rather than a depleting health bar seen in most fighting games.
lead
Melee was first released in Japan in November 2001, in the Americas in December 2001, and in Europe and Australia in May 2002.
lead

The game received widespread acclaim from critics, earning praise for its visuals, simple controls, gameplay, and orchestrated soundtrack, as well as several awards and acknowledgments from various publications; it is now considered one of the greatest video games ever made.
Gameplay
Most attacks inflict damage and can, if enough damage is dealt, knock back the enemy.
Gameplay
Unlike other games of the same genre, in which moves are entered by button-input combinations, most moves in Super Smash Bros.
Gameplay
Most stages have a theme relating to a Nintendo franchise or a specific Nintendo game and are interactive to the player.
Gameplay
For example, the Mushroom Kingdom stage is from Super Mario Bros, and the Temple stage is from The Legend of Zelda.
Gameplay
Although the stages are rendered in three dimensions, players can only move on a two-dimensional plane.
Single-player
"All-Star Mode" is an unlockable feature that requires the player to defeat every character in the game while having only one stock and three health supplements between battles.
Multiplayer

The two most common multiplayer modes are “Time mode”, where the player or team with the most KOs and least falls wins after a predetermined amount of time, and "Stock mode", a battle in which the last player or team with lives remaining wins.
Trophies
The trophies range from the well-known to the obscure, and even characters or elements only released in Japan.
Trophies
Super Smash Bros. had a similar system of plush dolls; however, it only included the 12 playable characters.
Playable characters
Melee features 25 (26 if Zelda and Sheik are considered separate) characters, 13 (14 with Zelda and Sheik separate) more than its predecessor.
Playable characters
Fourteen are available initially, while the other 11 characters require completing specific tasks to become available.
Development and release
The game was one of the first games released on the GameCube and highlighted the advancement in graphics over the Nintendo 64.
Development and release
The project proposal/initial design document for the game was completed on July 5, 1999.
Development and release
The game was in development for 13 months, beginning around autumn 2000, and Sakurai called his lifestyle during this period "destructive" with no holidays and short weekends.
Development and release
Unlike the experimental first Super Smash Bros., he felt great pressure to deliver a quality sequel, claiming it was the "biggest project I had ever led up to that point".
Development and release

Despite the stressful development cycle, in a 2010 interview, Sakurai proudly called Melee "the sharpest game in the series... it just felt really good to play", even compared to its successor, Super Smash Bros.
Development and release
Initially, the development team wanted to replace Ness with Lucas, the main character of Mother 3, but retained Ness in consideration of delays.
Development and release

Video game developer Hideo Kojima originally requested the inclusion of Solid Snake to Sakurai, and Yuji Naka of Sonic Team requested the inclusion of Sonic the Hedgehog to Sakurai, but neither characters were added as the game was too far in development.
Development and release
Nintendo presented the game at the Electronic Entertainment Expo 2001 as a playable demonstration.
Development and release
The next major exposition of the game came in August 2001 at Space World, when Nintendo displayed a playable demo that updated from the previous demo displayed at E3.
Development and release
Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu reported that Nintendo advertised the game in between showings of Pokémon 4Ever across movie theaters in Japan.
Development and release
In January 2003, Melee was re-released as part of the Player's Choice program, a marketing label used by Nintendo to promote video games that have sold more than a million copies.
Development and release
In August 2005, Nintendo bundled the game with the GameCube for $99.99.
Music
In 2002, Enterbrain released a soundtrack in Japan titled Dairantou Smash Brothers DX Orchestra Concert.
Music
Shogo Sakai took over as the game's composer in place of Hirokazu Ando on February 14, 2001.
Reception
Melee received critical acclaim from reviewers, most of whom credited Melee ' s expansion of gameplay features from Super Smash Bros.
Reception
Caleb Hale from GameCritics.com noted that while it was "every bit as good as its Nintendo 64 predecessor" he also felt "the game doesn't expand much past that point".
Reception
Gaming journalists have welcomed the roster of 26 Nintendo characters, as well as the trophy system, which Nintendo Spin labeled as "a great addition to this game".
Sales
When released in Japan, it became the fastest selling GameCube game with 358,525 units sold in the week ending November 25, 2001.
Sales
This success continued as the game sold more than a million units only two months after its release, making it the first GameCube title to reach a million copies.
Sales
The game also sold well in North America, where it sold 250,000-copies in nine days.
Sales
Melee was the 19th best-selling video game in 2001 according to the NPD Group.
Sales
By July 2006, it had sold 3.2 million copies and earned $125 million in the United States alone.
Sales
Next Generation ranked it as the fifth highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Sales
Approximately 4.06 million units have been sold in the country as of December 27, 2007.
Sales
With a software-to-hardware ratio of 3:4 at one time, some have attributed the increasing sales of the GameCube near the launch date to Melee.
Sales
As of March 10, 2008, Super Smash Bros.
Sales
Melee is the best-selling GameCube game, with more than seven million copies sold worldwide.
Awards and accolades
During the 5th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Super Smash Bros.
Awards and accolades
Melee for " Console Fighting Game of the Year " and " Outstanding Achievement in Animation ", which were ultimately awarded to Dead or Alive 3 and Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee, respectively.
Awards and accolades
GameFAQs placed it sixth in a poll of the 100 best games ever and was in the final four of the "Best.
Awards and accolades

In the 200th issue of Electronic Gaming Monthly, the editors selected Melee as the 92nd most influential game in their "Top 200 Games of Their Time" list, defining Melee as "Billions of things to unlock, plus Yoshi pummeling Pikachu with a bat".
Awards and accolades
Melee the 16th best game ever to appear on a Nintendo console, and selected it as the 2001 "Game of the Year".
Awards and accolades

IGN named it the third best GameCube game of all-time in 2007 as a part of a feature reflecting on the GameCube's long lifespan, citing it as "the grand stage of fighters, much like Mario Kart is for racing fans".
Awards and accolades
The game was ranked 58th in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s "100 Greatest Nintendo Games Ever" feature.
Awards and accolades
In 2019, Game Informer ranked it as the 2nd best fighting game of all time.
Awards and accolades
Edge magazine ranked the game 91st on their 100 best Video Games in 2007.
Competitive scene
Many consider it to be the most competitively viable game in the series.
Competitive scene

Melee version NTSC was first released on the GameCube in 2001 in Japan and later North America, Nintendo ran the first ever Melee tournament named Premium Fight most likely from August 25 to August 27, 2001.
Competitive scene
Several professional Melee players including Christopher "KillaOR" McKenzie, Isai Alvarado, and Ken were seen in the 2005 "I'm a Professional Gamer" episode of the MTV reality series True Life.
Competitive scene
From 2004 to 2007, Major League Gaming sponsored Melee on its Pro Circuit.
Competitive scene
Ken Hoang, also known as "The King of Smash" was considered to be the game's best player from 2003 to 2006, and has won over $50,000 from Smash tournaments.
Competitive scene
Melee was also included in the Evolution Championship Series (Evo) in 2007, a fighting game tournament held in Las Vegas.
Competitive scene
Melee was hosted at Evo 2013 after a charity vote to decide the final game to be featured in its tournament lineup.
Competitive scene
Due to the large turnout and popularity that year, Evo again included Melee at their 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018 events.
Competitive scene
The competitive Smash community was featured in a 2013 crowd-funded documentary called The Smash Brothers.
Competitive scene

The film detailed the history of the professional scene and profiled seven prominent Melee players including Hoang, Azen, Jason "Mew2King" Zimmerman, Isai, PC Chris, KoreanDJ, and Evo 2013 and Evo 2014 champion, Joseph "Mang0" Marquez.

fcube_pocket_critters_collosseum.title: Pokémon Colosseum
sents: lead
Pokémon Colosseum is a role-playing video game developed by Genius Sonority and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
A spin-off of the in the Pokémon series, it was released on November 21, 2003 in Japan, March 22, 2004 in North America and May 14, 2004 in Europe.
lead
Unlike previous titles' random encounters with Pokémon, Colosseum allows the player to steal ("snag") the Pokémon of other Pokémon Trainers.
lead
The game also features single-player and multiplayer battle modes.
lead
Set in the desert region of Orre, the player controls Wes, a former member of Team Snagem.
lead
Throughout the game, Wes rescues "Shadow Pokémon"—Pokémon who have had their hearts darkened by Team Cipher, an antagonistic organization—via snagging.
lead
Rui, a non-player character, serves as Wes's sidekick and identifies Shadow Pokémon.
lead
Pokémon Colosseum was exhibited at E3 2003 and featured Pokémon models ported from the Nintendo 64 's Pokémon Stadium and Pokémon Stadium 2.
Gameplay
Pokémon Colosseum is a 3D role-playing game viewed from a third-person perspective.
Gameplay
Most battles are of the "double battle" format, which means two Pokémon on each side at one time.
Gameplay
Unlike most Pokémon games, Colosseum does not feature random encounters.
Gameplay
Only specifically designated "Shadow Pokémon", whose hearts have been artificially closed, can be Snagged.
Gameplay
Once a Pokémon's gauge is empty, the player may "Purify" the Pokémon by bringing him or her to Celebi 's shrine in Agate Village, or by using a rare "Time Flute" item.
Gameplay
Purifying Shadow Pokémon is desirable because while in that status, they will often disobey the player, they cannot gain experience points, and their moves are at first restricted to "Shadow Rush".
Gameplay

In the single-player battle mode, the player competes at Colosseums—stadiums used throughout the game for Pokémon battles—and earns "Poké Coupons", another currency which can be used to buy rare items.
Gameplay
The first can use Pokémon obtained in the story mode, or from the Game Boy Advance games.
Gameplay
Players two through four, however, can only use Pokémon from the Game Boy Advance games.
Characters
The game's player protagonist is by default named Wes (レオ, Reo, Leo), but as with most Pokémon games, the player can change his name.
Characters
Wes's Starter Pokémon are Espeon and Umbreon, two fox-like Pokémon who start at level 25 and 26, respectively.
Story
With Espeon and Umbreon, Wes's first opponent is a Trainer named Willie.
Story
Battle, Wes and Rui find that Cipher has already taken over the first section of the mountain.
Story

After battling nine other Trainers, Wes battles another Cipher Admin, Dakim, who attacks the Area 1 leader Vander because he holds a relic called a Time Flute that has the ability to summon Celebi to the Relic Stone.
Story
Once defeated, Nascour tries to leave, only to be interrupted by Es Cade, who reveals that he is really none other than Evice, the head of Cipher, and battles Wes.
Development and release

Just as Nintendo 64 predecessors Pokémon Stadium and Pokémon Stadium 2 had served as home console counterparts to the first- and second-generation handheld titles, Colosseum had a similar role for the third generation.
Development and release
The new concept for Pokémon Colosseum was influenced by RPGs such as Final Fantasy VII and Persona 2 over the Pokémon mold.
Development and release
Genius Sonority ported most of the models and animations of first- and second-generation Pokémon from Stadium and Stadium 2.
Development and release
Genius Sonority based most of Orre on the real-life city of Phoenix, Arizona.
Development and release
A preview for the game was hosted at E3 2003.
Development and release

Upon completion of development, Colosseum received a rating of "E" (Everyone) from the Entertainment Software Rating Board, "All Ages" from Computer Entertainment Rating Organization, and "3+" from Pan European Game Information.
Development and release
The game was released on November 21, 2003, in Japan; March 22, 2004, in North America, and May 14, 2004, in Europe.
Development and release
The disc also updates the software in Ruby and Sapphire to remove a "berry glitch" discovered in 2003.
Critical response
Pokémon Colosseum was generally well-received upon release, with respective scores of 73/100 and 73.46% from aggregators Metacritic and GameRankings.
Critical response
During the 8th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Pokémon Colosseum for " Console Children's Game of the Year ".
Critical response
Critics praised Colosseum as the first true 3D role-playing installment in the Pokémon series and for its darker tone.
Critical response

Gamers Hell reviewer John K. called it "certainly a step in the right direction to a good 3D Pokémon game", although he felt that the limited number of Pokémon and lack of a true overworld detracted from the experience.
Critical response
IGN staff writer Craig Harris said that the adaptation of the Pokémon RPG formula to the 3D zeitgeist "does a decent enough job" and is "a bit more linear and straightforward".
Critical response
In 2006, Nintendo Power listed Colosseum as the 121st greatest video game to appear on a Nintendo console.
Sales
Three weeks before its release, pre-orders of Pokémon Colosseum made it the best-selling game on Amazon.com.
Sales
In the game's first week of release in the United Kingdom, it boosted the GameCube's market share from 16% to 32%.
Sales
It was the best-selling GameCube game of May 2004, and fourteenth among all consoles.
Sales
In 2005, the game was certified as part of Nintendo's Player's Choice line in North America, representing at least 250,000 copies sold.
Sales
As of 2007, the game has sold over 1.15 million copies in the United States and 656,270 in Japan.
Legacy
Pokémon Colosseum spawned a high-profile tournament in the United Kingdom entitled "Pokémon Colosseum Battlemaster 2004".
Legacy
The first round of battles was held at Toys "R" Us locations, with later battles taking place in movie theaters.
Legacy
A manga adaptation of Colosseum ' s plot was printed in 2004 issues of the Japanese magazine CoroCoro Comic and titled Pokémon Colosseum Snatcher Leo (ポケモンコロシアムスナッチャーズレオ).
Legacy
The game was followed by a 2005 sequel entitled Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness.

fcube_pocket_critters_xd_gale_of_d.title: Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness
sents: lead
Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness is a role-playing video game in the Pokémon series developed by Genius Sonority and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo.
lead
It was released for the GameCube on August 4, 2005, in Japan; October 3, 2005, in North America; November 10, 2005, in Australia; and November 18, 2005, in Europe.
lead
Pokémon XD is the successor to the GameCube title Pokémon Colosseum and takes place in Orre, the setting of Pokémon Colosseum ' s adventure mode.
lead
All of the Game Boy Advance Pokémon games can connect to this game through trading and Battle Mode.
lead

Pokémon XD was first announced in March 2005 as a new GameCube game and not a sequel to Colosseum, though later developments as well as two promotional demo versions confirmed the game would be similar to its predecessor.
lead
Shadow Pokémon, first introduced in Colosseum, are a major gameplay element, and a Shadow Lugia is featured on the game's box art.
lead
Munchlax and Bonsly, two Pokémon from the fourth generation of main Pokémon games, make debut appearances in Pokémon XD.
lead
The game garnered mixed to positive reviews among critics, with common criticisms being directed at similarities to and re-used assets from Colosseum.
Shadow Pokémon
In this game there are 83 different Shadow Pokémon to collect.
Shadow Pokémon
Shadow moves can be either physical or special, which is the only type of move that was capable of this in Generation III.
Shadow Pokémon
Once the player has obtained 82 of the Shadow Pokémon, Miror B. will appear one final time with the final obtainable Shadow Pokémon in the game.
Purifying Shadow Pokémon
The Purification Chamber allows the player to place anywhere from 1 to 4 Pokémon in a circle and a Shadow Pokémon is placed in the center of this circle.
Mt. Battle
Battle area is an area that is accessible early on in the game and is a 100 trainer challenge.
Mt. Battle
The 100 battles are split into 10 battles in 10 different zones with the trainers in each zone being stronger than the ones in the zone before.
Mt. Battle
When the player defeats an Area Leader the first time the player gets a special item.
Poke Spots
At these 3 locations 9 different wild Pokémon can be captured and they can be traded for rare Pokémon.
Development and marketing
In March 2005, Nintendo of America executive Reggie Fils-Aimé said that Pokémon XD would be a new GameCube game, but not a sequel to Colosseum.
Development and marketing
Japanese gaming magazines Famitsu and CoroCoro Comic later gave screenshots and information that revealed that the game would have 3D graphics similar to those of its predecessor, Pokémon Colosseum.
Reception
Pokémon XD received mixed to positive reviews, usually scoring 6–7 out of 10 (8.6 out of 10 was its highest score).
Reception
Another common complaint were the Poké Spot areas, regarded as very limited and small compared to Ruby and Sapphire.
Reception
While discussing the mixed quality of the Pokémon console games, Retronauts recalled it as an example.
Reception
Like its predecessor, Pokémon XD was a commercial success, selling over 1 million units as of March 31, 2006.

fcube_pocket_critters_box_ruby_sap.title: Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire
sents: lead
Pokémon Omega Ruby and Pokémon Alpha Sapphire are 2014 remakes of the 2002 Game Boy Advance role-playing video games Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire, also including features from Pokémon Emerald.
lead
The games are part of the sixth generation of the Pokémon video game series, developed by Game Freak and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS.
lead

Announced in May 2014, the games were released in Japan, North America and Australia on 21 November 2014, exactly twelve years after the original release date of Ruby and Sapphire, while the European release was the following week.
lead
Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire received generally positive reviews from critics.
lead
As of 31 March 2023, a combined total of 14.57 million copies have been sold worldwide, ranking them as the fourth-best-selling Nintendo 3DS titles of all time.
Gameplay
The games introduced a unique mechanic for Kyogre and Groudon dubbed "Primal Reversion", akin to the broader Mega Evolution feature.
Setting and story
Aside from the gameplay, 21 new Mega Evolutions were added since Pokémon X and Y, as well as "primal reversions" for Groudon and Kyogre, which function similarly.
Release

Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire were released in Japan, North America and Australia on 21 November 2014, exactly twelve years after the original release date of Ruby and Sapphire, while the European release was the following week.
Release
They are the third remake pairs in the franchise following Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen for the Game Boy Advance in 2004 and Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver for the Nintendo DS in 2009.
Release

As with Pokémon X and Y, the games include all official translations, unlike previous generations where games contained only certain languages depending on the region or country they were originally distributed.
Reception
GameSpot ' s Peter Brown praised the 3D visuals and the super training mechanic, but believed the game failed to fully resolve general issues in the game formula.
Reception
IGN ' s Kallie Plagge also praised the game's 3D reinvention of Hoenn and online functionality.
Reception
At the 2014 Game Awards it was nominated for Best Remaster, but lost out to Grand Theft Auto V.
Sales
The games sold 3,040,000 copies in their first three days of sale.
Sales
Of the total sales, 1,534,593 copies were sold in Japan, the rest were sold in North America and Australia.
Sales
Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire had the biggest launch in the series history in the United Kingdom, beating the previous record held by Pokémon Black and White.
Sales
By the end of 2014, the games had sold 2.4 million copies in Japan.
Sales
As of 31 March 2023, a combined total of 14.57 million copies have been sold worldwide, ranking them as the fourth-best-selling Nintendo 3DS titles of all time.

fcube_brother_s_mansion.title: Luigi's Mansion
sents: lead
Luigi's Mansion is a 2001 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo.
lead

The game was a launch title for the GameCube and was the first game in the Mario franchise to be released for the console; it was released in Japan on September 14, 2001, in North America on November 18, 2001, in Europe on May 3, 2002, and in Australia on May 17, 2002.
lead
It is the third video game in which Luigi is the main character instead of Mario, after Mario Is Missing! and Luigi's Hammer Toss.
lead
Players control him as he explores a haunted mansion, searches for Mario and deals with ghosts by capturing them through a vacuum cleaner supplied by Professor E.
lead
Luigi's Mansion received a positive critical reception overall, with reviewers praising the gameplay, setting, and soundtrack, though its short length was criticized.
lead
The game has sold over 3.3 million copies, and is the fifth-best-selling GameCube game of all time.
lead
It was one of the first games to be re-released as a Player's Choice title on the system, and achieved a cult following.
lead
The game was followed by two sequels – Luigi's Mansion: Dark Moon, released for the Nintendo 3DS in 2013, and Luigi's Mansion 3, which was released for the Nintendo Switch in 2019.
Gameplay
Gadd – the Poltergust 3000, a specially modified, high-powered vacuum cleaner; and the Game Boy Horror, a play on Nintendo's Game Boy Color.
Gameplay
To capture ghosts, Luigi must first stun a ghost with his flashlight, revealing its heart.
Gameplay
Rooms will usually have treasure hidden within, which can be either coins, bills, gold bars, pearls, or gems, hidden within objects and even in chests that appear when rooms are cleared.
Gameplay
Boos can only be located in cleared rooms.
Gameplay
Completing the game once unlocks a second mode called the "Hidden Mansion", which features a stronger Poltergust and stronger ghosts.
Plot
Luigi has been notified about winning a mansion in a contest he never entered.
Plot
Gadd entrusts Luigi with his ghost-hunting equipment, the Poltergust 3000 vacuum cleaner and Game Boy Horror communication device, as the latter re-enters the mansion to find Mario.
Plot

Working his way through each of the darkened floors, halls and locked rooms, Luigi recaptures the escaped portrait ghosts and discovers that Mario has been trapped inside of a painting by King Boo and held captive in a secret ritualistic altar in the mansion's basement.
Plot

While recapturing the last of the sheltered ghosts, Luigi finds the key that unlocks the door to the altar and confronts King Boo, who, now disdainful over Luigi capturing his subjects, pulls Luigi into the painting.
Plot
Gadd's laboratory, he informs Luigi that the mansion (which is also an illusion) has ceased to exist as they turn King Boo into a painting along with the last of the recaptured portrait ghosts.
Development
The game was revealed at Nintendo Space World 2000 as a technological demo designed to show off the graphical capabilities of the GameCube.
Development
A newer version of the game, more closely related to the final version, was revealed at Nintendo Space World 2001.
Development
Older concepts, such as a role-playing game -like system which made real-time changes to rooms, as well as a cave area located under the mansion, were scrapped due to the inclusion of the new ideas.
Development
Luigi's Mansion received an award for its audio by BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Awards in 2002.
Development

All GameCube systems support the display of stereoscopic 3D, and Luigi's Mansion was planned to utilize this feature; however, 3D televisions were not widespread at the time, and it was deemed that compatible displays would be too cost-prohibitive for the consumer.
Reception
Commercially, Luigi's Mansion is the most successful GameCube launch title and the best-selling game of November 2001.
Reception
It sold 257,000 units during its first week on sale in the United States.
Reception
According to Nintendo, the game was a large driving force behind the GameCube's launch sales and sold more copies in its opening week than Super Mario 64 had managed to sell.
Reception
Despite meager sales in Japan at around 348,000 units in total, it became the fifth best-selling GameCube game in the United States, with sales of roughly 2.19 million units.
Reception
In total it sold 3.33 million copies worldwide by 2020.
Reception
The Japanese video game publication Famitsu awarded the game with a gold rating, and noted that the control system, while tricky at first, works well.
Reception
GameSpot later named Luigi's Mansion the most disappointing game of 2001.
Reception
Luigi's Mansion was awarded the 2002 BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Award for audio.
Reception
The game placed 99th in Official Nintendo Magazine 's 100 greatest Nintendo games of all time.
Legacy
Gadd has reappeared in other Mario games, such as Mario Party 6 and Mario & Luigi: Partners in Time.
Legacy

King Boo has also reappeared in other games, either as a boss (including Super Mario 64 DS and Super Princess Peach) or a playable character (including Mario Kart: Double Dash and Mario Super Sluggers).
Legacy
It appeared in Mario Kart: Double Dash!!, Mario Kart DS, Mario Kart 7, Mario Kart 8 (Deluxe), Mario Power Tennis, Mario Super Sluggers, Mario Hoops 3-on-3, Mario Sports Mix, Super Smash Bros.
Legacy
A direct sequel for the Nintendo 3DS, Luigi's Mansion: Dark Moon, was released in March 2013, almost twelve years after the release of Luigi's Mansion, to celebrate the Year of Luigi.
Legacy
In 2015, Nintendo released Luigi's Mansion Arcade, an arcade game based on Luigi's Mansion: Dark Moon developed by Capcom and published by Sega.
Legacy
The game uses the same plot as Dark Moon, but goes for a first-person, on-rails gameplay style, and utilizes a special vacuum-based controller.
Legacy
A third installment, titled Luigi's Mansion 3, was released for the Nintendo Switch on October 31, 2019.
3DS remake
A remake of Luigi's Mansion for the Nintendo 3DS, co-developed by Nintendo and Grezzo, was announced on March 8, 2018, and released on October 12, 2018.
3DS remake

Several years prior to the remake's official announcement as a commercial project, Shigeru Miyamoto designed a working prototype of the game running on a 3DS development kit to test the system's hardware and 3D functionality, which ultimately led to the development of Luigi's Mansion: Dark Moon.
3DS remake
The remake has amiibo functionality and supports gyroscopic controls, the Circle Pad Pro accessory, the C-Stick on New Nintendo 3DS models, and stereoscopic 3D.
3DS remake
All regional releases of the remake also incorporate elements from the PAL version's Hidden Mansion, increasing the difficulty of the second quest in the North American and Japanese versions.
3DS remake
If the player scores high enough in the Hidden Mansion, they will achieve Rank S, one level higher than A, and be shown an even more luxurious version of Luigi's new mansion after the credits.
3DS remake
As of 2018, it has sold 90,410 copies in Japan, making it the third best-selling Nintendo 3DS release of 2018 behind WarioWare Gold and Detective Pikachu.
3DS remake

Critical reception to the remake was generally positive; reviewers appreciated the effort put into the revamped visuals and many believe the core experience to largely hold up 17 years after the original release.
3DS remake
Outlets also spoke positively about the implementation of stereoscopic 3D and the two screens as well as the new content such as the boss rush mode and the PAL Hidden Mansion.

fcube_eternal_dorkness_sanity_s_re.title: Eternal Darkness
sents: lead
Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem is a 2002 action-adventure video game developed by Silicon Knights and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
It was produced and directed by Denis Dyack.
lead
The game follows the story of several characters across a period of two millennia and four different locations on Earth, as they contend with an ancient evil who seeks to enslave humanity.
lead
The gameplay distinguishes itself with unique "sanity effects", visual and audial effects that confuse the player and often break the fourth wall.
lead
Development began on Eternal Darkness after Nintendo, impressed with Silicon Knights' Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain (1996), contacted the company to propose a collaboration on an original mature title.
lead
Silicon Knights based their concept around Lovecraftian horror and the Eternal Champion concept, and decidedly avoided making a survival horror game.
lead
It was originally planned for the Nintendo 64, and was mostly completed before development was moved to Nintendo's forthcoming home console, the GameCube.
lead
It was the first game published by Nintendo to receive an M (Mature) rating from the Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB).
Gameplay
Decapitating most enemies effectively blinds them.
Gameplay
Some of the more common enemies vary very little in appearance, usually only changing in hue and aesthetics, but may have some behavioral differences.
Gameplay
The story features multiple paths that can be taken at the end of the first chapter.
Gameplay
Some changes include slight differences in puzzles and items, but most changes revolve around enemy placement, which will determine how the player engages them.
Gameplay
Magick can be used by most characters and consists of spells that can be used to damage opponents, protect characters and heal them, and be used to solve certain puzzles.
Gameplay
This robust mechanic of experimentation has been praised by game critics as unique, and something that sets the magick system in this apart from most magic systems of most other game titles.
Gameplay
Stronger effects include bleeding on walls and ceilings, entering a room that is unrealistic before finding that the character never left the previous room, or the character suddenly dying.
Story
The story moves between these locations, with each chapter occurring during a different time period (between 26 B.C. and 2000 A.D.), and from the perspective of a different character.
Plot
In 2000 AD, Alexandra Roivas returns to her family's estate in Rhode Island after her grandfather, Edward Roivas, her only living relative, is found brutally murdered.
Plot
Alex decides to investigate the mansion for clues, and stumbles upon a secret room containing a book bound with human skin called the Tome of Eternal Darkness.
Plot
Deciding to read it, she finds it contains accounts of various people in the past, beginning with the story of Pious Augustus in 26 BC.
Plot
In 565 AD, a young swordsman named Karim, ventures to the Forbidden City to locate a treasure for a woman that he loves.
Plot
In 1460 AD Roberto Bianchi, a Venetian architect traveling through the region, is captured by Pious under the guise of a warlord.
Plot
Centuries later in 1991 AD, a Canadian firefighter named Michael Edwards works with his team to extinguish several major oil fires in the Middle East, following the end of the Gulf War.
Plot
A few months later, Michael delivers the artifact to Edward Roivas in secret, telling him that he "won't last a night".
Plot
First, though, Pious orders the assassination of Charlemagne, so his movement cannot impede his plans.
Plot
In 814 AD, a Frankish messenger named Anthony, who stumbles upon the plot, travels to the then small monastery in order to warn him of the danger to his life.
Plot
In 1485 AD a Franciscan friar named Paul Luther, visiting the region to view a holy relic at the cathedral, finds himself accused of murdering a fellow friar by the local Inquisition.
Plot
In 1916 AD, During World War I, Oublié Cathedral is converted into a field hospital.
Plot
In 1150 AD, Pious travels to a temple in Angkor Thom, Cambodia in order to deal with Mantorok.
Plot
Now only Mantorok remains, slowly dying.
Development
The project's origins can be traced back to the mid-1990s when Nintendo staff saw Silicon Knights' game Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain (1996) at an E3 gaming convention.
Development
The game was originally in development for the Nintendo 64 (N64).
Development
The team used 3D Studio Max for modelling and Photoshop for textures.
Development
By 2000, much of development had been completed, and it was presented and playable at industry trade shows.
Development
When the September 11 attacks occurred, Silicon Knights opted to remove the character Joseph De Molay, a Templar knight, from the game.
Release

Short films
In 2002, Nintendo and Hypnotic, a film entertainment company, established a filmmaking contest in which contestants submitted ideas that would be later funded into short films if selected.

Short films
The grand prize for the contest was $20,000, and was selected by a panel of industry experts.
Short films
The finalists were unveiled between May 23 and July 4, 2002.
Reviews and sales

AllGame editor Scott Alan Marriott described Eternal Darkness as "fun" and "certainly worth playing".
Reviews and sales
In Japan, the game has sold 17,748 copies as of December 31, 2006.
Retrospective

In 2006, Nintendo Power ranked Eternal Darkness as the 101st top game on Nintendo systems, while the readers of IGN had it voted as the 96th best video game of all time on all systems; in 2009, Official Nintendo Magazine had it listed as the 48th best Nintendo game.

Both X-Play and Game Informer in 2007 in 2006 ranked it as the fifth scariest game of all time.

In other lists, ScrewAttack ranked the fake "Corrupt Data" sanity effect as the ninth top "OMGWTF" moment in gaming in 2008, while Alex Roivas was included among the 50 greatest heroines in video games by Tom's Games in 2007 and ranked as the 40th greatest heroine in video game history by Complex in 2013.
Retrospective

IGN included Eternal Darkness on their 2008 list of "horror franchises that should rise from the grave", GamesRadar included Eternal Darkness among the games "with untapped franchise potential" in 2009, and UGO included it on a similar list of games "that need sequels" in 2010.
Legacy
Alex Roivas makes a cameo appearance in the 2018 fighting game Super Smash Bros.
Cancelled sequel
In 2006, Dyack said "absolutely yes" in response to the question of a possible sequel.
Cancelled sequel
At Microsoft's Spring 2008 Showcase, Dyack said there was a "strong chance" they would return to the Eternal Darkness brand.
Cancelled sequel
In 2011, Silicon Knights said they were refocusing on one of their most requested titles for the next generation of consoles.
