Any possibility for a sequel from Silicon Knights ended in 2013 when Silicon Knights filed for bankruptcy and closed its offices.
Shadow of the Eternals

In May 2013, Precursor Games, staffed by many former Silicon Knights members, had begun a crowdfunding campaign on their website, seeking $1.5 million to create a spiritual successor to Eternal Darkness under the title Shadow of the Eternals, to be released for Microsoft Windows and Wii U.
Shadow of the Eternals
The game was to be released in twelve 2-4 hour long episodes, with Dyack acting as the game's chief creative officer.
Shadow of the Eternals
The same month, a secondary fundraising campaign was launched on Kickstarter, aiming to receive $1.35 million within 36 days.
Shadow of the Eternals

Eventually, being only halfway through their campaign in early June, the company decided to shut down both funding campaigns whilst refunding all the accumulated money back to their contributors, and promised to relaunch a new campaign a few weeks later.
Shadow of the Eternals
Another Kickstarter campaign was launched in July, aiming for a $750,000 goal this time.
Shadow of the Eternals
Instead of twelve episodes, the game was intended to be released as one 8-10 hour experience.
Shadow of the Eternals
Though Nintendo still owns the rights to Eternal Darkness and the patent for the game's unique "Sanity Meter", Precursor Games was in communication with Nintendo, who was supportive of the project.
Shadow of the Eternals
Kyle Hilliard of Game Informer wrote that he was not surprised the game was put on hold, as it has been "plagued with issues" since its first announcement.

In January 2018, QEE was quietly shut down and the production of Shadow of the Eternals was cancelled.

fcube_resident_weevil_0.title: Resident Evil (1996 video game)
sents: lead
Resident Evil is a 1996 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation.
lead
It is the first game in Capcom's Resident Evil franchise.
lead
Players control Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine, members of the elite task force S.T.A.R.S., who must escape a mansion infested with zombies and other monsters.
lead
Resident Evil was conceived by the producer Tokuro Fujiwara as a remake of his 1989 horror game Sweet Home (1989).
lead
It went through several redesigns, first as Super NES game in 1993, then a fully 3D first-person PlayStation game in 1994 and finally a third-person game.
lead
Gameplay consists of action, exploration, puzzle solving and inventory management.
lead

Resident Evil established many conventions seen later in the series, and in other survival horror games, including the inventory system, save system, and use of a vitals-monitoring system instead of a health counter.
lead
Resident Evil was praised for its graphics, gameplay, sound, and atmosphere, although it received some criticism for its dialogue and voice acting.
Gameplay
The game is presented with real-time 3D polygonal characters and objects, superimposed over pre-rendered backdrops with fixed camera angles.
Gameplay

The player's health, represented by an electrocardiogram, goes down whenever the player is caught by a zombie or other hazard - if they run out, the character dies, resulting in a game over and forcing the player to restart from their last save, although herbs and first aid spray can be used to heal.
Plot

On July 24, 1998, when a series of bizarre murders occur on the outskirts of the fictional Midwestern town of Raccoon City, the Raccoon City Police Department's S.T.A.R.S. team are assigned to investigate.
Plot
Eventually, the player character discovers a secret underground laboratory containing Umbrella's experiments.
Plot
After activating the lab's self-destruct system, the player character reaches the heliport and manages to contact Brad for extraction, at which point the Tyrant may confront them one last time.
Plot

If at least the partner survives, the Tyrant is defeated and the mansion destroyed, otherwise the mansion remains intact and the Tyrant remains loose in the forest if the partner or team member is left to permanently die.
Design
Resident Evil was created by a team of staff members who would later become part of Capcom Production Studio 4.
Design
The inspiration for Resident Evil was the earlier Capcom horror game Sweet Home (1989), itself a video game adaption of the Japanese horror film of the same name.
Design
Part of the inspiration for limited ammunition came from the MSX port of the game Alcazar: The Forgotten Fortress, according to scenario writer Kenichi Iwao.
Design
The idea of having limited ammunition was inspired by the limited amount of supplies in the game's randomized dungeons.
Production
Production began in 1993, and the game took three years to develop.
Production
During the first six months of development, Mikami worked on the game alone, creating concept sketches, designing characters, and writing over 40 pages of script.
Production
The project was originally planned for the Super NES, before moving development to the PlayStation in 1994.
Production
Koji Oda was working on the Super NES version, after having worked on Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts (1991).
Production
Oda revealed that the setting was originally more of a hellish place, before being changed to a more realistic setting.
Production
Several of the Resident Evil mansion's pre-rendered backdrops were inspired by The Overlook Hotel, the setting for the 1980 horror film, The Shining.
Production
Mikami also cited the 1978 film Dawn of the Dead as a negative inspiration for the game.
Production
The game was initially conceived as a fully 3D first-person update of Sweet Home (influenced by the game's first-person battles), with action and shooting mechanics.
Production

A first-person prototype was produced, and initially featured a supernatural, psychological Japanese horror style similar to Sweet Home, before opting for an American zombie horror style influenced by George Romero films.
Production
During production, Mikami discovered Alone in the Dark (1992), which influenced him to adopt a cinematic fixed-view camera system.
Production
Mikami said that, if it was not for Alone in the Dark, Resident Evil would have had a first-person view instead.
Production
A first-person perspective was not used again for the mainline Resident Evil series until Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (2017).
Production

A later prototype featured cooperative gameplay, but this feature was eventually removed, as Mikami said it "technically...wasn't good enough." Early footage of this co-op prototype was revealed in 1995.
Production
A later demo made for the 1995 V Jump Festival presentation in Japan featured real-time weapon changes, with the co-op mode removed and rudimentary character models and textures.
Production
An early 1996 preview in Maximum Console magazine featured a graveyard and a slightly different version of the final boss.
Production
The graveyard, which was removed from the final game, eventually made it into the 2002 remake.
Production
Another feature that was removed from the final game was the real-time weapon changing, from the earlier 1995 V-Jump demo.
Production
The PlayStation was chosen as the lead platform because the development team felt it was the most appropriate for the game in terms of things such as the amount of polygons.
Production
The development team had upwards of 80 people towards the end of the game's development.
Production
A Saturn version was finally unveiled at the April 1997 Tokyo Game Show, at which Capcom also showed a demo for the sequel on PlayStation.
Production
Fujiwara said the game was originally targeted towards a core audience and he only expected it to sell around 200,000 copies, before the game went on to sell millions.
English localization
Among others, the 1992 video game Bio-Hazard Battle and the New York alternative metal band Biohazard were already using the name.
English localization
Despite these tweaks, the game was ultimately released on the PlayStation as one of the first games to receive the Mature rating from the Entertainment Software Rating Board.
Releases
Resident Evil was initially released for the PlayStation in Japan on March 22, 1996, in North America on April 1, and in Europe on August 16.
Windows
The Windows version, released in December 1996, featured the uncensored footage from the Japanese version, and the opening intro is in full color rather than black and white.
Windows
Support for 3D accelerator cards were added, allowing for much sharper graphics.
Windows
Two new unlockable weapons were added, a MAC-10 for Jill and an FN Minimi for Chris.
Windows
The original Windows version was re-released on June 26, 2024 by GOG.com to include quality of life improvements and enhanced compatibility.
Sega Saturn

The Japanese version is the most gore-laden of all the platforms; after decapitating a crawling zombie with a kick, the head remains on the floor, and Plant 42 can cut the character before the game over screen; though the live-action footage is censored in the U.S. version.
Director's Cut
A second version for the PlayStation, Resident Evil: Director's Cut, was released in September 1997.
Director's Cut
Director's Cut was produced to compensate for the highly publicized delay of the sequel, Resident Evil 2, and was originally bundled with a playable pre-release demo of that game.
Director's Cut

The main characters, as well as Rebecca, are given a new wardrobe and the player's handgun is replaced by an improved model where any shot fired has a random chance of decapitating a zombie, killing it instantly.
Director's Cut
Director's Cut was included in the lineup for the PlayStation Classic, which was released on December 3, 2018.
Director's Cut
It was made available on PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 on June 13, 2022.
Director's Cut Dual Shock Ver.
(デュアルショックver.), co-produced by Keiji Inafune, was released in August 1998.
Director's Cut Dual Shock Ver.
The symphonic music was credited to composer Mamoru Samuragochi, although he admitted in 2014 that he directed his orchestrator Takashi Niigaki to ghostwrite the new soundtrack.
Director's Cut Dual Shock Ver.
In 1998, Capcom USA released the game under PlayStation's Greatest Hits label.
Game Boy Color version

A Game Boy Color version of the game, developed by the Software House HotGen, was supposed to be released in late 1999 or early 2000, until Capcom decided to cancel this project citing that the port was poor quality due to the Game Boy's limited hardware.
Game Boy Color version
In January 2012, an anonymous individual claimed to have an EPROM cartridge of the GBC version and requested $2,000 before he was willing to leak the playable ROM.
Deadly Silence
The DS version also includes updated play mechanics: the 180-degree turn introduced in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, along with the knife button and tactical reload from Resident Evil 4.
Deadly Silence
Gameplay and combat are otherwise uncensored, thus making this the first of 11 DS games to ever be rated Mature 17+ by the ESRB.
Deadly Silence
"Knife Battle" sequences, viewed from a first-person perspective, are also added, in which the player must fend off incoming enemies by swinging the knife via the stylus.
Deadly Silence
The first is a cooperative mode in which each player must help each other solve puzzles and escape the mansion together.
Deadly Silence
The other is a competitive mode in which the objective is to get the highest score out of all the players by destroying the most monsters, with the tougher monsters being worth more points.
Reception
The original PlayStation version of Resident Evil was critically acclaimed, receiving an aggregated rating of 91 out of 100 at Metacritic based on eight reviews.
Reception
Among those who praised the game was GameSpot, describing it as "one of those rare games that's almost as entertaining to watch as it is to play".
Reception
Famitsu gave it ratings of 9, 10, 10 and 9 out of 10, adding up to 38 out of 40.
Reception
This made it one of their three highest-rated games of 1996, along with Super Mario 64 (which scored 39/40) and Tekken 2 (which scored 38/40).
Reception
Resident Evil was also one of only ten games to have received a Famitsu score of 38/40 or above up until 1996.
Reception
Sushi-X remarked that it, "at first glance, may appear to be a clone of Alone in the Dark, but in reality, it is a totally new experience".
Reception
After trading blows with the first zombie, you'll quickly become hesitant to turn down any uncharted corridors in the mansion."
Reception
The Director's Cut was positively received as well, with most critics regarding the advanced mode and the bundled Resident Evil 2 demo as the highlights.
Sales
Shortly after release, it became the best-selling PlayStation game ever at the time.
Sales
In Japan, the game sold 1.016 million units in 1996 which made if the 4th best-selling game of the year, only trailing Pocket Monsters, Tekken 2 and Super Mario RPG.
Sales
In the United States, the game sold over 1 million copies by early September 1996, becoming a system-seller for the PlayStation and increasing its install base at the time.
Sales
In Europe, the game shipped 230,000 units on its first day of release, with 21,500 sold on its first weekend in the United Kingdom where it was one of the fastest-selling CD releases up until then.
Sales
The game went on to sell at least more than 300,000 units in Europe by December 1996.
Sales
By December 1997, the game had sold about 4 million units worldwide and grossed more than $200,000,000 (equivalent to $389,000,000 in 2023).
Sales

According to Capcom's investor relations website, the original version of Resident Evil has sold over 2.75 million copies, while the Director's Cut version (including the Dual Shock edition) sold an additional 2.33 million copies.
Sales
All PlayStation versions of the game have sold a combined 5.08 million units worldwide.
Accolades
Resident Evil was the first game to be dubbed a " survival horror ", a term that it coined for the genre.
Accolades
Game Informer referred to the original Resident Evil as "one of the most important games of all-time" in 2007.
Accolades
In 2012, Time named it one of the 100 greatest video games of all time.
Accolades

That same year, the game ranked as one of G4TV 's top video games of all time for how it has "launched one of the most successful series in gaming history and provided one of its most memorable scares." Resident Evil was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2024.
Accolades
Stuff ranked it as the 3rd best PlayStation game of all time.
Sequels
The series has become Capcom 's biggest franchise.
Sequels
The events of the game were also retold in Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles, originally released for the Wii in 2007.
Novelization
Perry in 1998 as the first book in her series of Resident Evil novels.
Novelization

The book also takes liberty with some of the original source materials; the most notable difference being the inclusion of an original character named Trent, an insider from the Umbrella Corporation who provides Jill with information about the Spencer Mansion prior to the events of the mansion incident.
Novelization

Overall, despite having been written before the retcon introduced in the Resident Evil remake and Resident Evil Zero, the book still maintains overall similarity to what the story warped into in the early 2000s.
Remake
In 2002, Resident Evil was remade for the GameCube as part of an exclusivity agreement between Capcom and Nintendo that spanned three new games.
Remake

A remastered version of the remake, featuring high definition graphics, was released as a download for the PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Windows, Xbox 360, Xbox One in 2015 then later for Nintendo Switch in 2019, with a limited edition PlayStation 3 version released at retail in Japan.
Cultural impact
GameSpot listed Resident Evil as one of the 15 most influential video games of all time.
Cultural impact
Resident Evil is credited with sparking a revival of the zombie genre in popular culture since the late 1990s, leading to a renewed interest in zombie films during the 2000s.
Cultural impact
In 2013, George Romero said it was the video games Resident Evil and The House of the Dead "more than anything else" that popularised zombies in early 21st-century popular culture.
Cultural impact

In a 2015 interview with Huffington Post, screenwriter-director Alex Garland credited the original Resident Evil video game as a primary influence on his script for the horror film 28 Days Later (2002), and credited the first Resident Evil game for revitalizing the zombie genre.
Cultural impact
Shaun of the Dead (2004) star and co-writer Simon Pegg also credits the original Resident Evil game with starting the zombie revival in popular culture.
Cultural impact
The Resident Evil film adaptations also went on to become the highest-grossing film series based on video games, after they grossed more than $1 billion worldwide.
Cultural impact
The zombie revival trend was popular up until the mid-2010s, before zombie films declined in popularity by the late 2010s.

Kennedy on a mission to rescue the US president's daughter, Ashley Graham, who has been kidnapped by a religious cult in rural Spain.

lead
In a departure from the fixed camera angles and slower gameplay of previous Resident Evil games, Resident Evil 4 features a dynamic camera system and action-oriented gameplay.

President's daughter, who has been abducted by a mysterious cult.

Legacy

Resident Evil 4 is regarded as one of the most influential games of the 2000s, particularly due to its influence in redefining the third-person shooter genre by introducing offset camera angles that do not obscure action.
Legacy
In 2019, Game Informer called Resident Evil 4 "the most important third-person shooter ever" and said it "innovated two genres", inspiring developers of both survival horror and shooter games.
Legacy
While working on The Last of Us, Naughty Dog took cues from Resident Evil 4, particularly the tension and action.
Legacy

Dead Space designers Ben Wanat and Wright Bagwell stated that their game was originally intended to be System Shock 3 before the release of Resident Evil 4 inspired them to go back to the drawing board.
Legacy

Cory Barlog cited Resident Evil 4 as an influence on the God of War series, including God of War II (2007) and particularly God of War (2018), which was influenced by Resident Evil 4 ' s "combination of poised camera exploration and scavenging".
Legacy

Resident Evil Village is heavily influenced by Resident Evil 4 with its own director stating, "If Resident Evil 7 was like a reboot that inherited the DNA of the original Resident Evil, then you could say that this time we're doing the same for Resident Evil 4.
Legacy
Some critics have included the Regenerator in retrospective "top" lists of the scariest or most memorable monsters in video games.
Legacy
A remake of Resident Evil 4 was released on March 24, 2023 on PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S.
Legacy
The remake was also announced for the iPhone 15 Pro, to be released between late 2023 to early 2024.
Legacy
A dismissal was filed on February 7, 2022 with the District of Connecticut to end the lawsuit.

fcube_resident_weevil_funcube.title: Resident Evil
sents: lead
Resident Evil, known as Biohazard in Japan, is a Japanese horror game series and media franchise created by Capcom.
lead
It consists of survival horror, third-person shooter and first-person shooter games, with players typically surviving in environments inhabited by zombies and other mutated creatures.
lead
The franchise has expanded into other media, including a live-action film series, animated films, television series, comic books, novels, audiobooks, and merchandise.
lead
Resident Evil is the highest-grossing horror franchise.
lead
The first Resident Evil game was created by Shinji Mikami and Tokuro Fujiwara for PlayStation, and released in 1996.
lead
It is credited for defining the survival horror genre and returning zombies to popular culture.
lead
With Resident Evil 4 (2005), the franchise shifted to more dynamic shooting action, popularizing the "over-the-shoulder" third-person view in action-adventure games.
lead
The franchise returned to survival horror with Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (2017) and Resident Evil Village (2021), which used a first-person perspective.
History

The development of the first Resident Evil, released as Biohazard in Japan, began in 1993 when Capcom 's Tokuro Fujiwara told Shinji Mikami and other co-workers to create a game using elements from Fujiwara's 1989 game Sweet Home on the Family Computer (Famicom) in Japan.
History
Resident Evil made its debut on the PlayStation in 1996 and was later ported to the Sega Saturn.
History

The first entry in the series was the first game to be dubbed a " survival horror ", a term coined for the new genre it initiated, and its critical and commercial success led to the production of two sequels, Resident Evil 2 in 1998 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis in 1999, both for the PlayStation.
History
A port of Resident Evil 2 was released for the Nintendo 64.
History
The fourth game in the series, Resident Evil – Code: Veronica, was developed for the Dreamcast and released in 2000, followed by ports of Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
History

The next three games in the series—a remake of the original Resident Evil and the prequel Resident Evil Zero, both released in 2002, as well as Resident Evil 4 (2005)—were all released initially as GameCube exclusives.
History
Resident Evil 4 was later released for Windows, PlayStation 2, and Wii.
History
A trilogy of GunCon -compatible light gun games known as the Gun Survivor series featured first-person gameplay.
History
The first, Resident Evil Survivor, was released in 2000 for the PlayStation and PC but received mediocre reviews.
History
The subsequent games, Resident Evil Survivor 2 – Code: Veronica and Resident Evil: Dead Aim, fared somewhat better.
History
Dead Aim is the fourth Gun Survivor game in Japan, with Gun Survivor 3 being the Dino Crisis spin-off Dino Stalker.
History
In a similar vein, the Chronicles series features first-person gameplay, albeit on an on-rails path.
History
Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles was released in 2007 for the Wii, with a sequel, Resident Evil: The Darkside Chronicles released in 2009 (both were later ported to the PlayStation 3 in 2012).
History

Resident Evil Outbreak is an online game for the PlayStation 2, released in 2003, depicting a series of episodic storylines in Raccoon City set during the same period as Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
History
It was the first in the series and the first survival horror game to feature cooperative gameplay.
History
The town served as a critical junction for the series' progression as one of the main catalysts to Umbrella's downfall and the entry point for some of the series' most notable characters.
History

At the Sony press conference during E3 2009, Resident Evil Portable was announced for the PlayStation Portable, described as a new game being developed with "the PSP Go in mind" and "totally different for a Resident Evil game".
History
In 2009, Resident Evil 5 was released for PlayStation 3, Windows and Xbox 360, becoming the best selling game of the franchise despite mixed fan reception.
History
Capcom revealed the third-person shooter Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon City, which was developed by Slant Six Games for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and Windows and released in March 2012.
History
A survival horror game for the Nintendo 3DS, Resident Evil: Revelations, was released in February 2012.
History
In October of the same year, the next numbered entry in the main series, Resident Evil 6, was released to mixed reviews, but enthusiastic pre-order sales.
History

In 2013, producer Masachika Kawata said the Resident Evil franchise would return to focus on elements of horror and suspense over action, adding that "survival horror as a genre is never going to be on the same level, financially, as shooters and much more popular, mainstream games.
History
A series of team-based multiplayer games were developed beginning with the poorly received Umbrella Corps, which was released in June 2016.
History

Resident Evil: Resistance was released in April 2020, followed by Resident Evil Re:Verse in October 2022, with both being available for free to those who bought Resident Evil 3 and Village respectively.
History
The next mainline game, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard was released for Windows, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in January 2017.
History
Set in a dilapidated mansion in Louisiana, the game uses a first-person perspective and emphasizes horror and exploration over action, unlike previous installments.
History
The first-person perspective continued in the eighth mainline game Resident Evil Village.
History
Released in May 2021, the game, set in a mysterious European village, is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard although it incorporates more action elements inspired from Resident Evil 4.
History
A new generation of remakes of older entries began in 2019 with a remake of Resident Evil 2, being released for the PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One.
History
The remake outsold the original game within a year, selling over five million copies.
History
Following in the success of the Resident Evil 2 remake, Capcom revealed a remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis in December 2019, known as Resident Evil 3.
History
In June 2022, a remake of Resident Evil 4 was announced and released on March 24, 2023 for PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC.
Story overview
The STARS team is mostly decimated by zombies and other BOWs, leaving only a handful of survivors, including Chris Redfield, Jill Valentine, and Albert Wesker.
Story overview
Chris and Jill explore the zombie-infested mansion and uncover a secret underground Umbrella research facility.
Story overview
Most of the city's residents are infected and become zombies.
Story overview
Resident Evil 6 features Leon and Chris meeting for the first time in the video game series.
Story overview
Ethan, Mia, and their newborn daughter, Rosemary, are relocated to Eastern Europe but are abducted by a cult.
Tank controls
The first game introduced a control scheme that the player community has come to refer to as " tank controls " to the series.
Tank controls
While the first three entries in the series featured this control scheme, the third, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, saw some action-oriented additions.
First-person shooter gameplay and VR
Resident Evil 7 is the first main Resident Evil game to use the first-person perspective and to use virtual reality.
First-person shooter gameplay and VR
The eighth main-series game, Resident Evil Village, also features a first-person perspective.
First-person shooter gameplay and VR
A VR version of Resident Evil 4 was released on the Oculus Quest 2 on October 21, 2021.
Live-action films
From 2002 to 2016, six live-action Resident Evil films were produced, all written and produced by Paul W.
Live-action films
Despite a negative reaction from critics, the live-action film series has made over $1 billion worldwide.
Live-action films

The series holds the record for the "Most Live-Action Film Adaptations of a Video Game" in the 2012 Guinness World Records Gamer's Edition, which also described it as "the most successful movie series to be based on a video game."
Live-action films
A reboot, Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City, was released on November 24, 2021, with Johannes Roberts as writer/director.
Animated films
The first computer animated film for the franchise was Biohazard 4D-Executer.
Television
Resident Evil: Infinite Darkness, a four-part CG anime series, premiered on July 8, 2021, on Netflix.
Television
An eight episode live-action series, two plotlines set in 2022 and 2036 follow Albert Wesker and his daughters navigating Umbrella's experiments in New Raccoon City.
Merchandise
Over the years, various toy companies have acquired the Resident Evil license, with each producing their own unique line of Resident Evil action figures or models.
Merchandise

Some models included the STARS Beretta featured in Resident Evil 3, and the Desert Eagle in a limited edition that came with other memorabilia in a wooden case, along with the Gold Lugers from Code: Veronica and the "Samurai Edge" pistol from the Resident Evil remake.
Merchandise
The guide describes and summarizes all of the key events that occur in Resident Evil Zero, Resident Evil, Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, and Code: Veronica.
Merchandise

A second Archives book was later released in December 2011 and covers Resident Evil 4, Resident Evil 5, the new scenarios detailed in Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles and Resident Evil: The Darkside Chronicles, and the 2008 CGI movie, Resident Evil: Degeneration.
Merchandise
Halloween Horror Nights 2013, held at Universal Orlando, featured a haunted house titled Resident Evil: Escape from Raccoon City, based on Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
Novels

The first Resident Evil novel was Hiroyuki Ariga's novella Biohazard: The Beginning, published in 1997 as a portion of the book The True Story of Biohazard, which was given away as a pre-order bonus with the Sega Saturn version of Biohazard.
Novels
Perry has written novelizations of the first five games, as well as two original novels taking place between games.
Novels
While no official English translation of these novels has been published yet, the last two books were translated into German and published in 2006.
Novels
There was also a Japanese novelization of the first film, unrelated to DeCandido's version, written by Osamu Makino.
Novels
The books are a two-part direct novelization of the game and are published in Japanese and German only.
Novels
The first novel, titled Biohazard: The Umbrella Chronicles Side A in Japan and Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles 1 in Germany, was released on December 22, 2007.
Novels
The second novel, titled Biohazard: The Umbrella Chronicles Side B in Japan and Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles 2 in Germany, was published in January 2008.
Comics
In 1998, WildStorm began producing a monthly comic book series based on the first two games, Resident Evil: The Official Comic Magazine, which lasted five issues.
Comics
The first four issues were published by Image, while Wildstorm themselves published the fifth and final issue.
Comics

In Hong Kong, there has been officially licensed Biohazard manhua adaptations of Biohazard 0 by publisher Yulang Group, Biohazard 2 by Kings Fountain, Biohazard 3 Supplemental Edition by Cao Zhihao and, Biohazard 3 The Last Escape, and Biohazard Code: Veronica by Lee Chung Hing published by Tinhangse Publishing.
Comics
In 2009, Wildstorm began publishing a Resident Evil comic book prequel to Resident Evil 5, which centers on two original members of the BSAA, Mina Gere and Holiday Sugarman.
Comics
Written by Ricardo Sanchez and illustrated by Kevin Sharpe and Jim Clark, the first issue was published on March 11, 2009.
Comics
On November 11, 2009, the third issue was released, and the fourth was released March 24, 2010.
Reception and legacy
Most of the games in the prominent Resident Evil series have been released to positive reviews.
Reception and legacy

Some of the games, most notably Resident Evil, Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 4, have been bestowed with multiple Game of the Year honors and often placed on lists of the best video games ever made.
Reception and legacy
That same year, G4tv called it "one of the most successful series in gaming history."
Commercial performance
By December 2022, around 135 million Resident Evil games had been sold.
Commercial performance
The first two Resident Evil games had collectively sold approximately 11 million units worldwide by March 1999.
Commercial performance
By early 2001, the series had sold 17 million units worldwide, earning more than $600 million.
Commercial performance
By 2011, it had sold about 46 million copies and was estimated to have grossed at least $1.3 billion.
Commercial performance
It is recognized by Guinness World Records as the best-selling survival horror series, with Resident Evil 2 remake being the best-selling survival horror game as of 2023.
Commercial performance
Seven of the top ten best-selling horror games in North America are Resident Evil games.
Commercial performance
The 2023 Resident Evil 4 remake sold more than three million copies in its first two days of release.
Commercial performance
It sold four million copies in its first two weeks, making it one of the fastest-selling Resident Evil games.
Commercial performance
In Japan, it was the best-selling retail game in its first week, selling 89,662 copies on PlayStation 5 and 85,371 on PlayStation 4.
Commercial performance
The Resident Evil film series was the highest-grossing film series based on video games by 2012.
Commercial performance

By 2011, the films had grossed over $600 million at the box office, bringing the franchise's estimated revenue to at least more than $1.9 billion in combined video game sales and box office gross up until then.
Commercial performance
As of 2020, the films have grossed more than $1.3 billion in box office and home video sales.
Commercial performance
The success of the video games and films have made Resident Evil the highest-grossing franchise in the horror and zombie genres.
Cultural impact
GameSpot listed the original Resident Evil as one of the fifteen most influential video games of all time.
Cultural impact
According to Kim Newman in the book Nightmare Movies (2011), "the zombie revival began in the Far East" mainly due to the 1996 Japanese zombie games Resident Evil and The House of the Dead.
Cultural impact
George Romero, in 2013, said it was the video games Resident Evil and House of the Dead "more than anything else" that popularised his zombie concept in early 21st-century popular culture.
Cultural impact

In a 2015 interview with Huffington Post, screenwriter-director Alex Garland credited the Resident Evil series as a primary influence on his script for the horror film 28 Days Later (2002), and credited the first Resident Evil game for revitalizing the zombie genre.
Cultural impact

Screenwriter Edgar Wright cited Resident Evil 2 as a primary influence on his zombie comedy film Shaun of the Dead (2004), with the film's star and co-writer Simon Pegg also crediting the first game with starting the zombie revival in popular culture.
Cultural impact

The Resident Evil films, 28 Days Later and the Dawn of the Dead remake all set box office records for the zombie genre, reaching levels of commercial success not seen since the original Dawn of the Dead (1978).
Cultural impact

Since then, zombie films have declined in popularity during the late 2010s, but zombie video games have remained popular, as seen with the commercial success of the Resident Evil 2 remake and Days Gone in 2019.

fcube_killer8.title: Killer7
sents: lead
Killer7 is a 2005 action-adventure game developed by Grasshopper Manufacture and Capcom and published by Capcom for the GameCube and PlayStation 2.
lead
The game was written and directed by Goichi Suda and produced by Hiroyuki Kobayashi.
lead
The game follows an elite group of assassins called the "killer7".
lead
The assassins, physical manifestations of a man named Harman Smith, perform hits on behalf of the United States government.
lead
Through these missions, the killer7 uncover a deeper conspiracy regarding the role of Japan in U.S. politics and secrets about the nature of their organization.
lead
Killer7 features first-person shooter elements and a unique on rails control scheme, but the core adventure-style gameplay has been compared to Myst and Snatcher.
lead
Killer7 was Suda's first game released outside Japan.
lead
It initially received mixed reviews due to its unconventional control scheme, linear gameplay, and complex noir plot.
Gameplay
The player controls the on-screen character, a member of the killer7 group, from a third-person view using the gamepad.
Gameplay
The gameplay consists of elements of first-person shooter and action-adventure game with restricted movement (i.e.
Gameplay
Some puzzles require the talents of a specific killer7 member.
Gameplay
Combat in Killer7 occurs when the player encounters enemies called "Heaven Smiles".
Gameplay
The player must switch to a first-person viewpoint and scan the surroundings to reveal Smiles.
Gameplay
While in first-person view, movement is disabled and the analog stick aims the character's gun.
Gameplay
Completing the game unlocks a new difficulty called Killer8 where the character Young Harman (a young version of Harman Smith) can be played along with the original seven personalities.
Gameplay
Killer8 is more difficult than the original mode with most enemies able to kill the player with one attack.
Gameplay

Completing Killer8 unlocks a comical Hopper7 mode where the first level can be replayed with weaker enemies that wear grasshopper masks, mirroring the logo for the game's developer Grasshopper Manufacture.
Setting
Killer7 takes place in an alternate version of Earth in the early 21st century.
Setting
The UN Party seized control of the Japanese government through the wisdom of the "Yakumo Cabinet Policy", a secret document which details how to run the "ideal nation".
Setting
The interaction between Japan and the US is a central source of conflict in Killer7.
Characters

The player controls the members of a group of assassins called the "killer7." The group is led by an elderly man in a wheelchair named Harman Smith (Dwight Schultz), who exhibits "Multifoliate Personae Phenomenon".
Characters

The killer7 were temporarily incapacitated in an incident 50 years ago, in which the members of the group were systematically tracked and killed while performing a job at the Union Hotel in Pennsylvania.
Characters

In this capacity, he receives orders from the frail Harman when his consciousness is "awake" and accepts jobs from Christopher Mills (Bart Flynn), who hires the killer7 on behalf of the US government.
Characters
Iwazaru, a man in a bondage suit, and Travis Bell, the killer7's first target, are the main remnant psyches who aid them throughout the game.
Plot
The game opens with a conversation between Garcian Smith and Christopher Mills about a new job for the killer7.
Plot
In the subsequent missions, the killer7 target a number of individuals on behalf of the US government or for personal reasons.
Plot
After a volley of two hundred intercontinental ballistic missiles are fired at Japan, the US government contracts the killer7 to eliminate Toru Fukushima (Jim Ward), the head of the UN Party.
Plot
In the end, the killer7 defeat the two UN Party members who had been reanimated by Kun Lan as Japan is destroyed by the missiles.
Plot
In their final mission, the killer7 seek Matsuken, who leads the 10 million UN Party members who live in the US.
Plot
At the top, he discovers that his true identity is Emir Parkreiner, the one who killed the killer7 at the Union Hotel over 50 years ago.
Plot
Three years later, Garcian, now living as Emir, arrives at Battleship Island in Japan to destroy the last Heaven Smile.
Plot
Regardless of the player's choice, Garcian finds that the last Heaven Smile is Iwazaru, whose real identity is Kun Lan, and kills him.
Development
Development for Killer7 began in mid-2002 as part of the Capcom Five, a set of games overseen by Shinji Mikami and intended to be exclusive to the GameCube.
Development
Killer7 ' s gameplay mechanics were finalized late in development because most resources went to story and visual work.
Development

Director Suda51 wrote the scenario based on a plot he conceived together with Mikami, and later decided on the unconventional control scheme as a deconstruction of how gamers play and to "create new expression".
Development
The long development process culminated in several delays, the last of which was due to an artistic desire to release the game on July 7 (7/7).
Development
The game was finally released on July 5, two days earlier than previously stated.
Development
A lot of the content in Killer7 was cut due to feedback from both Mikami and internal testing.
Development
About 2/3 of the map size and plot were drastically reduced and according to Suda, the cinematics in total was three hours long as opposed to the now one-hour duration.
Development
Suda51 drew influence from film noir, particularly the theme of multiple personality disorder, and called Killer7 a " hardboiled action-adventure ".
Development
Hiro Sugiyama, Peter Saville, and American comic book artists, such as Adrian Tomine, inspired the artistic design and aesthetic.
Development
Suda51 noted the inclusion of cel animation in Western and Japanese anime styles was meant to legitimize video games as an art form by competing with traditional art forms in their stage.
Development
Kobayashi commented that Killer7 is "styled more as an interactive story than a traditional game." Suda also drew from yakuza film Battles Without Honor and Humanity: Hiroshima Deathmatch.
Development

The game reflects his interest in professional wrestling; Suda51 included a luchador character, Mask de Smith, and conducted interviews and attended promotional events while wearing a lucha libre mask.
Development
Reflecting on his work, Suda51 considers Killer7 his proudest achievement.
Reception and legacy
Killer7 received divided reviews and sparked debates about depictions of sex and violence in video games and the status of video games as art.
Reception and legacy
James Mielke of 1UP.com likened the game's high-contrast art style to noir and neo-noir film such as Se7en.
Reception and legacy
He found that despite poor pacing and stilted gameplay, the "quirky scripting and edgy plot" were strong draws, and called Killer7 one of the "most artfully designed footnotes in gaming history".
Reception and legacy

Eurogamer ' s Kristan Reed was keenly aware of the game's limited appeal, calling it "a concept game, an arthouse game, a simple game, an often beautiful game, but most certainly never an everyman's game".
Reception and legacy

Greg Kasavin of GameSpot praised the unity of "great-looking camera work with simple controls" and compared its "thought-provoking" storyline to Metal Gear Solid, while a GamePro reviewer criticized those features, calling the controls limited, the cel-shading dull, and the story incoherent.
Reception and legacy

IGN ' s Matt Casamassina likened the control scheme to "old-school adventure games like Myst and Snatcher " and commended Suda51 for making a "cult hit", "erupting with style, mood and undiluted craziness".
Reception and legacy
Nevertheless, IGN called it the 94th best PlayStation 2 game.
Reception and legacy
Nintendo Power claimed that Killer7 is a "highly rewarding" experience for dedicated gamers.
Reception and legacy
Charles Herold of The New York Times was less forgiving and commented that the lack of new features beyond the first hour made the remaining experience boring and annoying.
Reception and legacy
Despite its mixed reception, a number of video game publications recognized Killer7 ' s unconventional gameplay and innovative style.
Reception and legacy

At GameSpot ' s "Best and Worst of 2005" awards, the game was nominated for Best Story, Best GameCube Game, Most Outrageous Game, Most Gratuitous Use of F------ Swearing, and won Best New Character (Harman Smith) and Most Innovative Game.
Reception and legacy
IGN similarly nominated it for Game of the Year, Most Innovative Design, and Best Artistic Design and awarded it Best Adventure Game, Best Story, and Best Game No One Played.
Reception and legacy
IGN later named Killer7 the 20th best GameCube game of all time.
Reception and legacy
The game had a large presence at the 2005 Nintendo Power Awards, winning Best New Character (Harman Smith).
Reception and legacy

In August 2005, Jack Thompson, an activist who campaigns against video games, demanded that the Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB) change its rating for Killer7 from "M" (for Mature, ages 17 and up) to "AO" (for Adults Only, ages 18 and up).
Reception and legacy
Casamassina rebutted that the scene in question involved two fully clothed adults and that a similar scene in a film would garner "only a PG-13 or, worst, R-rating".
Reception and legacy
Reviewers quickly identified Killer7 as a cult game with limited appeal.
Reception and legacy
IGN lamented that its experimental style was not conducive to high sales, naming it GameCube's Best Game No One Played in their 2005 awards.
Reception and legacy
IGN ' s Casamassina later placed it fourth in his Top 10 Tuesday: Underrated and Underappreciated Games feature.
Reception and legacy
Despite modest sales, Killer7 ' s cult success prompted the development of remakes of Suda51's older Japan-only games, The Silver Case and Flower, Sun, and Rain.
Reception and legacy
In 2007, Grasshopper Manufacture released Suda51's No More Heroes to critical and commercial success.
Reception and legacy
Dan Smith later made a guest appearance in Suda51's 2019 game Travis Strikes Again: No More Heroes.
Reception and legacy
The 2021 Nintendo 3DS game Gal Galaxy Pain features a laugh in homage to Heaven Smiles that can be heard during the game over screen and when hovering over the game's icon on the 3DS home menu.
Music
Killer7 Original Sound Track was released on June 20, 2005 by Scitron Digital Contents.
Music
It features 55 compositions by Masafumi Takada and 6 by Jun Fukuda across two discs.
Music
Takada said in a 2008 interview that Killer7 is his favourite own soundtrack.
Comic book
In 2006, Devil's Due Publishing released a comic book adaptation of Killer7, written and drawn by Kinetic Underground staff.
Comic book
The planned 12-issue limited series was cancelled after four issues.
Comic book
Players who preordered Killer7 through EB Games received a special "Issue #0" as a bonus, and "Issue #½" was available at the 2005 San Diego Comic-Con.
Comic book

Writer Arvid Nelson described the story as a "mutant cross-breeding of John Woo and Quentin Tarantino ", and Devil's Due President Josh Blaylock commented that Killer7 ' s style was perfect for the comic book medium.
Possible sequel
Since its inception, fans have been anticipating a Killer7 sequel.
Possible sequel
Suda made it clear that it will "probably never happen" as Capcom holds the rights to the IP.
Possible sequel
In a 2010 interview, he exclaimed that Killer7 is "part of his soul" and is certainly interested in making a sequel.
Possible sequel

In 2012, Suda revealed a new game titled Killer Is Dead; word quickly spread that it was a follow-up to Killer7 since the game shares similar concept with an assassin protagonist, complex plot and cel-shaded graphics.
Possible sequel
Suda later clarified that Killer Is Dead is an original game and has no relation to Killer7.
Possible sequel
During a panel at 2016's PAX East, Suda expressed his interest to remaster Killer7 and has begun talks with the game's publisher, Capcom.
Possible sequel
On March 17, 2018, during HOPPER'S Vol.
Possible sequel
5 an event celebrating Grasshopper Manufacture's 20th anniversary, Suda verbally announced to attendees that there are plans to remaster both Killer7 and Flower, Sun, and Rain.
Possible sequel
Suda later posted on his Twitter account stating that the Killer7 remaster will be out within 10 years.
Possible sequel
At the 2018 MomoCon, Suda announced a remastered version of Killer7 for Windows which was released on November 15, 2018.

fcube_skies_of_arcadio_legends.title: Skies of Arcadia
sents: lead
Skies of Arcadia is a 2000 Dreamcast role-playing video game developed by Overworks and published by Sega.
lead
Players control Vyse, a young air pirate, and his friends as they attempt to stop the Valuan Empire from reviving ancient weapons with the potential to destroy the world.
lead

Skies of Arcadia uses traditional Japanese role-playing game systems such as turn-based battles and experience points, but puts greater focus on exploration, with the player flying an airship in 3D space.
lead
The development team included staff who had contributed to the Panzer Dragoon, Phantasy Star, Sonic the Hedgehog and Sakura Wars series.
lead
Skies of Arcadia received critical acclaim upon release and is frequently regarded as one of the best games for the Dreamcast, although the game underperformed commercially.
lead
A port for the GameCube, Skies of Arcadia Legends, was released in 2002.
Gameplay
Gameplay is similar to early 3D Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest games; the player engages enemies in turn-based battles to earn experience points, making their characters stronger.
Gameplay
The overworld is divided into six regions, traversed by flying airships in 3D space; "Discoveries", hidden locations, reward the player with extra benefits.
Gameplay
Getting through the end of the maze generally culminates in a last boss battle to be won prior to exiting.
Setting
The most advanced, the Silver Civilization, used their Gigas to summon the Rains of Destruction, which pulled meteors from the orbiting moons and crashed them down onto the planet's surface.
Setting
The catastrophic destruction stopped the rampage of the Gigas, as well as nearly destroyed the other five civilizations, thus ending the war.
Setting
A seal was placed on the Silver Gigas to prevent it from being used again, and the Moon Crystals were hidden away, while each civilization worked on rebuilding itself.
Characters
The other two main characters, Aika and Fina, are mandatory characters for the party through most of the game.
Story
Upon the Silver Civilization learning of this plan, they send Fina to find the Moon Crystals first.
Development
The title was changed to Eternal Arcadia in 2000, retained for the Japanese release.
Development

Producer Rieko Kodama had worked on Phantasy Star 1, 2 and 4, and the first two Sonic the Hedgehog games for the Sega Genesis, while scenario writer Shuntaro Tanaka had written the stories for the first two Sakura Wars RPGs.
Development
The soundtrack was composed by Yutaka Minobe and Tatsuyuki Maeda; Maeda had composed music for Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
Development
Expectations were high, as Team Andromeda's prior game, Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998), had received critical acclaim, and the Dreamcast had few well-reviewed JRPGs.
Development
After production moved to the Dreamcast, the motif of traveling the skies was set, inspired by the Age of Discovery.
Development
The Japanese Dreamcast release date was set for September 14, 2000, but delayed to October 5, 2000, so the team could create a paid "trial version" for concurrent release.
Localization
The localization was completed in four months, with 80- to 100-hour work weeks, on a script of over 2,000 pages.
Localization
Skies of Arcadia was released in English in North America on November 14, 2000, and in English, German, French and Spanish in Europe on April 21, 2001.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port

In October 2001, shortly after Sega's announcement that it would abandon the Dreamcast to make software for other consoles, Sega announced that it would port Skies of Arcadia to GameCube and PlayStation 2.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port
Development was announced to begin in January 2002, with Sega initially aiming for a mid-2002 release.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port
In August 2002, Sega announced that the PS2 version was cancelled in favor of focusing on the GameCube release, which was, as of October 2002, 80% complete.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port

Skies of Arcadia Legends was released on the GameCube in Japan on December 26, 2002, in North America on January 28, 2003, and in Europe on May 23, 2003, with Infogrames distributing for the latter territory.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port
A port for Windows was announced in early 2004, but never released.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 33 out of 40.
Reception
A reviewer of GameFan gave it 99%, calling it "By far my favorite RPG of all time thanks to its great story, looks, and battle system.
Reception
GameSpot praised the visuals, stating that they were "some of the most painstakingly detailed ever seen in a role-playing game".
Reception
Four-Eyed Dragon of GamePro called it "a Dreamcast role-playing game worth playing to the very end.
Reception
The game was a finalist for the "Best Dreamcast Game" and "Best Role-Playing Game" awards at GameSpot ' s Best and Worst of 2000 Awards, both of which went to NFL 2K1 and Chrono Cross, respectively.
Reception

The game was also nominated for the "Best Console RPG" and "Best New Game Character" (Vyse) awards at The Electric Playground ' s Blister Awards 2000, both of which went to Valkyrie Profile and Ulala from Space Channel 5, respectively.
Reception
Game Informer later listed it as one of the top 10 Dreamcast games.
Reception

In a 2017 retrospective from Metacritic on the highest-rated exclusive games (at time of release) per platform, Skies of Arcadia placed third for the Dreamcast, behind Soulcalibur and Jet Grind Radio.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.
GameCube port
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 32 out of 40.
GameCube port
Fennec Fox of GamePro stated that "there's no need to harp on the battles too much---they're the only blemish on what's otherwise the Dreamcast's (and now GameCube's) best RPG.
GameCube port
The graphics are dated but effective, and the musician was obviously overdosing on 1930s adventure serials when composing the over-the-top score.
GameCube port
The story, though, is the best part---Vyse and crew are the most extroverted RPG heroes ever, and there's none of that Final Fantasy -style self-abhorrence present.
Cancelled entries
In addition to the cancelled PlayStation 2 and PC releases of the game, a sequel to the game was considered by Sega in the early 2000s, but did not begin full production.
Cancelled entries

In September 2002, after the completion of Legends, Skies of Arcadia producer Rieko Kodama stated that the team was still interested in creating a sequel, but that work had still not started on it, though had it started, she felt that the GameCube would have been the most likely platform for its release.
Cancelled entries
In February 2003, Overworks president Noriyoshi Ohba announced that a Skies of Arcadia sequel had entered the planning stages.
Cancelled entries

Starting in 2010, Sega began a campaign of releasing HD remasters of Dreamcast games digitally on PlayStation Network and Xbox Live for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 consoles, including games such as Sonic Adventure, Crazy Taxi, Sonic Adventure 2 and Jet Set Radio.
Cancelled entries
In 2012, Sega brand manager Ben Harborne stated that a Skies of Arcadia HD was a likely next release, after Shenmue, as they were the most frequently requested titles for re-release.
Cancelled entries
As recently as 2020, main developer staff Kenji Hiruta expressed interest in returning to the series as well.
In other media
Multiple characters from the game later appeared in Sega's 2008 video game Valkyria Chronicles, another title directed by Shuntaro Tanaka.
In other media
"Vyse Inglebard" and "Aika Thompson" appear as optional members of Squad 7 and are listed on each other's "Like" list.
In other media
The three also appeared in the Japan-only Valkyria Chronicles III in 2011 as well.
In other media

Vyse also appears in the Sonic the Hedgehog comic book adaptation of Transformed featured in Sonic Universe #45, and again in the Sonic comics for the "World Unite" Sega character crossover story arc.

fcube_tales_of_symphonica.title: Tales of Symphonia

Composer(s): Motoi Sakuraba Shinji Tamura Takeshi Arai

sents: lead
Tales of Symphonia is an action role-playing video game developed by Namco Tales Studio and published by Namco for the GameCube.
lead
The fifth main installment of the Tales series, it was released in Japan on August 29, 2003, in North America on July 13, 2004 and in Europe on November 19, 2004.
lead
In Japan, the game was ported for the PlayStation 2 with additional content and was released on September 22, 2004.
lead
The game takes place in a fictional world called Sylvarant and follows Lloyd Irving.
lead
Lloyd accompanies his childhood friend, Colette Brunel, who is destined to go on a journey to save their world.
lead
As their journey progresses, they learn that saving Sylvarant endangers Tethe'alla, a world parallel to their own.
lead
The game's central theme is an "RPG that resonates with you" (君と響きあうRPG, Kimi to Hibikiau RPG).
lead
Tales of Symphonia received generally positive reviews upon release.
Gameplay
The overworld map is a 3D model, featuring a scaled-down version of the game's fictional world which the player travels through to reach the game's locations.
Gameplay
The battle screen is a 3D representation of an area, in which the player commands the characters in battles against CPU-controlled enemies.
Setting
4000 years prior, a war was waged by an evil race known as the Desians, who were sealed away by the legendary hero Mithos via a pact with the world's goddess Martel.
Setting

The Chosen's pilgrimage is complicated by the presence of the Renegades, a group that deliberately dresses in Desian garb and has assassinated Sylvarant's Chosen for the past 800 years, preventing Martel's awakening.
Setting
Although normally only those of elven blood can cast magic, humans such as Kratos and Zelos can gain the same ability by ingesting the powdered ore "Aionis".
Characters

Yggdrasill's secret identity is that of the legendary hero Mithos, an ageless half-elven boy who seeks to revive his older sister Martel, whom he propped up as a goddess following her death in the ancient war.
Development and release

On May 8, 2002, Namco and Nintendo announced at a Tokyo press conference that they would collaborate on a number of titles for the GameCube, including a new installment in the Tales series slated for a July 2003 release.
Development and release
Originally developed under the title Tales of Phantasia, its final title was revealed to be Tales of Symphonia in February 2003.
Development and release

An April 2003 edition of Famitsu revealed the game had been in development for two years, most of the development staff previously worked on Tales of Eternia, the game would have the most main characters in a Tales game to date, and would be the first 3D game in the series.
Development and release
A North American localization was confirmed at E3 2003.
Development and release
A conference by Namco on June 9, 2003 revealed the game would be on two disks and its theme song would be "Starry Heavens" by J-pop group Day After Tomorrow.
Development and release
The game was released in Japan on August 29, 2003, and was localized in North America, Australia, and Europe on July 13, 2004, November 18, 2004, and November 19, 2004, respectively.
Development and release
The game was re-released in North America under the Player's Choice label on July 19, 2004.
Development and release
During the second week of April 2004, Weekly Shōnen Jump announced a PlayStation 2 port of Tales of Symphonia.
Development and release
2013"), which is also performed by the band's lead singer, Misono, in the PS3 version in both the Japanese and Western releases, as well as the PC and Remastered versions.
Development and release
It was released exclusively in Japan on September 22, 2004, and re-released under the PlayStation 2 the Best label on July 7, 2005.
Scenario
Takumi Miyajima, the game's writer, explained Tales of Symphonia was planned to create a "unique symphonia", dependent on the player's choices and the affection system.
Scenario
Miyajima wrote many scenarios, with the most significant events centered on Zelos Wilder.
Scenario
Originally, Zelos' death was supposed to be canon.
Scenario

His survival would have been dependent on the affection system: He would die early on if he was ranked the lowest in the affection system, would die at the end if he ranked in the middle, and would only survive if he ranked the top.
Scenario
While generally a self-contained story, Symphonia apparently takes place within either the same or a similar timeline to the first Tales game, Tales of Phantasia.
Sequel and Chronicles release
A direct sequel, Tales of Symphonia: Dawn of the New World, was announced on July 20, 2007, for the Wii.
Sequel and Chronicles release
Tales of Symphonia Chronicles was announced on June 1, 2013, for the PlayStation 3.
Comics
The first anthology collection, Tales of Symphonia Comic Anthology, consists of five volumes which were released between November 25, 2003, and February 25, 2006, by Ichijinsha.
Comics
It consists of five volumes released between November 25, 2003, and December 25, 2006, by Ichijinsha.
Comics
A third anthology collection entitled BC Anthology Collection Tales of Symphonia had two volumes published by Mag Garden in February 2005 and 2007.
Comics
The fourth anthology collection is BC Anthology Collection Tales of Symphonia Yonkoma Short Comic Collection and consisted of a single volume which was released by Mag Garden on October 10, 2007.
Comics
It consisted of two volumes which were released by Square Enix on May 27, 2005, and September 16, 2005.
Comics
The sixth anthology collection is Tales of Symphonia Comic Anthology: The Best is a single volume released on June 5, 2010, by Ichijinsha.
Comics
The first four chapters were serialized between the April and July 2005 editions of Monthly Comic Blade.
Comics
Six volumes were released: the first was released on August 10, 2005, and the last two were released on July 10, 2007.
Books
The first novel series is titled Tales of Symphonia and is written by Kiyoshi Yuki.
Books
It consisted of three novels released between November 21 and December 20, 2003, by Shueisha.
Books
It consists of four volumes released between December 20, 2003, and June 19, 2004, by Enterbrain.
Books
An after story by the same author was released on September 18, 2004.
Books
Two strategy guides under the V Jump Books brand were published by Shueisha: the Gamecube guide was released on August 29, 2003, and the PS2 on September 22, 2004.
Books
Namco Bandai Games released two official strategy guides on October 1, 2003, and October 27, 2004, for the Gamecube and PS2 respectively.
Books
Tales of Symphonia Illustration: Kosuke Fujishima's Character Work is a book by the game's designer, Kōsuke Fujishima, and was released on January 26, 2004, by Ichijinsha.
Books
Tales of Symphonia Official Scenario Book was released on June 26, 2008, by Namco Bandai.
Books
Tales of Symphonia The Animation Visual Complete Picture Book is an art book for the anime released on March 28, 2013, by ASCII Media Works.
Audio CDs
Drama CD: Tales of Symphonia (A Long Time Ago) 1, 2, and 3 are stories preceding the game.
Audio CDs
They were released between July 23, 2004, and September 24, 2004.
Audio CDs
Drama CD: Tales of Symphonia Anthology 1 (Rodeo Ride Tour) First Part and Second Part follow Sheena Fujibayashi and Zelos Wilder as they tour the world a year after the events of the main game.
Audio CDs
The two CDs were released on May 25, 2005, and June 24, 2005.
Audio CDs
Tales of Symphonia Comic Market 78 and Tales of Symphonia Comic Market 79 are side stories with guest characters from Tales of Vesperia and Tales of Graces, respectively.
Audio CDs
Tales of Symphonia Original Soundtrack was published by DigiCube on October 1, 2003, and consists of 4 discs.
Audio CDs
The soundtrack was re-released on October 27, 2004, by King Records (Japan) for the PS2 port of Tales of Symphonia.
Animation
It consists of four episodes which were released direct-to-video on four separate DVDs on June 8, August 10, October 24, and December 21 of 2007.
Animation
They were later released in a Blu-ray Disc collection on September 26, 2008.
Animation
The series later rereleased on Universal Media Disc between June 25 and July 23, 2010.
Animation
On May 8, 2010, the series were aired on AT-X as a promotion to the sequel of the series.
Animation

The sequel series, Tales of Symphonia the Animation: Tethe ' alla Episode (テイルズ オブ シンフォニア The Animation テセアラ編, Teiruzu Obu Shinfonia The Animation: Teseara hen), was announced during Tales of Festival 2008.
Animation
It consists of four episodes which were released on March 25, May 26, September 23, 2010, and February 25, 2011.
Animation

All four episodes received an early screening: The first was screened on March 13, 2010, in Fukuoka and was hosted by Music Plaza Indo; The second on May 4, 2010, in Tokushima, Tokushima by Ufotable; the third on September 17, 2010, in Yokohama by Animate; and the fourth on February 20, 2011, in Roppongi by Toho.
Animation
The first two episodes were later aired on September 12, 2010, on AT-X.
Animation
Ending theme of the 4th episode is "Tethe’alla: Tsui no Kodomo-tachi" (対の子どもたち) by Akiko Shikata.
Animation
It consists of three episodes released directly to DVD and Blu-ray on November 23, 2011, June 20, 2012, and October 24, 2012.
Animation

All three episodes had early screenings: the first was screened between September 23 and September 25, 2011, by Cinema Sunshine in Ikebukuro; the second on May 3, 2012, in Tokushima by Ufotable; and the third is on September 29, 2012, by Cinema Sunshine in Ikebukuro.
Animation
A Blu-ray box set containing all three series was announced on June 1, 2013, and released on November 6, 2013.
Reception

Jonathan Metts of Planet GameCube said that although the game "clings to many of the well-worn RPG elements", its distinct battle system, story, and visual presentation allowed it to stand on equal footing with the most recent Final Fantasy titles.
Reception

Metts explained that it "strikes a perfect balance between the strategy of traditional menu-based RPG battles and the fast, skill-based action found in a weapons-based fighting game like Soul Calibur ".
Reception

Irwin negatively compared the amount of backtracking in the game's vast overworld to The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, but was thankful for the various modes of transportation that were continuously introduced.
Reception
Irwin, comparing the puzzles to The Legend of Zelda, welcomed them as breaks from the frequent exploration and battles, as well as an expansion of the game's appeal to a broader audience.
Reception
Juba proclaimed the game's world to be "one of the most stunning ever experienced", likening the presentation to " Windwaker -meets-anime".
Reception
Smith, however, disliked the lack of detail and facial expression in the character models, remarking that "the rare occasions where they do show emotion come across as disturbingly jarring".
Reception
The settings were admired for their detail and variety, with some commenting that the background art transitioned well into a 3D format from the classic Tales titles.
Reception

Jastrzab was stunned by the lack of slowdown during the game's chaotic action segments, Turner was also amazed by the consistently high framerate, which he regarded as "a great bonus in a time when most RPGs are content to chug at 30 ".
Reception

Juba, Turner, and Irwin respectively described Sakuraba's score as "pretty mellow", "a typically fine piece of work", and "pleasantly decent", though Irwin remarked that the musical variety was relegated to dialogue-oriented events, with the battle and overworld themes taking up most of the playtime.
Reception

Fahey noted that his praise of the voice acting was rare as he was not a fan of dubbing, and was slightly disappointed that the skits were not voiced as well, which he said resulted in them feeling drawn-out.
Reception

Jastrzab argued that the story held a "never-ending" depth underneath its surface, which he said was highlighted by the variety of plot outcomes that arose from subtle decisions by the player, though he warned of the script's excessive moralizing.
Remastered

Glen Fox of Gamezebo, upon establishing that Tales of Symphonia is his personal favorite video game, denounced the remaster as "a complete and utter mess", and expressed bafflement as to why Bandai Namco would allow "one of its most treasured releases from yesteryear" to be released in such a state.
Remastered
While Shkreli found the combat to be enjoyable without being overwhelming, he experienced difficulty with enemies approaching from multiple angles due to the 2D plane.
Remastered
Shkreli said that the story's "interesting and innovative" twists were still exciting, especially by the game's last third.
Sales and awards
Over 100,000 copies were sold in the United States during the first two weeks after its release.
Sales and awards
In December 2007, Namco announced that the GameCube version had sold 953,000 copies worldwide, and the PlayStation 2 port had sold 486,000 copies in Japan.
Sales and awards
The bargain reissue for the PlayStation 2 in 2005 sold almost 50,000 copies in Japan by the end of 2006.
Sales and awards
Its total worldwide sales for the GameCube and PS2 have reached 1.6 million units as of 2008, making it the best-selling Tales title to date.
Sales and awards
It was also the best-selling Tales title overseas, with more than half of its sales coming from outside Japan, having sold 600,000 units in North America and 250,000 in Europe as of 2008.
Sales and awards
The 2016 PC release sold more than 250,000 copies on Steam, as of April 2018.
Sales and awards
The game is estimated to have sold 2.4 million copies worldwide across all platforms, making it one of the best-selling titles in the franchise.
Sales and awards
GameSpot named it the best GameCube game of July 2004, and nominated it for the year-end "Best Role-playing Game" award across all platforms.
Sales and awards
The game has appeared on many top game rankings and received a Japan Game Awards in 2003 for excellence.
Sales and awards
During the 8th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Tales of Symphonia for " Console Role-Playing Game of the Year ".
Sales and awards
The January 2009 issue of Game Informer listed it at #24 in its "Top 25 GameCube Games".
Sales and awards
Nintendo Power ranked Tales of Symphonia 107th in a list of "Top 200 Nintendo Games Ever".
Sales and awards
IGN users placed it 75th in a Top 100 Games list, while GameFAQs users put it at 81st in a similar list.
Sales and awards
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.

fcube_batten_kaitos.title: Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean

Artist(s): Nakaba Higurashi Shinji Noguchi Yasuyuki Honne

sents: lead
Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean is a role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and tri-Crescendo and published by Namco for the GameCube.
lead

In it, the player assume the role of a " guardian spirit " – an unseen player avatar – who guides protagonist Kalas and his party of companions in an adventure across an aerial floating island-based kingdom in the clouds.
lead
The game is focused around the concept of "Magnus" – magical cards that capture the "essence" of items found in the in-game world.
lead
The concept is used as a plot device, for in-game item management, and as a basis for the card-themed battle system.
lead
The game was noted for its unique battle system, which included aspects of turn-based and action-based battle systems, collectible card games, and poker.
lead
Developed specifically for the GameCube due to its lack of JRPGs in its game library, the game was generally well received by critics, but received lukewarm sales.
lead
Despite this, a prequel, Baten Kaitos Origins was green-lit and released at the end of the GameCube's lifespan, receiving a similar reception itself.
lead
Outside of the cancelled Baten Kaitos DS, no further entries have been announced or released, with the team largely focusing on other projects, like the Xenoblade Chronicles games.
Gameplay

Battles are both turn-based and action-based; each character has both an offensive and defensive turn, where they have a brief number of seconds to quickly play a limited number of cards from their pre-build deck.
Gameplay

Each Magnus has a spirit number in the corner ranging from 1–9; playing same-number groupings or numbers used in gradual succession (1-2-3-4) result in an increased damage effect; cards with multiple numbers allow for the player to select the more beneficial option.
Gameplay

Experience points are accumulated by winning battles, but may only be applied to a character upon visiting blue flowers across the world, which teleports the party to a church, where one may " pray " to apply the experience points.
Setting and characters
Overtime, this causes humans to evolve and grow wings, allowing for limited flight.
Setting and characters
Kalas is considered a bit of a hooligan, and an outcast due to only have one wing, with the other being replaced by a mechanical wing.
Plot
Together, they inadvertently release the first of the "End Magnus", which is quickly seized by members of the Alfard Empire, a hostile nation on one of the islands.
Plot
One is found in Diadem, but is stolen from them immediately.
Plot
A temporary arrest for being suspected of kidnapping Miran resident Lady Melodia causes them again to lose the only End Magnus they had obtained there.
Plot
The party then learns of one last hope of stopping Melodia and Malpercio: the Magnus of Life.
Plot
Geldoblame felt Kalas was too human, and only had one wing, and ordered his death.
Plot
A final battle with Geldoblame ensues, and Kalas and Xelha defeat him, but the battle uses the last of Xelha's strength and she dies in Kalas's arms just after confessing her love.
Development

The game's developer, Monolith Soft, was initially founded in October 1999 after its founder, Tetsuya Takahashi, left his previous employer, Squaresoft, after the company refused to green-light funding for a second entry of Takahashi's first major project, Xenogears.
Development
The game's initial concept was created in 2001, with development beginning six months later.
Development

Monolith Soft, at the time only really known for the Xenosaga games, clarified after its announcement that while they would be utilizing their development experience from creating said games, the game would not have any actual connection to the Xenosaga series.
Development
The game was co-developed by Tri-Crescendo, and was the company's first venture into full-fledged video game development, previously only dealing with music and sound in video games.
Development
Game development approximately consisted of a staff of about 50 people over the course of an 18-month time period, leading to a cumulative 2 years process from inception to finish.
Development

The game was primarily developed to have 3D character models moving over 2D hand drawn art for the game's general world, to increase the level of detail that could be shown onscreen with the Gamecube's processing power.
Development
Honne wished to experiment with other art styles as well, including an entirely 2D segment with 8-bit graphics.
Development

The game was always designed to have six playable characters, 3 playable at a time, and between 40 and 50 key non-playable characters, feeling that anymore than that was taxing on the system's hardware, and made it difficult to programm all the different possibilities that can occur in-game.
Development
Honne noted that Kalas was most difficult to design, in balancing his wings, cape, and generally garish clothing, which they felt were necessary for his personality.
Development
Kato insisted that the character Mizuti speak with a certain accent, to the point that he sat in on her, and only her, voice acting recording sessions.
Development

Early character designs initially had larger, anime -styled eyes, but more realistic eye proportions were eventually given to better meld with the 3D character designs, and to better appeal to Western markets.
Development
The soundtrack album was published by Team Entertainment on December 17, 2003.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
In a February 2023 Nintendo Direct, an HD Remaster of the game, Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster, was announced for the Nintendo Switch for release in mid-2023.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
The release bundles Baten Kaitos and Baten Kaitos Origins (originally released as Baten Kaitos 2 in Japan) together as one release.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
The remaster does not add or remove any story content from either title, although it only features Japanese voice acting; the English voice acting has been removed.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
The game features improved graphics and resolution, widescreen display, and a stabilized framerate of 30 frames per second.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

New features include new options to alter the battle system, including eliminating random battles, an "auto-battle" function, a "1 hit kill" option, and a simplified, faster post-battle results screen.
Reception

At Metacritic, which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the game has an average score of 80 out of 100, which indicates "generally favorable reviews" based on 48 reviews.
Reception
GameSpot agreed with the notion, stating that it was " a beautiful game with a captivating world, a unique art style and... a great place to go for a nice fairy tale ".
Reception
Baten Kaitos received a runner-up position in GameSpot ' s 2004 "Best Role-playing Game" award category across all platforms, losing to Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door.
Impact and other releases

Publisher Namco had set a sales-goal of 500,000 copies sold worldwide, and initial sales figures fell well-short of it; it had sold only 80,000 copies in Japan after 2 weeks, and only 161,000 copies in North America after its first month and a half on the market.
Impact and other releases

It also sold poorly in comparison to Tales of Symphonia, Namco's other JRPG released along the same time period for the GameCube; which had sold 290,000 copies in Japan, and 285,000 copies in North America.
Impact and other releases
Despite this, the game was still considered to have accumulated a " cult following " in the years following its release.
Impact and other releases

Initially, the only other releases came in the form of two separate novelizations of the game released in Japan; Baten Kaitos: The Destruction of Truth and the Lie of the Promise and Baten Kaitos: Castle of Storms.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3
Prior to Origins release, in December 2004, another title, Baten Kaitos DS, was on Nintendo 's list of upcoming games scheduled for their then-upcoming Nintendo DS platform, alongside a Xenosaga DS.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3
While the Xenosaga title was later released as Xenosaga I & II, the Baten Kaitos DS title was never further detailed, and later disappeared from Namco's own list of upcoming games in October 2005.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3

In August 2006, when Monolith Soft's president was questioned about the title, responded that the team was "strongly willing to develop ", but that questions on the project needed to be directed to their publisher, Namco.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3
In 2011, Eurogamer published a report of a number game titles rumored to be in development, including a Baten Kaitos 3 being in development for the Nintendo 3DS.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3
