The report mentioned a 2011 Tokyo Game Show reveal, and while many of the rumored titles surfaced, a Baten Kaitos title did not.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3
In 2018, Honne revealed that a Baten Kaitos 3 had entered pre-production planning shortly after the conclusion of development on Origins/2, though his details differed greatly from the 3DS reports.
Cancelled entries Baten Kaitos DS and Baten Kaitos 3
The game never entered production, but game design documents and concept art had been created.
Future
The series has largely lay dormant since the release of Origins in 2006.
Future

Meanwhile, Tri-Crescendo went on to develop and release Eternal Sonata in 2007 for the Xbox 360 (and later PlayStation 3), a project company founder Hiroya Hatsushiba stated was only possible due to the experience of co-developing Baten Kaitos.
Future
In 2014, the Baten Kaitos Origins music track "The Valedictory Elegy" appeared in Nintendo's cross over video game Super Smash Bros. for Wii U.

fcube_batten_kaitos_origins.title: Baten Kaitos Origins

Developer(s): Monolith Soft tri-Crescendo logicalbeat Co.,Ltd (HD Remaster)

sents: lead
Baten Kaitos Origins, released in Japan as Baten Kaitos II, is a 2006 role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and Tri-Crescendo for the GameCube.
lead
It is a prequel to Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean (2003).
lead

Similar to the first entry, the player assume the role of a " guardian spirit " – an unseen player avatar – who guides protagonist Sagi and his party of companions in an adventure across an aerial floating island -based kingdom in the clouds.
lead

The game retains the original's focus around the concept of "Magnus" – magical cards that capture the "essence" of items found in the in-game world, where the concept is still used as a plot device, for in-game item management, and as a basis for the card-themed battle system, albeit with minor tweaks.
lead
Unlike the first game, which was published by then-Monolith Soft owner Namco, Origins was published by Nintendo, and was not released in Europe.
lead
It was released in February 2006 in Japan, and in North America in September 2006.
lead
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster, which includes Baten Kaitos Origins, was released on the Nintendo Switch on September 15 2023 and on Steam on June 18, 2024.
Gameplay
The game plays as a traditional JRPG and very similarly to the first Baten Kaitos game, albeit with some changes and adjustments.
Gameplay
Quest Magus, on the other hand, are treated like most in-game RPG items, and can be used to interact with the game's environment.
Settings and characters
The game is a prequel to the original Baten Kaitos game, taking place in the same fictional world twenty years prior to the events of the first game.
Settings and characters
The player plays the role of an unseen guardian spirit who can communicate to Sagi, the main character, who is a "spiriter" - a rare type of person who can communicate with said spirits.
Settings and characters
Communication is limited to pre-set dialogue tree option selections.
Plot

Geldoblame, as Verus's most loyal devotee, is devastated and driven mad by Verus's betrayal, but discovers that he is now Emperor due to the deaths of Verus and Baelheit's entire cabinet in the destruction of Tarazed.
Development and release

The original Baten Kaitos was originally conceived as the start of a new series for the relatively newly created Monolith Soft, which up to that point, had largely focused on the company's flagship Xeno series.
Development and release
The game was first announced as Baten Kaitos 2 in September 2005 at the Tokyo Game Show.
Development and release
Despite being a prequel, the game retained its 2 moniker even through its final release in Japan, while being renamed to Origins in its North American release.
Development and release
Development took approximately 18 months with a staff of around 50 employees.
Development and release

The game runs on the same game engine as the original, retaining the style of 3D characters over 2D art backgrounds, with fully 3D battles, a format popularized during the original PlayStation 's time.
Development and release
The originals restrictive leveling up system was scrapped entirely, as is the need to heal characters outside of battle.
Development and release
While the original had over 1,000 collectible "Magnus" cards, Origins was cut down to 655, and no opening CG movie was produced.
Development and release
Motoi Sakuraba returned from the original Baten Kaitos to arrange and compose the game's soundtrack; a total of 61 individual tracks of music are included within the game.
Development and release
Unlike the first Baten Kaitos game, which was published by Namco, Origins was published by Nintendo, and translated and localized by 8-4.
Development and release
Originally planned for release in December 2005 in Japan, it was later delayed several months later to February 2006.
Development and release
The North American version was released six months later in September 2006.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
In February 2023 Nintendo Direct, an HD Remaster of the game, Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster, was announced for the Nintendo Switch for release in mid-2023.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
The release bundles the original Baten Kaitos and Baten Kaitos Origins (originally released as Baten Kaitos 2 in Japan) together as one release.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
The remaster does not add or remove any story content from either title, although it only features Japanese voice acting; the English voice acting has been removed.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
The game features improved graphics and resolution, widescreen display, and a stabilized framerate of 30 frames per second.
Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

New features include new options to alter the battle system, including eliminating random battles, an "auto-battle" function, a "1 hit kill" option, and a simplified, faster post-battle results screen.
Reception
At Metacritic, it received an average score of 73 out of 100, which indicated "generally favorable reviews", based on 21 reviews.
Reception
They later described it as "one of the last great gems" on the GameCube, naming it their "Game of the Month" for September 2006.
Reception
Baten Kaitos Origins debuted at number 15 on the weekly games sales charts in Japan, with roughly 14,000 units sold in the first week.
Legacy
To date, Baten Kaitos Origins is the last entry into the Baten Kaitos series.
Legacy
An entry for the Nintendo DS was announced concurrently to Origins, but development was halted and the game was never released.
Legacy
In 2011, Eurogamer published a report of a Baten Kaitos 3 being in development for the Nintendo 3DS.
Legacy
The game was to be revealed at the 3DS event at the 2011 Tokyo Game Show, but while many of the rumored titles surfaced, a Baten Kaitos title did not.
Legacy
In 2018, Honne revealed that a Baten Kaitos 3 had entered pre-production planning shortly after the conclusion of development on Origins/2, though his details differed greatly from the 3DS reports.
Legacy
The game never entered production, but game design documents and concept art was created.
Legacy
An arrangement of the battle theme of this game, "The Valedictory Elegy" appears in the 2014 fighting game Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U, composed by Origins composer Motoi Sakuraba.

fcube_chibi_robbo.title: Chibi-Robo! (video game)

Designer(s): Sayoko Yokote Ryosuke Sumida Hiroyuki Takanabe Alberto Gonzalez
Programmer(s): Masaru Hori Shunsuke Yoshida Junko Muroyama

sents: lead
Plug Into Adventure! is a 2005 platform - adventure video game developed by Skip Ltd. and published by Nintendo for the GameCube console.
lead
It was released in Japan in 2005, and in North America and Europe the following year.
lead
Originally conceived as a point-and-click adventure game, it was put on developmental hold until Nintendo producer Shigeru Miyamoto gained interest in the title and overhauled its production.
lead
The player takes on the role of the eponymous Chibi-Robo, a 10-centimeter-tall robot owned by the Sanderson family.
lead

Gameplay revolves around navigating a household and collecting "Happy Points" by completing various tasks from housework to helping solve the dilemmas of the Sanderson family and the numerous living toys that inhabit their household.
lead
Every action consumes energy, requiring the player to recharge using electrical outlets.
lead
Chibi-Robo! was generally well received, with praise for the premise, the charming storyline, and sound design.
lead
However, some gameplay mechanics and the quality of the graphics drew some criticism.
Plot
Each of the one million Chibi-Robos in the world is supposed to collect "Happy Points" by doing good deeds for their owners and must occasionally charge their batteries at electrical outlets.
Gameplay
The player's exploration is limited by a timer representing a full day or full night.
Gameplay

The gear available from Citrusoft includes the "Chibi-Copter", used to reach far-off points or fly down from a high place safely; the "Chibi-Blaster", used to eliminate obstacles and fend off the hostile Spydorz; and the "Chibi-Radar", used to detect hidden objects.
Development
Chibi-Robo! was announced in early 2003 with publishing rights held by Bandai.
Development
Its original projected release date was June 2003 in Japan and spring 2004 in North America.
Development

Despite the game's overall happy attitude, the game designers put some emphasis on serious topics such as divorce, loneliness, pollution, and loss, in which Nishi said: "If we only concentrate on cheerful fun, we'll lose depth.
Development
Limited Soundtrack, a CD released alongside an official 142-page guidebook and published by Shogakukan in Japan in August 2005.
Reception
Official Nintendo Magazine ranked it the 88th best game available on Nintendo platforms.
Reception
The staff felt that it was the GameCube's "last classic".
Reception

Critics Greg Mueller of GameSpot, Mathew Kumar of Eurogamer, Bryn Williams of GameSpy, Shane Satterfield of G4, and Matt Casamassina of IGN all applauded the game's charming setting, compelling storyline, and complex characters.
Reception

Kumar heeded Chibi-Robo! as "honestly one of the most touching games I've played in ages" in which the player often becomes engrossed in "events that pan out like miniature plays, with love triangles (nay, love dodecahedrons) between toys, and some scenes with a real pathos behind them".
Reception
James Mielke of 1UP.com similarly enjoyed the "near-constant sense of discovery" and the tiny details included by Skip with earning Happy Points and Moolah.
Reception
Satterfield proclaimed that although the gameplay is somewhat varied, most of it is constituted by the tedious location and collection of objects for the non-player characters.
Reception

Jeremy Zoss of Game Informer was displeased with the game as whole and wrote that it was "not a platformer, but more of a 3D adventure game composed entirely of fetch-quests and repetitive menial labor".
Reception
Casamassina encountered low-polygon 3D models and a below-average frame rate; Satterfield stated the game operated at " Dreamcast level".
Reception
However, Mueller noted that switching to the top-down or first-person viewpoints and the ability to center the camera behind Chibi-Robo alleviates most of its problems.
Reception
According to Media Create, the GameCube version was the fourth best-selling game in Japan for its week ending June 26, 2005 with nearly 29,000 copies sold.
Reception
The game managed to sell 97,879 units in Japan alone by the end of 2005.
Reception
The Wii port of the game did not fare as well; it only sold 11,000 copies in Japan for the week ending June 14, 2009 and a total of 38,573 copies throughout the remainder of that year.
Legacy
Chibi-Robo! received a sequel in 2007 for the Nintendo DS called Chibi-Robo!: Park Patrol, which follows a different Chibi-Robo as it attempts to revitalize a park.
Legacy
Happy Richie Ōsōji!, saw an Exclusively in Japan release in 2009.
Legacy
The remake was released in Japan on June 11, 2009, but Nintendo of America did not permit an English release.
Legacy
Photo Finder, was released in 2013 for the Nintendo 3DS.
Legacy
Zip Lash was released in October 2015 for the Nintendo 3DS.

fcube_plumber_kart_double_dish.title: Mario Kart: Double Dash
sents: lead
Mario Kart: Double Dash is a 2003 kart racing video game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
It is the fourth main entry in the Mario Kart series.
lead
Similar to previous titles, Double Dash challenges Mario series player characters to race against each other on 16 Mario -themed tracks.
lead
The game introduced a number of gameplay features, such as having two riders per kart.
lead
Double Dash released in November 2003 and received positive reviews from critics.
lead

It attained an aggregated score of 87 out of 100 on Metacritic; reviewers praised the graphics, new gameplay features, character and item rosters, arcade aesthetic and track design, but the audio received mixed reactions.
lead
It was commercially successful, with more than 3.8 million copies sold in the United States, and more than 802,000 copies sold in Japan.
lead
It is the second best-selling GameCube game of all-time, selling around 7 million copies worldwide, behind Super Smash Bros.
Gameplay
Each pair of characters has a unique item that others cannot receive and are picked up in the same way as standard items; for example, only Mario and Luigi can launch fireballs against other racers.
Modes
A player who sets a new time record can enter their initials after the trophies are awarded.
Modes
The Time Trial is a single-player mode in which the player can race over a set number of laps to record the fastest completion time.
Modes
In the Versus mode, two or more human players can race against each other on any given track, with the race concluding when all but the last-place racer finish the race.
Modes

In "Balloon Battle", each player has three balloons, with one being lost when a player is hit by a weapon or hazard; players who lose all their balloons are eliminated, with victory going to the last player standing.
Modes

In "Bob-omb Blast", players gain points by attacking other players with Bob-ombs and lose points when hit by opponents' Bob-ombs, with the winner being the first to reach three or four points depending on the number of players.
Development and release
Mario Kart: Double Dash was first shown at E3 2001 as a seven-second video clip.
Development and release
The clip featured Mario and Luigi driving their karts on a bump mapped 3D surface with no background.
Development and release
In April 2003, Nintendo released the first pictures and details of the game, as well as revealing the title to be Mario Kart: Double Dash.
Development and release
At E3 2003, a playable demo was available.
Development and release
An updated demo with some additions was shown at the Games Convention in August 2003.
Development and release
The Gamers' Summit announced the North American release date to be November 17, 2003.
Reception
Nintendo Power gave the game a perfect score, and said the graphics were of "3-D perfection" and the controls and game mechanics "rival those of any racing game".
Reception
GMR ' s Andrew Pfister said, " Mario Kart: Double Dash is the most fun you'll have with a game this year.
Reception
Leeper, Davis and Metts warned of the repetitive character voices, with Metts mentioning that the player characters each had a single first-place victory comment.
Reception
Considering the 7-year gap since Mario Kart 64, Davis stated that he was "a little disappointed with the limited scope of the game".
Sales
In its first seven weeks of sales, Double Dash sold 1 million units, making it the fastest-selling GameCube game up to that point.
Sales
By July 2006, the game had sold 2.2 million copies and earned $105 million in the United States.
Sales
Next Generation ranked it as the 12th highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Sales
The game ultimately sold 3.8 million units in the United States, and over 802,000 units in Japan.
Sales
According to the NPD Group, Double Dash was the best-selling game of November 2003.
Sales
It is also the third best-selling GameCube game in Australia and was rereleased under the label of Players Choice only in that region.
Sales
Joystiq reported in February 2009 that the game had sold nearly seven million copies worldwide.
Awards
The game received the "Multiplayer Game" award from ITV 's Game Stars in 2004.
Awards
During the AIAS ' 7th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Double Dash received a nomination for " Console Racing Game of the Year ".
Awards
In 2009, the game placed 63rd in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s 100 greatest Nintendo games of all time.
Awards
In 2021, Kotaku ranked the game second best Mario Kart game, praising the two-player co-op mode and track design.

fcube_plumber_party_6.title: Mario Party 6
sents: lead
Mario Party 6 is the sixth installment in the Mario Party series of board game -style party video games by Nintendo and is the third game in the series made for the GameCube.
lead
It was released in Japan on November 18, 2004; in North America on December 6, 2004; in Europe on March 18, 2005; and in Australia on September 15, 2005.
lead
It is the first GameCube game to make use of a microphone add-on.
lead
Mario Party 6 received mixed reviews from critics, with praise for the day-and-night system, boards, and minigames, but criticism for the microphone feature and its perceived lack of originality.
lead
Mario Party 6 is followed by Mario Party Advance and Mario Party 7.
Gameplay
In Mario Party 6, up to four players take turns moving on board game -style stages, often playing multiplayer minigames to earn coins and stars.
Gameplay
The object of the game is to amass the most coins and stars before completing a set number of turns.
Gameplay
This is the first game to take out the coin bonus star, replacing it with the Orb star, which is awarded to the player that used the most Orbs.
Gameplay
All 10 playable characters from Mario Party 5 return in this game: Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Princess Daisy, Wario, Waluigi, Toad, Yoshi, Koopa Kid, and Boo.
Orbs
Unlike in Mario Party 5, the player does not have to pay to use Orbs on his or herself and may find coins in Orbs.
Orbs
Roadblock type Orbs are one-use only and trigger when passed.
Orbs
Space type Orbs transform a space into a character space and only work if a rival lands on the space.
Orbs
Special Orbs are used automatically to protect players' coins or stars from being stolen from Pink Boo and Chain Chomp, occurrences exclusive to certain boards.
Solo Mode
The player may also choose a teammate (for 2 vs 2 minigames).
Solo Mode
The dice block for Solo Mode only has the numbers 1–6 on it, unlike Party Mode where the dice blocks have numbers ranging from 1–10.
Solo Mode
At the end of the board, there is an exclusive rare minigame space, where the player receives a rare minigame without needing to play it.
Solo Mode
If the player goes past the rare minigame space, they fall off the board and lose all of the minigames they have acquired.
Solo Mode
To win, the player must land on the rare minigame space, or quit (without getting a rare minigame).
Minigames
There are 82 minigames in Mario Party 6.
Minigames
New to this edition are mic and rare minigames.
Minigames
The majority of rare games are usually obtained by stopping on the space at the end of Solo Mode, although one is purchased in the Star Bank.
Minigames
The minigames are divided into 4-player, 1-vs.-3, 2-vs.-2, Battle, Duel, DK, Bowser, Mic and Rare.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 3 eights and a 7 for a total of 31 out of 40.
Reception

Retrospectively, the game has been called by some critics as one of the best games in the series, citing the day-and-night system as an innovation that sets Mario Party 6 apart from other games in the series.
Reception
During the 8th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Mario Party 6 for " Console Children's Game of the Year ".
Reception
Mario Party 6 sold 1.63 million copies, making it the worst-selling home console Mario Party game.

fcube_plumber_party_7.title: Mario Party 7
sents: lead
Mario Party 7 (Japanese: マリオパーティ7, Hepburn: Mario Pāti Sebun) is a party video game developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo for the GameCube in November 2005.
lead

The seventh main installment in the Mario Party series, it makes use of the microphone peripheral introduced in Mario Party 6, and features twelve characters, including two new unlockable characters: Birdo and Dry Bones.
lead
Koopa Kid was omitted as a playable character, after being playable in the two previous games.
lead
Mario Party 7 was the fourth and last game in the series released for the GameCube and was followed by Mario Party 8 for the Wii in May 2007.
Gameplay
The goal of Mario Party 7 is to gather stars, but each board requires it in a different way.
Gameplay
For the first time ever in the Mario Party series, eight players may participate in either Party Cruise or Deluxe Cruise (the 8-player equivalent of the Mini-Game Cruise).
Gameplay

Players are split into teams of two and are required to share a controller, with the first player using the L button and the Control Stick in mini-games, while the second player uses the R button and the C-stick.
Gameplay
There are 88 minigames in Mario Party 7, the most in the series up to this point.
Gameplay
Like all except Mario Party 2, no minigames from previous editions appear.
Gameplay
There are nine types of minigames in the game: 4-player, 1-vs.-3, 2-vs.-2, Battle, Duel, 8-player, DK, Bowser, and Rare.
Gameplay
For 4-player and 1-vs.-3, there are an additional five minigames that can be played with the microphone.
Gameplay
In 8-player minigames, one player uses the Control Stick and L, and the other player uses the C stick and R.
Gameplay

After each minigame, the meter on the screen will increase by 20% and when the meter is full, Bowser will appear and hinders the players depending on which board that the characters are currently playing.
Gameplay
"Bowser Time!" may only occur once, or up to nine times, depending on the number of turns played.
Plot
When the player beats all the other boards, Bowser invites the player to the last board of the game, "Bowser's Enchanted Inferno".
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of two eights and two sevens for a total of 30 out of 40.
Reception
IGN gave the game a 7 out of 10, stating solely it was "a slumber party".
Reception
The game sold 1.86 million copies worldwide.

fcube_plumber_golf_toadstool_tours.title: Mario Golf: Toadstool Tour

Producer(s): Shinji Hatano Hiroyuki Takahashi Shugo Takahashi
Programmer(s): Haruki Kodera Toru Takamatsu Kazunori Mimori

sents: lead

Mario Golf: Toadstool Tour, known in Japan as Mario Golf: Family Tour (マリオゴルフ ファミリーツアー, Mario Gorufu Famirī Tsuā), is a 2003 sports game developed by Camelot Software Planning and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
It is the sequel to the 1999 Nintendo 64 title Mario Golf, and is the third game in the Mario Golf series.
lead
It was released in North America on July 28, 2003, in Japan on September 5, 2003, and in PAL regions in 2004.
lead
Toadstool Tour is a golf game featuring characters and elements from the Mario series.
lead
There are 16 playable characters in total, each with a set of golfing statistics defining their style of play.
lead
The game's main mode involves the player competing in tournaments to obtain new features, although there are alternative modes consisting of a training session and variations to the golf format.
lead
This includes "Ring Attack", requiring the player to hit the ball through rings of varying sizes while remaining on or under par.
lead
The game also features connectivity with Mario Golf: Advance Tour using the Nintendo GameCube Game Boy Advance cable.
Gameplay
The opportunities are only available once an envelope appears beside a character portrait in the selection screen.
Development and release
The game was displayed as a playable demonstration in the E3 convention of 2003.
Development and release
Toadstool Tour became part of the Player's Choice label in 2004, which offers a reduced price to games that have sold more than one million copies.
Reception
Eurogamer 's Tom Bramwell commented that "Mario Golf hasn't really grown much since its time on the N64", despite enjoying the game's course design and "sense of fun".
Reception
The game's multiplayer offerings were highly regarded by most reviewers.
Reception
GameSpot otherwise welcomed the game's visuals, however, arguing that the recurring Mario characters "never looked better".
Reception
Matt Casamassina acknowledged the characters' voiced taunts, saying "the muttering, complaining Waluigi, never fails to bring a smile to our faces".
Sales and awards
GameSpot named Toadstool Tour the best GameCube game of July 2003.
Sales and awards
By July 2006, Toadstool Tour had sold 830,000 copies and earned $26 million in the United States.
Sales and awards
Next Generation ranked it as the 72nd highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Sales and awards
Combined sales of Mario sports games released in the 2000s reached 2.5 million units in the United States by July 2006.
Sales and awards
Toadstool Tour sold 1.03 million units in North America as of December 27, 2007.

fcube_plumber_superstar_basebrawl.title: Mario Superstar Baseball

Composer(s): Ayako Yamaguchi Masasi Sugiyama Nobuhiro Ohuchi Kenichi Takahara Toshio Kajino

sents: lead
Mario Superstar Baseball is a 2005 sports video game developed by Namco and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
The game was created in the vein of other Mario sports games such as Mario Golf: Toadstool Tour and Mario Power Tennis.
lead
A sequel, Mario Super Sluggers, was released for the Wii in 2008.
lead

Gameplay mainly focuses on the player assuming the role of many Mario series characters to challenge any opposing teams compatible in the Challenge Mode, the final being Bowser, having baseball matches to see who will win the Cup of the mode.
lead

Other playable modes include Exhibition Mode, in which players choose the leader and the other rosters in the team and challenge another team to a single baseball game, and Minigames where the player must complete a certain mission.
lead

A common power-up in the game is a charged swing, a hit by a baseball bat performed by a character that will give the ball a strong hit, causing the length of a normal hit baseball to be twice as powerful.
lead
The game received generally favorable reviews from critics.
Exhibition Game
Players can choose which team bats first.
Exhibition Game
Players can also choose how many innings the game will last, and pick their choice out of six unique stadiums.
Challenge

It is a single-player mode where the player selects a pre-built team and must defeat all the other teams; at first Bowser's team is the last team to beat for the cup, and must be unlocked before the player can use him.
Challenge
Players of a different color can't be recruited and can only be played in minigames and playing with the teams they start on.
Challenge
Another way to recruit characters is by a mercy win; if either team is leading by at least 10 runs at the end of an inning, the game is called out of mercy to the losing team.
Challenge

After every game or minigame, Bowser Jr. will wander around the map; if the player runs into him, they will be forced to play a game in the bottom of the 9th inning, with the player randomly chosen as visitor or home.
Challenge
Beating Bowser Jr. earns the player 100 coins to use in the shop, while losing costs the player half of their coins.
Challenge
Bowser Jr.'s team also has players from disbanded teams that the player can recruit; in which case the only mission objective is "Win the game."
Challenge
There is a shop located on the map for purchasing power-ups, each worth a certain number of coins that the player earns from the minigames or Bowser Jr.
Challenge
Other power-ups offer a temporary boost to a stat for all characters on their team, but they only last for one game, win or lose.
Challenge
The game rules that cannot be changed are as follows: Your team bats first, and the Star Skills and mercy are turned on.
Reception
The game was met with positive reception, as GameRankings gave it a score of 76.70%, while Metacritic gave it 76 out of 100.
Reception
Robert Workman of GameDaily praised the game, writing, "...I found to grow on me." IGN praised the game, while noting its inconsistent production values GameSpot awarded the game an 8 out of 10.

fcube_super_plumber_strykers.title: Super Mario Strikers

Producer(s): Justin Dowdeswell Ken Yeeloy Kensuke Tanabe

sents: lead
Super Mario Strikers, known in Europe and Australia as Mario Smash Football, is a 2005 sports video game developed by Next Level Games and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
The game's developers had worked on NHL Hitz Pro before development of Strikers, which served as an influence for the fast-paced and physical nature of the game.
lead
This was also the last Mario game to be released on the GameCube in Japan and North America.
lead
Strikers is a sports game incorporating characters and themes from the Mario franchise.
lead
The game features the basic aspects and objectives of a football game, although no referees are present and characters can legitimately shove others out of possession of the ball.
lead
As in other games such as Mario Power Tennis, the player can use Mario -themed items such as bananas and red shells to hinder the opposition and gain the advantage.
lead
Each team's captain can use "Super Strikes" that, if timed accurately, will result in two points scored for the striker's team.
lead
Each team comprises a goal keeper, a main Mario character (captain), and three of the same secondary Mario characters known as "sidekicks".
Gameplay
Strikers follows the basic gameplay featured in most football video games, including the ability to dash, tackle players, and lob the ball.
Gameplay
The game also features "Perfect" passes and shots, which trigger in sequence if both a pass and shot are applied close to the opponent's goal.
Gameplay
The most powerful shot possible is the "Super Strike", which only the captain can make and will account for two points if successful.
Gameplay
Training sessions come in the form of "Strikers 101", where the player can practice individual aspects such as shooting and dashing.
Development
Strikers was developed by Next Level Games, who revealed the game at the E3 conference of 2005 in the form of a playable demonstration.
Development

In an interview, game director Mike Inglehart and marketing director Grace Kim revealed that Strikers was originally intended to be a more realistic Mario sports game, but the development team opted for an "over-the-top" style after numerous consultations with Nintendo.
Reception
Despite enjoying the variety and appearance of Strikers ' stadia, GameSpot noted only cosmetic differences among them, and criticised a lack of physical features to make them more interesting.
Reception
Despite this, Eurogamer remarked that it was deeper than first anticipated, while IGN lauded the game's "tight controls" and use of Super Strikes.
Reception
GameSpot thought the menu music had "some nice flair to it", despite noting sounds such as Luigi 's goal celebration that, while charming when first heard, became tedious.
Reception

In Japan, Famitsu gave the game a score of three sevens and one six for a total of 27 out of 40; Famitsu Cube + Advance, on the other hand, gave it a score of one nine, two eights, and one seven, for a total of 32 out of 40.
Awards and sales

In GameSpot's E3 2005 coverage, this game was given the award "Best Sports Game," and was nominated a finalist for "Best Game of Show." It received GameSpy 's "Game of the Year 2005" awards for "Best GameCube Sports", "Best GameCube Multiplayer", and was ranked second for all the GameCube games in 2005.
Awards and sales
Super Mario Strikers sold 950,000 copies in North America as of December 27, 2007.

fcube_legend_of_zeldo_the_wind_wak.real: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
fcube_legend_of_zeldo_the_wind_wak.title: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
sents: lead
The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker is an action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
An installment in The Legend of Zelda series, it was released in Japan on December 13, 2002, in North America on March 24, 2003, and in Europe on May 2, 2003.
lead
The game is set on a group of islands in a vast sea, a departure for the series.
lead
The player controls series protagonist Link as he attempts to save his sister from the sorcerer Ganondorf and becomes embroiled in a struggle for the Triforce, a sacred wish-granting relic.
lead

Aided by allies including pirate captain Tetra – an incarnation of Princess Zelda – and a sentient sailboat named the King of Red Lions, Link sails the ocean, explores islands, and traverses dungeons to acquire the power necessary to defeat Ganondorf.
lead
Wind, which facilitates sailing, plays a prominent role and can be controlled with a magic conductor's baton called the Wind Waker.
lead
The Wind Waker was directed by Eiji Aonuma and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka.
lead
It retains the basic 3D gameplay of its predecessors, Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask, but the team chose to avoid the realistic graphics of previous games.
Gameplay
The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker is an action-adventure game with role-playing elements.
Gameplay
The game world comprises 49 gridded sections of the " Great Sea ", each containing an island or island chain.
Wind and sailing
The first melody, the "Wind's Requiem", enables Link to change the wind's direction, allowing him to sail anywhere.
Background and setting

According to The Legend of Zelda: Hyrule Historia, Nintendo's official Legend of Zelda chronology, The Wind Waker takes place in the "New World" timeline, one of several parallel timelines in which Zelda games are set following the events of Ocarina of Time.
Plot
The King of Red Lions reveals himself to be Daphnes Nohansen Hyrule, the last King of Hyrule, and Tetra is his heir, Zelda, keeper of the Triforce of Wisdom.
Game design
Nintendo's Zelda team initiated plans for a new game early in the development of the GameCube system, before Majora's Mask was completed for the Nintendo 64 in 2000.
Game design
The team hastily created a brief clip of Link fighting Ganondorf for a demonstration at the 2000 Space World exposition, where Nintendo announced the GameCube.
Game design
To achieve this look, they used cel shading on 3D models, giving the look of an interactive cartoon.
Game design
The developers built the game with Alias/Wavefront 's Maya 3D tool and a custom game engine.
Game design
Nintendo presented a demo clip of the new game at the 2001 Space World.
Game design
Miyamoto introduced a playable demo at the next year's Electronic Entertainment Expo (E3), alongside another upcoming Zelda title for the GameCube, Four Swords Adventures.
Game design
The game received the 2002 Game Critics Awards for Best Console Game at E3.
Game design
The E3 demo also introduced new features, such as the ability to connect to the Game Boy Advance and receive help from Tingle.
Game design
Development continued through late 2002, with targeted release dates of December in Japan and early 2003 in North America.
Game design
On October 15, 2002, Nintendo revealed the game's Japanese subtitle, Kaze no Takuto (Wind Baton), to emphasize the role of wind in the game.
Game design
The company announced the English title, The Wind Waker, on December 2 the same year.
Music
Koji Kondo, the primary composer for The Legend of Zelda series, contributed to the score but did not serve as sound director.
Music
Much of the score is inspired by traditional Irish music and is overall lighter and more upbeat than previous scores in the series.
Music
Scitron Digital Content released a two-disc, 133-track soundtrack album, The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker Original Sound Tracks, on March 19, 2003.
Release and promotion
The Wind Waker was released on December 13, 2002, in Japan, on March 24, 2003, in North America, and on May 2, 2003, in Europe.
Release and promotion
To promote the release, Nintendo offered a bonus disc as a pre-order incentive which included a GameCube port of Ocarina of Time as well as its previously unreleased expansion, Ura Zelda.
Release and promotion

Ura Zelda, largely an adaptation of Ocarina of Time with some changes, including new dungeon challenges, had been developed for the Nintendo 64's 64DD peripheral, but was shelved when that system failed.
Release and promotion
To avoid this issue in Europe, Nintendo released the item only in two-disc packages with The Wind Waker.
Release and promotion
In May 2003, Nintendo bundled The Wind Waker with limited edition GameCubes in North America and Europe.
Release and promotion
On November 17 that year, Nintendo launched another promotion via a compilation disc, The Legend of Zelda Collector's Edition.
Release and promotion
The disc includes ports of the original Legend of Zelda, Zelda II: The Adventure of Link, Ocarina of Time, and Majora's Mask, as well as a Wind Waker demo and two featurettes.
Release and promotion

Never sold commercially, the Collector's Edition was included in another GameCube bundle and was made available to existing GameCube owners who either registered their system or subscribed to Nintendo Power.
Release and promotion
The compilation became a coveted item among fans; in the United Kingdom and Ireland, the 1000 allotted copies were claimed within minutes.
Wii U version
In 2013, Nintendo developed a high definition re-release of The Wind Waker, The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker HD, for the Wii U.
Wii U version
Some weapons, like the bow, can be aimed using the GamePad's gyroscope, as in Ocarina of Time 3D.
Wii U version

Wii U version
A redemption code for a digital copy of The Legend of Zelda: Hyrule Historia was also included.
Critical reception
Review aggregator website Metacritic calculated a score of 96/100 based on 80 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim".
Critical reception

It was the fourth game to receive a perfect score from the Japanese magazine Famitsu, and additionally earned perfect scores from Computer and Video Games, Game Informer, Game Pro, Nintendo Power, and Planet GameCube.
Critical reception
In particular, critics appreciated the characters' unique expressiveness, and found that the fine details and environments added richness to the game world.
Critical reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s reviewers found the animation quality unparalleled in games and wrote that " The Wind Waker ' s new look is as effective as it is unique".
Critical reception
Steve Thomason of Nintendo Power wrote that though he was initially skeptical, the visuals worked "brilliantly, framing the most enjoyable game play experience I've had since Ocarina of Time ".
Critical reception
The heavy emphasis on sailing was the game's most common criticism, especially later in the game when Link must trek around the ocean to collect Triforce pieces.
Critical reception
Gerstmann wrote that while the main quest "starts out in a very brisk manner", by the last third of the game, the "focus on sailing... is pretty tedious".
Critical reception
IGN gave it the Readers' Choice award for 2003 and named it Best Adventure Game for the GameCube.
Critical reception
The game was ranked 157th in Electronic Gaming Monthly's "The Top 200 Video Games of Their Time" in 2006.
Audience response and sales
The Wind Waker generated the most successful pre-order campaign in Nintendo history at the time.
Audience response and sales
The overall market remained strong in North America, but The Wind Waker ' s sales were slow there and had declined markedly by the time they reached one million.
Audience response and sales
The Wind Waker sold 4.6 million copies, far below the 7.6 million record set by Ocarina of Time.
Audience response and sales

Nintendo of America attributed the game's comparatively weak North American sales in large part to the cel-shaded graphics, which turned off many players, particularly older teenagers who made up The Legend of Zelda ' s traditional audience.
The Wind Waker HD
The Wind Waker HD was critically acclaimed; Metacritic calculated a score of 90/100 based on 70 reviews.
The Wind Waker HD
The game's first week sales in Japan were 30,000 physical copies.
The Wind Waker HD
In the week following the release of Wind Waker HD, sales of the Wii U console increased by 685% in the UK.
The Wind Waker HD
As of September 2023, it has worldwide sales of 2.37 million units.
Sequels and other media
Nintendo initially planned a direct sequel for the GameCube, developed by Aonuma's Zelda team under the working title Wind Waker 2.
Sequels and other media
Wanting to continue The Wind Waker ' s story and art style, in 2007 Aonuma produced Phantom Hourglass, which follows Link and Tetra as they explore new reaches of the Great Sea.
Sequels and other media
Spirit Tracks (2009) is set roughly a century later and features a new Link and Zelda, the latter a descendent of Tetra, as they traverse New Hyrule with a magical train.
Sequels and other media
Toon Link also returned in indirectly related Legend of Zelda games such as Four Swords Adventures (2004), The Minish Cap (2005), and Tri Force Heroes (2015).
Sequels and other media
Conductors of the concert tour The Legend of Zelda: Symphony of the Goddesses have used custom-made Wind Waker batons.
Sequels and other media
The Wind Waker also influenced 2017's Breath of the Wild, which features a similarly stylized art design, but with more realistic proportions.
Later reputation
Nintendo Power named The Wind Waker the fourth best game to ever appear on a Nintendo console, while Official Nintendo Magazine placed it 12th.
Later reputation
UGO listed The Wind Waker on their list of the "Top 50 Games That Belong On the 3DS".
Later reputation
Nintendo Power named The Wind Waker the second best GameCube game of all time, behind only Resident Evil 4.
Later reputation
In 2013, Keza MacDonald of IGN wrote that The Wind Waker had outlived its initial reception and become "popularly considered among the very best Zeldas ".

The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess is a 2006 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube and Wii.
lead

Originally planned for release exclusively on the GameCube in November 2005, Twilight Princess was delayed by Nintendo to allow its developers to refine the game, add more content, and port it to the Wii.
lead
The Wii version was a launch game in North America in November 2006, and in Japan, Europe, and Australia the following month.
lead
The GameCube version was released in December 2006 as the final first-party game for the console.
lead
The story focuses on series protagonist Link, who tries to prevent Hyrule from being engulfed by a corrupted parallel dimension known as the Twilight Realm.
lead
To do so, he takes the form of both a Hylian and a wolf, and he is assisted by a mysterious imp named Midna.
lead
The game takes place over a century after Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask, in an alternate timeline from The Wind Waker.
lead
Twilight Princess was critically acclaimed upon its release, received numerous game of the year awards, and has been called one of the greatest video games ever made.
Gameplay
The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess is an action-adventure game focused on combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving.
Gameplay
While L-targeting, projectile-based weapons can be fired at a target without the need for manual aiming.
Gameplay

In the GameCube version, players can control the camera freely, without entering a special "lookaround" mode required on the Wii; however, in the GameCube version, only two of Link's secondary weapons can be equipped at a time, as opposed to four in the Wii version.
Plot

The pair reaches the depths of Gerudo Desert to use the Mirror of Twilight, the only known way that connects Hyrule amd the Twili's realm, only to discover Zant has destroyed it into fragments; only the true ruler of the Twili can permanently destroy it.
Inception as a GameCube game
In 2003, Nintendo announced a new The Legend of Zelda game for the GameCube by the same team that had created the cel-shaded The Wind Waker.
Inception as a GameCube game
Just as the original Legend of Zelda game was inspired by J.

Tolkien 's The Lord of the Rings novels, the aesthetic of Twilight Princess was inspired by the Lord of the Rings films, as they had just come out and were very popular at the time.
Inception as a GameCube game
In four months, Aonuma's team managed to present realistic horseback riding, which Nintendo later revealed to the public with a trailer at E3 2004 that was met with enormous praise.
Inception as a GameCube game
The game was scheduled to be released the next year and was no longer a follow-up to The Wind Waker; a true sequel to it was released for the Nintendo DS in 2007, in the form of Phantom Hourglass.
Inception as a GameCube game

Originally, Link was planned to be a wolf from the game's start to bluntly contrast the Ocarina of Time formula, but this was changed so that new players could be eased into the Zelda series' traditional gameplay and narrative formula.
Inception as a GameCube game
From a gameplay perspective, the Twilight Realm portions of the game were vaguely inspired by the fact that prior Zelda games had always distinctively separated dungeons from the overworld.
Transition to the Wii
Aonuma had anticipated creating a Zelda game for what would later become the Wii, but had assumed that he would need to complete Twilight Princess first.
Transition to the Wii
Aonuma felt confident this was the only way to proceed, but worried about consumers who had been anticipating a GameCube release.
Transition to the Wii
Developing two versions would mean delaying the previously announced 2005 release, still disappointing the consumer.
Transition to the Wii
At E3 2005, Nintendo released a small number of Nintendo DS game cards containing a preview trailer for Twilight Princess.
Transition to the Wii
A prototype was created that used a swinging gesture to control the sword from a first-person viewpoint but was unable to show the variety of Link's movements.
Transition to the Wii
At E3 2006, Nintendo confirmed that both versions would be available at the Wii launch, and had a playable version of Twilight Princess for the Wii.
Transition to the Wii
To solve this, sword controls were transferred back to gestures—something E3 attendees had commented they would like to see.
Music and sound
Kondo's piece was chosen as music for the E3 2005 trailer and for the demo movie after the title screen.
Music and sound

Midna has the most voice acting—her on-screen dialogue is often accompanied by a babble of pseudo-speech, which was produced by scrambling English phrases sampled by Japanese voice actress Akiko Kōmoto.
Music and sound
He originally envisioned a full 50-person orchestra for action sequences and a string quartet for more "lyrical moments", though the final product used sequenced music instead.
Music and sound

Both six- and seven-track versions of the game's soundtrack were released on November 19, 2006, as part of a Nintendo Power promotion and bundled with replicas of the Master Sword and the Hylian Shield.

Versions 3.3 and 3.4 of the Wii Menu prevented copying exploited save files onto the console until circumvention methods were discovered, and version 4.0 of the Wii Menu patched the vulnerability.

Wii U version
Announced during a Nintendo Direct presentation on November 13, 2015, it features enhanced graphics and Amiibo functionality.
Wii U version
The idea for a high-definition version of Twilight Princess first originated during the production of Breath of the Wild.
Wii U version
After its release, which was developed internally at Nintendo in only six months, the Zelda team settled on an HD remaster of Twilight Princess.
Wii U version

At the time, most of the Zelda team was preoccupied with Breath of the Wild, so Nintendo sought a partnership with an external development studio, the Australia-based Tantalus Media, to work on Twilight Princess HD.
Wii U version
A commitment to "preserving the feel of the original" inspired several design decisions, such as keeping the frame rate at 30 frames per second.
Wii U version
A CD containing 20 musical selections from the game was available as a GameStop preorder bonus in North America; it is included with the limited-edition bundle in other regions.
Wii U version
A three-disc original soundtrack consisting of 108 pieces from the game was released in Japan in July 2016.
Reviews
It received perfect scores from major publications such as 1UP.com, Computer and Video Games, Electronic Gaming Monthly, Game Informer, GamesRadar and GameSpy.
Reviews
On the review aggregator Metacritic, Twilight Princess holds scores of 95/100 for the Wii version and 96/100 for the GameCube version, indicating "universal acclaim".
Reviews
GamesRadar praised Twilight Princess as "a game that deserves nothing but the absolute highest recommendation".
Reviews
Cubed3 hailed Twilight Princess as "the single greatest videogame experience".
Reviews
Regarding the Wii version, GameSpot ' s Jeff Gerstmann said the Wii controls felt "tacked-on", although 1UP.com said the remote-swinging sword attacks were "the most impressive in the entire series".
Wii U version
Twilight Princess HD holds a score of 86/100 at the review aggregator Metacritic, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.
Wii U version
The title received the Nintendo Game of the Year award at the Golden Joystick Awards in November 2016.
Awards
Twilight Princess received Game of the Year awards from GameTrailers, 1UP.com, Electronic Gaming Monthly, Game Informer, GamesRadar, GameSpy, Spacey Awards, X-Play and Nintendo Power.
Awards
The game placed 16th in Official Nintendo Magazine ' s list of the 100 Greatest Nintendo Games of All Time.
Awards
Nintendo Power ranked the game as the third-best game to be released on a Nintendo system in the 2000s decade.

In North America, the game was sold with three of every four Wii purchases during its first week.

The Wii version sold 412,000 copies in the United States during November 2006, representing 87% of Wii launch sales that month, the highest attach rate for a launch game since Super Mario 64 launched with the Nintendo 64 in 1996.
Sales
It went on to become America's fifth-best-selling game of 2006 with 1.5 million copies sold for the Wii and GameCube in the US that year.
Sales

In the United Kingdom, the Wii version received a Platinum sales award from the Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 300,000 copies in the UK.
Sales
The game had sold 5.82 million copies on the Wii as of March 2011, and 1.32 million on the GameCube as of March 2007.
Sales

Wii U version
The remaster sold 52,282 copies during its first week of release in Japan, which placed it at second place in the video-game sales charts.
Wii U version
The following week, it came in at number 9 on the charts, selling an additional 7,705 copies.
Wii U version
By comparison, 30,264 copies of The Wind Waker HD were sold in its first week in Japan.

In the first week of Twilight Princess HD ' s United Kingdom release, the remaster was the second-best-selling game and the best-selling game released for a single platform in the country.

In the United States, it was the third-best-selling game sold in brick-and-mortar retailers throughout March 2016, according to market-research firm The NPD Group.

As of December 2022, the game has sold 1.17 million copies worldwide.

Legacy
While the manga adaptation began almost ten years after the initial release of the game on which it is based, it launched only a month before the release of the high-definition remake.
Legacy
Viz Media began releasing an English localization of the series in 2017 and was finished in March 2022.
Legacy

The Legend of Zelda, originally released in Japan as The Hyrule Fantasy: Zelda no Densetsu, is an action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo.
lead

The first game of The Legend of Zelda series, it is set in the fantasy land of Hyrule and centers on an elf -like boy named Link, who aims to collect the eight fragments of the Triforce of Wisdom in order to rescue Princess Zelda from Ganon.
lead
The player controls Link from a top-down perspective and navigates throughout the overworld and dungeons, collecting weapons, defeating enemies and uncovering secrets along the way.
lead
Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, it was originally released in Japan as a launch title for the Family Computer Disk System in February 1986.
lead

More than a year later, North America and Europe received releases on the Nintendo Entertainment System in cartridge format, being the first home console game to include an internal battery in the US for saving data.
lead
This version was later released in Japan in 1994 under the title The Hyrule Fantasy: Zelda no Densetsu 1.
lead
The game was ported to the GameCube and Game Boy Advance, and was available via the Virtual Console on the Wii, Nintendo 3DS and Wii U.
lead
It was also one of 30 games included in the NES Classic Edition system, and is available on the Nintendo Switch through the Nintendo Switch Online service.
Gameplay
The Legend of Zelda incorporates elements of action, adventure, and role-playing genres.

Link begins the game equipped only with a small shield, but can enter a cave and receive a sword from an old man who advises, " It's dangerous to go alone!
Gameplay
Some are easily accessible, while others are hidden beneath obstacles such as rocks, trees, and waterfalls.
Gameplay

Each dungeon has a unique maze-like layout of rooms connected by doors and secret passages, often barred by monsters (which must be defeated) or by blocks (which must be moved to gain entrance).
Gameplay

The game may be completed by traversing any given dungeon on the overworld and is largely flexible to players, although gameplay steadily increases in difficulty, and some rooms can only be passed by using items gained in previous locations.
Gameplay
There are dungeons with secret entrances which must be uncovered while freely wandering the overworld after acquiring useful items.
Gameplay
The game world contains 600 separate scenes, with the overworld consisting of over 97 scenes and the underworld consisting of nine multi-scene labyrinths.

Although more difficult "replays" were not unique to Zelda, few games offered completely different levels upon the second playthrough.

By starting a new file with the name entered as "ZELDA", this mode can instead be accessed without needing to beat the game first.

Setting
In this era, Hyrule has been reduced to a small kingdom where the residents now live in caves, setting the background for The Legend of Zelda.

In an attempt to prevent him from acquiring the Triforce of Wisdom, Princess Zelda splits it into eight fragments and hides them in secret underground dungeons.

Rather than merely simplifying matters for players, Miyamoto forced the player to listen to the old man who gives the player their sword, and encouraged interaction among people to share their ideas with each other to find the various hidden secrets, a new form of gaming communication.

With The Legend of Zelda, Miyamoto wanted to flesh out the idea of a game "world" even further, giving players a "miniature garden that they can put inside their drawer".

lead

lead

The game's story focuses on an alien pilot, Captain Olimar, who crash lands on a mysterious planet and must make use of a native species called "Pikmin" to find his ship's missing parts in order to escape within 30 days.
lead

Players take control of Olimar and direct the different varieties of Pikmin to explore the game's various levels, overcoming obstacles and hostile creatures, in order to find and recover the missing ship parts.
lead
Pikmin was well-received by critics and was commercially successful, selling over one million copies worldwide.
lead
It spawned a series of sequels, starting with Pikmin 2, which was released in 2004.
lead
The game was ported to Wii in 2008 in Japan and 2009 for the rest of the world as part of the New Play Control! series, while a high-definition remaster was released for Nintendo Switch in 2023.

Red Pikmin are the first type found in the game, resistant to fire and the strongest type of Pikmin with respect to combat.
Gameplay
Blue Pikmin are the only ones that are able to survive in water and throw Pikmin of other colors across it.

Only one hundred Pikmin, whether planted or plucked, can be on the ground at a time.

With the exception of the first day, which lasts until the player finds the first ship part, all days in the game are about thirteen minutes in length, which can prematurely end at the player's request or if Olimar's health, replenished at his spacecraft, is depleted from attacks by native creatures.
Gameplay
Collecting all thirty grants the best ending, while collecting at least the twenty-five mandatory parts within the 30-day time limit grants the normal ending.

Olimar regains consciousness after the crash and realizes that his life support will only function for another 30 days, after which he will succumb to the planet's oxygen (poisonous to his species).
Plot

If all ship parts are collected within 30 days, Olimar bids the Pikmin farewell and successfully returns home; the Pikmin, with better survival skills, are able to defend themselves against the planet's other hostile creatures.

If Olimar does not collect all 30 parts but manages to collect the 25 necessary parts for successful escape, Olimar hastily leaves the planet at the end of the final day and manages to return home.

lead

lead

lead

When a treasure is found, the Pikmin carry it back to the Hocotate Ship, where it will be placed into the ship's cargo hold and its worth calculated.

Plot
The money from these treasures is enough to start paying off the debt, which is now reduced to 10,000.

In the process of finding treasure, they encounter White and Purple Pikmin, two new species that Olimar had never encountered before.
