However, the voice acting and the departure from the traditional Star Fox -style gameplay received some criticism.
Gameplay

The game is played from a third-person perspective with full camera control in most areas and the ability to use a first-person perspective for looking around a location, with the players able to use a widescreen mode, provided that their console is hooked up to a television set that has widescreen capabilities.
Gameplay
The first style of gameplay is Adventure Mode, which is the main mode, and operates in a similar manner to that of The Legend of Zelda series, especially Ocarina of Time.
Gameplay
As a tool, the staff can be used to open containers, operate mechanisms, or lift up stones to uncover hidden caves and boulders to find items.
Gameplay

In this mode, the player decides where on Dinosaur Planet they wish to go; at the beginning of the game, the planet itself, the game's overworld, is only accessible, but upon unlocking a planet segment during the Adventure Mode, the player gains access to travelling there via Arwing.
Gameplay

In order to visit a place, the player must fly through a set number of gold rings; each segment has around 10 gold rings, and the player will need to fly through more to reach later areas, or be forced to repeat the segment.
Story
After releasing the first one, however, a mysterious being sends Krystal into the spirit's path, trapping her in a floating crystal atop the palace until all the spirits can be returned.
Story
When Fox finds the last spirit, he discovers that it is guarded by Scales himself.
Development
Star Fox Adventures had its origins in two separate projects, one of these being Dinosaur Planet, a Nintendo 64 game unrelated to the Star Fox series.
Development

According to lead engineer Phil Tossell, development of Dinosaur Planet began after the release of Diddy Kong Racing (1997), with two teams to work on Dinosaur Planet and Jet Force Gemini toward the end of the Nintendo 64's lifespan.
Development
The game was changed many times during early development before Rare settled on the eventual idea of an open world adventure-game based around two interwoven stories.
Development
Dinosaur Planet was intended to be Rare's last game for the Nintendo 64 and was adorned with gameplay and cinematics introduced by Ocarina of Time.
Development
Dinosaur Planet initially utilised the Nintendo 64's Expansion Pak and was housed in a 512- megabit (64 megabyte) cartridge, which is the largest size the console would have.
Development
Bayliss said that Rare developed Dinosaur Planet in earnest, including preparation of a large E3 2000 demonstration, without considering that Nintendo already had the Star Fox property.
Development
The Dinosaur Planet demo caught Miyamoto's attention, noticing the similarities of Rare's anthropomorphic design of Sabre to Nintendo's Fox McCloud design were striking.
Development

Just prior to E3 2000, Nintendo asked Rare to keep discussion of Dinosaur Planet quiet and arranged a meeting with Rare to see about a "marriage" of Dinosaur Planet and their Star Fox Adventures concept during the event.
Development
The two agreed to the idea of Star Fox Adventures: Dinosaur Planet as a Nintendo 64 game, maintaining as much of Rare's work.
Development

Likewise, for Star Fox 64, although the game certainly appeals to children somewhat, I think Miyamoto felt that leaning fully into that would be going too far, and he wanted to add some more mature touches where possible.
Development
The team later realised the potential of using the Star Fox licence in hopes of boosting awareness, and switch development from the Nintendo 64 to the then-upcoming GameCube console as a launch game.
Development

According to Imamura, he and Miyamoto were looking to add "sex appeal" to the Star Fox franchise, as Miyamoto wanted the series to have mature elements where possible, and that Krystal's new design was inspired by Vampirella, a comic book character known for wearing risqué outfits.
Development

Of all games converted away from Nintendo 64 in its late market span, IGN called this possibly the biggest departure, having expected it to be one of the platform's killer apps, and side-by-side comparing its "amazing graphical upgrades" on GameCube.
Development
With the Star Fox theme established, Rare begun re-working the game for the then-upcoming GameCube and was subsequently met with little interference from Nintendo.
Development
During development, the team was invited to Nintendo's headquarters in Kyoto to discuss progress and certain changes; in return Imamura came to stay at Rare's Twycross studio to oversee development.
Development
Tossell stated that "without a doubt", Nintendo strengthened their relationship through trust and respect, though Nintendo only had a 49% stake of the company at the time.
Development
In February 2021, a late development version of Dinosaur Planet for the Nintendo 64 dated December 2000 was leaked online, having been acquired from a collector in Sweden.
Development
The build features a unique model for Fox instead of Sabre, indicating that Miyamoto's intervention happened before the decision was made to transition the game to GameCube.
Development
Star Fox Adventures is the only Rare game released for the GameCube.
Development
Shortly after its release, Microsoft purchased Rare for £375 million, ending most of Rare's association with Nintendo.
Development
Rare continued developing games for the Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS after the acquisition.
Reception
It sold over 200,000 copies in Japan following its release, and was the fastest-selling GameCube game at the time.
Reception
By July 2006, it had sold 800,000 copies and earned $30 million (~$ 43.6 million in 2023) in the United States.
Reception
Next Generation ranked it as the 73rd highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.
Reception
Combined sales of Star Fox games released during the 2000s reached 1.2 million units in the United States by July 2006.
Reception
Star Fox Adventures was eventually designated a Player's Choice game by Nintendo, signifying over 250,000 copies sold, and was thus available at a reduced retail price.
Reception

Edge wrote that the "visual splendour is immense", whilst in a similar fashion Matt Casamassina of IGN noted that the game is a "perfect companion" to The Legend of Zelda series, to which Adventures is often compared.
Reception
NGC Magazine said that the accents of most of the characters did not suit that of the Star Fox world, in particular they noted the use of a Scottish accent for the Warpstone Master was "awful".
Reception
Casamassina asserted that Fox was "clearly only on 'Dinosaur Planet' at Nintendo's request, not because he belongs".
Reception

NGC Magazine similarly expressed concern on why Fox was added to the game, adding that Adventures was "one game Fox himself would probably want to forget" and further speculating that Nintendo only added the Star Fox license to prevent Dinosaur Planet from appearing on the Xbox.
Reception
GameSpot named Star Fox Adventures the second-best GameCube game of September 2002.

fcube_star_vixen_assault.title: Star Fox: Assault

Director(s): Toshiyuki Nakanishi Hideki Okazaki Yutaka Yoshida
Producer(s): Tsuyoshi Kobayashi Shigeru Miyamoto Takaya Imamura
Writer(s): Yoshihiko Arawi Ayumu Shindo Kazuya Hatazawa

sents: lead
Star Fox: Assault is a 2005 third-person shooter game developed by Namco and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead
It is the fourth released title in the Star Fox series.
lead
The game was released on 15 February 2005 in North America, on 24 February 2005 in Japan, on 29 April 2005 in Europe, and on 16 June 2005 in Australia.
lead
The game is set after the events of Star Fox Adventures, and follows Fox McCloud and his team attempting to save the Lylat System from the enemy insectoid beings called Aparoids.
lead
It contains orchestral arrangements of music from Star Fox 64 as well as original tracks created specifically for the game.
lead
When Assault was initially announced by Nintendo and Namco, it was also rumored that an arcade game was under development, but it was never officially revealed to the public.
Gameplay
Arwing missions are similar to those of the first two games in the series.
Gameplay

Playing on foot essentially turns the game into a 3D third-person run 'n' gun shooter; the player starts armed with a standard blaster gun and can acquire a variety of other weapons scattered throughout each stage.
Gameplay
Whenever damage is taken from enemies or hazards, the shield or health meter depletes; depleting the meter completely will cause the vehicle to be destroyed or the player to lose a life.
Multiplayer

This mode starts off very limited, with only a few playable characters, weapons, items, and maps; but many more can be unlocked by either playing a certain number of multiplayer games or achieving certain accomplishments in-game.
Story
During the battle, Oikonny's flagship is destroyed by an insectoid creature, which attacks the Star Fox team.
Story
Beltino explains the creature is a member of a race of robotic insectoids called Aparoids, one of which ravaged the Cornerian fleet 17 years prior.
Story
The Memory Unit Pigma had stolen is then sent to Beltino for analysis.
Story
Star Fox and Star Wolf travel to the Aparoid Homeworld, only to discover the planet's core is blocked by a regenerative shield.
Development
Star Fox: Assault was first informally announced on May 8, 2002, several months before the release of its predecessor, Star Fox Adventures.
Development

Star Fox: Assault was meant to be a return to the series' roots, after Star Fox Adventures being a notable departure from the series' usual 3D Rail shooter gameplay in favor of an action adventure styled title.
Development

The game's development, unusually, began with its multiplayer battle mode, as Imamura desired to improve upon the battle mode that was present in St ar Fox 64, which was described as being a last-minute bonus.
Development
At E3 2004, EGM, the same magazine that wrote poorly about it a year before, wrote a follow-up that said the game looked "much better than...a year ago".
Development
Assault was then scheduled for a November 2004 release, but was delayed to the beginning of 2005.
Development
The last "acceleration style" control scheme was included to harken back to the Nintendo 64 controller, where the player presses the R trigger to accelerate, feeling that older fans would enjoy it.
Development
Most of the score pieces use themes from Star Fox 64, composed by Koji Kondo and Hajime Wakai.
Reception
In Electronic Gaming Monthly, two of the reviewers gave it an 8 out of 10.
Reception
Play Magazine gave the game 8 out of 10.
Reception
The game became enough of a commercial success for it to be included in Nintendo's Player's Choice line, which also includes Star Fox 64 and Star Fox Adventures.

fcube_donkey_kongaa.title: Donkey Konga
sents: lead
Donkey Konga is a series of rhythm video games developed by Namco and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
lead

A spin-off of the Donkey Kong series, they are played with a special controller called the DK Bongos that resemble two small bongo drums, but can optionally be played with the standard GameCube controllers.
lead
Donkey Konga was developed by the team that were responsible for developing the Taiko no Tatsujin series.
lead
The tracks include songs such as " Louie Louie ", " We Will Rock You ", " Shining Star ", " Rock Lobster ", " Losing My Religion ", and Hungarian Dance#5 in G Minor.
lead
There are tracks from the Mario series, The Legend of Zelda series, and other Nintendo related music.
lead

The Japanese, North American, and PAL region versions have different track lists, and in the North American version of the first two games, almost all of the licensed non-Nintendo/traditional songs are shortened covers.
lead
The first two games have around 30 tracks each, depending on the region, while Donkey Konga 3 has 58.
Plot
At first they are against this, but then they realize if they can become successful in playing the bongos, they could afford as many bananas as they wish, so they start practicing.
Donkey Konga 2

Donkey Konga 2, marketed in Japan as "Donkey Konga 2: Hit Song Parade!", is the 2004 sequel to Donkey Konga for the Nintendo GameCube, a video game where the player must pound on a special, barrel-like controller called the DK Bongos along with a selected song.
Donkey Konga 2
The main selling point of Donkey Konga 2 is over 30 new tracks to play with Bongos.
Donkey Konga 3
Donkey Konga 3 is a music video game in the Donkey Kong series developed by Namco and published by Nintendo.
Donkey Konga 3

Before the second installment was released in North America, Nintendo and Namco had already started plans for the third game in the series, which, unlike the first two Donkey Konga games, was eventually released only in Japan on March 17, 2005.
Donkey Konga 3
Donkey Konga 3 features a total of 57 tracks (none repeated from the previous games), over 20 tracks more than the first two games.
Donkey Konga 3
35 of these tunes are the usual classical, pop, and game selections, but an extra 21 tunes from Famicom games are included.
Donkey Konga
Donkey Konga won an award at the Game Developers Conference for the best "Innovation" in 2005.
Donkey Konga 2
Donkey Konga 2 received "average" reviews according to Metacritic.

dc_skies_of_arcadio.title: Skies of Arcadia
sents: lead
Skies of Arcadia is a 2000 Dreamcast role-playing video game developed by Overworks and published by Sega.
lead
Players control Vyse, a young air pirate, and his friends as they attempt to stop the Valuan Empire from reviving ancient weapons with the potential to destroy the world.
lead

Skies of Arcadia uses traditional Japanese role-playing game systems such as turn-based battles and experience points, but puts greater focus on exploration, with the player flying an airship in 3D space.
lead
The development team included staff who had contributed to the Panzer Dragoon, Phantasy Star, Sonic the Hedgehog and Sakura Wars series.
lead
Skies of Arcadia received critical acclaim upon release and is frequently regarded as one of the best games for the Dreamcast, although the game underperformed commercially.
lead
A port for the GameCube, Skies of Arcadia Legends, was released in 2002.
Gameplay
Gameplay is similar to early 3D Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest games; the player engages enemies in turn-based battles to earn experience points, making their characters stronger.
Gameplay
The overworld is divided into six regions, traversed by flying airships in 3D space; "Discoveries", hidden locations, reward the player with extra benefits.
Gameplay
Getting through the end of the maze generally culminates in a last boss battle to be won prior to exiting.
Setting
The most advanced, the Silver Civilization, used their Gigas to summon the Rains of Destruction, which pulled meteors from the orbiting moons and crashed them down onto the planet's surface.
Setting
The catastrophic destruction stopped the rampage of the Gigas, as well as nearly destroyed the other five civilizations, thus ending the war.
Setting
A seal was placed on the Silver Gigas to prevent it from being used again, and the Moon Crystals were hidden away, while each civilization worked on rebuilding itself.
Characters
The other two main characters, Aika and Fina, are mandatory characters for the party through most of the game.
Story
Upon the Silver Civilization learning of this plan, they send Fina to find the Moon Crystals first.
Development
The title was changed to Eternal Arcadia in 2000, retained for the Japanese release.
Development

Producer Rieko Kodama had worked on Phantasy Star 1, 2 and 4, and the first two Sonic the Hedgehog games for the Sega Genesis, while scenario writer Shuntaro Tanaka had written the stories for the first two Sakura Wars RPGs.
Development
The soundtrack was composed by Yutaka Minobe and Tatsuyuki Maeda; Maeda had composed music for Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
Development
Expectations were high, as Team Andromeda's prior game, Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998), had received critical acclaim, and the Dreamcast had few well-reviewed JRPGs.
Development
After production moved to the Dreamcast, the motif of traveling the skies was set, inspired by the Age of Discovery.
Development
The Japanese Dreamcast release date was set for September 14, 2000, but delayed to October 5, 2000, so the team could create a paid "trial version" for concurrent release.
Localization
The localization was completed in four months, with 80- to 100-hour work weeks, on a script of over 2,000 pages.
Localization
Skies of Arcadia was released in English in North America on November 14, 2000, and in English, German, French and Spanish in Europe on April 21, 2001.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port

In October 2001, shortly after Sega's announcement that it would abandon the Dreamcast to make software for other consoles, Sega announced that it would port Skies of Arcadia to GameCube and PlayStation 2.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port
Development was announced to begin in January 2002, with Sega initially aiming for a mid-2002 release.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port
In August 2002, Sega announced that the PS2 version was cancelled in favor of focusing on the GameCube release, which was, as of October 2002, 80% complete.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port

Skies of Arcadia Legends was released on the GameCube in Japan on December 26, 2002, in North America on January 28, 2003, and in Europe on May 23, 2003, with Infogrames distributing for the latter territory.
Skies of Arcadia Legends port
A port for Windows was announced in early 2004, but never released.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 33 out of 40.
Reception
A reviewer of GameFan gave it 99%, calling it "By far my favorite RPG of all time thanks to its great story, looks, and battle system.
Reception
GameSpot praised the visuals, stating that they were "some of the most painstakingly detailed ever seen in a role-playing game".
Reception
Four-Eyed Dragon of GamePro called it "a Dreamcast role-playing game worth playing to the very end.
Reception
The game was a finalist for the "Best Dreamcast Game" and "Best Role-Playing Game" awards at GameSpot ' s Best and Worst of 2000 Awards, both of which went to NFL 2K1 and Chrono Cross, respectively.
Reception

The game was also nominated for the "Best Console RPG" and "Best New Game Character" (Vyse) awards at The Electric Playground ' s Blister Awards 2000, both of which went to Valkyrie Profile and Ulala from Space Channel 5, respectively.
Reception
Game Informer later listed it as one of the top 10 Dreamcast games.
Reception

In a 2017 retrospective from Metacritic on the highest-rated exclusive games (at time of release) per platform, Skies of Arcadia placed third for the Dreamcast, behind Soulcalibur and Jet Grind Radio.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best JRPGs of All Time" list.
GameCube port
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 32 out of 40.
GameCube port
Fennec Fox of GamePro stated that "there's no need to harp on the battles too much---they're the only blemish on what's otherwise the Dreamcast's (and now GameCube's) best RPG.
GameCube port
The graphics are dated but effective, and the musician was obviously overdosing on 1930s adventure serials when composing the over-the-top score.
GameCube port
The story, though, is the best part---Vyse and crew are the most extroverted RPG heroes ever, and there's none of that Final Fantasy -style self-abhorrence present.
Cancelled entries
In addition to the cancelled PlayStation 2 and PC releases of the game, a sequel to the game was considered by Sega in the early 2000s, but did not begin full production.
Cancelled entries

In September 2002, after the completion of Legends, Skies of Arcadia producer Rieko Kodama stated that the team was still interested in creating a sequel, but that work had still not started on it, though had it started, she felt that the GameCube would have been the most likely platform for its release.
Cancelled entries
In February 2003, Overworks president Noriyoshi Ohba announced that a Skies of Arcadia sequel had entered the planning stages.
Cancelled entries

Starting in 2010, Sega began a campaign of releasing HD remasters of Dreamcast games digitally on PlayStation Network and Xbox Live for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 consoles, including games such as Sonic Adventure, Crazy Taxi, Sonic Adventure 2 and Jet Set Radio.
Cancelled entries
In 2012, Sega brand manager Ben Harborne stated that a Skies of Arcadia HD was a likely next release, after Shenmue, as they were the most frequently requested titles for re-release.
Cancelled entries
As recently as 2020, main developer staff Kenji Hiruta expressed interest in returning to the series as well.
In other media
Multiple characters from the game later appeared in Sega's 2008 video game Valkyria Chronicles, another title directed by Shuntaro Tanaka.
In other media
"Vyse Inglebard" and "Aika Thompson" appear as optional members of Squad 7 and are listed on each other's "Like" list.
In other media
The three also appeared in the Japan-only Valkyria Chronicles III in 2011 as well.
In other media

Vyse also appears in the Sonic the Hedgehog comic book adaptation of Transformed featured in Sonic Universe #45, and again in the Sonic comics for the "World Unite" Sega character crossover story arc.

dc_jetset.title: Jet Set Radio
sents: lead
Jet Set Radio (originally released in North America as Jet Grind Radio) is a 2000 action game developed by Smilebit and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
lead
The player controls a member of a youth gang, the GGs, as they use inline skates to traverse Tokyo, spraying graffiti, challenging rival gangs, and evading authorities.
lead
Development was headed by director Masayoshi Kikuchi, with art by Ryuta Ueda.
lead

The team drew influence from late 1990s Japanese popular culture such as the rhythm game PaRappa the Rapper and the anti-establishment themes in the film Fight Club, and 1980s American hip hop culture such as graffiti.
lead
The environments were based on Tokyo shopping districts in Shibuya and Shinjuku, with graffiti designed by artists including Eric Haze.
lead
Jet Set Radio was the first game to use a cel-shaded art style, developed in response to the team's disappointment with the abundance of sci-fi and fantasy Sega games.
lead
Jet Set Radio received acclaim and is considered one of the best games of its decade for its graphics, soundtrack and gameplay.
lead
It won several awards and was nominated for many others.
Gameplay
The first is to tag every graffiti point in each area previously tagged by a rival gang before the timer runs out while evading the authorities.
Plot
After the GGs defeat Poison Jam, Noise Tanks, and Love Shockers in turf wars, they each drop a piece of a mysterious vinyl record.
Plot
Professor K says that the mysterious vinyl record collected is The Devil's Contract and has the power to summon a demon.
Plot
Poison Jam explains that the Rokkaku CEO, Goji Rokkaku, plans to use the record to make a contract with the demon and take over the world.
Plot
In a twist, Combo reveals that The Devil's Contract is an old record with no demonic powers and that wealth had driven Goji to insanity.
Development
The development team consisted of fewer than 25 developers, with an average age of under 25.
Development
The game was announced at the 1999 Tokyo Game Show and drew media attention for its cel-shaded style.
Development
Ueda wanted to create something "cool" that dealt with popular culture and was completely unlike the team's previous game, the 1998 role-playing game Panzer Dragoon Saga.
Development
Ueda was particularly inspired by a demonstration of the PlayStation rhythm game PaRappa the Rapper at the 1996 Tokyo Game Show: "I think that's the first game with pop culture like that.
Development
After that I decided to make a true game, not just a visual experience, that was actually for adults." The anti-establishment themes of the 1999 film Fight Club were another influence.
Development
Smilebit developed a new cel-shading technique not used at the time as it would not have been possible on the Dreamcast or PlayStation 2.
Development
Jet Set Radio was one of the earliest games to feature an open 3D world, which presented the team's biggest challenge.
Development
The settings were inspired by Japanese locations such as the Tokyo shopping districts of Shibuya and Shinjuku, which Smilebit photographed to use as references.
Soundtrack
The 2012 port omits "Yappie Feet" and "Many Styles" for licensing reasons.
Soundtrack
Most of the soundtrack was composed by Hideki Naganuma, with additional tracks by Richard Jacques, Deavid Soul, Toronto, and B.B.
Soundtrack
In 2012, Naganuma said Jet Set Radio and its sequel had been his favorite projects.
Soundtrack

A soundtrack CD, Jet Grind Radio Music Sampler, was given to those who pre-ordered the game in the United States, featuring 10 tracks from the game, 4 of which do not appear in any version of Jet Set Radio.
Soundtrack
The soundtrack CD, Jet Set Radio Original Soundtrack (UPCH-1048), featured 19 tracks including a data track from the game and was distributed by Polydor Records on December 20, 2000, in Japan.
Soundtrack

For the HD release, a new soundtrack CD titled Jet Set Radio: Original Soundtrack with Bonus Tracks from JSRF, was distributed by Sumthing Else on September 18, 2012, for North America and Europe, containing a total of 17 tracks, 10 from the game and 7 additional tracks from the sequel, Jet Set Radio Future.
Soundtrack

A second soundtrack for the HD version, Jet Set Radio: Sega Original Tracks, was distributed by Sega, containing 15 tracks and was released on iTunes on October 3, 2012 alongside Jet Set Radio Future: Sega Original Tracks.
Promotion and release
Jet Set Radio was released in Japan on June 29, 2000.
Promotion and release
In North America, it was released on October 31 as Jet Grind Radio due to trademark problems for "Jet Set" in the United States at the time.
Promotion and release
The PAL version was released later on November 24 under the original name.
Promotion and release

Sega chose five finalists and flew them into San Francisco, California on October 21, where they competed to make graffiti art pieces on a canvas within a 3 and a half-hour timeframe for a prize of $5000.
Alternative versions
This version was released on October 18, 2001, in Japan via Dreamcast Direct (later renamed Sega Direct) and included a T-shirt featuring the protagonist Beat for those who pre-ordered.
Mobile versions
The first, Typing Jet, a side-scrolling game in which players escape police, was released for Japanese mobile phones by Sega on June 22, 2001.
Mobile versions
It was followed by a remake for Game Boy Advance developed by Vicarious Visions and published by THQ in North America on June 26, 2003, and in Europe on February 20, 2004.
Mobile versions

The Game Boy Advance version uses the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 engine and an isometric perspective, and it emulates the cel-shaded graphics of the Dreamcast game, with some original stages and shortened songs.
High-definition remaster
In 2012, high-definition ports developed by BlitWorks were released for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, Windows, PlayStation Vita, iOS, and Android.
High-definition remaster
The game was made backwards-compatible with the Xbox One in May 2016.
High-definition remaster
In North America, the PS3 version was released on September 18, with PlayStation Plus members able to purchase it early on September 11.
High-definition remaster
The PS3 version was released in Europe the following day alongside The Xbox Live Arcade and Windows version for both North America and Europe.
High-definition remaster

The PlayStation Vita version was scheduled for release on October 16, but was delayed for development optimization reasons; it was released on November 20 in North America and in Europe the following day.
High-definition remaster
The PS3, Xbox 360, and PlayStation Vita versions were released in Japan simultaneously on February 20, 2013.
High-definition remaster
The iOS and Android versions were released in North America and Europe on November 29, 2012.
High-definition remaster
Japan received the iOS version on December 20, 2012 and Android on January 30, 2013.
High-definition remaster
The smartphone versions were delisted as of 2015 due to compatibility problems with iOS updates.
Critical reception
The camera controls were commonly criticized, but most reviewers said the overall quality outweighed them.
Critical reception
DC-UK also praised it for resembling a 2D cartoon in 3D space, and considered it ground-breaking.
Critical reception
GamePro wrote that the visuals were unique and that the stylized design was convincing and fun.
Critical reception
GamesRadar+ praised how it is a joy to play even 12 years after its release.
Critical reception

Eurogamer also gave positive statements, calling the visual style "timeless", and complimented the HD remaster, stating "12 years on and this is a surprisingly rigorous game built of oddball delights, then, and the HD updating has only enhanced its charms.
Critical reception
Game Informer further elaborated that in retrospect, the originally released visual style blinded them from its faulty gameplay.
Critical reception
Across all versions of the game combined, including the original and re-releases sales of Jet Set Radio surpassed 1 million copies worldwide.
Accolades
Jet Set Radio won the Best Console Game at the E3 Game Critics Awards in 2000 and was the runner up for Best in Show at the same event.
Accolades
The game won the category of "Excellence in Visual Arts" award, received a "Game Spotlights Award" and was nominated for Game of the year at the 2001 Game Developers Choice Awards.
Accolades
Gamers' Republic awarded it "Best 3D Game Design" in its 2000 Year in Review.
Accolades
The game was also featured in 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
Legacy
Jet Set Radio is recognized as one of the first games to feature cel-shaded graphics, with exaggerated shapes, thick lines, and flat, bright colors.
Legacy
A sequel, Jet Set Radio Future, was released for the Xbox in 2002, early in the system's life cycle.
Legacy
In 2009, an early antagonist in the game, Captain Onishima, was ranked 95th in IGN's "Top 100 Videogame Villains" list.
Legacy
In 2021, Sega teased the possibility of a Jet Set Radio reboot, and announced Beat as a playable character for Super Monkey Ball Banana Mania.
Legacy
Sega announced a new Jet Set Radio game at the Game Awards 2023.

dc_space_channel_6.title: Space Channel 5
sents: lead
Space Channel 5 is a music video game developed and published by Sega.
lead
Originally released for the Dreamcast (1999 in Japan, 2000 worldwide), it was later ported to the PlayStation 2 (2002 in Europe, 2003 in Japan and North America).
lead
A version for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) was published in 2003 as a Western exclusive.
lead
Following space-faring reporter Ulala as she investigates an alien invasion, players engage in rhythm-based combat where Ulala mimics the actions of rivals in time to musical tracks.
lead
The game was conceived by Tetsuya Mizuguchi, who was told to create something aimed at a female audience.
lead
Production lasted two years, with a staff of around 20 that included company veterans and newcomers to game development.
lead
The music, composed by Naofumi Hataya and Kenichi Tokoi, drew inspiration from big band music.
lead
Ken Woodman 's "Mexican Flyer" had informed the musical style and acted as the theme song.
Synopsis and gameplay

Space Channel 5 is a music video game in which players take on the role of Ulala, a reporter working for the titular news channel in a 1960s-styled science fiction future filled with competing news channels.
Synopsis and gameplay
The invasion is revealed to have been staged by Space Channel 5 boss Chief Blank to drive up ratings for the channel.
Synopsis and gameplay
During boss battles, Ulala has a health meter represented on-screen as hearts; a heart is lost for each mistake.
Development

The concept for Space Channel 5 originated when Tetsuya Mizuguchi —then known for his work on racing games—was contacted by Sega to develop a game for the Dreamcast aimed at a female casual gaming demographic.
Development
Other sources of inspiration were the music of the 1950s and 60s, and the music videos of Peter Gabriel and Michael Jackson that were showing on MTV during the 80s.
Development
This concept originated in 1993, with full production beginning in 1998 following extensive internal planning and approval by Sega senior staff.
Development
Production was handled by Sega AM9, later known as United Game Artists.
Development
Beginning with a small team of ten, it eventually expanded to 27 members as development progressed.
Development
The game was Mizuguchi's first time working on a game aimed exclusively at the home console market, as his earlier work had first been developed for arcade.
Design

To make the game more interesting, Mizuguchi drew inspiration from the rhythm troope Stomp; a particular piece which inspired him was a segment where a performer would have the audience copy their clapping, with the rhythm becoming more complex over time.
Design
The name of the game's aliens "Morolians" was a derivation of the surname of artist Mayumi Moro; it came about as the team often used her last name around the office.
Design
A key aspect of the game was that while the gameplay involved shooting, Ulala never actually killed anyone, allowing the game to be approachable to a wider range of players.
Design
The game content filled just over 99% of the Dreamcast GD-ROM disc.
Design
An early tech demo was put together for the game; in this prototype version, the player character was a man, and only the most basic elements of its gameplay and theme were in place.
Design
A later version featured a prototype design for Ulala.
Design
Mizuguchi was inspired by the contrasting styles of orchestral music and science fiction setting used in Star Wars.
Design
Kazdal said that one of Ulala's key design inspirations was the titular lead of the science fiction film Barbarella (1968).
Music
The music for Space Channel 5 was composed by Naofumi Hataya and Kenichi Tokoi of Sega's music label WaveMaster.
Music
The musical style, inspired by big band jazz of the 1950s and 60s, was one of the earliest elements to be decided upon.
Music
Music production ran simultaneously with the game's production, with the sound team at first using concept art and in-production gameplay.
Music
The final total of in-game music was estimated at 70 minutes.
Music
The game's main theme was "Mexican Flyer", composed by Ken Woodman in 1966.
Music
A soundtrack album for the game was published by Marvelous Entertainment and distributed by VAP on February 21, 2000.
Music
The album featured 22 tracks, including a remix of "Mexican Flyer".
Music
Tracks from Space Channel 5 were included in the compilation album Space Channel 5 20th Anniversary: Gyungyun Selection by UMA on December 18, 2019.
Voice cast
Most of the voice roles were performed by members of the game's staff.
Voice cast
Professionals Show Hayami and Kae Iida were hired for the roles of rival reporters Jaguar and Pudding respectively, with Iida originally being planned for the role of Ulala.
Voice cast

Mizuguchi initially wanted to refuse the request, as the game was only a month away from completion, but the team wanted to include Jackson, so they substituted a Morolian-controlled NPC character for a model based on Jackson and added moves based on the singer's famous dance moves.
Release
Space Channel 5 was first announced at the September 1999 Tokyo Game Show.
Release
The game was released in Japan on December 16, 1999.
Release
In the US, Sega conducted a contest in Universal City, California titled Space Channel 5 Ulala-a-like Contest.
Release
The contestants were girls between the ages of 9 and 21 who competed to who could resemble Ulala the best.
Release
The contestants were able to meet with Ulala portrayed by Kelly Preston and the winner won $500 and a Dreamcast.
Release
The game was released internationally in 2000; it was published in North America on June 6, and in Europe on October 8.
Release
Following their exit from the console market, Sega began moving the Space Channel 5 franchise onto other systems, beginning with the PlayStation 2.
Release
The PS2 version released in Europe on March 15, 2002; and in Japan on December 12 of that year.
Release
In North America, the PS2 port was bundled with its sequel and published in the region by Agetec.
Release
In Japan, the PS2 version has since become a rarity, fetching high resale prices.
Release
A remake for the Game Boy Advance titled Space Channel 5: Ulala's Cosmic Attack was also produced.
Release
The game was released as a Western exclusive in 2003; it was published on June 17 in North America and September 12 in Europe.
Dreamcast
During its first week, it sold through just over 44% of its stock with over 41,000 units.
Dreamcast
It eventually sold over 93,600 units in Japan, being among the region's top 40 best-selling Dreamcast titles.
Dreamcast
At a 2002 conference, the game was declared a success by its staff, finding a wide audience among both hardcore and casual gamers.
Dreamcast
In contrast during a 2005 interview, Mizuguchi said that the game was not a commercial success.
Dreamcast
According to video game review aggregator GameRankings, the Dreamcast version earned a score of 84% based on 34 reviews.
Dreamcast
Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu gave the game a score of 29 points out of 40.
Dreamcast
Pat Garratt of Computer and Video Games gave the game a perfect score, calling it a unique game and "absolute must for every DC owner".
Dreamcast
GameSpot ' s Jeff Gerstmann said Space Channel 5 was worth playing for its unconventional art style and music, with his main complaints being repetitive gameplay and lack of unlockables.
Dreamcast
IGN gave both the Japanese original and the Western release near-perfect scores, praising the presentation while criticizing the short length and timing issues.
Dreamcast
Space Channel 5 was nominated for awards in four categories at the 1999 Japan Game Awards.
Dreamcast
Space Channel 5 and Sega AM9 were nominated at the 2002 BAFTA Awards in the "Best Audio" category, losing to Luigi's Mansion.
Dreamcast

In anniversary retrospectives and lists of favorite Dreamcast titles from multiple websites including Gamasutra and IGN, Space Channel 5 has been remembered as one of the most unique titles on the system for its gameplay design and art direction.
Dreamcast
1UP.com, in an article about Mizuguchi's work with United Game Artists, "highlight" on the Dreamcast and described as "unlike anything before it."
PlayStation 2
The PlayStation 2 port was met with a similarly positive response.
PlayStation 2

GameRankings gave the North American release a score of 79% based on 7 reviews; and Metacritic gave it a score of 79 out of a possible 100 from 16 reviews, indicating a "generally favorable" reception.
PlayStation 2
Electronic Gaming Monthly said that the mixture of music and unique style gave the game "an infectious, addictive quality".
PlayStation 2
GamePro called the Special Edition package "easily the best bargain for the PS2 this side of ".
PlayStation 2
Game Informer called the release "a great package crammed with more value and personality than most rhythm games".
PlayStation 2
Douglass Perry of IGN, comparing the game to its sequel that formed part of the package, felt that the first was the inferior game due to lacking the later additions and polishing.
PlayStation 2
PlayStation Magazine felt that the original game's flaws were only exacerbated when contrasted with its sequel.
Game Boy Advance
By contrast, the Game Boy Advance port received a Metacritic score of 55 out of 100 based on 15 reviews, indicating "mixed or average" reception.
Game Boy Advance
For Frank Provo of GameSpot, the biggest problem was the unresponsive controls, as otherwise, the game was a laudable conversion of the game for the GBA.
Game Boy Advance
GameZone said that the difficulties with controlling Ulala and presentation made the game suitable only for hardcore series fans.
Game Boy Advance
Game Informer was also positive, saying that there could be no better version of Space Channel 5 on the platform.
Sequels
A sequel to Space Channel 5 was planned from an early stage, but production was put on hold until Western sales figures came in.
Sequels
The sequel, Space Channel 5: Part 2, was announced in October 2001.
Sequels
The PS2 version was released in mainland Europe the following year.
Sequels
In North America, the game was released as part of Space Channel 5: Special Edition by Agetec.
Sequels
It was the last game produced by United Game Artists prior to Sega's internal restructuring in 2003.
Sequels
Part 2 was later given a high-definition port to Microsoft Windows, Xbox 360, and PlayStation 3.
Sequels
It was released first as part of the Dreamcast Collection in February 2011, then as a standalone digital release in October of the same year.
Sequels
Beginning in 2016 as an experimental collaboration with Sega and KDDI titled Space Channel 5 VR: Ukiuki Viewing Show, the project saw a strong fan response for a full game.
Sequels
Titled Space Channel 5 VR: Kinda Funky News Flash, the player takes the role of novice reporters assisting Ulala during a new invasion report.
Sequels
Originally scheduled for release on PlayStation VR, SteamVR, HTC Vive and Oculus Quest during December 2019, the game was delayed into the following year to improve its quality.
Sequels
All versions were released between February and November 2020.
Additional media and cameos
Ulala was used in a collaboration between MTV and Sega to present the "Best Video" award at the MTV Video Music Award ceremony in 2000.
Additional media and cameos
A CGI television adaptation of Space Channel 5 was originally planned from SuperMega Media.
Additional media and cameos
A film adaptation of the series was announced in August 2022.
Additional media and cameos
Sega's Sonic Team studio also created a mobile application called Ulala's Channel J for Japanese Vodafone devices in July 2001.
Additional media and cameos
The application consisted of several minigames, most themed after the series and specifically Space Channel 5: Part 2.
Additional media and cameos
Some featured 3D graphics that required higher-specification devices to play.
Additional media and cameos
The game shut down in September 2005, with some of its content merged into the Sonic Cafe mobile service.
Additional media and cameos
In 2001, Palisades Toys produced themed merchandise; these included a lunch box, and figures of game characters including boss characters Evila, Pudding, the Morolians, and several variants of Ulala.
Additional media and cameos
Japanese action figure company Figma produced two Ulala figures based on her main looks from Space Channel 5 and its sequel in 2017.
Additional media and cameos
United Game Artists' next game Rez featured the Morolian character as a secret playable character.
Lawsuit
In 2003, Space Channel 5 and its protagonist Ulala were the subject of a lawsuit against Sega from Deee-Lite vocalist Kierin Magenta Kirby.
Lawsuit

In July 2000, a Sega affiliate contacted Kirby to determine if she was interested in promoting the game in England, utilizing the 1990 Deee-Lite song " Groove Is in the Heart "; Kirby rejected the offer.
Lawsuit
During the lawsuit, Sega showed that the game and character had been created and released in Japan between 1997 and 1999.
Lawsuit
Kirby was obliged to pay Sega's legal fees of $608,000 (reduced from $763,000 on request).
Lawsuit
"Groove Is in the Heart" was later licensed for use in Sega's 2008 Wii port of Samba de Amigo, used in a section of the game where the Ulala character appears.

dc_space_channel_6_part_2.title: Space Channel 5: Part 2

Composer(s): Naofumi Hataya Kenichi Tokoi Tomoya Ohtani Mariko Nanba
Platform(s): Dreamcast, PlayStation 2, PlayStation 3, Microsoft Windows, Xbox 360

successor: Space Channel 5 VR: Kinda Funky News Flash

sents: lead
Space Channel 5: Part 2 is a music video game developed by United Game Artists.
lead
A direct sequel to the 1999 game Space Channel 5, the game was published for Dreamcast and PlayStation 2 in Japan in February 2002 by Sega.
lead
The PS2 version released worldwide in 2003 by SCEE (Mainland Europe) and Agetec (North America).
lead
The game later received a high-definition port to Microsoft Windows, Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in 2011 from Sega.
lead
In a space age future, reporter Ulala takes on a group called the Rhythm Rogues and their leader Purge when they unleash a dancing madness on the galaxy.
lead
As Ulala, players engage in rhythm-based combat through scripted levels where Ulala mimics the actions of rivals in time to musical tracks.
lead
Alongside the single-player story campaign, there exists an endurance mode called Ulala's Dance and a multiplayer option for both modes.
lead

Part 2 was produced over two years by many of the same staff; it was the team's last game prior to being merged with Sonic Team, and the last produced by Tetsuya Mizuguchi prior to leaving Sega in 2003.
Synopsis and gameplay

In the music video game Space Channel 5: Part 2, players take on the role of Ulala, a reporter working for the titular news channel in a 1960s-styled science fiction future filled with competing news channels.
Synopsis and gameplay
The Rhythm Rogues kidnap Space President Peace, steal transmitters from other news stations to amplify their dancing signal, and destroy Space Channel 5's base.
Synopsis and gameplay
Players control Ulala through six 3D levels, with some levels having specific gimmicks such as band instrument-based battles or mimicking picture poses.
Synopsis and gameplay
Ratings, shown in the bottom left-hand corner of the screen, increase with each good performance and discovering secret moves.
Synopsis and gameplay
An additional mode outside the main campaign is "Ulala's Dance", a 100-stage endurance battle where Ulala only has a single heart.
Synopsis and gameplay
Successful performance in Ulala's Dance, in addition to finding hidden moves in standard levels, unlocks costumes and accessories for Ulala.
Synopsis and gameplay
Part 2 also supports multiplayer; one player controls the directional pad, while the other controls the action buttons.
Development
A sequel to Space Channel 5 was planned from an early stage, but production was put on hold until Western sales figures came in.
Development
As with the first game, production was handled by Sega's subsidiary studio United Game Artists.
Development

While the original game was developed first for Dreamcast and production was focused on this version, Part 2 saw simultaneous development for Dreamcast and PS2 and was the second game developed by the team for Sony's console.
Development
Space Channel 5: Part 2 was the last title developed by United Game Artists prior to Sega's internal restructuring in 2003, when it was incorporated into the newly formed Sonic Team studio.
Development
While the first game used polygonal real-time models over FMV sequences, the environments in Part 2 were fully 3D.
Development
Based on feedback from the first game, the team added more extras such as alternate costumes and accessories.
Development
To ensure creative control over the voice performances and foreseeing last-minute changes, the game's staff voiced the characters as with the first game.
Development
The game featured an appearance from Michael Jackson, who played himself as a character called Space Michael and is voiced only in English across both the Japanese and English voices.
Development
Having previously appeared in the first game as a brief cameo after being impressed by a pre-release version, he was given a much-expanded role in the sequel.
Development

The first game's director, Takashi Yuda, returned to voice the character Fuze; as did Ulala's respective actresses in Japanese (United Game Artists staff member Mineko Okamura) and English (Apollo Smile).
Music
The music for Part 2 was co-composed by Naofumi Hataya, Kenichi Tokoi, Tomoya Ohtani and Mariko Nanba.
Music
Hataya and Tokoi returned from the first game, with Hataya also acting as sound producer.
Music
The game was Ohtani's third project as a composer after his work on Sonic Adventure 2 and ChuChu Rocket!.
Music
Nanba was brought aboard the project in May 2001, and was initially overwhelmed by both the project and the game's musical style.
Music
Same as with the first game, the music was influenced by big band jazz of the 1960s and 70s.
Music
The main theme was "Mexican Flyer", composed by Ken Woodman in 1966, returning from the first game.
Music
The first rhythm battle created was against rival reporter Pudding, who uses a guitar.
Music
The two albums, respectively titled Chu!! and Hey!!, were published on April 10 and 24, 2002 by Marvelous Entertainment and distributed by VAP.
Music
Two remix albums were also released, featuring both arrangements of tracks from Part 2 and short audio dramas; Uki Uki Non-Stop Mega Mix on June 21 and Moji Moji Can't Stop Remix on June 24.
Music
Tracks from Part 2 were included in the compilation album Space Channel 5 20th Anniversary: Gyungyun Selection by UMA on December 18, 2019.
Release
The game was officially announced by Sega for both Dreamcast and PS2 in October 2001 shortly before that year's Tokyo Game Show.
Release
The game was released in Japan on February 14, 2002, for both Dreamcast and PS2.
Release
The PS2 version later received a budget PS2 the Best release on December 12.
Release
The PS2 version was co-published in Europe as a standalone release by Sega and Sony.
Release
The PS2 version released in mainland Europe on February 12, 2003.
Release
Part 2 only released in North America as part of the Special Edition release including the original Space Channel 5.
Release
Part 2 later received a high definition port as part of Sega's Dreamcast Collection.
Release
This version released on Microsoft Windows and Xbox 360 on February 22, 2011 in North America and February 25 in Europe.
Release
The game later received a standalone digital release for 360 on October 4 and PlayStation 3 on October 5.
Release
The console version released in Japan for both platforms on October 5.
Release
The Steam version was patched in 2014, fixing technical and control issues, and including achievements.
Reception
Upon its debut in Japan, Part 2 reached the top of sales charts.
Reception

According to Mizuguchi, the game sold around 50,000 copies during its first week, then remained steady in the charts in subsequent weeks rather than the expected sharp drop-off of other games experiences.
Reception
Unlike both Space Channel 5 and the studio's other title Rez, Part 2 for the PS2 was a commercial success; 150,000 units were sold in Japan alone.
Reception
Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu gave both versions of the game a score of 35 points out of 40.
Reception
Andrew Reiner provided a second opinion for Game Informer stating that Part 2 —while not as memorable as the original—was still highly enjoyable.
Reception
Brad Shoemaker of GameSpot, despite mechanical similarities, cited Part 2 as the better entry of the two due to added mechanics and the broader range of music despite uneven voice acting and singing.
Reception
Nich Maragos of 1UP.com praised the music, stating it was better than its predecessor for providing more variety and matching the music to the tone of its scenes.
Reception
Maragos further elaborated when reviewing the game for GMR calling the music tighter, and the animation and gameplay improved to the point that he wished the first game had been similar.
Reception
IGN ' s Douglass Perry said that Part 2 fixed the first game's faults and added new elements to enhance the gameplay.
Reception
Peter Garden of Play Magazine enjoyed the sequel far more than its predecessor, citing the upgrade to full 3D graphics and improvements to input responses.
Reception
Reviews of the Dreamcast Collection version were less positive, though most criticisms focused on the collection as a whole.

dc_rezz.title: Rez (video game)
sents: lead
Rez is a musical rail shooter game developed by United Game Artists and published by Sega for the Dreamcast and PlayStation 2.
lead
It was released in Japan in 2001, followed by releases to the United States and Europe in 2002.
lead
The game was ported to Xbox 360 as Rez HD by Q Entertainment and HexaDrive in 2008.
lead

A virtual reality -compatible expanded version dubbed Rez Infinite was co-developed and released through 2016 to 2023 by Enhance Games, Resonair and Monstars for PlayStation 4, Windows, Android, Oculus Quest and PlayStation 5.
lead
Following a hacker's journey into a malfunctioning AI system, the game has players controlling their avatar as they shoot down numerous enemies.
lead
The gameplay and projectile hits sync with the music and have vibration feedback for different controllers, aiming to create a sense of synesthesia.
lead
The narrative is told using little description and no dialogue and includes thematic references to the journey of life and technological singularity.
lead
The game was conceived by Tetsuya Mizuguchi during 1994 and 1995, drawing inspiration from European disco music.
Gameplay
Destroying data nodes in each level raises the "layer level" to a maximum number of 10.
Gameplay
There are five levels, dubbed Areas, although at the start only four can be accessed.
Gameplay
Achieving 100% leveling score for the first four areas of the game unlocks Area 5.
Gameplay
The player character can assume six forms at different power levels, with a seventh unlocked for Area 5.
Gameplay
The lowest possible is Level 00, and if hit again in this state the game ends.
Gameplay
The player raises their level using Progress Nodes, which appear after a certain number of enemies are destroyed.
Gameplay
There are singular Progress Nodes and X3 Progress Nodes that fill three bars on the level meter.
Gameplay
Each area's completion is scored by Analyzation (data nodes accessed), Shot Down (enemies destroyed) and Support Item (support nodes collected).
Production
The original concept for Rez originated between 1994 and 1995.
Production
During research work in Europe on Sega Rally Championship 2, Mizuguchi and a few friends attended the open-air music event Street Parade.
Production

In 1998, Mizuguchi was approached about forming a dedicated team to work on new innovative titles for Sega's new Dreamcast console; his first project along these lines was Space Channel 5, and during its production he made plans for Rez.
Production
As with Space Channel 5, Mizuguchi wanted to draw in casual gamers from across demographics, along with people who would normally not play games.
Production
Production proper began in 1999 following the completion of Space Channel 5.
Production
The final title was meant to be a contraction of "Resolve", but during a studio visit from Edge Magazine staff, he was inspired to connect it to the concept of "de-rezzing" from the 1982 movie Tron.
Production
Production of the game began on Dreamcast, but during development a version was put into motion for the PlayStation 2 (PS2) which would release simultaneously with the Dreamcast version.
Production
Rez was the first Sega-produced game released on the PS2, and one of Sega's last first-party titles for the Dreamcast.
Production
According to technical officer Ryuichi Hattori, a lot of problems stemmed from it being the team's first PS2 title.
Game design
The first concept for the gameplay of Rez was that when the player shot something down, it would create a sound in synch with the background music, coupled with a vibration through the controller.
Game design
The game's software was developed entirely from scratch, causing issues for the team, particularly due to the PS2 release.
Game design
The first working prototype featured a figure running through a cyberspace environment, while a later build used a fighter jet.
Game design

The vibration feedback made use of the Dreamcast vibration pack, the DualShock 2 controller for PS2, and a custom controller created by Mizuguchi's team for the game dubbed the Trance Vibrator that could be used with the PS2 version.
Game design
The Trance Vibrator was Mizuguchi's idea, starting as a joke to enhance the visual mechanics of the game.
Game design
While the standard controllers gave good vibration feedback, it only fed into the hands.
Art design and scenario
Kazdel, who worked on Space Channel 5, was on board as a character artist and graphics co-designer with Ryutaro Sugiyama.
Art design and scenario
One of the game's earliest visual inspirations was the work of Wassily Kandinsky, a 19th-century artist whose abstract work made a profound impression on Mizuguchi and his work.
Art design and scenario
The early plans had levels directly inspired by Kandinsky's artwork, but Mizuguchi decided against this.
Art design and scenario

One of the principle inspirations was Kandinsky's theories on synesthesia, sensations created by the combination of different sensory inputs that had already inspired Mizuguchi's work on Space Channel 5.
Art design and scenario

A major decision for the team was using wire frame graphics for everything from character models to environments, paying homage to early video game graphics such as were seen in the 1983 Star Wars game and Missile Command.
Art design and scenario
The decision to use this style was described by Yokota as "quite interesting", as his work on Panzer Dragoon had been aiming for the highest realism possible.
Art design and scenario
All but Area 5 were created using the same methodology; the wire frame was in the level foreground, while any particle effects and other visual elements were placed in the background area.
Art design and scenario
The first four levels had different visual themes and two key colors each.
Art design and scenario
Kazdel described this last area as Yokota's "personal trip out level".
Art design and scenario
Mizuguchi's first ideas for the game's plot, which is delivered through "sensory" means rather than being driven by text and narration, was to form a connection between life and music.
Art design and scenario
The narrative poem shown during Area 5 was written by Yokota.
Music
It drew inspiration from the soundtracks of Xenon 2 Megablast (1989) and Xevious (1983), along with Haruomi Hosono 's 1984 Super Xevious remix single.
Music
Mizuguchi listened to the early versions of tracks, picking "Rock is Sponge" as most suitable.
Music
Freeland also created his track "Fear" as an original piece, inspired by Mizuguchi's description of the game as being inspired by the artwork of Kandinsky.
Music
For the album release, the team asked each composer to create a new remix that was the "highest" form of the track that had been mixed and synced to gameplay.
Music
The soundtrack album, titled Rez / Gamer's Guide to..., was co-published in collaboration with United Game Artists by Musicmine, an imprint of Universal, and independent record company Third Ear.
Music
The soundtrack was released January 23, 2002.
Music
The Rez soundtracks were Third Ear's first major commercial release, with one of its founders using contacts within Sega to get the publishing contract.
Release
The game was first announced at E3 2001 under its working title "K-Project".
Release
The game was announced under its official title the following month at the Shibuya-AX Sony PlayStation 2 party.
Release
Sega acted as publisher for the Dreamcast version worldwide and the PS2 version in Japan and North America.
Release
The game was released in Japan for both PS2 and Dreamcast on November 22, 2001.
Release
A special "Absolute Set" edition, limited to 500 units, was sold exclusively through the Tsutaya store chain.
Release
The Japanese versions also included a Morolian alien from Space Channel 5 as a secret playable character if players had save data from Space Channel 5.
Release
While the Dreamcast version was localised into English for a European release, it went unreleased in North America.
Release
The PS2 version was marketed and published in Europe as part of Sony's deal with Sega to distribute multiple titles in the region.
Release
The game released on January 8, 2002, in North America, and February 20 in Europe.
Release
The Trance Vibrator was offered for a limited time through Sega's American online store.
Rez HD
A high-definition remaster for Xbox 360, titled Rez HD, was developed by Mizuguchi's studio Q Entertainment and HexaDrive.
Rez HD
The game was released through Xbox Live Arcade on January 30, 2008.
Rez HD
Rez HD was HexaDrive's first job as a company.
Rez HD
For the conversion, the team adjusted the aspect ratio, and raised the framerate from 30 to 60 per second.
Rez Infinite
Rez Infinite is an expanded release of Rez, first announced in December 2015 for PlayStation 4 (PS4).
Rez Infinite
The biggest addition to the game for Infinite was "Area X", which was built from scratch using Unreal Engine 4 and unlocked after playing the original for one hour.
Rez Infinite
The team received additional marketing support from 8-4.
Rez Infinite
Mizuguchi decided on two points; first to have particles generated from impacts so players could see a visualisation of the sounds and music, and second that players could roam freely.
Rez Infinite
The PS4 version released on October 13, 2016.
Rez Infinite
The release, co-created by Iam8bit, also featured a large book detailing the making of both Rez and Rez Infinite, with extensive interviews with Mizuguchi and other staff members.
Rez Infinite
A version for Microsoft Windows was released on August 9, 2017.
Rez Infinite
Mizuguchi planned for a Windows version from an early stage, beginning development using Windows before bringing it over into the PS4 environment.
Rez Infinite
A port to PlayStation 5, with compatibility with the PlayStation VR2, was released on February 22, 2023.
Rez Infinite
Owners of the PS4 version were offered an upgrade to the PS5 version at a discounted price.
Original release
Sega originally shipped Rez in fairly small quantities.
Original release
In Japan, the PS2 version sold just under 37,600 units.
Original release
By 2003, the PlayStation 2 version had sold over 100,000 copies in North America.
Original release
In their PS2 version review, Famitsu praised its combination of rail shooter and music genre mechanics while also praising the visual design.
Original release
The Dreamcast version was given one point less than the PS2 version, with a reviewer citing the added gameplay immersion from the Trance Vibrator as the reason for the PS2 version's higher score.
Original release

Edge reviewed both versions, preferring the PS2 version due to experiencing slowdown on the Dreamcast release, but lauding both for their visual design and blend of absorbing musical and visual elements.
Later releases

Giving Rez HD a perfect score, Sam Kennedy of 1Up.com felt that the release proved the original was ahead of its time, saying its stylised graphics had hardly aged and that the graphical and audio updates showed off the game as its best.
Later releases
Erik Brudvig of IGN praised the upgrade to the game, citing it as unique among the Xbox Live library and worth trying for any gamer, while admitting its niche appeal and lack of new content.
Later releases
Simon Parkin, writing for Eurogamer, also gave the port a perfect score and noted that modern gamers would be more appreciative of the title than those when it first released.
Later releases
Both the PS4 and PC versions of Rez Infinite received "generally favourable" reviews, earning scores of 89 points out of 100 on review aggregate Metacritic.
Later releases
Chris Carter of Destructoid praised the game's unique nature, and IGN ' s Vince Ingenito called it the most complete version of Rez with or without the VR functions.
Later releases
Edge called it the best VR-based title of 2016, and Phil Savage of PC Gamer lauded the range of graphics option alongside the aesthetic upgrades and new content.
Accolades and retrospectives

At the 2002 NAVGTR awards, Rez was nominated in the "Outstanding Innovation in Game Play" category, and was nominated for " Console Action/Adventure Game of the Year " at the 6th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.
Accolades and retrospectives
It also won GameSpot ' s 2002 "Best Graphics (Artistic) on PlayStation 2" award, and was nominated in the "Best Game No One Played on PlayStation 2" category.
Accolades and retrospectives
As part of a feature on Mizuguchi's career and work, James Mielke of 1Up.com considered Rez underrated in its time and having aged well compared to its contemporaries.
Accolades and retrospectives
The game would go on to receive "Runner Up" in the category of "Electronic - Puzzle and Classic" in Games ' s annual "The Games 100".
Accolades and retrospectives
In 2009, Edge ranked the game #49 on its list of "The 100 Best Games To Play Today", calling it "Astonishing to watch uniquely absorbing to play".
Accolades and retrospectives
In 2012, Rez was listed on Time 's list for the 100 greatest video games of all time.
Accolades and retrospectives
Rez was chosen as one of the Dreamcast games to be shown at the Smithsonian American Art Museum 's 2012 exhibition, The Art of Video Games.
Accolades and retrospectives
Rez HD was rated the 13th best Xbox Live Arcade of all time by IGN in a September 2010 listing.
Accolades and retrospectives
In 2023, a poll by GQ conducted among a team of video game journalists across the industry ranked Rez the 99th best video game of all time.
Accolades and retrospectives
At The Game Awards 2016, Rez Infinite was nominated for "Best Music/Sound Design" and won "Best VR Game".
Accolades and retrospectives
At the 2017 British Academy Games Awards, the game was nominated in the "Audio Achievement" category.
Legacy
Mizuguchi envisioned Rez as being the first in a trilogy of similar titles.
Legacy
According to a 2017 interview, Area X was seen by him partly as a prototype for the conceptual third title.

dc_crazy_taxy.title: Crazy Taxi (video game)
sents: lead
Crazy Taxi is a racing video game developed and published by Sega.
lead
It is the first game in the Crazy Taxi series.
lead
The game was first released in arcades in 1999 and then was ported to the Dreamcast in 2000.
lead
Gameplay is based on picking up taxi customers and driving to their destination as quickly as possible.
lead
Reception to Crazy Taxi has been mostly positive.
lead

lead

In the three time-limited settings, play continues for the designated period of time, after which the cab automatically stops and no more points can be scored.

These ports originally were to force a 4:3 aspect ratio, with widescreen monitors showing blue bars on either side of the screen, resulting in featuring full widescreen support for these ports.

Crazy Taxi was brought to the App Store on iOS devices in October 2012.

Patent 6,200,138 – "Game display method, moving direction indicating method, game apparatus and drive simulating apparatus" – in 2001.
Development and marketing
The mechanics in the "138 patent" describe an arcade cabinet similar to Sega's previous arcade game Harley-Davidson & L.A.
Development and marketing
Riders (1997) but also describe the arrow navigation system and pedestrian avoidance aspects that were used in Crazy Taxi.

Custom soundtracks can also be used on the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 via their system firmware.

In Japan, the Dreamcast, PS2 and GameCube versions sold 155,714 units.

lead

Capcom Fighting Collection: Arcade Classics for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4 and Windows.

It notably marks the series' debut on Nintendo platforms, the first time the classic entries have been made available on PC, as well as the first general re-releases for Marvel Super Heroes, Clash of Super Heroes and New Age of Heroes since the original Origins compilation and the remaster of Marvel vs.

Cannon Spike, originally released in Japan as Gunspike (ガンスパイク, Gansupaiku), is a multi-directional shooter arcade game released in 2000 by Psikyo and later in the same year for the Dreamcast by Capcom.
lead
It uses Capcom-designed characters and runs on Sega's Naomi Hardware.
lead
Cannon Spike is similar to games like Smash TV and Capcom's Commando, although with primary focus on boss fighting.
lead
Cannon Spike is noted as the last game released for Dreamcast in Europe, published by Bigben Interactive and exclusively sold at retail in Game outlets.
lead
The international title, Cannon Spike, is the name of a trademark attack performed by Cammy, a character from the Street Fighter series of video games and one of the protagonists of this title.
Characters
The game features seven playable characters, each of which originates from or is inspired by other Capcom games.
Characters
Predator respectively; and the secret characters Baby Bonnie Hood from Darkstalkers and Mega Man.

The use of the super special requires a Special Token, occasionally dropped by a defeated enemy and always dropped by a defeated ally in 2-player mode.
Reception
Greg Orlando of NextGen said that the game was "not quite artillerific, but it is a mindlessly fun way to murder some time." In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 30 out of 40.
