Also in Japan, Game Machine listed the arcade version in their 15 November 2000 issue as the second most-successful arcade game of the month.

dc_daytuna_usa.title: Daytona USA

Programmer(s): Daichi Katagiri Koki Koiwa Hideomi Miyauchi
Platform(s): Arcade, Sega Saturn, Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3 (PSN), Xbox 360 (XBLA), Xbox One

sents: lead
Daytona USA is an arcade racing game developed by Sega AM2 and released by Sega in March of 1994.
lead
Inspired by the popularity of the NASCAR motor racing series in the US, the game has players race stock cars on one of three courses.
lead
It was the first game to be released on the Sega Model 2 arcade system board.
lead
Daytona USA is one of the highest-grossing arcade games of all time.
lead
Sega partnered with GE Aerospace to develop the Model 2, which renders 3D graphics capable of texture filtering and texture mapping.
lead
Daytona USA was developed by AM2 after a meeting of the heads of Sega's regional offices to decide on a game to debut the Model 2 hardware.
lead
The concept was suggested by Tom Petit, president of Sega's American arcade division, with input from AM2 director Toshihiro Nagoshi, who became the game's director and producer.
lead
Sega aimed to outperform Namco 's Ridge Racer (1993).
Gameplay
Players begin in last place and compete against a field of up to 39 computer-controlled cars, dependent on the course selected.
Gameplay
Adaptive difficulty is used; the first lap of each race measures the skill of the player and adjusts the difficulty of opponents accordingly.
Gameplay
Daytona USA 's arcade version on the Model 2 is capable of displaying up to 300,000 texture-mapped polygons per second, nearly double that of the previous Model 1.
Gameplay
In multiplayer, only the lead driver needs to reach a checkpoint before time runs out.
Gameplay
The PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions included online multiplayer with up to eight players.
Development
In September 1992, Sega partnered with the engineering division GE Aerospace to create its new arcade system board, the Model 2.
Development
At the second meeting, GE Aerospace executives brought a tape demonstrating the hardware's 3D graphics simulating the Daytona International Speedway.
Development
GE estimated that their sale of the Model 2’s graphics technology accelerated Sega's arcade hardware development by 14 months.
Development
The heads of Sega's regional offices began discussing ideas for games to demonstrate the Model 2's capabilities.
Development
Sega's previous board, the Model 1, had debuted in 1992 with Virtua Racing, which was popular in Japan and Europe.
Development
Tom Petit, president of Sega's American arcade division Sega Enterprises USA, suggested that NASCAR would be an attractive brand to use for a Model 2 game in the US.
Development

Petit and Sega Enterprises USA chief of finance Masahiro Nakagawa began negotiations with representatives of the Daytona 500 at Daytona International Speedway for a license to develop a game based on the race.
Development
Sega mandated that Daytona USA had to be better than Namco 's 1993 racing game Ridge Racer and it had to achieve higher sales.
Development

Ridge Racer had reached the top of arcade sales charts at the end of 1993 and beginning of 1994, and it had received highly favorable reviews of its graphics, especially in comparison to Virtua Racing.
Development
Development was handed to Sega AM2, a development division headed by Yu Suzuki, who had led development on popular racing games including Hang-On, Out Run, and Virtua Racing.
Development
AM2 director Toshihiro Nagoshi was given direct responsibility for the project, with Nagoshi and Suzuki serving as producers.
Development
The game was Nagoshi's first project as a director.
Development
While in the US for a meeting on the Model 2, Nagoshi was given tickets to a NASCAR race, and later recalled that it was a new experience for him because it was not a known style of racing in Japan.
Development
AM2 split into two teams: one focused on Daytona USA while the other developed Virtua Fighter.
Development
Game planner Makoto Osaki said he purchased a sports car and watched the NASCAR film Days of Thunder more than 100 times.
Development
Unlike Virtua Racing 's Model 1 hardware, the Model 2 is capable of displaying surface detail on its 3D graphics with texture mapping.
Development
As this was new for the developers, trial and error was used to find the most effective approach.
Development
Katagiri said there was no need to develop software for rendering because the Model 2 hardware handled this.
Development

A hidden track, "Pounding Pavement", was inspired by " Hotel California " by the Eagles and is accessible by holding the fourth view perspective button while selecting the beginner track in the arcade version.
Development
This was the only way to include vocals, due to technical limitations of the Model 2.
Release

Prior to release, a prototype had debuted at the Amusement Machine Show in Tokyo in August 1993, and it was tested in select Japanese arcades the same month; Petit states this was done to measure how the games would be received by the public.
Release

The complete version of Daytona USA was released in Japan in March 1994, and made its North American debut the same month at Chicago's American Coin Machine Exposition (ACME); it was subsequently released worldwide in April 1994.
Release

The standard game was released in a twin-seat cabinet and a deluxe cabinet fitted with detailed seats on top of subwoofers; Sega originally planned to use actual car seats, but management determined the seats were too difficult to enter and exit.
Release
Daytona USA debuted at number two on arcade operator publication RePlay ' s "Player's Choice" chart and stayed on the list for five years, with 16 months at number one.
Release
Daytona USA was rereleased in 1996 in arcades as Daytona USA: Special Edition, designed as a smaller, more affordable cabinet.
Release
Around the time of the worldwide release, Sega announced releases for its Saturn and 32X consoles, but a year later, Sega announced their intention to focus solely on the Saturn.
Release
In early 1995, Sega AM2's Saturn division split into three departments, each charged with converting a different arcade game to the Saturn: Virtua Fighter 2, Virtua Cop, and Daytona USA.
Release
Due to slow progress on the Daytona USA conversion, several members of the Virtua Fighter 2 team were reassigned to Daytona USA.
Release
AM2 completed the conversion in April 1995.
Release
In Japan, two separate Windows releases were done in September and December 1996, with the first released version supporting specific graphics cards such as Leadtek 's WinFast GD400.
Release
A Windows version was released in Europe on November 14, 1996, and in North America in December of the same year.
Remakes and sequels
Daytona USA: Championship Circuit Edition, a reworked and expanded version of Daytona USA, was released in 1996 for the Saturn.
Remakes and sequels
An enhanced arcade remake, called Sega Racing Classic, was released in 2010 and is the first title in the series not branded with the Daytona name as Sega no longer owned the rights at the time.
Remakes and sequels
Another enhanced version was released digitally for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2012, as Daytona USA.
Remakes and sequels
The Xbox 360 version was later made compatible with Xbox One.
Remakes and sequels
Daytona USA 2: Battle on the Edge, an arcade-exclusive sequel using the Sega Model 3 hardware, was released in 1998.
Remakes and sequels
Daytona USA 2001, a remake of Daytona USA and Championship Circuit Edition, was released in 2001 for the Dreamcast, with graphical upgrades, online multiplayer, and new courses.
Remakes and sequels
Daytona Championship USA, also referred to as Daytona USA 3, debuted in late 2016 as an arcade exclusive; it was the first Daytona -branded arcade game in 18 years.
Arcade
In Japan, it was the ninth highest-grossing arcade game of 1994, and the highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1995.
Arcade
In the United Kingdom, it topped the dedicated arcade charts for six months in 1994, from May to October.
Arcade
Retro Gamer 's Nick Thorpe said that though Daytona USA is considered anecdotally one of the most successful arcade games for its multiplayer and longevity, exact figures were difficult to find.
Arcade

In 2015, IGN 's Luke Reilly said that the game is "perhaps the most recognisable arcade racing game of all time and the highest-grossing sit-down cabinet ever" and noted the continued presence of Daytona USA cabinets in arcades and bowling alleys.
Saturn
The Saturn version received a positive reception, with high scores from most critics, though a number of them criticized it for graphical issues.
Retrospective
Daytona USA was named one of the best games of all time by Next Generation in 1996, GamesMaster in 1996, Computer and Video Games in 2000, EGM in 1997 and 2001, Yahoo! in 2005, and Empire in 2009.
Retrospective
It was named one of the best coin-op games by EGM in 1997 and by Killer List of Videogames, and one of the best retro games by NowGamer in 2010 and EGM in 2006.
Retrospective
Edge named it the 70th "best game to play today" in 2009.
Retrospective
In 2015, IGN named it the sixth-most influential racing game, asserting that it "remains a shining example of arcade racing done oh so right".
Retrospective
According to aggregator Metacritic, the Xbox 360 version received "generally favorable reviews" and the PlayStation 3 version received "mixed" reviews.
Retrospective
1Up.com 's Ray Barnholt praised this version but expressed disappointment at the lack of new features.

dc_adventure.title: Sonic Adventure
sents: lead
Sonic Adventure is a 1998 platform game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
lead
It was the first main Sonic the Hedgehog game to feature 3D gameplay.
lead

It follows Sonic the Hedgehog, Miles "Tails" Prower, Knuckles the Echidna, Amy Rose, Big the Cat, and E-102 Gamma in their quests to collect the Chaos Emeralds and stop Doctor Robotnik from unleashing Chaos, an ancient evil.
lead
Controlling one of the six characters—each with their own abilities—players complete levels to progress the story.
lead
Sonic Adventure retains many elements from prior Sonic games, such as power-ups and the ring -based health system.
lead
Players can play minigames such as racing and interact with Chao, a virtual pet.
lead
Sonic Team began developing Sonic Adventure in 1997, after the cancellation of the Sega Saturn game Sonic X-treme.
lead
Led by director Takashi Iizuka and producer Yuji Naka, the team strove to reinvent Sonic for the 3D era of video games.
Gameplay
Sonic Adventure is a 3D platform game with action and role-playing elements.
Gameplay
Through exploration, the player discovers entrances to levels called Action Stages, some of which must be opened using keys hidden in the Adventure Field.
Gameplay
Some minigames can only be accessed with particular characters.
Gameplay
Canisters containing power-ups, such as speed shoes, additional rings, invincibility, and protective shields, are also hidden in levels.
Gameplay
Each character starts with a limited number of lives, and the player loses a life if the character drowns, gets crushed, or is hit without any rings in their possession.
Gameplay
Lives can be replenished by collecting 100 rings or a 1-up.
Gameplay
Players may also discover Chao Gardens, hidden, protective environments inhabited by Chao, a virtual pet.
Gameplay
Eggs that can produce special types of Chao are hidden throughout the Adventure Fields.
Plot

When a tribe of echidnas sought to steal the power of the Emeralds, breaking the harmony they had with the Chao, Chaos retaliated by using the Emeralds' power to transform into a monstrous beast, Perfect Chaos, and wipe them out.
Plot
Knuckles, the only remaining echidna, sets out to find the shards of the Master Emerald and repair it.
Plot
Although Sonic disrupts Robotnik's plans, Chaos manages to absorb all the Chaos Emeralds and transforms into Perfect Chaos; it rebels against Robotnik and destroys Station Square.
Background
During the early 1990s, Sega was one of the most successful video game companies due to the rise of its Genesis console.
Background
Genesis sales were driven by the popularity of Sega's flagship franchise of 2D platform games, Sonic the Hedgehog.
Background
After the completion of Sonic & Knuckles in 1994, Naka returned to Japan to work with Sonic Team.
Background
STI began developing Sonic X-treme for the Sega Saturn, planned as the first Sonic the Hedgehog game to feature full 3D gameplay.
Background
X-treme suffered a series of setbacks and was canceled in 1996.
Background
Naka wanted a 3D Sonic game, but felt that only Sonic Team should undertake the endeavor; his refusal to let STI use the Nights game engine was instrumental in X-treme ' s cancellation.
Conception
In August 1996, shortly after the completion of Nights into Dreams, Iizuka proposed Sonic Adventure as a role-playing-style Sonic game with a greater emphasis on storytelling.
Conception
Sonic Team started to work on it in April 1997 on the Saturn with a 20-strong team.
Conception
Sonic Team created the first prototype using the Nights engine, but the Saturn's limited capabilities made development difficult.
Conception
One of the largest video games created at the time, the team had grown to 60 after 10 months, and over 100 developers worked on the game in total.
Conception
Sonic Team undertook development in conjunction with the Dreamcast, aiming to release the game in December 1998, even if it meant making improvements after release.
Characters and art
As such, Yuji Uekawa redesigned each character to suit the transition to 3D and to give them "new, edgy, more Western" design.
Characters and art
Hoshino noted that the characters' longer limbs made it easier to recreate their 2D poses in 3D.
Characters and art
Chaos was originally intended to have realistic blue scales in his final form, but this was abandoned because of the technological constraints of the Dreamcast.
Characters and art
While some Sonic games, such as 1993's Sonic CD, contained limited voice work, Sonic Adventure was the first Sonic game to feature extensive voice acting.
Characters and art
Iizuka recalled that the only element they agreed on was to avoid using an anime voice actor, favoring a film actor with an "over-the-top" voice.
Characters and art
In an interview celebrating his 30th anniversary as a voice actor, Kanemaru said one reason he was cast was because of his ability to speak English.
Characters and art
Eggman", to western audiences; he accomplished this by having Sonic insult Robotnik when they meet for the first time in-game.
Characters and art
The character Tikal was inspired by Peru and took her name from the Guatemalan ruins.
Characters and art
The 3D visuals were created using a Voodoo2 graphics chip.
Design
One of the biggest challenges the Adventure designers faced was transitioning Sonic ' s 2D style to 3D.
Design
The designers created models for the stages before testing it as the player character, resulting in trial and error.
Design
One particular difficulty was defeating enemies; in the 2D games, enemies were beaten simply by jumping on them, but this was harder to achieve in a 3D game.
Design
The team also wanted to add elements unexpected in a platform game; for example, the level in which Tails sandboards was inspired by a group of sandboarders in Ica, Peru.
Design
Some levels reference past Sega games, such as Ice Cap (1994's Sonic the Hedgehog 3) and the Tornado levels (1995's Panzer Dragoon).
Design
Sonic Adventure was the first time Amy was playable in a Sonic platformer, and Iizuka aimed to use her to add tension, such as hiding from pursuers, that Sonic's gameplay could not offer.
Design

Because Sonic Adventure had a stronger emphasis on storytelling than previous games in the series, the team implemented hub worlds to "draw the players deeper into the world." The hub worlds' emphasis on exploring to find new areas and power-ups was inspired by The Legend of Zelda.
Music
Adventure was Senoue's first project as sound director and its scope meant he had many more responsibilities, including schedule management, compared to his previous games.
Music

Iizuka noted that Sonic Team's primary goal with Adventure was "to evoke the essence of Sonic by going from 2D to 3D", and felt the music needed to exceed fan expectations due to previous Sonic soundtracks' popularity.
Music

Despite the different styles, Senoue did retain some music from the Genesis Sonic games: the music for the Windy Valley and Twinkle Park levels were rearranged from Sonic 3D Blast (1996), while the level clear jingle was taken from Sonic 3.
Music
He chose to reuse his 3D Blast tracks because he felt they were strong enough to be more widely heard, as they were only used for the Genesis version (which was not released in Japan).
Music
Sonic Adventure marked Senoue's first collaboration with Gioeli; the two later formed the band Crush 40 (originally known as Sons of Angels), and continue to make music together.
Music
Iizuka was inspired to use "Open Your Heart" as the final boss music by films, which he noted often use main themes during dramatic events.
Music
A two-disc soundtrack, Sonic Adventure "Digi-LOG Conversation" Original Sound Track, was released in Japan in January 1999.
Music
In May 2011, the soundtrack was rereleased to commemorate the Sonic franchise's 20th anniversary.
Music
A two-volume digital soundtrack was also released on iTunes and Spotify in September 2014 and January 2017, respectively.
Music
Brave Wave Productions released a vinyl LP version of the soundtrack including interviews with Senoue and Iizuka in 2018.
Release
Sonic Adventure was kept a secret during production, though screenshots were leaked in mid-1998 and plans for a 3D Sonic game had long been rumored.
Release
The team showed off several dynamic elements, such as a chase sequence from the first level and Tails's sandboarding sequence.
Release
On December 23, 1998, Sonic Adventure was released in Japan.
Release
The promotion began on July 15, 1999, and took place at 1,055 Hollywood Video stores across the country.
Release
The localized version was released in North America on September 9, 1999, as a launch title, and in Europe on October 14, 1999.
Release
Before release, Sega projected to sell a million copies of Sonic Adventure.
Release
Sonic Adventure is the bestselling Dreamcast game; by August 4, 2006, it had sold 2.5 million copies, including 440,000 in Japan and 1.27 million in the US.
Release
In Europe, it sold 86,000 copies during its first five days on sale.
Release
Most copies were unaffected, and customers with defective copies could trade for working ones at retailers.
Reception
As the first fully 3D Sonic platform game, Sonic Adventure was highly anticipated.
Reception
The game was a finalist for " Outstanding Achievement in Visual Engineering " during the 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, which ultimately went to Unreal Tournament.
Reception
IGN called it the most graphically impressive platform game released up to that date, praising its cinematic sequences and describing it as "engrossing, demanding, and utterly awe-inspiring".
Reception
GameSpot agreed and said only Soulcalibur ' s graphical quality surpassed that of Sonic Adventure.
Reception
Edge felt the graphical features showed off the Dreamcast's potential to the fullest and that the game was "perfect" as a showcase for the system.
Reception
IGN thought the cutscenes were repetitive and voiced strong disapproval of the voice acting, declaring it "a complete joke" and "downright awful".
Reception
IGN had a particular distaste for Tails's voice, and retrospectively called it among the most annoying to feature in a video game.
Reception
GameSpot admired the straightforward, linear approach to the 3D platform genre and particularly praised it for keeping the basic gameplay of the original Genesis games.
Reception
Retrospectively, 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die called its environments vast and twisted, stating it "brilliantly" captured traditional Sonic elements.
Reception
Some critics compared Sonic Adventure to Super Mario 64 —Nintendo's "groundbreaking" 1996 game that propelled the Nintendo 64 and the 3D platform genre.
Reception

Edge said Sonic Adventure was a worthy rival to Super Mario 64, but AllGame wrote that Sonic Adventure was not as ambitious and that those looking for exploration would be disappointed with its linear gameplay.
Reception

According to Next Generation, "Expert gamers may beat the game in only a day or two but, even then, the ride is worth the price of admission." AllGame wrote that the game was an impressive showing of the Dreamcast's potential and that it was among the best of the series.
Reception
Arcade and CVG speculated the game could save the Dreamcast, which had not sold well by the end of 1998.
Sonic Adventure DX
In 2001, Sega announced it would transition from a first-party to a third-party software publisher, in response to the international failures of the Saturn and Dreamcast.
Sonic Adventure DX

Wanting to reach new players by creating an enhanced version of one of its older games, in June 2003 Sega released Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut, a port of Sonic Adventure for the GameCube and Windows.
Sonic Adventure DX
GameSpot was disappointed the rerelease did not address the problems of the original version, irritated the graphics were only marginally different, and dissatisfied with its collision detection.
HD version
In September 2010, Sega rereleased Sonic Adventure as a downloadable game for the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, followed by a Windows release in March 2011 via Steam.
HD version
The game was also included in the Dreamcast Collection compilation in 2011 and is backwards-compatible with the Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S.
HD version
Reviews of the 2010 rerelease were generally unfavorable, with criticism directed at the perceived lack of effort put into the port.
HD version
In 2024, the game was released on Steam in Japan, having never been made available in the region previously through the platform.
Legacy
With most contemporary 3D platform games focusing on exploration and collecting items, Sonic Adventure stood out with its linear gameplay.
Legacy
According to GamesRadar, as one of the first sixth-generation console games, it changed the industry "forever".
Legacy
Joystiq wrote that both Adventure and the original Sonic the Hedgehog had innovated—in 3D and 2D games, respectively—through effective linear level design and by feeling "good to play".
Legacy

In 2009, GamePro listed Sonic Adventure as the seventh-best platform game of all time, saying that it had not aged well in certain aspects but that its core gameplay remained among the best of the Sonic series.
Legacy
The first level in the 2006 Sonic the Hedgehog reboot heavily references Sonic Adventure ' s Emerald Coast stage.
Legacy
To celebrate the Sonic series's 20th anniversary in 2011, Sega released Sonic Generations, which reused aspects from past games in the franchise.
Legacy

The Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and Windows versions contain reimagined versions of the Speed Highway level and the Perfect Chaos boss fight, and the Nintendo 3DS version contains a remake of Emerald Coast.
Legacy
Several characters that first appeared in Sonic Adventure appeared in later games.
Legacy
Big is widely considered by video game journalists the worst character in the Sonic franchise, and was named one of the worst game characters in a poll conducted by 1UP.com.
Legacy
On October 4, 1999, Sega announced that a sequel to Sonic Adventure was in development.
Legacy
Sonic Adventure 2 made its debut at E3 2000 and was released in June 2001.
Legacy
A concept for Sonic Adventure 3 was reworked into the 2008 game Sonic Unleashed.
Legacy
The comic offered an explanation for the altered character designs and established that Station Square was hidden beneath Sonic's planet, Mobius.

dc_sonik_adventura_2.title: Sonic Adventure 2
sents: lead
Sonic Adventure 2 is a 2001 platform game developed by Sonic Team USA and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
lead

It features two good-vs-evil stories: Sonic the Hedgehog, Miles "Tails" Prower, and Knuckles the Echidna attempt to save the world, while Shadow the Hedgehog, Doctor Eggman, and Rouge the Bat attempt to conquer it.
lead

The stories are divided into three gameplay styles: fast-paced platforming for Sonic and Shadow, multidirectional shooting for Tails and Eggman, and action-adventure exploration for Knuckles and Rouge.
lead
Like previous Sonic the Hedgehog games, the player completes levels while collecting rings and defeating enemies.
lead
Outside the main gameplay, they can interact with Chao, a virtual pet, and compete in multiplayer battles.
lead
After Sonic Adventure (1998), Sonic Team was downsized and a portion of the staff moved to San Francisco to establish Sonic Team USA.
lead
They worked on Adventure 2 for a year and a half, with Takashi Iizuka directing and Yuji Naka producing.
lead
Developed during a tumultuous period in Sega's history, Adventure 2 had a significantly smaller development team than the first game.
Gameplay
Sonic Adventure 2 is a 3D platform game divided into two campaigns: Hero and Dark.
Gameplay
Adventure 2 has the health system found in many other Sonic games.
Gameplay
Adventure 2 has 180 emblems, earned for a variety of tasks.
Gameplay
Each level has five missions; only the first is required to continue the campaign, and other missions include completing a harder version of a level and collecting 100 rings.
Gameplay
Collecting all the emblems unlocks a 3D version of the Green Hill Zone stage from the original Sonic the Hedgehog.
Plot

Doctor Eggman learns of a secret weapon from the diary of his grandfather, Professor Gerald Robotnik, and infiltrates a high-security Guardian Units of Nations (GUN) facility to revive it with a Chaos Emerald.
Plot
On the ARK, Tails reveals he has made a counterfeit Chaos Emerald to destroy the Eclipse Cannon.
Plot
Sonic tries to trick Eggman with the fake emerald, but Eggman deduces the plan and jettisons him in an escape pod rigged with explosives.
Plot
Sonic uses the power of the fake emerald to escape; Shadow is sent to intercept him.
Plot
Eggman sneaks away with the last emerald and arms the Eclipse Cannon.
Plot
Shadow catches up with Sonic and Knuckles in the core as they encounter the Biolizard, a colossal lizard and prototype Ultimate Lifeform.
Conception
Sonic Adventure, the first 3D platformer in Sega's Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, was developed by Sonic Team and released for the Dreamcast in Japan in 1998.
Conception
The Adventure team was downsized, and in 1999, 12 Sonic Team members, including Adventure ' s director Takashi Iizuka, relocated to San Francisco, California to establish Sonic Team USA.
Conception
Sega directed a team of 11—significantly smaller than Adventure ' s team of 120—to begin working on Sonic Adventure 2 after they spent six months localizing Adventure for the West.
Conception
As with the first game, Iizuka directed Adventure 2 while Yuji Naka, the Sonic franchise's co-creator, produced it.
Conception
Shiro Maekawa, who wrote portions of Sega's Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998) and joined Sonic Team during Adventure ' s production, conceived and wrote Adventure 2 ' s story.
Conception
Because Adventure 2 would be the first Sonic game released during the 21st century, Maekawa wanted a substantial portion of the story to take place in space.
Conception
Maekawa drew influence from the manga and anime he had enjoyed since childhood, including Please Save My Earth (1986–1994).
Conception
As Maekawa disliked Sonic as a character, he used Adventure 2 as an opportunity to revise him to suit his tastes.
Design

Iizuka summarized Sonic Adventure 2 ' s development as "trying to make the impossible possible", as Sonic Team USA had to overcome the challenge of creating a game comparable in scope to the first Adventure with less than a tenth of the staff.
Design

Despite this, he considered Adventure 2 the most fun Sonic game to develop, as the small team meant "we were able to condense all the good elements from the previous game, and deliver a story and game that was satisfying to players everywhere".
Design
Whereas Sonic Team had tried to include as much content as possible in Adventure, for Adventure 2 they only concentrated on the elements they deemed necessary.
Design

The levels, drawn from Maekawa's story and setting, were inspired by San Francisco and other American locations, such as Yosemite National Park (where the team vacationed) and the San Francisco Bay Area.
Design
The staff frequently received parking tickets from authorities; as a joke, they included the authorities' cars in a level where Sonic could destroy them.
Design
The month Adventure 2 was to be released to manufacturing, one artist suggested adding Green Hill Zone, the original Sonic the Hedgehog ' s first stage.
Design
Sonic Team USA gave Sonic more abilities, such as grinding on rails, to add rhythm to ensure the gameplay was not only about speed.
Music
Senoue, Kumatani and Tokoi returned from Adventure, while Ohtani made his first contributions to a Sonic game.
Music
Senoue began writing in April 2000; he worked closely with Sonic Team USA regarding Adventure 2 ' s structure, design, and characters.
Music
Tokoi said the soundtrack explores more genres than the first game's, and other genres include pop-punk, glam metal, and orchestral arrangements.
Music
Senoue reused most of the character theme lyrics from the first Adventure, but wrote new music.
Music
Poley wrote and performed "Escape from the City", the first level's theme.
Music
While he enjoyed studio work, Senoue described the last three months as chaotic, as he had to travel between Tokyo, San Francisco and Los Angeles within weeks to write and record music.
Marketing
Sega announced Sonic Adventure 2 at E3 2000 with a trailer premiere behind closed doors and a press release.
Marketing
Sega showcased Adventure 2 further at E3 2001 in May.
Marketing

According to Ken Penders, one of the series' writers, the creative team was unable to adapt the story in full due to Sonic Team's desire for secrecy; they were only able to work from the demo and a few screenshots.
Marketing
Adventure 2 was initially set to be released in February 2001, but was ultimately released in North America on June 19 and worldwide on June 23.
Marketing

In Japan, Sega offered a limited edition "Birthday Pack" for two days that included the game, a gold disc containing Sonic music, a commemorative gold coin, and a 17-page booklet detailing the series' history.
GameCube port

Peter Moore, the president and chief operating officer of Sega of America, said the Dreamcast would need to sell five million units in the US by the end of 2000 to remain a viable platform, but Sega fell short of this goal with three million units sold.
GameCube port
On January 31, 2001, Sega announced it was discontinuing the Dreamcast to become a third-party developer, although it remained committed to releasing first-party Dreamcast software through 2001.
GameCube port
The third-party transition made Adventure 2 one of the last major Dreamcast exclusives and the final Sonic game for a Sega console.
GameCube port
Sonic Team kept the project a secret until its reveal at Nintendo Space World in August.
GameCube port
Battle was released in Japan on December 20, 2001, in North America on February 11, 2002, in Europe on May 3, 2002, and in Australia on May 17, 2002.
Sales
The Dreamcast version of Sonic Adventure 2 sold more than 84,000 copies during its first week in Japan (a franchise record), and a total of around 500,000 copies worldwide.
Sales
In Japan, it sold almost 50,000 copies during its first month, and had sold 192,186 by December 23, 2002.
Sales
In North America, it was the bestselling GameCube game between January and August 2002, selling 465,000 copies.
Sales
By August 2002, it had sold more than a million copies worldwide.
Sales
Cumulative sales reached 1.7 million, and by July 2006, it had earned $44 million in the US.
Sales
According to Next Generation, it was the 42nd-bestselling game for the GameCube, PlayStation 2, or Xbox between January 2000 and July 2006 in the US.
Sales
It is one of the bestselling GameCube games and the bestselling third-party GameCube game.
Reception

Anthony Chau of IGN called it one of the best Sonic games: "If this is the last Sonic game in these declining Dreamcast years, it's satisfying to know that the DC didn't go out with a bang, but with a sonic boom." In 2022, IGN named it one of the best Dreamcast games.
Reception
According to Chau, the game had "some of the best textures ever seen" and was one of the most beautiful Dreamcast games.
Reception

Despite high review scores for the Dreamcast version, the GameCube version released six months later received mixed reviews: respective Metacritic and GameRankings scores of 73 percent and 72.33 percent.
Accolades
Sonic Adventure 2 received several accolades, including the 2001 IGN's Editors' Choice Award.
Post-release
Development on the next game, Sonic Heroes (2003), began at Sonic Team USA shortly after Adventure 2 ' s completion.
Post-release
Heroes became the first multiplatform Sonic game when it was released for the GameCube, PlayStation 2, and Xbox in late 2003.
Post-release

Another 2003 Sonic Team game, Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg, uses an updated version of the Adventure 2 engine, and Ohtani, who first composed Sonic music for Adventure 2, became the series' sound director with Sonic the Hedgehog (2006).
Post-release

Sega's discontinuation of the Dreamcast made Sonic Adventure 2 the last Sonic game that Sonic Team—which had worked with Sega hardware teams to take advantage of their consoles—produced with the benefits of first-party development.
Post-release
Iizuka described the loss of first-party development benefits as the greatest challenge of the third-party transition, as his team "no longer the ability to control what we need to make our games".
Post-release
The division developed Nights: Journey of Dreams (2007) before it was merged back into the Japanese Sonic Team in 2008.
Soundtracks

Marvelous Entertainment released a collection of Sonic Adventure 2 songs, Cuts Unleashed Sonic Adventure 2 Vocal Collection, on August 18, 2001, before releasing the full two-disc soundtrack album, Multi-dimensional Sonic Adventure 2 Original Sound Track, on September 5.
Soundtracks
Tokyopop released a soundtrack in the US on February 5, 2002, ahead of the GameCube version's release, featuring 26 tracks selected by Senoue and US-exclusive remixes.
Soundtracks
On November 30, 2011, Sega released the soundtrack on iTunes via its Wave Master label to coincide with the franchise's 20th anniversary.
Rerelease

Sega released a port of Sonic Adventure 2 as a downloadable game for the PlayStation 3 (via PlayStation Network) and Xbox 360 (via Xbox Live Arcade) on October 2, 2012, and for Windows (via Steam) on November 20.
Rerelease

The port followed a similar reissue of the first Adventure in 2010 and was branded as part of Sega Heritage, a 2012 initiative in which Sega rereleased popular games from its back catalog on modern consoles.
Rerelease
The rerelease features high-definition graphics and widescreen support, though some cutscenes are still presented in 4:3.
Rerelease

In 2017, the PlayStation 3 version was made playable on the PlayStation 4 and Windows via the cloud gaming service PlayStation Now, and the Xbox 360 version was made backward compatible with the Xbox One.
Retrospective assessments
While IGN praised the gameplay variety, Kotaku noted that many only like the Sonic and Shadow levels; retrospective reviewers have criticized the other characters as frustrating and cumbersome.
Retrospective assessments

VentureBeat wrote that Adventure 2 did not hold up to modern standards, finding its camera and reliance on trial-and-error design outdated, and Destructoid said it was only redeemed by how engaging the Chao Garden was.
Retrospective assessments
A Vice writer, while playing Adventure 2 for the first time in a decade, said that " been forced to reconcile my nostalgia with the harsh reality that it is not a terrific game".
Retrospective assessments
VentureBeat wrote that it was more worth remembering for its historical significance as the last Sonic game for a Sega console than it was worth replaying.
Retrospective assessments

Following Adventure 2, Sonic ' s critical standing began to decline, which VentureBeat attributed to Sega "depending on stupid gimmicks to sell their most iconic property" following the third-party transition.
Retrospective assessments

The Escapist wrote that subsequent Sonic games, such as Sonic the Hedgehog, Sonic Unleashed (2008), and Sonic Forces (2017), attempted to replicate the Adventure 2 format of varied gameplay styles, but failed because they did not develop each style fully.
Retrospective assessments

VentureBeat said Adventure 2 ' s alternate gameplay styles were natural additions to Sonic whereas those in subsequent games, such as Unleashed ' s Werehog segments and Sonic and the Black Knight ' s (2009) swordplay, were not.
City Escape
Sonic Adventure 2 ' s first level, City Escape, has been described as one of the best opening stages in a video game.
City Escape

Red Bull said it was "unquestionably Sonic ' s finest hour since the days", and Destructoid called it a perfect introduction to modern Sonic gameplay that encapsulates the strengths of the Adventure games.
City Escape
Sega produced two remixes in 2021: a Sonic 30th Anniversary Symphony remix in June and a funk remix in December.
City Escape
Poley described "Escape from the City" as his biggest hit, though he does not receive any royalties.
City Escape
Generations, which commemorates the franchise's 20th anniversary, features reimagined versions of levels from past Sonic games, including 2D and 3D reimaginings of City Escape.
City Escape

The 2D version features the "Classic" iteration of Sonic racing the truck as it moves between the background and foreground, while the 3D version features shortcuts that take advantage of Generations ' s mechanics.
City Escape

Kotaku regarded Generations ' s City Escape as one of the most impactful moments of 2011, and PCMag considered it a highlight, a "prime example" of Sonic Team drawing inspiration from the franchise's history.
Influence

Sonic Adventure 2 ' s GameCube port introduced Sonic to a new audience of Millennials and, alongside the compilation Sonic Mega Collection (2002), built a new fanbase following Sega's third-party transition.
Influence

For this reason, The Escapist regarded it as possibly the most important Sonic game and said that while some later Sonic games were better, " didn’t do nearly as much to energize or even create a new fanbase".
Influence
Sonic Frontiers (2022) features levels that recreate the layouts of the Adventure 2 stages Metal Harbor, Green Forest, and Sky Rail, and Sonic's Soap shoes are available as DLC.
Influence
According to PC Gamer, Shadow is the most famous modern Sonic character.
Influence
In 2005, Naka said Sonic Team had determined Shadow was the most popular Sonic character excluding Sonic himself, a finding reaffirmed in a 2009 Sega poll.
Influence
A 2024 rerelease of Generations was bundled with Shadow Generations, a Shadow game that features recreations of Adventure 2 levels and bosses.
Influence
Rouge also became a recurring character; a 2006 Sega poll found her the tenth-most-popular Sonic character.
Influence
"Live & Learn" remains a popular Sonic song, and Crush 40 performed a remix featuring the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra as the finale of the Sonic 30th Anniversary Symphony.
Influence
The plot of Adventure 2 was adapted in the second season of the anime series Sonic X (2003–2006).
Influence
The live-action feature film Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (2024) draws inspiration from Adventure 2.

dc_sonik_shuffle.title: Sonic Shuffle
sents: lead
Sonic Shuffle is a Sonic the Hedgehog -themed party game developed and published by Sega for the Dreamcast in 2000.
lead

The game plays like a board game much in the same vein as Nintendo 's Mario Party series, with up to four players moving their characters across a game board filled with a variety of spaces which can trigger different events.
lead
Some spaces will launch minigames that pit the players against each other in short competitive events.
lead
Sega contracted Hudson Soft, the developers of Mario Party, to assist with development.
lead
For the game's graphics, they used the same cel shading technique used in their earlier game Jet Set Radio (2000).
lead
An online multiplayer mode was planned, but it was pulled so the game could launch in time for the 2000 holiday season.
lead
Although critics praised the graphics, the game's excessive load times and poorly explained, overly complex minigames were found to be significantly detrimental to the overall experience.
lead
Critics classified Sonic Shuffle as an inferior clone of Mario Party.
Gameplay
The players can choose to play as one of these four characters, or Big the Cat, E-102 Gamma, Super Sonic, and a Chao if unlocked later.
Gameplay
Each character has unique abilities they can use to traverse the game boards.
Gameplay
Players take turns moving across the board in an effort to collect the most Precioustones; this is done by picking cards and moving the amount of spaces specified on it.
Gameplay
Each player is dealt seven cards at a time, and their deck is visible on their personal VMU screen in their controller, keeping it a secret from other players.
Gameplay
The most common spaces increase or subtract the player's ring count.
Gameplay
The goal of each game is to collect the most Precioustones.
Development and release
Sonic Shuffle was developed by Sega, with assistance from the Hudson Soft team behind Mario Party (1998), and supervision from Sonic Team.
Development and release
Most sources attributed Sega as the developer although some attributed the game to Sega's internal development team Smilebit.
Development and release
Smilebit had previously developed Jet Set Radio (2000) for the Dreamcast which was well regarded for its cel shaded visuals.
Development and release
Sega revealed that a Sonic Adventure spin-off was in development alongside Sonic Adventure 2 in October 1999.
Development and release
The game was revealed in the June 2000 issue of Electronic Gaming Monthly (EGM) with the tentative title Sonic Square, shortly before the E3 trade fair that year.
Development and release
Sega had planned to reveal information about Sonic Adventure 2 to EGM for the issue, but decided the game was not ready to be shown, and shared Sonic Square instead.
Development and release
Support for online multiplayer through SegaNet was planned, it was ultimately cut so the game could ship ahead of the 2000 holiday season.
Development and release
Sonic Shuffle was released for the Dreamcast in North America on November 14, 2000, in Japan on December 21, and in Europe on March 9, 2001.
Development and release
The game was expected to appear in the 2002 compilation Sonic Mega Collection, but was ultimately not included.
Reception
GameSpot noted that it was possible to play through an entire game without ever playing a minigame, and felt that they were "a test of who can decipher the needlessly bewildering gameplay first".
Reception
Although it's the only party game for Dreamcasters, Sonic Shuffle deals a great hand for all to play."
Reception
Most reviewers praised the colorful and cartoon styling of the cel shaded graphics.
Reception
Under the dark shadow of Sonic Adventure 2, this tepid, diluted affair will have difficulty proving itself, even to franchise stalwarts".

dc_shenmoo_ii.title: Shenmue II
sents: lead
Shenmue II is a 2001 action-adventure game developed by Sega AM2 and published by Microsoft Game Studios and Sega.
lead
It was directed, produced and written by Yu Suzuki.
lead
Like the original Shenmue (1999), Shenmue II consists of open-world environments, brawler battles and quick-time events.
lead
It features a day-and-night system, variable weather effects, non-player characters with daily schedules, and various minigames.
lead
The player controls the teenage martial artist Ryo Hazuki as he arrives in Hong Kong in 1987 in pursuit of his father's killer.
lead
His journey takes him to Kowloon and the mountains of Guilin, where he meets a girl who is part of his destiny.
lead
Some of Shenmue II was developed alongside the original Shenmue, which was the most expensive video game ever developed at the time.
lead

The game was released in Japan and Europe for the Dreamcast in 2001, while an enhanced port was released in Western markets for the Xbox in 2002; the Dreamcast version was not released in North America, where Microsoft Game Studios secured console exclusivity.
Gameplay
Most of the game is spent exploring the game's open world, searching for clues, examining objects and talking to non-player characters for information.
Gameplay
The game features a 3D fighting system similar to Sega's Virtua Fighter series; Ryo can fight multiple opponents at once and practice moves to increase their power.
Gameplay
Unlike the first Shenmue, taking a job is not part of the main story, and the player can choose how to earn money—for example, by gambling, arm wrestling, street fighting or running a pachinko stand.
Gameplay
Ryo can spend money on items such as capsule toys or 1980s arcade games including Hang-On, After Burner, Space Harrier and Out Run.
Gameplay
The Dreamcast version allows the player to import their save data from the first Shenmue, transferring money, items and martial arts moves.
Plot
In 1987, the teenage martial artist Ryo Hazuki arrives from Japan in Wan Chai, Hong Kong on the trail of his father's killer, Lan Di, of the criminal Chi You Men organization.
Development
Shenmue II was developed by Sega AM2 and directed by Yu Suzuki.
Development

Part of the game was developed in tandem with the first Shenmue, which was most expensive video game ever developed at the time and is reported to have cost Sega US$70 million; in 2011, Suzuki said the figure was closer to $47 million including marketing.
Release
Shenmue II was released for Dreamcast in 2001 in Japan and Europe.
Release
The Japanese version included Virtua Fighter 4 Passport, promoting Sega's upcoming Virtua Fighter 4.
Release
By 2003, the Dreamcast version had sold 100,000 copies, a tenth of the original game's sales.
Release
The company released an enhanced port for the Xbox console on October 29, 2002.
Release
An anime adaptation of the first two Shenmue games premiered on February 6, 2022.
Ports
Sega released remastered versions of Shenmue and Shenmue II games for Windows, Xbox One, and the PlayStation 4 on 21 August 2018.
Reception
GamesRadar felt that, like the first game, Shenmue II had some uninteresting elements, but praised the expanded scale and action.
Reception
Shenmue II was voted the tenth-best game of all time by IGN readers in 2008.
Reception
In 2013, Den of Geek named Shenmue and Shenmue II the best Dreamcast games, and in 2014 Empire ranked Shenmue II the 51st-best game of all time.
Sequel
After the commercial failure of the first two games, Shenmue III entered a period of development hell lasting over a decade.
Sequel
In September 2011, Suzuki left Sega to focus on his development studio, Ys Net.
Sequel
In June 2015, he launched a successful Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign to develop Shenmue III with Ys Net for the PlayStation 4 and Windows, having licensed the rights from Sega.

dc_phantasy_starr_online.title: Phantasy Star Online
sents: lead
Phantasy Star Online is an online role-playing game (RPG) developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega in 2000 for the Dreamcast.
lead

It was the first successful online RPG for game consoles; players adventure with up to three others over the internet to complete quests, collect items and fight enemies in real-time action RPG combat.
lead
The story is unrelated to previous games in the Phantasy Star series.
lead
Before Phantasy Star Online, online gaming was limited to western PC games, particularly RPGs such as Diablo, Ultima Online, and EverQuest.
lead
Believing online play was the future, Sega chairman Isao Okawa instructed Sonic Team to develop an online game for the Dreamcast, produced by Yuji Naka.
lead
Sonic Team's experiments led to the development of ChuChu Rocket!, the first online Dreamcast game.
lead
Using what they learned from the project, and taking significant inspiration from Diablo, Sonic Team built Phantasy Star Online.
lead

As Japanese internet service providers charged for dial-up access per minute, and high-speed connections were not yet widely available, Okawa personally paid for free internet access bundled with Japanese Dreamcasts.
Gameplay
After organizing a team, players are transported to their own instance of the hub spaceship Pioneer 2, where they can buy and sell items, store money and items, heal, and browse quests.
Gameplay
Quests, taken on Pioneer 2, task players with specific challenges; once completed, the team returns to Pioneer 2 to collect their reward.
Plot
Threatened by the imminent destruction of their home planet, thousands of refugees arrive at planet Ragol aboard the spaceship Pioneer 2.
Plot
As they establish contact with colonists sent ahead on Pioneer 1, an enormous explosion shakes the planet.
Plot
Adventurers from Pioneer 2 land to investigate the explosion and search for Rico Tyrell, daughter of the head of Pioneer 2.
Development
By the late 1990s, the popularity of online gaming on personal computers had grown substantially in the west, but was almost nonexistent in Japan, where consoles were more popular.
Development
None of Sega's development studios wanted the project, as they were occupied with their own ventures, such as Jet Set Radio (2000) and the Sakura Wars series.
Concept
Sonic Team began experimenting with the Dreamcast's network capabilities after completing Sonic Adventure in 1998.
Concept
Their network experiments became ChuChu Rocket!, released in 1999 as the first online game for the Dreamcast.
Concept

Because of the lack of Japanese online games, and the developers' experience with the genre, Naka looked to western games for inspiration, and studied three online RPGs popular at the time: Diablo (1996), Ultima Online (1997), and EverQuest (1999).
Concept
Diablo was a 2D game, however, and Sonic Team wanted to develop a 3D game with the same degree of smoothness and gameplay.
Art and setting
The art style was "comic-like" at first, but became more realistic.
Art and setting
One of artist Satoshi Sakai's early concept drawings of a dragon reminded Naka of Sega's Phantasy Star series; which had been dormant since Phantasy Star IV (1993) for the Genesis.
Art and setting
Naka had served as main programmer on Phantasy Star (1987) and Phantasy Star II (1989).
Art and setting

Since few of the Phantasy Star IV staff still worked at Sega, the art team felt little obligation to adhere to the previous games' style, retaining only the science fiction look and some enemy and item names.
Music
The soundtrack was composed by Hideaki Kobayashi using a Roland JV-2080 synthesizer, with live orchestration on some tracks, including the theme song.
Online functionality
Sonic Team had conceived their 1998 Saturn game Burning Rangers as an online game for four players, but abandoned the idea due to insurmountable network problems.
Online functionality
In Japan, Sonic Team gave beta versions to 10,000 users who pre-ordered the game, so they could work with a variety of equipment and internet services to eliminate problems.
Online functionality
One of the biggest challenges was bridging the language barrier between global players.
Online functionality
Sonic Team felt that developing a universal language system would be the largest barrier to a global gaming network.
Online functionality
The system had about 2000 words near the end of development, and Naka found it difficult to add more words to satisfy all player needs.
Online functionality
Japanese and English were easier to implement because the only concern is the word location in the sentence, whereas Spanish and French have grammatical gender.
Online functionality
Sega initially prepared 20 network servers to accommodate 20,000 online users for game's launch, with room to add more servers as necessary.
Online functionality
The clock system divides each 24 hours into 1000 beats, with one beat equaling one minute and 26.4 seconds.
End of production
Phantasy Star Online was planned for release in March 2000, but was delayed so more features could be added.
End of production
The team planned 18 character types, and had male and female sketches for each, but settled on nine.
Promotion

"As one of the most anticipated games for RPG fans and Dreamcast owners alike, Sonic Team's Phantasy Star Online represents what could be the pinnacle of current next-generation gaming, roleplaying or otherwise."
Promotion
Sega unveiled Phantasy Star Online at the 1999 Tokyo Game Show with a gameplay demonstration.
Promotion
Naka called it the " killer app " for the Dreamcast as it used all aspects of the system, most importantly the modem.
Promotion
As the first online RPG for consoles, Phantasy Star Online was highly anticipated.
Promotion

Computer and Video Games wrote that the Dreamcast was quickly becoming the platform for innovative games, and wrote that Phantasy Star Online was "arguably the most revolutionary - not the mention most ambitious - console game ever".
Promotion
GameSpot believed it would "change the way we think of RPGs" and could possibly be "the most exciting console RPG ever created".
Promotion
Video Gamer called it the "Dreamcast's most ambitious project yet".
Promotion
The first 100,000 people to pre-order the game in Japan received Phantasy Star Online branded dog tags.
Promotion
A limited edition in Japan including a branded memory card was canceled and the memory card sold separately on Sega's website.
Promotion
Early copies of the game included a demo for Sonic Adventure 2.
Launch
Phantasy Star Online was released in Japan on December 21, 2000.
Launch
While subscriptions would be free in North America, in Japan the game included a 30-day free trial, after which Japanese players were required to purchase 30-day or 90-day subscriptions.
Launch
In North America, which Naka believed would be the biggest market, Phantasy Star Online was released on January 30, 2001.
Launch
It sold 75,000 copies there on the first day and was the bestselling game that week.
Launch
Phantasy Star Online sold 500,000 copies in Japan and one million worldwide, meeting Sega's expectations almost exactly.
Launch
Before its western launch, nearly 100,000 players had registered.
Launch
By April 2001, over 235,000 players had registered worldwide: 130,000 in Japan, 70,000 in North America, and 35,000 in Europe.
Launch
The peak number of users connected simultaneously was 26,000.
Launch
Phantasy Star Online suffered problems common with other online games, with players cheating and selling rare items online.
Launch
Sonic Team announced they would ban players found cheating or disrupting other players, starting in May 2001.
Launch
In Japan, a special "Fan Cup" quest was held from March 23 to April 6, developed with the game magazine Famitsu.
Launch
In the event, over 70,000 players competed for the fastest time; the winner received a cash prize and a rare game item.
Ver. 2
2 also adds a challenge mode, which places teams in a stage with starting equipment and stats; if a teammate dies, the mission ends.
Ver. 2
2 in under six months, releasing it on June 7, 2001, in Japan and September 25, 2001, in North America.
Ver. 2
2 was ported to Windows in Japan and released on December 20, 2001.
Episode I & II
On January 31, 2001, following years of losses, Sega announced it would discontinue the Dreamcast and restructure as a third-party developer.
Episode I & II

Phantasy Star Online: Episode I & II comprises two "episodes": Episode I is a port of Ver 2 with improved graphics, whereas Episode II comprises entirely new content, which Naka described as a true sequel.
Episode I & II
A Chao resembling Tails, a character from the Sonic games, can be imported into Sonic Advance and Sonic Adventure 2: Battle.
Episode I & II
Sonic Team ran a beta trial for some players who had pre-ordered Episode I & II, starting on May 31, 2002.
Episode I & II
The game sold 70,000 copies within the first month in Japan, and by October had sold over 100,000.
Episode I & II
It was released in North America in October, and in Europe on March 7, 2003.
Episode I & II
ASCII Corporation developed a keyboard controller for the game, released only in Japan, though plans were announced for a keyboard controller to be released in America.
Episode I & II
Episode I & II was ported to Xbox on April 15, 2003.
Blue Burst
A new version for Windows, Phantasy Star Online Blue Burst, was released in Japan on July 15, 2004, following an open beta that began on May 22.
Blue Burst

It features enhancements including a system allowing players to communicate across different servers; the most significant change is that the game is online-only, with user data stored on the servers, reducing cheating.
Blue Burst
In January 2005, Blue Burst was released in China, Sega's first online game there.
Server closure
The North American Dreamcast servers operated until September 30, 2003.
Server closure
The North American and Japanese GameCube servers as well as the Japanese Dreamcast servers were shut down on March 30, 2007, following a month of free service.
Server closure
The Japanese Xbox servers were shut down on January 31, 2007, and the North American servers followed on April 22, a week earlier than the announced date of April 30.
Server closure
The North American and European Blue Burst servers were shut down following a free period lasting from January 12, 2008, until the server's closing on March 31, 2008.
Server closure
This was followed by the shutdown of the Japanese Blue Burst servers on December 27, 2010, the last official Sega servers.
Server closure
Hobbyists have developed private servers, and so the game retains a cult following and can still be played online.
Reception
2, Dreamcast Magazine (UK) felt that it would renew interest in the game for those that enjoyed it, but would not convert new players.
Reception
GameSpot named Phantasy Star Online the best Dreamcast game and eighth-best console game of 2001.
Reception
Episode I & II was a runner-up for GameSpot ' s 2002 "Best Role-Playing Game on GameCube" award, which ultimately went to Animal Crossing.
Legacy
As the first online role-playing game for home consoles, Phantasy Star Online is considered a landmark game.
Legacy
VentureBeat dubbed it "one of the most important games in console gaming evolution".
Legacy
IGN named it one of the best RPGs of all time for being the first online experience for many gamers.
Legacy

1UP.com called Phantasy Star Online one of the most revolutionary games of the 2000s, crediting it for creating "an entire pantheon of multiplayer dungeon crawlers that continue to dominate the Japanese sales charts" and making "both online gaming and the concept of fee-based services a reality for consoles".
Legacy
Hiroshi Matsuyama, president of CyberConnect2 and developer of the.hack series, cited the game as an influence.
Legacy
Later Phantasy Star games, such as Phantasy Star Universe (2006), share similar gameplay with Phantasy Star Online but failed to reach the same critical and commercial success in the West.
Legacy
Phantasy Star Online 2 was released in Japan in 2012, and localized for the west in 2020.
Legacy
Phantasy Star Online 2 made over 900 million dollars since its release.

By the late 1990s, the popularity of online gaming on personal computers had grown substantially in the west, but was almost nonexistent in Japan, where consoles were more popular.
Development
None of Sega's development studios wanted the project, as they were occupied with their own ventures, such as Jet Set Radio (2000) and the Sakura Wars series.
Concept
Sonic Team began experimenting with the Dreamcast's network capabilities after completing Sonic Adventure in 1998.
Concept
Their network experiments became ChuChu Rocket!, released in 1999 as the first online game for the Dreamcast.
Concept

Because of the lack of Japanese online games, and the developers' experience with the genre, Naka looked to western games for inspiration, and studied three online RPGs popular at the time: Diablo (1996), Ultima Online (1997), and EverQuest (1999).
Concept
Diablo was a 2D game, however, and Sonic Team wanted to develop a 3D game with the same degree of smoothness and gameplay.
Art and setting
The art style was "comic-like" at first, but became more realistic.
Art and setting
One of artist Satoshi Sakai's early concept drawings of a dragon reminded Naka of Sega's Phantasy Star series; which had been dormant since Phantasy Star IV (1993) for the Genesis.
Art and setting
Naka had served as main programmer on Phantasy Star (1987) and Phantasy Star II (1989).
Art and setting

Since few of the Phantasy Star IV staff still worked at Sega, the art team felt little obligation to adhere to the previous games' style, retaining only the science fiction look and some enemy and item names.
Music
The soundtrack was composed by Hideaki Kobayashi using a Roland JV-2080 synthesizer, with live orchestration on some tracks, including the theme song.
Online functionality
Sonic Team had conceived their 1998 Saturn game Burning Rangers as an online game for four players, but abandoned the idea due to insurmountable network problems.
Online functionality
In Japan, Sonic Team gave beta versions to 10,000 users who pre-ordered the game, so they could work with a variety of equipment and internet services to eliminate problems.
Online functionality
One of the biggest challenges was bridging the language barrier between global players.
Online functionality
Sonic Team felt that developing a universal language system would be the largest barrier to a global gaming network.
Online functionality
The system had about 2000 words near the end of development, and Naka found it difficult to add more words to satisfy all player needs.
Online functionality
Japanese and English were easier to implement because the only concern is the word location in the sentence, whereas Spanish and French have grammatical gender.
Online functionality
Sega initially prepared 20 network servers to accommodate 20,000 online users for game's launch, with room to add more servers as necessary.
Online functionality
The clock system divides each 24 hours into 1000 beats, with one beat equaling one minute and 26.4 seconds.
End of production
Phantasy Star Online was planned for release in March 2000, but was delayed so more features could be added.
End of production
The team planned 18 character types, and had male and female sketches for each, but settled on nine.
Promotion

"As one of the most anticipated games for RPG fans and Dreamcast owners alike, Sonic Team's Phantasy Star Online represents what could be the pinnacle of current next-generation gaming, roleplaying or otherwise."
Promotion
Sega unveiled Phantasy Star Online at the 1999 Tokyo Game Show with a gameplay demonstration.
Promotion
Naka called it the " killer app " for the Dreamcast as it used all aspects of the system, most importantly the modem.
Promotion
As the first online RPG for consoles, Phantasy Star Online was highly anticipated.
Promotion

Computer and Video Games wrote that the Dreamcast was quickly becoming the platform for innovative games, and wrote that Phantasy Star Online was "arguably the most revolutionary - not the mention most ambitious - console game ever".
Promotion
GameSpot believed it would "change the way we think of RPGs" and could possibly be "the most exciting console RPG ever created".
Promotion
Video Gamer called it the "Dreamcast's most ambitious project yet".
Promotion
The first 100,000 people to pre-order the game in Japan received Phantasy Star Online branded dog tags.
Promotion
A limited edition in Japan including a branded memory card was canceled and the memory card sold separately on Sega's website.
Promotion
Early copies of the game included a demo for Sonic Adventure 2.
Launch
Phantasy Star Online was released in Japan on December 21, 2000.
Launch
While subscriptions would be free in North America, in Japan the game included a 30-day free trial, after which Japanese players were required to purchase 30-day or 90-day subscriptions.
Launch
In North America, which Naka believed would be the biggest market, Phantasy Star Online was released on January 30, 2001.
Launch
It sold 75,000 copies there on the first day and was the bestselling game that week.
Launch
Phantasy Star Online sold 500,000 copies in Japan and one million worldwide, meeting Sega's expectations almost exactly.
Launch
Before its western launch, nearly 100,000 players had registered.
Launch
By April 2001, over 235,000 players had registered worldwide: 130,000 in Japan, 70,000 in North America, and 35,000 in Europe.
Launch
The peak number of users connected simultaneously was 26,000.
Launch
Phantasy Star Online suffered problems common with other online games, with players cheating and selling rare items online.
Launch
Sonic Team announced they would ban players found cheating or disrupting other players, starting in May 2001.
Launch
In Japan, a special "Fan Cup" quest was held from March 23 to April 6, developed with the game magazine Famitsu.
Launch
In the event, over 70,000 players competed for the fastest time; the winner received a cash prize and a rare game item.
Ver. 2
2 also adds a challenge mode, which places teams in a stage with starting equipment and stats; if a teammate dies, the mission ends.
Ver. 2
2 in under six months, releasing it on June 7, 2001, in Japan and September 25, 2001, in North America.
Ver. 2
2 was ported to Windows in Japan and released on December 20, 2001.
Episode I & II
On January 31, 2001, following years of losses, Sega announced it would discontinue the Dreamcast and restructure as a third-party developer.
Episode I & II

Phantasy Star Online: Episode I & II comprises two "episodes": Episode I is a port of Ver 2 with improved graphics, whereas Episode II comprises entirely new content, which Naka described as a true sequel.
Episode I & II
A Chao resembling Tails, a character from the Sonic games, can be imported into Sonic Advance and Sonic Adventure 2: Battle.
Episode I & II
Sonic Team ran a beta trial for some players who had pre-ordered Episode I & II, starting on May 31, 2002.
Episode I & II
The game sold 70,000 copies within the first month in Japan, and by October had sold over 100,000.
Episode I & II
It was released in North America in October, and in Europe on March 7, 2003.
Episode I & II
ASCII Corporation developed a keyboard controller for the game, released only in Japan, though plans were announced for a keyboard controller to be released in America.
Episode I & II
Episode I & II was ported to Xbox on April 15, 2003.
Blue Burst
A new version for Windows, Phantasy Star Online Blue Burst, was released in Japan on July 15, 2004, following an open beta that began on May 22.
Blue Burst

It features enhancements including a system allowing players to communicate across different servers; the most significant change is that the game is online-only, with user data stored on the servers, reducing cheating.
Blue Burst
In January 2005, Blue Burst was released in China, Sega's first online game there.
Server closure
The North American Dreamcast servers operated until September 30, 2003.
Server closure
The North American and Japanese GameCube servers as well as the Japanese Dreamcast servers were shut down on March 30, 2007, following a month of free service.
Server closure
The Japanese Xbox servers were shut down on January 31, 2007, and the North American servers followed on April 22, a week earlier than the announced date of April 30.
Server closure
The North American and European Blue Burst servers were shut down following a free period lasting from January 12, 2008, until the server's closing on March 31, 2008.
Server closure
This was followed by the shutdown of the Japanese Blue Burst servers on December 27, 2010, the last official Sega servers.
Server closure
Hobbyists have developed private servers, and so the game retains a cult following and can still be played online.
Reception
2, Dreamcast Magazine (UK) felt that it would renew interest in the game for those that enjoyed it, but would not convert new players.
Reception
GameSpot named Phantasy Star Online the best Dreamcast game and eighth-best console game of 2001.
Reception
Episode I & II was a runner-up for GameSpot ' s 2002 "Best Role-Playing Game on GameCube" award, which ultimately went to Animal Crossing.
Legacy
As the first online role-playing game for home consoles, Phantasy Star Online is considered a landmark game.
Legacy
VentureBeat dubbed it "one of the most important games in console gaming evolution".
Legacy
IGN named it one of the best RPGs of all time for being the first online experience for many gamers.
Legacy

1UP.com called Phantasy Star Online one of the most revolutionary games of the 2000s, crediting it for creating "an entire pantheon of multiplayer dungeon crawlers that continue to dominate the Japanese sales charts" and making "both online gaming and the concept of fee-based services a reality for consoles".
Legacy
Hiroshi Matsuyama, president of CyberConnect2 and developer of the.hack series, cited the game as an influence.
Legacy
Later Phantasy Star games, such as Phantasy Star Universe (2006), share similar gameplay with Phantasy Star Online but failed to reach the same critical and commercial success in the West.
Legacy
Phantasy Star Online 2 was released in Japan in 2012, and localized for the west in 2020.
Legacy
Phantasy Star Online 2 made over 900 million dollars since its release.

dc_seaguy.title: Seaman (video game)

sents: lead
Seaman is a virtual pet video game developed and published by Vivarium for the Dreamcast.
lead
It was originally released in Japan in 1999, with a North American release by Sega in 2000.
lead
It is one of the few Dreamcast games to take advantage of the microphone attachment.
lead
The game developed a cult following for its dark humor, bizarre aesthetics, and innovative gameplay.
lead
A sequel called Seaman 2 was released in Japan for the PlayStation 2 in 2007.
lead
Additionally, a PC spin-off called SeaMail was released for Microsoft Windows, with the Seaman being able to interact with the user's applications from the desktop.
lead
A version of Seaman for the Nintendo 3DS was also planned, however it was cancelled during development.
Gameplay
Seaman is considered a unique video game because it contains limited action.
Gameplay
The Seaman begins its first days of life as a Mushroomer, a form which consists of a well-developed optic organ and a flagellum.
Gameplay
During this stage, the Seaman becomes capable of speech but can only communicate in gibberish by reiterating comments made through microphone input.
Gameplay
As the Gillmen mature, they develop scales and more advanced speaking abilities, but they will soon kill one another until only two remain.
Gameplay
The aquarium is also transformed into a terrarium: most of the water is gone, there is new land, and new breathable oxygen.
Story and setting
In March 1996, the French government established the Anthro-Bio-Archeological Research Institute (ABARI), headquartered in Paris.
Story and setting
Gassé, and most of the modern day research of the Seaman specimens has taken place there.
Story and setting
In 1997, the ABARI announced there was a strong possibility that these Seaman species were closely related to the origins of ancient civilizations in Egypt.
Story and setting
On October 6, 1998, one of Gassé's formaldehyde specimens is discovered at the University of Paris.
Story and setting
On February 15, 1999, parts of Gassé's journal and note entries were found in the Masuda family storehouse in the city of Matsusaka in Mie Prefecture, Japan.
Story and setting
In July 2000, an expedition team embarked for Egypt in the first major research of Seamen in the wild.
Development and release
It was conceived and designed by Saito, who originally came up with the concept of a joke when one of his coworkers was creating a tropical fish simulator.
Development and release
Seaman was intended to be developed for the Nintendo 64DD, but was instead made for the Dreamcast.
Development and release
The prototype was initially developed on a Macintosh computer, with a year-and-a-half spent on converting it into a Dreamcast game.
Development and release

A limited-edition demo version titled Christmas Seaman was released in Japan on December 16, 1999, and available for only ten days either through the Sega Direct online store or as part of an exclusive red Dreamcast pack-in.
Development and release
In 2001, Seaman was re-released in Japan for the PlayStation 2 as Seaman: Kindan no Pet - Gaze Hakushi no Jikken Shima, the first edition of which came with a microphone.
Reception
As of February 1, 2004, the Dreamcast version of Seaman sold 399,342 copies in Japan, making it the third best-selling Dreamcast game in the region at the time.
Reception
The PlayStation 2 version of the game sold 305,632 in Japan as of November 2, 2008.
Reception
It received an Excellence Award for Interactive Art at the 1999 Japan Media Arts Festival and received the Original Game Character of the Year award at GDC 2002.
Reception
In 2008, Game Informer named the game one of the top ten weirdest games of all time.
Reception

Greg Orlando reviewed the Dreamcast version of the game for Next Generation, praising the game and stating, "the gentle art of conversation meets Resident Evil – and the Dreamcast gets its most bizarre title ever".
Reception
The Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Seaman for the "Console Innovation" award during the 4th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards.

Grandia II is a role-playing video game developed by Game Arts originally for the Dreamcast console as part of their Grandia series.
lead
Initially released in Japan by Game Arts in August 2000, the game was published by Ubi Soft in North America in December 2000 and in Europe in February 2001.
lead

lead
However, it was designed around creating a more "mature" product than the previous title and the first in the series to feature fully three-dimensional graphics.

The system supports limited movement during a battle; an invisible barrier prevents characters from wandering outside the arena.

If the critical lands during the opponent's action phase, it will "cancel" the opponent's move and push the opponent's icon substantially backward along the IP gauge, delaying the opponent from taking action.

Special moves and spells can be learned with Skills Coins and Magic Coins and have a maximum level of 5.

Spells can be cast instantly if a character has skills equipped, giving a +100% bonus to the element of that particular spell.

In the last scene, Ryudo says goodbye to Granasaber and buries it under a tree in a remote area.

Destroyed, broken into pieces, and sealed after the Battle of Good and Evil.

For instance, when a party member defeats the last enemy standing while using the weapon or accessory Warp effect, the character's color scheme vanishes, and only a bright white model is left.

On the PC port, there is a glitch in the first fight with Millenia.

On May 11, 2015, GungHo America president Jun Iwasaki revealed to GameSpot that Grandia II will be receiving an HD remaster on Steam and GOG.com.

The game received a remastered version on the Nintendo Switch as part of the Grandia HD Collection on August 16, 2019.

Changes in the remaster include enhanced details to UI / sprites / texture art, visual enhancements to original cinematic videos, widescreen support and customizable resolutions (PC only), Japanese and English audio, and additional French and German localization.
Ports
The remaster was released in Japan and received Japanese language support in other regions, along with various fixes, on March 25, 2020.
Dreamcast version

The original Dreamcast release of Grandia II received a largely positive response during its initial release in Japan, earning a 9.75 out of 10 rating from Dreamcast Magazine, as well as a 35 out of 40 from Weekly Famitsu, which earned it the magazine's editor's choice Platinum award.

Famitsu DC rated the game 26 out of 30 based on three reviews.
Dreamcast version
Despite good reception, sales of the game remained relatively low in the region, with an estimated 184,863 copies sold.
Dreamcast version
It received an aggregate score of 88.81% on GameRankings and 90/100 on Metacritic.
Dreamcast version
Electronic Gaming Monthly granted the game a 9 out of 10, earning it a Gold Award.
PlayStation 2 and PC ports
The PlayStation 2 rerelease of Grandia II in 2002 experienced lower sales than the Dreamcast version in Japan despite a higher install base, selling approximately 42,060 copies in its first month.

GameSpot called the Dreamcast release "technically superior", but the new version was recommended to those who did not play the original and that it was still "well worth playing".
