PlayStation 2 and PC ports

And the characters all have huge eyes and no mouths." But the reviewer added that Grandia II "still manages to be fun, maybe even just because it's so different than most of the dark, dreary and serious RPGs that find their ways to our favorite platform."

dc_record_of_lodess_war.title: Record of Lodoss War
sents: lead
Record of Lodoss War (Japanese: ロードス島戦記, Hepburn: Rōdosu-tō Senki, lit.
lead

"Lodoss Island War Chronicle") is a franchise of fantasy novels by Ryo Mizuno based on the work he originally created for a world called Forcelia as a rules-free setting for role-playing games (RPGs).
lead
There have since been multiple manga, anime and video game adaptations, several of which have been translated into English.
lead
The plots generally follow the conventions and structure of the RPG systems including Dungeons & Dragons and Sword World RPG, in which several characters of distinct types undertake a specific quest.
Origins

Record of Lodoss War was created in 1986 by Group SNE as a Dungeons & Dragons "replay" serialized in the Japanese magazine Comptiq from September 1986 to September 1989 issues, though they also used the setting with other systems such as Tunnels & Trolls and RuneQuest.
Origins
Many shorter Lodoss scenarios and replays were published in the Comp RPG magazine (initially a supplement of Comptiq) that ran from 1991 to 1994.
Origins
An example of such a character is the female elf Deedlit in Record of Lodoss War, who was played by science fiction novelist Hiroshi Yamamoto during the RPG sessions.
Origins

The popularity of the Record of Lodoss War replays was such that the Dungeon Master Ryo Mizuno started to adapt the story into some of the earliest Japanese-language domestic high fantasy novels in 1988.
Origins
When the replay series went on to become a trilogy, Group SNE had to abandon the Dungeons & Dragons rules and create their own game, dubbed Record of Lodoss War Companion and released in 1989.
Origins

RPG Replay Record of Lodoss War I (ＲＰＧリプレイ ロードス島戦記I, RPG Ripurei Rōdosu-tō Senki I) (November 1989) — Parn's party, retake played according to the Record of Lodoss War Companion rules and incorporating elements from the novelization.
Origins

RPG Replay Record of Lodoss War II (ＲＰＧリプレイ ロードス島戦記II, RPG Ripurei Rōdosu-tō Senki II) (September 1990) — Orson's party, retake played according to the Record of Lodoss War Companion rules and incorporating elements from the novelization.
Origins
RPG Replay Record of Lodoss War III (ＲＰＧリプレイ ロードス島戦記III, RPG Ripurei Rōdosu-tō Senki III) (July 1991) — Spark's party, played according to the Record of Lodoss War Companion rules.
Origins
RPG Replay Record of Lodoss War: Spark, the Heroic Knight (RPGリプレイ ロードス島戦記 英雄騎士スパーク, RPG Ripurei Rōdosu-tō Senki Eiyū Kishi Supāku) (April 1998) — illustrated by Izubuchi.
Origins
Three prequel Legend of Lodoss replay volumes based on a draft by Ryo Mizuno, written by Hiroshi Takayama and Group SNE, with illustrations by Retsu Tateo and Tatsumi Minegishi were published.
Origins

Before being published as light novels, the first two RPG replays were serialized in Comptiq under the title TRPG Magazine Live New Record of Lodoss War: Demon Wars (TRPG誌上ライブ 新ロードス島戦記 魔神戦争, TRPG Shijō Raibu Shin Rōdosu-tō Senki Majin Sensō).
Origins
RPG Replay Legend of Lodoss 1: Invasion of the Demons (ＲＰＧリプレイ ロードス島伝説１ 魔神襲来, RPG Ripurei Rōdosu-tō Densetsu 1 Majin Shūrai) (November 1994) — serialized from August 1993 to July 1994 issues.
Origins
RPG Replay Legend of Lodoss 2: Summoning of the Demons (ＲＰＧリプレイ ロードス島伝説２ 魔神召喚, RPG Ripurei Rōdosu-tō Densetsu 2 Majin Shōkan) (October 1995) — serialized from September 1994 to September 1995 issues.
Origins

Mizuno's novelizations were published by Kadokawa Shoten between 1988 and 1993, and followed by two collections of short stories in 1995, High Elf Forest: Deedlit's Tale and The Black Knight, all with illustrations done by Izubuchi.
Origins
The Black Knight was re-released in 1998, with illustrations by Masato Natsumoto.
Origins
The first volume of the novelizations, The Grey Witch, was published in English by Seven Seas Entertainment in 2018.
Origins

The first volume forms the basis for the first eight episodes of the Record of Lodoss War original video animation (OVA) series, as well as both Record of Lodoss War: The Grey Witch manga series (by Yoshihiko Ochi and Tomomasa Takuma, respectively).
Origins

The Record of Lodoss War: Chronicles of the Heroic Knight TV series is a more faithful adaptation of volumes three to four and six to seven, with the manga drawn by Masato Natsumoto also adapting from volumes six and seven.
Origins
The first of two collections of short stories was adapted into the Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit's Tale manga series by Setsuko Yoneyama.
Origins
In 2019, he released a novel sequel Record of Lodoss War: The Crown of the Covenant (ロードス島戦記 誓約の宝冠, Rōdosu-tō Senki: Seiyaku no Hōkan).
Origins
The novel takes place 100 years after the events of the original series, with Deedlit as the lead protagonist.
Plot
Record of Lodoss War recounts the adventures of a youth by the name of Parn, the son of a dishonored knight.
Plot

Volumes three to seven, all but volume five adapted into the anime Chronicles of the Heroic Knight, continue the adventures of Parn for the first eight episodes, but then focus on Spark and his adventures to complete a quest tasked onto him to protect Neese, the daughter of Slayn and Leylia.
Plot
Spark and his fiance Neese remain the protagonists of the Record of Lodoss War Next Generation series and become the rulers of Marmo after Ashram´s group vacates the island.
Plot
The Legend of Crystania setting places the former villain Ashram into the seat of a would-be hero who is placed under a spell by an "animal god" of Crystania.
Anime
2014 Record of Lodoss War: Is That Delicious?
Anime
On April 14, 2017, Funimation announced their license to both the OVA series and the Chronicles of the Heroic Knight TV series for the United States.
Anime
Subsequently, they released the OVA on both Blu-ray and DVD and the TV series on DVD in one set on July 18, 2017.
Related media

Legend of Crystania (はじまりの冒険者たち レジェンド・オブ・クリスタニア, Hajimari no Bōkensha-tachi: Legend of Crystania), a series of RPGs and novels adapted to film, OVAs, manga and a video game, that focus on Crystania, the land to which Ashram and Pirotess migrated after the Lodoss series.
Related media
Rune Soldier, a more comedic series from the same creator set in the same world as Record of Lodoss War, but on the Alecrast continent.
Audio drama
The Demons of Wind and Flame (風と炎の魔神, Kaze to Honō no Majin), released in 4 CD collections.
Books on tape
The first three are original stories.
Reception
The novel series has sold over 10 million copies in Japan.
Reception
Australian magazine Hyper reviewed Chronicles of the Heroic Knight in 1999.

dc_illbled.title: Illbleed
sents: lead
Illbleed is a survival horror game developed by Crazy Games and released for the Dreamcast in 2001.
lead
It was published by Crazy Games in Japan and Amusement Interface Associate (AIA) in North America.
lead
The game follows Eriko Christy, a high school student who explores a horror-themed amusement park to find her missing friends.
lead
The player explores six haunted house attractions based on fictional horror films, detecting and neutralizing hidden traps and enemies which can harm or frighten Eriko and her friends.
lead
Crazy Games was known as Climax Graphics until a month before Illbleed ' s release.
lead
As Climax Graphics, they developed and published Blue Stinger (1999), an action-adventure game for the Dreamcast.
lead

The team wanted to explore horror themes in their next game, and so drew inspiration from haunted house attractions and horror films to create an original scenario that would differentiate it from other horror games.
lead
Illbleed was released in the months following Sega 's discontinuation of the Dreamcast.
Gameplay
In Illbleed, the player explores six stages, each an amusement park attraction themed after a different fictional horror film, and complete objectives unique to each one.
Gameplay
Marking enemies grants the player a first strike advantage when entering battle.
Gameplay
Engaging enemies places the game into a combat mode with unique controls, in which the player must neutralize the enemy or escape by calling for a helicopter from a helipad.
Plot
Its creator, the horror film producer Michael Reynolds, offers a reward of $100 million to anyone who can successfully reach the end of the park.
Development
The team began working on Illbleed after completing their first Dreamcast game, Blue Stinger (1999), which was published by Sega in Japan.
Development
At the time, horror media was undergoing a renaissance as a result of the success of films such as Ring (1998) and Spiral (1998) in Japan, and Scream (1996) in the United States.
Release
A playable demo was demonstrated at E3 that year and at the Tokyo Game Show in September 2000.
Release

Although Crazy Games originally expected Sega to localize the game due to Blue Stinger ' s success, Sega of America dropped Illbleed from its localization lineup in mid-2000, citing a crowded first-party release schedule.
Release
Former Jaleco executives founded Amusement Interface Associate (AIA) and its subsidiary AIA USA in early 2001, which ultimately localized the game.
Release
Crazy Games self-published Illbleed in Japan on March 29, 2001 for the Dreamcast, two months after Sega announced it was discontinuing the platform.
Release
Crazy Games also released an action figure of Eriko Christy, which was limited to 1,000 figures.
Release
Illbleed was a commercial failure, only selling 50,000 copies worldwide, a tenth of Blue Stinger ' s sales.
Release
Despite the port of Illbleed reportedly being 90% complete, the ports were canceled due to Nishigaki's death in 2004 and the Xbox's poor performance in Japan.
Reception
Next Generation described the survival horror genre as becoming "almost as ubiquitous as first-person shooters ", and felt Illbleed successfully set itself apart.
Reception
GameSpy agreed, saying the genre needed some kind of innovation, and felt that Illbleed ' s new gameplay elements and unique humor made it original.
Reception
The most-praised elements included the campy B movie style, twisted dark humor, and gratuitous use of blood.
Reception
GameSpot called the offbeat presentation Illbleed ' s most redeeming quality, writing that "gratuitous use of luscious, spurting blood sets its B movie tone perfectly".
Reception
To me, the negative reviews of the game did not affect me at all." The game has amassed a cult following.

Defender of the Future received generally positive reviews from critics.
lead

The same style of movement is kept with slight alterations for the 3-D environment.

One of the most major complaints against the graphics is the high level of fog; other reviewers have said that visibility in the ocean is often much reduced from what it is above the surface.

While the team did not take motion capture of actual dolphins, they consulted videos of dolphins in movement and spent "more than a year" to develop "a unique skeleton animation system" to achieve the "desired lifelike results".

dc_soul_caliper.title: Soulcalibur (video game)
sents: lead
Soulcalibur is a weapon-based 3D fighting game developed by Project Soul and produced by Namco.
lead
It is the second game in the Soulcalibur series, preceded by Soul Edge.
lead
Originally released in arcades on July 30, 1998, it ran on the Namco System 12 hardware, and was ported to the Dreamcast console in 1999 with new features and improved graphics.
lead
The game centers on the pursuit of the legendary weapon known as Soul Edge, now in the possession of a warrior known as Nightmare, who slaughters countless people to satisfy the blade's bloodlust.
lead
Other warriors pursue him either to claim the weapon for themselves or to destroy it, end his mass murder, and free him of its curse.
lead
Developed closely with Namco 's Tekken development team, it is one of the few home console ports that outdid their arcade parent performance-wise.
lead
The title brought many innovations to the fighting game genre that include a heavy emphasis on weapons and a unique eight-way movement system.
lead
Soulcalibur received unanimous critical applause upon release; it is the second-highest-rated video game of all time, with a 98 rating on Metacritic.
Gameplay
One of the biggest innovations introduced by Soulcalibur to the gameplay system of its predecessor, Soul Edge, is the eight-way run.
Gameplay
Previous 3D fighters had only limited movement along the third axis, with sidesteps and rolls providing useful but unsustained lateral movement.
Characters
Soulcalibur was originally planned to be a dramatic overhaul, with all new characters apart from Mitsurugi from Soul Edge.
Characters
The arcade version featured a staggered Time Release system for hidden characters akin to the Tekken series as well as codes that could be entered on the Namco website.
Characters
For example, new character Maxi has a fighting style and move set influenced by Soul Edge's Li Long (the only of the original starting characters not to return).
Characters
In fact, Soulcalibur only added one original playing style, belonging to Ivy.
Characters
Consequently, Namco has been working since Soulcalibur to gradually separate the individual styles of the characters in order to make each one unique.
Plot
For the next 25 years, he stayed dormant on the remnants of a Spanish port town, taking the souls of those who reached him during their search of the sword.
Plot
Three years after those events, in 1586 AD, Soul Edge uses Siegfried as its host, and now Siegfried is Nightmare, a knight wearing azure armor and sporting a hideously deformed right arm.
Development
Producer Hiroaki Yotoriyama decided to give the sequel a new name instead of just calling it Soul Edge 2 in order to have a fresh start and take the series in a new direction.
Development
Inspired by an internal Namco prototype featuring a character able to run openly in a field, the eight-way run system was implemented.
Development
The team for the arcade version of Soulcalibur consisted of roughly sixty people working on Namco's System 12 hardware, while the team developing the home port was reduced to about forty.
Development

The biggest technological change to the Dreamcast port was to render all of the game's stages in full 3D polygons, whereas the far backgrounds in the arcade original were flat, two-dimensional images.
Release
The game was originally released in the Japanese arcades on July 30, 1998, with releases in North America and Europe following later the same year.
Release
A Gamest Book series guide book Soul Calibur Skill Up Manual (ソウルキャリバー スキルアップマニュアル) was published by Shinseisha on September 27, 1998.
Dreamcast
The Dreamcast port of Soulcalibur was released in Japan on August 5, 1999; and in North America and Europe as launch titles, on September 9, 1999, and November 26, 1999, respectively.
Dreamcast
The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur is one of the first examples of a home conversion of a game being graphically superior to its original arcade counterpart.
Dreamcast

Among the differences were the improved graphics (including the addition of 3D backgrounds), tweaked gameplay, new game modes, new costumes, and the inclusion of an extra character, Cervantes de Leon.
Xbox 360 (Xbox Live Arcade)
In 2008, Namco Bandai Games announced a port of Soulcalibur would be released for the Xbox 360.
Xbox 360 (Xbox Live Arcade)
The port was based on the European Dreamcast version and was made available for download on Xbox Live Arcade on July 2, 2008.
Xbox 360 (Xbox Live Arcade)
While the game included HD updated graphics and various Live leaderboards, online play was absent which makes it an exception amongst most games ported to Xbox Live Arcade.
iOS (iPad, iPhone, iPod Touch)
On January 19, 2012, Namco Bandai released a port of Soulcalibur for Apple 's iOS platform.
Android
On November 20, 2013, Namco Bandai released a port of Soulcalibur for the Android platform.
Reception
In Japan, Game Machine listed Soulcalibur on their September 1, 1998 issue as being the third most-successful arcade game of the month.
Reception
The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur sold in excess of one million copies by December 1999, and 1.3 million by 2002.
Reception
It won the 1999 E3 Game Critics Award for "Best Fighting Game".
Reception

The game received universal critical acclaim, garnering perfect 10/10 scores from GameSpot and IGN, and was for nearly a decade the last game to receive a perfect rating from IGN, until the release of Grand Theft Auto IV in 2008.
Reception
It is the second game ever to get a perfect 40/40 from Japanese gaming magazine Famitsu (the first being The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time).
Reception

As of 2017, game review aggregator website GameRankings has the Dreamcast version ranked as the seventh best-reviewed game of all time, as well as being the highest-scoring title in the fighting game genre.
Reception
The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur also holds a score of 98, making it one of the highest-rated video games of all time across all consoles and platforms, on Metacritic.
Retrospective
In 2009, IGN ranked Soulcalibur as the fifth best Dreamcast game, while ScrewAttack ranked it sixth.
Retrospective
In 2005, GameSpot ranked Soulcalibur as the sixth best launch title yet, calling it "not only one of the greatest launch games or one of the greatest fighters, but one of the greatest games ever.
Retrospective
Period." In 2022, Cultured Vultures ranked Soulcalibur as the best Dreamcast game of all time.
Retrospective
Game Informer (2001): "The Top 100 Games of All Time" (74th place).
Retrospective
IGN (2003): "Top 100 Games" (38th place).
Retrospective
Retro Gamer (2004): "Top 100 Games" (75th place).
Retrospective
IGN (2005): "Top 100 Games" (43rd place).
Retrospective
IGN (2006): "Readers' Choice The Top 100 Games Ever" (sixth place).
Retrospective
Electronic Gaming Monthly (2006): "The Greatest 200 Videogames of Their Time" (22nd place).
Retrospective

Retrospective
Cinema Blend (2008): "Top 10 Best Fighting Games of All Time" (fourth place).
Retrospective
UGO.com (2010): "Top 25 Fighting Games of All Time" (second place).
Retrospective
Complex (2011): "The 50 Best Fighting Games of All Time" (fifth place).

dc_dead_or_alivish_2.title: Dead or Alive 2

Mode(s): Up to 2 players simultaneously (Arcade) Up to 4 players simultaneously (Dreamcast/PlayStation 2)

sents: lead
Dead or Alive 2 (Japanese: デッドオアアライブ2, Hepburn: Deddo oa Araibu To~ū, abbreviated as DOA2) is a 1999 fighting game developed by Team Ninja and published by Tecmo.
lead
It debuted in Arcades in 1999 and was later ported for the Dreamcast and the PlayStation 2 in 2000.
lead
It is the second main entry in the Dead or Alive fighting series.
lead
Several enhanced editions of the game were released, including the updates Dead or Alive 2 Millennium and Dead or Alive 2 Hardcore.
lead

The game's plot focuses on the evil tengu, Gohyakumine Bankotsubo, who escaped from the tengu world into the human world, and the Dead or Alive tournament's change in purpose and significance after the murder of DOATEC's founder and CEO, Fame Douglas.
lead
Dead or Alive 2 received universal acclaim, strong sales, and is considered one of the greatest fighting games of all time.
lead

It improved upon the gameplay system by including many new features, it improved upon and popularized the concept of multi-tired environments and improved upon the graphics engine of its predecessor by utilizing the Sega NAOMI hardware.
lead
In 2004, Dead or Alive 2 was remade for the Xbox as part of Dead or Alive Ultimate.
Gameplay

In Dead or Alive 2, the basis of the entire fighting system is the circular relationship between three types of moves: blows, throws, and holds; blows beating throws, throws beating holds, and holds beating blows.
Gameplay
A major difference between DOA2 and other fighters was in the safety and non-punishability of attacks, both upon hitting and upon being blocked.
Gameplay
Most blows in DOA2 can be punished on hit and block by each character's faster throws, making blow-based offense very risky.
Gameplay
In DOA2, fights can occur on either water or ice; when a character is on such a surface, all non-knockdown, non-launching attacks will induce a stun on any successful hit.
Gameplay
DOA2' s Tag Battle Mode offers Tag Throws which are special throws unique to pairs of characters.
Characters
Dead or Alive 2 features a total of 15 fighters, 14 playable fighters and the unplayable Kasumi X.
Characters
The ten returning veterans from the first DOA game are Ayane, Bass Armstrong, Bayman (unlockable), Gen Fu, Jann Lee, Kasumi, Leifang, Ryu Hayabusa, Tina Armstrong, and Zack.
New
In order to fulfill the last words of Rolande, Leon enters the tournament, aspired to be the strongest man on earth.
Plot
Fame Douglas, founder and CEO of DOATEC was killed at the end of the 20th century.
Plot

Kasumi, who won the first tournament was captured by the DOATEC Super-human Development Project and was unwillingly used in the organization's attempt to develop a physical body with superhuman abilities.
Development and release
The gameplay and graphics were enhanced and based on a better game engine than the one used in the first game, as all resources went into the characters and the stages.
Development and release
Dead or Alive 2 was first released in the arcades on October 16, 1999.
Development and release
An update titled Dead or Alive 2 Millennium was released in arcades worldwide in 2000.
Development and release
Dead or Alive 2 featured the song "Exciter" by punk band, Bomb Factory, in its opening sequence.
Development and release
Both "Exciter" and "Deadly Silence Beach" can be found on the self-titled mini-album, Bomb Factory, and on the Dead or Alive 2 Original Sound Trax ~PlayStation 2 Version~.
Home versions
Nine different versions (excluding DOA2 Ultimate on Xbox and the two PSN releases) of Dead or Alive 2 were released: two for the arcade market, and the others were home versions.
Home versions
Tomonobu Itagaki and Team Ninja were constantly enhancing the game for both the Dreamcast and PlayStation 2 as they worked towards their vision of the "ultimate fighting game".
Home versions
The Dreamcast port was first released in North America on February 29, 2000.
Home versions
Unlike home ports of the first Dead or Alive game, there were no unlockables in this release.
Home versions
Team Ninja immediately started working on the console version as Tecmo planned to be listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in March 2000.
Home versions

Since the development environment for the Dreamcast was very convenient and the NAOMI hardware being the same as the Dreamcast, the team manage to complete the Dreamcast port in February 2000 as planned.
Home versions
Dead or Alive 2 was the only game that Tecmo published on the Dreamcast.
Home versions
Dead or Alive 2 was released as a launch title for the PlayStation 2 in Japan on March 30, 2000.
Home versions
The game engine of the PlayStation 2 port ran using Field Rendering instead of Frame Rendering, thus the PlayStation 2 port appeared much more aliased than the Dreamcast port.
Home versions
Itagaki and his team were only given two months initially to produce the first PlayStation 2 port.
Home versions

Itagaki was greatly disappointed in how the PlayStation 2's development environment was not as convenient as the Dreamcast's, and felt that he couldn't complete the PlayStation 2 version as planned in March 2000.
Home versions
The European Dreamcast version was released on April 28, 2000.
Home versions
Acclaim developed the Shadow Man video game and published Dead or Alive 2 in Europe.
Home versions
The Japanese Dreamcast version (known as the Limited Edition) was released on September 28, 2000.
Home versions
The most notable addition was that Bankotsubo and Bayman were now unlockable, playable in all but Story Mode.
Home versions
The new stages from the PlayStation 2 version were not included, in favor of new versions of Burai Zenin and L's Castle stages from the first game.
Home versions
On October 25, 2000, Tecmo released DOA2: Hardcore (DOA2: Dead or Alive 2 in Europe) as a launch title for the PlayStation 2 in America and on December 15, 2000 in Europe.
Home versions
Survival Mode now only took place in the "Danger Zone" arena.
Home versions
Overall gameplay speed was increased, and the entire game (including cutscenes) now ran at a full 60 frames-per-second (in the Dreamcast version, the game ran at 60fps, while cutscenes ran at 30).
Home versions

English voice-overs (provided by Brian Vouglas, Donna Mae Wong, Gina Rose, Jeremy Hou, John Parsons, Lucy Kee, Roger Jackson, Sally Dana, Terry McGovern, Timothy Enos, and Zoe Galvez) were added in addition to the original Japanese voice-overs, making it the first game in the series to have English voice-overs.
Home versions
Kasumi can be unlocked as a trainable 'monster' in Monster Rancher 4 by going to the Shrine, and inserting the DOA2: Hardcore disk in the PS2.
Home versions
Tecmo followed up on the release of Hardcore in the US and Europe with the release of DOA2: Hard*Core in Japan.
Home versions

This was the last Dead or Alive game to be released for a Sony system, as the series became exclusive to the Xbox until the release of Dead or Alive Paradise, Dead or Alive: Dimensions, and Dead or Alive 5 respectively.
Merchandise
Two soundtrack CDs were released in 2000 by Wake Up in Japan: Dead or Alive 2 Original Sound Trax (KWCD-1001) and Dead or Alive 2 Original Sound Trax ~PlayStation 2 Version~ (KWCD-1004).
Merchandise
Two guide books for the game were published in North America by Prima Games (Dead or Alive 2: Prima's Official Strategy Guide and DOA2: Hardcore: Prima's Official Strategy Guide).
Re-release
On August 22, 2012, a software emulated version of DOA2: Hard*Core was made available as a downloadable game on the Japanese PlayStation Network.
Re-release
The North American version was released to the US PlayStation Network on March 24, 2015.
Reception
Dead or Alive 2 was "universally acclaimed", scoring 91% and 91/100 on GameRankings and Metacritic.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu scored the game a 34 out of 40.
Commercial
Dead or Alive 2 brought more than $2 million profit in sales.
Commercial
In Japan, Game Machine listed Dead or Alive 2 on their December 15, 1999 issue as being the second most-successful arcade game of the month.
Commercial
The PlayStation 2 version would top the Japanese charts on release, coming in number 2 during Week 14 in 2000.
Commercial
The Dreamcast version also top the Japanese charts on release, coming in number 2 during Week 40 in 2000.
Critical
Dead or Alive 2 is considered one of the best fighting games in the genre in terms of gameplay and expanded game modes.
Critical
On GameRankings, the Dreamcast version was met with universal acclaim, while the PS2 version was very well received.
Critical
Famitsu scored the Dreamcast version 32/40 and the PS2 version 34/40.
Critical
Main criticism was the poor English voice dub used in the updated version for the PS2 titled DOA2: Hardcore, much like other English dub Japanese video games.
Critical
For the original Dreamcast and PlayStation 2 versions, Greg Orlando of Next Generation rated it 5 stars out of 5, and stated that "You'd have to be Dead and Buried not be enjoy Dead or Alive 2.
Critical

Mielke called the fast combat the best thing about Dead or Alive 2, also praising the game's Tag Battle mode and stating how "no other 3D (or even 2D) fighter matches DOA2 for sheer intensity and speed.
Critical
This game is for hard-core gamers only." Overall, calling Dead or Alive 2 "superb" and "excellent".
Critical

For the Hardcore version, Jeff Lundrigan of Next Generation rated it 5 stars out of 5, and stated that "This is the best-looking, most full-featured, most packed-with-extras version of one of the best fighting games ever made.
Critical

Buy it, period." David Smith of IGN gave it an 8.7 out of 10, calling DOA2: Hardcore "the best version around", stating how he always preferred Dead or Alive ' s speed, balance, character design, and levels, even if Tekken may be the majority choice.
Critical
Gamespot scored it 8.9 out of 10, saying how the game "looks simply amazing", and that "the animation is smooth, but the character models are what really stand out".
Critical
Game Pro rated DOA2: Hardcore 5 out of 5, calling it a must have PlayStation 2 game for fighting enthusiasts.
Critical

Vargas of PSX Nation gave it an 8 out of 10, stating that DOA2: Hardcore "takes better advantage of the PS2 than Tekken Tag Tournament, IMHO, with incredible physics, realistic fighters and fast action not seen in any other modern brawler".
Awards

During the AIAS ' 4th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Dead or Alive 2 was honored with the " Console Fighting Game of the Year " award, and also received a nomination in the " Animation " category.
Awards
IGN awarded it "Best PS2 Fighting Game of 2000" during their Best of 2000 Awards.
Awards
The game was nominated for "Best Fighting Game" at E3 ' s Game Critics Awards.
Legacy
Dead or Alive 2 was notable for improving and popularizing the concept of multi-tiered environments.
Legacy
Dead or Alive 2' s interactive multi-tiered environments offered all kinds of features that made the game feel so alive.
Legacy
Dead or Alive 2 appears in the 2002 film Run Ronnie Run, where the character, Jerry Trellis (portrayed by E.J.
Legacy
The game also appears in the 2002 film One Hour Photo, where the character, Jake Yorkin (portrayed by Dylan Smith), is playing the game in his bedroom.
Remake
Dead or Alive Ultimate is a remake of DOA and DOA2 for the Xbox with a greatly improved graphics engine.
Remake
As it was created after Dead or Alive 3, it takes elements and mechanics from both its original iteration and successor.
Remake
The action of 3D-axis movement is as free-formatted as DOA3, and Hitomi, as well as Tengu are now playable characters (albeit outside story mode), but other elements have been kept intact from DOA2.
Remake
The biggest set of changes instituted in Dead or Alive Ultimate are online play over Xbox Live and the inclusion of slopes, which are a type of environmental hazard.

lead
It is a futuristic combination of squash and Breakout, and is a single player game.
lead
It is one of the few Dreamcast games to be released in a DVD-style case, rather than a jewel case.
lead
A reimagining titled C-Smash VRS released for PlayStation VR2 and Meta Quest on June 23, 2023, and Pico 4 on April 4, 2024.

In the Dreamcast version, the first seven stages of every playthrough are the same, starting at station 707 ("Welcome"), and advancing by 10 (717, 727, etc.) to station 777 ("Nami").
