The Dreamcast version also produces a unique code at the end of each playthrough, directing the player to enter the code at a now defunct website at the official Cosmic Smash website to be entered into a worldwide leaderboard (though on console, the game was only released in Japan).
Gameplay
At last update, the highest score on the third-party leaderboard was a two-way way of 590,678,903—both entries by an English player named "Alex" with a listed age of 11.
Gameplay
The top three scores on the leaderboard are almost ten times the total of the fourth place score of 60,018,465.

dc_choo_choo_rocket.title: ChuChu Rocket!

Platform(s): Dreamcast, Game Boy Advance, iOS, Android

sents: lead
ChuChu Rocket! is an action puzzle game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega.
lead
Released for the Dreamcast in 1999, it was the first game for the system to support online console gaming.
lead
Players must place arrows on a board to lead mice into escape rockets while avoiding cats.
lead
The game features single-player modes in which a player must save all the mice on a board, and a multiplayer mode in which players battle to collect the most mice.
lead

Directed and produced by Yuji Naka, ChuChu Rocket! was developed in part to test the online functionality of the Dreamcast and Sega's servers, and test the Dreamcast's processing power by displaying many characters at once.
lead
The knowledge gained from the network portion of the project helped Sonic Team in their development of Phantasy Star Online (2000).
lead
ChuChu Rocket! topped the Japanese sales charts its first week on sale in November 1999.
lead
When it arrived in the United States, Sega held an online tournament where players could battle against Sega and Sonic Team employees.
Gameplay
Up to three arrows can be placed by a player at any time; placing a fourth arrow will make the player's oldest arrow vanish, and all arrows fade away over time.
Gameplay
In the puzzle mode, the player is provided a limited set of arrows to place on the field to save all the ChuChus in play.
Gameplay
In the challenge mode, players are given 30 seconds to save the ChuChus in play without any arrow limitations as in puzzle mode.
Gameplay
ChuChu Rocket! is notable for being the first Dreamcast online multiplayer game.
Gameplay
Servers for the game's online functionality were brought back online by fans in 2016.
Development
Director and producer Yuji Naka conceived the game as a way to use the power of the Dreamcast to create 100 sprites moving at once.
Development
' s purpose was to test the capabilities of online multiplayer gaming on the Dreamcast; the team used what they learned to help drive the development of Phantasy Star Online (2000).
Development
A NAOMI arcade version of the game was also planned, but later scrapped.
Promotion and release
Sega announced ChuChu Rocket! on September 2, 1999 as Sonic Team 's second game for the Dreamcast after Sonic Adventure (1998).
Promotion and release

Prior to the game's release in Japan in November 1999, Sega promoted the game with a website dedicated to ChuChu Rocket!, and a 15-second commercial advertising the game was solicited to television stations across the country, with the commercial also made available to download through the website.
Promotion and release

ChuChu Rocket! released in Japan on November 11, 1999 and climbed to the top of the Japanese sales charts in its first week on sale, selling 35,000 copies and knocking the PlayStation release of Chrono Trigger off the top spot.
Promotion and release
In January 2000, Sega of America announced it would bring ChuChu Rocket! to North America on March 2, 2000, three months earlier than the original anticipated release in June.
Promotion and release
Prior to the North American release of the game, a Shockwave demo featuring 30 levels from the game's puzzle mode was made available to play on personal computers through Sega's website.
Promotion and release
ChuChu Rocket! was released in North America on March 7, 2000, a week later than had been announced earlier.
Promotion and release
It retailed for $29.99 in America — below the average for new Dreamcast games.
Promotion and release
Sega held an online tournament on March 25, 2000 where players could battle with members of Sonic Team, the Dreamcast network team, and other Sega employees in online matches.
Promotion and release
The European and PAL versions were not released until months after the North American release, on June 9, 2000.
Promotion and release
At the time of the game's release in Europe, Dreamarena had over 25,000 subscribers, despite the absence of online play beforehand.
Ports
A port of ChuChu Rocket! was released as a launch game for the Game Boy Advance in Japan on March 21, 2001.
Ports
The release garnered interest as the first game Sega published for a Nintendo system.
Ports
Players can use Game Link Cables to connect up to four systems together to play using only one cartridge.
Ports
Sonic Team also selected 2,500 of the 17,000 custom puzzles uploaded to the Dreamcast servers to include in the game.
Ports
This version of ChuChu Rocket! was re-released on the Wii U in Japan on October 21, 2015.
Ports
ChuChu Rocket! was also included as part of a 2-in-1 Sonic Advance cartridge for the Gameboy Advance released on 11 November 2005.
Ports
Sega released iOS and Android ports of ChuChu Rocket! in 2010 and 2011.
Reception
The most common complaints were in regards to the game's network component.
Reception

However, praise was given for the ability to hook up four Game Boy Advances and play multiplayer using only one cartridge, and also for the inclusion of 2,500 user-created stages uploaded to the Dreamcast servers.
Legacy
A follow-up to ChuChu Rocket!, Dee Dee Planet, was in development and scheduled for release on the Dreamcast in 2001.
Legacy
In 2021, a near-complete beta copy of the game was obtained and leaked onto the internet.
Legacy
In the original GameCube release of Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg (2003), a limited version of the Game Boy Advance port can be unlocked and played via the GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable.
Legacy
Minigames inspired by ChuChu Rocket! were included in Sega Superstars (2004) and Sega Superstars Tennis (2008).
Legacy
Universe, developed by Hardlight, was released on September 19, 2019 for iOS, macOS and tvOS as a launch game for Apple Arcade.

dc_bangai_oh.title: Bangai-O
sents: lead
Bangai-O is a multidirectional shooter developed by Treasure and released in 1999 on the Nintendo 64 in Japan.
lead
It was ported to the Dreamcast worldwide shortly after with some gameplay changes and updated graphics and audio.
lead
The game places the player in control of a weaponized mech that can hover across large stages and fire at enemies all around them.
lead
The player must reach the end of each stage and defeat the boss, while avoiding hazards scattered across the map such as enemy mechs and gun turrets.
lead
The initial ideas for Bangai-O came from Treasure programmer Mitsuru Yaida who wanted to challenge himself by programming an extreme number of bullets on the screen at once.
lead
Journalists agree that Yaida was most likely inspired by the 1984 Japanese computer game Hover Attack.
lead
The team developed the game with a focus on creating enjoyable gameplay, and opted for simple graphical effects to preserve the game's speed.
lead
Bangai-O was released on the Nintendo 64 and was limited to a run of 10,000 copies because of publisher Entertainment Software Publishing 's belief it had niche appeal.
Gameplay
The player can fly freely around each of the game's 44 stages, and must find and destroy the boss in each stage to advance.
Gameplay
Destroyed enemies and objects yield fruit which replenishes a meter that is used to power the "scatter bomb" attack.
Gameplay
Hitting all 100 shots on enemies will open a small portal to a shop where the player can get upgrades such as improved shot damage.
Gameplay
The Dreamcast version of Bangai-O, released after the initial Nintendo 64 version, features significant differences in gameplay which results in a more streamlined experience.
Gameplay
In the Dreamcast version, the bullets are stronger, and destroying objects and enemies refills the bomb attack meter instead of fruit which now only add to the player's score.
Gameplay
In the Dreamcast version, up to 400 missiles can be shot at once in comparison to 100 on the Nintendo 64.
Development
Even though Yaiman and other staff behind the game have not identified the game, industry analysts agree that the game is almost certainly Hover Attack (1984) for Japanese computers.
Development
Yaiman began thinking about the programming challenges involved in detecting when the bullets collide with other objects, and started work on a prototype.
Development
One of the artists on the team, Koichi Kimura, had just finished working on Guardian Heroes (1996), another 2D game.
Development
With more powerful development hardware available, he wanted to challenge himself the possibilities and limits of 2D graphics.
Release
Treasure announced Bangai-O for the Nintendo 64 in June 1999.
Release
Because of the game's niche appeal, the publisher Entertainment Software Publishing (ESP) only shipped 10,000 units.
Release
The Dreamcast version was first released in Japan on December 9, 1999.
Release
By February 2000, publishers were researching the possibility of localizing the Dreamcast version for Western audiences.
Release
In December, industry newcomer Conspiracy Entertainment announced they were localizing Bangai-O along with another Dreamcast game, Record of Lodoss War (2000).
Release
The Dreamcast version was planned for release on February 27, 2001, but was eventually released on March 21.
Reception
Bangai-O received positive reviews for its initial Nintendo 64 release.
Reception
Critics enjoyed the manic and unique gameplay that they believed was characteristic of Treasure's video games.
Reception
Most compared it to older shoot 'em ups and action games.
Reception
Eric Mylonas of GameFan called it a mix between the free-floating gameplay of Sub-Terrania (1994) and the rotating shooting action of Omega Boost (1999).
Reception
Bartholow and Martin Kitts (N64 Magazine) both praised the level design for forcing the player to change their tactics level to level.
Reception
Kitts and Mylonas wrote that it looked and played like a Super NES game and pointed out how some effects were reminiscent of the 16-bit system's Mode 7 rotation effects.
Reception
Rick Mears (GameFan) wrote that it felt like Robotron (1982) with its unique control style, and called it an "old school 2D treat".
Reception
Although the game was not in 3D like most other games at the time, critics felt the 2D graphics were satisfactory enough.
Reception
Reviews for the Dreamcast version carried the same sentiments as the Nintendo 64 version in regards to the frantic and unique gameplay.
Reception
Human Tornado of GamePro said, "This well-designed 2D shooter will satisfy fans of old-school arcade ation games, but Bangai-O doesn't break any new ground.
Reception
Despite never having been reviewed, the Dreamcast version was nominated at The Electric Playground ' s 2001 Blister Awards for "Best Console Shooter Game", but lost to Halo: Combat Evolved.
Sequels
The first, Bangai-O Spirits, was released for the Nintendo DS in 2008, and the second, Bangai-O HD: Missile Fury, was released exclusively on the Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade in 2011.
Sequels
The games feature most of the same core gameplay ideas as the first game, but evolve on them with more weapons and gameplay elements.

dc_giga_wyng_2.title: Giga Wing 2
sents: lead

Giga Wing 2 (ギガウイング2, Giga Uingu Tsū) is a 2000 vertical scrolling shooter arcade game developed by Takumi and published by Capcom on Sega's NAOMI arcade system board and later ported in 2001 to the Dreamcast console.
lead
The arcade version is notable both for its excessive scores (scores in the quintillions are not unheard of), and for using a horizontally aligned monitor (much like Treasure Co.
lead
Ltd 's Radiant Silvergun), something that is considered rare for a vertical shooter.
Dreamcast version
Online ranking service was ended on 10 December 2003.
Soundtrack
The soundtrack to Giga Wing 2 was released on CD, bundled with the soundtrack to Mars Matrix, both composed by the Japanese composer Yasushi Kaminishi -上西 泰史- (上西泰史).
Reception
In Japan, Game Machine listed Giga Wing 2 on their March 1, 2001 issue as being the most-successful arcade game of the month.
Reception
The Dreamcast version received "average" reviews, a bit more positive than the first Giga Wing, according to the review aggregation website Metacritic.
Reception
For a mere $20, you get plenty of mindless old-school fun, albeit for a relatively short time".
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 27 out of 40.

dc_mars_matrics.title: Mars Matrix
sents: lead
Mars Matrix: Hyper Solid Shooting, or simply Mars Matrix (マーズマトリックス, Māzu Matorikkusu), is a vertically scrolling shooter arcade game developed by Takumi and released in 2000.
lead
The game was published by Capcom and run on their CPS-2 arcade system board.
lead
Mars Matrix was later ported to the Dreamcast video game console in 2001.
lead
The arcade version uses a horizontally aligned monitor, despite being a vertically scrolling game.
Plot
In 2100, millions of people were starving due to massive food shortages and has caused civil wars around the world.
Plot
In 2309, a Declaration of Independence has been sent to Earth.
Controls
Shot power increases with level (max 8), which depends on EXP points.
Controls
Piercing Cannon: By not pressing A button for at least 1 second, press A.
Controls
Mosquito: When GHB is full, A button is hold for 1/4 to 1/2 second.
Fighter
Each fighter has a 10x12 pixel hit box at the front of the unit.
Fighter
The fighter can only be destroyed by colliding with enemy bullet, not other objects.
Items
1UP: Increases player's life stock by 1.
Experience system
Combo meter can be depleted if player's fighter fails to capture a cube for a prolonged time period, or if player's fighter is destroyed.
Stages
Time: Depends on how many seconds left after destroying last boss in the completed stage.
Ports
Despite the claim of perfect conversion, the base scores for enemy units are different.
Ports
The bug where player's score cannot go beyond 999,999,999,990 points was fixed by adding 2 extra digits in the score table.
Soundtrack
Mars Matrix & Giga Wing 2 Original Soundtrack Box was released by Suleputer.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 31 out of 40.
Reception
Also in Japan, Game Machine listed the arcade version in their July 15, 2000 issue as the seventh most-successful arcade game of the year.

dc_karouss.title: Karous
sents: lead
Karous (カラス, karasu, "raven") is a vertical-scrolling shooter video game developed by MileStone Inc. for the Sega NAOMI platform and released in Japanese arcades on November 15, 2006.
lead
The game was later ported to the Sega Dreamcast, becoming the system's last officially licensed title when it was released in Japan on March 8, 2007.
Gameplay
The weapon system is based on Radio Allergy, but it uses a unique D.F.S. bomb system.
Gameplay
Enemies destroyed by the barrier provide more experience points to the player.
Gameplay
The player's shot, sword, shield can be upgraded by using experience items dropped from enemies, with a maximum of 100 levels.
MileStone Shooting Collection Karous Wii
On April 8, 2008, a Nintendo Wii version of the game was released in Japan, titled MileStone Shooting Collection: Karous Wii.
Reception
Famitsu gave the Dreamcast version a review of 6, 6, 6, 7, while Edge gave it 6 out of 10.
Reception
The game marks the last official third-party release for the Dreamcast platform.

dc_radirgee.title: Radirgy
sents: lead
Radirgy is a shoot 'em up video game developed by MileStone Inc. and released for the Sega NAOMI arcade platform in 2005.
lead
The story follows schoolgirl Shizuru Kamigusa in an age filled with radio waves which she is allergic to.
lead
She must save her father, who is developing a remedy for her sickness, from terrorists who have taken control of his company.
lead
The game features bullet hell gameplay elements and a distinct cel shaded graphical style.
lead
Radirgy was ported in 2006 to the Dreamcast, PlayStation 2, and GameCube for release in Japan—of which the latter two featured additional gameplay modes.
lead
O~3 Entertainment planned to localize the GameCube version in North America under the title Radio Allergy, but the release was canceled.
lead
The game was later localized for the Wii in a compilation of MileStone shooters, Ultimate Shooting Collection.
lead
Critics found the game challenging and unique, but overall an average experimental shooter.
Gameplay
Most of the bullets come in patternless waves with the exception of bosses which feature more structured patterns.
Gameplay
In order to use the ABSNET shield, the player must fill a gauge by gathering blue items which drop from destroyed enemies.
Release
After first releasing on the arcade Sega NAOMI platform, Radirgy was ported to the Dreamcast, and later the PlayStation 2 and GameCube.
Release
The PlayStation 2 version featured a more difficult mode called "Okawari Mode" and the GameCube release had a special score attack mode titled "Manpuku Mode".
Release
In January 2007, O~3 Entertainment announced that it would be localizing Radirgy in February for North America exclusively for the GameCube under the new title of Radio Allergy.
Reception
They found the game to not carry the depth of Ikaruga, another GameCube shooter, but still believed the game was "solid" especially for the retail price of $20.
Sequels
Another title, Radirgy de Gojaru!, was released for the Nintendo 3DS in 2014 in Japan.
Sequels
Radirgy 2 was released for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and PlayStation 5 in March 2024.

dc_psyvariarr_2.title: Psyvariar 2
sents: lead
Psyvariar 2: The Will to Fabricate (サイヴァリア2: THE WILL TO FABRICATE) is a vertically scrolling shoot 'em up developed by SKONEC Entertainment and distributed by Success.
lead
It is the sequel to the 2000 title, Psyvariar.
lead
The game was initially developed for the Sega NAOMI arcade platform, and was released in Japanese arcades in November 2003.
lead
A Dreamcast version was released on February 26, 2004, and ports to both the PlayStation 2 and Xbox were released later that year.

dc_kaos_field.title: Chaos Field

Programmer(s): Jirō Hamaya Manabu Matsumoto Takahiro Kawachi

sents: lead
Chaos Field is a 2004 vertically scrolling shooter arcade video game developed by MileStone.
lead
The game consists entirely of boss battles, featuring five stages with three bosses each.
lead
The player can choose to play as one of three characters, each with their own ship that has a unique primary weapon.
lead
The player can flip the environment at will between two parallel worlds.
lead
Chaos Field is the first game from MileStone, a company founded by former Compile employees looking to develop high quality shooters similar to those Compile was known for in the past.
lead
The game experienced a troubled development cycle due to a lack of organization and the number of employees involved.
lead
After its release in Japanese arcades, it was ported to the Dreamcast, PlayStation 2, and GameCube in Japan.
lead
The GameCube version was also released in North America, and included a mode that adds small waves of enemies between the bosses.
Gameplay
The player can choose to play as one of three characters, each with their own ship that has a unique primary weapon: a spread shot, a lock-on laser, or bolts of lightning.
Gameplay
The player only gets one life per credit, but can take several hits before losing a life.
Development and release
Chaos Field was the first game developed by MileStone Inc., who were desiring to make a shooter of their own.
Development and release
The company was founded by former Compile employees in 2003 after Compile went bankrupt.
Development and release

Most of the staff originally joined Compile because of the company's positive reputation with shooting games like the Aleste series, but were left unsatisfied from Compile's growing focus on other franchises like Puyo Puyo.
Development and release
The team had a working prototype by September 2003 but scrapped this iteration and started anew when they determined it did not feel right.
Development and release
Chaos Field was first released in Japanese arcades on May 25, 2004.
Development and release
The team also had experience with developing for the GameCube and PlayStation 2, and so created ports for those platforms as well.
Development and release
The GameCube version, Chaos Field Expanded, was released in February 2005 in Japan by Sega, with a North American version published by O~3 Entertainment in December that year.
Development and release
Chaos Field is included in the Wii compilations Ultimate Shooting Collection (2009) and Milestone Shooting Collection 2 (2010).
Reception
Some critics like IGN only recommended Chaos Field to hardcore fans of the genre who desired to attain the highest scores, and pointed casual players to Ikaruga.

dc_ikaruka.title: Ikaruga

Platform(s): Arcade, Dreamcast, GameCube, Xbox 360, Windows, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4

sents: lead
' Japanese grosbeak ') is a shoot 'em up developed by Treasure.
lead
It is the spiritual sequel to Radiant Silvergun (1998) and was originally released in Japanese arcades in December 2001.
lead
The story follows a rebel pilot named Shinra as he battles an enemy nation using a specially designed fighter called the Ikaruga which can flip between two polarities, black and white.
lead
This polarity mechanism is the game's key feature and the foundation for its stage and enemy design.
lead
All enemies and bullets in the game are either black or white.
lead
Bullets which are the same color as the player are absorbed while the others will kill the player.
lead
The game features both single-player and cooperative modes.
lead
Development on Ikaruga began during director Hiroshi Iuchi's off-hours while Treasure was busy developing Sin and Punishment (2000).
Gameplay
When white, the ship will absorb white bullets fired by enemies and store their power until released with a special attack.
Gameplay
If an enemy is destroyed with the same polarity as the player, the ship will expel energy which can be absorbed or, if the player changes polarities too quickly, present a fatal danger.
Gameplay
Ikaruga does not feature any pick-ups or power-ups, instead, the player can only rely on their standard firing weapon and a homing laser.
Gameplay
The power of the attack increases one level for every 10 enemy bullets absorbed.
Gameplay
Each level is equal to one laser, with a maximum of 12 which can be stored.
Gameplay
A homing laser is 10 times more powerful than a standard shot.
Gameplay
The player will earn 100 points for their first chain bonus, and double the amount for each bonus thereafter.
Gameplay
If certain conditions are met, a prototype mode is unlocked which limits the number of bullets the player has.
Synopsis

Hidden in a secret underground bunker and launched via the transportation device called "The Sword of Acala", Ikaruga is the first fighter to be built with both energy polarities, and is capable of successfully switching between the two.
Synopsis
Kagari's fate at the end of the game is the same as Shinra's, dying as her ship is destroyed in the final attack against the object.
Development
Development of Ikaruga began while Treasure 's Sin and Punishment (2000) was still in development.
Development

Since company resources were allocated for Sin and Punishment, director Hiroshi Iuchi worked on Ikaruga at home on his spare time and developed a prototype with help from programmer Atsutomo Nakagawa.
Development
Ikaruga shares basic shooter gameplay elements with an earlier Treasure shooter, Radiant Silvergun (1998).
Development
Another source of inspiration was the defense system in Shinrei Jusatsushi Taromaru (1997) for the Sega Saturn.
Development
Iuchi reused sprites from Radiant Silvergun so he could finish the prototype quickly.
Development
A unique feature to the original design was a limited ammo supply.
Development
Gameplay ideas in the prototype version were later included in a special bonus mode in the final game.
Development
Originally, Radiant Silvergun was intended to be a trilogy, and Ikaruga began development as a direct sequel, codenamed "Project RS-2".
Development
The game's pacing follows a "mountain" and "valley" approach, in which the music and action will peak, followed by a melancholy atmosphere, only to build up tempo again.
Development
By the time development was finished, 5 Treasure staff had worked on the game, as well as 3 support staff from G.rev which was raising funds to develop its own shooter, Border Down (2003).
Release
Ikaruga was targeted to Treasure's core fanbase, as pleasing them was the team's first priority.
Release
Ikaruga was first released in arcades in Japan on 20 December 2001.
Release
A Dreamcast port was released exclusively in Japan on 5 September 2002.
Release
Although not yet published in the West, Ikaruga began to garner a cult following in North America among import gamers.
Release

On August 15, 2002, it was announced that Infogrames ' Japanese division had picked up the publishing rights to a GameCube version of the game and would release the title in January 2003 under the Atari brand name.
Release
The game was released in Japan on January 16, 2003.
Release
The game was released in North America on April 15, and in Europe on May 9, branded under the Atari label as in Japan.
Release
On 12 September 2007, Microsoft announced they were planning on releasing Ikaruga on Xbox Live Arcade for the Xbox 360.
Release
It was released on 9 April 2008, and included new features such as leaderboards, achievements, and the ability to record and replay playthroughs.
Release
Treasure later released Ikaruga on the arcade distribution platform, NESiCAxLive, on 8 August 2013.
Release

In October 2013, Treasure placed the title into the Steam Greenlight process to bring the game (based on the Xbox 360 version) to Microsoft Windows, with hopes to bring their other titles to the platform later.
Release
The game was released on Steam on 18 February 2014.
Release
It was also published by Nicalis for the Nintendo Switch on 29 May 2018, supporting both horizontal and vertical screen orientations.
Release
In June 2018, Ikaruga was also released on the PlayStation 4.
Release
On 22 November 2019, Nicalis announced that physical copies were in production for both the Nintendo Switch and the PlayStation 4.
Reception and legacy
In February 2002, Game Machine listed the game as being the fifth most popular arcade game in Japan at the time.
Reception and legacy
Critics agreed that Ikaruga ' s game design was "innovative", "clever", and "unique".
Reception and legacy
Reception of the Xbox 360 and Windows ports was similar to the GameCube version.
Reception and legacy
Topher Cantler of Destructoid gave Ikaruga a perfect score and dubbed it a "work of art".
Reception and legacy
Ikaruga continues to be one of the most revered shooters of all time.
Reception and legacy
The Xbox 360, Windows, and Switch ports have received positive reviews.
Reception and legacy
IGN voted Ikaruga the 3rd greatest 2D shooter of all time.
Reception and legacy
The Dreamcast and GameCube versions sold 33,860 physical units in Japan.
Reception and legacy
The Xbox Live Arcade version sold 137,088 digital units on the Xbox 360, as of 2011.
Reception and legacy
The PC version has sold 128,543 digital units on Steam, as of 1 July 2018.

gen_starr.title: Phantasy Star IV
sents: lead
Phantasy Star IV: The End of the Millennium is a 1993 role-playing video game by Sega for the Sega Genesis.
lead
It was first released in Japan and later in Europe and North America in 1995.
lead
It is the fourth and final game in the original Phantasy Star series, concluding the story of the Algol Star System.
lead
Phantasy Star IV kept many of the gameplay elements of the previous game, including turn-based battles, overhead exploration, and magic spells.
lead
It received mixed reviews upon its release but has since been considered one of the greatest video games of all time.
Gameplay
The instruction manual for the American version states that there are 15 possible combination-attacks.
Gameplay
Occasionally, the "secret technique" Feeve, a useless technique accessible through hacking, is mistaken for the "lost 15th combo".
Plot
Phantasy Star IV takes place 1,000 years after the events of Phantasy Star II and 1,000 years before the era of Phantasy Star III.
Plot

Joined by others along the way, they connect the world's troubles to a cult leader called Zio, "The Black Magician", whose aims appear to be total annihilation of not only Motavia but of the whole Algol solar system.
Release
The game was released in Japan in December 1993, North America in February 1995 and the United Kingdom and Europe in December, 1995.
Release
End of the Millennium was the first Phantasy Star title not to be localized to Brazil by Tec Toy.
Release
In the United States, the game retailed for just under $100.
Release
Phantasy Star IV was the last Phantasy Star game until Phantasy Star Online (2000), which has a mainly unrelated story.
Ports and remakes
The game was ported as part of Phantasy Star Collection for the Sega Saturn, released only in Japan.
Ports and remakes
There was a Windows port released in 2004, as well as its inclusion in the Sega Genesis Collection, Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection, Sega Genesis Classics, and the Sega Genesis Mini.
Ports and remakes
Sega Ages planned a remake for the PlayStation 2 console, having revamped the first two games: Phantasy Star Generation 1 and Phantasy Star Generation 2.
Reception
Nintendo Life ' s Corbie Dillard said that one could not have asked for a better end to the 16-bit series.
Reception

IGN called it one of the definitive 16-bit role-playing games, stating the "storyline and characters are deep and engaging", the "attractive anime -style cutscenes steal the show visually", and the gameplay is both "classic and unique at the same time".
Reception

Tor.com described it as "an ambitious JRPG that is the perfect end to the series, taking the best elements of each of the previous games and weaving together a 'phantastic' journey." Eurogamer stated that it is "epic in scope" and recommended that "anyone with a fondness for JRPGs should investigate this at once".
Reception
In 2007, IGN ranked Phantasy Star IV as the 61st best game ever made.
Reception

In 2012, IGN placed Phantasy Star IV at number 59 in their Top 100 RPGs of all time, citing the elegantly simple mechanics and the game's influence on Phantasy Star Online (which they ranked as number 23 on the list).
Reception
In 2009, Nintendo Power labelled the title, along with Phantasy Star II, as one of the greatest RPGs of all time.
Reception
Complex ranked the game number 2, behind only Gunstar Heroes, in its list of the best Sega Genesis games.

gen_shining_farce.title: Shining Force

Developer(s): Climax Entertainment, Sonic! Software Planning Amusement Vision (GBA)
Writer(s): Masaki Wachi Kenji Orimo Haruki Kodra Hiroyuki Takahashi
Platform(s): Sega Genesis, Game Boy Advance, iOS, Microsoft Windows

sents: lead
Shining Force is a 1992 turn-based tactical role-playing game for the Sega Genesis console.
lead
It is the second entry of the Shining series of video games, following Shining in the Darkness.
lead
While primarily a traditional fantasy -themed game, it contains some science fiction elements.
lead

The game has been repeatedly re-released: in Sega Smash Pack Volume 1 for the Dreamcast and Sega Smash Pack 2 for Microsoft Windows, in Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, and as a standalone game for the Wii Virtual Console and Microsoft Windows via Steam.
lead

Additionally, in 2004 a remake was released for the Game Boy Advance under the title Shining Force: Resurrection of the Dark Dragon and in 2010 the game was released for iOS but was discontinued in 2015.
lead
It was re-released again on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in 2021.
Gameplay
As is most common for the RPG genre, units become stronger by fighting enemies or by performing other actions in battle, such as healing allies.
Gameplay
Although there are no "generic" units, except on the enemy side, most characters contribute little or nothing to the plot upon joining the player army.
Gameplay
A unit can be promoted to another class at any level between 10 or 20.
Gameplay
Upon promotion the character's level resets to 1 and statistics are reduced by a fixed amount, although they begin higher if the character had been promoted to a higher level.
Development and release
Despite being the sequel to the successful Shining in the Darkness, Sega allotted only a minimal budget to the development of Shining Force.
Development and release

In fact, when asked about the game, lead Shining Force developer Hiroyuki Takahashi remarked: "The tempo of that title was so bad that it wasn't something I even wanted to play." Takahashi recalled that Shining Force was chiefly inspired by Dragon Quest.
Development and release
The game was released for Wii via Virtual Console in Japan on July 10, 2007, in North America on July 23, 2007, and on August 3, 2007.
Reception
Mega placed the game at #33 in their Top Mega Drive Games of All Time.
Retrospective

In 2004, readers of Retro Gamer voted this "truly unique RPG masterpiece" 86th top retro game, with the staff additionally calling it "one of the greatest Megadrive games of all time and a definite office favourite."
Remake
The game was remade in 2004 for the Game Boy Advance under the title Shining Force: Resurrection of the Dark Dragon.
Remake
GameSpot named Resurrection of the Dark Dragon the best Game Boy Advance game of July 2004.

gen_shining_farce_ii.title: Shining Force II
sents: lead
Shining Force II (シャイニング・フォースII 古えの封印, Shainingu Fōsu Tsū: Inishie no Fūin, lit.
lead
"Shining Force II: The Ancient Seal") is a tactical role-playing game for the Mega Drive/Genesis console developed by Sonic!
lead
Software Planning and published by Sega in 1993.
lead
Its storyline is not directly connected to the original Shining Force, although a Game Gear title Shining Force Gaiden: Final Conflict links the two games' plots.
lead
The game is much longer than Shining Force, and contains more free roaming.
lead
There is no chapter system, so the player can return to previously visited parts of the world.
lead
There are also two different ways of promoting certain characters.
lead
After the game's initial release, Shining Force II saw re-releases and remasters on consoles and PCs.
Gameplay
While roaming through town or moving throughout the world, one can find both visible and hidden treasures and interact with certain objects.
Gameplay
Some of these characters are hidden, requiring specific events to occur before they will join the force.
Gameplay
Once a unit reaches level 20, that character has the ability to advance to a more powerful class through promotion.
Gameplay
Some characters have two different classes they may be promoted to, one of which is only accessible using a special hidden item.
Shining series continuity
Shining Force II takes place somewhere in the area of 40–70 years after Shining Force Gaiden: Final Conflict, and is set in the same lands of Parmecia and Grans.
Shining series continuity
Artifacts from Final Conflict such as the Caravan and Nazca Ship make return appearances, and several monsters, most notably the Kraken, still terrorize the lands.
Development
Despite being the fifth game in the successful Shining series, Sega allotted the same budget for Shining Force II as it had for the first game in the series, Shining in the Darkness.
Development
Shining Force II' s planning and development was intertwined with first two Shining Force Gaiden games.
Reception

Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s Mike Weigand commented that the story "could use a few more twists and turns", but that the music is good, the control configuration is very user-friendly, and the game improves on the first Shining Force with bigger areas to explore.
Reception

He summarized that "This will definitely appeal to fans of the first one, and to RPG fans in general." Stan Hojnacki of the Santa Cruz Sentinel recommended the game, describing it as "a worthy sequel to a popular first edition."
Reception
In 1997, Electronic Gaming Monthly listed it as the 60th best console video game of all time, citing the compelling story and the cerebral challenge of the battles.
Reception

In 2007 IGN named it one of the top 100 video games of all time at number 48, citing its refreshing simplicity among tactical RPGs and its underlying challenge, and Retro Gamer included it among the top ten Mega Drive games.

gen_landstalkur.title: Landstalker
sents: lead
Landstalker: The Treasures of King Nole is an action role-playing that was developed by Climax Entertainment and released for the Sega Genesis in 1992 in Japan and 1993 elsewhere.
lead
Players take on the role of the treasure hunter Nigel as he navigates a three-dimensional world through an isometric viewpoint, solving puzzles and fighting enemies.
lead
The game was a critical and commercial success.
lead
A spinoff called Lady Stalker: Challenge from the Past was released in Japan for the Super NES in 1995.
lead
A sequel was in the planning stages but was cancelled.
lead
Dark Savior and Alundra are considered spiritual successors.
lead
Nigel is a playable character in Time Stalkers.
lead
It has been re-released several times: on the Wii 's Virtual Console in 2007, Steam in 2011, on the Sega Genesis Mini in 2019, and on the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in 2023.
Gameplay
There are a variety of items throughout the game, most of which either increase or restore health and attacking power or are important to advancing the plot or solving puzzles.
Plot

The game's intro starts in Gamul Date 312 where Nigel, a treasure hunter who is 88 years old, far older than he appears, is shown traversing a dungeon of rolling boulders and moving platforms called Jypta Ruins to acquire the Statue of Jypta.
Plot
Once Nigel spends most of his money on a bird to carry him to the island, Friday admits that while she doesn't know the exact location of the treasure she has a "feeling" where it is.
Plot

The player controls Nigel from here on where he and Friday, who accompanies him for the entire game, first journey through a dungeon until they fall into a river and end up in the care of the red-furred bear-people of Massan.
Plot
Nigel frees the townspeople, and they give him a legendary sword they found but had hidden from the Duke.
Plot
In the original ending in the Japanese and European version the treasure vanishes after Gola's last stand.
Reception
The game was reviewed in 1995 in Dragon #217 by Jay & Dee in the "Eye of the Monitor" column.
Reception
Jay gave the game 3 out of 5 stars, while Dee gave the game 4 out of 5 stars.
Reception
The game was praised in the Australian-based Megazone magazine, where it received a 9 out of 10.
Reception
In GameFan ' s annual Megawards, Landstalker won the awards for Most Innovative New Game (Sega) and Best Action/RPG, and was a nominee for the Best Music (Genesis) and Game of the Year awards.
Reception
Mega placed the game at #5 in their Top Mega Drive Games of All Time.
Reception
In 2017, Gamesradar ranked the game 24th on their: "Best Sega Genesis/Mega Drive games of all time."

gen_beyond_oasys.title: Beyond Oasis
sents: lead
The Story of Thor, known in North America as Beyond Oasis, is a 1994 action-adventure game developed by Ancient and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis.
lead
The game was produced and had music written by Yuzo Koshiro.
lead
The Story of Thor was later released in various emulated collections.
lead
A prequel, The Story of Thor 2, was released for the Sega Saturn in 1996.
Gameplay
The game has action adventure elements similar to The Legend of Zelda series.
Reception
Game Informer gave the game a "very good" score of 8.75/10.
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly gave it a 38/50 (7.6/10 average), praising the vast game world and strong plot twists.
Reception

IGN gave the Virtual Console re-release an 8/10, calling it "very stylish," and expressing "surprise" that despite a lack of polish in certain areas, its "unique" mechanics "deserve to be mentioned alongside such classics as Secret of Mana ".
Reception
In 2017, GamesRadar rated Beyond Oasis 38th on their Best Sega Genesis/Mega Drive games of all time, giving praise to the game's graphics and sound.

gen_ranger_y.title: Ranger X
sents: lead
Ranger X is a side scrolling run and gun video game for the Sega Genesis.
lead
Developed by GAU Entertainment and published by Sega, the game was released in 1993.
Gameplay
The jet pack allows for short periods of flight, the duration of which is limited by the jet pack's temperature.
Gameplay
Unlike the pulse rifle, the special weapons drain a power bar, which can only be recharged when Ranger X is in a bright light source.
Gameplay
The game is split across several levels, each of which is introduced via a wire frame 3D cutscene detailing a specific target objective.
Development and release
Hiraiwa stated that the choice of colors reflects the music's tone, which lead him to write 23 songs with a rock and progressive rock touch as he did not want music feel similar to each other.
Reception
Similar sentiments were echoed in Sega Force Mega and GamePro, who felt that "the unique dual action of flying and riding a motorcycle gives this game a step up against over other shooters".

gen_vektorman.title: Vectorman
sents: lead
Vectorman is a 2D action platformer video game developed by BlueSky Software and published by Sega.
lead
The game was released for the Sega Genesis in late 1995 in North America and Europe.
lead

In subsequent decades, the game was re-released across many Sega-themed video game compilations, and on its own across the Wii Virtual Console, Steam, and the Sega Forever line of mobile game releases.
lead
A sequel, Vectorman 2, was released in 1996, but despite several abandoned attempts at making a Vectorman 3, no further games have been released.
Gameplay
Collecting "multipliers" may also be collected to increase damage dealt by attacks; for example, collecting a 2X multiplier leads attacks to cause double the damage.
Plot
The game takes place in a future where the Earth has been largely destroyed by humans through pollution.
Development and release
BlueSky Software 's development relationship with Sega began in the early 1990s.
Development and release
After successfully developing and releasing Starflight and Joe Montana Football in 1991, BlueSky Software signed an exclusivity contract to develop video games for their Sega Genesis platform.
Development and release

Sega published two of their Jurassic Park games; a video game adaption of the original Jurassic Park film released in 1993, and a sequel game, Jurassic Park: Rampage Edition, the following year, both for the Sega Genesis.
Development and release

After completion of the two games, Sega turned to them to create a game centered around pre-rendered 3D models in its levels and character designs, as an answer to Nintendo 's popular 1994 release Donkey Kong Country.
Development and release
Vectorman originally started as a 3D tech demo created by tools programmer Karl Robillard, inspired by vector ball demos for the Amiga.
Development and release

While Sega had been finding success with the Genesis platform in the early 1990s, by 1995, they had lost momentum; Donkey Kong Country was a huge hit, while the launches of the Sega 32x and the Sega Saturn had not gone well.
Development and release
Rather than the typical singular character sprite, Vectorman's body consists of 23 individual sprites programmed to move in unison.
Development and release

The "sphere-only" character approach characters would have allowed for more varied perspectives and scaling, including the changing of viewpoints, but this was eliminated upon the creation of more detailed character models.
Development and release

With the emphasis on smooth animations, the team had worked on the idea of having more "windup" and "aiming" type animations while shooting, but the added delay in action from the extra animations hampered the game's playability, and the idea was scrapped.
Development and release
The game's villain, Warhead, was originally named Raster; the dynamic of Vectorman versus Raster would have mirrored how vector graphics are the opposite of raster graphics.
Development and release
Karpp said that the level had a unique look but was not fun to play because Vectorman could not freely explore and the lack of room to maneuver made it difficult to line up shots at flying enemies.
Development and release
For the moving flags on the first level, the team referenced video footage of the flags on top of BlueSky's building during a windy day to make the animation look believable.
Development and release
The techno soundtrack was inspired by the works of Kraftwerk, Orbital, and The Prodigy, as well as Goa mixes.
Development and release
The resulting soundtrack was described as "slower and moodier" than most platformer games from the 16-bit era.
Development and release
A year after the game's release, the game's soundtrack was released under the name Sega Tunes: Vectorman CD, featuring higher sound quality arrangements of the songs originally aimed for by Holland.
Development and release
The game was released on the Sega Genesis on October 24, 1995 in North America and on November 30, 1995 in Europe, with a marketing budget of $12 million.
Development and release
The game wasn't released further until the mid-2000s, after Sega became a third-party video game developer, and the game appeared on a number of Sega-themed game compilations.
Development and release
It appeared on Sonic Gems Collection (2005), Sega Genesis Collection (2006), and Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection (2009).
Development and release
The game was also re-released on various digital download services, including the Wii Virtual Console in 2008, on Steam in 2010, and as part of the Sega Forever service in 2018.
Development and release
In 2019, the game was included on the Sega Genesis Mini console.
Reception
The game was a commercial success in the US, with it being one of the best-selling video games of the 1995 holiday season.
Reception

Vectorman sold 500,000 copies in the US by the end of the year, making it among Sega's top selling games of the year, though short of Nintendo's concurrent holiday, Donkey Kong Country 2, which moved 900,000 copies.
Reception
Publications noted that the game's graphic's were comparable to early-generation PlayStation 1 games being released around the same time period.
Reception

The four reviewers of Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the first Vectorman a score of 8.25 out of 10, unanimously praising the advanced graphics and animation, large levels with numerous hidden areas, strong audio, and ability to change into different forms.
Legacy
In 1996, a sequel, Vectorman 2 was released for the Sega Genesis.
Legacy

During the same year, Sega of America entered into a deal with Los Angeles-based Ideal Entertainment for the motion picture, television and merchandising rights to the first game, though no television or film ever entered development.
Legacy
Multiple attempts at making a Vectorman 3 were made in the late 1990s and early 2000s, though all were cancelled by Sega prior to release.

gen_vektorman_2.title: Vectorman 2
sents: lead
Vectorman 2 is a 2D action platformer developed by BlueSky Software and published by Sega.
lead
Released one year after the original Vectorman, the game retains the game's core gameplay while expanding its mechanics.
lead
Multiple attempts to create a Vectorman 3 were proposed to Sega, with none of them coming to fruition.
Gameplay
The gameplay is similar to the first Vectorman game.
Gameplay
The game consists of 22 levels; more than the original game's 16, but levels in the game are generally shorter and smaller than ones found in the original.
Story
After saving Earth in the previous game, Vectorman's spaceship is targeted and destroyed by a missile.
Story
Unlike the post-apocalyptic setting of the first game, Vectorman traverse a wide range of modern settings until coming across the source infestation: the evil Black Widow Queen.
Development

In the early 1990s, BlueSky Software, after a series of successfully developed games for the Sega Genesis video game console, Sega signed a contract with them to exclusively develop their next games for the platform.
Development

A sequel was immediately greenlit, though the game would feature a rushed development cycle; the lifespan of the Sega Genesis was already coming to an end by the time of the late 1995 release of the original Vectorman, and despite continued good sales, new releases were becoming increasingly rare in 1996.
Development
The original's main programmer, Richard Karp, was busy with other projects, and had to be replaced with Keith Freiheit, who had been a lead programmer on the first Jurassic Park game adaption.
Development
Leaked prototype copies of the game showed many test and unfinished level designs not featured in the final game, along with an alternate unused " game over " screen.
Development
While enemies in the first game tended to have a more robotic, metal feel, enemies in Vectorman 2 have more of an organic feel.
Development
The game was released on November 15, 1996; with it and Sonic 3D Blast being of the last games Sega games published for the Sega Genesis platform.
Development
The game was not released further until the mid-2000s, after Sega became a third-party video game developer, and the game appeared on a number of Sega-themed game compilations.
Development
Vectorman 2 was released on Sonic Gems Collection (2005), Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection (2009), and the Sega Genesis Mini 2 (2022).
Reception
Electronic Gaming Monthly gave Vectorman 2 a 7.25 out of 10.
Reception
Sushi-X, in contrast, said that the levels are surprisingly small, making it a disappointment compared to the first game.
Reception
GamePro gave it a 4.5/5 in graphics and a 5/5 in every other category.
Reception
The reviewer said that compared to the first game, it "has cleaner graphics, more sound and voice effects, and faster, smoother gameplay.
Abandoned sequels
Multiple attempts at making a Vectorman 3 were made in the late 1990s and early 2000s, though all were cancelled by Sega prior to release.

gen_alisha_dragun.title: Alisia Dragoon
sents: lead
Alisia Dragoon is a 1992 platform game developed by Game Arts for the Sega Genesis.
lead
The player controls Alisia, a young woman who is on a quest to avenge her father and save the world.
lead
She can fire lightning from her hands and summon four faithful beasts to aid her.
lead
Alisia Dragoon was published outside of Japan by Sega.
lead
Despite the acclaim the game received, it was not a commercial success.
lead
The game was later made available on the Sega Genesis Mini and Nintendo Switch Online.
Gameplay
Only one pet can fight alongside Alisia in her quest, but the player can select any of the four (or none) as the active companion at any time.
Gameplay
These enhancement items are placed throughout the first seven stages, mostly in hidden locations.
Plot
Similar to most action games on the Sega Genesis, the plot in Alisia Dragoon is simple and short.
Plot
Although the world has not fully recovered from the devastating effects of Baldour's last visit, Baldour's aide Ornah manages to transport his dormant cocoon back to Earth.
Development
In 1992, Japanese animation studio Gainax was in a collaboration with Game Arts, the makers of the Lunar role-playing games, to produce an action video game.
Development

Several of its founders had worked on Hayao Miyazaki 's animated films, and the influences of Miyazaki's 1984 science fiction animated film Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind were evident in certain levels of the game.
Development
The composition of the soundtrack was delegated to Mecano Associates, who had produced the music for other works from Game Arts, such as the action games Fire Hawk: Thexder 2 and Silpheed.
Development

Game Arts, however, did most of the work in producing Alisia Dragoon, adapting the artwork into environments and creatures that can be rendered by the console hardware and writing them as lines of software code.
Reception

Rignall agreed with Leadbetter on the game's difficulty, which along with the secret rooms and power-ups to be discovered made Alisia Dragoon an excellent action platform game that had long-lasting appeal.
Reception

Of the hundreds of Genesis games, Mega magazine rated Alisia Dragoon among the top 100 games, calling it " the best dragon-based platform game around." Despite the positive sentiments, sales of the game outside Japan were weak.

gen_dynamite_heady.title: Dynamite Headdy

Composer(s): Katsuhiko Suzuki Yasuko Koji Yamada Aki Hata Norio Hanzawa

sents: lead
Dynamite Headdy is a platform video game developed by Treasure and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis in 1994.
lead
The game follows a puppet named Headdy in his efforts to stop an evil puppet king from taking over his world.
lead
Headdy can throw his head at enemies to defeat them and use it to pull himself to various areas and move objects.
lead
The player can find a wide variety of "heads" which act as power-ups that provide different effects and alter gameplay.
lead
Critical reception to Dynamite Headdy was positive.
lead
Critics highlighted the game's originality and creativity in distinguishing it among other games in the platform genre.
lead
They also commended Treasure for demonstrating their technical expertise with impressive graphical effects and building on the success of their earlier game Gunstar Heroes (1993).
lead
In reviews from the time and in retrospect, Dynamite Headdy is cited as one of the best games on the Genesis, and has since been included in multiple compilations of classic Genesis games.
Gameplay
Some of these power-ups last for only a short time.
Development and release
Up to this point in his five-year career, Kimura had only worked on projects using the pre-existing works of others.
Development and release
The game's visual design was inspired by Western animation and the work of film director Terry Gilliam.
Development and release
Dynamite Headdy was originally released in Japan on 5 August 1994 for the Sega Genesis, with North American and European releases following in September and October respectively.
Development and release
The game was included along with Gunstar Heroes and Alien Soldier in Sega Ages 2500: Gunstar Heroes Treasure Box, a compilation released for the PlayStation 2 in 2006 in Japan.
Development and release
The game saw a digital re-release on the Wii via the Virtual Console in July 2007.
