sat_panzer_dragun.title: Panzer Dragoon (video game)

Developer(s): Sega (Team Andromeda) Land Ho! (PS2) MegaPixel Studio (remake)

sents: lead
Panzer Dragoon is a 1995 rail shooter game for the Sega Saturn, developed and published by Sega.
lead
It is the first game in the Panzer Dragoon series.
lead
The game follows hunter Keil Fluge, who becomes the rider of a powerful dragon.
lead
The player moves an aiming reticle (representing the dragon's laser and Kyle's gun) and shoots enemies while the dragon flies through 3D environments on a predetermined track.
lead
As one of six games available at the Sega Saturn's surprise North American launch, Panzer Dragoon was the first game created by Team Andromeda.
lead
It was also the directorial debut of Yukio Futatsugi, who was 25 years old at the time of release.
lead
Panzer Dragoon received positive reviews in 1995 and in retrospective coverage.
lead
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it game of the month and the best Saturn game of the year, and named it the 140th-best game of all time in 2006.
Gameplay
The only time the game pauses is during boss battles.
Gameplay
The player has a full, 360-degree field of view, and can quickly look left, right, forward, and behind the dragon.
Gameplay

Two weapons are available: the rider's handgun, which can be fired with a single button press when an enemy enters the aiming reticle, and the homing laser fired by the dragon, which can lock on up to eight enemies by moving the reticle over them while holding down the fire button.
Plot
From the newly created hole, an armored, blue dragon flies down the cavern with a rider across its shoulders, being chased by an even bigger black dragon as the cavern is destroyed in an explosion.
Plot
During the first level of the game, Keil and his dragon fly through a drowned city, where they encounter a small Imperial patrol ship.
Plot
During the fifth level, they defeat a large armada of the most powerful Imperial ships over a forested area.
Plot
During this, they are both waylaid by the creatures and machines seen attacking the Imperial fleet around the tower while also being fired on by Imperial defenses.
Development
Panzer Dragoon was created in the early 1990s as the Japanese video game company Sega was preparing to release its Saturn console.
Development

In 1993, as the Saturn lacked third-party games, Sega asked its developers for game ideas; according to art director Manabu Kusunoki, Sega asked for shooting game ideas to add variety to the Saturn's launch library.
Development
Twenty-three-year-old Yukio Futatsugi, who had joined Sega only two years before, proposed several concepts, including Panzer Dragoon.
Development
Futatsugi became the head of Team Andromeda, a development team that Sega assembled for the project in early 1994 and was built around the duo formed by Futatsugi and Kusunoki.
Development
Team Andromeda wanted to create a fully 3D arcade game, having worked on similar games such as Out Run which were not truly 3D.
Development
With influences including Space Harrier, Starblade, Star Fox, and RayForce, the project became a 3D rail shooter.
Development
Usually, in 3D shooters, the player rides a 3D object like a jet fighter or a tank.
Development
With this basic concept in mind, the creators had 3 months to define a visual identity and a setting for their game, prior to development.
Development
The first presentation video featured a green dragon, in line with traditional European / medieval depictions, however the team quickly decided to change it and make it "more sci-fi".
Development
The overall fantasy look of the game's world, which mixed natural and technological elements, was also chosen in order to set it apart from classic science-fiction 3D games of the time.
Development
The team wanted a famous artist to make the game's cover art.
Development
The Saturn's hardware was new to the team, and it was their first attempt at creating an original environment.
Development

It was also Futatsugi's first year working as a full developer at Sega, so he was only able to do simple things while having a clear vision of what he wanted, which helped him to keep the overall style pure, with stark and minimalist cutscenes.
Development
Working on new hardware proved difficult for the young team, and the game ended up missing the initial deadline given by Sega, which was the Saturn Japanese launch on November 1994.
Development

One of the problems was that the Saturn hardware was only finalized in mid-1994, and without actual Saturn prototype to test their progress, the programmers initially had to work with hypothetical hardware performance.
Development
Team Andromeda created its own graphics library and mapping tools instead of using Sega's, in order to make the most of their first game on the new system.
Development
The game's graphics and cutscenes were done with Softimage, and the 3D elements were programmed on SGI workstations using OpenGL.
Development
The programmers were eventually able to transition to the debug Saturn they had received, but the process was difficult and the game had a very low frame rate at first, before it increased to approx.
Development

The first two levels that the team programmed, a desert (level 2) and a forest (level 5), did not have any objects or anything besides sand and forest effects, again because the team was unsure how far the hardware could be pushed.
Development
Keeping CPU limitations in mind, simple tornado effects were added to level 2, so that it did not look too bland.
Releases

Panzer Dragoon was released in Japan on March 10, 1995, North America on May 11, 1995 as one of the six launch games for the North American release, and Europe on August 30, 1995, on the Sega Saturn console.
Releases
It was followed by Panzer Dragoon II Zwei (1996) and Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998), both for Saturn, and Panzer Dragoon Orta (2002) for Xbox.
Releases
In 1997, a software rendered version was released, requiring at least an Intel Pentium P5 processor.
Releases
An updated version of Panzer Dragoon was included in the Japan-only Sega Ages 2500 collection for PlayStation 2 in 2006.
Releases

The port was handled by development studio Land Ho!, and features the original Saturn game and an "arrange" version with anti-aliasing filter, better texturing, and improved 3D models for the dragon and some enemies.
Reception
Panzer Dragoon received positive reviews, both in 1995 and in retrospective coverage.
Reception
As one of the first Saturn games, Panzer Dragoon was highly anticipated by journalists after its appearance in promotional material.
Reception
In contrast, a reviewer from Maximum said that the game was much too easy even on the highest difficulty setting, greatly reducing its already low longevity.
Reception

He also said the gameplay would be too simplistic for many players, with its on-rails shooting and selection of only two weapons, but was overall very positive in his assessment of the game, highly praising the 360 degrees of rotation and most especially the textured 3D graphics of the enemies, settings, and bosses.
Reception
Famitsu magazine's Reader Cross Review gave the game a 9 out of 10 in April 1995.
Reception
Film director Steven Spielberg approached Team Andromeda to say he was impressed by the game's presentation at the 1995 E3 show.
Reception
James Mielke from online game magazine 1UP.com gave Panzer Dragoon a retroactive review of 8/10 for what the game offered in 1995, but gave it a modern score of 6/10.
Accolades
It was named "Best Saturn Game of 1995" by Electronic Gaming Monthly in their 1996 Buyers' Guide.
Accolades
Panzer Dragoon ranked 140th in EGM ′s "The Greatest 200 Videogames of their time" feature published in 2006.
Accolades
In 1996, GamesMaster ranked the game 5th on their "The GamesMaster Saturn Top 10."
Remake
A remake of Panzer Dragoon was developed by MegaPixel Studio and published by Forever Entertainment in March 2020 for Nintendo Switch.
Remake
It was released on Stadia on June 1, with Windows, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Amazon Luna versions later in 2020.

sat_panzer_dragun_ii_zwo.title: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei
sents: lead
Panzer Dragoon II Zwei is a 1996 rail shooter game for the Sega Saturn, developed and published by Sega.
lead
The second entry in the Panzer Dragoon series and a prequel to the original game, the story follows Lundi and his dragon companion, Lagi, as they pursue an airship of the Ancient Age.
lead
The player controls an aiming reticle representing the dragon's laser and Lundi's gun, shooting enemies while the dragon travels through 3D environments on a fixed track.
lead
Levels can have multiple pathways, and the dragon grows stronger over the course of the game based on the player's score.
lead
Production of Zwei began in 1995 in parallel with the role-playing video game Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998), with a small staff and little assistance from Sega.
lead
In response to player criticism of the original Panzer Dragoon, the team reduced the overall difficulty and expanded the story elements.
lead
The soundtrack, composed by Yayoi Wachi, influenced the musical direction of later entries in the series.
lead
Zwei was acclaimed by critics and journalists, with many praising it as superior to the original Panzer Dragoon.
Gameplay
Panzer Dragoon II Zwei is a single-player rail shooter which spans seven levels, with each after the first including a boss encounter.
Development
Encouraged by the success of the first Panzer Dragoon (1995), Sega began planning two sequels for the Saturn: the rail shooter Zwei, and the role-playing video game Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998).
Development
Development of Zwei began in mid-1995, several months after Panzer Dragoon was released.
Development
As they used the first game's engine, production took less than twelve months.
Development
Series creator Yukio Futatsugi originally oversaw both projects' narratives, but as his attention shifted onto Saga, Zwei ' s story became the responsibility of Katsuhiko Yamada.
Development
Kentaro Yoshida was the art director and designer, with art contributions and oversight from Manabu Kusunoki, the artist for the first Panzer Dragoon.
Development
The Emperor's design was inspired by Harkonnen, a main antagonist of the novel Dune.
Development
The transition from ground to air was difficult to display, as the Saturn could only show one scrolling layer, so the team made use of camera transitions to mask the change.
Development

A notable element was the water effects, which were created using a combination of parallax scrolling and layers, allowing a look impossible on the 3D-focused PlayStation without exceeding the hardware limits of the Saturn.
Development
The dragons were inspired by different creatures and machines from classic science fiction.
Development

Iwate had to work around the Saturn's limited 3D ability when creating the models, with Suto and Nakanishi sometimes clashing with Iwate over his complex models and movements when they tried to run them on Saturn hardware.
Music
In contrast to the purely orchestral and electronic score of the first game, Zwei added ethnic elements.
Music
Panzer Dragoon Saga composer Saori Kobayashi credited Wachi's shift away from the first game's musical style with shaping her future compositions for the series.
Music
A soundtrack album was published by PolyGram on April 25, 1996.
Music
An arrange album created in collaboration music company Cube, Panzer Dragoon II Zwei Original Arrange Album "Alternative Elements", was published by NEC Avenue on April 21.
Music
The original Japanese album was released digitally worldwide on February 14, 2018, alongside the other Panzer Dragoon soundtracks to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Saga.
Release
Panzer Dragoon II Zwei was announced in Japan and teased at the promotional event "Toshimaen VS Sega Saturn" in December 1995.
Release
Production was said to be 30% complete by January 1996.
Release
In the West the finished game was shown off at the May 1996 Electronic Entertainment Expo.
Release
Zwei was released on March 22 of that year in Japan, on April 17 in North America, and on May 10 in Europe.
Release
For the cover art CGI graphics were used, in contrast to the first game's Japanese cover, which was drawn by Giraud.
Release
A PC version was announced in 2007 and planned for release on online video game service GameTap, but GameTap closed its North American offices in 2010 and changed focus to newer PC games.
Release
GameTap staff said that Saturn emulation was challenging, speaking in reference to a planned PC port of Saga that likewise never saw release due to GameTap's closure in 2015.
Release
Following the releases of Saga for the Saturn and Panzer Dragoon Orta (2002) for the Xbox, the series went dormant due to low overall sales, with Sega licensing out later projects.
Release
Remakes of both Panzer Dragoon and Zwei were announced in 2018, published by Forever Entertainment and developed by their internal MegaPixel Studio under license from Sega.
Release
The Zwei remake was originally announced for a 2021 release date, but in June of that year it was postponed to an unspecified date.
Release
Scenes from Zwei are also planned for Panzer Dragoon Voyage Record, a virtual reality rail shooter based on sequences from the first three Panzer Dragoon games.
Reception
Panzer Dragoon II Zwei was critically acclaimed upon release, with a score of 88% on the review aggregation site GameRankings based on five reviews.
Reception

A reviewer for Next Generation said that while the gameplay makes only minimal innovations to the restrictive on-rails format, the game keeps the player hooked though its gorgeous visuals and absorbing story.
Reception
Panzer Dragoon II Zwei was a runner-up for Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s Shooter Game of the Year (behind Alien Trilogy) and Best Graphics of the Year (behind Super Mario 64).
Reception

The following year they ranked it number 90 on their "100 Best Games of All Time", citing its atmospheric levels and evolving dragon, as well as how, like the original, it represented a true 3-D evolution for the shooter genre through the player ability to rotate the perspective.
Reception

IGN staff writer Levi Buchanan ranked Panzer Dragoon II Zwei fifth in his list of the top 10 Sega Saturn games, saying that "The original Panzer Dragoon that flanked the Saturn at launch was nothing short of revelation.

sat_panzer_dragun_saga.title: Panzer Dragoon Saga
sents: lead
Panzer Dragoon Saga, known in Japan as Azel: Panzer Dragoon RPG, is a 1998 role-playing video game (RPG) developed by Team Andromeda and published by Sega for the Sega Saturn.
lead

The third entry in the Panzer Dragoon series, it replaced the rail shooter gameplay of the previous games with RPG elements such as random encounters, semi- turn-based battles and free-roaming exploration.
lead
The player controls Edge, a young mercenary who rides a dragon and encounters a mysterious girl from a vanished civilization.
lead
Sega felt an RPG was critical to compete against the PlayStation and Final Fantasy.
lead
Development began in early 1995 alongside Panzer Dragoon II Zwei (1996).
lead

The project was arduous and repeatedly delayed; incorporating the Panzer Dragoon shooting elements with full 3D computer graphics and voice acting, both unusual features in RPGs at the time, pushed the Saturn to its technical limits and strained team relations.
lead
Two staff members died during development, which the director, Yukio Futatsugi, attributed to stressful working conditions.
lead
Panzer Dragoon Saga is one of the most acclaimed Saturn games and is listed among the greatest video games, earning praise for its story, graphics, and combat.
Gameplay
For example, it has few travel sequences and side quests, requires little management of inventories or skill trees, and has only one playable character, Edge.
Gameplay
It can be completed in under 20 hours, making it much shorter than most RPGs at the time.
Battle system
A radar indicates safe, neutral and dangerous areas, with the front and rear quadrants typically posing the most danger.
Battle system
Weak points can sometimes be attacked only from dangerous areas, and enemy attack patterns may change mid-battle, forcing the player to adapt.
Battle system
Certain berserks are available only in certain dragon configurations, and the dragon learns some types of berserks more quickly in different forms.
Development
In March 1995, following completion of the original Panzer Dragoon, the producer, Yoji Ishiji, suggested making an RPG to explore the Panzer Dragoon world, as this had been praised in reviews.
Development
The director, Yukio Futatsugi, said Saga was the most difficult Panzer Dragoon game to develop, as many of its features, such as fully 3D environments, were unusual for RPGs at the time.
Battle design
Mukaiyama expected his job to be simple, but found problems with Kondo's prototype: there was no strategic element, as the player had no reason to change positions.
Battle design
The team estimated that having the dragon morph in real time would be too difficult to implement, but a programmer surprised them with a working prototype.
Story
Although Edge is not a silent protagonist, Futatsugi minimized his dialogue outside cutscenes to focus on Azel's story, who he felt was the most important character.
Story
Sega estimated that the script amounted to more than 1,500 pages of Japanese text.
Story
Panzerese is only used in the introduction and end sequences, with the rest of the dialogue in Japanese.
Story
The biggest change was in the depiction of the relationship between Edge and Azel.
Story
Lucich felt Panzer Dragoon Saga featured one of the first meaningful love stories in a video game.
Art
Her oversized jacket, belonging to her master, Craymen, was inspired by British mod fashion, which Yokota had seen in the 1979 film Quadrophenia.
Soundtrack
A soundtrack album was released by Marvelous Entertainment in February 1998.
Soundtrack
In January 2018, an anniversary edition, Resurrection: Panzer Dragoon Saga, was released by Brave Wave Productions on CD, vinyl and download formats.
Team
Kusunoki recalled "endless disputes", particularly between experienced Panzer Dragoon developers and newcomers who wanted to explore new ideas.
Team
The programmers wanted to build on the technically sophisticated shooting of Zwei, whereas the artists wanted to explore the potential of 3D to showcase their characters.
Team
Sega lacked experience managing large teams; it was the largest team Futatsugi had managed, and he recalled pressure to "domineer" over the staff.
Team
Two staff members died during development: one from a motorcycle accident, which Futatsugi attributed to stress, and another from suicide.
Team
Futatsugi said it was the most difficult project he had ever worked on, and that "all we could do was carry on and finish the game – it was out of my hands".
Release
Panzer Dragoon Saga was released in Japan in January 1998 as Azel: Panzer Dragoon RPG.
Release
European and North American releases followed on 17 April and 5 May, making Saga one of the last Saturn games published by Sega outside Japan.
Release
In the UK, the first disc was released as a demo with Sega Saturn Magazine; in 2010, GamesRadar+ named it one of the greatest demos of all time.
Release
Sega planned Panzer Dragoon Saga to compete with the PlayStation RPG Final Fantasy VII, believing that having the best RPG would win the console war, and aimed to sell 1.5 million copies.
Release
Final Fantasy VII sold almost 10 million copies, but sales of Panzer Dragoon Saga worldwide were low.
Release
One of the Panzer Dragoon Saga localizers, Chris Lucich, said it was a "strange transitional period" for Sega of America, which had shrunk from more than 2,000 employees to 200.
Release
Sega initially produced only 20,000 North American copies of Panzer Dragoon Saga.
Release
In Europe, only around 1,000 copies were made.
Release
The Sega Europe employee David Nulty, who received a production credit, advocated for the release in Europe, saying he felt it was "one of the most epic-feeling games the Saturn ever had".
Release
As Panzer Dragoon Saga received almost no marketing in the west beyond limited print advertisements, the localizers sent screenshots to bloggers, hoping to generate word-of-mouth interest.
Release
Sega allotted around only ten copies to the press and focused on hardcore game media, feeling other outlets would not be interested.
Release
At the request of the producer Yu Suzuki, who was developing the Dreamcast RPG Shenmue (1999), Sega held a meeting with the developers to discuss the failure.
Reception
At the review aggregator website GameRankings, Panzer Dragoon Saga has a score of 92%, the highest of any Saturn game.
Reception
In 2007, Game Informer wrote that "critically, the game was a smash hit, lauded as one of the year's best, and generally considered the Saturn's finest title".
Reception
Next Generation described "some of the most beautiful locations ever seen in an RPG...
Reception
It is flawlessly executed, limited only by the hardware (and barely that at all) and medium."
Reception
At the 2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, Panzer Dragoon Saga was nominated for " Console Role-Playing Game of the Year " and "Console Game of the Year".
Retrospective

In 2007, Game Informer called Panzer Dragoon Saga one of the greatest games ever made, and praised the use of dramatic camera angles and animations to make the battles cinematic "even by modern standards".
Retrospective
In a 2007 retrospective, 1UP rated it 9/10, describing it as "the greatest RPG you've never played" and one of the most unique RPGs, and praised the leap from shooter to RPG.
Retrospective
Reviewing it in 2008, Retro Gamer praised the fusion of action and RPG elements, and wrote: "If you can find and afford it, you won't be disappointed with this seminal title."
Retrospective
In the 2013 book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die, Jason Brookes wrote that only the cutscenes had aged poorly and that many aspects remained more impressive than modern RPGs.
Retrospective
Brookes, 1UP and Retro Gamer praised the story's restraint and lack of cliché.
Retrospective

John Szczepaniak, the author of The Untold History of Japanese Game Developers, said in 2018 that no game story had impressed him more and that the primitive graphics assisted the sense of an ancient, alien world.
Retrospective
In a 2018 article for The Ringer, Ben Lindburgh praised the complexity of the characters, saying none were "truly heroic".
Retrospective

In a 2008 article for Gamasutra, Kurt Kalata found that while the visual design was "still lovely", the graphics showed the Saturn's 3D limitations, with low-resolution textures, "boxy" character models, frequent slowdown and compressed video.
Retrospective
Nonetheless, Kalata concluded that Panzer Dragoon Saga was "still thoroughly entrancing" and that its battle system made it "completely worth it".
Retrospective
Panzer Dragoon Saga was named one of the best games of all time by Computer and Video Games in 2000, Electronic Gaming Monthly in 2001 and 2006, IGN readers in 2005, IGN in 2007 and G4 in 2012.
Retrospective
1UP placed it #1 in its 2005 list of cult classic games, and Game Informer ranked it #1 in its 2006 list of the "top 10 rare RPGs you need".
Retrospective
In 2008, IGN named it the greatest Saturn game, and wrote: " Panzer Dragoon Saga was the swan song to end all swan songs...
Retrospective
In 2017, Jeff Grubb of VentureBeat said it was arguably the best Sega game and expressed hope for a rerelease.
Legacy
Sega disbanded Team Andromeda after Panzer Dragoon Saga 's completion and reassigned some staff to Smilebit, which developed the final Panzer Dragoon game, Orta (2002), for the Xbox.
Legacy
Meanwhile, Ueda worked on Jet Set Radio (2000), Sakai worked on Phantasy Star Online (2000) and Yokota worked on Rez (2001), all for Dreamcast.
Legacy

Though few developers have cited Panzer Dragoon Saga as an influence, the Ringer journalist Ben Lindburgh drew parallels to Horizon Zero Dawn (2017) and the games of Fumito Ueda, particularly The Last Guardian (2016).
Legacy
Lindburgh wrote that these games "are regarded as distinctive and original games, and Saga got to some of the same territory first".
Legacy
As of 2018, English-language copies of Panzer Dragoon Saga sold for hundreds of US dollars on the used market, with factory-sealed copies selling for more than a thousand.
Legacy
According to The Ringer, "Its scarcity has conferred a cult-classic status that's become part of its appeal...
Legacy
In 2009, the game-downloading service GameTap said it had non-exclusive rights to distribute it, but, as Saturn emulation is difficult, there was not enough demand to make it a priority.

sat_saga_rally_championship.title: Sega Rally Championship

Platform(s): Arcade, Sega Saturn, Windows, N-Gage, Game Boy Advance, PlayStation 2

sents: lead
Sega Rally Championship is a 1994 racing game developed and published by Sega.
lead
Originally released for arcades using the Sega Model 2 board, ports were published for the Sega Saturn in 1995 and Microsoft Windows in 1997.
lead
The Sega Rally Championship simulates driving on different surfaces, with different friction properties, with the car's handling changing accordingly.
lead
As the first racing game to incorporate this feature, Sega Rally Championship is considered to be one of the milestones in the evolution of the racing game genre.
lead
It was also an early rally racing game and featured cooperative gameplay alongside the usual competitive multiplayer.
lead
The game spawned the Sega Rally series, in addition to inspiring Colin McRae Rally (1998) and Initial D Arcade Stage (2002).
Gameplay

In this mode, it is impossible to reach first-place position by the end of the first track; thus, the player must try to overtake as many opponent cars as possible on each track (while staying within the time limit), and gain the lead over several tracks.
Gameplay

If, at the end of the third stage, the player is in first place, they will advance to the extra fourth stage called "Lakeside" (on the Saturn version, this course may then be played in time attack and split-screen multiplayer modes).
Development
While the game featured only three cars—the Toyota Celica GT-Four, Lancia Delta Group A, and a hidden Lancia Stratos —it was distinguished by its "stylized handling" and some tuning options.
Development
Senior programmer Riyuchi Hattori added: "Originally there was talk of using another car from Toyota, but we couldn't find a good one.
Development
The Sega Saturn version of the game had to be almost completely remade, only referencing the graphics of the arcade version, which required detailed planning.
Development

For similar reasons, a split screen was used for multiplayer mode instead of the Saturn link cable; the developers also felt it was important that multiplayer be available to all owners of the Saturn game, not only those who had also purchased a link cable.
Release

In Japan, the Sega Saturn version of the game shared the full title of its arcade counterpart, Sega Rally Championship 1995, because it was released on December 29, 1995; the year was dropped from the title of the North American and European SegaSaturn version.
Release
The European release was scheduled for December 1995, in time for the crucial Christmas shopping season, but it did not appear until the end of the following January.
Arcade
In Japan, Game Machine listed it on their April 1, 1995 issue as being the second most-successful dedicated arcade game of the month.
Arcade
It went on to be the second highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1995 in Japan.
Arcade
In the United States, it was one of the top six best-selling arcade games of 1995, receiving the Platinum Award from the American Amusement Machine Association (AAMA).
Home conversions
The Sega Saturn version would go on to sell 1.2 million copies.
Home conversions
In Japan, Sega Rally Championship topped the charts on release, coming in number 1 during Week 52 in 1995.
Home conversions

Game Informer ' s Reiner and Andy gave Sega Rally Championship scores of 8/10 and 8.5/10, making note of technical improvements over the Saturn version of Sega's Daytona USA, which Andy nonetheless felt was the better game.
Home conversions
Game Informer ' s Paul was more effusive, rating the Saturn port 9.25/10 for its "far better racing feel" and superior graphics to Daytona.
Home conversions
Both of the sports reviewers for Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the Saturn version an 8.5 out of 10, saying it "has all of the action and adventure of its arcade cousin.
Home conversions

Maximum decreed the conversion to be "every bit as good as anyone could have ever hoped", stating that aside from the frame rate being reduced to 30 frames per second, it is essentially identical to the arcade version.
Home conversions
Mark Clarkson of Computer Gaming World found the biggest problem was that, being a port of an arcade game, it lacks the longevity expected of a PC game, though he judged it to be fun while it lasted.
Accolades

In 1996, Next Generation listed it as number 57 on their "Top 100 Games of All Time", citing the "heavier", more realistic feel of the car when compared to other racing games, and the generally realistic controls.
Accolades
In 1996, GamesMaster ranked the game number 1 on their "The GamesMaster Saturn Top 10".
Accolades
In the same issue, they also rated the game 24th in its "Top 100 Games of All Time".
Accolades

In 1999, Next Generation listed Sega Rally as number 19 on their "Top 50 Games of All Time", commenting that, "one of the best Model 2 games, Sega Rally is some of the best fun you can have in a car without having to pretend that you've run out of gas".
Accolades
Sega Rally Championship was named the best racing game of all time by Retro Gamer magazine, which ranked it at the top of its "Top 25 Racing Games Ever" list.
Accolades

In Guinness World Records: Gamer's Edition 2009 the Saturn version of the game made it to 44th position in the list of the Top 50 Console Games, due to its "distinct handling style and superb track design".
Accolades

IGN staff writer Levi Buchanan ranked Sega Rally Championship 6th in his list of the top 10 Sega Saturn games, saying: "Yes, the Dreamcast version is much better and the current-gen sequel... is stunning, but this Saturn arcade port was one of the top reasons to stick by SEGA as it flailed through the 32-bit days".
Accolades

Some publications and fan-voted lists have considered it to be one of the best games of all time, including Next Generation in 1996, or Electronic Gaming Monthly in 1997, Computer and Video Games in 2000, Edge in 2007, and NowGamer in 2010.
Accolades
In 2024, The Guardian would rank Sega Rally Championship as the 3rd best Sega arcade game.
Impact
In 2010, Codemasters cited Sega Rally Championship as a strong influence on their first Colin McRae Rally game (1998).
Impact

According to Guy Wilday, producer of the first four Colin McRae Rally games, the "basic premise for the game was based around" Sega Rally ' s car handling which "remains excellent to this day and it’s still an arcade machine I enjoy playing".

sat_virtuo_cop_2.title: Virtua Cop 2
sents: lead
Virtua Cop 2 is a light gun shooter arcade game, released in 1995 and developed internally at Sega by their AM2 studio.
lead
It was ported to the Sega Saturn in 1996, PC in 1997, and Sega Dreamcast in 2000.
lead
It was bundled with Virtua Cop in Virtua Cop: Elite Edition for PlayStation 2 in 2002.
lead
This game was known as Virtua Squad 2 for the North American PC release.
lead
The game was succeeded by Virtua Cop 3.
Gameplay
As with the first Virtua Cop, players earn extra points for "justice shots", meaning shooting an enemy's gun hand to disarm them without killing them.
Characters
Janet Marshall (Janet) - A newly installed special VCPD detective in the Virtua Cop special investigations squad (although the only female cop in the squad), Janet fights for her deceased partner.
Plot
The final, fourth member of the E.V.I.L Inc. gang, international terrorist Joe Fang is believed to have been killed in a helicopter crash, though his body was never found.
Plot
The vice-president of the Virtua City Bank is killed in shady circumstances that are only officially termed accidental.
Plot
The missing funds amount to more than the GNP of most small countries.
Development
When questioned about Sega AM2 's plans for Virtua Cop 2 in a February 1995 interview, AM2 manager Fumio Kurokawa stated "We're not sure if there will be VC2.
Development
The Saturn version was demonstrated at the May 1996 Electronic Entertainment Expo, at which point only the first level was in a playable state.
Development
Development was slowed because AM2's resources were prioritized for the Saturn versions of Fighting Vipers and Virtua Fighter Kids.
Development
Virtua Cop 2 was re-released in 2001 as part of the Sega Smash Pack: Volume 1 compilation for Dreamcast.
Development
The game was later bundled with Virtua Cop in Japan and Europe on the PlayStation 2 as Virtua Cop: Elite Edition (Virtua Cop Rebirth in Japan) on August 25 and November 29, 2002, respectively.
Arcade
In Japan, Game Machine listed Virtua Cop 2 on their November 1, 1995 issue as being the second most-successful dedicated arcade game of the month.
Arcade
It went on to become the highest-grossing dedicated arcade video game of 1996 in Japan.
Arcade
It was reported to have sold 7,000 arcade cabinets worldwide by 1996, including 4,000 units in Japan and 3,000 units overseas.
Saturn
Next Generation elaborated, "Taking the game one step closer to the feel of a big budget action movie, Virtua Cop 2 seems to have more 'movement' to it....
Saturn

Tom Ham wrote in GameSpot, "While the first Virtua Cop set a new standard for light gun shooters, Sega and the AM2 team have delivered an incredible sequel that takes the concept to a whole new level."
Saturn

In 1997, they named the Saturn version number 98 on their "100 Best Games of All Time", citing its addition of branching levels and innovative stage design to the series' revolutionary use of polygonal enemies which move realistically and react differently depending on where they are shot.

sat_virtuo_cop.title: Virtua Cop
sents: lead
Virtua Cop (known as Virtua Squad for the North American Windows version) is a 1994 light gun shooter game developed by Sega AM2 and designed by Yu Suzuki.
lead
It was originally an arcade game on the Sega Model 2 system, and was ported to the Sega Saturn in 1995 and Windows in 1996.
lead
The Saturn version included support for both the Virtua Gun and Saturn mouse, as well as a new "Training Mode" which consists of a randomly generated shooting gallery.
lead
Virtua Cop was notable for its use of real-time 3D polygon graphics with texture mapping, with Sega advertising it as "the world's first texture mapped, polygon action game ".
lead
Emphasizing the real-time nature of the game, enemies would react differently depending on where they were shot.
lead
It was one of the first games to allow the player to shoot through glass.
lead
Its name is derived from its 3D graphical style, which was previously used in Virtua Racing and Virtua Fighter, and later Virtua Striker.
lead

It was influential on later shooter games, with 3D polygons being adopted by subsequent light gun shooters such as Time Crisis (1995) and The House of the Dead (1996) instead of the digitized sprites previously used in the genre, as well as inspiring the first-person shooter GoldenEye 007 (1997).
Gameplay
Played in a first-person perspective, players must use a light gun (or a joypad in the Sega Saturn version) to shoot criminals and advance through the game.
Development
The game's targeting reticles and zooming camera were inspired by a commercial for Pokka Kilimanjaro coffee.
Development
A division of Sega AM2 began work on the Saturn version in April 1995.
Development
Along with the Saturn version of Virtua Fighter 2, it was one of the first games to make use of the Sega Graphics Library operating system.
Development

The Saturn version features a full-motion video sequence of Michael and James driving on the dockyard before confronting Kong; designer Kazufumi Ohashi originally animated Kong flipping the bird, which Isono rejected, moving Ohashi to work on the training mode instead.
Development
In June, the team displayed a playable demo of the Saturn version's first level at the Tokyo Toy Show.
In other games
The default gun, the Guardian, can be used in Ghost Squad; however, it can only be obtained by playing the IC Card or Evolution versions.
Arcade
In Japan, Game Machine listed it on their November 1, 1994 issue as being the second most-successful upright/cockpit arcade cabinet of the month.
Arcade
In North America, RePlay reported Virtua Cop to be the fifth most-popular arcade game in April 1995.
Arcade
It went on to become the highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1995 in Japan, and one of America's top ten best-selling arcade video games of 1995.
Arcade

Computer and Video Games also gave it a positive review, calling it "a classy title" and praising the 3D graphics, "excellent" animation, weapon power-ups, and the gameplay in both single-player and multiplayer modes.
Arcade

Games World magazine called it an "excellent fun" game, comparing it favorably with the shooters Operation Wolf (1987) and Lethal Enforcers (1992) as well as the film Reservoir Dogs (1992), while Dave Perry said the Virtua Fighter like 3D targets made it a "more challenging and satisfying" shooter.
Arcade
There was initially some skepticism over its introduction of 3D polygons in a genre that previously used realistic digitized sprites, most notably Konami 's Lethal Enforcers.
Arcade

In 1996, Next Generation listed the Virtua Cop series (which then consisted of just Virtua Cop and the arcade version of Virtua Cop 2) at number 82 on their "Top 100 Games of All Time", praising the skill and realism invoked by the enemies' differing reactions to being shot in different places.
Saturn
Upon release of the Saturn version, the game sold over 300,000 copies in its first week of release in Japan.
Saturn
Its Japanese sales reached 455,396 units by the end of 1995, and 482,362 units in total.
Saturn
In the United States, it sold more than 500,000 bundled copies by December 1996, bringing total sales to more than 982,362 copies sold in Japan and the United States.
Saturn

Game Informer ' s Reiner, Andy, and Paul gave the Saturn version scores of 8.5, 8.25 and 7.5 out of 10, praising the game as one of the best in its genre but noting that it lacked longevity for a console release.
Saturn
Similarly to EGM's reviewers, he remarked that the game is a near-perfect arcade port but too short and completely lacking in replay value, though he nonetheless gave it an overall recommendation.
Saturn

Game Players gave the Saturn version of Virtua Cop the award for "Best Shooter" of 1995, calling it "beyond entertaining — it's therapeutic." In 1996, GamesMaster rated the Saturn version 4th on their "The GamesMaster Saturn Top 10."
PC
Next Generation voiced similar criticisms: "It's noticeably slower on the majority of PCs than in the arcade or on Saturn, running at speed only on the most high-end Pentiums.
PC
Worse, played without a light gun using only the mouse, the game loses a major part of its appeal..." They concluded that the game felt out of place on PC.
Legacy
Virtua Cop was a major influence on both light gun shooters as well as first-person shooters.
Legacy
When it was released in 1994, the game broke new ground by introducing the use of 3D polygons to the shooter genre.
Legacy

Virtua Cop was also the primary influence on the seminal first-person shooter GoldenEye 007, which was originally envisioned as an on-rails light gun shooter akin to Virtua Cop before it ended up as an off-rails first-person shooter.
Legacy

According to creator Martin Hollis: "We ended up with innovative gameplay, in part because we had Virtua Cop features in a FPS: A gun that only holds 7 bullets and a reload button, lots of position-dependent hit animations, innocents you shouldn’t kill, and an aiming mode.

neo_metal_slog_2.title: Metal Slug 2
sents: lead
Metal Slug 2 is a run and gun video game developed by SNK.
lead
It was originally released in 1998 for the Neo-Geo MVS arcade platform as the sequel to the 1996 game Metal Slug.
lead
The original version of the game had extensive slowdown and performance issues, eventually leading SNK to release a modified version in 1999 titled Metal Slug X: Super Vehicle-001 (メタルスラッグX).
lead
It has been ported to the Neo Geo CD, PlayStation, Virtual Console, iOS and Android, and to the Wii, PlayStation Portable and PlayStation 2 (as part of the Metal Slug Anthology).
lead
The game added several new features to the gameplay of the original Metal Slug, such as new weapons, vehicles and the ability to transform the character.
lead
It received generally positive reviews.
lead
It was followed by Metal Slug 3 released in 2000.
Gameplay
Gameplay in Metal Slug 2 is similar to the previous game; the player must shoot constantly at a continual stream of enemies in order to reach the end of each level.
Gameplay
The tank is known as the SV-001 ("SV" stands for Super Vehicle), which increases the player's offense and considerably adds to their defense.
Gameplay
Metal Slug 2 introduces the ability for characters to transform during the course of the game.
Gameplay
As well as doubling the number of available player characters from two to four, Metal Slug 2 introduces in-game characters to help the player in battle.
Gameplay
The first is Hyakutaro Ichimonji, a prisoner who, when rescued, will fight alongside the player, throwing Hadouken balls at enemies, or roundhouse kicking them if they get within melee range.
Metal Slug X
An upgraded version of Metal Slug 2, titled Metal Slug X, was released in March 1999 for the Neo Geo MVS.
Metal Slug X
The game used a modified version of the engine from Metal Slug 3, which eliminated the slowdown problems of the original.
Metal Slug X
It is now possible for the player character to become fat by collecting food items in every stage after Mission 2; in the original game, the obese transformation was only possible in Mission 4.
Metal Slug X
Several new weapons are included: Stones, Iron Lizard, Enemy Chaser, Super Grenade, Drop Shot, a new Golden Metal Slug, which is available in Mission 3, and the Armor piercer, available in Mission 4.
Metal Slug X
The original art for Metal Slug is shown at the end of the game while the credits are rolling, instead of the black screen used in Metal Slug 2.
Later releases
Home versions of Metal Slug 2 were released for the Neo Geo AES in April 1998, and the Neo Geo CD in June as well.
Later releases
Metal Slug X was ported to the Neo Geo AES in May 1999 and the PlayStation in January 2001.
Later releases
The PlayStation version was released in North America and PAL regions by Agetec and features the same "Combat School" mode featured in the Neo Geo CD versions of the first two games.
Later releases
In 2006, Metal Slug Anthology (titled Metal Slug Complete in Japan) was released for the Wii, PlayStation 2 and PSP.
Later releases
This compilation includes the original Metal Slug, and all of its arcade sequels (including Metal Slug 2 and Metal Slug X) up to Metal Slug 6.
Later releases
The AES version of Metal Slug 2 was released in October 2008 for the Wii Virtual Console.
Later releases
Both Metal Slug 2 and Metal Slug X were also included in Metal Slug Collection PC, which was released in Europe in 2009.
Later releases
In 2013, versions of both games were released for iOS and Android.
Later releases
The original arcade version of Metal Slug X became available on Nintendo Switch via ACA Neo Geo in 2017.
Reception
Upon their initial appearance, both Metal Slug 2 and Metal Slug X received generally positive reviews.
Reception
For example, the iOS version of Metal Slug 2 holds an aggregate score of 77% on GameRankings, based on 5 reviews, and 76 out of 100 on Metacritic, based on 6 reviews.
Reception
When Metal Slug 2 was released on the Virtual Console in 2008, IGN 's Lucas M.
Reception

Eurogamer 's Dan Whitehead scored the game 7 out of 10, criticizing the price: "The Metal Slug Anthology collates seven games from the series on disc, and can now be bought for just over twice the price of this solitary offering.
Reception
Eurogamer's Tom Bramwell scored the 2001 PlayStation version of Metal Slug X 8 out of 10.
Reception
GameSpot 's Ryan Davis scored it 8.2 out of 10, writing: "What really separates Metal Slug X from the rest of the crowd is its tongue-in-cheek presentation.
Reception
In a retrospective review, Neo-Geo.com scored Metal Slug X 10 out of 10: " Metal Slug X is different enough in many small ways that if you're a completist, you'll still want MS2 in your collection.
Commercial performance

Instrumental in defeating Morden during the first coup were Cpt.

Most of its subsequent ports and re-releases have also seen good reviews.

This is not a $40 value unless you absolutely must have this game on your Xbox.

Two-player spins it out for a while, and there are Hard and Very Hard modes, but at £15 if you shop around Metal Slug 3 arguably transcends the usual rental recommendation.

You can try and collect all the extras (Japanese radish and Chinese cabbage are all there for the taking), but there's no getting away from the fact that there's not enough in here to warrant shelling out full whack, no matter how perfect a slice of arcade action it may be".

a26_pitfell.title: Pitfall!
sents: lead
Pitfall! is a video game developed by David Crane for the Atari Video Computer System (later renamed Atari 2600) and released in 1982 by Activision.
lead
The player controls Pitfall Harry, who has a time limit of 20 minutes to seek treasure in a jungle.
lead
The game world is populated by enemies and hazards that variously cause the player to lose lives or points.
lead
Crane had made several games for both Atari, Inc. and Activision before working on Pitfall! in 1982.
lead
He started with creating a new realistic-style walking animation for a person on the Atari 2600 hardware.
lead
After completing it, he fashioned a game around it.
lead
He used a jungle setting with items to collect and enemies to avoid, and the result became Pitfall!
lead
Pitfall! received mostly positive reviews at the time of its release praising both its gameplay and graphics.
Gameplay
Similar to Superman (1979) and Adventure (1980), the game does not feature side-scrolling, but instead loads one screen at a time, with a new screen appearing when Harry moves to the edge.
Gameplay

The player starts the game with 2000 points and can collect a total of 32 treasure hidden among 255 different scenes to increase their total, ranging from a money bag worth 2000 points, to a diamond ring worth 5000 points.
Development
Crane had previously worked at Atari, Inc. in the late 1970s developing games for the Atari Video Computer System, later released as the Atari 2600.
Development
The system became known as the Atari 2600 after the release of the Atari 5200 in 1982.
Development
When he was turned down, Crane and other Atari programmers left the company to form Activision in 1979.
Development
Crane described his own game-design philosophy involved making the Atari 2600 do new and unexpected things.
Development
Crane said he "used this technique to lead me in a new direction of game design, and some of the tricks were to me as much as an accomplishment as solving the Rubik's Cube the first time".
Development
Early development of Pitfall! started with Crane trying to create realistically animated graphics on the Atari 2600.
Development
The jungle setting of the game was influenced by the 1981 film Raiders of the Lost Ark.
Development
The process involved what Crane said was "a lot of trial-and-error".
Development

When asked if the arcade game Donkey Kong (1981) had inspired his game, Crane responded he did not draw any parallels to Pitfall! at the time and had already developed elements in his game that were present in both games such as a human character, paths and ladders.
Development
Crane commented that "The entire [game design] process took about 10 minutes.
Development
About 1000 hours of programming later the game was complete." Much of Crane's time was spent optimizing and compressing the code so that it would fit into a four kilobyte ROM cartridge.
Development
Unlike Haunted House (1982) or Raiders of the Lost Ark (1982) where the environments were hard-coded into the game, Pitfall! was generated constantly by code.
Development
Each number in the counter used 8 bits to load certain details such as the background, trees, ground and object patterns, allowing 255 screens to occupy fewer than 50 bytes of ROM.
Release
Pitfall! was released for the Atari 2600 in September 1982.
Release
The game was later released for the Intellivision in November 1982.
Release
To promote the game, Activision created a five-week long promotion on November 15, 1982, and ending December 13, 1982 in various markets across the United States for a chance to win $5,000 in gold.
Release

In January 1984, it was announced that Pitfall! would be released along with other Acitivision titles such as River Raid, Megamania, and Beamrider for the Atari 5200, ColecoVision, Commodore 64, and MSX.
Release
Pitfall! was subsequently released for the Colecovision in February, the Atari Computer and Atari 5200 in March, and the Commodore 64 in June.
Release
These include Activision Classics (1998) for the PlayStation, Activision Anthology (2002) for PlayStation 2, and for portable devices as Activision Hits Remixed in 2006 for the PlayStation Portable.
Release
The game was also a secret extra in Activision published titles such as Pitfall: The Mayan Adventure (1994), Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare (2016) and Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War (2020).
Reception
In Blip, the reviewer stated that the game was similar to Donkey Kong (1981), but that "this is one case where inspiration didn't lead to imitation.
Reception
In JoyStik How to Win at Video Games, the game was awarded five stars and listed in their top ten games of the year in January 1983.
Reception
The Atari 2600 version of Pitfall! was awarded "Best Adventure Video Game" at the 4th annual Arkie Awards in 1983.
Reception

Reviewing the Intellivision version in March 1983, Phil Wiswell wrote in Video Games that it was the same game in every aspect as the Atari 2600 version, but criticized the release for not taking advantage enough of Intellivision's graphical capabilities.
Reception
Electronic Games in their "1983 Software Encyclopedia" issue gave it a seven out of ten rating for the Intellivision, noting that the game "requires more arcade-type skills than intuition or logic".
Reception
Pitfall! was the highest selling video game from late 1982 to the first quarter of 1983.
Reception
It is one of the best-selling games on the Atari 2600, with over four million copies sold .
Retrospective reviews

Later 1980s reviews continued to praise the game, such as an anonymous reviewer in Computer Games who gave the game an A-rating in their 1985 game guide, praising the graphics as "gorgeous and cartoony" declaring it a "terrific game for action fans".
Retrospective reviews
Scott Alan Marriott of the online game database AllGame wrote that the variety of threats you encounter on each screen made Pitfall! one of the most exciting and best-looking games on the Atari 2600.
Retrospective reviews

Brett Alan Weiss included the game in his book The 100 Greatest Console Video Games 1977-1987 (2014), and criticized that the Atari 5200 version of the game had poor controls and the Intellivision version for requiring a second button for letting go of vines.
Retrospective reviews

Weiss found the ColecoVision designed by Action Graphics to be the best of the three versions with improved visuals over the Atari 2600 game, but that it failed to take true advantage of the systems graphic capabilities.
Retrospective reviews

Pitfall! has been included in several best-of video games lists from various publications, such as Electronic Fun with Computers & Games in 1984, Flux (1995) where it placed 33rd, Game Informer (2001) where it placed 41st and Time in 2012.
Legacy
Pitfall! was described by authors Montfort and Bogost in Racing the Beam as an important early platform game, a game genre made famous by Super Mario Bros.
Legacy
Unlike Mario or Pac-Man who originated in arcade games, Pitfall Harry was the first popular video game character originating in home consoles.
Legacy
The character was featured on licensed merchandise and led to Pitfall Harry appearing on the cartoon show Saturday Supercade which aired from 1983 to 1985 on CBS.
Follow-ups
Sega released Pitfall II: Lost Caverns (1985) to arcades which incorporated elements of both Pitfall! and Pitfall II: Lost Caverns Atari 2600 games.
Follow-ups
The 2012 release was similar to the game Temple Run (2011).
Follow-ups
Pitfall! remained the game that Crane has been most associated with, stating in 2012 that "I suppose that's not a bad problem to have, It's not a dark shadow.

a26_pitfell_ii_lost_caverns.title: Pitfall II: Lost Caverns

Platform(s): Atari 2600, Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit, ColecoVision, Commodore 64, IBM PCjr, Apple II, MSX, ZX Spectrum

sents: lead
Pitfall II: Lost Caverns is a video game developed by David Crane for the Atari 2600.
lead
It was released in 1984 by Activision.
lead
The player controls Pitfall Harry, who must explore in wilds of Peru to find the Raj Diamond, and rescue his niece Rhonda and their animal friend Quickclaw.
lead
The game world is populated by enemies and hazards that variously cause the player to lose points and return to a checkpoint.
lead
(1982), one of the best-selling Atari 2600 video games.
lead
Crane said the Atari 2600 hardware was out of date when developing the sequel, which led to him creating a custom computer chip called the Display Processor Chip for Pitfall II: Lost Caverns.
lead
This allowed for more complex graphics and background music in the game.
lead
It became the top selling console game of the year and was ported to other consoles and home computers.
Gameplay
When the player is hit by an enemy, Harry returns to the last red cross he found.
Development
(1982) was a major success for Activision and was the company's best selling release at the time.
Development

"at a time when the Atari 2600 should have been replaced by a new gaming system." He had training as an electronics engineer and felt that the Atari 2600 "needed a boost" and designed a custom computer chip called the Display Processor Chip that was unique to Pitfall II: Lost Caverns.
Development
The chip allowed for additional graphic capabilities for the Atari 2600 and a music circuit.
Development
The chip contained special indexing registers that reduced the processing time for graphics operation by over 40%.
Development

Crane spoke about the developing the game and its graphics for the Atari 2600 at the Winter Consumers Electronics Show, stating that he would "stack Pitfall II against software in any other computer under $10,000.
Development
This made the game the first Atari 2600 game with a full scored polyphonic musical track.
Development
The main theme in the game plays the bass through one channel, two channels play the melody and harmony while the last channel plays percussion sounds.
Development
The ports of the game for the Atari 800 and Atari 5200 were written by Mike Lorenzen, using Crane's original code with new graphics routines for the Atari hardware.
Development
The ColecoVision port was written from scratch by Robert Rutowski, and the Commodore 64 version was written from scratch by Tim Shotter.
Development
Both the Atari 800 and Atari 5200 versions of the game included more areas to explore than the original Atari 2600 version.
Development
Lorenzen found time during production to create new levels that appear after the first game was completed.
Release
The game debuted at 9th place on Billboard ' s list of top 20 selling video games.
Release
Activision's national sales manager stated that the sales of the game exceeded the company's expectations by 25% to 30%.
Release
The game had a higher retail price ($34.95) than the usual game for the system due to Display Processor Chip.
Release

Activision had reported slumping sales with operating loss of $4.1 million on $13.2 million in sales in the second quarter of 1984 and sought to remedy this with the release of Pitfall II: Lost Caverns.
Release
By the end of the 1984, the game became the highest selling console game of year.
Release

At the June 1984 Consumer Electronics Show, Activision did not reveal any new games for Atari 2600 or Intellivision and showed older games in new formats, including Pitfall II: Lost Caverns for Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit computers, ColecoVision, IBM PCjr, and the Coleco Adam.
Release
The game was released for Atari 5200 in November 1984.
Release
The versions for the IBM PC Jr. were released in the fourth quarter of 1984.
Release
These include Activision Anthology (2002) for PlayStation 2, and for portable devices as Activision Hits Remixed (2006) for the PlayStation Portable.
Release
The game is available hidden feature in both Pitfall: The Lost Expedition (2004) and Call of Duty: World War 2 (2017).
Contemporary
Pitfall II: Lost Caverns received positive reception from Lou Hudson of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, Bill Kunkel of Electronic Games, and the publication The Video Game Update.
Contemporary
The three complimented the graphics, with Kunkel stating that it was "the kind of videogame that would be impressive if presented on a 48K computer.
Contemporary

Kunkel concluded that the game "offers the most remarkable breadth of any 2600 video game yet produced." while The Video Game Update stated that "We have the opportunity to play and review hundreds of games every year, and there are very few that we feel must become part of your personal collection.
Contemporary
Blanchet also noted that the games score was annoying as it never stopped.
Contemporary
In January 1985, Pitfall II won the award for Program of the Year for the Atari 2600 from Computer Entertainer magazine in their 1984 Awards of Excellence.
Retrospective

Skyler Miller of AllGame awarded the game 4 1/2 stars out of 5, stating that the game was not as innovative as the original game, but that it expanded upon the original to create one of the systems most accomplished game.
Retrospective
Brett Weiss included the game in his book The 100 Greatest Console Video Games, 1977-1987 (2014) stating the game was even better than Pitfall! noting that it offered a variety of fresh features.
Retrospective

John Harris of Game Developer wrote found the game was not quite as fun to play in 2007 as it was when it was first developed, but declared it to be one of the most advanced games for the Atari 2600, comparing its gameplay to the later Nintendo game Metroid (1986).
Retrospective
Harris noted innovative elements such as being among the first games to include a checkpoint system.
Retrospective
In their list of the top 25 Atari 2600 games, Stuart Hunt and Darran Jones of Retro Gamer magazine listed Pitfall II: Lost Caverns in the number one spot.
Retrospective
(1981), River Raid (1982), Ghostbusters (1984), Little Computer People (1985) and Alter Ego (1986), as one of the best games from Activision's classic period.
Legacy

Following the release of Pitfall II: Lost Caverns, the Atari 2600 was at the end of its first lifecycle as a system for new games and no other games for it were developed using Crane's Display Processor Chip.
Legacy

Crane was often asked if he would develop at third Pitfall game, he stated that "after one sequel, I was happy to move on to other ideas." Following work on Pitfall II, Crane began work developing games for the Commodore 64, starting with Ghostbusters (1984).
Legacy
Sega developed an arcade game titled Pitfall II: The Lost Caverns (1985) which featured gameplay elements from both of Crane's Pitfall games.

lead

lead

lead

lead

The game's environments were stated to be inspired by works by Hayao Miyazaki, with the game using an anime art style due to Killspace's experience with it.

While saying it was "tailor-made" for shooter fans wanting a challenge, he found it difficult to recommend even for $10.

a26_combot.title: Combat (video game)
sents: lead
Combat is a 1977 video game by Atari, Inc. for the Atari Video Computer System (later renamed the Atari 2600).
lead
In the game, two players controlling either a tank, a biplane, or a jet fire missiles at each other for two minutes and sixteen seconds.
lead
Points are scored by hitting the opponent, and the player with the most points when the time runs out wins.
lead
Variations on the gameplay introduce elements such as invisible vehicles, missiles that ricochet off of walls, and different playing fields.
lead
The game was being made while the Atari 2600 was still in development.
lead
Combat was based on Atari's popular arcade game Tank.
lead
It was initially developed by Steve Mayer and Ron Milner.
lead
Joe Decuir later tested it on the developing Atari Video Computer System hardware, and Larry Wagner completed the game while adding the two plane variations to the game.
Gameplay
The player with the most points at the end of a two minutes and sixteen second round wins.
Gameplay
The original 1977 Atari VCS (Video Computer System) has six switches in front, including left and right difficulty switches and a game select switch.
Development
Combat was programmed while the Atari 2600 hardware was still under development.
Development
The original version was a tank game made on the early prototype Atari 2600 hardware engineered by Mayer and Ron Milner from Cyan Engineering, a consulting firm that Atari purchased in 1975.
Development
The VCS hardware was designed to be capable of playing Atari's popular arcade games Pong (1972) Pong Doubles (1973), Quadrapong (1974), Gran Trak 10 (1974), Tank (1974), and Jet Fighter (1975).
Release
Combat was bundled with most Atari 2600 consoles from 1977 to 1982.
Release
The only systems not bundled with the game were those marketed by Sears under its Telegames label, which were sold with Air-Sea Battle (1977) under the title Target Fun as the pack-in game.
Release
According to Weekly Television Digest from October 17, 1977 the Atari VCS was shipped to all major market areas by August 1977.
Release
The system became known as the Atari 2600 only after the release of the Atari 5200 in 1982.
Release
Combat was re-released in various compilation formats, such as the Atari 80 in One for Windows in 2003 and the Atari Anthology for PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2004.
Release
It was also released on portable devices as part of Atari Classics Evolved (2007) for the PlayStation Portable and Atari Greatest Hits (2011) for iOS.
Release
In 2010, it was made available as part of Microsoft 's Game Room for the Xbox 360.
Reception

From contemporary reviews, Video compared the Atari VCS's launch titles, and gave tank pong the highest rating of the variations on Combat with a seven-and-one-half rating for Tank-Pong and Invisible Tank Pong, six-and-one-half for invisible tank game, and six for all the other variations.
Reception

In the British publication TV Gamer from August 1983, Sonya Bradford found the controls took time to get used to and that the game "becomes a bit monotonous, which is not helped by the poor graphics."
Reception
In 1995, Flux magazine ranked Combat #48 on their list of "Top 100 Video Games".
Reception

In 2012, PCMag included Combat in their "The Greatest Atari Games of All Time" list, with writer Eric Griffith noted the dated graphics by 2012 standards, while finding that the game felt "pretty magical in the 70s."
Legacy
A sequel to Combat went into development for the Atari 2600 and was to be titled Combat Two.
Legacy
The game was officially announced but was never officially released for the system.
Legacy
An incomplete prototype of the game surfaced in 1999 by former Atari Age magazine editor Steve Morgenstern.
Legacy
Physical copies of the game were made for sale in limited quantity at the 2001 Classic Gaming Expo.
Legacy
The prototype was released as part of the Atari Flashback 2 dedicated console in 2005.
Legacy
Combat Two was included as part of the Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration (2022) compilation for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Steam, and Xbox One.

a26_missive_command.title: Missile Command

Platform(s): Arcade, Atari 2600, Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit, Atari ST, Game Boy, Lynx

sents: lead
Missile Command is a 1980 shoot 'em up arcade video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. and later licensed to Sega for Japanese and European releases.
lead
It was designed by Dave Theurer, who also designed Atari's vector graphics game Tempest from the same year.
lead
The game was released during the Cold War, and the player uses a trackball to defend six cities from intercontinental ballistic missiles by launching anti-ballistic missiles from three bases.
lead
Atari brought the game to its home systems beginning with the 1981 Atari VCS conversion by Rob Fulop.
lead
Numerous contemporaneous clones and modern remakes followed.
lead
Atari's 1981 port to the Atari 8-bit computers was reused for the Atari 5200 (1982) and built into the Atari XEGS (1987).
Plot
As a regional commander of three anti-missile batteries, the player must defend six cities in their zone from being destroyed.
Gameplay
There are three batteries, each with ten missiles; a battery becomes useless when all its missiles have been launched or if it is destroyed by enemy fire, whichever occurs first.
Gameplay
The missiles of the central battery fly to their targets at much greater speed; only these missiles can effectively kill a smart bomb at a distance.
Gameplay
Enemy weapons are only able to destroy three cities during one level.
Gameplay
A level ends when all enemy weaponry is destroyed or reaches its target.
Gameplay

At the conclusion of a level, the player receives bonus points for all remaining missiles and cities; at preset score intervals, the player earns a bonus city that can be used to replace a destroyed one at the end of the current level.
Gameplay
The scoring multiplier begins at 1x and advances by 1x after every second level, to a maximum of 6x; this multiplier affects both target and bonus values.
Gameplay
The game inevitably ends once all six cities are destroyed and the player neither has any in reserve nor earns one during the current level.
Gameplay
Like most early arcade games, there is no way to "win"; the enemy weapons become faster and more prolific with each new level.
Development
At this time, games were usually developed by a single programmer with a deadline of 6 months.
Development

Dave Theurer, who was free after finishing Atari Soccer as a junior programmer, was offered the project, loosely defined as "radar screen showing missiles fired from the USSR toward the US, which is defended by the player".
Development
The game would be purely defensive and never put players in situations where they would be the aggressor.
Development
Only a crazy person would sling nuclear weapons without context, right?".
Development
The only possible game outcome of total destruction was also a message on the futility of war.
Development
The game would also be the first color game made by Atari.
Development
As the deadline was approaching, the programmers started crunching heavily and Theurer suffered from nightmares of being destroyed by a nuclear blast.
Development
A common observation at Atari at the time was that no programmer ever succeeded at having their first game released.
Development

Coin-op games had to go through early "field tests" where Atari would pay an arcade owner to place their prototype in the arcade for a few days so that the developers could observe player behaviour and reaction, find bugs and ensure the players were understanding the game and having fun.
Development
The game was an instant hit but the extra indicator panel was distracting the player and taking their attention from the screen, thus was scrapped entirely.
Reception
Missile Command was a commercial success for Sega in Japan, where it was among the top-ten highest-grossing arcade video games of 1980.
Reception
In 1983, Softline readers named Missile Command for the Atari 8-bit computers eighth on the magazine's Top Thirty list of Atari programs by popularity.
Reception

In a retrospective review, Brett Weiss of Allgame gave the arcade version a perfect score of 5 out of 5, in terms of controls, frenetic gameplay, sound effects, theme, and strategic aiming and firing.
Reception
In 1995, Flux magazine ranked the arcade version 24th on their "Top 100 Video Games".
Ports
Missile Command was ported to the Atari 2600 in 1981.
Ports
On level 13, if the player uses all of his or her missiles without scoring any points, at the end of the game the city on the right will turn into "RF" – the initials of the programmer Rob Fulop.
Ports
This Easter egg is originally documented in Atari Age (Volume 1, issue #2) in a letter to the editor by Joseph Nickischer, and is the second one publicly acknowledged by Atari.
Ports
Missile Command was released for Atari 8-bit computers in 1981 and an identical version for the Atari 5200 in 1982.
Ports
The same Atari 8-bit port was later used in the 1987 Atari XEGS as a built-in game that boots up if there isn't a cartridge or keyboard in the console.
Re-releases
The game was released for Microsoft Windows 3.x as part of the Microsoft Arcade package in 1993.
Re-releases
Accolade released a version for the Game Boy in 1995, as part of their Arcade Classics series.
Re-releases
The game is included in the Midway Games published Arcade's Greatest Hits: The Atari Collection 1 for the Sega Saturn, Super Nintendo Entertainment System, and the PlayStation.
Re-releases
It is also included in Atari Arcade Hits 1, Atari Greatest Hits, Atari Anniversary Edition and Atari: 80 Classic Games in One!.
Re-releases

The game appears as a bonus unlockable minigame in the PlayStation 2 and Xbox versions of Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines, that can be unlocked once it has been played on a hidden computer in one of the levels.
Re-releases
The game has also been made available for the Xbox and PlayStation 2 (in both arcade and Atari 2600 versions) as part of Atari Anthology in 2004.
Re-releases
The game is included in Retro Atari Classics and Atari Greatest Hits Volume 1 for the Nintendo DS.
Re-releases
Both the arcade and 2600 versions are part of Atari Vault (2016).
Re-releases
Both the Atari 2600 and Atari 7800 version was released on the Evercade as part of Arcade Collection 1 and 2 in 2020.
Re-releases
The arcade, Atari 2600 and Atari 5200 versions were included in Atari 50 (2022) for the Atari VCS, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S.
Sequels
In late 1980, a two-player sequel Missile Command 2 was field tested but never released, although at least one prototype appeared in an arcade in Santa Clara, California.
Sequels
In 1992, Atari developed a prototype of an arcade game called Arcade Classics for their 20th anniversary, which included Missile Command 2 and Super Centipede.
Sequels
Despite its name, however, this version was not the unreleased sequel, but an enhanced remake of the first game.
Sequels
In 1981, an enhancement kit was made by General Computer Corp. to convert Missile Command into Super Missile Attack.
Sequels

In 1982, Atari released a game called Liberator, which was seen by some as being a sequel to Missile Command with the situation essentially reversed; in Liberator, the player is the one attacking planetary bases from orbit.
Updated versions
An updated version called Missile Command 3D was released for the Atari Jaguar in 1995.
Updated versions
Hasbro Interactive released a 3D remake of Missile Command for Microsoft Windows and PlayStation in 1999.
Updated versions
Missile Command: Recharged with high-definition graphics was released via Xbox Live Arcade for the Xbox 360 on July 4, 2007.
Updated versions
Missile Command was released for the iPhone and iPod Touch for US$5 on September 23, 2008.
Updated versions
In March 2020, Atari released a new remake, Missile Command: Recharged, on mobile platforms.
Updated versions
On May 27, the remake also made it to Nintendo Switch as well as home computers via Steam, later on released as a launch title on the Atari VCS.
Updated versions
An updated version of the game was announced in 2018 for the Intellivision Amico.
Updated versions

While neither the Intellivision Amico version of Missile Command nor the Amico console itself have yet released, a mobile version was announced in late 2023, as part of Intellivision's Amico Home initiative.
Clones

Contemporary Missile Command clones include Missile Defense (1981) for the Apple II, Stratos (1982) for the TRS-80, Missile Control (1983) for the BBC Micro, Repulsar (1983) for the ZX Spectrum, and Barrage (1983) for the TI-99/4A.
Clones
Silas Warner programmed the 1980 clone ABM for the Apple II several years before writing Castle Wolfenstein.
Clones
Similarly, John Field programmed the Missile Command -like game ICBM (1981), then went on to create Axis Assassin, one of the first five games published by Electronic Arts.
Clones
Atomic Command, a clone of Missile Command, is playable on the Pip-Boy interface in the Fallout 4 video game.
In popular culture
Missile Command was referenced in the 1980 episode "Call Girl" of the TV sitcom Barney Miller, which features a detective who is hooked on the game.
In popular culture
In the 1991 film Terminator 2: Judgment Day, John Connor plays the game in an arcade, echoing the film's theme of a future global nuclear war.
In popular culture
The documentary High Score (2006) follows William Carlton, a Portland, Oregon gamer, on his quest to beat the Missile Command high score record for Marathon settings.
In popular culture
In the 2010 open world survival horror video game, Deadly Premonition, the game is mentioned by the protagonist Francis York Morgan, while driving.
In popular culture
In the 2008 episode " Chuck Versus Tom Sawyer " of the NBC show Chuck, a weapons satellite access code is hidden in the (fictitious) kill screen of Missile Command by its programmer, Mr.
In popular culture
In the 1982 film Fast Times at Ridgemont High, Missile Command ' s "The End" screen is used to help illustrate the film's ending.
In popular culture
The game is shown in the opening title sequence of the 2013 FX television series The Americans.
In popular culture
Fallout 4 features a holotape called Atomic Command where the player must defend landmarks across the United States from atomic bombs.
Film connection and adaptation

The gameplay of Missile Command, specifically, the contrails left by incoming ICBMs, and the visuals of cities being destroyed by nuclear warheads on a video display screen, strongly resembles the opening nuclear war scenes from the 1977 film, Damnation Alley.
Film connection and adaptation
In February 2010, Atari was talking with several studios to turn Missile Command into a film.
Film connection and adaptation
20th Century Fox acquired the rights to bring Missile Command to film the following year.
Film connection and adaptation
In May 2016, Emmett/Furla/Oasis Films closed a deal to partner with Atari to produce and finance both Centipede and Missile Command.
Marathon settings
In 1981, Floridian Jody Bowles played a Missile Command arcade game for 30 hours at The Filling Station Eatery in Pensacola.
Marathon settings
Bowles scored 41,399,845 points with one quarter using Marathon settings, besting the previous known record, according to Atari spokesman Mike Fournell.
Marathon settings
The record was broken when Victor Ali of the United States scored 80,364,995 points in 1982.
Marathon settings
Beginning on March 15, 2013, Victor Sandberg of Sweden scored 81,796,035 points live on Twitch after 56 hours of play.
Marathon settings
On December 27 of the same year, Sandberg started a 71-hour and 41 minute game with a score of 103,809,990—10 points short of getting an additional 176 cities.
Tournament settings
On July 3, 1985, Roy Shildt of Los Angeles set a world record in tournament-set Missile Command, with a score of 1,695,265, as verified by Twin Galaxies.
Tournament settings
This score, as well it earning his induction into the Video Game Hall of Fame, were published in the 1986 Guinness Book of World Records.
Tournament settings
After more than 20 years, on March 9, 2006, UK -based gamer Tony Temple set a new world record of 1,967,830 points, also with Tournament settings as confirmed by Twin Galaxies.
Tournament settings

Temple's score was published in the 2008 Guinness Book of World Records Gamer's Edition, although Guinness noted that the score was controversial due to Temple playing on game settings that increased cursor speed and was therefore easier than those of Roy Shildt, the previous record holder.
Tournament settings
Tony Temple increased his world record on two occasions, culminating in a score of 4,472,570 in 2 hours and 57 minutes–verified on September 9, 2010.
Tournament settings
This is the first verified time that a player passed wave 256 under tournament settings; the game difficulty starts over at wave 1 again.

f64_clay_fightur_sculptor_s_cut.title: ClayFighter (video game)

Developer(s): Visual Concepts (Super NES) Ringler Studios (Genesis) Danger Productions (animation)
Designer(s): Gregory A. Thomas Matthew Crysdale Jason G. Andersen Jeffrey J. Thomas

sents: lead
ClayFighter is a fighting game released for the Super NES in November 1993 and ported to Sega Genesis in June 1994.
lead
The game is a parody of Street Fighter.
lead
In 2009, the Genesis version was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console.
lead
Most of the game features a circus theme focused more on humor.
lead
It features claymation -style graphics that were created by photographing and digitized actual clay models.
lead
The game was one of the two "clay"-themed game franchises made by Interplay Productions, the second being a platformer released for the SNES titled Claymates.
lead
In July 2020, Megalopolis Toys made a partnership with Interplay to release a line of 6-inch action figures based on the games.
Characters
The first opponent in single player mode, she fights at an open-air opera theatre.
Characters
In 1-player mode, he will fight in two overflowing taffy factories.
Characters
Boss only attacks with projectiles copied from other characters and a grab attack.
Development
ClayFighter ' s design was originally made to compete with fighting games such as Mortal Kombat, but without the heavy violence and gore that was becoming controversial.
Development
In May 1994, Interplay released ClayFighter: Tournament Edition for the SNES.
Development
The Genesis version of ClayFighter was released on the Wii Virtual Console in Europe on February 6 and in North America on May 25, 2009.
Development
A port of ClayFighter for the Atari Jaguar was reportedly in the works by Interplay but it was never released.
Sequels
ClayFighter was followed by the Tournament Edition update in 1994.
Sequels
