Two sequels were also produced: ClayFighter 2: Judgment Clay for the SNES in 1995 and ClayFighter 63⅓ for the Nintendo 64 in 1997, the latter of which had its own special edition with ClayFighter: Sculptor's Cut in 1998, which was only available as a rental game at Blockbuster Video stores in North America.
Sequels
The Sculptor's Cut edition included four additional characters (High Five, Lady Liberty, Lockjaw Pooch, and Zappa Yow Yow Boyz) who were cut out of the original release for 63⅓.
Sequels
Sculptor's Cut is widely considered to be the rarest game released for the Nintendo 64, with only 20,000 copies ever produced.
Sequels
In March 2015, Interplay revealed that a remastered ClayFighter was to be released sometime in 2016 and developed in partnership with Drip Drop Games.
Sequels
The game was to include more than 20 characters and 20 "familiar" environments, unique "Claytalities" and new mechanics like double-jumping, air-dashing, counters, and reversals.
Sequels
The game has since been cancelled, as in 2016 Interplay sold the intellectual rights to ClayFighter and many other titles as well.
Reception
ClayFighter was awarded Best Street Fighter Wannabee of 1993 by Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Reception
ClayFighter sold 200,000 copies by the end of 1994.

f64_stunto_racer_64.title: Stunt Racer 64
sents: lead
Stunt Racer 64 is a racing video game developed by Boss Studios and published by Midway.
lead
The game was released exclusively in North America on October 3, 2000 for the Nintendo 64.
Game modes
Contest Mode - One player selects one of four characters, each with their own unique cars.
Game modes
Placing first in a race allows the player to keep all money earned, second place allows half of the money earned to be kept, and no money is kept for places 3–6.
Game modes
When a first-place overall finish is attained, the player races one-on-one against the league owner, with the prize of the league owner's car.
Cars
When a career is first started in Contest Mode, the player selects one of four starter characters, each with their own car: Warbird Light, Z-Bucket, Stottlemeyer, and Del Raye.
Cars
Cash prizes can later be used to purchase the rest of these starter cars if desired, along with other cars that are available by purchase only.
Development
Stunt Racer 64 was originally planned for retail release, including in Europe, but these plans were canceled as a result of missed deadlines.

f64_boomerman_64_the_second_atta.title: Bomberman 64: The Second Attack!

Composer(s): Tomohiko Kira Yasunori Mitsuda Hidenobu Otsuki Tomori Kudo Hiroyo Yamanaka Yoshitaka Hirota Kenji Hiramatsu

sents: lead
Bomberman 64: The Second Attack! is a 1999 action video game, the sequel to 1997's Bomberman 64.
Gameplay
In many aspects, the game plays identically to Bomberman 64, with features such as the ability to make bombs bigger.
Gameplay
As opposed to the circular explosions of the first Nintendo 64 title, the explosions in The Second Attack are the traditional cross "+" shape.
Story
Once Bomberman defeats most of the knights, the way opens to Warship Noah, the cause of the black hole and the headquarters of the BHB army.
Story
If Bomberman goes to the final confrontation without defeating all bosses first, Sthertoth will be impossible to defeat, resulting in a bad ending.
Story
Bomberman was in possession of the Fire Stone, the last one they were missing.
Reception
Although the new bomb types add variety, most of the puzzles don't require much thought".
Reception
Bomberman 64: The Second Attack! also introduces a cute little sidekick for the hero, who is occasionally helpful and who may "evolve" and grow in power if given the proper attention."

f64_pocket_critters_puzzle_leagu.title: Pokémon Puzzle League
sents: lead
Pokémon Puzzle League is a puzzle video game in the Puzzle League series developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Released in North America on September 25, 2000, and in Europe on March 2, 2001, its Puzzle League -based gameplay has a focus on puzzle-based strategy in the game's grid-based format.
lead
To advance to new levels, players are required to combat the game's trainers and gym leaders, similar to the ones featured in Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow.
lead
One of several games based on the Pokémon anime, it features lead protagonist Ash Ketchum, his Pikachu, his companions Brock and Misty, the Kanto Gym Leaders, and other characters from the series.
lead

As the development process of video games as a whole changed drastically from the 2D era of the fourth generation of video game consoles to the 3D era of the fifth generation, so did the development of Pokémon Puzzle League.
lead

The increased capabilities for artificial intelligence (AI) compelled the developers to create multiple levels of difficulty for the game, and it was implemented successfully in all but the 3D modes of the game, in which the AI becomes erratic at times.
lead
Local multiplayer capabilities are also available for one-on-one Puzzle League battles.
lead
Pokémon Puzzle League received mostly positive reviews from critics.
Gameplay
Unlike its predecessors, Pokémon Puzzle League features a 3D mode in addition to the traditional 2D mode.
Gameplay
In this mode, gameplay takes place on a cylinder with an effective width of 18 blocks, compared to the six-block width of the flat 2D field.
Gameplay
The game features the ability to battle against AI opponents, though their abilities are limited when using the 3D gameplay style.
Gameplay
In "1P Stadium", players control Ash Ketchum as they compete to defeat a series of increasingly difficult opponents and become the Puzzle Master.
Gameplay
"2P Stadium" allows two players to choose one of 15 Pokémon trainers to play as, and battle one another using different gameplay rulesets.
Characters

The 16 playable characters in Pokémon Puzzle League are directly taken from the Pokémon anime, including characters that originally debuted in previous Pokémon games, such as Misty, Brock, and Giovanni.
Characters
Ash Ketchum is the only playable character in the 1P Stadium mode, whereas other characters are available in the 2P Stadium mode.
Characters

Ash's rival Gary Oak 's Pokémon, a Nidoran♀, Growlithe, and Krabby, appear fully evolved into Nidoqueen, Arcanine, and Kingler when playing 1P Stadium on Hard difficulty or higher, although these evolved forms are not available when playing as Gary in 2P Stadium.
Characters
Each character has a unique set of three Pokémon to battle with and a specific theme music; these differences are purely cosmetic and do not affect gameplay.
Plot

During the tournament, Ash challenges Gary, his first rival, before defeating seven of the eight of the Kanto region gym leaders and earning their badges, learning from them of a legendary undefeated competitor known as the Puzzle Master.
Plot
After battling Tracey and Team Rocket, Ash challenges the supposed Puzzle Master, Giovanni, and defeats him to win the last badge.
Development
The game's engine was originally built for an unpublished Panel de Pon title for Nintendo 64; this version was ultimately released as part of the Nintendo Puzzle Collection compilation for GameCube.
Development
The in-game soundtrack is primarily composed of instrumental arrangements of tracks from the 1999 soundtrack album Pokémon 2.B.A.
Development
Other featured tracks include an arrangement of "Catch Me If You Can" from Pokémon: The First Movie ' s short feature Pikachu's Vacation, and other instrumental tracks from the Pokémon anime.
Reception

It may not be up to Puzzle Fighter 2 Turbo standards, but it's one of the best puzzlers on N64." Miss Spell of GamePro said the game "is designed for young gamers, encouraging creative puzzle-solving—something parents will love.
Reception
Pokemon and puzzle game fans will appreciate this fun and challenging N64 game."
Reception
The game was nominated for the "Best Console Puzzle Game" award at The Electric Playground ' s Blister Awards 2000, which went to Mr.

f64_ogre_battel_64.title: Ogre Battle 64
sents: lead
Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber is a real-time tactical role-playing game developed by Quest Corporation and localized by Atlus USA for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Though conceptually similar to Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen, significant gameplay tweaks were implemented to change the game's overall flow.
lead
Ogre Battle 64 is the third game in the series, the first two being Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen, and Tactics Ogre.
lead
Gaidens have been released in Japan, on Game Boy Advance and Neo Geo Pocket Color.
lead
Unlike earlier Ogre Battle games, which feature Queen song titles, "Person of Lordly Caliber" is an original title.
lead
Ogre Battle 64 was released in PAL regions for the first time via the Wii Virtual Console in 2010.
Unit formations
Magnus, the protagonist, commands a battalion of up to 50 troops.
Unit formations
Any character can be dubbed leader, minus most non-human entities, soldiers and basic classes like the Fighter or Amazon.
Storyline structure and objectives
Most objectives require capturing an enemy stronghold with any unit or defeating a particularly strong unit.
Battle

Much like other real time tactics games, Ogre Battle 64 has automatic combat between two outfits, however what makes the gameplay unique is that when two parties battle, the screen view switches to an isometric view of a pre-rendered battlefield, which is very reminiscent of typical RPG video game battles.
Classes
Many classes are most efficient in certain positions of a unit.
Classes
All classes are divided into 3 major groups: male, female, and non-human.
Development
Ogre Battle 64 was the first Ogre title developed by Quest after Matsuno and other staff left for Square.
Development
Production began sometime prior to 1997 for Nintendo 64 (N64), at which point it was known only as Ogre Battle Saga.
Development
During this stage, the developers were debating whether to release it as a standard cartridge, as a title for the disc-based 64DD, or both.
Development
While apparently planned for the 64DD, it later settled into being a standard cartridge-based game.
Development
It was credited as having the second-largest N64 cartridge at 320 megabits.
Development
The team created the character models to appear realistic, using 3D graphics to create them.
Music
Matsuo had previously held a minor composing role for the original Ogre Battle, but for Ogre Battle 64 he was given a far larger role.
Music
For Sakimoto and Iwata, Ogre Battle 64 was their only work for the N64 platform.
Music
Sakimoto commented later than he found transferring his music into the N64 sound environment hard due to his lack of knowledge with the hardware.
Music
A soundtrack album was released by Datam Polystar in August 1999.
Release
The game was announced in April 1997 as Ogre Battle 3, with a planned completion date of March 1998.
Release
Originally planned to release under that title, the game was officially retitled to Ogre Battle 64 in June 1999.
Release
The Western version shipped in limited quantities, a fact attributed to lack of manufactured chips in the game's cartridge which made it playable.
Release
It was later re-released for the Wii through the Virtual Console market place on March 24, 2010; this marked the title's debut in PAL regions.
Release
It was later released through the Virtual Console for the Wii U on February 16, 2017.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 33 out of 40.
Reception
Vicious Sid of GamePro said, "Beneath Ogre Battle 64 ' s intimidating interface and plodding pace lies a wealth of strategy: If you choose to enlist, be sure to pack plenty of patience."
Reception
The game won the award for "Best Strategy Game" at GameSpot ' s Best and Worst of 2000 Awards, and was nominated for the "Best Game No One Played" award, which went to Samba de Amigo.
Reception

The staff noted that the game's sales had "fallen prey to console of origin, the N64." The game was also nominated for the "Best Console Strategy Game" and "Gamers' Choice: N64" awards at The Electric Playground ' s Blister Awards 2000, both of which went to Front Mission 3 and Perfect Dark, respectively.
Reception
It was rated the 111th best game made on a Nintendo System in Nintendo Power ' s Top 200 Games list.
Reception
In 2023, Time Extension included the game on their "Best Nintendo 64 Games of All Time" list.

f64_worms_armageddoon.title: Worms Armageddon

Platform(s): Microsoft Windows Dreamcast PlayStation PlayStation 4 PlayStation 5 Game Boy Color Nintendo 64 Nintendo Switch Xbox One Xbox Series X/S

sents: lead
Worms Armageddon is a 1999 turn-based strategy video game developed and published by Team17 as part of the Worms series.
lead
It was originally released for the Microsoft Windows operating system, and was later ported to the PlayStation, Dreamcast, Nintendo 64, and Game Boy Color.
lead
In the game, the player controls a team of up to eight earthworms tasked with defeating an opposing team using a wide range of weapons at their disposal.
lead
The game takes place on a destructible and customizable two-dimensional board and is characterized by cartoonish graphics and a unique brand of humour.
lead
The third installment in the series, Worms Armageddon was originally developed as an expansion pack to Worms 2 (1997) and initially titled Wormageddon before it was released as a standalone game.
lead
As a result the game is very similar to Worms 2 but has a new single-player mode and adds a number of new content as well as being released on a wider variety of platforms.
lead
Worms Armageddon was acclaimed by critics, who praised the refined gameplay and stylized graphics, and it has been featured in a number of "greatest games of all time" lists.
lead
Worms Armageddon on PC is still updated periodically, most recently in 2020.
Gameplay
During a single turn, a team can only move one of their worms (unless an item that allows the team to select their worm is used).
Development
Worms Armageddon was originally intended to be an expansion pack to Worms 2, but it was eventually developed as a standalone game.
Development
The game was eventually ported to Dreamcast and PlayStation in December 1999, Game Boy Color in January 2000, and Nintendo 64 in March 2000.
Development
The Nintendo 64 version is one of the first Nintendo 64 games to feature a terrain editor and generator.
Development
Worms Armageddon was initially released on the Steam platform for a limited time as the preorder bonus for Worms Revolution.
Development
Worms Armageddon was released onto the Steam store as a standalone game on 20 March 2013.
Development
Despite its age, Worms Armageddon still receives periodic updates, mainly from two programmers known as Deadcode and CyberShadow, recruited by Team17.
Development
The latest update was on 16 July 2020.
Reception

Among his only criticisms are that the AI-controlled worms do not utilize their full arsenals and that the player would wish that there were more weapons, more diverse graphics and sound, and more content.
Reception
Matthew Pierce of PC Gamer UK commended Team17 for addressing the problems of single-player (i.e. the missions and AI) that the original Worms and Worms 2 had always been criticized for.
Reception

Chris Hudak of The Electric Playground gave it a perfect ten, calling it "a gaming masterpiece." Tom Chick of GamePro said, "For all its similarities to previous cans of Worms, Armageddon is still a classic example of the joy of computer gaming.
Reception

Cindy Vanous of Computer Games Strategy Plus gave it a similar score of four stars out of five, saying, "In short, it seems that Team 17 figured out every detail that might have detracted even slightly from Worms 2, then recreated the game without those tiny flaws.
Reception
The result is eminently playable and often hysterical—in fact, the only thing serious in Armageddon is its strategy."
Reception

Every development house could learn something by taking a few pages from Team 17's book." Cam Shea of Hyper gave it 79%, saying, "if this is the kind of no frills PC port we can expect for the Dreamcast, don't toss out your N64 just yet.
Reception
Many publications gave the Nintendo 64 version favorable reviews while it was still in development months before its U.S. release date.
Reception
The PlayStation version received a "Gold" sales award from the Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 200,000 units in the UK.
Awards

The staff wrote that the game "put up one hell of a fight and should not be overlooked by fans of the genre." The console versions were nominated for the same category at GameSpot ' s Best and Worst of 2000 Awards, which went to Ogre Battle 64.
Legacy
18 on their list of the top 20 Nintendo 64 games of all time.
Legacy
13 on their list of the top 50 PlayStation games of all time.
Legacy
68 on their list of the top 100 video games of all time.
Legacy

Team17 chose to base the source code of the 2016 game Worms W.M.D entirely on that of Worms Armageddon, because fans frequently told them upon questioning that Worms Armageddon was their favourite game in the series.
Legacy
Additionally, the 2009 game Worms 2: Armageddon was named in honor of Worms Armageddon despite not being a direct sequel.
Legacy

In 2022, the PlayStation versions of Worms Armageddon and Worms World Party were added to the PlayStation Store as part of the first batch of downloadable PlayStation titles; the games run on emulation on the PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5, but do not feature trophies.

f64_indianna_bones_and_the_infer.real: Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine
f64_indianna_bones_and_the_infer.title: Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine

Platform(s): Microsoft Windows Nintendo 64 Game Boy Color

sents: lead
Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine is an action-adventure video game by LucasArts released in 1999.
lead
The first 3D installment in the series, its gameplay focuses on solving puzzles, fighting enemies, and completing various platforming sections.
lead
The story is set in 1947, after the events of Indiana Jones and the Iron Phoenix, and puts the eponymous protagonist, the adventurer Indiana Jones, against the Soviet Union.
lead

In a race for a mythological Babylonian power source, he joins forces with the Central Intelligence Agency and collects four pieces of the Infernal Machine, an ancient device that allegedly opens a portal to another dimension.
lead
The title was designed, written, and directed by Hal Barwood, who considered the Indiana Jones franchise a perfect fit for the action-adventure genre.
lead

Initially developed for the Microsoft Windows operating systems, the game later received an enhanced Nintendo 64 port jointly developed with Factor 5 released exclusively in North America, as well as a 2D version for the Game Boy Color created by HotGen.
lead
Infernal Machine received generally favorable reviews, having been praised for its detailed storyline and sophisticated level designs, though widely criticized for its unwieldy control scheme.
Gameplay
The player sees Indiana Jones from a third-person perspective and controls him through 17 levels of a fully polygonal 3D world.
Plot
The story of the game is set in 1947 and depicts archaeologist and adventurer Indiana Jones returning to his digging career after his involvement in World War II.
Plot
A bonus level sees Jones return to the Peruvian temple from the opening of the film Raiders of the Lost Ark, discovering another golden idol in a secret room.
Development
Based on this notion, he decided for the game to be an action-adventure, as he was particularly fond of the genre and its use of 3D worlds.
Development
Originally, UFOs were planned to be used as a plot device, though George Lucas vetoed the idea, still reserving it for a then undeveloped fourth installment.
Development
Developed for Windows 95 and 98, the game uses a modified version of the Sith engine adapted for a third-person view by lead programmer Paul LeFevre.
Development
Apart from John Williams ' "Raiders March", the soundtrack was newly composed by Clint Bajakian and consists of about 130 original pieces.
Development
However, a team of eight Factor 5 employees teamed up with artists, level designers and a programmer from LucasArts to port Infernal Machine to the Nintendo 64.
Development
Development of this version commenced in early March 1999 and was finished in October 2000.
Development

Over the course of these 19 months, several improvements were made to the game, such as enhanced real-time lighting, controls, camera and particle systems, as well as added lock-on targeting and assigning items to three of the C buttons of the Nintendo 64 controller.
Development
The port was only released in North America and was exclusive to the LucasArts Company Store, a majority of the stock being distributed for rental at the Blockbuster chain of stores.
Development
Originally scheduled for March 2001, the PAL version became subject to continuous monthly delays and was eventually cancelled in September 2001.
Development
A Dreamcast port was announced a for fall 2000 release but this was also cancelled.
Development
A 2D version of Infernal Machine with top-down perspective gameplay was developed for the Game Boy Color by HotGen also in early 2001.
Development
In October 2018, GOG.com re-released Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine as a downloadable game for personal computers.
Reception

Ellis, Blevins, and Mark Hill of PC Zone also praised Infernal Machine for its levels, calling them "excellently designed" and including "some of the most brilliant layouts seen in a game of this type".
Reception
Ryan of GameSpot found many of the puzzles in the game to focus too heavily on platforming and went on to state that they become "quite repetitive - even predictable" after the first few levels.
Reception
The most criticized aspect of the PC game across the majority of reviews, however, are the controls.
Reception

Peter Silk of Adventure Gamer gave the PC version a perfect five stars out of five, saying that it was "in my opinion the best attempt yet to make adventure games appeal to a mainstream audience because it does not achieve this by 'dumbing-down' the plot or puzzles for action fans.
Reception

The man in the hat is back to reclaim the role he never should have lost." Jason Lambert of GameZone gave the same PC version 8.7 out of 10, saying, "If you loved playing Tomb Raider and you really loved the Indiana Jones movie series, then you will love this game.
Reception
Despite its enhancements, the Nintendo 64 version fared about as well with critics as the PC original, receiving "generally favorable reviews" according to the review aggregation website Metacritic.
Reception
The control scheme of the port was well received by Matt Casamassina of IGN for the addition of C button item management and Z-targeting, both inspired by Ocarina of Time.
Reception

Casamassina was impressed with the texture work and lighting, and found the title to be "one of the prettiest" on the Nintendo 64, even more so by employing the Expansion Pak to achieve high-resolution graphics.
Reception
Hyper ' s Fish gave it 84%, saying, "Whilst Infernal Machine isn't the greatest third-person action adventure, it's certainly a nice one to add to your N64 collection.
Reception
The N64's twitchy analog stick causes some accuracy problems, but, overall, Machine provides perfect Indy-style adventure fun."
Reception
Suzi Sez of GameZone gave it 8.5 out of 10, saying, "This game is not for the faint-hearted!
Reception
Fast-paced action will greet you on the very first scene and will follow you throughout the perilous journey to find the Infernal Machine!
Reception
Nintendo Power compared it to the N64 version saying it that it has much depth and far fewer control problems, and described it more as a puzzle game.

f64_dooom_64.title: Doom 64

Developer(s): Midway Studios San Diego Nightdive Studios (re-release)

sents: lead
Doom 64 is a first-person shooter game by Midway.
lead
It was first released for the Nintendo 64 in 1997, as the second spin-off game in the Doom series after Final Doom (1996), and the fourth game in the series overall.
lead
A remastered port was developed by Nightdive Studios and published by Bethesda Softworks for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One in March 2020, and for Stadia in May 2020.
lead
Doom 64 was developed from 1994 by Midway Studios San Diego under supervision of id Software, the main developer of the Doom franchise, and was tentatively titled Doom: The Absolution.
lead
It has a customized version of the Doom engine, enabling new kinds of level geometry, and dynamic colored lighting.
lead
It has new sprite graphics for weapons and monsters.
lead

Doom 64 received positive reviews from critics, praising its graphics, level design, soundtrack, and general atmosphere, with some criticizing the lack of new gameplay elements compared to the previous games of the series.
lead
It gained a cult following, with several fan-made PC source ports and mods.
Gameplay
Doom 64 ' s gameplay is similar to that of earlier Doom games.
Gameplay

The player must advance through 28 story levels (and 4 secret levels) by battling demons, collecting weapons and keys, and activating switches to reach the level's exit while surviving deadly ambushes and traps.
Gameplay
The Doom engine and gameplay elements were customized, and all visual assets such as weapon and monster graphics are unique to Doom 64.
Weapons
It had originated in the Doom Bible in 1992, and was planned for the original Doom in 1993, but never appeared.
Weapons
Its appearance in Doom 64 is its only official appearance prior to Doom Eternal, in which it is spelled "Unmaykr".
Weapons

The first artifact increases the laser speed, the second artifact adds a second laser, and the third artifact allows the weapon to fire three simultaneous lasers which can automatically aim separately from one another, allowing the weapon to attack three different enemies at once with huge amounts of rapid damage.
Plot
As the only experienced survivor of the Doom episodes, the Marine is sent in alone to exterminate them.
Plot
In the Lost Levels from the 2020 remaster, the story continues as the Mother Demon was revealed to have a sister called the "Resurrector".
Development
Doom 64 was developed by Midway Games at its San Diego studio. id Software, the primary developer of the Doom franchise, supervised the project.
Development
Its tentative title of The Absolution was changed to Doom 64 for brand recognition, and reused as the name of the last level.
Development
The environments were built from 3-dimensional polygon models, and the enemies were created by pre-rendering sprites with SGI workstations.
Development
The Nightmare Imp was originally developed for the PlayStation version of Doom and appeared in a near-complete beta of the game, but was removed just prior to release for unknown reasons.
Development

Doom 64 was slated to be a North American launch game, but near the deadline id Software expressed dissatisfaction with many of the level designs, so Midway postponed the game until April 1997 while redesigning the levels.
Development

Nintendo's then-recent decision to remove the ability to run over animals from the Nintendo 64 version of Cruis'n USA raised concerns about the possibility of censoring Doom 64, but Midway vice president of software Mike Abbot said Nintendo had not voiced any concerns about the game's violent content.
Development
The original Doom 64 team was working on a potential sequel titled Doom Absolution designed only for two-player deathmatches soon after the first game was released, but canceled it.
Development
Because id Software was impressed with the team's work on Doom 64, they were assigned to the Nintendo 64 version of Quake at this time.
Development
Midway shipped Doom 64 on March 27, 1997, for release on April 4.
Reception
By the time Doom 64 was released, the original Doom had been converted to nearly every platform capable of running it.
Reception
Critics agreed that Doom 64 was by far the best-looking Doom to date, exceeding even the PC version.
Reception
A Next Generation critic remarked that "even the most skillful Doom fans will have their hands full.
Reception
Most critics praised the game's musical score for its atmospheric effect.
Reception
Doom 64 has garnered a cult following, with multiple fan-made PC source ports compatible with PC WAD files.
Reception

Most prominently, Doom 64 TC (2003) is a massive collaborative PC fan port led by Samuel Vilarreal to add numerous enemy variants and levels; and Doom 64 EX (2008) is a source port to re-create the original experience made by Vilarreal, who had worked on Doom 64 TC and a Nintendo DS port of Doom 64.
Reception
Patrick Klepek from Kotaku described it as the most underrated Doom game.
Reception
Others praised the game for some of the best and most unique level designs, and for its darker and more sinister tone in contrast to the intense and aggressive action of the original Doom.
Re-release
Versions of Doom 64 for PC, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One by Nightdive Studios were released on March 20, 2020, and for Stadia on May 12, 2020.

f64_mega_robo_man_64.title: Mega Man Legends (video game)
sents: lead
Mega Man Legends is a 1997 action-adventure game released by Capcom.
lead
It is the first game in the Mega Man Legends sub-series of Mega Man games from Capcom, and the second major 3D polygonal Mega Man title released in the franchise, following Mega Man: Battle & Chase.
lead
It was released for PlayStation in 1997 in Japan, and in 1998 in North America.
lead
A Nintendo 64 port was released in 2000 with the same title, but it was renamed Mega Man 64 for the North American release in 2001.
lead
It was also ported to Windows in 2001, and PlayStation Portable in 2005, the latter only in Japan.
lead
It was last released as a PS one Classic through North American PlayStation Network in 2015.
lead
Legends stars a different spiritual incarnation of Mega Man named Mega Man Volnutt, the game's player character.
lead
Mega Man Volnutt is a "Digger," a person in charge of investigating ruins from a flooded Earth.
Gameplay
Although the only way to move in the game is on foot, once Roll Caskett repairs a support car, she is able to directly take Mega Man to specific areas.
Gameplay
Small shards of them can be exchanged for money, and in the game, enemies that are destroyed will often drop these Refractor Shards.
Gameplay

Buster Parts can be equipped to upgrade four stats of the Buster Gun; Attack (how strong it is), Rapid (how fast it fires), Range (how far the shots go), and Energy (how many shots can be fired before pausing).
Gameplay
The only way to refill them in the field is an item that can be bought, but only one can be carried.
Gameplay
Only one special weapon can be equipped at a time, and the only way to switch is to talk to Roll, unlike the original series.
Setting and characters
Because of the flooding, only a few sparse islands exist and energy sources are rare.
Setting and characters
The game's antagonists are the Bonne family, pirates who want to steal Kattelox's secret treasure in order to become rich.
Story
Kattelox's mayor, Amelia, tells Mega Man the Bonnes are searching for the island's secret treasure and that legend says if somebody obtains it, a great disaster will befall the island.
Story
Inside, Mega Man unlocks the island's largest ruin, the Main Gate, hoping to find the reason why Reaverbots from the island are being activated.
Story
Even with Juno's physical body gone, his last words transfer his backup data into the systems of Eden and confirm the Carbon Purification Process.
Development and release
One of the earliest showings of Legends around the world took place at the Electronic Entertainment Expo in Atlanta, Georgia in June 1997 under the title Mega Man Neo.
Development and release
The game was released in Japan on December 18, 1997, while a re-release with the label of "PlayStation the Best" was published on May 4, 1999.
Development and release
In December 1997, Capcom USA's president, Bill Gardner, told IGN that Mega Man Legends would be ported to the Nintendo 64.
Development and release
In January 1998 the game was renamed "Mega Man Nova" as the general consensus did not find the previous name appealing, only to revert it just two weeks later due to trademark issues.
Development and release
The title Mega Man Legends was decided and confirmed in March 1998.
Development and release
By April 1998, the English adaptation of the game was finished, but Capcom decided to delay its release until September of the same year, believing it would fit better during the holiday seasons.
Development and release

The English localization removed an option from the original game in which Mega Man protects Tron from a dog chasing her; in the Japanese version, Mega Man can either kick or calm the dog, while in the English release he can only calm the dog.
Development and release
The PC port of the game was first announced by Capcom at the Tokyo Game Show in April 2000 alongside Dino Crisis and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
Development and release
The PlayStation Portable version of Mega Man Legends was released in Japan on August 4, 2005.
Development and release
It was re-released on December 21, 2006, and January 29, 2009, with the latter also including the PSP port of Mega Man Legends 2.
Development and release
The PlayStation original became part of the PS one Classics program on September 29, 2015.
Development and release
Likely owing to licensing issues, this release is only available through North American PlayStation Network, limited to PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita.
Development and release
The sound designers found it a challenge to make the sounds for the game, with one of them, Toshio Kajino, having never worked on a Mega Man title.
Development and release
On February 21, 1998, Capcom published a CD of the game called Rockman Dash Original Soundtrack (「ロックマンDASH」 オリジナル・サウンドトラック).
Reception
Since its release, Mega Man Legends has received moderately positive critical response from video game publications although the ports for Nintendo 64 and PC received from mixed to negative comments.
Reception
The PC and Nintendo 64 version had lower averages of 33.67% and 63.94%, respectively.
Reception

On Metacritic, the Nintendo 64 port holds an aggregate 59 out of 100 based on six reviews The jump from a 2D platform video game series to a 3D action-adventure game was well received, as reviewers compared it with other video game franchises whose changes were overall negative.
Reception
On the other hand, the game's difficulty received mixed reviews with focus on the boss battles, but praise in the addition of a tutorial mode later added to the Nintendo 64 port.
Reception

Next Generation reviewed the PlayStation version of the game, rating it three stars out of five, and stated that "first impressions can be a killer, and the game just doesn't possess the most outstanding graphics or mechanics to hook the merely curious after just one play.
Reception
The N64 port, however, received criticism by Famitsu for being too similar to the original game.
Reception
IGN commented that the PlayStation game "was a poor experience", asking "why Capcom decided to make Nintendo 64 owners suffer through it unchanged".
Reception
The PC version received a more negative review; GameSpot gave it a "bad" 3.6 out of 10 stating gamers would find the PlayStation port more worthwhile.
Reception
Similarly to Famitsu ' s review of the Nintendo 64 port, GameSpot complained about the lack of additions to the PC port.
Reception
The PC's conversions of the cutscenes during the game were found to have a mistake which makes a character start a dialogue while another one is still talking.
Reception

In a 2007 retrospective of the Mega Man series, Jeremy Parish of 1UP.com ranked Mega Man Legends as "Worth it!", with praise focused on the setting, the plot, the English voice acting and the boss battles.
Reception

Allgame mentioned that while the game "had some significant problems that kept it from being anything more than a diversion" with its most notable one being the controls which were improved in the sequel.
Reception
Mega Man's design was third in GamePro ' s "The 8 Worst Game Character Makeovers Ever" in which the author Patrick Shaw commented that having Mega Man without a helmet "just doesn't work".
Reception
GamesRadar's article "Gaming's most absurdly oversized limbs" featured the game as an example of games with characters' oversized arms.
Reception
In 2008, Joystiq 's Wesley Fenlon listed Mega Man Legends as a potential game to be ported for the Wii with comments focused in the game's and the console's controls.
Reception
In December 1998, a Capcom representative stated that Mega Man Legends became a very popular game.

f64_mystikal_ninja_starring_goem.title: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon

Composer(s): Shigeru Araki Yusuke Kato Saiko Miki Yasumasa Kitagawa

sents: lead

Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon is a platform action-adventure video game released by Konami for the Nintendo 64 on August 7, 1997 in Japan, April 16, 1998 in North America, and April 18, 1998 in Europe.
lead
The second Goemon game released in North America and Europe, it follows The Legend of the Mystical Ninja and features hybrid elements of platform games and action-adventure games.
lead
The story follows Goemon 's struggles to prevent the Peach Mountain Shoguns gang from turning Japan into a Westernized fine arts theater.
lead
The plot calls for three cinematic musical features and battles between giant robots; like other Ganbare Goemon games, it is peppered with surrealist humor and anachronisms.
lead
Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon sold nearly 200,000 units worldwide.
lead
Reviewers praised its graphics, gameplay, and humorous plot, while criticizing its virtual camera and questioning how accessible its references and jokes would be to Western audiences.
Gameplay
Players control only one of the four characters at a time but can cycle through them with the press of a button.
Gameplay
If the player loses all lives, the game restarts at the last point saved or at the beginning of the game if a Controller Pak is not used.
Story
Goemon travels to Iyo but finds the Hot Springs closed; the only entrance is a mouse hole.
Story
The hidden man aboard the peach ship at Oedo comes out calling himself Spring Breeze Dancin '.
Story
Goemon investigates reports of stolen food in the village while Yae undergoes training to become a mermaid.
Story
After sidestepping grills and swimming through gallons of soup, Goemon confronts Poron, the final weirdo, who jokes that he lost the last miracle item in Zazen Town.
Story
Goemon locates Omitsu and learns that Dancin' and Lily can be found past a rigid gate, accessible only with the help of Wise Man.
Development and audio
It was first titled Ganbare Goemon 5, then Legend of the Mystical Ninja.
Development and audio
Originally made with a two-player mode, this feature was scrapped months before the Japanese release.
Development and audio
A 60–70% complete build of the game was featured at E3 in June 1997, suffering from graphical clipping and camera issues.
Development and audio
Konami later presented a mostly finished build at the Tokyo Game Show in September 1997.
Development and audio
Its release in the United States was planned for winter 1997, then February 1998, but was ultimately delayed to two more months.
Development and audio
Mystical Ninja featured a cartridge size of 128 megabits, designed to be much larger than most of its peers and predecessor games to allow high quality musical numbers and voice samples.
Development and audio
The musical numbers, with forty tunes from the game and one remix of I Am Impact, were released October 3, 1997 on CD.
Development and audio
The soundtrack was later extracted from Read-only memory and presented in Nintendo Ultra 64 Sound Format on May 9, 2005; it is one of the most downloaded releases at USF Central.
Development and audio
In 2018, the 8-Bit Big Band recorded a cover of the song "I am Impact!"
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 28 out of 40.
Reception
Reviewers praised the game's story and setting for its quirky, unique flavor.
Reception
A reviewer for The News Tribune considered the presentation "a terrific upgrade from the Super Nintendo version" but the play control "not as fluid as it is in Super Mario 64 ".
Reception
64 Lightland found the game prone to slowdown, and decried the inability to pause the game during Impact battles.
Reception
The work done on the release is a trimuph for Konami that augurs well for the future" (#58, May 1998).
Reception

Kraig Kujawa of Electronic Gaming Monthly elaborated that the unexpected shifts in gameplay style and perspective keep the adventure feeling fresh, and serve to provide some of the most humorous moments in the game.
Reception

GameSpot said that though Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon borrows heavily from Super Mario 64, its gameplay is more varied and, due to it having the most memory of any Nintendo 64 cartridge to date, it has a much wider variety of textures.
Reception

Early conversations with village residents only add to the confusion." The News Tribune countered that the strange localization often compounded the surrealist humor through the use of weird, unusual English and grammar.
Reception

GamePro said the game "never gets anywhere near exciting" and has a bland story, but succeeds well enough on the platforming front to make an acceptable holdover for RPG enthusiasts who could not wait for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
Reception
IGN concluded that it would hold over gamers until the release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but advised them to rent before buying.
Reception
The Dallas Morning News likewise concluded that the game "will please N64 owners starving for a decent adventure game...
Reception
The game sold 55,000 units in America and 141,000 units in Japan.
Sequels
Featuring gameplay similar to the Super Famicom entry Ganbare Goemon 3: Shishijūrokubē no Karakuri Manji Gatame, the game presented a story in which Yae had been kidnapped by the Black Ship Gang.
Sequels
In 1999, Konami released Goemon's Great Adventure on the Nintendo 64 (a 2.5D side-scroller with multiplayer support).
Sequels
Reviewers gave it high marks for recreating the feel of the older, 16-bit Goemon games and considered it the best side-scroller for the Nintendo 64.
Sequels
The final Goemon entry for the Nintendo 64 was Goemon Mononoke Sugoroku, released in Japan on December 25, 1999.
Sequels

After a series of sequels on the PlayStation line of consoles, Konami returned to the medieval, quirky Japanese themes of Mystical Ninja and its brethren on June 23, 2005 with Ganbare Goemon: Tōkai Dōchū Ōedo Tengu ri Kaeshi no Maki for the Nintendo DS.

f64_goemon_s_great_adventura.title: Goemon's Great Adventure

Composer(s): Shigeru Araki Yasumasa Kitagawa Hirotaka Kurita Yusuke Kato Nobuyuki Akena

sents: lead
Goemon's Great Adventure, known as Mystical Ninja 2 Starring Goemon in Europe, is a video game developed and released by Konami for the Nintendo 64 on December 23, 1998.
lead
It is the fourth game in the Ganbare Goemon series released in North America and Europe, following Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon, released two years earlier.
lead
Featuring platform gameplay in 2.5D, it returns the series to a side-scrolling format.
lead
The quirky story highlights Goemon's quest to stop the evil Bismaru, who has stolen Wise Man's resurrection machine.
lead
Goemon and his friends must journey through five worlds to battle the revived Dochuki, prince of the underworld, and destroy the captured device.
lead
Each world is designed with Japanese styles and themes, and Goemon's Great Adventure continues the series' tradition of offbeat, surreal humor.
lead
The game was received well, with more than 160,000 copies sold worldwide.
lead
Reminiscent of older, 16-bit games, the side-scrolling system was lauded by reviewers, who also praised the two-player cooperative mode.
Gameplay
Though the game is linear like its 16-bit predecessors, certain non-linear elements exist—such as a secret village and multiple paths through a world map.
Gameplay
Individual stages are populated by monsters, obstacles, items (such as Ryō currency or dumplings), and occasionally bosses, who are stronger than most enemies.
Gameplay
The game ends if all lives are lost, at which point it reverts to the beginning or the last point at which the player saved his or her progress with a Controller pak.
Characters
Bismaru, a cross-dressing nun (who first appeared in Ganbare Goemon 3), steals Wise Man's resurrection machine to revive Dochuki, an ancient prince of the underworld.
Promotion

Konami heavily promoted the Ganbare Goemon series for the Christmas season of 1998, as three games were due to be released— Goemon's Great Adventure and the PlayStation release Ganbare Goemon: Kuru Nara Koi!
Promotion
Ayashige Ikka no Kuroi Kage would premiere on December 23, 1998, and Ganbare Goemon: Tengu-tou no Gyakushuu! for the Game Boy Color would enter the market on January 14, 1999.
Promotion
Great Adventure and its PlayStation counterpart were both shown to fans at the 1998 Tokyo Game Show, where children flocked to play them.
Promotion

News of an English translation and North American release was first provided by a Konami employee in September 1998, and the finished game appeared at the 1999 Electronic Entertainment Expo, though without the theme song sequence.
Promotion
It was originally slated to be named Mystical Ninja: Goemon 2 in North America; this title was kept in some form for the PAL release, entitled Mystical Ninja 2: Starring Goemon.
Promotion
To generate interest and incentive for the North American release, Konami included $20 rebates for Goemon's Great Adventure or Castlevania 64 in copies of Hybrid Heaven.
Audio
In normal stages, at night a stage's unique theme slows down and segues into a night theme particular to all levels in a world map.
Audio
And thanks to this project, I've come down with the Goemon syndrome—the disease most dreaded by composers wherein all the songs one writes are Japanese-style.
Audio
A 68-track soundtrack was released by Konami on January 22, 1999.
Critical reception

Goemon's Great Adventure sold over 160,000 copies worldwide and received favorable reviews, earning an 8 out of 10 at IGN, an A at 1UP.com, a 3.5 out of 5 at GamePro, and a metascore of 80% at GameRankings.
Critical reception

The 2.5D system received much fanfare; GamePro stated that it made the game "more exciting than any old 2D scrollers." Nintendo noted that the game looks "more realistic than any 16-bit platformer, but...plays just like one".
Critical reception
The only problem with control occurs when playing as the mermaid...maneuvering a beached whale might be easier." Great Adventure ' s graphics impressed critics.
Critical reception
The sound effects of the game mirrored ones used in 16-bit Ganbare Goemon games, although increased in sampling rate and variety.
Critical reception
IGN's Schneider remarked that Goemon's Great Adventure would have benefitted from more role-playing game elements as exemplified in Ganbare Goemon 3: Shishijūrokubē no Karakuri Manji Gatame.
Critical reception
Jason Leung of Nintendo Power wrote, "finally, a sidescroller done right for the N64".
Critical reception
All in all, this title is a solid, challenging 2-D action/platform game for a system that is woefully short on the genre...
Critical reception

Next Generation reviewed the Nintendo 64 version of the game, rating it three stars out of five, and stated that " Goemon's Great Adventure emerges as a much better game than its predecessor - and, like the Crash Bandicoot series, shows that not every game needs to be in full 3D to be fun."
Sequels
As of 2012, Goemon's Great Adventure is the last Ganbare Goemon game to date that has been translated to English and released overseas.
Sequels
The next and final Goemon game for the Nintendo 64 is Goemon Mononoke Sugoroku, released exclusively in Japan on December 25, 1999.
Sequels
Konami followed with Bouken Jidai Katsugeki Goemon, a game for the PlayStation 2 released on December 21, 2000, and other PlayStation games in 2001.
Sequels
The now-defunct company Working Designs attempted to bring Bouken Jidai Katsugeki to English audiences as Mystical Ninja Goemon beginning in May, 2002.
Sequels
Motivated to promote a series "that's never quite received the recognition it deserves here ", Working Designs demonstrated the game in its booth at E3 a month later.
Sequels
Mystical Ninja Goemon remained on the studio's release list until its closing in 2005; it is rumored that Sony canceled the game's release due to subpar graphics.
Sequels
The medieval, quirky, Japanese themes were revived on June 23, 2005 with Ganbare Goemon: Tōkai Dōchū Ōedo Tengu ri Kaeshi no Maki for the Nintendo DS.

f64_roket_robot_on_wheels.title: Rocket: Robot on Wheels
sents: lead
Rocket: Robot on Wheels is a platform game developed by Sucker Punch Productions and published by Ubi Soft for the Nintendo 64.
lead

It marked the first game developed by Sucker Punch, and their only game that it released on a Nintendo console, as Sucker Punch would be associated more closely with Sony Interactive Entertainment in its later years.
lead
In it, the player controls Rocket, the titular robot.
lead
Rocket: Robot on Wheels was the first game on a home platform to use a realistic physics engine to drive the gameplay.
lead
The player can solve puzzles dealing with mass, inertia, friction, and other physical properties.
Gameplay
Each world, along with the hub, contains 12 tickets and 200 tokens to collect.
Gameplay
Each world has at least one vehicle that is used for solving puzzles and getting tickets; for example, the first world has a hot-dog-shaped car that the player can drive.
Plot
Rocket gives chase and begins exploring the many areas of the park, working to find the stolen tickets and tokens so he can catch Jojo and rescue Whoopie before Gavin returns.
Development
After Sucker Punch's founders left Microsoft and formed the studio, they decided to develop a game for the Nintendo 64.
Development
Without development kits or tool libraries, they developed a prototype of the game using a PC.
Development
The developers pitched the prototype to Nintendo and received development kits, but Nintendo refused to publish the game.
Development
Ironically they pitched the game to Sony Computer Entertainment, who was impressed with it, but they stipulated the game still be released on N64 and later ported to the PlayStation.
Development
Nervous about both the concept not being mascot-centric and a potential game being on their biggest competitor's system, Sony declined.
Development

Eventually the team went to E3 1999 to present the game themselves, which produced positive coverage in gaming magazines such as Next Generation, catching the attention of Ubi Soft, who finally agreed to publish the game.
Reception

The realism of the gameplay, set in the surreal world of a cartoony theme park, makes this a game well worth any gamer's time." However, Boba Fatt said in another review that the game's interface "is far more challenging than its puzzles or obstacles, making Rocket just one long, unrewarding exercise in tedium."
Reception
The game was listed as the "18th Best Nintendo 64 Game of All Time" in Nintendo Power ' s 20th anniversary issue.

f64_snowbooard_kids_2.title: Snowboard Kids 2

Designer(s): Shigeru Maekawa Katsumi Suzuki Hitomi Fukaumi
Composer(s): Tomohiko Sato Isao Kasai Sayuri Yamamoto

sents: lead
Snowboard Kids 2 is a snowboarding video game developed by Racjin and published by Atlus.
lead
It is the sequel to Snowboard Kids and was itself followed by a sequel, SBK: Snowboard Kids.
Gameplay
Snowboard Kids 2 retains the core gameplay of its predecessor, while making changes to game mechanics.
Gameplay
Four new characters are introduced, along with five returning characters from the first game, for a total of nine characters.
Gameplay
Only the six starter characters can be used in story mode, while all nine characters can be used in battle mode once the remaining three are unlocked.
Reception
Time Extension included the game on their "Best Nintendo 64 Games of All Time" list.

f64_starr_warz_rogue_squadron.title: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron

Programmer(s): Thomas Engel Holger Schmidt Amit Shalev

successor: Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader

sents: lead
Star Wars: Rogue Squadron is an arcade-style flight action game co-developed by Factor 5 and LucasArts.
lead
The first of three games in the Rogue Squadron series, it was published by LucasArts and Nintendo and released for Microsoft Windows and Nintendo 64 in December 1998.
lead

The game's story was influenced by the Star Wars: X-wing – Rogue Squadron comics and is set in the fictional Star Wars galaxy, taking place primarily between events in the films Star Wars and The Empire Strikes Back.
lead
The player controls Luke Skywalker, commander of the elite X-wing pilots known as Rogue Squadron.
lead
As the game progresses, Skywalker and Rogue Squadron fight the Galactic Empire in 16 missions across various planets.
lead
Gameplay is presented from the third-person perspective and game objectives are divided into four categories: search and destroy, reconnaissance, rescue, and protect.
lead
The player can control five craft and each offers a unique armament arrangement, as well as varying degrees of speed and maneuverability.
lead
Bonus power-ups that improve these crafts' weapons or durability are hidden in different levels throughout the game.
Gameplay
Each of the game's 16 levels introduces mission objectives that must be completed to progress to the next level.
Gameplay
Each vehicle offers a unique armament arrangement, as well as varying degrees of speed and maneuverability.
Gameplay
Nine bonus power-ups are hidden in different levels throughout the game.
Gameplay
Each benchmark contains five categories: completion time, number of enemies destroyed, shot accuracy, number of friendly craft and structures saved and number of bonuses collected.
Gameplay
Acquiring these medals promotes the player's rank and helps unlock hidden content.
Unlockable content
One is the T-16 Skyhopper in "Beggar's Canyon", and an AT-ST is playable in a basic demonstration level unlocked only via passcode.
Unlockable content
A playable model of a 1969 Buick Electra 225 based on a car owned by the game's sound designer, Rudolph Stember, is included in the game as an Easter egg.
Unlockable content
During Rogue Squadron ' s development, Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace — the first Star Wars film in more than 15 years — was less than one year from its scheduled release date.
Unlockable content
To take advantage of this marketing opportunity, Factor 5 included content from the upcoming film in Rogue Squadron.
Unlockable content
Because the game was scheduled to be released six months before the film, Factor 5 was required to keep the ship's inclusion a secret.
Unlockable content
As a result, most of the game's development team at Factor 5 and LucasArts were not informed of its inclusion.
Unlockable content
The code has been named the Nintendo 64 's most well-hidden code because of the length of time before its discovery.
Setting
The game's first fifteen levels occur six months after the Battle of Yavin — as depicted in A New Hope — and before the events of The Empire Strikes Back.
Setting

As the Empire gathers strength for an all-out assault on the Rebel forces, Luke Skywalker and Wedge Antilles form Rogue Squadron, a group comprising twelve of the most skilled X-wing pilots from the Rebel Alliance.
Development
After the success of Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire on the Nintendo 64 in 1996, LucasArts began planning a follow-up.
Development
At the time, Factor 5 was developing a game engine to create large terrain maps for their planned sequel to LucasArts' Rescue on Fractalus!
Development
After LucasArts signed a three-game exclusivity deal with Nintendo, Factor 5 was allowed to convert their work on the new Fractalus sequel into a Star Wars game instead.
Development
The game's focus would be flight combat; this direction was inspired by a level of Shadows of the Empire in which the player flies a snowspeeder during the Battle of Hoth.
Development
Factor 5 designed the game engine, the music, and worked closely with Nintendo, while LucasArts produced the game's content and ensured it was faithful to Star Wars canon.
Development
Factor 5 initially pitched a concept to allow gamers to play through missions similar to the fans' favorite action sequences from the Star Wars films.
Development
LucasArts began developing the story and gameplay in a setting that would include characters from the films participating in new, original missions using Factor 5's terrain map engine as the base.
Development
In May 1998, a demo of the game was displayed at E3, but the game was so incomplete at the time that Tosti considered it a tech demo.
Development
Late in development, the team realized that they were developing the game with a Nintendo 64 memory expansion in place at all times.
Development
Unable to run the game on a standard Nintendo 64, they began working on compression techniques to allow the game to run within the confines of the standard console.
Development
At the same time, Factor 5 appealed to Nintendo to release the newly developed memory Expansion Pak commercially.
Development
However, after Iguana Entertainment also wanted to use the Expansion Pak to achieve a higher display resolution for Turok 2: Seeds of Evil, Factor 5 was given the green light.
Development
Ultimately, Rogue Squadron was made to run on a standard Nintendo 64 but the Expansion Pak increases its resolution from 320 × 240 to 640 × 480.
Development
Lucasfilm was hesitant to grant access to the Star Wars library of sound effects to Factor 5 sound designer Rudolph Stember.
Development
As a compromise, the company provided Stember with sounds sampled at the relatively low rate of 22 kHz, half the standard rate.
Development
The Factor 5 drivers use Nintendo 64 processors, but tax them less; advanced compression techniques were employed.
Development
As a result, the game includes over 80 minutes of high-quality stereo sound.
Development
In November 1998, a month before the game's scheduled release, LucasArts announced the worldwide agreement with Nintendo concerning three new Star Wars video games.
Development
Rogue Squadron was the first game released under this agreement.
Reception
The Nintendo 64 version received mostly positive reviews, and received an aggregate score of 85 percent from both GameRankings and Metacritic.
Reception
IGN's Matt Casamassina said that the game was the best-looking Nintendo 64 game to date.
Reception
Powered by the new Factor 5 audio drivers, Rogue Squadron features about 40 minutes of speech and 40 minutes of music.
Reception
IGN awarded the game three sound awards, including Sound Effects, Best Voice, and Best Overall Sound of 1998 on the Nintendo 64.
Reception
The game earned a nomination for " Game of the Year " at the AIAS ' 2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards (now known as the D.I.C.E.
Reception
Although nearly identical, the game's PC version garnered lower review scores than its Nintendo 64 counterpart, with an aggregated GameRankings score of 80 percent.
Reception
Directly comparing the two versions, AllGame 's Brad Cook wrote that the PC version's handling is more difficult than the N64 version.
Reception
In contrast to its opinion of the N64 version, IGN's PC review was not enthusiastic about the game's visuals.
Sales

When Rogue Squadron was released in early December 1998, the title's Nintendo 64 incarnation was the second-highest-selling video game for the first half of the month (behind Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time) and the holiday season.
Sales
PC Data, which tracked sales in the United States, reported that Rogue Squadron sold 584,337 units and earned $29.3 million in revenue by the end of 1998.
Sales
This made it the country's ninth-best-selling Nintendo 64 release of the year.
Sales
Delayed until after Christmas in the United Kingdom, the game was released mid-January and debuted as the second-best-selling game of the month, ahead of Ocarina of Time.
Sales
In August 1999, Nintendo added the title to its best-selling Player's Choice collection, while the PC version was re-released as a part of the LucasArts Archive Series in May 2001.
Sales
The PC version was also released via digital distribution in 2015.
Sales
The Nintendo 64 version sold over 1 million copies in the United States, and over 44,000 in Japan.
Sales
Rogue Squadron ' s retail success was not anticipated by the game's producer Julian Eggebrecht, who said that the game sold "about 100 times better than anybody expected".

f64_starr_warz_episode_i_racer.title: Star Wars Episode I: Racer

Publisher(s): LucasArts Nintendo (N64, GBC) Aspyr (2020 ports) THQ Nordic (Playstation 4 and Switch retail)
Designer(s): Jon Knoles Eric Johnston Brett Tosti
Programmer(s): Eric Johnston Mark Blattel Darren Johnson

sents: lead
Star Wars Episode I: Racer is a 1999 racing video game based on the podracing sequence in the film Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace.
lead
The game features all of the racers and race course on Tatooine from The Phantom Menace.
lead
It adds several new courses, on Tatooine and various planets.
lead
It has several single player modes, including a tournament mode.
lead
The format of multiplayer mode varies by platform.
lead
Jake Lloyd and Lewis MacLeod, who portrayed Anakin Skywalker and Sebulba in The Phantom Menace, reprise their film roles in the game.
lead
Episode I: Racer received generally positive reviews from critics.
lead
Several major media outlets listed it as one of the top Star Wars video games.
Gameplay
The podracer will also be destroyed if one or both engines sustain severe damage from colliding into too many walls or obstacles, requiring the player to steer carefully to avoid falling behind.
Gameplay
Time Attack pits the player character against the clock, racing along to try to achieve the fastest time on the given course.
Gameplay
The Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast versions feature a two player splitscreen mode, and the Windows and Macintosh versions allow play over a local area network (LAN).
Development
Star Wars Episode I: Racer was developed and published by LucasArts for Windows in May 1999.
Development
Tools included 3D Studio Max, Alias Wavefront, and Autodesk Softimage.
Development
Multiple graphical application programming interfaces (APIs) were tested, including 3dfx Glide, OpenGL, and Direct3D.
Development

Ultimately the game shipped with only Direct3D support because according to project lead Brett Tosti, when testing Glide and OpenGL the developers "didn't see any performance increases so didn't add support".
Development
The team had to develop a physics simulation from only a few short film clips given to them.
Development

The game was originally titled Star Wars: Podracer; however, the subtitle was changed to Episode I Racer when LucasArts learned that another company owned the trademark for games with "Pod" in the title.
Development
Actor Jake Lloyd, who portrayed Anakin Skywalker in Star Wars Episode I: The Phantom Menace, promoted the game at E3 1999 and provided voice-over in the game.
Development
Several of the game's other locales had never appeared in prior Star Wars games.
Development
During an IGN interview with Tom Byron of LucasArts at E3 1999, the question of online play was brought up.
Development
The game was supported by a $10 million marketing budget.
Release
Episode I: Racer was later ported and released for several other platforms: Nintendo 64 Dreamcast, and Game Boy Color.
Release
The announced PlayStation version of the game was never released.
Release
The Nintendo 64 version received a special edition Star Wars Episode I: Racer hardware bundle, including the standard gray and black console and a copy of the game.
Release

Though the Nintendo 64 cartridge can optionally take advantage of Nintendo's Expansion Pak memory unit to display additional textures, the limited capacity of the cartridge resulted in the removal of all pre-rendered cutscenes of the Windows and Macintosh versions.
Release

The Game Boy Color hardware is technically incapable of rendering the 3D graphics used in the other versions, so the game instead features one-on-one racing duels on abbreviated, linear tracks using an overhead 2D view.
Release
The game was re-released online via the DRM-free GOG.com store in May 2018.
Release

On October 18, 2019, the Nintendo 64 version was officially re-released in both a standard and Collector's Edition set with approval by Disney and Lucasfilm in limited quantities by Limited Run Games.
Release
On March 26, 2020, the Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4 versions were announced for May 12, 2020.
Release
The PlayStation 4 version was delayed by two weeks, with a new release date of May 26, 2020.
Release

On May 11, 2020, exactly one day before the Switch version's release, both the PlayStation 4 and the Nintendo Switch versions were eventually rescheduled for June 23, 2020 release due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Reception
GameRankings gave it a score of 75.78% for the Nintendo 64 version; 75.42% for the Dreamcast version; 73.79% for the PC version; and 69.44% for the Game Boy Color version.
Reception
In March 2004, GMR rated Episode I: Racer the fifth-best Star Wars game of all time.
Reception
In 2015, PC Gamer listed it 3rd in their list of top Star Wars games.
Reception
That same year, it placed 10th in Rock Paper Shotgun 's top Star Wars games list.
Reception
In Game Informer' s 2016 list of the 30 best Star Wars video games, Racer ranked 11th.
Reception
As of 2011, the game holds the Guinness world record for the best-selling sci-fi racing game, with worldwide sales of 3.12 million units, followed by other series like Wipeout and F-Zero.
Reception
The editors of Computer Gaming World nominated Racer for their 1999 "Racing Game of the Year" award, which ultimately went to Need for Speed: High Stakes.
Reception
During the AIAS ' 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards (now known as the D.I.C.E.
Reception
Star Wars Episode I: Racer also nominated for the Blockbuster Entertainment Award in the "Favorite Nintendo 64 Game" category, although it lost to Donkey Kong 64.

f64_body_harvezt.title: Body Harvest
sents: lead
Body Harvest is a 1998 action-adventure video game developed by DMA Design and published by Gremlin Interactive for the Nintendo 64.
lead

It was intended to be a launch title for the system, but was delayed due to its original publisher, Nintendo, having issues with the game's violent themes, and eventual dropping of the title, leaving DMA to find a new publisher.
lead
Gremlin would later acquire the rights to the game and released it in Europe, while Midway Games released it in North America.
lead

In Body Harvest, players assume the role of a genetically engineered soldier, Adam Drake, who must investigate and eliminate an alien attack force that has been returning once every 25 years to "harvest" the human population of Earth for their organic material.
lead

Being in possession of a time travel device, Drake must return to the past and battle in five areas over a 100-year period that covers World War I –era Greece, World War II –era Indonesia in the 1940s, the United States in the 1960s, Russia in the 1990s, and the near future (2016).
lead
The game is non-linear, as players can go anywhere and do anything within the limits of the game's boundaries.
Plot
The opening text tells of how an alien force has harvested the population of Earth over a 100-year time period.
Plot
Every 25 years, they land and imprison whole areas in shields that prevented anyone from leaving and any outside help getting in.
Plot

After repeating this several times, they teleport back to their homeworld, an artificially created comet, before returning exactly 25 years later as it has completed its orbit around the nearby star systems back to earth.
Plot
Greece was the first targeted area in 1916, southern Spain was second, eastern Canada was third, and the south island of Japan was fourth.
Plot
In 1941, the first targeted area was the Indonesian island Java.
Plot
Finally, in 1991, the Siberia region of Russia was targeted.
Plot
The player only has to stop the aliens in the first area that they target in order to save every future targeted area of that time period.
Plot
The opening cutscene shows Station Omega, an orbital space station containing Earth's last survivors.
Plot
The year is 2016 and the aliens have returned to destroy the last remnant of the human race.
Gameplay
Generally, only Harvester aliens deliberately kill civilians, but the player must be careful not to shoot or run down any civilians in the process of rescuing them.
Gameplay

The player must react to Harvester Waves quickly, as if the aliens manage to harvest 8 humans in a single wave they will create an extremely dangerous 'Mutant' creature, which immediately attacks the player regardless of location.
Gameplay
Adam can still fire most weapons from within a vehicle, although many vehicles are equipped with powerful weapons of their own.
Gameplay
Each vehicle has a unique combination of top speed, armor and fuel capacity, inviting players to consider their options carefully.
Gameplay

With thorough exploration, rarer items can be found including alien artifacts and 'weapon crystals', three of which combine to form a technologically advanced powerful laser weapon unique to that level.
Gameplay
To do this, the player must first destroy a number of Alien Processors, which act as sub-bosses.
Gameplay
Once the Shield Generator itself has been destroyed, the player immediately faces that level's boss.
Development

Body Harvest was one of 13 games demoed at the Nintendo 64's unveiling at the 1995 Shoshinkai show, though it was not in playable form and was described by journalists as one of the most incomplete of the 13 games.
Development
The development team were very enthusiastic about the Nintendo 64 as a development platform.

f64_glovur.title: Glover (video game)
sents: lead

Glover is a 1998 puzzle-platformer developed by Interactive Studios and published by Hasbro Interactive for the Nintendo 64 and Windows in 1998, and for the PlayStation in 1999 (branded under Hasbro Interactive's Atari Interactive label).
lead
The game follows a magical, four-fingered glove named Glover in his quest to restore the Crystal Kingdom by retrieving crystals that were lost.
lead
The Nintendo 64 and Windows versions received generally positive reviews while the PlayStation version garnered negative reviews.
lead
A sequel titled Glover 2 was planned but was eventually cancelled.
lead
A second updated Windows port was released in 2022 and a port for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S is in development.
Gameplay
If the ball gets destroyed or Glover loses all three hearts, Glover loses one life and must start from the beginning of the stage or from the last checkpoint.
Plot
After the last crystal is brought back, they all return to the castle spires where they belong.
Development
The game was originally announced at E3 1998, later it was reported that the game was 60% completed in August 1998.
Development
Two months later in October, the game was reported to be 70% completed.
Development
On September 15, 1998, it was announced that Nintendo would handle distribution of the Nintendo 64 version in Europe.
Reception
For the Nintendo 64 version, Glover received generally positive reviews by critics.
Reception
Matt Casamassina of IGN praised the Nintendo 64 version, specifically on its gameplay and sound.
Reception

Paul Hales of PC Zone gave it a 67% stating, "It's all good, clean, harmless fun in reasonably 3D rendered landscapes." Edge magazine gave the game a 7 out of 10 stating it was not all that original but also stated that the game provides regular surprises that make it an entertaining game.
Reception
Despite positive reviews for the Nintendo 64 version, the PlayStation version was heavily panned by critics.
Reception
Matt Whine of IGN gave the PlayStation version a "Terrible" 2.6.
Reception

Miguel Lopez of GameSpot also criticized this version, stating that " Glover, despite its interesting play mechanics, seems to have lost its soul in the port from the N64." PC Zone gave the game 56%, stating, "There's no denying Glover is bizarre, but at the same its not particularly interesting.
Cancelled sequel
In July 1999, Interactive Studios announced a sequel titled Glover 2 was being developed after the first one was released.
Cancelled sequel
The game was set to continue where the story of the first game left off and would have a more complete story that would unravel as the game progressed.
Cancelled sequel
Gameplay features of Glover 2 would have been similar to the original game with enhancements for hand/ball physics, enhanced graphics, and a new multiplayer mode.
Cancelled sequel

The game was expected to release in mid-1999 for the Nintendo 64, then PlayStation and Dreamcast the following year, but it ended up getting cancelled along with another N64 game from Interactive Studios, Frogger 2.
Cancelled sequel
In October 2011 it was reported that Nesworld.com acquired a prototype cartridge of the game and had released a ROM hack and a video of the game.
Cancelled sequel
On February 25, 2015, James Steele, a programmer formerly of Interactive Studios, released a blog entry detailing the reasoning of the cancellation of the game.
Cancelled sequel
Publisher Hasbro had planned on acquiring 150,000 units of N64 cartridges for the game.
Cancelled sequel
An employee of Hasbro in charge of ordering the cartridges bumped the amount to 300,000 units.
Cancelled sequel
Hasbro was left with approximately 150,000 units as retailers didn't want any additional stock, costing Hasbro roughly half-a-million dollars' worth of stock that could not be sold.
Cancelled sequel
Hasbro was forced to take a loss on all of the extra cartridges it ordered and decided to cancel the project due to its financial situation along with the bad reputation the situation had caused.
Cancelled sequel
The game was around 80–85% completed before development ceased.
Cancelled sequel
In 2018, indie studio Golden Mushroom claimed that it would be working on a sequel to Glover for Nintendo Switch.
Re-releases
In 2017, Piko Interactive, a game company focused on re-releasing old video games, physically acquired several properties from Atari SA including Glover.
Re-releases
The company stated their intent to produce a re-release of Glover for newer platforms such as Steam, as well as finish and release the Nintendo 64 version of Glover 2.
Re-releases
On March 7, 2022, Piko announced a remaster of Glover for modern computers built using the game's original source code.
Re-releases
It was released via GOG.com and Steam on April 20, 2022, and will eventually be released on the upcoming Bleem!
Re-releases

On October 26, 2022, during the QUByte Connect 2022 presentation, a port of Glover for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S, was announced to be in development by QUByte Interactive, in collaboration with Limited Run Games.

f64_boomerman_hero.title: Bomberman Hero

Designer(s): Hideyuki Kubota Katsumi Miyashita Norio Ookubo

sents: lead
Bomberman Hero is a platforming video game and the second Bomberman game for the Nintendo 64.
lead
A further departure from the 16-bit Bomberman titles after Bomberman 64, it gives Bomberman more character moves, and has more levels, bosses, and weapons.
lead
However, in a break from the Bomberman series formula, it lacks a multiplayer mode.
lead
This game was released on the Wii Virtual Console service in 2011.
Gameplay
A unique feature is that it is possible to play with an extra advancement, such as a jet pack or a submarine.
Gameplay
Salt bombs only harm slugs, which are invulnerable to all other weapons.
Gameplay
Much of the game's replay value is in the sub-mission of scoring the number of target points per stage, which awards Bomberman a certain number of stage points (1 through 5) at the end of each level.
Gameplay
Stages can be replayed, in order to secure the highest possible score within the stage.
Gameplay
Getting a perfect score on every planet (or rather, a gold medal on each one) will award mini-games to be accessed on the options screen.
Plot
A princess steals a secret data disk from an evil empire, and she safely smuggles out the information through a robot, but is captured herself.
Plot
Bomberman chases after the Garaden Empire to save the Princess, but the Empire claims back the disks to rebuild their leader, Bagular, whose body was destroyed in Super Bomberman 3.
Plot
For the first three worlds, Bomberman chases after Princess Millian only to find that she has been transported to the next world.
Plot
If a perfect score is achieved on every level and all the Adok bombs are collected, a new cut-scene takes place after the destruction of Garaden Star.
Reception
The game received the Player's Choice label, indicating sales of at least one million units.

f64_chameleoon_twist.title: Chameleon Twist

Programmer(s): Hideyuki Nakanishi Masataka Imura Takashi Isugioka Masaki Kimura Masaomi Ishimoto
Composer(s): Takashi Sugioka Takashi Makino Yuuji Nakao Nobutoshi Ichimiya Koki Tochio Tsutomu Washijima Hiroshi Takami Fumihiko Yamada

sents: lead

Chameleon Twist (カメレオンツイスト, Kamereon Tsuisuto) is a 1997 video game developed by Japan System Supply, published by Japan System Supply in Japan, and published by Sunsoft in North America and Europe for the Nintendo 64.
lead
Though disliked by critics due to its easy gameplay, repetitive music, and awkward camera angles, Chameleon Twist was followed by a sequel titled Chameleon Twist 2.
lead
This 3D platform game has players take on the role of one of four anthropomorphic chameleons, and travel across six themed worlds.
lead
The chameleon's elongated tongue can be used as a weapon, a means to traverse gaps, or as a way to leap onto platforms.
lead
Once the tongue is unrolled, it can be guided in any direction using the analog stick.
lead
A five-room training area lets players practice the controls.
lead
The single-player game involves progressing through predominately indoor environments, each culminating in a boss battle, while collecting hearts to replenish health.
Multiplayer
Battle Royal has players vying to be the last chameleon left standing on a suspended platform, while Time Trial rewards the chameleon that stays on the platform the longest.
Release
The game was originally only planned for release in Japan, but Sunsoft and Nintendo thought children in the U.S. would enjoy the title.
Reception
Really, it's a pretty innocuous little game and probably worth a rental if you have an itch for another 3D N64 platformer.
Reception
The game held a score of 59% on the review aggregation website GameRankings based on eight reviews.
Reception
In Japan, Famitsu gave it a score of 28 out of 40.

f64_buck_bumbleo.title: Buck Bumble
sents: lead
