f64_mortel_kombot_trilogy.title: Mortal Kombat Trilogy

Developer(s): Avalanche Software (PS1) Williams Entertainment (N64) Point of View (Win, MS-DOS, Saturn)
Artist(s): John Tobias Steve Beran Tony Goskie
Platform(s): Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Sega Saturn, MS-DOS, Windows, R-Zone, Game.com
Mode(s): Up to 2 players simultaneously (8 on N64)

sents: lead

Mortal Kombat Trilogy is a fighting game released by Midway in 1996 as the second and final update to Mortal Kombat 3 (the first being Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3) for the PlayStation, Nintendo 64, Sega Saturn and PCs.
lead
Further versions were also released for the Game.com and R-Zone.
lead
It features a similar basic gameplay system and the same story as Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3, but adds characters and stages restored from Mortal Kombat and Mortal Kombat II.
lead
New additions to the game included the "Aggressor" bar.
lead
The Brutality mechanic was introduced with this installment.
lead
The game was met with positive to mixed reviews upon release.
Gameplay
Some were simple edits of existing moves (such as Stryker throwing two grenades instead of one), while others were unused animations never implemented in their intended previous games.
Gameplay
Sub-Zero 's famous "Spine Rip" Fatality reappears in the game but is completely censored, as the screen blacks out with only the "Fatality" text visible.
Gameplay

All of the battle arenas that were featured in MKII, MK3, and UMK3 are available in MKT, but only four backgrounds from the original Mortal Kombat are featured (Courtyard, Goro's Lair, the Pit, and the Pit Bottom).
Gameplay
The PC, PlayStation, and Sega Saturn versions lack The Hidden Portal and Noob's Dorfen stages from MK3, while the Nintendo 64 version lacks Kahn's Arena and the Bank from MKII and MK3, respectively.
Characters

Along with the Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 roster, including those who were originally hidden and specific console exclusives in previous iterations, Trilogy adds Raiden and Baraka exactly as they appeared in Mortal Kombat II, with added running animations especially created for Mortal Kombat Trilogy.
Characters

The actors of both characters were Carlos Pesina as Raiden (except for one sprite, which was portrayed by Sal Divita, who portrayed Sektor, Cyrax, Cyborg Smoke and Nightwolf), and Richard Divizio as Baraka (which also portrayed Kano and Kabal, including Noob Saibot only in MK3), respectively.
Characters

Johnny Cage was also added to the roster, this time portrayed by Chris Alexander (replacing Daniel Pesina, Carlos' brother, who was legally at odds with Midway), making him the only character exclusive to this version of the game.
Characters
He kept his moves from MKII except for the Split Punch, which was excluded since none of the characters from MK3 / UMK3 had graphics for getting hit in the groin.
Characters

Bosses Goro, Kintaro, Motaro and Shao Kahn are also playable characters from the start (except for the Nintendo 64 version, where only Motaro and Shao Kahn are included and must be unlocked via a cheat menu).
Characters
The PC, PlayStation and Saturn versions also contain alternate versions of Jax, Kung Lao, Kano and Raiden as they appeared in the first two titles.
Characters
Two new secret characters appear as well, depending on the version of the game.
Characters

Most versions have Chameleon, a semi-transparent ninja who rapidly switches between all the other male ninjas (Classic Sub-Zero, Scorpion, Noob Saibot, Human Smoke, Rain, Reptile, and Ermac) during combat, portrayed by John Turk (who also portrayed unmasked Sub-Zero and Shang Tsung).
Characters
The Nintendo 64 version replaced him with a female character named Khameleon, who switches between the female ninjas instead (Kitana, Mileena, and Jade), portrayed by Becky Gable.
Development
When we going to release Ultimate MK3 on consoles, it seemed odd to release it on the Playstation without doing something "special" for it.
Development
Since the PS1 had so much space (CD drive) we decided to include the MK1 and MK2 assets and call it MK Trilogy.
Development
Most of the background music tracks from MKII and MK3 remained intact, especially for the CD-ROM versions of the game.
Development
All of the music taken from MK3 on the CD-ROM MKT games is noticeably slowed down in both speed and pitch.
PlayStation
With each revision, aspects of the gameplay were refined, producing gameplay closer to that of Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 for the arcade.
PlayStation
Many of the infinite combos and bugs found in the game only existed in earlier revisions.
PlayStation
After beating the PlayStation version of the game, the final message in the credits says " MK4 coming in 1997".
PlayStation
The PlayStation version of the game exhibits a number of bugs when played on a PlayStation 2 or PlayStation 3 console which causes the game to freeze at certain points.
Nintendo 64
The Nintendo 64 port is based on the Windows PC and PlayStation versions of Mortal Kombat 3 and the Sega Saturn version of Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3.
Nintendo 64
This edition includes 3-on-3 simultaneous battles as an exclusive feature.
Nintendo 64
This version only uses music from MK3 and is of considerably lower quality than the CD versions.
Nintendo 64
For some MK3/UMK3 backgrounds, the incorrect background track is used compared to one used for arcade UMK3.
Nintendo 64
Due to cartridge limitations, only 30 characters are included, instead of the 37 featured in the other console versions.
Nintendo 64

The N64 port lacks Goro and Kintaro; the classic versions of Jax, Kung Lao, Kano, and Raiden; as well as the unmasked Sub-Zero (however, the masked Sub-Zero can perform both Sub-Zeros' special moves).
Nintendo 64
Chameleon is replaced with the secret character Khameleon, a grey female ninja that randomly switches between Kitana, Mileena and Jade.
Nintendo 64

The N64 version of the game, like MK3 and UMK3, provides the player with an "Ultimate Kombat Kode" screen after a single-player game is over, where a 6-digit code can be entered to unlock Human Smoke and Khameleon for normal play.
Nintendo 64
Further, the "new" characters: Noob Saibot, Rain, Baraka, Rayden, Johnny Cage, and Khameleon use italicized Arial, but with greater spacing than the original MK3 characters.
Nintendo 64
The N64 game also includes a new stage, the Star Bridge, made of the Pit II's background with a star-filled sky.
Nintendo 64

In the N64 version, the Graveyard stage has more names on the gravestones near the front: besides those of the original Midway design team for MK3, names of the team at Williams Entertainment were added, and the date of death on the stones was changed to the creators' birthdates.
Nintendo 64
In development for the N64 game, both The Bank and Kahn's Arena backgrounds were included, seeming to be building on the UMK3 version made for the Saturn previously.
Nintendo 64
In Kahn's Arena, both Raiden and Baraka (where Kano and Sonya in MK2, respectively) were held captive by Kahn if not actively participating in the fight.
Nintendo 64
Since this was only seen in beta versions and not in the final game, the reason for their capture is unknown as well as any impact on the story.
Nintendo 64
In this version, there are two secret menus, because not all the playable characters are unlocked from the start.
Nintendo 64

Nightwolf has a very different Friendship move exclusive to this version, which he pulls out 3 hatchets and begins to juggle, as opposed to turning into Raiden since this character became playable in this game (although in the other versions, Nightwolf retains his original MK3 Friendship move).
Sega Saturn

The Sega Saturn version, converted by Point of View and released almost a year after the PlayStation and Nintendo 64 versions, is a straight conversion of the PlayStation version without any substantial changes in content.
MS-DOS and Windows
The game was re-released digitally on GOG.com on 15 August 2022.
Game.com
The game includes a multiplayer mode, accessible only with the compete.com game link cable (to link two Game.com consoles together).
Game.com

Only 13 characters (Cyrax, Ermac, Jade, Mileena, Sektor, Kitana, Motaro, Nightwolf, Noob Saibot, Raiden, Rain, Reptile and Shao Kahn) and 10 Kombat Zones remain in this version (screenshots of early releases showed a different assortment of characters).
Reception
Brazilian magazine SuperGamePower gave the Nintendo 64 version 4.8 out of 5, and regarded it as the best Mortal Kombat game.
Reception
French magazine Super Power gave the N64 game 91%, favoring it over the PlayStation version.
Reception

And while he complimented the Nintendo 64 version's large selection of play modes, he said it is conspicuously missing frames of animation from the arcade games, and that the characters left out of this version are "favorites".
Reception

However, he held that the arcade games themselves are too aged to merit an appearance on the Nintendo 64, referring to them as five years old (in actuality, Mortal Kombat 3 was barely a year old at the time, and even the oldest in the series was four years old).
Reception

Mortal Kombat Trilogy was said to be a "particularly horrible game" among the Nintendo 64 library by Forbes, but was honored in Nintendo Power Awards '96, coming second in the category "Best Tournament Fighting Game".
Reception
Though Electronic Gaming Monthly never reviewed the PlayStation version of Mortal Kombat Trilogy, they ran a four-page feature comparing it to the Nintendo 64 version.
Reception
Shawn Smith picked the Nintendo 64 version as the one to buy, saying that the major bugs in the PlayStation version outweigh the Nintendo 64 version's various shortcomings.
Reception

The other three members of the review team all voted for the PlayStation version, particularly citing the additional characters and the lower price ($49.99 as compared to $69.99 for the Nintendo 64 version).
Reception
The Saturn version arrived nearly a year (over a year in some countries) after the PlayStation and Nintendo 64 versions and received comparatively little attention.
Reception
Released at a time when the Nintendo 64's popularity was burgeoning and there were few competing games for the system, the Nintendo 64 version of Mortal Kombat Trilogy saw impressive sales figures.
Reception

According to a later IGN retrospective, Mortal Kombat Trilogy "offered something no fan could ignore: It brought every character from the series into the fold, along with most of the levels, making for one massive game that had enough to please everyone.
Reception

Sure, some of the balance went out the window with the massive cast, but it was a small price to pay to make the Mortal Kombat family whole again, and it gave fans the closure they needed for Midway to move on to Mortal Kombat 4."

f64_bio_f_r_e_a_k_z.title: Bio F.R.E.A.K.S.
sents: lead
Bio F.R.E.A.K.S. is a 3D fighting video game released by Midway in 1998.
lead
It was originally planned for arcades.
lead

Prototypes of the game were tested at arcades, but the final arcade release was canceled (although a ROM image of the prototype was eventually dumped and works in MAME) and the game was later released for the PlayStation, Nintendo 64 and Microsoft Windows.
Plot

To prevent further conflict and hopefully reunite America, the Secret Games Commission (SGC) is formed, working with the remaining members of government to organize a fighting tournament to settle disputes between GI-Corps.
Gameplay
The game uses a fully polygonal fighting engine, with 8 different fighters, and 2 boss fighters.
Gameplay
Damage from powerful attacks can add up, causing a limb to be destroyed as well.

f64_fighturs_destiny.title: Fighters Destiny
sents: lead
Fighters Destiny, known in Japan as Fighting Cup (ファイティングカップ, Faitingu Kappu) is a 1998 video game developed by Genki and Opus Corp for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It closely models the 3D fighting game standard set by Sega 's Virtua Fighter, but integrates a unique point scoring system.
lead
The game's generic characters and unoriginal presentation have been panned by critics, but reviewers praise its point system and consider it to be one of the best fighting games on the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was followed by a 2000 sequel Fighter Destiny 2.
Gameplay
In most fighting games, the objective is to deplete the opponent's health gauge.
Gameplay

By default, knocking the character off the fighting platform (a "Ring Out") is worth one point, taking down an opponent with a throw nets the player two points, while a typical K.O. is worth three points, as well as taking the opponent down with a counterattack, and executing a "special" is worth four points.
Gameplay
By default setting, the first fighter to score seven points wins the match.
Gameplay
"Specials" can only be executed when the opponent is in Piyori condition.
Reception and sales

As with Mace: The Dark Age just a few months earlier, critics widely deemed Fighters Destiny the best fighting game on the Nintendo 64 to date, while noting that this was largely because the others were uniformly weak.
Reception and sales
However, while most critics described Mace as simply the best of a mediocre set, Fighters Destiny was more commonly referred to as the first genuinely worthwhile fighting game for the Nintendo 64.
Reception and sales
Jeff Gerstmann wrote in GameSpot, "The unique scoring system and variety of modes make Fighters Destiny a winner.
Reception and sales
The scoring system was commonly cited as both the game's best feature and the one which most sets it apart from other fighting games.
Reception and sales

A few also found the variety of possible fighting styles an important aspect; GamePro commented that "You can do multi-hit combos, throws, counters, and juggles as in most fighting games, but you can also execute lock moves and holds like in a wrestling game.
Reception and sales
Fighters Destiny held a 77% on the review aggregation website GameRankings at the time of the site's 2019 closure, based on 12 reviews.
Reception and sales
Until the arrival of Tekken 3 for PlayStation, Fighters Destiny is the fighting game to play."
Reception and sales
The game missed its initial Christmas release date and was greeted with lukewarm sales figures, selling only 18,000 copies in the first two months after its North American release.
Reception and sales

In an effort to boost sales, Infogrames Entertainment (the parent company of Fighters Destiny international distributor Ocean Software) shaved US$20 off the price tag, dropping the game's price to US$49.99.
Sequel

A sequel to Fighters Destiny, titled Fighter Destiny 2 (dropping the plural form of the first word) and known in Japan as Kakutō Denshō: F-Cup Maniax (格闘伝承 ~F-Cup Maniax~, Kakutō Denshō ~F-Kappu Mēniakkusu~, lit.
Sequel
"Fighting Tradition: F-Cup Maniax"), was released in 1999-2000.
Sequel
There are several new characters added, but most are direct replacements of previous characters and retain almost all of their moves.
Reception
Fighter Destiny 2 received more mediocre reviews than the original Fighters Destiny according to Metacritic.
Reception
In Japan, however, Famitsu gave it a score of 30 out of 40.

f64_gauntleto_legends.title: Gauntlet Legends

Publisher(s): Atari Games/Midway Games SNK (Japanese version) Midway (home versions) Epoch Co., Ltd. (Japanese N64 version)
Producer(s): Mark Stephen Pierce - Executive ProducerMike Hally - Producer

sents: lead
Gauntlet Legends is an arcade game released in 1998 by Atari Games and Midway Games.
lead
It is a fantasy themed hack and slash styled dungeon crawl game, a sequel to 1985's popular Gauntlet and 1986's Gauntlet II and marks the final game in the series to be produced by Atari Games.
lead
Its unusual features for an arcade game included passwords and characters that could be saved, enabling players to play over the course of a long period.
lead
The game was given an expansion called Gauntlet Dark Legacy, which featured new characters to play and new levels.
Gameplay
Skorne, fearing the power of the Runestones, scattered them throughout the four realms, so that they could never be used against him.
Gameplay
The players must find three rune stones on each kingdom in order to defeat Skorne in the Underworld (in the arcades only), and one from the battle grounds (home versions only).
Gameplay
The initial arcade version had a contest by which the first 500 players to complete the game and send in the supplied validation code would win a free Gauntlet Legends shirt.
Gameplay
Character progression is saved through a password system; a player can progress all four characters to a maximum level of 99, and each of their attributes to a maximum of 999.
Ports
The first home console port of Gauntlet Legends was released for the Nintendo 64 in September 1999 in North America.
Ports
This port saw a European release by the end of the year, and it was the exclusive platform for the Japanese release in the following year, on April 7, 2000.
Ports
Though it was originally planned to be released in 1999 alongside the Nintendo 64 version, the PlayStation port was released in 2000 for North America and Europe.
Ports
Unlike the other versions, this release only supports one or two players, as it omitted multitap support.
Ports
The Dreamcast port was also released in 2000 for North America and Europe.
Reception
Dan Elektro of GamePro said, "Overall, Gauntlet Legends takes advantage of the 3D space and uses it as much more than a gimmick.
Reception

Gauntlet deserved an update—and the legend has been treated with befitting respect." In Japan, Game Machine listed the game in their March 1, 1999 issue as the sixth most-successful dedicated arcade game of the previous year.
Reception
Greg Orlando of NextGen said of the Dreamcast version, "Four controllers and one Legends make for party-game excitement of the highest order."
Reception

Vicious Sid of GamePro said of the N64 version in one review, " Gauntlet Legends is not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but it's an impressive port of a polished arcade game that manages to cram in some extra playability to boot.
Reception

During the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences ' 3rd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards, the Nintendo 64 version was nominated for the " Console Action Game of the Year " award, which went to Crazy Taxi.
Reception
Likewise, the same console version was a nominee for CNET Gamecenter ' s 1999 "Nintendo 64" award, which went to Rayman 2: The Great Escape.

f64_rampageo_world_tour.title: Rampage World Tour

Developer(s): Game Refuge (Arcade) Midway Studios San Diego (PlayStation) Point of View (Saturn, Windows) Saffire (N64) Digital Eclipse (Game Boy)
Platform(s): Arcade, PlayStation, Saturn, Nintendo 64, Game Boy Color, Windows

sents: lead
Rampage World Tour is an arcade video game released by Midway Games in 1997 as the sequel to Rampage.
lead
It was developed at Game Refuge by Brian Colin and Jeff Nauman, who designed the 1986 original.
lead
Ports were released for the Sega Saturn, Nintendo 64, Game Boy Color, PlayStation, and Microsoft Windows.
lead
It was re-released on Midway Arcade Treasures 2 and included in Rampage: Total Destruction.
Plot
In the last levels, Scumlabs CEO Eustace DeMonic turns himself into a monster in an attempt to combat George, Lizzie, and Ralph, but is defeated during a battle on a lunar base.
Plot
After this, the only surviving Scumlabs employee Dr.
Plot
Elizabeth Veronica tries to disintegrate the monsters with a ray gun on her spaceship, but it only shrinks them to a miniature size, and they wind up inside her ship.
Gameplay
Like in the first Rampage game, the goal of every stage is to destroy all the buildings in each city while avoiding or destroying the military forces.
Gameplay
In the first level, Peoria, a tourism billboard cycles through different regions in the country (Northeast, Southwest, etc.).
Gameplay
After getting a World Tour power-up, the next few levels take place in a foreign location until a Scumlabs plant is destroyed.
Gameplay

The game will not end until every Scumlabs city has been destroyed, which may cause some erratic traveling around towards the end of the game (including multiple world tour trips if the players have missed or purposely kept from getting world tour flags).
Gameplay
Though it was announced that the PlayStation version would also support three players, both the PlayStation and Saturn versions allow only two players.
Gameplay

Three player support apparently was programmed into the port at one point and pulled at the last minute, since a review of the PlayStation version in Electronic Gaming Monthly describes three player gameplay.
Gameplay
The Nintendo 64 conversion includes full three-player functionality.
Release
The game would never be released in Japan.
Reception

Critics agreed that the console ports are nearly arcade-perfect, though some criticized the PlayStation and Saturn versions for supporting only two players instead of the three supported in the arcade version.
Reception

Despite the meagre improvements to the update, the very same criticisms can be levelled at Rampage World Tour." Even Smith showed a loss of enthusiasm in his review of the later Nintendo 64 version, now stating that the game is fun at first but quickly grows old.
Reception

Next Generation reviewed the Nintendo 64 version of the game, and stated that "Despite the three-player mode, no amount of graphic flash or nostalgia can improve a style of gameplay whose day has passed."

f64_shadowz_of_the_empire.title: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire (video game)

Programmer(s): Eric Johnston Mark Haigh-Hutchinson Mark Blattel
Series: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire

sents: lead
Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire is a third-person shooter video game developed by LucasArts and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 in 1996 and published by LucasArts for Windows in 1997.
lead
It is primarily a third-person shooter, with multiple types of vehicular combat sequences.
lead
The player controls the mercenary Dash Rendar to help Luke Skywalker and rescue Princess Leia from Prince Xizor.
lead
It is part of the Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire multimedia project and has a backstory between The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi.
lead
Tracks from the multimedia project's soundtrack are in the musical score.
lead
The game received mixed reviews from critics.
lead
Shadows of the Empire was the third-best-selling Nintendo 64 game for 1997, with more than one million copies sold.
Gameplay
Each level is timed and up to three challenge points are awarded for performing specific actions or finding hidden tokens, to unlock rewards.
Gameplay
Rendar controls the turret of his ship, the Outrider, in 360 degree space battles to destroy a specific number of enemy ships.
Plot
Dash pilots a snowspeeder into battle, and returns to Echo Base when the shield generator is destroyed, just as the Millennium Falcon leaves.
Plot
Luke informs Dash of a secret imperial supercomputer aboard the Imperial Freighter Suprosa, containing unknown important Imperial construction plans for the Death Star II.
Development
There was considerable pressure to finish the game in time for the Christmas 1996 deadline.
Development
The work on Shadows of the Empire project started in late 1994 with the idea of making a side story to the movies.
Development
LucasArts used the level editor of the Jedi engine, previously used on its games Star Wars: Dark Forces and Outlaws, to create the game's 3D environments.
Development
The game was originally planned to have 19 levels, Nintendo Power reported a reduction to 12 levels, and the final release has 10 levels.
Development
LucasArts's choice to be an early adopter of the Nintendo 64 came from what company leaders believed were missed opportunities for revenue on game consoles.
Development
When work began on Shadows of the Empire, the Nintendo 64 hardware had not been finalized by Silicon Graphics (SGI) and Nintendo.
Development

Therefore, SGI approximated the console's performance and functionality profile using a US$140,000 SGI Onyx supercomputer with the RealityEngine 2 graphics subsystem with the Performer 3D API — the architecture which had originally inspired SGI's design of the Nintendo 64.
Development
Two LucasArts developers already had extensive experience with the SGI platform, which eased the prototyping of the game for approximately 18 months until the Nintendo 64 hardware was finalized.
Development
Eventually, Nintendo 64 hardware cards were released for SGI Indy workstations, and given to the team to replace the software-based profile on Onyx.
Development
For a prototype controller with which to test the game, they were delivered a modified SNES controller with a primitive analog joystick and Z trigger, designed by Konami.
Development

For maximal secrecy under strict nondisclosure agreement, the core team was not allowed to speak to anyone else about the hardware or the project, and the controller prototype was concealed within a cardboard box that the team members could place their hands into.
Development
For the console version, due to limited cartridge space, the score was sampled down to 16-bit at 11 kHz in mono.
Development
After some discussion, Nintendo agreed to increase the cartridge space from 8 MB to 12 MB, giving the developers enough room to sample roughly 15 minutes of music on the cartridge.
Development
It is unique among Nintendo 64 games for using a digitized orchestral soundtrack, instead of synthesized music like that in Star Wars: Rogue Squadron.
Development
When supplemented with a 3D acceleration card, the Windows version runs at a resolution of 640 x 480 pixels.
Development
The Nintendo 64 version runs at a 320 x 240 resolution with hardware based blending and anti-aliasing features to make the difference in resolution less obvious.
Development

After the game's demonstration at the 1996 Electronic Entertainment Expo met with mixed reactions, LucasArts canceled its plans to release it with the Nintendo 64 North American launch, postponing it until December to give the production team a few more months for quality.
Release
Shadows of the Empire was released on December 2, 1996, for the Nintendo 64, three months after the console's launch.
Release

With the developer reporting more than one million copies sold by 1997, It is the third top-selling Nintendo 64 game for that year (September 1996 to August 1997) and the third top-selling game on any system for the 1996 Christmas shopping season.
Release
A version for Windows 95 was released on September 17, 1997.
Release
In coming decades, compatibility problems arose, so the game was re-released for 64-bit Windows systems on May 3, 2016, through Good Old Games.
Release
On July 26, 2019, the Nintendo 64 version was re-released in both a standard and Collector's Edition in limited quantities by Limited Run Games.
Reception
The most common comment was that the opening Battle of Hoth is outstanding, but all the other levels are mediocre.
Reception

The third-person shooter stages (which comprise the majority of the game) drew the strongest criticism, with reviews describing poor controls and camera angles which either give a cripplingly limited view or block the action with Dash's own body.
Reception
The other three reviewers for EGM were less enthusiastic, with Sushi-X in particular summarizing the game as "a poor first-person shooter on top of an awesome Hoth battle sequence".
Reception
Most critics were amazed by the Battle of Hoth level, particularly its success in recreating the scene from The Empire Strikes Back as an interactive experience.
Reception
EGM named Shadows of the Empire a runner-up for Nintendo 64 Game of the Year, behind Super Mario 64.
Reception

Though noting little competition for this category, because only eight Nintendo 64 games were released in the US in 1996, they called the game "a tour-de-force that all Star Wars fans must check out".

f64_wipeoout_64.title: Wipeout 64
sents: lead
Wipeout 64 is a 1998 futuristic racing game developed by Psygnosis and published by Midway for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It is the third game in the Wipeout series and remains the only one published on a Nintendo console.
lead
At the time of the game's release, developer Psygnosis had been owned for five years by Sony Computer Entertainment, for whose hardware all subsequent Wipeout games have been released exclusively.
lead

Set in 2098, a year after Wipeout 2097, Wipeout 64 introduced several new elements to the Wipeout series including analogue control which benefited from the Nintendo 64's controller, new weapons, teams, and tracks.
lead
The game received generally positive reviews from critics.
lead

Comparing the game with F-Zero X, which was released a month earlier, many critics praised the game for its individuality among the Wipeout series, its graphics, offering more tracks and racing craft, unique atmosphere and "superior track design".
lead
However, the game was criticised for its slow frame rate, and opinion is divided whether Wipeout 64 is a 'true sequel' to Wipeout 2097.
Gameplay
Most aspects of the gameplay did not differ from the previous two titles.
Gameplay
Wipeout is based on a futuristic anti-gravity setting where pilots would race against each other or computer-controlled AI opponents to finish in the highest position possible.
Gameplay
Wipeout 64 provides most of the same features as Wipeout 2097 along with new weapons unique to each team.
Gameplay
Exclusive to Wipeout 64 is an unlockable weapon power-up called the "Cyclone" which allows the player to strengthen the power of their weapons.
Gameplay
Unlike its predecessors that allowed split-screen between two players, Wipeout 64 introduces split-screen for a maximum of four players for the first time.
Gameplay

Wipeout 64 also introduces a new addition named Challenge Mode where the player has to complete sets of challenges in predefined classes and tracks through either getting the fastest time in a Time Trial, the highest placing in a race, or eliminating the most opponents through a weaponry-based deathmatch.
Gameplay
Most of the tracks in Wipeout 64 feature mirrored layouts of circuits from select tracks in Wipeout and Wipeout XL, set in different locations.
Development
Wipeout 64 was developed by Liverpudlian developer Psygnosis.
Development
After rumors that several publishers had approached Psygnosis about developing a Wipeout installment for the Nintendo 64, Psygnosis officially announced Wipeout 64 in April 1998.
Development
Development began in February 1998 and it took a total estimated amount of eight months to complete the game.
Development
Psygnosis originally intended to publish the game themselves with Sony Music Entertainment handling the distribution for Europe, but in September, Midway obtained publishing and distribution rights.
Development
It is a rare N64 title with noticeable load times, disguised by the request 'Please Wait', due to sound decompression times.
Development
Wipeout 64 utilized the N64's analogue stick, making ships more responsive than the series' predecessors.
Development
Rather than creating a full-fledged sequel to Wipeout 2097, Psygnosis decided to use Wipeout 2097 and tweak its design.
Development
Senior producer Andy Satterthwaite stated that Wipeout 64 is a brand-new game and not a port of its predecessor, due to changes to the game structure, new race tracks, and new features.
Development
During development, Psygnosis were impressed with the precision of the Nintendo 64 controller's control and were able to make the aircraft curve turns without sacrificing speed.
Audio

Despite the limited capacity of a game cartridge, Wipeout 64 fit nine music tracks, mostly by composers Rob Lord & Mark Bandola (credited as "PC MUSIC" in-game), with additional tracks by Fluke and Propellerheads.
Reception
The game received an aggregate score of 84/100 from Metacritic.
Reception
IGN remarked that Wipeout 64 was a superior game to F-Zero X.
Reception

Despite the considerable praise, a negative review came from Joe Fielder of GameSpot, saying that regarding the graphics, the visuals in Wipeout 64 did not meet the par set by Wipeout 2097 that was released for the PlayStation two years prior.
Reception

Most reviews compared the game with F-Zero X which was released a month earlier, with the general assumption that Nintendo 's own futuristic racer offered more tracks and racing craft, but Wipeout 64 contained superior track designs and atmosphere.
Reception
GameSpot criticized the game, saying that " WipeOut 64 isn't horrible, it just feels like the developer's first effort for the system at times – which it is".
Reception

"Sayewonn" of Gaming Age praised its new innovations, especially its analogue control, saying that "adapting analogue controls was the biggest improvement racing games made and Wipeout 64 demonstrates that beautifully".
Reception
Sayewonn also noted that the game still had a "learning curve", noting that "it's not as brutal as the first game but definitely harder than the far easier XL ".
Reception
Despite being complimentary of Wipeout 64, both GameSpot and Gaming Age recommended purchasing F-Zero X instead.
Reception

Gamepro, in addition, compared the game to Extreme-G2 and F-Zero X: "While Extreme G-2 may match Wipeout in content, it simply can't compete when trying to match W64 ' s speed and F-Zero X isn't even in the same league".
Reception
Opinion is divided on whether Wipeout 64 simply merges the good points of the previous two games, or is different enough to be considered a sequel in its own right.
Reception
Pop-up and a slow frame rate are repeatedly mentioned as problems, but only when the screen is split up to three or four times in multiplayer mode.

f64_extreme_go.title: Extreme-G
sents: lead
Extreme-G is a futuristic racing video game developed by Probe Entertainment and published by Acclaim Entertainment, featuring an original trance soundtrack.
lead
It was released for the Nintendo 64 in 1997, and was released in Japan on May 29, 1998.
lead
Despite the crowded field of Nintendo 64 racing games, Extreme-G was met with moderately positive reviews and was a commercial success.
lead
A sequel, Extreme-G 2, was released in 1998, followed by two additional games: Extreme-G 3 (2001) and XGRA: Extreme-G Racing Association (2003).
lead
In 2024, the game was re-released through the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack through Throwback Entertainment, who purchased the rights to the game in 2006.
Gameplay
As with all Extreme-G games, futuristic racing pilots race plasma -powered bikes in an intergalactic Grand Prix at speeds over 750 km/h.
Gameplay
The main game mode (Extreme Contest) features three championships: Atomic (four tracks), Critical Mass (eight tracks) and Meltdown (full 12 standard tracks).
Gameplay
The player must come first in each championship to progress.
Gameplay
Winning championships on the various difficulty levels will open up the hidden bikes, levels and cheats.
Reception
Most critics remarked that the techno soundtrack is unoriginal but does its job of enhancing the mood of the intense races.
Reception
Most reviews concluded that while a handful of shortcomings keep Extreme-G from being a top-ranked game, it was impressive enough to recommend.
Reception
GamePro, for instance, wrote that Extreme G will keep N64 racers sated until F-Zero 64 debuts.
Reception
Similarly, Peer Schneider of IGN opined that it can't compete with Wave Race 64 and Top Gear Rally in terms of graphics, physics and control, but ultimately recommended it for action and racing fans.
Reception
According to N64 Magazine, Extreme-G was a commercial success, selling 700,000 copies by October 1998.

f64_top_gear_rallie.title: Top Gear Rally
sents: lead
Top Gear Rally is a 1997 racing video game developed by Boss Game Studios and released for the Nintendo 64.
lead

A follow-up to Kemco ' s original Top Gear game, it features a championship mode where a single player must complete six seasons of two to four races, as well as a multiplayer mode where two players may compete against each other via a split-screen display.
lead
The game's tracks combine both road and off-road surfaces and can be played in different weather conditions, including night, fog, rain, and snow.
lead
Players may customize their car with different tire grips and adjust its suspension stiffness and steering sensitivity.
lead
An option that allows players to custom paint their cars is also included.
lead

Top Gear Rally was conceived after Boss created a non-interactive demonstration running on Silicon Graphics workstations that featured two- and four-wheel drive vehicles racing through different driving conditions.
lead
The game features a physics engine with a functioning suspension that reacts to a variety of challenging terrain.
lead
Although the cars featured in the game are fictitious, they were modeled after real vehicles.
Gameplay
Tracks are relatively open and may include hidden shortcuts, and each of them can be played in sunny, nocturnal, foggy, rainy, or snowy conditions.
Gameplay

In Championship mode, a single player must complete six seasons of two to four races in different weather conditions, with each race requiring the player to overtake 19 opponents controlled by the game's artificial intelligence.
Gameplay

A total of nine cars and four tracks are included in the game, in addition to two bonus cars and a hidden track that can be unlocked by completing the game and finishing first in every race during the last season of the Championship mode.
Development and release
Development of the game started in July 1996, after the company created a non-interactive demonstration that featured two- and four-wheel drive vehicles racing through different driving conditions.
Development and release
The demonstration was enough to convince Nintendo of America that Boss could develop a game for the Nintendo 64 console.
Development and release
A level editor, which would let players create their own tracks, and a Battle Mode similar to the combat-based races of Super Mario Kart, were originally planned to be included in the game.
Development and release

The developers opted to limit the multiplayer mode to two players because simultaneous four-player racing would have forced them to compromise on either the draw distance or their target frame rate of 30 frames per second.
Development and release

Although Boss did not have licenses to use automobile manufacturing brands, the cars featured in the game were modeled after real vehicles such as the Ford Escort, the Toyota Celica, the Toyota Supra, and the Porsche 959.
Development and release
The soundtrack was composed by Barry Leitch and produced in 8-bit samples.
Development and release
Top Gear Rally was originally intended to be released in the first quarter of 1997.
Development and release
In January 1997, nearly 50% of the game was complete, and by May around 80% of the game was complete.
Development and release
In North America, the game was published by Midway and released in September 30, 1997.
Development and release
The Japanese version, which was released on December 5, 1997, includes a built-in EEPROM in the Nintendo 64 Game Pak that allows players to save their progress without the need of a Controller Pak.
Reception
Top Gear Rally received generally positive reviews from critics, who considered it superior to MRC: Multi-Racing Championship —another Nintendo 64 game that shares similar features.
Reception

Graphically, N64 Magazine stated that Top Gear Rally rivals most arcade games of the time, while GamePro noted details such as the reflective mud in the game's jungle track and the fact that cars can be damaged.
PC port
Top Gear Rally was ported by Boss to Microsoft Windows in 1999.
PC port
Unlike the Nintendo 64 version, Boss Rally features three more cars and an additional track, and comprises three gameplay modes: Championship, Time Attack, and Quick Race.

f64_cruiz_n_world.title: Cruis'n World
sents: lead
Cruis'n World is a 1996 racing game developed by Midway Games and published by Nintendo.
lead
It is the sequel to the 1994 arcade racer Cruis'n USA.
lead
A port for the Nintendo 64 developed by Eurocom was released in 1998, and was the best received of the Cruis'n ports.
lead
Cruis'n World allows players to race on various tracks around the world.
lead
The game also features more cars than Cruis'n USA.
lead
This game introduced stunts to the Cruis'n series.
lead
They served to dodge obstacles, take close curves, and gain extra seconds of time.
Development
The development of the Nintendo 64 version started in 1996 after the development of the Nintendo 64 version of Cruis'n USA.
Development
Eugene Jarvis had admitted that Williams Entertainment 's port of Cruis'n USA was not good, so they promised the game to be an arcade perfect port.
Development
In early 1997, Nintendo announced that Cruis'n World would be coming to the Nintendo 64 in the fall, but the game was silently delayed until 1998.
Reception
The game was displayed at the 1996 AMOA show, where it won the award for Most Innovative New Title.
Reception
On review aggregation site GameRankings it held a score of 63% based on 14 reviews.
Reception
Next Generation reviewed the Nintendo 64 version of the game, rating it two stars out of five, criticising the game having minimal technique and difficulty.

f64_cruiz_n_usa.title: Cruis'n USA
sents: lead
Cruis'n USA is a racing video game developed by TV Games Inc. and published by Nintendo.
lead
It was first released in arcades in 1994 by Midway Games, with a port to the Nintendo 64 developed by Williams Electronics released in 1996.
lead
It is the first game in the Cruis'n series and features races set in locations across the continental United States.
lead

Cruis'n USA is branded as the first release of the "Ultra 64" platform collaboration between Midway and Nintendo, although it was based on the Midway V-unit arcade hardware, predating the Killer Instinct arcade hardware which would become the Nintendo 64.
lead
The home port was published by Nintendo as part of the deal.
lead
The arcade version was critically and commercially successful, drawing favorable comparisons to Sega 's Daytona USA.
lead
The Nintendo 64 version received poor reviews, but was also commercially successful.
lead
It was released on Wii 's Virtual Console in Europe on March 28, 2008, making it the first third party developed Nintendo 64 game to be released on the service.
Gameplay
Like in most racing games, players race down one-way courses consisting of streets vaguely based on real-life locations.
Gameplay
In each race, players must reach first place to advance to the next track, and there is a time limit to reach the goal, which can be extended by driving through checkpoints.
Gameplay
Unlike most racing games, there is the option to change the music by pressing the music button.
Vehicles
Bonus cars consist of a 1991 Chevrolet Caprice police car, a school bus, and a Jeep Wrangler labeled as an All Terrain Vehicle.
Development

In early 1994, Nintendo signed a licensing agreement with WMS Industries, Midway's parent company, which allowed Midway to release two arcade games advertised as the first version of Ultra 64 hardware and formed a joint venture named "Williams/Nintendo" to port those two games to its consoles.
Development
Eugene Jarvis, who had developed Defender (1981) and Robotron: 2084 (1982) for Williams Electronics, served as lead developer.
Development

Along with Killer Instinct, created by Rare, the arcade original was showcased at the June 1994 Consumer Electronics Show as running on Ultra 64 branded arcade hardware, sharing the branding of Nintendo's upcoming home console, codenamed Ultra 64.
Development
Cruis'n USA runs on a Midway V-Unit, which is very different from what would become the Silicon Graphics based Nintendo 64.
Development

The Midway V-unit consists of a 50 MHz TMS32031 CPU, a 10 MHz ADSP-2115 DSP for sound, and a custom 3D chip that can render perspective-correct but unfiltered quads at a high resolution (512 × 400 pixels).
Development
Williams Entertainment, the developers of the Nintendo 64 version, had to downgrade most of the arcade graphics to accommodate home console hardware.
Development

Originally announced as a Nintendo 64 launch game along with Killer Instinct Gold, less than a month before launch day it was pulled from the lineup and returned to Williams for retooling because it did not meet Nintendo's quality standards.
Development
Several elements of the game, such as the ability to run over animals, and depictions of Bill and Hillary Clinton, were censored from the Nintendo 64 version.
Development
During the last couple of months of development, people sent letters or emails about the censorship.
Reception

In the United States, RePlay reported Cruis'n USA to be the second most-popular deluxe arcade game in November 1994, and Play Meter listed the title to be the second most-popular arcade game in December 1994.
Reception
It was one of America's top five best-selling arcade video games of 1994, receiving a Diamond Award from the American Amusement Machine Association (AMAA).
Reception
It went on to be America's highest-grossing dedicated arcade cabinet of 1995.
Reception
The Nintendo 64 version met with mostly negative reviews, and earned a GameRankings score of 50.63% based on 16 reviews.
Reception
Next Generation concluded that "this half-hearted, rough-shod conversion is exactly what Nintendo 64 doesn't need".
Reception
GameSpot ' s Jeff Gerstmann and GamePro ' s Air Hendrix had more mixed reactions than most.
Reception
Gerstmann praised the controls when using the Nintendo 64 controller's analog stick, but concluded the game to be a major disappointment.
Reception

Air Hendrix, while heavily criticizing elements like the pop-up in the two-player mode and lack of variety in general, said it is essentially a faithful conversion of the arcade game and worth trying out as a rental, though not an outright purchase.
Reception

Kujawa's co-reviewer Dean Hager said the game "certainly fails to show off the processing power of the N64", and Shneider said it lacked excitement and was "probably doomed to be the nadir of N64 racing games for many years to come."
Reception

Despite the negative reviews, the Nintendo 64 version of Cruis'n USA saw strong sales, thanks largely to a combination of the console's popularity and the small library of games available for it at the time.
Reception
It was the sixth best-selling video game of the 1996 Christmas shopping season according to TRST data, with three of the five higher-selling games also being Nintendo 64 games.
Reception
By the end of 1997 it had sold over a million copies.
Reception
In 1995, Flux magazine ranked the arcade version 63rd on its "Top 100 Video Games."

f64_rooad_rash_64.title: Road Rash 64

Artist(s): Chris Adams Ben Ridgway Dane Shears Brian Walker

sents: lead
Road Rash 64 is a racing video game developed by Pacific Coast Power and Light and published by THQ for the Nintendo 64.
lead
The game is the fifth of seven entries in the Road Rash series of video games, the only entry to be published by THQ and the only to be released for the Nintendo 64 platform.
Gameplay
The ultimate goal is to place first in the race, and do damage to others, in order to gain more money to upgrade the player's motorcycle.
Development
Unlike most games in the series, it was not developed or published by Electronic Arts, but rather by Pacific Coast Power and Light and published by THQ respectively.
Development
The game was originally thought to be a straight port of the game Road Rash 3D for the PlayStation.
Development

With the addition of the Expansion Pak in the Nintendo 64 system, alternate graphics options, wide screen, letterboxed, and high resolution settings, were available to choose from in addition to the default graphics setting.

f64_nffl_blitz.title: NFL Blitz

Platform(s): Arcade, Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Game Boy Color, Microsoft Windows, Dreamcast, PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube, Game Boy Advance, PlayStation 3, Xbox 360

sents: lead
NFL Blitz is a series of American football themed video games originally released by Midway featuring National Football League (NFL) teams.
lead
It began as a 1997 arcade game NFL Blitz that was ported to home consoles and spawned a series of sequels.
lead

Rather than being designed as a realistic interpretation of the sport of football, like Madden NFL or NFL 2K, the Blitz series was created as an over-the-top, exaggerated version of the sport, inspired by Midway's own NBA Jam basketball games.
lead

In 2005, after losing the NFL license, Midway relaunched the Blitz series as Blitz: The League, depicting fictional players and teams in a fictional league with slightly more realistic (though still exaggerated) on-field play and a focus on the seedy behind-the-scenes lives of the players.
lead

Following the dissolution of Midway, EA Sports acquired the rights to the Blitz name and relaunched the series on PlayStation Network and Xbox Live with a new entry in the series simply titled NFL Blitz.
lead
The game took the series back to the original style of Blitz, but removed the late hits due to input by the NFL.
Gameplay
Not only were there fewer players, but positions were flexible at best.
Gameplay
2002 saw an increase to eight players and NFL Blitz Pro (released in 2003) increased to the full eleven.
Gameplay
Extra point attempts are claimed to be automatic, but there are rare misses.
Gameplay
For most releases, a first down would mean players would have to go 30 yards, instead of ten.
Gameplay
Plays such as "Da Bomb" allowed for a quarterback to accurately throw the ball most of the length of the field at will and receivers could make impossible catches.
Gameplay
Where other games had to keep normal tackling and stops, Blitz players were able to stop a play in a variety of unique ways.
Gameplay
One of the most common was for a defensive player to grab his opponent and spin him around and fling him to the ground, sometimes giving them extra yards in the process.
Gameplay
The NFL, however, made Midway tame most of the more violent or insane aspects of the game as the license progressed.
Gameplay
Subsequent releases stripped down "excessive celebrations" and late hits until the game was almost one of the sims to which it was originally opposed.
Games
Beginning in 1997, Midway released a new entry in the series each year.
Games
However, after the commercial failure of the more simulation-oriented Blitz Pro, Midway did not release a Blitz in 2004 for the first time since the series began.
Games
After losing the NFL license to Electronic Arts, Midway brought back the original Blitz style play with 2005's Blitz: The League.
Games
The celebrations and the violent aspects returned and were ramped up to levels that the NFL never allowed.
Games
As a result of the mature themes in the title, The League is the first and only professional football franchise to ever receive the "Mature" rating from the ESRB and was banned in Australia.
Games
A sequel, Blitz: The League II was released on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on October 13, 2008.
Games
In 2000 Midway released a spinoff to Blitz based on the Arena Football League titled Kurt Warner's Arena Football Unleashed for the PlayStation.
Reception
Gamerankings.com gives the PlayStation 2 release a score of 75% and the Xbox release a score of 77%.
Reception
GameSpot.com gave both PS2 and Xbox versions an 8.6/10.

f64_ken_griffo_jr_s_slugfest.title: Ken Griffey Jr.'s Slugfest
sents: lead
Ken Griffey Jr.'s Slugfest is a 1999 baseball video game developed by Angel Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was released in May 1999 only in North America.
lead
A Game Boy Color port developed by Software Creations was released in June 1999.
lead

Featuring real-life player Ken Griffey Jr., it is a sequel to Major League Baseball Featuring Ken Griffey Jr., released for the Nintendo 64, which itself was preceded by Software Creation's Ken Griffey Jr.
lead
Presents Major League Baseball and Rare 's Ken Griffey Jr.'s Winning Run, both released for the Super NES.
lead
This version of the game contains actual player names, unlike the original.
lead
It contains Season, Exhibition, World Series and Home Run Derby modes.
Gameplay
The batting feature in this game is set up differently from most other baseball video games.
Gameplay
The fielding portion of this game makes use of the c-directional pad on the Nintendo 64 controller.
Gameplay
For example, c-right represents first base, c-up represents second base, c-left represents third base, and c-down represents home plate.
Gameplay
Every pitcher has his own unique set of pitches and no pitcher can throw all the pitches.
Gameplay
The speed of the pitches can range anywhere from 37 mph to 103 mph.
Reception
The Nintendo 64 version received favorable reviews, while the Game Boy Color version received mixed reviews, according to the review aggregation website GameRankings.

f64_waiolae_country_club_golf.title: Waialae Country Club: True Golf Classics
sents: lead
Waialae Country Club: True Golf Classics is a golf video game developed by T&E Soft and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 in 1998.
lead

It is part of the True Golf Classics series (New 3D Golf Simulation in Japan) Although set at the same real life golf course, it is a different game than True Golf Classics: Waialae Country Club, released in 1991 for the Super NES.
lead

It was preceded by the game Masters '98: Haruka Naru Augusta, which was released in Japan in 1997; although both have very similarly styled graphics and gameplay, they are set at different golf courses.
lead
The game gained speedrunning notoriety in March 2021 after YouTuber Kurtis Conner made a video in which he broke the world record speedrun time.
Reception
The graphics received negative reviews, citing how poor the graphics were for how late the game was released in the Nintendo 64's life cycle.

f64_army_men_sarge_z_heroes.title: Army Men: Sarge's Heroes
sents: lead
Army Men: Sarge's Heroes is a third-person shooter video game and the fourth entry in The 3DO Company 's Army Men series (1998–2003), which are based on the green plastic figures of the same name.
lead
Its Nintendo 64 and PlayStation versions were developed and published by The 3DO Company.
lead
The port for the Dreamcast was developed by Saffire and published by Midway, while another for Microsoft Windows was published by GT Interactive.
lead
Excluding the 1999 North American release for the Nintendo 64 version, the game was released in 2000.
lead

The primary single-player mode depicts the Green Army, led by Colonel Grimm, fighting against General Plastro's Tan Army, which have found portals to Our World (the human world) that contain useful weapons when fighting in Their World (the world where the plastic soldiers reside).
lead

In 3D battlefields of both worlds, the player acts as plastic soldiers, either the titular Sargent Hawk or one of five members of a group of the army's best troops he leads, the Bravo Company, completing a variety of missions, such as rescues, capturing blue spies, killing enemies and destroying portals.
lead
In the game's multi-player modes, tan, gray or blue soldiers are options for playable characters.
lead
The game features variations of 13 weapons.
Gameplay
Army Men: Sarge's Heroes is a third-person shooter where players take the role of soldiers in 3D battlefields.
Gameplay

It has the feel, pace, weapons and level design of classic arcade shooters like Ikari Warriors (1986) and Guerrilla War (1987), and also features elements of GoldenEye (1997), Command & Conquer (1995), and platform video games.
Gameplay
On the Green Army's base, the game's first mission is the leader of the Bravo Company that did not get captured, Sargent Hawk, getting Grimm, his mentor, to an escape chopper.
Gameplay
The Nintendo 64 and PlayStation versions have 14 missions with up to five objectives each, the Dreamcast 16 missions with three-to-four objectives each, totaling to 40.
Gameplay
Other options are to view the character from the front or first-person, activated with the press of a button.
Gameplay
The 3D spaces can theoretically be traversed at the player's own free will, but the missions can be completed by following a path with no requirement for backtracking.
Gameplay

With control that heavily uses context-sensitive buttons like a previously released Nintendo 64 game, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998), the player can jump, climb, latch onto ledges, drop and roll, crawl, crouch, strafe, and sneak up to enemies and attack them typical in stealth games.
Gameplay
Sharp, a Morter Man with a surfer dude personality; Thick, the M-60 Machine Gunner with a strong aim but low intelligence; and Scorch, a Flamethrower so mentally-unstable he loves being near fire.
Gameplay
In single player, Sarge and whoever is rescued are the only playable characters; in a mission, a rescued soldier assists for the remainder of a mission, which ends prematurely if they die.
Gameplay
Some tasks can be only be achieved with certain equipment; soldiers on mountaintops can only be killed with snipers, and those in bunkers with grenades.
Gameplay
All weapons besides the default M16 rifle are out of the soldiers' bag if a life is lost.
Gameplay
In a Family Mode borrowed from 3DO's BattleTanx (1998), players can individually choose the difficulty level of the choice of weapons, i.e. ones that are quicker to adapt to.
Background
In the late 1990s, following the failure of the 3DO Interactive Multiplayer console, The 3DO Company transitioned to developing and publishing only software.
Background

The move started with the Nintendo 64 multiplayer game Battletanx and the tactical PC game Army Men (based on the green plastic toy soldiers of the same name), both developed by separate teams, released around the same time in 1998, and landing in the top-ten of sales charts.
Background
Potato Head and Slinky Dog, caused by a film that featured them, Toy Story (1995).
Background

Before Army Men: Sarge's Heroes, the series had covered multiple genres and platforms with two tactics games, the first game and its sequel Army Men II (1999) which were both released for PC and the Game Boy Color, and a PlayStation third-person shooter, Army Men 3D (1999).
Background

Wrote Joe Fielder of GameSpot, Army Men 3D, the series' first console entry, "lacked a great deal of spit and polish but had enough going deep down to make you hope for a sequel, albeit one that was much improved".
Conception and design
Justin Bates, Ben Lopez and Jon "Pan" Oakley were only credited as designer on the Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast releases, James Farley only on the PlayStation.
Conception and design

Hawkins and Mendheim established Sarge's Heroes as the franchise's inaugural character-oriented action-adventure game, taking inspiration from the style of Super Mario (1985–present) and incorporating mission design akin to GoldenEye (1997).
Conception and design
A PlayStation version was announced a month later on April 6, with the clarification that it would not be a sequel to Army Men 3D but another version of the previously announced Nintendo 64 game.
Conception and design

This direction was influenced by the Mutant League games he worked on at EA, which included Mutant League Football (1993) and Mutant League Hockey (1994) and spawned a cartoon show of the same name (1994–1996).
Conception and design
The only character from a predecessor was the titular protagonist, who was in Army Men 3D.
Conception and design

Although parts of the game would be fighting in the semi-realistic environments of Army Men and Army Men 3D, "I wanted to have these soldiers fighting on kitchen countertops, in a bathtub and under a Christmas tree " as well.
Conception and design
Fury and his Howling Commandos (1963–1981) and war films like The Dirty Dozen (1976) were inspirations for the characters.
Conception and design
Barney Fife from The Andy Griffith Show (1960–1968) inspired the inclusion of a timid character.
Production
On the Nintendo 64, the technical director was Dan Geisler, an industry veteran who created EA's Road Rash (1991).
Production
In the late 1990s, The 3DO Company attempted to have a prolific output with far less money than EA when trying to enter the software market.
Production
Mendheim improved himself from these experiences, learning how to make games that looked and felt high-value with limited resources.
Production

Although he has never revealed the start and end dates of development, he reported Army Men: Sarge's Heroes was done under a year, and in the last two months, members of the team were working 16–18 hours a day, not going home on some days.
Production
Mendheim, in 2022, felt the game needed three more months to fix issues of the camera and difficulty balance.
Production
A pre-alpha version of the Nintendo 64 game was reviewed in a "Hands On" feature by IGN, published on March 5, 1999.
Production
Next Generation ' s June 1999 insider coverage of the game concluded development was "pretty far along for a fall release date".
Presentation
In the end, more than 150 hand-drawn animations were completed for the project.
Presentation
A "Hands On" preview feature from IGN on March 5, 1999, described its animation as "disney-style", with "Realistic movements and funny death animations".
Presentation
Charnes was a main artist and Kennedy and Groark only additional artists on the Nintendo 64.
Presentation
For the Nintendo 64 game, Animatek was an additional artist.
Presentation

Although Mendheim felt the Nintendo 64 could render in-game graphics better, the PlayStation had the capacity to play video files, influencing the creation of video cutscenes for the PlayStation version.
Presentation
Susan Blu was the only other voice actor, playing Vikki.
Release and promotion
On the night of March 4, 1999, The 3DO Company held a hidden "pre- E3 bash" in San Francisco.
Release and promotion

Army Men, in its second year of existence in 1999, saw five games: Army Men II, Army Men 3D, Army Men: Sarge's Heroes, Army Men: Air Attack and Army Men: Toys in Space, the latter three released at the end of the year.
Release and promotion
Army Men: Sarge's Heroes was the first Nintendo 64 Army Men game, released in 1999 in North America on September 28 and Australia in November.
Release and promotion
On the PlayStation, Army Men: Sarge's Heroes was released in 2000, on February 23 in North America and August 17 in Europe.
Critical response
On GameRankings, average ratings of versions of the game range from 49% to 62%.
Concept

The toys alternating between both universes intrigued IGN ' s Dean Austin and Electronic Gaming Monthly ' s (EGM) John Davison as unusually ambitious for the contemporary era of gaming, and N64 Magazine ' s Jess Bickham as a "inspiring" combination of GoldenEye and the Micro Machines series (1991–2017).
Concept

In the memory of Tom Chick of CNET Gamecenter, the only other times a toy-sized playable character in massive settings had been tried was in a few maps of PC games, such as a library in Sin ' s (1998) deathmatch mode, and Unreal ' s (1998) DMBreakfast map.
Gameplay

The Electric Playground ' s Miguel Lopez called Army Men: Sarge's Heroes "unexquisite torture" to play, while AllGame ' s Shawn Sackenheim explained the "cheap thrill" of the training mission was the game's most fun.
Gameplay
Wrote Boyer, the perfect precision of the auto-aim made progression "mindless", with the occasional aggravation from a sudden death by an enemy that pops up out of nowhere.
Controls and camera
Praise was limited to a comment by Chick, who called the button layout "very good".
Controls and camera

Scary Larry of GamePro also targeted the traversal control; although switching weapons was always reliable and movements like strafing, crouching and rolling were only a bit harder, traversing was jerky to the point of being useless of getting out of enemy fire.
Controls and camera
The most condemned specific of the control was turning.
Controls and camera
Wrote Sackenheim, the Nintendo 64 control setup was the same as the PlayStation's, meaning holding left and right on the analog stick turned the camera, making the character turning more cumbersome.
Controls and camera
Perry derided the absence of backing off, meaning taking a long time to turn around before moving forward was the only way to get out of a bombardment of shooting enemies in front.
Controls and camera
As a consequence, to avoid the shots of a bombardment of enemies, the easy-to-use auto-aim of the default weapon was not only useful but also necessary, according to Austin, Axel, Boyer and Lopez.
Controls and camera
A few critics explained the biggest cause of frustration was the combination of controls and camera problems.
Controls and camera
Now, you only have to maneuver two or three awkward circles around it, and it’s yours.
Weapons
When it came to weapons, Army Men: Sarge's Heroes was mostly praised for its high quantity and variety, N64 Magazine ' s Jes Bickham calling them "mostly fun".
Weapons
Richie Shoemaker of the UK edition of Official Dreamcast Magazine called its weapon variety lesser than Toy Commander (1999), which was more focused on vehicles than combat.
Weapons

Adam negatively described the shooting cursor of the first-person perspective as too slow, and PlayStation Pro ' s Will Johnston and Mega Fun ' s Georg called close-up combat so inaccurate the enemy was just as likely to injure the player character as vice versa.
Weapons
Axel did however, enjoy the auto-aim of the M16 and admitted the snipper was his favorite weapon.
Weapons
Perry called mines useless for blowing up a tank, stating it would take at least 45 minutes as a result of poor collision detection and the number of mines required for an explosion (four to five).
Technical flaws
In Perry's play-through, he faced enemies that would attack if their back was only approached, and those that did nothing even if several bullets were being shot close behind.
Technical flaws
The N64 and PS1 versions were reported to have an abundance of fog and pop-ups caused by a low draw distance, hindering navigation and detracting from the experience.
Technical flaws
Mahood wrote that it was hard to see 20 feet away of the player character, Jake the Snake 50 feet.
Technical flaws
A small minority of reviews commented on the framerate, choppy on the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation versions, and consistent for the Dreamcast.
Technical flaws
In a Nintendo 64 review for Superjuegos, De Lucar claimed that on single-player, it was choppy but not to the point of being unplayable, while it was worse in two-player.
Graphics
Perry, CNET Gamecenter critic Tom Chick, and GameSpot writer Joe Fiedler called the graphics weaker than 3D games released in the previous few years, N64 Gamer ' s Arthur Adam on par.
Graphics
On the Nintendo 64, Sackenheim considered the explosion effects a success, suggesting players would "crack a smile", if not be amazed, by them.
Graphics
Reviewers of the Nintendo 64 version were amazed by the use of lighting and shining effects on the soldiers' surface material, truly realized with the Game Pak activated.
Graphics
The animations were also acclaimed by Smith, Adam and Chick, who called them as "smooth and graceful" as GoldenEye 007.
Graphics
Some reviewers were disappointed with the scarcity of props in the 3D spaces, although Austin and Axel clarified it was much less of a problem in the human world.
Differences between versions

A reviewer for the US edition of Official Dreamcast Magazine, Chris Charla, cited it as part of a trend of Dreamcast ports where only some aspects of the visuals were "photo-realistic" and others on par with the PlayStation.
Differences between versions

Anthony Chau of IGN opined the graphics were "just plain old and average", failing to meet the standards of even a first-generation Dreamcast game, Sonic Adventure (1998), as well as games released on the console the year before, Shenmue (1999) and Quake III Arena (1999).
Comparisons to other games
Conversely, Rybicki was disappointed by how poor he perceived Sarge's Heroes to be in comparison to Army Men 3D, concluding that the inclusion of real world levels was the only superior aspect.
Comparisons to other games

Andy, the Game Hombre of Game Informer, a fan of Army Men 3D, critique'd Sarge's Heroes ' difference from the predecessor as too small, elaborating that first-timers to the series would be entertained but players of the previous game will get the same experience, except new missions.
Comparisons to other games
Jake the Snake did, however, find it inferior to Medal of Honor (1999) and Syphon Filter 2 (2000).
Commercial performance

When announcing the release of a PlayStation port, Hawkins announced Army Men: Sarge's Heroes as the best-selling game in the series so far, and doing better than most other 3DO games, such as Battletanx and games in the company's Might and Magic (1996–2003) and High Heat (1998–2003) properties.
Commercial performance

Upon its October 1999 release, the Nintendo 64 version debuted at number four on Video Software Dealers Association 's console game rental chart, above Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace (1999) but below the chart-topping Pokémon Snap (1999) and two PlayStation games, Driver (1999) and WCW Mayhem (1999).
Commercial performance

In Patrick Hickey Jr.'s feature on the development of the game in the 2022 book The Mind Behind Playstation Games, it was reported that its Nintendo 64 and PlayStation versions combined sold 1.3 million units.
Commercial performance
In an interview conducted for the book, Mendheim stated it was a number-one hit on the Nintendo 64 chart and a top-ten hit for that of the PlayStation.
Legacy
Many later Army Men games, including 3DO's final game for the franchise Army Men: RTS (2002), would star all of the characters introduced in Army Men: Sarge's Heroes.
Legacy
A spin-off game starring Vikki, Portal Runner (2001), was released on the PlayStation 2.
Legacy

Army Men: Sarge's Heroes spawned two sequels of its own: Army Men: Sarge's Heroes 2 (2000) and Army Men: Sarge's War (2004), the latter of which was developed and released after The 3DO Company's selling of the franchise to Global Star Software.
Legacy
Zoey Hendley, in 2021, noted its prolific output as more than that of franchises like Guitar Hero (2005–2015).
Legacy

Hickey Jr. explained retrospective players and writers debate which Army Men had the longest staying power, but he felt the arcade-style gameplay and child-friendly plot of Army Men: Sarge's Heroes made it the most accessible.
Legacy

Digital Cybercherries ' shooter game Hypercharge: Unboxed (2020), conceived out of the development team's session of watching Small Soldiers (1998) on television, was partially influenced by Army Men: Sarge's Heroes.

f64_tetrisphure.title: Tetrisphere
sents: lead
Tetrisphere is a puzzle video game developed by H2O Entertainment and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
lead
It was released in North America on August 11, 1997, and in PAL regions in February 1998.
lead
The game, originally named Phear, was slated for release on the Atari Jaguar in early 1995, but was reworked into a Tetris game for the N64 after Nintendo obtained its publishing rights.
lead
Tetrisphere is a variant on Tetris in which various shapes are shifted across a wrapped three-dimensional grid resembling a sphere, and then destroyed.
lead
The objective of the game changes depending on the mode but generally consists of removing layers of shapes to reach the playing field's core.
lead
Despite very little domestic advertising, Tetrisphere enjoyed moderately good sales and a mostly favorable critical reception.
lead
Reviewers praised the game's originality and the musical score composed by Neil Voss.
Gameplay
In most Tetris titles, a player's score is incremented as a result of completing "lines", where a row of brick pieces that is without gaps is removed from the 2D playing field.
Gameplay
The only exception is that the pieces involved (including the original three) must abide by the rules which dictate which pieces are "touching".
Gameplay
First, is that if a combo is started with a power piece, the combo takes longer to finish.
Gameplay
The combo multiplier starts at 1x, and it has a maximum multiplier of 20x.
Gameplay
If a combo results in 20 or more pieces being removed, no power pieces will appear on the sphere.
Gameplay
Whenever a life is lost, any unused magic is lost, the combo multiplier resets to 1x, and the speed meter resets to a full blue timer.
Gameplay
Finally, a hidden "Lines" mode exists, where pieces cannot be dropped.
Development
Tetrisphere was developed by H2O Entertainment, a game development company founded by Steve Shatford, Christopher Bailey, and Michael Tam, which was based in Calgary, Alberta, Canada.
Development
Nintendo reportedly secured the rights to Phear after seeing the game showcased at WCES '95, and it was announced as a Nintendo 64 game at Nintendo Space World that same year.
Development
H2O, which had completed a reverse takeover with Canadian Entech Resources Inc., began working exclusively for Nintendo during the game's development.
Development
Around the time the company went public, Nintendo announced that Tetrisphere would be released in October 1996, boosting the company's stock.
Development
"That was the first they had heard of the release date," the Canadian Business magazine said.
Development
"We weren't able to disclose any information," H2O developer Michael Tam said.
Development
The game was developed on Silicon Graphics Indy, Indigo and O2 workstations.
Development
The graphics were created with SoftImage running on Indigo and O2 workstations.
Development
The game was written in the C programming language and compiled to target 'Ultra64' development boxes for testing and bug tracking.
Development
Senior developers improved the engine so that only part of the sphere is visible at any time, thus reducing the render load on the N64 hardware.
Development
The framerate was increased, allowing for a two-player mode not present in the first version.
Development
The North American release of Tetrisphere was ultimately delayed until August 1997, when it became the first puzzle game available on the Nintendo 64.
Development
The techno -style soundtrack for Tetrisphere was composed by Neil Voss using FastTracker 2 on a Pentium PC.
Development

Voss explained that Tetrisphere features only stereophonic sound because " for a game where the action is all around you, it could enhance gameplay and the immersive experience." Voss was also able to simulate surround sound.
Reception

Next Generation dissented with the majority, stating that "Graphically, Tetrisphere doesn't live up to most other Nintendo 64 games - the most obvious flaw is an annoying pop-up as the player rotates the globe."
Reception
Out of 42 titles, Tetrisphere ranked at number 27 in terms of sales for Nintendo games in 1997.
Reception
H2O Entertainment announced that the game had sold 430,000 copies worldwide as of March 31, 1998.
Reception
Nintendo Power ranked Tetrisphere at number 50 on its list of "100 Best Nintendo Games of All Time" in September 1997.
Reception
IGN considered the game's soundtrack to be the fourth best of any N64 game.

f64_toy_storie_2.title: Toy Story 2 (video game)
sents: lead
Toy Story 2 is a 1999 side-scrolling platform game for Game Boy Color based on the film of the same name.
lead
The game was developed by Tiertex Design Studios and published by THQ.
lead
It was released in November 1999 in North America with the European version releasing the following year.
lead

Superman: The New Superman Adventures, commonly referred to as Superman 64, is an action-adventure video game developed and published by Titus Interactive for the Nintendo 64 and based on the television series Superman: The Animated Series.
lead
Released in North America on May 29, 1999, and in Europe on July 23, it is the first 3D Superman game.
lead

In the game, Lex Luthor has trapped Jimmy Olsen, Lois Lane, and Professor Hamilton in a virtual reality version of Metropolis that he created with the help of Brainiac, leaving it up to Superman to save them and break apart the virtual world.
lead

The game shifts between outdoor levels where the player flies through rings while saving civilians, and indoor levels where the player looks for access cards, activates computers, and fights villains such as Brainiac, Mala, Metallo, Darkseid, and Parasite.
lead
The development of Superman began in 1997 and was largely hampered by constraints between Titus and the game's licensors, Warner Bros. and DC Comics, leaving little room for polishing the gameplay.
lead
BlueSky Software attempted to redo the game for the PlayStation, but this version was ultimately canceled, as Titus's license with Warner Bros had expired by the time it was completed.
lead

With three E3 presentations and positive press coverage before its release, Superman 64 was released to strong sales and positive consumer reception; however, critical reviews were extremely negative, panning its unresponsive controls, technical flaws, repetitive gameplay, overuse of distance fog, and poor graphics.
lead
It is widely considered one of the worst video games ever made.
Gameplay

Superman's other superpowers, including Heat Vision, Freeze Breath, X-Ray Vision, Super Speed, and Reprogrammation (where Superman reprograms an enemy to help fight off other enemies), are only accessible through the collection of power-ups in certain levels and have limited reserves.

The penultimate ride stage and the penultimate regular stage are only playable on Normal and Superman modes, and the concluding ride stage and regular stage only on Superman mode.

In early 1997 Titus signed a licensing deal with Warner Bros. to make games based on Superman: The Animated Series for the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, and Game Boy.
Development

Caen's initial plan was for a style of gameplay only Tomb Raider (1996) had tried before, a 3D open world action-adventure video game involving real-time strategy where players really behave as a superhero.
Development

As he explained, "it would stretch the Nintendo 64 to its limits, feature Superman's ability to fly and fight, and include his every superpower", but it would be too much for the Nintendo 64's limitations.
Development
Only a few days after the deal was made, the Warner Bros. licensing team changed.
Development
The first demand was to make Superman "a Sim City -like game, where Superman would be like the mayor of Metropolis", instead of an action game.
Development
Warner Bros. only got more coercive after Titus rejected the idea, going against any decision of the French developer.
Development
Often, their reasoning for rejection was that Superman would never do the things Titus proposed.
Development
Although the ring stages were originally supposed to be tutorial stages, they became a part of regular gameplay due to the other changes.

Animation World Network, however, was more optimistic, claiming that the game appeared to have "stunning 3D environments, various fight levels and rescue operations".
Pre-release publicity
At the time of the 1997 E3 showing, the release date was set for late 1997, but was delayed.

Superman was one of only five Nintendo 64 games presented at the 1999 Tokyo Game Show.

After the critical failure of the N64 version, Titus gave BlueSky Software the reins to completely redesign Superman for the PlayStation.
