The game received approval from Sony, but the license from Warner Bros. had expired and Titus was unable to secure a new one, resulting in the game's cancellation in 2000.

All of this contradicted Superman 64 ' s contemporaneous critical reputation, filled with claims of being one of the worst games of all time.

sents: lead
The Super NES CD-ROM (commonly abbreviated to SNES-CD) is an unreleased add-on for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) video game console.
lead
It was built upon the functionality of the cartridge -based SNES by adding support for a CD-ROM -based format known as Super Disc.
lead
The SNES-CD was developed in a joint venture between Nintendo and Sony and was publicly announced in 1990.
lead
Sony also planned to release it as a hybrid console, the Play Station and planned to use their Super Disc for video and other multimedia.
lead
A separate partnership with Philips led to the development of a CD-ROM/XA format add-on for SNES, and separately yielded a few Nintendo-themed games on the CD-i format.
lead
Eventually the three companies agreed on a common CD standard.
lead
The project moved to a 32-bit system and specifications were completed near end 1992, but by the summer of 1993, Nintendo quietly canceled the addon entirely.
lead
After the SNES-CD was canceled, Sony developed its own new and unrelated console using the PlayStation name.
History

Sony was uninterested in the video game business, so most of his superiors did not approve of the project, but Kutaragi found support in Sony executive Norio Ohga and the project was allowed to continue.
History
Development of the format started in late 1988, when Nintendo signed the contract with Sony.
History

Nintendo had become suspicious of Sony's growth, because of the combination of the audio chip, Sony's PlayStation hybrid console, and Sony's rapid expansion beyond its electronics origins into music, movies, and most recently software.
History
In 1992, a deal was reached allowing Sony to produce SNES-compatible hardware, with Nintendo retaining control and profit over the games.
History
The organizations never repaired their rift, although Sony executives remained convinced that remaining with the more experienced Nintendo was the best course of action.
Prototype
In July 2015, it was reported that one of the original Nintendo PlayStation prototypes had been found.
Prototype
The prototype was reportedly abandoned by former Sony Computer Entertainment CEO Ólafur Jóhann Ólafsson during his time at Advanta.
Prototype
A former Advanta worker, Terry Diebold, acquired the device as part of a lot during Advanta's 2009 bankruptcy auction.
Prototype
The prototype came with a Sony/PlayStation-branded version of the standard Super Famicom controller (model number SHVC-005).
Prototype

In March 2016, retro-gaming website RetroCollect reported that it (and influential members of online emulation communities) had received (from an anonymous source) a functional disc boot ROM for the SNES-CD.
Prototype
Diebold had given the unit to hardware hacker Benjamin Heckendorn, to examine around 2017.
Prototype
The prototype was auctioned by Diebold in February 2020, with an initial price of US$15,000, but the auction quickly exceeded $350,000 within two days.
Prototype

It was sold for $360,000 to Greg McLemore, an entrepreneur and founder of Pets.com, who has a large collection of other video game hardware and plans to establish a permanent museum for this type of hardware.
Technical specifications
Heckendorn's July 2016 teardown video provides technical specifications of the prototype.
Technical specifications
The specifications from the prototype are different from those published in the March 1993 edition of Electronic Gaming Monthly (EGM).
Legacy
The main game in development for the SNES-CD platform launch was Square 's Secret of Mana, whose planned content was cut down to the size suitable for cartridge and released on that medium instead.
Legacy

A tentative reconciliation in late 1992 gave better terms to Nintendo for game royalties while allowing Sony royalties for all other software and the rights to produce SNES-compatible hardware, such as the PlayStation.
Legacy
Sony released the PlayStation in December 1994 in Japan and September 1995 in North America and Europe.
Legacy

This CD-only console successfully competed with Nintendo's cartridge-based Nintendo 64 and other CD-based consoles such as the Fujitsu FM Towns Marty, the NEC PC-FX, the SNK Neo Geo CD, the Panasonic 3DO Interactive Multiplayer, and the Sega Saturn, causing it to become the console leader.
Legacy

The broken partnership with Sony has often been cited as a mistake by Nintendo, effectively creating a formidable rival in the video game market as a consequence of Sony's and Kutaragi's shrewd determination to break into the market.
Legacy
Nintendo, still convinced of the faster load times and stronger anti-piracy of the cartridge, did not release an optical disc -based console until the GameCube in 2001.

sents: lead
The Atari Jaguar is a home video game console developed by Atari Corporation and released in North America in November 1993.
lead
Part of the fifth generation of video game consoles, it competed with the 16-bit Sega Genesis, the Super NES and the 32-bit 3DO Interactive Multiplayer that launched the same year.
lead
Powered by two custom 32-bit processors – Tom and Jerry – in addition to a Motorola 68000, Atari marketed it as the world's first 64-bit game system, emphasizing its 64-bit bus used by the blitter.
lead
The Jaguar launched with Cybermorph as the pack-in game, which received divisive reviews.
lead
The system's library ultimately comprised only 50 licensed games.
lead
Development of the Atari Jaguar started in the early 1990s by Flare Technology, which focused on the system after cancellation of the Atari Panther console.
lead
The Jaguar was an important system for Atari after the company shifted its focus from computers - having ceased development of its Atari ST - back to consoles.
lead
However, the multi-chip architecture, hardware bugs, and poor tools made writing games for the Jaguar difficult.
Development
Atari Corporation's previous home video game console, the Atari 7800, was released in 1986.
Development
Around 1989 work began on a new console leveraging technology from their Atari ST computers.
Development
Originally named the Super XE - following the Atari XE Game System - it eventually became the Atari Panther using either 16 or 32-bit architecture.
Development
The team had claimed that they could not only make a console superior to the Genesis or the Super NES, but they could also be cost-effective.
Development

Work on the Jaguar design progressed faster than expected, so Atari canceled the Panther project in 1991 to focus on the more promising Jaguar, and rumors were already circulating of a 1992 launch and its 32-bit or even 64-bit architecture.
Development
Support for Atari's legacy 8-bit products were dropped to fully focus on developing the Jaguar console, while their line of ST computers were dropped during the Jaguar's release in 1993.
Development
The Atari Jaguar was unveiled in at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in June 1993, calling it a "multi-media entertainment system".
Launch
The Jaguar was launched on November 23, 1993, at a price of $249.99, under a $500 million manufacturing deal with IBM.
Launch
The system was initially available only in the test markets of New York City and San Francisco, with the slogan "Get bit by Jaguar", claiming superiority over competing 16-bit and 32-bit systems.
Launch
A nationwide release followed six months later, in early 1994.
Launch
Atari reported that it had shipped 17,000 units as part of the system's initial test market in 1993.
Launch
By the end of 1994, it reported that it had sold approximately 100,000 units.
Launch

Atari had "ventured late into third-party software support" for the Jaguar while competing console 3DO 's "18 month public relations blitz" would result in "an avalanche of software support", the magazine reported.
Launch
Jaguar did eventually earn praise with games such as Tempest 2000, Doom, and Wolfenstein 3D.

With only one or two exceptions – Tempest 2000 is cited most frequently – there have just been no truly great games for the Jaguar up to now." Bit count controversy

Atari tried to downplay competing consoles by proclaiming the Jaguar was the only "64-bit" system; in its marketing in the American market the company used the tagline do the math!, in reference to the 64 number.
Bit count controversy
This claim is questioned by some, because the Motorola 68000 CPU and the Tom and Jerry coprocessors execute 32-bit instruction sets.
Arrival of Saturn and PlayStation
In early 1995, Atari announced that it had dropped the price of the Jaguar to $149.99, to be more competitive.
Arrival of Saturn and PlayStation
These aired for most of 1995, but did not sell the remaining stock of Jaguar systems.
Arrival of Saturn and PlayStation

In a 1995 interview with Next Generation, then-CEO Sam Tramiel declared that the Jaguar was as powerful, if not more powerful, than the newly launched Sega Saturn, and slightly weaker than the upcoming PlayStation.
Arrival of Saturn and PlayStation

Next Generation received a deluge of letters in response to Tramiel's comments, particularly his threat to bring Sony to court for price dumping if the PlayStation entered the U.S. market at a retail price below $300.
Arrival of Saturn and PlayStation
Tramiel and Next Generation agreed that the PlayStation's Japanese price converts to approximately $500.
Decline

Figures from the NPD Group showed that at the end of year 1995, the Jaguar had statistically a share of zero percent of the "sold through" units (which are systems purchased by consumers) in the 32-bit market, which was also lower than the one percent held by its struggling rival 3DO.
Decline
From the introduction of Jaguar in late 1993 through the end of 1995, Atari sold approximately 125,000 units of Jaguar.
Decline
As of December 31, 1995, Atari had approximately 100,000 units of Jaguar in inventory.
Decline
The filing confirmed that Atari had abandoned the Jaguar in November 1995 and in the subsequent months were concerned chiefly with liquidating its inventory of Jaguar products.
Decline
On April 8, 1996, Atari Corporation agreed to merge with JTS, Inc. in a reverse takeover, thus forming JTS Corporation.
Decline
After the merger, the bulk of Jaguar inventory remained unsold and would be finally moved out to Tiger Software, a private liquidator, on December 23, 1996.
Decline
On March 13, 1998, JTS sold the Atari name and all of the Atari properties to Hasbro Interactive.
Technical specifications
Jaguar provides these blocks with a 64-bit data path to external memory devices, and is capable of a very high data transfer rate into external dynamic RAM.
Technical specifications
Design specs for the console allude to the GPU or DSP being capable of acting as a CPU, leaving the Motorola 68000 to read controller inputs.
Technical specifications
Atari's Leonard Tramiel also specifically suggested that the 68000 not be used by developers.
Technical specifications
In practice, however, many developers use the Motorola 68000 to drive gameplay logic due to the greater developer familiarity of the 68000 and the adequacy of the 68000 for certain types of games.
Technical specifications
Most critically, a flaw in the memory controller means that certain obscure conventions must be followed for the RISC chips to be able to execute code from RAM.
Technical specifications
The system was notoriously difficult to program for, not only because of its two-processor design but development tools were released in an unfinished state and the hardware had crippling bugs.
Processors

Tom chip, 26.59 MHz Graphics processing unit (GPU) – 32- bit RISC architecture, 4 KB internal RAM, all graphical effects are software-based, with additional instructions intended for 3D operations Object Processor – 64-bit fixed-function video processor, converts display lists to video output at scan time.

It runs the lightgun games Area 51 and Maximum Force, which were released by Atari as dedicated cabinets or as the Area 51 and Maximum Force combo machine.

Other games were developed but never released: 3 On 3 Basketball, Fishin' Frenzy, Freeze, and Vicious Circle.

The only peripherals and add-ons released by Atari for the Jaguar are a redesigned controller, an adapter for four players, a CD console add-on, and a link cable for local area network (LAN) gaming.

Sold independently, however, it was never bundled with the system.

Players directly dial each other for online play, only compatible with Ultra Vortek which initializes the modem by entering 911 on the key pad at startup.

The program was deemed a spiritual successor to the Atari Video Music, a visualizer released in 1976.

Jaguar CD
A prototype, described by journalists as resembling a bathroom scale, was unveiled at the 1995 Winter Consumer Electronics Show, but the console was canceled before production.

After Atari's merger with JTS in 1996, all prototypes of the headset were allegedly destroyed.
Jaguar VR

However, two working units, one low-resolution prototype with red and grey-colored graphics and one high-resolution prototype with blue and grey-colored graphics, have since been recovered, and are regularly showcased at retrogaming -themed conventions and festivals.
Jaguar VR
Only one game was developed for the Jaguar VR prototype: a 3D-rendered version of the 1980 arcade game Missile Command, titled Missile Command 3D, and a demo of Virtuality's Zone Hunter was created.
Unlicensed peripherals
It was originally slated to be released early in the Jaguar's life, in the second quarter of 1994, but was not actually released until mid-1995.
Reception
The Jaguar won GameFan ' s "Best New System" award for 1993.
Reception
The small size and poor quality of the Jaguar's game library became the most commonly cited reason for its failure in the marketplace.
Reception
The pack-in game Cybermorph was one of the first polygon -based games for consoles, but was criticized for design flaws and a weak color palette, and compared unfavorably with the SNES's Star Fox.

Jaguar did eventually earn praise with games such as Tempest 2000, Doom, and Wolfenstein 3D.

With only one or two exceptions – Tempest 2000 is cited most frequently – there have just been no truly great games for the Jaguar up to now." Game Players also stated the despite being 64-bit, the Jaguar is much less powerful than the 3DO, Saturn, and PlayStation, even when supplemented with the Jaguar CD.

With such a small library of games to challenge the incumbent 16-bit game consoles, Jaguar's appeal never grew beyond a small gaming audience.

Digital Spy commented: "Like many failed hardware ventures, it still maintains something of a cult following but can only be considered a misstep for Atari."

Telegames continued to publish games for the Jaguar after it was discontinued, and for a time was the only company to do so.

On May 14, 1999, Hasbro Interactive announced that it had released all patents to the Jaguar, declaring it an open platform; this opened the doors for extensive homebrew development.

Following the announcement, Songbird Productions joined Telegames in releasing unfinished Jaguar games alongside new games to satisfy the cult following.

The 64DD is a magnetic floppy disk drive peripheral for the Nintendo 64 game console developed by Nintendo.
lead
It was announced in 1995, prior to the Nintendo 64's 1996 launch, and after numerous delays was released in Japan on December 13, 1999.
lead
The "64" references both the Nintendo 64 console and the 64 MB storage capacity of the disks, and "DD" is short for "disk drive" or "dynamic drive".
lead

Plugging into the extension port on the underside of the console, the 64DD allows the Nintendo 64 to use proprietary 64 MB magnetic disks for expanded and rewritable data storage, a real-time clock for persistent game world design, and a standard font and audio library for further storage efficiency.
lead
Its games and hardware accessories let the user create movies, characters, and animations to use within various other games and shared online.
lead
The system could connect to the Internet through a dedicated online service, Randnet, for e-commerce, online gaming, and media sharing.
lead

Describing it as "the first writable bulk data storage device for a modern video game console", Nintendo designed the 64DD as an enabling technology platform for the development of new genres of games and applications, several of which were in development for several years.

The 64DD is notable in part for two years of many launch delays, which created an interdependent cascade of delays and complications of many other business processes and product launches for Nintendo and its partners, and the cancellation of Space World 1998 due to lack of completed 64DD software.

IGN reported in June 1999 that many called it "the most elusive piece of vaporware to date".

On May 30, 1997, Nintendo issued a press conference announcing the first 64DD launch delay, rescheduled to March 1998 with no comment on an American release schedule.
Delays
On June 9, 1997, Nintendo and Alps Electric announced their manufacturing partnership for the still tentatively titled 64DD.
Delays

Delays

Reportedly featuring at least twenty games in development including Donkey Kong 64 and the sequel to Super Mario 64, the device retained its projected Japanese launch window of "at least" March 1998, and received its first American launch window of early 1998.
Delays
At Space World from November 21–24, 1997, the 64DD was shown prominently but its delay was extended from March 1998 to June 1998, with no mention of an international launch.

And whether or not it was ever a serious mainstream contender is now open for debate", and wondered if 64DD would become "just an interesting footnote to the Nintendo 64 story".

But it's an accessory and we all know the history of selling add-ons in this marketplace, and to be successful we'd have to get a 60%-to-80% penetration of this 64DD into the installed base of N64 to be considered a success.

We can't just have 10% or 20% of people buy it, otherwise it wouldn't make any sense to continue software support for it.

(laughs)" To illustrate the fundamental significance of the 64DD to all game development at Nintendo, Itoi said, "I came up with a lot of ideas because of the 64DD.

Known third-party 64DD developers included Konami, Culture Brain, Seta, Japan System Supply, Titus, Infogrames, Rare, Paradigm Entertainment, Ocean, and Factor 5.

Nintendo's 64DD delay track record still has a few openings for more entries.

The Japanese launch was delayed to June 1998, later adjusted by the apologetic announcement on April 3, 1998, that it would launch "within the year".

In June 1999, IGN reported that month's completion of Randnet and the modem, as having "breathed new life into what many have called the most elusive piece of vaporware to date".

IGN said Nintendo "is surprisingly confident about the 64DD and is predicting to sell the full initial shipment of 500,000 before year's end".

As of Space World 1999 in August, Nintendo had set Randnet's launch date at December 1, 1999, but reportedly had not yet set a launch date for the 64DD.

Nintendo's 64DD booth demonstrated eight launch games, including DT Bloodmasters with a data transfer (DT) cable from Game Boy Color to 64DD.

The 64DD was launched on December 13, 1999, exclusively in Japan, as a package called the Randnet Starter Kit including six games bimonthly through the mail, and one year of Internet service.
Launch
Later, very limited quantities of the individual 64DD and games were released to stores.
Discontinuation

On August 25, 2000, Space World was signified by the launches of the GameCube and Game Boy Advance, and by what IGN considered to be the unofficial discontinuation of the 64DD, jokingly calling it "DeaDD".
Discontinuation
In October 2000, Nintendo announced the impending discontinuation of the 64DD and Randnet, with 15,000 active subscribers.

Only ten 64DD disks were ever released, including three third-party games and one Internet application suite.
Discontinuation
Most planned 64DD games were either released on increasingly larger Nintendo 64 Game Pak, ported to other consoles like the PlayStation or GameCube, or canceled entirely.
Hardware

The dual storage strategy of the Nintendo 64 plus the 64DD combines the traditional high speed cartridges, which are low-capacity, non-writable, and expensive but very fast along with the introduction of proprietary mass storage disks, which are large-capacity, rewritable, and cheap but only moderately fast.
Hardware

Complementing its proprietary and copy-protected cartridge strategy, the proprietary 64 MB disk format was Nintendo's faster, more flexible, and copy-protected answer to the commodity Compact Disc format, which is cheaper to produce but is much slower, read-only, and easier to copy on personal computers.
Hardware

The most advanced CD technology delivered by the contemporaneous Sega Saturn and Sony PlayStation game consoles can hold at least 650 megabytes (MB) of information with a peak 300 kB/s throughput and more than 200 ms seek speed.
Hardware

This compares to the Nintendo 64's cartridge 's 4 to 64 MB size and 5 to 50 MB/s of low latency and instantaneous load times, and the 64DD's 64 MB disk size and 1 MB/s peak throughput with 75 ms average seek latency.
Hardware

As an example of variable storage strategies, Nintendo determined that the development of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time would be retargeted from 64DD disk format alone, to the much faster cartridge format plus expansions on the cheaper floppy disk, to optimize performance and cost.
Hardware

Nonetheless, the 64DD disk format would serve as significant storage size expansion upon its 1999 launch when 32 MB cartridges were the norm and on into future years when only three 64 MB cartridges would ever be released for Nintendo 64.

The service was accessed at an additional dialup fee of up to ¥20 per minute, initially local only to Tokyo.

The service later eliminated the monthly payment model in favor of an annual prepaid model, at ¥30,000 (US$290) for one year for outright purchase and ¥39,600 (US$380) for the first year of lease-to-own.

The final Starter Kit subscription title Polygon Studio was suddenly delayed and then released on August 29, 2000.

One of the most substantial series of games to include Randnet support is the Mario Artist series, which allowed online users to swap their artwork creations with others.

Because the 64DD hardware package was primarily sold with a mandatory subscription to Randnet, the service was fairly popular among the limited 64DD user base.
Randnet
The Randnet service closed on February 28, 2001 and Nintendo's equity partnership with RandnetDD Co., Ltd. was liquidated from June 30, 2001 to January 31, 2002.

Software load times are described as "minimal", where the most complex possible point of the system's library reaches about five seconds.

The site says that the 64DD popularity was inherently limited, due in part to its limited release in Japan, a country which had a limited adoption of the Nintendo 64 and of dialup Internet connectivity.

But it provides new users with a "simple network functions as first baby steps into the vast world of the Internet".

Because these items were sold only as a soon-discontinued bundle, all with such ultimately limited application, he found the disks' cheaper prices to be aggregated back up to the level of cartridges.

The Family Computer Disk System, commonly shortened to the Famicom Disk System, or just Disk System, is a peripheral for Nintendo 's Family Computer home video game console, released only in Japan on February 21, 1986.
lead
It uses proprietary floppy disks called "Disk Cards" for cheaper data storage and it adds a new high-fidelity sound channel for supporting Disk System games.
lead

Fundamentally, the Disk System serves simply to enhance some aspects already inherent to the base Famicom system, with better sound and cheaper games — though with the disadvantages of high initial price, slow speed, and lower reliability.
lead
However, this boost to the market of affordable and writable mass storage temporarily served as an enabling technology for the creation of new types of video games.
lead

This includes the vast, open world, progress-saving adventures of the best-selling The Legend of Zelda (1986) and Metroid (1986), games with a cost-effective and swift release such as the best-selling Super Mario Bros.
lead
2, and nationwide leaderboards and contests via the in-store Disk Fax kiosks, which are considered to be forerunners of today's online achievement and distribution systems.
lead
By 1989, the Famicom Disk System was inevitably obsoleted by the improving semiconductor technology of game cartridges.
lead
The Disk System's lifetime sales reached 4.4 million units by 1990, making it the most successful console add-on of all time, despite not being sold outside of Japan.
History
By 1985, Nintendo's Family Computer was dominating the Japanese home video game market, selling over three million units within a year and a half.
History
The add-on itself was produced by Masayuki Uemura and Nintendo Research & Development 2, the same team that designed the Famicom itself.
History
Following several delays, the Famicom Disk System was released on February 21, 1986, at a retail price of ¥15000 (US$80).
History
The same day, Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda as a launch title, alongside disk re-releases of earlier Famicom games.
History
The Famicom Disk System sold over 300,000 units within three months, jumping to over 2 million by the end of the year.
History
Nintendo remained confident the Disk System would be a sure-fire success, and ensured that all future first-party releases would be exclusive to the peripheral.
History
These kiosks allowed customers to bring in their disk games and have a new game rewritten onto them for a ¥500 fee; blank disks could also be purchased for ¥2000.
History
Nintendo of America announced plans to release the Disk System for the Famicom's international counterpart, the Nintendo Entertainment System, however these plans were eventually scrapped.
History
Most common was the quality of the Disk Cards; Nintendo removed the shutters on most Disk System games to reduce costs, instead placing them in a wax sleeve and clear plastic shell.
History

Four months after the Disk System was released, Capcom released a Famicom conversion of Ghosts 'n Goblins on a 128k cartridge - larger than the Disk Card's 112k capacity - which, as a result, made consumers and developers less impressed with the Disk System's technological features.
History
The Disk System's vague error messages, long loading times, and the poor quality of the rubber drive belt that spun the disks are also cited as attributing to its downfall.
History
By 1989, advancements in technology made cartridge games much cheaper and easier to produce, leaving the Famicom Disk System obsolete.
History
Nintendo officially discontinued the Famicom Disk System in 1990, selling around 4.4 million units total.
History
Disk writing services were still kept in operation until September 30, 2003, while technical services were provided up until October 31, 2007.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
Widespread copyright violation in Japan's predominantly personal-computer-based game rental market inspired corporations to petition the government to ban the rental of all video games in 1984.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
With games then being available only via full purchase, demand rose for a new and less expensive way to access more games.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks

In 1986, as video gaming had increasingly expanded from computers into the video game console market, Nintendo advertised a promise to install 10,000 Famicom Disk Writer kiosks in toy and hobby stores across Japan within one year.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
To write an existing disk with a new game from the available roster was ¥500 (then about US$3.25 and 1/6 of the price of many new games).
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
Instruction sheets were given by the retailer, or available by mail order for ¥100.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
In 1987, Disk Writer kiosks in select locations were also provisioned as Disk Fax systems as Nintendo's first online concept.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
Players participated in a nationwide leaderboard, with unique prizes.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
The kiosk service was very popular and remained available until 2003.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks

In subsequent console generations, Nintendo would relaunch this online national leaderboard concept with the home satellite-based Satellaview subscription service in Japan from 1995 to 2000 for the Super Famicom.

The RAM Adapter contains 32 kilobytes (KB) of RAM for temporarily caching program data from disk, 8 KB of RAM for tile and sprite data storage, and an ASIC named the 2C33.
Technology
Finally, embedded in the 2C33 is an 8KB BIOS ROM.

Batteries usually last five months with daily game play.

The Disk System's Disk Cards are somewhat proprietary 71 mm × 76 mm (2.8 × 3 in) 56K-per-side double-sided floppy.

They are a slight modification of Mitsumi 's Quick Disk 71 mm 2.8 in square disk format which is used in a handful of Japanese computers and various synthesizer keyboards, along with a few word processors.

Games
Some are FDS exclusives, some are Disk Writer exclusives, and many were re-released years later on the cartridge format such as The Legend of Zelda for NES in 1987, and for Famicom in 1994.

2 originated from a disk-only game called Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic.

sents: lead
The Satellaview is a satellite modem peripheral produced by Nintendo for the Super Famicom in 1995.
lead

Containing 1 megabyte of ROM space and an additional 512 kB of RAM, Satellaview allowed players to download games, magazines, and other media through satellite broadcasts provided by Japanese company St.GIGA.
lead
Its heavy third-party support included Squaresoft, Taito, Konami, Capcom, and Seta.
lead
To use Satellaview, players purchased a special broadcast satellite (BS) tuner directly from St.GIGA or rented one for a six-month fee.
lead
It attaches to the expansion port on the bottom of the Super Famicom.
lead
Satellaview is the result of a collaboration between Nintendo and St.GIGA, the latter known in Japan for its "Tide of Sound" nature sound music.
lead
By 1994, St.GIGA was struggling financially due to the Japanese Recession affecting the demand for its music; Nintendo initiated a "rescue" plan by purchasing a stake in the company.
lead
Satellaview was produced by Nintendo Research & Development 2, the same team that designed the Super Famicom, and was made for a more adult-oriented market.
History
Founded in early 1990, St.GIGA was a satellite radio subsidiary of the Japanese satellite television company WOWOW Inc., based in Akasaka, Tokyo.
History

Credited as the world's first digital satellite radio station, it was maintained by Hiroshi Yokoi and best known for its "Tide of Sound" broadcasts, which were high-quality digital recordings of nature sounds accompanied by a spoken word narrator known as the "Voice".
History
By 1994, St.GIGA struggled financially due to the Japanese Recession reducing consumer spending on ambient music and satellite systems.
History
Nintendo purchased a 19.5% stake in St.GIGA in May, as a way to "rescue" the company and help to successfully restructure it.
History
Satellaview development began shortly after the acquisition, reportedly in production alongside the Virtual Boy and Nintendo 64.
History

Nintendo stressed to video game publications that much of Satellaview's content, specifically St.GIGA broadcasts, were primarily for adults, with video games constituting only a small portion of airtime.
History
Nintendo officially announced Satellaview on December 21, 1994, at a retail price of ¥14,000, or US$150 (equivalent to $310 in 2023).
History
The peripheral was designed by Nintendo Research & Development 2, the same team that had designed the Super Famicom.
History

Though Nintendo was in a slump due to falling Super Famicom game sales and the Virtual Boy's failure, its management remained confident in Satellaview's success and would help calm any consumer concerns; company president Hiroshi Yamauchi expected to sell roughly 2 million Satellaview units each year.
History
Pre-orders were available beginning February 25, 1995.
History
Broadcasting services for Satellaview launched on April 1, and the peripheral was released on April 23.
History

Satellaview was never released outside Japan, which some publications cited as being due to expensive costs of digital satellite broadcasting, and due to a supposed lack of appeal to American consumers.
History

When the service first launched, St.GIGA had a number of issues regarding broadcasting video games and video game-related services through the Satellaview service, such as legal issues with other companies and technical restraints of the time.
History

In June 1996, Nintendo announced a potential partnership with Microsoft to release a similar service for Windows, which would combine St.GIGA's broadcasting services with dial-up Internet; this was never launched.
History
By March 1997, St.GIGA reported that Satellaview had 116,378 active users.
History
By mid 1998, Nintendo's relationship with St.GIGA began to deteriorate.
History

St.GIGA refused a debt-management plan created by Nintendo to reduce the firm's capital, though having ¥8.8 billion in debt, and had also failed to apply for a government digital satellite broadcasting license by a deadline.
History
This led to Nintendo halting all production of new games and content for the peripheral beginning March 1999, and to cancel content and services via a new BS-4 satellite.
History
St.GIGA continued to supply content for Satellaview, broadcasting reruns of older content and making the service only for video games.
History

Satellaview was fully discontinued on June 30, 2000, due to a severe lack of outside support and a dwindling player base, dropping by nearly 60% from its peak in 1997 to about 46,000 active subscribers.
Technical specifications
A Satellaview device attaches to the expansion port on bottom of a Super Famicom, similar to the 64DD or the Sega CD.
Technical specifications
The peripheral expands the Super Famicom with 1 MB of ROM space and 512 kB of RAM.
Technical specifications
Game and broadcast information is stored on 8 MB memory packs, inserted into the top of a special application cartridge.
Technical specifications
A vintage user purchased (or rented for six months at ¥5,400) a BS tuner from St.GIGA, paid monthly fees to St.GIGA and Nintendo, and bought a satellite dish.
Technical specifications

The requisite system cartridge, titled BS-X: Sore wa Namae o Nusumareta Machi no Monogatari (commonly translated as BS-X: The Town Whose Name Was Stolen), serves as both an interactive menu system and as its own game.
Games and services
A total of 114 games were released for Satellaview; some are remakes or updates of older Family Computer and Super Famicom games, and others were created specifically for the service.
Games and services
Nintendo's popular franchises include Kirby, F-Zero, Fire Emblem, The Legend of Zelda, and Super Mario Bros.
Games and services
The previously unreleased Special Tee Shot, later reworked into Kirby's Dream Course, was released.
Games and services

Third-party games include Squaresoft's Radical Dreamers and Treasure Conflix, Pack-In-Video's Harvest Moon, Chunsoft 's Shiren the Wanderer, Jaleco's Super Earth Defense Force, and ASCII's Derby Stallion '96.
Games and services
Unlike other Satellaview games, SoundLink games could only be played on a live schedule.
Reception and legacy
Nintendo World Report liked its uniqueness which will likely never be replicated on modern video game consoles, and its library of games and services.
Reception and legacy
Shacknews listed it among Nintendo's most innovative products for its technological accomplishments and pioneering of online gaming.
Reception and legacy
Kill Screen labeled Satellaview as "perhaps one of the most crucial early experiments in combining games with storytelling", specifically the Soundlink games and voice acting.
Reception and legacy
In 1999, Nintendo released a spiritual successor to Satellaview for Nintendo 64, the 64DD and its Randnet Internet service.
Reception and legacy
Originally announced in 1995, a year prior to console launch, Randnet had many similar features, such as a Nintendo newsletter and online gaming, plus chat and email.
Reception and legacy
Nintendo attempted to have St.GIGA transition from Satellaview to the 64DD, however, when St.GIGA refused, Nintendo instead partnered with Japanese media company Recruit to form Randnet.
Reception and legacy
Satellaview has a large cult following since the late 2000s due to most of its content having been lost after the service was closed.

Fans have created custom private servers that work with the official BS-X application cartridge, and translated certain games such as those from the Legend of Zelda series.

The Sega Saturn is a home video game console developed by Sega and released on November 22, 1994, in Japan, May 11, 1995, in North America, and July 8, 1995, in Europe.
lead
Part of the fifth generation of video game consoles, it is the successor to the successful Genesis.
lead
The Saturn has a dual- CPU architecture and eight processors.
lead
Its games are in CD-ROM format, including several ports of arcade games and original games.
lead
Development of the Saturn began in 1992, the same year Sega's groundbreaking 3D Model 1 arcade hardware debuted.
lead
The Saturn was designed around a new CPU from the Japanese electronics company Hitachi.
lead
Another video display processor was added in early 1994 to better compete with the 3D graphics of Sony 's forthcoming PlayStation.
lead
The Saturn was initially successful in Japan but not in the United States, where it was hindered by a surprise May 1995 launch, four months before its scheduled release date.
Background

In the early 1990s, Sega had success with the Genesis (known as the Mega Drive in most countries outside of North America), backed by aggressive advertising campaigns and the popularity of its Sonic the Hedgehog series.
Background

Sega also had success with arcade games; in 1992 and 1993, the new Sega Model 1 arcade system board showcased Sega AM2 's Virtua Racing and Virtua Fighter (the first 3D fighting game), crucial to popularizing 3D polygonal graphics.
Background
The Model 1 was expensive, so several alternatives helped bring Sega's newest arcade games to Genesis, such as the Virtua Processor chip used for Virtua Racing, and the 32X add-on.
Development

In 1993, Sega and the Japanese electronics company Hitachi formed a joint venture to develop a new CPU for the Saturn, which resulted in the creation of the "SuperH RISC Engine" (or SH-2) later that year.
Development
Sega considered making CD-ROM-based and cartridge-only versions of the Saturn, but discarded the idea due to concerns over the lower quality and higher price of cartridge games.
Development

Kalinske, Sony Electronic Publishing's Olaf Olafsson, and Sony America's Micky Schulhof had discussed development of a joint "Sega/Sony hardware system", which never materialized due to Sega's desire to create hardware for both 2D and 3D visuals and Sony's competing notion of focusing on 3D technology.
Development
In April 1994, Acclaim Entertainment announced it would be the first American publisher to produce software for the Titan.
Development
In January 1994, Sega began to develop the 32X add-on for the Genesis, as a less expensive entry into the 32-bit era.
Development
The 32X would not be compatible with the Saturn, but Sega executive Richard Brudvik-Lindner pointed out that the 32X would play Genesis games, and had the same system architecture as the Saturn.
Development
According to Sega of America research and development head Joe Miller, the 32X familiarized development teams with the dual SH-2 architecture also used in the Saturn.
Launch
Sega released the Saturn in Japan on November 22, 1994, at a price of ¥ 44,800.
Launch
Though Sega had wanted to launch with Clockwork Knight and Panzer Dragoon, the only other first-party game available at launch was Wan Chai Connection.
Launch
Boosted by the popularity of Virtua Fighter, Sega's initial shipment of 200,000 Saturn units sold out on the first day.
Launch
Meanwhile, Sega released the 32X on November 21, 1994, in North America, December 3, 1994, in Japan, and January 1995 in PAL territories, at less than half of the Saturn's launch price.
Launch
Half a million Saturn units were sold in Japan by the end of 1994 (compared to 300,000 PlayStation units), and sales exceeded 1 million within the following six months.
Launch
In March 1995, Sega of America CEO Tom Kalinske announced the Saturn's launch in the U.S. on "Saturnday" (Saturday), September 2, 1995.
Launch

At the first Electronic Entertainment Expo (E3) in Los Angeles on May 11, 1995, Kalinske gave a keynote presentation in which he revealed the release price of $399 (including a copy of Virtua Fighter), and described the features of the console.
Launch

Sony subsequently unveiled the retail price for the PlayStation; Olaf Olafsson, the head of Sony Computer Entertainment America (SCEA), summoned Steve Race to the stage, who uttered "$299", and then walked away to applause.
Launch
The Saturn's release in Europe also came before the previously announced North American date, on July 8, 1995, at £ 399.99.
Launch

The PlayStation launched in Europe on September 29, 1995; by November, it had already outsold the Saturn by a factor of three in the United Kingdom, where Sony had allocated £20 million of marketing during the holiday season compared to Sega's £4 million.
Launch
The Saturn's U.S. launch was accompanied by a reported $50 million advertising campaign including coverage in publications such as Wired and Playboy.
Launch
The early rescheduling yielded only six launch games (all published by Sega) because most third-party games were scheduled around the original launch date.
Launch

Virtua Fighter ' s relative lack of popularity in the West, combined with a release schedule of only two games between the surprise launch and September 1995, prevented Sega from capitalizing on the Saturn's early timing.
Launch
Although the System 11 is technically inferior to Sega's Model 2 arcade board, its lower price made it attractive to smaller arcades.
Launch
Following a 1994 acquisition of Sega developers, Namco released Tekken for the System 11 and PlayStation.
Launch
Tekken surpassed Virtua Fighter in popularity due to its superior graphics and nearly arcade-perfect console port, becoming the first million-selling PlayStation game.
Launch
On October 2, Sega announced a Saturn price reduction to $299.
Launch

High-quality Saturn ports of the Sega Model 2 arcade hits Sega Rally Championship, Virtua Cop, and Virtua Fighter 2 (running at 60 frames per second at a high resolution) were available by the end of the year and were generally regarded as superior to competitors on the PlayStation.
Launch
An informal survey of retailers showed that the Saturn and PlayStation sold in roughly equal numbers during the first quarter of 1996.

Prior to the Western launch, Sega reduced the price of the Dreamcast to ¥19,900, effectively making it unprofitable but increasing sales.
North America

According to Stolar, president of EA at the time, Larry Probst, wanted exclusive rights as the only sports brand on Dreamcast, which Stolar could not accept due to Sega's recent US$10 million purchase of the sports game developer Visual Concepts.
North America
Let's take the conservative estimate of 250,000 Dreamcast units at presage—that's a quarter of a million units at $200.
North America
This could be a $60 to 80 million 24-hour period.
North America
What has ever sold $60 to 80 million in the first 24 hours?
North America
The Dreamcast launched in North America on September 9, 1999, at a price of $199, which Sega's marketing dubbed "9/9/99 for $199 ".
North America

Eighteen launch games were available in the US Sega set a new sales record by selling more than 225,132 Dreamcast units in 24 hours, earning $98.4 million in what Moore called "the biggest 24 hours in entertainment retail history".
North America
On November 4, Sega announced it had sold over one million Dreamcast units.
Europe
Sega released the Dreamcast in Europe on October 14, 1999, at a price of £200.
Europe
By Christmas of 1999, Sega of Europe had sold 500,000 units, six months ahead of schedule.
Europe
The price was dropped to £149.99 from September 8, 2000, with sales at around 800,000 in Europe at this point.
Europe
We have reached 80 or 90 per cent of them now and the market is screaming for a price reduction.
Europe
Sales did not continue at this pace, and by October 2000, Sega had sold only about one million units in Europe.
Australia and New Zealand
Through the regional distributor Ozisoft, the Dreamcast went on sale in Australia and New Zealand on November 30, 1999, at a price of A$ 499.
Australia and New Zealand

There were severe problems at launch; besides a severe shortage of the consoles, only six of the thirty planned launch games were available for purchase on day one with no first-party software included, and additional peripherals were not available in stores.
Australia and New Zealand

The poor launch, combined with a lack of advertising and a high price point, produced lackluster sales in Australia; two large retail chains reported a combined total of 13 console sales over the first few days after launch.
Competition
Though the Dreamcast launch was successful, Sony held 60 percent of the overall video game market share in North America with the PlayStation at the end of 1999.
Competition
On March 2, 1999, Sony revealed the first details of the PlayStation 2 (PS2), which Ken Kutaragi said would allow video games to convey unprecedented emotions.
Competition

Sony estimated the PS2 could render 7.5 million to 16 million polygons per second, whereas independent estimates ranged from 3 million to 20 million, compared to Sega's estimates of more than 3 million to 6 million for the Dreamcast.
Competition
US Dreamcast sales—which exceeded 1.5 million by the end of 1999 —began to decline as early as January 2000.
Competition

Poor Japanese sales contributed to Sega's ¥42.88 billion ($404 million) consolidated net loss in the fiscal year ending March 2000, which followed a loss of ¥42.881 billion the previous year and marked Sega's third consecutive annual loss.
Competition
Moore became the president and chief operating officer of Sega of America on May 8, 2000.
Competition
On September 7, 2000, Sega.com launched SegaNet, the Dreamcast's internet gaming service, at a subscription price of $21.95 per month.
Competition

Although Sega had previously released only one Dreamcast game in the US that featured online multiplayer, ChuChu Rocket!, the launch of SegaNet combined with the release of NFL 2K1, with a robust online component, was intended to increase demand for the Dreamcast in the US market.
Competition
Prior to the launch of SegaNet, Sega had already offered a $200 rebate to any Dreamcast owner who purchased two years of internet access from Sega.com.
Competition

To increase SegaNet's appeal in the US, Sega dropped the price of the Dreamcast to $149 (compared to the PS2's US launch price of $299) and offered a rebate for the full $149 price of a Dreamcast, and a free Dreamcast keyboard, with every 18-month SegaNet subscription.
Decline
Moore said that the Dreamcast would need to sell 5 million units in the US by the end of 2000 to remain a viable platform; Sega fell short of this goal, with some 3 million units sold.
Decline
Instead of an expected profit, for the six months ending September 2000, Sega posted a ¥17.98 billion ($163.11 million) loss, with a projected year-end loss of ¥23.6 billion.
Decline
This estimate more than doubled to ¥58.3 billion, and in March 2001, Sega posted a consolidated net loss of ¥51.7 billion ($417.5 million).
Decline

While the PS2's October 26 US launch was marred by shortages, this did not benefit the Dreamcast as much as expected; many consumers continued to wait for a PS2, while the PSone, a remodeled version of the original PlayStation, became the bestselling console in the US at the start of the 2000 holiday season.
Decline

What effectively happened is the PlayStation 2 lack of availability froze the marketplace." Eventually, Sony and Nintendo held 50 and 35 percent of the US video game market, while Sega held only 15 percent.
Decline
According to Bellfield, Dreamcast software sold at an 8-to-1 ratio with the hardware, but the small install base meant this did not produce enough revenue to keep it viable.
Decline
We were selling 50,000 units a day, then 60,000, then 100,000, but it was just not going to be enough to get the critical mass to take on the launch of PS2.
Decline
On May 22, 2000, Okawa replaced Irimajiri as president of Sega.
Decline
Sega also announced a price reduction to $99 to eliminate its unsold inventory, which was estimated at 930,000 units as of April 2001.
Decline
After a further reduction to $79, the Dreamcast was cleared out of stores at $49.95.
Decline

Okawa, who had previously loaned Sega $500 million in 1999, died on March 16, 2001; shortly before his death, he forgave Sega's debts to him and returned his $695 million worth of Sega and CSK stock, helping Sega survive the transition to third-party development.
Aftermath and reaction
Despite the discontinuation of Dreamcast hardware, Sega continued to support the system and had stated that more than 30 new titles were confirmed for release for the remainder of 2001.
Aftermath and reaction
In the United States, official game releases continued until the end of the first half of 2002.
Hardware
The Dreamcast measures 190 mm × 195.8 mm × 75.5 mm (7.48 in × 7.71 in × 2.97 in) and weighs 1.5 kg (3.3 lb).
Hardware
Its 100 MHz NEC PowerVR2 rendering engine, integrated with the ASIC, can draw more than 3 million polygons per second and use deferred shading.
Hardware

Sega estimated the Dreamcast's theoretical rendering capability at 7 million raw polygons per second, or 6 million with textures and lighting, but noted that "game logic and physics reduce peak graphic performance".
Hardware
The Dreamcast can output approximately 16.77 million colors simultaneously and displays interlaced or progressive scan video at 640 × 480 video resolution.
Hardware
The Dreamcast has 16 MB main RAM, along with an additional 8 MB of RAM for graphic textures and 2 MB of RAM for sound.
Models
The R7, a refurbished Dreamcast, was originally used as a network console in Japanese pachinko parlors.
Models
Another model, the Divers 2000 CX-1, is shaped similarly to Sonic's head and includes a television and software for teleconferencing.
Models
A Hello Kitty version, limited to 2000 units, was targeted at female gamers in Japan.
Controllers and accessories
The original Japanese model and all PAL models have a transfer rate of 33.6 kbit/s, and consoles sold in the US and in Japan after September 9, 1999, feature a 56 kbit/s dial-up modem.
Controllers and accessories
Broadband service was enabled through the later release of a broadband accessory in 2000 in Japan, and early 2001 in the US.
Storage
Iomega announced a Dreamcast-compatible zip drive storing up to 100 MB on removable discs, but it was never released.
Game library
In North America, it launched with 19 games, including the highly anticipated Sonic Adventure, Soulcalibur, and NFL 2K.
Game library
In Europe, it was planned to launch with 10 games; this increased to 15 after the launch was delayed.
Game library
Some indie developers continued to release games, such as 2007's Last Hope, developed by the German studio NG:Dev.Team.
First-party games
Sonic Team's Sonic Adventure, the first fully 3D platform game starring Sega's mascot Sonic the Hedgehog, was considered the "centerpiece" of the Dreamcast launch.
First-party games
At 2.5 million copies, it is the best-selling Dreamcast game.
First-party games

Incorporating a simulated day-and-night cycle with variable weather, non-player characters with regular schedules, the ability to pick up and examine detailed objects, and introducing the quick-time event in its modern form, Shenmue went over budget and was rumored to have cost Sega over $50 million.
First-party games
Visual Concepts' NFL 2K football series and its NBA 2K basketball series were critically acclaimed.
First-party games
After Sega sold Visual Concepts for $24 million in 2005, the NBA 2K series continued with publisher Take-Two Interactive.
Network services
The service launched the week of October 28, 1998, with its feature set expanded in the weeks preceding the Dreamcast's launch in Japan on November 27, 1998.
Network services
Much of its infrastructure was developed by ISAO Corporation, which was spun-off from Sega on November 26, 1999.
Network services
Dricas persisted until March 7, 2000, when the service was consolidated into ISAO's multi-platform online service, isao.net.
Network services
Isao.net maintained online services and game servers for the Dreamcast until Sega ceased operation of the online servers for Phantasy Star Online, along with its GameCube port, on March 31, 2007.
Network services

Sega announced a partnership with AT&T on August 4, 1999, making the AT&T WorldNet service the preferred ISP for Dreamcast in the United States, and an agreement making Excite@Home as the exclusive portal partner for SegaNet.
Network services
SegaNet launched on September 7, 2000, and originally offered a rebate for a free Dreamcast and keyboard with a two-year contract.
Network services
Because of the Dreamcast's discontinuation, Sega announced they would discontinue the service on July 20, 2001, less than 11 months after launch.
Network services
Dreamarena was a free dial-up -based online gaming service provided for Dreamcast consoles in Europe, launching with the debut of the Dreamcast in Europe on October 14, 1999.
Network services
After the discontinuation of the Dreamcast, Sega closed Dreamarena on February 28, 2002.
Reception and legacy
At the beginning of 2000, five Electronic Gaming Monthly reviewers scored the Dreamcast 8.5, 8.5, 8.5, 8.0, and 9.0 out of 10.
Reception and legacy
In 2001, the Electronic Gaming Monthly reviewers scored it 9.0, 9.0, 9.0, 9.0, and 9.5 out of 10.
Reception and legacy

In 2013, Edge named the Dreamcast the tenth-best console of the last 20 years, highlighting innovations including in-game voice chat, downloadable content, and second-screen technology through the use of VMUs.
Reception and legacy

The staff of Edge agreed with this assessment of Dreamcast games, including Sega's arcade conversions, stating that the system "delivered the first games that could meaningfully be described as arcade perfect".

dc_saga_dreamcaster_resident_we.real: Sega Dreamcast Resident Evil Code: Veronica Edition (Japan)
dc_saga_dreamcaster_resident_we.title: Resident Evil – Code: Veronica
sents: lead
Resident Evil – Code: Veronica is a survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom and originally released for the Dreamcast in 2000.
lead
It is the fourth main installment in the Resident Evil series and the first to debut on a separate platform from the PlayStation.
lead
The story takes place three months after the events of Resident Evil 2 (1998) and the concurrent destruction of Raccoon City as seen in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis (1999).
lead
It follows Claire Redfield and her brother Chris Redfield in their efforts to survive a viral outbreak at a remote prison island in the Southern Ocean and a research facility in Antarctica.
lead

The game retains the traditional survival horror controls and gameplay of previous installments; however, unlike the pre-rendered backgrounds of previous games, Code: Veronica uses real-time 3D environments and dynamic camera movement.
lead
After producer Shinji Mikami and his team learned they would be unable to port Resident Evil 2 to the Sega Saturn, they began development on an original game, which became Code: Veronica.
lead

Although labeled a spin-off, it was designed as the true sequel to Resident Evil 2; the title " Resident Evil 3 " was given to what was originally another spin-off game being developed in tandem for the PlayStation.
lead
Claire was designed with a tougher appearance than in Resident Evil 2, with the reason being her past experiences in Raccoon City built her toughness and confidence.
Gameplay
Unlike previous games in the series which used pre-rendered backgrounds, Code: Veronica uses real-time 3D environments.
Gameplay
The camera will follow, pan, and zoom as the player navigates their character through the environment, similar to Capcom's own Dino Crisis (1999).
Gameplay
The player can only hold a limited number of items at a given time; other items must be stored in storage boxes located throughout the game.
Gameplay
At this point, the game must be continued from the last save point.
Plot

In December 1998, three months after escaping from Raccoon City (seen in Resident Evil 2) prior to its eventual destruction (seen in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis), Claire Redfield raids an Umbrella Corporation facility in Paris in search of her brother, Chris Redfield.
Plot
Eventually, the pair manages to find a seaplane and use it to escape, only for Alfred to pursue them and switch their plane to autopilot, directing it towards another Umbrella facility in Antarctica.
Plot

Before he dies, Alfred frees his sister, Alexia, who had been in cryogenic sleep within the facility after injecting herself with the T-Veronica virus, an experimental virus that the Ashford family had developed 15 years ago.
Plot
Once there, Chris frees his sister and helps her to search for Steve, only for them to find that he had been experimented with and injected with the T-Veronica virus.
Development
With the success of Resident Evil 2 in 1998, Capcom began more Resident Evil projects across multiple consoles.
Development
Code: Veronica originated from an unsuccessful attempt to port Resident Evil 2 to the Sega Saturn.
Development
Around the same time, a side-story game for the PlayStation starring Jill Valentine in the events leading up to Resident Evil 2 was being developed.
Development

According to IGN, Sony bartered for limited exclusivity on the " Resident Evil 3 " title, and thus the side-story was branded as Resident Evil 3 and the true sequel was labeled a spin-off and titled Code: Veronica.
Development

While previous games are set in the United States and have a corresponding American feel to them, Code: Veronica is set in the Southern Ocean and Antarctica and carries a European gothic horror inspired design.
Development
During in-game cutscenes, the polygon count is increased to nearly 2,500 polygons, especially on character faces.
Development
Claire was given a tougher appearance in Code: Veronica than in Resident Evil 2, the reason being her experiences in Resident Evil 2 built her toughness and confidence to handle any situation.
Development
Mikami described Code: Veronica as 50 to 60% of his perfect vision for Resident Evil in February 2001, and he cited that future Resident Evil projects may make up the other half.
Development
By the time Resident Evil 3 was released, development on Code: Veronica was nearing completion.
Development
Much of Code: Veronica ' s 70-person development staff was outsourced because Capcom resources had been tied up working on Resident Evil 3.
Development
Capcom Production Studio 4 still handled art direction and character design.
Development
By September 1999, Sega was sending some of its own developers to help add final touches to the game.
Release
Code: Veronica was confirmed to be in development as early as August 1998 and was promoted as the true sequel to Resident Evil 2.
Release
It was officially revealed on October 6, 1998, by Capcom R&D chief Yoshiki Okamoto.
Release
Capcom of Japan stated that they were hoping to sell the game to roughly one third of all Dreamcast users, which they estimated would total to around one million copies.
Release
In July 1999, Capcom of Japan announced their shipment expectations for the Japanese Dreamcast version were at 400,000 copies.
Release
Journalists were skeptical if this was only the initial shipment, or evidence that Capcom overestimated sales of the Dreamcast, given their initial sales estimate was one million.
Release
Capcom initially planned to have Code: Veronica released around the same time as Resident Evil 3 and, more importantly, the Dreamcast launch in North America on September 9, 1999.
Release
To make up for the game's absence, Capcom announced they would release a port of Resident Evil 2 for the Dreamcast that December.
Release
Pre-ordered copies came with a unique numbered tag, special red packaging, and a unique title screen.
Release
Limited Dreamcast system bundles were also released to commemorate the game's release.
Release
The "Claire Version", limited to 1,800 copies, consisted of the Code: Veronica game, a pink system, pink controller, and a VMU.
Code: Veronica X
This led to an expanded version, titled Code: Veronica X in the West and Code: Veronica Kanzenban in Japan, on the PlayStation 2 in 2001.
Code: Veronica X
While the core game remained unchanged, several graphical alterations were also made, most notably in the character model for Steve Burnside (who was given a different hairstyle).
Code: Veronica X
A high-definition remastered version of Code: Veronica X was released in September 2011 for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.
Code: Veronica X
An emulated version for the PlayStation 3 was released as a PS2 Classic in July 2012 in Japan and in May 2014 in Europe.
Code: Veronica X
Another emulated PS2 version was released for the PlayStation 4 in May 2017.
Code: Veronica X
The Xbox 360 version was added to the Xbox One backwards-compatible library in February 2019.
Reception
Derek Williams of AllGame called it the best game for the system along with Soulcalibur (1999).
Reception
A critic from Game Revolution found it to be the best of all the horror games on the Dreamcast, towering the likes of The House of the Dead 2 (1999), Zombie Revenge (1999), and Carrier (2000).
Reception
Most reviewers found the graphics as being some of the very best on the Dreamcast and being a testament to the power of its hardware.
Reception
The use of music and sound was called "top-notch" and "perfect".
Reception
Reviews for the PlayStation 2 release of Code: Veronica X were mostly positive.
Reception
Critics shared similar opinions to the Dreamcast reviews, but some complaints were drawn from it being a mostly unmodified port of an 18-month-old Dreamcast game.
Reception
GameSpot 's Joe Fielder pointed out that Sony's Extermination (2001) and Capcom's own Onimusha: Warlords (2001) had been released during this gap with better controls.
Sales
Code: Veronica outsold Shenmue (1999) within its first week on shelves in February 2000.
Sales
In total, the Dreamcast version sold almost 450,000 units in the United States and 1.14 million copies worldwide.
Sales
The PlayStation 2 version of Code: Veronica X had sold 900,000 copies and earned $27 million in the United States by July 2006, outselling Resident Evil 4.
Sales
The PS2 version went on to sell 1.4 million copies worldwide, for a total of 2.54 million units sold worldwide for both the Dreamcast and PS2 versions.
Sales
Next Generation ranked it as the 63rd-highest-selling game launched for the PlayStation 2, Xbox or GameCube between January 2000 and July 2006 in the United States.
Sales
Combined console sales of Resident Evil franchise released in the 2000s reached 3 million units in the United States by July 2006.
Legacy
Game Informer ranked Code: Veronica as 69th in their "Top 100 Games of All Time" in 2001.
Legacy
GamesRadar named it the 14th-best Dreamcast game of all time.
Legacy
Resident Evil Survivor 2 – Code: Veronica (2001) for Naomi-based arcades and PlayStation 2 follows the story of Code: Veronica from a first-person view with light gun shooter -style gameplay.
Legacy
Similarly, another light gun game, Resident Evil: The Darkside Chronicles (2009) was released for the Wii and features sequences set in Code: Veronica along with Resident Evil 2.
Legacy
A demo version of a fan remake of the game was released in 2021.

pst_playstatia_net_yaroza_black.title: Net Yaroze
sents: lead
The Net Yaroze (ネットやろうぜ, Netto Yarōze) is a development kit for the PlayStation video game console.
lead
It was a promotion by Sony Computer Entertainment to computer programming hobbyists which launched in June 1996 in Japan and in 1997 in other countries.
lead
It was originally called "Net Yarouze", but was changed to "Net Yaroze" in late 1996.
lead
Yarōze means "Let's do it together".
lead

Conceived by PlayStation creator Ken Kutaragi and priced at around $750 US, the Net Yaroze (DTL-H300x) package contained a special black-colored debugging PlayStation unit, a serial cable for connecting the console to a personal computer, and a CD containing PlayStation development tools.
lead

The user has to provide a personal computer (an IBM PC compatible or Macintosh; NEC PC-9801 was also supported in Japan) to write the computer code, compile it, and send the program to the PlayStation.
lead
The Net Yaroze was neither the first nor only official consumer console development kit.
lead
The PC-Engine Develo predates it, and the WonderWitch followed it.
Contents
The Access Card, a dongle which must be placed in memory card port 1 in order to boot programs which were loaded from a PC.
Versions
The Japanese version is sometimes unofficially referred to as DTL-3000 rather than DTL-H3000.
Versions
The Net Yaroze was only available for purchase by mail order; but Sony also provided it to universities in the UK, France (EPITA), and Japan.
Versions
LightWave 3D was another consumer-level PlayStation development tool.
Versions
The Yaroze's primary RAM was the same as the consumer's model (2 megabytes).
Games produced

Many games made by hobbyists on the Net Yaroze were released on various demo discs that came along with the Official UK PlayStation Magazine (as well as other official PlayStation magazines in PAL regions) from 1997 to 2004.
Games produced
The last Official UK PlayStation Magazine issue, number 108, featured a compilation with many Net Yaroze games.
Games produced
A promotional disc, limited to a thousand copies and featuring a number of user-developed games, was produced by SCEE and sent to PAL-zone Yaroze owners.
Games produced
An updated version of Time Slip was later released for Xbox Live Arcade in February 2011 and Windows in January 2012.
Games produced
Others such as Magic Castle by Kaiga were pitched to various publishers but went unreleased until it was distributed online in 2021 by one of the original staff members.

pst2_playstatia_2_linuks_kit.title: Linux for PlayStation 2
sents: lead
Linux for PlayStation 2 (or PS2 Linux) is a kit released by Sony Computer Entertainment in 2002 that allows the PlayStation 2 console to be used as a personal computer.
lead
It included a Linux -based operating system, a USB keyboard and mouse, a VGA adapter, a PS2 network adapter (Ethernet only), and a 40 GB hard disk drive (HDD).
lead
An 8 MB memory card is required; it must be formatted during installation, erasing all data previously saved on it, though afterwards the remaining space may be used for savegames.
lead
It is strongly recommended that a user of Linux for PlayStation 2 have some basic knowledge of Linux before installing and using it, due to the command-line interface for installation.
lead
The official site for the project was closed at the end of October 2009 and communities like ps2dev are no longer active.
Distribution
PlayStation and Sony ended their support of hobbyist programmers with the support of Linux on the PlayStation 3 being discontinued.

odd_pyoneer_lazeractive.title: LaserActive

Type: Converged device, home video game console

sents: lead
The LaserActive (レーザーアクティブ, RēzāAkutibu) is a converged device and fourth-generation home video game console capable of playing LaserDiscs, Compact Discs, console games, and LD-G karaoke discs.
lead
It was released by Pioneer Corporation in 1993.
lead
In addition to LaserActive games, separately sold add-on modules (called "PACs" by Pioneer) accept Mega Drive/Genesis and PC Engine/TurboGrafx-16 ROM cartridges and CD-ROMs.
lead
Pioneer released the LaserActive model CLD-A100 in Japan on August 20, 1993, at a cost of ¥89,800, and in the United States on September 13, 1993, at a cost of $970.
lead

An NEC-branded version of the LaserActive player known as the LD-ROM² System, or model PCE-LD1, was released in December 1993, which was priced identically to the original system and also accepted Pioneer's PAC modules.
PAC modules
In the headings below, the Japanese model number occurs first, followed by the North American model number.
LaserActive 3-D Goggles

The LaserActive 3-D Goggles (model GOL-1) employ an active shutter 3D system compatible with at least six 3D-ready LD-ROM software titles: 3-D Museum (1994), Vajra 2 (1994), Virtual Cameraman 2 (1994), Dr.
LaserActive 3-D Goggles
Paolo No Totteoki Video (1994), Goku (1995), and 3D Virtual Australia (1996), the last software title published for the LaserActive.
LaserActive 3-D Goggles
The goggles are also compatible with the Master System, and are interchangeable with the SegaScope 3-D Glasses.
LaserActive 3-D Goggles
A goggle adapter (model ADP-1), packaged and sold separately from the 3-D Goggles, enables the user to connect one or two pairs of goggles to the CLD-A100.
Games
An LD-ROM had a capacity of 540 MB (where digital audio would have normally been stored) with 60 minutes of analog audio and video.
Contemporary devices
In the early 1990s, a number of consumer electronics manufacturers designed converged devices around CD-ROM technology.
Contemporary devices
Some comparable systems are the Commodore CDTV, Philips CD-i, 3DO Interactive Multiplayer, and Tandy Video Information System.
Reception
Computer Gaming World in January 1994 stated that although LaserActive was "a better product in many ways" than 3DO, it lacked software and the NEC and Sega control packs were too expensive.

odd_4do_fz_1_panasonik.title: 3DO Interactive Multiplayer

Display: 320×240 @ 60 Hz, 384×288 @ 50 Hz; 16-bit palettized color (from 24-bit) or 24-bit true color.
Sound: Panasonic FZ-1 "Clio" DSP: 16-bit stereo @ 44.1 kHz, 4-Channel Dolby Surround

sents: lead
The 3DO Interactive Multiplayer, also referred to as simply 3DO, is a home video game console developed by The 3DO Company.
lead

Conceived by entrepreneur and Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, the 3DO was not a console manufactured by the company itself, but a set of specifications, originally designed by Dave Needle and RJ Mical of New Technology Group, that could be licensed by third parties.
lead
Panasonic produced the first models in 1993, and further renditions of the hardware were released afterwards by GoldStar, Sanyo, Creative Labs, and Samsung Electronics in 1997.
lead

Despite having a highly promoted launch (including being named Time magazine's "1993 Product of the Year"), the oversaturated console market and the system's mixed reviews prevented it from achieving success comparable to competing consoles from Sega and Sony, rendering its discontinuation by 1996.
lead
In 1997, The 3DO Company sold its "Opera" hardware to Samsung.
Conception
The 3DO Interactive Multiplayer was originally conceived by The 3DO Company, founded on September 12, 1991 by Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins.
Conception
To game publishers, the low US$3 royalty rate per game was a better deal than the higher royalties paid to Nintendo and Sega when making games for their consoles.
Conception
The 3DO hardware itself was designed by Dave Needle and RJ Mical (designers of the Amiga and Atari Lynx), starting from an outline on a restaurant napkin in 1989.
Licensing model
The 3DO Company lacked the resources to manufacture consoles, and instead licensed the hardware to other companies for manufacturing.
Licensing model
Trip Hawkins recounted that they approached every electronics manufacturer, but that their chief targets were Sony and Panasonic, the two largest consumer electronics companies in the world.
Licensing model
According to former Sega CEO Tom Kalinske The 3DO Company was engaged in very serious talks for Sega to become involved with the 3DO.
Licensing model
Panasonic launched the 3DO with its FZ-1 model in 1993, though Goldstar and Sanyo would later manufacture the 3DO as well.
Licensing model

Companies who obtained the hardware license but never actually sold 3DO units include Samsung, Toshiba, and AT&T, who went so far as to build prototype AT&T 3DO units and display them at the January 1994 Consumer Electronics Show.
Licensing model

The manufacturers had to make a profit on the hardware itself, whereas most major game console manufacturers, such as Sega and Sony, sold their systems at a loss, with expectations of making up for the loss with software sales.
Licensing model
The 3DO was priced at US$699, far above competing game systems and aimed at high-end users and early adopters.
Licensing model
Hawkins has argued that 3DO was launched at $599, and not "higher myths that are often reported".
Licensing model
In a later interview, Hawkins clarified that while the suggested retail price was $699, not all retailers sold the system at that price.
Licensing model
Goldstar, Sanyo, and Panasonic's later models were less expensive to manufacture than the FZ-1 and were sold for considerably lower prices.
Licensing model
For example, the Goldstar model launched at $399.
Licensing model

In addition, after six months on the market, the price of the FZ-1 had dropped to $499, leading some to contend that the 3DO's cost was not as big a factor in its market failure as is usually claimed.
Competition
Both 3DO and Philips, seeking to pioneer the broader concept of interactive entertainment, aimed to sell in the order of one million units during 1994 and into 1995.
Launch and performance
The launch of the platform in October 1993 received a great deal of attention in the press as part of the " multimedia wave" in the computer world at the time.
Launch and performance

Return Fire, Road Rash, FIFA International Soccer, and Jurassic Park Interactive had been slated for launch releases but were pushed to mid-1994 due to the developers' struggles with the then-cutting-edge hardware.
Launch and performance
The only 3DO software available at launch was the third-party game Crash 'n Burn.
Launch and performance
Panasonic also failed to manufacture an ample supply of the console in time for launch day, and as a result most retail stores only received one or two units.
Launch and performance
By mid-November, the 3DO had sold 30,000 units.
Launch and performance
The system was released in Japan in March 1994 with an initial lineup of six games.
Launch and performance
The Japanese launch was moderately successful, with 70,000 units shipping to 10,000 stores.
Launch and performance
Computer Gaming World reported in January 1994 that 3DO "is poised for an avalanche of software support to appear in the next 12 months", unlike the Atari Jaguar and Pioneer LaserActive.
Launch and performance
The 3DO's claim to the title of most advanced console on the market was lost with the 1994 Japanese launches of the Sony PlayStation and Sega Saturn.
Launch and performance
The 3DO Company responded by emphasizing their console's large existing software library, lower price (both the Panasonic and Goldstar models were $299 by this time), and promised successor: the M2.
Launch and performance
To assure consumers that the 3DO would still be supported, the M2 was initially announced as an add-on for the 3DO.
End of 3DO
Unlike Panasonic, Goldstar initially produced only 3DO hardware, not software.
End of 3DO
This made it difficult to manage competitive price drops, and when the price of the Goldstar 3DO dropped to $199 in December 1995, the company took a loss of more than $100 on each sale.
End of 3DO

This lack of a profitable business model, combined with Panasonic acquiring exclusive rights to the M2 technology, were cited as the two chief reasons for Goldstar dropping support for the 3DO in early 1996.
End of 3DO

During the second quarter of 1996 several of the 3DO's most loyal software supporters, including the software division of The 3DO Company themselves, announced they were no longer making games for the system, leaving Panasonic as the only company supporting active software development for the 3DO.
End of 3DO
The 3DO system was eventually discontinued towards the end of 1996, with a complete shutdown of all internal hardware development and divestment of the M2 technology.
End of 3DO
The 3DO Company restructured themselves around this same time, selling off their hardware division to become a multi-platform company focused on software development and online gaming.
End of 3DO
After selling the Opera hardware to Samsung in 1997, the hardware was revived in South Korea for another two years.
End of 3DO
The 3DO platform had achieved more attention in South Korea, where LG had opened a '3DO Plaza' in Seoul on its 1994 launch and many games had been localized.
End of 3DO
The initial high price is considered to be one of the many issues that led to the 3DO's failure, along with lack of significant funding that larger companies such as Sony took advantage of.
End of 3DO
In an interview shortly after The 3DO Company dropped support for the system, Trip Hawkins attributed its failure to the model of licensing all hardware manufacturing and software to third parties.
Licensed systems
A number of different manufacturers produced the 3DO system.
Licensed systems

Panasonic FZ-1 R·E·A·L 3DO Interactive Multiplayer (Japan, Asia, North America and Europe) – The first 3DO system, which was initially priced at $699.99 in the U.S. and ¥ 79,800 (1994) (equivalent to ¥ 82,875 or US$ 760 in 2019) in Japan.
Licensed systems
The price was reduced to $399.99 in the fall of 1994.
Licensed systems

Panasonic FZ-10 R·E·A·L 3DO Interactive Multiplayer (Japan, North America and Europe) – Released on November 11, 1994 (a year after the FZ-1), it is a redesigned slimmer and lighter model that replaced the FZ-1 in Panasonic's portfolio.
Licensed systems
The FZ-10 featured a top loading CD tray and an internal memory manager.
Licensed systems
The controller is also smaller and lighter than the one included with the FZ-1 as it lacks a headphones connector.
Licensed systems
Panasonic N-1005 3DO CD Changer "ROBO" (Japan only) – An FZ-1 custom console, fitted with a five disc CD drive.
Licensed systems
GoldStar GDO-101 Alive 3DO Interactive Multiplayer (South Korea) – Released in mid-1994, this model is similar in physical appearance to the Panasonic model.
Licensed systems
GoldStar GDO-101M 3DO Interactive Multiplayer (North America and Europe) – A version of the GDO-101 for foreign markets.
Licensed systems
