GoldStar GDO-202 3DO Interactive Multiplayer (Korea and Europe) – An updated version of the GDO-101.
Licensed systems
CD-ROM drive replaced with one similar to that of the FZ-1 style.
Licensed systems
GoldStar GDO-203 3DO Alive II (South Korea only) – Replaced the GDO-202 in late 1995, but was discontinued shortly thereafter.
Licensed systems
Sanyo IMP-21J TRY 3DO Interactive Multiplayer (Japan only) – Released in March 1995, this model has the pickup head on the tray (resembling a laptop optical drive).
Licensed systems
Creative 3DO Blaster – A PC ISA expansion card with a double-speed CD-ROM drive and a controller that enables compatible Windows-based PCs to play 3DO games.
Licensed systems
Arcade – American Laser Games utilized 3DO-based hardware for a number of arcade titles.
Licensed systems
DMB-800 – Manufactured exclusively for the Korean market, after the purchase of the Opera hardware in 1997 by Samsung.
Hardware
The original edition of the console, the FZ-1, was referred to in full as the 3DO REAL Interactive Multiplayer.
Hardware
The console had advanced hardware features at the time: an ARM60 32-bit RISC CPU, a custom graphics processor with a math co-processor, and a custom 16-bit DSP with a 20-bit ALU.
Hardware
The 3DO included the first light synthesizer in a game console, converting CD music to a mesmerizing color pattern.
Hardware
The 3DO is one of few CD-based units that feature neither regional lockout nor copy protection, making it easy to use illegal copies or homebrew software.
Hardware

Although there is no regional lockout for 3DO systems, a few Japanese games cannot be played on non-Japanese 3DO consoles due to a special kanji font which was not present in the English language console firmware.
Technical specifications

Resolution 640×480 (interpolated), 320×240 (actual) 60 Hz for NTSC version, and 768×576 (interpolated), 384×288 (actual) 50 Hz for PAL version with either 16-bit palettized color (from 24-bit) or 24-bit truecolor.
Technical specifications
Dual pixel engine (CEL engine) capable of producing 9–16 million pixels per second (36–64 megapix/s interpolated), distorted, scaled, rotated and texture mapped.
Technical specifications
Custom 16-bit digital signal processor (DSP) with 16-bit I/O and registers but a 20-bit ALU and accumulator, embedded in the CLIO chip.
Technical specifications
13 DMA channels of digital input, to be sampled, and distorted by the DSP.
Audio and video
The 3DO output is compatible with most existing video console switches, including those made for the NES/SNES, Sega Master System/Genesis, & NEC Turbo Grafix RF.
Audio and video
S-Video The 3DO also offers an S-Video connector for enhanced picture quality on more advanced televisions.
Power
Some models (Panasonic 3DO FZ-1, Sanyo TRY 3DO, and Goldstar 3DO) have hardwired power cords, others (Panasonic 3DO FZ-10) use an IEC 60320 C7 "figure 8" power cord.
Power
All North American model specifications are AC 120 V 60 Hz 30 W.
Basic accessories
Most 3DO systems shipped with a standard controller, as well as A/V and power cables.
Basic accessories

The 3DO controllers were unusual in that the system base unit contained only one controller port and the controllers could be physically daisy chained together via a port on the back of each controller.
Basic accessories
All controllers for each 3DO console are compatible with one another.
Basic accessories
World International Trading Corporation also released an adapter that allows Super NES controllers to be used with the 3DO.
Light gun
The only light gun released for the 3DO was the Gamegun, a product of third-party developer American Laser Games.
Light gun
Despite this, no fewer than 10 games with light gun support were produced for the system.
Light gun
Most of these were arcade ports from American Laser Games (including Mad Dog McCree), but Virgin Interactive and Digital Pictures also released 3DO light gun games.
Light gun
The 3DO Gamegun uses the same design as the Gamegun released for the Sega CD: an orange " Old West " revolver.
Light gun
Select Gameguns house a controller port so that another Gamegun may be daisy-chained for two-player gameplay, which is supported in most of American Laser Games's 3DO titles.
Light gun

Though no light gun was released for the 3DO in Japan, the Japanese localizations of Demolition Man and Corpse Killer retain light gun support, and could be played by Japanese gamers using imported Gameguns.
Mouse
The Panasonic FZ-JM1 and Logitech 3DO mouse are identical aside from their markings.
Mouse
Fewer than 20 games supported its use, some of which were optimized for the standard controller or light gun rather than the mouse.
Mouse
The Panasonic mouse was also bundled with Konami's Policenauts Limited Edition in Japan which came with a Policenauts mouse pad.
Other
The Panasonic FZ-EM256 is a 256 KB Expandable Memory Unit that plugs into the 3DO expansion port on the back of the console.
Other
The Panasonic 3DO Karaoke Mixer allows 3DO owners to play a standard music CD, turn the vocals down, plug in one or two microphones and sing over the music.
Games
The 3DO version of arcade title Samurai Shodown was the only port with faithful graphics for some time, and the 3DO Super Street Fighter II Turbo was the first port with its CD-quality audio.
Games

Since its release coincided with the arrival of the modern first-person shooter, the 3DO also had some of the earliest members of the genre as exclusives, such as Escape from Monster Manor, the previously mentioned Killing Time, and PO'ed, as well as ports of Wolfenstein 3D and Doom.
Games
The 3DO was one of the first CD-ROM consoles, and some early titles on the 3DO frequently attempted to use interactive movie -style gameplay.
Games

Such titles rendered all or nearly all of their graphics in full motion video, which necessitated that any interactive influence from the player be limited to a greater extent than other games of the time.
Games
Night Trap, D, Mad Dog McCree, and The Daedalus Encounter are among the more famous examples of full motion video driven games.
Reception
The 3DO was awarded Worst Console Launch of 1993 by Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Reception
In a special Game Machine Cross Review in May 1995, Famicom Tsūshin would score the 3DO Real console a 26 out of 40.
Legacy
The 3DO Company designed a next-generation console that was never released due to various business and technological issues.
Legacy
The M2 project, which began as an accelerator add-on for the 3DO, was to use dual PowerPC 602 processors in addition to newer 3D and video rendering technologies.

fes_console.title: Nintendo Entertainment System

Also known as: Family Computer/Famicom (Japan) Hyundai Comboy (South Korea) Samurai Electronic TV Game System (India) Dendy (Post-Soviet countries) Nintendo Entertainment System (PAL A/PAL B/Southeast Asia)
Sound: APU, 5 channels: 2 pulse wave, triangle wave, white noise, DPCM

sents: lead
The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) is an 8-bit home video game console produced by Nintendo.
lead
It was first released in Japan on 15 July 1983 as the Family Computer (Famicom).
lead
It was released in US test markets as the redesigned NES in October 1985, and fully launched in the US the following year.
lead
The NES was distributed in Europe, Australia, and parts of Asia throughout the 1980s under various names.
lead
As a third-generation console, it mainly competed with Sega 's Master System.
lead
The NES was designed by Masayuki Uemura.
lead
Nintendo's president, Hiroshi Yamauchi, called for a simple, cheap console that could run arcade games on cartridges.
lead
The controller design was reused from Nintendo's portable Game & Watch hardware.
Background
The video game industry experienced rapid growth and popularity from the late 1970s to the early 1980s, marked by the golden age of arcade games and the second generation of consoles.
Background
Games like Space Invaders (1978) became a phenomenon across arcades worldwide, while home consoles such as the Atari 2600 and the Intellivision gained footholds in the American market.
Background

Uemura's main challenge was economic rather than technological; Yamauchi wanted the system to be affordable enough for widespread household adoption, aiming for a price of ¥9,800 (less than $75) compared to existing machines priced at ¥30,000 to ¥50,000 ($200 to $350).
Inception
The team designed the cartridges to store 2,000 bytes of random-access memory (RAM), significantly more than Atari's 256 bytes.
Development

The controller designs were reused from the Game & Watch machines, although the Famicom design team originally wanted to use arcade-style joysticks, even dismantling some from American game consoles to see how they worked.
Development
Katsuya Nakawaka attached a Game & Watch D-pad to the Famicom prototype and found that it was easy to use and caused no discomfort.
Japanese release

The console was released on July 15, 1983, as the Home Cassette Type Video Game: Family Computer, for ¥14,800 (equivalent to ¥18,400 in 2019) with three ports of Nintendo's successful arcade games Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye.
Japanese release

Following a product recall and a reissue with a new motherboard, the Famicom's popularity soared, becoming the bestselling game console in Japan by the end of 1984 in what came to be called the "Famicom Boom".
Japanese release

Nintendo launched the system with only first-party games, but after being approached by Namco and Hudson Soft in 1984, agreed to produce third-party games for a 30% fee for console licensing and production costs.
North American release
Atari's CEO Ray Kassar was fired the next month, so the deal went nowhere, and Nintendo decided to market its system on its own.
North American release
Subsequent plans for the Nintendo Advanced Video System likewise never materialized.
North American release

By the beginning of 1985, more than 2.5 million Famicom units had been sold in Japan, and Nintendo soon announced plans to release it in North America as the Advanced Video Entertainment System (AVS) that year.
North American release
The Famicom hardware first made its North American debut in the arcades, in the form of the Nintendo VS.
North American release
System became a major success in North American arcades, becoming the highest-grossing arcade machine of 1985 in the United States.
North American release

Renamed the "Nintendo Entertainment System" (NES), the new and cost-reduced version lacked most of the upscale features added in the AVS but retained many of its audiophile-inspired design elements, such as the grey colour scheme and boxy form factor.
North American release

Disappointed with the cosmetically raw prototype part they received from Japan, which they nicknamed "the lunchbox", Nintendo of America designers Lance Barr and Don James added the two-tone gray, the black stripe, and the red lettering.
North American release

Nintendo seeded these first systems to limited American test markets starting in New York City on October 18, 1985, and followed up in Los Angeles in February 1986; the American nationwide release came on September 27, 1986.
North American release
WoW salesman Jim Whims distinctly recalled delivering an ultimatum: "if you want to sell Teddy Ruxpin and you want to sell Lazer Tag, you're gonna sell Nintendo as well.
North American release
The system's launch represented not only a new product, but also a reframing of the severely damaged home video game market in North America.
North American release
The most famous example is Lucasfilm Games 's attempts to port the comedy-horror game Maniac Mansion to the NES, which Nintendo insisted be considerably watered down.
North American release
Though at first, the American public exhibited limited excitement for the console itself, peripherals such as the light gun and R.O.B. attracted extensive attention.
Other markets
The first consisted of mainland Europe (excluding Italy) where distribution was handled by several different companies, with Nintendo responsible for manufacturing.
Other markets
The NES saw an early launch in Europe in 1986 although most of the European countries received the console in 1987.
Other markets
The release in Scandinavia was on September 1, 1986, where it was released by Bergsala.
Other markets
In the Netherlands, it was released in the last quarter of 1987 and was distributed by Bandai BV.
Other markets
In France, it was released in October 1987, and in Spain most likely in 1988 through distributor Spaco.
Other markets
One of the most successful local clones was the Phantom System, manufactured by Gradiente, which licensed Nintendo products in the country for the following decade.
Bundles and redesigns

The Deluxe Set was launched in the 1985 test markets, retailing at US$179.99 (equivalent to $550 in 2023), including R.O.B., a light gun called the NES Zapper, two controllers, and the two Game Paks Gyromite and Duck Hunt.
Bundles and redesigns
The Control Deck bundle was first released in 1987 at $89.99 with no game, and $99.99 bundled with the Super Mario Bros. cartridge.
Bundles and redesigns
The Action Set, released April 14, 1988, for $109.99, has the Control Deck, two controllers, an NES Zapper, and a dual Game Pak containing both Super Mario Bros. and Duck Hunt.
Bundles and redesigns
In 1992, the Challenge Set was released for $89.99 with the console, two controllers, and a Super Mario Bros.
Bundles and redesigns
The Basic Set retailed at US$89.99; it included only the console and two controllers, and no pack-in game.
Bundles and redesigns

Released in October 1993 in North America and 1994 in Australia, this final bundle retailed for $49.99 and A$69.99 (A$79.99 with the pack-in game) respectively, and was discontinued with the NES in 1995.
Discontinuation
On August 14, 1995, Nintendo discontinued the Nintendo Entertainment System in both North America and Europe.
Discontinuation
In North America, replacements for the original front-loading NES were available for $25 in exchange for a broken system until at least December 1996, under Nintendo's Power Swap program.
Discontinuation
The Game Boy and Super NES were covered for $25 and $35 respectively.
Discontinuation
On May 30, 2003, Nintendo announced the discontinuation of the Famicom in September alongside the Super Famicom and the disk rewriting services for the Famicom Disk System.
Configurations

One variant was a television set with an integrated Famicom; originally released in 1983 as the My Computer TV in 14-inch (36 cm) and 19-inch (48 cm) models, it was later released in the United States in 1989 as a 19-inch model named the Video Game Television.
Hardware clones
A range of Famicom clones was marketed in Argentina during the late 1980s and early 1990s with the name Family Game, resembling the original hardware design.
Hardware clones
Many of the clone vendors have included built-in copies of licensed Nintendo software, which constitutes copyright infringement in most countries.
Design flaws
Nintendo would ship the necessary replacement parts only to shops that had enrolled in the authorization program.
Design flaws

With the release of the top-loading NES-101 (New-Style NES) in 1993 toward the end of the NES's lifespan, Nintendo resolved the problems by switching to a standard card edge connector and eliminating the lockout chip.
Lockout
The original NES released for Western countries in 1985 contains the 10NES lockout chip, which prevents it from running cartridges unapproved by Nintendo.
Lockout

The inclusion of the 10NES was a direct influence from the 1983 video game crash in North America, partially caused by a market flooded with uncontrolled publishing of games of poor quality for the home consoles.
Lockout
Nintendo did not want to see that happen with the NES and used the lockout chip to restrict games to only those they licensed and approved for the system.
Lockout
Such regions include North America; most of continental Europe (PAL-B); Asia; and the British Isles, Italy, and Australasia (PAL-A).
Lockout

Problems with the 10NES lockout chip frequently result in one of the console's most common issues: the blinking red power light, in which the system appears to turn itself on and off repeatedly because the 10NES would reset the console once per second.
Lockout
In other cases, the console turns on but only displays a solid white, gray, or green screen.
Technical specifications

The console's main central processing unit (CPU) was produced by Ricoh, which manufactured different versions between NTSC and PAL regions; NTSC consoles have a 2A03 clocked at 1.79 MHz Tooltip megahertz, and PAL consoles have a 2A07 clocked at 1.66 MHz.
Technical specifications
The console's graphics are handled by a Ricoh 2C02, a processor known as the Picture Processing Unit (PPU) that is clocked at 5.37 MHz.
Technical specifications
The console's standard display resolution is 256 × 240 pixels, though video output options vary between models.
Technical specifications
The original Famicom features only radio frequency (RF) modulator output, and the NES additionally supports composite video via RCA connectors.
Controllers
Though the original button layout was retained, the shape of the redesigned controller—nicknamed the " dog bone " controller—resembles that of the Super Famicom and SNES.
Controllers
The original NES controller has become one of the most recognizable symbols of the console.
Controllers
Nintendo has mimicked the look of the controller in several other products, from promotional merchandise to limited edition versions of the Game Boy Advance.
Japanese accessories
The Famicom 3D System, an active shutter 3D headset peripheral released in 1987, enabled the ability to play stereoscopic video games.
Japanese accessories
A dial-up modem was never released for the NES after a partnership with Fidelity Investments.
Famicom Disk System

Partnering with Mitsumi to develop a floppy disk add-on for the Famicom based on the latter's Quick Disk format, Nintendo officially released it as the Family Computer Disk System in Japan on February 21, 1986, at a retail price of ¥15,000.
Famicom Disk System
Though selling close to two million units for all of 1986, Nintendo only managed to increase the total to 4.4 million units by 1990, falling well short of internal projections.
Famicom Disk System
Most of its games were re-released with workarounds on cartridge for both the Famicom and NES, without the enhanced audio.
Famicom Disk System
Although the last game for the Disk System was released in December 1992, Nintendo continued repair and rewrite services for it until September 2003.
NES Test Station
The television it is connected to (typically 11" to 14") is meant to be placed atop it.
Game Pak
The NES uses a 72-pin design, as compared with 60 pins on the Famicom.
Game Pak

All licensed NTSC and PAL cartridges are a standard shade of gray plastic, with the exception of The Legend of Zelda and Zelda II: The Adventure of Link, which were manufactured in gold-plastic carts.
Game Pak
Nintendo also produced yellow-plastic carts for internal use at Nintendo Service Centers, although these "test carts" were never made available for purchase.
Game Pak
For promotion of DuckTales: Remastered, Capcom sent 150 limited-edition gold NES cartridges with the original game, featuring the Remastered art as the sticker, to different gaming news agencies.
Third-party licensing
Acclaim Entertainment, a fledgling game publisher founded by former Activision employees, was the first major third-party licensee in the United States to sign on with Nintendo in late 1987.
Third-party licensing

The global 1988 shortage of DRAM and ROM chips reportedly caused Nintendo to only permit an average of 25% of publishers' requests for cartridges, with some receiving much higher amounts and others almost none.
Third-party licensing

Nintendo and the FTC settled the case in April 1991, with Nintendo required to send vouchers giving a $5 discount off to a new game, to every person that had purchased an NES game between June 1988 and December 1990.
Third-party licensing
Consoles from Nintendo's rivals in the post-SNES era had always enjoyed much stronger third-party support than Nintendo, which relied more heavily on first-party games.
Unlicensed games
Companies that refused to pay the licensing fee or were rejected by Nintendo found ways to circumvent the console's authentication system.
Unlicensed games
Most of these companies created circuits that use a voltage spike to temporarily disable the 10NES chip.
Unlicensed games
Nintendo successfully sued Tengen for copyright infringement.
Unlicensed games
Tengen's antitrust claims against Nintendo were never decided.
Game rentals
Nintendo lost the lawsuit, but did win on a claim of copyright infringement.
Game rentals
Blockbuster was banned from including photocopies of original, copyrighted instruction booklets with its rented games.
Reception
Compute! reported in 1989 that Nintendo had sold seven million NES systems in 1988 alone, almost as many as the number of Commodore 64s sold in its first five years.
Reception

"Computer game makers scared stiff", the magazine said, stating that Nintendo's popularity caused most competitors to have poor sales during the previous Christmas and resulted in serious financial problems for some.
Reception
In June 1989, Nintendo of America's vice president of marketing Peter Main, said that the Famicom was present in 37% of Japan's households.
Reception
By 1990, 30% of American households owned the NES, compared to 23% for all personal computers.
Reception
In the early 1990s, gamers predicted that competition from technologically superior systems such as the 16-bit Sega Genesis would mean the immediate end of the NES's dominance.
Reception

Nintendo produced new Famicom units in Japan until September 25, 2003, and continued to repair Famicom consoles until October 31, 2007, attributing the discontinuation of support to insufficient supplies of parts.
Reception
By 1990, the Master System was the highest-selling console in Europe, though the NES was beginning to have a fast-growing user base in the United Kingdom.
Legacy

The NES was released two years after the video game crash of 1983, when many retailers and adult consumers regarded electronic games as a passing fad, so many believed at first that the NES would soon fade.
Legacy
Super Mario Bros. is the forerunner of side-scrolling games, while The Legend of Zelda had mostly influenced action-adventure games and helped popularizing the save data in video games.
Emulation
The first emulator was the Japanese-only Pasofami.
Emulation
The first version of NESticle, an unofficial MS-DOS -based emulator, was released on April 3, 1997.
Re-release

On July 14, 2016, Nintendo announced the November 2016 launch of a miniature replica of the NES, named the Nintendo Entertainment System: NES Classic Edition in the United States and Nintendo Classic Mini: Nintendo Entertainment System in Europe and Australia.
Re-release
The emulation-based console includes 30 permanently bundled games from the vintage NES library, including the Super Mario Bros. series and The Legend of Zelda series.
Re-release
However, Nintendo announced in September 2017 that the NES Classic Mini would return to production on June 29, 2018, only to be discontinued again permanently by December of that year.

fes_fes_action_set.title: NES Play Action Football
sents: lead
NES Play Action Football is a football video game developed by Tose and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It was released in 1990 in North America only.
lead
The game was also ported to the Game Boy as Play Action Football, and received a follow-up on the Super NES titled Super Play Action Football in 1992 in North America only.
lead
It was released on the Wii Virtual Console in North America on September 10, 2007.
lead
The Virtual Console version was available as a Club Nintendo bonus download from August 19 to September 2, 2012.
Overview
The game used an isometric view, presenting the game at an angle to make it appear 3-D, and the game allowed a very large number of moving objects (all the players) to be on screen at the same time.
Overview
Another feature was the use of primitive digitized voices for such actions as "Touchdown!" or "First down!" and "Ready!
Overview
To allow teammates to select plays without showing the competitors, it included a NES Play Action Football 4 player play card.

fes_fes_top_loader_fes_101.title: Toploader
sents: lead
Toploader are an English rock band from Eastbourne, East Sussex, formed in 1997, with over two million album sales and several top 20 hits both home and abroad.
lead
Their debut album, Onka's Big Moka, sold over one million units and peaked in the top 5 of the UK Albums Chart, where it remained for six months.
lead
It earned them four nominations at the 2001 Brit Awards.
lead
They are recognised most of all for their cover of King Harvest's US hit "Dancing in the Moonlight" written by Sherman Kelly, which became a global hit for the band.
lead
Their second album, Magic Hotel, reached number 3 in the UK Albums Chart.
lead
The band reunited in 2009; they continue to tour and record music.
Formation and early start (1997–1998)
Named after a joint-rolling technique, Toploader's live career began playing with Coldplay and Muse in small venues across the UK.
Formation and early start (1997–1998)
On 20 July 2000 they backed Bon Jovi at the original Wembley Stadium, becoming the last British band to play there before it was demolished and redeveloped.
Commercial success (1999–2001)
By 1998, Toploader had been picked up by S2 Records, a subsidiary of Sony Music, and signed a six-album deal.
Commercial success (1999–2001)
On 7 May 1999, the band made their first live TV performance on TFI Friday, hosted by Chris Evans.
Commercial success (1999–2001)
Later that same year their debut album, Onka's Big Moka, was released on 11 November and became a huge hit.
Commercial success (1999–2001)
On 24 June 2000, Toploader played at the Glastonbury Festival, as part of the Saturday line-up.
They struggled with a backlash from the UK music press and their single, "Time of My Life", could only make it into the Top 20.
Because of the negative reception and the album not meeting the same success as the first, they were dropped by S2.
Julian Deane retired as a musician and in 2007 he founded Raygun Music, a Brighton based management company, that serves both as a record label and publisher.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
Six years later, Toploader reformed and signed a one-album deal with Underdogs Music for their third album, which was released in June 2011.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
The album's title was Only Human, and the first single from it, "Never Stop Wondering", was released on 14 March 2011.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
Another single, "A Balance to All Things" (featuring a remix from Ash Howes), followed on 20 June 2011.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
On 28 April 2012, they performed at the University of Gloucestershire Student Union Summerball.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
They also performed at Aberystwyth University's May Ball on 11 May 2012.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
During 2012 the band agreed to act as patrons for a UK-based children's charity called 'Time Is Precious'.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
In November 2012 they performed a gig in Frome, Somerset with all proceeds going to the charity, which helps ill children and their families.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
In 2013, Toploader released a new single "Turn It Around", co-written with Eg White and produced by Andrew Green, as part of a four-song EP.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
In the summer of 2013 they headlined the LeeStock Music Festival in Suffolk and the AmpRocks Festival in Bedfordshire.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
On 12 May 2017, Toploader's fourth album, Seeing Stars was released on Big Lake Music, a sub-label of India Media Group; "Roll with the Punches" was chosen as the lead single.
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
Toploader appeared on Ant & Dec's Saturday Night Takeaway on 18 March 2023 as part of the "Sing-a-long Live" segment, where they performed "Dancing in the Moonlight".
Reforming and later work (2009–present)
The band performed at the 2023 Conservative Party conference in Manchester on 3 October 2023 and the 2023 Labour Party Conference in Liverpool on 11 October.

fes_funicom_3d_system.title: Famicom 3D System
sents: lead
The Famicom 3D System is a Japan-exclusive accessory for the Nintendo Family Computer released in 1987.
Overview
The 3D System consists of a pair of active shutter glasses and an adapter to connect them to the Famicom's third player expansion port.
Overview
The glasses are connected to the adapter via dual 3.5 mm jacks.
Overview
Games would play in conventional 2D until a "3D mode" was activated by use of the select button.
Twin Famicom 3D System
Sharp Corporation released their own branded version of the 3D System called the Twin Famicom 3D System.
Twin Famicom 3D System
Though marketed towards users of Sharp's Twin Famicom, it was equivalent to the 3D System with only cosmetic differences.
Reception and legacy
The 3D System was a commercial failure and, as a result, was never released outside Japan.
Reception and legacy
Criticisms included the clunkiness of the glasses and the limited selection of compatible titles.
Reception and legacy
Eight years later, in 1995, Nintendo again ventured into stereoscopic gaming with the commercially unsuccessful Virtual Boy.
Reception and legacy

In the following years, Nintendo experimented in stereoscopic 3D with both the GameCube and Game Boy Advance SP systems, but these features were not released commercially due to cost and technical limitations.
Reception and legacy
In 2011, Nintendo released the 3DS handheld capable of displaying stereoscopic 3D images without the need for special glasses.

fes_funicom_network_system.title: Famicom Disk System

Memory: 32 kB disk cache 8 kB game RAM
Sound: 1 extra channel of wavetable synth facilitated by Ricoh 2C33

sents: lead

The Family Computer Disk System, commonly shortened to the Famicom Disk System, or just Disk System, is a peripheral for Nintendo 's Family Computer home video game console, released only in Japan on February 21, 1986.
lead
It uses proprietary floppy disks called "Disk Cards" for cheaper data storage and it adds a new high-fidelity sound channel for supporting Disk System games.
lead

Fundamentally, the Disk System serves simply to enhance some aspects already inherent to the base Famicom system, with better sound and cheaper games — though with the disadvantages of high initial price, slow speed, and lower reliability.
lead
However, this boost to the market of affordable and writable mass storage temporarily served as an enabling technology for the creation of new types of video games.
lead

This includes the vast, open world, progress-saving adventures of the best-selling The Legend of Zelda (1986) and Metroid (1986), games with a cost-effective and swift release such as the best-selling Super Mario Bros.
lead
2, and nationwide leaderboards and contests via the in-store Disk Fax kiosks, which are considered to be forerunners of today's online achievement and distribution systems.
lead
By 1989, the Famicom Disk System was inevitably obsoleted by the improving semiconductor technology of game cartridges.
lead
The Disk System's lifetime sales reached 4.4 million units by 1990, making it the most successful console add-on of all time, despite not being sold outside of Japan.
History
By 1985, Nintendo's Family Computer was dominating the Japanese home video game market, selling over three million units within a year and a half.
History
The add-on itself was produced by Masayuki Uemura and Nintendo Research & Development 2, the same team that designed the Famicom itself.
History
Following several delays, the Famicom Disk System was released on February 21, 1986, at a retail price of ¥15000 (US$80).
History
The same day, Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda as a launch title, alongside disk re-releases of earlier Famicom games.
History
The Famicom Disk System sold over 300,000 units within three months, jumping to over 2 million by the end of the year.
History
Nintendo remained confident the Disk System would be a sure-fire success, and ensured that all future first-party releases would be exclusive to the peripheral.
History
These kiosks allowed customers to bring in their disk games and have a new game rewritten onto them for a ¥500 fee; blank disks could also be purchased for ¥2000.
History
Nintendo of America announced plans to release the Disk System for the Famicom's international counterpart, the Nintendo Entertainment System, however these plans were eventually scrapped.
History
Most common was the quality of the Disk Cards; Nintendo removed the shutters on most Disk System games to reduce costs, instead placing them in a wax sleeve and clear plastic shell.
History

Four months after the Disk System was released, Capcom released a Famicom conversion of Ghosts 'n Goblins on a 128k cartridge - larger than the Disk Card's 112k capacity - which, as a result, made consumers and developers less impressed with the Disk System's technological features.
History
The Disk System's vague error messages, long loading times, and the poor quality of the rubber drive belt that spun the disks are also cited as attributing to its downfall.
History
By 1989, advancements in technology made cartridge games much cheaper and easier to produce, leaving the Famicom Disk System obsolete.
History
Nintendo officially discontinued the Famicom Disk System in 1990, selling around 4.4 million units total.
History
Disk writing services were still kept in operation until September 30, 2003, while technical services were provided up until October 31, 2007.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
Widespread copyright violation in Japan's predominantly personal-computer-based game rental market inspired corporations to petition the government to ban the rental of all video games in 1984.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
With games then being available only via full purchase, demand rose for a new and less expensive way to access more games.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks

In 1986, as video gaming had increasingly expanded from computers into the video game console market, Nintendo advertised a promise to install 10,000 Famicom Disk Writer kiosks in toy and hobby stores across Japan within one year.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
To write an existing disk with a new game from the available roster was ¥500 (then about US$3.25 and 1/6 of the price of many new games).
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
Instruction sheets were given by the retailer, or available by mail order for ¥100.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
In 1987, Disk Writer kiosks in select locations were also provisioned as Disk Fax systems as Nintendo's first online concept.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
Players participated in a nationwide leaderboard, with unique prizes.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks
The kiosk service was very popular and remained available until 2003.
Disk Writer and Disk Fax kiosks

In subsequent console generations, Nintendo would relaunch this online national leaderboard concept with the home satellite-based Satellaview subscription service in Japan from 1995 to 2000 for the Super Famicom.
Technology
The RAM Adapter contains 32 kilobytes (KB) of RAM for temporarily caching program data from disk, 8 KB of RAM for tile and sprite data storage, and an ASIC named the 2C33.
Technology
Finally, embedded in the 2C33 is an 8KB BIOS ROM.
Technology
The Disk Cards used are double-sided, with a total capacity of 112 KB per disk.
Technology
Batteries usually last five months with daily game play.
Technology
The Disk System's Disk Cards are somewhat proprietary 71 mm × 76 mm (2.8 × 3 in) 56K-per-side double-sided floppy.
Technology

They are a slight modification of Mitsumi 's Quick Disk 71 mm 2.8 in square disk format which is used in a handful of Japanese computers and various synthesizer keyboards, along with a few word processors.
Games
There are about 200 games in the Famicom Disk System's library.
Games
Some are FDS exclusives, some are Disk Writer exclusives, and many were re-released years later on the cartridge format such as The Legend of Zelda for NES in 1987, and for Famicom in 1994.
Games
The most notable FDS originals include The Legend of Zelda, Zelda II: The Adventure of Link, Kid Icarus, Metroid, and Akumajō Dracula (Castlevania).
Games
2 originated from a disk-only game called Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic.
Games
The final FDS game release was Janken Disk Jō in December 1992, a rock paper scissors game featuring the Disk System mascot, Disk-kun.
Legacy
Within its library of 200 original games, some are FDS-exclusive and many were re-released one or two years later on cartridges for Famicom and NES, though without the FDS's additional sound channel.

fes_funicom_data_recordr.title: Famicom Data Recorder
sents: lead
Famicom Data Recorder (HVC-008) is a compact cassette tape data interface introduced in 1984, for the Famicom which had been introduced in 1983.
lead
It is compatible with four Famicom games, for saving user-generated content to tapes.
lead
As Nintendo's first rewritable storage medium, it was replaced by the Famicom Disk System in 1986.
History
Based on the read-only memory cartridge medium, the premium cost of easy-to-use solid-state data storage technology, such as battery-backed memory, drove the 1980s market to seek cheaper compromises.
History
Manufactured by Matsushita/Panasonic for Nintendo, the cassette tape drive was released in 1984 only in Japan for ¥9,800.
Operation
The Famicom Data Recorder is powered either by a 6 volt adapter or 4 AA batteries.
Operation
The Recorder has two data ports that use a conventional 3.5mm mono phone connector.
Operation
The Data Recorder set includes an instruction manual, a data cable, a Nintendo-branded compact cassette, a 6 volt AC adapter, and a carrying handle that extends from the front bezel.

fes_family_basik_keyboard.title: Family BASIC
sents: lead
Family BASIC is a consumer product for programming on the Family Computer video game console.
lead
Family BASIC was launched on June 21, 1984, to consumers in Japan by Nintendo, in cooperation with Hudson Soft and Sharp Corporation.
lead
A second version titled Family BASIC V3 was released on February 21, 1985, with greater memory and new features.
Overview

The first edition of the Family BASIC application cartridge is bundled with a computer style keyboard and instructional textbook, and requires a cassette tape recorder to save user-generated BASIC programs.
Overview
1984-1985, are Family BASIC development componentry, or appear in premade Family BASIC games.
Overview
Like Integer BASIC and Tiny BASIC, the Family BASIC interpreter only supports integers.
Development
Family BASIC was released in Japan by Nintendo for the Family Computer on June 21, 1984, in Japan.
Development

Two revisions of Family BASIC were produced — the first, "v.2.1", was released shortly after production of the game begun, and the second, "v.3.0", was released in early 1985. v.3.0 features expanded memory and several minigames built-in to the programming cartridge, indicated by a red cartridge shell.
Reception
Family BASIC was commercially successful, with more than 400,000 units sold by the end of the 1980s.
Reception
In IGN's 2013 retrospective of the Famicom's library that was lost to audiences outside Japan, Lucas Thomas called Family BASIC "a legitimate home computing solution".
Legacy
Cho Ren Sha 68K designer Koichi "Famibe No Yosshin" Yoshida used Family BASIC to create two shoot 'em up games titled Zacner and Zacner II.
Legacy
This inspired him to create his own handmade Famicom game development hardware, and make Game Freak 's debut game Quinty, later released as Mendel Palace (1990).

fes_r_o_b_b_robotic_operating_pa.title: R.O.B.
sents: lead
(Robotic Operating Buddy) is a toy robot accessory for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES).
lead
It was launched in July 1985 as the in Japan, and October 1985 as R.O.B. in North America.
lead
Its short lifespan yielded only two games in the Robot Series: Gyromite and Stack-Up.
lead
"the world's only interactive robot".
lead
The NES's extensive marketing plan immediately and successfully centered on R.O.B., with the October 1985 test market launch in Manhattan, New York.
lead
This was Nintendo's debut in the North American video game console market, which eventually revitalized the entire video game industry.
lead
R.O.B. was quietly discontinued a few years later, and is now remembered as a successful Trojan Horse of marketing.
lead
He is a cameo or playable character in many Nintendo games such as the Super Smash Bros. series.
Development
But the entire American video game industry, which had been devastated by the video game crash of 1983, first needed a relaunch.
Development

The Family Computer Robot, a recent niche entry in the Famicom's aftermarket accessory lineup in Japan on July 26, 1985, is a mechanized toy robot with working arms and crude eyesight, resembling "a cross between E.T. and R2-D2".
Development

You no longer have to fight only the aliens on the screen; you have a robot to contend with as well." Computer Entertainer called it "the world's only interactive robot", because no other video game system or home computer package ever had one, greatly distinguishing the NES to retailers and consumers alike.
Development
Nintendo of America staff received the first R.O.B. shipment from Japan, initially thrilled with anticipation while unboxing and using the robot.
Development

Howard Phillips remembered, "The technology was so cool! [...] like voodoo magic [...] But then his actual motion was just hysterically slow." Nintendo marketing executive Gail Tilden recalled, "That thing was definitely like watching grass grow.
Development

But again, like Rock 'em Sock 'em Robots, I wouldn't want to do it for 40 hours." Tasked with all of the NES's naming and branding, the sole marketing staff member Gail Tilden said the name was "originally going to be OTTO, which was a play on the word 'auto'", but she settled on Robotic Operating Buddy, or R.O.B.
Development
As the centerpiece of the new NES platform, R.O.B. was revealed at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago in June 1985.
Development
Our new video robot is the first of a long line of winners to come from Nintendo." and that R.O.B. is the "star of a new Entertainment System that's programmed to make you rich".
Release

Nintendo anticipated that R.O.B.'s flair for futurism, personality, and physicality was so crucial to the success of the NES, that the toy was featured prominently in much of the advertising media of the system and its game library, even more than any particular game and even with only one robot game.
Release

The toy robot is the highlighted accessory within the first and most premium NES consumer product offering, the Deluxe Set boxed bundle of Control Deck, R.O.B., Zapper light gun, Gyromite, and Duck Hunt.
Release
The NES was launched as the Deluxe Set, in the October 1985 test market of New York City, then in further test markets including Los Angeles, Chicago, and San Francisco, and finally nationwide.
Release
Soon in 1985 came the second and final entry in the Robot Series, Stack-Up, packaged separately along with its own physical game pieces.
Release
The NES was soon sold much more popularly in the form of only the Control Deck and Super Mario Bros. — without R.O.B.
Hardware

The patent underlying the R.O.B. product was filed by Gunpei Yokoi as "photosensing video game control system", with the same optical electronics as a Zapper, and likewise only functions correctly with a cathode ray tube (CRT) television and not an LCD.
Games
Only two officially licensed games were published for R.O.B., which comprise Nintendo's Robot Series: Gyromite and Stack-Up.
Games
Computer Entertainer reported Nintendo's supposed plans as stated prior to CES June 1985, for four more nondescript Robot Series games, but they were never released.
Gyromite
Hector cannot jump, so he can only collect dynamite by descending upon it.
Aftermarket
In 2014, independent game developer Retrozone produced a limited release NES cartridge titled 8-Bit X-Mas 2014.
Reception

In January 1986, an independent research firm commissioned by Nintendo delivered a survey of 200 NES owners, showing that the most popular given reason for buying an NES was because children wanted the robot—followed by good graphics, variety of games, and the uniqueness and newness of the NES package.
Reception
The creation and marketing of R.O.B. as a "Trojan Horse" after the video game crash of 1983 was placed fifth in GameSpy's twenty-five smartest moves in gaming history.
Reception
Yahoo! ranked R.O.B. as one of the craziest video game controllers and noted the unfortunate fact that the peripheral only worked with two games.
Reception

By 1987, the two-year-old R.O.B. and Robot Series had received none of Nintendo's promised updates while the rest of the NES's library had exploded with classic flagship franchise-building hits like Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, and Metroid.
Reception

In 1987, Mark Seeley of Crash! magazine visited a toy fair in England to observe a playthrough of Gyromite with R.O.B., saying of the struggling demonstrator that he had "never seen anything so complicated and difficult in all my life".
Legacy

R.O.B. has made cameo appearances in many video games, such as StarTropics (1990) for NES, F-Zero GX (2003), the WarioWare series, The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (2015, 3DS), and the Star Fox series.
Legacy
Brawl, Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U, and Super Smash Bros.
Legacy
As part of Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U, R.O.B. has two Amiibo figurines, uniquely produced in both the gray and white NES color scheme and the red and white Famicom color scheme.

fes_zapper.title: NES Zapper

Predecessor: Video Shooting Series light gun for Famicom

sents: lead
The Zapper is an electronic light gun accessory launched within the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) in North America on October 18, 1985.
lead

It is a cosmetic redesign by Nintendo of America 's head designer Lance Barr, based on Gunpei Yokoi 's Video Shooting Series light gun (光線銃シリーズガン), which had been released in Japan for the Famicom on February 18, 1984.
lead
The Zapper requires compatible NES games, such as Duck Hunt, Wild Gunman, and Hogan's Alley.
lead
Its internal optical sensor allows the player to aim at a television set and accurately shoot at in-game targets.
lead
The Zapper bridged Nintendo's existing library of hit arcade light-gun shooter games into the NES's launch library.
lead
As distinct toys, the Zapper and R.O.B.
lead
(Robotic Operating Buddy) were key to the identity of the NES bundle, for positioning the NES's 1985–1986 launch into the North American toy market instead of into the crashed video game market.
Design
The Video Shooting Series light gun was designed for Famicom by Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada of Nintendo R&D1, modeled realistically after a revolver.
Design
The Video Shooting Series light gun is a double-action revolver with a moving hammer, which is automatically fired with a loud bang when the trigger is pulled without needing to cock the hammer.
Design
In 1988, the Federal Toy Gun Law required that toy guns be distinct from real guns, so the orange revision was released in 1989.
History
The Video Shooting Series light gun was released for Famicom in Japan on February 18, 1984, bundled with Wild Gunman, and a holster accessory was released.
North America

In January 1985, at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show (CES), Nintendo of America presented the Advanced Video System, a prototype American redesign of the Famicom, which was pitched as a high-end piece of consumer electronics.
North America

The NES ports of Nintendo's existing hit arcade games Duck Hunt and Hogan's Alley were used to position the NES as a gun game instead of a video game system, and Nintendo Research & Development 1 developed the R.O.B.
North America
On October 18, 1985, the NES was launched in the New York City test market, bundled with the Control Deck, Zapper, R.O.B., two controllers, Duck Hunt, and Gyromite.
North America

After successful launch in New York, the NES was gradually rolled out to other major markets in the United States, starting with Los Angeles in February 1986 and followed by other major American cities, culminating in the nationwide launch in July 1986.
North America
In June 1986, the original launch bundle was rebranded as the Deluxe Set, and a cheaper bundle was launched with two controllers and Super Mario Bros.
North America
In January 1988, at the Winter CES, the orange Zapper revision was announced (as had been required by the Federal Toy Gun Law of 1987) within the new Action Set bundle of the NES.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
In 1988, the Video Shooter was released in the United States by Placo Toys.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
When the gun is fired, a red light on the back of the gun is illuminated to indicate that a shot has been fired.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
In late 1988, the Video Blaster was released in North America by Camerica.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
On February 20, 1989, Bandai released the Hyper Shot in Japan.
Accessories and third-party counterparts

When used with Space Shadow, the Hyper Shot can output game audio from its built-in speaker and use haptic feedback to simulate the recoil of firing a gun; while the Hyper Shot can be used as a controller and light gun for any game, Space Shadow is the only game to support the speaker and haptic feedback.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
Space Shadow requires the Hyper Shot and cannot be played with other light guns, as the game expects button input to come from the Famicom expansion port (which only the Hyper Shot can provide).
Accessories and third-party counterparts
In 1989, Nexoft released The Dominator ProBeam in the United States, a wireless version of the NES Zapper.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
In 1990, Konami released the LaserScope, a headset accessory for use with the NES Zapper, in the United States and Japan.
Accessories and third-party counterparts
In the United States, Laser Invasion came with a coupon for a $5 discount for the LaserScope.
Gameplay
The Japan-only Space Shadow was bundled with, and can uniquely use the speakers and haptic feedback of, the Hyper Shot light gun.
Operation
The Zapper can only be used on CRT displays; it will not work on LCDs, plasma displays or other flat panel displays due to display lag.
Reception
In July 1988, Computer Entertainer opined that Freedom Force was Sunsoft 's "best game yet.
Reception
Most of its survey respondents who own a game console also had a light gun.
Reception

In August 1988, Antic magazine praised the Zapper's accuracy compared to the poor horizontal accuracy of the Atari XG-1 light gun, saying "if something is lined up in sights, that's exactly what you hit".
Reception
In the 2001 book The Ultimate History of Video Games, Steven L.
Reception
Kent argues that "most of the 500 retailers who sold the NES that Christmas might not have taken the merchandise if it were not for a risky offer made by Arakawa himself—a money-back guarantee."
Legacy
The Wii U game Splatoon and its Nintendo Switch sequels Splatoon 2 and Splatoon 3 all include several N-ZAP weapons, which are heavily based on the Zapper's design.
Legacy
The N-ZAP '85 and N-ZAP '89 use the gray and orange colors of the Zapper respectively.
Legacy
The N-ZAP '83 appears in Splatoon and Splatoon 2 only, with the red and gold from the original Famicom controller, but shaped like the Zapper.

fes_power_padd.title: Power Pad
sents: lead
The Power Pad (known in Japan as Family Trainer, and in Europe and briefly in the United States as Family Fun Fitness) is a floor mat game controller for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
It is a gray mat with twelve pressure-sensors embedded between two layers of flexible plastic.
lead
It was originally developed by Bandai.
lead
Bandai first released the accessory in 1986 as the Family Trainer pack for the Famicom in Japan, and later released in the United States.
lead
Nintendo released it in 1988 as the Power Pad, along with the game World Class Track Meet, which was a rebranding of an earlier game.
Overview
The Power Pad was originally released by Bandai as the Family Trainer in Japan in 1986, and as the Family Fun Fitness both in North America and Europe in 1987 and 1988 respectively.
Overview
In 1988, Nintendo acquired the rights from Bandai for the accessory in North America and renamed it the Power Pad, with the remaining Family Fun Fitness mats recalled from stores.
Overview
There are two illustrated sides to the pad: Side A, which is rarely used, has eight buttons, while side B has twelve buttons numbered 1-12.
Revival
In 2007, Namco Bandai Games announced that the Power Pad would see a reappearance for the original Wii.
Compatible games
The following is a list of all 11 video games which were created for use with the accessory.
Compatible games
The games were developed by Human Entertainment except for the last three entries in the series.

fes_mitt.title: Power Glove

Controller input: 1 Crosshead A B Action Buttons Start Select Buttons Turbo Buttons

sents: lead
The Power Glove is a controller accessory for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
The Power Glove gained public attention due to its early virtual reality mechanics and significant marketing.
lead
However, its two games did not sell well, as it was not packaged with a game, and it was criticized for its imprecise and difficult-to-use controls.
Development
The Power Glove was originally released in 1989.
Development
Zimmerman built the first prototype that demonstrated finger flex measurement and hand position tracking using a pair of ultrasonic transmitters.
Design and functionality
The glove has traditional NES controller buttons on the forearm as well as a program button and buttons labeled 0–9.
Design and functionality
The design of the Glove was based on RoboCop from the 1987 film of the same name.
Design and functionality
The ultrasonic speakers take turns transmitting a short burst (a few pulses) of 40 kHz sound and the system measures the time it takes for the sound to reach the microphones.
Design and functionality
The only dimension it cannot calculate is the pitch of the hand, since the hand can pitch without moving the location of the two ultrasonic speakers.
Games
Two games were released with specific features for use with the Power Glove: Super Glove Ball, a faux-3D puzzle maze game; and Bad Street Brawler, a beat 'em up.
Games
Since no Power Glove-specific games ever retailed in Japan, the Power Glove was sold only as an alternative controller.
Games
Two more games, Glove Pilot and Manipulator Glove Adventure, were announced but never released.
Games

Another unreleased game, Tech Town or Tektown, is a virtual puzzle solving game in which the player moved a robotic hand around a deserted space station type of setting, using the glove to open doors and to pick up and use tools.
Games
The Power Glove was adopted by the emerging virtual reality community in the 1990s to interact with 3D worlds in a cheaper way to the popular high end DataGlove produced by VPL Research.
Reception
The Power Glove sold nearly one million units and was a commercial success.
Reception
Only two games were specially constructed for the Power Glove, and many users had no practical use for it for other noteworthy games of its time.
Reception

Consumer complaints also noted the poor connection signal between the glove and the console, build quality of the materials, and high price point for 1989 (retail price was $100, approximately $250 in 2024).
In popular culture
The Power Glove is featured in the 1989 film The Wizard, wielded by antagonist Lucas Barton (Jackey Vinson), who infamously declares, "I love the Power Glove - it's so bad."
In popular culture
The Power Glove is parodied in the 1991 horror film Freddy's Dead: The Final Nightmare, complete with Krueger saying, "Now I'm playing with power!"
In popular culture
In 2013, a documentary titled The Power of Glove was put into development.
In popular culture
The Power Glove appears in the hacking scene in the 2015 movie Kung Fury.
In popular culture
The Power Glove was featured in the 2021 movie 8-Bit Christmas, and New York Times writer Calum Marsh describes the Power Glove's "awfulness" as what "sets the plot in motion".
In popular culture
The 2023 superhero film Blue Beetle features the Power Glove in its climax.
Modern influences
Essential Reality's P5 controller, released in 2002, was a PC input device that borrows elements from the Power Glove and U-Force.

fes_fes_four_scour.title: NES Four Score
sents: lead
The NES Four Score is a multitap accessory created by Nintendo in 1990 for the Nintendo Entertainment System.
lead
Select games can utilize it to enable up to four-player gameplay.
lead
The NES Four Score is similar to the previously introduced NES Satellite, a device that allows four players to connect to the NES and extends the range using infrared wireless communication.
lead
Prior to the advent of NES multitap support, the NES games supporting more than two players required the players to pair up and then alternate turns while sharing the same pair of NES controllers.
lead
Some games that originally featured support for more than two players, such as some arcade titles, support only two simultaneous players in their NES versions.
lead
The NES Four Score plugs into both controller ports on the NES console and allows input of up to four NES controllers.
lead
On the NES Four Score, there is an option to switch between two-player and four-player modes, and there are turbo A and B buttons that give any of the connected controllers a rapid-fire boost.
lead
The NES Four Score can also be used as a controller extension cable because the wire which leads from the accessory to the NES is several feet in length.
4-Players Adaptor
The 4-Players Adaptor is a licensed peripheral released for the Famicom in Japan by Hori.
4-Players Adaptor

The adapter also features a switch that allows the first two players to use external controllers in lieu of the standard Famicom controllers, giving each player the choice to use an external controller.

fes_fes_satellyte.title: NES Satellite
sents: lead
The NES Satellite is a Nintendo Entertainment System multiplayer adaptor accessory (multitap), created by Nintendo and released in 1989 as a part of the NES Sports Set.
lead
With select supporting games, the Satellite allows up to four players to play the NES, potentially simultaneously.
lead
Additionally, it acts as a wireless range extender adaptor for all wired controllers, with the use of portable, battery-powered, infrared technology.
lead
While a normal controller has a range of 7.6 feet, the NES Satellite expands the usable range to 15 feet.
lead
A small infrared receiver plugs into the two controller ports on the front of the NES.
lead
The main Satellite unit is powered by six C-cell batteries and must have a line of sight to the receiver.
lead
The unit has four controller ports which accommodate any type of wired NES controllers.
lead
The unit provides " Turbo " selectors for both the A and B buttons.

fes_fes_max.title: NES Advantage
sents: lead
The NES Advantage is an arcade style controller manufactured by Asciiware and released by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1987.
lead
The device is meant to rest on a flat surface at a comfortable level, such as a tabletop or the floor, with the player seated behind it.
lead
This way, it can be used like an arcade game joystick —with the left hand using the joystick and the right hand operating the buttons.
Features
The slow motion feature was unique at release, though it became a popular feature on later controllers.
Features
By toggling a switch between "Player 1" and "Player 2", the Advantage can be shared with another player for games where two players alternate gameplay.
In popular culture

In the 1989 television series Captain N: The Game Master, the main character Kevin Keene can be seen in a live-action sequence playing Punch-Out!!, and another one playing The Adventures of Bayou Billy, both with an NES Advantage.
Reception
Upon the Advantage's initial release in 1987, it was well received as a great way to get the "arcade experience" at home.
Reception
Since its successful release in the '80s, the NES Advantage has received little media attention, but has continued to be regarded as one of the best NES accessories ever produced.

fes_game_jeannie_fes.title: Game Genie
sents: lead
Game Genie is a line of video game cheat cartridges originally designed by Codemasters, sold by Camerica and Galoob.
lead
The first device in the series was released in 1990 for the Nintendo Entertainment System, with subsequent devices released for the Super NES, Game Boy, Genesis, and Game Gear.
lead

All Game Genie devices temporarily modify game data, allowing the player to do things unintended by developers such as, depending on the game, cheating, manipulating various aspects of games, and accessing unused assets and functions.
lead
Five million units of the original Game Genie products were sold worldwide, and most video game console emulators for the platforms it was on feature Game Genie code support.
lead
Emulators that have Game Genie support also allow a near-unlimited number of codes to be entered whereas the actual products have an upper and lower limit, between three and six codes.
lead

In 1993, Codemasters began development on a "Game Genie 2", with Galoob to market and distribute the device in North America, but no Game Genie devices were released for the fifth generation of consoles.
lead
Other companies have produced similar hacking devices such as the Code Breaker, Action Replay, and Game Shark.
lead
The Game Genie brand was later revived by the company Hyperkin, who released cheat systems for newer consoles.
Operation and design

Most published codes give the player some form of invulnerability, infinite ammunition, level skipping, or other modifications that allow the player to be more powerful than intended by the developers.
Operation and design
In other cases, codes can make the game more difficult or even unlock game features that developers had scrapped and rendered unreachable in normal play.
Operation and design
The Game Genie is covered by US Patent #5112051, "Interfacing device for a computer games system", filed 30 May 1990.
Operation and design
This patent expired on 30 May 2010, according to current US patent law.
Super NES
The Super NES edition is incompatible with certain games, such as Star Fox and Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars, as these games use pins that went unused in most games.
Super NES
It also has problems with the SNS-101, as only two codes can be used at a time.
Super NES
There are three known versions of the SNES Game Genie (v1, v1.1, v2).
Super NES
When comparing the PCBs of v1 and v2, v2 has much fewer components.
Super NES
All three versions look exactly the same on the outside, but when v1.1 is booted up, it will have dashes present before any code is entered.
Super NES
The only way to tell v1 and v2 apart is by opening the case and checking the PCB.
Sega Genesis

On the Genesis/Mega Drive, the Game Genie can function as a country converter cartridge since most of these games are only " locked " to their respective regions by the shape of the cartridges and/or a set of a few bytes in the header of the ROM.
Sega Genesis
The unit is also not compatible with Sega 32X cartridges (see "legal issues" below).
Legal issues
Nintendo sued Galoob in the case Galoob v.
Legal issues
Around the time of the lawsuit from Galoob, Nintendo tried to use other methods to thwart the Game Genie, using ROM checksum in later titles intended to detect the cheat modifications.
Game Genie 2
A fully working prototype of the device was completed, but was not brought to market due to changes in market conditions.
Game Genie 2
One prototype is known to remain in existence, in the possession of Richard Aplin, one of its original creators.

fes_u_farce.title: U-Force
